practice.stem: A school club used a light trap to compare the number of moths in a garden in March and in June. They set the trap on one night in each month. On the March night it was windy and the moon was full; the June night was calm and cloudy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the club cannot conclude that more moths are active in June than in March.
parts.answer: Weather and moonlight affect how many moths fly and are attracted to the light; because conditions differed, the difference may be caused by these variables rather than the month; only one night each, so results may not be representative.
parts.working: B1 uncontrolled variables (wind, moonlight, temperature) affect moth catches; B1 only one night in each month/no replicates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways to make the comparison more reliable.
parts.answer: Trap on several nights in each month and calculate a mean; choose nights with similar weather and moon phase (or record them); use the same trap, lamp and times each night.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid improvements.

practice.stem: Two students used kick sampling to compare invertebrates at two sites on a stream. At site 1, one student kicked the stream bed for about 30 seconds. At site 2, the other student kicked for about 2 minutes and over a larger area.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the results from the two sites cannot be compared fairly.
parts.answer: Sampling effort was different (time and area), so more animals would be caught at site 2 whatever the true abundance; the two students may also kick with different force.
parts.working: B1 different time/area sampled; B1 different operators/force – numbers caught depend on effort, not only on the site.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the kick sampling should be standardised.
parts.answer: Kick for the same time (e.g. 60 s, timed with a stopwatch) over the same area (e.g. 1 m² marked out), with the net held the same distance downstream, by the same person, and repeat three times at each site.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: same timed duration; same area/distance; same person/same kicking method; same net/mesh size; replicates at each site.

practice.stem: Students compared seaweed cover on two rocky shores near Karachi. On each shore they chose five places that looked typical, placed a 1 m² quadrat at each and estimated by eye the percentage cover of each seaweed species. One shore was sampled at low tide on a morning, the other in the afternoon a week later when the tide was coming in.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three limitations of this method and suggest an improvement for each.
parts.answer: Percentage cover estimated by eye is subjective – use a quadrat divided into 100 small squares/point quadrat, and the same person to estimate. Quadrats placed where the student chose – use random coordinates (or regular intervals along a belt transect). Only 5 quadrats – sample more (e.g. 20) until the running mean levels off. Some species may be misidentified – use an identification key/photograph. Samples taken at different states of the tide or on different days – sample at the same time on the same day.
parts.working: 1 mark per limitation and 1 mark per matching improvement, for three pairs (max 6).

practice.stem:
Soil cores were taken from a woodland and a field and placed in Tullgren funnels, with a 60 W bulb above each, to drive small animals down into a beaker of ethanol. Results: woodland 46 animals, field 19 animals.
The students noted that: the woodland core was deeper than the field core; the soil in the field core dried and cracked within a few hours, and some soil fell into the beaker; the funnels were left for 4 hours only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each of the three notes, explain how it could affect the results.
parts.answer: Deeper woodland core: larger volume of soil, so more animals regardless of habitat. Rapid drying/heating: animals in the field soil may die before they move down, and soil falling in makes counting harder – fewer counted. 4 hours: too short for all animals to move out, so both counts are underestimates (and possibly by different amounts).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest three improvements to the method.
parts.answer: Use a corer to take cores of the same depth and diameter (same volume); use a lower-power bulb or raise it to dry the soil gradually; put a mesh in the funnel to hold soil; leave for longer (e.g. 48 hours); take several cores from each habitat.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

practice.stem:
A student tested the viability of stored seeds by placing 20 seeds on damp filter paper in each of five Petri dishes and counting the seeds that germinated after 7 days.
Dish: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Seeds germinated: 16, 15, 17, 6, 16
The student noticed afterwards that dish 4 had been placed next to a window and its filter paper had dried out.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and explain how the student should deal with it when calculating the mean.
parts.answer: Dish 4 (6 seeds); it should be left out of the mean (because there is a known cause), giving a mean of 16 seeds per dish, or the dish should be repeated.
parts.working: B1 dish 4; B1 exclude from mean (mean = 16.0) / repeat that dish.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean percentage germination excluding the anomalous result.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two improvements to the method so that all dishes are kept in the same conditions.
parts.answer: Keep all dishes in an incubator/same dark cupboard at a controlled temperature; add the same volume of water to each dish and cover with lids to stop drying.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: incubator/constant temperature; same light; lids/sealed to prevent drying; same volume of water added and topped up.

practice.stem: To investigate air pollution, students counted lichen species on one tree at each of six sites at increasing distances from a brick kiln. They used whatever tree was nearest to each measuring point: some were mango, some were eucalyptus. They recorded lichens on whichever side of the trunk they could reach.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the results may not show the true effect of distance from the kiln.
parts.answer: Different tree species have bark with different pH, texture and water-holding, which affects which lichens grow; the side of the trunk (aspect) affects light and moisture; only one tree per site, so the result may be unrepresentative.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: tree species not standardised – bark pH/texture differs; aspect of trunk not standardised – light/moisture differ; height on trunk not standardised; one tree per site/no replicates; other sources of pollution (roads) not considered.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest three improvements.
parts.answer: Use the same tree species at all sites; record on the same side (e.g. north side) and at the same height (e.g. 1.0–1.5 m) using a quadrat; sample several trees at each site and calculate a mean.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Birds in a city park were counted by 'point counts': an observer stands at a point for 10 minutes and records every bird species seen or heard. One observer, an expert, counted at points in the north of the park at 7 a.m.; a second observer, a beginner, counted in the south of the park at 1 p.m. The north had more bird species.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest three reasons why the difference between the two parts of the park may not be real.
parts.answer: Observers differ in skill at identifying birds by sight and song; birds are much more active and singing in the early morning than at midday; different weather/noise/visibility at the two times.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: observer skill/experience; time of day/bird activity; weather/temperature; noise (traffic, people) at midday; number of points different.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the survey design should be changed.
parts.answer: The same observer (or both observers at all points) should count in both areas at the same time of day, on several days, with the same number of points and same duration.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: same observer/both observers in both areas; same time of day; repeated on several days; same number of points/duration.

practice.stem: Students measured the surface flow rate of a stream by timing a float over a distance of 5.00 m, measured with a tape measure. One reading was 8.0 s. The uncertainty in starting and stopping the stopwatch is estimated as ±0.2 s and the uncertainty in the distance as ±0.05 m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the flow rate for this reading in m s⁻¹. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the time and in the distance.
parts.answer: Time 2.5 %; distance 1.0 %

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two ways to reduce the uncertainty in the flow rate.
parts.answer: Time over a longer distance (e.g. 10 m) so the timing error is a smaller fraction; repeat several times and take a mean; use a flow meter.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: longer distance; repeats and mean; same person timing/start and stop at marked points; use an electronic flow meter.

practice.stem:
Students used mark–release–recapture to estimate the number of land snails in a garden. They noted three problems:
1: water-based paint used to mark the shells washed off in rain
2: bright paint was put on the top of the shell, where birds could see it
3: the second sample was taken 20 minutes after release, close to the release point

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each problem, explain how it would affect the population estimate (too high or too low).
parts.answer: 1: marked snails in the second sample are fewer than they should be, so the estimate is too high. 2: if marked snails are eaten more, fewer marked are recaptured, so the estimate is too high. 3: marked snails have not mixed, so recapturing near the release point gives too many marked snails (estimate too low) – or too few if sampling elsewhere (too high).
parts.working: 1 mark each: (1) too high; (2) too high; (3) explained either way – not randomly mixed, so ratio not representative.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an improvement for each problem.
parts.answer: 1: use waterproof, non-toxic paint/permanent marker and check it does not rub off in a trial. 2: mark on the underside or in an inconspicuous place / use a dull colour. 3: leave a longer time (e.g. 24 h) for mixing and sample from the whole area.
parts.working: 1 mark per improvement.

practice.stem:
Ecologists used live traps baited with grain to estimate the number of gerbils in an area of the Thar desert by mark–release–recapture. They considered these possible problems:
1 Gerbils that have been caught once learn that the traps contain food and return to them.
2 Gerbils that have been caught once avoid the traps afterwards.
3 Many young gerbils were born and left their burrows between the first and second samples.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each problem, state whether the population estimate would be too high or too low, and explain why.
parts.answer: 1: Too low – marked gerbils are over-represented in the second sample, so the proportion marked is too large. 2: Too high – marked gerbils are under-represented in the second sample, so few recaptures are recorded. 3: Too high – new unmarked animals dilute the marked proportion in the second sample (the population also no longer matches the one marked).
parts.working: 1 mark for each direction and 1 mark for each explanation linked to the proportion of marked animals in the second sample.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the design could reduce problems 1 and 3.
parts.answer: Use different trap positions or unbaited traps / traps of a different type for the second sample; take the second sample soon after (e.g. after 1–2 days, once marked animals have mixed) and outside the breeding season.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A student wanted to estimate the density of a rare orchid on a hillside. The orchids grow as widely spaced single plants. She placed ten 0.25 m² quadrats at random and found orchids in only two of them (1 plant and 2 plants).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean density of orchids per m² from her results.
parts.answer: 1.2 plants per m²
parts.working: B1 3 plants ÷ (10 × 0.25 m²) = 1.2 per m².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this estimate is unreliable.
parts.answer: With so few plants found, a single plant more or less in a quadrat would change the estimate greatly; most quadrats contain zero, so the sample is too small and the area sampled (2.5 m²) is a tiny fraction of the hillside.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: very few individuals counted; large proportion of zeros/high variability; total area sampled very small; one extra plant changes estimate by 0.4 per m².

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the method should be changed for a sparse species such as this.
parts.answer: Use much larger quadrats (e.g. 5 m × 5 m) or count all plants within belt transects, and sample many more of them; or count every plant in a defined area.
parts.working: B1 larger quadrats/plots; B1 more samples/larger total area or complete count.

practice.stem: A student concluded that the diversity of aquatic plants is higher in Lake A than in Lake B. Lake A was sampled in late summer with 12 samples, and Lake B in early spring with 4 samples. Simpson's index of diversity was 0.82 for Lake A and 0.64 for Lake B.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the student's conclusion.
parts.answer: D is higher in Lake A, which supports the conclusion; however the lakes were sampled in different seasons – many aquatic plants have not grown or are not visible in early spring, so diversity in B is underestimated; fewer samples in B means rarer species are more likely to be missed; no measure of variability or statistical test, so the difference may not be significant; conclusion therefore not valid.
parts.working: B1 data do show higher D in A; B1 season is a confounding variable – fewer plants visible/growing in spring; B1 unequal sampling effort – fewer samples misses rare species; B1 no replicates per lake/statistical test or error bars – significance unknown; max 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the comparison should be improved.
parts.answer: Sample both lakes in the same month (preferably at several times of the year), using the same number of samples taken at random with the same method; calculate D for each sample and use a t-test to compare means.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: same season/date; same number of samples/same method; replicate D values and statistical test (t-test).

practice.stem:
Students recorded plants in a grassland. They could not tell apart two similar species of grass, so they counted them together as 'grass'. A botanist later identified the plants and found 18 of species 1 and 12 of species 2.
Other species: 25, 20, 15, 10

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Simpson's index of diversity, D = 1 − Σ(n/N)², using the students' grouping (30 'grass' plus the four other species) and using the botanist's identifications. Give your answers to 3 decimal places.
parts.answer: Students: D = 0.775; botanist: D = 0.818

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how errors in identification can affect estimates of biodiversity and suggest how they could be reduced.
parts.answer: Grouping two species together reduces species richness and makes one group seem more dominant, so D is underestimated; misidentification can also split one species into two and overestimate D; use identification keys/photographs, check specimens with an expert, train recorders, or record unknowns as 'species A', 'species B' consistently.
parts.working: B1 lumping species underestimates richness/D; B1 effect explained (dominance/evenness changed); B1 improvement – keys/expert checking/voucher specimens/training/DNA barcoding.

practice.stem:
The number of bird species was recorded during one-hour counts in four areas of natural forest and four areas of farmland in the foothills near Abbottabad. All counts were made in the same week.
Forest: 24, 21, 26, 23
Farmland: 11, 9, 14, 10

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of bird species in each habitat.
parts.answer: Forest 23.5; farmland 11.0
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State a conclusion and say whether the data support it strongly. Give a reason.
parts.answer: More bird species live in forest than farmland (about twice as many); the data support this well because every forest count is higher than every farmland count (ranges do not overlap), though only four areas of each were sampled.
parts.working: B1 forest has more bird species; B1 ranges do not overlap/consistent, with a valid caveat (small sample/no statistical test) for full credit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest an explanation for the difference.
parts.answer: Forest has more layers of vegetation and more plant species, giving more niches – food (insects, fruits, seeds), nesting sites and shelter; farmland is uniform crops, often sprayed with pesticides.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: more niches/habitat structure; more varied food; nesting sites/shelter; pesticides/disturbance on farmland.

practice.stem:
Samples were taken at five sites on a river above and below the outfall of a town's sewage pipe.
Site: 200 m upstream, 50 m upstream, 50 m downstream, 200 m downstream, 1000 m downstream
Number of invertebrate taxa: 14, 13, 4, 6, 11
Dissolved oxygen / mg dm⁻³: 8.9, 8.7, 3.1, 4.6, 7.8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the results.
parts.answer: Upstream there are 13–14 taxa and oxygen is high (8.7–8.9 mg dm⁻³); just below the outfall both fall sharply (4 taxa, 3.1 mg dm⁻³); further downstream both gradually recover (11 taxa and 7.8 mg dm⁻³ at 1000 m), but not to upstream values.
parts.working: B1 high taxa and oxygen upstream; B1 sharp fall immediately below outfall, with data; B1 gradual recovery downstream, not fully, with data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an explanation for the fall in dissolved oxygen and number of taxa below the outfall.
parts.answer: Sewage contains organic matter that is decomposed by aerobic bacteria; the bacteria multiply and use up oxygen in respiration; invertebrates that need high oxygen (e.g. mayfly and stonefly nymphs) die or move away, leaving only a few tolerant taxa.
parts.working: B1 organic matter/sewage decomposed by bacteria; B1 bacterial respiration uses oxygen (high BOD); B1 oxygen-sensitive species die/leave, only tolerant species remain.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether these data prove that the sewage caused the fall in the number of taxa. Give a reason.
parts.answer: No – it is a correlation from one survey; other factors (e.g. toxic chemicals in the sewage, change in stream bed) could be responsible; but the pattern is consistent with the sewage being the cause.
parts.working: B1 no + reason (correlation/other variables not measured/single sample).

practice.stem:
The number of occupied nests of a vulture species was counted in one study area of Pakistan every two years. The veterinary drug diclofenac, which poisons vultures that feed on the carcasses of treated cattle, was banned for veterinary use in 2006.
Year: 2000, 2002, 2004, 2006, 2008, 2010, 2012, 2014, 2016
Occupied nests: 410, 260, 130, 70, 45, 40, 48, 62, 75

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in occupied nests between 2000 and 2010. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the changes in the number of nests after the ban.
parts.answer: The number continued to fall for about four years after the ban (to 40 in 2010), then rose slowly to 75 by 2016 – still less than one fifth of the number in 2000.
parts.working: B1 continued to fall until 2010; B1 slow increase from 2010 to 75 in 2016, with comparison to 2000.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the number of nests did not increase immediately after the ban.
parts.answer: Stocks of diclofenac were still used illegally or human diclofenac was used on cattle; vultures take several years to mature and lay only one egg a year, so populations recover slowly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: continued (illegal) use of the drug/stocks remaining; slow reproduction (late maturity, one egg per year); too few adults left to breed; other threats such as food shortage or habitat loss.

practice.stem:
Parthenium hysterophorus is an invasive weed in Pakistan. Wheat seeds were watered with different concentrations of an extract made from Parthenium leaves.
Extract concentration / %: 0, 2.5, 5, 10, 20
Germination / %: 95, 90, 78, 52, 20
Mean root length after 7 days / mm: 32, 27, 19, 9, 3

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two conclusions that can be drawn from these results.
parts.answer: As the concentration of leaf extract increases, the percentage germination of wheat decreases; and root length decreases (from 32 mm with no extract to 3 mm at 20 %).
parts.working: 1 mark each, with data quoted for one.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how these results could help to explain why Parthenium spreads in fields and grassland.
parts.answer: Parthenium leaves release chemicals that inhibit germination and growth of other plants, so it reduces competition from crops and native plants and can take over the area.
parts.working: B1 releases inhibitory chemicals (allelopathy) into the soil; B1 reduces growth of competitors so Parthenium outcompetes them.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the effect in a field may be less than in this experiment.
parts.answer: In the field the chemicals are diluted by rain or broken down by soil microorganisms, so concentrations are lower.
parts.working: B1 dilution/breakdown/adsorption to soil.

practice.stem:
Belt transects were used to sample butterflies at six urban and six rural sites near Lahore. Simpson's index of diversity was calculated for each site.
Urban: mean D = 0.62, 95 % confidence interval ± 0.07
Rural: mean D = 0.81, 95 % confidence interval ± 0.05

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student concluded that butterfly diversity is higher in rural sites than in urban sites. Use the data to evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: Mean D is higher in rural sites (0.81 vs 0.62). The 95 % confidence intervals (rural 0.76–0.86, urban 0.55–0.69) do not overlap, so the difference is significant and the conclusion is supported for these sites. But only 6 sites of each type, sampled in one season/year, in one city, so it may not apply generally.
parts.working: 1 mark: rural higher with data. 1 mark: CIs do not overlap so significant. 1 mark: limitation – few sites / one season / one region.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why butterfly diversity is lower in urban areas.
parts.answer: Fewer flowering plants/nectar sources and larval food plants; habitat loss and fragmentation by buildings and roads; pollution/pesticide use; higher temperature/light at night.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
The ratio of shell height to shell base length was measured for limpets on an exposed rocky shore (strong waves) and a sheltered shore. 25 limpets were measured on each shore.
Exposed shore: mean ratio 0.42; 95 % confidence interval ± 0.05
Sheltered shore: mean ratio 0.51; 95 % confidence interval ± 0.06
A student concluded that limpets on exposed shores have significantly flatter shells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the range covered by each 95 % confidence interval.
parts.answer: Exposed 0.37 to 0.47; sheltered 0.45 to 0.57.
parts.working: B1 both.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the student's conclusion.
parts.answer: The mean ratio is lower on the exposed shore, so shells there are on average flatter; but the 95 % confidence intervals overlap (0.45–0.47), so it cannot be concluded that the difference is significant; a t-test (or more limpets) is needed; only one shore of each type was studied.
parts.working: B1 mean lower on exposed shore; B1 CIs overlap so difference may not be significant/may be due to chance; B1 further point: need t-test / larger sample / only one shore of each type so cannot generalise.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a flatter shell might be an advantage on an exposed shore.
parts.answer: A flatter shell has less resistance to waves, so the limpet is less likely to be dislodged.

practice.stem:
Earthworm density and soil pH were measured at six sites on a farm. Spearman's rank correlation coefficient was 0.77. The critical value at p = 0.05 for n = 6 is 0.886.
A student concluded: 'There is a significant positive correlation between soil pH and earthworm density, so adding lime to raise the soil pH will increase the number of earthworms.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the value of the correlation coefficient shows.
parts.answer: 0.77 is less than the critical value 0.886, so the null hypothesis (no correlation) cannot be rejected; the positive correlation is not significant and could be due to chance (p > 0.05).
parts.working: B1 0.77 < 0.886 so accept/do not reject the null hypothesis; B1 correlation not significant/probability due to chance more than 5 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the student's conclusion.
parts.answer: The first part is wrong because the correlation is not significant; only six sites were sampled, so the test has little power and more sites are needed; even a significant correlation would not show that pH causes the change – another variable (e.g. organic matter, moisture, soil type) could affect both, so an experiment adding lime to some plots and not others would be needed before recommending liming.
parts.working: B1 correlation not significant so 'significant' is incorrect; B1 small sample (n = 6)/more sites needed; B1 correlation does not show causation – confounding variable named or experiment (limed and unlimed plots) needed to support the recommendation.

practice.stem:
Students compared the number of insect species caught in pan traps on 10 organic farms and 10 conventional farms. Organic farms: mean 23.4 species; conventional farms: mean 20.1 species. A t-test gave t = 1.65. The critical value of t at p = 0.05 with 18 degrees of freedom is 2.10.
The students concluded that organic farming increases insect diversity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what the t-test result shows.
parts.answer: t = 1.65 is less than 2.10, so the null hypothesis (no difference between the means) is accepted; the difference between the means is not significant and could be due to chance (p > 0.05).
parts.working: B1 1.65 < 2.10 so accept null hypothesis; B1 difference not significant/probability of being due to chance is more than 5 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the students' conclusion.
parts.answer: The conclusion is not supported: although the mean is higher on organic farms, the t-test shows the difference is not significant; even if it were, the farms may differ in other ways (crop type, hedges, location), so the cause cannot be identified; more farms or repeat sampling might detect a smaller difference.
parts.working: B1 not supported because difference not significant; B1 other variables between farms not controlled; B1 suggestion – larger sample/repeat in other seasons/matched pairs of farms.

practice.stem:
In 100 random quadrats in an area of scrub, a student recorded whether shrub species S and herb species H were present.
Both present: 34; S only: 16; H only: 16; neither: 34
If the two species were distributed independently, the expected number of quadrats with both present would be 25. A chi-squared test for association gave χ² = 12.96. The critical value at p = 0.05 with 1 degree of freedom is 3.84.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the null hypothesis for this test.
parts.answer: There is no association between the presence of S and H – they are distributed independently of each other.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the result shows, including the type of association.
parts.answer: 12.96 > 3.84, so the null hypothesis is rejected; there is a significant association between the two species; it is a positive association because they are found together (34) more often than expected (25).
parts.working: B1 comparison with critical value, reject null; B1 significant association (probability due to chance < 5 %); B1 positive, because observed 'both' > expected.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a biological reason for this association.
parts.answer: The herb grows in the shade or moister soil under the shrub, or the shrub protects it from grazing; or both need the same soil conditions.
parts.working: B1 any valid reason.

practice.stem:
Simpson's index of diversity of the plants was measured in five fields grazed by different numbers of sheep.
Sheep per hectare: 0, 2, 4, 8, 12
Simpson's index, D: 0.52, 0.71, 0.78, 0.60, 0.38

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between grazing intensity and plant diversity.
parts.answer: Diversity increases from no grazing to a peak at 4 sheep per hectare (D = 0.78), then decreases at higher grazing to its lowest value of 0.38 at 12 sheep per hectare.
parts.working: B1 increase to a maximum at 4 sheep ha⁻¹; B1 decrease above that, with data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest explanations for the low diversity at 0 and at 12 sheep per hectare.
parts.answer: With no grazing, a few tall, fast-growing grasses outcompete and shade out smaller plants; moderate grazing keeps these dominant grasses short so many species can coexist; very heavy grazing and trampling kill most species, leaving only a few that tolerate grazing.
parts.working: B1 no grazing – competitive dominant species exclude others; B1 moderate grazing reduces dominance; B1 heavy grazing – only tolerant species survive/trampling/bare ground.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why only one field at each grazing level limits the conclusions that can be drawn.
parts.answer: Differences between fields (soil, slope, history) could cause the differences in D; without replicates, reliability cannot be judged or statistics used.

practice.stem: Lichen diversity on tree trunks was recorded at seven distances (5 m to 200 m) from a busy road. Spearman's rank correlation between distance from the road and lichen diversity gave rs = 0.86. The critical value for n = 7 at p = 0.05 is 0.79.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student concluded that pollution from vehicles on the road causes the decrease in lichen diversity. Evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: The significant positive correlation shows lichen diversity increases with distance from the road (rs = 0.86 > 0.79), which is consistent with pollution from traffic. However, correlation does not prove causation; other variables also change with distance, e.g. dust, light, humidity, trampling, tree species or bark pH; pollution was not measured; only one road and 7 points, so the conclusion is tentative.
parts.working: 1 mark: correlation significant and positive, supports link. 1 mark: correlation ≠ causation. 1 mark: named confounding variable(s) changing with distance. 1 mark: pollution not measured / small sample / one road.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one further measurement that would test whether vehicle pollution is the cause.
parts.answer: Measure the concentration of nitrogen dioxide/sulfur dioxide (or particulates) in the air at each distance and correlate with lichen diversity.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
A marine protected area (MPA) with a ban on fishing was set up on a reef. Fish density was surveyed by divers just before the ban and 5 years later, both inside the MPA and at a similar reef nearby where fishing continued.
Mean fish per 100 m² (inside MPA): before 22, after 41
Mean fish per 100 m² (fished reef): before 24, after 23

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in fish density at each site. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: MPA: +86.4 %; fished reef: −4.17 %
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why data from the fished reef were collected as well as from the MPA.
parts.answer: The fished reef is a control: it shows what would have happened without protection (e.g. effects of sea temperature or a good breeding year), so the change in the MPA can be linked to the fishing ban.
parts.working: B1 control/comparison; B1 rules out factors that would affect both reefs (weather, temperature, recruitment).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate the claim that the fishing ban caused the increase in fish density.
parts.answer: Supports: big increase inside MPA while the control stayed almost the same, and the reefs were similar at the start. Limitations: only one MPA and one control reef; only one survey before and after – year-to-year variation unknown; no SD/statistical test; fish may have moved into the MPA from elsewhere rather than the population increasing.
parts.working: B1 support from data; max 2 for limitations: single replicate of each; few surveys/no measure of variability or test; movement of fish/divers' counts may vary; other differences between sites.

practice.stem:
Seeds of a wild melon were stored for 10 years under four conditions. Their germination at the start was 95 %.
Seed moisture 5 %, stored at −20 °C: 91 % germination after 10 years
Seed moisture 5 %, stored at 5 °C: 84 %
Seed moisture 12 %, stored at −20 °C: 52 %
Seed moisture 12 %, stored at 5 °C: 47 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the data, compare the effects of seed moisture and storage temperature on seed viability.
parts.answer: Both lower moisture and lower temperature give higher germination; moisture has the larger effect: reducing moisture from 12 % to 5 % raises germination by 37–39 percentage points, while reducing temperature from 5 °C to −20 °C raises it by only 5–7; the best condition is 5 % moisture at −20 °C, which loses only 4 percentage points.
parts.working: B1 both factors affect viability in the same direction; B1 moisture has a bigger effect, with calculated differences; B1 best conditions identified.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why seeds with 12 % moisture lost viability even at −20 °C.
parts.answer: With more water, ice crystals form in the cells when frozen and damage membranes/cells.
parts.working: B1 ice crystal damage (or higher residual metabolic activity).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two limitations of these data for deciding how a seed bank should store all its seeds.
parts.answer: Only one species was tested – others may respond differently; no information on number of seeds or replicates, so reliability is unknown; only two levels of each factor and one storage time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid limitations.

practice.stem:
In a captive breeding programme for a rare deer, the inbreeding coefficient (F) of each fawn was calculated from the studbook. F = 0 means the parents were unrelated; F = 0.25 means the parents were full siblings.
F: 0, 0.125, 0.25, 0.375
Number of fawns born: 40, 22, 11, 4
Percentage surviving to one year: 78, 70, 55, 50

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between inbreeding and survival.
parts.answer: As F increases, survival to one year decreases, from 78 % for F = 0 to 50 % for F = 0.375; the largest fall is between F = 0.125 and 0.25.
parts.working: B1 negative relationship; B1 data quoted.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why inbreeding might reduce survival.
parts.answer: Related parents are more likely to carry the same harmful recessive alleles; offspring are more likely to be homozygous recessive and express the harmful phenotype (inbreeding depression), e.g. weaker immunity.
parts.working: B1 shared alleles/increased homozygosity; B1 harmful recessive alleles expressed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate how strongly these data support the conclusion that inbreeding reduces survival in this deer.
parts.answer: Clear trend supports it; but very few fawns at high F (4 at F = 0.375, so one fawn changes survival by 25 percentage points); no statistical test; other factors (mother's age, year, enclosure, disease outbreaks) not controlled; data from one programme only.
parts.working: B1 trend consistent/supports; B1 small sample sizes at high F, with figure; B1 other variables not controlled/no statistical test.

practice.stem:
Two populations of a small freshwater fish live in two separate river systems. Males in population 1 have red fins; males in population 2 have yellow fins. Some biologists think they are two species.
Evidence:
1 Mitochondrial DNA sequences differ by 0.4 %. In this genus, pairs of recognised species usually differ by 3–8 %.
2 In aquaria, fish from the two populations mated and produced fertile offspring.
3 In aquaria, females chose males from their own population in 70 % of trials.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the evidence to discuss whether the two populations should be classified as separate species.
parts.answer: Against: DNA difference (0.4 %) is far smaller than between recognised species, suggesting recent separation; they interbreed to give fertile offspring, which fits the biological species definition of one species. For: different fin colour and females prefer own-population males, so some behavioural isolation is developing. Conclusion: probably one species (possibly two subspecies/populations undergoing speciation), as they are not reproductively isolated.
parts.working: B1 small DNA difference compared with typical species; B1 fertile offspring – same species by biological species concept; B1 colour and mate preference suggest partial/behavioural isolation beginning; B1 balanced conclusion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the result of evidence 2 might not apply in the wild.
parts.answer: In the wild the populations are geographically isolated and never meet; even if they met, mate choice, different breeding times or habitats might prevent mating; in aquaria fish have no choice of mates.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid points.

practice.stem: On a sandy beach the plants change from bare sand near the high-tide line, through low creeping plants, to taller grasses and shrubs further inland.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a belt transect could be used to investigate how the plant species change from the high-tide line inland.
parts.answer: Lay a tape measure at right angles to the shore from the high-tide line inland; place a 1 m² quadrat at regular intervals (e.g. every 5 m) along the tape; in each quadrat record each species present and its percentage cover; continue to the end of the vegetation zone; repeat with two more transects at randomly chosen positions along the beach; record an abiotic factor (e.g. distance, soil moisture or salinity) at each quadrat.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: tape from high-tide line inland/perpendicular to shore; quadrats at regular intervals (stated); quadrat size stated; identify species (key); percentage cover/abundance measured (grid); same method at each point; repeat transects at random positions; abiotic factor measured at each quadrat; results presented as kite diagram.

practice.stem: A student wants to estimate the number of woodlice living under logs in a garden.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how mark–release–recapture could be used to estimate the population.
parts.answer: Collect as many woodlice as possible from under the logs in a set time; count them and mark each with a small dot of non-toxic, waterproof paint on the back; release them where they were found; after 1–2 days collect again from the same logs for the same time; count the total caught and the number marked; population = (first sample × second sample) ÷ number of marked recaptures.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: first sample collected and counted; marked with non-toxic/waterproof marker that does not make them more visible to predators; released at the same place; time allowed to mix (e.g. 24 h); second sample collected in same way/same effort; count marked and unmarked; Lincoln index formula given.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two assumptions of this method.
parts.answer: No births, deaths, immigration or emigration between samples; marked animals mix fully with the population; marks are not lost and do not affect survival.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: A student wants to compare the number of small soil animals (mites and springtails) in soil from woodland and from a playing field.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method using Tullgren funnels to compare the number of soil animals in the two habitats.
parts.answer: Take soil cores of the same volume (same diameter and depth, using a corer) from several random places in each habitat; place each core on a mesh in a funnel; put a lamp (e.g. 25 W) at a fixed distance above; collect animals in a beaker of 70 % ethanol under the funnel; leave for the same time (e.g. 48 h); count animals using a hand lens/microscope; calculate a mean per core for each habitat.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: same volume of soil/corer; several samples per habitat chosen at random; mesh/gauze in funnel; lamp above to dry/heat soil from the top; animals move down into ethanol/collecting vessel; same lamp power, distance and time; count/identify using microscope; mean calculated and compared/t-test.

practice.stem: A seed bank must check whether stored seeds of a wild chickpea are still alive. The test is to see what proportion of the seeds germinate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to carry out a germination test on a batch of stored seeds.
parts.answer: Take a random sample of seeds from the batch (e.g. 4 replicates of 50); place them on moist filter paper or agar in Petri dishes with lids; keep at a suitable constant temperature (e.g. 20 °C) in an incubator; keep moist with the same volume of water; count the seeds with an emerged radicle after a fixed time (e.g. 14 days); calculate percentage germination for each dish and the mean.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: random sample/replicates; known number of seeds per dish; damp filter paper/agar, lids to prevent drying; constant temperature (incubator); same light conditions; criterion for germination (radicle visible) and fixed time; percentage germination and mean calculated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why seeds that do not germinate should be checked before being recorded as dead.
parts.answer: Some may be dormant (alive but not germinating, e.g. hard seed coat), so a cut test or tetrazolium stain is used to see if the embryo is alive.
parts.working: B1 dormancy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to compare the species richness of plants in a grazed area and an ungrazed (fenced) area of hillside.
parts.answer: Choose two areas of similar slope, aspect and soil; mark out each with tapes as axes; use random number coordinates to place 1 m² (or 0.25 m²) quadrats; use at least 20 quadrats in each area (or until a running mean levels off); count the number of different plant species in each quadrat, using an identification key; also record abundance/percentage cover if Simpson's index is to be calculated; sample both areas at the same time of year; calculate mean species per quadrat and compare with a t-test.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: areas matched for other variables (slope, aspect, soil); random sampling method with coordinates; quadrat size stated; sufficient number of quadrats (≥10, ideally 20+); DV species per quadrat identified with key; same time/season; abundance recorded for Simpson's index; means calculated; t-test to compare.

practice.stem:
A footpath crosses a grassland in a national park. Walkers trample the vegetation on and near the path.
Plan an investigation to find out how trampling affects plant species diversity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method for this investigation.
parts.answer: Lay transects at right angles across the path, extending e.g. 5 m on either side; place quadrats (e.g. 0.5 m × 0.5 m) at fixed intervals (e.g. every 0.5 m) along each; identify all species and count or estimate percentage cover in each quadrat; repeat with several transects at random points along the path; choose a section where slope, aspect and soil are similar; measure trampling intensity (e.g. soil compaction with a penetrometer, or count walkers); calculate Simpson's index for each distance from the path; use Spearman's rank to test correlation between distance (or compaction) and D.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any seven of: transect perpendicular to path; quadrats at stated regular intervals; size of quadrat stated; species identified using a key; abundance recorded (count/cover); several transects, positions chosen randomly; similar slope/soil/aspect/away from other disturbances; measure of trampling (compaction, footfall count); Simpson's index; Spearman's rank correlation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a suitable null hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is no correlation between distance from the path and plant species diversity.

practice.stem: A plant breeder wants to find out how salt concentration affects the growth of seedlings of a wild wheat relative. She has seeds, a 1.0 mol dm⁻³ sodium chloride solution, distilled water, sand in pots and normal laboratory apparatus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method for this investigation.
parts.answer: Make a range of salt concentrations by diluting the stock, e.g. 0, 25, 50, 100, 150, 200 mmol dm⁻³ (volume stock + water to fixed total); plant the same number of seeds (from the same batch) at the same depth in identical pots of washed sand; water each pot with the same volume of its solution at fixed times; keep all pots in the same light and temperature (growth room); use at least three pots per concentration; after a fixed time (e.g. 21 days) wash out the seedlings, dry them in an oven at 80 °C to constant mass and weigh; calculate mean dry mass per seedling for each concentration.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any seven of: at least five concentrations including 0; dilution method; same seed batch/size; same volume of solution, same frequency; replicates (≥ 3 pots); controlled temperature/light/same pot and sand volume; fixed growth period; dependent variable – dry mass (or root/shoot length) measured appropriately; dry to constant mass; mean calculated; graph of mean against concentration.

practice.stem: Leaves of the invasive weed Parthenium are thought to release chemicals that slow the growth of other plants. A student wants to test the effect of different concentrations of Parthenium leaf extract on the root growth of radish seedlings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how she could carry out this investigation.
parts.answer: Grind a known mass of fresh leaves (e.g. 20 g) with 100 cm³ distilled water and filter to make a stock extract (20 %); dilute to give a range, e.g. 0, 2.5, 5, 10, 20 %; place 10 radish seeds on filter paper in each Petri dish and add the same volume (5 cm³) of one concentration; distilled water as control; three dishes per concentration; cover and keep in the dark at 25 °C; after 5 days measure the root length of each seedling with a ruler; calculate mean root length; plot against concentration.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any seven of: method of making extract (mass/volume); serial or proportional dilution, at least five concentrations; control with distilled water; same number of seeds per dish; same volume of solution; replicates; constant temperature/dark; fixed time; root length measured in mm with ruler/thread; mean calculated; statistical test or graph.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a precaution to make sure that any effect is caused by chemicals in the extract and not by its osmotic effect.
parts.answer: Measure the solute potential/concentration of the extracts and include controls of sugar or mannitol solutions with the same water potential.
parts.working: B1 osmotic control/matching water potential.

practice.stem: A fish farm releases waste water into a stream. An environmental officer wants to find out whether the invertebrate community below the outfall is less diverse than above it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan a field investigation to compare the invertebrate diversity above and below the outfall.
parts.answer: Choose sampling sites above and below the outfall with the same depth, flow rate and stream-bed type; at each site take several (e.g. 5) kick samples at random points; for each kick sample, disturb a 1 m² area for 60 s with the net held downstream; empty into a white tray and identify and count all invertebrates using a key; return animals to the stream; calculate Simpson's index of diversity for each sample; compare mean D above and below using a t-test; measure dissolved oxygen and temperature at each site.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any seven of: sites above and below (several distances); matching depth/flow/substrate; random positions; standardised kick sampling (time, area, net); replicates; identification with key/count; return animals; Simpson's index; t-test comparing means; abiotic measurements (oxygen, temperature, nitrate); same day/time.

practice.stem: Brick kilns in Punjab release sulfur dioxide and soot. Lichens are sensitive to air pollution. A student wants to find out whether the cover of lichens on walls changes with distance from a brick kiln.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method for this investigation.
parts.answer: Choose sites at regular distances from the kiln (e.g. 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4 km) along roads in one direction (downwind); at each site choose walls of the same material and age, facing the same direction; place a 10 cm × 10 cm quadrat grid at the same height on several (e.g. 5) walls; estimate percentage cover of lichens in each; calculate mean cover per site; use Spearman's rank to test for correlation between distance and lichen cover.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: at least five distances stated; same direction from kiln/downwind; walls of same material/aspect/height/age; quadrat with grid for % cover; replicates at each distance; identify lichen types/count species; mean calculated; Spearman's rank correlation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Spearman's rank correlation is more suitable than a t-test for analysing the results.
parts.answer: The investigation looks for a correlation between two variables (distance and cover) measured at many sites, not a difference between two groups.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan a field investigation into how the abundance of a fern changes with light intensity from the inside of a woodland into an open field.
parts.answer: Lay a tape from inside the wood, across the edge and into the field; place quadrats at regular intervals (e.g. every 2 m) along the tape – a belt or interrupted belt transect; in each quadrat record the abundance of the fern as percentage cover or number of fronds; measure light intensity at ground level in each quadrat with a light meter, at the same height and at the same time of day (or several readings averaged); repeat with two or three more transects at random positions along the wood edge; also record soil moisture/temperature as other variables; plot abundance against light intensity.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: transect line across the edge; quadrats at regular intervals (belt/interrupted belt); abundance measure (% cover, count); light meter readings at each quadrat; same time of day / weather / height of meter; repeat transects; record other variables (soil moisture, pH, temperature); at least 10 sampling points; plot scatter graph of abundance against light.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the statistical test that should be used to analyse the results and explain your choice.
parts.answer: Spearman's rank correlation – to test for a correlation between two variables (light intensity and abundance) whose data may not be normally distributed.
parts.working: 1 mark: Spearman's rank with reason (testing correlation between two variables).

practice.stem: Leaves on a forest floor are broken down by soil invertebrates (such as earthworms and millipedes) and by microorganisms. An ecologist wants to find out how much of the breakdown is caused by invertebrates, and how temperature affects it. She can use 'litter bags' with different mesh sizes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation using litter bags to separate the contributions of invertebrates and microorganisms to leaf breakdown.
parts.answer: Use bags with coarse mesh (e.g. 5 mm, allowing invertebrates in) and fine mesh (e.g. 0.05 mm, excluding invertebrates but allowing microorganisms); fill each with the same dry mass of the same leaves (e.g. 5.0 g, dried at 60 °C); bury pairs at random positions in the same leaf litter; replicate (e.g. 10 of each); retrieve after fixed times (e.g. 30, 60, 90 days); clean, dry to constant mass and weigh; percentage mass loss in fine bags = microbial; difference between coarse and fine = invertebrate contribution.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: two mesh sizes with reason; same species/mass of dried leaves; dried to constant mass before and after; placed at random/same site; replicates; fixed retrieval times; percentage mass loss calculated; invertebrate contribution = coarse − fine; t-test to compare.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the effect of temperature could be investigated in the laboratory, and one disadvantage of doing this in the laboratory.
parts.answer: Place bags of leaves with the same soil and invertebrates in containers kept in incubators at different temperatures (e.g. 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 °C) with the same moisture; disadvantage – laboratory conditions do not reproduce the natural community, moisture changes and rainfall.
parts.working: B1 incubators/water baths at ≥ 5 temperatures with other conditions controlled; B1 disadvantage.

practice.stem: Leaf-eating snails in a garden are offered the leaves of a native plant and the leaves of an invasive plant. A student wants to test whether the snails prefer to eat one species.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan a laboratory investigation to test whether the snails show a preference.
parts.answer: Cut discs of the same area (e.g. 2 cm diameter, cork borer) from leaves of the same age of each species; place one disc of each at opposite ends of a container lined with damp paper; add one snail that has been starved for 24 h; record which disc it eats first, or the area of each disc eaten after a set time (e.g. 12 h, by tracing on graph paper); use a new snail each time and many replicates (e.g. 30); swap the sides of the two discs between trials; keep in the dark at constant temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: same area/mass of leaf from each species; same leaf age/position; snails starved for the same time; one snail per trial/new snail each time; discs placed equally distant, position swapped/randomised; fixed time; measure area eaten (grid) or first choice; many replicates; same temperature/light/humidity; return snails afterwards.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name a statistical test to analyse the 'first choice' results and state the expected numbers if 30 snails had no preference.
parts.answer: Chi-squared test; 15 snails choosing each species.
parts.working: B1 chi-squared; B1 15 and 15.

practice.stem: A student wants to compare the diversity of phytoplankton (microscopic algae) in two ponds: one in a park and one on a farm where fertiliser runs into the water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how she could collect, identify and count the phytoplankton and compare their diversity.
parts.answer: At each pond take water samples of a fixed volume (e.g. 1 dm³) from several random points at the same depth, at the same time of day; concentrate the phytoplankton by passing each sample through a plankton net/filter or letting it settle, into a fixed final volume; take a fixed volume (e.g. 0.1 cm³) onto a counting slide (haemocytometer or Sedgwick-Rafter cell); identify cells using a key at ×400 and count each species in a set number of fields; calculate Simpson's index for each sample; compare mean D of the two ponds with a t-test; measure nitrate/phosphate in each pond.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any seven of: fixed sample volume; random sampling points, same depth/time; replicates; concentration method; known subsample volume on counting chamber; microscope with stated magnification; identification key; counts of each species; Simpson's index; t-test; measure nitrate/phosphate/light.

practice.stem:
Ladybirds are being considered as a biological control agent for aphids on a vegetable crop grown in polytunnels.
Plan an experiment to find out whether adding ladybirds reduces the number of aphids on the plants.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the experiment, including the controls you would use.
parts.answer: Use many plants of the same variety and age, each placed in a fine-mesh cage; add the same number of aphids to each (e.g. 50) and allow them to settle; randomly assign cages to treatments: with ladybirds (e.g. 2 adults per cage) and without ladybirds; include cages with the same mesh to control for cage effects; keep cages in the same polytunnel conditions (temperature, light, watering); after a fixed time (e.g. 7 days) count aphids on each plant (hand lens); replicate (e.g. 10 cages per treatment); compare mean numbers with a t-test.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any seven of: same plant variety/age/size; same starting number of aphids; cages to keep insects in/out; control without ladybirds; random allocation; same number/species/starvation of ladybirds; same conditions; fixed time; counting method; replicates; t-test or comparison of means; ethical/risk point (ladybirds native, not released into wild).

practice.stem: Duckweed (Lemna) is a small floating plant that reproduces by producing new fronds. A student grew duckweed in beakers of pond water placed at different distances from a lamp and counted the number of fronds after 10 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: light intensity (distance from the lamp). Dependent: number of fronds (after 10 days).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three variables that should be kept constant and explain why one of them must be controlled.
parts.answer: Temperature (use a heat filter/water bath, as temperature affects the rate of photosynthesis and growth); volume and source of pond water/mineral ions; starting number of fronds; type of beaker; time; wavelength of light.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three variables; 1 mark for a valid reason linked to one of them.

practice.stem: A conservation nursery is investigating the effect of temperature on germination of seeds of an endangered tree. Seeds will be placed in Petri dishes in incubators at 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30 °C, and the percentage that germinate after 21 days will be recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three variables that should be standardised and describe how each would be standardised.
parts.answer: Number of seeds per dish – count 25 seeds into each; water – add the same volume (5 cm³) of distilled water to identical filter paper; light – keep all incubators dark; seed source – use seeds from the same batch and storage conditions; time – count after exactly 21 days.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three variable + method pairs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why each temperature should be tested with several dishes.
parts.answer: To identify anomalous results and calculate a mean, so the results are more reliable.

practice.stem: In an investigation of whether chemicals from the leaves of an invasive plant inhibit germination, lettuce seeds were watered with leaf extract. Another set of lettuce seeds was watered with distilled water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the purpose of the dishes watered with distilled water.
parts.answer: They are a control: they show how many seeds germinate without the extract, so any difference can be attributed to the extract.
parts.working: B1 control/baseline; B1 allows comparison so effect is due to extract alone.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a further control that would show whether the effect was due to chemicals specific to the invasive plant, rather than to any leaf extract.
parts.answer: Water seeds with extract made in the same way from leaves of a native plant (or a plant known to have no inhibitory chemicals) at the same concentration.
parts.working: B1 extract from a different (native/non-inhibitory) plant; B1 same concentration/method of preparation.

practice.stem: Students used pitfall traps to compare the number of spiders in an orchard and in an area of natural scrub.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: habitat (orchard or scrub). Dependent: number of spiders caught (per trap).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe three ways to standardise the trapping so that the two habitats can be compared fairly.
parts.answer: Same size and type of trap (e.g. 250 cm³ plastic cup); same number of traps in each habitat; left for the same length of time on the same nights; no bait or the same bait in all; rims set level with the soil.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

practice.stem: A student wants to find out whether leaves from the shaded inside of a neem tree's crown are larger than leaves from the sunny outside.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable, and suggest how the dependent variable could be measured.
parts.answer: Independent: position/light (shade or sun). Dependent: leaf (leaflet) area or length; measure by drawing round the leaf on 1 mm graph paper and counting squares (or measuring length with a ruler).
parts.working: B1 IV; B1 DV; B1 method of measurement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two variables that should be standardised when choosing leaves, and explain why.
parts.answer: Same tree (genetic differences); same age/position along the shoot, e.g. the fifth leaf from the tip (leaves grow as they age); same height above ground.
parts.working: 1 mark each for variable + reason, any two.

practice.stem: A student wants to find out whether the number of mayfly larvae in streams flowing into Rawal Lake is related to the concentration of dissolved oxygen in the water. She will use a kick-sampling net for 1 minute at each site and measure dissolved oxygen with a meter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent and dependent variables.
parts.answer: Independent: dissolved oxygen concentration (site). Dependent: number (abundance) of mayfly larvae.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a field study the other variables cannot be controlled. Name three variables that might affect the number of mayfly larvae and describe how the student could take account of them.
parts.answer: Any three: water temperature; flow rate; type of stream bed (stones vs mud); depth; pH; shading. Choose sites that are similar in these variables (e.g. same depth and stone size), and measure them at each site (thermometer, flow meter, pH probe) so that their effects can be considered.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three variables (max 3). 1 mark for: choose similar sites or measure and record them to take into account.

practice.stem: Students want to compare bird diversity in two parks in Islamabad. They cannot control conditions in the parks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest four variables that could affect the number of bird species recorded and describe how the students could take account of each.
parts.answer: Time of day – count in both parks at the same time (early morning); weather – count on days with similar weather and record it; observer skill – same observers in both parks; duration/area – same number and length of point counts; season – survey both parks in the same week.
parts.working: 1 mark for each variable with a matching way of standardising or recording it, max 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why, in a field study, some variables are measured and recorded rather than controlled.
parts.answer: Field conditions such as temperature, wind and cloud cover cannot be changed by the investigator; recording them allows the investigator to judge whether they could have affected the results and to choose comparable days.
parts.working: B1 cannot be controlled/manipulated in the field; B1 recording allows their effect to be taken into account/conditions matched.

practice.stem: An investigation compares the number of earthworms per m² in a field that has received farmyard manure every year and in a neighbouring field that has received only chemical fertiliser.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest three abiotic variables, other than the type of fertiliser, that could differ between the two fields and could affect the number of earthworms.
parts.answer: Soil moisture content/drainage; soil pH; soil texture (clay or sand); soil compaction or how recently it was ploughed; soil temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: soil moisture/drainage; pH; soil type/texture; compaction/ploughing/cultivation; soil temperature; slope/aspect.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the effect of these variables could be taken into account when choosing and sampling the fields.
parts.answer: Choose two fields next to each other with the same soil type, slope and crop and the same ploughing history; measure moisture, pH and temperature at every sampling point (on the same day) to show they are similar, or to allow their effect to be considered.
parts.working: B1 select fields matched for soil type/slope/crop/cultivation; B1 measure and record these variables at each sampling point to check they are similar.

practice.stem: In a test of salt tolerance in wild rice, a student planned to use these salt concentrations: 0, 10 and 400 mmol dm⁻³. She will grow one seedling at each concentration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest a more suitable range and interval of concentrations, giving reasons.
parts.answer: At least five concentrations spread evenly from 0 to about 200 mmol dm⁻³ (e.g. 0, 50, 100, 150, 200); with only three very unevenly spaced values, the trend between 10 and 400 would not be seen, and 400 mmol dm⁻³ might kill all seedlings.
parts.working: B1 at least five, evenly spaced, values; B1 reason: shows the pattern/trend, extreme value may kill all/no information between.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why using one seedling at each concentration is not enough, and how the seedlings should be allocated to treatments.
parts.answer: Seedlings vary genetically and in size, so one seedling may not be typical; use several (e.g. 5) per concentration, and allocate seedlings to treatments at random so that differences are not systematic.
parts.working: B1 variation between individuals/need replicates for reliability; B1 random allocation.

practice.stem: A survey found that trees close to busy roads in a city had fewer lichen species than trees in quiet streets. A student concluded that air pollution from vehicles reduces lichen diversity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a confounding variable.
parts.answer: A variable other than the independent variable that also changes between the conditions and affects the dependent variable, so it could explain the results.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two possible confounding variables in this survey and explain how each could affect lichen diversity.
parts.answer: Tree species – busy roads may be lined with a different species whose bark pH/texture suits fewer lichens; tree age – roadside trees may be younger, with less time for lichens to colonise; light/shading or humidity – busy roads are more open and drier; dust or road salt.
parts.working: 1 mark for each variable and 1 mark for each linked explanation.

practice.stem: In sea turtles, the sex of the hatchlings depends on the temperature of the sand during incubation. A conservation hatchery wants to find the effect of incubation temperature on the proportion of female hatchlings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent and dependent variables.
parts.answer: Independent: incubation temperature. Dependent: percentage (proportion) of hatchlings that are female.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest three variables that should be controlled and how.
parts.answer: Moisture content of the sand – same volume of water added/same sand; depth of eggs – same depth in identical containers; eggs from several clutches divided equally among temperatures (to control for clutch/parent effects); time of incubation/humidity in incubators.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three variable + method.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one ethical consideration for this investigation.
parts.answer: Use temperatures within the natural range so that hatching success and the sex ratio of released turtles are not harmed; release all hatchlings to the sea.

practice.stem: Some populations of a grass grow on spoil heaps from an old copper mine, where the soil contains a high copper concentration. A researcher wants to compare copper tolerance of the mine population with a population from a nearby pasture. She collects seeds from both populations, grows the seedlings for 4 weeks in ordinary compost, then places cuttings in solutions with and without copper and measures root growth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the plants are first grown from seed in the same compost, rather than being dug up from the two sites and tested directly.
parts.answer: Plants dug up from the mine may already have been affected by their environment (acclimatised or damaged), so any difference could be environmental rather than genetic; growing both in the same conditions means differences in tolerance must be inherited.
parts.working: B1 removes environmental effects/acclimatisation; B1 so differences are genetic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the dependent variable should be expressed to allow fair comparison between plants of different sizes.
parts.answer: As a tolerance index: root growth in copper solution ÷ root growth of a similar cutting in solution without copper (× 100), so each plant is compared with its own growth without copper.
parts.working: B1 ratio/percentage of growth in copper to growth without copper; B1 accounts for differences in vigour/size between plants.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two other variables that must be controlled.
parts.answer: Concentration of other mineral ions in the solutions; temperature and light; size/age of cuttings; time in solution; aeration of solutions.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: In a field trial, cotton plants were enclosed in mesh cages. Some cages had parasitic wasps added to control whiteflies; others had no wasps. A scientist noticed that the whiteflies in all the caged plants grew more slowly than on uncaged plants in the same field.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the cages might affect whitefly numbers even without wasps.
parts.answer: Cages change the microclimate – shade, temperature, humidity and wind – and keep out (or keep in) other predators; so whitefly growth differs from uncaged plants.
parts.working: B1 altered microclimate (named factor); B1 exclusion of other predators/immigration of whiteflies.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the treatment without wasps must also be caged, and why uncaged plants are useful as an additional comparison.
parts.answer: Caged plants without wasps control for the effect of the cage itself, so the only difference between treatments is the presence of wasps; uncaged plants show how whiteflies behave in natural field conditions, so it can be judged whether the caged results represent the field.
parts.working: B1 cage control so only one variable (wasps) differs; B1 any difference then due to wasps; B1 uncaged plants show natural conditions/effect of cage on population.

practice.stem: A microbiologist isolated two single-celled prokaryotes, J and K, from a hot spring at 70 °C. To help decide whether each belongs to the Bacteria or the Archaea, she tested the effect of the antibiotic penicillin, which prevents the formation of peptidoglycan cell walls, by spreading each organism on agar plates with paper discs containing penicillin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest the result expected for an archaean and explain your answer.
parts.answer: No clear zone (growth right up to the disc), because archaea have no peptidoglycan in their cell walls, so penicillin has no target.
parts.working: B1 no inhibition zone; B1 no peptidoglycan.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the controls and standardised variables needed for this test to be valid.
parts.answer: Discs soaked in sterile water (no penicillin) as a negative control; a known bacterium sensitive to penicillin tested at the same time as a positive control; same concentration and volume of penicillin on each disc; same volume of culture spread; incubate at the organisms' growth temperature (e.g. 70 °C) for the same time; aseptic technique to avoid contamination.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: negative control disc (water/solvent only); positive control organism; same antibiotic concentration/volume/disc size; same culture density/volume; same incubation temperature and time; aseptic technique.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why this test alone is not enough to place an organism in a domain.
parts.answer: Some bacteria are naturally resistant to penicillin (e.g. those lacking a cell wall or with resistance genes), so rRNA sequencing or membrane lipid analysis is also needed.

practice.stem: Researchers are investigating the effect of salinity on the growth of seedlings of the mangrove Avicennia marina, for a restoration project in the Indus delta. They consider measuring growth as (1) increase in stem height, (2) increase in fresh mass, or (3) final dry mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate each of the three measures of growth.
parts.answer: Height: quick and non-destructive, so the same plant can be measured repeatedly, but ignores growth in leaves and roots and thickness. Fresh mass: includes the whole plant but water content varies with salinity and time of day, so it is unreliable. Dry mass: the best measure of organic material/biomass, but plants must be killed, so separate plants are needed for each time point.
parts.working: B1 height – non-destructive but only one dimension; B1 fresh mass – variable water content (especially relevant with salinity); B1 dry mass – most valid measure of biomass; B1 dry mass destructive/needs more plants.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the dry mass would be determined accurately.
parts.answer: Wash off sediment, heat in an oven at about 80–90 °C, and weigh repeatedly until the mass is constant.
parts.working: B1 oven at suitable temperature (not so hot that tissue burns); B1 dry to constant mass.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
The shell lengths of eight dog-whelks (sea snails) on a rocky shore were measured.
Shell length / mm: 32, 35, 29, 38, 31, 34, 36, 33

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean shell length.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the standard deviation, s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: M1 deviations from 33.5 squared, Σ(x − x̄)² = 58; M1 58 ÷ 7 = 8.286; A1 √8.286 = 2.88 mm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the standard deviation shows about the data.
parts.answer: It measures the spread of the lengths around the mean – most shells are within about 2.9 mm of 33.5 mm.
parts.working: B1 spread/variation about the mean.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Four ecological investigations are described.
1 Is the number of moth species caught in a light trap correlated with night-time temperature? The data are not normally distributed.
2 Is the mean leaf length of a shrub different in a sunny and a shaded habitat? The data are normally distributed.
3 Do woodlice in a choice chamber show a preference for damp or dry conditions?
4 Is the wing length of a bird species linearly correlated with its body mass? Both are normally distributed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the most suitable statistical test for each investigation.
parts.answer: 1 Spearman's rank correlation; 2 t-test; 3 chi-squared test; 4 Pearson's correlation coefficient.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: The lengths of 16 pine needles from a tree were measured. Mean = 18.4 mm; standard deviation = 3.2 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard error of the mean, SE = s ÷ √n.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the 95 % confidence interval of the mean, using mean ± 2 × SE.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the 95 % confidence interval tells you.
parts.answer: There is a 95 % probability that the true mean needle length for the tree lies within this range.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: A student wants to know whether the mean number of lichen species per tree differs between two villages, and plans to use a t-test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a suitable null hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the mean number of lichen species per tree in the two villages.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a probability of 0.05 when deciding whether a result is significant.
parts.answer: If the probability of getting a difference this large by chance alone is 5 % or less, the null hypothesis is rejected; so there is a 5 % (1 in 20) chance of wrongly concluding there is a real difference.
parts.working: B1 5 %/1 in 20 probability the difference is due to chance; B1 below this, reject the null hypothesis/the difference is significant.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two conditions that the data should meet for a t-test to be used.
parts.answer: Data are continuous/measured (interval) and approximately normally distributed; samples are independent and similar in size/variance; sample sizes are less than about 30 per group (for the t-test as used here).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: normal distribution; continuous/interval data; independent samples; similar variances; small samples (< 30).

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
The lengths of ten leaflets from the sunny side and ten from the shaded side of a neem tree were measured.
Sun / mm: 52, 48, 55, 50, 47, 53, 49, 51, 46, 54
Shade / mm: 61, 58, 64, 57, 62, 59, 66, 60, 63, 58

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate t, using t = |x̄₁ − x̄₂| ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂). The standard deviations are s(sun) = 3.03 mm and s(shade) = 2.94 mm. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 both means; M1 √(3.03²/10 + 2.94²/10) = 1.335; A1 7.71 (accept 7.72 from unrounded standard deviations).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The critical value of t at p = 0.05 with 18 degrees of freedom is 2.10. State a conclusion.
