parts.answer: 7.71 > 2.10, so reject the null hypothesis: shade leaflets are significantly longer than sun leaflets (probability the difference is due to chance < 5 %).
parts.working: B1 comparison and rejection of null hypothesis; B1 conclusion in context.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
60 woodlice were placed in the centre of a choice chamber with four equal sections. After 15 minutes their positions were recorded.
Dark and damp: 27; dark and dry: 14; light and damp: 12; light and dry: 7

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: E = 15 in each section; χ² = 14.53
parts.working: M1 expected 15 each; M1 (O − E)²/E values 9.6, 0.067, 0.6, 4.267; A1 14.53.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of degrees of freedom and use the critical value 7.82 (p = 0.05) to state a conclusion.
parts.answer: 3 degrees of freedom; 14.53 > 7.82 so reject the null hypothesis – the woodlice are not distributed randomly and prefer dark, damp conditions.
parts.working: B1 df = 3; B1 conclusion, significant preference (dark and damp).

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
The nitrate concentration and the number of frog species breeding in nine village ponds were recorded.
Nitrate / mg dm⁻³: 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 18, 22, 27, 35
Frog species: 7, 6, 7, 5, 4, 4, 2, 3, 1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n(n² − 1)). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 ranks with ties averaged (7, 7 → 8.5; 4, 4 → 4.5, ranking from lowest); M1 d² values; M1 Σd² = 232; A1 −0.93.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The critical value for n = 9 at p = 0.05 is 0.700. State a conclusion.
parts.answer: 0.93 > 0.700 (ignoring the sign), so there is a significant negative correlation – ponds with more nitrate have fewer frog species.
parts.working: B1 comparison and reject null; B1 significant negative correlation in context.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
The mass of single seeds was measured for a wild and a cultivated population of a grain crop.
Wild: mean 42.0 mg, standard deviation 6.0 mg, n = 36
Cultivated: mean 47.5 mg, standard deviation 7.5 mg, n = 25

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard error and the 95 % confidence interval (mean ± 2 × SE) for each population.
parts.answer: Wild: SE = 1.0 mg, 95 % CI 40.0–44.0 mg. Cultivated: SE = 1.5 mg, 95 % CI 44.5–50.5 mg.
parts.working: M1 SE = s ÷ √n; A1 1.0 and 1.5; M1 ± 2 SE; A1 both intervals.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the confidence intervals suggest about the difference between the populations.
parts.answer: The intervals do not overlap (44.0 < 44.5), so the difference in mean seed mass is likely to be significant – cultivated seeds are heavier; a t-test would confirm this.
parts.working: B1 no overlap; B1 difference likely significant/not due to chance.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
The wing length and body mass of eight house sparrows were measured. Both variables are normally distributed.
Wing length / mm: 74, 76, 73, 78, 75, 77, 79, 76
Body mass / g: 27.1, 28.0, 26.5, 29.2, 27.8, 28.3, 30.1, 28.9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Pearson's correlation coefficient, r = (Σxy − n x̄ ȳ) ÷ ((n − 1) sₓ s_y). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 means; M1 standard deviations; M1 Σxy and substitution; A1 0.96.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The critical value for 8 pairs at p = 0.05 is 0.707. State a conclusion.
parts.answer: 0.96 > 0.707, so there is a significant positive linear correlation between wing length and body mass.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
A wetland plant was counted in four zones of equal area around a pond. The total was 120 plants.
Zone 1: 28; zone 2: 41; zone 3: 19; zone 4: 32

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the null hypothesis.
parts.answer: The plants are distributed evenly (randomly) across the four zones; any difference from the expected numbers is due to chance.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of χ², using χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value at p = 0.05 for 3 degrees of freedom is 7.82. Explain what the result shows.
parts.answer: 8.33 > 7.82, so reject the null hypothesis; the difference between observed and expected numbers is significant – the plants are not evenly distributed (more in zone 2, fewer in zone 3).
parts.working: 1 mark: χ² greater than critical value, reject null. 1 mark: distribution significantly different from even / not due to chance.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Simpson's index of diversity was calculated for five transects at each of two sites on a hillside: site 1 is a protected forest reserve and site 2 is a forest where firewood is cut.
Site 1: 0.72, 0.68, 0.75, 0.70, 0.66
Site 2: 0.58, 0.63, 0.55, 0.61, 0.60

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and standard deviation for each site. Give the standard deviations to 3 decimal places.
parts.working: B1 both means; B1 s(site 1) = 0.035; B1 s(site 2) = 0.030.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate t using t = |x̄₁ − x̄₂| ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: t = 5.24 (5.21 if unrounded standard deviations are used)

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of t at p = 0.05 is 2.31. State the degrees of freedom and a conclusion, and suggest a reason for the difference.
parts.answer: df = 8; 5.24 > 2.31 so reject the null hypothesis – diversity is significantly higher in the protected reserve; firewood cutting removes trees and shrubs, destroying habitats/niches and favouring a few disturbance-tolerant species.
parts.working: B1 df = 8; B1 significant difference, reserve higher; B1 valid reason.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: In 100 quadrats, plant species A was present in 60 and plant species B in 40. Both were present together in only 16 quadrats.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected number of quadrats for each combination (both present, A only, B only, neither) if the two species were distributed independently.
parts.answer: Both 24; A only 36; B only 16; neither 24
parts.working: M1 expected both = 60 × 40 ÷ 100 = 24; A1 all four expected values.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The observed numbers were: both 16; A only 44; B only 24; neither 16. Calculate χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: With 1 degree of freedom the critical value at p = 0.05 is 3.84. State the conclusion and the type of association, and suggest a biological reason.
parts.answer: 11.11 > 3.84 so reject the null hypothesis; there is a significant negative association – the species occur together less often than expected; e.g. they compete for the same resources, one releases inhibitory chemicals, or they need different soil conditions.
parts.working: B1 significant association; B1 negative because observed 'both' (16) < expected (24); B1 biological reason.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
A student counted a rare beetle in 12 quadrats in each of two meadows, and planned to compare the means with a t-test.
Meadow 1 counts: 0, 0, 3, 0, 1, 0, 0, 8, 0, 2, 0, 0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and standard deviation of the meadow 1 counts. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why a t-test is not suitable for these data.
parts.answer: The standard deviation is about twice the mean, and most counts are zero with a few large values, so the data are strongly skewed, not normally distributed; a t-test assumes normal distribution; counts are discrete and the samples small.
parts.working: B1 SD > mean indicates skew (values cannot be negative); B1 many zeros/not normally distributed; B1 t-test requires normally distributed data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the investigation could be changed to compare the beetle's occurrence in the two meadows.
parts.answer: Record presence or absence in many more quadrats and use a chi-squared test on the numbers of quadrats with and without the beetle in each meadow (or use larger quadrats).

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Hatchling turtles were weighed at two hatcheries: hatchery P, where eggs are buried in natural beach sand, and hatchery Q, where eggs are kept in polystyrene boxes.
P (n = 12) / g: 23.1, 24.5, 22.8, 25.0, 23.9, 24.2, 22.5, 23.6, 24.8, 23.3, 24.0, 23.7
Q (n = 10) / g: 21.9, 22.6, 23.0, 21.5, 22.8, 22.1, 23.4, 21.8, 22.4, 22.9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and standard deviation of each sample. Give the means to 2 decimal places and the standard deviations to 3 decimal places.
parts.working: B1 both means; B1 s(P); B1 s(Q).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate t, using t = |x̄₁ − x̄₂| ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂), and state the number of degrees of freedom.
parts.working: M1 substitution; A1 4.56; B1 df = 12 + 10 − 2 = 20.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of t at p = 0.05 with 20 degrees of freedom is 2.09. State a conclusion.
parts.answer: 4.56 > 2.09, so hatchlings from the beach-sand hatchery are significantly heavier.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
The abundance of a fern was recorded at 5 m intervals from the edge of a forest into a field, using a scale: 5 = abundant, 4 = common, 3 = frequent, 2 = occasional, 1 = rare.
Distance / m: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45
Abundance score: 5, 5, 4, 4, 3, 3, 3, 2, 1, 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Spearman's rank correlation, not Pearson's correlation coefficient, must be used for these data.
parts.answer: The abundance scores are ordinal (ranked categories), not measurements on an interval scale, and cannot be normally distributed; Spearman's uses ranks so is suitable.
parts.working: B1 ordinal/categorical scale; B1 Pearson's requires normally distributed interval data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n(n² − 1)). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value for n = 10 at p = 0.05 is 0.648. State a conclusion.
parts.answer: 0.92 > 0.648 (ignoring sign) so there is a significant negative correlation: fern abundance decreases with distance from the forest edge.

practice.stem: Students will collect invertebrates by kick-sampling in a shallow, fast-flowing stream in the hills and measure the water temperature and flow rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three hazards of this fieldwork and suggest a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Slipping or falling into the stream/drowning – work in pairs, wear boots with grip, stay in shallow water, check water level and weather. Infection from contaminated water (e.g. bacteria from animal urine or sewage) – wear gloves, cover cuts, wash hands. Sunburn/heat stroke – hat, sunscreen, drinking water. Insect or snake bites – long sleeves, look before placing hands. Getting lost – tell someone the route and return time.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard with a matching precaution (max 3).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the overall level of risk and give a reason.
parts.answer: Medium – working in or near flowing water has a risk of serious harm, although it can be reduced by the precautions.
parts.working: 1 mark: level with justification (accept low with good justification of shallow water and supervision).

practice.stem: A class will sample seaweeds and animals on a rocky shore near Karachi, using quadrats along a transect from the low-water mark up the shore.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three hazards of this fieldwork and suggest a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Rising tide cutting off the group – check tide tables, start as the tide goes out and finish well before low water ends; slippery, seaweed-covered rocks causing falls – wear shoes with good grip, walk carefully, no running; large waves sweeping people off rocks – check the weather/sea forecast, stay away from exposed edges; sunburn/heat stroke – hats, sunscreen, drinking water; cuts from barnacles or shells – wear gloves and shoes.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard and 1 mark for a matching precaution, any three pairs.

practice.stem: Students used Tullgren funnels with 60 W lamps to extract small animals from soil samples into beakers of 70 % ethanol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three hazards in this practical and suggest a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Hot lamp – burns: allow to cool before touching, keep away from paper; ethanol is flammable – keep away from the hot lamp and naked flames, use a small volume; soil may contain bacteria such as Clostridium tetani (tetanus) – wear gloves, cover cuts, wash hands; glassware breaking – handle with care, sweep up with a brush; electrical equipment near liquids – keep cables and liquids apart.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard and 1 mark for each matching precaution, any three pairs.

practice.stem: Students will go pond dipping in a village pond that is also used by buffalo and has rats living on its banks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two biological hazards and one physical hazard, and suggest a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Leptospirosis (Weil's disease) from water contaminated with rat urine – cover cuts with waterproof plasters, wear gloves, wash hands; faecal bacteria from buffalo dung – do not touch face/eat, wash hands with soap; drowning/falling in – stay on a firm bank, kneel, work in pairs, nets with long handles, teacher supervision.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard and 1 mark for each precaution; two biological and one physical.

practice.stem: In a laboratory germination test, students place seeds on filter paper moistened with sodium chloride solutions (up to 0.2 mol dm⁻³) in Petri dishes, and later measure roots with a ruler. The seeds have been treated by the seed company with a fungicide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two hazards in this investigation and a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Fungicide on seeds may be toxic/irritant – wear gloves and wash hands, do not eat; dilute salt solution – low hazard but can irritate eyes, wear eye protection; glass Petri dishes breaking – use plastic dishes or handle carefully.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard and 1 mark for each matching precaution, any two pairs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the overall level of risk and give a reason.
parts.answer: Low – the chemicals are dilute and the only significant hazard (fungicide) is easily controlled with gloves.

practice.stem: A team will survey reptiles and plants in the Thar desert in May, walking along transects during the day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three hazards and suggest a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Heat stroke and dehydration – work early in the morning, carry plenty of water, wear hats; venomous snakes and scorpions – wear boots and long trousers, do not put hands under rocks, carry a first-aid kit and know the nearest hospital; getting lost – use GPS/map, work in groups, tell someone the route and return time; sunburn – sunscreen, long sleeves.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard and 1 mark for each matching precaution, any three pairs.

practice.stem: To compare bacteria from two soils, students will spread diluted soil suspensions on nutrient agar plates and count the colonies.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Explain why each of these precautions is used:
(i) the plates are incubated at 25 °C, not 37 °C
(ii) the lids are held on with two short pieces of tape, not sealed all round
(iii) the plates are not opened after incubation
(iv) all plates are autoclaved before disposal
parts.answer: (i) 37 °C is human body temperature, which favours growth of human pathogens; (ii) allows oxygen in so anaerobic bacteria (which include many dangerous pathogens) are not encouraged, while preventing accidental opening; (iii) colonies may include pathogens, and opening could release spores/bacteria; (iv) high temperature and pressure kill all microorganisms and spores so waste is safe.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other precaution needed when spreading the suspensions.
parts.answer: Aseptic technique: flame the spreader after dipping in ethanol and keep the ethanol away from the flame / disinfect benches / wash hands.

practice.stem: A school club traps moths overnight in a garden using a light trap with a mercury vapour lamp connected to the mains electricity supply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three hazards and suggest a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Ultraviolet light from the lamp can damage eyes – do not look at the lamp, use a shielded lamp or UV-blocking glasses; electric shock if rain wets the lamp or cable – use a residual current device (RCD) and rain guard, outdoor cables; hot lamp can burn skin or crack if rain falls on it – allow to cool, use rain guard; tripping over cables in the dark – use torches, mark/tape down cables.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard and 1 mark for each matching precaution, any three pairs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way to reduce harm to the moths.
parts.answer: Place egg-box shelters in the trap, empty it early the next morning, identify moths quickly and release them in cover away from birds.

practice.stem: In a mark–release–recapture study, wild mice are caught in baited live traps, marked by clipping a small patch of fur, and released.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two risks to the people handling the mice and a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Bites – wear thick gloves/handle with a bag; diseases carried by rodents (e.g. hantavirus, leptospirosis) – gloves, wash hands, avoid stirring up dust from nests.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a risk with precaution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest three ways the study should be designed to protect the welfare of the mice.
parts.answer: Check traps often (e.g. every few hours) so mice do not suffer from heat, cold or hunger; put bedding and food in the trap; handle quickly and gently; use a marking method that causes no pain and does not make them more visible to predators; release at the point of capture; avoid trapping when females are feeding young.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

practice.stem: A student plans to compare the leaves of a rare orchid growing in two valleys by collecting 20 whole plants from each valley.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this plan is a risk to the organisms being studied and suggest how the investigation should be changed.
parts.answer: Removing 40 plants could reduce a small population and remove reproductive individuals, increasing the risk of local extinction; measure leaves on living plants in place (non-destructive), photograph them with a scale, or take one small leaf from each plant only if allowed.
parts.working: B1 removal of plants threatens rare population/reduces reproduction; B1 non-destructive measurement in the field; B1 permission/permit from the authorities or use photographs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other permission or ethical point the student should consider.
parts.answer: Permission from the landowner or park authority/wildlife department; avoid trampling and disturbing the habitat.

practice.stem:
A risk assessment lists these activities:
1 measuring the girth of trees with a tape in a park
2 collecting water samples from a fast-flowing river in flood
3 counting snails on a garden wall
4 using a sweep net in long grass where ticks are common

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assign a level of risk (low, medium or high) to each activity and justify each choice.
parts.answer: 1 low – little chance of injury; 2 high – risk of drowning/being swept away, severe harm likely; should not be done; 3 low – minimal hazard, wash hands; 4 medium – tick bites can transmit diseases, so long trousers tucked into socks, check skin afterwards.
parts.working: 1 mark each for level with valid justification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a safer way to collect a water sample from the river in activity 2.
parts.answer: Wait until the flood has passed, or take the sample from a bridge or bank using a bottle on a long pole/rope, with a partner and no one entering the water.

practice.stem: A class will survey crabs and mangrove seedlings on the mudflats of a mangrove creek near Karachi at low tide, in June. A student's risk assessment says: 'Hazard: getting muddy. Precaution: wear old clothes. Risk: low.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate this risk assessment.
parts.answer: It is incomplete and the risk is underestimated: it misses the incoming tide cutting off the group or flooding the creek channels; sinking and getting stuck in soft mud; cuts from oyster shells, barnacles and sharp mangrove roots (pneumatophores), which can become infected in dirty water; heat stroke and sunburn in June; bites from crabs. 'Old clothes' do not control any real hazard – suitable footwear, gloves and checking tide tables are needed; the risk should be medium, and there is no plan for supervision, first aid or emergencies.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: tide hazard missing (check tide tables/times); soft mud/getting stuck missing; cuts from shells/roots and infection missing; heat/sun hazard missing (June); precaution given does not reduce any harm – boots/gloves needed; risk rating underestimated with reason; no emergency plan (supervision, phone, first aid, working in pairs).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two changes to the plan of the fieldwork itself to reduce the risk.
parts.answer: Time the survey to start just after high tide as the water falls and finish well before the tide returns; work only on firm mud near the edge, using boards to stand on and a fixed route; work in pairs with a supervisor; survey early in the morning to avoid the hottest part of the day.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: timing linked to tide tables; stay on firm ground/boards/marked route; work in pairs/supervision/head count; early-morning timing to avoid heat; first-aid kit and clean water to wash cuts.

practice.stem: An entomology club traditionally killed collected insects in 'killing jars' containing ethyl ethanoate (ethyl acetate) on cotton wool, then pinned them for a reference collection.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the hazards of using ethyl ethanoate and suggest precautions.
parts.answer: Highly flammable – no naked flames; vapour harmful/irritant if inhaled – use in a well-ventilated place/outdoors, keep lids on, small volumes; irritant to eyes – eye protection; keep the jar labelled and stored securely.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: flammability + precaution; harmful vapour/inhalation + ventilation; eye/skin irritant + goggles/gloves; storage/labelling.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether killing insects is justified for a school survey of insect diversity, and suggest an alternative.
parts.answer: Killing reduces local populations, may include rare species, and raises ethical concerns; it may be justified when species cannot be identified alive and a reference collection is needed for accuracy; alternative – identify alive in the field with keys, photograph with a scale, use pooters and release; only a few specimens of common species collected.
parts.working: B1 harm to populations/ethics; B1 justification for scientific accuracy/identification; B1 alternative (photograph, identify and release, minimal collection).

practice.stem: A student suggests collecting water from a canal just below a sewage outfall, culturing it on agar at 37 °C in the school laboratory to count faecal bacteria, and comparing the count with water from upstream.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this plan is unsafe for a school laboratory.
parts.answer: Sewage contains human pathogens (e.g. Salmonella, E. coli O157, cholera bacteria); incubating at 37 °C encourages these pathogens to multiply to very high numbers; handling and disposing of large numbers of pathogens needs a specialist laboratory with higher containment.
parts.working: B1 sewage contains pathogens; B1 37 °C selects for/grows human pathogens; B1 school labs do not have suitable containment/disposal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a safer way for the student to compare the pollution of the water above and below the outfall.
parts.answer: Use a biotic index of invertebrates collected by kick sampling, or measure dissolved oxygen with a meter, or use commercially prepared test kits (e.g. nitrate/ammonia strips); wear gloves and wash hands after handling the water.
parts.working: B1 safer method (biotic index/oxygen/chemical test kits); B1 suitable precaution when collecting.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the level of risk of sample collection from the bank and justify it.
parts.answer: Medium – risk of infection from contaminated water and falling in, but it can be reduced with gloves, waterproof plasters and working from a firm bank.

practice.stem: Two methods are proposed to survey birds in a wetland reserve: (1) mist-netting, in which fine nets catch birds that are then identified, weighed and released by trained bird ringers; (2) point counts, in which observers record birds seen or heard from fixed points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the risks of the two methods to the birds and to the investigators.
parts.answer: Mist-netting: birds can be injured, stressed or die if nets are not checked often or in bad weather; requires licensed trained handlers; investigators risk pecks/scratches and diseases (e.g. avian influenza) – gloves, hand washing. Point counts: no handling, so almost no risk to birds; investigators face only general fieldwork risks (wet ground, insects, sun).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: mist-netting injury/stress to birds; need for trained/licensed ringers and frequent net checks; zoonotic disease/handling injury to people; point counts no contact so minimal risk to birds; point counts low risk to observers (general field hazards).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest when the extra risk of mist-netting could be justified.
parts.answer: When data can only be obtained by handling birds, e.g. body mass, age, moult or ringing to follow survival and migration, or to identify similar-looking species; and the benefit to conservation outweighs the small risk.
parts.working: B1 data not obtainable otherwise (mass, ringing, close identification); B1 conservation benefit outweighs risk when done by trained people.

practice.stem: An ecologist plans to measure Simpson's index of diversity of plants in quadrats at 100 m intervals from 100 m to 1000 m from a cement factory, where dust from the factory settles on the vegetation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a testable hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: Species diversity of plants increases as distance from the cement factory increases.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the null hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is no correlation between distance from the factory and plant species diversity.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the results and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Diversity will be lowest near the factory and increase with distance, because dust settling on leaves near the factory blocks light and stomata (and changes soil pH), so only a few tolerant species survive there.
parts.working: 1 mark: prediction (diversity increases with distance). 1 mark: explanation (dust reduces photosynthesis / alters soil pH; only tolerant species survive).

practice.stem: A student will germinate seeds of a wild rice in sodium chloride solutions of 0, 50, 100, 150 and 200 mmol dm⁻³ and record percentage germination.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a testable hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: As salt concentration increases, the percentage germination of wild rice seeds decreases.
parts.working: B1 directional relationship between IV and DV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the null hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is no relationship (correlation) between salt concentration and percentage germination.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the biological reason for your hypothesis.
parts.answer: Higher salt concentration lowers the water potential of the solution, so less water enters the seed by osmosis; the seed cannot take up enough water to activate enzymes and germinate (salt ions may also be toxic).
parts.working: B1 lower water potential outside, less water uptake by osmosis; B1 water needed to activate enzymes/hydrolyse food stores for germination.

practice.stem: A park manager stopped mowing one half of a large lawn. Two years later, students will compare plant species diversity in the mown and unmown halves.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a hypothesis and a null hypothesis for this comparison.
parts.answer: Hypothesis: plant species diversity is higher in the unmown half than in the mown half. Null hypothesis: there is no difference in mean plant species diversity between the mown and unmown halves.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the statistical test that would be used to test the null hypothesis, if the diversity values are normally distributed.
parts.answer: t-test

practice.stem: Mayfly nymphs absorb oxygen through gills on their abdomen. A student will measure dissolved oxygen and count mayfly nymphs at ten stream sites.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the relationship between dissolved oxygen and the number of mayfly nymphs, and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Positive correlation – more mayfly nymphs where dissolved oxygen is higher; the nymphs need a high oxygen concentration for aerobic respiration, and with low oxygen they cannot absorb enough through their gills, so they die or move away.
parts.working: B1 positive correlation; B1 need oxygen for aerobic respiration; B1 low oxygen → death/migration/fewer survive.

practice.stem:
Statements from a student's plan:
1 'Lichens are sensitive to sulfur dioxide.'
2 'Lichen cover will be lower on walls 100 m from the factory than on walls 2 km away.'
3 'There is no correlation between distance from the factory and lichen cover.'
4 'Lichen cover increases as distance from the factory increases.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which statement is: (i) the null hypothesis, (ii) a testable hypothesis, (iii) a specific prediction, (iv) background information.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Brine shrimps are placed in a long tube; one half is lit and the other half is dark. After 10 minutes the number of shrimps in each half will be counted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the null hypothesis that would be tested with a chi-squared test.
parts.answer: There is no difference between the numbers of brine shrimps in the light and dark halves (any difference from equal numbers is due to chance).

parts.label: b
parts.text: If 50 brine shrimps are used, state the expected number in each half under the null hypothesis.

practice.stem:
A researcher is investigating whether nitrate from farmland affects aquatic plant diversity. She considers two designs:
Design 1: measure nitrate and Simpson's index in 12 ponds across a district.
Design 2: compare Simpson's index in 10 ponds next to fertilised fields with 10 ponds in an unfarmed reserve.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a null hypothesis suitable for each design.
parts.answer: Design 1: there is no correlation between nitrate concentration and Simpson's index of plant diversity. Design 2: there is no difference between the mean Simpson's index of ponds next to fertilised fields and ponds in the reserve.
parts.working: 1 mark each – correlation for design 1, difference in means for design 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the statistical test for each design, assuming design 1 data are not normally distributed and design 2 data are normally distributed.
parts.answer: Design 1: Spearman's rank correlation; design 2: t-test.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: On many trees in a forest in Murree, a student notices that more moss grows on the north side of the trunks than on the south side.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest a hypothesis to explain this observation.
parts.answer: The north side of the trunk receives less direct sunlight, so it stays damper/has higher humidity, which mosses need.
parts.working: B1 linked to light/moisture/temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Make a prediction from your hypothesis that could be tested by measurement.
parts.answer: Bark moisture content (or air humidity next to the bark) will be higher on the north side than on the south side, and moss cover will be greater where bark moisture is higher.
parts.working: B1 measurable variable predicted to differ; B1 linked to moss cover.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how you would test the prediction.
parts.answer: On several (e.g. 15) trees of the same species, measure bark moisture with a moisture meter (or humidity with a probe) and moss percentage cover in a 10 cm × 10 cm grid quadrat at the same height on the north and south sides; compare with a paired t-test or correlate moisture and cover with Spearman's rank.
parts.working: B1 measurements on both sides of many trees at same height; B1 suitable analysis.

practice.stem: Limpets cling to rocks on the shore. A student thinks that on exposed shores, where waves are strong, limpets have flatter shells (a lower height ÷ base length ratio) than on sheltered shores.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a hypothesis and a null hypothesis for the investigation.
parts.answer: Hypothesis: the mean shell height ÷ base ratio is lower on exposed shores than on sheltered shores. Null: there is no difference in mean shell ratio between exposed and sheltered shores.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the biological reasoning behind the hypothesis.
parts.answer: A flatter shell has a smaller surface facing the waves, so less drag; limpets with flatter shells are less likely to be dislodged and survive to reproduce, so natural selection favours them on exposed shores (or they grow flatter in response to waves).
parts.working: B1 reduced drag/less likely to be washed off; B1 better survival/selection on exposed shores.

practice.stem: Parthenium hysterophorus has invaded grazing land in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. An ecologist will compare native plant species in paired 1 m² quadrats: one inside a Parthenium patch and one 5 m outside it, at 20 patches.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a hypothesis and predict the results if your hypothesis is correct.
parts.answer: Hypothesis: Parthenium reduces native plant species richness. Prediction: in most pairs the number of native species will be lower in the quadrat inside the patch than in the quadrat outside it.
parts.working: B1 hypothesis; B1 prediction linked to the paired design.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the quadrats are placed in pairs close to each other.
parts.answer: Each pair shares similar soil, slope, grazing and rainfall, so the main difference between them is the presence of Parthenium; this controls for differences between sites.
parts.working: B1 other variables similar within pairs; B1 so difference can be attributed to Parthenium.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a lower native richness inside patches would not, on its own, show that Parthenium caused it.
parts.answer: Parthenium may simply invade places that already had few native species (e.g. disturbed or overgrazed ground) – the cause and effect could be the other way round.

practice.stem: A fence has been built to keep goats out of an area of hillside grassland that was previously heavily grazed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how plant species diversity inside the fence will change over the next 10 years and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Diversity will first increase as grazing-sensitive species recover and flower; later it may decrease as tall, fast-growing grasses and shrubs become dominant and shade out smaller species (succession/competition).
parts.working: B1 initial increase; B1 reason – grazing-sensitive species recover/seed; B1 later decrease due to competitive dominant species/succession without disturbance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a control that should be used when testing this prediction.
parts.answer: Similar unfenced areas nearby, still grazed, surveyed at the same times.

practice.stem:
Many mangrove seedlings planted in the Indus delta die in their first year. Two hypotheses are proposed:
H1: seedlings die because the soil water is too salty.
H2: seedlings die because crabs eat them.
Survival after one year: open plots at low salinity 34 %; open plots at high salinity 30 %; plots with crab-proof mesh at low salinity 81 %; plots with crab-proof mesh at high salinity 76 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to evaluate the two hypotheses.
parts.answer: H2 is strongly supported: excluding crabs more than doubles survival (34 → 81 % at low salinity, 30 → 76 % at high salinity, an increase of about 46–47 percentage points); H1 is only weakly supported: high salinity lowers survival by only 4–5 percentage points, with or without crabs; crabs are the main cause of death, though salinity may have a small effect that needs a statistical test.
parts.working: B1 crab exclusion large increase, with figures; B1 H2 supported; B1 salinity small effect, with figures; B1 H1 weakly supported/may not be significant – need replicates/statistics.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the mesh itself could have affected the results, and how this could be tested.
parts.answer: Mesh may shade seedlings or reduce wave damage/trap sediment; test with a 'partial cage' control – mesh with gaps large enough for crabs to enter, so the only difference is crab access.
parts.working: B1 mesh alters other conditions (shading, water flow, sediment); B1 control of mesh with openings/roof-only cage.

practice.stem: Frogs from two neighbouring valleys look identical but their mating calls are different. A biologist proposes the hypothesis that they are two separate species.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Make three predictions that would be expected to be true if the hypothesis is correct.
parts.answer: Females will respond (move towards) only to calls of males from their own valley; in mixed captive groups they will not interbreed, or hybrids will be infertile/inviable; DNA sequences (e.g. mitochondrial genes) will differ more between the valleys than within each valley, by an amount similar to that between other recognised frog species.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three testable predictions: call preference/behavioural isolation; no interbreeding or infertile hybrids; greater genetic difference between than within populations; no gene flow where ranges meet.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a result that agrees with a prediction does not prove the hypothesis.
parts.answer: The result could have another explanation (e.g. call differences due to local learning or temperature, or populations recently separated but still able to interbreed); further evidence could still contradict the hypothesis, so it is supported, not proved.
parts.working: B1 alternative explanations possible; B1 hypotheses can only be supported/falsified, not proved.

practice.stem: A botanist has records of the altitudes at which an alpine flower was found on a mountain in Gilgit-Baltistan in 1975. She will survey the mountain again this year to test the hypothesis that climate warming has caused the species to move to higher altitudes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a null hypothesis and two predictions that follow from the hypothesis.
parts.answer: Null: there is no difference between the altitudes at which the flower is found in 1975 and now. Predictions: the lowest altitude at which the species grows is higher now than in 1975; the mean (or upper limit) altitude of the population is higher now.
parts.working: B1 null; 1 mark each for two predictions about lower limit, mean or upper limit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons, other than climate warming, why the survey might find the flower at higher altitudes.
parts.answer: Grazing or land use change has removed it from lower slopes; the new survey may search higher areas more thoroughly (different sampling effort/methods); trampling or collecting at lower, more accessible sites.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one additional piece of evidence that would strengthen the link with climate warming.
parts.answer: Temperature records showing warming over the same period, or similar upward shifts in many other species on the same and other mountains.

practice.stem: In green turtles, eggs incubated at higher sand temperatures produce more female hatchlings. A conservation team is concerned that shade from new beach buildings will cool some nesting sites.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a hypothesis about the effect of shading on the sex ratio of hatchlings and a prediction that could be tested at the hatchery.
parts.answer: Hypothesis: shaded nests have a lower sand temperature, so they produce a lower proportion of female hatchlings. Prediction: if half of a set of clutches is incubated under shade cloth, those nests will have a lower mean temperature and fewer female hatchlings than unshaded nests.
parts.working: B1 hypothesis linking shade, temperature and sex ratio; B1 testable prediction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the team should record sand temperature in every nest, not just whether it is shaded.
parts.answer: Temperature is the actual factor that determines sex; shade may affect other factors (moisture), and temperature varies between nests for other reasons, so recording it allows the relationship between temperature and sex ratio to be analysed directly.
parts.working: B1 temperature is the causal variable; B1 shade is only an indirect/variable proxy – allows correlation analysis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why, for conservation, a population producing almost only female hatchlings could be a problem.
parts.answer: Too few males for mating in future, reducing reproductive success and genetic diversity.

practice.subtopic: Genetic crosses (mono/dihybrid, sex linkage, codominance, epistasis)
practice.stem: In a species of flowering plant grown in a research garden in Faisalabad, the allele for purple flowers, F, is dominant to the allele for white flowers, f.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the terms 'dominant' and 'homozygous'.
parts.answer: Dominant: an allele that is expressed in the phenotype of a heterozygote (whenever it is present). Homozygous: having two identical alleles of a gene (at the same locus on a pair of homologous chromosomes).
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A purple-flowered plant of unknown genotype is crossed with a white-flowered plant. Use genetic diagrams to show how the offspring would show the genotype of the purple-flowered plant.
parts.answer: Test cross with ff. If FF × ff: gametes F and f; all offspring Ff, purple. If Ff × ff: gametes F, f and f; offspring Ff : ff = 1 purple : 1 white. Any white offspring shows the parent is Ff; all purple (in a large sample) suggests FF.
parts.working: B1 key to alleles and parental genotypes; B1 gametes; B1 offspring genotypes and phenotypes for both crosses; B1 conclusion linking ratio to genotype.

practice.subtopic: Genetic crosses (mono/dihybrid, sex linkage, codominance, epistasis)
practice.stem: The ABO blood group gene has three alleles: Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant and both are dominant to Iᴼ. In a family in Peshawar, the father has blood group A and the mother has blood group B. Their first child has blood group O.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the genotypes of the father and the mother. Explain how you know.
parts.answer: Father IᴬIᴼ; mother IᴮIᴼ; the group O child is IᴼIᴼ, so must have received an Iᴼ from each parent.
parts.working: B1 both genotypes; B1 reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Draw a genetic diagram to show the possible blood groups of their children and state the probability that their next child has blood group AB.
parts.answer: Gametes: Iᴬ, Iᴼ and Iᴮ, Iᴼ. Offspring: IᴬIᴮ (AB), IᴬIᴼ (A), IᴮIᴼ (B), IᴼIᴼ (O) in 1 : 1 : 1 : 1. Probability AB = 1/4 (0.25).
parts.working: B1 gametes; B1 four genotypes with phenotypes; B1 1/4.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why blood group AB shows codominance.
parts.answer: Both alleles are expressed in the heterozygote: both antigen A and antigen B are present on the red cells.

practice.subtopic: Genetic crosses (mono/dihybrid, sex linkage, codominance, epistasis)
practice.stem: In shorthorn cattle, the allele Cᴿ gives red hair and the allele Cᵂ gives white hair. Heterozygous cattle, CᴿCᵂ, are roan: they have a mixture of red hairs and white hairs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this is an example of codominance.
parts.answer: Both alleles are expressed in the heterozygote – red and white hairs are both present.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A farmer crossed roan bulls with roan cows and 24 calves were born. Draw a genetic diagram and state the expected numbers of red, roan and white calves.
parts.answer: Gametes Cᴿ, Cᵂ from each parent; offspring CᴿCᴿ red : CᴿCᵂ roan : CᵂCᵂ white = 1 : 2 : 1; expected 6 red, 12 roan, 6 white.
parts.working: B1 parental genotypes and gametes; B1 offspring genotypes; B1 phenotypes/1 : 2 : 1; A1 6, 12, 6.

practice.subtopic: Genetic crosses (mono/dihybrid, sex linkage, codominance, epistasis)
practice.stem: Albinism in humans (no melanin in the skin, hair or eyes) is caused by a recessive allele a. Normal pigmentation is caused by the dominant allele A. Two parents with normal pigmentation each carry one copy of the a allele.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use a genetic diagram to show the genotypes and phenotypes of the possible children, and state the probability that a child has albinism.
parts.answer: Parents Aa × Aa; gametes A and a from each parent; offspring 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa; 3 normal : 1 albino; probability of albinism = 1/4 (25 %).
parts.working: 1 mark: parental genotypes Aa × Aa with gametes A and a from each; 1 mark: offspring genotypes 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa; 1 mark: probability of albinism 1/4 (25 %).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the probability that both of their first two children have normal pigmentation.
parts.working: 1 mark: each child has probability 3/4 of normal pigmentation; multiply (3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16).

practice.subtopic: Genetic crosses (mono/dihybrid, sex linkage, codominance, epistasis)
practice.stem: Haemophilia A is caused by a recessive allele, Xʰ, of a gene on the X chromosome. A woman whose father had haemophilia marries a man without haemophilia. Neither of them has haemophilia.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the genotypes of the woman and the man.
parts.answer: Woman XᴴXʰ (carrier – she inherited Xʰ from her father); man XᴴY.
parts.working: B1 both.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Draw a genetic diagram to show the possible genotypes and phenotypes of their children.
parts.answer: Gametes: Xᴴ, Xʰ (mother); Xᴴ, Y (father). Children: XᴴXᴴ unaffected female; XᴴXʰ carrier female; XᴴY unaffected male; XʰY male with haemophilia.
parts.working: B1 gametes including Y; B1 four genotypes; B1 phenotypes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate (i) the probability that a son of this couple has haemophilia, and (ii) the probability that any child of this couple will be a son with haemophilia.
parts.working: B1 1/2 (half of sons); B1 1/4 (one of four equally likely children).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why haemophilia is much more common in males than in females.
parts.answer: Males have only one X chromosome, so one recessive allele causes the condition (no second allele to mask it); females need two copies.

practice.subtopic: Genetic crosses (mono/dihybrid, sex linkage, codominance, epistasis)
practice.stem: In a species of tomato, red fruit (R) is dominant to yellow fruit (r) and tall stem (T) is dominant to dwarf stem (t). The two genes are on different chromosomes. Two plants heterozygous for both genes were crossed and 320 offspring were produced.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the genotypes of the gametes that each parent can produce, and explain why there are four types.
parts.answer: RT, Rt, rT, rt; the genes are on different chromosomes, so they assort independently in meiosis (metaphase I/anaphase I), giving four combinations in equal numbers.
parts.working: B1 four gametes; B1 independent assortment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the expected numbers of each phenotype among the 320 offspring.
parts.answer: red tall 180; red dwarf 60; yellow tall 60; yellow dwarf 20
parts.working: M1 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio; M1 320 ÷ 16 = 20 per sixteenth; A1 all four numbers.

practice.subtopic: Genetic crosses (mono/dihybrid, sex linkage, codominance, epistasis)
practice.stem: In summer squash, fruit colour is controlled by two genes on different chromosomes. A dominant allele W prevents any pigment forming, so the fruit is white. In ww plants, allele Y (dominant) gives yellow fruit and yy gives green fruit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the phenotypes of plants with genotypes WwYy, wwYy and wwyy.
parts.answer: WwYy white; wwYy yellow; wwyy green.
parts.working: B1 all three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Two WwYy plants are crossed and 160 plants are grown from the seeds. Calculate the expected number of white, yellow and green plants. Show your reasoning.
parts.answer: white 120; yellow 30; green 10

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how this cross differs from the 9 : 3 : 4 ratio seen in Labrador coat colour.
parts.answer: Here the epistatic allele is dominant (one W masks the other gene), giving 12 : 3 : 1; in Labradors the epistatic allele is recessive (ee needed to mask), giving 9 : 3 : 4.
parts.working: B1 dominant vs recessive epistasis; B1 ratios linked.

practice.subtopic: Genetic crosses (mono/dihybrid, sex linkage, codominance, epistasis)
practice.stem: Coat colour in rabbits is controlled by one gene with four alleles. In order of dominance: C (full colour) > cᶜʰ (chinchilla, silver-grey) > cʰ (Himalayan, white with dark extremities) > c (albino).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A chinchilla rabbit with genotype cᶜʰc is crossed with a Himalayan rabbit with genotype cʰc. Draw a genetic diagram to show the expected genotypes and phenotypes of the offspring, and state the phenotypic ratio.
parts.answer: Gametes cᶜʰ, c and cʰ, c. Offspring: cᶜʰcʰ chinchilla; cᶜʰc chinchilla; cʰc Himalayan; cc albino. Ratio 2 chinchilla : 1 Himalayan : 1 albino.
parts.working: B1 gametes; B1 four genotypes; B1 phenotypes; A1 ratio 2 : 1 : 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of different genotypes possible for this gene in the rabbit population.
parts.working: B1 4 homozygotes + 6 heterozygotes = 10.

practice.subtopic: Genetic crosses (mono/dihybrid, sex linkage, codominance, epistasis)
practice.stem: In domestic cats, a gene on the X chromosome controls orange or black fur. Xᴼ gives orange fur and Xᴮ gives black fur. The alleles are codominant: a female XᴼXᴮ is tortoiseshell (patches of orange and black).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A tortoiseshell female is mated with a black male. Draw a genetic diagram to show the phenotypes of the kittens and their sexes.
parts.answer: XᴼXᴮ × XᴮY; gametes Xᴼ, Xᴮ and Xᴮ, Y; kittens: XᴼXᴮ tortoiseshell female; XᴮXᴮ black female; XᴼY orange male; XᴮY black male.
parts.working: B1 parental genotypes and gametes; B1 offspring genotypes; B1 phenotypes with sexes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the probability that a kitten from this cross is tortoiseshell.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why tortoiseshell cats are almost always female.
parts.answer: Tortoiseshell needs both Xᴼ and Xᴮ, so two X chromosomes are needed; males (XY) have only one X chromosome so can be only orange or black (rare XXY males can be tortoiseshell).
parts.working: B1 needs two X chromosomes/both alleles; B1 males XY have one X.

practice.subtopic: Genetic crosses (mono/dihybrid, sex linkage, codominance, epistasis)
practice.stem: In sweet peas, purple flowers need at least one dominant allele of gene C and at least one dominant allele of gene P. Any plant that is cc or pp, or both, has white flowers. Two plants, both heterozygous for both genes (CcPp), were crossed and 224 seeds were grown.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the expected phenotypic ratio of the offspring and name this type of gene interaction.
parts.answer: 9 purple : 7 white; complementary gene interaction (both genes must be dominant for purple).
parts.working: 1 mark: 9 purple : 7 white; 1 mark: complementary gene action (two genes interact to give one phenotype). Do not accept codominance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the expected number of purple-flowered plants among the 224 offspring.
parts.working: 1 mark: purple = 9/16 of offspring; 1 mark: 224 × 9/16 = 126.

practice.subtopic: Genetic crosses (mono/dihybrid, sex linkage, codominance, epistasis)
practice.stem: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is caused by a recessive allele d on the X chromosome. The dominant allele D gives normal muscle. A woman who is a carrier (heterozygous) marries a man who has the disorder.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Draw a genetic diagram to show the genotypes and phenotypes of their children, including the sex of each child.
parts.answer: Mother XᴰXᵈ (normal carrier) × father XᵈY (affected); gametes Xᴰ and Xᵈ from the mother, Xᵈ and Y from the father; children XᴰXᵈ (carrier daughter), XᵈXᵈ (affected daughter), XᴰY (normal son), XᵈY (affected son).
parts.working: 1 mark: correct parental genotypes and gametes; 1 mark: all four child genotypes with sex and phenotype.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the probability that a child of this couple is an affected daughter, and the probability that a child is an affected son.
parts.answer: Affected daughter 1/4 (25 %); affected son 1/4 (25 %).
parts.working: 1 mark: affected daughter = XᵈXᵈ = 1/4; 1 mark: affected son = XᵈY = 1/4.

practice.subtopic: Genetic crosses (mono/dihybrid, sex linkage, codominance, epistasis)
practice.stem: In a cereal plant, the allele for coloured grain (C) is dominant to colourless grain (c), and the allele for smooth grain (S) is dominant to wrinkled grain (s). A plant heterozygous for both genes, CcSs, which had received C and S from one parent and c and s from the other, was crossed with a plant with colourless, wrinkled grains. Offspring: coloured smooth 86; colourless wrinkled 82; coloured wrinkled 17; colourless smooth 15.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the ratio of phenotypes expected if the two genes assorted independently.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the results differ from this ratio.
parts.answer: The genes are linked – on the same chromosome (close together); C and S, and c and s, tend to be inherited together, so parental phenotypes (coloured smooth, colourless wrinkled) are most common; the small numbers of coloured wrinkled and colourless smooth are recombinants produced by crossing over between the loci in prophase I.
parts.working: B1 linkage/same chromosome; B1 parental combinations inherited together; B1 recombinants from crossing over (chiasmata).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of offspring that are recombinants.

practice.subtopic: Genetic crosses (mono/dihybrid, sex linkage, codominance, epistasis)
practice.stem: Coat colour in Labrador retriever dogs is controlled by two genes on different chromosomes. Gene B/b: B gives black pigment, b gives chocolate (brown) pigment. Gene E/e: at least one E allele allows pigment to be deposited in the hair; ee dogs are yellow whatever their B/b alleles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name this type of gene interaction and explain why.
parts.answer: Epistasis (recessive epistasis); the homozygous recessive ee genotype at one locus masks the expression of the B/b gene at another locus.
parts.working: B1 epistasis; B1 ee masks/prevents expression of B/b.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Two black dogs, both BbEe, are mated many times. Use a genetic diagram to show the expected phenotypic ratio of their puppies.
parts.answer: Gametes: BE, Be, bE, be from each parent. 16 combinations: B_E_ 9 black; bbE_ 3 chocolate; B_ee 3 yellow and bbee 1 yellow, so 9 black : 3 chocolate : 4 yellow.
parts.working: B1 gametes; B1 Punnett square/16 genotypes; B1 genotypes linked to phenotypes; A1 9 : 3 : 4.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Over several litters the dogs had 64 puppies. Calculate the expected number of yellow puppies.

practice.subtopic: Genetic crosses (mono/dihybrid, sex linkage, codominance, epistasis)
practice.stem: In the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, white eyes are caused by a recessive allele, Xʷ, on the X chromosome (red eyes Xᵂ). Vestigial wings are caused by a recessive allele, v, of a gene on an autosome (normal wings V). A red-eyed female with normal wings, genotype XᵂXʷ Vv, is crossed with a white-eyed male with normal wings, genotype XʷY Vv.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the probability that an offspring fly will be white-eyed with vestigial wings. Show your working.
parts.working: M1 P(white eyes) = 1/2 (XʷXʷ or XʷY from XᵂXʷ × XʷY); M1 P(vv) = 1/4; A1 1/2 × 1/4 = 1/8.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 400 offspring were counted. Calculate the expected number of white-eyed flies with vestigial wings, and the expected number of these that are female.
parts.answer: 50 white-eyed vestigial; 25 of them female
parts.working: B1 400 × 1/8 = 50; B1 half are XʷXʷ females = 25.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a male fly cannot pass the Xʷ allele to his sons.
parts.answer: Sons receive the Y chromosome from their father (and their X from the mother).

practice.subtopic: Genetic crosses (mono/dihybrid, sex linkage, codominance, epistasis)
practice.stem: In an insect, two genes are inherited independently. Gene A is autosomal: AA and Aa give long antennae; aa gives short antennae. Gene B is on the X chromosome: XᴮXᴮ, XᴮXᵇ and XᴮY give red eyes; XᵇXᵇ and XᵇY give brown eyes. A female with genotype AaXᴮXᵇ is crossed with a male with genotype AaXᴮY.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the probability that an offspring is a female with long antennae and red eyes. Show your working.
parts.answer: 3/8 (0.375): P(long antennae) = 3/4; P(female) = 1/2 and all females are red-eyed, so 3/4 × 1/2 = 3/8.
parts.working: 1 mark: P(long antennae) = 3/4 (AA or Aa); 1 mark: P(female) = 1/2 and every female carries at least one Xᴮ, so all are red-eyed; 1 mark: 3/4 × 1/2 = 3/8.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The cross produces 320 offspring. Calculate the expected number of females with long antennae and red eyes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The lac operon of Escherichia coli contains a promoter, an operator and three structural genes. State what is meant by a structural gene and a regulatory gene.
parts.answer: Structural gene: codes for a protein (e.g. an enzyme) that has a function in the cell other than controlling other genes. Regulatory gene: codes for a protein (e.g. a repressor or transcription factor) that controls the expression of other genes.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the lac operon is kept switched off when lactose is absent.
parts.answer: The regulatory gene (lacI) is transcribed and translated to make the repressor protein; the repressor binds to the operator; this prevents RNA polymerase from binding to the promoter/moving along, so the structural genes are not transcribed.
parts.working: B1 repressor made by regulatory gene; B1 binds operator; B1 RNA polymerase blocked, no transcription of structural genes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the enzyme encoded by lacZ.
parts.answer: β-galactosidase

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a transcription factor in a eukaryotic cell.
parts.answer: A protein that binds to DNA (at a specific base sequence, e.g. a promoter) and controls whether a gene is transcribed; by increasing or decreasing the binding of RNA polymerase.
parts.working: B1 protein binding to DNA/promoter; B1 switches transcription on or off/helps or blocks RNA polymerase.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why different cell types in the same plant, such as guard cells and root hair cells, make different proteins although they contain the same genes.
parts.answer: Different transcription factors are active in different cell types, so different genes are switched on (transcribed) and others are switched off.
parts.working: B1 same genes but different genes expressed; B1 due to different transcription factors (or signals) in each cell type.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A single base substitution in the gene for β-globin changes the codon for the sixth amino acid so that glutamic acid is replaced by valine. Explain why this may change the shape of the haemoglobin molecule, but why the number of amino acids in the polypeptide is unchanged.
parts.answer: The altered codon codes for a different amino acid, valine, which has a hydrophobic side group instead of the charged side group of glutamic acid. This changes the interactions that determine how the polypeptide folds, so the shape of the protein changes. A substitution keeps the reading frame and the number of codons, so the polypeptide still has the same number of amino acids.
parts.working: 1 mark: different amino acid because the codon has changed; 1 mark: different R group (hydrophobic instead of charged) alters bonding and folding (tertiary structure); 1 mark: a substitution keeps the reading frame and number of amino acids the same.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what a promoter is, and explain why RNA polymerase must bind to it before transcription can begin.
parts.answer: A promoter is a sequence of DNA, upstream of a gene, to which RNA polymerase (and transcription factors) bind to start transcription. RNA polymerase must bind here so that it is correctly positioned to begin transcribing the gene.
parts.working: 1 mark: promoter is a DNA sequence upstream of the gene where RNA polymerase/transcription factors bind; 1 mark: binding positions RNA polymerase at the start of the gene so transcription can begin.

practice.stem: Mutant strains of E. coli were grown in a medium with no lactose and then in a medium with lactose. The amount of β-galactosidase was measured.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Strain 1 has a mutation in the regulatory gene so that the repressor protein cannot bind to the operator. Predict and explain the amount of β-galactosidase made in each medium.
parts.answer: Large amount in both media (made all the time/constitutive); the repressor cannot bind the operator, so RNA polymerase can always bind to the promoter and transcribe lacZ, even without lactose.
parts.working: B1 high in both; B1 repressor cannot block operator; B1 RNA polymerase transcribes structural genes continuously.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Strain 2 has a mutation in the regulatory gene so that the repressor still binds to the operator but cannot bind lactose (allolactose). Predict and explain the amount of β-galactosidase made in each medium.
parts.answer: Little or none in both media; normally lactose binds the repressor and changes its shape so it leaves the operator; this repressor cannot bind lactose, so it stays on the operator and the genes are never transcribed.
parts.working: B1 none/very low in both; B1 lactose normally changes repressor shape; B1 repressor stays bound, no transcription.

practice.stem: When a barley grain absorbs water, the embryo releases gibberellin (GA). GA causes cells of the aleurone layer to make amylase, which hydrolyses starch in the endosperm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline how gibberellin causes the gene for amylase to be transcribed in an aleurone cell.
parts.answer: GA binds to a receptor protein (GID1) in the cell; the GA–receptor complex binds to DELLA proteins; this causes DELLA to be broken down (ubiquitination and destruction by proteasomes); DELLA normally binds to and inhibits a transcription factor (PIF); the freed transcription factor binds to the promoter of the amylase gene and RNA polymerase transcribes it.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of the points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the production of amylase is important for germination.
parts.answer: Amylase hydrolyses starch to maltose/glucose; the sugars are respired by the embryo to release energy (ATP) for growth, and used to build new cells (cellulose).
parts.working: B1 starch → maltose/glucose; B1 for respiration/growth of embryo.

practice.stem: A bacterium makes the amino acid tryptophan using five enzymes coded by genes in one operon. When tryptophan was added to the growth medium, the concentration of these enzymes fell to almost zero within 20 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether the tryptophan-synthesising enzymes are repressible or inducible, and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Repressible; their synthesis is switched off (repressed) when the end product, tryptophan, is present.
parts.working: B1 repressible; B1 reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how tryptophan could switch off transcription of this operon.
parts.answer: Tryptophan binds to an (inactive) repressor protein, changing its shape so it can bind to the operator; this blocks RNA polymerase so the genes are not transcribed.
parts.working: B1 tryptophan binds repressor and activates it; B1 repressor binds operator, blocks transcription.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the advantage to the bacterium of controlling these genes in this way.
parts.answer: The bacterium does not waste energy, ATP and amino acids making enzymes (and tryptophan) when tryptophan is already available.
parts.working: B1 saves energy/resources; B1 only made when needed.

practice.stem: In eukaryotes, genes are not organised into operons. Each gene has its own promoter, and transcription starts only when the correct transcription factors and RNA polymerase have bound.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the three structural genes of the lac operon are always transcribed together, while three genes coding for enzymes of one pathway in a eukaryote may be switched on separately.
parts.answer: In the lac operon the three genes share one promoter and operator and are transcribed as one mRNA; in eukaryotes each gene has its own promoter, so each can be controlled by its own transcription factors.
parts.working: B1 shared promoter/operator, one mRNA; B1 separate promoters/separate transcription factors in eukaryotes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A mutation changes the base sequence of the promoter of a eukaryotic gene so that a transcription factor that activates the gene can no longer bind. Suggest the effect on the cell.
parts.answer: RNA polymerase does not bind/transcription is not started, so no (or little) mRNA and protein is made from that gene; the cell lacks the protein, e.g. an enzyme, so its function is lost.
parts.working: B1 no transcription/RNA polymerase not recruited; B1 protein not made and consequence.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way in which a transcription factor may be activated in response to a signal reaching a cell.
parts.answer: A hormone/signal binds a receptor, which leads to the transcription factor being changed (e.g. phosphorylated) or released from an inhibitor (as when GA causes DELLA breakdown).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how methylation of cytosine bases in the promoter of a gene can switch the gene off without changing the base sequence of the DNA.
parts.answer: Methyl groups are added to cytosine bases in the promoter. This blocks the binding of transcription factors and RNA polymerase, or recruits proteins that pack the chromatin tightly, so transcription is reduced. The methyl pattern is copied when DNA replicates, so it is passed to daughter cells.
parts.working: 1 mark: methyl groups are added to cytosine in the promoter; 1 mark: this blocks binding of transcription factors or RNA polymerase (or condenses chromatin); 1 mark: the pattern is copied on replication so it is inherited by daughter cells (epigenetic).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the steroid hormone oestrogen can alter transcription in a target cell.
parts.answer: Oestrogen is lipid-soluble, so it diffuses through the cell-surface membrane. It binds to a receptor protein in the cytoplasm or nucleus to form a hormone–receptor complex. The complex enters the nucleus and binds to a specific DNA sequence near a gene, acting as a transcription factor. This increases (or decreases) transcription of the gene, so more (or less) mRNA and protein are made.
parts.working: 1 mark each: oestrogen is lipid-soluble and crosses the cell-surface membrane; it binds to an intracellular receptor forming a complex; the complex enters the nucleus and binds to DNA as a transcription factor; transcription is changed so mRNA and protein levels change.

practice.stem: A mutant strain of Escherichia coli has a mutation in the promoter of the lacZ gene. Its RNA polymerase cannot bind to this promoter. The strain was grown in a medium with lactose present and in a medium with no lactose, and β-galactosidase activity was measured.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the β-galactosidase activity in each medium, and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: No β-galactosidase is made in either medium. RNA polymerase cannot bind the promoter, so lacZ is not transcribed whether or not lactose is present, and the repressor and lactose have no effect.
parts.working: 1 mark: no (zero or negligible) enzyme in lactose medium; 1 mark: none in no-lactose medium; 1 mark: RNA polymerase cannot bind the promoter, so lacZ is not transcribed regardless of lactose or repressor.

practice.stem: A culture of E. coli growing without lactose was transferred at time 0 to a medium containing lactose and no glucose. β-galactosidase activity (arbitrary units): 0 min – 2; 2 min – 2; 5 min – 15; 10 min – 50; 20 min – 120; 30 min – 190.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of increase in β-galactosidase activity between 10 and 20 minutes, in arbitrary units per minute.
parts.answer: 7 units min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the increase in β-galactosidase activity after lactose was added.
parts.answer: Lactose (allolactose) enters and binds to the repressor; the repressor changes shape and can no longer bind to the operator; RNA polymerase binds to the promoter and transcribes lacZ, lacY and lacA (one mRNA); mRNA is translated into β-galactosidase (and lactose permease, which lets more lactose in, so activity rises faster).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: lactose binds repressor; shape change, released from operator; RNA polymerase binds promoter; transcription of structural genes; translation; permease increases uptake.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why there was no increase in activity in the first two minutes.
parts.answer: Time is needed for lactose to enter, for the repressor to be released and for transcription and translation to make new enzyme.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why β-galactosidase is described as an inducible enzyme.
parts.answer: It is made only when its substrate (lactose, the inducer) is present.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Semi-dwarf wheat varieties grown widely in Pakistan since the 1960s carry mutant alleles of the Rht genes, which code for DELLA proteins. The mutant DELLA proteins are not broken down when gibberellin binds to its receptor. Explain why these plants have short stems even though they make normal amounts of gibberellin.
parts.answer: The mutant DELLA is not degraded, so it remains bound to the transcription factors (PIFs); genes that promote stem elongation/cell division are not transcribed; so stems grow less in response to GA (GA-insensitive).
parts.working: B1 DELLA not degraded; B1 continues to inhibit transcription factors; B1 growth genes not transcribed/GA has no effect.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In peas, tall plants have the dominant allele Le, which codes for an enzyme that converts an inactive gibberellin into active GA₁. The recessive allele le has a single base substitution. Suggest why lele plants are short.
parts.answer: The substitution changes one amino acid in the enzyme; the enzyme's tertiary structure/active site is altered so it has (much) lower activity; less active GA₁ is made, so DELLA proteins are not broken down and stem elongation is reduced.
parts.working: B1 amino acid changed; B1 enzyme less active/active site shape changed; B1 less GA₁, DELLA remains, less elongation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one advantage to farmers of growing semi-dwarf wheat.
parts.answer: Short, strong stems are less likely to fall over (lodge) in wind/rain when carrying heavy heads of grain; more energy goes into grain, increasing yield.

practice.stem: A gene that is switched on by a transcription factor was monitored in a cell after a hormone signal was added at time 0. Relative mRNA concentration (arbitrary units): 0 min – 2.0; 30 min – 8.0; 60 min – 8.4; 90 min – 3.0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fold increase in mRNA concentration between 0 and 30 minutes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in mRNA concentration between 60 and 90 minutes. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the mRNA concentration falls between 60 and 90 minutes, even though the transcription factor may still be present.
parts.answer: The hormone signal has been removed or is no longer acting, so the transcription factor is inactivated and transcription falls; existing mRNA is also broken down by ribonucleases, so the amount of mRNA falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: transcription slows because the signal stops and the transcription factor is inactivated or removed; 1 mark: existing mRNA is hydrolysed (degraded) so its concentration falls.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a eukaryotic cell may need to stop the production of a protein very quickly once a signal has been removed, and suggest two mechanisms that allow it to do this.
parts.answer: The protein may be harmful or wasteful if its synthesis continues, so the cell needs a rapid response. Mechanisms include: the transcription factor is inactivated, so transcription stops; the mRNA is short-lived and is degraded; translation is blocked; or the protein is tagged and degraded.
parts.working: 1 mark: explanation that continued production is wasteful or harmful, so a fast response is needed; 1 mark each for any two mechanisms: transcription factor inactivated or removed; mRNA degraded quickly; translation repressed; protein tagged and degraded (proteasome).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a homologous pair of chromosomes.
parts.answer: Two chromosomes, one from each parent (maternal and paternal), that have the same genes at the same loci and are the same size and shape (centromere position); they may carry different alleles.
parts.working: B1 same genes at same loci; B1 one maternal and one paternal (may have different alleles).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the stage of meiosis in which (i) crossing over occurs and (ii) homologous chromosomes are separated.
parts.answer: (i) prophase I; (ii) anaphase I
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two ways in which the cells produced by meiosis differ from those produced by mitosis.
parts.answer: Meiosis gives haploid cells (half the chromosome number); four cells rather than two; cells genetically different from each other and from the parent cell.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Human body cells have 46 chromosomes. Explain why gametes have 23 chromosomes and why this matters for the zygote.
parts.answer: Meiosis halves the chromosome number, so each gamete is haploid (n = 23). Fusion of two gametes at fertilisation restores the diploid number (2n = 46) in the zygote.
parts.working: 1 mark: meiosis halves the chromosome number to the haploid number; 1 mark: fertilisation restores the diploid number in the zygote.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A gamete with 24 chromosomes is produced by non-disjunction in meiosis I of a human male. Explain how this happens, and state the chromosome number of the zygote formed when this gamete fertilises a normal egg.
parts.answer: In anaphase I the two members of a homologous pair fail to separate and move to the same pole. One gamete receives 24 chromosomes and the other receives 22. The zygote formed from the 24-chromosome gamete and a normal egg with 23 chromosomes has 47 chromosomes (trisomy).
parts.working: 1 mark: homologous chromosomes fail to separate (non-disjunction) at anaphase I; 1 mark: one gamete has 24 and the other 22; 1 mark: zygote has 47 chromosomes (trisomy, 2n + 1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences between prophase I of meiosis and prophase of mitosis.
parts.answer: Homologous chromosomes pair up (synapsis) to form bivalents in prophase I; crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids in prophase I. Neither happens in mitotic prophase.
parts.working: Any two, 1 mark each: homologous chromosomes pair (form bivalents) in prophase I only; crossing over (chiasmata) occurs in prophase I only; chromosomes do not pair in mitotic prophase.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how independent assortment in meiosis produces genetic variation among gametes.
parts.answer: At metaphase I each homologous pair lines up on the equator independently/randomly of other pairs; so the maternal and paternal chromosomes are shuffled into different combinations in each gamete.
parts.working: B1 random orientation of homologous pairs at metaphase I; B1 different combinations of maternal/paternal chromosomes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A plant species has a diploid number of 14. Calculate the number of genetically different gametes one plant could produce by independent assortment alone.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the number of different chromosome combinations possible in a zygote produced from two plants of this species, by independent assortment and random fertilisation (ignore crossing over).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the real number of genetically different gametes is far larger than your answer to (b).
parts.answer: Crossing over in prophase I exchanges sections between non-sister chromatids, producing new combinations of alleles on each chromosome.

practice.stem: A student examined squashed anther cells of an onion (2n = 16) undergoing meiosis. Cell P: pairs of homologous chromosomes (bivalents) lined up across the middle of the cell. Cell Q: two groups of chromosomes, each made of two chromatids, moving to opposite poles. Cell R: four groups of single chromatids, in two cells, being pulled to the poles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the stage of meiosis shown in each cell.
parts.answer: P metaphase I; Q anaphase I; R anaphase II
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of chromosomes that will be present in each nucleus at the end of meiosis.

parts.label: c
