parts.text: Explain why the separation of chromatids in meiosis II also contributes to genetic variation.
parts.answer: Because of crossing over, the sister chromatids of a chromosome are no longer identical; independent assortment of chromatids at metaphase II produces further new combinations in the four cells.
parts.working: B1 chromatids not identical after crossing over; B1 random arrangement at metaphase II.

practice.stem: An organism has a diploid number of 24. A primary spermatocyte of this organism undergoes meiosis to form four sperm cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of chromatids present in the cell at metaphase I.
parts.answer: 48 (24 chromosomes, each made of two sister chromatids).
parts.working: 1 mark: 24 chromosomes × 2 chromatids = 48.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of chromosomes in all four sperm cells.
parts.working: 1 mark: each sperm is haploid, with 12 chromosomes; 1 mark: 4 × 12 = 48.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how crossing over during prophase I produces new combinations of alleles on the same chromosome.
parts.answer: Homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis). Non-sister chromatids break at equivalent points and the segments are exchanged at chiasmata. Alleles that were previously on the same chromatid are now on different chromatids. After separation, the gametes contain recombinant chromosomes with new allele combinations.
parts.working: 1 mark each: homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis); non-sister chromatids exchange equivalent segments at chiasmata; alleles that were linked are now on different chromatids; the gametes carry recombinant chromosomes with new allele combinations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens to the chromosomes in anaphase I and in anaphase II of meiosis, and state how they differ.
parts.answer: In anaphase I, homologous chromosomes (each still made of two chromatids) are pulled to opposite poles. In anaphase II, the sister chromatids of each chromosome are separated and pulled to opposite poles. The difference is that anaphase I separates homologous pairs, whereas anaphase II separates sister chromatids.
parts.working: 1 mark: anaphase I homologous chromosomes move to opposite poles; 1 mark: anaphase II sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles; 1 mark: anaphase I separates homologues (each chromosome still has two chromatids), anaphase II separates chromatids.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why sexual reproduction produces more genetic variation in the offspring of a plant population than asexual reproduction does.
parts.answer: Sexual reproduction involves meiosis, which produces gametes with new combinations of alleles through independent assortment and crossing over. Fertilisation then combines gametes from two different parents at random, creating new genotypes. Asexual reproduction produces offspring that are genetically identical to the parent, apart from new mutations.
parts.working: 1 mark: meiosis gives new allele combinations (independent assortment and/or crossing over); 1 mark: random fertilisation combines gametes from different parents; 1 mark: asexual reproduction gives genetically identical offspring (variation only from mutation).

practice.stem: The mass of DNA in a nucleus of a cell from the testis of a mammal was measured during one meiotic division. Mass in arbitrary units: before the S phase (G1) – 20; end of interphase – 40; after telophase I – 20; after telophase II – 10.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the changes in mass of DNA shown by these data.
parts.answer: 20 → 40: DNA replicates in S phase of interphase, each chromosome now two chromatids; 40 → 20: at the end of meiosis I homologous chromosomes separate into two nuclei, so each nucleus gets half the DNA (still two chromatids per chromosome); 20 → 10: in meiosis II sister chromatids separate, giving haploid nuclei with half the DNA of the original G1 cell.
parts.working: B1 replication in S phase; B1 homologues separate in meiosis I; B1 chromatids separate in meiosis II; B1 final nuclei haploid with half the original DNA.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sperm cell fertilises an egg. State the DNA mass, in arbitrary units, of the zygote nucleus before it replicates, and explain the significance of this for the species.
parts.answer: 20; the diploid chromosome number (and DNA content) is restored at fertilisation, so it stays constant from generation to generation.
parts.working: B1 20; B1 diploid number restored/maintained between generations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how meiosis and fertilisation together produce genetic variation in the offspring of sexually reproducing organisms.
parts.answer: Points: in prophase I homologous chromosomes pair (bivalents); non-sister chromatids form chiasmata and exchange sections (crossing over); this produces new combinations of alleles on chromatids; at metaphase I homologous pairs line up randomly/independent assortment; giving 2ⁿ combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes; at metaphase II chromatids (no longer identical) assort independently; random fertilisation – any male gamete can fuse with any female gamete; mating between unrelated individuals combines different alleles; gametes haploid so zygote combines alleles from two parents.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six points; max 4 if fertilisation is not mentioned.

practice.stem: An organism has a diploid number of 4. It has two pairs of homologous chromosomes, one pair from each parent (maternal and paternal).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of genetically different gametes that can be formed by independent assortment alone.
parts.answer: 4 (2 pairs of chromosomes give 2² = 4 different gametes)
parts.working: 1 mark: 2 pairs of chromosomes give 2² = 4 different gametes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the probability that a gamete contains only maternal chromosomes, and explain your answer.
parts.answer: 1/4; each chromosome of a pair is independently maternal or paternal with probability 1/2, so (1/2) × (1/2) = 1/4.
parts.working: 1 mark: each chromosome of a pair is passed on with probability 1/2 independently; 1 mark: (1/2)² = 1/4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a pair of identical twins are genetically identical, but a pair of non-identical (fraternal) twins are genetically different from each other.
parts.answer: Identical twins develop from a single zygote that divides early, and the two embryos are produced by mitosis, so they have the same genome. Non-identical twins come from two different eggs fertilised by two different sperm; each gamete was formed by meiosis, so the combinations of alleles are different.
parts.working: 1 mark: identical twins come from one zygote; 1 mark: the embryos are produced by mitotic divisions so their genomes are identical; 1 mark: fraternal twins come from two separate zygotes; 1 mark: each gamete is formed by meiosis with random combinations, so the twins differ genetically.

practice.stem: In dogs, the diploid number is 78. During meiosis II in a male, one pair of sister chromatids failed to separate. This produced a sperm cell with 40 chromosomes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how this sperm cell came to have 40 chromosomes, and calculate the chromosome number of the zygote formed when it fertilises a normal egg.
parts.answer: In meiosis II, the sister chromatids of one chromosome fail to separate (non-disjunction), so one daughter cell receives both and the other receives neither. The dog’s normal haploid number is 39, so this sperm has 39 + 1 = 40 chromosomes and the other sperm has 38. A normal egg has 39 chromosomes, so the zygote has 40 + 39 = 79 chromosomes.
parts.working: 1 mark: sister chromatids (of one chromosome) do not separate at anaphase II (non-disjunction); 1 mark: the sperm has 40 chromosomes; 1 mark: zygote = 40 + 39 = 79.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A monohybrid cross between two heterozygous plants with purple flowers (dominant) is expected to give a 3 : 1 ratio. Calculate the expected number of white-flowered plants among 240 offspring.
parts.working: 1 mark: white is 1/4 of the expected offspring; 1 mark: 240 × 1/4 = 60.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the degrees of freedom for a chi-squared test comparing observed and expected numbers in four phenotypic classes, and explain how you obtained your answer.
parts.answer: 3 (number of classes − 1 = 4 − 1)
parts.working: 1 mark: 3 degrees of freedom; 1 mark: degrees of freedom = number of classes minus 1 (4 − 1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the expression χ² = Σ(O − E)² ÷ E, state what O and E represent, and explain why the difference is squared.
parts.answer: O is the observed number and E is the expected number in a class. The difference is squared so that positive and negative deviations do not cancel out.
parts.working: 1 mark: O = observed and E = expected numbers for each class; 1 mark: squaring prevents positive and negative differences cancelling (and makes the value always positive).

practice.stem: In a test cross, 180 offspring were counted: 96 with normal wings and 84 with short wings. The expected ratio is 1 : 1. The critical value for χ² with 1 degree of freedom at p = 0.05 is 3.84.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate χ² for these data. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark: expected 90 normal and 90 short; 1 mark: χ² = 0.80.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the conclusion.
parts.answer: 0.80 is less than 3.84, so accept the null hypothesis: the results are consistent with a 1 : 1 ratio.
parts.working: 1 mark: accept the null hypothesis because χ² < 3.84.

practice.stem:
A dihybrid cross between two plants heterozygous for flower colour and leaf shape was expected to give a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio. Observed offspring: 93, 29, 31 and 7 (total 160).
χ² = Σ (O − E)² ÷ E. Critical values at p = 0.05: 1 df – 3.84; 2 df – 5.99; 3 df – 7.82.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected numbers for each class.
parts.working: B1 all four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of χ². Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of degrees of freedom and explain what the result shows.
parts.answer: 3 degrees of freedom (4 classes − 1); 1.07 < 7.82, so the difference between observed and expected is not significant (p > 0.05); it is due to chance, and the results fit a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio.
parts.working: B1 3 df; B1 not significant, accept null/fits ratio.

practice.stem: In a cross, 180 offspring were counted: 136 with normal wings and 44 with short wings. The expected ratio is 3 : 1. The critical value for χ² with 1 degree of freedom at p = 0.05 is 3.84.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate χ² for these data. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark: expected 135 normal and 45 short; 1 mark: χ² = 0.03.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the conclusion.
parts.answer: The χ² value is far below 3.84, so the null hypothesis is accepted: there is no significant difference from the 3 : 1 ratio.
parts.working: 1 mark: accept the null hypothesis because χ² < 3.84.

practice.stem: In a test cross of a dihybrid, 200 offspring were counted: 52 with both dominant phenotypes, 48 with only the first dominant phenotype, 55 with only the second dominant phenotype and 45 with both recessive phenotypes. Independent assortment predicts a 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio. The critical value for χ² with 3 degrees of freedom at p = 0.05 is 7.82.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected number in each class.
parts.answer: 50 in each class (200 ÷ 4).
parts.working: 1 mark: 200 × 1/4 = 50 in each class.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate χ². Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark: correct substitution into Σ(O − E)² ÷ E for all four classes; 1 mark: χ² = 1.16.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the conclusion of the test.
parts.answer: 1.16 is less than 7.82, so accept the null hypothesis: the results are consistent with independent assortment.
parts.working: 1 mark: χ² is less than the critical value, so the data agree with independent assortment.

practice.stem: A student counted 10,400 newborn babies in a hospital: 5,400 were male and 5,000 were female. The null hypothesis is that the sex ratio is 1 : 1. The critical value for χ² with 1 degree of freedom at p = 0.05 is 3.84.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate χ² and state whether the null hypothesis is rejected. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: χ² = 15.38, which is greater than 3.84, so the null hypothesis is rejected: the sex ratio differs significantly from 1 : 1.
parts.working: 1 mark: expected 5,200 of each sex; 1 mark: χ² = 2 × (200)² ÷ 5,200 = 15.38; 1 mark: 15.38 > 3.84 so reject the null hypothesis.

practice.stem: In a sample of 200 students, 141 had free earlobes and 59 had attached earlobes. The expected ratio is 3 : 1 (free : attached). The critical value for χ² with 1 degree of freedom at p = 0.05 is 3.84.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate χ² for these data.
parts.working: 1 mark: expected 150 free and 50 attached; 1 mark: χ² = 2.16.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the conclusion.
parts.answer: Accept the null hypothesis: 2.16 is less than 3.84, so there is no significant difference from 3 : 1.
parts.working: 1 mark: χ² below critical value; the data are consistent with the expected ratio.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a chi-squared test should not be used if any expected value is less than 5, and suggest what a student could do instead.
parts.answer: When expected values are small, the χ² distribution is a poor approximation, so the calculated value is unreliable. The student could combine classes (where biologically sensible) or collect a larger sample so that all expected values are 5 or more.
parts.working: 1 mark: the χ² distribution is only a good approximation when expected values are large enough (≥ 5); 1 mark: combine classes or increase the sample size.

practice.stem:
A breeder in Karachi mated BbEe Labrador dogs (B black, b chocolate; ee dogs are yellow whatever their B/b alleles) and recorded 160 puppies over several years: 98 black, 22 chocolate, 40 yellow. The expected ratio is 9 black : 3 chocolate : 4 yellow.
χ² = Σ (O − E)² ÷ E. Critical values at p = 0.05: 1 df – 3.84; 2 df – 5.99; 3 df – 7.82.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the null hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the observed numbers and the numbers expected from a 9 : 3 : 4 ratio (any difference is due to chance).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate χ². Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State a conclusion, using the critical values.
parts.answer: 2 degrees of freedom; 2.84 < 5.99, so accept the null hypothesis: the difference is not significant and the results are consistent with recessive epistasis (9 : 3 : 4).
parts.working: B1 2 df and comparison; B1 not significant/consistent with 9 : 3 : 4.

practice.stem: Seeds of a plant were sorted into three colour classes: red 40, orange 35 and yellow 25 (total 100). The null hypothesis is that the three classes are equally frequent. The critical value for χ² with 2 degrees of freedom at p = 0.05 is 5.99.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate χ². Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark: expected 33.33 in each class; 1 mark: χ² = 3.50.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the conclusion.
parts.answer: 3.50 is less than 5.99, so accept the null hypothesis: no evidence that the classes are unequally frequent.
parts.working: 1 mark: accept the null since χ² < 5.99.

practice.stem: Two pink-flowered plants (heterozygous, showing incomplete dominance) were crossed and gave 400 offspring: 90 red, 214 pink and 96 white. The expected ratio is 1 : 2 : 1. The critical value for χ² with 2 degrees of freedom at p = 0.05 is 5.99.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate χ². Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark: expected values 100, 200 and 100; 1 mark: χ² = 2.14.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the degrees of freedom and the conclusion of the test.
parts.answer: 2 degrees of freedom (3 classes − 1). 2.14 is less than 5.99, so accept the null hypothesis: the results are consistent with a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio.
parts.working: 1 mark: df = 3 − 1 = 2; 1 mark: accept the null hypothesis because 2.14 < 5.99.

practice.stem: A student obtained χ² = 3.9 with 1 degree of freedom from a sample of 40 offspring. The observed proportions were then reproduced exactly in larger samples of 400 and 4,000 offspring.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the χ² value expected for the samples of 400 and 4,000 offspring if the proportions stay the same.
parts.answer: 39 for 400 offspring and 390 for 4,000 offspring
parts.working: 1 mark: χ² is proportional to the sample size when proportions are the same (×10 for 400); 1 mark: 390 for 4,000 (×100).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the larger samples give a significant result even though the proportions have not changed, and suggest what this shows about interpreting χ².
parts.answer: χ² increases with sample size, so a small deviation becomes significant when the sample is large. A significant χ² shows the deviation is unlikely to be due to chance, but not whether it is biologically important; the size of the difference must also be considered.
parts.working: 1 mark: χ² increases with n, so a small deviation becomes significant in a large sample; 1 mark: significance does not mean the difference is biologically large or important.

practice.stem: A test gives χ² = 4.5 with 1 degree of freedom. The critical values are 3.84 (p = 0.05) and 6.63 (p = 0.01).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the conclusion at the 5 % significance level and at the 1 % level. Explain what the result tells you about the probability of the deviation.
parts.answer: At 5 %: 4.5 > 3.84, so reject the null hypothesis; the deviation is significant. At 1 %: 4.5 < 6.63, so the result is not significant at this level. The probability of obtaining a deviation this large by chance (if the null hypothesis is true) lies between 1 % and 5 %.
parts.working: 1 mark: significant at 5 % (reject null); 1 mark: not significant at 1 % (4.5 < 6.63); 1 mark: probability between 0.01 and 0.05; 1 mark: the result is evidence against the null hypothesis but is not strongly significant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student has true-breeding pea plants with green pods (dominant) and true-breeding plants with yellow pods (recessive). She wants to test whether pod colour is controlled by one gene. Describe how she should set up the cross, which generation she should count, and how she should record the results.
parts.answer: Cross the true-breeding green-podded and yellow-podded plants to produce F1 offspring (all green). Self-pollinate (or cross) the F1 plants and count a large number of F2 offspring, recording pod colour in a table with totals and the ratio, then compare with the expected 3 : 1 ratio.
parts.working: 1 mark: true-breeding parents cross to give F1 (all green); 1 mark: F1 plants self-pollinated or crossed and a large number of F2 offspring counted; 1 mark: results recorded in a table of phenotypes with totals and ratio, compared with 3 : 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two variables that should be controlled when growing pea plants for a breeding experiment.
parts.answer: Any two: temperature; light; water and nutrients (growing medium); number of plants per pot (density); age of the plants when crossed.
parts.working: Any two, 1 mark each: temperature; light; water/nutrients/growing medium; density of plants or pot size; age of plants.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give one reason why the parents in a breeding experiment should be of the same age.
parts.answer: Age can affect fertility and the number or quality of gametes, which could bias the number of offspring of each phenotype.
parts.working: 1 mark: age affects fertility/gamete production, so differences in age would bias the results.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a student could find out whether seed colour in a bean plant is controlled by one gene, including how many seeds she should count.
parts.answer: Self-pollinate (or cross) a plant heterozygous for seed colour and collect the seeds. Count a large number of seeds (at least 100, ideally several hundred) from several pods/plants, recording each colour. Compare the observed numbers with the expected 3 : 1 ratio using a chi-squared test.
parts.working: 1 mark: cross or self-pollinate heterozygotes; 1 mark: count a large number (at least 100) of seeds from several plants/pods; 1 mark: compare with the expected 3 : 1 ratio using a chi-squared test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a dihybrid cross could be used to test whether two genes assort independently, including the number of offspring she should count and how she would analyse the results.
parts.answer: Use a random sample, for example by choosing students from a complete class list with random numbers, so that each student has an equal chance of selection. Test each student under the same lighting with the same test (for example Ishihara plates) and record sex and result. Obtain consent and keep results anonymous. Use a large sample of both sexes (at least 100 each if possible) and analyse with a chi-squared test. Avoid bias by testing all students in exactly the same way and recording each result on the same form.
parts.working: 1 mark: cross of heterozygotes for both genes (or test cross); 1 mark: large sample (several hundred offspring) counted; 1 mark: expected ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 (or 1 : 1 : 1 : 1) stated; 1 mark: χ² compared with critical value to decide independent assortment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher wants to find out whether red–green colour blindness is less common among women than men in a school in Lahore. Plan a survey, including how she would choose the sample, how she would test each student, and how she would avoid bias.
parts.answer: Use a random sample, for example by choosing students from a complete class list with random numbers, so that each student has an equal chance of selection. Test each student under the same lighting with the same test (for example Ishihara plates) and record sex and result. Obtain consent and keep results anonymous. Use a large sample of both sexes (at least 100 each if possible) and analyse with a chi-squared test. Avoid bias by testing all students in the same way and recording results blind to the sex of the student, where practical.
parts.working: Any five, 1 mark each: random sampling from a full list; large sample of both sexes; standard test (e.g. Ishihara plates) under the same conditions; record sex and result; consent/anonymity; same procedure for all to avoid bias; chi-squared analysis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a student could prepare and examine onion root-tip squashes to find the proportion of cells in each stage of meiosis, and explain how she would count enough cells to make a valid conclusion.
parts.answer: Cut the root tip, fix it, hydrolyse and stain it (for example in acetic orcein), then squash the tip gently on a slide under a coverslip to spread the cells. Examine several slides and count the stages seen in each field of view. Count at least 100 (ideally 200) cells in total, on several slides from different root tips, and calculate the percentage in each stage.
parts.working: Any five, 1 mark each: fixation/hydrolysis and staining; squashing to spread cells; examine several slides/root tips; count stages in a systematic way (fields of view); count at least 100 cells; calculate percentages per stage; use a range of samples.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student wants to test whether ultraviolet (UV) light increases the rate of mutation in a bacterial culture (for example, the rate of resistance to an antibiotic). Plan the investigation, including the control, how she would vary the UV dose, and how she would count the mutants.
parts.answer: Spread equal numbers of bacteria on several plates. Expose plates to different UV doses (for example 0, 5, 10, 20 seconds) for the same distance and light source, with a control of 0 seconds (no UV). Keep other conditions the same, use replicate plates for each dose, then incubate in the dark and count antibiotic-resistant colonies. Calculate the mean number of mutants per dose and plot against dose.
parts.working: Any five, 1 mark each: control with no UV; a range of UV doses; equal bacterial densities and replicate plates; same distance and time; counting resistant colonies on each plate; calculating means; incubation in the dark so light repair is not a factor.

practice.stem: A geneticist has two true-breeding stocks of Drosophila: one with normal (red) eyes and one with a new mutant eye colour, 'sepia-like'. She wants to find out whether the mutant allele is recessive, and whether the gene is on the X chromosome or on an autosome.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how she could carry out breeding experiments to answer these questions. Include the crosses, how the flies are handled, and the results she would expect for each possibility.
parts.answer: Points: collect virgin females (isolate within about 8 h of emerging) so the female parents have not mated; reciprocal crosses – mutant female × normal male and normal female × mutant male; anaesthetise flies (e.g. CO₂) to sex and score them; keep cultures at a constant temperature (e.g. 25 °C) on the same medium; remove parents before offspring emerge; if all F1 in both crosses are normal, mutant is recessive; if reciprocal crosses give the same results (all F1 normal), gene is autosomal; if mutant female × normal male gives normal females but all mutant males, the gene is X-linked; interbreed F1 to get F2 and score phenotypes by sex – autosomal recessive gives 3 : 1 in both sexes; use large numbers and test fit with χ².
parts.working: 1 mark each for any seven points; must include reciprocal crosses and the expected results for at least one possibility for full marks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a species of wheat, red grain (R) is dominant to white grain (r) and awned ears (A) are dominant to awnless ears (a); the two genes are on different chromosomes. Two plants, both heterozygous for both genes (RrAa), are available. Design a breeding programme to produce a true-breeding line with red grain and awned ears (RRAA), giving the crosses, the selection at each generation, and how you would confirm that the line breeds true.
parts.answer: Cross the two RrAa parents and grow a large F1 generation. Select plants with red grain and awned ears (R_A_). Self-pollinate or test cross the selected plants: a test cross with rraa identifies RRAA plants, because if all offspring are red and awned the parent is homozygous for both genes. Repeat the selection over successive generations until the selected line produces only red, awned offspring when self-pollinated. Confirm the line breeds true by growing several generations and checking that all offspring show the same phenotype. Use a large number of plants at each step to avoid losing rare genotypes.
parts.working: Any seven, 1 mark each: cross RrAa × RrAa; grow a large F1 population; select red awned plants (R_A_); self-pollinate or test cross selected plants to identify homozygotes (all red awned offspring from a test cross with rraa = RRAA); repeat selection over generations; keep only lines whose progeny are all red awned; confirm over several generations; use large numbers to avoid losing genotypes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A plant breeder finds that two genes controlling leaf shape and flower colour in a plant species may be linked on the same chromosome. Plan an investigation to test for linkage, including the crosses, the number of offspring to count, how you would calculate the percentage of recombinants, and what result would indicate linkage.
parts.answer: Cross a plant heterozygous for both genes with a homozygous recessive plant (test cross). Count a large number of offspring (several hundred) and record each phenotype. Identify parental (non-recombinant) and recombinant types. Calculate the percentage recombinants = recombinants ÷ total × 100. Independent assortment gives about 50 % recombinants; a much lower percentage indicates linkage.
parts.working: Any six, 1 mark each: test cross with homozygous recessive parent; large numbers of offspring; recording of each phenotype; identifying recombinant from parental types; percentage recombinants calculated; comparison with 50 % (independent assortment) to decide linkage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A biologist wants to know whether the frequency of the recessive allele for snail shell colour differs between two meadows. Plan a field study, including the sampling method, how she would identify each phenotype, how she would calculate allele frequency and how she would test for a difference.
parts.answer: Use random sampling in each meadow (for example random quadrats or points marked with random coordinates) and collect or count all snails in each sample. Score each snail for shell colour (recessive phenotype = homozygous recessive). Calculate the frequency of the recessive phenotype and take its square root to estimate the allele frequency q. Compare the two meadows using a chi-squared test on the numbers of recessive and dominant snails, with enough snails in each meadow to give expected values of 5 or more.
parts.working: Any six, 1 mark each: random sampling in each meadow; collect/count all snails in each sample; identify phenotypes accurately; recessive frequency = q²; q = √ recessive frequency; χ² test on counts with expected values at least 5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student wants to find out whether height in a crop variety is controlled by one gene or many genes. Plan an investigation that includes how she would select and measure plants, how many plants she would need, how she would present the data and which statistical measure she would use to describe the spread.
parts.answer: Measure the height of a large random sample of plants from a population (and of parents/F1 if available). Use a ruler to measure height to a stated precision. Present the data as a frequency histogram. A single gene would give discrete phenotypes; continuous variation suggests polygenic inheritance. Describe the spread using mean and standard deviation, and compare the distribution to the expectation.
parts.working: Any six, 1 mark each: random sample of plants; large sample (e.g. at least 100); accurate measurement to a stated precision; frequency histogram/ distribution; discrete vs continuous distribution to compare one-gene and many-gene hypotheses; mean and SD to describe spread; parents/F1 used for comparison.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher wants to test whether the sex ratio of offspring in a population of wild mice differs from 1 : 1. Plan the investigation, including sampling, sample size, how she would record the sex of each mouse, and how she would analyse the data.
parts.answer: Trap mice randomly across several sites and record the sex of each captured mouse, releasing them after recording to avoid harm. Use a large sample (for example several hundred mice) so that expected numbers are at least 5 in each class. Compare observed numbers with a 1 : 1 expectation using a chi-squared test with 1 degree of freedom, and compare the result with the critical value of 3.84 at p = 0.05.
parts.working: Any six, 1 mark each: random sampling across several sites; humane trapping and release; record sex of each mouse; sample size large enough for expected values of 5 or more; expected 1 : 1; chi-squared with 1 df compared with critical value 3.84.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student wants to find out whether beak length in a wild bird population is inherited. Plan an investigation using measurements of parents and their offspring, including how she would measure beak length, how she would analyse the relationship and what result would support inheritance.
parts.answer: Capture and measure the beak length of pairs of parents and their offspring using the same method (for example calipers to 0.1 mm), keeping measurements blind to the parents where practical. Plot offspring beak length against mean parental beak length. Calculate a correlation coefficient (Spearman if the data are not normal) and test for a significant positive correlation. A significant positive correlation supports inheritance.
parts.working: Any six, 1 mark each: measure parents and offspring using a consistent method; repeat on a large number of families; plot offspring against parents; calculate correlation (Spearman or Pearson); test significance; a significant positive correlation supports inheritance.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: The heights (cm) of six plants from one cross were: 42, 45, 39, 48, 44, 41.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean height. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the sample standard deviation (use n − 1). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark: Σ(x − mean)² = 50.83 (correct substitution); 1 mark: divide by n − 1 = 5 and take the square root to give 3.19 cm.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what the standard deviation of a set of measurements tells you about the data.
parts.answer: It measures how spread out the values are around the mean: a small standard deviation means most values are close to the mean (the data are consistent), and a large standard deviation means the values are more widely spread.
parts.working: 1 mark: a measure of the spread of values around the mean; 1 mark: small SD = values close together, large SD = values spread out.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard error of the mean for a sample with standard deviation 4.2 cm and n = 16. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark: SE = SD ÷ √n; 1 mark: 4.2 ÷ 4 = 1.05 cm.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student wants to compare the mean mass of seeds from two varieties of wheat, using independent samples. State the statistical test she should use, and state one assumption that the test makes.
parts.answer: An unpaired (independent samples) t-test. Assumption: the data in each sample are normally distributed (and the variances are similar), with random sampling.
parts.working: 1 mark: unpaired (independent-samples) t-test; 1 mark: one assumption, e.g. data normally distributed, random samples, similar variances.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a 95 % confidence interval for a mean is wider when the sample size is small than when it is large.
parts.answer: A small sample has a larger standard error, because SE = SD ÷ √n gets bigger as n gets smaller. The t-value is also larger for small samples, so the margin of error on each side of the mean is larger.
parts.working: 1 mark: smaller n gives a larger standard error (SE = SD ÷ √n); 1 mark: a larger t-value for small samples makes the interval wider.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
A student counted the kernels on one ear of maize produced by a test cross between a plant heterozygous for purple kernels (Pp) and a plant with yellow kernels (pp). There were 212 purple and 188 yellow kernels.
χ² = Σ (O − E)² ÷ E. Critical value at p = 0.05 for 1 df is 3.84.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a χ² test, not a t-test, is the appropriate statistical test for these data.
parts.answer: The data are counts in categories (frequencies of discrete phenotypes), compared with expected numbers from a predicted ratio; a t-test compares the means of two sets of continuous measurements.
parts.working: B1 categorical counts/observed vs expected; B1 t-test is for comparing means of continuous data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate χ² and state a conclusion.
parts.answer: χ² = 1.44; 1.44 < 3.84 (1 df), so the difference from 1 : 1 is not significant/due to chance; results fit the expected 1 : 1 ratio.
parts.working: B1 expected 200 each; B1 χ² = 1.44; B1 conclusion with 3.84.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: The mean stem length of a sample of 25 seedlings is 52.4 mm, with standard deviation 6.0 mm. For n − 1 = 24 degrees of freedom, the t-value for a 95 % confidence interval is 2.064.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard error of the mean.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the 95 % confidence interval for the mean. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark: margin = 2.064 × 1.2 = 2.48; 1 mark: interval 49.92 to 54.88 mm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what the interval means.
parts.answer: If the sampling were repeated many times, about 95 % of such intervals would contain the true population mean stem length.
parts.working: 1 mark: the interval is expected to contain the population mean in 95 % of repeated samples (not that 95 % of the data lie within it).

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: Two varieties of wheat were grown in the same field. Variety A: mean height 98.4 cm, SD 5.1 cm, n = 20. Variety B: mean height 92.7 cm, SD 4.6 cm, n = 20. The t-test formula is t = (mean A − mean B) ÷ √(SDA²/nA + SDB²/nB). The critical value at p = 0.05 with 38 degrees of freedom is 2.024.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of t. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark: difference of means = 5.7 cm and the denominator √(1.30 + 1.06) = 1.54; 1 mark: t = 3.71.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the difference in mean height is significant at p = 0.05, and give the conclusion in biological terms.
parts.answer: Yes: 3.71 is greater than 2.024, so the difference is significant; variety A is significantly taller than variety B on average.
parts.working: 1 mark: t > critical value so significant; 1 mark: variety A has a significantly greater mean height.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: Six plants were given different light intensities and their growth was measured. Light intensity (lux): 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60. Growth (mm): 5.1, 6.2, 7.0, 8.3, 9.9, 9.5. The critical value of Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient for n = 6 at p = 0.05 (two-tailed) is 0.886.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient, ρ. Give your answer to 2 decimal places. Use ρ = 1 − (6Σd²) ÷ (n(n² − 1)).
parts.working: 1 mark: ranks of growth: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 5 compared with light ranks 1 to 6; 1 mark: Σd² = 2; 1 mark: ρ = 1 − 12/210 = 0.94.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the correlation is significant at p = 0.05, and describe the relationship.
parts.answer: Significant: 0.94 is greater than 0.886. There is a strong positive correlation: growth increases as light intensity increases.
parts.working: 1 mark: 0.94 > 0.886 so significant; 1 mark: strong positive correlation between light and growth.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student finds that the standard deviation of a set of heights is 4.0 cm. Explain why the standard error of the mean for the same data is smaller, and explain why the standard error is more useful than the standard deviation when comparing two sample means.
parts.answer: The standard error equals the SD divided by √n, so it is smaller than the SD for any sample with more than one value. It measures how precisely the sample mean estimates the population mean, which is what is compared between two means in a t-test or confidence interval, whereas the SD describes spread among individuals.
parts.working: 1 mark: SE = SD ÷ √n so it is smaller than SD; 1 mark: SE measures uncertainty in the mean, not the spread of individuals; 1 mark: SE (with the difference between means) is used to judge whether means differ.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A breeder measures the height of the same 15 plants before and after applying a fertiliser. Explain why a paired t-test is more appropriate than an unpaired t-test for these data.
parts.answer: The two measurements come from the same plants, so each “before” value is linked to an “after” value. A paired test uses the differences for each plant, which removes the variation between individual plants and so is more sensitive to any effect of the fertiliser. An unpaired test would treat the samples as independent and would have less power to detect a difference.
parts.working: 1 mark: the data are linked (same plants measured twice); 1 mark: the paired test uses each plant’s difference, removing variation between plants; 1 mark: this makes it more sensitive to the fertiliser effect; 1 mark: an unpaired test ignores the pairing and would be less sensitive.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: Eight pairs of values were recorded for a correlation study: x = 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 17 and y = 4.1, 6.5, 5.2, 9.8, 8.9, 12.0, 11.1, 13.5. There are no tied values.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient, ρ, for these data. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the correlation and state how it would be expected to change if one of the largest y-values were removed.
parts.answer: A strong positive correlation: as x increases, y increases. Removing the largest y value would change the ranks of the remaining data only slightly and the correlation would remain positive and strong, although the value might change.
parts.working: 1 mark: strong positive correlation; 1 mark: a strong positive correlation would be expected to remain, changing only slightly.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: The mean number of leaves on plants in two treatment groups were: group A mean 14.2, 95 % confidence interval 13.1 to 15.3; group B mean 12.5, 95 % confidence interval 12.0 to 13.0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether the two confidence intervals overlap, and what this suggests about the difference between the two means.
parts.answer: They do not overlap: the upper limit of group B (13.0) is below the lower limit of group A (13.1). This suggests a significant difference between the population means.
parts.working: 1 mark: intervals do not overlap (13.0 < 13.1); 1 mark: suggests a significant difference between the two means.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why overlapping confidence intervals would not by themselves prove that there is no significant difference between two means.
parts.answer: Two intervals can overlap and still represent a significant difference when tested directly, because the test uses the difference between the means and the standard error of that difference. The overlap rule is a rough guide only.
parts.working: 1 mark: a formal test uses the difference between the means and its standard error, which can be significant even when intervals overlap; 1 mark: overlap is only a rough guide, not a test.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: Two samples have the same standard deviation of 10 units. The 95 % confidence interval for the mean is approximately ±1.96 × SD ÷ √n. Sample 1 has n = 25 and sample 2 has n = 100.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the width of the 95 % confidence interval for each sample, and state by what factor the width changes when n increases from 25 to 100.
parts.answer: Sample 1: 2 × 1.96 × 10 ÷ 5 = 7.84 units. Sample 2: 2 × 1.96 × 10 ÷ 10 = 3.92 units. The width is halved (factor 0.5).
parts.working: 1 mark: width for n = 25 is 7.84; 1 mark: width for n = 100 is 3.92; 1 mark: the width changes by a factor of 0.5 (it halves), because width ∝ 1/√n and √(100/25) = 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a researcher might still choose a sample of 25 rather than 100.
parts.answer: Collecting 100 samples costs more time and money, and the gain in precision may not justify it; a sample of 25 may be enough to answer the question.
parts.working: 1 mark: cost and time versus the benefit of narrower intervals.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student performs 20 independent t-tests on 20 different genes. None of the genes has a real effect. Each test uses significance level p = 0.05. Calculate the expected number of significant results, and the probability that at least one result is significant by chance.
parts.answer: Expected number of significant results = 20 × 0.05 = 1. Probability of no significant result in one test = 0.95; probability of none in 20 tests = 0.95²⁰ = 0.358; probability of at least one = 1 − 0.358 = 0.642, i.e. about 64.2 %.
parts.working: 1 mark: expected number = 20 × 0.05 = 1; 1 mark: P(no significant result in a test) = 0.95; 1 mark: P(no significant result in 20 tests) = 0.95²⁰; 1 mark: P(at least one) = 1 − 0.95²⁰ = 0.642; 1 mark: state 64.2 % and that the chance of a false positive increases with many tests.

practice.stem: A plant breeder thinks that seed coat colour in a variety of chickpea is controlled by one gene, with black seed coat dominant to cream. She crosses two plants that are both heterozygous.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the prediction she would make about the offspring if her hypothesis is correct.
parts.answer: 3 black : 1 cream (three-quarters black).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State a null hypothesis for a χ² test on her results.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the observed numbers of black and cream offspring and the numbers expected from a 3 : 1 ratio.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why she should grow a large number of offspring.
parts.answer: Ratios are probabilities; with large numbers, chance effects of random fertilisation are smaller and the test is more reliable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A breeder thinks that black coat (B) is dominant to brown coat (b) in a species of rabbit. State the expected phenotypic ratio of the offspring of two heterozygous black parents if the hypothesis is correct.
parts.answer: 3 black : 1 brown
parts.working: 1 mark: 3 black : 1 brown (Bb × Bb gives 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student compares the mean pod length of two bean varieties using a t-test. State the null hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is no difference between the mean pod length of the two bean varieties.
parts.working: 1 mark: no difference in mean pod length between the two varieties.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student hypothesises that a recessive condition is inherited on the X chromosome. State two predictions for the offspring of an affected male mated with a homozygous normal female, if the hypothesis is correct.
parts.answer: All sons are unaffected (they receive their X chromosome from their mother, not their father). All daughters are carriers (heterozygous, X from the father carrying the allele).
parts.working: 1 mark: all sons unaffected (they receive the father’s Y, not his X); 1 mark: all daughters are heterozygous carriers (they receive the affected X from their father).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a testable hypothesis, in the form "If … then …", for the inheritance of leaf margin in a plant in which smooth margins are dominant to serrated margins.
parts.answer: If leaf margin is controlled by one gene in which smooth is dominant to serrated, then a cross of two heterozygous smooth-leaved plants will produce smooth and serrated offspring in a ratio of 3 : 1.
parts.working: 1 mark: a clear if/then statement that names the gene, dominance and expected ratio.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a prediction should be written down before the data are collected.
parts.answer: Writing the prediction first prevents the results being interpreted to fit what is expected (bias). It also makes the test clear, so that a suitable statistical test and null hypothesis can be chosen before the results are known.
parts.working: 1 mark: avoids bias or fitting the interpretation to the results; 1 mark: allows the correct null hypothesis and test to be chosen in advance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two genes, A and B, are on the same chromosome and are completely linked. A plant with genotype AB/ab is test-crossed with a plant with genotype ab/ab. Predict the phenotypic ratio of the offspring, and contrast this with the ratio expected if the genes assorted independently.
parts.answer: Complete linkage: 1 AB/ab : 1 ab/ab, so a 1 : 1 ratio of two parental types only. Independent assortment: 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 of four phenotypes (AB, Ab, aB, ab).
parts.working: 1 mark: 1 : 1 ratio of the two parental types; 1 mark: no recombinant offspring when completely linked; 1 mark: independent assortment would give a 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio of four phenotypes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A breeder predicts that a mutant allele reduces seed mass. State a one-tailed alternative hypothesis and the corresponding null hypothesis for a t-test.
parts.answer: Alternative: the mean seed mass of mutant plants is less than that of wild-type plants. Null: there is no difference between the mean seed masses of mutant and wild-type plants.
parts.working: 1 mark: one-tailed alternative (mutant mean less than wild-type); 1 mark: null hypothesis of no difference in means.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student proposes that the dark pigment of a Himalayan rabbit’s extremities is produced more at lower temperatures. State a testable hypothesis, and describe the prediction she would test with shaved patches of fur.
parts.answer: Hypothesis: the enzyme that makes the dark pigment works more at lower temperatures, so dark pigment is produced more at cooler temperatures. Prediction: shaved patches kept at 15 °C will grow darker fur than patches kept at 30 °C.
parts.working: 1 mark: hypothesis linking low temperature to more pigment; 1 mark: testable prediction that cooler patches grow darker fur; 1 mark: a control such as the same patch size and fur type or the same time (or keeping all else constant).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A mutant plant with a new leaf shape is found. Its F1 offspring from a cross with a normal plant all have normal leaves. State the prediction for the F2 generation if the mutant allele is recessive, and describe a test cross that would confirm the hypothesis.
parts.answer: If the mutant allele is recessive, F2 offspring would show normal to mutant leaves in a 3 : 1 ratio. A test cross of a normal-leaved F2 plant that might be heterozygous with a mutant (homozygous recessive) plant would produce mutant offspring in a 1 : 1 ratio if the plant is heterozygous, and all normal offspring if it is homozygous dominant.
parts.working: 1 mark: F2 ratio 3 normal : 1 mutant; 1 mark: test cross with homozygous recessive plant; 1 mark: heterozygotes give 1 : 1 normal : mutant; 1 mark: homozygous dominant gives all normal offspring.

practice.stem: In Drosophila, a student crosses true-breeding red-eyed females with white-eyed males. White eyes are caused by a recessive allele. All the F1 flies have red eyes. She then crosses F1 females with F1 males and counts the F2 offspring. She hypothesises that the white-eye allele is on the X chromosome.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the predicted eye colour of the F2 females and the ratio of red-eyed to white-eyed F2 males if the hypothesis is correct.
parts.answer: All F2 females have red eyes. F2 males are red-eyed and white-eyed in a 1 : 1 ratio.
parts.working: 1 mark: F1 females are XᴿXʷ and F1 males are XᴿY; 1 mark: every F2 female receives Xᴿ from her father, so all are red-eyed; 1 mark: F2 males receive Xᴿ or Xʷ from their mother in equal proportion, giving 1 red : 1 white.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the proportion of F2 females with white eyes predicted if the white-eye allele were instead an autosomal recessive, and explain how the observed F2 females would distinguish the two hypotheses.
parts.answer: If autosomal, 1/4 of the F2 females would have white eyes (a 3 : 1 ratio in both sexes). Finding no white-eyed females would therefore support X-linkage.
parts.working: 1 mark: autosomal recessive predicts 3 red : 1 white in both sexes, so 1/4 of females are white; 1 mark: no white-eyed females in the F2 would support X-linkage and reject the autosomal hypothesis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a species of mouse, a yellow coat is caused by a dominant allele Y. Yellow homozygotes (YY) die before birth. Heterozygous yellow mice (Yy) are crossed with each other. Predict the phenotypic ratio of the surviving offspring, and state the hypothesis that explains it.
parts.answer: Each cross gives 1 YY : 2 Yy : 1 yy; the YY embryos die, leaving 2 yellow (Yy) : 1 non-yellow (yy), a 2 : 1 ratio among surviving offspring. Hypothesis: the dominant Y allele is lethal when homozygous.
parts.working: 1 mark: 1 YY : 2 Yy : 1 yy at fertilisation; 1 mark: YY embryos die, so survivors are in a 2 yellow : 1 non-yellow ratio; 1 mark: hypothesis that the Y allele is lethal when homozygous; 1 mark: the 2 : 1 ratio is the prediction that is tested against the counted surviving offspring.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher wants to know whether a recessive allele for a disease is more common in males than in females in a population. State a null hypothesis and an alternative hypothesis suitable for a test, and explain which type of test she would use.
parts.answer: Null hypothesis: the frequency of the allele (or of the disease) is the same in males and females. Alternative: the frequency differs between males and females. A chi-squared test of the numbers of affected and unaffected males and females, with 1 degree of freedom.
parts.working: 1 mark: null hypothesis of no difference in frequency between sexes; 1 mark: alternative hypothesis of a difference (two-tailed); 1 mark: chi-squared test; 1 mark: comparison of observed and expected numbers.

practice.stem: A student suspects that a pesticide increases the mutation rate in Drosophila. In a pilot study, the number of white-eyed mutants per 1000 flies was higher in a treated group than in a control group.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a testable hypothesis and a prediction that follows from it.
parts.answer: Hypothesis: exposure to the pesticide increases the rate of mutation (for example, to white-eyed mutants) compared with no exposure. Prediction: the treated group will show a higher number of mutants per 1000 flies than the control group.
parts.working: 1 mark: testable hypothesis about pesticide raising the mutation rate; 1 mark: prediction of more mutants per 1000 in the treated group.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the role of a control group, and describe one result that would falsify the hypothesis.
parts.answer: A control group (no pesticide, otherwise identical) shows the background mutation rate, so any extra mutants can be attributed to the pesticide. A result that falsifies the hypothesis would be no greater number of mutants in the treated group than in the control (or fewer), after a statistical test.
parts.working: 1 mark: control shows background rate so the effect of the pesticide can be identified; 1 mark: control kept identical except for the pesticide; 1 mark: falsifying result: treated group no higher (or lower) than control with no significant difference.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Continuous variation in human height is thought to be caused by many genes, each with a small additive effect. Write a hypothesis that could explain this, and predict how the distribution of offspring heights from two tall parents would compare with that from two short parents.
parts.answer: Hypothesis: height is polygenic, with many genes each adding a small amount to height so that many combinations give a continuous spread. Prediction: offspring of two tall parents would have a higher mean and a continuous distribution shifted towards greater height compared with offspring of two short parents, with a similar spread.
parts.working: 1 mark: hypothesis that many genes each have a small additive effect (polygenic); 1 mark: continuous distribution rather than discrete classes; 1 mark: offspring of tall parents have a higher mean than those of short parents; 1 mark: spreads similar but shifted.

practice.stem: Students will grow a non-pathogenic laboratory strain of E. coli on agar plates with and without lactose, and test for β-galactosidase activity using a colourless substrate that turns yellow when hydrolysed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards in this investigation and describe a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Any two hazards with matched precautions: bacteria could be contaminated with pathogens/cause infection – use aseptic technique, flame loops, tape lids (do not seal fully), do not open plates after incubation, incubate at 25–30 °C not 37 °C; cultures spilt – disinfect bench before and after with disinfectant; disposal – autoclave cultures before disposal; Bunsen burner/hot loop – burns, tie hair back; chemical substrate/irritant – wear gloves and eye protection.
parts.working: B1 each hazard; B1 each matching precaution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why plates are incubated at about 25 °C rather than 37 °C in school laboratories.
parts.answer: 37 °C (body temperature) favours growth of human pathogens that may have contaminated the plates.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one hazard and one precaution when preparing an onion root-tip squash using acetic acid stain.
parts.answer: Hazard: acetic acid is corrosive and irritates the eyes and skin. Precaution: wear eye protection and gloves and work in a well-ventilated area or fume cupboard.
parts.working: 1 mark: hazard identified (corrosive/irritant acetic acid); 1 mark: matching precaution (goggles, gloves, ventilation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Fruit flies are anaesthetised with carbon dioxide before being counted. Identify one hazard and one precaution.
parts.answer: Hazard: high concentrations of carbon dioxide are harmful and can cause dizziness or unconsciousness in people. Precaution: use the anaesthetic pad or gas only briefly, in a well-ventilated area, and do not inhale the gas directly.
parts.working: 1 mark: hazard: carbon dioxide harmful to people in high concentrations; 1 mark: precaution: ventilation, brief use, no direct inhalation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethanol is used to dehydrate a plant sample before staining. Identify one hazard and one precaution.
parts.answer: Hazard: ethanol is flammable and can ignite near a naked flame. Precaution: keep the bottle closed, use small volumes, and keep it away from Bunsen burners and other sources of ignition.
parts.working: 1 mark: flammable (ignites near naked flames); 1 mark: precaution such as keeping away from flames and using small volumes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student uses a scalpel to cut plant tissue for a microscope slide. Identify one hazard and one precaution.
parts.answer: Hazard: the blade can cut the fingers. Precaution: cut away from the body on a cutting board, use a sharp blade with a guard, and put used blades into a sharps container.
parts.working: 1 mark: cuts from the scalpel; 1 mark: cutting away from the body, using a sharps container, or a guarded blade.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Electrophoresis is carried out in a tank of buffer solution connected to the mains supply. Identify one hazard and one precaution.
parts.answer: Hazard: electric shock if the buffer spills or the leads are wet. Precaution: switch off the power before opening the lid or changing the leads, keep the leads dry, and do not place the tank near water.
parts.working: 1 mark: electric shock from the mains supply near liquid; 1 mark: switch off before handling, keep equipment dry.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethidium bromide is used to stain DNA in a gel and the gel is viewed under ultraviolet light. Identify two hazards and a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Hazard 1: ethidium bromide is toxic and a suspected mutagen, so it can damage DNA in cells. Precaution: wear gloves and dispose of the stained gel and solution as chemical waste. Hazard 2: ultraviolet light can damage the eyes and skin. Precaution: use a UV-blocking screen or visor and keep the viewing box closed.
parts.working: 1 mark each: ethidium bromide toxic/mutagenic; precaution: gloves and chemical waste disposal; UV damages eyes and skin; precaution: UV visor or closed transilluminator box.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student takes a blood sample from a finger with a lancet to extract DNA. Identify two hazards and a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Hazard 1: blood may carry infectious agents (for example hepatitis or HIV). Precaution: use gloves, use only one’s own finger, and dispose of blood-contaminated materials in a biohazard bag. Hazard 2: the lancet may cut or puncture the skin. Precaution: use a single-use lancet and dispose of it in a sharps container.
parts.working: 1 mark each: infection from blood; precaution gloves/own sample/biohazard disposal; puncture/cut from lancet; precaution single-use lancet and sharps disposal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Heat-stable DNA polymerase is used in a PCR. Each cycle requires the reaction tubes to be heated to 95 °C in a heating block. Identify two hazards and a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Hazard 1: burns from the hot heating block or from hot liquid and steam when tubes are removed. Precaution: use tongs or heat-resistant gloves and allow the block to cool before handling. Hazard 2: tube lids may pop open or liquid may spray from a tube. Precaution: use tube racks, close the tube lids firmly and check tubes for cracks before heating.
parts.working: 1 mark each: burns from the hot block or steam; precaution: tongs/heat-resistant gloves and cooling; spray or leak from tubes; precaution: closed lids, tube racks and checking tubes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student incubates a nutrient agar plate that she inoculated with bacteria from soil. Identify two hazards and a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Hazard 1: soil bacteria may include pathogens. Precaution: use only the non-pathogenic strain approved by the school, and do not open the plate. Hazard 2: the plate may leak or be contaminated when moved. Precaution: seal the plate with tape, incubate it inverted, and disinfect the bench afterwards.
parts.working: 1 mark each: pathogens in soil; precaution approved non-pathogenic strain/do not open; spill or contamination; precaution sealing, incubating inverted and disinfecting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A class sets up a PCR in the laboratory to amplify a gene from a plant sample. Identify three hazards and a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Hazard 1: contamination of the sample or of others’ DNA. Precaution: use separate pipettes and sterile tips, and work in a clean area. Hazard 2: sharp pipette tips can puncture skin. Precaution: dispose of tips in a sharps container. Hazard 3: reagents may be harmful if spilt or swallowed. Precaution: wear gloves and goggles and follow the safety data sheet.
parts.working: Any three hazard–precaution pairs, 1 mark each for the hazard and 1 mark for the precaution where stated: contamination (separate tips, clean area); sharp tips (sharps container); harmful reagents (gloves, goggles, safety data sheet).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student collects pond water and snails from a local pond for a genetics study of shell colour. Identify two hazards and a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Hazard 1: pond water may contain bacteria such as Leptospira or parasites. Precaution: wear gloves, wash hands thoroughly afterwards and cover any cuts. Hazard 2: slipping or falling into deep water near the bank. Precaution: work with a partner, stay on firm ground and use a sturdy net on a handle.
parts.working: Any two hazard–precaution pairs, 1 mark each for the hazard and 1 mark for its precaution (max 4): pathogens in water (gloves, hand washing, covering cuts); slipping into water (partner, stable ground, sturdy net).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A chemical mutagen is used to produce mutants in barley seeds for a genetics investigation. Identify two hazards and a precaution for each, and describe how the used mutagen and treated material should be disposed of.
parts.answer: Hazard 1: the mutagen may be toxic, carcinogenic and damage DNA. Precaution: work in a fume cupboard, wear gloves and goggles, and measure only the amount needed. Hazard 2: spills may contaminate the bench or skin. Precaution: keep a spill kit, wipe up spills at once and wash hands. Disposal: treated seeds and solutions go into labelled chemical waste and are not disposed of in the sink or the compost.
parts.working: Any two hazard–precaution pairs (1 mark each for hazard and precaution, max 4), plus 1 mark for disposal as chemical waste and not to the sink or compost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Students keep rabbits in a school laboratory to study the inheritance of coat colour. Identify two hazards to the students and a precaution for each, and state one precaution that protects the welfare of the rabbits.
parts.answer: Hazard 1: scratches and bites from the rabbits. Precaution: handle the animals correctly, wear gloves and wash hands afterwards. Hazard 2: infection from the animals or their droppings (zoonotic infection). Precaution: wash hands, keep food away from the animals and clean cages with an appropriate disinfectant. Welfare: follow the school's animal care rules and handle the animals only under supervision.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two hazards and their precautions (max 4); 1 mark for a welfare precaution such as following animal care rules or supervised handling.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student uses a mutagenic UV lamp to irradiate bacteria. Identify two hazards and explain how the investigation should be made safe for the student and for the class.
parts.answer: Hazard 1: UV light damages the eyes and skin. Precaution: use a closed UV cabinet and UV-blocking eye protection, and do not look directly at the lamp. Hazard 2: bacteria may be harmful if they escape. Precaution: use non-pathogenic strains, seal plates and handle them only in the closed cabinet. For safety, the whole class should be supervised and the procedure approved by the teacher.
parts.working: Any two hazard–precaution pairs (1 mark each for hazard and precaution, max 4), plus 1 mark for supervision or approval of the procedure.

practice.stem: Each human kidney contains about one million nephrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put these parts of a nephron in the order in which filtrate passes through them: distal convoluted tubule, Bowman's capsule, collecting duct, proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle.
parts.answer: Bowman's capsule → proximal convoluted tubule → loop of Henle → distal convoluted tubule → collecting duct
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 if one pair is reversed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the region of the kidney (cortex or medulla) in which the glomeruli are found and the region in which most of each loop of Henle is found.
parts.answer: Glomeruli: cortex; loops of Henle: medulla.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the blood vessel that brings blood to a glomerulus and the vessel that carries blood away from it.
parts.answer: Afferent arteriole in; efferent arteriole out.
parts.working: B1 both needed.

practice.stem: Ali plays cricket for three hours in Lahore on a hot afternoon. He sweats a lot and eats salty pakoras, but drinks very little.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the effect on the water potential of Ali's blood.
parts.answer: It decreases (becomes more negative).
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the changes in ADH secretion and in Ali's urine that follow.
parts.answer: More ADH is released from the posterior pituitary; the collecting ducts become more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed into the blood; a small volume of concentrated (dark) urine is produced.
parts.working: B1 more ADH. B1 more water reabsorbed in collecting duct / DCT. B1 small volume, more concentrated urine.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Ali then drinks a large glass of water. State how the volume of his urine will change over the next hour, and why.
parts.answer: The volume will increase (dilute urine); blood water potential rises, so less ADH is released and less water is reabsorbed in the collecting ducts.
parts.working: B1 more urine / dilute. B1 less ADH / collecting duct less permeable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student writes: 'Selective reabsorption happens in Bowman’s capsule and needs no energy because it is passive.' Identify the two errors in this statement and correct them.
parts.answer: Error 1: reabsorption happens mainly in the proximal convoluted tubule (and the rest of the tubule), not in Bowman’s capsule. Error 2: much reabsorption is active (uses ATP), e.g. active transport of glucose and sodium ions.
parts.working: 1 mark for the correct location; 1 mark for stating that the process is active and needs ATP (for example for sodium pumping or co-transport of glucose).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two substances that are reabsorbed completely from the proximal convoluted tubule under normal conditions.
parts.answer: Glucose and amino acids (any two).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: glucose, amino acids (accept these only; urea and water are only partly reabsorbed).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how ultrafiltration takes place in the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule.
parts.answer: The afferent arteriole is wider than the efferent arteriole, so blood in the glomerulus is at high hydrostatic pressure; water and small solutes are forced out through gaps (fenestrations) in the capillary endothelium; the basement membrane acts as the filter, holding back large proteins (relative molecular mass above about 69 000) and cells; the fluid passes between the podocytes' foot processes (filtration slits) into the capsule space.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: afferent wider than efferent; high hydrostatic pressure; pores / fenestrations in endothelium; basement membrane is the filter; large proteins and blood cells retained; podocytes with filtration slits; filtrate contains water, glucose, urea, ions, amino acids.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the filtrate in Bowman's capsule has a lower concentration of protein than blood plasma but the same concentration of glucose.
parts.answer: Proteins are too large to pass through the basement membrane, so they stay in the blood; glucose molecules are small and pass freely, so their concentration is the same as in plasma.
parts.working: B1 proteins too large / retained by basement membrane. B1 glucose small, filtered freely.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how glucose is reabsorbed from the filtrate in the proximal convoluted tubule.
parts.answer: Na⁺/K⁺ pumps in the basal membrane of the tubule cells actively pump Na⁺ out into the tissue fluid/blood, using ATP; this lowers the Na⁺ concentration inside the cell; Na⁺ diffuses into the cell from the lumen through cotransporter proteins that carry glucose with it (indirect active transport / cotransport); glucose then moves out of the cell into the blood by facilitated diffusion through the basal membrane.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: Na⁺/K⁺ pump on basal membrane; uses ATP / active; low Na⁺ concentration in cell; Na⁺ moves in by facilitated diffusion with glucose (cotransporter / symporter); glucose against its concentration gradient; glucose leaves by facilitated diffusion into capillaries.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the structure of the proximal convoluted tubule cells is adapted for reabsorption.
parts.answer: Microvilli on the luminal surface give a large surface area for transport proteins; many mitochondria supply ATP for active transport.
parts.working: B1 microvilli → large surface area. B1 many mitochondria → ATP for active transport. (Also accept: many cotransporter proteins / tight junctions.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a fall in the water potential of the blood is detected and how ADH is released.
parts.answer: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the fall in water potential (they lose water and shrink); neurosecretory cells (in the hypothalamus) send impulses so ADH is released from the posterior pituitary gland into the blood.
parts.working: B1 osmoreceptors in hypothalamus. B1 ADH released from posterior pituitary.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how ADH increases the permeability of the collecting duct to water.
parts.answer: ADH binds to receptors on the cell surface membrane of collecting duct cells; this activates adenylyl cyclase, producing cAMP as a second messenger; cAMP activates a protein kinase (cascade) that phosphorylates proteins; vesicles containing aquaporins move to and fuse with the luminal membrane; more aquaporins in the membrane allow more water to move out by osmosis.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: ADH binds to receptor (on membrane of collecting duct cells); adenylyl cyclase activated / cAMP produced (second messenger); protein kinase activated / phosphorylation; vesicles with aquaporins; vesicles fuse with luminal (cell surface) membrane; more water channels → more water reabsorbed by osmosis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this is an example of negative feedback.
parts.answer: The change (low water potential) triggers responses that reverse it – more water is reabsorbed so blood water potential rises back to the set point; as it returns to normal, less ADH is released.
parts.working: B1 response reverses the change / returns to set point. B1 less ADH once water potential is restored.

practice.stem: In a healthy adult the kidneys produce glomerular filtrate at a rate of 125 cm³ per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of filtrate produced per day in dm³.
parts.answer: 180 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: The person produces 1.5 dm³ of urine per day. Calculate the percentage of the filtrate that is reabsorbed. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a person with kidney failure who is treated by dialysis must limit how much water and salt they consume.
parts.answer: Their kidneys cannot remove excess water and salt (cannot form urine normally), so these build up in the blood between dialysis sessions, raising blood volume / pressure and causing oedema.
parts.working: B1 kidneys cannot excrete excess water / salt. B1 build-up → high blood pressure / oedema / fluid overload.

practice.stem:
In diabetes insipidus the posterior pituitary gland releases little or no ADH. A patient with this condition used a nasal spray of desmopressin, a drug that acts on the collecting duct in the same way as ADH. Her rate of urine production was measured.
Time after spray / h: 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12
Urine production / cm³ min⁻¹: 10.0, 6.5, 2.0, 1.2, 1.5, 4.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Before the spray, the patient produced urine at 10.0 cm³ min⁻¹. Calculate the volume of urine she would produce in one day at this rate, in dm³.
parts.answer: 14.4 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a person who makes no ADH produces a large volume of dilute urine.
parts.answer: Without ADH, few aquaporins are inserted into the luminal membranes of the collecting duct cells (vesicles containing aquaporins stay in the cytoplasm); so the collecting duct walls have low permeability to water; little water moves out by osmosis into the medulla (even though its water potential is low), so a large volume of dilute urine passes out.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: no ADH binding to receptors on collecting duct cells; few aquaporins in the luminal membrane; collecting duct (and DCT) walls less permeable to water; little water reabsorbed by osmosis into the medulla / blood; large volume of dilute urine.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the rate of urine production rises again between 8 h and 12 h after the spray.
parts.answer: The desmopressin is gradually broken down / removed from the blood; so fewer aquaporins remain in the collecting duct membranes, less water is reabsorbed and urine output increases – another dose is needed.
parts.working: B1 drug broken down / excreted / concentration falls. B1 aquaporins removed from membrane / less water reabsorbed.

practice.stem: A person's urine flow rate is 1.0 cm³ per minute. The inulin concentration is 25 g dm⁻³ in the urine and 0.20 g dm⁻³ in the plasma.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of glomerular filtrate formation in cm³ min⁻¹. Show your working.
parts.answer: 125 cm³ min⁻¹ (1.0 cm³ min⁻¹ × 25 g dm⁻³ ÷ 0.20 g dm⁻³ = 125 cm³ min⁻¹).
parts.working: M1 use of GFR = urine flow × (concentration in urine ÷ concentration in plasma); A1 125 cm³ min⁻¹ with units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why inulin is a suitable substance for this calculation.
parts.answer: Inulin is freely filtered at the glomerulus; it is neither reabsorbed nor secreted by the tubules, so all of it stays in the filtrate and its concentration in the urine depends only on the volume of water removed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: freely filtered; not reabsorbed; not secreted; so the amount in the urine depends only on the volume of filtrate lost.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why glucose concentrations could not be used in the same calculation.
parts.answer: Glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule, so its concentration in urine is not the same as in filtrate.
parts.working: 1 mark for stating that glucose is reabsorbed (so the urine concentration would not reflect the filtrate concentration).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Alcohol inhibits the release of ADH from the posterior pituitary gland. Predict the effect on the volume of urine and on the water potential of the blood. Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Urine volume increases and the water potential of the blood falls (becomes more negative / lower); less ADH means the collecting ducts are less permeable to water, so less water is reabsorbed and the blood loses water.
parts.working: 1 mark for increased urine volume and decreased (more negative) blood water potential; 1 mark for explaining that less ADH gives fewer aquaporins/less permeable collecting ducts so less water is reabsorbed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the hypothalamus and posterior pituitary restore the blood water potential when it falls below normal, for example after sweating.
parts.answer: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the fall in blood water potential; the hypothalamus stimulates the posterior pituitary to release more ADH, so the collecting ducts become more permeable to water, more water is reabsorbed and a small volume of concentrated urine is produced.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the change; more ADH released from the posterior pituitary; collecting ducts more permeable (more aquaporins); more water reabsorbed, giving small concentrated urine (negative feedback restores the water potential).

practice.stem:
