parts.label: c
parts.text: The urine had been diluted 1 in 5 before testing. Calculate the glucose concentration of the original urine.
parts.answer: 25 mmol dm⁻³

parts.label: a
parts.text: A stock solution of glucose has a concentration of 80 mmol dm⁻³. It is diluted 1 in 10, and then the diluted solution is diluted 1 in 4. Calculate the final concentration in mmol dm⁻³.
parts.answer: 2.0 mmol dm⁻³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume, in cm³, of the 80 mmol dm⁻³ stock solution needed to make 50 cm³ of 8.0 mmol dm⁻³ solution.
parts.answer: 5.0 cm³
parts.working: M1 volume of stock = 50 × 8.0 ÷ 80; A1 5.0 cm³ (with 45.0 cm³ of water).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A leaf with an area of 18.0 cm² loses 0.54 g of water in 3.0 hours. Calculate the rate of water loss per cm² per hour in g.
parts.answer: 0.01 g cm⁻² h⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why water loss per cm² per hour is more useful than total water loss when comparing leaves of different sizes.
parts.answer: It takes account of the leaf area, so leaves of different sizes can be compared fairly.
parts.working: 1 mark for correcting for leaf area / comparing rates fairly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The resting heart rate of a student is 68 beats per minute. After 5 minutes of step exercise it is 124 beats per minute. Calculate the percentage increase in heart rate. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the heart rate increases during exercise.
parts.answer: Muscles need more oxygen and glucose for respiration; the medulla increases the impulses to the sinoatrial node, so the heart beats faster and pumps more blood to the muscles.
parts.working: 1 mark for increased need for oxygen/glucose and removal of CO₂; 1 mark for nerve impulses from the medulla increasing heart rate (or adrenaline).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Three measurements of the width of a stomatal pore were 2.4 µm, 2.6 µm and 2.5 µm. Calculate the mean width.
parts.answer: 2.5 µm
parts.working: M1 sum ÷ 3; A1 2.5 µm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest what the spread of the three readings tells you about the measurements.
parts.answer: The readings are close together, so the measurements are precise.
parts.working: 1 mark for precise (close readings) / consistent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The glucose concentration in a dialysis bag fell from 10.0 mmol dm⁻³ to 6.5 mmol dm⁻³ in 30 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of fall in mmol dm⁻³ min⁻¹. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.117 mmol dm⁻³ min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one variable that must be kept constant for this rate to be compared with a second experiment.
parts.answer: The surface area or size of the dialysis bag, or the temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark for any one constant (bag size, temperature, volume of water).

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a microscope image, one division on the eyepiece graticule represents 0.01 mm. A stoma spans 4 divisions across its width. Calculate the width of the stoma in µm.
parts.answer: 40 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why the graticule must be calibrated before the measurements are made.
parts.answer: The divisions on the graticule differ with the magnification, so the real size of one division must be measured with a stage micrometer at that magnification.
parts.working: 1 mark for calibration converting divisions to real length at the magnification used.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Five potato cylinders were placed in sucrose solutions. The percentage change in mass was +4.0 % at 0.4 mol dm⁻³ and −2.5 % at 0.6 mol dm⁻³. Assuming the change is linear between these two points, calculate the sucrose concentration at which there is no change in mass. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.523 mol dm⁻³
parts.working: M1 0.4 + 0.2 × (4.0 ÷ (4.0 + 2.5)) (linear interpolation of the change from +4.0 % to −2.5 %); A1 0.523 mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why the result from linear interpolation is an estimate rather than an exact value.
parts.answer: The relationship is not necessarily linear between the two points, and only two points were used on either side of zero.
parts.working: 1 mark for relationship not known to be linear / small number of points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a potometer with a capillary tube of internal radius 0.40 mm, the bubble moved 25 mm in 20 minutes. Calculate the volume of water taken up in mm³ per hour. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 37.7 mm³ per hour
parts.working: M1 volume in 20 min = π × 0.40² × 25 = 12.57 mm³; M1 × 3 for one hour; A1 37.7 mm³ per hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The glucose concentration of a patient’s urine is 15 mmol dm⁻³ and the volume of urine per day is 1.8 dm³. Calculate the mass of glucose lost in the urine per day in g. (Mᵣ of glucose = 180)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the amount of glucose lost in the urine is not the same as the amount of glucose in the filtrate.
parts.answer: The glucose in the filtrate is partly reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule, so most is returned to the blood; only the glucose that is not reabsorbed (above the renal threshold) appears in urine.
parts.working: 1 mark for reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule; 1 mark for only the unreabsorbed glucose appearing in urine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A patient excretes 25 g of urea per day in 1.5 dm³ of urine. Calculate the concentration of urea in the urine in mol dm⁻³. (Mᵣ of urea = 60)
parts.answer: 0.278 mol dm⁻³
parts.working: M1 moles = 25 ÷ 60 = 0.417 mol; M1 concentration = 0.417 ÷ 1.5; A1 0.278 mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student uses a potometer to measure water uptake. Name two sources of error that could make the measured rate too low.
parts.answer: Any two of: an air leak at a joint in the potometer; air bubbles trapped in the water or capillary tube; the shoot not being cut under water so air enters the xylem.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two named sources of error that reduce the bubble movement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For each error you named in part (a), suggest one improvement to reduce it.
parts.answer: Seal all joints with vaseline and check for leaks before starting; re-cut the stem under water and fill the apparatus completely with water with no bubbles.
parts.working: 1 mark for an improvement matching each error (maximum 2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a random error and a systematic error, and give one example of each in an experiment that measures the length of stomata with an eyepiece graticule.
parts.answer: A random error is an unpredictable variation that makes readings scatter on either side of the true value (e.g. reading the edge of each pore differently); a systematic error is a consistent error that shifts all readings in one direction (e.g. an uncalibrated graticule).
parts.working: 1 mark for random error definition; 1 mark for systematic error definition; 1 mark for a correct example of each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student measures the mass of potato cylinders on a top-pan balance that reads to 0.1 g. The cylinders have a mass of about 2 g. Explain why this balance is unsuitable and suggest a better instrument.
parts.answer: A reading to 0.1 g is a large percentage uncertainty for a 2 g sample (about 5 %), so small changes in mass cannot be detected; an electronic balance reading to 0.001 g (or 0.01 g) gives a much smaller uncertainty.
parts.working: 1 mark for large percentage uncertainty; 1 mark for small mass changes cannot be detected; 1 mark for a balance reading to 0.001 g or 0.01 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Glucose test strips were read in two rooms with different lighting. Explain how this could make the readings unreliable and suggest how the lighting could be controlled.
parts.answer: The colour appears different under different light, so the readings matched to the chart are different even if the glucose concentration is the same; use the same light source (or a colorimeter) and read all strips in the same place.
parts.working: 1 mark for the colour appearance depending on light; 1 mark for a valid control (same light, colorimeter, same location).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest three variables in a leaf transpiration experiment that must be kept the same for all leaves and explain why one of them could affect results if it is not controlled.
parts.answer: Any three of: leaf size/area; leaf age; temperature; humidity; light intensity; air movement; the time of day. Example: leaf age affects stomatal number and cuticle thickness, so older leaves may lose water at a different rate.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three variables; 1 mark for explaining how one uncontrolled variable changes the transpiration rate.

practice.stem: Students used glucose test strips and a colour chart to estimate the glucose concentration in artificial urine samples.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two sources of error when glucose test strips are read by comparing their colour with a printed chart.
parts.answer: Colour matching is subjective / differs between people; the chart has only a few colour blocks, so the concentration is only known within a range; strip read too early or too late (colour keeps developing); lighting affects perceived colour; strips stored badly lose enzyme activity.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how each error could be reduced.
parts.answer: Use a reflectance meter / colorimeter or biosensor to read the strip; read at the exact time stated using a timer; same observer in standard lighting; use a chart with more intermediate colours; check strips with a control solution.
parts.working: 1 mark each for improvements matched to errors.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Students repeat each test three times and get identical colour readings each time. Explain why this does not show that the readings are accurate.
parts.answer: Identical readings show the method is repeatable (precise), but all readings could share the same systematic error, e.g. old strips or a misjudged colour, so they may not be close to the true value.
parts.working: B1 precision / repeatability is not accuracy – systematic error possible.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student counts the heart rate of a volunteer by feeling the pulse for 15 seconds and multiplying by four. Identify two sources of error and suggest how each could be reduced.
parts.answer: Miscounting beats or losing track of the count (or slow starting/stopping the timer by reaction time); reduce by using a second person to count, a longer time (e.g. 30 s or 60 s) or a heart rate monitor.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two sources (miscounting; reaction time of timing); 1 mark each for a valid improvement (longer count, second counter, heart rate monitor).

parts.label: a
parts.text: In an investigation of the water potential of potato cylinders, some cylinders were not blotted dry before they were weighed. Explain the effect on the calculated percentage change in mass and suggest two other sources of error.
parts.answer: Surface water adds to the measured final mass, so the percentage change is less negative (or more positive) than the true value; other errors: cylinders of unequal size or length; cylinders left in solution for different times.
parts.working: 1 mark for surface water increasing the final mass; 1 mark for the calculated change being too positive/too small; 1 mark each for two other valid sources (unequal cylinders; unequal times; temperature changes).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two students measure the length of the same stoma in the same field of view. Their answers are 2.8 µm and 3.6 µm. Suggest two reasons for this difference and state how the students could improve their measurements.
parts.answer: Different interpretation of where the edge of the pore is (judgement); parallax or focus differences between the two students; one student may have used a different magnification or graticule scale. Improve by agreeing the criteria, measuring several stomata each and taking a mean, and using the same calibrated graticule.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two reasons (judgement of edge; focus/parallax; different magnification or calibration); 1 mark for an improvement (agreed criteria, repeats, same calibration).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student insulates a beaker of hot water with a lid made of cardboard, but a small hole is left in the lid for the thermometer. Explain why the results may not show the true effect of insulation and suggest an improvement.
parts.answer: Heat is lost through the hole by convection and evaporation, so the water cools faster than it would with a fully sealed lid; the insulation effect is therefore underestimated. Improve by using a lid with a snug fit for the thermometer or a sealed insulating cover with a single small hole.
parts.working: 1 mark for heat loss through the hole (by convection or evaporation); 1 mark for the effect of insulation being reduced/underestimated; 1 mark for a valid improvement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student dips three different test strips from the same batch into the same glucose solution. Each strip gives the same colour, so the student concludes that the results are accurate. Explain why this conclusion may be wrong and suggest what else is needed to show accuracy.
parts.answer: Repeats show consistency (precision), not accuracy; a systematic error, such as a faulty strip batch or a strip that is read against a chart with the wrong calibration, could give the same wrong answer every time; compare the readings with a known standard solution.
parts.working: 1 mark for repeat readings show precision only; 1 mark for systematic error affecting all repeats; 1 mark for a known standard solution for comparison.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A biosensor glucose meter gave readings that drifted upwards over a 2-hour test session when the room temperature rose from 20 °C to 30 °C. Explain the likely cause of the drift and state one improvement to the experiment.
parts.answer: The enzyme activity and the electrode response change with temperature, so the current rises; the meter must be calibrated at the same temperature as the test, or the test carried out in a temperature-controlled room, and the meter checked with a control solution during the session.
parts.working: 1 mark for temperature affecting enzyme activity or electrode current; 1 mark for the reading changing as a result; 1 mark for an improvement: temperature control or recalibration; 1 mark for checking with a control solution during the session.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In an investigation of the effect of wind on transpiration, a fan is switched on for some potometer set-ups but its speed is not measured. Explain why this affects the reliability of the results and describe how the investigation could be improved.
parts.answer: The wind speed is not controlled or known, so the rate of transpiration cannot be linked to a measured variable; results at the same fan setting may vary; measure the wind speed with an anemometer at the leaf for each set-up and use the same fan setting and distance for all repeats.
parts.working: 1 mark for an unmeasured variable making the comparison unreliable; 1 mark for results being inconsistent between repeats; 1 mark for measuring wind speed; 1 mark for fixed fan settings and distance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A dialysis tube used to model diffusion of glucose has a small tear, which is not noticed. Explain the effect of this error on the calculated rate of glucose loss and on the starch test results.
parts.answer: The tear allows starch (large molecules) to escape as well as glucose, so starch would be detected in the outside water; the rate of glucose loss would be overestimated because diffusion is no longer through the membrane alone; the results would not show that the membrane is selectively permeable.
parts.working: 1 mark for starch being found outside (starch detected outside); 1 mark for glucose rate overestimated; 1 mark for the membrane no longer acting as a selective barrier; 1 mark for the results being unreliable as a model of selective filtration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student reads the distance moved by the bubble in a potometer to the nearest 5 mm by eye, and starts the stopwatch a few seconds after the bubble starts to move. Identify two sources of error and suggest an improvement for each.
parts.answer: Reading to the nearest 5 mm gives a large uncertainty in the distance moved (poor resolution); starting the stopwatch late gives a timing error; improvement: mark the start point and read with a ruler to 1 mm or use a longer time; start the timer when the bubble passes a mark.
parts.working: 1 mark for a resolution error from the coarse reading; 1 mark for a timing error (late start); 1 mark for a valid improvement for each (finer scale, marked start point, longer time).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student heats 200 cm³ of water to 80 °C in identical beakers, each wrapped in a different thickness of insulation, and records the temperature every minute. State the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent variable: thickness of insulation; dependent variable: temperature of the water (or the rate of cooling).
parts.working: 1 mark for independent variable; 1 mark for dependent variable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two variables that must be kept constant and explain why one of them must be controlled.
parts.answer: Any two of: volume and starting temperature of water; type and size of beaker; room temperature; time of readings. Explanation e.g. the volume of water changes the amount of heat to be lost, so the cooling rate would change.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two correct controlled variables; 1 mark for an explanation of why one changes the result.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In an investigation into the effect of humidity on transpiration using a potometer, state the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: relative humidity of the air around the shoot; dependent: rate of movement of the bubble (or volume of water taken up per minute).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a suitable control for this investigation.
parts.answer: An identical set-up kept at the normal ambient humidity, with the same temperature, light and air movement, so that any difference can be attributed to humidity; or an identical set-up with no shoot, to check for bubble movement caused by leaks or evaporation from the water.
parts.working: 1 mark for a set-up identical except for the humidity variable; 1 mark for a control without the plant to check for bubble movement not caused by the shoot.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student compares the mass change of potato cylinders in two sucrose solutions. Explain why the same mass of potato tissue must be used for each solution.
parts.answer: Mass of tissue is a variable; more potato tissue would absorb or lose more water and the total change in mass would be bigger, so a different tissue mass would make the comparison unfair.
parts.working: 1 mark for the amount of tissue changing the total change in mass; 1 mark for a fair comparison needing the same tissue mass / percentage change.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a suitable control for this investigation.
parts.answer: A cylinder placed in distilled water for the same time, to show the mass change when there is no solute.
parts.working: 1 mark for distilled water (or 0 mol dm⁻³ solution) as a control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student dips test strips in artificial urine for different times. Explain how the time between dipping and reading the strip must be standardised, and state one further variable that must be controlled.
parts.answer: The colour continues to develop, so the strip must be read at the same time after dipping (for example exactly 60 s) for each strip; temperature of the sample (or the light conditions) must be the same, because the enzyme reaction is temperature dependent.
parts.working: 1 mark for reading at a fixed time after dipping; 1 mark for the colour continuing to change so timing matters; 1 mark for one further variable (temperature, light, sample volume, strip batch).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what a control variable is, and give one example from an investigation using glucose test strips.
parts.answer: A control variable is a factor that is kept the same so it cannot affect the dependent variable; example: the volume of artificial urine tested or the time between dipping and reading the strip.
parts.working: 1 mark for a factor kept constant so it does not affect the result; 1 mark for a valid example.

practice.stem: A student plans to investigate the effect of different concentrations of abscisic acid (ABA) on stomatal closure using strips of lower epidermis peeled from Commelina leaves.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent and dependent variables in this investigation.
parts.answer: Independent: concentration of ABA. Dependent: stomatal pore width (or percentage of stomata open).
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the epidermal strips are first kept in light in a solution containing potassium chloride before ABA is added.
parts.answer: So that all the stomata are open at the start (K⁺ available for uptake and light stimulates opening); then any closure can be attributed to the ABA.
parts.working: B1 stomata open at start / standard starting condition. B1 so change is due to ABA.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State three variables that must be standardised and how one of them could be controlled.
parts.answer: Temperature (water bath / temperature-controlled room); light intensity (same lamp at the same distance); time in ABA solution; pH (buffer); leaves of the same age / same plant / same position; size of strip; volume of solution.
parts.working: B1 B1 two variables. B1 a valid method for controlling one of them. (Max 3: three variables, or two variables and one method.)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe a suitable control.
parts.answer: Strips placed in the same solution without ABA (0 mmol dm⁻³ ABA, same volume, same time).
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student tests the accuracy of a biosensor at different temperatures. State three variables that must be controlled and give a reason for each.
parts.answer: Any three of: glucose concentration (same standard for each run, since it changes the signal); volume of sample (affects the amount of glucose available); pH or buffer (affects enzyme activity); time of measurement (the reading changes over time); strip or meter batch (differences in enzyme loading).
parts.working: 1 mark each for a valid variable with a reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student measures heart rate before and after a 3-minute step exercise. Identify the independent and dependent variables.
parts.answer: Independent: time after exercise (or the stage of recovery); dependent: heart rate in beats per minute.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two variables that must be standardised in this investigation and explain how each could affect the results.
parts.answer: Height of the step and the rate of stepping (more work means a higher heart rate); age and fitness of the volunteer (affect resting heart rate and recovery).
parts.working: 1 mark each for two valid variables; 1 mark for explaining how each affects the heart rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A leaf area investigation uses leaves of different sizes from the same plant. State the independent and dependent variables.
parts.answer: Independent: leaf area (cm²); dependent: water loss per hour (g or cm³).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the leaves should be taken from the same plant, at the same height and of similar age.
parts.answer: Position and age affect light, stomatal density and cuticle thickness, so these factors would change the transpiration rate and make it hard to see the effect of leaf area.
parts.working: 1 mark for light/position/age affecting transpiration; 1 mark for the effect of leaf area being masked.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student investigates how the temperature of a biosensor solution affects the current. Write a suitable description of a control for this investigation.
parts.answer: A set-up kept at the same temperature as the test, with the same buffer, enzyme volume and measurement time, but with distilled water in place of the glucose solution; any current it produces is the background signal not caused by glucose.
parts.working: 1 mark for the same buffer, enzyme volume and timing; 1 mark for distilled water (no glucose) in place of glucose at the same temperature; 1 mark for the background signal being compared with or subtracted from the test readings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student compares the rate of cooling of water in two beakers of different diameter, both with the same insulation. Identify the independent variable, and explain why the volume and starting temperature of the water must be the same in both beakers.
parts.answer: Independent variable: diameter (size or surface area) of the beaker; the volume and starting temperature must be equal because the amount of water and its starting heat energy change the time taken to cool, so these would confound the effect of beaker size.
parts.working: 1 mark for beaker diameter/surface area as the independent variable; 1 mark for same volume (amount of heat energy/water); 1 mark for same starting temperature or confounding of the comparison.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student investigates the rate of diffusion of glucose across dialysis tubing using different concentrations of glucose solution inside the tubing. Identify the independent variable, the dependent variable, and two variables that must be controlled.
parts.answer: Independent: glucose concentration inside the tubing; dependent: rate of glucose diffusion out (or glucose concentration in the outer water over time); controls: the volume and length of the tubing, the volume of distilled water outside, temperature, the same type and size of tubing.
parts.working: 1 mark for independent; 1 mark for dependent; 1 mark each for two sensible controlled variables (maximum 2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the volume of distilled water outside the tubing must be kept the same.
parts.answer: A larger volume of water dilutes the glucose that diffuses out, so the concentration outside would be lower and the rate of diffusion appears slower.
parts.working: 1 mark for dilution affecting the measured concentration; 1 mark for the apparent rate of diffusion changing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student plans to test whether the number of stomata affects the rate of water loss by covering the lower surface of some leaves with petroleum jelly. Identify two possible confounding variables that the student must control, and explain how petroleum jelly could itself change the result.
parts.answer: Confounding variables: leaf size, leaf age, and the conditions around the leaves (temperature, humidity, air movement). Petroleum jelly also blocks water loss through the cuticle and epidermis of the lower surface, and it can change the leaf temperature, so any change would not be due to stomatal number alone.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two valid confounding variables; 1 mark for the jelly acting in another way besides blocking stomata (blocks cuticular or epidermal water loss, or changes leaf temperature).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two variables that the student could not easily control in humans, and describe how each could be reduced.
parts.answer: Any two of: food eaten before the test (reduce by fasting or a standard meal); age or fitness of the volunteers (use a group with similar age and fitness); stress or emotional state (rest before testing); time of day (test at the same time each day); the testing method (use the same meter and a trained operator).
parts.working: 1 mark each for two valid variables; 1 mark each for a sensible way to reduce each (4 marks in total).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student investigates the effect of light intensity on stomatal opening by placing a lamp at different distances from leaf strips. State the independent variable, explain how the light intensity is related to the distance of the lamp, and identify one confounding variable.
parts.answer: Independent variable: distance of the lamp from the leaf strip (light intensity is inversely proportional to distance squared, so light intensity can be calculated from the distance); confounding variable: heat from the lamp, which would change temperature and affect the stomata.
parts.working: 1 mark for independent variable (distance / light intensity); 1 mark for light intensity falling with the square of the distance; 1 mark for a valid confounder (heat or temperature from the lamp, or air movement).

practice.stem: A student will measure stomatal pore width in epidermal strips placed in ABA solutions of 0, 0.01, 0.1, 1.0 and 10 µmol dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a hypothesis for the effect of ABA concentration on stomatal pore width.
parts.answer: As ABA concentration increases, mean stomatal pore width decreases.
parts.working: B1 directional relationship.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student will use Spearman's rank correlation. Write a suitable null hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is no correlation between ABA concentration and stomatal pore width.
parts.working: B1 must say no correlation (not 'no difference').

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the results for strips placed in a solution of ABA at a very high concentration, and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Almost all stomata closed (pore width near zero); at high ABA concentration all receptors on guard cells are occupied, so maximum K⁺ loss and loss of turgor in every guard cell – further increase in ABA has no further effect.
parts.working: B1 stomata fully / nearly closed (levels off). B1 receptors saturated / maximum response.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a hypothesis for the effect of the length of a step exercise on the heart rate of a student.
parts.answer: The longer the step exercise, the greater the increase in heart rate; (or with a reason: longer exercise increases the demand for oxygen and so increases heart rate).
parts.working: 1 mark for a testable directional statement linking exercise length to heart rate; 1 mark for a reason (demand for oxygen and glucose).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a null hypothesis for the same investigation.
parts.answer: There is no correlation (no relationship) between the length of step exercise and the heart rate of a student.
parts.working: 1 mark for a statement of no difference/relationship.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student measures the water potential of potato cylinders in sucrose solutions. Write a null hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: There is no difference in the percentage change in mass of potato cylinders between sucrose solutions of different concentrations.
parts.working: 1 mark for no difference; 1 mark for linking it to percentage change in mass in different solutions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student measures stomatal density on the upper and lower epidermis of 10 leaves of a plant. Write a suitable null hypothesis and name a suitable statistical test to compare the two surfaces.
parts.answer: Null hypothesis: there is no difference in the stomatal density of the upper and lower surfaces of the leaves. Test: Student’s t-test (paired, since the same leaves are measured on both surfaces) or Wilcoxon signed-rank test for paired data.
parts.working: 1 mark for null hypothesis with no difference; 1 mark for a suitable paired test (paired t-test or Wilcoxon).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student measures the blood glucose concentration with a biosensor at several temperatures. Write a hypothesis for the effect of temperature on the current produced by the biosensor, with a reason.
parts.answer: The current increases as temperature rises up to the enzyme’s optimum temperature, because enzyme activity increases with temperature (more frequent collisions and more kinetic energy).
parts.working: 1 mark for a testable hypothesis with a direction; 1 mark for a reason based on enzyme activity and kinetic energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student plans to use a chi-squared test to compare the number of stomata that are open and closed in a leaf sample under two conditions. Write a suitable null hypothesis for this test.
parts.answer: There is no association between the light condition and the state of the stomata (open or closed).
parts.working: 1 mark for no association/relationship; 1 mark for linked to open/closed categories and two conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student predicts that people with a higher glucose concentration in their urine will produce a larger volume of urine. Write a suitable hypothesis for this prediction and state the reason.
parts.answer: The higher the glucose concentration in the urine, the greater the urine volume; the reason is that glucose in the filtrate that is not reabsorbed raises the solute concentration, so more water stays in the tubule by osmosis.
parts.working: 1 mark for a testable hypothesis with a direction (higher glucose, higher volume); 1 mark for an osmotic explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student predicts the rate of water loss from a potometer leaf set-up as the speed of a fan is increased from low to high. Write the prediction and explain it using the water potential gradient.
parts.answer: The rate of water loss increases as fan speed increases; moving air removes water vapour from around the stoma, keeping the water vapour concentration gradient steep, so diffusion out of the leaf is faster.
parts.working: 1 mark for increased rate with fan speed; 1 mark for moving air removing water vapour around the stoma; 1 mark for a steeper gradient and faster diffusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student plans to test the relationship between leaf area and water loss per hour using Spearman’s rank correlation. Write a suitable alternative hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is a correlation (positive) between leaf area and water loss per hour.
parts.working: 1 mark for a stated relationship; 1 mark for directional or non-directional statement that is testable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why Spearman’s rank correlation might be preferred to a Pearson’s test for this data.
parts.answer: The data may not be normally distributed or the relationship may not be linear; ranks do not depend on normal distribution.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid reason (non-normal data / non-linear relationship).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student predicts that doubling the duration of exercise will lengthen the time taken for the heart rate to return to its resting value. Explain whether this prediction is likely to be correct.
parts.answer: Not necessarily: recovery depends on factors such as the intensity of exercise and the fitness of the person; longer exercise may cause a larger oxygen debt and a longer recovery, but doubling the duration does not necessarily double the recovery time, so the prediction is unlikely to be exact.
parts.working: 1 mark for recovery depending on other factors such as intensity; 1 mark for longer exercise giving a larger oxygen debt/recovery; 1 mark for the relationship being not simply proportional.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student has measured the blood glucose concentration of a sample with a meter whose readings are known to be about 0.5 mmol dm⁻³ higher than the true value. Predict the effect on the results of comparing a diabetic patient’s readings with the target values and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: The readings would be systematically too high, so the patient might appear to have higher glucose than true; a repeated overestimate of 0.5 mmol dm⁻³ would make the patient seem outside the target range when they are not.
parts.working: 1 mark for readings too high; 1 mark for systematic error consistent across readings; 1 mark for a false impression of the patient’s control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the shape of the graph of percentage change in mass against sucrose concentration for potato cylinders, from 0 to 1.0 mol dm⁻³. Explain the shape using the movement of water by osmosis.
parts.answer: A curve or line that starts positive at 0 mol dm⁻³ (cylinders gain water) and falls, crossing zero at a concentration near the water potential of the potato cells, then becomes increasingly negative as the concentration rises; water moves in when the solution is more dilute and out when it is more concentrated.
parts.working: 1 mark for a downward-sloping curve (positive to negative); 1 mark for crossing zero at the concentration where water potentials are equal; 1 mark for osmosis explanation: water moves into the cells in dilute solutions and out in concentrated solutions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student predicts the results of dialysis tubing that is placed in water with a solution containing both glucose and a protein of large molecular size. Predict which substance will diffuse out of the tubing and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Glucose will diffuse out of the tubing into the water, but the large protein molecules will not pass through the pores of the dialysis tubing and will remain inside.
parts.working: 1 mark for glucose diffusing out; 1 mark for protein not passing through; 1 mark for the membrane pore size being smaller than protein molecules.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student plans a two-factor investigation of the effects of humidity and fan speed on transpiration. Write two predictions, one for each factor on its own, and a prediction for the interaction of the two factors.
parts.answer: Humidity: higher humidity reduces the transpiration rate. Fan speed: higher fan speed increases the transpiration rate. Interaction: the effect of the fan is larger at low humidity, because the air near the leaf is drier and the water potential gradient is greater; at high humidity the fan has less effect.
parts.working: 1 mark for humidity prediction; 1 mark for fan speed prediction; 1 mark for an interaction prediction; 1 mark for a reason (water potential gradient).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student predicts that doubling the amount of enzyme on a test strip will double the rate at which the colour appears, when glucose is in excess. State the assumption this prediction depends on and explain whether the prediction is likely to hold at high enzyme concentrations.
parts.answer: The assumption is that the enzyme is the rate-limiting factor (glucose is in excess and the substrate is not used up); at high enzyme concentrations the rate levels off because another factor (such as the chromogen or the amount of oxygen or peroxidase) becomes limiting, so the prediction would not hold.
parts.working: 1 mark for enzyme is the limiting factor (glucose in excess); 1 mark for the prediction being valid only up to a point; 1 mark for another substrate or co-factor becoming limiting so the rate levels off.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The heart rate of a volunteer was measured at rest and after 3 minutes of exercise: rest 68 beats per minute; 1 minute after exercise 124; 2 minutes after 110; 3 minutes after 92; 4 minutes after 78. Describe the pattern in the heart rate.
parts.answer: The heart rate rises to a peak of 124 beats per minute immediately after exercise and then falls steadily back towards the resting value.
parts.working: 1 mark for rise to a peak immediately after exercise; 1 mark for steady fall back towards resting rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase from the resting rate to the highest rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student concludes that exercise causes the heart rate to rise, based on the data for one volunteer. State two limitations of this conclusion.
parts.answer: Only one volunteer was tested, so the result may not apply to others; the volunteer’s fitness, age or emotional state may have affected the result; the measurement may have been made only once.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid limitations (small sample, individual variation, uncontrolled factors).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the student could make the conclusion stronger.
parts.answer: Test several volunteers of different ages and fitness, measure the heart rate at the same times, and calculate means with the range of the results.
parts.working: 1 mark for more volunteers; 1 mark for control of variables or repeats.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student measured the glucose uptake of cells in a solution over time: at 0 min 10.0 mmol dm⁻³; at 10 min 8.0; at 20 min 6.5; at 30 min 5.2. Describe the trend in the glucose concentration.
parts.answer: The glucose concentration falls over time, fastest at the start and slowing down as the time increases.
parts.working: 1 mark for falling concentration; 1 mark for rate of fall decreasing over time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student counted open stomata on 20 stomata in one leaf at three times after the leaf was placed in light: 0 min: 4 open; 30 min: 11 open; 60 min: 16 open. Describe the trend.
parts.answer: The number of open stomata increases with time in the light; the rate of opening is greatest between 0 and 30 minutes and slows down between 30 and 60 minutes.
parts.working: 1 mark for increase with time; 1 mark for the rate of opening slowing down.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of stomata open after 60 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two beakers of water at 80 °C were cooled for 10 minutes. The beaker with thin insulation cooled to 60 °C and the beaker with thick insulation cooled to 68 °C. Calculate the percentage fall in temperature for each beaker, and state which beaker is the better insulator.
parts.answer: Thin: 25 %; thick: 15 %. The thick insulation is the better insulator.
parts.working: M1 (80 − 60) ÷ 80 × 100 = 25 %; M1 (80 − 68) ÷ 80 × 100 = 15 %; A1 thick insulation is the better insulator (smaller fall in temperature).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State a conclusion that the data support and explain how the cooling curves would support this conclusion further.
parts.answer: Thicker insulation reduces the rate of heat loss from the water, so the temperature falls more slowly; cooling curves that are flatter for the thick insulation would show a lower rate of heat loss.
parts.working: 1 mark for conclusion (thicker insulation slows heat loss); 1 mark for flatter cooling curve showing lower rate of cooling.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student measured the percentage change in mass of potato cylinders in sucrose solutions: 0.2 mol dm⁻³: +6.0 %; 0.4 mol dm⁻³: +1.5 %; 0.6 mol dm⁻³: −2.0 %; 0.8 mol dm⁻³: −5.5 %. State the conclusion from these data about the water potential of the potato tissue.
parts.answer: The water potential of the potato cells is about equal to a sucrose concentration of about 0.4 to 0.5 mol dm⁻³ (the change is zero between these concentrations), so the potato cells have a water potential of about the same as this solution.
parts.working: 1 mark for zero change lying between 0.4 and 0.6 mol dm⁻³; 1 mark for the cell water potential being equal to the solution at that point; 1 mark for the data showing gain in dilute solution and loss in concentrated solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The mean rate of water uptake in a potometer was 1.2 mm³ per minute at 40 % humidity and 0.6 mm³ per minute at 80 % humidity. Describe the relationship between humidity and transpiration rate shown by these data.
parts.answer: As humidity increases, the rate of water uptake (transpiration) decreases; the rate at 80 % humidity is half the rate at 40 %.
parts.working: 1 mark for inverse relationship; 1 mark for quantitative statement (half/halved).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why these results can only be used to support a conclusion about two humidity levels.
parts.answer: Only two humidity levels were tested, so no pattern across the full range can be seen and the shape of the relationship is unknown.
parts.working: 1 mark for limited data points / only two levels.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two potato varieties were tested in sucrose solutions. Variety A reached zero change in mass at 0.45 mol dm⁻³ and variety B at 0.30 mol dm⁻³. Use these data to compare the water potential of the two varieties and suggest a conclusion.
parts.answer: Variety A has a more negative (lower) water potential than variety B: its cells match a more concentrated sucrose solution (0.45 mol dm⁻³ compared with 0.30 mol dm⁻³), so its cells hold water more strongly.
parts.working: 1 mark for A needing a higher concentration (0.45 > 0.30); 1 mark for zero change meaning the cell water potential equals the solution; 1 mark for the conclusion that variety A has the more negative water potential.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student finds that the mean percentage change in potato mass in 0.4 mol dm⁻³ sucrose has a range of ±0.5 %. State what this range tells you about the data and whether the mean is reliable.
parts.answer: The range shows the spread of the repeats; a small range relative to the change means the results are fairly consistent (precise), so the mean is a reliable estimate, but the range does not show accuracy.
parts.working: 1 mark for the range showing spread/precision; 1 mark for a reliable mean if the spread is small; 1 mark for precision not necessarily accuracy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The number of leaves that were still green after 10 days of drought was recorded for two varieties of wheat: variety X 18 of 25 leaves; variety Y 9 of 25 leaves. Calculate the percentage of leaves still green in variety X and in variety Y.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a conclusion from these data.
parts.answer: Variety X keeps more leaves green (and is more tolerant of drought) than variety Y.
parts.working: 1 mark for a conclusion linked to the data (variety X more drought tolerant).

practice.stem:
A volunteer drank 1.0 dm³ of water on one day and 1.0 dm³ of 0.9 % sodium chloride solution (about the same water potential as blood plasma) on another day. Urine was collected every 30 minutes.
Time period / min: 0–30, 30–60, 60–90, 90–120, 120–150, 150–180
Urine after water / cm³: 40, 160, 310, 220, 90, 50
Urine after salt solution / cm³: 40, 50, 60, 55, 45, 40

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and compare the effects of the two drinks on urine volume.
parts.answer: After water, urine volume rose sharply to a peak of 310 cm³ in the 60–90 min period and then fell back to 50 cm³; after salt solution, urine volume stayed low and almost constant (40–60 cm³).
parts.working: B1 water: large increase then decrease, with data. B1 salt solution: little change, with data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between the effects of the two drinks.
parts.answer: Pure water raises the water potential of the blood, so less ADH is released and less water is reabsorbed in the collecting ducts, giving a large volume of dilute urine; the 0.9 % salt solution has about the same water potential as blood plasma, so the blood water potential hardly changes and ADH secretion stays the same; the extra volume is removed slowly.
parts.working: B1 water raises blood water potential → less ADH. B1 less water reabsorbed → more urine. B1 isotonic salt solution: water potential unchanged so ADH unchanged.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two limitations of this investigation that make it hard to draw a firm conclusion.
parts.answer: Only one volunteer (no replicates); the two drinks were tested on different days so other factors (food, sweating, temperature, activity) may differ; no statistical analysis possible; urine volume only collected every 30 min.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student finds a strong positive correlation between the number of stomata per mm² and the water loss per hour in leaves from 12 different plant species. Explain why the student cannot conclude that stomatal number causes the greater water loss.
parts.answer: The species differ in other ways (leaf size, cuticle thickness, habitat), any of which could cause both the high stomatal number and the high water loss; correlation does not prove causation.
parts.working: 1 mark for correlation not proving causation; 1 mark for a confounding factor such as leaf size or cuticle thickness; 1 mark for other species differences affecting both variables.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one investigation that could test whether stomatal number causes water loss.
parts.answer: Use leaves from one species and vary stomatal number (e.g. by blocking stomata with petroleum jelly on one surface) while keeping leaf size and conditions the same; compare water loss.
parts.working: 1 mark for a single-species comparison; 1 mark for a controlled manipulation of stomatal number.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student plots a graph of heart rate against time after exercise. The graph shows an unexpected spike at 2 minutes. Describe how the student should decide whether the spike is an outlier, and explain whether it should be removed.
parts.answer: Check whether the spike is repeated in other repeats or volunteers; check the measurement for a miscount or error; an outlier may be removed only if there is a clear, recorded reason (measurement error); otherwise it is kept and reported.
parts.working: 1 mark for comparing with repeats/other volunteers; 1 mark for checking for a recording or counting error; 1 mark for removing only with a valid reason and reporting the decision.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student concludes from a set of biosensor readings that the glucose meter is accurate. The readings are close to each other but all are 0.6 mmol dm⁻³ above a standard solution of known concentration. Evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: The readings are precise (close together) but not accurate; they are consistently 0.6 mmol dm⁻³ too high, which indicates a systematic error such as a calibration fault; the conclusion is therefore not supported; the meter must be recalibrated and retested against several standards.
parts.working: 1 mark for precision not accuracy; 1 mark for systematic error (consistently too high); 1 mark for the conclusion not being supported; 1 mark for recalibration and testing against several standards.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student claims that a biosensor is more accurate than the laboratory method because the biosensor gave 5.0 mmol dm⁻³ and the laboratory gave 5.1 mmol dm⁻³ for a sample whose true value is 5.0 mmol dm⁻³. Evaluate this claim.
parts.answer: The claim is not supported: each method was tested on one sample only, so no repeats show precision; the difference of 0.1 mmol dm⁻³ is within the normal uncertainty of both methods; accuracy needs several repeats and standards, and a conclusion about which method is better needs the stated uncertainty of each method.
parts.working: 1 mark for one reading only (no repeats, no precision evidence); 1 mark for the difference being within likely uncertainty; 1 mark for the need for repeats or several standards; 1 mark for stating that the uncertainty of each method must be compared.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the function of the myelin sheath and name the cells that form it.
parts.answer: Insulates the axon so that depolarisation occurs only at the nodes of Ranvier, speeding up conduction; formed by Schwann cells.
parts.working: B1 insulation / speeds conduction (saltatory). B1 Schwann cells.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a resting potential of about −70 mV is maintained across the membrane of a neurone.
parts.answer: Na⁺/K⁺ pumps actively transport 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ in, using ATP; the membrane is more permeable to K⁺ than Na⁺ (K⁺ leak channels open), so K⁺ diffuses out; large negatively charged proteins/organic anions stay inside; so the inside is negative relative to the outside.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: Na⁺/K⁺ pump, 3 Na⁺ out : 2 K⁺ in; active transport / ATP; membrane more permeable to K⁺ / K⁺ diffuses out through open channels; few Na⁺ channels open so little Na⁺ diffuses back in; organic anions inside / inside more negative.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the direction in which an impulse travels along a motor neurone.
parts.answer: From the cell body (in the CNS) along the axon to the effector (muscle).
parts.working: B1

practice.stem:
A recording electrode inside an axon gave these readings of membrane potential during one action potential:
0 ms: −70 mV; 0.5 ms: −55 mV; 1.0 ms: +35 mV; 1.5 ms: −20 mV; 2.0 ms: −80 mV; 3.5 ms: −70 mV

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the resting potential of this axon.
parts.answer: −70 mV
parts.working: B1 −70 mV (reading at 0 ms and again at 3.5 ms).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the time interval during which the axon is depolarising most rapidly, and name the ion moving at this time and its direction.
parts.answer: Between 0.5 ms and 1.0 ms; sodium ions (Na⁺) diffuse into the axon.
parts.working: B1 0.5–1.0 ms (−55 to +35 mV). B1 Na⁺ moving in, through voltage-gated sodium channels.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the change in potential between 1.0 ms and 1.5 ms.
parts.answer: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels close and voltage-gated K⁺ channels open; K⁺ diffuses out, so the inside becomes less positive (repolarisation).
parts.working: 1 mark each: Na⁺ channels close / K⁺ channels open; K⁺ diffuses out down its electrochemical gradient, removing positive charge.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the potential at 2.0 ms is lower than the resting potential.
parts.answer: Hyperpolarisation: K⁺ channels are slow to close, so too many K⁺ ions leave.
parts.working: B1 K⁺ channels stay open briefly after resting potential is reached, so extra K⁺ diffuses out (hyperpolarisation).

practice.stem: A dentist in Lahore injects a local anaesthetic, lidocaine, near a nerve in the lower jaw before filling a tooth. Lidocaine blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in neurone membranes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where voltage-gated sodium channels are concentrated in a myelinated neurone.
parts.answer: At the nodes of Ranvier.
parts.working: B1 nodes of Ranvier (gaps between Schwann cells).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the patient feels no pain while the tooth is drilled.
parts.answer: Na⁺ cannot enter the sensory neurone, so the membrane cannot depolarise to threshold; no action potentials are generated or conducted; no impulses reach the brain (sensory area), so pain is not perceived.
parts.working: 1 mark each: no Na⁺ influx / no depolarisation; threshold not reached so no action potential; impulses do not reach the brain so no sensation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The patient's lip also feels numb and may droop slightly. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Lidocaine also blocks sodium channels in other sensory and motor neurones in the area (e.g. to the lip skin and lip muscles).
parts.working: B1 nearby sensory neurones (numbness) and/or motor neurones (drooping) are also blocked, because all neurones use the same type of channel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two differences between the structure of a motor neurone and a sensory neurone.
parts.answer: Motor: cell body at one end, inside the CNS, with many dendrites; long axon. Sensory: cell body part-way along, in a ganglion outside the CNS; long dendron and short axon.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two of: position of cell body (end vs part-way along/side branch); cell body in CNS vs in a ganglion just outside the CNS; motor has many dendrites on cell body, sensory has a long dendron/dendrite carrying impulses to the cell body; motor has long axon, sensory has short axon.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of a relay neurone.
parts.answer: Carries impulses from sensory neurones to motor neurones (within the CNS).
parts.working: B1 links/transmits impulses between sensory and motor neurones inside the brain or spinal cord.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the cells that wrap around the axon of a peripheral motor neurone and state one function of the layer they form.
parts.answer: Schwann cells; the myelin sheath insulates the axon so the impulse jumps between nodes (saltatory conduction), making conduction faster.
parts.working: B1 Schwann cells. B1 myelin insulates / prevents ion movement except at nodes / speeds up conduction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the changes in the membrane that cause the depolarisation and repolarisation phases of an action potential.
parts.answer: A stimulus opens some voltage-gated Na⁺ channels; when the threshold (about −50 mV) is reached, many more open and Na⁺ diffuses in rapidly, making the inside positive (to about +30 mV); the Na⁺ channels then close and voltage-gated K⁺ channels open; K⁺ diffuses out, so the potential falls back (repolarisation) and overshoots (hyperpolarisation) before the resting potential is restored.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open; threshold reached → more open (positive feedback); Na⁺ diffuses in → inside becomes positive; Na⁺ channels close; voltage-gated K⁺ channels open; K⁺ diffuses out → repolarisation; hyperpolarisation, then K⁺ channels close.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the importance of the refractory period.
parts.answer: During the refractory period a new action potential cannot be generated at that part of the membrane (Na⁺ channels inactive); this makes impulses travel in one direction only and keeps impulses separate (discrete), limiting the maximum frequency.
parts.working: B1 impulses travel in one direction only. B1 action potentials separate / discrete / limits frequency.

practice.stem: Electrodes were placed 0.90 m apart along a myelinated motor neurone in a volunteer's arm. An action potential took 15 ms to travel between them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of conduction in m s⁻¹.
parts.answer: 60 m s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how myelination allows such a high speed of conduction.
parts.answer: Myelin insulates the axon so ions cannot move across the membrane except at the nodes of Ranvier; depolarisation occurs only at the nodes; local circuits of current flow between nodes so the action potential 'jumps' from node to node (saltatory conduction), covering more distance per action potential.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: myelin insulates / prevents ion movement; depolarisation only at nodes of Ranvier; local circuits between nodes; saltatory conduction – impulse jumps; fewer depolarisations needed per length of axon.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why multiple sclerosis, in which the myelin sheath is damaged, causes muscle weakness.
parts.answer: Impulses are conducted more slowly or fail to reach the muscle, so muscle fibres are stimulated less.
parts.working: B1

practice.stem:
Concentrations of two ions inside and outside a resting giant axon (mmol dm⁻³):
K⁺: inside 400, outside 20
Na⁺: inside 50, outside 440

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times more concentrated K⁺ is inside the axon than outside, and how many times more concentrated Na⁺ is outside than inside.
parts.answer: K⁺: 20 times; Na⁺: 8.8 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how these concentration differences are set up and how they lead to a resting potential with the inside negative.
parts.answer: Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in; the membrane is more permeable to K⁺ (K⁺ leak channels) so K⁺ diffuses out faster than Na⁺ diffuses in; more positive charge leaves than enters, so the inside is negative.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: active transport by Na⁺/K⁺ pump, ATP; 3 Na⁺ out for 2 K⁺ in; more K⁺ channels open/membrane more permeable to K⁺; K⁺ diffuses out down its gradient; net loss of positive charge.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A respiratory inhibitor is added. Suggest what will happen to the resting potential over the next hour and explain why it does not disappear immediately.
parts.answer: The resting potential gradually falls towards zero; no ATP so the pump stops, but the existing ion gradients take time to run down by diffusion.
parts.working: B1 resting potential gradually lost / becomes less negative. B1 pump stops (no ATP) but gradients already present only slowly dissipate by leakage.

practice.stem: A basketball player in Karachi is 1.95 m tall. The sensory neurone from a touch receptor in the skin of his big toe to his spinal cord is 1.05 m long and conducts impulses at 60 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for an impulse to travel the length of this neurone. Give your answer in ms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how local currents cause an action potential to move along an unmyelinated axon.
parts.answer: Na⁺ entering at the depolarised region diffuses sideways inside the axon to the next region; this depolarises the next region to threshold; voltage-gated Na⁺ channels there open, creating a new action potential further along.
parts.working: 1 mark each: Na⁺ ions diffuse along the inside (local circuit) to the adjacent resting region; this region is depolarised to threshold; voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open there, so the action potential is regenerated next to the previous one.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the action potential cannot move back towards the receptor.
parts.answer: The region just behind is in its refractory period (Na⁺ channels cannot reopen yet).
parts.working: B1 the membrane just behind is refractory / Na⁺ channels inactivated.

practice.stem:
The speed of conduction along a sciatic nerve fibre from a frog was measured at different temperatures:
Temperature / °C: 10, 15, 20, 25
Speed / m s⁻¹: 12, 16, 21, 27

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in conduction speed between 10 °C and 25 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why conduction speed increases with temperature.
parts.answer: Ions have more kinetic energy so diffuse faster; channel and pump proteins change shape (open/close) faster / Na⁺/K⁺ pump (an enzyme) works faster.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two of: faster diffusion of Na⁺/K⁺ (more kinetic energy); voltage-gated channels open and close more quickly; faster active transport by Na⁺/K⁺ pump / more ATP from faster respiration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why conduction would stop at very high temperatures, such as 50 °C.
parts.answer: Channel proteins and pump proteins are denatured.
parts.working: B1 proteins (channels/pumps) denature, so ion movement cannot be controlled.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why conduction along a myelinated neurone uses less ATP per impulse than conduction along an unmyelinated neurone of the same length.
parts.answer: Ion movement occurs only at the nodes of Ranvier, so far fewer Na⁺ and K⁺ ions cross the membrane per impulse; fewer ions must then be pumped back by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump; less ATP is used.
parts.working: 1 mark each: depolarisation only at nodes (saltatory conduction); fewer ions move in total; less active transport/pumping to restore gradients so less ATP.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a high speed of conduction is an advantage in a motor neurone to the leg muscles of a cheetah.
parts.answer: Impulses reach the muscles quickly, so the muscles contract and respond rapidly; allows fast coordinated movement to catch prey.
parts.working: 1 mark each: rapid response/short delay; fast coordinated muscle contraction for chasing prey.

practice.stem:
Conduction speeds of axons from different animals:
Unmyelinated, diameter 2 µm: 1.2 m s⁻¹
Unmyelinated, diameter 20 µm: 4.0 m s⁻¹
Myelinated, diameter 2 µm: 12 m s⁻¹
Myelinated, diameter 20 µm: 100 m s⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to describe how myelination and axon diameter affect conduction speed.
parts.answer: Myelinated axons conduct much faster than unmyelinated axons of similar diameter (at 2 µm: 12 v 1.2 m s⁻¹; at 20 µm: 100 v 4.0 m s⁻¹); in both types, wider axons conduct faster.
parts.working: B1 myelinated faster, with data. B1 larger diameter → faster, in both.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why wider axons conduct impulses faster.
parts.answer: A wider axon has a lower resistance to the flow of ions inside it (larger cross-sectional area of cytoplasm); so local currents spread further and faster along the axon, depolarising the next region sooner.
parts.working: B1 lower resistance / less resistance to ion flow. B1 local currents spread further / faster.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The squid has some unmyelinated axons about 500 µm in diameter. Suggest an advantage of these giant axons to the squid, and why mammals do not need them.
parts.answer: Giant axons conduct fast enough for a rapid escape response without myelin; mammals achieve high speed with narrow myelinated axons, so many more axons can fit in a small space (e.g. nerves, spinal cord).
parts.working: B1 fast escape response. B1 myelination gives speed with small diameter / saves space and energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the all-or-nothing principle.
parts.answer: If a stimulus causes depolarisation to reach the threshold, an action potential is produced and it is always the same size; if threshold is not reached, no action potential is produced.
parts.working: B1 threshold must be reached. B1 action potentials all the same size (amplitude).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the nervous system distinguishes between a weak stimulus and a strong stimulus.
parts.answer: A stronger stimulus produces a higher frequency of action potentials (not bigger ones); it may also stimulate more receptors / neurones with different thresholds.
parts.working: B1 higher frequency of impulses. B1 more neurones / receptors stimulated.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The absolute refractory period of a neurone lasts 2.0 ms. Calculate the maximum number of action potentials that could pass along it in one second.

practice.stem:
Two toxins were applied separately to isolated axons.
Tetrodotoxin (TTX), from pufferfish, blocks voltage-gated sodium channels.
Tetraethylammonium (TEA) blocks voltage-gated potassium channels.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict and explain the effect of TTX on the response of the axon to a stimulus.
parts.answer: No action potential; Na⁺ cannot enter, so no depolarisation beyond a tiny local change and threshold is never reached.
parts.working: B1 no action potential. B1 no Na⁺ influx so no depolarisation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict and explain the effect of TEA on the shape of an action potential.
parts.answer: Depolarisation still occurs normally, but repolarisation is much slower so the action potential is prolonged/broader; K⁺ can only leave through leak channels; little or no hyperpolarisation.
parts.working: B1 depolarisation unaffected (Na⁺ channels work). B1 repolarisation slowed/action potential lasts longer. B1 K⁺ cannot leave through voltage-gated channels (only slow leakage); no hyperpolarisation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why TEA would reduce the maximum frequency of impulses the axon can carry.
parts.answer: Each action potential and refractory period lasts longer, so fewer can occur per second.
parts.working: B1 longer action potential/refractory period means a longer minimum gap between impulses.

practice.stem: Hyperkalaemia is a condition in which the concentration of K⁺ ions in the tissue fluid is higher than normal. It may occur in patients with kidney failure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the resting potential of neurones becomes less negative in hyperkalaemia.
parts.answer: The K⁺ concentration gradient across the membrane is reduced; so fewer K⁺ ions diffuse out through K⁺ leak channels; less net loss of positive charge, so the inside is less negative.
parts.working: 1 mark each: smaller K⁺ gradient (outside concentration higher); less K⁺ diffusion out; less positive charge lost, inside less negative.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how mild hyperkalaemia would affect the size of stimulus needed to produce an action potential. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: A smaller stimulus is needed; the resting potential is already closer to the threshold (about −55 mV).
parts.working: B1 smaller stimulus. B1 less depolarisation needed to reach threshold.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Severe hyperkalaemia keeps membranes partly depolarised for a long time. Suggest why this can stop neurones firing altogether.
parts.answer: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels become inactivated when the membrane stays depolarised; they cannot reopen until the membrane repolarises, so no action potentials (like a permanent refractory period).
parts.working: 1 mark each: sodium channels inactivated/stay closed; membrane cannot repolarise to reset channels so no new action potentials.

practice.stem: A nerve was stimulated at one point. Two recording electrodes were placed on the same nerve fibre, 45 mm and 105 mm from the stimulating electrode. The action potential reached the first electrode 0.9 ms after the stimulus and the second electrode 2.1 ms after the stimulus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of conduction between the two recording electrodes in m s⁻¹.
parts.answer: 50 m s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the speed is calculated from the two recording electrodes rather than from the stimulating electrode to the first recording electrode.
parts.answer: There is a delay at the stimulating electrode before an action potential is set up; using the difference between two recordings removes this delay, so only conduction time is measured.
parts.working: 1 mark each: delay/latency in starting the action potential at the stimulus site; difference cancels it out / measures only propagation time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest, with a reason, whether this fibre is myelinated.
parts.answer: Myelinated; 50 m s⁻¹ is much faster than unmyelinated mammalian/amphibian fibres (about 0.5–10 m s⁻¹).
parts.working: B1 myelinated, because the speed is high (saltatory conduction).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which of the following change in length when a sarcomere contracts: A band, I band, H zone.
parts.answer: I band and H zone become shorter; the A band stays the same length.
parts.working: B1 I band and H zone shorten. B1 A band unchanged.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the A band does not change in length.
parts.answer: The A band is the length of the myosin (thick) filaments, which do not shorten – the filaments slide past each other.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the protein that makes up the thin filaments and the protein that makes up the thick filaments.
parts.answer: Thin: actin (with troponin and tropomyosin); thick: myosin.
parts.working: B1 both needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three features of the ultrastructure of a striated (skeletal) muscle fibre.
parts.answer: Multinucleate; contains many myofibrils made of repeating sarcomeres; sarcolemma with T-tubules; extensive sarcoplasmic reticulum; many mitochondria.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: many nuclei (syncytium); myofibrils with sarcomeres/light and dark bands; sarcolemma/cell membrane with T-tubules; sarcoplasmic reticulum around myofibrils; many mitochondria; sarcoplasm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why muscle fibres contain many mitochondria.
parts.answer: Aerobic respiration produces a lot of ATP; ATP is needed for myosin heads to detach and recock, and for active transport of Ca²⁺ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
parts.working: 1 mark each: mitochondria are site of aerobic respiration/ATP production; ATP used for myosin head movement/detachment or Ca²⁺ pumping.

practice.stem:
The events below occur when a skeletal muscle contracts. They are not in the correct order.
P Myosin heads bind to actin, forming cross-bridges.
Q Ca²⁺ ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
R Acetylcholine binds to receptors on the sarcolemma.
S Ca²⁺ binds to troponin and tropomyosin moves away from the binding sites on actin.
T Depolarisation spreads along T-tubules.
U Myosin heads tilt, pulling actin towards the centre of the sarcomere (power stroke).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the letters in the correct order.
parts.answer: R, T, Q, S, P, U
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 if one pair is reversed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the role of ATP in the cycle of cross-bridge formation after the power stroke.
parts.answer: ATP binds to the myosin head, causing it to detach from actin; ATP is hydrolysed, re-cocking the head ready to bind again.
parts.working: 1 mark each: detachment of myosin head; hydrolysis of ATP returns head to its original position.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name each structure described.
(i) the cell surface membrane of a muscle fibre
(ii) the membrane-bound store of calcium ions in a muscle fibre
(iii) the line at each end of a sarcomere to which the thin filaments are attached
(iv) the region in the centre of a sarcomere that contains only thick filaments
parts.answer: (i) sarcolemma (ii) sarcoplasmic reticulum (iii) Z line (Z disc) (iv) H zone (H band)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which band of a sarcomere stays the same length during contraction.
parts.answer: The A band.
parts.working: B1 A band (the length of the thick myosin filaments).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the role of calcium ions and ATP in the contraction of a sarcomere.
parts.answer: Ca²⁺ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds to troponin; troponin changes shape and moves tropomyosin away from the myosin-binding sites on actin; myosin heads (carrying ADP and Pi) bind to actin forming cross-bridges; release of ADP and Pi causes the power stroke, pulling actin towards the centre (M line); ATP binds to the myosin head, causing it to detach from actin; hydrolysis of ATP by ATPase in the myosin head re-cocks the head ready to bind again.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: Ca²⁺ from sarcoplasmic reticulum; Ca²⁺ binds troponin; tropomyosin moves, exposing binding sites on actin; myosin heads bind → cross-bridges; power stroke when ADP + Pi released; actin pulled towards the M line / sarcomere shortens; ATP binds → myosin head detaches; ATP hydrolysed → head returns to original position.

parts.label: b
parts.text: After death, muscles become stiff (rigor mortis). Suggest why.
parts.answer: No ATP is made after death, so myosin heads cannot detach from actin; cross-bridges remain attached.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how an impulse arriving at a neuromuscular junction leads to depolarisation of the sarcolemma.
parts.answer: The action potential opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels in the presynaptic membrane and Ca²⁺ diffuse in; vesicles of acetylcholine move to and fuse with the presynaptic membrane, releasing ACh by exocytosis; ACh diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds to receptors on the sarcolemma (motor end plate); these ligand-gated channels open and Na⁺ diffuse in, depolarising the sarcolemma.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: Ca²⁺ channels open, Ca²⁺ enter; vesicles fuse, ACh released by exocytosis; ACh diffuses across cleft; binds to receptors on sarcolemma / motor end plate; Na⁺ channels open, Na⁺ enter; depolarisation / action potential in sarcolemma.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the role of T-tubules in muscle contraction.
parts.answer: T-tubules carry the depolarisation (action potential) deep into the muscle fibre; this causes the sarcoplasmic reticulum to release Ca²⁺ throughout the fibre, so all myofibrils contract at the same time.
parts.working: B1 carry action potential into fibre. B1 sarcoplasmic reticulum releases Ca²⁺ / all myofibrils contract together.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the role of acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction.
parts.answer: Hydrolyses (breaks down) acetylcholine in the cleft so the muscle fibre is not continuously stimulated / the receptors are freed.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two similarities and two differences between a neuromuscular junction and a cholinergic synapse between two neurones.
parts.answer: Similarities: both release acetylcholine by exocytosis after Ca²⁺ influx; both have ACh receptors (ligand-gated Na⁺ channels) on the postsynaptic membrane and acetylcholinesterase. Differences: NMJ postsynaptic membrane is the sarcolemma (muscle) not a neurone; NMJ is always excitatory and one impulse always triggers an action potential (no summation needed); NMJ postsynaptic membrane is folded with more receptors; NMJ is the end of the pathway (no further neurone).
parts.working: 1 mark each for two similarities (ACh; Ca²⁺ triggers vesicle exocytosis; receptors on postsynaptic membrane; AChE; one-way transmission) and two differences (muscle vs neurone postsynaptic cell; always excitatory; one impulse enough/no summation; folded postsynaptic membrane with many receptors).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why it is important that a single impulse at a neuromuscular junction is always enough to produce an action potential in the muscle fibre.
parts.answer: Ensures muscle responds reliably every time the motor neurone fires, giving precise control of movement.
parts.working: B1 reliable/precise response, no failure of contraction.

practice.stem: A rare mutation changes the troponin protein in some muscle fibres so that it can no longer bind calcium ions. All other proteins are normal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the roles of troponin and tropomyosin in a normal resting muscle fibre.
parts.answer: Tropomyosin covers the myosin-binding sites on actin; troponin holds tropomyosin in this blocking position.
parts.working: 1 mark each: tropomyosin blocks binding sites on actin; troponin attached to tropomyosin/holds it in place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict and explain the effect of the mutation on the ability of affected fibres to contract.
parts.answer: Affected fibres cannot contract; Ca²⁺ is released normally but cannot bind troponin; tropomyosin is not moved, binding sites stay covered, so no cross-bridges form.
parts.working: 1 mark each: no contraction; troponin cannot change shape/move tropomyosin; actin binding sites blocked so myosin heads cannot bind.

practice.stem: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease. Antibodies bind to acetylcholine receptors on the sarcolemma at neuromuscular junctions and cause many receptors to be destroyed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why people with myasthenia gravis have weak muscles that tire easily.
parts.answer: Fewer ACh receptors, so fewer Na⁺ channels open when ACh is released; depolarisation of the sarcolemma is smaller and may not reach threshold; fewer fibres produce action potentials/contract.
parts.working: 1 mark each: fewer receptors for ACh to bind; less Na⁺ entry/smaller depolarisation; threshold not reached in some fibres so fewer fibres contract.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The drug pyridostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase. Suggest how this drug improves muscle strength in these patients.
parts.answer: ACh is not broken down as quickly so it stays in the cleft longer and at a higher concentration; it binds repeatedly to the remaining receptors, giving greater depolarisation.
parts.working: 1 mark each: ACh remains in cleft longer/more ACh; more binding to remaining receptors so threshold reached.
