practice.stem: A myofibril in a relaxed biceps muscle is 10 mm long and is made of sarcomeres that are each 2.5 µm long. During a strong contraction each sarcomere shortens by 0.4 µm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of sarcomeres along the length of this myofibril.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how much the whole myofibril shortens, in mm, and the percentage shortening.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the myofibril can only shorten by a limited amount.
parts.answer: Shortening stops when the thin filaments meet/overlap in the centre and the thick filaments reach the Z lines; filaments cannot shorten themselves, they only slide.
parts.working: 1 mark each: filaments do not change length, they slide; limited by thick filaments hitting Z lines/actin filaments meeting.

practice.stem: In a relaxed skeletal muscle fibre, each sarcomere is 2.4 µm long, the A band is 1.6 µm long and the H zone is 0.6 µm long. During contraction each sarcomere shortens to 2.0 µm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total length of the I band within one relaxed sarcomere and within one contracted sarcomere.
parts.answer: Relaxed: 0.8 µm; contracted: 0.4 µm
parts.working: I band (both halves) = sarcomere length − A band. B1 2.4 − 1.6 = 0.8. B1 2.0 − 1.6 = 0.4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in sarcomere length. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the length of the H zone in the contracted sarcomere, and explain your answer.
parts.answer: 0.2 µm; the sarcomere shortened by 0.4 µm and this is taken up by the thin filaments sliding further into the A band, so the H zone (the part of the A band with no actin) shortens by 0.4 µm.
parts.working: M1 0.6 − 0.4. A1 0.2 µm with explanation that A band is constant and actin slides in.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why a muscle fibre produces less force when its sarcomeres are stretched to 3.6 µm.
parts.answer: Thin and thick filaments overlap very little or not at all, so few or no myosin heads can form cross-bridges with actin.
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: Organophosphate pesticides are sprayed on cotton crops in southern Punjab. Farm workers who handle them without protection may be poisoned. Organophosphates inhibit the enzyme acetylcholinesterase.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why organophosphate poisoning causes uncontrolled muscle twitching and spasms.
parts.answer: Acetylcholinesterase is inhibited, so acetylcholine is not broken down in the synaptic cleft; ACh stays bound to receptors on the sarcolemma; Na⁺ channels keep opening, so the sarcolemma is repeatedly depolarised and the muscle is stimulated continuously.
parts.working: B1 acetylcholinesterase inhibited / ACh not hydrolysed. B1 ACh remains bound to receptors / accumulates. B1 repeated / continuous depolarisation and contraction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why severe poisoning can lead to death by failure of breathing.
parts.answer: Breathing muscles (diaphragm and intercostal muscles) are skeletal muscles; continuous stimulation leads to spasm then paralysis (receptors desensitised), so ventilation stops.
parts.working: B1 diaphragm / intercostal muscles affected. B1 cannot contract and relax rhythmically / paralysis → no ventilation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Atropine, which blocks some types of acetylcholine receptor, is used as a treatment. Suggest how it helps.
parts.answer: It prevents excess acetylcholine from binding to (those) receptors, reducing overstimulation.
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: In a type of skeletal muscle, each thick (myosin) filament is 1.6 µm long and each thin (actin) filament extends 1.1 µm from the Z line. A sarcomere in a resting muscle is 2.8 µm long.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the length of the I band and the length of the H zone in this resting sarcomere.
parts.answer: I band 1.2 µm; H zone 0.6 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the sarcomere length at which the H zone just disappears.
parts.answer: 2.2 µm
parts.working: B1 2 × 1.1 = 2.2 µm (thin filaments meet in the centre).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the sarcomere length beyond which the thick and thin filaments would no longer overlap at all, and explain why the muscle could produce no force at this length.
parts.answer: 3.8 µm; no myosin heads can reach actin, so no cross-bridges can form.
parts.working: B1 1.6 + 2 × 1.1 = 3.8 µm. B1 no overlap of actin and myosin. B1 no cross-bridges/power strokes so no tension.

practice.stem: The common krait, a snake found in Pakistan, produces a venom containing α-bungarotoxin. This toxin binds almost irreversibly to acetylcholine receptors at neuromuscular junctions, but does not open them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a bite from this snake can cause paralysis of skeletal muscles.
parts.answer: Toxin blocks ACh receptors so ACh cannot bind; ligand-gated Na⁺ channels do not open; no depolarisation/action potential in the sarcolemma, so no Ca²⁺ release and no contraction (flaccid paralysis).
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: toxin occupies receptor binding sites; ACh cannot bind; no Na⁺ entry/no depolarisation of sarcolemma; no Ca²⁺ release from SR so no cross-bridges.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a drug that inhibits acetylcholinesterase is less effective against this venom than against a reversible receptor blocker.
parts.answer: Raising ACh concentration lets ACh compete with a reversible blocker, but the toxin is bound almost irreversibly, so extra ACh cannot displace it.
parts.working: 1 mark each: AChE inhibitor increases ACh in the cleft (competes); irreversible binding not displaced by ACh.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why victims may die even though the heart continues to beat.
parts.answer: Breathing muscles (diaphragm and intercostal muscles) are skeletal muscles and are paralysed, so ventilation stops.
parts.working: B1 diaphragm/intercostals paralysed → respiratory failure (cardiac muscle is myogenic).

practice.stem:
Muscle fibres were treated with glycerol so that their membranes became fully permeable to small molecules and ions. Their lengths were measured before and after placing them in different solutions.
Solution 1: ATP only → no change in length
Solution 2: Ca²⁺ only → no change in length
Solution 3: ATP and Ca²⁺ → fibres shortened by 22 %
Solution 4: ATP, Ca²⁺ and an inhibitor of myosin ATPase → no change in length

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the results for solutions 1 and 2.
parts.answer: Solution 1: without Ca²⁺, tropomyosin still covers the binding sites, so cross-bridges cannot form. Solution 2: Ca²⁺ exposes binding sites but there is no ATP to energise the myosin heads/allow cycling.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the results for solutions 3 and 4.
parts.answer: 3: Ca²⁺ uncovers binding sites and ATP allows repeated cross-bridge cycling, so filaments slide. 4: ATP cannot be hydrolysed by the myosin head, so no recocking/power strokes.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the glycerol treatment was needed for this experiment.
parts.answer: To let ATP and Ca²⁺ reach the myofibrils directly, bypassing the need for nerve stimulation and the sarcolemma.
parts.working: B1 substances can cross the membrane to reach the filaments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the Venus fly trap detects an insect and closes.
parts.answer: The insect touches sensitive trigger hairs on the inner surface of the lobes; bending a hair causes a receptor potential and an action potential; a second stimulation within about 20–30 s is needed (prevents closing for raindrops / debris); the action potentials spread across the lobes; ions (Ca²⁺) and water move quickly, so cells change turgor / outer cells expand; the lobes flip from convex to concave and the trap snaps shut in a fraction of a second.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: trigger / sensory hairs bent; action potential generated; two stimulations within a short time needed; action potential spreads across lobe; rapid ion and water movement / change in turgor / cell walls loosened; lobes change shape (convex → concave), trap closes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the trap only closes after two stimulations within a short time.
parts.answer: To avoid wasting energy closing on non-food objects such as raindrops or falling debris.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why Venus fly traps, which can photosynthesise, catch insects.
parts.answer: They grow in soils poor in nitrogen (and other minerals), so insects provide nitrogen (for amino acids / proteins).
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: A Venus fly trap closes its two lobes in about 0.3 s after an insect touches the trigger hairs. If the insect keeps moving, the lobes seal tightly and glands on the inner surface secrete digestive enzymes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this closure cannot be caused by cell growth.
parts.answer: Growth (cell division/elongation) takes hours or days; closure takes a fraction of a second.
parts.working: B1 growth is far too slow.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest the advantage of secreting enzymes only after the trapped insect has continued to stimulate the hairs.
parts.answer: Avoids wasting energy/enzymes on non-food objects (e.g. raindrops, debris); only secretes when live prey is definitely inside.
parts.working: 1 mark each: saves enzymes/ATP/resources; only when prey present (not false alarm).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the type of enzyme needed to digest the insect's muscle proteins and suggest how the plant uses the products.
parts.answer: Proteases (peptidases); amino acids absorbed and used as a source of nitrogen to make proteins/nucleotides.
parts.working: B1 protease. B1 amino acids/nitrogen for protein or nucleic acid synthesis (soil is poor in nitrogen).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where auxin is made in a shoot.
parts.answer: In the shoot tip (apical meristem).
parts.working: B1 tip/apex of shoot, young leaves.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the effect of auxin on cells in the zone of elongation just behind the shoot tip.
parts.answer: Auxin stimulates the cells to elongate; cell walls become more stretchable so cells take up water and grow longer.
parts.working: 1 mark each: cell elongation; walls loosened so cells expand by water uptake.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the membrane protein activated by auxin that moves hydrogen ions into the cell wall, and the wall proteins that are then activated by the low pH.
parts.answer: Proton pump (H⁺-ATPase); expansins.
parts.working: B1 proton pump/H⁺ pump. B1 expansins.

practice.stem:
The following events happen when a barley grain germinates. They are not in order.
A Gibberellin diffuses to the aleurone layer.
B Maltose and glucose are used by the embryo for respiration and growth.
C The grain absorbs water.
D Amylase is secreted into the endosperm.
E The embryo releases gibberellin.
F Genes for amylase are transcribed in aleurone cells.
G Starch is hydrolysed to maltose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the letters in the correct order.
parts.answer: C, E, A, F, D, G, B
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 one pair reversed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where in the barley grain the starch is stored.
parts.answer: In the endosperm.
parts.working: B1 endosperm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways in which plant hormones are transported, and compare this with the transport of animal hormones.
parts.answer: Plant hormones move from cell to cell by diffusion and active transport, and over longer distances in xylem or phloem; animal hormones are carried dissolved in blood plasma.
parts.working: 1 mark each: cell to cell (diffusion/active transport through cells); in xylem or phloem; animal hormones in blood plasma (no specialised gland in plants).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way in which plant hormones are similar to animal hormones in how they act on cells.
parts.answer: Both bind to specific receptors on/in target cells (and can change gene expression).
parts.working: B1 specific receptors / act at low concentration / change gene expression.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how auxin causes elongation of cells in a shoot.
parts.answer: Auxin binds to a receptor in/on the cell; this stimulates proton pumps in the cell surface membrane to pump H⁺ into the cell wall (ATP used); the pH of the cell wall falls; low pH activates expansins, which loosen the bonds between cellulose microfibrils; the wall becomes more extensible, so water enters by osmosis and the cell elongates (acid growth hypothesis).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: auxin binds receptor; proton pumps activated / H⁺ pumped into cell wall; cell wall pH lowered; expansins activated; bonds between cellulose microfibrils loosened / wall extensible; water enters by osmosis → cell elongates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student puts thin slices of shoot tissue in a buffer solution at pH 4.5 without auxin. Predict and explain what happens.
parts.answer: The cells elongate; the low pH activates expansins in the cell wall directly, mimicking the effect of auxin.
parts.working: B1 cells elongate / grow. B1 acidic conditions activate expansins without needing auxin.

practice.stem: When a wheat grain absorbs water, the embryo begins to produce gibberellin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how gibberellin causes the starch stored in the endosperm to be broken down.
parts.answer: The embryo releases gibberellin, which diffuses to the aleurone layer; gibberellin binds to a receptor and causes DELLA proteins to be broken down; DELLA proteins normally inhibit a transcription factor (PIF); the transcription factor can now bind to the promoter of the amylase gene, so amylase is synthesised; amylase is secreted into the endosperm and hydrolyses starch to maltose.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: gibberellin from embryo to aleurone layer; binds receptor; DELLA proteins broken down; transcription factor no longer inhibited / binds promoter; transcription of amylase gene; amylase hydrolyses starch to maltose (glucose).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the breakdown of starch helps the seedling to grow.
parts.answer: Maltose/glucose is used by the embryo in respiration to provide ATP for cell division and growth (and to make cellulose / new cells) until the seedling can photosynthesise.
parts.working: B1 sugars used in respiration / ATP. B1 for growth / until photosynthesis begins.

practice.stem: When gibberellin reaches an aleurone cell, it binds to a receptor. In the absence of gibberellin, a DELLA protein prevents a transcription factor from binding to the promoter of the amylase gene.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how gibberellin causes amylase to be produced.
parts.answer: Gibberellin–receptor complex causes the DELLA protein to be broken down; the transcription factor is released; it binds to the promoter, RNA polymerase transcribes the amylase gene; mRNA translated to amylase.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: DELLA broken down/degraded (marked for destruction by proteasome); transcription factor freed; binds promoter; transcription of amylase gene by RNA polymerase; translation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why this control mechanism is described as 'removing a brake' rather than 'pressing an accelerator'.
parts.answer: Gibberellin does not activate the gene directly; it removes a repressor (DELLA) that normally blocks transcription.
parts.working: B1 removes an inhibitor.

practice.stem:
Oat coleoptile tips were cut off and placed on agar blocks for 3 hours. Each block was then placed on one side of a decapitated coleoptile kept in the dark. After 2 hours the angle of curvature was measured.
Number of tips placed on the block: 0, 1, 2, 4, 8
Mean curvature / °: 0, 5, 10, 18, 21

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the coleoptiles curved away from the side on which the block was placed.
parts.answer: Auxin diffused from the tips into the agar, then into the coleoptile on one side only; cells on that side elongated more; so the coleoptile bent towards the other side.
parts.working: 1 mark each: auxin from tips enters block; auxin moves down one side only; more elongation on that side so curvature away.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the relationship between number of tips and curvature.
parts.answer: Curvature increases with number of tips, almost proportionally up to 4 tips; then increases less (levels off) from 4 to 8 tips.
parts.working: 1 mark each: positive relationship / roughly doubles 1→2 tips; levels off at high numbers.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the block with no tips was included.
parts.answer: Control to show that agar alone does not cause curvature.
parts.working: B1 control.

practice.stem: A gardener in Islamabad pinches off the tips of young chilli plants. The plants then grow many side branches and become bushier.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain this effect.
parts.answer: Auxin is made at the shoot tip and moves down the stem; it inhibits growth of the lateral buds (apical dominance); removing the tip removes this auxin so lateral buds grow into side shoots.
parts.working: 1 mark each: auxin produced at tip; auxin inhibits lateral buds (apical dominance); removal lowers auxin so side buds grow.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict what would happen if a paste containing auxin were placed on the cut tip, and give a reason.
parts.answer: Side branches would not grow (or grow much less); the auxin replaces that from the tip and still inhibits lateral buds.
parts.working: 1 mark each: lateral bud growth suppressed; supplied auxin acts like the natural tip.

practice.stem: In pea plants, the gene Le codes for an enzyme that converts an inactive gibberellin (GA20) into active gibberellin (GA1). The allele le is recessive. Plants with genotype le le are dwarf.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why plants with genotype le le are dwarf.
parts.answer: The recessive allele le codes for a non-functional (less active) enzyme; so inactive GA20 is not converted into active GA1; without GA1, DELLA proteins are not broken down and continue to inhibit transcription factors needed for stem elongation (cell elongation and division in internodes).
parts.working: B1 le gives non-functional enzyme. B1 no / little active GA1 produced. B1 DELLA proteins remain → growth genes not transcribed / short internodes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the height of le le plants sprayed with GA1 and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: They would grow tall (similar to Le plants), because GA1 is the active form, so the missing enzyme step is bypassed and DELLA proteins are broken down.
parts.working: B1 tall. B1 active GA supplied directly / missing enzyme not needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the phenotype of plants with genotype Le le and explain why.
parts.answer: Tall; Le is dominant – one functional allele produces enough enzyme to make active GA1.
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: Fusicoccin is a toxin made by a fungus that attacks almond and peach trees. It permanently activates the proton pumps in plant cell membranes. Vanadate is a substance that inhibits these proton pumps.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the effect of fusicoccin on the growth of stem segments in the absence of auxin. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Segments elongate rapidly even without auxin; H⁺ pumped into the cell walls lowers the pH; expansins are activated and loosen the bonds between cellulose microfibrils; cells take up water and extend.
parts.working: 1 mark each: elongation increases; H⁺ pumped into wall/low pH; expansins/wall loosening then water uptake.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the effect of vanadate on auxin-induced elongation and explain how this supports the acid-growth hypothesis.
parts.answer: Auxin no longer causes elongation; shows auxin acts through proton pumping (lowering wall pH).
parts.working: 1 mark each: elongation blocked; supports that proton pump activity is needed for auxin's effect.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why fusicoccin makes leaves wilt even when soil water is available.
parts.answer: Proton pumps in guard cells are activated so stomata open widely and stay open, causing excessive transpiration.
parts.working: B1 stomata kept open → water loss faster than uptake.

practice.stem:
Half-seeds of barley were placed on starch agar for 48 hours. The agar was then flooded with iodine solution and the diameter of the clear zone around each half-seed was measured.
Half with embryo: 14 mm
Half without embryo: 2 mm
Half without embryo + gibberellin (10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³): 9 mm
Half without embryo + gibberellin (10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³): 13 mm
Half without embryo + gibberellin (10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³) + an inhibitor of transcription: 2 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what the clear zones show.
parts.answer: Starch has been hydrolysed by amylase that diffused out of the half-seed.
parts.working: B1 starch broken down by amylase (no blue-black).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using all the data, explain the role of the embryo and of gibberellin.
parts.answer: Without the embryo almost no amylase is made; gibberellin can replace the embryo; so the embryo is the source of gibberellin; more gibberellin gives more amylase.
parts.working: 1 mark each: no embryo → little amylase; GA restores amylase production; effect increases with GA concentration (embryo supplies GA).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what the result with the transcription inhibitor shows.
parts.answer: Gibberellin acts by causing transcription of the amylase gene (new synthesis), not by activating amylase already present.
parts.working: 1 mark each: GA effect needs transcription; amylase is newly synthesised (gene expression switched on).

practice.stem:
Venus fly traps were touched twice on the trigger hairs with different time intervals between the two touches.
Interval / s: 5, 15, 30, 45, 60
Percentage of traps closing: 100, 95, 60, 10, 0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of the interval between touches on trap closure.
parts.answer: Up to 15 s almost all traps close; closure falls steeply between 15 and 45 s; none close at 60 s.
parts.working: 1 mark each: high closure at short intervals; decreases to 0 at 60 s (with data).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Each touch produces an action potential in the trap. Suggest an explanation for the results.
parts.answer: Each action potential raises the level of a signal (e.g. Ca²⁺ concentration) in the cells; one action potential alone is below the threshold for closure; if a second arrives before the signal has fallen back, the threshold is reached; the signal decays with time, so longer intervals fail.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: first action potential alone insufficient; it raises a signal such as Ca²⁺ concentration; second adds to it (summation) to reach threshold; signal decays over ~30 s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest an advantage of this 'counting' mechanism.
parts.answer: Prevents closure by single accidental stimuli (raindrops/debris), saving energy.
parts.working: B1 avoids false closures.

practice.stem:
Two mutant varieties of a cereal plant are studied.
Mutant X: produces a DELLA protein that cannot bind the gibberellin–receptor complex.
Mutant Y: produces no functional DELLA protein at all.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the height of each mutant compared with normal plants, and explain your predictions.
parts.answer: X: dwarf, because DELLA cannot be broken down, so it keeps blocking the transcription factors needed for growth genes. Y: tall (slender), because there is no DELLA to inhibit the transcription factors, so growth genes are always expressed.
parts.working: B1 X dwarf. B1 DELLA not degraded so transcription of growth genes stays blocked. B1 Y tall. B1 no repressor so growth genes transcribed regardless of GA.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the effect of spraying each mutant with gibberellin, giving a reason.
parts.answer: No change in either; X cannot respond because DELLA is not broken down; Y is already at maximum growth/has no DELLA to remove.
parts.working: 1 mark each with reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three differences between nervous and endocrine communication.
parts.answer: Nervous: electrical impulses along neurones (and chemical at synapses); endocrine: hormones (chemicals) carried in the blood. Nervous: very fast; endocrine: slower. Nervous: short-lived responses; endocrine: longer-lasting. Nervous: response localised to specific effectors; endocrine: can affect target cells widely throughout the body.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct comparative difference, max 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a hormone travelling in the blood affects only certain cells.
parts.answer: Only target cells have specific receptors complementary to the hormone.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the gland that secretes ADH into the blood.
parts.answer: Posterior pituitary gland.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each response, state whether it is controlled mainly by the nervous system, the endocrine system, or both. Give a reason in each case.
(i) blinking when dust blows towards the eye
(ii) breast development during puberty
(iii) the heart beating faster when a dog suddenly barks
parts.answer: (i) nervous: very rapid, short-lived, localised reflex. (ii) endocrine: slow, long-lasting changes over months (oestrogen). (iii) both: sympathetic nerves act within a second and adrenaline from the adrenal glands prolongs the effect.
parts.working: 1 mark each, with reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way in which the nervous and endocrine systems are similar.
parts.answer: Both use chemical signals that bind to specific receptors / both coordinate responses to stimuli.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each hormone of the menstrual cycle (FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone), state the gland or structure that secretes it and give one of its functions.
parts.answer: FSH – anterior pituitary – stimulates follicle development/oestrogen secretion. LH – anterior pituitary – triggers ovulation / formation of corpus luteum. Oestrogen – developing follicles (ovary) – repairs/thickens endometrium; controls FSH/LH. Progesterone – corpus luteum – maintains endometrium; inhibits FSH and LH.
parts.working: 1 mark per correct row (source and function).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two endocrine glands, and one hormone secreted by each.
parts.answer: e.g. pancreas (islets) – insulin/glucagon; adrenal gland – adrenaline; pituitary – ADH/FSH/LH; ovary – oestrogen/progesterone.
parts.working: 1 mark each correct gland + hormone pair.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how hormones are transported from endocrine glands to their target organs.
parts.answer: Dissolved in blood plasma.
parts.working: B1 in the blood (plasma).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why endocrine glands have a very good blood supply but no ducts.
parts.answer: Hormones are secreted directly into the blood (ductless); many capillaries carry hormones away quickly to the whole body.
parts.working: 1 mark each: secreted into blood not a duct; capillaries/rapid removal and distribution.

practice.stem: Some hormones, such as oestrogen and progesterone, are steroids. Others, such as insulin and ADH, are proteins or peptides.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why steroid hormones can bind to receptors inside the cytoplasm or nucleus of target cells, while peptide hormones bind to receptors on the cell surface membrane.
parts.answer: Steroids are lipid-soluble/non-polar, so they diffuse through the phospholipid bilayer; peptide hormones are large and polar/water-soluble, so they cannot cross; they act via receptors on the membrane (and second messengers).
parts.working: 1 mark each: steroid lipid-soluble crosses bilayer; peptides polar/large cannot cross; peptide uses surface receptor + second messenger/signalling cascade.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term endocrine gland.
parts.answer: A gland that secretes hormones directly into the blood (it has no duct).
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Adrenaline and insulin are both hormones. Adrenaline is released within seconds of a fright; the effects of insulin are needed over hours after a meal. Explain why the endocrine system, rather than the nervous system, is used for these responses.
parts.answer: Both hormones need to reach many different target cells throughout the body (e.g. liver, muscle, fat cells); blood carries hormones to all tissues; hormone effects (e.g. on enzymes or membrane transporters) last as long as the hormone remains, giving a longer, sustained response.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: many / widespread target cells; hormone reaches all tissues in blood; long-lasting effect; one hormone can produce several coordinated effects; nervous responses would be too short / localised.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the reflex withdrawal of a bare foot from a sharp thorn uses the nervous system.
parts.answer: It needs a very fast, localised response to prevent damage.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the concentrations of FSH and LH stay low during the days after ovulation.
parts.answer: After ovulation the follicle becomes the corpus luteum; it secretes large amounts of progesterone (and some oestrogen); progesterone inhibits secretion of FSH and LH by the anterior pituitary (negative feedback).
parts.working: 1 mark each: corpus luteum forms; secretes progesterone; negative feedback on anterior pituitary/hypothalamus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why menstruation begins if the egg is not fertilised.
parts.answer: The corpus luteum degenerates, so progesterone falls; the endometrium is no longer maintained and breaks down.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A combined contraceptive pill is taken daily for 21 days, followed by 7 days without hormone (or with inactive tablets). A progesterone-only pill is taken every day without a break.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why bleeding usually occurs during the 7 days without the combined pill.
parts.answer: Hormone (progesterone/oestrogen) levels fall; the endometrium is no longer maintained, so it breaks down (a withdrawal bleed).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Progesterone-only pills do not always prevent ovulation. Suggest two other ways in which they could prevent pregnancy.
parts.answer: Thicken cervical mucus so sperm cannot pass through; make the endometrium thin/unsuitable for implantation.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the progesterone-only pill must be taken at about the same time each day.
parts.answer: Synthetic hormone is broken down quickly, so its concentration must not fall too low between doses (or mucus thins).
parts.working: B1 hormone concentration must be kept above an effective level.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A neurotransmitter and a hormone are both chemical messengers. Give one similarity and three differences between them.
parts.answer: Similarity: both bind to specific receptors (complementary shape) on target cells. Differences: neurotransmitter crosses a tiny synaptic cleft by diffusion, hormone travels in the blood; neurotransmitter acts in milliseconds, hormone in seconds to hours; neurotransmitter affects one cell/very localised, hormone affects many target cells all over the body; neurotransmitter broken down quickly so short effect, hormone effect lasts longer.
parts.working: B1 similarity. 1 mark each for three differences.

practice.stem: A woman in Peshawar records the lengths of her last six menstrual cycles: 28, 30, 27, 29, 31 and 28 days. Ovulation usually happens about 14 days before the next menstruation starts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean cycle length, to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 28.8 days

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the mean to predict on which day of the next cycle ovulation is most likely. Explain your answer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Urine test strips detect LH. Explain why a positive LH test helps to predict ovulation more accurately than the calculation.
parts.answer: Ovulation follows the LH surge by about a day; the surge is measured directly in the current cycle, whereas cycle length varies from cycle to cycle.
parts.working: 1 mark each: LH surge triggers ovulation (shortly after); cycle lengths vary so average is approximate.

practice.stem:
Hormone concentrations in a woman's blood (arbitrary units):
Day of cycle: 2, 7, 12, 14, 17, 21, 26
FSH: 8, 6, 9, 15, 4, 3, 5
LH: 6, 5, 18, 50, 7, 4, 4
Oestrogen: 2, 6, 14, 10, 6, 9, 3
Progesterone: 1, 1, 1, 3, 12, 20, 4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the role of FSH and oestrogen in the first half of the menstrual cycle.
parts.answer: FSH from the anterior pituitary stimulates the development of a follicle in the ovary; the follicle secretes oestrogen; oestrogen stimulates repair/thickening of the endometrium; rising oestrogen initially inhibits FSH (negative feedback), then high oestrogen triggers the LH surge.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: FSH from anterior pituitary; stimulates follicle development; follicle secretes oestrogen; oestrogen thickens endometrium; oestrogen inhibits FSH; high oestrogen stimulates LH surge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the data, identify the day on which ovulation is most likely and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Day 14; LH concentration peaks on day 14 (LH surge, 50 units), which triggers ovulation.
parts.working: B1 day 14 (accept 14–15). B1 LH peak / surge causes ovulation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a contraceptive pill containing synthetic oestrogen and progesterone prevents pregnancy.
parts.answer: The hormones inhibit secretion of FSH and LH by the anterior pituitary (negative feedback); so follicles do not develop and no LH surge occurs, so ovulation does not happen.
parts.working: B1 FSH and LH secretion inhibited. B1 no follicle development / no ovulation. (Also accept: cervical mucus thickened.)

practice.stem:
After a sudden loud noise, a student's heart rate and blood adrenaline concentration were recorded.
Time after noise: 0 s, 2 s, 30 s, 1 min, 3 min, 10 min
Heart rate / beats min⁻¹: 72, 95, 110, 108, 96, 76
Adrenaline / arbitrary units: 1, 1, 6, 9, 5, 1.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the heart rate rose within 2 s although the adrenaline concentration had not yet changed.
parts.answer: The first increase is caused by the nervous system; impulses in sympathetic neurones to the SAN act within milliseconds; adrenaline takes time to be secreted and carried in the blood.
parts.working: 1 mark each: nervous (sympathetic) control is rapid; hormone needs secretion and transport in blood.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the heart rate remained high for several minutes.
parts.answer: Adrenaline secreted by the adrenal glands circulates in the blood and keeps stimulating the heart until it is broken down (e.g. in the liver).
parts.working: 1 mark each: adrenaline still present in blood; removed/broken down only slowly.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the data to suggest why both systems are needed to deal with danger.
parts.answer: Nervous system gives an immediate response; the endocrine system sustains and spreads the response to many organs (e.g. liver glycogenolysis, breathing) over minutes.
parts.working: 1 mark each: rapid initial response; longer-lasting, widespread response.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For most of the menstrual cycle, oestrogen inhibits secretion of LH. Shortly before ovulation, a high concentration of oestrogen instead stimulates a large release of LH. Explain why this is an example of positive feedback, and why it is useful.
parts.answer: A rise in oestrogen causes a rise in LH, which stimulates the follicle to produce even more oestrogen, so the change is amplified; this gives a sudden large LH surge that causes ovulation at the right time.
parts.working: 1 mark each: change increases further rather than being reversed; LH and oestrogen stimulate each other; produces rapid surge that triggers ovulation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why this positive feedback stops after ovulation.
parts.answer: The follicle has ruptured and becomes the corpus luteum, which makes mainly progesterone; progesterone inhibits LH (negative feedback).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: In an IVF clinic in Karachi, a woman is given daily injections of FSH for about 10 days. When ultrasound shows several large follicles, she is given a single injection of a hormone that acts like LH. Eggs are collected 36 hours later. After an embryo is placed in the uterus, she is given progesterone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the FSH injections are given.
parts.answer: FSH stimulates several follicles to develop at once (instead of one), so several eggs can be collected.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the LH-like injection is timed so that eggs are collected 36 hours later.
parts.answer: It mimics the LH surge which triggers final maturation of eggs and ovulation; eggs must be collected just before they would be released from the follicles.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why progesterone is given after the embryo is transferred.
parts.answer: To keep the endometrium thick and maintained so the embryo can implant; normal corpus luteum function may be inadequate after the treatment.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: The adrenal medulla releases adrenaline into the blood when it receives impulses from sympathetic neurones.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the adrenal medulla is said to link the nervous system and the endocrine system.
parts.answer: It is stimulated by nerve impulses (neurotransmitter from neurones) but its output is a hormone secreted into the blood.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Adrenaline cannot enter its target cells. Explain how it can still cause liver cells to release glucose within seconds.
parts.answer: Adrenaline binds to receptors on the cell surface membrane; activates a G protein and adenylyl cyclase, producing cAMP (second messenger); a cascade of enzymes (kinases) is activated, amplifying the signal and activating glycogen phosphorylase to break down glycogen.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: surface receptor; G protein / adenylyl cyclase; cAMP second messenger; enzyme cascade/amplification; glycogenolysis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the sequence of events at a cholinergic synapse, from the arrival of an action potential at the presynaptic knob to the production of an action potential in the postsynaptic neurone.
parts.answer: Depolarisation opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels and Ca²⁺ diffuse into the presynaptic knob; vesicles containing acetylcholine move to and fuse with the presynaptic membrane; ACh is released by exocytosis; ACh diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds to receptor proteins on the postsynaptic membrane; Na⁺ channels (ligand-gated) open and Na⁺ diffuse in, depolarising the postsynaptic membrane; if threshold is reached, an action potential is produced; acetylcholinesterase hydrolyses ACh.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: Ca²⁺ channels open / Ca²⁺ enter; vesicles fuse with presynaptic membrane; exocytosis of ACh; diffusion across cleft; binds to receptors on postsynaptic membrane; Na⁺ channels open, Na⁺ enter; depolarisation – threshold → action potential; ACh broken down by acetylcholinesterase; products reabsorbed and ACh resynthesised using ATP.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why presynaptic knobs contain many mitochondria.
parts.answer: To provide ATP for resynthesis of acetylcholine / packaging into vesicles / pumping Ca²⁺ out.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State the role of each of these in transmission at a cholinergic synapse.
(i) voltage-gated calcium ion channels in the presynaptic membrane
(ii) synaptic vesicles
(iii) receptor proteins in the postsynaptic membrane
(iv) acetylcholinesterase
parts.answer: (i) open when the action potential arrives, letting Ca²⁺ diffuse into the knob, which triggers vesicle fusion. (ii) store acetylcholine and release it by exocytosis. (iii) bind acetylcholine and open, allowing Na⁺ into the postsynaptic neurone. (iv) hydrolyses acetylcholine so the signal stops/receptors are freed.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens to acetylcholine after it has bound to the receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, including how it is recycled.
parts.answer: ACh leaves the receptor and is hydrolysed by acetylcholinesterase into choline and ethanoic acid (acetate); these diffuse back across the cleft; they are taken into the presynaptic knob; ACh is resynthesised (using acetyl coenzyme A and ATP) and packaged into vesicles.
parts.working: 1 mark each for four of: hydrolysis by AChE; into choline + ethanoate/acetate; diffuse back to presynaptic membrane; reabsorbed (active transport/uptake); ACh resynthesised using ATP; stored in vesicles.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of recycling acetylcholine.
parts.answer: Saves energy/materials; ACh supply is quickly restored for further impulses.

practice.stem: A presynaptic action potential produces a depolarisation of 6 mV in the postsynaptic neurone. The resting potential of the postsynaptic neurone is −70 mV and its threshold is −55 mV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depolarisation needed to reach threshold.
parts.answer: 15 mV

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the smallest number of presynaptic neurones that must fire at the same time to produce an action potential in the postsynaptic neurone.
parts.working: B1 15 ÷ 6 = 2.5, so 3 neurones needed (2 give only 12 mV).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name this type of summation, and describe the other type of summation.
parts.answer: Spatial summation; temporal summation is when one presynaptic neurone fires several impulses in rapid succession, so the depolarisations add up.
parts.working: B1 spatial. B1 temporal = repeated impulses from the same neurone close together in time.

practice.stem:
A student wrote these statements about a cholinergic synapse. Each contains one error.
1 Acetylcholine crosses the synaptic cleft by active transport.
2 The receptors for acetylcholine are found on the presynaptic membrane.
3 Sodium ions entering the presynaptic knob cause the vesicles to fuse with the membrane.
4 Acetylcholinesterase is found inside the synaptic vesicles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Rewrite each statement correctly.
parts.answer: 1 ACh crosses the cleft by diffusion. 2 The receptors are on the postsynaptic membrane. 3 Calcium ions entering the knob cause vesicle fusion. 4 AChE is in the synaptic cleft/on the postsynaptic membrane.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why impulses can only travel in one direction across a synapse.
parts.answer: Vesicles of neurotransmitter are only in the presynaptic knob; receptors are only on the postsynaptic membrane.
parts.working: B1 neurotransmitter released only from presynaptic side. B1 receptors only on postsynaptic membrane.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how synapses allow one neurone to influence many others, and many neurones to influence one, and state one benefit of each.
parts.answer: Divergence: one presynaptic neurone synapses with many postsynaptic neurones, so one signal can spread to several parts of the nervous system / several effectors; convergence: many presynaptic neurones synapse with one postsynaptic neurone, allowing information from several sources to be integrated (summed) and weak stimuli to be amplified.
parts.working: B1 divergence described. B1 convergence described. B1 a benefit of each (spread of signal / integration of information).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why repeated stimulation of the same synapse at a very high frequency can stop transmission.
parts.answer: Acetylcholine is used up faster than it can be resynthesised (vesicles depleted), so the synapse fatigues.
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: In a reflex arc, the total path from receptor to effector is 1.20 m and impulses travel at 100 m s⁻¹ along all the neurones. The time from stimulus to the start of depolarisation of the muscle fibre was 14.0 ms. The pathway includes two synapses and one neuromuscular junction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for conduction along the neurones, in ms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming the rest of the time is due to delays at the junctions, calculate the mean delay at each junction. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why there is a delay at each synapse.
parts.answer: Transmission is chemical: Ca²⁺ entry, exocytosis of vesicles, diffusion of ACh across the cleft and binding/opening of receptors all take time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two of these steps.

practice.stem: Botulinum toxin, made by the bacterium Clostridium botulinum, prevents synaptic vesicles from fusing with the presynaptic membrane at cholinergic synapses and neuromuscular junctions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why food poisoning by this toxin causes floppy (flaccid) paralysis.
parts.answer: No exocytosis so no ACh released; no ACh binds to receptors on the sarcolemma, so no depolarisation/action potential in muscle; muscles cannot contract and stay relaxed.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Doctors inject tiny amounts of this toxin into individual muscles to treat painful muscle spasms. Suggest why it is effective and why the injection must be repeated every few months.
parts.answer: It stops the overactive motor neurone signalling to that muscle only, so the spasm stops; the neurone eventually grows new terminals/replaces the damaged proteins, so the effect wears off.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
In an experiment, the duration and size of postsynaptic depolarisations were measured at a cholinergic synapse, before and after adding drug D.
Without drug D: peak depolarisation 20 mV, lasting 2 ms
With drug D: peak depolarisation 28 mV, lasting 15 ms

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest how drug D acts. Explain your answer using the data.
parts.answer: Drug D inhibits acetylcholinesterase; ACh is not broken down so it stays in the cleft longer and keeps binding receptors (longer depolarisation); ACh builds up to a higher concentration so more channels are open at once (larger peak).
parts.working: 1 mark each: AChE inhibitor; longer duration explained; larger amplitude explained.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one effect drug D would have on the muscles of a person exposed to it.
parts.answer: Prolonged contraction/spasms/twitching, then possible paralysis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The synaptic cleft at a cholinergic synapse is about 20 nm wide. Explain why it is important that the cleft is so narrow.
parts.answer: Diffusion is fast over a short distance, so transmission is quick; ACh stays concentrated enough to bind many receptors.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is important that acetylcholine is removed from the receptors very quickly.
parts.answer: Otherwise the postsynaptic membrane would stay depolarised/keep firing; removal allows the next impulse to be transmitted separately and stops continuous stimulation.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why presynaptic neurones that fire very frequently contain a large amount of rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus in their cell bodies.
parts.answer: To make and package proteins needed at the synapse (e.g. enzymes for ACh synthesis, channel proteins, vesicle membrane proteins) to replace those used.
parts.working: 1 mark each: protein synthesis (RER); packaging/vesicles (Golgi).

practice.stem:
Scientists studied a synapse between two neurones in a laboratory preparation.
Without drug X: presynaptic action potential normal; postsynaptic depolarisation 25 mV, action potential produced.
With drug X: presynaptic action potential normal; postsynaptic depolarisation 4 mV, no action potential.
With drug X, acetylcholine applied directly to the postsynaptic membrane: postsynaptic depolarisation 25 mV, action potential produced.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of drug X on the postsynaptic response.
parts.answer: Drug X reduces the depolarisation of the postsynaptic membrane from 25 mV to 4 mV, so no action potential is produced.
parts.working: B1 with data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the data to suggest how drug X acts. Explain your reasoning.
parts.answer: Drug X probably blocks the voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels in the presynaptic membrane (or prevents vesicle fusion); when acetylcholine was applied directly to the postsynaptic membrane the response was normal, so the receptors and Na⁺ channels still work; the presynaptic action potential is normal, so the drug acts between the arrival of the impulse and release of ACh – less ACh is released.
parts.working: B1 acts on presynaptic side / reduces ACh release (e.g. blocks Ca²⁺ channels). B1 postsynaptic response to applied ACh normal → receptors unaffected. B1 presynaptic action potential normal → conduction unaffected.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Nicotine has a similar shape to acetylcholine. Suggest how nicotine affects transmission at synapses with nicotinic receptors.
parts.answer: Nicotine binds to the acetylcholine receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, opening Na⁺ channels and causing depolarisation; it is not broken down by acetylcholinesterase, so it causes prolonged stimulation.
parts.working: B1 binds to ACh receptors / mimics ACh → depolarisation. B1 not hydrolysed by acetylcholinesterase → prolonged effect.

practice.stem: At some synapses in the brain, the transmitter released binds to receptors that are chloride ion channels. When these channels open, Cl⁻ ions diffuse into the postsynaptic neurone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the effect on the membrane potential of the postsynaptic neurone and explain why this makes an action potential less likely.
parts.answer: Inside becomes more negative (hyperpolarised, e.g. −75 mV); further from threshold; more excitatory input/greater depolarisation is needed to reach threshold.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A neurone receives input from one excitatory synapse and one of these inhibitory synapses at the same time. Explain why it may not produce an action potential even though the excitatory input alone would.
parts.answer: The hyperpolarisation from the inhibitory synapse cancels some of the depolarisation from the excitatory synapse (summation of opposite effects), so threshold is not reached.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why inhibitory synapses are important in the nervous system.
parts.answer: Allow integration/fine control, e.g. preventing unwanted responses or relaxing an antagonistic muscle.

practice.stem:
The peak postsynaptic depolarisation was measured at a synapse bathed in solutions with different calcium ion concentrations.
Ca²⁺ / mmol dm⁻³: 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0
Peak depolarisation / mV: 2, 5, 11, 18
When magnesium ions (Mg²⁺), which block calcium channels, were added to the 2.0 mmol dm⁻³ solution, the peak depolarisation fell to 3 mV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain the effect of calcium ion concentration on the postsynaptic response.
parts.answer: Higher Ca²⁺ gives larger depolarisation (2 mV to 18 mV); more Ca²⁺ diffuses into the presynaptic knob per impulse; more vesicles fuse and more ACh is released, so more receptor channels open.
parts.working: 1 mark each: trend with data; more Ca²⁺ influx; more ACh released/more Na⁺ channels opened.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the effect of Mg²⁺.
parts.answer: Mg²⁺ blocks Ca²⁺ channels so less Ca²⁺ enters; fewer vesicles release ACh so depolarisation is small.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of peak depolarisation at 4.0 mmol dm⁻³ to that at 1.0 mmol dm⁻³, and state whether the response is proportional to the Ca²⁺ concentration.
parts.answer: 3.6 : 1; not proportional (Ca²⁺ increased 4 times but response only 3.6 times).
parts.working: B1 18 ÷ 5 = 3.6. B1 not proportional, with reason.

practice.stem: Lambert–Eaton syndrome is an autoimmune disease in which antibodies attack the voltage-gated calcium ion channels in presynaptic membranes at neuromuscular junctions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why patients have muscle weakness.
parts.answer: Fewer Ca²⁺ channels so less Ca²⁺ enters the presynaptic knob; fewer vesicles fuse and less ACh is released; depolarisation of the sarcolemma may not reach threshold, so fewer muscle fibres contract.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Strength in these patients often improves briefly during repeated, rapid muscle activity. Suggest why.
parts.answer: With rapid repeated impulses, Ca²⁺ builds up inside the knob before it can be removed; so more ACh is released with each later impulse.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why this disease does not affect the heart rate directly.
parts.answer: Heartbeat is myogenic (started by the SAN), not dependent on neuromuscular junctions with skeletal muscle.

practice.stem: At some synapses the transmitter is not broken down by an enzyme in the cleft. Instead, it is taken back into the presynaptic neurone by transporter proteins (reuptake). Some antidepressant drugs block these transporters.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest how blocking reuptake affects transmission at these synapses.
parts.answer: Transmitter remains in the cleft longer and at a higher concentration; it continues to bind postsynaptic receptors; so the postsynaptic response is larger/longer-lasting (more frequent action potentials).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why such drugs often take several weeks to have their full effect, even though they block transporters within hours.
parts.answer: The nervous system adapts: e.g. the number of receptors or the amount of transmitter made changes slowly (gene expression/protein synthesis takes time).
parts.working: 1 mark each: slow changes in receptor/transmitter levels; protein synthesis/gene expression changes.

practice.stem: A boy in Faisalabad accidentally touches a hot tawa (griddle) and pulls his hand away immediately, before he feels the pain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the parts of the reflex arc in order, starting with the receptor.
parts.answer: Receptor (thermoreceptor/pain receptor in skin) → sensory neurone → relay (intermediate) neurone in the spinal cord → motor neurone → effector (biceps muscle).
parts.working: B1 receptor and sensory neurone. B1 relay neurone in spinal cord. B1 motor neurone and muscle as effector.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why reflex actions are fast.
parts.answer: Few synapses are involved (only two or three), and the impulse does not need to pass to the brain for a decision; myelinated neurones conduct quickly.
parts.working: B1 few synapses / short pathway. B1 brain not involved in initiating the response / no conscious decision (myelinated neurones).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why a reflex is described as involuntary.
parts.answer: It is automatic – it happens without conscious thought.
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: A doctor taps a patient's leg just below the kneecap. The lower leg kicks forward. This is the knee-jerk reflex. Only one synapse in the spinal cord is involved.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of receptor stimulated and the effector.
parts.answer: Stretch receptor (in the thigh muscle/muscle spindle); the quadriceps (thigh) muscle.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which type of neurone is missing from this reflex arc compared with a hand-withdrawal reflex.
parts.answer: Relay neurone.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why doctors test this reflex.
parts.answer: To check that the sensory and motor neurones and the spinal cord are working normally.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define each term: (i) receptor (ii) effector (iii) receptor potential
parts.answer: (i) a cell/structure that detects a stimulus (a change in the environment) and converts it to an electrical signal. (ii) a muscle or gland that carries out a response. (iii) a change in membrane potential of a receptor cell caused by a stimulus; its size depends on the stimulus strength.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why a receptor potential is described as graded but an action potential is not.
parts.answer: Receptor potential size varies with stimulus strength; action potential is always the same size (all-or-nothing).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Match each stimulus to the type of receptor that detects it, and give one example of a receptor cell or organ for each.
(i) light (ii) chemicals in food (iii) pressure on the skin (iv) temperature
parts.answer: (i) photoreceptor – rod/cone cells in the retina. (ii) chemoreceptor – taste bud cells/olfactory cells. (iii) mechanoreceptor – Pacinian corpuscle/touch receptor. (iv) thermoreceptor – nerve endings in the skin.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: When a person walks from a dim room into bright sunshine, their pupils constrict within a second.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the receptors and the effectors in this reflex.
parts.answer: Receptors: photoreceptors (rods/cones) in the retina. Effectors: circular muscles of the iris.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is an advantage that this response is a reflex.
parts.answer: It is very fast and automatic; protects the retina from damage by too much light before the brain consciously decides.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A girl in Multan steps on a sharp stone and lifts her foot before she feels the pain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where the cell bodies of the sensory neurone and the motor neurone are found.
parts.answer: Sensory: in a ganglion (dorsal root ganglion) just outside the spinal cord. Motor: in the grey matter of the spinal cord.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why she feels pain a short time after her foot has moved.
parts.answer: The relay neurone also passes impulses up the spinal cord to the brain; the path is longer and involves more synapses, so awareness comes after the motor response.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a chemoreceptor cell in a taste bud responds to sodium ions in food and how this results in impulses in a sensory neurone.
parts.answer: Na⁺ ions from salty food diffuse into the receptor cell through Na⁺ channels in its cell surface membrane; this depolarises the receptor cell (a receptor / generator potential); the bigger the stimulus, the bigger the receptor potential; if threshold is reached, the receptor cell releases neurotransmitter onto the sensory neurone; this depolarises the sensory neurone, producing action potentials that travel to the brain.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: Na⁺ diffuse in through channels; depolarisation / receptor potential; size depends on stimulus strength; threshold; neurotransmitter released to sensory neurone; action potentials in sensory neurone to the brain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a sensory receptor is described as a transducer.
parts.answer: It converts energy of one form (the stimulus, e.g. chemical) into electrical energy (a nerve impulse).
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why very salty food produces a stronger sensation of saltiness than slightly salty food.
parts.answer: More Na⁺ enters, giving a larger receptor potential and a higher frequency of action potentials in the sensory neurone (and more receptors stimulated).
parts.working: B1

practice.stem:
A pressure receptor in the skin was stimulated with increasing pressure and its receptor (generator) potential was measured. An action potential is produced in the sensory neurone only when the receptor potential reaches 10 mV.
Pressure / arbitrary units: 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8
Receptor potential / mV: 3, 7, 12, 18, 20

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between pressure and receptor potential.
parts.answer: Receptor potential increases with pressure; it rises steeply at low pressure and levels off at high pressure (only +2 mV from 4 to 8).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the lowest pressure in the table that would produce action potentials. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: 2 units; receptor potential (12 mV) is above threshold (10 mV); at 1 unit it is only 7 mV.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the receptor potential levels off at high pressure.
parts.answer: All the stretch-mediated ion (Na⁺) channels are already open.

practice.stem:
A constant stimulus was applied to a receptor for 10 s and the frequency of impulses in its sensory neurone was recorded.
Time / s: 0, 1, 2, 5, 10
Impulses per second: 40, 30, 20, 8, 5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in impulse frequency between 0 s and 10 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: This decrease is called adaptation. Suggest the advantage of adaptation to an animal.
parts.answer: Unchanging, unimportant stimuli (e.g. clothes on skin) are ignored; the nervous system is free to respond to new changes/danger.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the brain would detect that the stimulus had become stronger at 10 s.
parts.answer: Impulse frequency would increase (more action potentials per second).

practice.stem: In a hand-withdrawal reflex, the sensory neurone is 0.80 m long and conducts at 65 m s⁻¹. The motor neurone is 0.80 m long and conducts at 80 m s⁻¹. There are two synapses in the spinal cord and one neuromuscular junction, each with a delay of 0.6 ms. Ignore the conduction time in the very short relay neurone between the two spinal synapses. The muscle starts to shorten 10 ms after it is first depolarised.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total time from stimulus to the start of muscle shortening. Give your answer in ms to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A voluntary response to the same stimulus takes about 200 ms. Explain why the reflex is much faster.
parts.answer: Reflex involves few neurones and synapses (spinal cord only); the voluntary response involves the brain, many more synapses and decision-making.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Many people with long-term type 2 diabetes in Pakistan develop damage to sensory neurones in their feet (peripheral neuropathy). They are advised to inspect their feet every day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why damage to sensory neurones means a small cut or blister may go unnoticed.
parts.answer: Impulses from pain/touch receptors are not conducted to the brain (or are reduced), so the person does not feel the injury.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why these patients are also more likely to trip or lose balance.
parts.answer: Less sensory information about foot position/pressure from receptors; reflex adjustments of leg muscles are slower or absent.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Amiloride is a drug that blocks the sodium ion channels in the membranes of taste receptor cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the effect of amiloride on a person's ability to taste salt, and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Salt taste is reduced; Na⁺ cannot enter the chemoreceptor cells, so they do not depolarise (smaller receptor potential); less Ca²⁺ entry/less transmitter release, so fewer action potentials in the sensory neurone.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some salt taste remains even with a high dose of amiloride. Suggest one explanation.
parts.answer: There are other routes for Na⁺ entry/other receptors not blocked by amiloride, or not all channels are blocked.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why amiloride does not stop the person tasting sweet foods.
parts.answer: Sweet taste uses different receptors (receptor proteins for sugars), not Na⁺ channels.

practice.stem: A man whose spinal cord was completely cut in the neck region after a road accident in Lahore is still able to show the knee-jerk reflex, but he cannot feel the tap on his knee and cannot move his legs voluntarily.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the knee-jerk reflex still occurs.
parts.answer: The reflex arc passes only through the lower spinal cord below the injury; sensory and motor neurones and the synapse are undamaged.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why he cannot feel the tap.
parts.answer: Impulses cannot travel up the spinal cord past the injury to the brain (sensory cortex), so there is no conscious sensation.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why he cannot move his legs voluntarily even though his leg muscles and motor neurones work.
parts.answer: Impulses from the brain cannot pass down the spinal cord to the motor neurones.

practice.stem:
In a two-point touch test, two blunt points are pressed on the skin at different separations. The smallest separation at which a person can feel two separate points is recorded.
Fingertip: 2 mm
Palm: 10 mm
Forearm: 38 mm
Back: 42 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the separation threshold is on the back than on the fingertip.
parts.answer: 21 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the differences in the results in terms of touch receptors and sensory neurones.
parts.answer: Fingertips have a much higher density of touch receptors; each sensory neurone serves a small area (small receptive field); so two close points stimulate different neurones; on the back receptors are sparse and each neurone serves a large area, so both points may stimulate the same neurone and feel like one.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: receptor density; size of area served by one neurone; separate neurones needed for two sensations; brain interprets one neurone's signal as one point.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why it is an advantage for fingertips to have a low threshold.
parts.answer: Allows fine discrimination of texture/shape for manipulating objects precisely.

practice.stem: Capsaicin is the chemical that makes chillies hot. It binds to a receptor protein in the membranes of sensory nerve endings in the mouth. This receptor is a cation channel that is also opened by temperatures above about 43 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how eating chilli produces impulses that the brain interprets as burning heat.
parts.answer: Capsaicin opens the cation channels so Na⁺ (and Ca²⁺) diffuse in; the nerve ending depolarises (receptor potential) above threshold, producing action potentials; these travel along the same neurones used for heat, so the brain interprets them as heat.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: People in Pakistan who eat spicy food every day often become less sensitive to chilli. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Repeated stimulation desensitises the receptors / fewer receptors / channels inactivated.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Capsaicin creams are used to relieve some types of long-term pain. Suggest how they work.
parts.answer: After an initial burning, the sensory nerve endings become desensitised, so fewer pain impulses are sent.

practice.stem:
Students drank decaffeinated coffee to which different masses of caffeine had been added. Their reaction time to a light on a screen was measured 30 minutes later.
Caffeine / mg: 0, 50, 100, 150, 200
Mean reaction time / ms: 262, 248, 236, 233, 241

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of caffeine on reaction time.
parts.answer: Reaction time decreases as caffeine increases from 0 to 150 mg (262 to 233 ms), with the decrease getting smaller; at 200 mg reaction time increases again to 241 ms (still faster than with no caffeine).
parts.working: 1 mark each: decrease to 150 mg with data; increase at 200 mg.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in reaction time between 0 mg and 150 mg. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student concludes that 'the more caffeine you drink, the faster you react'. Explain why this conclusion is not supported.
parts.answer: At 200 mg the reaction time was slower than at 150 mg (and 100 mg), so it is not true for all doses.

practice.stem:
The leaflets of Mimosa pudica (touch-me-not, chhui-mui) fold up when touched and reopen later. The time taken for leaflets to reopen was recorded at different temperatures.
Temperature / °C: 15, 20, 25, 30, 35
Mean time to reopen / min: 32, 24, 17, 13, 15

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the results.
parts.answer: Time to reopen decreases from 32 min at 15 °C to a minimum of 13 min at 30 °C, then increases to 15 min at 35 °C.
parts.working: 1 mark each: decrease to 30 °C; slight rise at 35 °C (with data).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student concludes that the optimum temperature for reopening is exactly 30 °C. Explain why this conclusion cannot be made from these results.
parts.answer: Temperatures were only tested at 5 °C intervals; the true optimum could be anywhere between 25 °C and 35 °C; more temperatures (e.g. 1 °C intervals) are needed around 30 °C.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
A plant nursery in Lahore dipped stem cuttings of a rose variety into solutions of a synthetic auxin for 10 seconds before planting them. After three weeks the number of roots on each cutting was counted.
Auxin / mg dm⁻³: 0, 0.1, 1, 10, 100
Mean number of roots per cutting: 3, 6, 11, 14, 4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of auxin concentration on root formation.
parts.answer: Number of roots increases from 0 to 10 mg dm⁻³ (3 to 14 roots); at 100 mg dm⁻³ it falls to 4, only slightly more than with no auxin.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the concentration the nursery should use, and suggest why a higher concentration should not be used.
parts.answer: 10 mg dm⁻³ (in this range); 100 mg dm⁻³ inhibits rooting (high auxin concentrations inhibit root growth) and wastes auxin.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the cuttings without auxin still formed some roots.
parts.answer: Cuttings contain their own natural auxin (from buds/leaves).

practice.stem:
Oat coleoptiles were lit from one side for 4 hours. Twenty coleoptiles were used in each group.
Group 1: tip covered by a light-proof cap → 2 bent towards the light
Group 2: tip uncovered, lower part wrapped in foil → 18 bent towards the light
Group 3: nothing covered → 19 bent towards the light

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what can be concluded about the region of the coleoptile that detects light. Use the data to explain your answer.
parts.answer: The tip detects light; when only the tip is covered few bend (2/20), but covering the lower part has almost no effect (18/20, similar to 19/20).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The bending happens in the region below the tip. Suggest what this shows about the response.
parts.answer: A signal (auxin) must pass from the tip down to the growing region, where cells elongate.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why two coleoptiles with covered tips still bent.
parts.answer: Cap not fitted tightly/light leaked in, or natural variation.

practice.stem:
Percentage change in growth of roots and shoots of maize seedlings treated with auxin, compared with untreated seedlings:
Auxin concentration / mol dm⁻³: 10⁻¹², 10⁻¹⁰, 10⁻⁸, 10⁻⁶, 10⁻⁴, 10⁻³
Roots: +5, +20, −10, −40, −60, −70
Shoots: 0, +5, +30, +80, +40, −15

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of auxin concentration on the growth of roots and shoots.
parts.answer: Root growth is stimulated by very low concentrations (maximum +20 % at 10⁻¹⁰ mol dm⁻³) and inhibited at 10⁻⁸ mol dm⁻³ and above (−60 % at 10⁻⁴); shoot growth is unaffected or slightly stimulated at low concentrations, increases to a maximum (+80 %) at 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³ and is inhibited at 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ and above; roots are far more sensitive to auxin than shoots.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: root optimum at 10⁻¹⁰; root inhibition above about 10⁻⁸; shoot optimum at 10⁻⁶; shoot inhibition at high concentration; roots more sensitive than shoots (comparison with data).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student concludes: 'Auxin always increases plant growth.' Use the data to explain why this conclusion is not valid.
parts.answer: At high concentrations auxin inhibits growth (negative values: roots above 10⁻⁸, shoots at 10⁻³ and above); the effect depends on concentration and on the organ.
parts.working: B1 inhibition at high concentration with data. B1 effect depends on organ / concentration.

practice.stem:
A student studied the effect of caffeine on the heart rate of Daphnia (water fleas) at 20 °C.
Caffeine / %: 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8
Mean heart rate / beats min⁻¹: 220, 236, 251, 268, 270

parts.label: a
parts.text: The student concludes: 'Heart rate increases in proportion to caffeine concentration.' Evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: Heart rate increases with caffeine, but not in proportion: doubling 0.1 → 0.2 adds 15 beats, 0.2 → 0.4 adds 17, and 0.4 → 0.8 adds only 2, so it levels off; a proportional relationship would also pass through the origin, which it cannot (220 at 0).
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: positive trend agreed; not proportional — increases are not doubled; levels off at high concentration; intercept is not zero.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the results may not apply to humans.
parts.answer: Daphnia is an invertebrate with a different heart and nervous control; doses not comparable.

practice.stem:
Eight students recorded the hours they slept the night before and then did a computer reaction test.
Sleep / hours: 4.0, 5.0, 5.5, 6.0, 6.5, 7.0, 8.0, 9.0
Reaction time / ms: 285, 262, 270, 248, 251, 233, 228, 231

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship shown by these data.
parts.answer: Negative correlation: more sleep is linked with shorter reaction time (levelling off above about 7–8 hours).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student concludes that lack of sleep causes slower reactions. Give three reasons why this conclusion is not fully justified.
parts.answer: Correlation does not show causation; only eight students/one night (small sample); other variables not controlled (caffeine, time of day, practice, age, screen use); sleep hours self-reported/inaccurate; one test per student.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

practice.stem:
Dwarf pea plants were sprayed with gibberellin solution once a week for four weeks. Ten plants were used in each group. Mean increase in height ± standard deviation:
Water only: 18.2 ± 2.1 cm
Gibberellin 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³: 29.5 ± 4.8 cm
Gibberellin 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³: 33.0 ± 5.2 cm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the mean height increase is with 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ gibberellin than with water. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 1.8 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss what can be concluded about the effect of the two gibberellin concentrations. Refer to the standard deviations.
parts.answer: Both concentrations increase growth compared with water; the means ± SD for water (16.1–20.3) do not overlap with either gibberellin group, so this effect is likely to be real; the ranges for the two gibberellin concentrations overlap widely (24.7–34.3 and 27.8–38.2), so there may be no real difference between them; a statistical test (t-test) is needed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: gibberellin increases height; no overlap with control; overlap between the two GA groups so difference may not be significant; suggestion of t-test/more replicates.

practice.stem:
A student squeezed a spring-loaded clothes peg between thumb and forefinger as many times as possible, for five consecutive minutes without resting.
Minute: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Number of squeezes: 62, 51, 44, 39, 36

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in squeezes from minute 1 to minute 5. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the pattern and suggest a biological explanation.
parts.answer: Number of squeezes falls each minute, but the fall gets smaller; muscle fatigue: oxygen supply cannot meet demand so anaerobic respiration increases; lactate builds up and ATP supply for cross-bridge cycling and Ca²⁺ pumping falls.
parts.working: 1 mark each: pattern with decreasing rate of decline; ATP shortage/anaerobic respiration; lactate/acid build-up reduces contraction.

practice.stem:
Aleurone layers from barley grains were incubated in gibberellin solutions. A sample of each incubation liquid was then added to starch solution, and the time for the starch to disappear (no blue-black colour with iodine) was measured.
Gibberellin / mol dm⁻³: 0, 10⁻⁹, 10⁻⁸, 10⁻⁷, 10⁻⁶
Time / min: more than 60, 48, 30, 16, 12

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of starch breakdown, as 1000 ÷ time, for 10⁻⁸ and 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³ gibberellin. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 33.3 min⁻¹ and 83.3 min⁻¹ (arbitrary units)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State a conclusion from these results.
parts.answer: As gibberellin concentration increases, more amylase is released by the aleurone layer (faster starch breakdown), with the effect smaller between 10⁻⁷ and 10⁻⁶.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the result for 0 mol dm⁻³ cannot be used to calculate a rate.
parts.answer: The exact time is unknown (end point not reached within 60 min).

practice.stem:
Twelve students did a ruler-drop reaction test before and 20 minutes after drinking a cup of strong tea (contains caffeine).
Before: mean reaction time 0.203 s, 95 % confidence interval 0.190–0.216 s
After: mean reaction time 0.186 s, 95 % confidence interval 0.181–0.191 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the extent to which these results support the claim that drinking a cup of strong tea improves reaction time.
parts.answer: The mean reaction time after tea (0.186 s) was shorter than before (0.203 s), which supports the claim; but the 95 % confidence intervals overlap slightly (both include 0.190–0.191 s), so the difference may not be significant; the test was not blind and students may have improved with practice (order effect) – no control group drinking water or decaffeinated tea.
parts.working: B1 mean shorter after tea – supports. B1 confidence intervals overlap → difference may not be significant. B1 a design limitation (no control / practice effect / not blind / small sample).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the investigation could be improved to test the claim fairly.
parts.answer: Use a control group (or a separate session) drinking decaffeinated tea/water that looks and tastes the same, in random order, with students not knowing which drink they had; allow practice trials first; larger sample; use a t-test on the results.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem:
Nerve conduction speed in the legs was measured in adults with type 2 diabetes in a hospital in Faisalabad. Patients were grouped by years since diagnosis.
Years since diagnosis: 0–2, 3–5, 6–10, more than 10
