Number of patients: 34, 28, 22, 12
Mean conduction speed / m s⁻¹: 52, 49, 45, 40

parts.label: a
parts.text: A doctor claims that 'diabetes causes nerve damage that gets worse every year'. Discuss the extent to which these data support this claim.
parts.answer: Support: conduction speed falls as time since diagnosis increases (52 → 40 m s⁻¹), consistent with progressive damage. Limitations: no comparison group without diabetes; patients diagnosed longer ago are probably older and age itself slows conduction; grouped data so cannot show change every year; no measure of spread/statistical test; different and small group sizes (only 12 in last group); different individuals in each group (not followed over time); other factors such as blood glucose control not taken into account.
parts.working: B1 trend described with data. 1 mark each for up to three limitations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how a better study could test the claim.
parts.answer: Measure the same patients every year over many years (longitudinal), and compare with age-matched people without diabetes.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
The lowest concentration of sodium chloride solution that could be tasted (taste threshold) was found for 40 non-smokers and 40 smokers of the same age range.
Non-smokers: mean 0.012 mol dm⁻³, 95 % confidence interval 0.010–0.014 mol dm⁻³
Smokers: mean 0.019 mol dm⁻³, 95 % confidence interval 0.015–0.023 mol dm⁻³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what the confidence intervals allow you to conclude.
parts.answer: The intervals do not overlap, so the difference between the means is likely to be significant (not due to chance); smokers have a higher taste threshold (are less sensitive to salt).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the confidence interval for smokers is wider than for non-smokers.
parts.answer: Smokers' results are more variable (larger standard deviation), since sample sizes are equal.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the study does not prove that smoking damages salt receptors.
parts.answer: It is a correlation; smokers may differ in other ways (diet, salt intake, alcohol); no measurement of receptors themselves; habitual salty food could raise threshold.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two points.

practice.stem: A study compared 21 students who play action video games for more than 10 hours a week with 21 who never play. Mean reaction times were 182 ms and 214 ms. A t-test gave t = 3.9; the critical value at p = 0.05 for 40 degrees of freedom is 2.02.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the t-test result shows.
parts.answer: t (3.9) is greater than 2.02, so the null hypothesis is rejected; there is a significant difference in mean reaction time (probability of the difference being due to chance is less than 5 %).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A news website reports that 'playing video games makes your reactions faster'. Evaluate this claim.
parts.answer: There is a significant difference, but the study is comparative/correlational, so cause cannot be established; people with naturally fast reactions may choose to play games; groups may differ in age, sex, sleep, or practice with screens/keyboards; a controlled study training non-players would be needed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of these points.

practice.stem:
The time for Venus fly traps to close after two touches of the trigger hairs was measured at four temperatures. Five traps were tested at each temperature.
Temperature / °C: 10, 20, 30, 40
Mean closure time / s: 0.80, 0.42, 0.25, 0.31
Range / s: 0.71–0.92, 0.36–0.47, 0.21–0.30, 0.24–0.40

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain the effect of temperature on closure time between 10 °C and 30 °C.
parts.answer: Closure time decreases (0.80 to 0.25 s) as temperature rises; more kinetic energy so ions/water move faster across membranes; proton pumps/enzymes and ion channels work faster.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether the results show that closure is slower at 40 °C than at 30 °C.
parts.answer: Mean is higher at 40 °C (0.31 vs 0.25 s), but the ranges overlap (0.24–0.40 and 0.21–0.30), so the difference may not be real; only 5 traps; a statistical test is needed.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Reaction times of eight students to a sound were measured with a computer program:
245, 262, 238, 251, 270, 244, 259, 255 ms
Standard deviation s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1))

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean reaction time.
parts.answer: 253 ms

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the standard deviation. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the standard deviation tells you about these data.
parts.answer: How spread out the reaction times are around the mean.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
In 16 healthy adults, the simple reaction time (time to press a key after a light flashes) was measured. Mean = 312 ms; standard deviation = 24 ms.
Standard error SM = s ÷ √n. 95 % confidence interval = mean ± 2 × SM.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard error of the mean.
parts.answer: 6.0 ms

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the 95 % confidence interval.
parts.answer: 300 to 324 ms

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the 95 % confidence interval means.
parts.answer: It is a range that is likely to contain the true population mean: a 95 % confidence level means that about 95 % of intervals calculated this way from repeated samples would contain the true mean.
parts.working: B1 a range that estimates/likely contains the true population mean. B1 95 % confidence refers to repeated sampling (about 95 % of such intervals contain the true mean), not a 95 % probability for this one interval.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the most suitable statistical test for each investigation and give a reason.
(i) Is there a significant difference between mean reaction times of 15 left-handed and 15 right-handed students?
(ii) Is there a correlation between auxin concentration (8 concentrations) and mean root length?
(iii) Do the numbers of tall and dwarf plants in an F2 generation fit a 3 : 1 ratio?
parts.answer: (i) t-test: comparing two means of continuous, normally distributed data. (ii) Spearman's rank correlation: testing for a correlation between two variables (data need not be normally distributed). (iii) chi-squared test: comparing observed counts in categories with expected numbers.
parts.working: 1 mark each, test with reason.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: Two groups of 12 students measured their reaction times. Both groups had a mean of 230 ms. Group A had a standard deviation of 8 ms and group B had a standard deviation of 31 ms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which group's results are more variable and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Group B; larger standard deviation means values are more spread out from the mean.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the 95 % confidence interval for group A, using SM = s ÷ √n and mean ± 2 × SM. Give the limits to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: 225 to 235 ms

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why group B's results may be so variable.
parts.answer: Wider range of ages/sleep/caffeine/practice, or inconsistent method (e.g. different equipment, distractions).

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Reaction times (ms) of eight sprinters from a Lahore athletics club and eight students who do no regular sport:
Sprinters: 198, 205, 189, 210, 201, 195, 207, 192
Non-athletes: 221, 214, 230, 209, 226, 218, 235, 212
t = |x̄₁ − x̄₂| ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂)
Sprinters: s = 7.44 ms. Non-athletes: s = 9.13 ms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean for each group.
parts.answer: Sprinters 199.6 ms; non-athletes 220.6 ms

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of t. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of t at p = 0.05 for 14 degrees of freedom is 2.14. State the null hypothesis and what you can conclude.
parts.answer: Null hypothesis: there is no significant difference between the mean reaction times of sprinters and non-athletes. t = 5.04 > 2.14, so reject the null hypothesis: the difference is significant (sprinters react faster).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Eight students recorded how many hours they slept, then attempted a hand–eye coordination task and counted their errors.
Sleep / hours: 4.5, 5.0, 5.5, 6.0, 6.5, 7.0, 7.5, 8.0
Errors: 14, 11, 12, 9, 10, 6, 7, 4
rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n(n² − 1))

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The critical value for 8 pairs at p = 0.05 is 0.738. State what you can conclude.
parts.answer: |rs| = 0.929 > 0.738, so reject the null hypothesis; there is a significant negative correlation between hours of sleep and number of errors.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Tall pea plants (Le Le) were crossed with dwarf plants (le le). The F1 plants were self-pollinated. The F2 generation contained 312 tall plants and 88 dwarf plants.
χ² = Σ(O − E)² ÷ E

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected numbers of tall and dwarf plants for a 3 : 1 ratio.
parts.answer: 300 tall, 100 dwarf

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate χ².

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of χ² for 1 degree of freedom at p = 0.05 is 3.84. State what you can conclude.
parts.answer: 1.92 < 3.84, so accept the null hypothesis; the difference between observed and expected is not significant/due to chance; the results fit a 3 : 1 ratio.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Dwarf bean plants were treated with gibberellin or water. Mean final heights and standard errors:
Water: mean 18.2 cm, SM = 0.6 cm
Gibberellin: mean 41.5 cm, SM = 1.4 cm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the 95 % confidence interval (mean ± 2SM) for each group.
parts.answer: Water 17.0–19.4 cm; gibberellin 38.7–44.3 cm
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to state whether the difference between the means is likely to be significant. Explain.
parts.answer: Yes; the 95 % confidence intervals do not overlap, so the difference is unlikely to be due to chance.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: Nerve conduction speed in the median nerve was measured in 16 adult volunteers. Mean = 52.4 m s⁻¹, standard deviation = 4.8 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard error of the mean.
parts.answer: 1.2 m s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the 95 % confidence interval (mean ± 2SM).

parts.label: c
parts.text: A patient's conduction speed is 47.0 m s⁻¹. A student says that because this is outside the confidence interval the patient must have a nerve disorder. Explain why this reasoning is wrong.
parts.answer: The confidence interval describes where the population mean lies, not the range of normal individuals; individual values vary much more (SD 4.8, so about 43–62 m s⁻¹ covers most healthy people), and 47.0 is within normal variation.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Reaction times (ms) of ten volunteers of different ages in a computer reaction test:
Age / years: 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 55, 60, 65
Reaction time / ms: 212, 205, 230, 226, 241, 238, 255, 262, 249, 270
rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n(n² − 1))

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, rs. Show your working.
parts.answer: Ranks of reaction time: 2, 1, 4, 3, 6, 5, 8, 9, 7, 10; Σd² = 12; rs = 0.93
parts.working: M1 ranks correct for both variables (age ranks 1–10). M1 Σd² = 12. A1 rs = 1 − (6 × 12) ÷ (10 × 99) = 0.93.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The critical value of rs for 10 pairs at p = 0.05 is 0.648. State the null hypothesis and what you can conclude.
parts.answer: Null hypothesis: there is no correlation between age and reaction time. 0.93 > 0.648, so reject the null hypothesis: there is a significant positive correlation – reaction time increases with age.
parts.working: B1 null hypothesis (no correlation). B1 rs > critical value → significant positive correlation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this result does not prove that ageing causes slower reactions.
parts.answer: Correlation does not show cause; other factors (e.g. eyesight, practice, fitness) may vary with age; only one person of each age was tested.
parts.working: B1

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
The time taken for Mimosa leaflets to reopen after being touched was measured for ten plants at 20 °C and ten plants at 30 °C.
20 °C / min: 18, 22, 20, 25, 19, 23, 21, 24, 17, 22
30 °C / min: 14, 16, 13, 18, 15, 12, 17, 15, 16, 14

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and standard deviation for each temperature. Give the standard deviations to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 20 °C: mean 21.1 min, s = 2.60 min. 30 °C: mean 15.0 min, s = 1.83 min.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate t. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value at p = 0.05 for 18 degrees of freedom is 2.10, and at p = 0.001 it is 3.92. State the conclusion.
parts.answer: t = 6.07 > 3.92, so the difference is significant even at p = 0.001; reject the null hypothesis; leaflets reopen significantly faster at 30 °C.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Closure time of Venus fly traps was measured at eight temperatures.
Temperature / °C: 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30, 33, 36
Closure time / s: 0.62, 0.55, 0.50, 0.41, 0.43, 0.33, 0.30, 0.31

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a null hypothesis for a Spearman's rank test on these data.
parts.answer: There is no correlation between temperature and closure time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate rs, using rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n(n² − 1)). Give your answer to 3 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 ranks of closure time (smallest = 1): 8, 7, 6, 4, 5, 3, 1, 2. M1 Σd² = 164. A1 1 − 984 ÷ 504 = −0.952.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value for n = 8 at p = 0.05 is 0.738. Explain why a significant correlation does not show that temperature affects closure time at all temperatures.
parts.answer: The correlation only applies within 15–36 °C; at higher temperatures proteins denature so the trend would reverse; there is also a slight rise from 33 to 36 °C, so the trend may already be levelling off.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Ninety students were each tested with a visual, a sound and a touch stimulus. For each student the stimulus with the fastest reaction time was recorded.
Visual: 18 students; Sound: 31 students; Touch: 41 students

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the null hypothesis and calculate the expected number for each stimulus.
parts.answer: Null hypothesis: there is no difference in the number of students reacting fastest to each type of stimulus; expected = 30 each.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate χ². Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of degrees of freedom. The critical values are 5.99 (p = 0.05) and 9.21 (p = 0.01). State the conclusion.
parts.answer: 2 degrees of freedom; 8.87 > 5.99 so reject the null hypothesis at p = 0.05 (but not at p = 0.01); the type of stimulus significantly affects which gives the fastest reaction.
parts.working: B1 df = 2. B1 conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
The diameters of the clear zones (mm) produced on starch agar by six barley half-seeds without embryos, soaked in gibberellin, were:
15.2, 16.8, 14.9, 17.5, 16.1, 15.8
For six half-seeds with embryos, the mean was 13.6 mm and the 95 % confidence interval was 12.9–14.3 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean, standard deviation and standard error of the gibberellin group. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the 95 % confidence interval and compare it with the half-seeds with embryos.
parts.answer: 15.25–16.85 mm (15.3–16.8 mm); it does not overlap 12.9–14.3, so the gibberellin group produced significantly larger clear zones.
parts.working: B1 16.05 ± 0.80. B1 no overlap → significant difference.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
The two-point touch threshold on the fingertip was measured for eight guitar players and eight people who play no instrument.
Guitar players / mm: 2.1, 1.8, 2.4, 1.9, 2.2, 2.0, 1.7, 2.3
Non-players / mm: 2.4, 2.2, 2.6, 2.0, 2.5, 2.3, 2.7, 2.1
Both groups have a standard deviation of 0.245 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of t. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The critical value at p = 0.05 for 14 degrees of freedom is 2.14. State the conclusion.
parts.answer: 2.45 > 2.14, so the difference is significant; guitar players have a lower threshold (more sensitive fingertips).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the result might be different if the investigation were repeated with another sample of 8 + 8 people.
parts.answer: t is only just above the critical value; with small samples, chance variation between individuals could easily give t below 2.14; larger samples are needed to be confident.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A student wants to find out whether background noise affects reaction time. She has a computer program that shows a green square at random intervals and records the time taken to click the mouse, a sound-level meter and a speaker playing recorded traffic noise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method she could use. Include how she will vary the noise, what she will measure and how she will make the results reliable.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for six of: IV = noise level, e.g. 0 (quiet), 50, 60, 70, 80 dB, set with volume and checked with sound-level meter at the ear; DV = reaction time from program (ms); same volunteer(s) for all levels or several volunteers; same hand/mouse/chair/screen distance; practice trials before recording; at least 5 (e.g. 10) trials at each level and calculate a mean; random order of noise levels to avoid practice/fatigue effects; rest between sets; same time of day/no caffeine; quiet room with no other distractions; random interval between stimuli so clicks cannot be anticipated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the noise should not exceed about 85 dB.
parts.answer: Louder sounds could damage hearing (risk) / be uncomfortable.

practice.stem: Mung bean (moong) seeds are germinated on damp paper. A student wants to investigate the effect of auxin (IAA) concentration on root growth of the seedlings. She has a solution of IAA at 1 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how she should prepare a suitable range of IAA concentrations.
parts.answer: Serial dilution by factor of 10: e.g. 1 cm³ of stock + 9 cm³ distilled water to give 10⁻⁴, repeat to 10⁻⁵, 10⁻⁶, 10⁻⁷, 10⁻⁸; plus distilled water as a control.
parts.working: 1 mark each: tenfold serial dilution with volumes; at least five concentrations including a water control.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how she should carry out the investigation and collect results.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for five of: seedlings with roots of similar starting length (e.g. 5 mm) selected; measure initial root length with ruler; place e.g. 10 seedlings in a Petri dish on filter paper soaked with a fixed volume (e.g. 5 cm³) of each solution; same temperature (incubator 25 °C)/dark; same time (48 h); measure final root length and calculate mean change in length; repeat each concentration (three dishes); lids on to prevent evaporation.

practice.stem: Leaflets of Mimosa pudica fold when touched and later reopen. A student plans to investigate the effect of temperature on the time taken for leaflets to reopen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method for this investigation.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for six of: use plants of same age/size, same variety; place in temperature-controlled room/incubator/water bath around pot at e.g. 15, 20, 25, 30, 35 °C; allow time to acclimatise (e.g. 30 min) and check with thermometer; touch a leaf in a standard way (e.g. same glass rod, same force, same position, once); start stopwatch when touched; record time until leaflets fully reopen (define end point); same light intensity (lamp at fixed distance) and humidity; test several leaves/plants at each temperature (at least 5) and find a mean; leave time between tests on the same leaf.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the same leaf should not be tested twice in quick succession.
parts.answer: It may not have fully recovered; repeated touching can reduce its response (it may become less responsive/ not close fully).

practice.stem: A teacher wants students to investigate the effect of gibberellin concentration on the percentage germination of wheat seeds after 5 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the method the students should use.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for five of: range of GA concentrations (e.g. 0, 10⁻⁸, 10⁻⁷, 10⁻⁶, 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³) by serial dilution; same number of seeds (e.g. 50) from the same batch per dish; soak or place on filter paper with same volume of solution; dishes covered and kept at same temperature in the dark; define germination (radicle visible/≥ 2 mm); count germinated seeds daily or after 5 days and calculate percentage; three replicate dishes per concentration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the seeds should come from the same batch.
parts.answer: Seeds from different batches may differ in age, storage, viability, genetics, so this controls a variable affecting germination.

practice.stem: A student wants to investigate how the intensity of light from one side affects the curvature of oat coleoptiles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method she could use.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for five of: coleoptiles grown in the dark until a set length (e.g. 20 mm); same number (e.g. 10) per treatment; lamp placed at one side, different distances or a dimmer to vary intensity, measured with light meter; all other light excluded (box with a slit/dark room); same time of exposure (e.g. 3 h); same temperature (heat shield/water filter to stop the lamp heating); measure angle of curvature with a protractor from a photograph; calculate mean.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the coleoptiles must be grown in the dark before the experiment.
parts.answer: So they are straight/have not already bent towards light, and auxin is evenly distributed at the start.

practice.stem: Barley grains are used to make malt in breweries and bakeries. A student wants to find out how the concentration of gibberellin affects the production of amylase by the aleurone layer of barley grains.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to investigate the effect of gibberellin concentration on amylase production by barley grains, using starch agar plates.
parts.answer: Cut grains in half and use the endosperm halves without the embryo (so they make no gibberellin of their own); sterilise the surface (e.g. dilute bleach, then rinse); soak sets of half-grains in gibberellin solutions of e.g. 0, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10 mg dm⁻³ for a fixed time; place the same number of half-grains, cut surface down, on starch agar plates; incubate at the same temperature (e.g. 25 °C) for a fixed time (e.g. 48 h); flood with iodine and measure the diameter (or area) of the clear zone around each grain; at least 5 grains per concentration and calculate the mean.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: remove embryo (half-grains without embryo); at least five concentrations including 0; made by dilution / serial dilution; same soaking time and volume; surface sterilised / aseptic technique; same number of grains per plate; same temperature and time of incubation; iodine added; measure clear zone diameter / area; replicates and mean.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the embryo must be removed from each grain.
parts.answer: The embryo produces its own gibberellin; this would stimulate amylase production and mask the effect of the gibberellin supplied.
parts.working: B1 embryo makes gibberellin. B1 would affect results / not controlled.

practice.stem: Grip strength can be measured with a hand dynamometer (reading in kg). A student wants to investigate how the time spent repeatedly squeezing a hand gripper affects the maximum grip strength of the muscles of the forearm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method for this investigation, including how to make the results valid and reliable.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for seven of: measure maximum grip with dynamometer before exercise (mean of 3 with rest between); IV: duration of gripper exercise e.g. 0, 30, 60, 90, 120 s; squeeze at a fixed rate (e.g. metronome, one per second); measure maximum grip immediately after each period; full rest (e.g. 10 min) between durations so muscles recover, or different days; same hand, same arm position (e.g. elbow at 90°, seated); several volunteers of similar age/sex/fitness; same gripper; repeat and calculate mean; express as percentage of starting strength; no warm-up differences; stop if pain (risk).

practice.stem: A student wants to compare the taste threshold for salt (the lowest NaCl concentration that can be tasted) of students who add extra salt to their food with that of students who do not.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how she could prepare the solutions and find each person's taste threshold.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for five of: serial dilution of food-grade NaCl in bottled/distilled water (e.g. 0.1, 0.05, 0.025, 0.0125, 0.006 mol dm⁻³ or finer steps); fresh clean cups/sterile cotton buds for each person; present solutions in random/coded order including plain water (blind) or start from lowest; volunteer rinses mouth with water between samples; same volume and temperature of solution; record lowest concentration correctly identified as salty; repeat to confirm; no eating/smoking for 1 h before.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why each volunteer should not be told which cup contains which solution.
parts.answer: To prevent bias/guessing affecting the response (blind test).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify one safety or hygiene precaution.
parts.answer: Use food-grade salt and clean, single-use cups; do not use laboratory glassware; volunteers with high blood pressure/illness excluded; samples spat out.

practice.stem: The diameter of the pupil changes with light intensity. A student wants to investigate this using a lamp, a light meter and a camera that can photograph the eye next to a millimetre scale.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to investigate the effect of light intensity on pupil diameter.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for six of: darkened room; volunteer sits with head on chin rest at fixed distance from lamp; vary light intensity (dimmer or distance) and measure with light meter at eye level, at least 5 intensities; allow time to adapt (e.g. 1 min) at each intensity; photograph eye with mm scale beside it at same distance; measure pupil diameter from photo using scale; repeat (3 photos each) and calculate mean; same eye; several volunteers; random order or allow recovery.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the lamp should never be very bright or shone directly into the eye for a long time.
parts.answer: Could damage the retina.

practice.stem: Water fleas (Daphnia) are transparent, so their heart can be seen under a microscope. A student wants to investigate the effect of caffeine concentration on Daphnia heart rate. He has a 1 % caffeine solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how he should carry out the investigation.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for six of: dilute stock to give e.g. 0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4 % using pond water; place one Daphnia in a small volume of solution on a cavity slide with cotton fibres to restrict movement; leave for a fixed time (e.g. 5 min) to equilibrate; count heartbeats for 15 s using a tally counter, multiply by 4; same temperature (e.g. cold light source/not too long under microscope lamp); use a fresh Daphnia of similar size for each concentration (or rinse and rest); at least 5 Daphnia per concentration; mean heart rate calculated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one ethical point about this investigation and how it could be addressed.
parts.answer: Animals may be harmed — use the minimum number, short exposure, return them to pond water afterwards / use an invertebrate.

practice.stem: Segments of wheat coleoptiles, 10 mm long, elongate when floated in IAA (auxin) solution. A student wants to find out whether auxin acts by lowering the pH of the cell walls.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to test whether acidic conditions alone cause the same elongation as auxin.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for six of: cut segments of equal length (10 mm) from below the tip with a sharp blade; remove tip so no natural auxin; float in buffer solutions of different pH (e.g. 3.5, 4.5, 5.5, 6.5, 7.5) without auxin; plus a set in auxin solution at pH 6.5 (neutral buffer) and a buffer-only control at pH 6.5; same number of segments (e.g. 10) per dish; same volume of solution; same temperature in the dark; same time (e.g. 18 h); measure final length with ruler/graph paper or eyepiece graticule; calculate mean percentage increase; compare acid-only elongation with auxin elongation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the segments are kept in the dark.
parts.answer: Light can affect auxin distribution and growth, so it is a confounding variable.

practice.stem: A researcher wants to find out whether there is a correlation between age and the two-point touch threshold on the palm of the hand, using people aged 10 to 80 years from a town in Sindh.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the investigation should be carried out, including how participants are chosen and how the threshold is measured.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for six of: random or stratified sample across ages, e.g. at least 5 people in each decade (large sample); exclude people with diabetes/nerve disease or calloused hands; informed consent (and parental consent for children); use dividers/two-point tool; apply points at same pressure to same area of palm; participant's eyes closed; randomly alternate one and two points to check for guessing; start with large separation and decrease in 1 mm steps; threshold = smallest separation correctly felt as two in e.g. 3 out of 3 trials; same tester and room temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the statistical test that should be used and why.
parts.answer: Spearman's rank correlation (or Pearson's if both normally distributed); to test whether there is a significant correlation between two variables.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A botanical garden in Islamabad has 30 Venus fly trap plants. A student wants to investigate the effect of temperature on the time traps take to close after being stimulated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to obtain valid and reliable results.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for seven of: plants placed in growth chamber/ incubator at e.g. 15, 20, 25, 30, 35 °C with time to acclimatise (e.g. 1 h); same light intensity and humidity; select traps of similar size/age that have not closed recently; stimulate two trigger hairs in a standard way with a fine brush/hair, within e.g. 5 s; record with a high-speed video camera (or slow-motion phone) with a timer; measure time from second touch to complete closure (defined end point) frame by frame; one trap per plant per temperature or allow full reopening (e.g. 24 h) before reuse; use different traps for each temperature in random order; at least 5 traps per temperature; calculate mean and SD.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why each trap should not be tested many times.
parts.answer: Each closure uses energy and traps can only close a limited number of times before dying; repeated closure may change response time.

practice.stem: Dwarf pea plants respond to gibberellin. A student plans to test the hypothesis that the increase in height caused by gibberellin depends on its concentration. She has 60 dwarf pea seedlings, a gibberellin solution of 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ and a spray bottle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the method, including the experimental design and the measurements.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for six of: concentrations 0 (with same solvent/wetting agent), 10⁻⁸, 10⁻⁷, 10⁻⁶, 10⁻⁵, 10⁻⁴ by serial dilution; 10 seedlings per treatment, randomly assigned; seedlings same age/initial height (measure initial height); same volume sprayed (e.g. same number of sprays) at same time weekly; shield other plants when spraying; same soil, pot size, watering, light, temperature (randomise positions in greenhouse); measure height from soil to tip weekly for 4 weeks; calculate mean increase in height.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how she would decide whether the difference between two of the treatments is significant.
parts.answer: Use a t-test on the height increases of the two groups (calculate SD of each); compare t with the critical value at p = 0.05 for 18 degrees of freedom; if t is greater, the difference is significant.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A student believes that reaction time improves with practice. He has a computer reaction-time program.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to test this, including how he will control for fatigue and how the results will be processed.
parts.answer: See mark points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for six of: volunteers who have not used the program before; each volunteer does e.g. 10 blocks of 10 trials; record mean reaction time of each block; short fixed rest between blocks to reduce fatigue; same time of day, same hand, same screen distance; random stimulus intervals; several (e.g. 15) volunteers; plot mean reaction time against block number; use Spearman's rank to test correlation; compare first and last blocks with a t-test; second session another day to separate learning from fatigue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why reaction time might stop improving after many blocks.
parts.answer: There is a physiological limit (conduction time, synaptic delays), or fatigue/boredom balances learning.

practice.stem: In a nerve conduction study, an impulse travelled 360 mm along a nerve in 6.0 ms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of conduction in m s⁻¹.
parts.answer: 60 m s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how long, in ms, the impulse would take to travel 0.15 m at the same speed.
parts.answer: 2.5 ms

practice.stem: A student's mean reaction time was 0.284 s before a session of brisk exercise and 0.247 s immediately after.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in reaction time. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 13.0 % decrease

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert both reaction times to ms.
parts.answer: 284 ms and 247 ms

practice.stem: A student makes a stock solution of IAA (auxin), Mr = 175.2, at 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of IAA needed to make 250 cm³ of stock solution, in mg.

parts.label: b
parts.text: She makes a series of tenfold dilutions. State how many dilutions are needed to reach 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³, and how to make 10 cm³ of each dilution.
parts.answer: Four dilutions; 1 cm³ of the previous solution + 9 cm³ of distilled water.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Lengths of the roots of eight seedlings grown in 10⁻⁸ mol dm⁻³ auxin for 3 days:
23, 25, 22, 8, 24, 26, 21, 25 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and calculate the mean root length without it. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 8 mm is anomalous; mean = 23.7 mm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the range of the remaining results.
parts.answer: 5 mm

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason for the anomalous result.
parts.answer: Damaged seed/root, seed not viable or germinated late.

practice.stem: A microelectrode in a sensory neurone from a stretch receptor recorded 37 action potentials in 2.5 s when a muscle was stretched slightly, and 92 action potentials in 2.5 s when it was stretched more.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of impulses in each case, in Hz (impulses per second).
parts.answer: 14.8 Hz and 36.8 Hz

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the frequency is with the larger stretch. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 2.5 times

practice.stem:
In a ruler-drop test, a partner drops a metre rule and the student catches it as quickly as possible. The distance the ruler falls is d. Reaction time t = √(2d ÷ g), with d in metres and g = 9.81 m s⁻².
Distances before an energy drink / cm: 21, 19, 18, 23, 20

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean distance before the energy drink, in cm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the mean distance and the formula to calculate the mean reaction time before the drink. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: After the drink the mean distance was 17.0 cm. Calculate the reaction time and the percentage decrease in reaction time. Give the percentage to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 0.186 s; 8.3 % decrease
parts.working: B1 √(2 × 0.170 ÷ 9.81) = 0.186 s. B1 (0.203 − 0.186) ÷ 0.203 × 100 = 8.3 % (using unrounded times; 8.4 % from the rounded values is also accepted).

practice.stem:
The length of a coleoptile was measured every 2 hours after a block containing auxin was placed on its cut tip.
Time / h: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8
Length / mm: 12.0, 13.4, 15.1, 16.9, 18.2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of growth over the 8 hours, in mm h⁻¹. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.78 mm h⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the 2-hour interval with the fastest growth and calculate the rate in that interval.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in length over 8 hours. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

practice.stem:
A student counted the heartbeats of a Daphnia for 15 s before and after adding a caffeine solution.
Before: 55 beats in 15 s
After: 67 beats in 15 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the heart rate before and after in beats min⁻¹.
parts.answer: 220 and 268 beats min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in heart rate. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why counting for 15 s and multiplying by 4 gives a less accurate result than counting for a full minute.
parts.answer: Any miscount (e.g. one beat) is multiplied by 4; partial beats at start/end make a larger percentage error.

practice.stem: On an electron micrograph of a skeletal muscle fibre, one sarcomere measures 18 mm from Z line to Z line. The actual length of the sarcomere is 2.4 µm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the micrograph.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The H zone on the same micrograph measures 3.0 mm. Calculate its actual length in µm.
parts.answer: 0.4 µm

parts.label: c
parts.text: The micrograph shows the A band as 12 mm long. Calculate the actual length of the A band and the total actual length of the I band in this sarcomere.
parts.answer: A band 1.6 µm; I band 0.8 µm

practice.stem: A student has a 2.0 % caffeine stock solution and distilled water. She needs 20 cm³ of each of the following: 0.1 %, 0.2 %, 0.4 %, 0.8 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volumes of stock solution and water needed for each concentration.
parts.working: M1 volume of stock = 20 × (C ÷ 2.0). A2 all four correct (A1 for two or three correct).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total volume of stock solution needed.
parts.answer: 15 cm³

practice.stem: Extracts from barley aleurone layers were added to starch solution. The time for the starch to be completely broken down was 40 min for the extract from layers incubated in water and 10 min for the extract from layers incubated in gibberellin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of starch breakdown (1000 ÷ time, in arbitrary units) for each extract.
parts.answer: 25 and 100 arbitrary units

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in rate caused by gibberellin.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why 1000 ÷ time can be used as a measure of rate.
parts.answer: Rate is inversely proportional to the time taken for the same amount of starch to be broken down.

practice.stem:
The mean time for Mimosa leaflets to reopen was 21.1 min at 20 °C and 15.0 min at 30 °C.
The temperature coefficient Q₁₀ = rate at (T + 10) °C ÷ rate at T °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of reopening (1 ÷ time) at each temperature, in min⁻¹. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.0474 min⁻¹ and 0.0667 min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Q₁₀ for reopening between 20 °C and 30 °C. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Many enzyme-controlled processes have a Q₁₀ of about 2. Suggest why the Q₁₀ for reopening is lower.
parts.answer: Reopening depends partly on physical processes such as diffusion/osmotic water movement, which are less affected by temperature than enzyme reactions.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Coleoptile segments, each 10.0 mm long, were floated in either buffer alone or buffer with auxin for 18 hours. Mean final lengths: buffer alone 11.2 mm; buffer with auxin 14.8 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in length for each treatment.
parts.answer: Buffer 12 %; auxin 48 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the increase in length caused by auxin alone, and express it as a ratio of the increase with auxin to the increase without auxin.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of auxin-induced growth in µm h⁻¹.
parts.answer: 200 µm h⁻¹

practice.stem:
Barley grains were germinated in three dishes of 50 grains for each treatment.
Gibberellin: 46, 44, 47 germinated
Water: 31, 28, 34 germinated

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean percentage germination for each treatment. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Gibberellin 91.3 %; water 62.0 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times more grains failed to germinate in water than in gibberellin. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 4.4 times
parts.working: M1 failures: water 150 − 93 = 57; gibberellin 150 − 137 = 13. A1 57 ÷ 13 = 4.4.

practice.stem:
In a clinical test of the median nerve, the nerve was stimulated at the wrist and then at the elbow, and the time to the start of the response in a thumb muscle (latency) was recorded.
Stimulus at wrist: 3.4 ms
Stimulus at elbow: 7.8 ms
Distance between the two stimulation points: 24.0 cm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the conduction speed between the elbow and wrist. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the speed cannot be calculated simply as the distance from the wrist to the muscle divided by 3.4 ms.
parts.answer: The 3.4 ms includes the delay at the neuromuscular junction and the time for the muscle fibres to depolarise, not just conduction; subtracting two latencies cancels these delays.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the latency if the nerve were stimulated 12.0 cm above the elbow. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 10 ms

practice.stem: A student compares the reaction times of his dominant and non-dominant hands with a ruler-drop test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent and dependent variables.
parts.answer: Independent: whether the student uses the dominant or non-dominant hand. Dependent: distance the ruler falls (reaction time).
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three variables that should be standardised and explain how one of them could be controlled.
parts.answer: Starting position of the ruler (zero mark level with the top of the thumb); gap between thumb and finger (e.g. 2 cm); same person dropping the ruler; no warning before the drop / random delay; same time of day, posture, distractions.
parts.working: B1 B1 two valid variables. B1 method of control for one, e.g. use a fixed 2 cm gap marked on a card. (Max 3.)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the dropper should vary the time before releasing the ruler.
parts.answer: So the student cannot predict the drop and respond in anticipation; the test measures reaction to the stimulus.
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: A student investigates the effect of temperature on the time taken for Venus fly traps to close after their trigger hairs are touched twice.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: temperature. Dependent: time taken for the trap to close.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three variables that should be standardised and describe how one of them could be controlled.
parts.answer: e.g. size/age of trap, light intensity, humidity, way hairs are touched, time between the two touches, time since the trap last closed/fed; e.g. touch with the same fine brush, two touches 5 s apart timed with a stopwatch.
parts.working: B2 three variables (B1 for two). B1 one method of control.

practice.stem: Barley grains were soaked in gibberellin solutions of different concentrations, and the percentage that germinated in 4 days was recorded. One dish of grains was soaked in distilled water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the purpose of the dish soaked in distilled water.
parts.answer: It is a control; shows how many grains germinate without added gibberellin, so any increase can be attributed to the gibberellin.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two variables, other than those mentioned, that must be kept the same for all dishes.
parts.answer: e.g. number of grains, variety/batch of grains, temperature, volume of solution, light/dark, soaking time.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Volunteers did a computer reaction test, then drank 250 cm³ of an energy drink containing caffeine and repeated the test 30 minutes later.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three variables that should be controlled for each volunteer.
parts.answer: e.g. no other caffeine that day; same hand and mouse; same distance from screen; same time of day; same room/no distractions; same number of practice trials; same sleep/no exercise before.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a second group should drink a drink that looks and tastes the same but contains no caffeine.
parts.answer: Acts as a placebo/control; shows whether improvement is due to practice, the sugar/drink itself or expectation, rather than caffeine.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A student counts how many leaflets on a Mimosa leaf fold when the leaf tip is touched with different numbers of light taps (1 to 5 taps).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent and dependent variables.
parts.answer: IV: number of taps. DV: number of leaflets that fold.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two variables that should be controlled and why each could affect the results.
parts.answer: Force of each tap — stronger taps may cause more folding; time since the leaf was last touched — a recently touched leaf may not have recovered; also temperature/light/age of leaf.
parts.working: 1 mark each, with reason.

practice.stem: Moong seedlings were grown on filter paper soaked in different auxin concentrations at 25 °C for 2 days, and root length was measured.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of variable that temperature is in this investigation, and explain why it must be kept at 25 °C.
parts.answer: A standardised (controlled) variable; temperature affects rate of growth (enzymes/respiration), so changes would affect root length independently of auxin.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the student could keep the volume of solution available to each seedling the same throughout the 2 days.
parts.answer: Use the same volume per dish and cover the dishes (lids/cling film) to prevent evaporation.

practice.stem: Daphnia heart rate is counted under a microscope after placing the animal in a caffeine solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the temperature of the water around the Daphnia must be controlled, and describe how it could be done.
parts.answer: Daphnia is ectothermic so heart rate rises with temperature; microscope lamp heats the slide; use a cold light source/LED or a heat filter, limit time under the lamp, monitor temperature with a thermometer/keep in water bath before counting.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: reason (rate depends on temperature); lamp heating; method of control.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why each Daphnia should be left in the solution for the same time before counting.
parts.answer: Caffeine takes time to enter the body/reach the heart; effect may change with time of exposure, so time must be standardised.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Students measured the two-point touch threshold on the back of the hand of 20 volunteers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest three variables that must be standardised when applying the points, and explain why one of them matters.
parts.answer: Pressure applied; both points touching at exactly the same time; same area of skin; volunteer's eyes closed; skin temperature; e.g. greater pressure stimulates more receptors over a wider area, so two points may be felt at smaller separations.
parts.working: B3 three variables. B1 explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the tester should sometimes apply only one point.
parts.answer: To check whether the volunteer is guessing/to detect false reports of 'two'.

practice.stem: A student compares the grip strength of the dominant and non-dominant hand of 15 classmates using a hand dynamometer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest three variables that should be controlled.
parts.answer: Same dynamometer; same body position (standing, arm by side, elbow angle); same number of attempts and rest between attempts; time of day; no exercise beforehand; same encouragement.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the order in which the hands are tested should be varied between volunteers.
parts.answer: Testing one hand first every time could introduce fatigue or practice effects that bias the comparison; alternating/randomising order cancels this.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Coleoptile segments were floated in solutions to investigate the role of pH in auxin-induced elongation. The tip of each coleoptile was removed before the segments were cut.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the tips were removed.
parts.answer: Tips produce natural auxin, which would add to/confound the effect of the treatments.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why each solution was made with a buffer.
parts.answer: To keep the pH constant throughout the experiment; cells pump H⁺ which would otherwise change the pH of the solution.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a suitable control for the experiment testing whether auxin works at neutral pH.
parts.answer: Segments in the same neutral buffer without auxin.

practice.stem: Seedlings are placed in a box with a single opening facing a lamp, to study bending towards the light.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the lamp's heat must be controlled and suggest how.
parts.answer: Heat could cause uneven growth/drying on one side, making temperature a second variable; place a water filter/heat shield between lamp and box, or use an LED lamp.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why the box must exclude light from all other directions.
parts.answer: So that only the direction of the lamp's light affects bending.

practice.stem: A researcher wants to test whether caffeine tablets improve reaction time. 40 volunteers are available.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the researcher should use a placebo and a double-blind design, and why each is needed.
parts.answer: Half (randomly allocated) receive an identical-looking tablet without caffeine (placebo); this controls for the expectation effect/psychological effect of taking a tablet; double-blind: neither volunteers nor the person testing know who received which tablet (coded); prevents bias in how the test is run or results recorded.
parts.working: 1 mark each: placebo described; reason; double-blind described; reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why volunteers should be randomly allocated to the two groups.
parts.answer: To avoid systematic differences between groups (e.g. age, habitual caffeine use), so other variables are spread evenly.

practice.stem: In a field study in Sindh, the reaction times of 200 people aged 15–75 were recorded at community health camps to look for a correlation with age.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why it is not possible to control variables in the same way as in a laboratory experiment.
parts.answer: Age cannot be assigned by the researcher; participants differ in many other ways (health, sleep, eyesight, caffeine, education/computer use) that cannot be fixed.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest three ways the researcher could reduce the effect of these other variables.
parts.answer: Large sample size; record and exclude people with conditions such as diabetes or poor eyesight; same equipment, instructions and time of day; equal numbers of men and women in each age group/matching; ask about caffeine/sleep and analyse separately.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A student uses Venus fly traps from several plants. Some traps are newly opened and some have closed and reopened several times. Some have recently digested an insect.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why these differences are a problem for an investigation into the effect of light intensity on closure speed.
parts.answer: Trap age and recent activity/feeding may affect closure speed (energy reserves, cell turgor, ion gradients), so they are uncontrolled variables that could mask or mimic an effect of light.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the student could design the investigation so these variables do not bias the results.
parts.answer: Use only traps of similar age that have not closed or fed recently, or randomly allocate traps to light intensities so differences are spread evenly; record trap history; use large numbers.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Half-seeds of barley without embryos were placed on starch agar with gibberellin. A student found clear zones even on a control plate with boiled half-seeds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the boiled half-seeds were included as a control.
parts.answer: To show that any starch breakdown needs living aleurone cells (amylase made by the seed), not other factors.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why clear zones appeared around the boiled half-seeds, and how each problem could be prevented.
parts.answer: Bacteria or fungi on the seed surface secrete amylase onto the starch: surface-sterilise the seeds (e.g. brief dilute bleach, then rinse) and use sterile agar. Boiling was too brief, so some amylase was not denatured: boil for longer (e.g. 10 minutes) before use.
parts.working: 1 mark for each cause (max 2): microbes on the seed secreting amylase; incomplete denaturation of the enzyme by short boiling. 1 mark for each matching prevention (max 2): sterilise seeds and agar; boil for longer.

practice.stem: A student plans to investigate how temperature affects the time taken for Mimosa leaflets to reopen after being touched.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a suitable hypothesis.
parts.answer: As temperature increases (up to an optimum), the time taken for leaflets to reopen decreases.
parts.working: B1 states a testable relationship between IV and DV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give a biological explanation for your hypothesis.
parts.answer: Reopening depends on movement of ions and water into cells/active transport; higher temperature gives more kinetic energy and faster enzyme/pump activity.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A student wants to compare the mean reaction times of students who play a musical instrument and students who do not.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a null hypothesis suitable for a t-test.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the mean reaction times of students who play an instrument and those who do not.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the alternative hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is a significant difference between the mean reaction times of the two groups.

practice.stem: Auxin stimulates elongation of shoot cells at low concentrations, but high concentrations inhibit root growth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how root length of seedlings will change as auxin concentration increases from 10⁻¹² to 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³.
parts.answer: Root length decreases as auxin concentration increases: at the lowest concentrations the roots are only slightly shorter than the control, and at 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ they are much shorter. Roots are more sensitive to auxin than shoots, so they are inhibited at concentrations that promote shoot elongation.
parts.working: 1 mark each: root length falls as concentration rises (negative trend); inhibition at high concentrations, and roots already shorter at low concentrations because they are more sensitive than shoots.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the experiment should include a control with no auxin.
parts.answer: To compare each concentration with normal growth and see whether it stimulates or inhibits.

practice.stem: A student plans to add caffeine to the water around Daphnia and count the heart rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: As caffeine concentration increases, the heart rate of Daphnia increases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a prediction for the shape of a graph of heart rate against caffeine concentration, with a reason.
parts.answer: Heart rate rises then levels off (plateau); at high concentrations all receptors/targets are affected so no further increase (or toxic decrease).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Taste buds are replaced regularly, but the number of taste buds falls in older people.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a hypothesis about the relationship between age and the taste threshold for salt.
parts.answer: The taste threshold for salt increases with age (older people need saltier solutions to detect salt).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the biological reasoning behind your hypothesis.
parts.answer: Fewer taste buds/chemoreceptor cells means fewer receptor cells are stimulated at low concentrations; a higher concentration is needed to produce enough receptor potentials/impulses to be detected.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A student plans to compare reaction times when the stimulus is a sound (a beep) and when it is a light (a screen flashing), using a computer program and 20 volunteers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a hypothesis for this investigation and give a biological reason for it.
parts.answer: The mean reaction time will be shorter when a sound is used as the stimulus than when a light is used; because converting light into impulses in the retina involves a slower series of chemical reactions, whereas sound receptors are stimulated mechanically and respond faster.
parts.working: B1 directional hypothesis. B1 reasonable biological reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State a null hypothesis suitable for a t-test.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the mean reaction time to a sound stimulus and to a light stimulus.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a correlation test would not be appropriate for this investigation.
parts.answer: The investigation compares two groups / two conditions (categoric independent variable), not a relationship between two continuous variables.
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: Coleoptiles were lit from one side. In group P, a thin mica plate (impermeable to auxin) was inserted vertically into the tip on the shaded side, cutting off the shaded half of the tip from the region below. In group Q, the mica plate was inserted on the lit side in the same way.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict whether each group will bend towards the light. Explain your predictions.
parts.answer: P: little or no bending; auxin moves towards the shaded side but cannot pass down that side, so the shaded side does not elongate more. Q: bends towards the light (like normal); auxin that moved to the shaded side can pass down; shaded side elongates more.
parts.working: B1 P prediction. B1 P reason. B1 Q prediction. B1 Q reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the hypothesis that this experiment tests.
parts.answer: Bending towards light is caused by auxin moving down the shaded side of the coleoptile.

practice.stem: A student plans to compare reaction times to a touch on the shoulder and to a touch on the ankle, using a computer key press.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict which stimulus will give the longer reaction time and explain why.
parts.answer: Ankle; the sensory pathway from the ankle to the brain is longer, so conduction takes more time.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The difference in path length is about 1.2 m and conduction speed is about 60 m s⁻¹. Calculate the predicted difference in reaction time.
parts.answer: 20 ms

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the measured difference may be hard to detect.
parts.answer: 20 ms is small compared with the variation between trials (often ±20–30 ms) so many repeats are needed.

practice.stem: Plants heterozygous for a recessive allele that makes them unable to respond to gibberellin are crossed. A student counts the tall and dwarf offspring.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the expected ratio and the null hypothesis for a chi-squared test.
parts.answer: 3 tall : 1 dwarf; there is no significant difference between the observed and expected (3 : 1) numbers.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Of 240 offspring, predict the expected number of dwarf plants.

practice.stem: A student plans to measure nerve conduction speed in a volunteer's forearm before and after the arm has been cooled in cold water for 10 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a hypothesis and give a biological reason for it.
parts.answer: Cooling the arm will decrease conduction speed; at lower temperature ions diffuse more slowly; voltage-gated channels open and close more slowly (and Na⁺/K⁺ pump slower).
parts.working: B1 hypothesis. 1 mark each for two reasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict how the speed will change in the 20 minutes after the arm is removed from the water.
parts.answer: It will gradually increase back to the original value as the arm warms.

practice.stem: The pupil of the eye changes size depending on the brightness of the light.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a hypothesis about the effect of light intensity on pupil diameter.
parts.answer: As light intensity increases, pupil diameter decreases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the shape of a graph of pupil diameter against light intensity and explain the shape.
parts.answer: Diameter falls steeply at low intensities then levels off at high intensity, because the pupil has a minimum size (circular muscles fully contracted).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Two hypotheses are proposed to explain how auxin causes stem cells to elongate quickly.
Hypothesis 1: auxin lowers the pH of the cell wall.
Hypothesis 2: auxin increases synthesis of new cell wall material.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe an experiment that could distinguish between these hypotheses, and state the results predicted by each hypothesis.
parts.answer: Float segments in auxin solution in a strong neutral buffer (pH 7) versus auxin in unbuffered solution, and acid buffer (pH 4.5) without auxin. Hypothesis 1 predicts: no rapid elongation with auxin in neutral buffer, and elongation in acid buffer without auxin. Hypothesis 2 predicts: elongation with auxin even in neutral buffer, and no elongation in acid without auxin. (Alternatively inhibit cellulose synthesis.)
parts.working: B1 suitable experiment (buffer/acid/inhibitor). B1 control. B1 prediction for hypothesis 1. B1 prediction for hypothesis 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is possible for both hypotheses to be partly correct.
parts.answer: Rapid early elongation may be due to acidification while longer-term growth needs new wall synthesis.

practice.stem: A nerve contains many axons with different thresholds. A single stimulus of increasing voltage was applied and the total electrical response of the whole nerve was recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how the size of the total response will change as stimulus voltage increases from zero. Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: No response at very low voltage (below all thresholds); then the response increases as voltage increases, as more axons reach threshold; each axon gives an all-or-nothing action potential, so total depends on the number of axons firing; it reaches a maximum when all axons fire and does not increase further.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this does not contradict the all-or-nothing principle.
parts.answer: All-or-nothing applies to each individual axon; the nerve's graded response comes from different numbers of axons firing.

practice.stem: A student writes: 'Exercise is good for your reactions.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this is not a testable hypothesis, and rewrite it as one.
parts.answer: It does not name measurable variables or a direction/quantity; e.g. 'Mean reaction time to a visual stimulus is shorter after 10 minutes of moderate cycling than before it.'
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the results you would expect if your hypothesis is correct and if it is wrong.
parts.answer: Correct: significantly lower mean reaction time after exercise (t-test, p < 0.05). Wrong: no significant difference (or longer times).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A barley variety has a mutation in the DELLA protein so that it is not broken down when gibberellin binds to its receptor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the results of placing embryo-free half-seeds of this variety on starch agar containing gibberellin, compared with normal barley. Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Little or no clear zone with the mutant, but a large clear zone with normal barley; DELLA remains and keeps inhibiting the transcription factor; amylase gene not transcribed.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the effect of adding extra gibberellin to the mutant half-seeds.
parts.answer: No (or very little) increase; extra gibberellin cannot cause breakdown of the mutant DELLA.

practice.stem: A student measured reaction time with a computer program that flashes a red circle and records the time to press the space bar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two sources of error in this method.
parts.answer: Anticipation if the circle appears at regular intervals; distractions/noise; changes in attention or fatigue; keyboard delay; finger not resting on key in same position.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an improvement for each source of error you identified.
parts.answer: Random time intervals; quiet room/headphones; rest between sets; finger kept resting on the key; same keyboard.
parts.working: 1 mark each, matched.

practice.stem: The time for Mimosa leaflets to reopen was measured with a stopwatch by watching the leaf.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the end point is difficult to judge.
parts.answer: Leaflets reopen gradually, so deciding when they are 'fully open' is subjective.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two improvements to make the timing more accurate.
parts.answer: Define the end point (e.g. leaflets at 90 % of original angle); time-lapse video with a timer; same observer; compare with photo of the leaf before touching.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Seedling roots were measured with a 30 cm ruler marked in mm. Some roots were curved.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the curved roots may give inaccurate measurements and suggest an improvement.
parts.answer: A straight ruler underestimates a curved length; lay a piece of thread along the root then measure the thread / straighten gently on graph paper.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the uncertainty in each reading and explain why it is significant for roots that are only 5 mm long.
parts.answer: ±0.5 mm (half the smallest division); 0.5 ÷ 5 = 10 % error, which is large.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A student found it hard to count the heart rate of Daphnia because the heart beats more than 200 times a minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two ways to improve the accuracy of the counts.
parts.answer: Video the heart through the microscope and replay in slow motion; use a tally counter; count dots on paper with a pencil; count for longer (e.g. 30–60 s).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why repeating the count three times for each Daphnia improves reliability.
parts.answer: Allows anomalous counts to be identified and a mean calculated, reducing the effect of random counting errors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between random errors and systematic errors, with one example of each in a ruler-drop reaction test.
parts.answer: Random errors vary unpredictably between readings (e.g. reading the ruler at slightly different points, varying attention); systematic errors shift all readings in the same direction (e.g. always reading from the bottom of the thumb instead of the top, or the ruler's zero not at the fingers).
parts.working: 1 mark each: random definition; example; systematic definition; example.

practice.stem: Students use a ruler-drop test to measure reaction time, reading the distance the ruler falls at the top of the thumb.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three sources of error in the ruler-drop method.
parts.answer: Ruler not always released from the same height / zero not level with the thumb; distance read from where the thumb is, which is imprecise; the catcher may anticipate the drop; the ruler may not fall vertically; gap between finger and thumb varies; tiredness or learning over repeated trials.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest improvements to reduce two of these errors.
parts.answer: Use a clamp or marked starting line so the ruler starts at the same height; read the scale at the top of the thumb each time / use a ruler with larger divisions; vary the delay before dropping; use a computer reaction timer or light gate; give practice trials and rests between trials.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two improvements matched to errors.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the student does five practice trials before recording any results.
parts.answer: To reduce the learning (practice) effect, so improvement during the test does not distort the comparison.
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: The curvature of coleoptiles was measured by placing a protractor against each coleoptile while it was still growing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two problems with this method.
parts.answer: Difficult to align protractor with curved tip/parallax; coleoptile may be touched or damaged; the coleoptile continues to bend during measuring; different readers judge the angle differently.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an improved method.
parts.answer: Photograph (or trace a shadowgraph of) each coleoptile at the same time and measure the angle on the image with a protractor/software, using a standard reference line.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Ten volunteers each squeezed a hand dynamometer three times with their dominant hand. The readings for one volunteer were 38, 37 and 26 kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous reading and suggest a cause.
parts.answer: 26 kg; volunteer not gripping fully/fatigue/poor grip position/hand slipped.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways to improve the reliability of the results for all volunteers.
parts.answer: Practice attempt; standard posture; rest of e.g. 1 min between attempts; more attempts and use mean (excluding anomalies); standard encouragement; same time of day.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Clear zones around barley half-seeds on starch agar were measured with a ruler. Some zones were oval and had fuzzy edges.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest how the size of each clear zone should be measured to improve accuracy.
parts.answer: Measure two diameters at right angles and take the mean (or calculate area); use a ruler against a white background/through a hand lens; consistent judgement of edge (e.g. where blue-black colour starts).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why zones may be oval.
parts.answer: The half-seed is not round/enzyme diffuses unevenly; agar not level so uneven thickness.

practice.stem: In a test of the taste threshold for salt, volunteers tasted solutions starting from the most concentrated and working down to the weakest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this order could cause an error.
parts.answer: Receptors adapt to/salt remains from the strong solutions, so weak solutions may not be detected; the threshold would be overestimated.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two improvements.
parts.answer: Start with weakest solution and work upwards; rinse the mouth with distilled water between samples; wait a set time between samples; random order including water blanks.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A lamp was placed 10 cm from Mimosa plants in an investigation of light intensity. The temperature near the leaves rose from 24 °C to 31 °C during the experiment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how this temperature rise affects the validity of the investigation.
parts.answer: Temperature is not controlled, so it becomes a second variable; changes in response could be due to temperature rather than light intensity.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the investigation could be improved.
parts.answer: Use an LED (cool) lamp or a heat filter (water bath/glass tank) between lamp and plant; monitor temperature with a thermometer; carry out in a temperature-controlled room.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A thermometer used to set water baths for a temperature investigation on coleoptile growth always reads 2 °C higher than the true temperature.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of error and explain how it affects the results and conclusions.
parts.answer: Systematic error; every actual temperature is 2 °C lower than recorded; the pattern/trend is unchanged, but values such as the optimum temperature would be recorded 2 °C too high.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between the accuracy and the precision of the measurements in this case.
parts.answer: Readings may be precise (consistent, close together) but not accurate (not close to the true value).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and calculate the mean at 15 °C without it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the data, comment on the reliability of the results at 25 °C and 35 °C.
parts.answer: Results are quite variable (ranges 0.29–0.48 and 0.22–0.40) and the ranges overlap, so the difference between 25 °C and 35 °C may not be real; only five traps.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two improvements to the investigation.
parts.answer: More traps per temperature; video recording to time closure; traps of similar size/age; more temperatures; calculate SD/95 % CI or t-test.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: The time for starch to disappear (iodine test on drops taken every 30 s) was used to measure amylase activity. Times ranged from 12 min to 48 min.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in a time of 12 min and in a time of 48 min, if each time has an uncertainty of ±0.5 min. Give your answers to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the colour end point is a further source of error, and how it could be improved.
parts.answer: Judging when the blue-black colour has completely gone is subjective; use a colour standard/ colour chart or a colorimeter to measure absorbance.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Two-point thresholds were measured with dividers against a ruler marked in mm. Mean thresholds were 1.5 mm on the fingertip and 30 mm on the forearm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in each measurement, if each has an uncertainty of ±0.5 mm. Give your answers to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the fingertip measurements could be made more precise.
parts.answer: Use a two-point device/calipers with finer graduations (e.g. 0.1 mm or 0.5 mm steps); smaller steps between separations tested.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

subtopics.name: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

subtopics: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a peptide bond forms between two amino acids.
parts.answer: A condensation reaction between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amine group of the other; a molecule of water is removed; a C–N (peptide) bond forms, giving a dipeptide.
