parts.working: 1 mark each for: condensation; –COOH of one reacts with –NH₂ of other; water released; C–N bond / CONH link named.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the level of protein structure that is the sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide.
parts.answer: Primary structure
parts.working: B1 primary.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two types of bond, other than peptide bonds, that hold a protein molecule in its tertiary structure.
parts.answer: Any two of: hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds, hydrophobic interactions.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two; do not credit 'peptide' or 'glycosidic'.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about the R group of an amino acid is correct?
A It is the part of the amino acid that forms the peptide bond.
B It differs between amino acids and gives each amino acid its particular properties.
C It always contains a sulfur atom.
D It is removed as water when two amino acids join.
parts.answer: B It differs between amino acids and gives each amino acid its particular properties.
parts.working: The 20 amino acids share the amine and carboxyl groups and differ only in R. A is wrong: the peptide bond forms between the amine group of one amino acid and the carboxyl group of another; only cysteine (and methionine) R groups contain sulfur; the water removed comes from the –OH of the carboxyl and an H of the amine group.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the general structure of an amino acid. Name the groups attached to the central carbon atom.
parts.answer: A central carbon atom bonded to an amine group (–NH₂), a carboxyl group (–COOH), a hydrogen atom and an R group (side chain).
parts.working: 1 mark each: amine group –NH₂; carboxyl group –COOH; H atom and R group on the same central (α) carbon.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Glycine is the smallest amino acid. State what its R group is.
parts.answer: A single hydrogen atom (–H).
parts.working: B1 hydrogen atom.

parts.label: c
parts.text: When proteins are digested in the small intestine, peptide bonds are broken. Name this type of reaction and state the molecule that must be added for each bond broken.
parts.answer: Hydrolysis; one molecule of water per peptide bond.
parts.working: B1 hydrolysis; B1 water (one molecule per bond).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A technician in a hospital laboratory in Karachi compares haemoglobin and collagen. Give four differences between the two proteins, using these headings: shape of molecule, solubility in water, function, presence of a prosthetic group.
parts.answer: Shape: haemoglobin globular (compact, roughly spherical); collagen fibrous (long, rope-like). Solubility: haemoglobin soluble; collagen insoluble. Function: haemoglobin transports oxygen (metabolic role); collagen gives strength/structural support. Prosthetic group: haemoglobin has haem groups; collagen has none.
parts.working: 1 mark per correct comparison under each heading (both proteins needed for each mark).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two places in the human body where collagen is found.
parts.answer: Any two of: skin, tendons, ligaments, bone, cartilage, walls of arteries, cornea.
parts.working: Both needed for 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A solution of the enzyme amylase is heated to 90 °C for ten minutes. Which bonds in the enzyme are least likely to be broken?
A hydrogen bonds
B ionic bonds
C peptide bonds
D hydrophobic interactions
parts.answer: C peptide bonds
parts.working: Denaturation by heat breaks the weaker bonds holding the tertiary structure (hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions); the covalent peptide bonds of the primary structure stay intact. Hydrogen bonds (A) are the first to break, so A is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Haemoglobin is described as a globular protein with quaternary structure and a prosthetic group. Explain what is meant by each of the terms 'quaternary structure' and 'prosthetic group' for haemoglobin.
parts.answer: Quaternary: the molecule is made of more than one polypeptide chain – four chains (two α and two β) held together. Prosthetic group: a non-protein group permanently attached to the protein – the haem group (containing Fe²⁺) on each chain.
parts.working: B1 four polypeptides/two α + two β; B1 non-protein (haem) group attached to each chain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the structure of a haemoglobin molecule makes it soluble in water.
parts.answer: The polypeptides are folded so that hydrophobic R groups point into the centre of the molecule and hydrophilic R groups are on the outside, where they form hydrogen bonds with water.
parts.working: B1 hydrophobic R groups inside; B1 hydrophilic R groups outside/interact with water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the role of the iron ion in each haem group.
parts.answer: Each Fe²⁺ ion binds (reversibly) one oxygen molecule, so one haemoglobin carries up to four O₂.
parts.working: B1 binds O₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Human adult haemoglobin contains two α-chains of 141 amino acids each and two β-chains of 146 amino acids each. Calculate the number of water molecules released when all four polypeptides are made from free amino acids.
parts.working: M1 total amino acids = 2×141 + 2×146 = 574; each chain of n amino acids has n − 1 peptide bonds, so water = 574 − 4 = 570 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a cytoplasmic enzyme from a thermophilic bacterium found in a hot spring, a cysteine at position 52 forms a disulfide bond with another cysteine. A mutation replaces this cysteine with alanine, whose R group is –CH₃. Suggest and explain how this mutation could affect the enzyme's activity at high temperatures.
parts.answer: No disulfide bond can form (alanine has no –SH); the tertiary structure is less stable, so at high temperature the enzyme denatures more easily; the active site changes shape so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form and activity falls.
parts.working: B1 disulfide bond lost; B1 tertiary structure less stable/denatures at lower temperature; B1 active site shape changes, fewer ES complexes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A small polypeptide hormone is made of 85 amino acids. The mean relative molecular mass (Mr) of the free amino acids is 128, and the Mr of water is 18. Calculate the Mr of the polypeptide.
parts.working: 85 × 128 = 10880 (M1); 84 peptide bonds, so subtract 84 × 18 = 1512; Mr = 9368 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why replacing one amino acid in the primary structure of this polypeptide with a different amino acid may stop the hormone binding to its receptor.
parts.answer: The new R group may form different bonds (hydrogen, ionic, disulfide bonds or hydrophobic interactions) or fail to form the original ones, so the folding/tertiary structure changes; the shape of the part that binds to the receptor changes, so it is no longer complementary to the receptor.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: different R group / different properties (e.g. charge, polarity); different bonds formed or bonds lost between R groups; changed tertiary structure / folding; binding site no longer complementary in shape to receptor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Blood of a healthy adult contains 150 g of haemoglobin per dm³. The Mr of haemoglobin is 64500, and each haemoglobin molecule can carry up to four molecules of oxygen. One mole of oxygen occupies 24000 cm³ at room temperature. Calculate the maximum volume of oxygen, in cm³, that can be carried by the haemoglobin in 1 dm³ of blood. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the structure of haemoglobin allows each molecule to carry four oxygen molecules.
parts.answer: Haemoglobin has four polypeptide chains (quaternary structure: two α and two β); each chain has one haem group containing an iron (Fe²⁺) ion that binds one oxygen molecule.
parts.working: B1 four polypeptides each with a haem group; B1 each haem/Fe²⁺ binds one O₂.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Haem is described as a prosthetic group. State what this means.
parts.answer: A non-protein group that is permanently/tightly attached to a protein and needed for its function.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the α-helix and the β-pleated sheet, and name the bonds that hold them in shape.
parts.answer: α-helix: the polypeptide chain is coiled into a spiral; β-pleated sheet: lengths of the chain lie side by side folded in a zigzag sheet; both are held by hydrogen bonds between the C=O of one peptide group and the N–H of another along the backbone.
parts.working: B1 α-helix described as a coil/spiral; B1 β-sheet as parallel/antiparallel strands folded side by side; B1 hydrogen bonds between –C=O and –N–H groups of the backbone (not the R groups).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A cook in Lahore heats a solution of a globular protein to 80 °C. The protein loses its function, but its primary structure is unchanged. Explain these observations.
parts.answer: Heat increases the kinetic energy of the molecule so it vibrates; weak hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and hydrophobic interactions are broken, so the tertiary (and secondary) structure is lost and the 3D shape changes (denaturation); peptide bonds are strong covalent bonds and are not broken, so the sequence of amino acids is unchanged.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: increased kinetic energy / vibration; H bonds/ionic bonds/hydrophobic interactions broken; 3D shape/tertiary structure lost = denatured, so function lost; peptide (covalent) bonds not broken so primary structure kept.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Collagen is the main protein in tendons, which join muscles to bones. Describe the structure of a collagen fibre, from a single polypeptide to the fibre.
parts.answer: Each polypeptide is a left-handed helix with glycine as every third amino acid; three polypeptides wind together into a triple helix (tropocollagen), held by hydrogen bonds; glycine is small so the chains pack closely; molecules lie side by side with ends staggered; covalent cross-links form between adjacent molecules, making fibrils that combine into fibres.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: glycine every third position; three chains/triple helix; H bonds between chains; staggered ends; covalent cross-links between molecules; fibrils → fibres.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the staggered arrangement of collagen molecules increases the tensile strength of a tendon.
parts.answer: The ends of the molecules (the weak points) do not line up in one plane, so there is no single line of weakness; the load is spread along the overlapping molecules.
parts.working: B1 no line of weakness/ends not in line; B1 force spread across many molecules/cross-links.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A protein is made of three polypeptide chains containing a total of 450 amino acids. Two of the chains are joined to each other by one disulfide bond. How many peptide bonds are there in the protein?
A 446
B 447
C 448
D 449
parts.working: Each chain of n amino acids has n − 1 peptide bonds, so three chains have 450 − 3 = 447. The disulfide bond is not a peptide bond. 449 (D) treats the protein as a single chain.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In sickle cell anaemia, the amino acid glutamic acid at position 6 of each β-chain of haemoglobin is replaced by valine. Glutamic acid has a charged R group; valine has a non-polar R group. Which statement best explains why this change makes deoxygenated haemoglobin molecules stick together into long fibres?
A A non-polar R group now lies on the outer surface of the β-chain, so hydrophobic regions of neighbouring molecules associate.
B A polar R group now lies on the surface, so the molecules become more soluble in water.
C The haem groups can no longer hold an iron ion, so the chains collapse.
D The number of polypeptide chains in each molecule falls from four to three.
parts.answer: A A non-polar R group now lies on the outer surface of the β-chain, so hydrophobic regions of neighbouring molecules associate.
parts.working: Position 6 of the β-chain is on the surface of the molecule. Valine's non-polar R group creates a hydrophobic patch that binds to a complementary hydrophobic region of another deoxygenated molecule, so HbS polymerises. B is the reverse of what happens (solubility falls); haem and the four-chain structure are unchanged (C, D).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Every third amino acid in each polypeptide chain of collagen is glycine, whose R group is a single hydrogen atom. Explain why this is important for the structure of collagen.
parts.answer: Glycine is the smallest amino acid, so it can fit in the centre of the triple helix where the three chains are close together; this allows the three polypeptides to wind tightly together (and form many hydrogen bonds).
parts.working: B1 glycine small / small R group; B1 allows three chains to pack/coil tightly into the triple helix.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In one inherited form of brittle bone disease, a single glycine in one collagen chain is replaced by an amino acid with a larger R group. Suggest why bones of people with this mutation break easily.
parts.answer: The larger R group does not fit inside the triple helix, so the three chains cannot wind tightly and fewer hydrogen bonds form; the collagen molecules are less stable / cannot line up and cross-link properly into fibrils; so the fibres have lower tensile strength and the bone matrix is weaker.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: larger R group cannot fit in the centre of the helix; triple helix disrupted/fewer H bonds; molecules cannot pack/cross-link into fibrils normally; lower tensile strength of collagen in bone.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Vitamin C is needed to convert some proline residues in collagen into hydroxyproline, which forms extra hydrogen bonds between the three chains. Suggest why a person lacking vitamin C has bleeding gums and wounds that heal slowly.
parts.answer: Without hydroxyproline the triple helix is less stable, so collagen is weak/unstable; collagen in blood vessel walls and gum tissue is weak, so vessels break and bleed, and new tissue (scar tissue) made during healing lacks strong collagen.
parts.working: B1 fewer H bonds so collagen weak/unstable; B1 applied to blood vessel walls/gums or to new tissue in wound repair.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cooks in Pakistan rub raw papaya paste on meat before cooking. Papaya contains papain, an enzyme that catalyses the hydrolysis of peptide bonds. Explain why this makes the meat more tender.
parts.answer: Papain hydrolyses peptide bonds in muscle proteins and collagen, breaking them into shorter polypeptides/peptides; the fibrous proteins lose their strength, so the meat is softer.
parts.working: B1 peptide bonds hydrolysed → shorter chains; B1 collagen/fibrous proteins lose tensile strength.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The tertiary structure of a protein is partly held by an ionic bond between the R group of lysine (–NH₃⁺) and the R group of glutamic acid (–COO⁻). Explain why adding lemon juice, which lowers the pH to 2.5, can change the shape of this protein.
parts.answer: Lemon juice adds many H⁺ ions; the –COO⁻ group gains H⁺ and becomes uncharged –COOH; so the ionic bond between the R groups is broken (and hydrogen bonds may change), and the tertiary structure/3D shape changes.
parts.working: B1 high H⁺ concentration; B1 –COO⁻ becomes –COOH / loses charge; B1 ionic bond broken so tertiary structure/shape changes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the disulfide bonds in this protein are not broken by lemon juice.
parts.answer: Disulfide bonds are strong covalent bonds and are not affected by H⁺ ions/pH changes.
parts.working: B1 covalent/strong bonds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the difference between the structures of α-glucose and β-glucose.
parts.answer: In α-glucose the –OH group on carbon 1 is below the ring; in β-glucose it is above the ring (the H and OH on carbon 1 are reversed).
parts.working: B1 position of OH on carbon 1 reversed/below vs above the ring.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the bond that joins two α-glucose molecules to form maltose, and the type of reaction involved.
parts.answer: α-1,4 glycosidic bond; condensation reaction.
parts.working: B1 (α-1,4) glycosidic; B1 condensation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the name of the reaction that breaks maltose into glucose and name the reagent added in this reaction.
parts.answer: Hydrolysis; water is added.
parts.working: B1 hydrolysis; B1 water.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which polysaccharide is made of β-glucose units joined only by 1,4 glycosidic bonds?
A amylose
B amylopectin
C cellulose
D glycogen
parts.answer: C cellulose
parts.working: Cellulose is an unbranched chain of β-glucose joined by β-1,4 bonds. Amylose (A) is also unbranched with 1,4 bonds but is made of α-glucose.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which two monosaccharides join to form lactose, the sugar in milk?
A α-glucose and fructose
B two α-glucose molecules
C glucose and galactose
D β-glucose and fructose
parts.answer: C glucose and galactose
parts.working: Lactose is formed from glucose and galactose by a condensation reaction. A describes sucrose and B describes maltose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sugarcane grown in Sindh stores sucrose in its stems. Name the two monosaccharides that form sucrose.
parts.answer: α-glucose and fructose.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the bond that joins these monosaccharides and the type of reaction in which it forms.
parts.answer: Glycosidic bond; condensation reaction.
parts.working: B1 glycosidic; B1 condensation (water released).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Sucrose is a non-reducing sugar. State what this means in terms of a laboratory test.
parts.answer: It does not reduce Benedict's solution, so it gives no brick-red precipitate (stays blue) when heated with Benedict's solution unless it is first hydrolysed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of an amylose molecule.
parts.answer: A long unbranched chain of α-glucose molecules; joined by 1,4 glycosidic bonds; coiled into a helix (held by hydrogen bonds).
parts.working: 1 mark each: α-glucose; 1,4 glycosidic bonds/unbranched; helix/coiled.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the structure of amylose makes it suitable as an energy store in a rice grain.
parts.answer: Coiled helix is compact, so a lot of glucose is stored in a small space; it is insoluble, so it does not affect the water potential of the cells/does not cause osmosis; large molecule so it cannot leave the cell; can be hydrolysed to glucose for respiration.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two features each linked to a use.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Potato tubers store starch while human liver cells store glycogen. Compare the structure of amylopectin with the structure of glycogen.
parts.answer: Similarities: both made of α-glucose; both have α-1,4 glycosidic bonds in chains and α-1,6 bonds at branch points. Difference: glycogen is more highly branched (branches more frequent) and its chains between branches are shorter.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: both α-glucose; both 1,4 and 1,6 bonds; both branched; glycogen more branched/shorter chains.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the branched structure of glycogen suits it to be an energy store in an active animal.
parts.answer: Many branch ends (terminal glucose units) so enzymes can hydrolyse many glucose molecules at the same time – glucose is released quickly when needed; the molecule is compact so a lot is stored in a small space.
parts.working: B1 many ends for enzymes to act on/rapid hydrolysis; B1 compact.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two features of starch and glycogen, other than branching, that make them suitable storage molecules.
parts.answer: Any two of: insoluble so no effect on water potential/osmosis; large so cannot leave the cell; easily hydrolysed to glucose; compact/coiled.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The relative molecular mass (Mr) of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, is 180 and of water is 18. Calculate the Mr of a chain of ten glucose molecules joined by glycosidic bonds.
parts.working: M1 9 glycosidic bonds, so 9 water molecules removed; 10 × 180 − 9 × 18 = 1638 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student boiled a sucrose solution with Benedict's solution and it stayed blue. She then boiled a second sample with dilute hydrochloric acid, neutralised it with sodium hydrogencarbonate and repeated the Benedict's test. It turned brick-red. Explain these results.
parts.answer: Sucrose is a non-reducing sugar, so no colour change at first; acid hydrolyses the glycosidic bond, giving glucose and fructose; these are reducing sugars which reduce Cu²⁺ (blue) to copper(I) oxide (red precipitate).
parts.working: B1 sucrose non-reducing; B1 acid hydrolysis to glucose + fructose; B1 reducing sugars reduce Cu²⁺/form Cu₂O precipitate.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which pair of sugars are both reducing sugars?
A sucrose and glucose
B maltose and glucose
C sucrose and fructose
D sucrose and maltose
parts.answer: B maltose and glucose
parts.working: All monosaccharides (glucose, fructose) and the disaccharide maltose are reducing sugars. Every other option includes sucrose, which is non-reducing because its glycosidic bond links the reducing groups of both monomers.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A disaccharide X gives a brick-red precipitate when heated with Benedict's solution. When X is fully hydrolysed, two different monosaccharides are produced. What is X?
A maltose
B sucrose
C lactose
D amylose
parts.answer: C lactose
parts.working: Lactose is a reducing sugar and is made of two different monosaccharides (glucose and galactose). Maltose is reducing but gives only glucose; sucrose gives two different monosaccharides but is non-reducing; amylose is a polysaccharide, not a disaccharide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A food scientist completely hydrolyses 4.05 g of pure amylose into glucose. In a long chain, each glucose unit has an Mr of 162 (glucose minus water); free glucose has an Mr of 180. Calculate the mass of glucose produced. Ignore the water at the ends of the chain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the mass of glucose produced is greater than the mass of amylose that was hydrolysed.
parts.answer: A water molecule is added at each glycosidic bond during hydrolysis, so the products include the mass of the water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the enzyme in saliva that begins the hydrolysis of amylose and name the disaccharide it produces.
parts.answer: Amylase; maltose.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An enzyme removes glucose units one at a time from the free (non-reducing) ends of polysaccharide chains. Equal masses of three polysaccharides were incubated with this enzyme. Rate of glucose release / µmol min⁻¹: glycogen 8.4; amylopectin 3.1; amylose 0.6.
Calculate how many times faster glucose is released from glycogen than from amylose.
parts.answer: 14 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the differences in the rates of glucose release.
parts.answer: Amylose is unbranched, so each molecule has only one free end for the enzyme to act on; amylopectin is branched (1,6 glycosidic bonds), so it has many ends; glycogen is even more highly branched (branches closer together/more 1,6 bonds), so it has the most ends per unit mass; more ends means more enzyme molecules can act at the same time, so glucose is released faster.
parts.working: 1 mark each: amylose unbranched/one end; amylopectin branched via 1,6 bonds; glycogen more branched than amylopectin; more free ends → more enzyme–substrate complexes at once → faster release.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the rapid release of glucose from glycogen is an advantage to an animal.
parts.answer: Animals are active/move, so they may need glucose quickly for respiration to release energy (e.g. in muscles during exercise).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cotton fibres from Punjab are almost pure cellulose. Explain how the arrangement of β-glucose molecules in cellulose gives cotton fibres high tensile strength.
parts.answer: β-glucose joined by β-1,4 glycosidic bonds; alternate glucose units rotated by 180°, giving straight, unbranched chains; many hydrogen bonds form between –OH groups of neighbouring parallel chains; groups of chains form microfibrils, which group into fibres; the many hydrogen bonds together give great strength.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: β-1,4 bonds; alternate units inverted; straight unbranched chains; H bonds between adjacent chains; microfibrils/fibres; collectively strong.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Humans cannot digest cellulose although they digest starch. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Human digestive enzymes (amylases) are specific to α-glycosidic bonds; the β-1,4 bonds of cellulose do not fit the active site; humans do not make cellulase.
parts.working: B1 enzyme specificity/active site shape fits α bonds only; B1 no cellulase made.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A glycogen molecule in a liver cell contains 30000 glucose units, with one 1,6 glycosidic bond for every 10 glucose units. Calculate the number of 1,6 glycosidic bonds and the number of 1,4 glycosidic bonds in the molecule.
parts.working: 1,6 bonds = 30000/10 = 3000 (B1); total glycosidic bonds in one branched molecule = 30000 − 1 = 29999 (M1); 1,4 bonds = 29999 − 3000 = 26999 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Each branch point adds one free end to the molecule. Calculate the number of free (non-reducing) ends.
parts.working: 3000 branches + the original chain end = 3001.

parts.label: c
parts.text: After a meal, liver cells convert glucose into glycogen. Explain why liver cells store glycogen rather than glucose.
parts.answer: Glycogen is insoluble, so it does not lower the water potential of the cell / no osmotic water entry; it cannot diffuse out of the cell; it is compact, so much glucose is stored in a small volume; branched so glucose can be released quickly when needed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A cellulose molecule from a cotton fibre has an Mr of 810018. The Mr of glucose is 180 and of water is 18. Calculate the number of glucose units in the molecule.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why cellulose molecules form straight chains, while amylose forms a helix.
parts.answer: In cellulose the β-glucose units are joined by β-1,4 glycosidic bonds, and every other glucose is rotated/inverted by 180°; so the chain is straight, whereas the α-1,4 bonds of amylose make the chain turn into a helix.
parts.working: B1 β-glucose with alternate units inverted; B1 straight chain vs α-1,4 bonds giving a helix.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Buffaloes in Punjab digest cellulose with the help of microorganisms that make the enzyme cellulase. Suggest why cellulase cannot hydrolyse starch.
parts.answer: Enzymes are specific; the active site of cellulase is complementary in shape to the β-1,4 linked chain of cellulose, not to α-1,4 linked starch, so starch cannot bind / no enzyme–substrate complex forms.
parts.working: B1 active site shape complementary to cellulose/β-1,4 bonds only; B1 starch (α-glucose/α-1,4 bonds) does not fit/bind.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A potato cell stores 1.8 g of glucose units. An amylose molecule in the cell is made of 2000 glucose units (Mr 324018). The Mr of glucose is 180. Calculate how many times more molecules there would be if this 1.8 g were stored as free glucose instead of as amylose molecules of this size. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: About 1.8e+03 times (≈ 1800)
parts.working: number of molecules is proportional to mass/Mr: (1.8/180) ÷ (1.8/324018) = 324018/180 (M1) = 1800.1 ≈ 1.8e+03 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to explain why plant cells store carbohydrate as starch rather than as glucose.
parts.answer: Osmotic effect depends on the number of solute molecules; storing glucose would greatly lower the water potential of the cell, so water would enter by osmosis (cell could swell/burst or metabolism disturbed); starch has far fewer molecules and is insoluble, so it has almost no effect on water potential.
parts.working: B1 water potential depends on number of solute particles; B1 glucose would lower water potential → water enters by osmosis; B1 starch insoluble/few molecules → little osmotic effect.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a triglyceride is formed.
parts.answer: One glycerol molecule joins to three fatty acids by condensation reactions; three ester bonds form; three molecules of water are released.
parts.working: B1 glycerol + 3 fatty acids; B1 condensation/water removed (3 molecules); B1 ester bonds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Ghee is solid at room temperature in Lahore in winter, while sunflower oil is liquid. Explain this difference in terms of the fatty acids they contain.
parts.answer: Ghee contains mainly saturated fatty acids with no C=C double bonds, so the straight chains pack closely and the fat is solid; sunflower oil contains many unsaturated fatty acids whose C=C double bonds cause kinks, so chains cannot pack closely and the lipid is liquid.
parts.working: B1 saturated – no C=C, pack closely; B1 unsaturated – C=C, kinks, cannot pack closely.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of a fatty acid.
parts.answer: A hydrocarbon chain (of carbon and hydrogen atoms) attached to a carboxyl group (–COOH).
parts.working: B1 hydrocarbon chain; B1 carboxyl group.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the difference between a saturated and an unsaturated fatty acid.
parts.answer: A saturated fatty acid has no C=C double bonds in its hydrocarbon chain; an unsaturated fatty acid has one or more C=C double bonds.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the bond formed when a fatty acid joins to glycerol, and state how many water molecules are released when one triglyceride molecule is made.
parts.answer: Ester bond; three water molecules.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Phospholipids contain a phosphate group. Name the element, other than carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, that is present in the phosphate group.
parts.answer: Phosphorus (P).
parts.working: B1 phosphorus. Triglycerides contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Lung surfactant is made largely of phospholipid. State what surfactant does in the alveoli.
parts.answer: It reduces surface tension in the thin layer of water lining the alveoli, so the alveoli do not collapse and the surface area for gas exchange is kept large.
parts.working: B1 reduces surface tension of the water film lining the alveoli (prevents collapse).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why triglycerides are insoluble in water.
parts.answer: Triglycerides are non-polar / have no charged groups; so they cannot form hydrogen bonds with water molecules (water molecules are more attracted to each other).
parts.working: B1 non-polar/uncharged; B1 cannot form hydrogen bonds with water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three roles of triglycerides in animals.
parts.answer: Any three of: energy store; thermal insulation (e.g. blubber, fat under skin); protection of organs (e.g. fat around kidneys); buoyancy in aquatic animals; source of metabolic water when oxidised.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Camels in the Thar desert store fat in their humps. Suggest two ways this fat helps a camel survive a long journey without food or water.
parts.answer: It is a store of energy that can be respired when there is no food; oxidation (respiration) of fat releases metabolic water.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the small intestine, triglycerides are digested by lipase. Name the type of reaction and the products when a triglyceride is completely digested.
parts.answer: Hydrolysis; glycerol and three fatty acids.
parts.working: B1 hydrolysis; B1 glycerol; B1 fatty acids.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Bile salts break large fat droplets into many small droplets. Suggest why this speeds up the digestion of fat.
parts.answer: Small droplets have a larger total surface area; so more lipase molecules can bind to triglycerides at the same time (more enzyme–substrate collisions/complexes).
parts.working: B1 larger surface area; B1 more enzyme–substrate complexes/collisions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of a phospholipid molecule and state how it differs from a triglyceride.
parts.answer: Glycerol joined by ester bonds to two fatty acids; the third –OH of glycerol is joined to a phosphate group; this differs from a triglyceride, where all three positions carry fatty acids.
parts.working: B1 glycerol + two fatty acids; B1 phosphate group (on third carbon); B1 difference stated (one fatty acid replaced by phosphate).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why phospholipids form a bilayer when they are mixed with water.
parts.answer: The phosphate head is hydrophilic/polar and attracted to water; the fatty acid tails are hydrophobic/non-polar and repelled by water; in a bilayer the heads face the water on both sides and the tails point inwards, away from water.
parts.working: B1 hydrophilic head; B1 hydrophobic tails; B1 heads face water, tails face inwards.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Tripalmitin is a triglyceride found in palm oil. It is made from glycerol (Mr 92) and three palmitic acid molecules (Mr 256 each). The Mr of water is 18. Calculate the Mr of tripalmitin.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of water, in g, released when 0.50 mol of tripalmitin is made.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Palmitic acid is a saturated fatty acid. Suggest why palm oil is semi-solid at a room temperature of 25 °C, while sunflower oil is liquid.
parts.answer: Palm oil has a high proportion of saturated fatty acids, whose straight chains pack closely together, so the molecules are held together more strongly and the melting point is higher; sunflower oil has many unsaturated fatty acids with kinks at C=C bonds, so they cannot pack closely.
parts.working: B1 saturated chains straight/pack closely → higher melting point; B1 unsaturated have kinks/cannot pack closely.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The table shows four fatty acids, each with 18 carbon atoms.
fatty acid: stearic / oleic / linoleic / linolenic
number of C=C double bonds: 0 / 1 / 2 / 3
melting point / °C: 69 / 13 / −5 / −11
Describe the relationship shown by these data.
parts.answer: As the number of C=C double bonds increases, the melting point decreases; the largest fall is from 0 to 1 double bond (69 °C to 13 °C, a fall of 56 °C).
parts.working: B1 more double bonds → lower melting point; B1 quoted data with units, e.g. biggest drop between stearic and oleic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the relationship.
parts.answer: Each C=C double bond causes a kink/bend in the hydrocarbon chain; so the molecules cannot pack closely together and the attractions between them are weaker, so less energy is needed to melt them.
parts.working: B1 kinks at C=C; B1 cannot pack closely/weaker attractions → lower melting point.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Vanaspati (vegetable ghee) is made by adding hydrogen to vegetable oils. Suggest why this turns a liquid oil into a solid fat.
parts.answer: Hydrogen is added across C=C double bonds, making the fatty acids (more) saturated, so the chains are straighter, pack closely and the melting point rises above room temperature.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When phospholipids are added to a mixture of oil and water, they collect as a single layer at the boundary between the oil and the water. Describe and explain how the phospholipid molecules are arranged in this layer.
parts.answer: The hydrophilic phosphate heads point into the water and the hydrophobic fatty acid tails point into the oil; because heads are attracted to (form hydrogen bonds with) water and tails are repelled by water but mix with non-polar oil.
parts.working: B1 arrangement; B1 explanation in terms of hydrophilic/hydrophobic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In water alone, phospholipids form a bilayer. Explain why a bilayer forms rather than a single layer.
parts.answer: In water both sides are aqueous; the tails must be kept away from water, so two layers form with tails facing inwards towards each other and heads facing the water on both sides.
parts.working: B1 water on both sides; B1 tails inwards, heads outwards.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why phospholipids with unsaturated fatty acid tails make a membrane more fluid than phospholipids with saturated tails.
parts.answer: Unsaturated tails have kinks, so the phospholipids cannot pack closely; there are weaker attractions between the tails, so they can move more freely.
parts.working: B1 kinks/cannot pack closely; B1 move more freely.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The molecular formula of tripalmitin is C₅₁H₉₈O₆ and of glucose is C₆H₁₂O₆. Calculate the ratio of hydrogen atoms to oxygen atoms in each molecule. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: tripalmitin 16.3 : 1; glucose 2.0 : 1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why oxidising 1 g of triglyceride in respiration releases about twice as much energy as oxidising 1 g of glucose.
parts.answer: Triglycerides have many more C–H bonds/hydrogen atoms per unit mass and relatively little oxygen; so more hydrogen is available for oxidation (to form water) and more energy (ATP) is released per gram.
parts.working: B1 more H / C–H bonds per gram (less O); B1 more hydrogen oxidised → more energy/ATP.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why a hibernating brown bear stores lipid rather than glycogen before winter.
parts.answer: Lipid stores more energy per gram, so the bear carries less mass for the same energy (or lipid also insulates / produces metabolic water).

practice.stem: Some migratory birds fly from Central Asia to wetlands in Sindh each autumn. Before the journey they build up large fat stores. Complete oxidation releases about 39 kJ per gram of triglyceride and about 17 kJ per gram of carbohydrate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bird stores 40 g of triglyceride. Calculate the mass of carbohydrate that would release the same energy. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to (a) to explain why lipid is a better energy store than carbohydrate for a flying bird.
parts.answer: The same energy is stored in less than half the mass, so the bird carries less extra mass in flight.
parts.working: B1 less mass for same energy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two other advantages to the bird of storing triglycerides rather than glycogen.
parts.answer: Any two of: triglycerides are insoluble so do not affect water potential of cells; oxidation releases a lot of metabolic water (useful on long flights without drinking); fat stored under skin gives thermal insulation; glycogen is stored with water, adding mass.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A mustard (sarson) seed has a dry mass of 2.5 mg. 42% of its dry mass is triglyceride and 18% is carbohydrate. Oxidation releases 39 J per mg of triglyceride and 17 J per mg of carbohydrate. Calculate the total energy, in J, stored in these two reserves. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbohydrate, in mg, that would be needed to store this same amount of energy. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Mustard seeds are small and are spread by wind and water. Use your answers to explain the advantage to these seeds of storing most of their energy as lipid.
parts.answer: The seed stores the same energy in 1.50 mg of reserves instead of 2.86 mg, i.e. about 1.9 times less mass; a lighter seed is dispersed further, and still has enough energy for germination until the seedling can photosynthesise.
parts.working: B1 comparison using the figures (less mass for same energy); B1 link to dispersal/germination.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Fish of the same species were kept for six weeks at 5 °C or at 25 °C. The percentage of unsaturated fatty acids in the phospholipids of their cell membranes was 72% at 5 °C and 55% at 25 °C. Explain the advantage of this change to fish living in cold water.
parts.answer: At low temperatures phospholipids have less kinetic energy and membranes become less fluid/more rigid; unsaturated tails have kinks so they cannot pack closely, which keeps the membrane fluid; so membrane proteins (channels, carriers, enzymes) can still move/function and transport (and processes like endocytosis) continue.
parts.working: B1 cold reduces fluidity; B1 unsaturated tails kinked/pack loosely → fluid; B1 membrane functions maintained (named).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student wrote: 'A phospholipid is a triglyceride in which one fatty acid has been replaced.' Explain whether this statement is a correct description of how phospholipids and triglycerides are related, and state one way in which their functions differ.
parts.answer: It is an acceptable description of structure: both have a glycerol backbone with ester-linked fatty acids, but in a phospholipid a phosphate-containing group replaces one fatty acid; functions differ: triglycerides are mainly energy stores/insulation, phospholipids form membranes (bilayers).
parts.working: B1 structural comparison with phosphate group replacing one fatty acid; B1 functional difference.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sample of ghee was fully hydrolysed with lipase. The fatty acids released were exactly neutralised by 12.0 cm³ of 0.05 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide; one mole of NaOH neutralises one mole of fatty acid. Calculate the number of moles of fatty acid released.
parts.answer: 6.0e-04 mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming that all the triglyceride had an Mr of 806, calculate the mass of triglyceride that was hydrolysed, in g. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the pH of the mixture falls as hydrolysis proceeds.
parts.answer: Each fatty acid released has a carboxyl group (–COOH) that can release H⁺ ions into the solution; as more ester bonds are hydrolysed, more H⁺ is produced and the pH falls.
parts.working: B1 carboxyl groups release H⁺ ions; B1 more fatty acids released (more hydrolysis) → more H⁺ → lower pH.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A fat substitute is made by joining 8 fatty acid molecules (Mr 280 each) to one sucrose molecule (Mr 342) by ester bonds. The Mr of water is 18. Calculate the Mr of the fat substitute.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Lipase hydrolyses the ester bonds in triglycerides but cannot hydrolyse this fat substitute. Suggest why.
parts.answer: The fat substitute has a different (much larger, bulkier) shape from a triglyceride, with eight fatty acids around a sucrose core; it does not fit/is not complementary to the active site of lipase, so no enzyme–substrate complex forms.
parts.working: B1 different/bulky shape; B1 not complementary to active site / no ES complex.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why eating foods made with this fat substitute could help a person to lose body mass.
parts.answer: It is not digested, so it is not absorbed and supplies no energy; the person takes in less energy than they use, so stored fat is respired.
parts.working: B1 not digested/absorbed so no energy; B1 energy intake less than use → stored lipid used.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which property of water explains why sweating cools a farm worker in the hot summer in Multan?
A high specific heat capacity
B high latent heat of vaporisation
C cohesion between water molecules
D maximum density at 4 °C
parts.answer: B high latent heat of vaporisation
parts.working: Evaporating sweat needs a lot of energy to break the hydrogen bonds between water molecules; this heat is taken from the skin. A high specific heat capacity (A) resists temperature change but does not by itself remove heat from the body.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why is a water molecule described as polar?
A The oxygen atom attracts the shared electrons more strongly than the hydrogen atoms, so the oxygen end is slightly negative and the hydrogen ends are slightly positive.
B The hydrogen atoms contain more protons than the oxygen atom.
C Each water molecule carries an overall negative charge.
D Water molecules ionise completely into H⁺ and OH⁻ ions.
parts.answer: A The oxygen atom attracts the shared electrons more strongly than the hydrogen atoms, so the oxygen end is slightly negative and the hydrogen ends are slightly positive.
parts.working: Oxygen is more electronegative, giving δ− on O and δ+ on each H, although the molecule has no overall charge (C is wrong). Only a tiny fraction of water molecules ionise (D).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the maximum number of hydrogen bonds that one water molecule can form with other water molecules.
parts.answer: Four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how sodium chloride dissolves in water.
parts.answer: Water molecules are polar; the slightly negative oxygen of water molecules is attracted to Na⁺ ions and the slightly positive hydrogens are attracted to Cl⁻ ions; the ions become surrounded by water molecules and separate/move apart from the crystal.
parts.working: B1 water polar/δ+ and δ−; B1 correct attractions to both ions; B1 ions surrounded/separated by water molecules.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name two substances that are transported dissolved in blood plasma.
parts.answer: Any two of: glucose, amino acids, urea, mineral ions (e.g. Na⁺), hormones (e.g. insulin), carbon dioxide (as hydrogencarbonate ions).
parts.working: Both needed for 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the latent heat of vaporisation of water.
parts.answer: The energy needed to change a given mass (1 g/1 kg) of liquid water into water vapour (without a change in temperature).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why water has a high latent heat of vaporisation.
parts.answer: Water molecules are held together by many hydrogen bonds; a lot of energy is needed to break these bonds so that molecules can escape as vapour.
parts.working: B1 hydrogen bonds between molecules; B1 much energy needed to break them.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one example of how this property helps to keep a plant or an animal cool.
parts.answer: Evaporation of water from leaves during transpiration, or evaporation of sweat from the skin, removes a lot of heat energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why glucose dissolves in water but triglycerides do not.
parts.answer: Glucose has many –OH groups, which are polar; these form hydrogen bonds with water molecules, so glucose dissolves; triglycerides are non-polar (mostly hydrocarbon chains) and cannot form hydrogen bonds with water, so they do not dissolve.
parts.working: B1 glucose polar/–OH groups; B1 forms H bonds with water; B1 triglycerides non-polar/no H bonds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why lipids are carried in the blood combined with proteins.
parts.answer: Lipids are insoluble in water/plasma, so they need to be attached to (water-soluble) proteins to be transported.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other.
parts.answer: Water is a polar molecule: oxygen is slightly negative (δ−) and the hydrogens slightly positive (δ+); the δ+ hydrogen of one molecule is attracted to the δ− oxygen of a neighbouring molecule.
parts.working: B1 polar/dipole, O δ− and H δ+; B1 attraction between H of one molecule and O of another.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The specific heat capacity of water is 4.2 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹. Calculate the energy, in kJ, needed to raise the temperature of 5.0 kg of water in a fish tank by 3.0 °C.
parts.answer: 63 kJ

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the high specific heat capacity of water is important for organisms living in a lake.
parts.answer: A large input of energy is needed to change the temperature of water (many hydrogen bonds to break), so the lake temperature stays fairly stable; enzymes of aquatic organisms work in a stable environment/organisms are protected from sudden changes in air temperature.
parts.working: B1 temperature changes slowly/stable; B1 stable conditions for enzymes/organisms.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which observation is a direct result of the high specific heat capacity of water?
A The temperature of Dal Lake in Kashmir changes much less between day and night than the temperature of the air above it.
B A labourer is cooled when sweat evaporates from his skin.
C Glucose is carried in solution in blood plasma.
D Ions such as K⁺ are surrounded by water molecules in the cytoplasm.
parts.answer: A The temperature of Dal Lake in Kashmir changes much less between day and night than the temperature of the air above it.
parts.working: A high specific heat capacity means a lot of energy is needed to change the temperature of water, so large bodies of water stay at a stable temperature. B is due to the high latent heat of vaporisation; C and D are due to solvent properties.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Water is a reactant in many reactions in living organisms. Name two hydrolysis reactions that happen during digestion in humans.
parts.answer: Any two of: starch → maltose (amylase); maltose → glucose (maltase); proteins/polypeptides → amino acids (proteases); triglycerides → fatty acids and glycerol (lipase); sucrose → glucose + fructose; lactose → glucose + galactose.
parts.working: 1 mark each (substrate and product, or substrate and enzyme).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why metabolic reactions in cells take place in solution in water.
parts.answer: Water dissolves the substrates/reactants (and enzymes), so the molecules can move freely; this allows them to collide and react / form enzyme–substrate complexes.
parts.working: B1 solvent so molecules free to move; B1 collisions / ES complexes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The specific heat capacity of air is 1.0 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ and its density is 1.2 kg m⁻³. The specific heat capacity of water is 4.2 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ and its density is 1000 kg m⁻³. Calculate the energy, in kJ, needed to raise the temperature of 1 m³ of each by 1 °C, and how many times more energy water needs.
parts.answer: air 1.2 kJ; water 4200 kJ; 3500 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Along the coast at Karachi, air temperatures range from about 18 °C to 35 °C during the year, while the sea-surface temperature ranges from about 22 °C to 29 °C. Use your answer to (a) to explain why marine organisms live in a more stable environment than land organisms.
parts.answer: Water needs much more energy to change its temperature (high specific heat capacity, because energy is used to break hydrogen bonds), so the sea gains or loses heat with only small temperature changes; marine organisms therefore experience a narrower temperature range, so their enzymes work steadily.
parts.working: B1 much more energy needed / high SHC linked to H bonds; B1 smaller temperature fluctuation for organisms (with data or enzyme link).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The table shows the boiling points of four small molecules.
molecule: H₂O / NH₃ / H₂S / CH₄
Mr: 18 / 17 / 34 / 16
boiling point / °C: 100 / −33 / −60 / −162
Using these data, explain why water is a liquid at the temperatures at which most organisms live.
parts.answer: Water has a much higher boiling point than molecules of similar or larger Mr (e.g. H₂S, Mr 34, boils at −60 °C); this is because water molecules form many hydrogen bonds with each other, which need much energy to break; so water stays liquid between 0 °C and 100 °C, the range in which most organisms live.
parts.working: B1 comparison using data; B1 hydrogen bonding between water molecules (stronger/more than in the others); B1 liquid between 0 and 100 °C / at body temperatures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why it is important for organisms that water is a liquid rather than a gas at their body temperature.
parts.answer: It can act as a solvent/transport medium and as the medium for metabolic reactions inside cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Lakes in Gilgit-Baltistan freeze over in winter but fish survive beneath the ice. Explain how the properties of water allow this.
parts.answer: Ice is less dense than liquid water (hydrogen bonds hold molecules in an open lattice), so ice floats and forms at the surface; the ice layer insulates the water below, so it does not freeze; water below remains liquid (densest near 4 °C at the bottom), so fish can live and move.
parts.working: B1 ice less dense/floats; B1 open lattice due to H bonds; B1 ice insulates/water below stays liquid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the solvent properties of water make it a good transport medium in the blood plasma.
parts.answer: Water is polar, so ions and polar molecules (e.g. glucose, amino acids) dissolve in it; water molecules cluster around ions (δ− O around cations, δ+ H around anions), keeping them separated in solution; dissolved substances are carried in the plasma to cells.
parts.working: B1 polar; B1 named solutes dissolve/ions surrounded by water molecules; B1 carried in solution to/from cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A labourer working in Multan in June produces 1200 g of sweat in one hour. 80% of the sweat evaporates from his skin. The latent heat of vaporisation of water at skin temperature is 2.4 kJ g⁻¹. Calculate the energy, in kJ, removed from his body in one hour by evaporation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The labourer's body mass is 65 kg and the specific heat capacity of his body is 3.5 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹. Calculate the rise in his body temperature if this energy were not removed. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why sweating is less effective at cooling the body on a humid day in Karachi than on a dry day in Multan.
parts.answer: In humid air the water vapour concentration gradient between skin and air is smaller, so less sweat evaporates; sweat drips off without evaporating, so the latent heat is not removed from the body.
parts.working: B1 less evaporation in humid air; B1 cooling only happens when water evaporates (latent heat taken from skin).

parts.label: a
parts.text: On a hot afternoon, a maize leaf absorbs 30 J s⁻¹ more energy from the Sun than it loses by other means. The latent heat of vaporisation of water at leaf temperature is 2.45 kJ g⁻¹. Calculate the mass of water, in g, the leaf must transpire in one hour to remove this extra energy. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the evaporation of water from the leaf removes heat energy.
parts.answer: Energy (heat) from the leaf is used to break hydrogen bonds between water molecules so that they evaporate; the water molecules with the most energy leave as vapour, carrying the energy away, so the leaf cools.
parts.working: B1 energy used to break hydrogen bonds; B1 heat taken from leaf / high-energy molecules escape.

parts.label: c
parts.text: In very dry soil in the Thar, the maize plant closes its stomata. Suggest why the leaf temperature may then rise high enough to damage its enzymes.
parts.answer: With stomata closed transpiration stops, so there is no evaporative (latent heat) cooling; the leaf continues to absorb solar energy, its temperature rises and enzymes may be denatured.
parts.working: B1 little/no evaporation so no cooling; B1 temperature rises → enzymes denatured.

parts.label: a
parts.text: To remove 500 kJ of heat by evaporation, calculate the mass of water and the mass of ethanol that would have to evaporate. Latent heat of vaporisation: water 2.4 kJ g⁻¹; ethanol 0.85 kJ g⁻¹. Give your answers to the nearest gram.
parts.answer: water 208 g; ethanol 588 g

parts.label: b
parts.text: Ethanol (C₂H₅OH) has one –OH group per molecule. Water (H₂O) can form up to four hydrogen bonds per molecule. Use this information to explain the difference in latent heat of vaporisation.
parts.answer: Each water molecule forms more hydrogen bonds than an ethanol molecule (which has only one –OH and a non-polar ethyl group); more energy is needed to break the hydrogen bonds per gram of water, so water has the higher latent heat.
parts.working: B1 more hydrogen bonds per water molecule / per gram; B1 more energy needed to separate molecules.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why evaporation of water is a more efficient way for a mammal to lose heat than evaporation of any other liquid it could produce.
parts.answer: Because of its high latent heat, a large amount of heat is lost for only a small loss of water/body fluid, which reduces the risk of dehydration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 70 kg person contains about 42 kg of water. Calculate the energy, in kJ, needed to raise the temperature of this water by 1 °C. Specific heat capacity of water = 4.2 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: At rest the person's metabolism releases heat at 100 J s⁻¹. Calculate how long, in minutes, it would take for this heat to raise the temperature of the body water by 1 °C if no heat were lost. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 29.4 minutes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why the high specific heat capacity of water is important for enzyme-controlled reactions in the body.
parts.answer: Body temperature changes only slowly even when heat production or the environment changes, because much energy is needed to break hydrogen bonds before water warms; enzymes therefore stay close to their optimum temperature and are not denatured, so reaction rates are stable.
parts.working: B1 temperature changes slowly/stable; B1 enzymes stay near optimum / not denatured.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student crushes a peanut and shakes it with ethanol. She then pours the ethanol into a test-tube of water. Which result shows that lipid is present?
A a milky-white emulsion forms
B a brick-red precipitate forms
C the mixture turns purple
D the mixture turns blue-black
parts.answer: A a milky-white emulsion forms
parts.working: Lipid dissolves in ethanol; in water it comes out of solution as tiny droplets, giving a milky-white emulsion. B is a positive Benedict's test, C a positive biuret test and D a positive iodine test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to carry out the Benedict's test on a solution of fruit juice and describe a positive result.
parts.answer: Add an equal volume (e.g. 2 cm³) of Benedict's solution to the juice; heat in a water-bath at about 80–100 °C for a few minutes; a positive result is a colour change from blue to green, yellow, orange or brick-red (precipitate).
parts.working: B1 equal/excess volume Benedict's; B1 heat in water-bath (stated temperature/time); B1 blue → green/yellow/orange/brick-red.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The blue colour of Benedict's solution is due to copper(II) ions, Cu²⁺. Explain what happens to these ions in a positive result.
parts.answer: The reducing sugar donates electrons to/reduces Cu²⁺ ions to Cu⁺ ions; these form an insoluble brick-red precipitate of copper(I) oxide.
parts.working: B1 Cu²⁺ reduced to Cu⁺ by the sugar; B1 red precipitate of copper(I) oxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to test a slice of potato for starch, and give the result if starch is present.
parts.answer: Add a few drops of iodine in potassium iodide solution to the cut surface; colour changes from orange-brown to blue-black.
parts.working: B1 iodine (in KI) solution; B1 orange/brown → blue-black.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the iodine solution changes colour when it meets starch.
parts.answer: Iodine molecules fit inside the helix of amylose, forming a blue-black complex.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A slice from an unripe banana turned dark blue-black with iodine, but a slice from a ripe banana turned only pale blue. Suggest why.
parts.answer: During ripening starch is hydrolysed to sugars (e.g. glucose, sucrose); so the ripe banana has less starch, giving a paler colour.
parts.working: B1 starch broken down/hydrolysed; B1 into sugars, so less starch present.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to carry out the biuret test on a sample of milk.
parts.answer: Add sodium hydroxide solution (or biuret reagent) to the milk, then a few drops of dilute copper(II) sulfate solution and mix (no heating needed).
parts.working: B1 sodium hydroxide; B1 dilute copper(II) sulfate (or biuret reagent containing both).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the colour change for a positive result.
parts.answer: Blue to purple/violet/lilac.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A solution of free amino acids gives a negative result with the biuret test. Explain why.
parts.answer: The biuret reagent reacts with peptide bonds, and free amino acids have no peptide bonds.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student tested an unknown solution X. Results: Benedict's test (heated) – stayed blue; biuret test – stayed blue; iodine test – stayed brown; boiled with dilute acid, neutralised, then Benedict's test – orange-red precipitate. Which substance is in X?
A glucose
B protein
C starch
D sucrose
parts.answer: D sucrose
parts.working: Only a non-reducing sugar gives a negative first Benedict's test but a positive test after acid hydrolysis, so X contains sucrose. Glucose (A) would give a positive first Benedict's test.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A solution contains glucose and sucrose. One sample is heated with Benedict's solution. A second sample is boiled with dilute hydrochloric acid, neutralised and then heated with the same volume of Benedict's solution. The second sample gives more precipitate. What is the reason?
A Hydrolysis of sucrose releases glucose and fructose, which are reducing sugars.
B The acid makes Benedict's solution more sensitive to glucose.
C Boiling with acid converts glucose into starch.
D Sucrose is a reducing sugar that only reacts at a high temperature.
parts.answer: A Hydrolysis of sucrose releases glucose and fructose, which are reducing sugars.
parts.working: Acid hydrolyses the glycosidic bond in sucrose, producing two reducing monosaccharides, so there is more reducing sugar than in the first sample. Sucrose itself is non-reducing (D); acid neutralisation does not change the reagent's sensitivity (B).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a student could show that a sample of sugarcane juice contains a non-reducing sugar.
parts.answer: First test a sample with Benedict's solution (heat) – it stays blue (or record colour); boil a fresh sample with dilute hydrochloric acid; cool and neutralise with sodium hydrogencarbonate/sodium hydroxide (check with pH/indicator paper); heat with Benedict's solution – an orange/brick-red colour (or more precipitate than the first test) shows a non-reducing sugar was present.
parts.working: 1 mark each: Benedict's test first gives negative/baseline result; boil with dilute acid (hydrolysis); neutralise with alkali/hydrogencarbonate; Benedict's again positive/stronger.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the sample must be neutralised before the second Benedict's test.
parts.answer: Benedict's test only works in alkaline conditions / acid would react with the reagent, so a false negative could be obtained.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student tested four foods. The results were:
food P: Benedict's brick-red; iodine orange-brown; biuret blue; emulsion test clear
food Q: Benedict's blue; iodine orange-brown; biuret blue; emulsion test milky-white
food R: Benedict's blue; iodine blue-black; biuret blue; emulsion test clear
food S: Benedict's blue; iodine orange-brown; biuret purple; emulsion test clear
The foods were egg white, honey, cooking oil and potato. Identify P, Q, R and S.
parts.answer: P honey; Q cooking oil; R potato; S egg white.
parts.working: 1 mark each: P honey (reducing sugar); Q cooking oil (lipid); R potato (starch); S egg white (protein).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Food R was also boiled with acid, neutralised and tested with Benedict's solution. Suggest the result and explain it.
parts.answer: Orange/brick-red; acid hydrolyses starch (glycosidic bonds) into reducing sugars such as glucose/maltose.
parts.working: B1 positive result; B1 starch hydrolysed to reducing sugars.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A clinic in Peshawar screens urine samples for glucose using Benedict's solution. Describe how a set of colour standards could be used to estimate the glucose concentration of a sample.
parts.answer: Make glucose solutions of known concentration (e.g. 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 %) by dilution of a stock; test the same volume of each with the same volume of Benedict's, heated in a water-bath at the same temperature for the same time; test the urine in the same way; compare its colour with the standards and estimate the concentration as that of the closest match (or between two).
parts.working: 1 mark each: range of known concentrations; same volumes; same temperature and time; compare colour of sample with standards/estimate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one limitation of this method and suggest how it could be overcome.
parts.answer: Judging colours is subjective / colours of adjacent standards are hard to tell apart; use a colorimeter (after removing precipitate) or use more standards closer together.
parts.working: B1 limitation; B1 matching improvement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the emulsion test, the sample is shaken with ethanol before water is added. Explain why the ethanol must be added first.
parts.answer: Lipids dissolve in ethanol but not in water; when the ethanol solution is added to water the lipid comes out of solution as tiny droplets, forming the emulsion.
parts.working: B1 lipid soluble in ethanol; B1 insoluble in water → droplets/emulsion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the test-tube must be clean and dry before the ethanol is added.
parts.answer: Water already in the tube would make lipid come out of solution early / contamination could give a false result.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a suitable control for this test and state why it is needed.
parts.answer: Shake ethanol (with no sample) and add it to water in the same way; to show that the ethanol and water alone do not form a cloudy emulsion, so cloudiness is due to lipid.
parts.working: B1 ethanol + water without food; B1 shows cloudiness is caused by lipid.

practice.stem: A student made glucose solutions of 0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0 % and tested 2 cm³ of each with 2 cm³ of Benedict's solution in a boiling water-bath, timing how long each took to first show a colour change. She then tested a sample of sugarcane juice in the same way.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two variables, other than the volumes, that the student must keep the same for every tube.
parts.answer: Any two of: temperature of the water-bath; concentration of Benedict's solution; size/type of test tube; the colour change taken as the end-point; starting temperature of the solutions.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid standardised variables (do not credit heating time – it is the dependent variable).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how she could use her results to estimate the concentration of reducing sugar in the juice.
parts.answer: Plot a graph of time for colour change against glucose concentration (calibration curve); test the juice under identical conditions and record its time; read the concentration that matches this time from the curve.
parts.working: B1 calibration curve/graph from standards; B1 test juice in same way; B1 read concentration from graph (or compare with nearest standard).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The juice changed colour faster than the 1.0 % solution. Suggest what she should do to find its concentration.
parts.answer: Dilute the juice by a known factor (e.g. 1 cm³ juice + 9 cm³ water), test again so it falls within the range of the standards, then multiply the reading by the dilution factor.
parts.working: B1 dilute by known factor; B1 multiply result by dilution factor.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the colour change method gives only a semi-quantitative result, and one improvement.
parts.answer: Judging the colour/end-point by eye is subjective; use a colorimeter to measure absorbance/transmission (or filter and weigh the precipitate).
parts.working: B1 subjective colour judgement; B1 colorimeter (or other valid quantitative method).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sample of sugarcane juice was diluted 1 in 50 with distilled water. Before acid hydrolysis, the diluted juice gave the same Benedict's colour as a 0.05 % glucose standard. After acid hydrolysis and neutralisation (without changing the volume), it matched a 0.33 % glucose standard. Assume that all reducing sugars react like glucose. Calculate the concentration of reducing sugar in the undiluted juice before hydrolysis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of reducing sugar that came from the hydrolysis of sucrose in the undiluted juice.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hydrolysis of 342 g of sucrose produces 360 g of glucose plus fructose. Calculate the sucrose concentration of the undiluted juice. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why matching colours with glucose standards may give an inaccurate value for fructose produced by hydrolysis.
parts.answer: Fructose may not reduce Benedict's solution at exactly the same rate/extent as glucose, so equal concentrations may not give equal colours.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Starch solution was mixed with amylase solution at 35 °C. Samples were removed at intervals and tested:
0 min: iodine blue-black; Benedict's blue
10 min: iodine blue-black (paler); Benedict's green
30 min: iodine orange-brown; Benedict's orange
Explain these results.
parts.answer: At 0 min only starch present, no reducing sugar; amylase hydrolyses glycosidic bonds in starch to maltose (a reducing sugar); at 10 min some starch remains but some maltose has formed, so iodine is paler and Benedict's green; by 30 min all starch is hydrolysed (no blue-black), and more reducing sugar is present, so Benedict's is orange.
parts.working: 1 mark each: amylase hydrolyses starch; product maltose is reducing; 10 min partial hydrolysis linked to both tests; 30 min all starch gone and more reducing sugar.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A biuret test on the mixture gave a purple colour at every time. Explain why.
parts.answer: Amylase is a protein (enzyme), and its concentration does not change, so peptide bonds are always present.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a sample taken at 30 min was boiled immediately before the Benedict's test was carried out on a further sample.
parts.answer: To denature the amylase and stop the reaction at that time, so the result represents that time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Lactose-free milk is made by adding the enzyme lactase to milk, which hydrolyses lactose into glucose and galactose. Ordinary milk and lactase-treated milk were tested with Benedict's solution in the same way. Predict and explain the difference in the results.
parts.answer: Both give a positive result because lactose is itself a reducing sugar; the lactase-treated milk gives more precipitate/a colour further towards red; because each lactose molecule is hydrolysed into two reducing sugar molecules (glucose and galactose), so there are about twice as many reducing sugar molecules.
parts.working: B1 both positive (lactose reducing); B1 treated milk gives stronger result; B1 one lactose → two reducing monosaccharides.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a positive Benedict's result for the treated milk does not, on its own, prove that all the lactose has been hydrolysed.
parts.answer: Lactose itself also gives a positive result, so any remaining lactose would still react; a positive result shows reducing sugar is present but cannot distinguish lactose from glucose/galactose (would need a quantitative comparison or a glucose-specific test).
parts.working: B1 lactose also reducing; B1 cannot distinguish / needs quantitative method or specific test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student used the biuret test and a colorimeter calibration curve to measure the protein concentration of egg white. Undiluted egg white gave an absorbance above the highest standard, so it was diluted 1 in 25. The diluted egg white contained 4.4 mg cm⁻³ protein according to the calibration curve. Calculate the protein concentration of the undiluted egg white, in mg cm⁻³ and as a percentage (g per 100 cm³).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the undiluted egg white could not be measured directly from the calibration curve.
parts.answer: Its reading was outside the range of the standards, and the relationship cannot be assumed to continue beyond the highest standard (extrapolation is unreliable).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student then boiled some egg white until it was solid. Explain why boiled egg white still gives a purple colour with biuret reagent.
parts.answer: Boiling denatures the protein by breaking hydrogen/ionic bonds and hydrophobic interactions; peptide bonds are not broken, and the biuret reagent detects peptide bonds.
parts.working: B1 denaturation does not break peptide bonds; B1 biuret detects peptide bonds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student has a stock solution of albumin at 10 mg cm⁻³ and distilled water. Describe how she could make a serial dilution to give five solutions, each half the concentration of the one before, starting with the stock solution. State the concentration of each solution.
parts.answer: Concentrations: 10, 5, 2.5, 1.25, 0.625 mg cm⁻³. Method: put e.g. 10 cm³ of stock in the first tube; transfer 5 cm³ of stock to a second tube and add 5 cm³ of distilled water, mix; transfer 5 cm³ of this to a third tube and add 5 cm³ water, mix; repeat for the remaining tubes.
parts.working: B1 correct concentrations; B1 transfer 5 cm³ of previous solution; B1 add 5 cm³ distilled water; B1 mix thoroughly before the next transfer / use syringe or pipette for accurate volumes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student has samples of bread, rice, banana, chickpeas and sugar. Describe how she could test each sample for starch and record the results. You should include a control.
parts.answer: Crush/grind a small, equal amount of each food, mix with a little water; place a sample of each on a white tile/spotting tile; add 2 drops of iodine in KI solution to each; record colour (blue-black = starch; orange-brown = no starch) in a table; control: water (or sugar solution known to have no starch) with iodine, which stays orange-brown (or a known starch solution as positive control).
parts.working: 1 mark each for four of: preparation of samples; iodine solution; colour change described; control; results table.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a student could find out whether sugarcane juice contains a reducing sugar, a non-reducing sugar or both. Include the safety precautions she should take.
parts.answer: Test a sample of juice with an equal volume of Benedict's solution in a water-bath (about 90 °C) for 5 minutes: red/orange = reducing sugar; boil a fresh sample with dilute HCl for 2 minutes; cool and neutralise with sodium hydrogencarbonate until fizzing stops (or check with pH paper); then do Benedict's test; more precipitate/colour change after hydrolysis than before = non-reducing sugar present. Safety: eye protection; use a test-tube holder/heat-resistant gloves; point tubes away from people; care with acid.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: Benedict's test with heating described; acid hydrolysis; neutralisation; comparison of results to decide; one safety precaution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an experiment to compare the specific heat capacity of water and cooking oil. You are provided with a 12 V immersion heater of known power, a polystyrene cup, a balance, a thermometer and a stopclock.
parts.answer: Weigh 100 g of water into the polystyrene cup (insulated, with lid); record starting temperature; switch on heater for a fixed time (e.g. 3 minutes), stirring; record the highest temperature reached; repeat with 100 g of oil starting at the same temperature; calculate SHC = energy supplied (power × time) ÷ (mass × temperature rise) and compare; repeat 3 times for each and find mean.
parts.working: 1 mark each for five of: same mass using balance; insulation/lid; same heater/time; starting and final temperature measured (stirring); same starting temperature; SHC formula used; repeats/mean.

practice.stem: A student has a 2.0 % starch solution and distilled water. She needs 10 cm³ each of 2.0, 1.6, 1.2, 0.8 and 0.4 % starch solutions to investigate the iodine test with a colorimeter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volumes of 2.0 % starch solution and of distilled water needed to make 10 cm³ of each concentration. Present your answer as a list.
parts.working: M1 volume of stock = (required % ÷ 2.0) × 10; A1 at least three correct; A1 all correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why this is called a proportional dilution rather than a serial dilution.
parts.answer: Each solution is made directly from the stock solution in a different ratio, not by diluting the previous solution by the same factor each time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how she could show that the colour change depends on starch, not on the water.
parts.answer: Include a control of 10 cm³ distilled water (0 % starch) with iodine solution.
parts.working: B1 0 % starch control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find the protein concentration of a sample of soy milk using the biuret test and a colorimeter. You are provided with a 10 mg cm⁻³ albumin solution, biuret reagent, distilled water and a colorimeter.
parts.answer: Make standards of 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 mg cm⁻³ by proportional dilution (e.g. for 10 cm³: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 cm³ of stock made up to 10 cm³ with water); add the same volume of biuret reagent (e.g. 2 cm³) to 2 cm³ of each standard; leave for the same time (e.g. 10 minutes) at room temperature; zero colorimeter with water + biuret blank, use a green/yellow filter; measure absorbance of each standard, 3 times; plot calibration curve of absorbance against concentration; treat diluted soy milk in the same way and read concentration from the curve, multiplying by any dilution factor.
parts.working: 1 mark each for six of: range of ≥5 concentrations; how dilutions made; same volumes of sample/reagent; same time; blank/zero; filter colour; repeats; calibration curve; unknown read from curve (×dilution factor).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation into the effect of temperature on the time taken for egg albumin solution to become opaque (cloudy). Your plan should include the independent variable, how the dependent variable will be measured, and the variables to be standardised.
parts.answer: IV: temperature, at least five values e.g. 55, 60, 65, 70, 75, 80 °C using thermostatically controlled water-baths checked with a thermometer; DV: time taken for the albumin to become opaque, judged when a black cross/printed mark behind the tube can no longer be seen (or when absorbance reaches a set value in a colorimeter), timed with a stopclock; standardise: albumin concentration (same egg white batch, same dilution), volume (e.g. 5 cm³), tube size, pH; place each tube of albumin in the bath and start timing as soon as tube is placed in bath; repeat 3 times at each temperature and calculate mean; rate = 1/time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for six of: ≥5 temperatures with suitable range; water-bath and thermometer; end-point method that is objective; timing; standardised concentration; standardised volume; repeats and mean; rate as 1/time.

parts.label: a
