parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to present the mean lipid content of seeds of five species (sunflower, mustard, sesame, maize, wheat) as a bar chart.
parts.answer: Species on the x-axis and mean lipid content / % on the y-axis with a linear scale starting at zero; bars of equal width, separated by gaps (data are discrete categories); each bar labelled with the species.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: axes correct with label/units; scale from zero; equal-width bars; gaps between bars; bars labelled.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Equal masses of water and of cooking oil were heated with identical heaters:
time / s: 0, 60, 120, 180, 240
water temperature / °C: 20.0, 22.4, 24.9, 27.3, 29.8
oil temperature / °C: 20.0, 25.1, 30.0, 35.2, 40.1
Describe the results shown by these data.
parts.answer: Both temperatures rise steadily (linearly) with time; oil rises faster than water; after 240 s the oil has risen by 20.1 °C and the water by 9.8 °C, about twice as much.
parts.working: B1 both increase steadily; B1 oil faster; B1 data quoted with units.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Biuret calibration data:
protein / mg cm⁻³: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10
absorbance: 0.00, 0.11, 0.24, 0.35, 0.47, 0.60
Explain why the student should draw a straight line of best fit through the origin rather than joining the points.
parts.answer: The points lie close to a straight line, so random errors make individual points scatter; a line of best fit averages out these errors, and the origin is a real data point (no protein = zero absorbance after zeroing).
parts.working: B1 points scatter due to random error / best fit averages; B1 origin justified.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The gradient of the best-fit line through the origin is 0.0593 absorbance units per mg cm⁻³. A sample of soy milk has an absorbance of 0.3. Calculate its protein concentration. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 5.1 mg cm⁻³

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bar chart shows the mean reducing sugar content of guava, apple and mango juice, with error bars of ±2 standard errors. State what these error bars represent.
parts.answer: The 95 % confidence interval – the range within which we can be 95 % confident the true (population) mean lies.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The error bars for guava and apple overlap, but those for apple and mango do not. Explain what can be concluded.
parts.answer: Guava and apple: the difference between their means may be due to chance (not significant); apple and mango: the difference is likely to be significant (real).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A graph of water temperature against heating time is a straight line passing through (60 s, 24.0 °C) and (240 s, 33.0 °C). Calculate the gradient, giving the units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The heater supplied 50 J s⁻¹ to 250 g of water. Use the gradient to calculate the specific heat capacity of water, c = power ÷ (mass × gradient).
parts.answer: 4.0 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why it is better to use the gradient of the line than a single pair of readings.
parts.answer: The gradient uses all the data/the best-fit line, reducing the effect of random error in individual readings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The protein content of 40 individual chickpea seeds was measured, and the results were grouped into classes: 18.0–18.9, 19.0–19.9, 20.0–20.9, 21.0–21.9 and 22.0–22.9 % protein. The frequencies were 4, 9, 15, 8 and 4. State the type of chart that should be drawn and explain why the bars should touch.
parts.answer: A histogram; protein content is a continuous variable, so there are no gaps between the classes.
parts.working: B1 histogram; B1 continuous data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the modal class and describe the shape of the distribution.
parts.answer: Modal class 20.0–20.9 % (15 seeds); the distribution is roughly symmetrical/normal, with most seeds near the middle and few at the extremes (4 in each end class).
parts.working: B1 modal class; B1 shape.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Glucose standards gave the following colorimeter readings after Benedict's test:
glucose / %: 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8
reading: 0.00, 0.16, 0.33, 0.47, 0.55
A fruit juice gave a reading of 0.62. Explain why the student cannot use the graph to find the glucose concentration of the juice.
parts.answer: 0.62 is higher than the highest standard (0.55), so the concentration would have to be found by extrapolation; the curve is already levelling off (0.47 → 0.55), so its shape beyond 0.8 % is unknown.
parts.working: B1 outside range/extrapolation; B1 line not linear/levelling off so unreliable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the increase in reading per 0.2 % glucose between 0.0 and 0.4 % and between 0.6 and 0.8 %, and suggest why it is smaller at higher concentrations.
parts.answer: 0.165 per 0.2 % (0–0.4 %); 0.08 per 0.2 % (0.6–0.8 %); Benedict's reagent (Cu²⁺) is becoming used up/limiting at high glucose concentrations.
parts.working: B1 both values; B1 reagent limiting.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Starch and sugar content (g per 100 g) of bananas during ripening:
day: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8
starch: 20, 16, 10, 5, 2
sugar: 1, 5, 11, 15, 18
The student plotted both sets of data on one graph. Describe how she should arrange the axes and distinguish the two lines.
parts.answer: Day on the x-axis; one y-axis for both if same units and range (g per 100 g, 0–20), or a second y-axis on the right labelled clearly; different symbols (e.g. × and ⊙) and a key; points joined by ruled lines.
parts.working: B1 axes; B1 key/different symbols.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming straight lines between the plotted points, calculate the day on which the starch and sugar contents were equal, and the value at that time. Give both answers to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: between days 2 and 4 starch falls 3 g per day from 16 and sugar rises 3 g per day from 5 (M1); 16 − 3t = 5 + 3t → t = 1.833 days after day 2 (M1); day 3.83, value 10.50 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the total of starch + sugar is not constant during ripening.
parts.answer: Some sugar is used in respiration (and water content changes), so carbohydrate is lost/total mass changes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Absorbance of starch–iodine mixtures:
starch / g dm⁻³: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
absorbance: 0.00, 0.21, 0.40, 0.57, 0.68, 0.73, 0.75
Describe the shape of the graph of absorbance against starch concentration and state the range of concentrations that is suitable for a calibration curve.
parts.answer: Approximately linear (straight) from 0 to about 2–3 g dm⁻³, then the gradient decreases and the curve levels off towards 0.75; only the linear part, about 0–3 g dm⁻³, is suitable.
parts.working: B1 shape; B1 suitable range.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the curve levels off at high starch concentrations.
parts.answer: Iodine becomes limiting (all used up), so no more complex forms; the solution is so dark that almost no light passes through, so the colorimeter cannot detect further increases.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mean increase in absorbance per g dm⁻³ between 0 and 2 g dm⁻³, and between 4 and 6 g dm⁻³.
parts.answer: 0.20 and 0.035 per g dm⁻³
parts.working: Both needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student plotted a graph of the time taken for albumin to turn opaque against temperature. Her graph had these features:
• the x-axis was labelled 'temp' and the y-axis 'time'
• the y-axis scale went 0, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 s with equal spacing
• points were plotted as large dots
• a smooth curve was drawn from the origin through the points and continued past the last point
• the plotted points used only about one quarter of the grid.
Identify five faults and state how each should be corrected.
parts.answer: 1 Axis labels lack units → temperature / °C and time / s. 2 Non-linear y-axis scale → use a uniform linear scale. 3 Large dots hide the exact position → use small crosses or encircled dots. 4 Line drawn through the origin and extrapolated beyond the data → draw only between first and last points (no data at 0 °C). 5 Small use of grid → choose scales so data occupy more than half of the grid in each direction.
parts.working: 1 mark per fault with its correction (max 5).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mean reducing sugar (g per 100 g) of potatoes stored for 0, 3, 6, 9 and 12 days was 0.12, 0.25, 0.31, 0.44, 0.52. Each mean is from 4 potatoes; the standard deviations were 0.02, 0.018, 0.03, 0.024, 0.028. Calculate the value of 2 × SE (SE = s/√n) for day 3 and day 6, and state whether the error bars for these two days overlap.
parts.answer: day 3: ±0.018; day 6: ±0.030; bars 0.268 (top of day 3) and 0.280 (bottom of day 6) – they do not overlap
parts.working: SE = s/2 (M1); 2SE = 0.018 and 0.030 (A1); compares 0.268 with 0.280 → no overlap (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the student should join the points with ruled straight lines rather than draw a line of best fit through the origin, and suggest what the non-overlapping error bars indicate.
parts.answer: There is no reason to assume a straight-line/proportional relationship and day 0 is not zero sugar (0.12), so the line should not pass through the origin; points joined point-to-point show the actual data; non-overlapping 95 % CIs suggest the increase between days 3 and 6 is significant.
parts.working: B1 justification of joining points/not through origin; B1 significance of non-overlap.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Iodine solution turned blue-black on a cut potato but stayed orange-brown on a cut ripe grape. Explain these results.
parts.answer: Potato cells store carbohydrate as starch, which forms a blue-black complex with iodine; ripe grapes store carbohydrate as sugars (glucose/fructose), which do not react with iodine.
parts.working: B1 potato contains starch; B1 grape contains sugars not starch.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two equal cubes of fresh beetroot of the same size were placed in test-tubes of water, one at 5 °C and one at 60 °C. Red pigment left the beetroot much faster in the hot water. Explain these results.
parts.answer: Heat increases the kinetic energy of the water and pigment molecules, so the pigment diffuses out faster; heat also damages the cell surface and vacuole membranes (denaturing membrane proteins and making the phospholipid bilayer leaky), so the red pigment escapes from the vacuole more quickly.
parts.working: B1 more kinetic energy → faster diffusion/movement of pigment; B1 heat denatures membrane proteins/damages membranes; B1 membranes become more permeable, so pigment leaves the vacuole and cell.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Raw egg white is a clear liquid, but when an egg is fried, the white becomes solid and opaque. Explain this change.
parts.answer: Heat breaks hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and hydrophobic interactions in the albumin; the proteins lose their tertiary structure/unfold (denature); the unfolded chains tangle and bond together, forming an insoluble solid that scatters light.
parts.working: B1 bonds broken; B1 denaturation/loss of 3D shape; B1 aggregation/insoluble.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A boy in Gilgit feels much colder when he comes out of a swimming pool on a windy day than when he is dry. Explain why.
parts.answer: Water on his skin evaporates (faster in wind); water has a high latent heat of vaporisation, so evaporation removes a lot of heat energy from his skin (to break hydrogen bonds).
parts.working: B1 evaporation; B1 high latent heat removes much heat from skin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A salad dressing of oil and lemon juice separates into two layers when left to stand. Explain why.
parts.answer: Oil (triglycerides) is non-polar and cannot form hydrogen bonds with water; water molecules are more attracted to each other, so the oil forms a separate layer (on top, as it is less dense).
parts.working: B1 oil non-polar/no H bonds with water; B1 water molecules attract each other, oil separates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: When egg yolk, which contains phospholipids, is added and shaken, the dressing stays mixed. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Phospholipids have a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails; they surround tiny oil droplets with tails in the oil and heads facing the water, so the droplets stay dispersed (emulsion).
parts.working: B1 hydrophilic/hydrophobic parts; B1 orientation around droplets keeps them apart.

practice.stem: Samples of egg albumin solution were held at different temperatures for 10 minutes, cooled, and the cloudiness (turbidity) measured with a colorimeter. Turbidity (arbitrary units): 20 °C – 0.05; 40 °C – 0.06; 60 °C – 0.21; 70 °C – 0.68; 80 °C – 0.95; 90 °C – 0.97.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the results.
parts.answer: Up to 40 °C turbidity stays low – albumin keeps its tertiary structure and stays dissolved (hydrophilic R groups outside); between 60 and 80 °C turbidity rises sharply – increased kinetic energy breaks hydrogen and ionic bonds, the protein denatures and unfolds; hydrophobic R groups become exposed so the molecules clump together and come out of solution (coagulate), making it cloudy; by 80–90 °C nearly all protein is denatured, so turbidity levels off.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: low/unchanged at low temperature with reason; denaturation – H/ionic bonds broken; hydrophobic groups exposed/coagulation/insoluble; plateau as all denatured.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When ethanol was added to a clear solution of a globular protein, the protein formed a white precipitate. Explain this result.
parts.answer: In water, hydrophobic R groups are folded inside and hydrophilic R groups are on the outside, which keeps the protein soluble; ethanol is less polar than water and disrupts hydrophobic interactions and hydrogen bonds; the protein unfolds/denatures and the exposed hydrophobic regions stick together, so it comes out of solution.
parts.working: B1 normal arrangement of R groups/solubility; B1 ethanol disrupts hydrophobic interactions/H bonds; B1 denatures/aggregates.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When lemon juice is added to warm milk, the milk protein casein forms solid curds (as in paneer making). Explain this result.
parts.answer: Lemon juice contains acid (H⁺ ions) that lowers the pH; the H⁺ ions neutralise the negative charges on casein molecules; without charges to repel each other, the molecules come together/bond and precipitate as curds (the change in charge also breaks ionic bonds and changes shape).
parts.working: B1 H⁺/lower pH; B1 charges on R groups changed/neutralised; B1 molecules no longer repel → aggregate/precipitate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Potato discs were placed in either 5 % glucose solution or a 5 % starch suspension for 1 hour. The discs in glucose lost 8 % of their mass; the discs in starch gained 3 % of their mass, the same as discs in distilled water. Explain these results.
parts.answer: 5 % glucose solution has many dissolved solute molecules, so its water potential is lower than that of the potato cells; water left the cells by osmosis (mass decrease); starch is insoluble/has very few, very large molecules, so the suspension has almost the same water potential as pure water, which is higher than the cells, so water entered (mass increase like water).
parts.working: B1 glucose lowers water potential; B1 osmosis out of cells; B1 starch insoluble/few molecules → behaves like water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two trays, one of water and one of dry soil, each 2 cm deep, were left in the sun for 2 hours. The temperature of the water rose by 6 °C and that of the soil by 15 °C. Explain this result and suggest why it is important for aquatic organisms.
parts.answer: Water has a high specific heat capacity, because much of the energy absorbed is used to break hydrogen bonds between water molecules rather than increasing their kinetic energy; so the water warms less than soil for the same energy; aquatic organisms live in a stable temperature, so enzymes stay near their optimum/no denaturation.
parts.working: B1 high SHC; B1 linked to hydrogen bonds; B1 importance for organisms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student chewed a small piece of bread for 2 minutes. Before chewing, an extract of the bread stayed blue with Benedict's solution; after chewing it turned orange. Explain these results.
parts.answer: Saliva contains amylase; amylase hydrolyses glycosidic bonds in starch; producing maltose, which is a reducing sugar and gives a positive Benedict's test.
parts.working: B1 salivary amylase; B1 hydrolysis of starch; B1 maltose is reducing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Collagen in tendons does not dissolve in water. However, when collagen is boiled for a long time it forms gelatin, which dissolves in hot water and forms a gel (jelly) when cooled. Explain these observations.
parts.answer: In collagen, three polypeptides form a triple helix held by many hydrogen bonds, and molecules are joined by covalent cross-links into fibrils/fibres, so it is insoluble; long boiling breaks the hydrogen bonds (and some cross-links), so the chains separate into single polypeptides (gelatin) that dissolve in hot water; on cooling, hydrogen bonds re-form between parts of the chains, forming a network that traps water molecules – a gel.
parts.working: 1 mark each: structure of collagen explains insolubility; heat breaks H bonds/cross-links → separate chains; gelatin chains soluble/interact with water; on cooling H bonds re-form a network trapping water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Samples of dried seeds were burnt in a calorimeter. Energy released per gram: sunflower 25 kJ; groundnut 24 kJ; wheat 15 kJ; rice 14 kJ. Explain these results.
parts.answer: Sunflower and groundnut seeds store mainly lipid (triglycerides), while wheat and rice store mainly starch; lipids contain more C–H bonds and less oxygen per gram than carbohydrates; so more energy is released per gram when they are oxidised.
parts.working: B1 oil seeds vs starch seeds; B1 more C–H bonds/H and less O in lipids; B1 more energy per gram.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The accepted value for pure triglyceride is about 39 kJ g⁻¹. Suggest two reasons why the values for sunflower and groundnut seeds are lower.
parts.answer: The seeds are not pure lipid (they also contain protein, carbohydrate, fibre and water); heat is lost to the surroundings in the calorimeter/incomplete combustion.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Blood from a person with sickle cell anaemia was placed in a sealed slide and the oxygen was removed. After 30 minutes, many red blood cells had become sickle-shaped. When oxygen was supplied again, most cells returned to a normal shape. Explain these results.
parts.answer: In HbS, a glutamic acid (charged) is replaced by valine (non-polar) on the surface of the β-chains; when deoxygenated, the shape of HbS exposes a hydrophobic region that binds to the valine of another molecule; HbS molecules polymerise into long insoluble fibres that distort the cell into a sickle shape; when oxygen binds again, the haemoglobin changes shape, the fibres dissolve and the cell returns to normal.
parts.working: 1 mark each: amino acid change and R group property; deoxygenated HbS sticks together (hydrophobic interaction); fibres/polymers distort cell; reoxygenation reverses it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A length of dialysis (Visking) tubing was filled with a mixture of starch and glucose solutions and placed in a beaker of distilled water. After 30 minutes, the water outside gave a positive Benedict's test but a negative iodine test. In a second experiment, amylase was also placed inside the tubing with starch only; after 30 minutes, the water outside gave a positive Benedict's test. Explain these results.
parts.answer: The tubing is partially permeable, with pores that let small molecules through but not large ones; glucose molecules are small and diffused out down a concentration gradient, so the water outside contained reducing sugar; starch molecules are too large to pass through, so no starch was outside (negative iodine); in the second experiment amylase hydrolysed starch into maltose, which is small enough to diffuse out and is a reducing sugar.
parts.working: 1 mark each: partially permeable/pore size; glucose small → diffuses out; starch too large; amylase converts starch to maltose that diffuses out.

practice.stem: A student investigates how the concentration of hydrochloric acid used to hydrolyse sucrose affects the concentration of reducing sugar produced. Each tube contains 5 cm³ of 2 % sucrose solution and 1 cm³ of acid; it is heated, neutralised, tested with Benedict's solution, and the absorbance of the remaining blue solution is measured with a colorimeter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: concentration of hydrochloric acid; dependent: concentration of reducing sugar produced (measured as the absorbance of the solution after the Benedict's test).
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two variables that should be standardised and describe how to standardise one of them.
parts.answer: Any two of: temperature during hydrolysis (thermostatically controlled water-bath at a set temperature, e.g. 90 °C); time of heating with acid (stop-clock); volume/concentration of sucrose solution; volume and concentration of Benedict's solution; heating time and temperature in the Benedict's test; amount of sodium hydrogencarbonate used to neutralise.
parts.working: B1 two variables; B1 method for one.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a suitable control and state its purpose.
parts.answer: A tube of 5 cm³ sucrose solution heated with 1 cm³ distilled water instead of acid, then treated in the same way; shows that reducing sugar is produced by acid hydrolysis and that the sucrose solution was not already contaminated with reducing sugar.
parts.working: B1 control described (water instead of acid); B1 purpose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student compares the reducing sugar content of juice from guava, apple and mango using the Benedict's test and a colorimeter. Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: type of fruit (juice). Dependent: absorbance/colour after the Benedict's test (reducing sugar concentration).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three variables that should be standardised.
parts.answer: Any three of: volume of juice; volume (concentration) of Benedict's solution; temperature of water-bath; heating time; dilution of juice; time between heating and reading; same colorimeter filter.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student compares the starch content of two rice varieties, Basmati and a short-grain variety, using iodine solution and a colorimeter. Suggest how she should standardise the rice samples before testing.
parts.answer: Grind the rice to a fine powder (same particle size) and use the same mass (e.g. 1.0 g) of each, mixed with the same volume of water and boiled for the same time to release the starch.
parts.working: B1 same mass; B1 same preparation (grinding/boiling/water volume).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the colorimeter must be set to zero absorbance using a tube of water and iodine solution with no rice.
parts.answer: Iodine solution itself absorbs some light; zeroing with this blank means any absorbance measured is due only to the starch–iodine complex.
parts.working: B1 iodine/water absorbs light; B1 readings then due to starch only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student uses the biuret test to compare the protein content of milk from four shops. Describe a negative control and a positive control for this investigation.
parts.answer: Negative: distilled water (instead of milk) with biuret reagent – stays blue. Positive: a known protein solution, e.g. albumin, with biuret reagent – turns purple.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the purpose of each control.
parts.answer: Negative control shows that the reagent alone (or water) does not give purple, so purple is due to protein; positive control shows the reagent is working/what a positive looks like.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student compares the lipid content of almonds, walnuts and peanuts using the emulsion test. She records how cloudy the water becomes using a scale from 0 to 5. State the independent and dependent variables.
parts.answer: Independent: type of nut. Dependent: cloudiness of the emulsion (score 0–5).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how she should standardise two variables.
parts.answer: Use the same mass of crushed nut (weighed on a balance); the same volume of ethanol and of water (measured with a syringe/graduated pipette); shake for the same time; read cloudiness after the same time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two variables with how they are standardised.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student compares the specific heat capacities of water and cooking oil. She heats each liquid with an electric heater and measures the temperature rise after 4 minutes. Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: type of liquid. Dependent: temperature rise (°C) after 4 minutes.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three variables that must be kept constant.
parts.answer: Any three of: mass of liquid; power of heater; heating time; starting temperature; type/insulation of container; stirring.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student investigates the effect of temperature on the denaturation of egg albumin. She uses water-baths at 40, 50, 60, 70 and 80 °C and measures the cloudiness of the albumin after 5 minutes with a colorimeter. Describe how she should ensure that the albumin is at the correct temperature for exactly 5 minutes.
parts.answer: Use thermostatically controlled water-baths, checking temperature with a thermometer; place the albumin in the bath only after the bath is at temperature and in thin-walled tubes; start timing when the tube is placed in the bath and remove/cool in ice water at exactly 5 minutes.
parts.working: B1 thermostatic bath checked with thermometer; B1 timing/cooling method.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the samples should all be cooled to the same temperature before their cloudiness is measured.
parts.answer: Temperature could affect the cloudiness/absorbance reading or denaturation could continue while hot; cooling makes readings comparable.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a suitable control and explain its purpose.
parts.answer: Albumin kept at room temperature (or 20 °C) for 5 minutes and measured in the same way; shows the cloudiness of undenatured albumin, so any increase is due to heating.
parts.working: B1 control; B1 purpose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student investigates how the time for which starch is boiled with dilute hydrochloric acid affects the amount of reducing sugar produced. She takes samples after 0, 5, 10, 15 and 20 minutes. Explain why each sample must be neutralised as soon as it is removed.
parts.answer: Neutralising stops the hydrolysis, so each sample represents exactly that boiling time; and Benedict's test needs alkaline conditions.
parts.working: B1 stops reaction at that time; B1 Benedict's needs alkaline conditions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two variables, other than temperature, that she should standardise, and explain why one of them would affect the results if it varied.
parts.answer: Concentration of acid; volume of acid; starch concentration/volume; volume of Benedict's. E.g. a higher acid concentration would hydrolyse glycosidic bonds faster, giving more reducing sugar in the same time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two variables; 1 mark for an explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Gelatin is made from collagen. Fresh kiwi fruit contains a protease. A student adds 2 cm³ of fresh kiwi extract to 10 cm³ of warm gelatin solution and records whether it sets when cooled to 10 °C. Describe a control for this experiment.
parts.answer: Add 2 cm³ of boiled (and cooled) kiwi extract to 10 cm³ of the same gelatin solution and cool to 10 °C in the same way.
parts.working: B1 boiled extract (or water); B1 same volumes/conditions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the control you described is better than using 2 cm³ of water.
parts.answer: Boiled extract contains all the same substances as fresh extract (e.g. acids, sugars, colour) except the active enzyme (denatured); so any difference must be due to the enzyme, whereas water only controls for dilution.
parts.working: B1 same substances except active enzyme; B1 so the difference is due to the enzyme.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two variables that should be standardised.
parts.answer: Any two of: gelatin concentration; volumes; temperature of incubation/cooling; time; ripeness/source of kiwi.
parts.working: Both needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student wraps the bulbs of four thermometers in equal pieces of cotton wool. She soaks one in water, one in ethanol, one in salt solution, and leaves one dry. She records the fall in temperature after 10 minutes beside an electric fan. State the purpose of the dry cotton wool.
parts.answer: It is a control: it shows the change in temperature caused by the fan/air alone, without evaporation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify three variables that should be standardised in this experiment, and explain why one of them must be controlled.
parts.answer: Any three of: volume of each liquid; mass/thickness of cotton wool; starting temperature of liquids; distance from fan/fan speed; humidity/room temperature; time. E.g. the fan speed affects the rate of evaporation, so it would change the cooling independently of the liquid.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three variables; 1 mark for the explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student compares the tensile strength of cotton threads (made of cellulose) from three brands by adding 50 g masses until each thread breaks. State three variables she must keep the same.
parts.answer: Any three of: length of thread; diameter/thickness (or number of strands); how the masses are added (gently, same rate); humidity/dryness of thread; clamp/knot method; temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the student should test at least five threads of each brand.
parts.answer: Threads vary (e.g. weak points), so repeats allow a mean to be calculated and anomalous results to be identified, making the results more reliable.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest an improvement to the way the masses are added.
parts.answer: Use smaller increments (e.g. 10 g) near the breaking point so the breaking load is measured more precisely, adding them gently to avoid jerking.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student compared reducing sugar in three brands of honey. She diluted brand A 1 in 10, brand B 1 in 20 and brand C 1 in 10. She heated the tubes in a beaker of water over a Bunsen burner: A for 3 minutes, B for 5 minutes and C for 4 minutes. She concluded that brand B contains most reducing sugar. Identify two uncontrolled variables and explain how each could affect her conclusion.
parts.answer: (1) Dilution: brand B was diluted 1 in 20 but brands A and C 1 in 10, so the tubes do not contain equal amounts of honey and the colours cannot be compared fairly. (2) Heating time: B was heated for 5 minutes, A for 3 and C for 4, so more copper(II) ions may be reduced in B, giving more precipitate even if its sugar content is no higher. (The water temperature was also not controlled over a Bunsen burner.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two uncontrolled variables identified (dilution; heating time); 1 mark for each correct explanation of how it could change the conclusion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how she should control the temperature during heating.
parts.answer: Use a thermostatically controlled water-bath set at e.g. 90 °C, checked with a thermometer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A nutrition researcher wants to compare the protein content of masoor daal grown in two different districts. Suggest three variables, other than district, that could affect protein content of the daal, and describe how she could control or take account of each.
parts.answer: Variety (use the same variety from both districts); age/storage time of the seeds (use seeds harvested in the same season and stored the same time); water content (dry the samples to constant mass and express protein per g dry mass); also fertiliser use (record and choose farms with similar practice).
parts.working: 1 mark each for a variable with a sensible way to control or account for it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why protein content should be expressed per gram of dry mass rather than per gram of fresh mass.
parts.answer: Samples may contain different amounts of water; water adds mass but no protein, so a wetter sample would appear to have less protein per gram; dry mass gives a fair comparison.
parts.working: B1 water content varies; B1 so per fresh mass is not a fair comparison.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Milk protein (casein) precipitates as curd when the pH of milk is lowered, as when paneer is made with lemon juice. A student plans to add buffer solutions of pH 3.5, 4.0, 4.5, 5.0, 5.5 and 6.0 to milk and measure the dry mass of curd formed. Explain why the student should use buffer solutions rather than different volumes of lemon juice.
parts.answer: Buffers keep a fixed, known pH; different volumes of lemon juice would change the total volume of the mixture and add different amounts of other substances (e.g. sugars, citric acid), so pH would not be the only variable.
parts.working: B1 buffers give known/constant pH; B1 lemon juice volume varies/adds other substances.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three other variables that must be standardised and give a suitable value for one of them.
parts.answer: Any three of: volume of milk (e.g. 50 cm³); type/source of milk (same batch); volume of buffer; temperature (e.g. 40 °C in a water-bath); time before filtering; drying method/time (to constant mass).
parts.working: 1 mark each for three variables (one must include a suitable value).

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a colorimeter assay of starch using iodine, a student uses the same volume of iodine solution for all samples. Explain why the iodine must be in excess in every tube.
parts.answer: So that the colour (absorbance) depends only on the amount of starch; if iodine ran out, tubes with more starch could not form more starch–iodine complex and absorbance would stop increasing.
parts.working: B1 starch must be the limiting factor; B1 otherwise absorbance levels off/underestimates high concentrations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why readings should be taken at a fixed time after mixing iodine with the starch sample.
parts.answer: The colour may develop or fade with time (or precipitate may settle), so reading at different times would change the absorbance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the same filter and the same cuvette (or matched cuvettes) should be used for every reading.
parts.answer: Different filters let through different wavelengths, which are absorbed by different amounts; cuvettes may differ in thickness/scratches, so the path length/light transmission would change; either would change absorbance for the same concentration.
parts.working: B1 filter wavelength; B1 cuvette path length/scratches.

practice.stem:
An electron micrograph of a chloroplast from a mango leaf shows:
A: two membranes surrounding the whole organelle
B: stacks of flattened membrane discs, joined to each other by single membranes (intergranal lamellae)
C: a fluid-filled matrix around the membranes
D: large, pale, oval granules in the matrix, made of the plant's main storage polysaccharide

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name structures A, B, C and D.
parts.answer: A chloroplast envelope (double membrane); B granum (stack of thylakoids); C stroma; D starch grain.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept 'thylakoids' for B.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where in the chloroplast (i) the light-dependent stage and (ii) the Calvin cycle take place.
parts.answer: (i) thylakoid membranes (grana); (ii) stroma.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The stroma also contains circular DNA and 70S ribosomes. Suggest the function of these.
parts.answer: To make some of the chloroplast's own proteins (e.g. part of rubisco / photosystem proteins).
parts.working: 1 mark: protein synthesis within the chloroplast / codes for and makes chloroplast proteins.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the internal structure of a chloroplast is adapted for the light-dependent stage of photosynthesis.
parts.answer: Many thylakoid membranes stacked into grana give a large surface area; they hold the photosystems, electron carriers and ATP synthase; the small thylakoid space lets a proton gradient build up quickly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: large surface area of thylakoid membranes / grana; photosystems (chlorophyll) held in membranes; electron transport chain in membrane; ATP synthase in membrane; small volume of thylakoid space for steep H⁺ gradient.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the stroma is adapted for the light-independent stage.
parts.answer: It contains the enzymes of the Calvin cycle, e.g. rubisco, and surrounds the thylakoids so ATP and reduced NADP diffuse only a short distance to it.
parts.working: 1 mark: enzymes of Calvin cycle / rubisco in stroma. 1 mark: close to thylakoids, short diffusion distance for ATP and reduced NADP (or contains RuBP / CO₂ dissolved).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why chloroplasts in leaf palisade cells store carbohydrate as starch rather than as glucose.
parts.answer: Starch is insoluble so it does not lower the water potential of the cell / affect osmosis; it is compact and does not leave the chloroplast.
parts.working: 1 mark insoluble / osmotically inactive; 1 mark compact / large store in small space / cannot diffuse out.

practice.stem: Pigments from fenugreek (methi) leaves were separated by thin-layer chromatography. The solvent front moved 9.5 cm from the origin. A yellow-green spot moved 6.4 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the Rf value of the yellow-green spot. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: Rf = distance moved by pigment ÷ distance moved by solvent front = 6.4 ÷ 9.5 (M1) = 0.67 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Carotene has an Rf value of 0.94 in this solvent. Calculate how far carotene moved from the origin. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 8.9 cm

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the colour of the spots formed by carotene and by chlorophyll a.
parts.answer: Carotene: orange (yellow-orange); chlorophyll a: blue-green.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Chlorophyll a is called the primary pigment. Explain what this means.
parts.answer: Chlorophyll a is found in the reaction centre of each photosystem; it is the pigment that is photoactivated and emits electrons, so it converts light energy into chemical energy.
parts.working: 1 mark: in reaction centre (P680/P700). 1 mark: emits (excited) electrons / directly involved in the light reactions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two accessory pigments and state their role.
parts.answer: Any two of chlorophyll b, carotene, xanthophyll; they absorb light of other wavelengths (that chlorophyll a absorbs poorly) and pass the energy to chlorophyll a in the reaction centre.
parts.working: 2 marks for two named accessory pigments; 1 mark for absorbing a wider range of wavelengths and passing energy to the reaction centre.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the two regions of the visible spectrum that chlorophyll a absorbs most strongly.
parts.answer: Blue-violet (about 430 nm) and red (about 660 nm).
parts.working: Both needed for 1 mark.

practice.stem:
A student extracted pigments from spinach leaves and separated them by paper chromatography. The solvent front moved 8.0 cm from the origin. Four spots were seen, which had moved 3.6 cm, 5.2 cm, 5.7 cm and 7.6 cm.
Reference Rf values in this solvent: carotene 0.95; xanthophyll 0.71; chlorophyll a 0.65; chlorophyll b 0.45

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the Rf value of each spot. Give each answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent front. 2 marks all four correct; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the reference table to identify the pigment in each spot.
parts.answer: Spot 1 chlorophyll b; spot 2 chlorophyll a; spot 3 xanthophyll; spot 4 carotene.
parts.working: 2 marks all four; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the pigments separate on the chromatography paper.
parts.answer: The pigments have different solubilities in the solvent and different attraction (adsorption) to the paper; more soluble/less attracted pigments are carried further by the solvent.
parts.working: 1 mark: differ in solubility in solvent. 1 mark: differ in affinity for/adsorption to paper, so travel different distances.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between an absorption spectrum and an action spectrum.
parts.answer: An absorption spectrum shows how much light of each wavelength is absorbed by a pigment (or pigments); an action spectrum shows the rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength of light.
parts.working: 1 mark: absorption = amount of light absorbed at each wavelength. 1 mark: action = rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Chlorophyll a absorbs very little light between 450 nm and 550 nm, yet the rate of photosynthesis at 480 nm is still quite high. Explain why.
parts.answer: Accessory pigments such as carotene and xanthophylls (and chlorophyll b) absorb light at these wavelengths (blue-green); they pass the energy to chlorophyll a in the reaction centre of the photosystem; so light at these wavelengths is still used for photosynthesis.
parts.working: 1 mark: accessory pigments named (carotenoids/chlorophyll b). 1 mark: absorb blue/blue-green light around 450–500 nm. 1 mark: transfer energy to primary pigment / reaction centre chlorophyll a.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why most leaves appear green.
parts.answer: Green light (about 500–560 nm) is absorbed least by the pigments, so it is reflected or transmitted to the eye.
parts.working: 1 mark: green wavelengths reflected/not absorbed.

practice.stem: Leaf pigments were spotted at one corner of a square sheet of chromatography paper. Solvent 1 was run up the paper until its front was 10.0 cm from the origin. One spot, X, had moved 6.0 cm and looked brownish-green. The paper was dried, turned through 90° and run in solvent 2, whose front moved 8.0 cm. Spot X split into two spots that had moved 2.4 cm and 5.6 cm in the second direction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the Rf value of spot X in solvent 1 and the Rf values of the two new spots in solvent 2.
parts.answer: Solvent 1: 0.60. Solvent 2: 0.30 and 0.70.
parts.working: M1 for distance ÷ solvent front; A1 for all three values.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why spot X contained two pigments but they only separated in solvent 2.
parts.answer: The two pigments had the same (very similar) solubility in solvent 1 and the same attraction to the paper, so they moved together; in solvent 2 their solubilities differ, so they move at different speeds and separate.
parts.working: 1 mark: separation depends on solubility in solvent / adsorption to paper; 1 mark: similar in solvent 1 so same Rf; 1 mark: different in solvent 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the pigment spots must be identified by Rf value rather than by the distance moved.
parts.answer: Distance moved depends on how far the solvent travels, which differs between runs; Rf is a ratio that stays constant for a pigment in a given solvent.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
The chlorophyll content of leaves from the sunny top and the shaded base of a large mango tree was measured (mg per g of leaf).
Sun leaves: chlorophyll a 2.4, chlorophyll b 0.8
Shade leaves: chlorophyll a 2.1, chlorophyll b 1.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of chlorophyll a to chlorophyll b for each type of leaf. Give each answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Sun leaves 3.0; shade leaves 2.1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Chlorophyll b is found mainly in the light-harvesting (antenna) complexes of the photosystems. Suggest how the lower ratio in shade leaves is an advantage to the tree.
parts.answer: Shade leaves have relatively more light-harvesting pigment around each reaction centre; so they absorb more of the dim light (including wavelengths that chlorophyll a absorbs poorly); more energy is funnelled to the reaction centres, so the rate of photosynthesis in low light is higher.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: larger antenna / more light harvesting per reaction centre; absorbs wider range / more of the scarce light; more energy passed to chlorophyll a / more photoactivation, so more ATP and reduced NADP in low light.

practice.stem:
Chinar (plane) tree leaves in the hills turn orange in autumn. Pigment content (µg per cm² of leaf) was measured every two weeks.
Week: 0, 2, 4, 6
Chlorophyll: 42, 30, 14, 4
Carotenoids: 9.0, 8.4, 7.6, 6.8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in chlorophyll and in carotenoids between week 0 and week 6. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Chlorophyll 90.5 %; carotenoids 24.4 %
parts.working: 1 mark each; percentage decrease = (start − end) ÷ start × 100.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the data to explain why the leaves change colour from green to orange.
parts.answer: Chlorophyll is broken down much faster than carotenoids; green chlorophyll no longer masks the yellow-orange carotenoids, which now absorb blue light and reflect yellow/orange.
parts.working: 1 mark: chlorophyll falls faster / carotenoids mostly remain. 1 mark: carotenoids no longer masked so orange colour seen.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the rate of photosynthesis of these leaves changes over the six weeks. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: It decreases, because there is much less chlorophyll a (and fewer photosystems) so less light energy is absorbed and fewer electrons are emitted from reaction centres.
parts.working: 1 mark: decreases; 1 mark: less chlorophyll a / reaction-centre pigment so less light absorbed / less ATP and reduced NADP.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three structural features that chloroplasts and mitochondria have in common.
parts.answer: Double membrane (envelope); their own circular DNA; 70S ribosomes; ATP synthase in an internal membrane; an internal fluid with enzymes (stroma / matrix).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two structural differences between a chloroplast and a mitochondrion.
parts.answer: Chloroplast has separate internal thylakoid membranes stacked into grana, while the mitochondrial inner membrane is folded into cristae; chloroplast contains photosynthetic pigments (chlorophyll) and starch grains, mitochondria do not; chloroplasts are usually larger.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid comparative differences (both organelles must be referred to).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the ATP synthase in the chloroplast faces the stroma.
parts.answer: Protons are pumped into (and accumulate in) the thylakoid space and flow back through ATP synthase into the stroma; ATP is made on the stroma side, where it is used in the Calvin cycle.
parts.working: 1 mark: H⁺ diffuse from thylakoid space to stroma through ATP synthase; 1 mark: ATP released into stroma where Calvin cycle needs it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of a photosystem and explain how it captures light energy.
parts.answer: A photosystem is a cluster of pigment molecules held by proteins in the thylakoid membrane; a light-harvesting system (antenna complex) of accessory pigments and chlorophyll molecules surrounds a reaction centre; pigments absorb photons and pass energy from molecule to molecule towards the reaction centre; the reaction centre contains a pair of chlorophyll a molecules (P680 in PSII, P700 in PSI) which, when excited, emit an electron to an electron acceptor.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: in thylakoid membrane, pigments + proteins; light-harvesting/antenna complex of many pigments; energy transferred to reaction centre; reaction centre = chlorophyll a (P680/P700); excited electron emitted / passed to electron acceptor (photoactivation).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some red seaweeds live in coastal seas at depths where most red and blue light has been absorbed by the water and mainly green light remains. These seaweeds contain a red accessory pigment called phycoerythrin. Suggest how phycoerythrin helps them to grow at these depths.
parts.answer: Phycoerythrin absorbs green light (it looks red because it reflects red); the absorbed energy is passed to chlorophyll a in the reaction centres, so the seaweed can still photosynthesise using the light available at depth.
parts.working: 1 mark: absorbs green light / wavelengths that reach that depth. 1 mark: energy passed to reaction centre chlorophyll so photosynthesis continues.

practice.stem:
Chloroplasts were broken open and separated into a thylakoid fraction and a stroma fraction. Each was incubated under different conditions.
Tube 1: thylakoids, light, water — oxygen released
Tube 2: stroma, light, water — no oxygen released
Tube 3: stroma, dark, CO₂ + ATP + reduced NADP — CO₂ fixed into sugars
Tube 4: stroma, dark, CO₂ only — almost no CO₂ fixed

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the results for tubes 1 and 2.
parts.answer: Thylakoids contain the photosystems and electron transport chains; in light, photolysis of water releases oxygen (tube 1); the stroma has no photosystems, so no oxygen is produced (tube 2); without light, no photoactivation and no oxygen.
parts.working: 1 mark: thylakoids are site of light-dependent stage / photosystems. 1 mark: photolysis of water in light releases O₂. 1 mark: stroma lacks photosystems/chlorophyll so no O₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the results for tubes 3 and 4.
parts.answer: The stroma contains the Calvin cycle enzymes (rubisco); ATP and reduced NADP, normally supplied by the light-dependent stage, were added, so CO₂ could be fixed even in the dark (tube 3); without ATP and reduced NADP, GP cannot be reduced to triose phosphate and RuBP cannot be regenerated, so fixation stops quickly (tube 4).
parts.working: 1 mark: stroma contains Calvin cycle enzymes/rubisco. 1 mark: ATP and reduced NADP are the products of the light-dependent stage needed, so light not directly required. 1 mark: without them GP not reduced / RuBP not regenerated so fixation stops.

practice.stem: A mutant of a barley plant cannot make chlorophyll b. In bright sunlight it grows almost as fast as normal plants, but in dim light it grows much more slowly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the mutant grows more slowly in dim light.
parts.answer: Chlorophyll b is an accessory pigment in the light-harvesting system; it absorbs wavelengths (e.g. about 450–480 nm and 640 nm) that chlorophyll a absorbs poorly; without it less light energy is absorbed and passed to the reaction centres; in dim light, light intensity is the limiting factor, so less photoactivation, less ATP and reduced NADP, a slower Calvin cycle and less growth.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: chlorophyll b = accessory pigment / in antenna complex; absorbs other wavelengths; passes energy to chlorophyll a in reaction centre; light is limiting in dim light so rate falls (fewer electrons, less ATP / reduced NADP).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the mutant grows almost normally in bright sunlight.
parts.answer: In bright light there is plenty of light energy even with fewer pigments, so light is no longer the limiting factor; another factor such as CO₂ concentration or temperature limits the rate in both plants.
parts.working: 1 mark: light not limiting / enough absorbed by chlorophyll a and carotenoids; 1 mark: rate limited by CO₂ / temperature in both.

practice.stem:
A filament of a green alga was placed on a microscope slide with aerobic bacteria that move towards oxygen. Light was passed through a prism so that each part of the filament received a different band of wavelengths. After 10 minutes the bacteria next to each part were counted.
400–450 nm: 38 bacteria
450–500 nm: 30 bacteria
500–550 nm: 6 bacteria
550–600 nm: 8 bacteria
600–650 nm: 20 bacteria
650–700 nm: 42 bacteria
700–750 nm: 3 bacteria

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the number of bacteria can be used to compare the rate of photosynthesis at different wavelengths.
parts.answer: Photosynthesis releases oxygen from photolysis of water; the aerobic bacteria move towards (gather where) oxygen is released, so more bacteria where the rate of photosynthesis is higher.
parts.working: 1 mark: oxygen made in light-dependent stage / photolysis; 1 mark: bacteria attracted to / cluster at highest O₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the data to explain why the bacteria were most numerous at 400–450 nm and 650–700 nm and few at 500–550 nm.
parts.answer: Chlorophyll a and b absorb strongly in blue-violet and red light, so most photoactivation and photolysis there; green light (500–550 nm) is absorbed least (mostly reflected/transmitted), only a little by carotenoids, so little oxygen.
parts.working: 1 mark: blue and red absorbed by chlorophylls; 1 mark: more light absorbed → more electrons/photolysis → more O₂; 1 mark: green poorly absorbed / reflected.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The data form a type of spectrum. Name this spectrum and suggest one limitation of the method.
parts.answer: Action spectrum. Limitation: bacteria counts are an indirect measure (bacteria may also respond to light, temperature or nutrients / move slowly / O₂ diffuses between regions, the light bands may differ in intensity).
parts.working: 1 mark: action spectrum; 1 mark: any valid limitation.

practice.stem: Seedlings were grown on a herbicide that stops the synthesis of carotenoids but not of chlorophyll. In bright light the new leaves were white. In very dim light the new leaves were pale green.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Carotenoids protect chlorophyll from damage by excess light energy. Use this information to explain the results.
parts.answer: Without carotenoids, excess absorbed light energy is not dissipated safely; chlorophyll is damaged/destroyed (photo-oxidised) in bright light so the leaves are white; in dim light little excess energy is absorbed, so chlorophyll survives and the leaves are green.
parts.working: 1 mark each: carotenoids normally absorb / remove excess energy (or harmful reactive oxygen); bright light destroys chlorophyll so white; dim light less damage so chlorophyll stays.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest and explain the effect of the herbicide on the rate of photosynthesis of the pale green leaves, even in dim light.
parts.answer: Rate is lower: carotenoids are accessory pigments that absorb blue-green light (about 450–500 nm) and pass energy to chlorophyll a, so fewer wavelengths are absorbed and less light energy reaches reaction centres.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower rate; 1 mark: carotenoids absorb other wavelengths / pass energy to reaction centre.

practice.stem:
The rate of photosynthesis of a cucumber plant was measured at two CO₂ concentrations. Temperature was kept at 25 °C.
Light intensity / arbitrary units: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10
Rate at 0.04 % CO₂ / arbitrary units: 0, 3.2, 5.4, 5.9, 6.0, 6.0
Rate at 0.10 % CO₂ / arbitrary units: 0, 3.2, 6.1, 8.8, 10.4, 10.8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a limiting factor.
parts.answer: The factor that is in shortest supply (furthest from its optimum) and so restricts the rate of a process; increasing it increases the rate.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the factor limiting the rate of photosynthesis at 2 arbitrary units of light intensity at both CO₂ concentrations. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Light intensity; at low light intensity the rate is the same at both CO₂ concentrations and rises as light intensity increases.
parts.working: 1 mark: light intensity. 1 mark: rate same for both CO₂ levels / rate increases with light intensity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the factor limiting the rate at 10 arbitrary units of light intensity in 0.04 % CO₂. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide concentration; the rate has levelled off so increasing light has no effect, but the rate is higher at 0.10 % CO₂.
parts.working: 1 mark: CO₂ concentration. 1 mark: plateau with light, but higher rate at higher CO₂ (data quote: 6.0 vs 10.8).

practice.stem: A wheat field near Lahore was studied on a clear winter day. The rate of photosynthesis was very low at 07:00 and rose steadily until about 11:00.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three environmental factors that can limit the rate of photosynthesis.
parts.answer: Light intensity; carbon dioxide concentration; temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept 'water' or 'chlorophyll' alone as these are not the three syllabus limiting factors.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest which factor limited the rate at 07:00. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Light intensity; the sun is low in the early morning so little light is absorbed, little ATP and reduced NADP are made, and the rate rises as light increases during the morning.
parts.working: 1 mark: light intensity; 1 mark: low light → little photoactivation / rate rises as light increases.

practice.stem:
The rate of photosynthesis of a sugar beet leaf was measured at 0.04 % CO₂ and two temperatures.
Light intensity / arbitrary units: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10
Rate at 15 °C: 0, 2.8, 4.6, 5.0, 5.0, 5.0
Rate at 25 °C: 0, 2.8, 5.3, 7.4, 8.1, 8.1

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the factor limiting the rate at a light intensity of 2 units. Give a reason from the data.
parts.answer: Light intensity; the rate is the same (2.8) at both temperatures, so temperature is not limiting, and the rate rises as light increases.
parts.working: 1 mark light intensity; 1 mark same rate at both temperatures / rate increases with light.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the factor limiting the rate at 15 °C and a light intensity of 10 units. Give a reason from the data.
parts.answer: Temperature; the rate has levelled off at 5.0, so more light has no effect, but it is higher (8.1) at 25 °C.
parts.working: 1 mark temperature; 1 mark plateau and higher rate at 25 °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest the factor limiting the rate at 25 °C and a light intensity of 10 units.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide concentration.
parts.working: 1 mark (accept amount of rubisco / chlorophyll as alternative).

practice.stem: Many vegetable farmers in southern Punjab grow tomatoes in polythene tunnels during winter. Some burn natural gas in heaters inside the tunnels at night and in the early morning.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two ways in which burning gas inside the tunnel can increase the rate of photosynthesis.
parts.answer: It raises the temperature, so the enzymes of the Calvin cycle (e.g. rubisco) work faster; combustion releases CO₂, which raises the CO₂ concentration for fixation by rubisco.
parts.working: 1 mark each: higher temperature / more kinetic energy for enzymes; more CO₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: On hot afternoons the farmers roll up the sides of the tunnels. Suggest why.
parts.answer: To stop the temperature rising above the optimum (enzymes denature / stomata close); and to let fresh air in so the CO₂ concentration, used up by photosynthesis, does not limit the rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: prevents overheating / temperature above optimum; 1 mark: replaces CO₂ used up.

practice.stem:
A tomato grower compared yields in two greenhouses. One had normal air (0.04 % CO₂) and the other was enriched to 0.10 % CO₂. Light and temperature were the same.
Normal air: 9.6 kg of tomatoes per m²
Enriched: 14.2 kg of tomatoes per m²

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in yield in the enriched greenhouse. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why increasing the CO₂ concentration increases the yield.
parts.answer: CO₂ is often the limiting factor in bright light; more CO₂ means rubisco fixes more CO₂ with RuBP; more GP and triose phosphate are made, so more sugars/biomass are produced (faster growth, more fruit).
parts.working: 1 mark: CO₂ was limiting. 1 mark: more CO₂ combines with RuBP (via rubisco) / faster Calvin cycle. 1 mark: more triose phosphate → more sugars, starch, growth.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the grower also keeps the greenhouse warm in winter, and why there is no benefit in raising the CO₂ concentration further on dull, cloudy days.
parts.answer: Warmth increases the rate of enzyme-controlled reactions (Calvin cycle), so temperature does not limit the rate; on dull days light intensity is the limiting factor, so extra CO₂ cannot increase the rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: warmth so temperature is not limiting / enzymes faster. 1 mark: on dull days light is limiting.

practice.stem:
Rates of photosynthesis of a cotton leaf were measured at different temperatures in high light and high CO₂.
Temperature / °C: 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40
Rate / arbitrary units: 2.1, 3.4, 5.0, 6.6, 7.8, 5.2, 1.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of temperature on the rate of photosynthesis shown by these results.
parts.answer: The rate increases from 10 °C to a maximum (optimum) at 30 °C (from 2.1 to 7.8 units), then decreases sharply at 35 °C and 40 °C (to 1.5 units at 40 °C).
parts.working: 1 mark: increases to optimum at 30 °C. 1 mark: then decreases above 30 °C; data quote with units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the effect of temperature on the rate of photosynthesis between 10 °C and 30 °C and above 30 °C.
parts.answer: Below the optimum, rising temperature gives enzymes (e.g. rubisco) and substrates more kinetic energy; more frequent collisions / more enzyme–substrate complexes form, so the Calvin cycle is faster. Above the optimum, enzymes begin to denature: hydrogen bonds break and the active site changes shape, so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form; stomata may close at high temperature, reducing CO₂ uptake.
parts.working: 1 mark: Calvin cycle/light-independent stage is enzyme-controlled. 1 mark: more kinetic energy, more collisions / E–S complexes. 1 mark: above optimum enzymes denature, active site shape changes. 1 mark: stomatal closure reduces CO₂ entry (or increased photorespiration not required).

practice.stem:
The rate of photosynthesis of a citrus leaf in bright light was measured at different CO₂ concentrations at 20 °C and 30 °C.
CO₂ / %: 0.01, 0.03, 0.05, 0.07, 0.09
Rate at 20 °C: 1.5, 4.0, 5.6, 6.0, 6.0
Rate at 30 °C: 1.6, 4.4, 7.1, 9.0, 9.6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in rate when the temperature is raised from 20 °C to 30 °C at 0.07 % CO₂. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why raising the temperature has almost no effect on the rate at 0.01 % CO₂.
parts.answer: At 0.01 % CO₂ the CO₂ concentration is the limiting factor; rubisco can only fix as much CO₂ as is available, so speeding up the enzymes by raising temperature does not increase the rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: CO₂ is limiting; 1 mark: rate depends on CO₂ supply to rubisco, not on enzyme speed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate at 20 °C levels off above 0.07 % CO₂.
parts.answer: CO₂ is no longer limiting; temperature now limits, as the Calvin cycle enzymes (rubisco) are working at their maximum rate at 20 °C (enzyme molecules have limited kinetic energy).
parts.working: 1 mark: another factor (temperature) limiting; 1 mark: enzyme rate limited by kinetic energy at 20 °C.

practice.stem:
A lettuce grower in Murree covers a greenhouse with shade netting. One layer of netting lets through 60 % of the light falling on it. The rate of photosynthesis of the lettuce leaves (µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹) was measured at different light intensities (µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹) at 22 °C and normal CO₂:
Light: 0, 200, 400, 600, 800, 1000, 1200
Rate: −1.0, 6.0, 11.0, 14.0, 15.0, 15.0, 15.0
At midday the light outside the greenhouse is 1800.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the light intensity reaching the leaves at midday under one layer of netting and under two layers of netting.
parts.answer: One layer: 1080; two layers: 648 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the data to explain why one layer of netting does not reduce the rate of photosynthesis at midday, but two layers do.
parts.answer: With one layer (1080) the light is still above about 800, where the rate has levelled off at 15.0, so light is not the limiting factor (CO₂ or temperature limits); with two layers (648) the light is below 800, on the rising part of the curve (rate about 14), so light becomes the limiting factor and the rate falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: rate levels off (15.0) from about 800 so light not limiting above this; 1 mark: 1080 is above this so rate unchanged / another factor (CO₂, temperature) limits; 1 mark: 648 is below it so light limits and rate is lower (about 14).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one benefit to the grower of using one layer of netting in summer.
parts.answer: It lowers leaf temperature and water loss (less wilting / stomatal closure, less heat damage) without reducing the rate of photosynthesis.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Measurements were made on cotton leaves in a field near Faisalabad on a hot June day.
Time: 06:00, 09:00, 12:00, 15:00, 18:00
Light / µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹: 150, 1200, 2000, 1700, 300
Leaf temperature / °C: 28, 34, 42, 41, 33
Rate of CO₂ uptake / µmol m⁻² s⁻¹: 8, 30, 22, 20, 10

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the factor limiting the rate at 06:00. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Light intensity; it is very low (150) and the rate rises as light increases during the morning.
parts.working: 1 mark factor; 1 mark data-based reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The rate at 12:00 is lower than at 09:00 even though the light is brighter. Suggest two explanations.
parts.answer: Leaf temperature (42 °C) is above the optimum, so Calvin cycle enzymes such as rubisco start to denature / lose activity; the leaves lose water in the heat, so stomata partly close, less CO₂ diffuses into the leaf and CO₂ becomes limiting; (also more respiration at high temperature reduces net uptake).
parts.working: 2 marks per explanation: cause (high temperature / stomatal closure / respiration) + effect on photosynthesis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why raising the temperature from 15 °C to 25 °C has little effect on the rate of photosynthesis in dim light but a large effect in bright light.
parts.answer: In dim light, light intensity is limiting: the light-dependent stage makes little ATP and reduced NADP, and the photochemical reactions are hardly affected by temperature, so warming has little effect. In bright light, ATP and reduced NADP are plentiful and the rate is limited by the enzyme-controlled Calvin cycle; higher temperature gives rubisco and other enzymes more kinetic energy, more enzyme–substrate complexes, so the rate rises.
parts.working: 1 mark: dim light – light limiting; 1 mark: light absorption / photoactivation not temperature dependent / ATP & reduced NADP supply limits; 1 mark: bright light – Calvin cycle (enzyme) limiting; 1 mark: more kinetic energy → more successful collisions / ESCs.

practice.stem:
A piece of pondweed was placed in hydrogencarbonate solution and a lamp was placed at different distances. The number of bubbles released per minute was counted.
Distance / cm: 10, 15, 20, 30, 40
Bubbles per minute: 17, 16, 15, 8, 4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Light intensity is proportional to 1/d², where d is the distance from the lamp. Calculate the relative light intensity (10 000/d²) for each distance.
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark for three or four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the relationship between relative light intensity and the rate of oxygen production.
parts.answer: Rate increases as light intensity increases from 6.25 to 25 (from 4 to 15 bubbles per minute) but levels off at higher intensities (16–17 bubbles per minute at 44.4 and 100).
parts.working: 1 mark: increases at low intensity. 1 mark: levels off/plateaus at high intensity with data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two factors that may be limiting the rate when the lamp is 10 cm away and explain why the lamp's heat might be a source of error.
parts.answer: CO₂ (hydrogencarbonate) concentration; temperature; (number of chloroplasts/amount of chlorophyll or enzyme). A lamp close to the plant warms the water, so temperature changes as well as light intensity, which also affects the rate (the independent variable is no longer the only factor changing).
parts.working: 1 mark each for two limiting factors (CO₂ concentration, temperature, amount of chlorophyll/rubisco). 1 mark: heat raises water temperature, which changes rate – use a heat shield/LED/water bath.

practice.stem:
Oxygen released by a piece of Elodea was collected for 10 minutes under five conditions.
A: low light, 0.01 % CO₂, 20 °C – 0.40 cm³
B: high light, 0.01 % CO₂, 20 °C – 0.42 cm³
C: high light, 0.05 % CO₂, 20 °C – 1.10 cm³
D: high light, 0.05 % CO₂, 30 °C – 1.65 cm³
E: low light, 0.05 % CO₂, 30 °C – 0.44 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen release in condition C in mm³ per minute.
parts.answer: 110 mm³ per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use conditions A, B and C to identify the factor limiting the rate in condition A. Explain your reasoning.
parts.answer: CO₂ concentration. Raising light (A → B) hardly changes the rate (0.40 → 0.42 cm³), so light is not limiting; raising CO₂ in high light (B → C) greatly increases it, so CO₂ was limiting in B and, since A and B are almost the same, in A as well.
parts.working: 1 mark CO₂; 1 mark A vs B comparison; 1 mark B vs C comparison.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use conditions C, D and E to identify the factors limiting the rate in conditions C and E.
parts.answer: C: temperature (raising temperature from 20 °C to 30 °C in D increases the rate from 1.10 to 1.65 cm³). E: light intensity (E has the same CO₂ and temperature as D but much lower rate).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
An indoor vertical farm in Islamabad grows lettuce under LED lights. The rate of photosynthesis (µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹) was measured at 22 °C.
Light 200 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹, CO₂ 400 ppm: 8.2
Light 400, CO₂ 400 ppm: 11.0
Light 400, CO₂ 1000 ppm: 14.6
Light 200, CO₂ 1000 ppm: 9.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in rate (i) when light is doubled at 400 ppm CO₂, (ii) when CO₂ is raised to 1000 ppm at light 400, and (iii) when CO₂ is raised to 1000 ppm at light 200. Give each answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why raising the CO₂ concentration has a much smaller effect at light 200 than at light 400.
parts.answer: At light 200, light intensity is the main limiting factor; the light-dependent stage supplies only a little ATP and reduced NADP; so GP cannot be reduced and RuBP regenerated faster, and extra CO₂ cannot be fixed much faster. At light 400 more ATP and reduced NADP are available, so CO₂ becomes limiting and extra CO₂ raises the rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: light limiting at 200; 1 mark: ATP / reduced NADP supply restricts Calvin cycle (RuBP regeneration); 1 mark: at 400 CO₂ limiting.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The farm currently runs at light 200 and 400 ppm. Suggest which single change the manager should make first, giving a reason from the data.
parts.answer: Increase the light intensity: it gives a 34.1 % increase compared with only 9.8 % for adding CO₂.
parts.working: 1 mark for choice with comparison of data (also accept discussion of electricity cost against yield).

practice.stem: A plant was kept at a very low CO₂ concentration (0.005 %) and 25 °C. The light intensity was increased in steps, but the rate of photosynthesis did not change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, with reference to the light-independent stage, why increasing the light intensity did not increase the rate.
parts.answer: CO₂ is the limiting factor; rubisco can only fix a little CO₂ with RuBP, so little GP is formed; only a little ATP and reduced NADP are therefore used to reduce GP to triose phosphate; ADP and NADP are not regenerated fast enough, so extra light cannot increase the light-dependent stage either; RuBP accumulates because it is regenerated but not used.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: CO₂ limiting; little CO₂ fixed by rubisco / little GP; little ATP and reduced NADP used; NADP / ADP not regenerated so light-dependent stage cannot go faster; RuBP builds up.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the effect of raising the CO₂ concentration to 0.04 % at the highest light intensity used.
parts.answer: The rate would increase (because CO₂ is no longer limiting at that light intensity).
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Microalgae are grown for biofuel in shallow outdoor ponds. In a dense culture the light intensity (arbitrary units) fell with depth:
Surface: 1800; 5 cm: 450; 10 cm: 110; 15 cm: 28

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the light intensity at 10 cm as a percentage of the surface value. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate of photosynthesis per cell is much lower at 15 cm than near the surface.
parts.answer: Light intensity is very low at 15 cm because cells above absorb (shade) the light; light is the limiting factor, so less photoactivation, less ATP and reduced NADP, and a slower Calvin cycle.
parts.working: 1 mark: self-shading / light absorbed by cells above; 1 mark: light limiting → less ATP / reduced NADP.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The ponds are kept shallow (about 25 cm) and the water is kept moving by paddle wheels. Suggest two reasons why the paddles increase the total yield.
parts.answer: Cells are moved between the dark depths and the bright surface, so all cells get some light; mixing spreads dissolved CO₂ (and nutrients) so CO₂ does not become limiting near the surface; it stops cells settling or overheating at the surface.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by photolysis of water and give the equation for it.
parts.answer: The splitting of water using light energy (at photosystem II): 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂
parts.working: 1 mark: splitting of water by light (energy). 1 mark: correct balanced equation (accept H₂O → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ + ½O₂).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens to each product of photolysis.
parts.answer: Electrons replace those lost from the chlorophyll in photosystem II; protons (H⁺) build up in the thylakoid space and are then used (with electrons) to reduce NADP; oxygen diffuses out of the leaf (or is used in respiration).
parts.working: 1 mark each: e⁻ replace electrons lost by PSII; H⁺ reduce NADP (after contributing to gradient for ATP synthesis); O₂ by-product released / used in respiration.

practice.stem:
Five statements describe events in non-cyclic photophosphorylation, in the wrong order.
P: light energy is absorbed by photosystem II
Q: excited electrons pass to an electron acceptor and then along a chain of electron carriers
R: energy released by the electrons is used to pump H⁺ into the thylakoid space
S: the electrons are excited again at photosystem I
T: the electrons combine with NADP and H⁺ to form reduced NADP

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the letters in the correct order.
parts.answer: P, Q, R, S, T
parts.working: 1 mark for the full correct sequence.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the source of the electrons that replace those lost from photosystem II.
parts.answer: Water, split by photolysis.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the enzyme that uses the H⁺ gradient produced in R, and state its product.
parts.answer: ATP synthase; ATP (from ADP and inorganic phosphate).
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept 'ATPase'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the precise location of the light-dependent stage in a chloroplast.
parts.answer: The thylakoid membranes (of the grana and intergranal lamellae).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the three products of non-cyclic photophosphorylation and state what happens to each.
parts.answer: ATP – used in the Calvin cycle (to reduce GP and regenerate RuBP); reduced NADP – used to reduce GP to triose phosphate; oxygen – diffuses out of the leaf (or is used in respiration).
parts.working: 1 mark for each product with its fate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the light-dependent stage stops if the supply of NADP runs out.
parts.answer: NADP is the final electron acceptor; without it electrons cannot leave photosystem I, so the carriers stay reduced and electron flow (and photolysis) stops.
parts.working: 1 mark final electron acceptor; 1 mark electron flow stops / no more electrons accepted from PSII / no photolysis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe cyclic photophosphorylation.
parts.answer: Only photosystem I is involved; light excites electrons in the reaction centre chlorophyll of PSI; they pass to an electron acceptor and along electron carriers; they return to PSI (not to NADP); energy released pumps H⁺ into the thylakoid space and ATP is made by ATP synthase (chemiosmosis).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of the listed points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one product of non-cyclic photophosphorylation that is not made by cyclic photophosphorylation.
parts.answer: Reduced NADP (or oxygen).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation by giving four differences.
parts.answer: Cyclic involves PSI only; non-cyclic involves PSI and PSII. Cyclic produces ATP only; non-cyclic produces ATP and reduced NADP. Cyclic involves no photolysis of water / no O₂ released; non-cyclic involves photolysis and releases O₂. In cyclic, electrons return to PSI; in non-cyclic, electrons end up on NADP (electrons from water replace those lost from PSII).
parts.working: 1 mark for each difference, max 4: photosystems involved; products (ATP only vs ATP + reduced NADP); photolysis/oxygen; fate of electrons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one similarity between cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation.
parts.answer: Both make ATP by chemiosmosis using ATP synthase / both use an electron transport chain in the thylakoid membrane / both involve PSI and photoactivation of chlorophyll.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Two cultures of a green alga were given water and carbon dioxide containing different isotopes of oxygen. ¹⁸O is a heavy, non-radioactive isotope.
Culture 1: water labelled with ¹⁸O, normal CO₂ – the oxygen gas released contained ¹⁸O
Culture 2: normal water, CO₂ labelled with ¹⁸O – the oxygen gas released contained almost no ¹⁸O

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what these results show about the source of the oxygen released in photosynthesis.
parts.answer: It comes from water, not from carbon dioxide.
