parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the process that releases this oxygen and state where it happens.
parts.answer: Photolysis of water; at photosystem II, on the thylakoid-space (lumen) side of the thylakoid membrane.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest where the ¹⁸O from the labelled CO₂ in culture 2 would be found after an hour of photosynthesis.
parts.answer: In organic compounds made in the Calvin cycle, e.g. GP, triose phosphate, sugars / starch (and some in water).
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: The herbicide DCMU binds to a protein in photosystem II and stops electrons passing from photosystem II to the electron transport chain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict and explain the effect of DCMU on the release of oxygen by a leaf in light.
parts.answer: Oxygen release stops; photosystem II cannot pass on its electrons, so it cannot accept new electrons from water and photolysis stops.
parts.working: 1 mark prediction; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why DCMU stops the production of reduced NADP.
parts.answer: Electrons reaching NADP come from photosystem II via photosystem I in non-cyclic flow; with no electrons flowing from PSII, PSI has no replacement electrons for NADP.
parts.working: 1 mark: electrons for NADP come from PSII/water; 1 mark: none reach PSI to replace those given to NADP.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a little ATP can still be made in DCMU-treated chloroplasts in light, but the plant still dies.
parts.answer: Cyclic photophosphorylation around photosystem I still works, making ATP; but there is no reduced NADP, so GP cannot be reduced to triose phosphate – no sugars are made and the plant starves.
parts.working: 1 mark cyclic photophosphorylation continues; 1 mark no reduced NADP → Calvin cycle stops / no carbohydrate.

practice.stem: Paraquat is a herbicide that takes electrons from photosystem I before they can reach NADP. It then passes them to oxygen, making reactive substances that damage membranes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the effect of paraquat on the production of reduced NADP. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Reduced NADP production falls / stops, because the electrons are diverted to paraquat instead of to NADP (via NADP reductase).
parts.working: 1 mark prediction; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why oxygen release by photolysis may continue for a time after paraquat is applied.
parts.answer: Electrons still flow from PSII to PSI and on to paraquat, so PSII keeps losing electrons and water keeps being split to replace them.
parts.working: 1 mark electron flow continues (paraquat is an electron acceptor); 1 mark PSII electrons replaced by photolysis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why paraquat kills leaves faster in bright light than in dim light.
parts.answer: More light means more electron flow, so more electrons reach paraquat and more damaging reactive substances are made.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: In non-cyclic photophosphorylation, assume that each electron moving from water to NADP needs one photon absorbed at photosystem II and one photon absorbed at photosystem I. Two electrons are needed to reduce one molecule of NADP.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The equation for photolysis is 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂. Calculate the number of photons needed to release one molecule of oxygen.
parts.answer: 8 photons
parts.working: 4 electrons per O₂ (M1); 4 × 2 photons = 8 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Making one molecule of glucose in the Calvin cycle uses 12 molecules of reduced NADP. Calculate the minimum number of photons absorbed by non-cyclic photophosphorylation to supply this reduced NADP.
parts.answer: 48 photons
parts.working: 12 × 2 = 24 electrons (M1); 24 × 2 = 48 photons (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the true number of photons absorbed per glucose is higher than your answer to (b).
parts.answer: Extra ATP is needed (the Calvin cycle uses 3 ATP per 2 reduced NADP), so some cyclic photophosphorylation also absorbs photons; some absorbed energy is lost as heat / fluorescence.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: extra ATP via cyclic; energy losses (heat/fluorescence); some light absorbed by pigments not transferred to reaction centres.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain three ways in which the light-dependent stage makes the H⁺ concentration in the thylakoid space higher than in the stroma.
parts.answer: Photolysis of water releases H⁺ inside the thylakoid space; energy from electrons moving along the electron transport chain is used to pump H⁺ from the stroma into the thylakoid space; H⁺ are removed from the stroma when NADP is reduced.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this H⁺ gradient is used to make ATP.
parts.answer: H⁺ diffuse down their concentration (electrochemical) gradient from the thylakoid space into the stroma through ATP synthase; this flow drives the enzyme to join ADP and Pi (chemiosmosis).
parts.working: 1 mark facilitated diffusion through ATP synthase; 1 mark ADP + Pi → ATP / chemiosmosis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the events of non-cyclic photophosphorylation in the thylakoid membrane.
parts.answer: Light absorbed by photosystem II; chlorophyll a in the reaction centre is photoactivated and emits excited electrons to an electron acceptor; electrons are passed along an electron transport chain of carriers to photosystem I, losing energy; this energy is used to pump H⁺ into the thylakoid space; light excites PSI, whose electrons pass to a second carrier and then reduce NADP (with H⁺) to form reduced NADP; electrons from PSII replace those lost by PSI; photolysis of water supplies electrons to PSII, releasing H⁺ and O₂; H⁺ diffuse back through ATP synthase (chemiosmosis), producing ATP from ADP and Pi.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: light absorbed by PSII; photoactivation – electrons excited and emitted; electron acceptor; ETC, electrons lose energy; H⁺ pumped into thylakoid space / proton gradient; PSI excited; electrons reduce NADP (NADP reductase) to reduced NADP; PSII electrons replace those lost from PSI; photolysis replaces electrons in PSII, O₂ released; chemiosmosis through ATP synthase; ATP formed from ADP + Pi.

practice.stem: Isolated thylakoids were kept in the dark in an acidic buffer at pH 4.5 until the thylakoid space reached pH 4.5 (step 1). They were then transferred, still in the dark, to a buffer at pH 8.0 containing ADP and phosphate (step 2). ATP was produced for a short time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the concentration of H⁺ is in a solution at pH 4.5 than at pH 8.0. (pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]). Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: About 3200 times (3.2 × 10³)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why ATP was made in step 2 even though the thylakoids were in the dark.
parts.answer: The thylakoid space had a high H⁺ concentration (pH 4.5) compared with the outside (pH 8.0), so there was a proton gradient across the membrane; H⁺ diffused out through ATP synthase; the flow of protons drove the phosphorylation of ADP to ATP (chemiosmosis); light is normally needed only to generate the gradient.
parts.working: 1 mark: proton/H⁺ gradient across thylakoid membrane. 1 mark: H⁺ diffuse through ATP synthase (channel). 1 mark: energy from proton flow used to make ATP from ADP + Pi – chemiosmosis, light not directly needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A chemical that makes the thylakoid membrane permeable to H⁺ was added to illuminated chloroplasts. Predict and explain the effect on ATP production and on the reduction of NADP.
parts.answer: ATP production falls (stops) because H⁺ leak back across the membrane, so no proton gradient forms to drive ATP synthase; reduction of NADP continues because electron flow along the chain still occurs.
parts.working: 1 mark: ATP production decreases, no proton gradient. 1 mark: NADP still reduced / electron transport continues.

practice.stem:
Rates of oxygen release by a suspension of green algal cells were measured under three light treatments of equal total intensity.
Light of 680 nm only: 6.0 units
Light of 710 nm only: 2.0 units
680 nm and 710 nm together: 11.2 units
Photosystem II absorbs strongly up to about 680 nm; photosystem I also absorbs at longer wavelengths up to about 710 nm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of the rate with both wavelengths together to the sum of the rates with each wavelength alone. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate with 710 nm light alone is so low.
parts.answer: 710 nm light excites mainly photosystem I; photosystem II is hardly activated, so there is little photolysis and little non-cyclic electron flow (mainly cyclic, which releases no oxygen).
parts.working: 1 mark PSI only activated; 1 mark little PSII activity / photolysis so little O₂.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate with both wavelengths together is greater than the sum of the separate rates.
parts.answer: Non-cyclic photophosphorylation needs both photosystems working together in series; with both wavelengths, PSII and PSI are both excited, so electrons flow from water through both photosystems to NADP at a much faster rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: two photosystems work in series; 1 mark: both activated together → full non-cyclic flow / more photolysis.

practice.stem:
A suspension of isolated thylakoids (total volume 2.0 cm³, containing 0.05 mg chlorophyll) was placed in an oxygen electrode with potassium ferricyanide, an artificial electron acceptor. No NADP was present. The light was switched on at 1 minute.
Time / min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
Oxygen / µmol dm⁻³: 250, 250, 268, 286, 304

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen release in µmol dm⁻³ per minute after the light was switched on.
parts.answer: 18 µmol dm⁻³ per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen release in µmol per mg chlorophyll per hour. (1 cm³ = 0.001 dm³)
parts.answer: 43.2 µmol per mg chlorophyll per hour

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why oxygen was released even though there was no NADP, and predict what would happen without ferricyanide.
parts.answer: Ferricyanide accepts electrons in place of NADP (it is reduced), so electrons keep flowing from PSII and water keeps being split, releasing oxygen. Without it, the electron carriers would quickly all become reduced, electron flow and photolysis would stop, and oxygen release would stop almost at once.
parts.working: 1 mark ferricyanide = electron acceptor; 1 mark electron flow / photolysis continues; 1 mark prediction with reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare chemiosmosis in the thylakoid membrane of a chloroplast with chemiosmosis in the inner membrane of a mitochondrion. Give one similarity and three differences.
parts.answer: Similarity: in both, electrons passing along an electron transport chain release energy to pump H⁺ across a membrane, and H⁺ flow back through ATP synthase to make ATP. Differences: source of energy – light (photoactivated chlorophyll) in chloroplasts, oxidation of reduced NAD/FAD in mitochondria; H⁺ are pumped into the thylakoid space in chloroplasts but into the intermembrane space in mitochondria; final electron acceptor – NADP in chloroplasts, oxygen in mitochondria; ATP is made in the stroma vs in the matrix; water is split in chloroplasts but formed in mitochondria.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid similarity; 1 mark each for any three comparative differences.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why ATP made in the chloroplast is not the main source of ATP for active transport in a root hair cell.
parts.answer: Root hair cells have no chloroplasts (no light underground); chloroplast ATP is used in the Calvin cycle in the stroma, and ATP for the rest of the cell comes from respiration in mitochondria.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the enzyme that catalyses the fixation of carbon dioxide in the Calvin cycle.
parts.answer: Rubisco (ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Copy and complete the table to show the number of carbon atoms in each molecule.
RuBP | GP | triose phosphate
parts.answer: RuBP 5; GP 3; triose phosphate 3
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark for two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Outline how GP is converted to triose phosphate, naming the products of the light-dependent stage that are needed.
parts.answer: GP is reduced to triose phosphate using hydrogen from reduced NADP and energy from ATP.
parts.working: 1 mark: reduction (by reduced NADP). 1 mark: ATP provides energy / phosphate.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two uses of triose phosphate in the plant.
parts.answer: Any two: regenerating RuBP; making glucose/sucrose/starch/cellulose; making lipids (glycerol and fatty acids); making amino acids.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A suspension of algal cells in bright light was given carbon dioxide containing radioactive carbon (¹⁴CO₂). Samples were killed in hot ethanol after different times and the radioactive compounds were identified.

parts.label: a
parts.text: After 2 seconds almost all of the radioactivity was in one compound. Name this compound and explain why it is labelled first.
parts.answer: Glycerate 3-phosphate (GP); CO₂ combines with RuBP (catalysed by rubisco) and the 6C product immediately splits into two molecules of GP.
parts.working: 1 mark GP; 1 mark explanation (carbon fixation by rubisco).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the samples were killed in hot ethanol.
parts.answer: To denature the enzymes immediately, so the reactions stop at that exact time.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one compound that would become radioactive later than the compound in (a).
parts.answer: Triose phosphate (then hexose / sucrose / starch / RuBP / amino acids).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the two stages of the Calvin cycle that use ATP.
parts.answer: Reduction of GP to triose phosphate; regeneration of RuBP from triose phosphate.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the stage that uses reduced NADP and the role of reduced NADP in it.
parts.answer: Reduction of GP to triose phosphate; it provides hydrogen (electrons) to reduce GP.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what happens to the NADP and ADP made in the Calvin cycle.
parts.answer: They return (diffuse) to the thylakoids to be reduced / phosphorylated again in the light-dependent stage.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: This question is about six turns of the Calvin cycle, in which six molecules of CO₂ are fixed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State how many molecules of RuBP combine with CO₂.
parts.working: One RuBP per CO₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how many molecules of GP and of triose phosphate are formed.
parts.answer: GP 12; triose phosphate 12
parts.working: Each 6C intermediate gives 2 GP; each GP is reduced to one triose phosphate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Ten of the triose phosphate molecules are used to regenerate RuBP. Show by counting carbon atoms that this is enough to regenerate all the RuBP used.
parts.answer: 10 × 3 = 30 carbon atoms; 6 RuBP × 5 = 30 carbon atoms, so the numbers match.
parts.working: 1 mark each calculation.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State what the other two triose phosphate molecules can be used to make.
parts.answer: One molecule of a hexose (e.g. glucose), which can be made into sucrose, starch or cellulose.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the following word equation for carbon fixation: ribulose bisphosphate + carbon dioxide → ……
parts.answer: Two molecules of glycerate 3-phosphate (GP) (via an unstable 6C intermediate).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where in the chloroplast carbon fixation takes place.
parts.answer: The stroma.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the Calvin cycle is called the light-independent stage even though it stops within a minute of darkness.
parts.answer: Its reactions do not use light directly; but they need ATP and reduced NADP from the light-dependent stage, which stop being made in the dark, so the cycle soon stops.
parts.working: 1 mark no direct use of light; 1 mark depends on ATP / reduced NADP from light-dependent stage.

practice.stem: Cells of a single-celled green alga were kept in bright light with plenty of CO₂, and the concentrations of glycerate 3-phosphate (GP) and ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP) were measured. The light was then switched off. During the next minute the GP concentration increased and the RuBP concentration decreased.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the changes in the concentrations of GP and RuBP after the light was switched off.
parts.answer: No light means no ATP or reduced NADP from the light-dependent stage; GP cannot be reduced to triose phosphate, so GP accumulates; RuBP is still used up as it combines with CO₂ (to form GP); RuBP cannot be regenerated from triose phosphate because there is no ATP (and no TP being made), so RuBP falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: no ATP/reduced NADP. 1 mark: GP not converted to TP so GP rises. 1 mark: RuBP still used in fixation of CO₂. 1 mark: RuBP not regenerated (needs ATP/TP) so falls.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a second experiment the light was kept on, but the CO₂ concentration was suddenly reduced. Predict the changes in GP and RuBP concentrations and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: RuBP rises and GP falls; less CO₂ is available to combine with RuBP, so RuBP is not used but is still regenerated from TP; GP is still converted to TP but less is formed.
parts.working: 1 mark: RuBP increases and GP decreases (both needed). 1 mark: less CO₂ fixed with RuBP while regeneration / GP reduction continue.

practice.stem: A spinach leaf of mass 2.4 g contains 18 mg of soluble protein per gram of leaf. Rubisco makes up 25 % of this soluble protein.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of rubisco in the whole leaf. Give your answer in mg to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Rubisco catalyses only a few reactions per second, which is very slow for an enzyme. Suggest why leaves contain such a large amount of rubisco.
parts.answer: Each molecule fixes CO₂ slowly, so a very large number of rubisco molecules is needed to fix CO₂ fast enough to keep up with the ATP and reduced NADP made in bright light (and to make enough sugar for growth).
parts.working: 1 mark: low turnover so many molecules needed; 1 mark: to achieve a high overall rate of CO₂ fixation / match the light-dependent stage.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why plants that are short of nitrate fix less carbon dioxide.
parts.answer: Nitrate is needed to make amino acids and so proteins such as rubisco; less rubisco means less CO₂ fixation.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A potato tuber stores 120 g of starch. Treat the starch as glucose units (C₆H₁₀O₅, Mr 162). Fixing one molecule of CO₂ and regenerating RuBP uses 3 ATP and 2 reduced NADP. Ignore any ATP used to join the glucose units together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of glucose units in the stored starch. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of CO₂ fixed, ATP used and reduced NADP used in the Calvin cycle to make this starch. Give each answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: CO₂ 4.44 mol; ATP 13.3 mol; reduced NADP 8.89 mol
parts.working: 6 CO₂ per glucose unit: 0.7407 × 6 = 4.44 (1 mark); × 3 = 13.3 ATP (1 mark); × 2 = 8.89 reduced NADP (1 mark). Allow follow-through from (a).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The starch is made in the tuber from sucrose that was carried from the leaves. Suggest why triose phosphate is converted to sucrose rather than to glucose for transport.
parts.answer: Sucrose is a non-reducing sugar, so it is less reactive and is not used up (respired) on the way; it is soluble so it can be carried in phloem sap without being used by the cells it passes.
parts.working: 1 mark non-reducing / less reactive / not metabolised in transit; 1 mark soluble / transported in phloem.

practice.stem: Leaves in bright light were treated with a substance that inhibits the enzyme that converts GP to triose phosphate. Light and CO₂ supply were not changed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict and explain the changes in the concentrations of GP, triose phosphate and RuBP in the next few minutes.
parts.answer: GP rises, because it is still made from RuBP and CO₂ but cannot be converted; triose phosphate falls, because it is no longer made but is still used (to regenerate RuBP, make sugars); RuBP falls, because it is still used to fix CO₂ but cannot be regenerated without triose phosphate.
parts.working: 1 mark for all three predictions; 1 mark each for explanations of GP, triose phosphate and RuBP.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest what happens to the concentration of reduced NADP in the stroma. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: It rises, because reduced NADP is used only in the reduction of GP, which has stopped, while the light-dependent stage keeps making it (until NADP runs out).
parts.working: 1 mark rise; 1 mark explanation.

practice.stem: Triose phosphate made in the Calvin cycle can be used to make many organic compounds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two carbohydrates made from triose phosphate and state the use of each in a plant.
parts.answer: Any two of: sucrose – transport in phloem; starch – energy store; cellulose – cell walls; glucose – respiration.
parts.working: 1 mark each named carbohydrate with a correct use.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Triose phosphate can be used to make amino acids and lipids. State one other substance (or element) the plant needs to make amino acids, and name the two parts of a triglyceride that triose phosphate can form.
parts.answer: Nitrogen as nitrate (or ammonium) ions (also sulfur for some amino acids); glycerol and fatty acids.
parts.working: 1 mark nitrate / nitrogen; 1 mark each for glycerol and fatty acids.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the Calvin cycle, fixing one molecule of CO₂ and regenerating RuBP uses 3 molecules of ATP and 2 molecules of reduced NADP. Calculate the number of molecules of ATP and of reduced NADP needed to make one molecule of sucrose (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁).
parts.answer: 36 ATP and 24 reduced NADP
parts.working: M1: sucrose has 12 carbon atoms, so 12 CO₂ must be fixed. A1: 12 × 3 = 36 ATP and 12 × 2 = 24 reduced NADP.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the Calvin cycle, including the regeneration of RuBP.
parts.answer: In the stroma, CO₂ combines with RuBP (5C); catalysed by rubisco; forming an unstable 6C compound that splits into two molecules of GP (3C); GP is reduced to triose phosphate using reduced NADP; and ATP; five out of every six triose phosphates are used to regenerate RuBP; using ATP; one in six is used to make glucose and other organic compounds.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: CO₂ + RuBP; rubisco; two GP formed (via unstable 6C intermediate); GP reduced to TP; reduced NADP and ATP used; most TP (5/6) regenerates RuBP; ATP used in regeneration; some TP leaves to make sugars, amino acids, lipids.

practice.stem: Making one mole of glucose in the Calvin cycle uses 18 moles of ATP and 12 moles of reduced NADP. Hydrolysis of one mole of ATP releases 30.5 kJ. Oxidation of one mole of reduced NADP releases 220 kJ. Complete oxidation of one mole of glucose releases 2870 kJ.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total energy supplied by ATP and reduced NADP to make one mole of glucose.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the efficiency with which this energy is stored in glucose. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The overall efficiency of photosynthesis, from light energy reaching a leaf to energy in glucose, is much lower than your answer to (b). Suggest three reasons.
parts.answer: Some light is reflected, transmitted or hits non-photosynthetic parts; only certain wavelengths are absorbed (green poorly); energy is lost as heat in electron transport and ATP synthesis; some glucose is used in respiration; other factors (CO₂, temperature) limit the rate so not all light is used.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

practice.stem:
Algal cells in light were given ¹⁴CO₂ for 2 seconds and then transferred to normal CO₂ (a pulse–chase experiment). The percentage of the total radioactivity in four groups of compounds was measured.
Time after start / s: 2, 5, 10, 30, 60
GP: 85, 60, 40, 20, 12
Triose phosphate: 10, 25, 30, 25, 18
RuBP: 0, 5, 12, 20, 20
Hexose phosphates and sucrose: 5, 10, 18, 35, 50

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the radioactivity that was not in GP at 10 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the data show the order in which these compounds are made.
parts.answer: GP has most label first (85 % at 2 s), so it is the first product of fixation; triose phosphate rises next (peak about 10 s) as GP is reduced; label in sugars rises steadily later (to 50 %) and RuBP becomes labelled only after triose phosphate, so both are made from triose phosphate.
parts.working: 1 mark GP first; 1 mark TP second / intermediate; 1 mark sugars and RuBP last, made from TP.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the percentage in GP falls after 2 seconds even though fixation continues.
parts.answer: No more ¹⁴CO₂ is supplied (chase with unlabelled CO₂), so new GP is unlabelled; labelled GP is converted to triose phosphate and then to other compounds.
parts.working: 1 mark: new GP is unlabelled; 1 mark: labelled GP is used up / converted.

practice.stem: During a drought, the stomata of a wheat crop close for much of the day while the leaves are still brightly lit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why stomatal closure reduces the rate of the Calvin cycle.
parts.answer: Less CO₂ diffuses into the leaf, so the CO₂ concentration in the air spaces and stroma falls; rubisco fixes less CO₂ with RuBP, so less GP and triose phosphate are formed.
parts.working: 1 mark less CO₂ enters; 1 mark less fixation by rubisco / less GP.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a slower Calvin cycle affects non-cyclic photophosphorylation.
parts.answer: Less reduced NADP and ATP are used, so less NADP and ADP are returned to the thylakoids; with no NADP to accept electrons, electron flow from PSI (and hence from PSII and water) slows; electrons may instead flow round PSI by cyclic photophosphorylation.
parts.working: 1 mark less NADP regenerated; 1 mark non-cyclic flow / photolysis slows; 1 mark switch to cyclic flow (or excess light energy may damage chlorophyll).

practice.stem:
Algal cells were kept in bright light at 0.01 % CO₂. At 0 s the CO₂ concentration was suddenly raised to 0.10 %; light intensity and temperature were not changed. The concentrations of GP and RuBP (arbitrary units) were measured.
Time / s: 0, 10, 20, 30, 40
GP: 0.8, 1.3, 1.7, 1.9, 1.9
RuBP: 2.0, 1.4, 1.0, 0.85, 0.85

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of increase in GP concentration during the first 20 s, in units per second.
parts.answer: 0.045 units per second

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in RuBP concentration between 0 s and 40 s. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the changes in GP and RuBP, including why both concentrations level off after 30 s.
parts.answer: More CO₂ is available, so rubisco combines CO₂ with RuBP faster and GP is made faster than it is reduced, so GP rises; RuBP is used faster than it is regenerated from triose phosphate, so RuBP falls; the reduction of GP (and regeneration of RuBP) is limited by the supply of ATP and reduced NADP from the light-dependent stage; a new steady state is reached when the rates of GP formation and GP reduction are equal (lower RuBP slows fixation to match), so both level off.
parts.working: 1 mark more CO₂ fixed by rubisco / GP formed faster; 1 mark RuBP used faster than regenerated; 1 mark GP reduction / RuBP regeneration limited by ATP and reduced NADP; 1 mark new steady state – formation and use balance.

practice.stem: A student wants to find the effect of temperature on the rate of photosynthesis of the pondweed Cabomba. She has a gas syringe connected to an inverted funnel, water baths, 1 % sodium hydrogencarbonate solution and an LED lamp.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline a method she could use. Include how she will vary the temperature, measure the rate and keep other variables constant.
parts.answer: Place a known mass/length of Cabomba under the funnel in a beaker of 1 % NaHCO₃ inside a water bath; use at least five temperatures, e.g. 15, 20, 25, 30, 35 °C, checked with a thermometer; leave 5 minutes to equilibrate at each temperature; LED at a fixed distance (e.g. 10 cm) in a darkened room; collect gas for a fixed time (e.g. 10 min) and read the volume on the gas syringe; rate = volume ÷ time (÷ mass); repeat three times at each temperature and calculate a mean.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: water baths with stated range (≥5 values); thermometer to check; equilibration time; measure volume of gas in syringe over fixed time; rate calculation; same plant / same mass; fixed light intensity (distance, LED, dark room); same NaHCO₃ concentration and volume; replicates and mean.

practice.stem: In a Hill reaction investigation, a colorimeter is used to follow the loss of blue colour from DCPIP when it is mixed with a chloroplast suspension in light.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the colorimeter should be set up and used to take readings.
parts.answer: Choose a red / orange filter (light about 600 nm), which blue DCPIP absorbs most strongly; zero (calibrate) the colorimeter with a cuvette containing chloroplast suspension and buffer but no DCPIP; use the same cuvette and wipe it, place it the same way round each time; take absorbance readings at fixed time intervals (e.g. every 30 s) starting when the light is switched on.
parts.working: 1 mark each: red/complementary filter; blank with chloroplast suspension (no DCPIP); clean cuvette / same orientation; readings at regular intervals.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the blank must contain chloroplasts as well as buffer.
parts.answer: The green chloroplasts also absorb light, so the blank cancels their absorbance and only the DCPIP colour is measured.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A student wants to compare the rate of photosynthesis of leaves taken from the sunny and shaded sides of a guava tree using the floating leaf disc method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the leaf discs should be prepared and how the rate would be measured.
parts.answer: Cut discs with the same cork borer from leaves of similar age from each side, avoiding large veins; put discs in a syringe with 0.2 % NaHCO₃ and pull the plunger with the tip sealed to remove air so the discs sink (infiltration); place ten discs in a beaker of the same NaHCO₃ solution under a lamp at a fixed distance; record the time for each disc (or for half the discs) to float; rate = 1 ÷ time; repeat with fresh discs.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five: same borer / disc size; similar age / position; avoid veins; vacuum infiltration with NaHCO₃; fixed light / temperature; time to float recorded; rate as 1/t; repeats.

practice.stem: A student needs 50 cm³ of each of these sodium hydrogencarbonate solutions: 0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1.2, 1.6 %. She has a 2.0 % stock solution and distilled water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of stock solution and of distilled water needed for each concentration.
parts.answer: 0.2 %: 5 cm³ stock + 45 cm³ water; 0.4 %: 10 cm³ stock + 40 cm³ water; 0.8 %: 20 cm³ stock + 30 cm³ water; 1.2 %: 30 cm³ stock + 20 cm³ water; 1.6 %: 40 cm³ stock + 10 cm³ water
parts.working: Volume of stock = required concentration ÷ stock concentration × 50. 3 marks all correct; 2 marks for 3–4 correct; 1 mark for 1–2 correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one piece of apparatus that would measure these volumes accurately.
parts.answer: A graduated pipette / burette / syringe (or 50 cm³ measuring cylinder for the water).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the student should also set up a tube containing 0 % sodium hydrogencarbonate (distilled water only).
parts.answer: The 0 % tube shows how much photosynthesis occurs with no added CO₂ (only CO₂ from respiration / dissolved CO₂), so any increase can be linked to the added hydrogencarbonate.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis of an aquatic plant such as Elodea. Your plan should include how you would measure the rate and how you would control other variables.
parts.answer: Cut a piece of Elodea of fixed length (e.g. 8 cm) and place it upside down in a boiling tube of 1 % sodium hydrogencarbonate solution (excess CO₂); stand the tube in a beaker of water at 25 °C as a heat shield/water bath; place a lamp (LED) at distances 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30 cm (or measure light intensity with a light meter); leave 5 minutes at each distance to acclimatise; collect the gas in a photosynthometer/capillary tube for a fixed time (e.g. 5 min) and measure the volume/length of bubble; repeat three times at each distance and calculate means; carry out in a darkened room so the lamp is the only light source.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: IV light intensity varied by lamp distance (≥5 values) or light meter; same plant piece/length, same species; NaHCO₃ in excess for CO₂; temperature controlled with water bath/heat shield/LED; acclimatisation time at each new intensity; DV measured as volume of gas (photosynthometer/syringe) in fixed time (not just bubble count); darkened room / no other light; at least 3 repeats and mean; rate = volume ÷ time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline a method using leaf discs to investigate the effect of the colour (wavelength) of light on the rate of photosynthesis.
parts.answer: Cut discs from the same leaf with a cork borer, avoiding large veins; infiltrate the discs with 0.2 % sodium hydrogencarbonate solution by drawing them into a syringe and pulling the plunger to remove air, so they sink; place ten discs in the same volume of hydrogencarbonate solution in each of several beakers; illuminate each with a different colour of LED (red, blue, green, white), each at the same light intensity measured with a light meter and the same distance; keep temperature constant with a water bath; record the time for five of the ten discs to float; repeat three times and use 1/time as a measure of rate.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: discs same size and from same plant/leaf; infiltration with NaHCO₃ using syringe so discs sink; same number of discs and volume of solution; different colours via filters/LEDs; same light intensity (light meter) or same distance and lamp; constant temperature; DV time for (e.g.) half of the discs to float; rate = 1/t; repeats and mean; control in dark.

practice.stem: Plan an investigation into the effect of light intensity on the rate of the Hill reaction, using a chloroplast suspension, DCPIP solution, an LED lamp, a light meter and a colorimeter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a plan for this investigation.
parts.answer: Prepare chloroplast suspension (blend leaves in ice-cold isotonic buffer, filter, centrifuge, resuspend; keep on ice); vary light intensity by placing the LED at, e.g., 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 cm (or dimmer) and measure intensity with the light meter at the tube position; same volume of DCPIP and of suspension in each tube, mix at time zero; same temperature (water bath / LED gives little heat); read absorbance (red filter) every 30 s for 5 min or record the time to reach the absorbance of a colourless standard; control tube kept in the dark (wrapped in foil) and tube with buffer instead of chloroplasts; three repeats at each intensity; calculate rate as change in absorbance per minute (or 1/time) and plot against light intensity.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any seven: suspension preparation kept cold; ≥5 light intensities with method; light meter used; fixed volumes / chloroplast concentration; temperature controlled; colorimeter method (filter / endpoint); dark control; no-chloroplast control; repeats + mean; rate calculation and graph.

practice.stem: Algal balls are made by mixing green algae with sodium alginate and dropping the mixture into calcium chloride solution. Hydrogencarbonate indicator is yellow when CO₂ concentration is high, red at atmospheric CO₂ and purple when CO₂ is low.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation, using algal balls and hydrogencarbonate indicator, into the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis.
parts.answer: Make balls of equal size with a syringe; put the same number (e.g. 15) into identical bottles with the same volume (e.g. 10 cm³) of red indicator; put bottles at, e.g., 5 different distances from an LED lamp (measure intensity with a light meter / use 1/d²); keep temperature constant (water bath, LED, heat filter); after a fixed time (e.g. 60 min) measure indicator colour with a colorimeter at about 550 nm (or compare with pH colour standards); include a bottle wrapped in foil and a bottle with indicator but no balls; repeat three times and take means; rate = change in absorbance ÷ time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: equal ball size / number; same indicator volume / start colour; ≥5 light intensities; light measurement; temperature control; fixed time; colorimeter / colour standards; controls; repeats.

practice.stem: A student plans to investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of photosynthesis using algal balls in hydrogencarbonate indicator.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the algal balls and the indicator should be kept at the test temperature for 10 minutes before the experiment starts.
parts.answer: So that the algae and the solution reach the test temperature (equilibrate); otherwise the actual temperature at the start would be different and the rate would not match the stated temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student could vary temperature over a suitable range and keep it constant.
parts.answer: Use thermostatically controlled water baths at, e.g., 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 °C (at least five values); check with a thermometer and adjust; use an LED or heat filter so the lamp does not warm the bottles.
parts.working: 1 mark range of ≥5 temperatures; 1 mark water bath + thermometer; 1 mark avoid heating by lamp.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the student should also set up a bottle of algal balls covered in foil at each temperature.
parts.answer: Respiration also changes the CO₂ concentration and increases with temperature; the dark bottle measures respiration so that it can be allowed for (gross = net + respiration).
parts.working: 1 mark respiration affects indicator / increases with temperature; 1 mark allows correction / comparison.

practice.stem: A student wants to find out whether chlorophyll content differs between the youngest leaves at the tip of a shoot and older leaves lower down the stem.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student could extract the chlorophyll and use a colorimeter to compare the chlorophyll content of the leaves.
parts.answer: Cut discs of the same total area / weigh the same mass of leaf from each position; grind with the same volume of ethanol (propanone) and sand; filter / centrifuge and make up to the same final volume; measure absorbance with a red filter (about 660 nm), zeroing with ethanol alone; compare absorbance (higher = more chlorophyll) or read concentration from a calibration curve made with known chlorophyll dilutions; repeat with leaves from several plants.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five: same mass / area; same solvent volume; grinding / filtering; red filter / suitable wavelength; blank with solvent; calibration curve; replicates from several plants.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the extracts should be kept in the dark and measured quickly.
parts.answer: Chlorophyll breaks down in light (photo-oxidation) / ethanol evaporates, changing the concentration.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: To study the Hill reaction, a chloroplast suspension is prepared by blending spinach leaves in an ice-cold buffer solution that has the same water potential as the leaf cells. DCPIP is a blue dye that becomes colourless when it is reduced.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the leaves are blended in a buffer solution that is ice-cold and has the same water potential as the leaf cells.
parts.answer: Ice-cold: slows enzyme activity (e.g. enzymes that damage chloroplasts) / reduces damage. Same water potential: prevents water entering or leaving chloroplasts by osmosis, so they do not burst or shrink. Buffer keeps pH constant so proteins are not denatured.
parts.working: 1 mark for ice-cold reason. 1 mark for same water potential or buffer reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Plan an investigation into the effect of temperature on the rate of the Hill reaction, using a chloroplast suspension and DCPIP.
parts.answer: Prepare chloroplast suspension by blending spinach leaves in ice-cold buffer, filtering and centrifuging, then resuspending the pellet; set up tubes with the same volume of chloroplast suspension and the same volume and concentration of DCPIP; equilibrate tubes in water baths at five temperatures, e.g. 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 °C; place each tube at the same distance from the same lamp; measure the time for the blue DCPIP to become colourless, or measure absorbance with a colorimeter (red filter) every 30 s; rate = 1/time; controls: tube kept in the dark and tube with boiled chloroplasts; three repeats at each temperature and calculate means.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: method for extracting chloroplasts (blend, filter, centrifuge); same volumes/concentrations of DCPIP and suspension; ≥5 temperatures with thermostatic water bath; equilibrate before mixing; constant light intensity (same lamp, same distance); DV time to decolourise or colorimeter reading against colour standard; rate = 1/t; control in dark or with boiled chloroplasts; repeats and means.

practice.stem: DCPIP is blue in neutral and alkaline solutions but turns pink in acidic solutions, and colourless when reduced.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation into the effect of pH on the rate of the Hill reaction, using a chloroplast suspension and DCPIP. Include how you would make sure that the effect of pH on the colour of DCPIP does not affect your results.
parts.answer: Use buffer solutions of, e.g., pH 5, 6, 7, 8, 9; add the same volume of chloroplast suspension (prepared in ice-cold isotonic buffer) and DCPIP to each; same light intensity (LED at fixed distance), same temperature (water bath, 20 °C); time to decolourise / colorimeter readings at intervals; for each pH, make a colour standard / blank of that buffer with DCPIP but no chloroplasts and one with reduced (colourless) DCPIP, so the end-point is judged against the correct colour for that pH (or zero the colorimeter for each pH); control tubes in the dark at each pH; three repeats; rate = 1/time or change in absorbance per minute; plot against pH.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any seven: ≥5 pH values with buffers; same volumes; light controlled; temperature controlled; method of measuring rate; colour standard / blank at each pH (needed to gain full marks); dark control; repeats; rate calculation / graph.

practice.stem: The light compensation point is the light intensity at which the rate of photosynthesis equals the rate of respiration, so there is no net exchange of CO₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to estimate the light compensation point of a green alga using algal balls and hydrogencarbonate indicator.
parts.answer: Same number and size of algal balls in identical tubes of red indicator; expose tubes to a range of low light intensities (e.g. 0–500 lux in steps, using neutral density filters / layers of muslin / distance) measured with a light meter; constant temperature (water bath, LED); after a fixed time measure the colour change with a colorimeter compared with a control tube of indicator without balls; tubes that go yellow have net respiration, purple have net photosynthesis; the compensation point is the intensity where the colour does not change (interpolate on a graph of change in absorbance against light intensity); repeat and narrow the range around the estimate.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: equal balls / indicator; range of low light intensities and how; light meter; temperature control; colorimeter / colour comparison; interpretation of yellow/purple; compensation point where no change, by graph interpolation; repeats / refined range.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the compensation point measured at 30 °C would be higher than at 20 °C.
parts.answer: Respiration increases more with temperature (at low light photosynthesis is light-limited and hardly changes), so a higher light intensity is needed for photosynthesis to balance the faster respiration.
parts.working: 1 mark respiration faster at 30 °C; 1 mark more light needed to balance it.

practice.stem: A student wants to compare the pigments in young green leaves and old yellowing leaves of the same pipal tree.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan a chromatography investigation to compare the pigments in the two types of leaf. Include how you would make the comparison fair and how you would identify the pigments.
parts.answer: Grind the same mass of each leaf type with the same volume of propanone (and a little sand) in a mortar; filter; spot each extract on a pencil origin line 2 cm from the bottom of a TLC plate (or paper), spot repeatedly with drying in between to make a small concentrated spot, same number of applications for each; place in a covered tank with solvent below the origin; run until solvent front nearly reaches the top; mark the front in pencil; measure distances and calculate Rf values; identify pigments by colour and comparison of Rf with known values / standards; compare the number, size and intensity of spots (or scrape spots and measure absorbance); repeat; safety – propanone flammable, no flames, ventilation.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any seven: same mass / volume for extraction; pencil origin; small concentrated spot with same number of applications; covered tank, solvent below origin; mark front; Rf calculation; identification by Rf / colour / standards; quantitative comparison (spot intensity / colorimetry); repeat; safety.

practice.stem: Plan an investigation into the effect of carbon dioxide concentration on the rate of photosynthesis of Elodea, using a photosynthometer (capillary tube attached to a syringe) and sodium hydrogencarbonate solutions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a plan, including a hypothesis, the range of concentrations, how to measure the rate, the variables to control and how you would analyse the results.
parts.answer: Hypothesis: as CO₂ concentration increases the rate increases, then levels off. Make 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 % NaHCO₃ by diluting a stock; use the same piece of Elodea (cut end upwards, known length / mass), acclimatised for 5 min in each solution; lamp (LED) at a fixed distance in a darkened room; water bath at 25 °C; collect gas for 5 min, draw the bubble into the capillary and measure its length; volume = πr²l; rate = volume ÷ time (÷ mass); three repeats and mean; identify anomalies; plot mean rate against concentration with error bars (SD) or calculate correlation (Spearman's rank).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any eight: hypothesis; ≥5 concentrations with dilution; same plant / acclimatisation; constant light (method); constant temperature (method); volume of gas measured in capillary (πr²l) over fixed time; rate calculation; repeats + mean; graph with axes / error bars or statistical test; anomalies dealt with.

practice.stem:
Gas from a piece of pondweed was collected in a gas syringe. Readings (cm³) were taken every 2 minutes for 10 minutes:
0, 0.18, 0.37, 0.55, 0.74, 0.92

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of gas production over the 10 minutes in cm³ per minute.
parts.answer: 0.092 cm³ per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: The experiment was repeated twice more, giving totals of 0.88 cm³ and 0.96 cm³ in 10 minutes. Calculate the mean total volume of the three trials.
parts.answer: 0.92 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the readings show about the rate during the 10 minutes.
parts.answer: The rate is constant (about 0.18–0.19 cm³ every 2 minutes).
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Leaf discs were placed in two concentrations of sodium hydrogencarbonate under a lamp, and the time for each disc to float was recorded.
0.5 %: 420 s, 390 s, 450 s
1.0 %: 250 s, 270 s, 260 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean time to float at each concentration.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of photosynthesis as 1000 ÷ mean time for each concentration. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why 1 ÷ time can be used as a measure of rate.
parts.answer: Rate is inversely proportional to the time taken: the shorter the time to float, the faster oxygen is produced.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: The rate of oxygen production by an aquatic plant was 6.5 mm³ per minute in tap water and 9.1 mm³ per minute in 0.5 % sodium hydrogencarbonate solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in rate when sodium hydrogencarbonate was added. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student calculated the percentage decrease from the higher rate to the lower rate and obtained a different answer. Calculate this value to 1 decimal place and explain why it differs.
parts.answer: 28.6 %; the change is divided by a different (larger) starting value.
parts.working: 1 mark value; 1 mark explanation.

practice.stem: A leaf in a sealed chamber took up carbon dioxide at a rate of 4.2 cm³ per hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert this rate to mm³ per minute. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 70.0 mm³ per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of CO₂ taken up in 25 minutes, in cm³.
parts.answer: 1.75 cm³

practice.stem: An aquatic plant with a fresh mass of 2.5 g was placed in a photosynthometer. In 5 minutes, the gas collected formed a bubble 18 mm long in a capillary tube with an internal radius of 0.4 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of gas collected, using volume = π r² l. Give your answer in mm³ to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 9.05 mm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of gas production per gram of plant in mm³ min⁻¹ g⁻¹. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.72 mm³ min⁻¹ g⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the rate of gas production underestimates the true rate of photosynthesis.
parts.answer: Some oxygen produced is used in respiration by the plant (or dissolves in the water), so not all is collected.
parts.working: 1 mark: oxygen used in respiration / dissolves in water.

practice.stem: For DCPIP solutions, a calibration graph showed that absorbance = 0.084 × concentration (concentration in µmol dm⁻³). In a Hill reaction tube the absorbance was 0.63 at the start and 0.21 after 5 minutes in light.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of DCPIP at the start and after 5 minutes.
parts.answer: 7.5 and 2.5 µmol dm⁻³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of DCPIP reduction in µmol dm⁻³ per minute.
parts.answer: 1.0 µmol dm⁻³ per minute

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why a calibration graph is needed rather than using absorbance directly.
parts.answer: To convert absorbance into actual concentrations so rates can be given in standard units and compared with other experiments.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
The absorbance of a DCPIP and chloroplast mixture in light was measured every minute.
Time / min: 0, 1, 2, 3
Absorbance: 0.82, 0.70, 0.59, 0.47

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of decrease in absorbance per minute over the 3 minutes. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 0.12 per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in absorbance over the 3 minutes. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why absorbance decreases.
parts.answer: Electrons from the light-dependent stage reduce DCPIP; reduced DCPIP is colourless, so it absorbs less red light.
parts.working: 1 mark DCPIP reduced by electrons from chloroplasts; 1 mark colourless so less light absorbed.

practice.stem: A sealed flask with an aquatic plant and an oxygen sensor was kept in light for 20 minutes: the oxygen in the flask increased by 0.84 cm³. It was then kept in the dark for 20 minutes: the oxygen decreased by 0.18 cm³. Temperature was the same throughout.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of net photosynthesis and the rate of respiration in cm³ of oxygen per minute.
parts.answer: Net 0.042 cm³ min⁻¹; respiration 0.009 cm³ min⁻¹
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of gross photosynthesis in cm³ of oxygen per minute.
parts.answer: 0.051 cm³ min⁻¹
parts.working: Gross = net + respiration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one assumption you made in (b).
parts.answer: That the rate of respiration in the light is the same as in the dark.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
A light meter was used to measure the light intensity at different distances from a small lamp.
Distance / cm: 10, 20, 30, 40
Light intensity / lux: 12 000, 3000, 1330, 750

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each distance, calculate light intensity × distance². Give each answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 1.20 × 10⁶ for every distance (30 cm: 1 197 000 ≈ 1.20 × 10⁶)
parts.working: 2 marks all four; 1 mark two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what your answers show.
parts.answer: The product is constant, so light intensity is inversely proportional to distance squared (inverse square law).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answer to (a) to calculate the light intensity at 25 cm.
parts.answer: 1920 lux

practice.stem: Chlorophyll was extracted from 0.50 g of leaf into 80 % propanone and made up to 20.0 cm³. The absorbance was 0.31 at 645 nm and 0.72 at 663 nm. Total chlorophyll concentration (mg dm⁻³) = 20.2 × A₆₄₅ + 8.02 × A₆₆₃.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total chlorophyll concentration of the extract. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 12.0 mg dm⁻³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the chlorophyll content of the leaf in mg per g. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.48 mg g⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why absorbance is measured at 663 nm and 645 nm.
parts.answer: These are red wavelengths absorbed strongly by chlorophyll a (663 nm) and chlorophyll b (645 nm).
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
A Hill-reaction experiment measured the time for DCPIP to be decolourised by a chloroplast suspension at two temperatures.
20 °C: 240 s, 252 s, 246 s
30 °C: 150 s, 156 s, 300 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and explain why it should not be included in the mean.
parts.answer: 300 s at 30 °C; it is far from the other two readings (150 and 156 s), so it is probably due to an error (e.g. wrong volume or tube shaded) and would distort the mean.
parts.working: 1 mark: 300 s at 30 °C identified with reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean time at each temperature, leaving out the anomalous result, and then the rate of reaction as 1000/mean time. Give rates to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 20 °C: mean 246 s, rate 4.07; 30 °C: mean 153 s, rate 6.54 (rates as 1000/s)
parts.working: 1 mark: mean 246 s. 1 mark: mean 153 s (anomaly excluded). 1 mark: rates 4.07 and 6.54.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in rate from 20 °C to 30 °C. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

practice.stem: The outline of a bean leaf was drawn on 1 cm² grid paper. It covered 38 whole squares and 16 squares that were partly covered. The leaf took up 0.69 mg of CO₂ in 15 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Estimate the area of the leaf, counting each partly covered square as half a square.
parts.answer: 46 cm²

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of CO₂ uptake in mg cm⁻² h⁻¹. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.060 mg cm⁻² h⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Convert your answer to mg dm⁻² h⁻¹ (1 dm² = 100 cm²).
parts.answer: 6.0 mg dm⁻² h⁻¹

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why rates of photosynthesis are expressed per unit area of leaf.
parts.answer: Leaves differ in size, so dividing by area allows fair comparison between leaves / species.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A potted plant released 36 cm³ of oxygen (measured at room temperature and pressure) during a period of light. One mole of gas occupies 24 dm³ at room temperature and pressure. The equation for photosynthesis is 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. The Mr of glucose is 180.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of oxygen released.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of glucose, in mg, that this represents.
parts.answer: 45 mg

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the actual increase in dry mass of the plant was less than this.
parts.answer: Some glucose was used in respiration (and some oxygen measured is net, some dissolved / used) / some used for other processes.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Algal balls in hydrogencarbonate indicator were placed in bright light. As CO₂ was removed the indicator changed from red towards purple and its absorbance at 550 nm increased.
Time / min: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20
Absorbance: 0.3, 0.38, 0.46, 0.54, 0.58

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of change of absorbance between 0 and 15 minutes, in absorbance units per minute.
parts.answer: 0.016 per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate between 15 and 20 minutes and suggest why it is lower.
parts.answer: 0.008 per minute; CO₂ in the indicator has been used up and is now limiting photosynthesis (the indicator approaches its purple limit).
parts.working: 1 mark value; 1 mark explanation.

practice.stem: A gas syringe can be read to ±0.05 cm³. A student collected 1.20 cm³ of oxygen and timed the collection with a stopwatch to ±0.5 s over 60 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the volume and in the time. Give your answers to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: Volume 4.2 %; time 0.83 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which measurement contributes most to the uncertainty in the rate and suggest how the student could reduce it.
parts.answer: Volume; collect gas for longer (or use a brighter light) so a larger volume is collected, e.g. 2.40 cm³ gives only 2.1 %.
parts.working: 1 mark volume; 1 mark method of increasing volume measured.

practice.stem: A student uses a photosynthometer to measure the volume of gas given off by a piece of pondweed in sodium hydrogencarbonate solution when a lamp is placed at different distances.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation.
parts.answer: Independent: light intensity (distance of lamp). Dependent: volume of gas (oxygen) produced per minute.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three variables that should be standardised and explain how each could be kept constant.
parts.answer: Temperature – water bath / heat shield / LED lamp; CO₂ concentration – same concentration and volume of sodium hydrogencarbonate solution, in excess; plant – same piece/length of the same species; time of collection – stopwatch; background light – darkened room.
parts.working: 1 mark for each variable with a valid method (max 3).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the sodium hydrogencarbonate solution should be in excess.
parts.answer: So that CO₂ concentration is not a limiting factor and does not fall during the experiment; only light intensity limits the rate.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A student investigates the effect of light intensity on the Hill reaction. Tubes containing chloroplast suspension and DCPIP are placed at different distances from an LED lamp, and the time for the blue colour to disappear is recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: light intensity (distance from lamp). Dependent: time taken for DCPIP to decolourise (rate of DCPIP reduction).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three variables that should be standardised and how each could be kept constant.
parts.answer: Temperature – water bath / LED that gives off little heat; volume and concentration of DCPIP – same pipette/syringe and same stock; volume and concentration of chloroplast suspension – same suspension, mixed before use; wavelength of light – same LED; pH – same buffer.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three variables with a method.

practice.stem: A student puts algal balls into bottles of hydrogencarbonate indicator kept at 10, 20, 30 and 40 °C under the same lamp.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent variable and suggest how the dependent variable could be measured.
parts.answer: Independent: temperature. Dependent: change in indicator colour, measured as absorbance with a colorimeter (or time to reach a colour standard).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why each bottle must contain the same number of algal balls of the same size.
parts.answer: The number of algal cells affects the total amount of photosynthesis and CO₂ removal; if the bottles differ, the colour change would not be due to temperature alone.
parts.working: 1 mark: more algae → faster colour change; 1 mark: otherwise not a fair test / not valid.

practice.stem: In a pondweed experiment the lamp is moved closer to the plant to increase light intensity. A student places a glass tank of water between the lamp and the plant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the tank of water is used.
parts.answer: It absorbs heat (infrared) from the lamp; so the temperature of the plant does not rise as the lamp is moved closer and temperature stays a controlled variable.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an alternative way to avoid this problem.
parts.answer: Use an LED lamp (gives off little heat) / place the plant in a thermostatically controlled water bath.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A student wants to compare the pigments in the leaves of two plants by paper chromatography.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four variables that must be kept the same for the two chromatograms.
parts.answer: Type and volume of solvent; type of chromatography paper / TLC plate; distance the solvent runs; temperature; mass of leaf and volume of propanone used for extraction; number of times the spot is applied (amount of extract); position of the origin line.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

practice.stem: A student investigates the effect of sodium hydrogencarbonate concentration (0.0 %, 0.1 %, 0.2 %, 0.4 %, 0.8 %) on the time taken for infiltrated leaf discs to float in bright light.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why all the leaf discs should be cut from the same plant and should avoid large veins.
parts.answer: Same plant: discs have similar chlorophyll content / genotype / age, so differences are due to CO₂ concentration. Avoid veins: veins have fewer chloroplasts and different density/air spaces, which would affect floating time.
parts.working: 1 mark: same plant – reduces variation in chlorophyll/genetics. 1 mark: veins differ in chloroplasts/buoyancy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a suitable control and explain what it shows.
parts.answer: Discs in distilled water with no sodium hydrogencarbonate (no added CO₂) under the same light; shows that floating depends on CO₂ for photosynthesis (discs should not float or float very slowly). Or discs in hydrogencarbonate kept in the dark – shows light is needed.
parts.working: 1 mark: valid control (no NaHCO₃ or dark). 1 mark: what it shows.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a change in temperature during the experiment would make the results less valid.
parts.answer: Temperature affects the rate of the enzyme-controlled reactions of photosynthesis (Calvin cycle), so the floating time would no longer depend only on CO₂ concentration.
parts.working: 1 mark: enzymes/rubisco affected by temperature. 1 mark: rate would change for a reason other than the independent variable.

practice.stem: A student made algal balls and placed them in red hydrogencarbonate indicator in light. The indicator turned purple after 40 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two control tubes the student should set up and state what each would show.
parts.answer: Indicator with no algal balls in the same light – shows that light alone (or air) does not change the indicator colour. Indicator with alginate balls containing no algae – shows that the alginate / calcium chloride does not change the colour. (Also: algal balls in a foil-covered tube – shows respiration makes the indicator yellow without light.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each control described; 1 mark for what each shows.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the controls must be kept at the same temperature and light intensity as the experimental tubes.
parts.answer: So that the only difference is the presence of algae; any difference in colour can then be due to algal photosynthesis.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A student measured the rate of photosynthesis of sun leaves (top of the canopy) and shade leaves (inner canopy) of a neem tree using leaf discs. She collected sun leaves at 08:00 and shade leaves at 14:00 and tested each batch on the day it was collected.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two variables that were not controlled in her method and explain how each could affect the results.
parts.answer: Time of collection: leaves at 14:00 may have different starch / water content or be more stressed (stomata closed) than at 08:00. Temperature / storage time: discs tested at different temperatures or after different times. Leaf age: sun and shade leaves may differ in age. (Also: different light during testing.)
parts.working: 1 mark each for two variables; 1 mark each for explanation of their effect.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how she should improve the method.
parts.answer: Collect both types of leaf at the same time from leaves of similar age (same node position) and test them together under the same light and temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark same time / age; 1 mark tested together under same conditions.

practice.stem: In a photosynthometer experiment the student moves the lamp to a new distance and waits 5 minutes before starting to collect gas.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the student waits 5 minutes.
parts.answer: The plant needs time to adjust (acclimatise) to the new light intensity so that the rate of photosynthesis becomes steady; gas already in the system from the previous intensity is not collected.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the student should take readings in a darkened room.
parts.answer: So that the only light reaching the plant is from the lamp and light intensity depends only on distance (background light varies).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A filament lamp is moved from 40 cm to 10 cm from a beaker containing pondweed. Explain why this changes two variables at once and why this makes the results less valid.
parts.answer: Moving the lamp closer increases light intensity and also heats the water (raises temperature); both light intensity and temperature affect the rate; so a change in rate cannot be attributed to light intensity alone.
parts.working: 1 mark: light intensity increases; 1 mark: temperature increases; 1 mark: confounding variable so conclusion not valid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student could monitor whether temperature changed.
parts.answer: Place a thermometer (or temperature probe) in the beaker and record the temperature at each distance.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A Hill reaction class experiment uses chloroplast suspension prepared by different groups. Results from different groups cannot be compared.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the concentration of chloroplasts should be standardised.
parts.answer: More chloroplasts means more photosystems / more electrons to reduce DCPIP, so a faster rate; differences in chloroplast concentration would hide the effect of the independent variable.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the chloroplast concentration of each suspension could be standardised.
parts.answer: Measure the absorbance (or chlorophyll content) of each suspension with a colorimeter and dilute with buffer until all have the same absorbance; or use the same mass of leaf in the same volume of buffer.
parts.working: 1 mark measure (colorimeter / chlorophyll); 1 mark dilute to same value.

practice.stem: A student investigated the effect of colour of light on photosynthesis by placing red, blue and green filters in front of the same lamp at the same distance from a pondweed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the light intensity reaching the plant may not be the same for each filter, and why this is a problem.
parts.answer: Filters absorb different amounts of light, so different intensities pass through; light intensity affects the rate, so differences may be due to intensity rather than wavelength.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the student could make sure that only the wavelength varies.
parts.answer: Measure the light intensity behind each filter with a light meter (sensitive across wavelengths) and adjust the lamp distance (or use coloured LEDs of equal output) so that the intensity is the same.
parts.working: 1 mark measure with light meter; 1 mark adjust to equal intensity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one other variable that the filters might change and suggest how to control it.
parts.answer: Temperature (dark filters absorb more heat) – use LEDs / heat filter / water bath.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: The CO₂ uptake of a leaf was measured by sealing it in a small transparent chamber and recording the falling CO₂ concentration with a sensor for 30 minutes in constant light.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the CO₂ concentration is not a controlled variable in this design.
parts.answer: The leaf removes CO₂ from the sealed chamber, so the concentration falls during the experiment; as CO₂ may be a limiting factor, the rate decreases with time.
parts.working: 1 mark falls over time; 1 mark affects rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways to improve the design so that CO₂ concentration stays constant.
parts.answer: Pass a steady flow of air of known CO₂ concentration through the chamber (open system) and measure the difference between incoming and outgoing air; measure only over a short time at the start when the change is small; use a larger chamber volume.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the temperature of the chamber should be monitored.
parts.answer: Light on a sealed chamber can warm it (greenhouse effect), and temperature affects the rate of photosynthesis and respiration.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A student compared the rate of photosynthesis of three species of houseplant by measuring the time for leaf discs from each to float.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the independent variable in this investigation is categoric, and state the type of graph that should be used.
parts.answer: Species are separate groups, not numerical values on a scale; bar chart (with error bars).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two variables that differ between species and cannot be standardised, and explain how the student should deal with them.
parts.answer: Leaf thickness / density of air spaces; chlorophyll content; stomatal density; leaf age. These cannot be made the same because they are part of what differs between species, so they should be measured and recorded (monitored) and taken into account when drawing conclusions, while choosing leaves of similar age / position.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two valid variables; 1 mark for 'measure / monitor and take into account (cannot conclude cause)'.

practice.stem: A student measured the volume of oxygen released by pondweed at 10, 20, 30 and 40 °C using a gas syringe.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Oxygen is less soluble in warm water than in cold water. Explain how this could affect the volumes measured.
parts.answer: At low temperature more of the oxygen produced dissolves in the water and is not collected; at high temperature less dissolves (and some dissolved gas may come out of solution), so the increase in volume with temperature is exaggerated.
parts.working: 1 mark: more dissolves at low temperature; 1 mark: rate under-estimated at low / over-estimated at high temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the student could reduce this effect.
parts.answer: Use water already saturated with oxygen (aerated) at each temperature before starting; equilibrate the water at each temperature and allow time before measuring; or measure dissolved oxygen with an oxygen probe instead.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: A student will add DCPIP to chloroplast suspensions kept at 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 and 35 °C in light and record how quickly the blue colour disappears.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: As temperature increases from 10 °C to 35 °C, the rate of DCPIP reduction by chloroplasts increases.
parts.working: 1 mark: testable, directional statement linking temperature and rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the null hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is no relationship between temperature and the rate of DCPIP reduction.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict and explain the results you would expect if the range were extended to 60 °C.
parts.answer: Rate increases up to an optimum (around 35–40 °C) because molecules have more kinetic energy and electron carrier/enzyme proteins work faster; above the optimum the rate decreases sharply because proteins in the photosystems/electron carriers are denatured and thylakoid membranes are damaged.
parts.working: 1 mark: increase then decrease (optimum). 1 mark: more kinetic energy / faster reactions below optimum. 1 mark: denaturation of proteins (photosystems, carriers) / membrane damage above optimum.

practice.stem: A student will measure the time taken for leaf discs to float when a lamp is placed 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 cm away.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a testable hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: As light intensity increases (lamp closer), the rate of photosynthesis increases, so the time taken for discs to float decreases.
parts.working: 1 mark: names both variables; 1 mark: direction of the relationship.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict how the results would change if the lamp were moved even closer than 10 cm. Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: The time would stop decreasing (level off), because another factor such as CO₂ concentration or temperature becomes limiting.
parts.working: 1 mark prediction; 1 mark limiting factor explanation.

practice.stem: A student wants to know whether the mean chlorophyll content of spinach leaves differs from that of lettuce leaves. She will use a t-test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a null hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the mean chlorophyll content of spinach leaves and lettuce leaves.
parts.working: 1 mark; must refer to mean and 'no (significant) difference'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the alternative hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is a significant difference between the mean chlorophyll content of spinach and lettuce leaves.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Three tubes of red hydrogencarbonate indicator are set up:
Tube A: algal balls in bright light
Tube B: algal balls wrapped in aluminium foil
Tube C: no algal balls, in bright light

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the colour of each tube after two hours.
parts.answer: A: purple; B: yellow; C: red (unchanged).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain your prediction for tube B.
parts.answer: In the dark the algae cannot photosynthesise but still respire; CO₂ released by respiration raises the CO₂ concentration (lowers pH), turning the indicator yellow.
parts.working: 1 mark respiration only; 1 mark CO₂ increases.

practice.stem: A student will measure the rate of oxygen production of Cabomba in sodium hydrogencarbonate solutions of 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0 % in bright light.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: As the concentration of sodium hydrogencarbonate (CO₂) increases, the rate of oxygen production increases.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the shape of the graph you would predict, and give a reason for the shape at the highest concentrations.
parts.answer: Rate rises steeply at first and then levels off (plateau); at high concentrations CO₂ is no longer limiting – light or temperature limits the rate.
parts.working: 1 mark shape; 1 mark reason.

practice.stem: A student plans to compare the rate of photosynthesis of pondweed in red light and green light of equal intensity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a hypothesis that could be tested.
parts.answer: The rate of photosynthesis is higher in red light than in green light.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the biological reason for your hypothesis.
parts.answer: Chlorophyll absorbs red light strongly but absorbs little green light (green is reflected), so more light energy is absorbed for the light-dependent stage in red light.
parts.working: 1 mark absorption difference; 1 mark more energy for photoactivation / light-dependent stage.

practice.stem: DCMU blocks the transfer of electrons from photosystem II to the electron transport chain. A student adds DCMU to a chloroplast suspension containing DCPIP and places it in light.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the effect of DCMU on the colour change of DCPIP compared with a tube without DCMU.
parts.answer: DCPIP stays blue (or decolourises much more slowly).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: DCPIP accepts electrons from the electron transport chain after photosystem II; with DCMU no electrons leave PSII to reach the chain, so DCPIP is not reduced.
parts.working: 1 mark DCPIP is an electron acceptor from the chain; 1 mark no electrons flow from PSII.

parts.label: c
