parts.text: Identify three hazards of this fieldwork and a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Drowning / falling into deep water – work in pairs, stay on firm banks, teacher supervision; infection from water-borne microorganisms (e.g. leptospirosis carried in rat urine) – wear gloves, cover cuts, wash hands before eating; slippery banks – suitable footwear; sharp objects in the water – do not reach in with bare hands.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three hazard–precaution pairs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one action to protect the pond environment.
parts.answer: Take only a small amount of plant and do not trample the bank / return unused organisms.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a hazard and a risk.
parts.answer: A hazard is something that could cause harm (e.g. a flammable solvent); risk is the likelihood that harm will actually occur and how severe it will be (e.g. the chance of a fire if the solvent is used near a flame).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how using a smaller volume of propanone reduces the risk but not the hazard.
parts.answer: Propanone is still flammable (hazard unchanged), but with less of it any fire would be smaller and less vapour builds up, so the likelihood and severity of harm are reduced.
parts.working: 1 mark hazard unchanged; 1 mark risk reduced with reason.

practice.stem: A student plans to use the herbicide DCMU (toxic and harmful to aquatic life) to block photosynthesis in a Hill reaction experiment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest three precautions for using DCMU in a school laboratory.
parts.answer: Use the lowest effective concentration and smallest volume; wear gloves and goggles; teacher prepares the solution / weighs solid in a fume cupboard; wash hands; label clearly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how waste DCMU solution should be disposed of, and why.
parts.answer: Collect in a labelled waste container for proper chemical disposal, not down the sink; because it is toxic to aquatic organisms and would harm plants and algae in waterways.
parts.working: 1 mark method; 1 mark reason.

practice.stem: A photosynthometer practical uses a glass capillary tube joined to a syringe, pondweed stems trimmed with a scalpel, 1 % sodium hydrogencarbonate solution, and a 150 W halogen lamp on the bench next to the beaker of water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards in this practical and state a control measure for each.
parts.answer: Halogen lamp becomes very hot – burns or fire if near paper – do not touch, keep paper away, allow to cool, or use an LED; mains lamp near water – electric shock – keep water and wet hands away from the lamp and socket; glass capillary tube may snap when pushed into tubing – cuts – lubricate with water / hold in a cloth, push gently; scalpel – cuts – cut on a tile away from fingers.
parts.working: 1 mark each hazard with control measure (max 2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why placing a tank of water between the lamp and the beaker reduces a hazard as well as improving the experiment.
parts.answer: The water absorbs heat, so the beaker and nearby objects do not get as hot (less risk of burns / scorching), as well as keeping the plant's temperature constant.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the risk assessment must be done before the practical starts.
parts.answer: So that hazards are identified and control measures (e.g. LED lamp, goggles, layout of bench) are in place before anyone can be harmed.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A student's risk assessment for a leaf-pigment practical reads: 'Hazards: none really. Precautions: be careful. Risk: low.' The method uses a scalpel to cut leaves, propanone and sand ground in a mortar, a hot plate to dry the chromatography plates, and a running solvent containing petroleum ether in a tank.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate this risk assessment and rewrite it properly for two of the hazards.
parts.answer: The assessment is inadequate: it does not name specific hazards, 'be careful' is not a control measure, and the risk level is not justified (flammable solvents are used near a heat source). Example rewrites: propanone / petroleum ether – highly flammable vapour could be ignited by the hot plate – keep solvents away from the hot plate, dry plates in air or in a fume cupboard, no flames; hot plate – burns – use tongs, label as hot, let it cool; scalpel – cuts – cut on a tile, away from fingers; solvent vapour – irritant / harmful if breathed – fume cupboard or good ventilation, keep tank lid on.
parts.working: 1 mark: evaluation of weaknesses (no hazards named / vague precaution / risk not justified); 1 mark each for hazard + risk and control in two rewrites (max 3).

practice.stem: A student plans to use a high-intensity LED panel (very bright blue-white light) close to the bench to drive photosynthesis at high light intensities.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the main hazard and explain the possible harm.
parts.answer: Very bright (blue) light can damage the retina / cause eye strain and temporary blindness (glare); prolonged staring may cause permanent eye damage.
parts.working: 1 mark hazard; 1 mark harm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two precautions.
parts.answer: Do not look directly at the LEDs; position the panel so light is directed away from faces or shield it; wear tinted safety glasses; switch off when not taking readings.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: Elodea (Canadian pondweed) is not native to Pakistan's rivers and spreads quickly if released. After a class practical, students have pondweed, used DCPIP solution and propanone left over.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how each should be disposed of, giving reasons.
parts.answer: Pondweed: do not put into drains, ponds or rivers – it could become invasive and outcompete native plants; dispose of in general waste / compost or dry it out. DCPIP: small, dilute amounts can usually be washed down the sink with plenty of water if local rules allow; otherwise collect as chemical waste. Propanone: collect in a labelled solvent residue bottle, do not pour down the sink because it is flammable and pollutes water.
parts.working: 1 mark pondweed method; 1 mark invasive reason; 1 mark DCPIP; 1 mark propanone with reason.

practice.stem: Chloroplasts are separated by spinning tubes of leaf extract in a bench centrifuge.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the tubes must be balanced in the centrifuge.
parts.answer: An unbalanced rotor vibrates strongly at high speed; it can damage the centrifuge, break tubes and throw out glass or liquid, causing injury.
parts.working: 1 mark vibration; 1 mark consequence.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how to balance the tubes.
parts.answer: Place tubes with equal volumes (masses) opposite each other; if there is an odd number, add a balance tube filled with water to the same level.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two other precautions when using a centrifuge.
parts.answer: Keep the lid closed and locked while spinning; do not open it until the rotor has completely stopped; use tubes that are not cracked; do not exceed the stated speed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

subtopics.name: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

subtopics: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the role of carbonic anhydrase in red blood cells?
A It catalyses the combination of oxygen with haemoglobin.
B It catalyses the reaction between carbon dioxide and water to form carbonic acid.
C It transports hydrogencarbonate ions out of the red blood cell.
D It catalyses the combination of carbon dioxide with haemoglobin to form carbaminohaemoglobin.
parts.answer: B It catalyses the reaction between carbon dioxide and water to form carbonic acid.
parts.working: B: carbonic anhydrase catalyses CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃, which dissociates into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻. D is wrong: carbaminohaemoglobin forms by CO₂ combining with amine groups of haemoglobin without this enzyme. C is done by a membrane transport protein (in exchange for Cl⁻).

practice.stem:
A stained blood smear is viewed with a light microscope. Four cells are described:
A – about 7 µm across, no nucleus, pale centre, red/pink.
B – about 12 µm across, nucleus with three lobes, granular cytoplasm.
C – about 8 µm across, large round nucleus filling almost the whole cell, a thin rim of cytoplasm.
D – about 18 µm across, large bean-shaped nucleus, plenty of cytoplasm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify cells A, B, C and D.
parts.answer: A red blood cell (erythrocyte); B neutrophil; C lymphocyte; D monocyte.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way in which the shape of cell A is related to its function.
parts.answer: Biconcave disc gives a large surface area to volume ratio for fast diffusion of oxygen (also: flexible to squeeze through capillaries; no nucleus leaves more room for haemoglobin).
parts.working: B1 any one valid structure–function link.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Cell D can leave the blood and develop into a macrophage. State the function of macrophages.
parts.answer: Phagocytosis of pathogens / cell debris, and presenting antigens to lymphocytes.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text:
As hydrogencarbonate ions diffuse out of a red blood cell into the plasma, which ion moves into the cell to keep the charges balanced?
A chloride ions
B hydrogen ions
C potassium ions
D sodium ions
parts.answer: A chloride ions
parts.working: The chloride shift: Cl⁻ diffuses in as HCO₃⁻ diffuses out, so the cell stays electrically neutral. B is wrong: H⁺ ions are formed inside the cell and stay there, where haemoglobin buffers them; they do not enter from the plasma.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the level of protein structure shown by a haemoglobin molecule and the number of polypeptide chains it contains.
parts.answer: Quaternary structure; four polypeptide chains (two α-globin and two β-globin).
parts.working: B1 quaternary; B1 four chains (accept 2 α + 2 β).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the role of the iron ion in each haem group.
parts.answer: The Fe²⁺ ion binds (reversibly) to one oxygen molecule.
parts.working: B1 Fe²⁺ combines with one O₂ / forms oxyhaemoglobin.

parts.label: c
parts.text: One red blood cell contains about 2.8 × 10⁸ haemoglobin molecules. Calculate the maximum number of oxygen molecules this red blood cell can carry.
parts.answer: 1.12 × 10⁹ oxygen molecules
parts.working: M1 4 O₂ per haemoglobin (one per haem); A1 4 × 2.8 × 10⁸ = 1.12 × 10⁹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences in appearance between a neutrophil and a lymphocyte in a stained blood smear.
parts.answer: Neutrophil has a lobed nucleus, lymphocyte a large round nucleus; neutrophil has much granular cytoplasm, lymphocyte only a thin rim of cytoplasm.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: lobed vs round nucleus; much vs little cytoplasm; granular cytoplasm in neutrophil; neutrophil usually larger.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one function of each type of cell.
parts.answer: Neutrophil: phagocytosis of bacteria. Lymphocyte: specific immune response, e.g. B-lymphocytes secrete antibodies / T-lymphocytes destroy infected cells.
parts.working: B1 phagocytosis; B1 antibody production or other correct lymphocyte role.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A patient in Multan with a bacterial infection has 11.2 × 10⁹ neutrophils per dm³ of blood. The normal value is 4.5 × 10⁹ per dm³. Calculate how many times greater the patient's count is, to 2 significant figures, and suggest a reason for the increase.
parts.answer: 2.5 times; more neutrophils are produced to engulf the bacteria.
parts.working: A1 11.2 ÷ 4.5 = 2.5; B1 more phagocytes to destroy bacteria.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A person starts running. Respiring muscle cells release more carbon dioxide into the blood.
What is the effect of this on the oxygen dissociation curve of haemoglobin and on oxygen release to the muscles?
A The curve shifts to the left and more oxygen is released.
B The curve shifts to the left and less oxygen is released.
C The curve shifts to the right and more oxygen is released.
D The curve shifts to the right and less oxygen is released.
parts.answer: C The curve shifts to the right and more oxygen is released.
parts.working: C: the Bohr shift – higher CO₂ partial pressure lowers the pH (more H⁺), reducing haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, so the curve moves right and oxyhaemoglobin unloads more oxygen at the same partial pressure. D wrongly links a right shift with less unloading.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how most carbon dioxide produced by respiring cells is carried in the blood.
parts.answer: CO₂ diffuses into red blood cells; carbonic anhydrase catalyses CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃; carbonic acid dissociates into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻; HCO₃⁻ diffuses out of the red cell into the plasma (and is carried as hydrogencarbonate in the plasma); Cl⁻ moves into the cell to balance the charge (chloride shift).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: CO₂ enters red blood cells; carbonic anhydrase; carbonic acid formed; dissociates to H⁺ and HCO₃⁻; HCO₃⁻ diffuses out into plasma; chloride ions move in (chloride shift).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the hydrogen ions formed in this process cause oxygen to be released from haemoglobin.
parts.answer: H⁺ bind to haemoglobin forming haemoglobinic acid; this changes the shape (tertiary/quaternary structure) of haemoglobin, lowering its affinity for oxygen, so oxyhaemoglobin releases oxygen.
parts.working: B1 H⁺ combine with haemoglobin / haemoglobinic acid formed. B1 reduces affinity for O₂ so oxygen unloaded (Bohr effect). (Also accept: H⁺ buffered, preventing a fall in blood pH.)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two other ways in which carbon dioxide is carried in the blood.
parts.answer: Combined with haemoglobin as carbaminohaemoglobin; dissolved in plasma.
parts.working: B1 both needed.

practice.stem:
When fully saturated, 100 cm³ of blood carries 20.0 cm³ of oxygen. Percentage saturation of haemoglobin:
Lungs (pO₂ 13 kPa): 97 %
Resting tissue (pO₂ 5 kPa): 70 %
Exercising muscle (pO₂ 2.5 kPa): 35 % on the normal curve; 20 % when the high CO₂ in the muscle is taken into account.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen released to resting tissues by 100 cm³ of blood.
parts.answer: 5.4 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how much more oxygen is released by 100 cm³ of blood in exercising muscle, when the Bohr shift is taken into account, than in resting tissue.
parts.answer: 10.0 cm³ more
parts.working: M1 exercising, shifted curve: (97 − 20) % × 20.0 = 15.4 cm³. A1 15.4 − 5.4 = 10.0 cm³.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the saturation at 13 kPa is hardly affected by the Bohr shift, but the saturation at 2.5 kPa is reduced from 35 % to 20 %.
parts.answer: At 13 kPa the curve is flat (plateau), so a shift to the right makes little difference and haemoglobin still loads fully in the lungs; at low partial pressures the curve is steep, so the lower affinity causes a large fall in saturation and much more unloading.
parts.working: B1 lungs: plateau / high pO₂, loading still nearly complete. B1 tissues: steep part of curve, small change in affinity gives large change in saturation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why does the oxygen dissociation curve of adult haemoglobin have an S (sigmoid) shape?
A Each haem group has a different, fixed affinity for oxygen.
B After the first oxygen molecule binds, the haemoglobin molecule changes shape so that further oxygen molecules bind more easily.
C Oxygen binds to the globin polypeptide chains first and to the haem groups later.
D Carbon dioxide leaves haemoglobin as oxygen binds, so its affinity for oxygen falls.
parts.answer: B After the first oxygen molecule binds, the haemoglobin molecule changes shape so that further oxygen molecules bind more easily.
parts.working: Cooperative binding: binding of the first O₂ changes the quaternary shape, raising the affinity of the other haem groups, so the curve rises steeply in the middle. D is wrong: losing CO₂ would raise, not lower, the affinity, and it does not explain the shape.

practice.stem:
P₅₀ is the partial pressure of oxygen at which haemoglobin is 50 % saturated. Values from one laboratory study (rounded):
human 3.6 kPa
llama (lives in the Andes at about 4,000 m) 2.9 kPa
house mouse 5.3 kPa

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what the lower P₅₀ value of the llama shows about its haemoglobin compared with human haemoglobin.
parts.answer: Llama haemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen; its dissociation curve lies to the left of the human curve.
parts.working: B1 higher affinity; B1 curve to the left / 50 % saturated at a lower pO₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this is an advantage to a llama living at 4,000 m.
parts.answer: The partial pressure of oxygen in the air and alveoli is low at altitude; llama haemoglobin can still load oxygen and become (almost) fully saturated in the lungs.
parts.working: B1 low pO₂ in alveoli at altitude; B1 haemoglobin still loads / is highly saturated, so enough O₂ is carried.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the haemoglobin of a mouse has a higher P₅₀ than human haemoglobin.
parts.answer: The mouse is small with a large surface area to volume ratio, so it loses heat quickly and has a high metabolic rate; it needs a high rate of aerobic respiration; haemoglobin with a lower affinity unloads oxygen more readily in the tissues.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: large SA:V / loses heat fast; high rate of respiration / metabolic rate; lower affinity so O₂ released more easily to tissues (at higher pO₂).

practice.stem: A woman in Lahore has iron-deficiency anaemia. Her blood contains 87 g of haemoglobin per dm³. A healthy woman of the same age has 145 g dm⁻³. When fully saturated, 1 g of haemoglobin combines with 1.34 cm³ of oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum volume of oxygen that 1 dm³ of blood can carry for the healthy woman and for the patient. Give your answers to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: Healthy woman 194 cm³; patient 117 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in the patient's haemoglobin concentration compared with the healthy woman.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The patient becomes tired and breathless when climbing stairs. Explain why.
parts.answer: Less haemoglobin, so less oxygen carried to muscles; less aerobic respiration / less ATP; more anaerobic respiration so lactate builds up; breathing rate rises to try to obtain more oxygen.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: less O₂ carried / delivered; less aerobic respiration / ATP; anaerobic respiration / lactate / oxygen debt; increased breathing / heart rate to compensate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Fetal haemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen than adult haemoglobin. State where its dissociation curve lies compared with the adult curve and explain why this is important for the fetus.
parts.answer: To the left of the adult curve; at the low partial pressures in the placenta, fetal haemoglobin is more saturated than maternal haemoglobin; so oxygen moves from the mother's oxyhaemoglobin to the fetal haemoglobin.
parts.working: B1 left. B1 placenta has low pO₂ / mother's haemoglobin unloads there. B1 fetal haemoglobin loads oxygen released by maternal haemoglobin.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Mature red blood cells have no nucleus and no mitochondria. Suggest how each of these features is an advantage for the transport of oxygen.
parts.answer: No nucleus: more space inside the cell for haemoglobin, so each cell carries more oxygen (and the cell can be a flexible biconcave disc). No mitochondria: the cell does not respire aerobically (it makes ATP by anaerobic respiration / glycolysis), so it does not use any of the oxygen it carries, and all of it can be delivered to the tissues.
parts.working: B1 no nucleus → more room for haemoglobin. B1 so more oxygen carried per cell (or: flexible / biconcave shape allowed). B1 no mitochondria → no aerobic respiration, so the oxygen carried is not used up by the red cell itself.

practice.stem: In winter, some families in Quetta heat closed rooms with gas or charcoal heaters. Incomplete combustion releases carbon monoxide. Hospitals treat patients who arrive with headaches and dizziness.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why breathing carbon monoxide reduces the oxygen supplied to tissues.
parts.answer: Carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin (at the haem/iron sites) to form carboxyhaemoglobin; it binds much more strongly than oxygen and is not easily released; so fewer sites are available to carry oxygen and less oxygen reaches respiring tissues (it also makes the remaining haemoglobin release oxygen less readily).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: forms carboxyhaemoglobin; binds to haem / same site as oxygen; binds more strongly / almost irreversibly; less haemoglobin available for oxygen transport; less oxygen delivered / less aerobic respiration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the first symptoms are headache and dizziness.
parts.answer: The brain has a high demand for oxygen for aerobic respiration, so it is affected first by reduced oxygen supply.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the patients were given pure oxygen to breathe.
parts.answer: A high partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli competes with carbon monoxide for haemoglobin, speeding the replacement of CO; and more oxygen dissolves in plasma, raising oxygen supply to tissues.
parts.working: B1 high pO₂ helps displace CO from haemoglobin. B1 more oxygen carried (dissolved / bound) to tissues.

practice.stem:
Myoglobin is a red pigment found in muscle cells. Percentage saturation with oxygen:
pO₂ 1 kPa: myoglobin 70 %, haemoglobin 10 %
pO₂ 2 kPa: myoglobin 85 %, haemoglobin 25 %
pO₂ 4 kPa: myoglobin 94 %, haemoglobin 60 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Myoglobin is a single polypeptide with one haem group. Explain why its oxygen dissociation curve is not S-shaped.
parts.answer: With only one haem group there is no cooperative binding: binding of oxygen cannot change the affinity of other haem groups, so the curve is hyperbolic.
parts.working: B1 only one haem / binds one O₂; B1 no cooperative binding / no change in shape that raises affinity of further sites.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the data to explain how myoglobin helps to supply oxygen to respiring muscle cells.
parts.answer: Myoglobin has a much higher affinity than haemoglobin (70 % vs 10 % saturated at 1 kPa); it takes oxygen from oxyhaemoglobin in muscle capillaries; it keeps a store of oxygen that it releases only when pO₂ in the muscle falls very low, e.g. during intense exercise.
parts.working: 1 mark each: higher affinity (data quoted); loads O₂ from haemoglobin at low pO₂; acts as a store, releasing O₂ only at very low pO₂.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The muscles of Weddell seals contain much more myoglobin than human muscle. Suggest the advantage of this.
parts.answer: Seals hold their breath during long dives; the large myoglobin store supplies oxygen for aerobic respiration in the muscles while no air is breathed.
parts.working: B1 long dives / breath-holding; B1 O₂ store for aerobic respiration (delays anaerobic respiration / lactate).

practice.stem: Acetazolamide is a drug that inhibits carbonic anhydrase. Some trekkers take it on the route to K2 base camp.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the effect of acetazolamide on the rate of formation of hydrogencarbonate ions in red blood cells passing through respiring tissues. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: The rate falls; carbonic anhydrase normally catalyses CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃, so without it far less carbonic acid forms to dissociate into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻.
parts.working: B1 slower / less HCO₃⁻; B1 carbonic anhydrase catalyses formation of carbonic acid, which dissociates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how acetazolamide could affect the release of oxygen to respiring tissues.
parts.answer: Fewer H⁺ ions are produced inside the red blood cell; fewer H⁺ combine with haemoglobin to form haemoglobinic acid; the Bohr shift is smaller, so less oxygen is unloaded at a given pO₂.
parts.working: 1 mark each: fewer H⁺; less haemoglobinic acid / less change in haemoglobin shape; smaller Bohr effect so less O₂ released.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why carbon dioxide is still removed from the tissues even when carbonic anhydrase is fully inhibited.
parts.answer: Some CO₂ dissolves in the plasma; some combines with haemoglobin as carbaminohaemoglobin; the uncatalysed reaction with water still happens slowly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: dissolved in plasma; carbaminohaemoglobin; slow uncatalysed formation of carbonic acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which valves are closed during ventricular systole, while blood is being pumped into the arteries?
A atrioventricular valves only
B semilunar valves only
C both atrioventricular and semilunar valves
D neither atrioventricular nor semilunar valves
parts.answer: A atrioventricular valves only
parts.working: A: when ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure the atrioventricular (tricuspid and bicuspid) valves close; when it exceeds arterial pressure the semilunar valves open so blood leaves. C is true only during the brief isovolumetric phase before ejection.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where the sinoatrial node (SAN) is found.
parts.answer: In the wall of the right atrium.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the heartbeat is initiated and coordinated after the SAN produces a wave of excitation.
parts.answer: Excitation spreads across both atria, which contract (atrial systole); a band of non-conducting tissue stops it spreading directly to the ventricles; the atrioventricular node (AVN) delays the impulse (about 0.1 s); excitation passes down the bundle of His / Purkyne tissue in the septum to the apex; the ventricles contract from the apex upwards.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: spreads over atrial walls → atria contract; non-conducting (fibrous) tissue between atria and ventricles; AVN; delay at AVN; Purkyne tissue / bundle of His down septum; to the apex, so the ventricles contract from the apex upwards.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why there is a delay at the AVN.
parts.answer: So the atria finish contracting and emptying blood into the ventricles before the ventricles contract.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the blood vessel that carries blood from the right ventricle and the vessel that brings blood into the right atrium from the body.
parts.answer: Pulmonary artery; vena cava (superior / inferior).
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of the tendons (chordae tendineae) attached to the atrioventricular valves.
parts.answer: They stop the valves turning inside out (being pushed into the atria) when the ventricles contract, preventing backflow of blood.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Mammals have a closed double circulation. Explain what is meant by a double circulation and why it is an advantage.
parts.answer: Blood passes through the heart twice in each complete circuit of the body – the pulmonary circuit (heart → lungs → heart) and the systemic circuit (heart → body → heart); blood returning from the lungs is pumped again, so it can be sent to the body at high pressure; low pressure to the lungs avoids damage, and oxygen is delivered quickly to tissues with high metabolic rates.
parts.working: B1 passes through heart twice per circuit / pulmonary and systemic circuits. B1 blood repressurised after lungs / high pressure to body. B1 lower pressure to lungs / rapid delivery of oxygen to supply high metabolic rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cardiac muscle is described as myogenic. State what this means.
parts.answer: It contracts without needing impulses from nerves; the heartbeat starts within the muscle itself (at the SAN).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by systole and by diastole.
parts.answer: Systole: contraction of the heart muscle (of atria or ventricles). Diastole: relaxation of the heart muscle, when the chambers fill.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: During atrial systole, state which valves are open and which are closed.
parts.answer: Atrioventricular (tricuspid and bicuspid) valves open; semilunar valves closed.
parts.working: B1 AV open; B1 semilunar closed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A red blood cell enters the right atrium from the vena cava. List, in order, the chambers, valves and blood vessels it passes through until it leaves the heart in the aorta.
parts.answer: Right atrium → tricuspid (right atrioventricular) valve → right ventricle → pulmonary semilunar valve → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → bicuspid (mitral, left atrioventricular) valve → left ventricle → aortic semilunar valve → aorta.
parts.working: B1 right side chambers + tricuspid in order; B1 pulmonary valve and pulmonary artery; B1 lungs, pulmonary vein, left atrium; B1 bicuspid, left ventricle, aortic valve.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the blood vessel that carries oxygenated blood into the heart.
parts.answer: Pulmonary vein

parts.label: a
parts.text: The chambers of the heart are full of blood. Explain why the heart muscle still needs its own blood supply from the coronary arteries.
parts.answer: The walls (especially the ventricle wall) are too thick for oxygen to diffuse in from the blood in the chambers fast enough; cardiac muscle contracts continuously and needs a constant supply of oxygen and glucose for aerobic respiration.
parts.working: B1 wall too thick / diffusion distance too long; B1 high demand for O₂ / glucose for respiration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest what happens to the heart muscle if a branch of a coronary artery becomes completely blocked.
parts.answer: The muscle supplied by that branch gets no oxygen, cannot respire aerobically, stops contracting and may die (a heart attack).
parts.working: B1 no O₂ to that part; B1 cells die / cannot contract.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Between which two times does the bicuspid (left atrioventricular) valve close? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Between 0.1 s and 0.2 s; ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure (1.0 → 8.0 kPa while atrial pressure is 0.6 kPa).
parts.working: B1 0.1–0.2 s. B1 ventricular pressure becomes higher than atrial pressure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Between which two times does the aortic semilunar valve open, and between which two times does it close?
parts.answer: Opens between 0.2 s and 0.3 s; closes between 0.4 s and 0.5 s.
parts.working: B1 opens 0.2–0.3 s (ventricle > aorta). B1 closes 0.4–0.5 s (aorta > ventricle).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The cycle shown lasts 0.8 s. Calculate the heart rate in beats per minute.
parts.answer: 75 beats per minute

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the aortic pressure does not fall to near zero between 0.5 s and 0.8 s.
parts.answer: The elastic tissue in the aorta wall is stretched during systole; it recoils during diastole, pushing blood onward and maintaining pressure (and the closed semilunar valve stops backflow).
parts.working: B1 elastic fibres stretched during ejection. B1 recoil maintains pressure / smooth flow (semilunar valve prevents backflow).

practice.stem: Hamza, a student, has a resting stroke volume of 70 cm³ and a cardiac cycle lasting 0.8 s. Bilal, a long-distance runner from Abbottabad, has a resting stroke volume of 95 cm³ and a resting heart rate of 52 beats per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cardiac output of each person in dm³ per minute.
parts.answer: Hamza: 5.25 dm³ min⁻¹; Bilal: 4.94 dm³ min⁻¹
parts.working: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate. B1 Hamza: heart rate = 60 ÷ 0.8 = 75; 70 × 75 = 5250 cm³ = 5.25 dm³. B1 Bilal: 95 × 52 = 4940 cm³ = 4.94 dm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how training has led to Bilal's larger stroke volume and explain how this allows a lower resting heart rate.
parts.answer: Training increases the size/thickness of cardiac muscle in the ventricle walls (and chamber volume); so more blood is ejected per beat; the same cardiac output needed at rest can be supplied with fewer beats per minute.
parts.working: B1 larger / stronger ventricular muscle. B1 more blood per contraction. B1 similar output needed at rest so fewer beats needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Purkyne tissue carries the wave of excitation down the septum to the apex of the ventricles before it spreads up the ventricle walls. Why is this an advantage?
A The atria and ventricles contract at the same time.
B The ventricles contract from the base upwards, pushing blood back into the atria.
C The ventricles contract from the apex upwards, pushing blood towards the arteries.
D The semilunar valves open before the ventricles contract.
parts.answer: C The ventricles contract from the apex upwards, pushing blood towards the arteries.
parts.working: Contraction starting at the apex squeezes blood upwards towards the aorta and pulmonary artery, emptying the ventricles fully. A is wrong: the AVN delay ensures the atria contract first.

practice.stem: The maximum pressure measured in the left ventricle of a healthy adult was 16.0 kPa. The maximum pressure in the right ventricle was 3.5 kPa.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the maximum pressure in the left ventricle is than in the right ventricle. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 4.6 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the right ventricle produces a much lower pressure than the left ventricle.
parts.answer: The right ventricle pumps blood only to the lungs, which are close to the heart; a lower pressure avoids damage to the thin-walled lung capillaries and avoids forming too much tissue fluid in the lungs; the left ventricle must pump blood through the whole body against much greater resistance.
parts.working: 1 mark each: right pumps to lungs only / short distance; high pressure would damage lung capillaries / cause fluid in alveoli; left pumps to whole body / more resistance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why both ventricles must pump the same volume of blood in each beat.
parts.answer: The two sides are in series in a double circulation; all blood from the lungs returns to the left side, so if volumes differed blood would build up in one circuit.
parts.working: B1 same blood passes through both circuits in turn; B1 otherwise blood accumulates in lungs or body.

practice.stem: An ultrasound scan of a patient in Islamabad measured the volume of blood in the left ventricle. At the end of diastole it was 128 cm³ and at the end of systole it was 52 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the stroke volume.
parts.answer: 76 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: The ejection fraction is the percentage of the end-diastolic volume that is pumped out in one beat. Calculate the ejection fraction to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The heart rate is 70 beats per minute. Calculate the cardiac output in dm³ per minute.
parts.answer: 5.32 dm³ min⁻¹

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the position of the bicuspid valve and of the aortic semilunar valve while the ventricle volume falls from 128 cm³ to 52 cm³, and explain why.
parts.answer: Bicuspid valve closed because ventricular pressure is higher than atrial pressure; aortic valve open because ventricular pressure is higher than aortic pressure.
parts.working: B1 bicuspid closed + reason; B1 aortic open + reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the wall of the left ventricle is thicker than the wall of the right ventricle.
parts.answer: The left ventricle pumps blood around the whole body (systemic circulation), which needs a much higher pressure to overcome resistance; the right ventricle pumps only to the nearby lungs and a high pressure would damage the lung capillaries.
parts.working: B1 left ventricle produces higher pressure for systemic circulation / long distance / more resistance. B1 right only to lungs, lower pressure needed / avoids damaging capillaries / tissue fluid build-up in lungs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the atrial walls are much thinner than the ventricle walls.
parts.answer: Atria only pump blood a short distance into the ventricles, at low pressure.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: A baby is born with a hole in the septum between the two ventricles. Suggest and explain the effect on the oxygen supplied to the baby's tissues.
parts.answer: The pressure is higher in the left ventricle, so during systole some oxygenated blood is pushed through the hole into the right ventricle and is pumped back to the lungs instead of to the body; less blood (and so less oxygen) leaves in the aorta per beat; the heart must beat faster / work harder to supply enough oxygen, and pressure in the pulmonary circulation rises. (If the hole is large, or blood flows right → left, deoxygenated blood mixes into the aorta and the oxygen concentration of systemic blood falls.)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: blood flows left → right because pressure is higher in the left ventricle; oxygenated blood returns to the lungs / mixes with blood in the right ventricle; smaller volume of oxygenated blood leaves in the aorta / less oxygen delivered to tissues per beat; heart works harder / faster rate / tiredness or breathlessness; raised pressure in pulmonary circulation; (if right → left flow) deoxygenated blood enters the aorta, lowering its oxygen concentration.

practice.stem:
A cricketer's heart rate rises from 72 beats per minute at rest to 160 beats per minute while bowling.
At rest: atrial systole lasts 0.10 s and ventricular systole 0.30 s.
At 160 beats per minute: atrial systole lasts 0.07 s and ventricular systole 0.22 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the length of diastole (the time when both atria and ventricles are relaxed) at rest and during exercise. Give your answers in seconds to 3 decimal places.
parts.answer: At rest 0.433 s; during exercise 0.085 s

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in the length of diastole.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why stroke volume may fall if the heart rate becomes very high, and why the heart muscle itself may then receive less oxygen.
parts.answer: Ventricles fill during diastole, so a very short diastole means less time to fill and a smaller volume pumped per beat; the coronary arteries supplying the ventricle muscle are squeezed during systole, so most coronary flow happens in diastole and shorter diastole reduces it.
parts.working: 1 mark each: less filling time; smaller end-diastolic volume so lower stroke volume; coronary flow mostly during diastole / vessels compressed in systole.

practice.stem: In a patient with complete heart block, the atrioventricular node (AVN) no longer conducts. The atria contract 75 times per minute but the ventricles contract only 35 times per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the atria and the ventricles beat at different rates.
parts.answer: The SAN still sets the rate of the atria; the wave of excitation cannot pass through the AVN and Purkyne tissue to the ventricles, so the ventricles contract with their own slower myogenic rhythm.
parts.working: B1 SAN still excites atria; B1 excitation not passed via AVN, ventricles beat at own (slower) myogenic rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest the effect on the patient's cardiac output and one symptom this could cause.
parts.answer: Cardiac output falls (fewer ventricular beats per minute); less oxygen reaches the brain and muscles, causing dizziness, fainting or tiredness.
parts.working: B1 lower cardiac output; B1 suitable symptom linked to less O₂ supply.

parts.label: c
parts.text: An artificial pacemaker is fitted. Its electrode stimulates the ventricle wall near the apex 70 times per minute. Suggest why the electrode is placed near the apex.
parts.answer: Excitation then spreads up from the apex, as it would from Purkyne tissue, so the ventricles contract from the bottom upwards and push blood up into the arteries.
parts.working: B1 imitates Purkyne tissue / spread from apex; B1 ventricles contract upwards, emptying into arteries.

practice.stem: In mitral valve disease, the bicuspid (left atrioventricular) valve no longer closes completely.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State when the bicuspid valve should be closed during the cardiac cycle and explain why.
parts.answer: During ventricular systole; pressure in the left ventricle is higher than in the left atrium, and the closed valve stops blood flowing back into the atrium.
parts.working: B1 ventricular systole; B1 prevents backflow into atrium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest and explain the effects of the leaking valve on the pressure in the left atrium and on the volume of blood entering the aorta in each beat.
parts.answer: Some blood is forced back into the left atrium during ventricular systole, so left atrial pressure rises; less of the ventricle's blood leaves through the aortic valve, so the volume entering the aorta per beat falls.
parts.working: 1 mark each: backflow into atrium in ventricular systole; atrial pressure higher; less blood into aorta / lower stroke volume to body.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Patients with this condition often become breathless. Suggest why.
parts.answer: High pressure in the left atrium is passed back to the pulmonary veins and lung capillaries; more tissue fluid forms in the lungs, which increases the diffusion distance for gas exchange.
parts.working: B1 raised pressure in pulmonary veins / lung capillaries; B1 fluid in lungs / less efficient gas exchange.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature of the wall of an artery allows it to stretch when blood enters and then recoil to keep blood flowing smoothly?
A a layer of squamous endothelium
B a thick layer containing elastic fibres
C semilunar valves along its length
D an outer layer of collagen fibres only
parts.answer: B a thick layer containing elastic fibres
parts.working: B: elastic fibres in the tunica media stretch as each pulse of blood enters and recoil between beats, evening out pressure. Valves are found in veins, not arteries. Collagen gives strength to resist bursting but does not provide recoil.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two differences between the structure of an artery and the structure of a vein.
parts.answer: Artery has a thicker wall (more smooth muscle and elastic fibres); artery has a narrower lumen relative to its wall; veins have valves (arteries do not, except at the base of the aorta and pulmonary artery); artery endothelium is folded.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two comparative differences.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the structure of a capillary is related to its function.
parts.answer: Wall is one cell thick (endothelium only), giving a short diffusion distance; pores / gaps between endothelial cells allow plasma (and white cells) to leave and form tissue fluid; very narrow lumen (about 7 µm) slows red blood cells and brings them close to the wall; large numbers give a large surface area for exchange.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three structure–function points.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why veins have valves.
parts.answer: Blood pressure in veins is low, so valves prevent blood flowing backwards (and help return blood to the heart when muscles squeeze the veins).
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which blood vessel carries deoxygenated blood away from the heart?
A aorta
B pulmonary artery
C pulmonary vein
D vena cava
parts.answer: B pulmonary artery
parts.working: The pulmonary artery takes deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. D is wrong: the vena cava carries deoxygenated blood towards the heart.

practice.stem:
Descriptions of three blood vessels seen in a section of tissue:
W – wall one cell thick, made of endothelium only; diameter about 8 µm.
X – narrow lumen; wall mostly smooth muscle with a few elastic fibres; diameter about 0.1 mm.
Y – thin wall with little muscle; wide lumen; valves present.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify vessels W, X and Y.
parts.answer: W capillary; X arteriole; Y vein
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the role of the smooth muscle in the wall of vessel X.
parts.answer: When it contracts the lumen narrows (vasoconstriction), reducing blood flow to the capillaries it supplies; when it relaxes the lumen widens and flow increases.
parts.working: B1 contracts → narrows lumen; B1 controls/reduces flow to capillary bed (or reverse for relaxation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: All blood vessels are lined with endothelium. Describe this tissue and suggest why its smooth surface is important.
parts.answer: A single layer of thin, flat (squamous) cells; a smooth lining reduces friction / resistance to blood flow.
parts.working: B1 description; B1 reduces friction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of each of these vessels: aorta, pulmonary vein, vena cava.
parts.answer: Aorta: carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the body. Pulmonary vein: carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. Vena cava: carries deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium.
parts.working: B1 each.

practice.stem:
A student examined three blood vessels in a thin slice of sheep tissue from a butcher in Rawalpindi.
Vessel P: wall thickness 1.2 mm, lumen diameter 4.0 mm, wall contains many elastic fibres.
Vessel Q: wall thickness 0.4 mm, lumen diameter 6.0 mm, flaps of tissue seen inside.
Vessel R: seen only with the microscope; wall one cell thick, lumen just wide enough for one red blood cell.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter for vessel P and for vessel Q. Give each answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify vessels P and Q and give a reason for each.
parts.answer: P is an artery – thick wall relative to lumen, with much elastic tissue; Q is a vein – thin wall, wide lumen, with valves.
parts.working: B1 P artery with reason. B1 Q vein with reason.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why vessel R cannot be measured with a ruler and identify it.
parts.answer: R is a capillary; its diameter (about 8 µm) is too small to measure with a ruler – it needs a microscope with an eyepiece graticule.
parts.working: B1 capillary. B1 microscopic size / needs graticule / microscope.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how arterioles can change the amount of blood flowing to a particular organ.
parts.answer: Arterioles have smooth muscle in their walls; contraction narrows the lumen (vasoconstriction), reducing flow to the organ; relaxation widens it (vasodilation), increasing flow.
parts.working: B1 smooth muscle in wall. B1 contraction narrows / relaxation widens lumen, changing flow.

parts.label: b
parts.text: During a cricket match, blood flow to leg muscles increases but blood flow to the gut decreases. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Leg muscles respire faster and need more oxygen and glucose (and removal of CO₂/heat), so their arterioles dilate; digestion is less urgent, so gut arterioles constrict and blood is redirected.
parts.working: B1 muscles need more O₂ / glucose / remove CO₂. B1 blood redistributed / limited cardiac output shared.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why large arteries contain a lot of collagen in their outer layer.
parts.answer: Collagen is strong and resists the high pressure, so the artery does not burst / overstretch.
parts.working: B1

practice.stem:
Mean blood pressure along the systemic circulation:
aorta 12.5 kPa; large arteries 12.0 kPa; small arteries 10.5 kPa; start of arterioles 9.5 kPa; start of capillaries 4.0 kPa; end of capillaries 2.0 kPa; venules 1.5 kPa; vena cava 0.4 kPa

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in mean blood pressure as blood passes through the arterioles.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the greatest fall in pressure occurs in the arterioles.
parts.answer: Arterioles have narrow lumens and muscular walls, giving high resistance (friction) to blood flow; their smooth muscle can constrict them further.
parts.working: B1 narrow lumen / high resistance; B1 friction with walls / constriction by smooth muscle.

parts.label: c
parts.text: In the aorta the pressure rises and falls between 10.7 kPa and 16.0 kPa with every heartbeat, but in the capillaries it is steady. Explain why.
parts.answer: Pressure in the aorta rises when the left ventricle contracts and falls in diastole; elastic fibres in artery walls stretch during systole and recoil during diastole, smoothing the flow; by the time blood reaches the capillaries, friction and the elastic recoil have evened out the pulses.
parts.working: 1 mark each: rise and fall linked to ventricular systole/diastole; elastic stretch and recoil smooths pressure; pulses damped / lost by friction in many small vessels.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how blood returns to the heart from the legs when a person walks.
parts.answer: Pressure in veins is low; contracting leg (skeletal) muscles squeeze the veins and push blood along; valves in the veins close to prevent backflow, so blood can only move towards the heart.
parts.working: 1 mark each: low pressure in veins; skeletal muscle squeezes veins; valves prevent backflow.

parts.label: b
parts.text: During a long flag ceremony at the Wagah border, a guard standing very still faints. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Without leg muscle contraction blood pools in the leg veins; less blood returns to the heart, so cardiac output falls and the brain receives too little blood / oxygen.
parts.working: B1 blood pools / less venous return; B1 less blood / O₂ to brain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a photomicrograph at a magnification of ×1200, the lumen of a capillary measures 9.0 mm across. Calculate the actual diameter of the lumen in µm.
parts.answer: 7.5 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Red blood cells have a diameter of about 7 µm. Suggest two consequences of this for gas exchange in the capillary.
parts.answer: Red blood cells pass in single file and touch / are close to the capillary wall, so the diffusion distance is short; they move slowly, giving more time for exchange.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: single file; close to wall / short diffusion path; slow flow / more time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why capillary walls have no smooth muscle or elastic fibres.
parts.answer: Blood pressure in capillaries is low and steady, so no need to withstand or smooth pressure; a wall of endothelium only keeps the diffusion distance short.
parts.working: B1 low / steady pressure; B1 thin wall for exchange.

practice.stem: A fish has a single circulation: the heart pumps blood to the gills, and from the gills blood flows straight on to the rest of the body.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the difference between a single circulation and a double circulation.
parts.answer: In a single circulation blood passes through the heart once in each complete circuit of the body; in a double circulation it passes through the heart twice, once for the lungs (pulmonary) and once for the body (systemic).
parts.working: B1 once per circuit; B1 twice – pulmonary and systemic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why blood reaches the body capillaries of a fish at low pressure.
parts.answer: Blood is pumped first through the gill capillaries; much pressure is lost by friction in these narrow vessels before it flows on to the body without returning to the heart.
parts.working: B1 passes through gill capillaries first; B1 pressure lost there / not re-pumped.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one advantage to a mammal of the blood returning to the heart after passing through the lungs.
parts.answer: The heart can raise the pressure again, so oxygenated blood reaches the tissues quickly at high pressure; this supports the high metabolic rate of an endotherm.
parts.working: B1 pressure raised again / faster delivery; B1 linked to high metabolic rate / maintaining body temperature.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the changes in blood pressure as blood flows from the aorta to the vena cava.
parts.answer: Pressure is highest and fluctuates (pulses) in the aorta and large arteries; it falls through the arterioles (largest fall) and the fluctuations disappear; it continues to fall through capillaries and venules, and is lowest (near zero) in the vena cava.
parts.working: B1 high and fluctuating in arteries. B1 large drop in arterioles, continues falling to lowest in veins / fluctuations lost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The speed of blood flow is lowest in the capillaries, although each capillary is very narrow. Explain why, and why this is an advantage.
parts.answer: There are so many capillaries that their total cross-sectional area is much larger than that of the arteries; the same volume per second flows through a larger total area, so speed falls; slow flow gives more time for exchange of substances (oxygen, glucose, CO₂) with tissues.
parts.working: B1 very large total cross-sectional area. B1 same volume flow spread over larger area → lower velocity. B1 more time for exchange / diffusion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the speed of blood increases again in the veins.
parts.answer: Capillaries join into fewer, larger vessels, so the total cross-sectional area decreases.
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: The cardiac output of a resting woman is 5.4 dm³ min⁻¹. The cross-sectional area of her aorta is 4.5 cm². The total cross-sectional area of all her capillaries is 3000 cm².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the flow rate of blood leaving the heart is 90 cm³ s⁻¹.
parts.answer: 5.4 dm³ min⁻¹ = 5400 cm³ ÷ 60 s = 90 cm³ s⁻¹
parts.working: B1 correct conversion shown.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Mean velocity = flow rate ÷ total cross-sectional area. Calculate the mean velocity of blood in the aorta and in the capillaries. Give both answers in mm s⁻¹.
parts.answer: Aorta 200 mm s⁻¹; capillaries 0.30 mm s⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: A capillary is 0.6 mm long. Calculate the time a red blood cell takes to pass through it.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the slow flow in capillaries is an advantage.
parts.answer: More time for exchange of oxygen, glucose and carbon dioxide by diffusion between blood and tissue fluid, so exchange is more complete.
parts.working: B1 more time; B1 for diffusion / exchange of named substances.

practice.stem: With age, the walls of the aorta and large arteries gain collagen and lose elastic fibres, so they become stiffer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest the effect on systolic (maximum) blood pressure in the aorta. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Systolic pressure rises, because the stiff wall cannot stretch to absorb the surge of blood from the left ventricle.
parts.working: B1 higher; B1 less stretching of the wall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest the effect on diastolic (minimum) blood pressure. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Diastolic pressure falls, because less elastic recoil occurs between beats to keep pushing blood forward and maintain pressure.
parts.working: B1 lower; B1 less recoil.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the left ventricle wall of such a person may become thicker over many years.
parts.answer: The ventricle has to contract more strongly to pump blood into the stiff, high-pressure arteries; the extra work makes the muscle enlarge.
parts.working: B1 works harder against higher pressure / resistance; B1 muscle grows.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A giraffe's head can be 2 m above its heart. Suggest why the left ventricle of a giraffe produces a much higher pressure than a human left ventricle.
parts.answer: Blood must be pushed up about 2 m against gravity to reach the brain; a higher pressure is needed to maintain flow to the brain.
parts.working: B1 against gravity / height to brain; B1 to keep enough blood flow to the brain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The arteries in a giraffe's lower legs have very thick muscular walls and narrow lumens. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Gravity adds to the pressure in the legs, so the arteries there carry blood at very high pressure; thick walls resist bursting and narrow lumens reduce the flow and pressure reaching the leg capillaries.
parts.working: B1 very high pressure in legs; B1 thick wall withstands it / narrow lumen limits flow to capillaries.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The skin on a giraffe's legs is thick and tight. Suggest how this helps to prevent fluid building up in the leg tissues.
parts.answer: Tight skin raises the pressure of the tissue fluid, which opposes the high hydrostatic pressure forcing fluid out of the capillaries, so less tissue fluid forms.
parts.working: B1 raises tissue fluid pressure; B1 reduces net outward filtration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two components of blood that are absent, or almost absent, from tissue fluid.
parts.answer: Large plasma proteins (e.g. albumin, fibrinogen); (red blood cells and platelets are also absent from tissue fluid).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: plasma proteins / albumin; fibrinogen / clotting proteins; red cells; platelets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why these components stay in the blood.
parts.answer: They are too large to pass through the small gaps between the endothelial cells of the capillary wall; so they are not forced out with water and small solutes.
parts.working: B1 too large; B1 gaps / pores in capillary wall.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by tissue fluid.
parts.answer: The fluid that surrounds and bathes the cells of a tissue, formed from plasma that has left the capillaries.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the role of tissue fluid in supplying glucose to a muscle cell.
parts.answer: Glucose leaves the blood in the fluid forced out of the capillary; it then diffuses (or moves by facilitated diffusion) from the tissue fluid into the muscle cell down a concentration gradient.
parts.working: B1 glucose carried out of capillary into tissue fluid; B1 then enters cell from tissue fluid by (facilitated) diffusion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Not all tissue fluid returns to the capillaries. Name the fluid formed when the excess enters the lymphatic vessels, and state where it eventually goes.
parts.answer: Lymph; it is returned to the blood in veins near the heart (the subclavian veins in the chest).
parts.working: B1 lymph; B1 returns to blood / veins.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how carbon dioxide produced by a respiring liver cell reaches the blood.
parts.answer: CO₂ diffuses out of the liver cell into the tissue fluid; it then diffuses through the thin capillary wall into the plasma; both steps are down a concentration gradient, kept steep because the blood flow carries CO₂ away.
parts.working: 1 mark each: diffuses from cell into tissue fluid; diffuses through capillary wall into blood; down a concentration gradient maintained by blood flow.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other waste substance that leaves a liver cell in the same way.
parts.answer: Urea
parts.working: B1 urea (do not accept water).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Red blood cells are not found in tissue fluid, but some white blood cells are. Explain why.
parts.answer: Red blood cells cannot pass through the capillary wall and stay in the blood; some white cells (e.g. neutrophils) can change shape and squeeze out between the endothelial cells.
parts.working: B1 red cells too large / cannot leave; B1 white cells squeeze between endothelial cells.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why it is an advantage for white blood cells to be able to enter tissue fluid.
parts.answer: They can reach pathogens that have entered the tissues, e.g. through a cut, and destroy them by phagocytosis.
parts.working: B1 reach site of infection in tissues; B1 phagocytosis / destroy pathogens.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how tissue fluid is formed at the arterial end of a capillary.
parts.answer: Hydrostatic (blood) pressure is high at the arterial end; it is greater than the tendency of water to enter by osmosis (plasma has a lower water potential due to proteins); so water and small solutes (glucose, ions, oxygen) are forced out through gaps in the capillary wall; large plasma proteins and red cells stay in the blood.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: high hydrostatic pressure; greater than the opposing water potential / osmotic effect; fluid forced out through gaps / pores in endothelium; small molecules leave (e.g. glucose, amino acids, ions); proteins / red blood cells remain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how much of this fluid returns to the blood at the venous end.
parts.answer: Hydrostatic pressure has fallen at the venous end; the plasma still has a lower water potential than tissue fluid because of the plasma proteins, so water moves back in by osmosis.
parts.working: B1 lower hydrostatic pressure. B1 water re-enters by osmosis down water potential gradient (due to plasma proteins).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what happens to the tissue fluid that does not return to the capillaries.
parts.answer: It drains into lymph capillaries / lymph vessels and is returned to the blood (in veins near the heart).
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: In one capillary, 0.8 mm long, the hydrostatic pressure of the blood falls steadily from 4.2 kPa at the arterial end to 1.5 kPa at the venous end. The plasma proteins draw water into the capillary with an effect equal to 3.3 kPa along the whole length. Ignore the pressures of the tissue fluid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net pressure at the arterial end and at the venous end of the capillary, and state the direction in which fluid moves at each end.
parts.answer: Arterial end 0.9 kPa outwards (fluid leaves the capillary); venous end 1.8 kPa inwards (fluid returns to the capillary).
parts.working: B1 0.9 kPa out; B1 1.8 kPa in.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the distance from the arterial end at which there is no net movement of fluid. Give your answer in mm to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 hydrostatic pressure must fall by 4.2 − 3.3 = 0.9 kPa out of a total fall of 2.7 kPa; A1 0.9 ÷ 2.7 × 0.8 = 0.27 mm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the plasma proteins cause water to move into the capillary.
parts.answer: Plasma proteins stay in the capillary and lower the water potential of the plasma below that of the tissue fluid; water moves into the capillary by osmosis down the water potential gradient.
parts.working: B1 proteins lower water potential of plasma; B1 osmosis into capillary.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A shopkeeper in Saddar stands behind his counter for ten hours. By evening his ankles are swollen. Explain why.
parts.answer: Gravity and pooling of blood raise the hydrostatic pressure in the leg veins and capillaries; more fluid is forced out at the arterial end and less returns at the venous end; tissue fluid builds up faster than the lymph vessels can remove it.
parts.working: 1 mark each: higher hydrostatic pressure in leg capillaries; more filtration / less reabsorption; lymph cannot drain it all.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why walking about at intervals reduces the swelling.
parts.answer: Contracting leg muscles squeeze the veins (and lymph vessels) and, with their valves, push blood and lymph towards the heart; this lowers venous and capillary pressure so less tissue fluid forms and more is drained.
parts.working: B1 muscle pump / valves move blood and lymph; B1 lower capillary pressure / more drainage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When the right ventricle is weak, blood builds up in the venae cavae and the pressure in the systemic veins rises. Explain why tissue fluid then builds up in the legs.
parts.answer: Raised venous pressure is passed back to the venous ends of the capillaries; the hydrostatic pressure there is higher than normal, so it is no longer much lower than the inward (osmotic) effect of the plasma proteins; less tissue fluid returns to the blood, so it accumulates.
parts.working: 1 mark each: higher pressure at venous end of capillaries; less net inward movement / less reabsorption by osmosis; fluid accumulates (oedema).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why weakness of the left ventricle instead causes fluid to collect in the lungs.
parts.answer: Blood backs up in the left atrium and pulmonary veins, raising pressure in the lung capillaries; more fluid is forced out into the lung tissue and alveoli.
parts.working: B1 pressure rises in pulmonary veins / lung capillaries; B1 more tissue fluid in lungs.

practice.stem: In an adult, about 20 dm³ of fluid leaves the blood capillaries each day and about 17 dm³ of it is reabsorbed into the capillaries.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the fluid leaving the capillaries that is returned to the blood by the lymphatic system.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of lymph flow in cm³ per hour.
parts.answer: 125 cm³ per hour

parts.label: c
parts.text: Lymphatic filariasis is a disease, spread by mosquitoes, in which parasitic worms block lymph vessels. Explain why an affected leg can swell enormously.
parts.answer: The excess tissue fluid that should drain into the lymph vessels cannot leave the tissue; it accumulates every day, so the leg swells (lymphoedema).
parts.working: B1 lymph cannot drain / excess fluid not removed; B1 accumulates continuously.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why lymph vessels contain valves.
parts.answer: Lymph is at very low pressure, so valves stop it flowing backwards and keep it moving towards the heart.

parts.label: a
parts.text: During exercise, the volume of tissue fluid in working muscles increases. Explain why.
parts.answer: Arterioles to the muscle dilate, so more blood enters the capillaries at higher hydrostatic pressure, forcing out more fluid; respiration produces solutes (e.g. lactate, ions) that lower the water potential of the tissue fluid; so less water returns to the capillaries.
parts.working: 1 mark each: arteriole dilation; higher hydrostatic pressure → more filtration; solutes from respiration lower water potential of tissue fluid / less reabsorption.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how increased lymph flow during exercise helps the muscle.
parts.answer: It removes the extra tissue fluid (and any leaked protein), so the fluid does not accumulate and the diffusion distance between capillaries and muscle cells stays short.
parts.working: B1 removes excess fluid; B1 keeps diffusion distance short / prevents swelling.

practice.stem: Some children in areas affected by famine have diets very low in protein. Their blood plasma contains less protein than normal, and their legs and abdomen become swollen with fluid (oedema).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a low concentration of protein in blood plasma causes tissue fluid to build up.
parts.answer: With less protein, the water potential of the plasma is higher (less negative); the water potential gradient from tissue fluid to plasma at the venous end is smaller; so less water returns to the capillaries by osmosis, and more fluid stays in the tissues than the lymph can remove.
parts.working: B1 plasma water potential higher / less negative. B1 less water re-enters by osmosis at venous end. B1 more tissue fluid remains / lymph system cannot drain it all.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why people with very high blood pressure can also develop swelling of the ankles.
parts.answer: Higher hydrostatic pressure in capillaries forces more fluid out (and less returns at the venous end); in the legs gravity also raises pressure in the veins/capillaries, so fluid accumulates in the ankles.
parts.working: B1 more fluid forced out by higher hydrostatic pressure. B1 less reabsorbed / gravity effect in legs.

practice.stem: Albumin is the main plasma protein and is made in the liver. A patient with severe liver disease has a plasma albumin concentration of 24 g dm⁻³; the normal value is 42 g dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in the patient's plasma albumin concentration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the low albumin concentration leads to fluid building up in the tissues.
parts.answer: Less protein in the plasma means its water potential is less negative / higher; the water potential gradient from tissue fluid into the capillary at the venous end is smaller; less water returns by osmosis, so tissue fluid accumulates (oedema).
parts.working: 1 mark each: plasma water potential higher; smaller gradient / less osmosis back into capillary; tissue fluid accumulates.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A doctor gives an infusion of albumin into a vein. Suggest why this can reduce the swelling for a short time.
parts.answer: The plasma water potential falls again, so more water is drawn back from the tissue fluid into the capillaries by osmosis; it is temporary because the liver still cannot make enough albumin.
parts.working: B1 lowers plasma water potential so more water returns; B1 temporary because cause (liver damage) remains / albumin is broken down.

practice.stem: When a wasp stings a child in Swat, cells in the skin release histamine. Histamine makes the arterioles in the area dilate and makes the walls of the capillaries more permeable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the release of histamine leads to swelling of the skin around the sting.
parts.answer: Capillary walls become more permeable, so plasma proteins leak out into the tissue fluid; the water potential of the tissue fluid falls / the difference in water potential between plasma and tissue fluid is reduced; less water returns to the capillaries by osmosis at the venous end; also dilated arterioles raise capillary hydrostatic pressure so more fluid is forced out; tissue fluid accumulates.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: more permeable capillaries; proteins enter tissue fluid; water potential gradient reduced; less reabsorption by osmosis; higher hydrostatic pressure from dilation; fluid accumulates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why holding a cold pack on the sting reduces the swelling.
parts.answer: Cold causes the arterioles supplying the area to constrict; less blood flows into the capillaries, so their hydrostatic pressure falls and less fluid is forced out.
parts.working: B1 vasoconstriction / less blood flow; B1 lower hydrostatic pressure, less tissue fluid formed.

practice.stem: After a road accident in Faisalabad, a man loses about 1 dm³ of blood and his arterial blood pressure falls.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest the effect of the blood loss on the hydrostatic pressure in the capillaries, and how this helps to restore the blood volume.
parts.answer: Blood pressure falls, so capillary hydrostatic pressure is lower; less fluid is forced out at the arterial end; the inward osmotic movement due to plasma proteins is now greater, so more tissue fluid moves into the capillaries and adds to blood volume.
parts.working: 1 mark each: lower capillary hydrostatic pressure; less filtration out; more water moves in by osmosis, increasing blood volume.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the concentration of plasma proteins in the patient's blood falls over the next few hours.
parts.answer: Water drawn in from the tissue fluid contains almost no protein, so it dilutes the plasma proteins that remain; the lost proteins take time to be replaced.
parts.working: B1 protein-free fluid dilutes plasma; B1 lost proteins not yet replaced.

practice.stem: In the brain, the endothelial cells of capillaries are joined by tight junctions, with no gaps between them. In the liver, the capillaries (sinusoids) have large gaps between the endothelial cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest how the tissue fluid around liver cells differs in composition from the tissue fluid around brain cells.
parts.answer: Tissue fluid in the liver contains much more plasma protein (and other large molecules) because they pass through the large gaps; tissue fluid in the brain contains very little protein.
parts.working: B1 more protein / large molecules in liver tissue fluid; B1 linked to gaps vs tight junctions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of each type of capillary for the organ it supplies.
parts.answer: Liver: liver cells can take up and release large molecules such as plasma proteins (e.g. albumin they make) and absorbed food molecules quickly. Brain: harmful substances, toxins and many pathogens in the blood are kept away from the neurones.
parts.working: B1 liver advantage; B1 brain advantage.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a drug made of large protein molecules may be very effective against a liver infection but have little effect on an infection in the brain.
parts.answer: The drug can pass through the gaps in liver capillaries into the tissue fluid, but it cannot cross the tight junctions of brain capillaries, so it does not reach the infected brain tissue.
parts.working: B1 reaches liver tissue; B1 cannot leave brain capillaries.

practice.stem: A student in Gujranwala wants to plan an investigation using classmates as volunteers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student could find out whether body position (lying down, sitting, standing) affects resting pulse rate.
parts.answer: Use the same volunteers for all three positions; take pulse at the wrist (or with a pulse monitor) after the person has been in the position for a set time, e.g. 3 min; count for 60 s (or 30 s × 2); keep other factors the same: no exercise or caffeine beforehand, same time of day, same room temperature; repeat each position at least three times / use at least 10 volunteers and calculate means.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: three positions as IV; pulse counted in set time / bpm; set time in position before reading; standardised variables (≥2); repeats / several volunteers + mean; order of positions varied or rest between.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why each person should stay still in the position for a few minutes before the pulse is taken.
parts.answer: So the pulse rate settles at a steady value after the change of position (any short-term change has passed).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the effect of breath-hold time on blood oxygen saturation could be investigated using a pulse oximeter clipped to a finger.
parts.answer: Volunteer sits and breathes normally until the SpO₂ reading is steady and records it; volunteer holds breath for set times, e.g. 10, 20, 30, 40 s (timed with a stopwatch); record the lowest SpO₂ reading during / just after each hold; rest until SpO₂ returns to normal between holds; keep the same finger, hand still and warm; repeat each time three times and calculate means.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: baseline reading; range of hold times; how SpO₂ recorded (lowest / at end); recovery between trials; standardised variables (finger, posture, no movement); repeats + mean.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the volunteer should not take deep breaths just before holding the breath.
parts.answer: Deep breathing (hyperventilation) changes blood CO₂ and oxygen levels before the hold; this would change the starting conditions so readings would not be comparable / it can be unsafe.
parts.working: B1 alters CO₂ / O₂ at start; B1 so not standardised (or safety).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to find out whether the tempo of music affects heart rate in teenagers.
parts.answer: Use the same piece of music played at different tempos (e.g. 60, 90, 120, 150 beats per minute) at the same volume through headphones; volunteer seated and resting for 5 min; measure resting heart rate with a pulse monitor; play each tempo for a set time (e.g. 3 min) and record heart rate at the end; rest with silence between tempos until heart rate returns to resting; same time of day, no caffeine; repeat with many volunteers and calculate means.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: range of tempos (same music); same volume; resting baseline; set listening time; heart rate measurement method; rest between; repeats / many volunteers + mean.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the order in which the tempos are played should be changed for different volunteers.
parts.answer: So that any effect of time / getting bored or relaxed during the session does not always affect the same tempo.

practice.stem: A student needs 20 cm³ of each of five ethanol solutions (0, 2, 4, 6 and 8 %) to study Daphnia heart rate. She has a 10 % ethanol stock solution and pond water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete a dilution table: for each concentration (0, 2, 4, 6 and 8 %), state the volume of 10 % stock and the volume of pond water needed.
parts.working: M1 volume of stock = (required % ÷ 10) × 20; A2 all five correct (A1 for three or four correct).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the apparatus you would use to measure the volumes accurately.
parts.answer: A graduated pipette or syringe (e.g. 10 cm³ or 20 cm³), not a beaker.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why pond water, not distilled water, is used to dilute the stock.
parts.answer: Daphnia live in pond water; distilled water would change the ion concentration / water potential and could itself affect the heart rate or harm the animals.

practice.stem: Students at a school in Peshawar want to find out how the intensity of exercise affects heart rate immediately after exercise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to investigate the effect of exercise intensity on heart rate. Your method should allow reliable results to be collected.
parts.answer: Use step-ups on a bench of fixed height at different rates set by a metronome (e.g. 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 steps per minute) for a fixed time (e.g. 3 min); measure resting pulse first (count at the wrist for 30 s, ×2) and wait until it returns to resting between trials; measure pulse immediately after each bout; use the same person (or a group matched for age, sex, fitness); repeat each intensity three times on different days or after full recovery and calculate means; record results in a table and plot heart rate against step rate.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: at least five intensities set precisely (metronome / treadmill speed); fixed duration of exercise; same step height; resting heart rate measured first; pulse counted for a stated time with a stated method (or pulse meter); measured immediately after exercise; allow return to resting rate between trials; same subject or matched subjects (age / sex / fitness / no caffeine); repeats and means; safety – stop if unwell / subjects in good health.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one ethical consideration when planning this investigation.
parts.answer: Volunteers must give informed consent and may withdraw at any time / people with heart or breathing problems should not take part.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the dependent variable and suggest one variable that cannot easily be controlled.
parts.answer: Dependent: heart rate (beats per minute); uncontrolled: e.g. emotional state / time since last meal / sleep.
parts.working: B1 both.
