parts.text: Predict how the heart rate of Daphnia will change if the temperature of the water is raised from 15 °C to 25 °C.
parts.answer: Heart rate will increase.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Daphnia is an ectotherm, so its body temperature follows the water temperature; molecules have more kinetic energy, so enzyme-controlled reactions (respiration, muscle contraction) are faster.
parts.working: B1 ectotherm / body temp = water temp; B1 more kinetic energy / faster enzyme reactions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict what would happen above about 35 °C and explain.
parts.answer: Heart rate would fall (and the Daphnia may die), because enzymes and other proteins begin to denature.
parts.working: B1 fall; B1 denaturation.

practice.stem: A student collects data on body mass and resting stroke volume for 12 adults.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: There is a positive correlation between body mass and resting stroke volume in adults.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the null hypothesis for Spearman's rank correlation test.
parts.answer: There is no correlation between body mass and resting stroke volume.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a biological reason for the hypothesis.
parts.answer: Larger people have larger hearts with bigger ventricles, so each beat ejects more blood (larger stroke volume).
parts.working: B1 larger heart / ventricle; B1 more blood pumped per beat.

practice.stem: A geneticist suspects that blood group O is more common in one of three cities. She records how many people in a sample from each city have blood group O.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the null hypothesis for a chi-squared test on these data.
parts.answer: There is no difference in the proportion of people with blood group O between the three cities / any difference is due to chance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the null hypothesis is used rather than the researcher's own hypothesis.
parts.answer: Statistical tests calculate the probability that the observed differences arose by chance if there were no real difference; the null hypothesis can then be rejected or accepted at p = 0.05.
parts.working: B1 test measures probability of chance result; B1 reject / accept at 0.05.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how increasing the partial pressure of carbon dioxide will affect the percentage saturation of haemoglobin at pO₂ 3 kPa.
parts.answer: Percentage saturation will decrease.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: CO₂ enters red blood cells and forms carbonic acid (catalysed by carbonic anhydrase), which dissociates into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻; H⁺ binds to haemoglobin, forming haemoglobinic acid, which lowers its affinity for oxygen; so more oxygen is released (Bohr shift).
parts.working: 1 mark each: carbonic acid → H⁺; H⁺ binds haemoglobin; lower affinity / curve shifts right.

practice.stem: A student plans to test whether compression socks reduce ankle swelling on long bus journeys from Karachi to Islamabad.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: Wearing compression socks reduces the increase in ankle circumference during long periods of sitting.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the biological basis for your hypothesis.
parts.answer: Sitting still raises hydrostatic pressure in the leg capillaries and veins, so more tissue fluid forms; compression socks increase the pressure in the tissue fluid outside the capillaries; so less fluid is forced out and more returns / lymph and venous return are helped.
parts.working: 1 mark each: high hydrostatic pressure when sitting; socks raise external / tissue fluid pressure; less net filtration / more drainage.

practice.stem: A student investigates the effect of caffeine on the heart rate of Daphnia by adding caffeine solution to Daphnia on a cavity slide and counting heartbeats.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a hypothesis, including the biological mechanism, that the student could test.
parts.answer: Increasing the concentration of caffeine increases the heart rate of Daphnia because caffeine stimulates the pacemaker (SAN-like region) to send waves of excitation more often.
parts.working: B1 IV and DV with direction; B1 mechanism.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the result for the control (pond water only) and explain why it is needed.
parts.answer: Heart rate should stay about the same over time; this shows that any increase is due to caffeine, not to handling, light or temperature.
parts.working: B1 no change; B1 reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothesis 1: 'Caffeine changes the heart rate of Daphnia.' Hypothesis 2: 'Caffeine increases the heart rate of Daphnia.' Explain the difference between them.
parts.answer: Hypothesis 1 is non-directional – it predicts a change in either direction; hypothesis 2 is directional – it predicts the direction of the change.
parts.working: B1 non-directional; B1 directional.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a scientist might choose hypothesis 2, and what evidence would be needed to support it.
parts.answer: Previous knowledge (caffeine is a stimulant) suggests an increase; the heart rate at higher caffeine concentrations must be significantly higher than in the control.
parts.working: B1 based on prior knowledge; B1 significant increase compared with control.

practice.stem: A team of climbers from Lahore spends 4 weeks at a base camp at 5,000 m in the Karakoram. Their red blood cell counts are measured every week.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how the red blood cell count of the climbers will change over the 4 weeks.
parts.answer: It will gradually increase.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Lower partial pressure of oxygen at altitude means haemoglobin is less saturated in the lungs, so less oxygen reaches tissues; the kidneys release a hormone that stimulates bone marrow to produce more red blood cells; more haemoglobin increases the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood; this takes days to weeks.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: low pO₂ / less saturation; stimulus to bone marrow (hormone from kidney); more haemoglobin / O₂ capacity; takes time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict what will happen to the count after the climbers return to sea level for several weeks.
parts.answer: It will gradually fall back towards the sea-level value.

practice.stem:
Hypothesis: 'Faster music increases heart rate.' Results (10 volunteers):
Tempo / beats per minute: 60, 90, 120, 150
Mean heart rate / bpm: 72, 72, 75, 77
Standard deviation: 6, 7, 6, 7

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether the results support the hypothesis. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Partly: the means show heart rate higher at 120 and 150 bpm than at 60 bpm, which supports it; but 90 bpm gives the same mean as 60 bpm and the standard deviations (about 6–7) are larger than most differences, so the differences may not be significant; a statistical test is needed.
parts.working: 1 mark each: overall trend supports; 60 = 90 not supported; SDs overlap / need statistical test.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the investigation could be improved to give stronger evidence.
parts.answer: Use more volunteers; randomise the order of tempos; rest between tempos; carry out a statistical test (e.g. t-test between 60 and 150).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how the myoglobin concentration in the swimming muscles of a sperm whale compares with that in the leg muscles of a cow. Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Higher in the whale; it dives for long periods without breathing; myoglobin stores oxygen in muscles and releases it at very low pO₂, allowing aerobic respiration to continue during the dive.
parts.working: B1 higher; B1 long dives; B1 oxygen store released at low pO₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a prediction about the colour of the whale's muscle compared with the cow's, giving a reason.
parts.answer: Darker (almost black-red), because myoglobin is a red pigment and there is much more of it.

practice.stem: During a football match in Lyari, a player's heart rate rises from 70 to 170 beats per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why heart rate increases during exercise.
parts.answer: Muscles respire faster, so they need more oxygen and glucose and produce more carbon dioxide; a higher heart rate increases cardiac output; so blood delivers oxygen and removes CO₂ faster.
parts.working: 1 mark each: more respiration / more O₂ needed; more CO₂ / heat produced; higher cardiac output / faster delivery.

practice.stem: Rings of artery and vein were stretched with the same mass. When the mass was removed, the artery ring recoiled by 94 % but the vein ring by only 52 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the lower elastic recoil of vein walls does not stop blood returning to the heart.
parts.answer: Veins carry blood at low pressure, so their walls do not need to recoil; valves stop blood flowing backwards; contracting skeletal muscles squeeze the veins and push blood towards the heart.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: low pressure, so no need for recoil; valves prevent backflow; skeletal muscle squeezes veins (muscle pump).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this property is important to the artery in the body.
parts.answer: The artery wall stretches when blood is pumped in during systole and recoils in diastole; this smooths the flow and maintains pressure between beats.
parts.working: B1 stretch in systole; B1 recoil maintains pressure / smooth flow.

practice.stem: Climbers resting at Fairy Meadows camp (about 3,300 m) and at 4,500 m on the way to Nanga Parbat had a mean SpO₂ of 90 % and 84 %. At sea level their SpO₂ was 98 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the climbers' blood oxygen saturation is lower at 4,500 m than at sea level.
parts.answer: Atmospheric pressure is lower, so the partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli is lower; haemoglobin loads less oxygen in the lungs.
parts.working: B1 lower pO₂; B1 less loading of haemoglobin.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why their heart rate at rest is higher at altitude.
parts.answer: Each dm³ of blood carries less oxygen, so to deliver the same amount of oxygen to tissues per minute the cardiac output must rise.
parts.working: B1 less O₂ per volume of blood; B1 more blood pumped per minute.

practice.stem: A national hockey player has a resting heart rate of 48 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 110 cm³. An untrained student has a resting heart rate of 75 and a stroke volume of 70 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cardiac output of each person in dm³ min⁻¹ and state what this shows.
parts.answer: Hockey player 5.28 dm³ min⁻¹; student 5.25 dm³ min⁻¹. Their resting cardiac outputs are almost the same, so the larger stroke volume of the athlete is balanced by a lower heart rate.
parts.working: B1 110 × 48 = 5280 cm³ min⁻¹ = 5.28 dm³ min⁻¹ and 70 × 75 = 5250 cm³ min⁻¹ = 5.25 dm³ min⁻¹; B1 similar output reached with fewer beats per minute.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how training increases stroke volume.
parts.answer: The ventricle wall muscle becomes thicker / stronger and the ventricle larger, so it fills with and ejects more blood in each beat.
parts.working: B1 stronger / thicker muscle; B1 larger chamber / more complete emptying.

practice.stem: A student's heart rate was still 110 beats per minute four minutes after a 200 m sprint.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why heart rate and breathing rate remain high for several minutes after exercise has stopped.
parts.answer: During intense exercise some anaerobic respiration produced lactate; extra oxygen is needed after exercise (oxygen debt) to oxidise lactate / convert it back to glucose in the liver; blood must also continue to remove CO₂ and heat, and restore oxygen stores in myoglobin.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: anaerobic respiration / lactate; oxygen debt; lactate removed using O₂; CO₂ / heat removal; restore myoglobin / ATP stores.

practice.stem:
Mean heart rate of Daphnia at different temperatures:
Temperature / °C: 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35
Heart rate / bpm: 110, 160, 215, 280, 300, 210

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the increase in heart rate between 10 °C and 25 °C.
parts.answer: Daphnia is an ectotherm, so the temperature of its tissues rises; enzymes and molecules have more kinetic energy, so respiration and muscle contraction are faster, and the pacemaker fires more often.
parts.working: B1 kinetic energy / more collisions; B1 faster enzyme-controlled reactions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the fall in heart rate at 35 °C.
parts.answer: Above the optimum, enzymes (and other proteins such as membrane channels) start to denature as hydrogen bonds break; fewer active sites function, so reactions slow.
parts.working: B1 denaturation; B1 change in active site / fewer enzyme–substrate complexes.

practice.stem: In a standing adult, mean arterial pressure was about 24 kPa in the feet and about 8 kPa in the head.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the blood pressure in the arteries of the feet is higher than in the arteries of the head when a person is standing.
parts.answer: The weight of the column of blood above the feet adds to the pressure produced by the heart (gravity); the head is above the heart, so blood must be pushed up against gravity and pressure is lower.
parts.working: B1 gravity / weight of blood column adds in feet; B1 against gravity to head.

parts.label: b
parts.text: When the person lies down, the pressures in the head and feet become almost equal. Explain why.
parts.answer: The head, heart and feet are at the same level, so gravity no longer adds or subtracts pressure.

practice.stem: Blood leaving a resting forearm muscle was 70 % saturated with oxygen. Blood leaving the same muscle during hand-grip exercise, at a similar pO₂, was 55 % saturated. The blood from the exercising muscle had a higher carbon dioxide concentration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the percentage saturation of the blood leaving the active muscle was lower than that leaving the resting muscle, although the pO₂ of the two muscles was similar.
parts.answer: Active muscle produces more CO₂ (and heat); CO₂ forms carbonic acid in red blood cells, which releases H⁺; H⁺ binds to haemoglobin and lowers its affinity for oxygen (Bohr effect), so more oxygen is unloaded.
parts.working: 1 mark each: more CO₂ in active muscle; H⁺ from carbonic acid binds haemoglobin; lower affinity / Bohr shift, more O₂ released.

practice.stem: A patient with severe anaemia (haemoglobin 70 g dm⁻³) has a resting heart rate of 98 beats per minute. After three months of iron treatment her haemoglobin is 130 g dm⁻³ and her resting heart rate is 74 beats per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the resting heart rate of the anaemic patient is higher than normal.
parts.answer: Less haemoglobin, so each dm³ of blood carries less oxygen; to supply the tissues with enough oxygen, more blood must be delivered per minute; cardiac output is raised by increasing the heart rate.
parts.working: 1 mark each: less haemoglobin / less O₂ per dm³; tissues need same O₂ supply; higher heart rate increases cardiac output.

practice.stem: A volunteer's capillary refill time was 1.8 s after her hand had been in water at 35 °C and 3.9 s after it had been in water at 10 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the capillary refill time is longer when the hand is cold.
parts.answer: Cold causes the smooth muscle in the walls of the skin arterioles to contract (vasoconstriction); the lumen narrows so less blood flows into the skin capillaries; so the capillaries take longer to fill again after being pressed.
parts.working: 1 mark each: arterioles constrict; less blood flow to capillaries; slower refill.

practice.stem:
Mean red blood cell counts of healthy adults:
Karachi (sea level): 5.0 million per mm³
Villages in Hunza living at about 2,500 m for many years: 5.7 million per mm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference in red blood cell count between the two groups.
parts.answer: The partial pressure of oxygen in the air is lower at high altitude; so haemoglobin is less saturated and less oxygen reaches tissues; over time the body responds by producing more red blood cells in the bone marrow, increasing the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood.
parts.working: B1 lower pO₂ at altitude. B1 less oxygen loaded / tissues receive less. B1 more red blood cells made (more haemoglobin), so more oxygen carried.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a disadvantage of having a very high red blood cell count.
parts.answer: The blood becomes more viscous, so the heart has to work harder / greater risk of blood clots.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: On Earth, gravity keeps more blood and tissue fluid in the legs. Suggest why astronauts' faces become puffy in space while their legs become thinner.
parts.answer: Without gravity, blood and fluid are no longer pulled down into the legs, so more is redistributed to the upper body and head; hydrostatic pressure in the head and face capillaries rises; more tissue fluid forms there, while less forms in the legs.
parts.working: 1 mark each: no gravitational pooling in legs; fluid shifts to head / upper body; higher capillary hydrostatic pressure in face → more tissue fluid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why astronauts may feel faint when they first stand up after returning to Earth.
parts.answer: Blood volume / leg vessel tone has adapted to weightlessness; on standing, blood pools in the legs, venous return and cardiac output fall, so less blood reaches the brain.
parts.working: B1 pooling in legs / less venous return; B1 less blood to brain.

practice.stem: Pakistani middle-distance runners trained for 3 weeks at a high-altitude camp. Their mean haemoglobin concentration rose from 148 to 157 g dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the increase in haemoglobin concentration over the 3 weeks.
parts.answer: At altitude the low pO₂ means less oxygen reaches the tissues; the kidneys detect low oxygen and release a hormone that stimulates red blood cell production in the bone marrow; more red blood cells means more haemoglobin per dm³; this takes days to weeks because new cells must be made and mature.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: low pO₂ / less O₂ to tissues; hormone from kidney; stimulates bone marrow; more red cells; time needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the increase helps the athletes when they return to compete at sea level.
parts.answer: Blood can carry more oxygen per dm³, so more oxygen is delivered to muscles; more aerobic respiration and less lactate, improving endurance.
parts.working: B1 higher O₂ carrying capacity; B1 more aerobic respiration / endurance.

practice.stem:
Blood of 20 heavy smokers and 20 non-smokers in Lahore was tested.
Mean carboxyhaemoglobin: smokers 7 %, non-smokers 1 %.
Mean red blood cell count: smokers 5.4 × 10⁶ mm⁻³, non-smokers 5.0 × 10⁶ mm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the smokers have a higher percentage of carboxyhaemoglobin.
parts.answer: Tobacco smoke contains carbon monoxide; CO binds to haem much more strongly than oxygen (and almost irreversibly), so it stays attached.
parts.working: B1 CO in smoke; B1 high affinity / binds strongly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the smokers also have a higher red blood cell count.
parts.answer: With some haemoglobin blocked by CO, less oxygen reaches the tissues; this stimulates the production of more red blood cells to compensate.
parts.working: B1 less O₂ delivered; B1 more red cells made in compensation.

practice.stem: When seals dive, their heart rate falls from about 100 to 10 beats per minute and the arterioles supplying their limbs and gut constrict.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest how slowing the heart and constricting the arterioles to the limbs helps a diving mammal to survive a long dive.
parts.answer: A slower heart uses less ATP / oxygen; constricting arterioles to limbs and gut reduces their blood flow, so oxygenated blood is kept for the brain and heart; the oxygen store lasts longer; limb muscles use myoglobin oxygen / anaerobic respiration.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: less O₂ used by heart; blood diverted to brain / heart; O₂ lasts longer; limbs rely on myoglobin / anaerobic respiration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: When a person puts their face in cold water while holding their breath, heart rate falls by about 10–25 %. Suggest why the fall is greater in cold water than in warm water.
parts.answer: Cold receptors in the face trigger the reflex more strongly (the reflex is a response to cold water on the face).

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: Systolic blood pressure (mmHg) of six nurses at a hospital in Hyderabad: 118, 124, 121, 130, 115, 126

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean systolic pressure, to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 122.3 mmHg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the standard deviation, to 2 decimal places, using s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)).
parts.answer: 5.47 mmHg
parts.working: M1 deviations from mean squared; M1 Σ = 149.33, ÷ 5 = 29.87; A1 √29.87 = 5.47.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the statistical test for each investigation:
(i) comparing mean haemoglobin concentration of 20 men and 20 women
(ii) testing for a relationship between age and systolic blood pressure in 15 people
(iii) comparing the numbers of people with blood groups A, B, AB and O in a sample with expected numbers.
parts.answer: (i) t-test; (ii) Spearman's rank correlation; (iii) chi-squared test
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one condition that data must meet for a t-test to be suitable.
parts.answer: Continuous data that are approximately normally distributed (with similar variance); two independent groups.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: A t-test compares the resting heart rates of 9 swimmers and 11 non-swimmers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of degrees of freedom.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The critical value of t for 18 degrees of freedom at p = 0.05 is 2.10. The calculated value is 2.45. State what this shows.
parts.answer: 2.45 > 2.10, so the probability that the difference is due to chance is less than 5 %; reject the null hypothesis – the difference between the means is significant.
parts.working: B1 comparison; B1 significant / reject null.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: The heart rates of 16 students after a 1 km walk have a standard deviation of 8.4 bpm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard error of the mean.
parts.answer: 2.1 bpm

parts.label: b
parts.text: The sample size is increased to 64 and s stays the same. Calculate the new standard error and explain what this shows.
parts.answer: 1.05 bpm; a larger sample gives a smaller SE, so the sample mean is a more reliable estimate of the population mean.
parts.working: B1 1.05; B1 larger n → more reliable mean.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: Resting heart rate (bpm) of nine students: 64, 70, 68, 75, 72, 66, 71, 69, 74

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and the standard deviation, each to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Mean 69.89 bpm; s = 3.59 bpm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the standard error of the mean (SE = s ÷ √n), to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the 95 % confidence interval (mean ± 2 × SE) and state what it means.
parts.answer: 67.50 to 72.28 bpm; we can be 95 % confident that the true mean resting heart rate of the population lies in this range.
parts.working: B1 limits; B1 meaning.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Heart rate after climbing five floors of stairs:
Group A (office workers, n = 25): mean 82 bpm, s = 6
Group B (security guards, n = 25): mean 76 bpm, s = 5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the 95 % confidence interval (mean ± 2SE, where SE = s ÷ √n) for each group.
parts.answer: Group A: 79.6 to 84.4 bpm; group B: 74.0 to 78.0 bpm

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what can be concluded from the two intervals.
parts.answer: They do not overlap, so the difference between the means is likely to be significant.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Resting heart rates (bpm) of two groups of five students:
Group X: 70, 72, 71, 69, 73
Group Y: 60, 82, 71, 65, 77

parts.label: a
parts.text: Both groups have a mean of 71 bpm. Calculate the standard deviation of each group to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the standard deviations show about the two groups.
parts.answer: Group Y's heart rates are much more spread out about the mean than group X's; so the mean represents group X much better / group X is more uniform.
parts.working: B1 Y more variable; B1 mean less representative for Y.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: For 12 students, a student calculated Spearman's rank correlation coefficient between hours of sleep per night and resting heart rate: rs = −0.54. The critical value for n = 12 at p = 0.05 is 0.59.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a conclusion from this result.
parts.answer: 0.54 < 0.59, so the correlation is not significant at p = 0.05; accept the null hypothesis of no correlation between hours of sleep and resting heart rate.
parts.working: B1 comparison; B1 not significant / accept null.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why Spearman's rank correlation was used rather than Pearson's correlation coefficient.
parts.answer: Spearman's does not require the data to be normally distributed or the relationship to be linear; it tests for a monotonic relationship using ranks, and the sample is small.
parts.working: B1 no assumption of normal distribution; B1 linear not needed / ranks / monotonic.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
100 men aged 50 were surveyed:
Smokers (50): 30 with high blood pressure, 20 normal
Non-smokers (50): 18 with high blood pressure, 32 normal

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected numbers for each of the four cells if smoking has no effect on blood pressure.
parts.answer: Smokers: 24 high, 26 normal; non-smokers: 24 high, 26 normal
parts.working: M1 expected = row total × column total ÷ grand total (50 × 48 ÷ 100); A1 all four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate χ², to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value for 1 degree of freedom at p = 0.05 is 3.84. State a conclusion.
parts.answer: 5.77 > 3.84, so there is a significant association between smoking and high blood pressure.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
For eight students, exercise intensity score and heart rate after exercise (bpm) were recorded:
Intensity score: 3.1, 4.5, 2.2, 5.8, 3.9, 6.4, 1.7, 5.0
Heart rate / bpm: 71, 78, 66, 85, 80, 82, 64, 76

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the ranking (lowest = 1) and calculate Σd².
parts.answer: Exercise ranks: 3, 5, 2, 7, 4, 8, 1, 6; Heart-rate ranks: 3, 5, 2, 8, 6, 7, 1, 4; Σd² = 10

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n(n² − 1)) to 2 decimal places, and state a conclusion given that the critical value for n = 8 at p = 0.05 is 0.74.
parts.answer: rs = 0.88; 0.88 > 0.74, so there is a significant positive correlation between exercise intensity and heart rate after exercise.
parts.working: B1 0.88; B1 conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Resting heart rates (beats per minute) of 10 students who train for football and 10 who do not:
Trained: 62, 58, 66, 60, 64, 59, 63, 61, 67, 60
Untrained: 68, 72, 65, 70, 74, 66, 71, 69, 75, 67
s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1));  t = |x̄₁ − x̄₂| ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard deviation for each group. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Trained: s = 2.98; untrained: s = 3.33

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of t. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of t at p = 0.05 with 18 degrees of freedom is 2.10. State what you can conclude.
parts.answer: 5.44 is greater than 2.10, so the null hypothesis is rejected: there is a significant difference between the mean resting heart rates (probability of the difference being due to chance is less than 5 %).
parts.working: B1 t > critical value so reject null hypothesis. B1 difference is significant / not due to chance at p < 0.05.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: Capillary refill time (s) of two groups of eight volunteers. Group C put one hand in water at 10 °C; group W put one hand in water at 30 °C: / Group C (10 °C): 3.6, 4.1, 3.8, 4.4, 3.2, 4.0, 3.9, 3.5 / Group W (30 °C): 2.1, 2.5, 1.9, 2.8, 2.2, 2.6, 2.0, 2.4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard deviation of each group, to 2 decimal places, using s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)).
parts.answer: Group C 0.38 s; group W 0.31 s.
parts.working: B1 means 3.81 s and 2.31 s used; B1 s = 0.38 and 0.31 (Σ(x − x̄)² = 0.99 and 0.69).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate t, to 2 decimal places, using t = |x̄₁ − x̄₂| ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of t for 14 degrees of freedom at p = 0.05 is 2.14. State what you can conclude.
parts.answer: 8.67 > 2.14, so reject the null hypothesis: capillary refill time is significantly longer at 10 °C than at 30 °C.
parts.working: B1 comparison with 2.14; B1 significant difference with direction.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: Altitude and mean red blood cell count of residents of nine villages in northern Pakistan: / Altitude / m: 300, 900, 1500, 1900, 2300, 2700, 3100, 3500, 4000 / Red blood cell count / million per mm³: 4.8, 5.1, 4.9, 5.4, 5.3, 5.7, 5.6, 6.0, 5.9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Rank both variables (lowest = 1) and calculate Σd².
parts.answer: Altitude ranks 1 to 9; red blood cell count ranks 1, 3, 2, 5, 4, 7, 6, 9, 8; Σd² = 8.
parts.working: M1 correct ranks; A1 Σd² = 8 (each d = ±1 for eight of the nine pairs and 0 for one).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n(n² − 1)).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value for n = 9 at p = 0.05 is 0.70. State a conclusion.
parts.answer: 0.93 > 0.70, so there is a significant positive correlation: higher altitude is associated with a higher red blood cell count.
parts.working: B1 comparison with 0.70; B1 significant positive correlation.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
100 children were tested for anaemia in each of three districts:
District P: 38 anaemic, 62 not anaemic
District Q: 25 anaemic, 75 not anaemic
District R: 22 anaemic, 78 not anaemic

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected number of anaemic and non-anaemic children in each district, if there were no difference between districts.
parts.answer: Anaemic 28.33; non-anaemic 71.67 in each district

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate χ² = Σ(O − E)² ÷ E, to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 sum of six terms (3.298 + 1.304 + 0.392 + 0.155 + 1.416 + 0.560); A1 7.12 (rounding each term first gives 7.13).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the degrees of freedom and, using the critical value 5.99 at p = 0.05, a conclusion.
parts.answer: df = (3 − 1)(2 − 1) = 2; 7.12 > 5.99, so the difference between districts is significant – anaemia is not equally common in the three districts.
parts.working: B1 df = 2; B1 conclusion.

practice.stem:
Systolic blood pressure (mmHg) of people eating a high-salt and a low-salt diet:
High salt (n = 14): mean 132.4, s = 11.2
Low salt (n = 12): mean 124.1, s = 9.6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate t, to 2 decimal places, using t = |x̄₁ − x̄₂| ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the degrees of freedom. The critical value of t at p = 0.05 for this number of degrees of freedom is 2.06. State a conclusion.
parts.answer: df = 24; 2.03 < 2.06, so the difference is not significant at p = 0.05 – accept the null hypothesis.
parts.working: B1 df 24; B1 conclusion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the researcher should not conclude that salt has no effect on blood pressure.
parts.answer: t is very close to the critical value; with larger samples the difference might prove significant (a non-significant result does not prove no effect).

practice.stem: Since 2016, many cases of typhoid in Sindh have been caused by strains of Salmonella Typhi that are resistant to several antibiotics (extensively drug-resistant typhoid).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a population of bacteria can become resistant to an antibiotic.
parts.answer: A random mutation produces an allele giving resistance (e.g. coding for an enzyme that breaks down the antibiotic); when the antibiotic is used it acts as a selection pressure; bacteria without the allele are killed, resistant bacteria survive and reproduce (binary fission), passing on the allele; the allele frequency increases over generations; (resistance alleles on plasmids can also pass between bacteria by horizontal gene transfer/conjugation).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: mutation (random, already present); antibiotic is the selection pressure; resistant survive and reproduce; allele passed to offspring; allele frequency increases; plasmid transfer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways in which the spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria can be reduced.
parts.answer: Any two of: use antibiotics only when needed/prescribed; complete the full course; avoid using antibiotics in animal feed; improve sanitation and clean drinking water; vaccination against typhoid; infection control/hand washing.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by stabilising, directional and disruptive selection.
parts.answer: Stabilising: individuals with intermediate phenotypes are favoured, extremes selected against; the mean stays the same and variation decreases. Directional: individuals at one extreme are favoured; the mean shifts in that direction. Disruptive: both extremes are favoured over the intermediate; can produce two distinct groups.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Human birth mass is an example of stabilising selection. Explain why.
parts.answer: Babies of very low birth mass have a higher death rate (less able to keep warm/more infections) and very high birth mass increases complications in birth; intermediate birth masses have the highest survival, so the mean is maintained and variation is reduced.
parts.working: B1 extremes have higher mortality; B1 intermediate favoured/mean maintained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a mutation that is harmful in one environment may be beneficial in another.
parts.answer: The mutation arises at random and is not caused by the environment. When the environment changes, the altered phenotype gives higher survival and reproduction, so the allele is passed on more often and its frequency increases.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: mutation is random and not caused by the environment; the environment changes (or the organism moves); the phenotype now gives an advantage / higher fitness; these individuals survive and reproduce more; the allele frequency increases.

practice.stem: Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It is a slow-growing organism that is treated with antibiotics.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the term 'selection pressure'.
parts.answer: Any environmental factor (for example a drug, predator or climate) that causes differences in survival and reproduction between individuals with different phenotypes.
parts.working: 1 mark: a factor that affects survival/reproduction, so that some phenotypes/alleles are favoured over others.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Tuberculosis (TB) is treated with a combination of several antibiotics taken together for at least six months, rather than with one antibiotic alone. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Resistance to any one drug arises from a rare mutation. A bacterium that is resistant to all the drugs at once would need several rare mutations together, which is very unlikely, so the combination is far less likely to select a resistant population.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: resistance to one drug needs a rare mutation; resistance to several drugs needs several mutations together, which is very unlikely; a drug still kills any bacteria with resistance to another drug; the combination makes resistant survivors rare.

practice.stem: Sahiwal cattle are a dairy breed from Punjab, valued for tolerating heat and resisting ticks. Breeders want to increase their milk yield.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how breeders could use artificial selection to increase the milk yield of Sahiwal cattle over many generations.
parts.answer: Measure milk yield of cows and select those with the highest yield; bulls cannot be measured directly, so select bulls whose mothers/daughters (progeny testing) have high yields; breed selected cows with selected bulls (e.g. by artificial insemination); select the highest-yielding offspring and breed them; repeat over many generations so the frequency of alleles for high yield increases.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of the points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why breeders should also keep selecting for heat tolerance while selecting for milk yield.
parts.answer: Selecting only for yield may reduce/lose alleles for heat tolerance or tick resistance, which are needed in Pakistan's climate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one difference between artificial selection and natural selection.
parts.answer: In artificial selection humans choose which individuals breed, for characteristics useful to humans; in natural selection the environment/selection pressures decide which survive and reproduce.

practice.stem: Maize farmers in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa buy new hybrid maize seed every year. The seed is produced by crossing two inbred (homozygous) lines.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the inbred lines are often small and produce low yields.
parts.answer: Repeated inbreeding increases homozygosity; harmful recessive alleles are more likely to be expressed in the homozygous state (inbreeding depression).
parts.working: B1 homozygous; B1 harmful recessive alleles expressed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the F1 hybrid plants are vigorous and uniform.
parts.answer: Hybrids are heterozygous at many loci, so harmful recessive alleles are masked (hybrid vigour); both parents are homozygous, so all F1 plants have the same genotype and are uniform.
parts.working: B1 heterozygous/hybrid vigour; B1 identical genotypes, uniform.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why farmers do not save seed from their hybrid crop to sow the next year.
parts.answer: Seed from F1 × F1 is the F2 generation; alleles segregate, producing many different genotypes, so plants are not uniform and many have lower yield.
parts.working: B1 segregation/variety of genotypes in F2; B1 not uniform/lower yield.

practice.stem: Stem rust is a fungal disease that can destroy wheat crops. Wheat breeders in Pakistan cross local high-yielding varieties with varieties that carry a resistance allele.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline how breeders could produce a high-yielding variety that is resistant to stem rust.
parts.answer: Cross a high-yielding variety with a resistant variety; grow offspring and expose them to the fungus, selecting plants that are resistant and have high yield; breed these together/backcross to the high-yielding parent for several generations, selecting each time, until the variety is true-breeding for both features.
parts.working: B1 cross the two varieties; B1 select resistant, high-yield offspring (test by infecting); B1 repeat for many generations/backcrossing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: New races of the stem rust fungus sometimes appear that can infect previously resistant wheat. Explain how this happens.
parts.answer: Mutation in the fungus produces a new allele allowing it to infect resistant wheat; widely planted resistant wheat is a selection pressure; fungi with the new allele reproduce, so the new race spreads/allele frequency increases.
parts.working: B1 mutation in fungus; B1 resistant wheat selects for it; B1 the new race survives, reproduces and spreads.

practice.stem: Rock pocket mice live in deserts in North America. Most mice living on pale sandy rock have pale fur; most mice living on dark lava flows have dark fur. Dark fur is caused by a dominant allele of the Mc1r gene. Owls, which hunt by sight, are their main predators.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how natural selection has led to most mice on lava flows having dark fur.
parts.answer: There is variation in fur colour in the population, caused by different alleles; owls see and catch pale mice more easily on dark rock (predation is the selection pressure); dark mice are camouflaged, so more survive and reproduce; they pass on the dark allele, so its frequency increases over generations.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: variation/alleles; predation as selection pressure; dark mice survive and reproduce; allele passed on/frequency increases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a new dominant mutation for dark fur could spread through a population faster than a new recessive mutation would.
parts.answer: A dominant allele is expressed in heterozygotes, so it shows in the phenotype immediately and is selected for at once; a recessive allele is hidden in heterozygotes and only selected when homozygous, which is rare at first.
parts.working: B1 dominant expressed in heterozygote/visible to selection; B1 recessive hidden until homozygous.

practice.stem: Cotton bollworms are pests of cotton in Punjab. Many farms grow Bt cotton, which produces a toxin from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis that kills bollworm larvae that feed on it. Farmers are advised to plant a 'refuge': a block of non-Bt cotton near each Bt field.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the refuge slows the spread of resistance to the Bt toxin in the bollworm population.
parts.answer: Non-Bt refuge plants let susceptible bollworms survive without exposure to the toxin. Resistance is rare and recessive, so resistant moths that mate with susceptible moths produce mostly heterozygous or susceptible offspring, which are killed on the Bt cotton. The resistance allele therefore stays at a low frequency.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: susceptible bollworms survive on refuge plants (no selection there); the resistance allele is rare and recessive; resistant adults mate at random with susceptible adults from the refuge; their offspring are heterozygous or susceptible and are killed by the Bt toxin; so the resistance allele frequency stays low and the toxin stays effective.

practice.stem: A population of 1,200 green lizards and 800 brown lizards lived in a mixed habitat. A bird predator fed on the lizards for one season. At the end of the season, 360 green lizards and 560 brown lizards had survived.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of each colour of lizard that survived. Give each answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Green: 30.0 %; brown: 70.0 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which colour was favoured by natural selection, and name the type of selection shown by these results.
parts.answer: Brown was favoured (70 % survived compared with 30 % of green). This is directional selection, because one extreme phenotype is favoured and the population shifts towards brown.
parts.working: 1 mark: brown (higher survival); 1 mark: directional selection (one phenotype favoured, the mean shifts).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the surviving lizards that were brown. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: 1 mark for 560 ÷ (360 + 560) = 0.6087; 1 mark for 60.9 %. Compared with 40 % of the population at the start, brown is more common among survivors.

practice.stem: Mosquitoes of the genus Anopheles transmit malaria. In one district, the same insecticide was sprayed in houses every year. The percentage of mosquitoes surviving a standard dose was: year 1 – 2 %; year 3 – 9 %; year 5 – 31 %; year 7 – 68 %. Spraying then stopped. In year 10 the survival was 40 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the change in survival between years 1 and 7.
parts.answer: Some mosquitoes already carried a resistance allele (from mutation) at a low frequency (2 % survival); the insecticide killed non-resistant mosquitoes – a selection pressure; resistant mosquitoes survived and reproduced, passing on the allele; the frequency of the resistance allele increased each generation (directional selection), so survival rose to 68 %.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: pre-existing allele/mutation; selection pressure; survivors reproduce; allele passed on; allele frequency increases; directional selection; use of data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why survival fell between year 7 and year 10.
parts.answer: Without insecticide there is no advantage to resistance; the resistance allele may carry a cost (e.g. lower fertility or slower development), so non-resistant mosquitoes are selected for/out-reproduce resistant ones and the allele frequency falls.
parts.working: B1 no selection for resistance; B1 resistant individuals at a disadvantage without insecticide.

practice.stem: Sickle cell anaemia is caused by the allele Hbˢ. People with genotype HbˢHbˢ have sickle cell anaemia; heterozygotes (HbᴬHbˢ) are mostly healthy and are less likely to die from severe malaria than HbᴬHbᴬ people. The Hbˢ allele is much more common in parts of Africa where malaria is common than in places without malaria.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the Hbˢ allele remains at a high frequency in areas where malaria is common.
parts.answer: HbˢHbˢ people often die young/have fewer children, so Hbˢ alleles are lost; HbᴬHbᴬ people are more likely to die of malaria, so Hbᴬ alleles are lost; heterozygotes have a selective advantage – they survive malaria and reproduce, passing on both alleles; so both alleles are kept in the population (balanced polymorphism/heterozygote advantage).
parts.working: 1 mark each for: selection against HbˢHbˢ; selection against HbᴬHbᴬ by malaria; heterozygote advantage; both alleles maintained.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the frequency of Hbˢ is falling slowly among descendants of people who moved from these areas to countries without malaria.
parts.answer: Malaria is no longer a selection pressure, so heterozygotes have no advantage; HbˢHbˢ individuals are still selected against, so the allele frequency falls slowly (slowly because most Hbˢ alleles are carried in heterozygotes, where they are not selected against).
parts.working: B1 no heterozygote advantage without malaria; B1 selection against homozygotes only, so slow decline.

practice.stem: On an island, a severe drought killed most plants that produce small, soft seeds, leaving mainly large, hard seeds. The mean beak depth of a population of seed-eating finches was 9.2 mm before the drought and 9.7 mm in the generation hatched after it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in mean beak depth. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of selection shown and explain how the change happened.
parts.answer: Directional selection; beak depth varies and is partly genetic (polygenic); during the drought only birds with deeper beaks could crack the large, hard seeds; so they survived and bred, while birds with shallow beaks starved; alleles for deep beaks were passed on, so the mean in the next generation increased.
parts.working: B1 directional; B1 variation with genetic basis; B1 deep-beaked birds survived/reproduced (food as selection pressure); B1 alleles passed on/mean shifted.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the change in mean beak depth would not have occurred if beak depth were controlled only by the environment.
parts.answer: Characteristics caused only by the environment are not inherited, so offspring would not show the change.

practice.stem: In a population of finches, a gene has two alleles, S and s. At birth, 500 individuals were counted: 80 were SS, 240 were Ss and 180 were ss. The probability of surviving to breed was 0.60 for SS, 0.80 for Ss and 0.90 for ss.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of each genotype that survived to breed.
parts.answer: SS: 48; Ss: 192; ss: 162; total surviving 402.
parts.working: 1 mark each: 0.60 × 80 = 48; 0.80 × 240 = 192; 0.90 × 180 = 162; total 402 (1 mark for total or consistent working).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of allele S among the survivors. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: 1 mark for counting S alleles: (2 × 48) + 192 = 288 out of 2 × 402 = 804 alleles; 1 mark for 0.358.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the change in the frequency of allele S from its value at birth (0.40) is evidence of natural selection.
parts.answer: The change follows genotype: SS survive worst (0.60) and ss best (0.90), so the survival differences between genotypes favour alleles of the ss type over S. This is systematic selection based on phenotype, not the random sampling changes expected from genetic drift.
parts.working: 1 mark: survival differs between genotypes (fitness differs); 1 mark: the change is predictable and systematic (directional), unlike random genetic drift.

practice.stem: Dachshunds were bred for a long body and short legs. Many now have spinal problems. Breeders in some lines select dogs for extreme, showy body shapes and mate closely related animals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why selecting for an extreme body shape can reduce the fitness of a breed.
parts.answer: The alleles that produce the extreme shape often have harmful side-effects (pleiotropy), or are linked to alleles that damage the spine. Breeders select the extreme trait, which also selects these harmful alleles, so they increase in frequency and reduce survival or reproduction.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: the trait has harmful side-effects / pleiotropy; harmful alleles are linked to the trait; selection for the trait also selects the harmful alleles; the harmful alleles increase in frequency; reduced survival or reproduction lowers fitness.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how close inbreeding increases the chance that harmful recessive alleles are expressed.
parts.answer: Close relatives share alleles inherited from a common ancestor, so their offspring are more likely to receive the same recessive allele from both parents and be homozygous for it. The harmful phenotype is then expressed.
parts.working: 1 mark: relatives share alleles; 1 mark: offspring more likely to be homozygous recessive, so the harmful allele is expressed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'species' using the biological species concept.
parts.answer: A group of organisms with similar features that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring, and are reproductively isolated from other such groups.
parts.working: B1 interbreed to produce fertile offspring; B1 reproductively isolated from other species.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the difference between allopatric speciation and sympatric speciation.
parts.answer: Allopatric: populations are separated by a geographical barrier. Sympatric: a new species forms in the same area without geographical separation (e.g. by polyploidy or behavioural isolation).
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences between genetic drift and natural selection.
parts.answer: Drift is random/due to chance, selection is non-random (depends on phenotype and environment); drift has most effect in small populations, selection acts in any size population; selection leads to adaptation, drift does not.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why both processes change the gene pool of a population.
parts.answer: Both change the frequency of alleles in the population from one generation to the next; alleles can be lost or become fixed.
parts.working: B1 change allele frequencies; B1 alleles lost/fixed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by 'reproductive isolation'.
parts.answer: Two populations can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring, so gene flow between them stops.
parts.working: 1 mark: no interbreeding (or no fertile offspring), so no gene flow.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one prezygotic barrier and one postzygotic barrier to reproduction, each with an example.
parts.answer: Prezygotic: for example different breeding seasons or habitats, or different courtship/song (no mating or no fertilisation). Postzygotic: for example hybrid offspring that are sterile (such as a mule) or fail to develop.
parts.working: 1 mark for a prezygotic barrier with a correct example; 1 mark for a postzygotic barrier with a correct example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways in which the allele frequencies of a population can change without natural selection.
parts.answer: Any two of: genetic drift (random change, especially in a small population); the founder effect; a bottleneck; migration (gene flow) in or out; mutation.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of the listed causes.

practice.stem: A species of freshwater fish lived in one large lake. Over thousands of years the water level fell and the lake split into two smaller lakes, one with clear, rocky water and one with muddy water and dense weed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how two separate species of fish could evolve from the original population.
parts.answer: The two populations are geographically isolated, so no gene flow/interbreeding between them; different mutations arise in each population; different selection pressures in each lake (e.g. food, predators, water clarity) favour different alleles; genetic drift may also change allele frequencies (especially in small populations); over many generations the gene pools become so different that the two populations could no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring even if they met (reproductive isolation) – allopatric speciation.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: geographical isolation; no gene flow; different mutations; different selection pressures (with example); drift; allele frequencies change; reproductive isolation/cannot produce fertile offspring.

practice.stem: Bread wheat (Triticum aestivum) is hexaploid with 2n = 42. It is thought to have arisen when tetraploid emmer wheat (2n = 28) hybridised with a wild grass, Aegilops tauschii (2n = 14).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of chromosomes in the hybrid formed from one gamete of each parent.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this hybrid was sterile.
parts.answer: The chromosomes from the two parents are not homologous, so they cannot pair up in prophase I of meiosis; viable gametes cannot be formed.
parts.working: B1 chromosomes not homologous/cannot pair; B1 meiosis fails/no functional gametes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a fertile hexaploid species could have formed from the hybrid in the same place as its parents, and why this is an example of sympatric speciation.
parts.answer: The chromosome number of the hybrid doubled (e.g. a failure of cell division/non-disjunction), giving 42; every chromosome now has a homologous partner, so meiosis works and fertile gametes form; the new plant cannot produce fertile offspring with either parent, so it is reproductively isolated without any geographical barrier.
parts.working: B1 chromosome doubling to 42; B1 homologues can pair/fertile; B1 reproductively isolated in same area.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by genetic drift.
parts.answer: A random (chance) change in allele frequencies in a population from one generation to the next, not caused by selection; it has a larger effect in small populations.
parts.working: B1 random/chance change in allele frequency; B1 greater effect in small populations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A storm carried six birds of one species to a remote island where none of that species lived. Over 200 years the island population grew to several thousand. Explain why the island population may show less genetic diversity and different allele frequencies from the mainland population (the founder effect).
parts.answer: The six founders carried only a small sample of the alleles in the mainland gene pool; by chance some alleles were absent and others at a higher frequency than on the mainland; the population grew from these few, so it has lower diversity; drift in the small early population changed frequencies further.
parts.working: B1 founders carry a small/non-representative sample of alleles; B1 some alleles lost/frequencies different by chance; B1 low diversity as population grows from few individuals/drift.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a population with low genetic diversity may be at greater risk of extinction.
parts.answer: Fewer alleles means less variation for natural selection to act on if the environment changes (e.g. a new disease).

practice.stem: Five individuals reached an island and founded a new population. At one gene locus, the 10 alleles carried by these founders included 6 copies of allele R and 4 copies of allele r. After many generations the population had 400 individuals and the frequency of allele R was 0.52.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of allele R in the founders.
parts.answer: 0.6 (6 out of 10 alleles).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in the frequency of allele R between the founders and the population of 400.
parts.answer: The frequency fell by 0.08 (from 0.60 to 0.52).
parts.working: 1 mark: 0.60 − 0.52 = 0.08 (a decrease).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the process that best explains this change, and explain why it is more likely in a small population.
parts.answer: Genetic drift (the founder effect is a special case of drift that happens when a new population is founded). A small population is a small random sample of the alleles in the original population, so chance changes in allele frequency are larger than in a large population.
parts.working: 1 mark: genetic drift (or founder effect) named; 1 mark: a small population is a random sample, so chance sampling changes are larger.

practice.stem: Two populations of a mammal were separated by a river. Their mitochondrial DNA was compared and they differed at 3.6 % of sites. Assume each lineage accumulates 0.6 % of sites changed per million years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time since the two populations separated, in millions of years.
parts.answer: 3.0 million years.
parts.working: 1 mark: total divergence 3.6 % is shared by two lineages each changing at 0.6 % per million years, so the combined rate is 2 × 0.6 = 1.2 % per million years; 1 mark: 3.6 ÷ 1.2 = 3.0 million years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one assumption made in this calculation.
parts.answer: The rate of mutation is constant over time and the same in both lineages, and the mutations are neutral (no selection).
parts.working: 1 mark: any sensible assumption about constant or equal mutation rate, or neutral mutations.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the time calculated is only an approximate estimate.
parts.answer: Mutation rates vary between lineages and over time, and natural selection can change the rate of accumulation.
parts.working: 1 mark: a named source of variation in the molecular clock (rate changes, selection, reversals or random chance).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a bottleneck reduces genetic variation in a population.
parts.answer: A sudden drop in population size (for example from disease or hunting) means only a few individuals survive. These survivors are a random sample of the original alleles, so some alleles are lost by chance and frequencies change at random. The population that follows has less genetic variation.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: a sudden large fall in population size; survivors are a small random sample; some alleles are lost by chance; allele frequencies change at random (drift); the gene pool has less variation.

practice.stem:
The first 12 amino acids of a conserved protein were compared in four mammal species (one-letter code):
Species A: MGDVEKGKKIFV
Species B: MGDVEKGKKLFV
Species C: MGDAEKGKKIFA
Species D: MSDVEKGRKIFV

parts.label: a
parts.text: Count the number of amino acids that differ between: (i) A and B; (ii) A and C; (iii) A and D.
parts.working: 1 mark for the first two correct; 1 mark for all three correct. Each position is compared one by one (12 positions).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage identity between species A and species D.
parts.answer: 83.3 % (10 of 12 amino acids are identical).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which pair of species is most closely related, and justify your answer.
parts.answer: A and B. They have the fewest differences (1), so fewer mutations have built up since they shared a common ancestor.
parts.working: 1 mark for the correct pair; 1 mark for justification: fewest differences means fewer mutations since divergence.

practice.stem: The amino acid sequence of a respiratory protein, 104 amino acids long, was compared between humans and four other species. Number of amino acid differences from the human sequence: species K – 0; species L – 1; species M – 12; species N – 21.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of amino acids in species M's protein that are identical to the human sequence. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how these data provide evidence about the evolutionary relationships of the species.
parts.answer: Differences in amino acid sequence result from mutations in DNA that build up over time; the fewer differences, the more recently the species shared a common ancestor; so K and L are most closely related to humans, and N is the most distantly related.
parts.working: B1 mutations accumulate over time; B1 fewer differences = more recent common ancestor; B1 correct order using data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why comparing DNA base sequences of the gene gives more information than comparing amino acid sequences.
parts.answer: The genetic code is degenerate, so some base changes do not change the amino acid; these silent mutations (and changes in introns/non-coding DNA) are detected only by DNA comparison.
parts.working: B1 degenerate code/silent mutations; B1 non-coding DNA also compared.

practice.stem:
Scientists compared a 30-base section of mitochondrial DNA from three populations of a mountain goat (markhor) from different valleys.
Population X: ATGCTAGCCTTAGGACATCCGTTAGCAATC
Population Y: ATGCTGGCCTTAGGATATCCGCTAGCAATT
Population Z: ATACTGGCTTTAGGATATCCACTGGCGATT

parts.label: a
parts.text: Count the number of base differences between X and Y, X and Z, and Y and Z.
parts.working: B2 all three correct (B1 for two).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to state which two populations are most closely related and explain your reasoning.
parts.answer: X and Y; they have the fewest base differences, so fewest mutations have built up since they shared a common ancestor/they separated most recently.
parts.working: B1 X and Y; B1 reasoning.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why mitochondrial DNA is useful for studying relationships between populations of the same species.
parts.answer: It is inherited only from the mother, so it does not undergo recombination/crossing over; it mutates relatively quickly, so differences build up even between closely related populations.
parts.working: B1 maternal inheritance/no recombination; B1 fast mutation rate.

practice.stem: A horse (2n = 64) and a donkey (2n = 62) can mate to produce a mule. Mules are strong and healthy but almost always sterile.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of chromosomes in a body cell of a mule.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why mules are sterile.
parts.answer: The mule has an odd number of chromosomes and the horse and donkey chromosomes are not all homologous; they cannot pair correctly in prophase I of meiosis; so gametes have unbalanced/incorrect chromosome sets and are not viable.
parts.working: B1 odd number/non-homologous chromosomes; B1 cannot pair in meiosis I; B1 viable gametes not formed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Horses and donkeys are separate species even though they can produce offspring. Explain why, and name this type of reproductive isolating mechanism.
parts.answer: Their offspring are sterile, so genes cannot pass between the two gene pools; postzygotic isolation (hybrid sterility).
parts.working: B1 offspring not fertile/no gene flow; B1 postzygotic/hybrid sterility.

practice.stem: A songbird lives in populations that form a ring around a large mountain range. Adjacent populations can interbreed. The populations at the two ends of the ring, where the ring closes, do not interbreed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a ring species provides evidence that speciation can be a gradual process.
parts.answer: Neighbouring populations around the ring can interbreed, so gene flow links them, and each population differs slightly from the next because of gradual changes in alleles and selection with distance. Where the ring closes, the two end populations are no longer able to interbreed with each other, so they behave as separate species, even though a chain of intermediate populations connects them.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: neighbouring populations interbreed (gene flow); differences build up gradually around the ring; alleles and selection change with distance/environment; the two ends can no longer interbreed; speciation occurs as a series of small steps, not a single event.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the two end populations are considered separate species even though they are linked through intermediate populations.
parts.answer: Because they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring, so they are reproductively isolated and gene flow between them has stopped.
parts.working: 1 mark: reproductive isolation / no fertile offspring between the ends.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the difference between continuous variation and discontinuous variation, giving one example of each in humans.
parts.answer: Continuous: a range of values with no distinct categories (e.g. height, mass); discontinuous: distinct categories with no intermediates (e.g. ABO blood group).
parts.working: B1 continuous description; B1 discontinuous description; B1 correct examples of both.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why continuous variation is usually affected by both genes and the environment.
parts.answer: It is controlled by many genes (polygenes) each having a small additive effect; the environment (e.g. diet) also affects how the genes are expressed, adding to the range of phenotypes.
parts.working: B1 polygenic/many genes with additive effect; B1 environment modifies phenotype.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one genetic cause and one environmental cause of variation between individuals of the same species.
parts.answer: Genetic: different alleles inherited from parents, mutation or sexual reproduction (independent assortment, crossing over, random fusion of gametes). Environmental: for example diet, light, temperature or disease.
parts.working: 1 mark for a correct genetic cause; 1 mark for a correct environmental cause.

practice.stem: The lengths of six seedpods taken from one plant were measured (cm): 12.4, 11.8, 13.1, 12.9, 11.5, 12.3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean length of the six seedpods. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark for the sum 74.0 cm; 1 mark for 74.0 ÷ 6 = 12.33 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method for collecting data that show the variation in leaf length across one tree.
parts.answer: Choose leaves at random from all parts of the tree (for example by picking branches using random numbers), measure at least 20 leaves from base to tip with a ruler to the nearest millimetre, using the same method each time, and record the lengths in a table. Calculate the mean and standard deviation.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: random selection of leaves from different parts of the tree; a sample of at least 20 leaves; a clear method for measuring (base to tip, same method, ruler to the nearest mm); recording in a table; calculating the mean and standard deviation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a larger sample gives a more reliable estimate of the mean of a population.
parts.answer: A larger sample reduces the effect of unusual individuals (outliers) and of chance sampling error, so the sample mean is more likely to be close to the true population mean.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: a larger sample reduces the effect of outliers; less sampling error (chance) so the mean represents the population better.

practice.stem:
The lengths (cm) of eight leaflets taken from one neem tree were: 6.2, 5.8, 7.1, 6.5, 6.9, 5.5, 6.0, 6.8.
Standard deviation s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and standard deviation of the leaflet lengths. Give the standard deviation to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: mean 6.35 cm; s = 0.57 cm

parts.label: b
parts.text: A second tree had leaflets with mean length 6.40 cm and standard deviation 1.20 cm. Explain what the two standard deviations show.
parts.answer: The means are similar but the second tree has a much larger spread of leaflet lengths/more variation around the mean; the first tree's leaflets are more uniform.
parts.working: B1 means similar; B1 larger SD = more spread/variation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why leaflets on one tree vary in length even though they all have the same genotype.
parts.answer: Environmental factors differ for each leaflet, e.g. light (shade), position, age.

practice.stem: A researcher compared the mass at birth of lambs from two breeds of sheep. She calculated t = 1.45 with 18 degrees of freedom. The critical value of t at p = 0.05 for 18 df is 2.10.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the null hypothesis that was tested.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the mean birth mass of lambs of the two breeds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the researcher can conclude, and explain your answer.
parts.answer: 1.45 < 2.10, so the probability that the difference is due to chance is greater than 0.05; accept the null hypothesis – there is no significant difference in mean birth mass.
parts.working: B1 t below critical value; B1 accept null/no significant difference.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two conditions that the data should meet for a t-test to be suitable.
parts.answer: Any two of: data are continuous measurements; data are approximately normally distributed; two independent samples being compared; samples should have similar variances; sample size less than about 30 per group.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: The wing lengths (mm) of ten beetles of one species were measured: 8.2, 9.1, 7.8, 8.6, 9.4, 8.0, 8.9, 7.5, 8.4, 9.0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean wing length.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the sample standard deviation, using n − 1. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark for the sum of squared deviations from the mean (about 3.43); 1 mark for √(sum ÷ 9) = 0.62 mm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the standard deviation tells you about the wing lengths.
parts.answer: The wing lengths are spread about 0.62 mm either side of the mean, so most beetles lie within about 0.6 mm of 8.49 mm.
parts.working: 1 mark: a typical spread around the mean (most values lie within one standard deviation of the mean).

practice.stem:
A botanist grew two groups of six wheat plants: group F with normal fertiliser and group N with no fertiliser. The dry masses of the plants (g) were:
Group F: 5.2, 4.9, 5.6, 5.1, 5.4, 5.0
Group N: 4.1, 4.6, 3.9, 4.4, 4.0, 4.3

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean dry mass of each group.
parts.answer: Fertiliser: 5.20 g; no fertiliser: 4.22 g.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate t using t = (x̄₁ − x̄₂) ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂), where s is the sample standard deviation (n − 1). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark for the two sample variances (about 0.068 and 0.070) and the denominator √(0.0113 + 0.0116) ≈ 0.151; 1 mark for t = 0.98 ÷ 0.151 = 6.49.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using a critical value of 2.23 (df = 10, 5 % level, two-tailed), state the conclusion and what it means for the null hypothesis.
parts.answer: The calculated t (6.49) is greater than 2.23, so the difference in mean dry mass is significant; the null hypothesis of no difference is rejected.
parts.working: 1 mark: significant (t greater than the critical value), so reject the null hypothesis that fertiliser has no effect on mean dry mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A t-test gives t = 1.42. The critical value at the 5 % level (two-tailed) is 2.10. State the conclusion and what happens to the null hypothesis.
parts.answer: The calculated t is smaller than the critical value, so the difference is not significant. The null hypothesis is not rejected (retained): there is no evidence of a real difference between the means.
parts.working: 1 mark: t (1.42) is less than 2.10, so not significant; 1 mark: the null hypothesis is retained / not rejected (any difference is likely due to chance). Do not say the hypothesis is proven true.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the standard deviation of a sample is calculated by dividing by n − 1 rather than by n.
parts.answer: The sample mean is used in the calculation, so the deviations from it are smaller than those from the true population mean. Dividing by n − 1 (the degrees of freedom) corrects this bias and gives a better estimate of the population standard deviation.
parts.working: 1 mark: the sample mean makes deviations (and variance) underestimate the population value; 1 mark: dividing by n − 1 corrects this, giving an unbiased estimate of the population value.

practice.stem:
Shell lengths (mm) of a species of land snail were measured on an exposed hillside and in a sheltered valley.
Hillside: 18.2, 19.5, 17.8, 20.1, 18.9, 19.4, 18.6, 19.9 (mean 19.05, s = 0.816)
Valley: 16.9, 17.5, 16.2, 18.0, 17.1, 16.6, 17.8, 16.4 (mean 17.06, s = 0.659)
t = |x̄₁ − x̄₂| ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂). Degrees of freedom = n₁ + n₂ − 2.
Critical values of t at p = 0.05: 12 df – 2.18; 14 df – 2.14; 16 df – 2.12.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of t. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of degrees of freedom and what the student can conclude.
parts.answer: 14 df; 5.36 > 2.14, so the difference between the mean shell lengths is significant (p < 0.05) – hillside snails have longer shells; reject the null hypothesis.
parts.working: B1 14 df and comparison with 2.14; B1 significant difference/reject null.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the result does not show that the difference is genetic.
parts.answer: The difference could be caused by environmental factors (e.g. food or calcium availability, temperature) rather than different alleles.

practice.stem:
Petal lengths (mm) were measured for wild poppy flowers from two fields.
Field X (7 flowers): 14.2, 13.8, 15.1, 14.6, 13.9, 14.4, 14.9
Field Y (9 flowers): 12.9, 13.4, 12.6, 13.8, 13.1, 12.8, 13.5, 13.0, 12.7

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean shell diameter of each group. Give each answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Field X: 14.41 mm; field Y: 13.09 mm.
parts.working: 1 mark each: 100.9 ÷ 7 = 14.41 mm; 117.8 ÷ 9 = 13.09 mm (check the sums of the readings before dividing).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate t, using t = (x̄₁ − x̄₂) ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark for the two sample variances and the denominator; 1 mark for the final t value (5.82).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using a critical value of 2.145 (df = 14, 5 % level, two-tailed), state whether the difference is significant.
parts.answer: Yes: 5.82 is greater than 2.14, so the difference in mean shell diameter is significant at the 5 % level.
parts.working: 1 mark: significant, with reason (calculated t greater than critical value).

practice.stem: Two populations of the same species have the same mean body mass of 25 g. The standard deviation is 0.4 g in population P and 1.9 g in population Q.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what the difference in standard deviation suggests about the selection acting on each population.
parts.answer: Population P (small SD) may be under stabilising selection: individuals near the mean are favoured and extreme phenotypes are removed. Population Q (large SD) may be under weaker or disruptive selection, or have more genetic variation, more environmental variation, or gene flow bringing in different alleles. The two populations are not shown to differ in mean, so the difference is in spread rather than in average value.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: P: stabilising selection removes extremes; Q: weak or disruptive selection / greater variation; genetic or environmental causes of variation; gene flow; the means are the same so the difference is in the spread; a test would compare survival of extreme individuals in each population.

practice.stem: Two samples of leaf length were taken from one population. Sample 1 had 4 leaves and standard deviation 2.0 cm. Sample 2 had 16 leaves and standard deviation 2.0 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of the standard error of the mean for the sample of 4 to that for the sample of 16. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which sample gives the more reliable estimate of the population mean, and explain why.
parts.answer: The sample of 16: a smaller standard error means the sample mean is a more precise estimate of the population mean.
parts.working: 1 mark: sample of 16 (smaller SE, because SE falls with the square root of n).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the five conditions that must be met for a population to be in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
parts.answer: (1) Very large population; (2) random mating; (3) no mutation; (4) no migration (no gene flow in or out); (5) no natural selection (all genotypes have equal survival and reproduction).
parts.working: 1 mark for each of the five conditions.

practice.stem: In a population of 400 pigeons, 16 are white. White colour is caused by a recessive allele w. The population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.

parts.label: a
