parts.working: B1 concentration decreases the further down / away from the leaves, with figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this concentration gradient produces mass flow of sap down the stem.
parts.answer: High sucrose concentration near the leaves gives a low water potential, so water enters by osmosis and hydrostatic pressure is high; lower sucrose near the roots means less water enters/water leaves, so pressure is lower; sap flows down the hydrostatic pressure gradient.
parts.working: B1 high solute concentration at top → lower water potential → water enters by osmosis; B1 high hydrostatic (turgor) pressure near source; B1 sap moves by mass flow from high to low pressure (towards the sink).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the sucrose concentration is still well above zero at the base of the stem.
parts.answer: Sucrose is still being carried on to sinks in the roots; it is only unloaded where it is used or stored.
parts.working: B1 sucrose not yet unloaded / still in transit to the root sinks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sugar beet root cells store sucrose at a concentration higher than that in the phloem sap. Explain why unloading sucrose into these cells needs energy.
parts.answer: Sucrose must move against its concentration gradient, so it is moved by active transport (using ATP / a proton gradient made with ATP).
parts.working: B1 against the concentration gradient; B1 active transport / co-transport needing ATP.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a potato tuber, sucrose is unloaded down a concentration gradient. Explain how the tuber keeps this gradient.
parts.answer: Sucrose entering the tuber cells is converted to starch (via glucose/fructose), keeping the sucrose concentration in the cells low, so sucrose keeps diffusing in.
parts.working: B1 sucrose converted into starch (insoluble); B1 so sucrose concentration in sink cells stays lower than in sieve tubes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one other way in which sucrose is used at a sink such as a root tip.
parts.answer: Respiration to release energy / to make cellulose for new cell walls.
parts.working: B1 respiration or synthesis of cellulose / other molecules for growth.

practice.stem: Scientists supplied one leaf of a cotton plant with carbon dioxide containing radioactive ¹⁴C. Aphids feeding on the stem were later removed, leaving their mouthparts (stylets) in the stem. Sap collected from stylets 72 cm below the leaf first contained ¹⁴C 1.5 hours after it was supplied.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of movement of the ¹⁴C in the phloem, in cm h⁻¹.
parts.answer: 48 cm h⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why aphid stylets are useful for studying the contents of sieve tubes.
parts.answer: The stylet penetrates a single sieve tube element; sap flows out under pressure without contamination from other cells, so pure phloem sap can be collected and analysed (and the flow shows the sap is under pressure).
parts.working: B1 enters one sieve tube/pure sap; B1 sap exudes under (hydrostatic) pressure.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the structure of sieve tube elements allows rapid mass flow of sap.
parts.answer: Sieve tube elements have no nucleus, few organelles and only a thin layer of cytoplasm, so little resistance to flow; they are joined end to end into long tubes; the end walls are perforated as sieve plates with large pores.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: few organelles/no nucleus; thin cytoplasm; end to end/continuous tube; sieve plates with pores.

practice.stem: A bean plant had eight leaves, numbered 1 (oldest, at the base) to 8 (youngest, at the top). Leaves 1–6 were fully expanded; leaves 7 and 8 were still growing. Leaf 5 was supplied with ¹⁴CO₂ for 30 minutes. After 4 hours, radioactivity was found in leaves 7 and 8, the shoot tip and the roots, but almost none in leaves 3 and 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why radioactivity was found both above and below leaf 5.
parts.answer: Leaf 5 is a mature source; sinks are present both above (shoot apex, young expanding leaves 7–8, which use sucrose for growth) and below (roots); sucrose moves by mass flow in different sieve tubes towards each sink.
parts.working: B1 leaf 5 is a source (photosynthesising, exporting sucrose); B1 young leaves/apex above and roots below are sinks; B1 transport in different sieve tubes / both directions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why almost no radioactivity was found in leaves 3 and 4.
parts.answer: These are mature leaves, which are sources themselves: they make more sucrose than they use and export it, so they do not import assimilates; their sucrose concentration/pressure is high so sap does not flow into them.
parts.working: B1 mature leaves are sources/photosynthesise for themselves; B1 high sucrose concentration / hydrostatic pressure, so no mass flow into them.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict how the distribution of radioactivity would differ if the plant had been flowering, with pods developing. Give a reason.
parts.answer: More radioactivity in the developing pods/seeds (and less in roots and young leaves), because developing seeds are strong sinks storing large amounts of assimilate.
parts.working: B1 more ¹⁴C in pods/seeds; B1 seeds/fruits are strong sinks (store starch, protein, oil), taking priority over roots/young leaves.

practice.stem: In a sieve tube of a squash plant, sap moved at 0.6 m h⁻¹. The sieve tube had a circular cross-section of internal radius 12 µm. The sap contained 0.5 mol dm⁻³ sucrose. Area of a circle = πr².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of sap passing through the sieve tube in one hour, in m³. Give your answer in standard form to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sucrose carried through the sieve tube in one hour, in µg. (1 m³ = 1000 dm³; Mr of sucrose = 342.) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two features of the sieve tube element that allow such fast flow.
parts.answer: No nucleus and very few organelles (no vacuole) leave the lumen open; sieve plates with large pores let sap pass from one element to the next; elements joined end to end form a continuous tube.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two features linked to low resistance: few organelles/no nucleus; sieve plate pores; continuous tube of elements end to end.

practice.stem:
Water potentials were estimated at a source (P) and a sink (Q) of a cotton plant.
location – xylem water potential / MPa – sieve tube sap water potential / MPa
P (source leaf) – −0.5 – −1.6
Q (developing boll) – −0.7 – −0.4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, in terms of water potential, why water moves from the xylem into the sieve tube at P.
parts.answer: At P the sieve tube sap (−1.6 MPa) has a lower (more negative) water potential than the xylem (−0.5 MPa), so water moves into the sieve tube by osmosis down the water potential gradient.
parts.working: B1 sieve tube water potential lower than xylem (quote figures); B1 osmosis down water potential gradient (through partially permeable membrane).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why water leaves the sieve tube at Q.
parts.answer: Sucrose is unloaded at Q, so the sieve tube water potential rises to −0.4 MPa, above the xylem (−0.7 MPa); water moves out by osmosis.
parts.working: B1 sucrose removed raises water potential of sap; B1 now higher than xylem so water leaves by osmosis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: During a drought the xylem water potential near P fell to −2.0 MPa. Suggest and explain the effect on translocation.
parts.answer: The xylem water potential is now lower than the sieve tube sap, so water does not enter (or leaves) the sieve tube at P; hydrostatic pressure at the source falls, so the pressure gradient and mass flow decrease.
parts.working: B1 water no longer enters / moves out of sieve tube; B1 lower hydrostatic pressure at source so slower mass flow/translocation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the apoplastic and symplastic pathways by which water crosses the cortex of a root.
parts.answer: Apoplast: water moves through the cell walls and spaces between cells, without crossing membranes. Symplast: water moves through the cytoplasm of cells, entering across the cell surface membrane and passing from cell to cell through plasmodesmata.
parts.working: B1 apoplast through cell walls/intercellular spaces; B1 symplast through cytoplasm; B1 via plasmodesmata.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the role of the Casparian strip in the endodermis.
parts.answer: The Casparian strip is a band of suberin in the endodermis cell walls that is impermeable to water; it blocks the apoplast pathway, so water (and ions) must enter the cytoplasm/cross a cell surface membrane, allowing the plant to control which ions reach the xylem.
parts.working: B1 suberin/waterproof, blocks apoplast; B1 forces water through cytoplasm/membranes, control of ion uptake.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change would increase the rate of transpiration from a wheat plant?
A a decrease in light intensity
B an increase in air humidity
C an increase in wind speed
D a decrease in air temperature
parts.answer: C an increase in wind speed
parts.working: Wind removes the humid layer of air near the stomata, making the water potential gradient between the air spaces and the outside air steeper. Higher humidity (B) reduces the gradient and so reduces transpiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how water enters a root hair cell from the soil.
parts.answer: The soil water has a higher water potential than the cytoplasm/vacuole of the root hair cell (which contains dissolved ions and sugars), so water moves in by osmosis through the partially permeable cell surface membrane.
parts.working: B1 soil water has higher (less negative) water potential than the cell; B1 osmosis across partially permeable membrane.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how root hairs increase the rate of water uptake.
parts.answer: They greatly increase the surface area of the root in contact with soil water.
parts.working: B1 large surface area (for osmosis).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Fields in parts of Punjab have become salty after years of irrigation. Explain why crops on these fields may wilt even when the soil is wet.
parts.answer: Dissolved salts lower the water potential of the soil water; the gradient into the root is reduced or reversed, so less water (or none) enters by osmosis and water may even leave the root cells.
parts.working: B1 salts lower soil water potential; B1 smaller/reversed water potential gradient so less water uptake by osmosis (water may be lost).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which property of water molecules is mainly responsible for the continuous column of water in a xylem vessel being pulled upwards as a whole?
A adhesion of water molecules to lignin in the vessel walls
B cohesion between water molecules caused by hydrogen bonding
C root pressure produced by active transport of ions
D the high specific heat capacity of water
parts.answer: B cohesion between water molecules caused by hydrogen bonding
parts.working: Hydrogen bonds between water molecules (cohesion) let the tension created by transpiration pull the whole column up. Adhesion (A) helps the water stick to the walls and resist gravity but does not by itself transmit the pull along the column; root pressure (C) only pushes water a short distance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term transpiration.
parts.answer: Loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata of the leaves.
parts.working: B1 loss of water vapour from leaves/stems (mainly via stomata).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the route by which water leaves a leaf, starting in a xylem vessel in a vein.
parts.answer: Water leaves the xylem and moves to mesophyll cells by osmosis or through cell walls (apoplast); it evaporates from the wet surfaces of mesophyll cell walls into the air spaces; water vapour diffuses through the air spaces; then out through the open stomata down a water vapour potential gradient into the air.
parts.working: 1 mark each: from xylem to mesophyll cells (apoplast/symplast/osmosis); evaporation from mesophyll cell wall surfaces; into air spaces; water vapour diffuses out through stomata (down a water potential / concentration gradient).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how water moves up the xylem from the roots to the leaves of a tall tree such as a chinar (Platanus orientalis).
parts.answer: Water evaporates from mesophyll cell walls into air spaces and diffuses out through stomata (transpiration); this lowers the water potential in the leaf, so water is drawn from the xylem; water molecules are held together by hydrogen bonds (cohesion), so a continuous column is pulled up under tension; adhesion of water to the lignified xylem walls helps; this is the cohesion–tension mechanism / transpiration pull.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: evaporation/transpiration from leaves; water potential gradient; cohesion by hydrogen bonding; tension/pull on column; adhesion to xylem walls; continuous column.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the diameter of a tree trunk becomes slightly smaller during the hottest part of a sunny day.
parts.answer: Transpiration is fastest then, so tension in the xylem is greatest; the water column pulls the xylem walls inwards, so the trunk narrows.
parts.working: B1 high transpiration/high tension; B1 xylem walls pulled inwards.

practice.stem: A student set up a potometer with a leafy shoot. The capillary tube had an internal radius of 0.5 mm. An air bubble moved 45 mm along the tube in 5 minutes. The volume of a cylinder is πr²l.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 7.07 mm³ min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate of water uptake measured by the potometer is not exactly the same as the rate of transpiration.
parts.answer: Some water taken up is used in photosynthesis or to keep cells turgid/in cell growth; some water may be produced in respiration; so uptake is not equal to loss.
parts.working: B1 water used in photosynthesis/turgor; B1 so uptake ≠ water lost by evaporation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two precautions when setting up the potometer.
parts.answer: Any two of: cut the shoot under water; assemble the apparatus under water so no air enters; seal joints with petroleum jelly/check airtight; dry the leaves; allow the shoot to equilibrate before taking readings.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: On a cool, still morning in a lawn in Islamabad, small droplets of liquid were seen at the tips of the grass blades. The air was saturated with water vapour. The droplets had disappeared by midday.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how root pressure is produced.
parts.answer: Cells of the endodermis/root actively transport mineral ions into the xylem, lowering the water potential of the xylem sap; water then enters the xylem by osmosis, creating a positive pressure that pushes water up.
parts.working: B1 active transport of ions into xylem (using ATP); B1 lowers water potential so water follows by osmosis, giving a pressure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why droplets were seen in the early morning but not at midday.
parts.answer: At night stomata are closed and humidity is high, so transpiration is very low; the xylem is not under tension and root pressure pushes water out through the leaf tips. At midday transpiration is fast, the xylem is under tension and water is pulled up, so it is not forced out.
parts.working: B1 night: little/no transpiration (stomata closed, humid, cool); B1 root pressure forces water out at leaf tips/hydathodes; B1 midday: high transpiration creates tension in xylem / cohesion-tension dominates, so no excess water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why root pressure alone cannot supply water to the top of a 20 m tree.
parts.answer: Root pressure is far too small to push a water column that high.
parts.working: B1 pressure produced is too low (only supports a column of a few metres).

practice.stem:
The transpiration rate of a wheat crop near Faisalabad was measured on a clear summer day.
time – transpiration rate / mm h⁻¹
02:00 – 0.05
06:00 – 0.12
10:00 – 0.68
14:00 – 0.92
18:00 – 0.35
22:00 – 0.05

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how transpiration rate changed over the 24 hours.
parts.answer: Very low (0.05) at night from 22:00 to 04:00; rose from 06:00 to a peak of 0.92 at 14:00; then fell to 0.35 at 18:00 and back to 0.05 by 22:00.
parts.working: B1 low at night and peak in the afternoon (14:00); B1 data quoted with units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the changes between 06:00 and 14:00.
parts.answer: Light causes stomata to open, so the stomatal aperture increases; temperature rises, increasing evaporation from mesophyll cell walls and the kinetic energy of water molecules; humidity falls, steepening the water potential gradient between leaf air spaces and air.
parts.working: B1 stomata open in light (aperture increases); B1 rising temperature increases evaporation/diffusion; B1 lower humidity gives steeper water potential/diffusion gradient.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the rate at 18:00 is still much higher than at 04:00 even though the stomata are only slightly open.
parts.answer: The air is still warm and dry at 18:00, so the diffusion gradient is steep; at 04:00 it is cool and humid.
parts.working: B1 temperature high / humidity low at 18:00 compared with night.

practice.stem: A student used a bubble potometer with a capillary tube of internal diameter 0.8 mm. At 20 °C the bubble moved 36 mm in 4 minutes. The room heater was then switched on; at 35 °C the bubble moved 63 mm in 3 minutes. Volume = πr² × distance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of water uptake at each temperature in mm³ min⁻¹. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 20 °C: 4.52 mm³ min⁻¹; 35 °C: 10.6 mm³ min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in rate from 20 °C to 35 °C.
parts.working: B1 (21 − 9) ÷ 9 × 100 = 133 % (same with volumes).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the effect of temperature on the rate of water uptake.
parts.answer: Higher temperature gives water molecules more kinetic energy, so more water evaporates from mesophyll cell walls and diffuses out faster; warm air can also hold more water vapour, lowering relative humidity and steepening the gradient; faster transpiration pulls water up the xylem faster.
parts.working: B1 more evaporation / faster diffusion (more kinetic energy); B1 steeper water vapour gradient OR more transpiration pull so more uptake.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why transpiration is described as an inevitable consequence of gas exchange in leaves.
parts.answer: Stomata must open to let CO₂ diffuse in for photosynthesis; the mesophyll cell surfaces must be moist for gases to dissolve and diffuse; so water evaporates from these surfaces and water vapour diffuses out through the same open stomata.
parts.working: B1 stomata open for CO₂ uptake; B1 moist cell surfaces / large surface area of mesophyll exposed to air spaces; B1 water vapour diffuses out of the open stomata.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways in which transpiration is useful to a plant.
parts.answer: It moves mineral ions up from the roots in the transpiration stream; evaporation cools the leaves; it supplies water to leaf cells for photosynthesis and turgor.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: transport of mineral ions; cooling by evaporation; supply of water to leaves (photosynthesis/turgor).

practice.stem: The rate of water loss from a potted maize plant was measured at 30 °C in a growth chamber at three relative humidities: 30 % – 4.6 g h⁻¹; 60 % – 2.9 g h⁻¹; 90 % – 0.8 g h⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the effect of relative humidity on the rate of water loss.
parts.answer: As humidity increases, rate of water loss decreases; the air outside the leaf contains more water vapour, so the water potential gradient (difference in water vapour concentration) between the air spaces and the outside air is smaller; so water vapour diffuses out of the stomata more slowly.
parts.working: B1 trend with figures; B1 smaller water potential/vapour gradient; B1 slower diffusion through stomata.

parts.label: b
parts.text: At 90 % humidity, the rate of water loss fell close to zero. Suggest one disadvantage to the plant of a very low rate of transpiration.
parts.answer: Less mineral ions (e.g. nitrate) carried to leaves in the transpiration stream / less evaporative cooling of leaves.

parts.label: c
parts.text: During a dry spell in Sindh, maize plants closed their stomata during the afternoon. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of this.
parts.answer: Advantage: reduces water loss, so the plant does not wilt. Disadvantage: less CO₂ diffuses in, so the rate of photosynthesis falls (and leaves may overheat).
parts.working: B1 each.

practice.stem:
Water potentials were measured along the pathway in a 25 m tall eucalyptus tree on a sunny afternoon.
soil −0.3 MPa; root xylem −0.6 MPa; leaf xylem −1.2 MPa; leaf mesophyll cells −1.5 MPa; air −95 MPa.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the formula pressure = ρgh, where ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³ and g = 9.81 m s⁻², to calculate the pressure difference in MPa needed just to hold a column of water 25 m high (1 MPa = 10⁶ Pa). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The measured difference in water potential between the root xylem and the leaf xylem was 0.6 MPa. Suggest why this is larger than your answer to (a).
parts.answer: Extra tension is needed to overcome the resistance/friction to water flow through the narrow xylem vessels, pits and cell walls, as well as to support the column against gravity.
parts.working: B1 resistance to flow / friction against vessel walls; B1 extra pressure gradient needed to move water at a rate, not just hold it still.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the low water potential of the air causes water to move up the xylem of the tree.
parts.answer: Air has a very low (very negative) water potential, so water vapour diffuses out of the leaf and water evaporates from mesophyll cell walls; water moves from the xylem into the leaf cells to replace it, creating tension in the xylem; cohesion between water molecules (hydrogen bonds) pulls the whole column up; adhesion to vessel walls helps.
parts.working: B1 water lost by evaporation/transpiration down the gradient to air; B1 creates tension/negative pressure in leaf xylem; B1 cohesion (H-bonds) means the column is pulled up as a whole (accept adhesion as extra point).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why an air bubble (embolism) stops water moving up that vessel.
parts.answer: The air bubble breaks the continuous column of water; cohesion can no longer transmit the tension from the leaves, so water below the bubble is not pulled up.
parts.working: B1 water column broken / not continuous; B1 cohesion-tension cannot act across the gap (no pull transmitted).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how pits in xylem vessel walls allow water transport to continue after an embolism.
parts.answer: Water can move sideways through pits into neighbouring vessels and pass around the blocked vessel, then back into the column above it.
parts.working: B1 lateral movement through pits to adjacent vessels; B1 bypasses the air-filled vessel.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Embolisms are more likely when the tension in the xylem is very high. Suggest why they are common in plants during a drought in the Thar Desert.
parts.answer: Dry, hot air and dry soil make the water potential gradient very steep, so tension in the xylem becomes very high; dissolved gas comes out of solution / the column breaks, forming bubbles.
parts.working: B1 low soil water and high transpiration give very high tension (very negative pressure); B1 column breaks / air drawn in / cavitation.

practice.stem:
Detached leaves of two species, X and Y, were kept in the same conditions for one hour.
leaf – leaf area / cm² – water lost / g h⁻¹ – stomatal density / mm⁻²
X – 45 – 0.81 – 220
Y – 120 – 1.56 – 310

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of water loss of each leaf in mg h⁻¹ cm⁻².
parts.answer: X: 18.0 mg h⁻¹ cm⁻²; Y: 13.0 mg h⁻¹ cm⁻²

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of water loss per stoma for each species, in µg h⁻¹. (1 mm² = 0.01 cm²) Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: X: 0.818 µg h⁻¹; Y: 0.419 µg h⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Species Y has more stomata per mm² but loses less water per cm². Suggest two features of leaf Y that could explain this.
parts.answer: Stomata sunken in pits or covered by hairs, which trap humid air and reduce the water vapour gradient; thicker cuticle; stomata partly closed / smaller pores.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: sunken stomata / hairs (humid layer, thicker boundary layer); smaller stomatal pores or partly closed stomata; thicker waxy cuticle; stomata only on lower surface / in grooves.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature is found in mature xylem vessel elements?
A cytoplasm and a nucleus
B sieve plates
C lignified walls with pits
D plasmodesmata linked to companion cells
parts.answer: C lignified walls with pits
parts.working: Mature xylem vessel elements are dead, empty tubes with lignified walls and pits for lateral movement of water. Sieve plates (B) are found in phloem sieve tubes.

practice.stem: A student looked at a transverse section of a young sunflower stem and a transverse section of a young sunflower root under a light microscope.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the arrangement of the xylem and phloem in the stem.
parts.answer: In vascular bundles arranged in a ring near the outside of the stem; in each bundle xylem is on the inside (towards the centre) and phloem on the outside.
parts.working: B1 ring of vascular bundles; B1 xylem inner, phloem outer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the arrangement of the xylem and phloem in the root.
parts.answer: In a central vascular cylinder (stele); xylem forms a central star/X shape with phloem in groups between the arms of the xylem.
parts.working: B1 central; B1 xylem star/cross shape with phloem between arms.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the tissue in the stem that lies between the epidermis and the vascular bundles.
parts.answer: Cortex (parenchyma; collenchyma may be present just below epidermis)
parts.working: B1 cortex.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about a mature phloem sieve tube element is correct?
A It has thick lignified walls with pits.
B It has no nucleus and is linked to a companion cell by plasmodesmata.
C It has no cytoplasm and no cell surface membrane.
D It has no end walls, so it forms a completely open tube.
parts.answer: B It has no nucleus and is linked to a companion cell by plasmodesmata.
parts.working: A mature sieve tube element loses its nucleus and most organelles but keeps a cell surface membrane and a thin layer of cytoplasm; plasmodesmata link it to its companion cell. D is wrong because the end walls remain as sieve plates with pores; open tubes with no end walls describe xylem vessels.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a transverse section of a dicotyledonous leaf, a vascular bundle is seen in the midrib. State whether the xylem is nearer the upper or the lower epidermis.
parts.answer: Nearer the upper epidermis (phloem is below it, nearer the lower epidermis).
parts.working: B1 upper (adaxial) side.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two functions of the xylem in a leaf.
parts.answer: Brings water to the leaf for photosynthesis and to replace water lost by transpiration; brings mineral ions (e.g. nitrate, magnesium); lignified tissue helps support the leaf blade.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: supplies water (photosynthesis / turgor / transpiration); supplies mineral ions; support.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the veins branch so that no mesophyll cell is far from a vein.
parts.answer: Water, ions and sucrose move between veins and mesophyll cells by diffusion/osmosis and through cell walls, which is slow over long distances; short distances keep supply and removal fast.
parts.working: B1 movement into/out of mesophyll by diffusion/osmosis (slow); B1 short diffusion distance so fast supply of water and removal of sucrose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each feature of a xylem vessel element, explain how it helps the vessel carry water: (i) no end walls; (ii) no cytoplasm or organelles; (iii) lignified walls; (iv) pits.
parts.answer: (i) forms a continuous, unbroken tube / column of water; (ii) less resistance, nothing blocks flow; (iii) strengthens wall so vessel does not collapse under tension, and makes it waterproof; (iv) water can move sideways into neighbouring vessels or cells.
parts.working: 1 mark per feature correctly explained.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one function of xylem other than transporting water.
parts.answer: Transport of mineral ions / support of the plant.
parts.working: B1 mineral ions or mechanical support.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the structure of a mature xylem vessel element with a sieve tube element. Give three differences.
parts.answer: Xylem: dead/no cytoplasm; lignified walls; no end walls (continuous tube); pits; no companion cells. Sieve tube: living with thin cytoplasm (no nucleus); cellulose walls not lignified; sieve plates with pores; associated with companion cells; plasmodesmata.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct paired difference, up to three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how lignin in xylem walls helps the transport of water.
parts.answer: Lignin strengthens the walls so the vessels do not collapse under the tension of the water column; it also makes walls waterproof and helps adhesion of water.
parts.working: B1 prevents collapse under tension; B1 waterproof/adhesion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the position of the xylem in a young dicotyledonous root compared with a young stem.
parts.answer: Root: xylem in the centre, often in a star/X shape, with phloem between its arms. Stem: xylem in a ring of separate vascular bundles near the outside, on the inner side of each bundle with phloem outside it.
parts.working: B1 root: central / star shape with phloem between arms; B1 stem: in vascular bundles arranged in a ring towards the outside, xylem on the inside of each bundle.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how each arrangement suits the forces acting on the organ.
parts.answer: A central core of strong lignified tissue in the root resists pulling forces as the shoot sways and the root anchors the plant; a ring of lignified tissue near the outside of the stem resists bending in the wind.
parts.working: B1 root – central strengthening resists pulling / tension; B1 stem – peripheral ring resists bending.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the layer of cells immediately surrounding the vascular tissue in a root.
parts.answer: Pericycle (with the endodermis outside it).
parts.working: B1 pericycle (accept endodermis).

practice.stem: An electron micrograph of phloem is described. A long cell with no nucleus has a cross wall at each end perforated by large pores (P); the inside of this long cell (Q) is mostly empty apart from a thin lining of cytoplasm against the wall. Beside it lies a narrow cell (R) with a large nucleus, dense cytoplasm, many ribosomes and many mitochondria. Fine channels (S) through the shared wall connect R with Q.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify structures P, Q, R and S.
parts.answer: P sieve plate; Q sieve tube element (lumen with thin layer of cytoplasm); R companion cell; S plasmodesmata.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why cell R has many mitochondria.
parts.answer: Mitochondria produce ATP by aerobic respiration; ATP is needed by the proton pumps that set up the H⁺ gradient used to load sucrose by co-transport.
parts.working: B1 ATP from (aerobic) respiration; B1 for active loading of sucrose / proton pumping.

practice.stem: Phloroglucinol in hydrochloric acid stains lignin red. Cellulose cell walls are not stained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which tissues in a transverse section of a sunflower stem would be stained red by this stain.
parts.answer: Xylem (vessel elements) and any sclerenchyma fibres (e.g. a cap of fibres outside the phloem).
parts.working: B1 xylem; B1 sclerenchyma / fibres.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the phloem would not be stained red.
parts.answer: Sieve tube elements and companion cells have cellulose walls that are not lignified.
parts.working: B1 phloem walls not lignified (cellulose only).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why lignin is important for the function of xylem vessels when transpiration is fast.
parts.answer: Fast transpiration puts the water in the xylem under great tension (negative pressure); the rigid lignified walls stop the vessels collapsing inwards, so the water column stays continuous.
parts.working: B1 water under tension/negative pressure; B1 lignin prevents the vessel from collapsing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Copy and complete the comparison of a sieve tube element and a companion cell for: nucleus; ribosomes; cell surface membrane; cytoplasm (amount and density).
parts.answer: Sieve tube element: no nucleus; no ribosomes; cell surface membrane present; only a thin layer of cytoplasm. Companion cell: nucleus present; many ribosomes; cell surface membrane present; dense cytoplasm.
parts.working: 1 mark per correct row (4 rows), with both cell types given in each row.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the companion cell keeps the sieve tube element alive.
parts.answer: Through the plasmodesmata it supplies proteins (made on its ribosomes), ATP and other substances that the sieve tube element cannot make because it has no nucleus or ribosomes.
parts.working: B1 supplies proteins / ATP / metabolites; B1 via plasmodesmata, because sieve tube element lacks nucleus and ribosomes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the structure of a companion cell is related to its function.
parts.answer: Many mitochondria – supply ATP for active transport/proton pumps; many plasmodesmata linking to the sieve tube element – allow sucrose to pass in and the companion cell to support the sieve tube; nucleus and dense cytoplasm/many ribosomes – carry out metabolic processes for the sieve tube element, which has no nucleus; cell surface membrane infolded (in some) – larger surface area for carrier/cotransporter proteins.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a feature linked to its function, up to four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a sieve tube element cannot survive without its companion cell.
parts.answer: The sieve tube element has no nucleus and few organelles/ribosomes, so it cannot make its own proteins or enough ATP; the companion cell provides these through plasmodesmata.
parts.working: B1 no nucleus/ribosomes, cannot make proteins; B1 companion cell supplies via plasmodesmata.

practice.stem: For water moving through a tube, the volume flowing per second is proportional to r⁴, where r is the tube's radius (other conditions the same).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many vessels of diameter 20 µm are needed to carry the same volume of water per second as one vessel of diameter 80 µm.
parts.answer: 256 vessels
parts.working: M1 rate ∝ r⁴ so ratio = (40 ÷ 10)⁴ (or (80 ÷ 20)⁴); A1 = 256.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Plants in cold or dry places often have narrow vessels. Suggest why, despite your answer to (a).
parts.answer: Narrow vessels are less likely to form air bubbles (embolisms) under high tension or when ice forms, and an embolism blocks only a small part of the total flow; many vessels give back-up routes.
parts.working: B1 narrow vessels resist embolism/cavitation (or freeze-thaw bubbles); B1 one blocked vessel removes only a small fraction of flow capacity / safer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why wide vessels in a tall tree need thick lignified walls.
parts.answer: The water inside is under high tension, so the wide wall must resist collapse.
parts.working: B1 resist collapse under tension (wider tubes collapse more easily).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why xylem vessel elements can work as dead, empty cells, whereas sieve tube elements must be living.
parts.answer: Water moves up the xylem passively by cohesion-tension, driven by evaporation; no membranes or energy are needed in the vessels, and empty tubes give least resistance. Translocation depends on loading sucrose, which needs living cells; a partially permeable cell surface membrane is needed so water enters by osmosis and hydrostatic pressure builds up for mass flow.
parts.working: B1 xylem flow passive / driven by transpiration (no ATP in vessels); B1 empty lumen = least resistance; B1 phloem needs a partially permeable membrane to let water in by osmosis / build hydrostatic pressure; B1 sucrose loading/unloading is active (living companion cells/sieve tubes).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the sieve tube element keeps a thin layer of cytoplasm and a cell surface membrane, but loses its nucleus and vacuole.
parts.answer: The membrane is needed for osmosis and to keep sucrose in; losing nucleus and vacuole leaves more space so sap flows with less resistance.
parts.working: B1 membrane retains solutes / allows pressure; B1 loss of large organelles reduces resistance to mass flow.

practice.stem: A sieve plate is a disc of diameter 20 µm at the end of a sieve tube element. It has 20 circular pores, each of diameter 1.0 µm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the sieve plate area that is open pore. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why sap can still move quickly through a sieve plate that is only about 5 % open.
parts.answer: The hydrostatic pressure gradient along the tube is large, so sap is pushed through the pores; the pores are wide enough and numerous enough that the sieve plate adds resistance but does not stop flow.
parts.working: 1 mark: large hydrostatic pressure gradient pushes sap through; 1 mark: pores are wide enough and many enough, so resistance stays low (sieve plates still add some resistance).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student wrote: 'Phloem sieve tubes are just like xylem vessels: both are tubes of cells joined end to end with their end walls removed, so both carry sap by the same mechanism.' Evaluate this statement.
parts.answer: Partly correct: both are long tubes formed from cells joined end to end. But sieve tubes keep perforated end walls (sieve plates), xylem vessels have no end walls; sieve tube elements are living with a membrane and thin cytoplasm, vessels are dead and empty; vessel walls are lignified, sieve tube walls are cellulose. Mechanisms differ: xylem by cohesion-tension (negative pressure, passive), phloem by mass flow under positive hydrostatic pressure set up by active loading; xylem moves water upwards only, phloem moves assimilates in either direction.
parts.working: B1 correct similarity (cells end to end forming tubes); then 1 mark each, max 4: sieve plates v no end walls; living with membrane v dead/empty; cellulose v lignified walls; tension (negative pressure) v positive hydrostatic pressure; passive v active loading; one direction v both directions.

practice.stem: A student is asked to make a low-power plan diagram of a transverse section through a root of Ranunculus (buttercup), as seen through a light microscope.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four rules the student should follow when drawing the plan diagram.
parts.answer: Any four of: draw no individual cells; use clear, continuous, sharp pencil lines; outline the different tissues only; draw in correct proportions; fill a large part of the space provided; no shading; label lines with a ruler that touch the tissue and do not cross; add a title/magnification if asked.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name three tissues that should be labelled on the plan diagram.
parts.answer: Any three of: epidermis; cortex; endodermis; pericycle; xylem; phloem.
parts.working: 2 marks for three; 1 mark for two.

practice.stem: A student is given a slide of a transverse section of a young sunflower stem and is asked to make a plan diagram.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three things the student should do, and two things the student should not do, when drawing a low-power plan diagram of this section.
parts.answer: Do: use a sharp pencil with clear, continuous lines; draw only the outlines of the tissue regions; keep the correct proportions of the tissues; make the drawing large (fill most of the space). Do not: draw individual cells; use shading; use sketchy or overlapping lines.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three 'do' points (sharp pencil / clear continuous lines; tissue outlines only; correct proportions; large size) and any two 'do not' points (no cells; no shading; no sketchy lines; no arrowheads on label lines).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name four tissues the student should label on the plan of this stem.
parts.answer: Any four of: epidermis, cortex, vascular bundle, xylem, phloem, pith (accept sclerenchyma / fibres).
parts.working: 2 marks for four correct; 1 mark for two or three.

practice.stem: A student's plan diagram of a transverse section of a buttercup root has these features: the stele is shaded in with pencil; some cortex cells are drawn individually; label lines have arrowheads and two of them cross; the word 'xylem' is written inside the drawing; the outer edge is made of several short, overlapping strokes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify four errors in this drawing and state how each should be corrected.
parts.answer: Shading – remove; individual cells drawn – show only tissue outlines; arrowheads on label lines – use plain lines that touch the tissue; label lines crossing – arrange lines so they do not cross; labels written on the drawing – write labels outside the drawing (with ruled lines); sketchy double lines – use single clear lines.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four errors with correction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three features that should be visible in a high-power drawing of three xylem vessel elements seen in longitudinal section.
parts.answer: The vessel elements joined end to end with no (or remnants of) end walls; the pattern of lignin thickening (e.g. spiral or rings) on the walls; pits in the walls; the empty lumen (no contents).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: elements end to end / continuous tube; lignin thickening pattern drawn accurately; pits; no cell contents; correct relative widths.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why a high-power drawing should show only a few cells.
parts.answer: So that detail of each cell can be shown accurately and large enough.
parts.working: B1 detail / accuracy of individual cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: List, in order from the upper surface, the tissue layers that should be outlined in a plan diagram of a transverse section through the blade of a dicotyledonous leaf.
parts.answer: Upper epidermis (with cuticle); palisade mesophyll; spongy mesophyll (with vascular bundle / vein); lower epidermis.
parts.working: B1 upper epidermis then palisade; B1 spongy mesophyll; B1 lower epidermis (accept vascular bundle within mesophyll).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the student should not draw the chloroplasts in this plan diagram.
parts.answer: A plan shows only the outlines of tissues, not cells or organelles.
parts.working: B1 plan diagrams show tissue regions only.

practice.stem: A student is asked to make a high-power drawing of a group of four adjacent cells from the palisade mesophyll layer of a leaf section. Each palisade cell contains many chloroplasts and has a large central vacuole.

parts.label: a
parts.text: List the features of a high-power drawing that an examiner would expect.
parts.answer: Exactly four cells drawn; each cell shared walls shown as double lines (cell walls of adjacent cells touching, showing both walls/middle lamella); cells drawn in correct proportion to each other and the size of the chloroplasts relative to the cells; chloroplasts drawn as outlines in the correct position (near the cell walls/surrounding the vacuole); clear unbroken lines, no shading; large drawing.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of the points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two structures that should be labelled on one of the cells.
parts.answer: Any two of: cell wall; chloroplast; cytoplasm; vacuole/tonoplast (nucleus if visible).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Using an eyepiece graticule, a student measured a transverse section of a root. The whole root was 120 eyepiece units across and the stele (vascular cylinder) was 30 eyepiece units across.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The student draws the outline of the whole root as a circle 90 mm in diameter. Calculate the diameter she should draw for the stele.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why measuring with the eyepiece graticule before drawing improves the plan.
parts.answer: It keeps the proportions of the tissues correct.
parts.working: B1 correct proportions/relative sizes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one feature of the endodermis that could be shown in a plan diagram and one that could only be shown in a high-power drawing.
parts.answer: Plan: the position of the endodermis as a thin ring around the stele. High-power: individual endodermal cells / thickened (Casparian strip) walls.
parts.working: B1 plan: outline/ring position; B1 high-power: individual cells or wall details.

parts.label: a
parts.text: List what the student should include in a high-power drawing of one stoma and the cells immediately around it, from an epidermal peel of a leaf.
parts.answer: Two kidney-shaped guard cells drawn to the correct shape and proportion; the pore between them; chloroplasts in the guard cells (and none, or very few, in ordinary epidermal cells); the nucleus of each guard cell if visible; the thicker inner walls of the guard cells; the outlines of neighbouring epidermal cells, in correct proportion.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: two guard cells correct shape; pore; chloroplasts in guard cells; nuclei; uneven wall thickness; adjacent epidermal cells in proportion; clear continuous lines, no shading.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two labels the student should add.
parts.answer: Guard cell; stomatal pore; chloroplast; epidermal cell; cell wall; nucleus.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: A student is drawing a longitudinal section of phloem at high power.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student should show the difference in width between the sieve tube element and its companion cell.
parts.answer: Draw the companion cell much narrower than the sieve tube element, with widths in the same ratio as in the specimen (measured with a graticule).
parts.working: B1 companion cell narrower, in correct proportion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three other features that should be shown in a high-power drawing of a sieve tube element and its companion cell in longitudinal section.
parts.answer: Sieve plate(s) at the ends of the sieve tube element; the companion cell running alongside with its nucleus; dense contents of companion cell compared with the almost empty sieve tube element; walls drawn as clear lines.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: sieve plate; nucleus in companion cell; companion cell contents dense; sieve tube lumen almost empty; cell walls clear; correct length relationship.

practice.stem: A student drew one vascular bundle from a stem section. The drawing is 75 mm wide. The actual width of the vascular bundle, measured with a calibrated eyepiece graticule, was 0.5 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the drawing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student adds a scale bar representing 100 µm. Calculate how long the scale bar should be on the drawing.
parts.answer: 15 mm

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a scale bar is more useful than writing the magnification if the drawing will be enlarged on a photocopier.
parts.answer: The scale bar is enlarged by the same factor as the drawing, so it stays correct; a written magnification would become wrong.
parts.working: B1 scale bar changes size with the drawing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four features of a good high-power drawing of three adjacent endodermal cells and the pericycle cells next to them.
parts.answer: Only the few cells asked for; large drawing; clear, continuous lines with no shading; correct shapes and relative sizes of the cells; cell walls shown with their thickness where visible (e.g. thickened endodermal walls); only structures actually seen drawn.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the student should draw what is seen on the slide rather than a textbook diagram.
parts.answer: Drawings are a record of the actual specimen; textbook diagrams may differ from it.
parts.working: B1 records actual observations / specimen may differ.

practice.stem:
Two students drew plan diagrams of the same buttercup root section, in which the stele is about one quarter of the root diameter.
Drawing A: large; cortex shown as many small circles (cells); stele drawn about half the root diameter; stele shaded; one label line ends in an arrow.
Drawing B: occupies about one third of the space given; cortex, endodermis and stele shown only as outlines; stele about one quarter of the root diameter; ruled label lines touching each tissue; no shading.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the rules for plan diagrams, decide which drawing is better. Give three reasons from the descriptions.
parts.answer: Drawing B is better (B1): it shows only tissue outlines with no cells; the stele is in correct proportion (about a quarter of the diameter); it has ruled label lines that stop at the tissue; it has no shading. Drawing A shows cells, is shaded, has the stele too large and a label line with an arrow.
parts.working: B1 B is better; then 1 mark each for three valid reasons comparing A and B.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Drawing B has one fault. Identify it and explain why it matters.
parts.answer: It is drawn very small (one third of the space), so detail and proportions are hard to show/check.
parts.working: B1 too small – drawings should fill most of the space so detail is clear.

practice.stem: In a vascular bundle, the actual width of the bundle was 0.40 mm and the width of the xylem region was 0.16 mm. A student drew the bundle 60 mm wide and drew the xylem 36 mm wide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of xylem width to bundle width in the specimen and in the drawing.
parts.answer: Specimen 0.40; drawing 0.60

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage error in the proportion of xylem in the drawing.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the width the student should have drawn for the xylem.
parts.answer: 24 mm

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest how the student could avoid this error in future drawings.
parts.answer: Measure the tissues with the eyepiece graticule (or ruler on the image) first and scale each measurement by the same factor.
parts.working: B1 measure first and scale / use graticule readings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The stem section is large and has twenty similar vascular bundles in a ring. The student is told to draw a plan of one sector containing three vascular bundles. Explain why this is acceptable and describe how the edges of the sector should be shown.
parts.answer: The section is symmetrical/repetitive, so a sector shows all the tissues and their arrangement; it allows a larger drawing with correct proportions; the cut edges of the sector should be shown as straight (ruled) lines from the centre, clearly not tissue boundaries.
parts.working: B1 sector is representative / shows all tissues because bundles are repeated; B1 allows drawing large enough to show proportions; B1 sector edges drawn as straight lines (e.g. from centre outwards) / not as tissue boundaries.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two tissues that must be included in the sector so that the plan represents the whole stem.
parts.answer: Epidermis and cortex at the outside, and pith at the centre (plus vascular bundles with xylem and phloem).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: epidermis; cortex; pith; vascular bundle with xylem and phloem.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write three annotations (short notes, not just labels) for a drawing of xylem vessel elements in longitudinal section, each linking a visible structure to its function.
parts.answer: Spiral/ring lignin thickening – strengthens wall so vessel does not collapse under tension but allows stretching as the stem grows; no end walls between elements – continuous column of water; empty lumen – low resistance to water flow; pits – water moves sideways to other vessels and cells.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three annotations naming a visible feature and its function.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between a label and an annotation.
parts.answer: A label names a structure; an annotation adds a note about it, e.g. its function or a detail.
parts.working: B1 annotation adds information / explanation beyond the name.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature would NOT normally be found in the leaves of a xerophytic plant?
A a thick waxy cuticle
B many stomata on an exposed upper surface
C a layer of hairs over the epidermis
D a small surface area
parts.answer: B many stomata on an exposed upper surface
parts.working: Many exposed stomata on the upper surface would increase water loss; xerophytes have fewer stomata, often sunken or on a protected lower or inner surface. A, C and D all reduce water loss. Distractor C may seem odd, but hairs trap a layer of humid air.

practice.stem: Marram grass (Ammophila) grows on coastal sand dunes. In dry weather its leaves roll up into a tube with the upper surface on the inside. The upper surface has deep grooves, many stiff hairs and all of the stomata. Large, thin-walled hinge cells lie at the base of the grooves.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how rolling of the leaf reduces water loss.
parts.answer: The stomata on the inner (upper) surface are enclosed in a space where humid air is trapped; this reduces the water potential gradient between the air spaces in the leaf and the air outside, so less water vapour diffuses out. Less surface is exposed to wind.
parts.working: B1 humid air trapped inside the roll; B1 smaller water potential / diffusion gradient (or less exposure to wind) so slower diffusion of water vapour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how hinge cells cause the leaf to roll in dry conditions.
parts.answer: When water is short, the large thin-walled hinge cells lose water and turgor; they shrink/become flaccid, so the leaf folds inwards along them.
parts.working: B1 hinge cells lose water / turgor; B1 so the leaf curls inwards.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one other feature of the inner surface that reduces water loss.
parts.answer: Hairs that trap moist air / stomata in pits or grooves.
parts.working: B1 hairs or sunken stomata/grooves.

practice.stem: Prickly pear cactus (Opuntia) grows in many hot, dry regions, including parts of Pakistan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how each feature helps the cactus survive in a hot desert: (i) leaves reduced to spines; (ii) a green, fleshy stem; (iii) a thick waxy layer on the stem.
parts.answer: (i) very small surface area for transpiration (also deters animals); (ii) stem carries out photosynthesis instead of leaves, and stores water in its tissues; (iii) waxy cuticle is waterproof, reducing evaporation from the surface.
parts.working: 1 mark each, linked to water conservation or survival.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Many cacti have a wide network of shallow roots. Suggest how this helps them.
parts.answer: They can quickly absorb rain water from the surface soil after brief showers before it evaporates.
parts.working: B1 rapid uptake of water from light rain / surface water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term xerophyte.
parts.answer: A plant adapted to survive in conditions where water is scarce (dry habitats).
parts.working: B1 plant adapted to dry conditions / low water availability.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The kikar tree (Vachellia nilotica, Acacia) of the Punjab and Sindh plains has leaves divided into many very small leaflets. Explain how small leaflets reduce water loss compared with one large leaf.
parts.answer: The total leaf surface area exposed to sun and wind is small, so there are fewer stomata and less surface from which water can evaporate; small leaflets also lose heat quickly and stay cooler, reducing evaporation.
parts.working: B1 smaller total surface area (fewer stomata exposed); B1 so less transpiration. Accept: small leaflets stay cooler, reducing evaporation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of a very long tap root for a desert tree.
parts.answer: It reaches water deep in the soil / near the water table.
parts.working: B1 reaches deep water.

practice.stem: Calotropis procera (aak) grows in the Cholistan and Thar deserts. Its leaves are thick, covered in a waxy layer and have many short hairs on both surfaces. It has a long, deep tap root.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each of the features described, explain how it helps the plant survive in a desert.
parts.answer: Thick waxy cuticle – reduces water loss by evaporation through the epidermis (cuticular transpiration); hairs – trap a layer of moist, still air near the stomata, reducing the water potential gradient so less water vapour diffuses out; deep tap root – reaches water deep in the soil/water table.
parts.working: 1 mark for each feature correctly explained.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two other adaptations, not mentioned above, that xerophytic plants may have to reduce water loss.
parts.answer: Any two of: sunken stomata/stomata in pits; rolled leaves with stomata inside; fewer or smaller stomata; small leaves/spines (reduced surface area); stomata open at night (CAM).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
Mean number of stomata per mm² of leaf surface.
plant – upper surface – lower surface
xerophyte – 0 – 145
mesophyte – 60 – 230

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the mesophyte's stomata that are on the lower surface. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compare the distribution of stomata in the two plants.
parts.answer: The xerophyte has no stomata on the upper surface and all of them on the lower surface; it also has fewer stomata in total (145 v 290 per mm²). The mesophyte has stomata on both surfaces.
parts.working: B1 xerophyte none on upper / all on lower v mesophyte both; B1 xerophyte fewer in total, with figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how this distribution reduces water loss in the xerophyte.
parts.answer: The lower surface is shaded and cooler, and less exposed to wind and direct sun, so evaporation and diffusion are slower; fewer stomata mean fewer pores for water vapour to escape.
parts.working: B1 lower surface cooler / shaded / less wind; B1 fewer pores so less diffusion of water vapour.

practice.stem:
The silvery leaves of a desert shrub are covered in dense hairs. Water loss was measured from leaves with hairs left intact and from similar leaves after the hairs had been carefully removed with adhesive tape.
intact – 2.1 mg cm⁻² h⁻¹
hairs removed – 3.4 mg cm⁻² h⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of removing the hairs.
parts.answer: Water loss increased from 2.1 to 3.4 mg cm⁻² h⁻¹ (by 1.3, about 62 %).
parts.working: B1 increase, with figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the hairs reduced water loss.
parts.answer: Hairs trap a layer of still, humid air next to the leaf surface; this raises the water potential just outside the stomata; the water potential gradient from leaf air spaces to air is smaller, so water vapour diffuses out more slowly. Hairs also reduce air movement over the stomata.
parts.working: B1 trap humid / still air; B1 reduced water potential (diffusion) gradient; B1 slower diffusion of water vapour out of stomata.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one other benefit of pale, dense hairs to a plant in strong sunlight.
parts.answer: They reflect light, keeping the leaf cooler so less evaporation (and less heat damage).
parts.working: B1 reflect sunlight / cooler leaf.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A desert plant keeps its stomata closed during the hottest part of the day. Explain how this reduces water loss, and why opening the stomata in the cool early morning loses relatively little water.
parts.answer: Closing the stomata at midday stops water vapour diffusing out when the air is hot and dry, so the gradient is steep. In the cool, humid morning the water potential gradient is small, so opening the stomata loses little water while CO₂ enters.
parts.working: B1 stomata closed → fewer open pores when the gradient is steep; B1 cooler, more humid morning air → smaller gradient, so little water is lost while CO₂ enters.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the stomata cannot stay closed all day without any cost to the plant.
parts.answer: Stomata must open to let CO₂ diffuse in for photosynthesis; if they stayed closed all day, the leaf could not make enough sugar for growth.
parts.working: B1 stomata must open for CO₂ uptake; B1 without CO₂ photosynthesis (and so growth) would slow or stop.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a spherical cactus stem of radius 10 cm. (Surface area of a sphere = 4πr²; volume = 4/3 πr³.)
parts.answer: 0.3 cm⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a flat leaf measuring 10 cm × 5 cm × 0.05 cm (treat it as a cuboid). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why a spherical, swollen stem is an advantage in a desert.
parts.answer: Its surface area to volume ratio is about 135 times smaller, so much less surface per unit volume through which water can be lost; a large volume stores water.
parts.working: B1 small SA:V means less surface for water loss relative to volume; B1 large volume stores water / comparison with figures.

practice.stem: Leaves of a dune grass on a beach near Gwadar were flat at 07:00 and tightly rolled at 13:00 on a hot, windy day. The next morning they were flat again.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the leaves were flat in the morning but rolled at midday.
parts.answer: In the morning it was cool and humid and the soil still moist, so hinge cells were turgid and the leaf flat; by midday transpiration exceeded water uptake, hinge cells lost water and turgor, so the leaf rolled.
parts.working: B1 morning – hinge cells turgid / plenty of water; B1 midday – high transpiration (hot, windy, dry) so water lost faster than taken up; B1 hinge cells flaccid → rolling.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage to the grass of rolling its leaves.
parts.answer: Less light falls on the photosynthetic surface and CO₂ uptake is reduced (stomata enclosed), so the rate of photosynthesis falls.
parts.working: B1 less light / CO₂ reaching mesophyll; B1 lower photosynthesis / slower growth.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which adaptation of a xerophytic leaf reduces transpiration mainly by keeping humid air close to the stomata?
A a thick waxy cuticle
B stomata in pits below the leaf surface
C a large number of stomata on the upper surface
D large air spaces in the spongy mesophyll
parts.answer: B stomata in pits below the leaf surface
parts.working: Sunken stomata trap still, humid air in the pit, reducing the water vapour gradient. A thick cuticle (A) reduces water loss across the epidermis itself rather than by humid air at the stomata.

practice.stem: In one desert plant, each stoma lies at the bottom of a pit. Water vapour must diffuse 30 µm from the stoma to the moving air at the leaf surface. In a related plant with stomata level with the surface, the distance is 10 µm (the thin layer of still air at the surface).

parts.label: a
parts.text: If the rate of diffusion of water vapour is inversely proportional to the length of the diffusion path, calculate the rate from a sunken stoma as a percentage of the rate from a stoma at the surface.
parts.working: M1 rate ∝ 1/distance so ratio = 10 ÷ 30; A1 = 33.3 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, in terms of water potential, why the air in the pit reduces water loss.
parts.answer: Water vapour collects in the still air of the pit, so the air there has a high water potential (high humidity); the gradient between the leaf air spaces and the air in the pit is small; the vapour must also diffuse further through still air before reaching moving air.
parts.working: B1 humid air trapped in pit; B1 higher water potential outside stoma → smaller gradient; B1 longer diffusion path / protected from wind.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Grey mangrove (Avicennia marina) grows in the Indus delta, in mud soaked with sea water, yet it has thick leaves with a waxy cuticle and other xerophytic features. Explain why.
parts.answer: Sea water has a high solute concentration so the water potential of the soil water is very low; it is hard for the roots to take in water by osmosis, as the gradient into the root is small; so the plant behaves as if in a dry habitat and must reduce transpiration.
parts.working: B1 high salt concentration in soil water; B1 very low (more negative) soil water potential, so little water uptake by osmosis; B1 so water must be conserved – features reduce transpiration (physiological drought).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the root cells of such a plant could still take in water from the salty mud.
parts.answer: By accumulating solutes (ions or organic solutes) in their cells so their water potential is lower than that of the sea water.
parts.working: B1 accumulate solutes / ions in root cells; B1 water potential of cells lower than soil water so osmosis inwards.

practice.stem:
Water loss from leaves of a desert shrub was measured with stomata open (in light) and with stomata fully closed (in the dark, after a treatment that closes stomata).
stomata open – 4.5 mg cm⁻² h⁻¹
stomata closed – 0.3 mg cm⁻² h⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of water loss that passes through the cuticle when the stomata are open, assuming the cuticular rate is the same in both conditions. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student concluded that 'a thick cuticle is the most important xerophytic adaptation'. Evaluate this conclusion using the data.
parts.answer: Not supported: with stomata open, over 93 % of water loss is through the stomata, so features that reduce loss through stomata (fewer, sunken, closing in heat) have the largest effect; the cuticle is important only when stomata are closed (in drought, it is then the main route); data are from one species / one set of conditions.
parts.working: B1 most loss (93.3 %) is stomatal when open; B1 so stomatal adaptations matter more while open; B1 cuticle becomes main route when stomata closed (or: only one species / no comparison with a thin cuticle).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Closing stomata during the hottest part of the day saves water. Explain two disadvantages of closing stomata for a desert plant.
parts.answer: CO₂ cannot diffuse in, so photosynthesis slows and less sugar is made for growth; less transpiration means less evaporative cooling, so leaf temperature rises and enzymes may be damaged; mineral ion supply in the transpiration stream is reduced.
parts.working: 2 marks per disadvantage: point + explanation. Any two of: less CO₂ uptake → less photosynthesis/growth; less cooling → overheating/enzyme denaturation; slower transpiration stream → less mineral ion transport.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how small leaves help to overcome one of these disadvantages.
parts.answer: Small leaves lose heat to the air quickly (thin boundary layer), so they stay cooler even with stomata closed.
parts.working: B1 small leaves cool more easily / lose heat faster.

practice.stem: Descriptions from a microscope slide set: Section X is roughly circular with a single ring of separate vascular bundles, each with xylem towards the centre and phloem towards the outside, and a large central pith. Section Y is circular with a central core of xylem shaped like a four-armed star, phloem between the arms, an endodermis around the core and a wide cortex; there is no pith.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which section is from a stem and which is from a root.
parts.answer: X is a stem; Y is a root.
parts.working: B1 both correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two observable differences between X and Y that support your answer, other than the presence of pith.
parts.answer: Any two of: vascular tissue in separate bundles in a ring (X) vs central stele (Y); xylem and phloem in same radius in X vs alternating in Y; endodermis visible in Y; xylem star shape in Y.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one feature that both sections have in common.
parts.answer: Both have xylem and phloem / epidermis / cortex.

practice.stem:
A student peeled the epidermis from both surfaces of a bean leaf and observed them at ×400.
Upper epidermis: cells with fairly straight walls; on average 2 stomata per field of view; cells large.
Lower epidermis: cells with wavy walls that fit together like jigsaw pieces; on average 14 stomata per field of view; cells smaller; each pair of guard cells has many green chloroplasts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a table to show three differences between the upper and lower epidermis peels.
parts.answer: Table with a feature column and 'upper epidermis' and 'lower epidermis' as headings: number of stomata – few (2 per field) v many (14 per field); shape of cell walls – straight v wavy; cell size – larger v smaller.
parts.working: B1 table with a feature column and both peels as headings; 1 mark each for any two correct differences (max 3).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one feature that is the same in both peels.
parts.answer: Both have guard cells containing chloroplasts / ordinary epidermal cells without chloroplasts / cells fitting together with no gaps.
parts.working: B1 any valid similarity from the descriptions.

practice.stem:
A student looked at a longitudinal section of a young stem and found two kinds of xylem vessel.
Vessel V: narrow; lignin deposited as separate rings or as a spiral, with unthickened wall between.
Vessel W: wider; walls almost entirely thickened with lignin except for many small, oval, unthickened areas.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two observable differences between vessel V and vessel W.
parts.answer: V has lignin in separate rings / a spiral with gaps of unthickened wall between; W is almost completely thickened with only small unthickened areas (pits). V is narrower than W.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two differences: pattern of lignin (rings/spiral v almost complete with pits); width (narrow v wide).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why vessels like V are found in parts of the stem that are still growing in length.
parts.answer: Rings/spiral thickening can stretch (like a coiled spring) as the cells around it elongate; complete thickening would prevent the stem growing / would break.
parts.working: B1 can stretch / extend; B1 because surrounding tissues are still elongating.

practice.stem:
Leaf F (from a shade tree in a well-watered garden): broad, thin, soft, dull green; thin cuticle; no hairs; stomata level with the lower surface.
Leaf G (from oleander, Nerium, on a roadside in Karachi): long, narrow, leathery and thick; thick shiny cuticle; many hairs on the lower surface; stomata in pits on the lower surface.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give one similarity and two differences between leaf F and leaf G.
parts.answer: Similarity: both are simple leaves with a midrib / both have a cuticle. Differences: F is broad and thin, G is narrow and thick; F has a thin cuticle, G thick and shiny; F has no hairs, G has many hairs on the lower surface; F stomata on surface, G in pits.
parts.working: B1 valid similarity; B1 + B1 any two differences stated for both leaves.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which leaf is more likely to come from a plant adapted to dry conditions? Give a reason based on your answer to (a).
parts.answer: G – thick cuticle / hairs / sunken stomata reduce water loss.
parts.working: B1 G with a reason.

practice.stem:
Two stomata were drawn from epidermal peels.
S1: two kidney-shaped guard cells, curved apart, with a wide oval pore between them; guard cells look swollen.
S2: two guard cells lying straight and close together; only a thin line between them; guard cells look less swollen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two observable differences between stoma S1 and stoma S2.
parts.answer: S1 has a wide, open pore; S2 has a closed (slit-like or no visible) pore. S1 guard cells look swollen/curved; S2 guard cells look straighter/thinner.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest which stoma came from a leaf kept in bright light and explain your answer.
parts.answer: S1 – stomata open in light (to allow CO₂ in for photosynthesis); guard cells become turgid and curve apart.
parts.working: B1 S1; B1 reason – open in light / turgid guard cells.

practice.stem: A student compared two leaf transverse sections. Leaf P (from a bean plant grown in a well-watered garden) has a thin cuticle, a flat blade, stomata level with the surface on the lower epidermis and a spongy mesophyll with large air spaces. Leaf Q (from a desert grass) is rolled into a tube with the lower surface outside; it has a thick cuticle on the outer surface, stomata in grooves on the inner surface lined with hairs, and a compact mesophyll with small air spaces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a table to show three observable differences between leaf P and leaf Q.
parts.answer: Table with column headings 'feature', 'leaf P', 'leaf Q'; differences such as: shape – flat vs rolled; cuticle – thin vs thick; position of stomata – level on lower surface vs in grooves on inner surface; hairs – absent vs present; mesophyll air spaces – large vs small.
parts.working: B1 table with ruled columns and headings for both leaves and feature; 1 mark per correct difference, up to three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest which leaf grows in a habitat with low water availability and give one reason from your table.
parts.answer: Leaf Q; e.g. rolled leaf traps humid air around stomata / thick cuticle.
parts.working: B1 Q with reason.

practice.stem:
Transverse sections of stems from two groups of the same species were stained so that lignified walls looked red.
Sun-grown: diameter 6.2 mm; 22 vascular bundles; a thick band of red-stained fibres outside each bundle; cortex 8–10 cells thick.
Shade-grown: diameter 3.8 mm; 15 vascular bundles; a thin band of red-stained fibres; cortex 4–5 cells thick.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a table to compare the two sections. Include three differences.
parts.answer: Table with a 'feature' column and columns for sun-grown and shade-grown stems: stem diameter (larger v smaller); number of vascular bundles (more v fewer); amount of red-stained tissue / fibres (more v less); epidermis/cortex (thicker v thinner) – using the data given.
parts.working: B1 table with appropriate headings (feature, sun, shade); B1 × 3 for three correct differences in comparative form.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why plants grown in shade have less lignified tissue.
parts.answer: They make less sugar by photosynthesis, so less is available to make cell wall materials such as lignin; plants in shade are often taller and thinner as they grow towards light.
parts.working: B1 less photosynthesis / fewer resources; B1 less material for lignified walls / growth in length rather than strength.

practice.stem:
Section H: very large air spaces separated by thin plates of cells; small amount of xylem with a few narrow vessels; very thin cuticle.
Section J: tightly packed cortex with few small air spaces; large amount of xylem with many wide vessels; thick cuticle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the xylem and air spaces in sections H and J.
parts.answer: H has much less xylem (a few small vessels) than J (many large vessels); H has very large air spaces throughout the cortex, J has few small air spaces; H has thin or no cuticle, J has a thick cuticle.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three comparative statements.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify which section comes from a water lily, which floats in a pond, and explain two pieces of evidence.
parts.answer: H. Large air spaces keep the petiole buoyant and let oxygen diffuse to submerged parts; little xylem because water is all around and little support is needed; thin cuticle as water conservation is not needed.
parts.working: B1 H; B1 + B1 any two linked explanations.

practice.stem:
A student observed a whole radish seedling root under a hand lens.
Region K (5–15 mm from the tip): covered in fine white hairs; translucent surface.
Region L (40–60 mm from the tip): no hairs; slightly brown, tougher surface layer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two observable differences between region K and region L of the root.
parts.answer: K has many root hairs, L has none; K epidermis cells are thin-walled, L has a darker, corky/thicker outer layer; K is near the tip, L further back.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why most water uptake happens in region K.
parts.answer: Root hairs give a large surface area; thin walls and no suberin, so water can enter easily by osmosis.
parts.working: B1 large surface area (root hairs); B1 thin / permeable outer walls.

practice.stem:
A student counted the vascular bundles in transverse sections of five stems from each of two species.
Species A: 18, 20, 19, 21, 20
Species B: 12, 11, 13, 12, 12

parts.label: a
parts.text: Draw a suitable results table and calculate the mean number of vascular bundles for each species.
parts.working: B1 table with stem number and species as headings, unit-free counts; B1 mean A = 98 ÷ 5 = 19.6; B1 mean B = 60 ÷ 5 = 12.0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one observable difference, other than the number of bundles, that the student should look for when comparing the two species.
parts.answer: Size/shape of bundles; amount of pith; thickness of cortex; position of fibres; whether bundles are in one ring.
parts.working: B1 any valid observable feature.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the student counted five stems of each species.
parts.answer: To show the variation and calculate a reliable mean / reduce the effect of an unusual stem.
parts.working: B1 reliability / representative mean.

practice.stem: A student has stained transverse sections of a young dicotyledonous root and a young stem of the same plant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three differences between the root section and the stem section that the student should record.
