parts.answer: Root: xylem central and star-shaped, stem: xylem in separate bundles in a ring; root: phloem between the arms of the xylem, stem: phloem outside the xylem in each bundle; root: no pith (or very small), stem: large pith; root: endodermis clearly visible around the stele; stem: no obvious endodermis; root: no cuticle/hairs on epidermis.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three paired differences.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two features that both sections share.
parts.answer: Both have an epidermis; both have a cortex of parenchyma; both have xylem and phloem.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem:
A student's table comparing a sun leaf and a shade leaf of the same tree is described.
Column headings: (blank) | 1 | 2
Row 1: thickness | 310 | 180
Row 2: palisade | present | present
Row 3: cuticle | thick | many stomata
Row 4: colour | green | green

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify four faults in the student's table and say how each should be corrected.
parts.answer: No heading for the features column – add 'feature'; specimens named only as 1 and 2 – use names (sun leaf, shade leaf); entries not comparative ('present' for both palisade) – describe the difference (one layer v two layers); unit missing from thickness – add µm in the heading; a feature that is the same for both included as a difference; one row compares different features (cuticle in one, stomata in the other).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four faults with corrections.

practice.stem:
Leaves were taken from the sunny south side and the shaded centre of a neem tree.
sun leaf: thickness 320 µm; two layers of palisade cells; 260 stomata per mm²; area 28 cm²
shade leaf: thickness 190 µm; one layer of palisade cells; 150 stomata per mm²; area 45 cm²

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the two leaves in three ways, using the data.
parts.answer: Sun leaf thicker (320 v 190 µm); two layers of palisade v one; more stomata (260 v 150 per mm²); smaller area (28 v 45 cm²).
parts.working: 1 mark each for three comparative statements with data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how two of these differences suit each leaf to its light conditions.
parts.answer: Sun leaf: two palisade layers use the high light intensity for more photosynthesis; more stomata allow more CO₂ in to match. Shade leaf: large thin blade captures as much of the dim light as possible.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two linked explanations.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why one leaf of each type is not enough to conclude that light causes these differences.
parts.answer: One leaf may be unusual (variation); other factors (age, height, water, temperature) may differ between the positions; repeats/many leaves are needed for a mean.
parts.working: B1 natural variation / sample size; B1 other variables not controlled (e.g. age, temperature, water).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The leaves of a dune grass were collected on two days. Sample 1 leaves were flat with the grooved upper surface exposed; sample 2 leaves were tightly rolled. Suggest two differences in weather between the two days and explain how they caused the difference.
parts.answer: Sample 2 day hotter and/or windier and/or drier (lower humidity, less soil water); transpiration was faster than water uptake, so hinge cells lost turgor and the leaves rolled; on the sample 1 day it was cooler/humid/rain, so hinge cells stayed turgid and leaves flat.
parts.working: B1 + B1 two weather differences (temperature, wind, humidity, rainfall); B1 hinge cells lose turgor on the dry day; B1 water loss > uptake / link to transpiration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one measurement (not a description) that could be used to compare rolled and flat leaves objectively.
parts.answer: Measure the width of the leaf (or the diameter of the roll) with a ruler/graticule; or the angle of the leaf halves.
parts.working: B1 any quantitative measurement.

practice.stem: A section of a square, ridged stem was stained with toluidine blue, which stains lignified walls blue-green and unlignified cellulose walls pink-purple. Each corner ridge has a large vascular bundle with a thick blue-green cap of fibres and a large group of blue-green xylem vessels. Smaller bundles between the ridges have a thin blue-green cap and a few vessels. The phloem, cortex and pith are pink-purple.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the colours to identify which tissues have lignified walls.
parts.answer: Xylem vessels and the fibre cap outside the phloem (both blue-green).
parts.working: B1 xylem; B1 fibres/sclerenchyma.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compare a vascular bundle at a corner ridge with a bundle between the ridges, and suggest a reason for the difference.
parts.answer: The ridge bundle has a larger cap of blue-green fibres and more xylem than the other bundle; the ridges are where the stem is strengthened, as the outer parts resist bending most.
parts.working: B1 more fibres/lignified tissue in ridge bundle; B1 more/larger xylem; B1 ridges at the edge give most resistance to bending / support.

practice.stem: A student calibrated an eyepiece graticule using a stage micrometer on which 1 division = 0.01 mm. At high power, 40 eyepiece graticule units lined up exactly with 25 stage micrometer divisions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the length of one eyepiece graticule unit in µm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A xylem vessel measured 12 eyepiece units across at the same magnification. Calculate its actual diameter.
parts.answer: 75 µm

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the graticule must be recalibrated if the student changes to a different objective lens.
parts.answer: The graticule scale stays the same size in the eyepiece but the specimen is magnified by a different amount, so each eyepiece unit represents a different actual length.

practice.stem: On a stage micrometer slide, 1 division = 10 µm. Using the ×40 objective, 50 eyepiece graticule units lined up exactly with 18 stage micrometer divisions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the length of one eyepiece unit in µm.
parts.answer: 3.6 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: A stoma measured 9 eyepiece units long. Calculate its actual length in µm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the eyepiece graticule must be calibrated rather than read directly.
parts.answer: The graticule is in the eyepiece, so the real distance one division represents depends on the magnification of the objective lens.
parts.working: B1 its divisions have no fixed real size / value changes with objective.

practice.stem: A student drew a pair of guard cells 48 mm wide. The actual width of the pair of guard cells was 0.12 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert the actual width to micrometres.
parts.answer: 120 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the drawing.
parts.working: M1 magnification = drawing size ÷ actual size, same units: 48 mm ÷ 0.12 mm; A1 ×400.

practice.stem: A photomicrograph of a stem section has a scale bar 20 mm long labelled 50 µm. A xylem vessel measures 34 mm across on the photomicrograph.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual diameter of the xylem vessel in µm.
parts.answer: 85 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the photomicrograph.

practice.stem: A root hair on a seedling of mustard was 0.75 mm long.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express 0.75 mm in micrometres.
parts.answer: 750 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student drew this root hair 60 mm long. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the formula linking image size, actual size and magnification.
parts.answer: magnification = image size ÷ actual size
parts.working: B1 (accept rearranged forms).

practice.stem: Nail-varnish impressions were taken of the lower surface of a chilli leaf. The diameter of the field of view at ×400 was 0.45 mm. Numbers of stomata in four randomly chosen fields of view: 31, 28, 34, 29. Area of a circle = πr².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the area of the field of view in mm². Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of stomata per mm² of lower epidermis. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: 192 per mm²

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why fields of view were chosen at random rather than where the stomata looked most numerous.
parts.answer: To avoid bias, so the sample is representative of the whole leaf.
parts.working: B1 avoid bias / representative.

practice.stem: Six xylem vessels in a stem section had these diameters in eyepiece units: 14, 17, 12, 15, 16, 13. At this magnification one eyepiece unit = 2.5 µm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean diameter of the vessels in µm. Give your answer to 4 significant figures.
parts.working: M1 mean = 87 ÷ 6 = 14.5 eyepiece units; A1 14.5 × 2.5 = 36.25 µm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the range of diameters in µm.
parts.answer: 30 µm to 42.5 µm

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why vessels cut exactly transversely should be chosen for measurement.
parts.answer: A vessel cut at an angle appears oval and wider than its true diameter.
parts.working: B1 oblique cut gives an oval/overestimated width.

practice.stem: With the ×10 objective, one eyepiece graticule unit was calibrated as 10 µm. The student then changed to the ×40 objective without recalibrating.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of one eyepiece unit with the ×40 objective.
parts.answer: 2.5 µm
parts.working: M1 magnification ×4 greater so each unit represents ¼ of the length; A1 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5 µm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sieve tube element is 8 eyepiece units wide with the ×40 objective. Calculate its width, and the number of eyepiece units it would cover with the ×10 objective.
parts.answer: 20 µm; 2 eyepiece units

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why measuring the sieve tube with the ×40 objective is more precise.
parts.answer: It covers more graticule units, so the uncertainty of reading (±½ unit) is a smaller percentage of the measurement.
parts.working: B1 more divisions / smaller percentage error.

practice.stem: A root hair of a wheat seedling has a radius of 6 µm and a length of 0.8 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Treating a root hair as a cylinder, calculate the surface area of its side in mm² (area of side of a cylinder = 2πrl). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: One centimetre of root carries 2000 root hairs. Calculate the total surface area of root hairs on this length of root, in mm². Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 60.3 mm²

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the importance of this surface area to the plant.
parts.answer: A very large surface area for water uptake by osmosis (and mineral ion uptake).
parts.working: B1 large surface area for absorption of water/ions.

practice.stem: A student made a drawing of xylem and phloem at a magnification of ×250.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the length of a scale bar representing 50 µm on this drawing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: On the same drawing a xylem vessel is 20 mm wide. Calculate its actual width in µm.
parts.answer: 80 µm

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why scientists usually give a scale bar on a micrograph instead of the magnification.
parts.answer: The scale bar stays correct if the image is enlarged or reduced (printed or on a screen).
parts.working: B1 remains valid when image size changes.

practice.stem: A student counted the stomata on the lower epidermis of a leaf of a guava tree in five fields of view at high power. The diameter of the field of view was 0.40 mm. Counts: 23, 19, 25, 21, 22.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of stomata per mm². Show your working and give your answer to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: 175 per mm²

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student drew a guard cell 60 mm long. The actual length of the guard cell was 150 µm. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the student counted stomata in five fields of view rather than one.
parts.answer: Stomata are not evenly spread over the leaf, so a mean of several fields gives a more representative/reliable estimate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty for a measurement of 8 eyepiece units read to ±0.5 unit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The same structure measured 32 eyepiece units at a higher magnification. Calculate the new percentage uncertainty, still ±0.5 unit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two other sources of error when measuring cells with an eyepiece graticule.
parts.answer: The cell edge may be blurred / hard to judge; the cell may not be cut through its widest part (section plane); parallax / lines not aligned; calibration itself has an uncertainty; cells shrink when the slide is prepared.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: In a longitudinal section of phloem, five sieve tube elements lying end to end, from one sieve plate to the sixth, spanned 62 eyepiece units. One eyepiece unit = 25 µm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean length of one sieve tube element in µm.
parts.answer: 310 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Estimate how many sieve tube elements make up a sieve tube 1 m long. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why measuring five elements together and dividing by five gives a more accurate mean length than measuring one element.
parts.answer: The reading uncertainty (±½ unit) is spread over five lengths, so it is a smaller percentage; it also averages variation between elements.
parts.working: B1 smaller percentage error / averages variation.

practice.stem:
Counts were made in one field of view of area 0.12 mm² on the lower epidermis of two leaves.
leaf P: 24 stomata, 136 other epidermal cells
leaf Q: 30 stomata, 220 other epidermal cells

parts.label: a
parts.text: The stomatal index = number of stomata ÷ (number of stomata + number of other epidermal cells) × 100. Calculate the stomatal index for each leaf.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the stomatal density (stomata per mm²) for each leaf.
parts.answer: P: 200 mm⁻²; Q: 250 mm⁻²

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Q has the higher stomatal density but the lower stomatal index.
parts.answer: Q's epidermal cells are smaller, so more cells (and more stomata) fit in each mm², but stomata make up a smaller proportion of the cells.
parts.working: B1 smaller epidermal cells in Q – density depends on cell size, index does not.

practice.stem: Using a stage micrometer (1 division = 10 µm), 40 eyepiece units lined up with 25 stage micrometer divisions at ×400. A guard cell measured 6 eyepiece units long.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of one eyepiece unit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the actual length of the guard cell.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The open pore is approximately an ellipse 4.0 eyepiece units long and 1.2 eyepiece units wide. Calculate the area of the pore in µm², using area of an ellipse = π × a × b, where a and b are half the length and half the width. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 147 µm²

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to set up a bubble potometer with a leafy shoot so that it gives valid readings.
parts.answer: Cut the shoot under water (at an angle) so no air enters the xylem; fill the potometer with water under water / with no air bubbles; fit the shoot into the tubing under water; seal joints with petroleum jelly so it is airtight; dry the leaves; let the shoot settle (equilibrate) for a few minutes before taking readings; introduce one air bubble at the end of the capillary.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: cut under water; assemble under water / no air bubbles; airtight seal (vaseline); dry leaves; equilibrate before timing; introduce a single bubble / reset with reservoir.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the rate of water uptake is then measured.
parts.answer: Measure the distance the bubble moves along the scale in a fixed time (e.g. 5 min) with a stop-clock; convert to volume using πr² of the capillary and divide by time.
parts.working: B1 distance moved in a measured time; B1 calculate volume (πr²l) per unit time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline a method to compare the number of stomata per mm² on the upper and lower surfaces of the leaves of a plant, using clear nail varnish, sticky tape and a microscope.
parts.answer: Paint a thin layer of nail varnish on a small area of each surface, away from the midrib; let it dry; peel it off with sticky tape and stick it on a slide; count the stomata in a field of view at ×400; measure/calculate the field of view area with a calibrated graticule or stage micrometer; count several (e.g. 5) random fields per surface and on several leaves of the same age; calculate the mean per mm².
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: nail varnish on both surfaces / same region of leaf; peel and mount; count stomata in field of view at high power; determine area of field of view; repeat several fields and leaves (same age/position); calculate mean density per mm².

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student wants to find out whether leaf area affects the rate of water uptake by a leafy shoot. Describe how she could change the leaf area and measure it.
parts.answer: Remove leaves one at a time (or cut off set fractions of leaves) from the same shoot; measure the total area of the remaining leaves by drawing round them on squared (graph) paper and counting squares (or from length × width with a correction factor); seal cut surfaces with petroleum jelly.
parts.working: B1 remove leaves / leaflets in steps; B1 measure area by tracing on graph paper (or image software); B1 seal cut surfaces / use same shoot.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three variables she should keep constant and how.
parts.answer: Temperature – keep in a room or water bath at constant temperature/thermometer; light intensity – lamp at fixed distance; air movement – no fan / closed windows; humidity – same room / measured with hygrometer; same shoot / same species.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three variables with a method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to compare the rates of water loss from detached leaves of two species, using only a balance, string and a stop-clock.
parts.answer: Choose leaves of similar age/size from each species; weigh each leaf; hang them on string in the same place (same temperature, light, air movement); reweigh at regular intervals (e.g. every 30 min for 4 h); calculate % loss in mass per hour (or loss per cm² of leaf area); use several (≥ 3) leaves of each species and find the mean.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: similar leaves; initial mass; same conditions; reweigh at intervals; percentage (or per area) loss; replicates and mean.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the results should be expressed as percentage change in mass.
parts.answer: The leaves have different starting masses, so percentage change allows a fair comparison.
parts.working: B1 different initial masses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to investigate the effect of humidity on the rate of transpiration of a leafy shoot. Your method should give valid and reliable results.
parts.answer: Use a potometer with one shoot; enclose the shoot in a clear plastic bag; vary humidity by placing in the bag a dish of silica gel / calcium chloride (dry), nothing, or wet paper towels / water (humid); measure the relative humidity in the bag with a hygrometer/humidity sensor; at least 5 different humidity values; allow 10 min to equilibrate at each; record bubble distance in a set time; repeat 3 times at each humidity and calculate the mean; keep temperature (thermometer, heat shield/water bath), light intensity (same lamp distance) and air movement constant; same shoot throughout.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: potometer + bag; method of changing humidity; measure humidity; ≥ 5 values; equilibrate before each reading; measurement of DV (distance/time → volume); repeats and mean; control temperature; control light; control air movement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation into the effect of light intensity on the mean width of stomatal pores in onion or bean leaf epidermis.
parts.answer: Keep plants or leaf pieces in the dark, then expose groups to different light intensities for the same time (e.g. 1 h), with the lamp at different distances (or measured with a light meter); use a heat filter / glass tank of water to keep temperature constant; peel lower epidermis quickly and mount in water; use a calibrated eyepiece graticule at ×400 to measure the width of 10 stomata chosen at random in each peel; calculate mean pore width; repeat with 3 plants; keep same plant species/age, temperature, humidity.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: range of ≥ 5 light intensities; how intensity is changed and measured; same exposure time; control temperature (heat filter); peel and mount method; graticule calibration; measure pores of several (≥ 10) random stomata; replicates/means; standardised leaf age/position.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation into the effect of temperature on the rate at which a dye moves up the xylem in celery stalks.
parts.answer: Cut stalks to the same length under water; stand cut ends in the same volume and concentration of dye (e.g. eosin or food colouring) in beakers in water baths at 5 temperatures (e.g. 10–40 °C); leave for a fixed time (e.g. 30 min); remove and cut stalk into 1 cm slices from the base until no dye is seen in the vascular bundles, or cut lengthways and measure height of dye with a ruler; rate = distance ÷ time; three stalks at each temperature; keep light intensity, humidity, number/size of leaves, stalk diameter constant.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: same length and leaf number; dye concentration and volume constant; water baths at ≥ 5 temperatures; fixed time; method of measuring distance dye travelled; calculate rate; replicates and mean; light/humidity controlled.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student wants to test whether living phloem is needed for sugars to leave a leaf. She will kill a ring of tissue on the leaf stalk (petiole) with steam, without harming the xylem's ability to carry water. Plan the investigation, including the control and how the results will be obtained.
parts.answer: Use a well-watered plant kept in the dark for 48 h to destarch the leaves; then steam a ring around the petiole of several leaves; leave untreated leaves on the same plant as controls; place plant in bright light for several hours then in the dark overnight (so starch would normally be exported as sucrose); remove leaves, boil in water then hot ethanol, rinse, and test with iodine solution; blue-black = starch; compare colour of steamed and untreated leaves (or use a colour chart / colorimeter on extracts); repeat on several plants.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: destarch first; steaming treatment on several leaves; untreated control leaves on same plant; light then dark period for export; starch test with iodine (boil, ethanol, rinse); comparison/quantification of colour; replicate plants; check leaves did not wilt (xylem intact).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an experiment to investigate the effect of sodium chloride concentration in the watering solution on water uptake by young maize plants grown in pots.
parts.answer: Use at least 5 concentrations of NaCl (e.g. 0, 25, 50, 75, 100 mmol dm⁻³) made by diluting a stock solution; water each pot with the same volume each day; at least 3 pots per concentration; seal soil surface with plastic so only transpiration loses water; weigh pots daily at the same time, mass loss = water lost (≈ uptake); or measure volume added to keep soil at a fixed mass; continue for a set time; control: same age/size plants, same soil type and mass, light, temperature, humidity; calculate mean mass loss per day per plant (or per cm² leaf area).
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: range of ≥ 5 concentrations incl. 0; preparation by dilution; replicates; same volume; cover soil; weighing method for uptake/loss; time intervals; controlled variables (≥ 2); calculation of rate/mean.

practice.stem: A student wants to investigate how wind speed affects the rate of transpiration of a leafy shoot of a hibiscus plant. She has a bubble potometer, an electric fan with one speed, a metre rule, a stop-clock and an anemometer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method she could use to carry out this investigation. Your method should allow her to collect valid and reliable data.
parts.answer: Any six of: cut the shoot under water and fit it to the potometer under water, airtight joints; vary wind speed by placing the fan at different distances (e.g. 25, 50, 75, 100, 125 cm) and measure the wind speed at the shoot with the anemometer; include a no-fan condition; allow the shoot to equilibrate for 5 min at each wind speed; measure the distance moved by the bubble in a set time (e.g. 5 min) with the scale/rule; reset the bubble with the reservoir; repeat at least three times at each distance and calculate a mean; keep light intensity (same lamp at fixed distance), temperature (fan may cool – monitor with thermometer) and humidity constant; use the same shoot throughout; convert distance to volume with πr²l and calculate rate per minute (per leaf area).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six valid points; detail must be specific.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation into the effect of air temperature on the rate of water uptake by a leafy shoot. Include how you would change temperature without changing other variables, and a risk assessment.
parts.answer: Potometer with shoot in a transparent box / incubator or room with thermostatic heater; ≥ 5 temperatures (e.g. 15–35 °C) measured with a thermometer next to the leaves; allow 15 min to equilibrate; fix light intensity with an LED lamp at a fixed distance (LEDs give little heat); keep humidity constant or measure it with a hygrometer (warm air in a closed box changes relative humidity) – e.g. use a humidifier/air flow; keep air movement constant (small fan at fixed speed, same at each temperature); record bubble distance in 5 min, three repeats at each temperature, reset bubble; calculate volume per minute (πr²l) and mean; same shoot; risk: glass capillary and sharp scalpel – cut away from body; electrical heater/lamp near water – keep apart, dry hands.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 7: method of changing temperature; ≥ 5 values in sensible range; measure temperature at leaves; equilibration; control humidity (and say why it is linked to temperature); control light with low-heat source; control air movement; DV measurement & calculation; repeats/mean; one risk with precaution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothesis: the dense hairs on the leaves of a desert plant reduce the rate of transpiration. Plan an experiment to test this hypothesis.
parts.answer: Choose pairs of leaves (or shoots) of the same age and size from the same plant; remove hairs from one leaf of each pair using adhesive tape; handle the other leaf in the same way (sham treatment, e.g. tape touched on lightly and lifted without removing hairs), so the leaves differ only in hairs; check removal with a hand lens; measure water loss: weigh detached leaves at intervals in identical conditions, or use a potometer for shoots; express as % mass loss or loss per cm² (area measured on graph paper); at least 5 pairs; keep temperature, humidity, light, air movement constant; check stomata not damaged by the tape (examine peels); analyse with a t-test (paired) to see if difference is significant.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 7: matched leaves; method of removing hairs; control treated similarly (sham treatment); check hairs removed / stomata undamaged; measure water loss (method + calculation); express per area or %; replicates; controlled variables (≥ 2); statistical test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan a field investigation to test whether xylem vessels in stems of the same shrub species are narrower in plants on a dry, stony hillside than in plants beside a stream.
parts.answer: Choose ≥ 10 plants at each site, selected at random (random numbers / grid); take stems of the same age/diameter and height above ground; cut thin transverse sections (or hand sections) and stain; measure the diameter of a fixed number (e.g. 20) of vessels per section with a calibrated eyepiece graticule, choosing vessels by a fixed rule (e.g. along a line from the centre) to avoid bias; calculate mean diameter for each plant then each site with SD; use a t-test for the difference between means; state null hypothesis; record other conditions (soil moisture with a probe, light) since only habitat differs; ethics – take small samples, permission.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 7: random sampling; sample size ≥ 10 per site; standardise stem age/position; sectioning/staining; calibrated graticule; unbiased choice of vessels; mean/SD; t-test with null hypothesis; measure soil moisture to confirm sites differ; ethics/permission.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student suggests that species with more stomata per mm² lose water faster. Plan how to collect data from 10 garden plant species to test for a correlation, and state how you would analyse it.
parts.answer: For each species: measure stomatal density by nail-varnish impressions of the lower and upper surfaces, counting 5 random fields of known area on 3 leaves; measure water loss from 3 detached leaves of similar age by weighing at intervals for a set time under the same conditions (same room, temperature, light, air movement), and express as mass lost per cm² per hour (leaf area from graph paper); calculate means; plot a scatter graph of density against rate; use Spearman's rank correlation; null hypothesis: no correlation; compare rs with critical value at p = 0.05 for n = 10.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 7: stomatal density method; area of field of view; replicate leaves/fields; water loss method; per unit area/time; controlled conditions; scatter graph; Spearman's rank; null hypothesis + critical value; species leaves of similar age.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation into whether the colour (wavelength) of light affects the rate of transpiration of a leafy shoot. Explain how you would make sure that only wavelength differs between treatments.
parts.answer: Use a potometer and the same shoot; place coloured filters (e.g. blue, green, red) between lamp and shoot, or use coloured LEDs; measure light intensity at the leaf with a light meter and adjust lamp distance (or LED power) so intensity is the same for each colour; control temperature with a heat filter/water tank and thermometer; keep humidity and air movement constant; allow 15–20 min for stomata to respond to each colour before readings; include white light and dark as references; take 3 readings at each colour and calculate mean rate; randomise order of colours.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 7: method of changing wavelength; same light intensity checked with meter; temperature controlled (heat filter); time for stomata to adjust; DV measurement; repeats/means; reference treatments (white/dark); randomised order; other variables (humidity, air movement) controlled.

practice.stem:
A potometer was used with a hibiscus shoot at different wind speeds produced by a fan.
wind speed / m s⁻¹ – rate of water uptake / mm³ min⁻¹
0 – 2.1
1 – 3.4
2 – 4.6
3 – 5.3
4 – 5.6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between wind speed and the rate of water uptake.
parts.answer: As wind speed increases the rate of water uptake increases, from 2.1 to 5.6 mm³ min⁻¹; the increase becomes smaller at higher wind speeds (levels off between 3 and 4 m s⁻¹).
parts.working: B1 positive relationship with figures; B1 levels off / smaller increases at higher speeds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the increase between 0 and 2 m s⁻¹.
parts.answer: Moving air removes the water vapour that collects outside the stomata, keeping the water potential gradient steep, so water vapour diffuses out faster; faster transpiration pulls more water up.
parts.working: B1 removes humid air / water vapour near leaf; B1 steeper gradient → faster diffusion → more uptake.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State a conclusion from these results.
parts.answer: Higher wind speed increases the rate of water uptake (transpiration) by the shoot, up to about 3–4 m s⁻¹.
parts.working: B1 conclusion stated, limited to this shoot/range.

practice.stem:
Dry blue cobalt chloride paper turns pink when it absorbs water. Squares of paper were clipped to the upper and lower surfaces of leaves of four species, and the time taken to turn pink was recorded.
species – upper surface / s – lower surface / s
R – 420 – 95
S – 300 – 160
T – 380 – 40
U – not pink after 1800 – 70

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the species that loses water fastest from its lower surface and give the evidence.
parts.answer: Species T – cobalt chloride paper on its lower surface turned pink fastest (40 s).
parts.working: B1 T with time quoted.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two conclusions about the distribution of water loss between the two surfaces.
parts.answer: In all four species the lower surface loses water faster than the upper surface (paper turns pink sooner); the difference is greatest in species U, which may have no stomata on its upper surface (paper not pink after 30 min).
parts.working: 1 mark each for two valid conclusions with reference to the data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the times for the upper surface are longer.
parts.answer: There are fewer stomata on the upper surface (and a thicker cuticle).
parts.working: B1 fewer stomata (or thicker cuticle) on upper surface.

practice.stem:
Celery stalks with different numbers of leaves were stood in dye solution for 30 minutes.
number of leaves – height reached by dye / cm
0 – 1.5
2 – 3.0
4 – 5.0
6 – 7.0
8 – 9.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of the number of leaves on the height reached by the dye.
parts.answer: The more leaves on the stalk, the higher the dye travelled in 30 minutes: 1.5 cm with no leaves rising to 9.0 cm with 8 leaves; from 2 leaves upwards the height rises steadily by about 1 cm per extra leaf (linear).
parts.working: B1 more leaves → greater height; B1 figures quoted.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain this result.
parts.answer: More leaves give a larger surface area with more stomata for transpiration; more water evaporates and is lost, so greater tension pulls water (and dye) up the xylem faster.
parts.working: B1 more leaves → more transpiration; B1 greater transpiration pull/tension so faster movement up xylem.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the dye still rose a little with no leaves.
parts.answer: Capillarity (adhesion to the narrow xylem walls) / some evaporation from the cut top of the stalk.
parts.working: B1 capillarity/adhesion or evaporation from stem surface.

practice.stem:
A complete ring of bark, including the phloem, was removed from a branch of an apricot tree in Gilgit. The xylem was not damaged. After three weeks, samples of bark were tested for sugar.
bark 5 cm above ring – 38 mg sugar per g
bark 5 cm below ring – 7 mg sugar per g
bark on an untreated branch – 19 mg sugar per g

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the sugar content of the bark above and below the ring after three weeks.
parts.answer: Above the ring the bark had much more sugar (38 mg g⁻¹) than below (7 mg g⁻¹).
parts.working: B1 comparison with figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What conclusion can be drawn about the transport of sugars in this branch?
parts.answer: Sugars are transported downwards from the leaves in the bark (phloem); removing the ring stops this, so sugars build up above the ring and fall below it.
parts.working: B1 sugars move down from leaves in the outer tissues (phloem); B1 blocked by ringing, so accumulate above.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the leaves above the ring stayed turgid.
parts.answer: The xylem (in the wood) was not removed, so water still reached the leaves.
parts.working: B1 xylem intact.

practice.stem:
Ten detached leaves were weighed every hour.
hour – mean mass of water lost during that hour / g
1 – 0.42
2 – 0.35
3 – 0.21
4 – 0.12
5 – 0.09
6 – 0.08

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the mean mass of water lost changed over the six hours.
parts.answer: Mass lost increased each hour but the rate slowed: 0.42 g in the first hour, falling to 0.08 g in the sixth hour.
parts.working: B1 cumulative loss rises; B1 rate of loss per hour falls with figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an explanation for the fall in the rate of water loss.
parts.answer: As the detached leaves lose water, guard cells lose turgor and stomata close; less water remains in the leaf so the water potential of the leaf falls, reducing the gradient.
parts.working: B1 stomata close as leaf wilts; B1 less water available / smaller gradient (water now lost mainly through cuticle).

practice.stem:
Four similar leaves were picked from a tree. Leaf A was untreated; leaf B had petroleum jelly on its upper surface; leaf C on its lower surface; leaf D on both surfaces. The leaves were hung up for 48 hours.
Initial mass / g: A 2.40, B 2.36, C 2.52, D 2.44
Final mass / g: A 1.62, B 1.65, C 2.37, D 2.38

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage loss in mass of each leaf. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 (initial − final)/initial × 100; A2 all four correct (A1 for two or three).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why percentage loss is used rather than loss in mass.
parts.answer: The leaves had different starting masses, so percentages allow a fair comparison.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what conclusions can be drawn from these results.
parts.answer: Most water is lost from the lower surface (blocking it reduced loss from 32.5 to 6.0 %); blocking the upper surface had little effect, so few stomata on the upper surface; the small loss from D shows a little water is lost through the cuticle/petroleum jelly or at the petiole; this suggests most stomata are on the lower surface.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three, with use of data in at least one.

practice.stem:
The transpiration rate of a potted sunflower was measured at different light intensities, with the temperature kept at 25 °C.
light intensity / klx – transpiration rate / g h⁻¹
0 – 0.3
10 – 1.1
20 – 1.8
30 – 2.1
40 – 2.2
50 – 2.2
60 – 2.2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the results.
parts.answer: Transpiration rate rose steeply from 0 to 20 klx (0.3 to 1.8), then more slowly to 30 klx (2.1), and stayed the same (2.2) from 40 to 60 klx.
parts.working: B1 increases with light intensity; B1 levels off at about 40 klx with figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate levels off above 40 klx.
parts.answer: Stomata are fully open above about 40 klx, so increasing light cannot increase stomatal aperture further; another factor (e.g. humidity, temperature, air movement) is now limiting.
parts.working: B1 stomata fully open / maximum aperture; B1 another factor now limits transpiration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student concluded: 'Light intensity is the main factor controlling transpiration'. Explain why this is not fully supported.
parts.answer: It only applies up to 40 klx; above that light has no effect; other factors were not tested (temperature, humidity, wind), so their relative importance is unknown; only one plant/species.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid points.

practice.stem:
The water loss of two wheat varieties was measured on 6 plants of each.
variety A: mean 3.1 g h⁻¹, standard deviation 0.6 g h⁻¹
variety B: mean 2.8 g h⁻¹, standard deviation 0.7 g h⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Can the student conclude that variety A loses more water than variety B? Explain your answer using the data.
parts.answer: No firm conclusion: although the mean for A (3.1) is higher than B (2.8), the ranges mean ± SD overlap widely (A 2.5–3.7, B 2.1–3.5), so the difference may be due to chance/variation; a statistical test (t-test) is needed.
parts.working: B1 not valid / cannot conclude; B1 mean ± SD ranges overlap (with figures); B1 difference may be due to chance – need t-test.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the investigation could be changed to give a clearer answer.
parts.answer: Use more plants of each variety (larger sample) / reduce variation by using plants of the same age and size.
parts.working: B1 larger sample size / standardise plants.

practice.stem:
An aphid feeding on a willow stem was cut away, leaving its stylet in a sieve tube. The total volume of sap that came out of the stylet was recorded.
time / h – total volume of sap / mm³
0 – 0
2 – 2.0
4 – 4.1
6 – 5.2
8 – 5.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the volume of sap collected changed with time.
parts.answer: Sap flowed out at a steady rate (about 1.0 mm³ h⁻¹) for the first 4 hours, then the rate fell and it almost stopped by 8 h.
parts.working: B1 steady at first, with figures; B1 then slowed/stopped.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the steady flow in the first 4 hours shows about the contents of sieve tubes.
parts.answer: The sap in sieve tubes is under positive (hydrostatic) pressure, so it is pushed out of the cut stylet without any sucking; this supports mass flow.
parts.working: B1 sap under pressure (turgor/hydrostatic); B1 evidence for mass flow / pressure flow.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the flow stopped.
parts.answer: The sieve plates / stylet became blocked (e.g. by callose or protein) / the source leaves stopped supplying sucrose in the dark.
parts.working: B1 blockage or reduced supply/pressure.

practice.stem:
Water uptake (by potometer) and water loss (by weighing) were measured at the same times for a potted tomato plant.
time – water loss / g h⁻¹ – water uptake / g h⁻¹
08:00 – 20 – 12
10:00 – 50 – 35
12:00 – 75 – 62
14:00 – 80 – 72
16:00 – 55 – 64
18:00 – 18 – 30

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the time at which water loss exceeded water uptake by the greatest amount, and calculate the difference.
parts.working: B1 10:00 (greatest excess of loss over uptake; 12:00 gives only 13); B1 50 − 35 = 15 g h⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe and explain the relationship between water uptake and water loss over the day.
parts.answer: Both rise to a peak in the early afternoon and then fall; in the morning loss is greater than uptake, because uptake lags behind loss – tension must build up in the xylem before water is pulled into the roots; in the late afternoon (16:00, 18:00) uptake exceeds loss as the plant replaces water lost earlier.
parts.working: B1 both follow the same pattern / peak around 14:00; B1 uptake lags behind loss (morning loss > uptake); B1 explanation – transpiration creates the pull; deficit made up later in the day.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what would happen to the leaves if uptake remained less than loss for several days.
parts.answer: The plant would lose turgor and wilt (stomata would close).
parts.working: B1 wilting / loss of turgor.

practice.stem:
Eight shrub species were grown in the same field and left unwatered for six weeks.
species – stomatal density / mm⁻² – plants surviving / %
A – 110 – 92
B – 145 – 85
C – 160 – 80
D – 190 – 64
E – 210 – 58
F – 240 – 41
G – 275 – 30
H – 300 – 22

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship shown.
parts.answer: As stomatal density increases, the percentage of plants surviving drought decreases (negative correlation).
parts.working: B1 negative correlation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why these data do not show that stomatal density causes the difference in survival.
parts.answer: Correlation is not causation; the species differ in other ways (root depth, cuticle thickness, leaf area, etc.) that could affect survival.
parts.working: B1 correlation does not prove cause; B1 other differences between species named.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the effect of stomatal density alone could be tested.
parts.answer: Compare plants of one species that differ only in stomatal density (e.g. varieties/mutants with altered density) under identical drought.
parts.working: B1 same species, differing only in stomatal density, same conditions.

practice.stem:
Rate of water uptake (mm³ min⁻¹) by a shoot at different temperatures, three trials each.
20 °C: 3.1, 2.9, 3.0
25 °C: 4.0, 4.3, 4.1
30 °C: 5.6, 7.9, 5.4
35 °C: 6.4, 6.7, 6.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and explain your choice.
parts.answer: 30 °C, trial 2 (7.9) – it is much higher than the other two trials at 30 °C (5.6, 5.4) and higher than the readings at 35 °C.
parts.working: B1 7.9 identified with reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate at each temperature, leaving out the anomalous result. Give answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: B1 at least two correct; B1 all correct, with 30 °C mean = (5.6 + 5.4) ÷ 2 = 5.5.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State a conclusion and say how confident you can be in it.
parts.answer: Rate of water uptake increases as temperature increases from 20 to 35 °C; fairly confident because the trend is consistent and repeats are close, but only 3 trials, one shoot, and an anomaly suggests some uncontrolled variable (e.g. air bubble / draught).
parts.working: B1 conclusion; B1 justified confidence statement (repeats close / limited sample / anomaly).

practice.stem:
Hypothesis: the rate of translocation increases with the concentration of sucrose supplied to a source leaf.
sucrose applied / mol dm⁻³ – rate of translocation / arbitrary units
0.0 – 4
0.2 – 11
0.4 – 18
0.6 – 24
0.8 – 27
1.0 – 27
1.2 – 28

parts.label: a
parts.text: Do the results support the hypothesis? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Partly: rate increases from 0 to 0.8 mol dm⁻³ sucrose applied to the leaf, supporting the idea that more sucrose loaded increases translocation; but above 0.8 the rate does not increase (plateaus), so it is not true over the whole range; only one plant / no repeats or variation shown.
parts.working: B1 supports at low concentrations, with data; B1 plateau above 0.8 does not fit a simple 'more sucrose = faster' prediction; B1 limitation – no repeats/statistics or range.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a biological reason for the plateau.
parts.answer: The co-transporter proteins in the companion cell membranes are all in use (saturated), so sucrose cannot be loaded any faster; or proton pumping/ATP supply is limiting.
parts.working: B1 carriers/co-transporters saturated; B1 so loading rate cannot increase further (or ATP/H⁺ gradient limiting).

practice.stem:
Radioactive sugar (¹⁴C) was supplied to a leaf. Radioactivity in the phloem sap was measured at three distances below the leaf, one hour and three hours after the label was supplied.
distance below leaf / cm – radioactivity at 1 h / arbitrary units – radioactivity at 3 h / arbitrary units
10 – 120 – 310
40 – 20 – 140
70 – 0 – 60

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the radioactivity at 3 hours changes with distance below the leaf.
parts.answer: It falls with distance: 310 at 10 cm, 140 at 40 cm and 60 at 70 cm.
parts.working: B1 radioactivity decreases as distance from the leaf increases; B1 quoted figures (310 → 140 → 60).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why there is no radioactivity at 70 cm after 1 hour but there is some after 3 hours.
parts.answer: The labelled sucrose must be carried down the phloem by mass flow; it takes time to reach 70 cm, so the label had not arrived after 1 hour but had after 3 hours.
parts.working: B1 labelled sucrose is moved from the source by mass flow, not instantly; B1 time is needed for the labelled sap to reach 70 cm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in radioactivity at 40 cm between 1 hour and 3 hours.

practice.stem:
Changes in the diameter of a poplar trunk and the tree's transpiration rate were recorded over 24 hours.
time – transpiration / arbitrary units – change in trunk diameter / µm
01:00 – 2 – +15
07:00 – 10 – +8
13:00 – 95 – −30
14:00 – 88 – −34
19:00 – 30 – −10

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between transpiration rate and trunk diameter.
parts.answer: When transpiration rate is high (midday), the trunk diameter is at its smallest; when transpiration is low (night), the diameter is largest; changes in diameter follow changes in transpiration.
parts.working: B1 inverse relationship; B1 data quoted (e.g. 14:00 smallest diameter at highest rate).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how these results support the cohesion-tension theory.
parts.answer: High transpiration creates tension (negative pressure) in xylem water; because water molecules are held together by cohesion and stick to vessel walls by adhesion, the tension pulls the walls inwards, so the trunk shrinks slightly; at night tension falls and the trunk expands.
parts.working: B1 transpiration produces tension in xylem; B1 cohesion/adhesion transmits tension to vessel walls; B1 walls pulled inwards → smaller diameter (reverse at night).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The minimum diameter occurred at 14:00, but the maximum transpiration rate occurred at 13:00. Suggest a reason for this delay.
parts.answer: It takes time for the tension to be transmitted down from the leaves to the trunk / for water stored in trunk tissues to be withdrawn.
parts.working: B1 lag for tension to travel down / withdrawal of stored water.

practice.stem: A piece of banana leaf had a mass of 14.2 g when picked. After 24 hours hanging in a classroom its mass was 12.5 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage loss in mass. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why the answer should be given to 1 decimal place rather than more.
parts.answer: The masses were measured to only 1 decimal place (3 significant figures), so more figures would suggest false precision.
parts.working: B1 matches precision of the raw data.

practice.stem: In a potometer, the capillary tube has an internal radius of 0.25 mm. The bubble moved 48 mm in 6 minutes. Volume of a cylinder = πr²l.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of movement of the bubble in mm min⁻¹.
parts.answer: 8.0 mm min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 1.57 mm³ min⁻¹

practice.stem: Distance moved by a potometer bubble in one minute, five trials (mm): 6.2, 5.8, 6.6, 6.0, 5.9.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean distance moved per minute.
parts.answer: 6.1 mm

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the range of the results.
parts.answer: 5.8 to 6.6 mm (a range of 0.8 mm)
parts.working: B1 lowest and highest values or the difference.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the mean is given to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: The raw readings were recorded to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: B1 same precision as data.

practice.stem: Radioactive sucrose moved 1.8 m down the stem of a sugarcane plant in 2.5 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of translocation in m h⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert your answer to cm min⁻¹.
parts.answer: 1.2 cm min⁻¹
parts.working: B1 72 cm h⁻¹ ÷ 60 = 1.2 cm min⁻¹.

practice.stem: A leaf of a pea plant has 45 stomata per mm² on its upper surface and 315 per mm² on its lower surface.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express the number of stomata on the upper surface to the number on the lower surface as a simple whole-number ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the leaf's stomata (per mm² of both surfaces) that are on the lower surface.

practice.stem: A potted chilli plant with its pot sealed in a plastic bag was weighed every hour. Its mass fell from 486.2 g to 481.4 g in 6 hours. The total area of one surface of all its leaves was 240 cm².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the pot and soil were sealed in a plastic bag.
parts.answer: So that water does not evaporate from the soil/pot; all mass lost is from the plant (transpiration).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of water loss in mg cm⁻² h⁻¹. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 3.33 mg cm⁻² h⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the rate is given per cm² of leaf area.
parts.answer: So plants with different leaf areas/sizes can be compared.

practice.stem: All the leaves from a shoot were traced on 1 cm² squared paper. 52 squares were completely covered and 18 squares were partly covered. Before the leaves were removed, the shoot had lost 0.732 g of water in 3 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Estimate the leaf area of the shoot by counting each part square as half a square.
parts.answer: 61 cm²

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of water loss in mg cm⁻² h⁻¹.
parts.answer: 4.0 mg cm⁻² h⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way to estimate the leaf area more accurately.
parts.answer: Use smaller squares (e.g. 1 mm²) / photograph on a grid and use image software / count only squares more than half covered.
parts.working: B1 any valid improvement.

practice.stem:
Four similar leaves were left for 24 hours. Mass of water lost:
A untreated – 1.20 g
B upper surface coated with petroleum jelly – 1.02 g
C lower surface coated – 0.30 g
D both surfaces coated – 0.06 g

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of water lost through the lower surface of the leaf in the untreated leaf, and express it as a percentage of the total loss.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the total loss through the upper surface.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what the loss of 0.06 g from leaf D represents.
parts.answer: Water lost through the petiole (cut end) / imperfect seal of the petroleum jelly / evaporation through the cuticle.
parts.working: B1 any valid route.

practice.stem:
Total volume of water lost from a shoot.
time / min – total volume lost / cm³
0 – 0.0
10 – 0.8
20 – 1.7
30 – 2.8
40 – 3.6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of water loss between 10 and 30 minutes.
parts.answer: 0.10 cm³ min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate over the whole 40 minutes.
parts.answer: 0.09 cm³ min⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the rate at exactly 20 minutes could be found from a graph of these results.
parts.answer: Plot cumulative volume against time and draw a smooth curve/line of best fit; draw a tangent to the curve at 20 min and calculate its gradient (change in y ÷ change in x).
parts.working: B1 tangent at 20 min; B1 gradient = Δy ÷ Δx.

practice.stem: Over 24 hours a potted maize plant took up 250 g of water and lost 244 g of water by transpiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the water taken up that was kept by the plant.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest what the water kept by the plant was used for.
parts.answer: Photosynthesis (as a reactant); growth – increasing cell volume / vacuoles; maintaining turgor; hydrolysis reactions.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: A gas-exchange instrument measured the transpiration of a cotton leaf of area 150 cm² as 4.0 mmol of water per m² per second.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of water lost by the leaf in one hour. (Mr of water = 18; 1 m² = 10 000 cm²) Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why scientists express transpiration per m² of leaf.
parts.answer: So leaves or plants of different sizes can be compared.
parts.working: B1 allows comparison regardless of leaf size.

practice.stem: The stalk of a growing melon fruit receives 0.6 cm³ of phloem sap per hour. The phloem in the stalk has a cross-sectional area of 0.05 cm², of which 25 % is sieve tube lumen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cross-sectional area of sieve tube lumen in the stalk.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean velocity of sap in the sieve tubes, in cm h⁻¹.
parts.answer: 48 cm h⁻¹
parts.working: M1 velocity = volume flow ÷ area; A1 0.6 ÷ 0.0125 = 48 cm h⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why using the whole phloem area would give a misleading value.
parts.answer: Only the sieve tube lumens carry the sap; using the whole phloem area (including companion cells, parenchyma, walls) would underestimate the velocity (12 cm h⁻¹).
parts.working: B1 only sieve tubes conduct, so velocity would be underestimated.

practice.stem: A single eucalyptus tree in a plantation near Lahore transpires about 120 dm³ of water per day in summer. The plantation has 400 trees per hectare.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of water, in m³, transpired by the plantation in 30 days. (1 m³ = 1000 dm³)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Express this as a depth of rainfall, in mm, over the hectare (1 hectare = 10 000 m²).
parts.answer: 144 mm

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why such plantations can lower the water table in dry areas.
parts.answer: The trees transpire more water than the rainfall replaces, so their deep roots draw down groundwater.
parts.working: B1 transpiration exceeds recharge from rain.

practice.stem: A potometer capillary has an internal radius of 0.3 mm. Scale readings of the bubble: start 12 mm; after 5 min 47 mm. The bubble was then reset to 5 mm by opening the reservoir tap, and after a further 5 min it read 41 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total distance moved by the bubble in the 10 minutes.
parts.answer: 71 mm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 2.01 mm³ min⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the bubble had to be reset half way through.
parts.answer: It had nearly reached the end of the scale/capillary, and must not enter the tubing holding the shoot.
parts.working: B1 reached end of scale / avoid air entering the shoot.

practice.stem: A student traced the outline of a leaf onto paper, cut out the shape and weighed it. The cut-out shape had a mass of 0.36 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paper of this type has a mass of 80 g per m². Calculate the area of the leaf in cm².
parts.answer: 45 cm²

parts.label: b
parts.text: The leaf lost 0.27 g of water in 2 hours. Calculate the rate of water loss in mg cm⁻² h⁻¹.
parts.answer: 3.0 mg cm⁻² h⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one source of error in measuring leaf area this way.
parts.answer: Paper thickness/mass per m² varies; inaccurate cutting; paper absorbs moisture changing its mass; the leaf tracing ignores folds/curvature.
parts.working: B1 any one valid source.

practice.stem: A student plans to investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of transpiration of a leafy shoot, using a potometer and a lamp.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent variable and the dependent variable, and how each would be measured or changed.
parts.answer: Independent: light intensity – changed by moving the lamp to different distances (or measured with a light meter). Dependent: rate of water uptake – distance moved by the air bubble in a set time.
parts.working: B1 IV with method; B1 DV with method.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how two other variables should be standardised.
parts.answer: Temperature – place a heat filter/glass tank of water between lamp and shoot, or use an LED lamp, and monitor with a thermometer; humidity/air movement – carry out in a closed room with no draughts; use the same shoot/species and same leaf area.
parts.working: 1 mark for each variable with a method of control, up to two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the lamp might affect the results in a way other than through light intensity.
parts.answer: A filament lamp releases heat, which increases temperature near the leaves and so increases evaporation/transpiration.

practice.stem: A student plans to stand celery stalks in dye solution at five different temperatures and measure how far the dye rises in 30 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: temperature of the water bath (dye solution). Dependent: the height/distance the dye moves up the stalk in a fixed time (or rate of movement).
parts.working: B1 IV temperature; B1 DV distance/rate of dye movement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three variables that should be standardised and how each would be kept the same.
parts.answer: Concentration and volume of dye – make up from one stock with a measuring cylinder; length of stalk/number of leaves – cut to same length, same leaf number; time in dye – stop-clock; light intensity – same lamp distance; humidity/air movement – same room.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three variables with a method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three variables that must be kept the same when comparing water loss from detached leaves of a guava tree and a mango tree.
parts.answer: Temperature; humidity; air movement; light intensity; time; age/position of the leaves on the tree; time since picking.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the leaves should be picked from the same side of each tree.
parts.answer: Sun and shade leaves differ (thickness, stomata), which would affect water loss.
parts.working: B1 position affects leaf structure / light exposure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student used the same leafy shoot in a potometer for every light intensity. Explain why this is better than using a different shoot each time.
parts.answer: Different shoots have different leaf areas, numbers of stomata and xylem, which would affect water uptake; using one shoot removes these differences, so changes are due to light only.
parts.working: B1 shoots differ (leaf area / stomata / size); B1 so only the IV changes / fairer comparison.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one disadvantage of using the same shoot for a long investigation.
parts.answer: The shoot may change over time (e.g. wilt, xylem blocked, stomata respond to time of day), so later readings are affected.
parts.working: B1 shoot changes with time / ages / gets blocked.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student compared the number of stomata per mm² on leaves from plants grown in sun and in shade. State three variables she should standardise when choosing leaves.
parts.answer: Species/variety; leaf age or position on the plant (e.g. 4th leaf from tip); part of the leaf sampled (e.g. halfway between midrib and edge); surface of leaf (lower); time of collection.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In an investigation, the phloem of some branches of a lemon tree was removed by ringing. Describe a suitable control.
parts.answer: Similar branches on the same tree (same size, number of leaves and fruits, same side) left un-ringed, or with bark cut and replaced, and treated otherwise the same.
parts.working: B1 un-ringed similar branches; B1 same tree/conditions/same handling.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the purpose of this control.
parts.answer: To show that any change (e.g. in fruit size) is caused by removing the phloem and not by other factors.
parts.working: B1 show effect is due to the ring/IV only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student changes humidity around a shoot by enclosing it in a plastic bag with different amounts of wet cotton wool. Explain why temperature might change with humidity and how this could affect the results.
parts.answer: Evaporation of water from the wet cotton cools the air in the bag (and a sealed bag may warm up in light); temperature affects rate of transpiration, so the change in rate could be due to temperature, not humidity.
parts.working: B1 evaporation causes cooling / bag warms; B1 temperature also affects transpiration rate – confounding variable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student could monitor and control temperature.
parts.answer: Place a thermometer/temperature probe inside the bag; place the apparatus in a constant-temperature room or water-jacketed chamber / use a heat filter between lamp and bag; record temperature at every reading.
parts.working: B1 measure inside bag; B1 method of keeping constant.

practice.stem: To investigate the effect of light intensity on transpiration, a student placed a 100 W filament lamp at 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 cm from a shoot in a potometer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the problem with this design.
parts.answer: Moving the lamp closer also raises the temperature of the shoot, so both light intensity and temperature change; it is not possible to tell which caused the increase.
parts.working: B1 lamp heats shoot / temperature changes; B1 so two variables change together (not valid).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways to solve this problem.
parts.answer: Place a glass tank of water / heat filter between the lamp and the shoot; use an LED lamp (little heat); keep the lamp at a fixed distance and change intensity with neutral-density filters or a dimmer, checking with a light meter; monitor temperature at the leaves.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: A scientist tests whether an inhibitor dissolved in ethanol reduces sucrose uptake by leaf discs floated on a buffered sucrose solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a suitable control for the inhibitor treatment.
parts.answer: Leaf discs from the same leaves in the same buffer and sucrose solution with the same volume of the solvent used for the inhibitor, but no inhibitor; same time and temperature.
parts.working: B1 same discs/solution without inhibitor; B1 includes solvent (vehicle) control.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why leaf discs for all treatments should be cut from the same leaves and mixed at random.
parts.answer: Leaves differ in age and sucrose-loading ability; random allocation of discs from all leaves spreads this variation evenly across treatments so it does not bias one group.
parts.working: B1 variation between leaves; B1 random allocation avoids bias.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student compared transpiration rates of rose bushes in two gardens, one in Murree and one in Karachi, on the same day. Explain why this is not a fair test of the effect of altitude.
parts.answer: Many variables differ between the gardens (temperature, humidity, wind, light, soil water, variety and age of bushes), not just altitude.
parts.working: B1 many uncontrolled variables; B1 named examples.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the student could make the comparison more valid.
parts.answer: Use the same rose variety of the same age; measure and record temperature, humidity, light and wind at each site; take measurements at the same time of day on several days; many plants per site.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each investigation, state whether the independent variable is continuous or categorical, and the type of graph to plot: (i) rate of transpiration of five different plant species; (ii) rate of transpiration at five temperatures.
parts.answer: (i) categorical – bar chart; (ii) continuous – line graph (plotted points joined with straight lines or a line of best fit).
parts.working: B1 each correct pair.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why points on a graph of rate against temperature should not be joined to zero if no reading was taken at 0 °C.
parts.answer: There is no evidence of the value at 0 °C, so it would be an extrapolation not supported by data.
parts.working: B1 no data there / extrapolation.

practice.stem: A scientist plans to measure the rate of sap exudation from aphid stylets on willow stems kept at different temperatures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two variables, other than temperature, that would be difficult to control in this investigation and explain how each could affect the results.
parts.answer: Aphid stylet blocking – flow may stop for reasons other than temperature; distance of stylet from source/sink – sap pressure and composition differ along the stem; age and health of plants/source leaf photosynthesis rate; time of day/light affecting sucrose loading; humidity affecting xylem water potential.
parts.working: 2 marks per variable: B1 variable; B1 how it affects rate of exudation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the effect of one of these variables could be reduced.
parts.answer: Insert stylets at the same distance from the source leaf / use plants of same age / keep same light conditions / discard samples where flow stops early.
parts.working: B1 valid method.

practice.stem: Cotton plants of cultivars P and Q were grown side by side in a field.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student wants to compare the rate of water loss from leaf discs of two cultivars of cotton. Explain why cutting discs with a cork borer is better than using whole leaves.
parts.answer: Discs all have the same surface area, so water loss can be compared directly; avoids variation in leaf size/shape and midrib.
parts.working: B1 standard area; B1 removes leaf size variation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discs cut from the same leaf are more similar than discs from different leaves. Explain how the student could use this to design the experiment, and what statistical test would match this design.
parts.answer: Use a paired design: from each of several plants take a leaf of the same position/age from each cultivar (or compare discs from the same leaf position), so each pair shares conditions; repeat for many pairs; analyse the differences within pairs (a paired t-test) – in an unpaired design use a t-test on independent samples.
parts.working: B1 pair/match samples (same age/position/conditions); B1 many replicates; B1 suitable statistical test (t-test, paired if matched).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A scientist will compare mean xylem vessel diameter in wheat grown with irrigation and wheat grown without irrigation (rain only). State four variables she must standardise and explain why one of them is important.
parts.answer: Variety/cultivar; growth stage/age of plants; position on plant sampled (e.g. same internode or leaf); soil type/fertiliser; time of sampling; method of sectioning and measuring. Explanation e.g. vessel diameter varies along a stem (often wider towards the base), so sampling different positions would give differences unrelated to water supply.
parts.working: 1 mark each for four variables (max 4); B1 one explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student set up a second potometer with no shoot, its tubing sealed with a stopper, alongside the potometer with the shoot. Explain why this is a useful control.
parts.answer: It shows whether the bubble moves for reasons other than water uptake by the shoot, e.g. leaks, evaporation, or expansion/contraction of the water as temperature changes.
parts.working: B1 checks for movement not caused by the shoot; B1 named cause (leak / temperature expansion / evaporation).

parts.label: b
parts.text: During the experiment the bubble in the control potometer moved 4 mm in the opposite direction to the one in which uptake moves it, as the room warmed. Explain this and say how the student should correct the readings from the potometer with a shoot.
parts.answer: Water expands as it warms, pushing the bubble back (away from the shoot); the same expansion would occur in the potometer with the shoot, making its readings too small; add 4 mm (adjusted for the same time and capillary) to the distance moved by the bubble in the potometer with the shoot.
parts.working: B1 thermal expansion of water; B1 underestimates uptake in the test potometer; B1 add the control movement to the test reading (correction).

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Rates of water loss from six potted coriander plants (g h⁻¹): 4.2, 3.8, 4.6, 4.0, 4.4, 3.6.
Standard deviation s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate.
parts.answer: 4.1 g h⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the standard deviation. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the standard deviation tells you about the data.
parts.answer: How spread out the values are around the mean (variation between plants).
parts.working: B1 spread / variability about the mean.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Twelve measurements of stomatal pore length had a mean of 9.6 µm and a standard deviation of 0.84 µm.
Standard error SE = s ÷ √n. 95 % confidence interval = x̄ ± 2 × SE.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard error of the mean. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between standard deviation and standard error.
parts.answer: SD measures the spread of the individual measurements around the mean; SE measures how precisely the sample mean estimates the true (population) mean, and it gets smaller as the sample size increases.
parts.working: B1 SD = spread of data; B1 SE = reliability/precision of the mean (depends on n).

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Sixteen readings of water uptake by a shoot gave a mean of 18.6 mm³ min⁻¹ and a standard deviation of 2.4 mm³ min⁻¹.
Standard error SE = s ÷ √n. 95 % confidence interval = x̄ ± 2 × SE.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the 95 % confidence interval for the mean.
parts.answer: 17.4 to 19.8 mm³ min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Another plant had a 95 % confidence interval of 20.5 to 22.9 mm³ min⁻¹. What does this suggest about the difference between the two plants?
parts.answer: The intervals do not overlap, so the difference between the means is likely to be significant (not due to chance).
parts.working: B1 no overlap; B1 difference likely real / significant.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: A t-test was used to compare the mean stomatal density of two varieties of rice, with 10 leaves of each variety. The calculated value of t was 3.46.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a null hypothesis for this test.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the mean stomatal densities of the two varieties.
parts.working: B1 no (significant) difference between means.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of degrees of freedom.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of t at p = 0.05 for this number of degrees of freedom is 2.10. State and explain the conclusion.
parts.answer: t = 3.46 is greater than 2.10, so reject the null hypothesis: the difference in mean stomatal density is significant (probability that it is due to chance is less than 5 %).
parts.working: B1 3.46 > 2.10 so reject null hypothesis; B1 difference significant / not due to chance (p < 0.05).

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Choose the most suitable statistical test for each investigation, from: t-test; Spearman's rank correlation; chi-squared test. (i) Is there a correlation between leaf area and the number of stomata per leaf in 12 plants? (ii) Is the mean xylem vessel diameter different in plants from two habitats? (iii) Do the numbers of aphids on the upper and lower surfaces of leaves differ from an expected 1 : 1 ratio?
parts.answer: (i) Spearman's rank correlation; (ii) t-test; (iii) chi-squared test.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Mean xylem vessel diameter (µm) in stems of seven well-watered and seven drought-treated sunflower plants.
watered: 12.4, 13.1, 11.8, 12.9, 13.5, 12.2, 12.7
drought: 10.9, 11.6, 10.4, 11.2, 11.8, 10.7, 11.3
Standard deviation s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)).
t = |x̄₁ − x̄₂| ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂); degrees of freedom = n₁ + n₂ − 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and standard deviation for each group. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Watered: mean 12.66, s = 0.57; drought: mean 11.13, s = 0.50
parts.working: B1 both means; B1 s watered 0.57; B1 s drought 0.50.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of t. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value at p = 0.05 for 12 degrees of freedom is 2.18. State a conclusion.
parts.answer: 5.33 > 2.18, so the difference is significant: drought-treated plants have significantly smaller vessel diameters (reject the null hypothesis).
parts.working: B1 compare with critical value and conclude correctly.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Height and mean xylem vessel diameter of nine young trees of one species.
height / cm: 45, 62, 38, 80, 55, 71, 90, 50, 66
vessel diameter / µm: 28, 35, 31, 44, 30, 41, 52, 33, 36
rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n(n² − 1)).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a null hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is no correlation between plant height and mean xylem vessel diameter.
parts.working: B1 no correlation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, rs. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of rs for n = 9 at p = 0.05 is 0.700. State a conclusion.
parts.answer: 0.92 > 0.700, so reject the null hypothesis: there is a significant positive correlation between height and vessel diameter.
parts.working: B1 correct conclusion with comparison.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: 100 aphids were placed on a bean plant. After 2 hours, 68 were on young, growing leaves and 32 were on old, mature leaves (equal leaf areas of each). χ² = Σ (O − E)² ÷ E.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the expected numbers if aphids show no preference.
parts.answer: 50 and 50

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate χ².

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of χ² for 1 degree of freedom at p = 0.05 is 3.84. State and explain a conclusion.
parts.answer: 12.96 > 3.84, so the difference from 1 : 1 is significant; aphids prefer the young leaves (perhaps because young leaves are sinks with sieve tubes rich in incoming sucrose and amino acids, or have thinner tissues).
parts.working: B1 significant / reject null; B1 aphids prefer young leaves (any sensible reason).

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Transpiration rate of 10 irrigated and 10 unirrigated sorghum plants.
irrigated: mean 24.5, standard deviation 2.8 mg cm⁻² h⁻¹
unirrigated: mean 19.2, standard deviation 3.4 mg cm⁻² h⁻¹
Standard error SE = s ÷ √n. 95 % confidence interval = x̄ ± 2 × SE.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the 95 % confidence interval for each group. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Irrigated: 22.7 to 26.3; unirrigated: 17.0 to 21.4 mg cm⁻² h⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: What can you conclude?
parts.answer: The intervals do not overlap, so the irrigated plants have a significantly higher mean transpiration rate.
parts.working: B1 no overlap → significant difference.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
The distance travelled by dye in 20 minutes in eight stems of a plant in a sunny position (cm): 22, 31, 18, 27, 35, 24, 29, 20.
Standard deviation s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and the standard deviation. Give the standard deviation to 3 significant figures.
