parts.label: b
parts.text: The same measurement on a shaded plant gave a mean of 14.2 cm and s = 1.9 cm. Compare the variability of the two sets of data.
parts.answer: The sunny plant's data are much more variable (s = 5.80 v 1.9; also larger relative to the mean).
parts.working: B1 comparison using s.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
A student measured the rate of transpiration of a potted plant at eight light intensities.
light intensity / klx: 5, 12, 20, 28, 35, 44, 52, 60
rate / cm³ h⁻¹: 0.8, 1.1, 1.0, 1.6, 2.1, 1.9, 2.6, 2.4
Spearman's rank correlation coefficient rs = 1 − (6Σd²) ÷ (n³ − n).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a null hypothesis for this test.
parts.answer: There is no correlation between light intensity and the rate of transpiration.
parts.working: B1 must say 'no correlation' (not 'no difference').

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate rs. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 ranks correct (rate ranks 1, 3, 2, 4, 6, 5, 8, 7); M1 Σd² = 6; A1 rs = 1 − 36/504 = 0.93.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of rs for n = 8 at p = 0.05 is 0.738. State a conclusion.
parts.answer: 0.93 > 0.738, so reject the null hypothesis; there is a significant positive correlation between light intensity and rate of transpiration.
parts.working: B1 compare/reject null; B1 significant positive correlation.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the result does not prove that higher light intensity causes faster transpiration.
parts.answer: Correlation does not show cause; another factor that changed with light intensity (e.g. temperature, if a lamp was used) could cause the increase.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Stomatal density (per mm²) of leaves from a shrub species on an exposed hilltop and in a sheltered valley.
hilltop (n = 6): 38, 45, 41, 50, 36, 44
valley (n = 8): 33, 40, 29, 37, 35, 31, 38, 34
Standard deviation s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)).
t = |x̄₁ − x̄₂| ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂); degrees of freedom = n₁ + n₂ − 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of t. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the degrees of freedom and use the critical values to state a conclusion. Critical values at p = 0.05: 10 df 2.23; 12 df 2.18; 14 df 2.14.
parts.answer: 12 df; 3.15 > 2.18, so the difference is significant – the hilltop plants have a significantly higher stomatal density (reject the null hypothesis).
parts.working: B1 df = 6 + 8 − 2 = 12; B1 correct conclusion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the result does not show that the difference is caused by exposure to wind.
parts.answer: Other factors differ between the sites (light, temperature, soil water, genetics), so cause cannot be shown from a field comparison.
parts.working: B1 other uncontrolled factors / correlation not cause.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Light intensity (klx) and transpiration rate (g h⁻¹) were recorded for a potted plant on ten occasions.
light: 12, 18, 18, 25, 30, 34, 34, 41, 47, 52
rate: 0.9, 1.4, 1.1, 1.8, 1.6, 2.4, 2.2, 2.0, 2.9, 2.7
rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n(n² − 1)).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate rs, using the mean of the tied ranks where values are equal. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The critical value of rs for n = 10 at p = 0.05 is 0.648. State a conclusion.
parts.answer: 0.93 > 0.648: significant positive correlation between light intensity and transpiration rate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Spearman's rank was used rather than a t-test.
parts.answer: The aim is to test for a correlation between two variables measured on the same plants, not a difference between two means.
parts.working: B1 correlation, not difference between groups.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: Ninety seedlings of a desert shrub were planted in each of three soil types (loam, sandy loam, sand) and left without watering. After 8 weeks, 85 seedlings had survived in total: loam 38, sandy loam 30, sand 17. χ² = Σ (O − E)² ÷ E.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected number surviving in each soil if soil type has no effect.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate χ². Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of χ² at p = 0.05 is 5.99 for 2 degrees of freedom. Explain why there are 2 degrees of freedom and state the conclusion.
parts.answer: Three categories − 1 = 2 df; 7.93 > 5.99 so soil type has a significant effect on survival (reject null hypothesis).
parts.working: B1 df = number of categories − 1; B1 conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Rates of water uptake (mm³ min⁻¹), five readings each.
shoot X: mean 15.4, standard deviation 3.2
shoot Y: mean 12.1, standard deviation 3.0
Standard error SE = s ÷ √n. 95 % confidence interval = x̄ ± 2 × SE.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard error of the mean for each shoot. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Shoot X: 1.43 mm³ min⁻¹; shoot Y: 1.34 mm³ min⁻¹
parts.working: M1 SE = s ÷ √n: 3.2 ÷ √5 = 1.43 (X) and 3.0 ÷ √5 = 1.34 (Y); A1 both correct with units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student drew error bars of ± 1 standard deviation and said 'the bars overlap, so the difference is not significant'. Another drew ± 2 SE bars. Explain which error bars are more useful and what the overlap shows.
parts.answer: ± 2 SE (95 % CI) bars show how reliable each mean is, so they are appropriate for judging whether means differ; SD bars show the spread of the data, not the reliability of the mean. Here the 95 % CIs are about 12.5 to 18.3 (X) and 9.4 to 14.8 (Y), which overlap (12.5 to 14.8), so the difference between the means may not be significant – a t-test or more replicates are needed.
parts.working: B1 2SE/CI bars show reliability of means; B1 SD shows variability, not suited to comparing means; B1 CIs overlap so no evidence of significant difference / need more data or a t-test.

practice.stem: A student used a potometer with a leafy shoot in still air at 20 °C. The student then placed a fan so that air blew across the leaves and repeated the measurement at 20 °C. Distance moved by the air bubble in 10 minutes: still air 14 mm; with fan 37 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of movement of the bubble in the experiment with the fan, in mm min⁻¹.
parts.working: B1 37 mm ÷ 10 min = 3.7 mm min⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the bubble moved further when the fan was blowing over the leaves.
parts.answer: Moving air carries away water vapour from around the leaf surface, so the water vapour concentration gradient between the leaf air spaces and the air outside stays steep. Water vapour diffuses out through the stomata faster, so transpiration increases and more water is drawn up the xylem, moving the bubble further.
parts.working: 1 mark: moving air removes water vapour from the leaf surface; 1 mark: steeper/maintained concentration gradient so faster diffusion out of stomata; 1 mark: more water lost by transpiration so more drawn up the xylem (transpiration pull).

practice.stem: Potato cylinders of equal size were weighed, placed in sucrose solutions for 1 hour, and weighed again. Percentage change in mass: 0.0 mol dm⁻³ +12.0 %; 0.2 mol dm⁻³ +4.0 %; 0.4 mol dm⁻³ −3.0 %; 0.6 mol dm⁻³ −9.0 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Estimate, by linear interpolation between the two nearest results, the sucrose concentration at which there was no change in mass. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 0.31 mol dm⁻³ (approximately)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the mass of the cylinders increased in 0.0 mol dm⁻³ sucrose.
parts.answer: Pure water has a higher water potential than the potato cells, so water enters the cells by osmosis across the partially permeable membranes. The cells become turgid and the cylinders gain mass.
parts.working: B1 water potential of the cells is lower than that of pure water; B1 water enters by osmosis so cells swell (turgid).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the cylinders lost mass in 0.6 mol dm⁻³ sucrose.
parts.answer: The sucrose solution has a lower (more negative) water potential than the cells, so water leaves the cells by osmosis. The cells lose turgor and the cylinders lose mass.
parts.working: B1 solution water potential lower than the cell contents; B1 water leaves by osmosis, cells become flaccid.

practice.stem: Leaves of two plants were detached and weighed, then left on the laboratory bench for 6 hours. Leaves of a tropical rainforest plant lost 42 % of their fresh mass. Leaves of a desert succulent lost 6 % of their fresh mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the percentage mass loss was for the rainforest leaves than for the succulent leaves.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the succulent leaves lost much less mass.
parts.answer: Any three of: a thick waxy cuticle reduces evaporation through the epidermis; few stomata, or stomata sunken in pits, reduce the area through which vapour can escape; stomata closed in the day so little vapour escapes at the hottest time; a small surface area to volume ratio; water-storing tissue keeps the cells turgid and reduces the water potential gradient.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: thick waxy cuticle; few or sunken stomata; stomata closed in the day; small surface area to volume ratio; water-storage tissue.

practice.stem: A student measured the rate of water uptake by a shoot at five temperatures in a potometer. Results (mm³ min⁻¹): 10 °C 2; 20 °C 5; 30 °C 9; 40 °C 12; 45 °C 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the rate of water uptake changes between 10 °C and 40 °C.
parts.answer: It increases steadily, from 2 to 12 mm³ min⁻¹, as the temperature rises.
parts.working: B1 rate increases with temperature (2 → 5 → 9 → 12 mm³ min⁻¹).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate fell between 40 °C and 45 °C.
parts.answer: At 45 °C the enzymes and proteins in the roots and guard cells are denatured, and the cell membranes are damaged, so active processes such as ion uptake are impaired. The stomata may also close, which reduces the pull of transpiration.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: enzymes/proteins denatured in roots or guard cells; membranes damaged and less selectively permeable; less active uptake of ions so less water taken up; stomata close, reducing transpiration pull.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in the rate from 40 °C to 45 °C.

practice.stem: Celery stalks were placed with their cut ends in eosin (red dye) solution. One group was kept in bright light and another in the dark, both at 25 °C. After 30 minutes the dye had risen 9.5 cm in the light group and 2.0 cm in the dark group. Sections showed the dye only in small groups of cells near the outside of the stalk.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the dye was found only in small groups of cells near the outside of the stalk.
parts.answer: The dye travels in the xylem; the xylem is in vascular bundles that are arranged near the outside (in a ring) in the stalk.
parts.working: B1 dye in xylem; B1 xylem in vascular bundles near outside.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between the light and dark groups.
parts.answer: In light, stomata open; more water vapour diffuses out of the leaves (higher transpiration); greater tension/transpiration pull in the xylem, so water and dye are drawn up faster; in the dark stomata are mostly closed, so transpiration and pull are low.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: stomata open in light; more transpiration; greater tension/cohesion pull; stomata closed in dark.

practice.stem: The sap in a sieve tube of a sunflower contains 0.30 mol dm⁻³ sucrose at 25 °C. Use ψₛ = −iCRT, where i = 1, R = 0.00831 MPa dm³ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and T = 298 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the solute potential of the sap, in MPa, to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The pressure potential in the sieve tube is +0.20 MPa. Calculate the water potential of the sap, and state the direction in which water moves between the xylem (−0.45 MPa) and the sieve tube.
parts.answer: Water potential = −0.74 + 0.20 = −0.54 MPa; water moves from the xylem into the sieve tube by osmosis, because the xylem has the higher water potential.
parts.working: M1 ψ = ψₛ + ψₚ = −0.74 + 0.20 = −0.54 MPa; A1 water moves from xylem (−0.45) to sieve tube (−0.54), down the water potential gradient.

practice.stem: Three bean plants were stood with their cut bases in eosin dye for 2 hours. Plant W (normal): dye reached 18 cm up the stem. Plant X: a complete ring of bark (phloem and cambium) was removed 5 cm above the base; dye reached 18 cm. Plant Y: a ring of xylem was cut out 5 cm above the base, with the bark and phloem left intact; dye reached only 5 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the results for plant X.
parts.answer: Water and dissolved dye move up the stem in the xylem, not the phloem. Removing the bark and phloem does not block the xylem, so the dye still rises to 18 cm.
parts.working: B1 transport of water/dye is in the xylem; B1 phloem removal does not interrupt the xylem, so dye still reaches 18 cm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the results for plant Y.
parts.answer: The xylem vessels are the route for the dye, so the cut-out ring of xylem blocks its movement; the dye cannot cross the gap and stops at 5 cm. Phloem does not carry water upwards.
parts.working: B1 xylem is the pathway and the gap breaks it so dye stops at the gap (5 cm); B1 phloem does not carry water/dye up the stem.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the conclusion the student can draw from the three plants.
parts.answer: Water (and dissolved dye) moves up the stem in the xylem, not in the phloem.
parts.working: B1 xylem conclusion.

practice.stem: Students measured the rate of water loss from a leaf (mg cm⁻² h⁻¹) in moving air: 0 m s⁻¹ 2.1; 1 m s⁻¹ 3.4; 2 m s⁻¹ 4.0; 3 m s⁻¹ 4.2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the rate of water loss from 0 to 3 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate levelled off between 2 and 3 m s⁻¹.
parts.answer: The layer of still air (boundary layer) next to the leaf is already as thin as it can become, so faster air cannot reduce it further. The water vapour gradient is close to its maximum, and the stomatal aperture now limits the rate of diffusion.
parts.working: 1 mark: boundary layer already at its minimum thickness so faster wind has little effect; 1 mark: water vapour gradient near maximum or stomata are the limiting factor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one variable that must be kept the same in this investigation.
parts.answer: Temperature (or humidity, light intensity, leaf area, type of leaf).
parts.working: B1 any one control variable that would affect transpiration.

practice.stem: A student claims that a potometer measures the rate of transpiration. In one test the shoot took up 4.8 cm³ of water in 2 hours, while the shoot's mass fell by 4.1 g over the same period (equivalent to 4.1 cm³ of water lost).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of water taken up that was not lost by transpiration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the water uptake can be greater than the water lost by transpiration.
parts.answer: Some of the water taken up is used in photosynthesis as a reactant, and some is retained in the tissues to maintain turgor and for growth. Only the water lost as vapour is measured by the mass change.
parts.working: B1 water used in photosynthesis (a reactant); B1 water retained in cells for turgor / growth so not lost as vapour.

practice.stem: A leaf of a plant was supplied with ¹⁴CO₂ in light. After 2 hours, radioactive sugar was detected in the phloem sap below the leaf and in the roots, but not in the xylem sap above the leaf.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the label was found in the phloem below the leaf but not in the xylem above it.
parts.answer: Sucrose made in photosynthesis is loaded into the sieve tubes and moved in the phloem. The xylem carries water and minerals upwards from the roots, so no labelled sugar enters it.
parts.working: B1 labelled sucrose is made and loaded into phloem sieve tubes; B1 xylem carries water/minerals from roots, not sugars from the leaf.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the labelled sugar reached the roots.
parts.answer: The roots are a sink, and sucrose moves from the source (the leaf) to sinks through the phloem by mass flow.
parts.working: B1 roots are a sink; phloem transports sucrose from source to sink.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict what would happen to the label in the roots if a ring of phloem below the leaf were removed.
parts.answer: Less labelled sugar would reach the roots, and the label would build up in the phloem above the ring.
parts.working: B1 phloem route blocked so less label reaches roots; label accumulates above the ring.

practice.stem: Two leaves were weighed for water loss in one hour in the same room. Leaf P had an area of 60 cm² and lost 0.42 g of water. Leaf Q had an area of 45 cm² and lost 0.33 g of water. Leaf P has stomata only on its lower surface; leaf Q has stomata on both surfaces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the water loss per cm² per hour for each leaf, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why leaf Q may lose more water per cm² than leaf P, even though the total difference is small.
parts.answer: Leaf Q has stomata on both surfaces, so there are more stomata per cm² of leaf and more pores for water vapour to escape through; leaf Q may also have a thinner cuticle.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: stomata on both surfaces / more stomata per cm²; thinner cuticle; more open stomata because of the shaded environment.

practice.stem: On a calm, humid night a student cut a sunflower stem 5 cm above the soil and joined the cut end to a vertical glass tube. Over 10 hours overnight, sap rose 8 cm up the tube.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate at which the sap rose, in mm h⁻¹.
parts.answer: 8 mm h⁻¹
parts.working: B1 80 mm ÷ 10 h = 8 mm h⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the rise would be different if the stem had been cut in dry air rather than under water.
parts.answer: Air would be drawn into the xylem vessels when the stem was cut, breaking the continuous water column (cohesion), so the sap would not rise as far, if at all.
parts.working: 1 mark: air enters the xylem vessels; 1 mark: the continuous water column is broken so pressure cannot push sap up.

practice.stem: Potato cells were placed in a 0.5 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution at 25 °C. The water potential of the potato cells was −0.9 MPa. Use ψ = −iCRT, where i = 1 for sucrose, R = 0.00831 MPa dm³ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and T = 298 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the water potential of the sucrose solution, in MPa, to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which way water moves between the cells and the solution, and explain why.
parts.answer: Water moves out of the cells into the solution by osmosis, because the solution has a lower (more negative) water potential (−1.24 MPa) than the cells (−0.9 MPa). Water moves from higher to lower water potential.
parts.working: B1 water moves out of the cells; B1 solution has a lower water potential than the cells, so water moves down the water potential gradient.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the cells lose turgor when water leaves them.
parts.answer: As water leaves, the cell contents shrink and the cell membrane pulls away from the cell wall, so the pressure potential falls and the cell becomes flaccid (plasmolysis).
parts.working: B1 pressure potential falls as the protoplast shrinks away from the wall / cell becomes flaccid.

practice.stem: Bean leaves were examined through the day. Stomata were closed at night, opened after dawn as light increased, and closed again when the soil dried out during the afternoon of a hot day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the movement of potassium ions causes the stomata to open in the morning.
parts.answer: Potassium ions are pumped into the guard cells by active transport, using ATP. The water potential of the guard cells falls, so water enters by osmosis and the guard cells become turgid. The uneven thickening of the walls causes the guard cells to bend apart, opening the pore.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: K⁺ actively transported into guard cells (ATP / proton pump); water potential falls; water enters by osmosis and guard cells swell/turgid; uneven wall thickening makes them bend apart, opening the stoma.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a shortage of water in the leaves closes the stomata, with reference to abscisic acid (ABA).
parts.answer: ABA is produced when the plant is short of water. It causes potassium ions to leave the guard cells, so their water potential rises, water leaves by osmosis, the guard cells lose turgor and the stomata close.
parts.working: 1 mark: ABA produced in drought and causes K⁺ to leave guard cells; 1 mark: water leaves by osmosis, guard cells lose turgor and stomata close.

practice.stem: A student set up two potometers using leafy shoots cut from the same plant. Shoot 1 was cut under water and the bubble moved 22 mm in 10 minutes. Shoot 2 was cut in air. Within 30 seconds the cut was exposed to air, and the bubble moved only 1 mm in the next 10 minutes, although the shoot looked healthy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of movement of the bubble in shoot 1, and the percentage reduction in the rate for shoot 2 compared with shoot 1.
parts.working: B1 shoot 1 rate = 2.2 mm min⁻¹; B1 percentage reduction = (22 − 1)/22 × 100 = 95.5 % (shoot 2 rate 0.1 mm min⁻¹).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why shoot 2 transpired so much less than shoot 1.
parts.answer: When shoot 2 was cut in air, air entered the xylem vessels. Air bubbles (an embolism) break the continuous water column, so cohesion is lost and the transpiration pull cannot be transmitted up the xylem, so little water is moved.
parts.working: 1 mark: air enters the xylem vessels when cut in air; 1 mark: continuous water column broken / cohesion lost; 1 mark: transpiration pull cannot be transmitted so little water is drawn up.

practice.stem: A student will count open stomata on leaf epidermis peels taken from a bean plant at different light intensities.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a hypothesis that could be tested.
parts.answer: As light intensity increases, the percentage of open stomata increases (or a valid null hypothesis).
parts.working: B1 relates both variables.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Sketch in words the shape of the graph you would predict, and give a biological reason.
parts.answer: The percentage of open stomata rises with light intensity then levels off (plateau) when nearly all are open; in light, guard cells take up K⁺ ions, water enters by osmosis and they become turgid, opening the pore.
parts.working: B1 rise then plateau; B1 reason linked to guard cell turgor/K⁺ uptake.

practice.stem: A student wants to investigate the effect of relative humidity on the rate of transpiration of a leafy shoot using a potometer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a suitable hypothesis for an investigation into the effect of relative humidity on the rate of transpiration of a leafy shoot.
parts.answer: As relative humidity increases, the rate of transpiration decreases, because the water potential (water vapour concentration) gradient between the leaf and the air is smaller, so less water vapour diffuses out through the stomata.
parts.working: B1 correct relationship (higher humidity → lower transpiration); B1 biological reason: smaller concentration gradient so slower diffusion of vapour through stomata.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict what will happen to the rate of transpiration if the plant is moved from a dim cupboard into bright sunlight, and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: The rate of transpiration will increase, because light makes the stomata open for photosynthesis, so more water vapour diffuses out of the leaf.
parts.working: B1 rate increases; B1 stomata open in light, allowing more water vapour to diffuse out.

practice.stem: A student predicts that the rate of water uptake will double when the temperature rises from 10 °C to 20 °C. Results: 10 °C 3.0 mm³ min⁻¹; 20 °C 5.5 mm³ min⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the rate of water uptake from 10 °C to 20 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Is the prediction supported? Give a reason.
parts.answer: No. The rate increased by 83 %, not 100 %, so it did not double.
parts.working: B1 prediction not supported: increase is less than 100 % (rate less than doubled).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a suitable null hypothesis for an investigation into the effect of sucrose concentration on the mass of potato cylinders.
parts.answer: There is no effect of sucrose concentration on the percentage change in mass of potato cylinders (no correlation between them).
parts.working: B1 states no relationship/effect between sucrose concentration and percentage change in mass.

practice.stem: A plant has been kept in bright light for a week, with its leaves making sucrose by photosynthesis. It is then moved into darkness.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict what happens to sucrose loading into the phloem at the leaves, and to the rate of mass flow in the phloem, over the next few hours. Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Loading of sucrose into the phloem falls and the rate of mass flow falls.
parts.working: B1 less sucrose is made by photosynthesis, so less is loaded into sieve tubes; B1 the sieve tube water potential rises, less water enters by osmosis, hydrostatic pressure falls and mass flow slows.

practice.stem: A student's hypothesis: 'Increasing the temperature increases the rate of transpiration.' Results: 15 °C 0.8 g h⁻¹; 25 °C 1.4 g h⁻¹; 35 °C 2.3 g h⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean increase in the rate of transpiration for each 10 °C rise between 15 °C and 35 °C.
parts.working: M1 (2.3 − 0.8) = 1.5 g h⁻¹ over two 10 °C steps; A1 1.5 ÷ 2 = 0.75 g h⁻¹ per 10 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether the data support the hypothesis.
parts.answer: The data support the hypothesis: the rate rises at each step (0.8 → 1.4 → 2.3 g h⁻¹). However, only three temperatures were tested with no repeats, so the pattern is not yet reliable and more temperatures and repeats are needed.
parts.working: 1 mark: data show a rise in rate with temperature, so supports the hypothesis; 1 mark: limitation - only three temperatures and no repeats, so cannot be sure of the pattern.

practice.stem: A tree with many leaves is compared with the same tree after all its leaves have been removed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the effect of removing all the leaves from the tree on the rate of water uptake by its roots, and explain your prediction using the cohesion–tension theory.
parts.answer: The rate of water uptake will fall. With no leaves there is little transpiration, so less tension (pull) is created in the xylem; the water column is pulled up less and less water is taken up by the roots.
parts.working: 1 mark: rate of water uptake falls; 1 mark: fewer leaves so less transpiration and less tension in the xylem; 1 mark: less water pulled up the column so less absorbed by roots.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the independent variable in this comparison.
parts.answer: The number (or area) of leaves on the tree.
parts.working: B1 number/area of leaves (leaf removal).

practice.stem: Leaf discs were treated with cyanide, which blocks respiration and so reduces ATP production. Sucrose loading into the phloem was measured in µmol. Control discs loaded 10.4 µmol; cyanide-treated discs loaded 2.1 µmol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a prediction for this experiment, based on the hypothesis that sucrose loading into the phloem requires ATP.
parts.answer: Leaf discs treated with cyanide will load less sucrose than untreated (control) discs.
parts.working: B1 cyanide inhibits respiration/ATP so loading is reduced compared with control.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in sucrose loading in the cyanide-treated discs compared with the control.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether the data support the hypothesis, and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Yes. Loading fell by about 80 % when respiration (ATP production) was blocked, which supports the idea that loading uses energy from ATP. A control with a different inhibitor would be needed to check cyanide acts only through ATP.
parts.working: 1 mark: data support hypothesis - loading fell sharply when ATP production blocked; 1 mark: an extra control or other inhibitor needed to confirm cyanide's effect is through ATP.

practice.stem: Plant A has many small stomata; plant B has few large stomata. The leaves of both plants have the same total stomatal pore area.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest a hypothesis comparing the transpiration rate of plant A and plant B.
parts.answer: Plant A, with many small stomata, will have a higher rate of transpiration than plant B, with few large stomata of the same total pore area, because diffusion through many small pores is faster per unit area (the diffusion gradients overlap less).
parts.working: 1 mark: plant A higher rate (testable comparison); 1 mark: many small pores diffuse faster per unit area than one large pore of the same total area.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one variable that must be kept the same in this comparison.
parts.answer: Total stomatal pore area (or leaf area, temperature, humidity, light intensity).
parts.working: B1 any one controlled variable.

practice.stem: A student plans to use a potometer to investigate the effect of wind speed on the rate of transpiration of a leafy shoot.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent and dependent variables in a potometer investigation of wind speed.
parts.answer: Independent variable: wind speed (m s⁻¹) from a fan. Dependent variable: distance moved by the bubble in a fixed time (rate of transpiration).
parts.working: B1 IV wind speed; B1 DV distance moved by bubble per time (rate of transpiration).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a prediction for this investigation, with a reason.
parts.answer: As wind speed increases, the rate of transpiration increases (up to a limit), because moving air removes water vapour from the leaf surface, keeping the diffusion gradient steep.
parts.working: B1 prediction: rate increases with wind speed, with biological reason.

practice.stem: A student predicts that the rate of transpiration will fall in a straight line as relative humidity rises. Results (arbitrary units): 40 % humidity – 5.0; 60 % – 3.8; 80 % – 2.0; 90 % – 1.8; 100 % – 1.7.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the student's prediction using the data.
parts.answer: The prediction is partly supported: the rate falls as humidity rises. But the fall is not linear: it is steepest between 60 % and 80 % (−1.8 units) and levels off at 90–100 % (−0.1 units between 90 % and 100 %). Near 100 % the water vapour gradient is almost zero, so transpiration cannot fall much further, and a small loss continues through the cuticle.
parts.working: 1 mark: rate falls as humidity rises (partly supported); 1 mark: not linear – the fall slows to a small change near 90–100 %; 1 mark: the gradient is near zero, so the rate approaches a minimum.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in the rate from 80 % to 100 % humidity.

practice.stem: A student's hypothesis: 'The rate of xylem flow in a stem is proportional to the cross-sectional area of its xylem.' Stem A: xylem area 2.0 mm², flow 3.6 mm³ h⁻¹. Stem B: xylem area 3.5 mm²; observed flow 5.9 mm³ h⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the flow predicted for stem B by the hypothesis, using stem A.
parts.working: B1 flow per mm² = 1.8; 1.8 × 3.5 = 6.3 mm³ h⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage difference between the predicted and observed flows for stem B, as a percentage of the predicted flow.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether the hypothesis is supported, and suggest one reason for the difference.
parts.answer: Broadly supported, since the observed flow is within about 6 % of the prediction. The difference could be due to differences in the diameter or number of xylem vessels per unit area, or to measurement error.
parts.working: 1 mark: hypothesis broadly supported (within 6 %); 1 mark: a valid reason, e.g. vessel diameter/number differs, or measurement error.

practice.stem: A student writes: 'Plants transpire because they have stomata.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the flaw in the statement and rewrite it as a testable hypothesis.
parts.answer: The statement is an explanation of a fact rather than a testable relationship between two variables. Testable hypothesis: as the stomatal density on a leaf increases, the rate of transpiration increases, because more pores allow more diffusion of water vapour out of the leaf.
parts.working: 1 mark: not testable / no measurable variables named; 1 mark: a hypothesis with an IV, DV and a biological reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the null hypothesis for your testable hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is no correlation between stomatal density and the rate of transpiration.
parts.working: B1 null hypothesis: no relationship/correlation.

practice.stem: In summer, a complete ring of bark (including the phloem and cambium, but not the xylem) is removed from around a tree trunk.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the effect of the ring on the thickness of the bark above the ring after 2 months, and explain.
parts.answer: The bark above the ring will swell and thicken, because sucrose and other phloem products moving down from the leaves cannot pass the ring and accumulate above it. Tissue below the ring receives less sugar and may shrink or die.
parts.working: 1 mark: swelling/thickening above ring; 1 mark: phloem sap (sucrose) cannot pass the ring so accumulates above; 1 mark: tissue below ring receives less sugar (shrinks or dies).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict what happens to the xylem flow above the ring, and explain.
parts.answer: The xylem flow above the ring continues, because the ring removes only the bark and phloem and leaves the xylem intact; water still moves up by the transpiration pull.
parts.working: 1 mark: xylem flow continues; 1 mark: ring removes only the phloem/bark, xylem intact so transpiration pull still moves water up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two sources of error that could make the bubble move too slowly in a potometer.
parts.answer: Any two of: an air leak at a joint of the apparatus; air bubbles already in the xylem of the shoot; a bubble that sticks in the capillary tube; a capillary tube with uneven bore (so the volume per mm is not constant).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid sources of error (leaks, air in xylem, bubble sticking, uneven bore).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the student should wait about 10 minutes after setting up the potometer before taking the first reading.
parts.answer: Cutting and handling the shoot disturbs it; the shoot needs time to reach a steady rate of water uptake, so early readings may be too fast or too slow and are not representative.
parts.working: 1 mark: disturbance from setting up or cutting affects uptake; 1 mark: time is needed to reach a steady (equilibrated) rate before readings are valid.

practice.stem: A student repeated the measurement of the distance moved by the bubble in 5 minutes three times with the same shoot. Readings: 4.2 mm, 4.6 mm and 4.4 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the range of the three readings as a percentage of their mean, and state whether the readings are reliable.
parts.answer: Range = 0.4 mm; 0.4 ÷ 4.4 × 100 = 9.1 %. The readings are close together, so the measurement is repeatable (reliable).
parts.working: B1 range 0.4 mm and 0.4 ÷ 4.4 × 100 = 9.1 %; B1 small spread, so the readings are reproducible (reliable).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one thing that these three readings cannot show about the measurement.
parts.answer: Whether the measurement is accurate, i.e. whether the mean is close to the true value (a systematic error would shift all three readings equally).
parts.working: B1 repeats show precision (reliability) only, not accuracy or systematic error.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest an improvement that would make the measurement of the bubble movement more reliable.
parts.answer: Measure over a longer time (for example 10 minutes), so the distance moved is larger and the percentage uncertainty in reading the ruler is smaller. Mark the start and end positions of the bubble carefully, reading the ruler at eye level.
parts.working: 1 mark: longer timing interval gives a larger distance and a smaller percentage error; 1 mark: precise marking and reading at eye level (avoiding parallax).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student could check that the potometer is airtight.
parts.answer: Seal all the joints with petroleum jelly and fill the apparatus with water. Check that no air bubbles appear and that the bubble does not move when the apparatus is set up, showing that there are no leaks.
parts.working: 1 mark: sealing joints and filling with water, with a test method; 1 mark: result to look for - no bubbles appear or the bubble does not move when no leaves are transpiring (no leaks).

practice.stem: Two students used the same potometer and shoot to measure water uptake in still air. Student 1 took readings straight after setting up; student 2 waited 10 minutes. Their mean rates were 12.8 and 9.1 mm min⁻¹. Student 1 noticed small air bubbles appearing at the joint between the shoot and the rubber tubing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why student 1's results were higher and less reliable.
parts.answer: The shoot had not equilibrated to the conditions/stomata had not adjusted; air leaking in at the joint makes the bubble move further, giving an overestimate; (the shoot may have been under extra tension from being cut).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest three improvements to the procedure to obtain more accurate and reliable results.
parts.answer: Any three of: cut the stem under water at a slant and fit it under water; seal joints with petroleum jelly and check for leaks; allow 5–10 min equilibration; measure at constant temperature/away from draughts; take at least three readings and calculate a mean, discarding anomalies; use a capillary of smaller radius for greater precision.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

practice.stem: Four mass-loss readings for potato cylinders in the same solution were: 0.12 g, 0.15 g, 0.14 g and 0.42 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and suggest a likely cause.
parts.answer: The anomalous result is 0.42 g. A likely cause is that the cylinder was not blotted dry, or was damaged, or was weighed incorrectly, so its mass was not due to the sucrose treatment.
parts.working: 1 mark: 0.42 g identified as anomalous; 1 mark: valid cause, e.g. not blotted dry, cylinder damaged, or weighing error.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean mass loss using only the concordant results, to 3 significant figures.

practice.stem: A student estimated the rate of water uptake from one reading: the bubble moved 6 mm in 5 minutes, giving a rate of 1.2 mm min⁻¹. The ruler has marks at 1 mm intervals and the start and end positions were judged by eye.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the distance, if the uncertainty of reading the ruler is ±0.5 mm and the distance is 6 mm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why one reading is not reliable, and suggest an improvement.
parts.answer: A single reading cannot show whether the result can be repeated, and any random error in that one reading is not averaged out. Repeat the measurement at least three times and calculate the mean and range.
parts.working: 1 mark: one reading cannot show reproducibility / random error not averaged out; 1 mark: repeat at least three times and calculate a mean (and range).

practice.stem: Two students recorded the time for the bubble to move 10 mm in the same potometer. Student 1 measured 4.0 min; student 2 measured 4.6 min.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage difference between the two students' times, as a percentage of student 1's time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State and explain the type of error most likely to cause the difference between the two readings.
parts.answer: Random error: each student judged the start and stop of the bubble differently and had a different reaction time with the stopwatch. Repeating and averaging the readings would reduce this error.
parts.working: 1 mark: random error; 1 mark: different judgement / reaction time when starting and stopping the timer, reduced by repeats and a mean.

practice.stem: Cobalt chloride paper turns from blue to pink when it contacts water. A student uses it to compare the transpiration rates of two leaves by placing a dry paper on each leaf.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one limitation of using cobalt chloride paper to compare the rates of transpiration of two leaves.
parts.answer: It only shows whether water vapour is present (a qualitative result); it does not measure how much water is lost. Judging the end of the colour change is also subjective.
parts.working: B1 qualitative only / no measurement of volume or mass lost / subjective end point.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an improvement that would give a quantitative measure of transpiration.
parts.answer: Weigh the plant or leaf at the start and end of the test (or at regular intervals) to measure the mass of water lost, or use a potometer to measure the distance the bubble moves.
parts.working: 1 mark: a quantitative method (mass loss balance or potometer); 1 mark: measured at set intervals so rate can be calculated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the difference between random error and systematic error.
parts.answer: Random error causes readings to vary unpredictably above and below the true value; systematic error shifts all readings consistently in one direction.
parts.working: B1 random: unpredictable variation about true value; systematic: consistent bias in one direction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of random error and one example of systematic error in a transpiration experiment.
parts.answer: Random: judging the bubble's position differently each time. Systematic: a ruler with a zero error, or a potometer joint that always leaks, so every reading is too small.
parts.working: 1 mark: valid random error example (judging bubble position, reaction time); 1 mark: valid systematic example (zero error, consistent leak, faulty timer).

practice.stem: A student measured the rate of water uptake in a potometer in a room with a window open, causing draughts across the apparatus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the draught could affect the readings.
parts.answer: Moving air removes water vapour from the leaf surface, so transpiration increases and the bubble moves faster. Draughts vary from one run to another, so the readings are inconsistent.
parts.working: 1 mark: moving air increases transpiration so readings are higher; 1 mark: draught varies between runs so readings are inconsistent (random error).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two improvements and explain why each would improve reliability.
parts.answer: Any two, each with a reason: shield the apparatus from the window or move it into a draught-free room, so air movement is the same in every run; keep the temperature and humidity constant (for example in a growth chamber), so the transpiration rate is controlled and readings can be repeated.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two valid improvements and 1 mark each for a reason that links it to reliability (controls a variable / reduces random variation).

practice.stem: A student concluded that wind speed increases transpiration, using one potometer reading at 0 m s⁻¹ (distance 6 mm) and one at 3 m s⁻¹ (distance 15 mm) in 5 minutes. The two readings were taken on different days, from different plants.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the student's conclusion.
parts.answer: The conclusion is not reliable. Each wind speed has only one reading, and the two readings came from different plants on different days, so plant size, leaf area, temperature and humidity may have varied. The difference could be due to these uncontrolled variables, not to the wind.
parts.working: 1 mark: only one reading each, so no mean or range; 1 mark: different plants/days, so uncontrolled variables (leaf area, temperature, humidity) may explain the difference; 1 mark: conclusion not valid until variables controlled and repeats made.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the variables could be controlled and how many repeats should be made.
parts.answer: Use the same plant and leaf area, with the same conditions on the same day. Repeat at least three times at each wind speed and calculate the mean rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: same plant / leaf area / conditions (controlled); 1 mark: at least three repeats at each wind speed, with a mean.

practice.stem: The bubble moved 25 mm (±1 mm) in 10 minutes (±0.5 min).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of movement of the bubble and the percentage uncertainty in the rate, as the sum of the percentage uncertainties in the distance and the time.
parts.answer: Rate = 2.5 mm min⁻¹ (25 ÷ 10). Percentage uncertainty in distance = 1 ÷ 25 × 100 = 4 %; in time = 0.5 ÷ 10 × 100 = 5 %; total = 9 %.
parts.working: B1 rate = 2.5 mm min⁻¹; B1 distance uncertainty 4 %; B1 total 4 % + 5 % = 9 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which measurement gives the largest percentage uncertainty, and suggest how to reduce it.
parts.answer: Timing gives the largest percentage uncertainty (5 %). Timing over a longer period (for example 20 minutes) means the same reaction-time error is a smaller percentage of the total time.
parts.working: 1 mark: time (5 %) is the largest; 1 mark: longer timing interval reduces the percentage error.

practice.stem: Potometer P has a capillary tube of internal diameter 0.5 mm. Potometer Q has a capillary tube of internal diameter 1.0 mm. A bubble moves 10 mm in each tube.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of water (mm³) represented by a movement of 10 mm in each tube. Use V = πr²h, where r is half the internal diameter. Give each answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Potometer P: 1.96 mm³ (π × 0.25² × 10); potometer Q: 7.85 mm³ (π × 0.5² × 10).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain which potometer gives the more sensitive measurement, and state one disadvantage of that tube.
parts.answer: Potometer P, with the narrower tube, is more sensitive: a given volume of water taken up moves the bubble further. A disadvantage is that the bubble is more likely to stick or be hard to move, so readings may be less reliable.
parts.working: 1 mark: P is more sensitive (same volume gives larger distance); 1 mark: disadvantage - bubble may stick or be slower to move / more affected by small errors.

subtopics.name: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

subtopics: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where glycolysis takes place in a cell.
parts.answer: Cytoplasm (cytosol).
parts.working: B1 cytoplasm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the main stages of glycolysis.
parts.answer: Glucose is phosphorylated using 2 ATP to form hexose (fructose) bisphosphate; this splits (lysis) into two triose phosphate molecules; each triose phosphate is oxidised by removal of hydrogen, which reduces NAD; each is converted to pyruvate, producing 2 ATP per triose phosphate by substrate-level phosphorylation (net gain 2 ATP per glucose).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: phosphorylation of glucose using 2 ATP; hexose bisphosphate formed; splits into 2 triose phosphates; dehydrogenation / oxidation of triose phosphate; NAD reduced (2 reduced NAD per glucose); pyruvate formed; 4 ATP produced, net gain of 2 ATP; substrate-level phosphorylation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why glycolysis would stop if there were no NAD available.
parts.answer: NAD is needed to accept hydrogen when triose phosphate is oxidised, so this step could not happen.
parts.working: B1 no hydrogen acceptor for oxidation of triose phosphate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State how pyruvate enters the mitochondrial matrix.
parts.answer: By active transport (across the mitochondrial membranes).
parts.working: B1 active transport.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what happens to pyruvate in the link reaction.
parts.answer: Pyruvate is decarboxylated (CO₂ removed) and dehydrogenated (hydrogen removed, reducing NAD); the remaining 2-carbon acetyl group combines with coenzyme A to form acetyl coenzyme A.
parts.working: B1 decarboxylation / CO₂ released; B1 dehydrogenation / NAD reduced; B1 acetyl group + coenzyme A → acetyl CoA.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why this stage is called the link reaction.
parts.answer: It links glycolysis (in the cytoplasm) to the Krebs cycle (in the matrix).
parts.working: B1 connects glycolysis and the Krebs cycle.

practice.stem:
Four events in aerobic respiration are listed.
P: glucose is phosphorylated using ATP
Q: acetyl coenzyme A is formed
R: oxaloacetate is regenerated
S: triose phosphate is oxidised by removal of hydrogen

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each event P, Q, R and S, name the stage of aerobic respiration in which it occurs.
parts.answer: P glycolysis; Q link reaction; R Krebs cycle; S glycolysis
parts.working: 2 marks for all four correct; 1 mark for two or three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the precise location in a eukaryotic cell of the stage in which event Q occurs.
parts.answer: Mitochondrial matrix
parts.working: B1 matrix of the mitochondrion (not just 'mitochondrion').

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why two ATP molecules are used at the start of glycolysis even though the aim of respiration is to make ATP.
parts.answer: Phosphorylation makes glucose more reactive / lowers the activation energy for splitting it into two triose phosphates; more ATP (4) is made later, so there is a net gain of 2 ATP.
parts.working: B1 phosphorylated glucose (hexose bisphosphate) is more reactive / less stable so it can be split; B1 4 ATP are produced later giving a net gain of 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of carbon atoms in each of these molecules: glucose, pyruvate, the acetyl group of acetyl coenzyme A, citrate and oxaloacetate.
parts.answer: glucose 6; pyruvate 3; acetyl group 2; citrate 6; oxaloacetate 4
parts.working: 2 marks all five correct; 1 mark for three or four correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of molecules of carbon dioxide released in the link reaction and in the Krebs cycle from one molecule of glucose, and state the total.
parts.answer: link reaction 2; Krebs cycle 4; total 6
parts.working: M1 2 pyruvate × 1 CO₂ = 2 in the link reaction; 2 turns × 2 CO₂ = 4 in Krebs; A1 total 6 (all six carbons of glucose leave as CO₂).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the process in which carbon dioxide is removed from a respiratory intermediate.
parts.answer: Decarboxylation
parts.working: B1 decarboxylation.

practice.stem: Coenzymes play an important part in the reactions of glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the role of NAD in these stages.
parts.answer: NAD accepts hydrogen (is reduced) when dehydrogenase enzymes remove hydrogen from intermediates; it carries the hydrogen to the electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane.
parts.working: B1 hydrogen acceptor / becomes reduced NAD in dehydrogenation; B1 carries hydrogen (protons and electrons) to the electron transport chain / cristae.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the role of coenzyme A.
parts.answer: It carries the acetyl (2C) group from the link reaction into the Krebs cycle.
parts.working: B1 combines with the acetyl group and transfers it to oxaloacetate / into the Krebs cycle.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one other hydrogen carrier, apart from NAD, that is reduced in the Krebs cycle.
parts.answer: FAD
parts.working: B1 FAD.

practice.stem:
A simplified Krebs cycle is described in words.
Step 1: acetyl coenzyme A (2C) combines with compound W (4C) to form a 6-carbon compound.
Step 2: the 6-carbon compound loses CO₂ and hydrogen, forming a 5-carbon compound.
Step 3: the 5-carbon compound loses CO₂ and hydrogen, forming a 4-carbon compound; ATP is also made.
Step 4: the 4-carbon compound is converted back to W, with further removal of hydrogen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name compound W and the 6-carbon compound formed in step 1.
parts.answer: W = oxaloacetate; 6-carbon compound = citrate.
parts.working: B1 oxaloacetate; B1 citrate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the steps in which decarboxylation occurs and state what is meant by dehydrogenation.
parts.answer: Steps 2 and 3 (6C → 5C and 5C → 4C); dehydrogenation is the removal of hydrogen atoms from a substrate, which are accepted by NAD or FAD.
parts.working: B1 steps 2 and 3; B1 removal of hydrogen (by dehydrogenase enzymes) – accepted by NAD/FAD.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The Krebs cycle does not use oxygen directly. Explain why it stops when oxygen is not available.
parts.answer: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain; without it reduced NAD and FAD cannot be reoxidised, so there is no NAD / FAD to accept hydrogen in the Krebs cycle.
parts.working: B1 oxygen is the final electron / hydrogen acceptor in the ETC; B1 NAD and FAD not regenerated so dehydrogenation in the Krebs cycle stops.

practice.stem: Succinate dehydrogenase is a Krebs cycle enzyme, bound to the inner mitochondrial membrane, that removes hydrogen from succinate and reduces FAD.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Malonate has a similar shape to succinate. Suggest how malonate inhibits succinate dehydrogenase.
parts.answer: It is a competitive inhibitor: it binds to the active site of succinate dehydrogenase, so succinate cannot bind and fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form.
parts.working: B1 binds to the active site (competitive inhibition); B1 prevents succinate binding / fewer E–S complexes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why adding malonate to isolated mitochondria reduces their uptake of oxygen.
parts.answer: The Krebs cycle slows / stops, so less reduced FAD (and NAD) is produced; fewer electrons enter the electron transport chain; less oxygen is needed as the final electron acceptor.
parts.working: B1 Krebs cycle slows / succinate not converted to fumarate; B1 less reduced FAD / NAD produced; B1 fewer electrons passed to oxygen at the end of the ETC, so less oxygen reduced to water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the effect of malonate could be reversed in the experiment.
parts.answer: Add a high concentration of succinate.
parts.working: B1 increase succinate concentration (out-competes inhibitor).

practice.stem: Thiamine (vitamin B1) is needed to make a coenzyme used by the enzyme complex that converts pyruvate to acetyl coenzyme A. People whose diet is mainly polished white rice can develop thiamine deficiency (beriberi).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest how thiamine deficiency affects the concentration of pyruvate in cells. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Pyruvate concentration rises, because the link reaction is slowed so pyruvate made in glycolysis is not converted to acetyl coenzyme A.
parts.working: B1 pyruvate increases; B1 because the enzyme (pyruvate dehydrogenase) of the link reaction works more slowly / pyruvate is not decarboxylated and dehydrogenated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Patients with thiamine deficiency often have high concentrations of lactate in the blood. Explain why.
parts.answer: Excess pyruvate is reduced to lactate by reduced NAD (lactate dehydrogenase), which regenerates NAD so that glycolysis can continue to supply ATP.
parts.working: B1 pyruvate converted to lactate; B1 this regenerates NAD / allows glycolysis to continue when the link reaction is limited.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why nerve cells and heart muscle are among the first tissues affected by thiamine deficiency.
parts.answer: They have a high demand for ATP and rely heavily on aerobic respiration of glucose / pyruvate; less acetyl CoA enters the Krebs cycle so less reduced NAD and ATP are produced.
parts.working: B1 high ATP demand (impulses, active transport, continuous contraction); B1 depend on aerobic respiration via the link reaction / Krebs cycle so ATP supply falls.

practice.stem: A liver cell completely oxidises 3.0 × 10⁶ molecules of glucose per second by aerobic respiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of molecules of reduced NAD produced per second in glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle together.
parts.answer: 3.0e+07 molecules per second (3.0 × 10⁷)
parts.working: M1 2 + 2 + 6 = 10 reduced NAD per glucose; A1 10 × 3.0 × 10⁶ = 3.0 × 10⁷ s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of molecules of carbon dioxide released per second.
parts.answer: 1.8e+07 (1.8 × 10⁷) per second

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of this carbon dioxide that is released in the Krebs cycle. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State why no carbon dioxide is released in glycolysis.
parts.answer: Glycolysis involves no decarboxylation: the 6C glucose is split into two 3C molecules, so all carbon atoms remain in pyruvate.
parts.working: B1 no decarboxylation / glucose (6C) → 2 pyruvate (2 × 3C), no carbon lost.

practice.stem: Isolated mitochondria were suspended in a buffer containing pyruvate, coenzyme A, NAD and a very small concentration of oxaloacetate. The rate of oxygen uptake was low. When extra oxaloacetate was added, the rate of oxygen uptake increased sharply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why only a small amount of oxaloacetate is needed in a cell for the Krebs cycle to continue for long periods.
parts.answer: Oxaloacetate is regenerated at the end of each turn of the cycle, so each molecule is used again and again (it is not used up).
parts.working: B1 oxaloacetate combines with acetyl CoA to form citrate; B1 it is regenerated at the end of each turn / reused.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why adding extra oxaloacetate increased the rate of oxygen uptake by the mitochondria.
parts.answer: More acetyl CoA can combine with oxaloacetate to form citrate, so more turns of the Krebs cycle per unit time; more reduced NAD and reduced FAD are produced; more electrons pass along the electron transport chain to oxygen, the final acceptor.
parts.working: B1 more citrate formed / more turns of Krebs cycle; B1 more dehydrogenation / more reduced NAD and FAD; B1 more electrons passed to oxygen via the electron transport chain so more O₂ used.

practice.stem:
The products of each stage of aerobic respiration per molecule of glucose (net values) are:
glycolysis: 2 reduced NAD, 0 reduced FAD, 2 ATP, 0 CO₂
link reaction: 2 reduced NAD, 0 reduced FAD, 0 ATP, 2 CO₂
Krebs cycle (two turns): 6 reduced NAD, 2 reduced FAD, 2 ATP, 4 CO₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the totals for one molecule of glucose: number of reduced NAD, reduced FAD, ATP (by substrate-level phosphorylation) and CO₂ produced.
parts.answer: reduced NAD 10; reduced FAD 2; ATP 4; CO₂ 6
parts.working: B1 NAD 10 and FAD 2; B1 ATP 4 (net) and CO₂ 6.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assume that each reduced NAD gives 2.5 ATP and each reduced FAD gives 1.5 ATP by oxidative phosphorylation. Calculate the maximum yield of ATP from one molecule of glucose.
parts.answer: 32 ATP

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the actual yield of ATP in a cell is usually lower than this.
parts.answer: Some protons leak back across the inner membrane without passing through ATP synthase; energy is used to transport pyruvate, ADP and phosphate into the mitochondrion (and ATP out); some reduced NAD from glycolysis passes its hydrogen to carriers giving less ATP.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: proton leak across inner membrane; energy (ATP / proton gradient) used for active transport of pyruvate, ADP, Pi, ATP; reduced NAD from cytoplasm gives fewer ATP; some energy released as heat.

practice.stem: Yeast cells were supplied with glucose in which all the carbon atoms were the radioactive isotope ¹⁴C, in well-aerated conditions. Samples were taken every few seconds and analysed for radioactive compounds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest the order in which radioactivity would first appear in pyruvate, acetyl coenzyme A, citrate and the 5-carbon compound of the Krebs cycle. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Pyruvate → acetyl coenzyme A → citrate → 5-carbon compound; glucose is broken down to pyruvate in glycolysis, pyruvate forms acetyl CoA in the link reaction, the acetyl group joins oxaloacetate to form citrate (6C), and citrate is then decarboxylated and dehydrogenated to the 5-carbon compound.
parts.working: B1 correct order; B1 explanation linked to glycolysis → link reaction → Krebs cycle (citrate formed before it is converted to the 5C compound). Note: labelled CO₂ would appear as early as acetyl CoA, from the link reaction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: When the experiment was repeated with yeast in the absence of oxygen, radioactivity appeared in pyruvate, ethanal, ethanol and CO₂, but not in citrate. Explain these results.
parts.answer: Without oxygen the ETC stops so reduced NAD is not reoxidised in mitochondria; the link reaction and Krebs cycle stop, so no citrate; pyruvate is decarboxylated to ethanal (releasing labelled CO₂) and ethanal is reduced to ethanol by reduced NAD, regenerating NAD for glycolysis.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: no oxygen as final acceptor → Krebs cycle / link reaction stop; so no citrate; pyruvate decarboxylated to ethanal (labelled CO₂); ethanal reduced to ethanol using reduced NAD; NAD regenerated so glycolysis continues.

practice.stem:
A cell was broken up and centrifuged to separate a mitochondria fraction from the cytoplasm (cytosol) fraction. Samples were placed in four tubes with an oxygen electrode. Oxygen uptake after 10 minutes:
tube 1: mitochondria + glucose — no oxygen uptake
tube 2: mitochondria + pyruvate — high oxygen uptake
tube 3: cytosol + glucose — no oxygen uptake
tube 4: mitochondria + cytosol + glucose — high oxygen uptake
All tubes contained NAD, ADP and phosphate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the result for tube 1.
parts.answer: Glycolysis enzymes are in the cytoplasm, not in mitochondria, so glucose cannot be converted to pyruvate; mitochondria cannot use glucose directly (no carrier for glucose in the mitochondrial membranes).
parts.working: B1 enzymes of glycolysis are in the cytosol / not in mitochondria; B1 glucose not converted to pyruvate so no substrate for the link reaction / Krebs cycle, so no reduced NAD for the electron transport chain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the result for tube 3.
parts.answer: Glycolysis can take place, producing pyruvate and reduced NAD, but there is no electron transport chain (it is on the inner mitochondrial membrane) so oxygen is not used.
parts.working: B1 glycolysis occurs / pyruvate is made; B1 no electron transport chain / cristae, so no oxygen used as final electron acceptor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use all four results to explain what tube 4 shows about the link between glycolysis and the mitochondria.
parts.answer: The cytosol converts glucose to pyruvate in glycolysis; the pyruvate is then taken into the mitochondria for the link reaction and Krebs cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation uses oxygen.
parts.working: B1 glucose → pyruvate in cytosol; B1 pyruvate enters mitochondria where link reaction / Krebs / electron transport (O₂ use) occur; both fractions needed.

practice.stem: In this question, assume that each reduced NAD produces 2.5 ATP and each reduced FAD produces 1.5 ATP by oxidative phosphorylation. Per molecule of glucose: glycolysis produces 2 reduced NAD and a net 2 ATP; the link reaction produces 2 reduced NAD; the Krebs cycle (two turns) produces 6 reduced NAD, 2 reduced FAD and 2 ATP.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of ATP molecules that can be credited to each stage (glycolysis, link reaction, Krebs cycle), including ATP later made from the reduced coenzymes formed in that stage.
parts.answer: glycolysis 7; link reaction 5; Krebs cycle 20

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the total ATP yield that can be credited to the Krebs cycle. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Most ATP credited to the Krebs cycle is not made in the Krebs cycle itself. Explain this statement.
parts.answer: Only 2 ATP are made directly by substrate-level phosphorylation in the Krebs cycle; the rest are made by oxidative phosphorylation (chemiosmosis via ATP synthase) on the inner membrane using the hydrogen carried by reduced NAD and reduced FAD.
parts.working: B1 only 2 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation in the matrix; B1 the rest by oxidative phosphorylation / electron transport chain / ATP synthase using reduced NAD and FAD.

practice.stem: In a rare inherited condition, the Krebs cycle enzyme that converts the 4C compound fumarate to malate is almost inactive. Fumarate accumulates in the cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest and explain the effect of this condition on the number of turns of the Krebs cycle per minute.
parts.answer: The number of turns falls, because malate and then oxaloacetate are not regenerated, so less acetyl CoA can combine with oxaloacetate to form citrate.
parts.working: B1 fewer turns / cycle slows; B1 oxaloacetate not regenerated so acetyl CoA cannot enter / less citrate formed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the cells produce less ATP by oxidative phosphorylation.
parts.answer: Fewer dehydrogenation reactions so less reduced NAD (and reduced FAD) is produced; fewer electrons pass along the electron transport chain, fewer protons are pumped and less ATP is made by ATP synthase.
parts.working: B1 less reduced NAD / FAD produced; B1 less electron transport / smaller proton gradient so less chemiosmosis / ATP synthase activity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the cells of affected people rely more on glycolysis and produce more lactate.
parts.answer: Glycolysis still produces some ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation; pyruvate that cannot be oxidised in the mitochondria is reduced to lactate, regenerating NAD so glycolysis can continue.
parts.working: B1 glycolysis provides ATP independent of the Krebs cycle; B1 pyruvate → lactate regenerates NAD.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the structure of a mitochondrion is related to its function in aerobic respiration.
parts.answer: Inner membrane folded into cristae → large surface area for electron carriers and ATP synthase; inner membrane impermeable to protons so a gradient can be maintained; small intermembrane space so proton concentration builds up quickly; matrix contains enzymes for the link reaction and Krebs cycle, and contains NAD, FAD and its own DNA and ribosomes to make some proteins.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: cristae give large surface area; for ETC / ATP synthase; inner membrane impermeable to H⁺; small intermembrane space for high H⁺ concentration; matrix enzymes for link reaction and Krebs cycle; matrix has coenzymes / NAD / FAD; own DNA and 70S ribosomes; outer membrane has transport proteins for pyruvate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Heart muscle cells have mitochondria with many more cristae than mitochondria in skin cells. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Heart muscle contracts continuously and needs a lot of ATP, so it needs more ETC and ATP synthase.
parts.working: B1 more ATP needed for constant contraction → more sites for oxidative phosphorylation.

practice.stem:
Five events in oxidative phosphorylation are listed in random order.
1 Protons diffuse back into the matrix through ATP synthase.
2 Reduced NAD releases hydrogen at the inner mitochondrial membrane.
3 Hydrogen atoms split into protons and electrons.
4 Electrons pass along a series of carriers.
5 Energy from electrons is used to pump protons into the intermembrane space.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the numbers 1 to 5 in the correct order.
parts.answer: 2, 3, 4, 5, 1 (events 4 and 5 happen together as electrons move down the chain, so 2, 3, 5, 4, 1 is also accepted)
parts.working: 2 marks for the correct order; 1 mark if only one event is out of place. Event 1 must come last, because the proton gradient has to be built by events 4 and 5 before protons flow back through ATP synthase.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the process in which ATP is made as protons move down their concentration gradient.
parts.answer: Chemiosmosis
parts.working: B1 chemiosmosis (accept oxidative phosphorylation).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why oxygen is described as the final electron acceptor.
parts.answer: It accepts electrons from the last carrier of the electron transport chain (and combines with protons to form water), allowing the chain to keep working.
parts.working: B1 receives electrons at the end of the chain / removes electrons from last carrier.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the part of the mitochondrion where each of the following is found: the electron transport chain; ATP synthase; the enzymes of the Krebs cycle; the highest concentration of protons.
parts.answer: electron transport chain: inner membrane / cristae; ATP synthase: inner membrane / cristae; Krebs enzymes: matrix; highest proton concentration: intermembrane space
parts.working: 2 marks all four correct; 1 mark two or three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the inner mitochondrial membrane must be impermeable to protons except through ATP synthase.
parts.answer: So that the proton gradient (high in intermembrane space, low in matrix) can be maintained; protons can only flow back through ATP synthase, so the energy of the gradient is used to make ATP from ADP and Pi.
parts.working: B1 maintains the proton (electrochemical) gradient; B1 protons only return through ATP synthase so ATP is made.

practice.stem: Measurements from electron micrographs of a liver mitochondrion gave an outer membrane area of 12 µm² and an inner membrane area of 58 µm².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of inner membrane area to outer membrane area. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the folding of the inner membrane into cristae increases the rate of ATP production.
parts.answer: Folding gives a larger surface area for more electron transport chains and ATP synthase molecules, so more oxidative phosphorylation can occur at once.
parts.working: B1 larger surface area; B1 more electron carriers / ATP synthase so more ATP made per unit time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one feature, other than cristae, that you would expect to see in a liver cell that has a high rate of aerobic respiration.
parts.answer: Many mitochondria per cell (accept large matrix containing many enzymes).
parts.working: B1 many mitochondria / large mitochondria.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the energy in reduced NAD is used to synthesise ATP by oxidative phosphorylation.
parts.answer: Reduced NAD gives hydrogen to the first carrier on the inner membrane; hydrogen splits into H⁺ and an electron; electrons pass along a chain of carriers in a series of redox reactions; energy released is used to pump H⁺ from the matrix into the intermembrane space; a proton gradient forms; H⁺ diffuse back through ATP synthase (chemiosmosis); this provides energy to combine ADP and Pi; oxygen is the final electron acceptor, combining with electrons and H⁺ to form water.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: NAD reoxidised / hydrogen released at inner membrane (cristae); H → H⁺ + e⁻; electrons passed along carriers (ETC), redox reactions; energy released pumps H⁺ into intermembrane space; proton (electrochemical) gradient; H⁺ flow back through ATP synthase by facilitated diffusion / chemiosmosis; ADP + Pi → ATP; oxygen final electron acceptor; forms water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The complete oxidation of one mole of glucose releases 2870 kJ. Hydrolysis of one mole of ATP releases 30.5 kJ. Using a yield of 32 ATP per glucose, calculate the efficiency of aerobic respiration. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens to the rest of the energy.
parts.answer: It is released as heat.
parts.working: B1 heat (helps maintain body temperature in mammals and birds).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Anaerobic respiration in muscle produces only 2 ATP per glucose. Calculate the efficiency of anaerobic respiration, assuming the same 2870 kJ per mole of glucose, and suggest why this comparison is not entirely fair.
parts.answer: 2.1 %; much of the energy is still in lactate, which can be oxidised later, so the energy is not all lost.
parts.working: B1 2 × 30.5/2870 × 100 = 2.1 %; B1 lactate still contains chemical energy / can be converted back to pyruvate and respired.

practice.stem: In actively respiring mitochondria, the pH of the intermembrane space was measured as 7.0 and the pH of the matrix as 7.8. pH = −log₁₀[H⁺].

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the proton concentration is in the intermembrane space than in the matrix. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 6.3 times
parts.working: M1 difference of 0.8 pH units so ratio = 10⁰·⁸; A1 6.3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this difference in proton concentration is produced.
parts.answer: Energy released as electrons pass along the electron transport chain is used by carrier proteins to pump protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space (active transport).
parts.working: B1 energy from electron transfer along carriers; B1 protons pumped from matrix to intermembrane space.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict what would happen to the pH of the matrix if ATP synthase were blocked while electron transport briefly continued. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: The matrix pH would rise slightly (become more alkaline) as protons continue to be pumped out but cannot return through ATP synthase.
parts.working: B1 pH rises / matrix more alkaline; B1 protons removed but no return route.

practice.stem: Rotenone is a pesticide that stops electrons passing from reduced NAD to the first carrier of the electron transport chain. Reduced FAD passes its electrons to a different carrier further along the chain. Isolated mitochondria were given either malate (whose oxidation produces reduced NAD) or succinate (whose oxidation produces reduced FAD), with and without rotenone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the effect of rotenone on oxygen uptake by mitochondria given malate. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Oxygen uptake falls to (almost) zero, because electrons from reduced NAD cannot enter the chain so no electrons reach oxygen.
parts.working: B1 oxygen uptake stops / falls greatly; B1 electrons from reduced NAD cannot enter / pass along the chain to oxygen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why mitochondria given succinate still take up oxygen in the presence of rotenone.
parts.answer: Reduced FAD donates electrons to a carrier after the point blocked by rotenone, so electrons still pass along the rest of the chain to oxygen.
parts.working: B1 FAD enters the chain at a later carrier / bypasses the blocked step; B1 electrons still reach oxygen.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why less ATP is made per molecule of succinate oxidised than per molecule of malate oxidised.
parts.answer: Electrons from reduced FAD pass through fewer proton pumps, so fewer protons are pumped into the intermembrane space; less ATP is made by ATP synthase (about 1.5 instead of 2.5).
parts.working: B1 fewer proton pumps / fewer protons pumped; B1 so fewer ATP produced by chemiosmosis.

practice.stem: Mitochondria were placed in a buffer containing pyruvate, oxygen and phosphate. The rate of oxygen uptake was 12 nmol min⁻¹. When ADP was added, the rate rose to 58 nmol min⁻¹. When all the ADP had been converted to ATP, the rate fell back to 12 nmol min⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times faster oxygen was taken up after ADP was added. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 4.8 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why oxygen uptake was low when no ADP was present.
parts.answer: Without ADP, ATP synthase cannot make ATP, so protons do not flow back into the matrix; the proton gradient builds up until pumping is very difficult; electron transport slows, so less oxygen is used.
parts.working: B1 ATP synthase needs ADP (and Pi) / no ATP synthesis; B1 protons do not return to the matrix so the gradient becomes very steep; B1 electron transport / proton pumping slows so less O₂ reduced.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why this effect is useful in a living muscle cell.
parts.answer: The rate of respiration automatically matches the demand for ATP: when ATP is used and ADP rises, respiration speeds up; when resting, substrate is not wasted.
parts.working: B1 respiration rate matches ATP demand / substrate is conserved at rest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assume that 10 protons are pumped into the intermembrane space for each reduced NAD oxidised, 6 protons for each reduced FAD, and that 4 protons must flow back into the matrix (including transport of ADP and phosphate) for each ATP made. Calculate the number of ATP made per reduced NAD and per reduced FAD.
parts.answer: reduced NAD 2.5 ATP; reduced FAD 1.5 ATP

parts.label: b
parts.text: One glucose molecule gives 10 reduced NAD, 2 reduced FAD and 4 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation. Use your answers to (a) to calculate the total ATP yield per glucose.
parts.answer: 32 ATP

parts.label: c
parts.text: In some cells about 15 % of the protons pumped leak back across the inner membrane without passing through ATP synthase. Calculate the new total ATP yield per glucose, assuming substrate-level phosphorylation is unchanged.
parts.answer: 27.8 ATP
parts.working: M1 oxidative phosphorylation yield 28 × 0.85 = 23.8; A1 23.8 + 4 = 27.8 ATP.

practice.stem: The compound 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP) makes the inner mitochondrial membrane permeable to protons. It was once sold as a slimming drug but caused deaths.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why DNP reduces the production of ATP.
parts.answer: Protons leak back into the matrix through the membrane instead of through ATP synthase, so the proton gradient is lost and ATP synthase cannot make ATP.
parts.working: B1 H⁺ return without passing through ATP synthase / proton gradient dissipated; B1 so less chemiosmosis / ADP not phosphorylated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the rate of oxygen uptake by the cells increased when DNP was added, and why the body temperature of people who took DNP rose.
