parts.answer: The electron transport chain continues (or speeds up) because there is no build-up of protons to slow it, so more oxygen is used as final acceptor; energy from electron transport is released as heat instead of being used to make ATP; cells respire more substrate to try to meet ATP demand.
parts.working: B1 ETC still runs / faster because back-pressure of proton gradient removed; B1 more oxygen reduced to water; B1 energy released as heat rather than trapped in ATP (more substrate respired).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Brown fat cells in newborn babies contain a protein that lets protons pass through the inner membrane. Suggest the advantage of this.
parts.answer: Generates heat to maintain body temperature.
parts.working: B1 produces heat (thermoregulation) instead of ATP.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cyanide binds to the last carrier in the electron transport chain so that electrons cannot be passed to oxygen. Explain why cyanide quickly stops ATP production in the mitochondria.
parts.answer: Electrons cannot leave the chain, so carriers stay reduced and the chain stops; no protons are pumped, so no proton gradient and ATP synthase stops; reduced NAD and FAD cannot be reoxidised, so the Krebs cycle and link reaction also stop.
parts.working: B1 electron flow along ETC stops (carriers remain reduced); B1 no H⁺ pumped / no proton gradient so no ATP synthesis by ATP synthase; B1 NAD / FAD not regenerated → Krebs cycle and link reaction stop.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the concentration of lactate in the blood rises in a person poisoned with cyanide.
parts.answer: Cells can only make ATP by glycolysis; to regenerate NAD, pyruvate is reduced to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase, so lactate accumulates.
parts.working: B1 cells rely on anaerobic respiration / glycolysis only; B1 pyruvate converted to lactate to reoxidise NAD.

practice.stem: Oligomycin is an antibiotic that blocks the proton channel of ATP synthase. A suspension of respiring mitochondria with plenty of substrate, ADP and phosphate was set up in an oxygen electrode. Oligomycin was added at 4 minutes. At 8 minutes the uncoupler DNP, which makes the inner membrane freely permeable to protons, was added.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict and explain the change in the rate of oxygen uptake after oligomycin was added.
parts.answer: Oxygen uptake falls to near zero; protons can no longer flow back through ATP synthase, so the proton gradient builds up; the gradient slows and then stops proton pumping, so electron transport stops and oxygen is no longer reduced.
parts.working: B1 rate falls (to near zero); B1 protons cannot return through ATP synthase / gradient builds up; B1 electron transport chain slows / stops so O₂ not used as final acceptor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict and explain the change in the rate of oxygen uptake and in ATP production after DNP was added.
parts.answer: Oxygen uptake increases again (rapidly) because protons leak back through the membrane, removing the gradient so electron transport and proton pumping restart; ATP production stays near zero because ATP synthase is still blocked and the proton gradient is dissipated; energy is released as heat.
parts.working: B1 oxygen uptake rises; B1 gradient dissipated so electron transport resumes; B1 no ATP made (ATP synthase blocked / gradient lost) / energy lost as heat.

practice.stem: A teenager had muscle weakness and tired very quickly. After a short walk, her blood lactate concentration was 6.5 mmol dm⁻³ (normal after the same walk: 1.5 mmol dm⁻³). A muscle biopsy showed mitochondria with very few, short cristae.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how having few cristae reduces the ATP available for muscle contraction.
parts.answer: Smaller surface area of inner membrane; fewer electron transport chains and ATP synthase molecules; less oxidative phosphorylation, so far less ATP per glucose (most ATP normally comes from oxidative phosphorylation).
parts.working: B1 smaller area of inner membrane; B1 fewer electron carriers / ATP synthase; B1 less oxidative phosphorylation / chemiosmosis so less ATP.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the high blood lactate concentration after mild exercise.
parts.answer: Reduced NAD cannot be reoxidised quickly by the electron transport chain; pyruvate accumulates and is reduced to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase to regenerate NAD; glycolysis continues to provide some ATP; lactate diffuses into the blood.
parts.working: B1 reduced NAD not reoxidised by ETC / Krebs and link slowed; B1 pyruvate converted to lactate, regenerating NAD; B1 allows glycolysis / ATP production to continue, lactate passes into blood.

practice.stem:
Mitochondria were isolated from locust flight muscle and from rat liver. Measurements:
flight muscle: oxygen uptake 460 nmol O₂ min⁻¹ per mg mitochondrial protein; cristae membrane area 7.2 m² per g of mitochondria
liver: oxygen uptake 95 nmol O₂ min⁻¹ per mg mitochondrial protein; cristae membrane area 2.4 m² per g of mitochondria

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the oxygen uptake per mg protein and the cristae area per gram are in flight muscle mitochondria than in liver mitochondria. Give each answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: oxygen uptake 4.8 times; cristae area 3.0 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student concluded that the difference in oxygen uptake is caused only by the difference in cristae area. Use the data to evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: The difference in oxygen uptake (4.8×) is larger than the difference in cristae area (3.0×), so cristae area alone cannot explain it; flight muscle may have a greater density of electron transport chains per unit area or more Krebs enzymes in the matrix / faster supply of substrate; correlation does not prove cause and only one sample of each.
parts.working: B1 ratios differ (4.8 vs 3.0) so other factors involved; B1 suggestion: more carriers / ATP synthase per µm², more matrix enzymes, more ADP available; B1 correlation not causation / data from one tissue sample each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why locust flight muscle needs mitochondria with such a high rate of oxygen uptake.
parts.answer: Flight muscle contracts very rapidly and continuously, needing a very high rate of ATP production by aerobic respiration.
parts.working: B1 very high and sustained ATP demand for rapid contraction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare anaerobic respiration in yeast with anaerobic respiration in mammalian muscle.
parts.answer: Similarities: both start with glycolysis, both reoxidise reduced NAD, both produce 2 ATP per glucose. Differences: yeast produces ethanol and CO₂, muscle produces lactate and no CO₂; yeast pathway has two steps (pyruvate decarboxylated to ethanal by pyruvate decarboxylase, then ethanal reduced to ethanol by alcohol dehydrogenase), muscle has one step (pyruvate reduced to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase); lactate can be converted back to pyruvate, ethanol is not converted back to pyruvate and is lost from the cells.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four, at least one similarity and one difference: both use glycolysis / net 2 ATP; both regenerate NAD; yeast ethanol + CO₂ vs muscle lactate; hydrogen acceptor ethanal vs pyruvate; enzymes named (pyruvate decarboxylase & alcohol dehydrogenase vs lactate dehydrogenase); decarboxylation only in yeast; lactate reconverted in liver vs ethanol not converted back.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the regeneration of NAD is essential for anaerobic respiration.
parts.answer: NAD is needed for glycolysis to continue (to oxidise triose phosphate), which is the only source of ATP.
parts.working: B1 so glycolysis can continue producing ATP.

practice.stem: In yeast cells without oxygen, pyruvate is converted to ethanol in two steps.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the 2-carbon intermediate formed in the first step and the other product of this step.
parts.answer: Ethanal; carbon dioxide
parts.working: B1 ethanal; B1 carbon dioxide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the second step, naming the enzyme involved.
parts.answer: Ethanal is reduced to ethanol by reduced NAD (which is oxidised to NAD), catalysed by alcohol dehydrogenase.
parts.working: B1 ethanal reduced to ethanol using reduced NAD; B1 alcohol dehydrogenase.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the net number of ATP molecules produced per glucose molecule by this pathway.
parts.working: B1 2 (from glycolysis).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why anaerobic respiration releases much less energy (ATP) per glucose molecule than aerobic respiration.
parts.answer: Only glycolysis takes place (2 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation); without oxygen as final electron acceptor the electron transport chain stops, so no oxidative phosphorylation; the link reaction and Krebs cycle cannot run; much of the energy remains in lactate or ethanol.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: only glycolysis / 2 ATP; no oxygen to accept electrons so no oxidative phosphorylation; no link reaction / Krebs cycle; energy remains in lactate / ethanol (not fully oxidised).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where in a cell anaerobic respiration takes place.
parts.answer: Cytoplasm (cytosol)
parts.working: B1 cytoplasm.

practice.stem: Naan and bread dough is made with flour, water, sugar and yeast and left in a warm place for an hour before baking.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the dough rises.
parts.answer: Yeast respires the sugar (anaerobically once oxygen in the dough is used up), producing carbon dioxide gas that is trapped as bubbles in the dough.
parts.working: B1 yeast respires sugar / glucose; B1 carbon dioxide released and trapped in dough.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the dough is left in a warm place rather than in a refrigerator.
parts.answer: Respiration is enzyme-controlled; at warm temperatures enzymes have more kinetic energy and more frequent enzyme–substrate collisions, so CO₂ is produced faster; in a refrigerator enzymes work very slowly.
parts.working: B1 enzymes of respiration; B1 faster rate at warmer temperature / more collisions (not denatured at room warmth).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what happens to the ethanol produced by the yeast when the dough is baked.
parts.answer: It evaporates (is driven off by the heat of the oven).
parts.working: B1 evaporates.

practice.stem: After a cricketer bowls a fast over, she continues to breathe deeply for several minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the oxygen debt.
parts.answer: The extra oxygen taken in after exercise, above the resting amount, that is needed to remove the lactate produced (and restore oxygen stores / ATP).
parts.working: B1 extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down / convert lactate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what happens to lactate after exercise.
parts.answer: Lactate is carried in the blood to the liver; it is oxidised back to pyruvate (regenerating reduced NAD); some pyruvate is oxidised in the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation to CO₂ and water; most is converted to glucose (and then glycogen) in the liver.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: carried in blood to liver; converted to pyruvate; some oxidised by aerobic respiration (Krebs cycle) to CO₂ and water; rest converted to glucose / glycogen.

practice.stem: Rice is grown in flooded paddy fields across Punjab and Sindh.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how rice plants are adapted to grow with their roots in flooded paddy fields with very little oxygen.
parts.answer: Aerenchyma (large air spaces) in stems and roots allow oxygen to diffuse from the leaves to the roots; roots tolerate high ethanol concentrations; roots have high levels of alcohol dehydrogenase so ethanol is broken down / anaerobic respiration continues; stems grow rapidly to keep leaves above water; shallow roots / leaves have water-repellent surfaces trapping air.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: aerenchyma / air spaces; oxygen diffuses to roots from aerial parts; root cells tolerant of ethanol; high alcohol dehydrogenase activity; respire anaerobically producing ethanol; fast-growing stems keep leaves above water; air film on leaf surfaces.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why rice roots can respire anaerobically for long periods but most crop roots cannot.
parts.answer: In most crops ethanol builds up to toxic levels, killing the root cells.
parts.working: B1 ethanol toxicity in other species / rice breaks down or tolerates ethanol.

practice.stem:
Yeast was grown in a sealed industrial fermenter containing sugar-cane molasses diluted with water, at a distillery making fuel ethanol. Readings:
time / h: 0, 4, 8, 12, 24, 48, 72
dissolved oxygen / % of starting value: 100, 40, 5, 0, 0, 0, 0
ethanol / g dm⁻³: 0, 0.2, 1.5, 6.0, 22, 60, 64

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain the changes in dissolved oxygen and ethanol concentration in the first 12 hours.
parts.answer: Oxygen falls rapidly to zero because yeast respires aerobically, using oxygen; little ethanol is produced while oxygen is present; once oxygen is used up (8–12 h) yeast respires anaerobically, so ethanol concentration starts to rise.
parts.working: B1 oxygen falls to 0 by 12 h as used in aerobic respiration; B1 ethanol low while O₂ present; B1 rises as O₂ runs out / anaerobic respiration (fermentation).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the ethanol concentration levels off between 48 and 72 hours.
parts.answer: Sugar is used up / becomes limiting; ethanol concentration becomes toxic and kills or inhibits the yeast (denatures enzymes / damages membranes).
parts.working: 1 mark each for: substrate (sugar) running out; ethanol toxic to yeast.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the fermenter is sealed after the start.
parts.answer: To keep oxygen out so the yeast respires anaerobically and produces ethanol (also prevents contamination).
parts.working: B1 keep anaerobic so ethanol produced.

practice.stem: In this question use these data. Complete aerobic oxidation of 1 mol of glucose releases 2870 kJ. Conversion of 1 mol of glucose to 2 mol of lactate releases 197 kJ. Hydrolysis of 1 mol of ATP releases 30.5 kJ; 2 mol of ATP are made per mol of glucose converted to lactate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the energy in glucose that is released when glucose is converted to lactate. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the energy released in lactate formation that is trapped in ATP. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answer to (a) to explain why lactate is not a waste of energy for the body.
parts.answer: Over 90 % of the energy of the glucose is still in the lactate; lactate is later converted to pyruvate / glucose in the liver and can be respired aerobically, so this energy is recovered.
parts.working: B1 most energy (about 93 %) remains in lactate; B1 lactate reconverted to pyruvate / glucose and used.

practice.stem: Dahi (yoghurt) is made by adding a little old yoghurt, which contains Lactobacillus bacteria, to warm milk and leaving it at about 40 °C for several hours. The milk sugar lactose is broken down to glucose and galactose, which the bacteria respire anaerobically.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the product of anaerobic respiration in Lactobacillus and explain why the pH of the milk falls.
parts.answer: Lactate (lactic acid); lactic acid releases hydrogen ions, lowering the pH.
parts.working: B1 lactate / lactic acid; B1 acid / H⁺ ions accumulate so pH falls.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why fermentation slows down and stops after some hours even though sugar is still present.
parts.answer: The low pH changes the ionic and hydrogen bonds in the bacteria's enzymes, changing the active site shape (denaturing them), so respiration and growth slow and stop.
parts.working: B1 pH becomes too low / acidic; B1 enzymes denatured / active site shape altered.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the milk is kept at about 40 °C rather than at 20 °C.
parts.answer: 40 °C is close to the optimum temperature of the bacteria's enzymes, so fermentation is faster.
parts.working: B1 near optimum temperature for bacterial enzymes / faster respiration.

practice.stem: Wheat fields in parts of Sindh sometimes become waterlogged after heavy rain or poor drainage. Wheat roots are not adapted to waterlogging.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why waterlogging causes the roots to respire anaerobically.
parts.answer: Water fills the air spaces between soil particles; oxygen diffuses very slowly through water so the roots receive too little oxygen for aerobic respiration.
parts.working: B1 air spaces filled with water; B1 little oxygen reaches roots (slow diffusion in water).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the leaves of the wheat plants turn yellow when the soil stays waterlogged for several days.
parts.answer: Anaerobic respiration produces little ATP; root cells take up mineral ions such as nitrate and magnesium by active transport, which needs ATP; less uptake, so less chlorophyll (and protein) can be made, leaves turn yellow.
parts.working: B1 less ATP from anaerobic respiration; B1 less active transport / uptake of mineral ions; B1 nitrate / magnesium needed for chlorophyll so less chlorophyll.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why root cells may die after long waterlogging.
parts.answer: Ethanol accumulates to toxic concentrations (or not enough ATP to maintain the cells).
parts.working: B1 ethanol toxicity / ATP shortage.

practice.stem: A sprinter's blood lactate concentration was measured before, during and after a 400 m race.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assuming aerobic respiration yields 32 ATP per glucose and anaerobic respiration 2 ATP, calculate how many times faster glucose must be broken down anaerobically to give the same rate of ATP production.
parts.answer: 16 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why blood lactate concentration rises during a 400 m sprint and continues to rise for a few minutes after the race.
parts.answer: During the sprint oxygen supply to muscles cannot meet demand, so muscle cells respire anaerobically and pyruvate is reduced to lactate; lactate diffuses into the blood; after the race lactate still diffuses out of muscle cells into the blood before the liver removes it.
parts.working: B1 insufficient oxygen supply to muscle / demand for ATP exceeds aerobic supply; B1 lactate produced from pyruvate (to regenerate NAD); B1 lactate continues to diffuse from muscle into blood after exercise (removal by liver slower).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe what happens to lactate after exercise.
parts.answer: Lactate is carried in the blood to the liver, oxidised back to pyruvate (using oxygen – the oxygen debt), which is either respired aerobically or converted to glucose / glycogen.
parts.working: B1 transported to liver; B1 converted to pyruvate, then respired or converted to glucose / glycogen (requires extra oxygen).

practice.stem: Crucian carp can survive for months in ponds covered by ice where there is almost no oxygen. Their muscles carry out lactate fermentation, but then convert the lactate to ethanol, which diffuses out of the fish across the gills into the water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the fish must regenerate NAD to survive without oxygen.
parts.answer: Glycolysis needs NAD to accept hydrogen when triose phosphate is oxidised; without regenerated NAD glycolysis would stop and no ATP would be made.
parts.working: B1 NAD needed as hydrogen acceptor in glycolysis; B1 otherwise glycolysis / ATP production stops.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest the advantage to the fish of converting lactate to ethanol rather than keeping the lactate.
parts.answer: Lactate would build up in the tissues and blood, lowering pH and denaturing enzymes; ethanol is a small (uncharged) molecule that can diffuse out across the gills into the large volume of water, so no toxic build-up occurs and long periods of anaerobic respiration are possible.
parts.working: B1 lactate accumulation lowers pH / is harmful; B1 ethanol diffuses out of the body through gills; B1 so anaerobic respiration can continue for months.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one disadvantage of this adaptation.
parts.answer: The energy remaining in ethanol is lost from the body (it cannot be later reconverted to glucose), so more glucose (glycogen store) is used.
parts.working: B1 energy in ethanol is lost / glycogen stores used up faster.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare lactate fermentation in mammals with ethanol fermentation in yeast, giving two similarities and two differences.
parts.answer: Similarities: both start with glycolysis producing 2 ATP; both regenerate NAD by reducing a product using reduced NAD; both occur in the cytoplasm. Differences: ethanol pathway releases CO₂, lactate pathway does not; ethanol pathway has two steps (via ethanal), lactate pathway one step; enzymes differ (pyruvate decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase vs lactate dehydrogenase); lactate pathway is reversible, ethanol pathway is not.
parts.working: Max 2 similarities, max 2 differences, 1 mark each from the list.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why lactate can be converted back to pyruvate but ethanol cannot be converted back to pyruvate.
parts.answer: In lactate formation no carbon is lost: lactate (3C) is simply reduced pyruvate and lactate dehydrogenase catalyses a reversible reaction; in ethanol formation CO₂ is removed (decarboxylation), so ethanol has only 2C and the reaction is irreversible.
parts.working: B1 lactate still has 3 carbons / reversible reduction; B1 ethanol pathway loses CO₂ so cannot be reversed.

practice.stem:
Samples were taken from two muscles of a sheep. Results:
muscle X: mitochondria 2 % of cell volume; lactate dehydrogenase activity high; myoglobin content low
muscle Y: mitochondria 9 % of cell volume; lactate dehydrogenase activity low; myoglobin content high

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest which muscle is better suited to short bursts of very rapid contraction. Explain your answer using the data.
parts.answer: Muscle X: high lactate dehydrogenase activity so pyruvate rapidly converted to lactate, regenerating NAD and allowing fast glycolysis / ATP production without waiting for oxygen; few mitochondria and little myoglobin show it does not rely on aerobic respiration.
parts.working: B1 muscle X; B1 high LDH allows rapid anaerobic respiration / NAD regeneration; B1 few mitochondria / low myoglobin so not dependent on oxygen supply.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why muscle Y can contract for long periods without fatigue.
parts.answer: Many mitochondria give a high rate of aerobic respiration (link reaction, Krebs, oxidative phosphorylation) producing much more ATP per glucose; myoglobin stores oxygen; little lactate produced so pH does not fall.
parts.working: B1 many mitochondria / aerobic respiration; B1 more ATP per glucose (about 32 vs 2); B1 myoglobin stores oxygen / little lactate accumulation.

practice.stem: During a 10-second sprint, a muscle broke down glucose anaerobically at 0.60 µmol per gram per second. During a long run, the same muscle broke down glucose aerobically at 0.050 µmol per gram per second. Assume 2 ATP per glucose anaerobically and 32 ATP per glucose aerobically.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of ATP production, in µmol per gram per second, in each case.
parts.answer: anaerobic 1.2 µmol g⁻¹ s⁻¹; aerobic 1.6 µmol g⁻¹ s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times faster glucose is used during the sprint than during the long run.
parts.answer: 12 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why anaerobic respiration can be used for only short periods even though it supplies ATP rapidly.
parts.answer: It uses glucose / glycogen 12 times faster for a similar ATP rate, so stores are quickly depleted; lactate accumulates and lowers pH, inhibiting enzymes and causing fatigue; an oxygen debt builds up.
parts.working: B1 glucose / glycogen used very quickly (wasteful); B1 lactate accumulation / low pH / fatigue; B1 oxygen debt must be repaid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define respiratory quotient (RQ).
parts.answer: RQ = volume of carbon dioxide produced ÷ volume of oxygen used in the same time.
parts.working: B1 CO₂ given out ÷ O₂ taken in.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
The equation for the complete oxidation of the lipid tripalmitin is
2C₅₁H₉₈O₆ + 145O₂ → 102CO₂ + 98H₂O
Calculate the RQ of tripalmitin. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the RQ you would expect for respiration of carbohydrate and of protein.
parts.answer: Carbohydrate 1.0; protein about 0.9.
parts.working: B1 carbohydrate 1.0; B1 protein 0.9 (accept 0.8–0.9).

practice.stem: In 30 minutes, germinating gram (chickpea) seeds took in 50 cm³ of oxygen and gave out 45 cm³ of carbon dioxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the respiratory quotient (RQ) of the seeds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest the main respiratory substrate being used. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Protein, because an RQ of about 0.9 is typical of protein (carbohydrate 1.0, lipid 0.7).
parts.working: B1 protein; B1 RQ 0.9 matches protein / between lipid 0.7 and carbohydrate 1.0.

practice.stem:
Oleic acid is a fatty acid found in olive oil and mustard (sarson) oil. Its complete oxidation is:
C₁₈H₃₄O₂ + 25.5O₂ → 18CO₂ + 17H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the RQ for the respiration of oleic acid. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the RQ of lipids is lower than the RQ of carbohydrates.
parts.answer: Lipids contain far fewer oxygen atoms relative to carbon and hydrogen than carbohydrates, so more oxygen must be taken in to oxidise the hydrogen to water and carbon to CO₂; oxygen uptake is greater than CO₂ output.
parts.working: B1 lipids contain relatively little oxygen / more H per C; B1 more O₂ needed relative to CO₂ released.

practice.stem: A simple respirometer consists of a boiling tube containing germinating seeds on a wire gauze above soda lime. The tube is connected by a three-way tap to a syringe and to a U-shaped capillary tube containing coloured liquid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the function of each of the following: the soda lime; the coloured liquid in the capillary; the syringe.
parts.answer: soda lime absorbs carbon dioxide; coloured liquid shows the change in gas volume (moves towards the seeds as oxygen is used); syringe resets the liquid to its starting position and measures the volume of oxygen used
parts.working: B1 each: absorbs CO₂; shows volume change / movement measured; resets liquid / measures volume.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the liquid moves towards the seeds.
parts.answer: The seeds take in oxygen; the carbon dioxide they release is absorbed by soda lime; so the volume (pressure) of gas in the tube decreases and the liquid is drawn towards the seeds.
parts.working: B1 oxygen used and CO₂ absorbed; B1 gas volume / pressure in tube decreases.

practice.stem: Yeast in a sealed flask of glucose solution produced 30 cm³ of carbon dioxide while taking in 12 cm³ of oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the RQ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the RQ is greater than 1.
parts.answer: Some of the yeast are respiring anaerobically, producing CO₂ (by decarboxylation of pyruvate to ethanal) without taking in any oxygen; so CO₂ output exceeds O₂ uptake.
parts.working: B1 anaerobic respiration / fermentation occurring; B1 CO₂ released without O₂ uptake.

practice.stem: Two respirometers contained equal masses of germinating sunflower seeds at 25 °C. Tube A contained potassium hydroxide solution; tube B contained water instead. In 20 minutes the liquid in the capillary of tube A moved 36 mm towards the seeds and in tube B it moved 9 mm towards the seeds. Both capillaries had the same diameter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the liquid moves towards the seeds in tube A.
parts.answer: The seeds take in oxygen for aerobic respiration; the CO₂ they release is absorbed by potassium hydroxide, so the volume of gas falls and the pressure decreases.
parts.working: B1 oxygen used in respiration; B1 CO₂ absorbed by KOH so gas volume / pressure in the tube decreases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the RQ of the seeds.
parts.working: M1 O₂ uptake = 36 mm; CO₂ output = 36 − 9 = 27 mm; A1 RQ = 27/36 = 0.75.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest which respiratory substrate the seeds were mainly using. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: A mixture of lipid and carbohydrate (or mainly lipid), because 0.75 is between 0.7 (lipid) and 1.0 (carbohydrate) and close to 0.7.
parts.working: B1 lipid (with some carbohydrate), RQ between 0.7 and 1.0 / close to 0.7.

practice.stem:
When the amino acid alanine is respired in the body, its nitrogen is removed as urea. The overall equation is:
2C₃H₇O₂N + 6O₂ → 5CO₂ + 5H₂O + CO(NH₂)₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the RQ for alanine. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why proteins are not normally the main respiratory substrate in a well-fed person.
parts.answer: Amino acids are mainly used to make proteins (enzymes, structural proteins); they are only respired when carbohydrate and lipid stores are low; their nitrogen must first be removed (deamination), producing urea.
parts.working: B1 needed for protein synthesis / growth; B1 only respired when carbohydrate and fat are scarce / must be deaminated first.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the RQ for alanine is closer to 1 than the RQ for a fatty acid.
parts.answer: Alanine contains more oxygen relative to its carbon and hydrogen than a fatty acid does.
parts.working: B1 higher proportion of oxygen in the molecule.

practice.stem: A respirometer contained 3.0 g of germinating maize grains and potassium hydroxide solution at 25 °C. After 15 minutes the liquid in the capillary was returned to its starting position using the syringe. The syringe reading changed from 0.80 cm³ to 0.44 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen uptake in cm³ per gram per hour.
parts.answer: 0.48 cm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the syringe reading decreased.
parts.answer: Oxygen was absorbed by the grains and CO₂ absorbed by the KOH, so gas volume fell; air from the syringe was pushed in to replace the lost volume, returning the liquid to its starting point.
parts.working: B1 volume of gas in tube reduced by oxygen uptake; B1 syringe plunger pushed in to restore level / volume pushed in equals O₂ used.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the results are expressed per gram of grains.
parts.answer: So that results from samples with different masses can be compared.
parts.working: B1 allows comparison between different masses / standardises.

practice.stem: During the month of Ramadan, a healthy adult who fasts from dawn to sunset had her RQ measured at different times. Just after the pre-dawn meal (sehri), it was 0.97. Late in the afternoon it was 0.74.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the change in RQ during the day.
parts.answer: After the meal the main substrate is carbohydrate (RQ close to 1.0); as the day goes on, blood glucose and liver glycogen are used up; the body switches to respiring more lipid (fat stores), so RQ falls towards 0.7.
parts.working: B1 RQ ≈ 1 shows carbohydrate; B1 carbohydrate / glycogen stores depleted during fast; B1 increasing use of lipid gives RQ near 0.7.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how her RQ would change in the hour after she breaks the fast with dates and a meal rich in rice. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: RQ rises back towards 1.0, because carbohydrate from dates (sugars) and rice (starch) is digested and becomes the main respiratory substrate.
parts.working: B1 RQ increases towards 1; B1 carbohydrate becomes main substrate.

practice.stem:
Germinating seeds were sealed in a 500 cm³ flask of air for two hours. A gas analyser gave these percentages by volume:
start: oxygen 21.0 %, carbon dioxide 0.04 %
after 2 hours: oxygen 17.2 %, carbon dioxide 3.9 %
Assume the total gas volume stayed at 500 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen used and the volume of carbon dioxide produced.
parts.answer: oxygen 19.0 cm³; carbon dioxide 19.3 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the RQ to 2 decimal places and suggest the respiratory substrate.
parts.answer: RQ = 1.02; carbohydrate
parts.working: M1 19.3 ÷ 19.0 = 1.02; A1 carbohydrate (RQ ≈ 1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the RQ might be slightly above 1.0 in this experiment.
parts.answer: Some anaerobic respiration in the centre of the seeds / as oxygen falls (or measurement error of the gas analyser).
parts.working: B1 some anaerobic respiration releasing CO₂ without O₂ uptake (accept measurement uncertainty).

practice.stem: A respirometer containing 5.0 g of germinating mung bean seeds and soda lime was kept at 30 °C. The coloured liquid in the capillary tube (internal radius 0.5 mm) moved 24 mm in 10 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen uptake in mm³ per gram per hour. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 22.6 mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a thermobarometer (an identical tube with glass beads instead of seeds) should be set up alongside the respirometer.
parts.answer: Changes in temperature or atmospheric pressure would make the liquid move even without respiration; the thermobarometer measures this movement so it can be subtracted (or used to correct the readings).
parts.working: B1 temperature / atmospheric pressure changes alter gas volume; B1 allows correction of readings for these changes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: During the first two days of germination of castor bean seeds, which store mainly lipid, the RQ was 0.71; by day 10, when the seedlings had green leaves, it was 0.98. Suggest an explanation.
parts.answer: At first the seeds respire stored lipid (RQ about 0.7); later the lipid stores are used up and the seedlings photosynthesise, so they respire carbohydrate (RQ about 1.0).
parts.working: B1 early: lipid stores respired; B1 later: carbohydrate (from photosynthesis / converted from lipid) respired.

practice.stem: Assume carbohydrate has an RQ of 1.0 and lipid an RQ of 0.70. When a mixture of substrates is respired, the overall RQ is the weighted mean of the RQs, weighted by the proportion of the oxygen used for each substrate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A tissue uses 60 % of its oxygen to respire carbohydrate and 40 % to respire lipid. Calculate the overall RQ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A migrating bird has an RQ of 0.79. Calculate the percentage of its oxygen used for carbohydrate respiration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why an RQ of 0.88 does not prove that a tissue is respiring protein.
parts.answer: The same value can be produced by a mixture of carbohydrate and lipid; RQ shows the overall ratio of CO₂ to O₂, not which molecules are respired.
parts.working: B1 mixture of carbohydrate and lipid gives same RQ; B1 RQ is an average / cannot identify substrates on its own.

practice.stem: Seeds of mustard (sarson) were studied as they ripened on the plant. Ripening seeds convert sugars from the leaves into stored oil (lipid). Their measured RQ was 1.3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the RQ of ripening oil seeds is greater than 1.
parts.answer: Carbohydrate contains much more oxygen relative to carbon and hydrogen than lipid; converting carbohydrate to lipid releases the extra oxygen within the molecules, and some carbon is lost as CO₂ (from decarboxylation, e.g. pyruvate → acetyl CoA) without oxygen being taken in; so CO₂ output is greater than O₂ uptake.
parts.working: B1 carbohydrate is oxygen-rich, lipid oxygen-poor; B1 conversion releases CO₂ (decarboxylation) without using O₂; B1 so CO₂ released > O₂ taken in.

parts.label: b
parts.text: When the same seeds germinate, the RQ is about 0.7 for the first few days. Explain why.
parts.answer: The stored oil (lipid) is the main respiratory substrate during early germination; lipids have an RQ of about 0.7.
parts.working: B1 lipid stores being respired; B1 lipid RQ ≈ 0.7.

practice.stem: A respirometer containing 2.5 g of germinating peas and soda lime was set up beside a thermobarometer (identical tube containing glass beads). The capillary tubes have an internal radius of 0.5 mm. In 15 minutes the liquid in the respirometer moved 18 mm towards the peas, while the liquid in the thermobarometer moved 3 mm away from the beads.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the liquid in the thermobarometer moved.
parts.answer: The temperature in the room rose / the atmospheric pressure fell, so the gas in the tube expanded and pushed the liquid away from the beads.
parts.working: B1 change in temperature or atmospheric pressure; B1 gas expanded so liquid pushed away.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected rate of oxygen uptake in mm³ per gram per hour. Use V = πr²l and give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 26.4 mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹
parts.working: M1 corrected distance 18 + 3 = 21 mm (the same expansion also acted against the respirometer reading); M1 V = π × 0.5² × 21 = 16.5 mm³; A1 16.5 ÷ 2.5 × 4 = 26.4.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the respirometer and thermobarometer should be placed in the same water bath.
parts.answer: So that both experience the same temperature (and pressure) changes, making the correction valid.
parts.working: B1 same conditions so correction is valid.

practice.stem: Two respirometers with soda lime and capillary tubes of internal diameter 1.0 mm were kept at 25 °C. In 20 minutes, the liquid moved 30 mm with 4.0 g of earthworms and 42 mm with 1.5 g of blowfly larvae (maggots).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen uptake of each animal in mm³ per gram per hour. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: earthworms 17.7 mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹; maggots 66.0 mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹
parts.working: M1 radius = 0.5 mm, V = πr²l: 23.6 mm³ and 33.0 mm³; M1 ÷ mass × 3 (per hour); A1 17.7 and 66.0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the rate per gram is for maggots than for earthworms. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 3.7 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one biological reason for the difference.
parts.answer: Maggots are actively feeding and growing rapidly so have a high metabolic rate (or earthworms have a lower activity / body contains more water and non-respiring tissue per gram).
parts.working: B1 any sensible: higher activity / growth rate of maggots; earthworm mass includes gut contents / water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of an ATP molecule.
parts.answer: Adenine (a base) joined to ribose (a pentose sugar) and three phosphate groups.
parts.working: B1 adenine + ribose; B1 three phosphate groups.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why ATP is described as the universal energy currency of cells.
parts.answer: It is used for energy transfer in all organisms / cells; hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and Pi releases energy in small, manageable amounts; it is water soluble and easily transported within cells; it is quickly re-made from ADP and Pi; one molecule type can be used by many different reactions.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: found in all living cells; hydrolysis releases a small, suitable amount of energy (about 30 kJ mol⁻¹); single step reaction, quick; soluble / moves easily in cell; easily regenerated; links energy-releasing and energy-requiring reactions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the two ways ATP is synthesised in respiration.
parts.answer: Substrate-level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation (chemiosmosis).
parts.working: B1 both named.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why all living organisms need a continuous supply of energy.
parts.answer: To carry out work such as active transport, movement and synthesis of large molecules (anabolic reactions), and to maintain body temperature in some animals; cells are constantly using energy so it must be continuously released from respiration.
parts.working: B1 energy needed for named work (any two of active transport, anabolic reactions / synthesis, movement / muscle contraction, nerve impulses, cell division); B1 used continuously so constant supply needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name four processes in a cell that use ATP.
parts.answer: Any four of: active transport (e.g. sodium–potassium pump); muscle contraction; protein synthesis (or DNA replication / synthesis of polysaccharides); cell division; movement of vesicles (endocytosis / exocytosis); phosphorylating glucose in glycolysis; nerve impulse transmission (restoring resting potential).
parts.working: 2 marks for four; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a word equation for the hydrolysis of ATP and name the enzyme that catalyses it.
parts.answer: ATP + water → ADP + phosphate (Pi) + energy; ATP hydrolase (ATPase)
parts.working: B1 equation with water and both products; B1 ATP hydrolase / ATPase.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hydrolysis of one ATP releases a small quantity of energy (30.5 kJ mol⁻¹). Explain why this is an advantage to a cell.
parts.answer: Energy is released in small, manageable amounts that match the needs of individual reactions, so little is wasted as heat; and it is released in a single quick step.
parts.working: B1 small amounts suited to cellular reactions / less wasted as heat; B1 released quickly in one step (one reaction).

parts.label: a
parts.text: ATP is a phosphorylated nucleotide. Name the three components of an ATP molecule.
parts.answer: Adenine (a base), ribose (a pentose sugar) and three phosphate groups.
parts.working: 2 marks all three; 1 mark for two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways in which ATP is similar to an adenine nucleotide in RNA and one way in which it differs.
parts.answer: Similar: both contain adenine; both contain ribose (and phosphate). Different: ATP has three phosphate groups, the RNA nucleotide has one (ATP is not part of a polynucleotide chain).
parts.working: B1 adenine; B1 ribose; B1 three phosphates vs one.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between substrate-level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation.
parts.answer: Substrate-level: a phosphate group is transferred directly from a phosphorylated intermediate to ADP, catalysed by an enzyme. Oxidative: ATP is made by ATP synthase using energy from a proton gradient set up by the electron transport chain (chemiosmosis).
parts.working: B1 direct transfer of phosphate from substrate molecule to ADP; B1 ATP synthase / proton gradient / chemiosmosis / electron transport.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For each type, state one stage of respiration where it occurs.
parts.answer: Substrate-level: glycolysis or Krebs cycle. Oxidative: electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae).
parts.working: B1 glycolysis / Krebs; B1 inner membrane / ETC.

practice.stem: Mean energy values of respiratory substrates (kJ g⁻¹): carbohydrate 15.8; lipid 39.4; protein 17.0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times more energy is released per gram from lipid than from carbohydrate. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 2.5 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why lipids release more energy per gram than carbohydrates when respired.
parts.answer: Lipids contain more hydrogen atoms per unit mass (fatty acids are long hydrocarbon chains); most energy comes from oxidising hydrogen in the ETC: more hydrogen means more reduced NAD/FAD, more protons pumped and more ATP; carbohydrates contain more oxygen and are already partly oxidised.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: more H atoms per gram in lipid; hydrogen carried by NAD / FAD to ETC; more protons pumped / greater proton gradient; more ATP produced by oxidative phosphorylation; carbohydrates contain proportionally more oxygen.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why migratory birds such as Siberian cranes that fly to Pakistan each winter store lipid rather than carbohydrate before migration.
parts.answer: Lipid gives more energy per unit mass, so the bird carries less weight for the same energy store (and produces metabolic water).
parts.working: B1 more energy per gram so lighter load (accept metabolic water).

practice.stem: Energy values: carbohydrate 15.8 kJ g⁻¹, protein 17.0 kJ g⁻¹, lipid 39.4 kJ g⁻¹. A student in Karachi ate 300 g of carbohydrate, 60 g of protein and 70 g of lipid in one day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total energy in the food eaten.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of this energy that came from lipid. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The energy values above are for complete respiration in the body. Suggest two reasons why the energy the body actually gains from this food is less than the value calculated in (a).
parts.answer: Not all the food is digested and absorbed, so some energy is lost in faeces; nitrogen from protein is excreted as urea, which still contains unoxidised energy; some energy is lost as heat during digestion and metabolism.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: incomplete digestion/absorption (energy lost in faeces); energy still in urea from protein; energy lost as heat.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Glucose is the main respiratory substrate but ATP, not glucose, is the immediate source of energy for cell processes. Give three reasons why ATP is better suited to this role.
parts.answer: ATP is hydrolysed in a single step, releasing energy immediately (glucose needs many steps); energy released in small, useful quantities (glucose would release too much at once, wasting heat); ATP is small and soluble so moves easily within the cell to where energy is needed; ATP is used in all cells / reactions (universal) and is quickly regenerated from ADP.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: one-step hydrolysis / immediate; small quantities; soluble / easily moved; universal / easily regenerated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why ATP is described as an immediate energy source rather than an energy store.
parts.answer: ATP is not stored in large amounts; it is made and used continuously (rapid turnover); it is unstable (readily hydrolysed) so cannot hold energy for long.
parts.working: B1 small quantities in cells / rapidly used and remade; B1 unstable / readily hydrolysed so not suitable for storage.

practice.stem:
Food factories test the cleanliness of surfaces using an ATP swab. The swab is mixed with the enzyme luciferase and its substrate luciferin; light is produced in proportion to the ATP present. Readings (relative light units, RLU) from a dairy plant in Lahore:
milk tank after cleaning: 46 RLU
milk tank before cleaning: 3600 RLU
conveyor belt after cleaning: 820 RLU
The plant's pass limit is 150 RLU.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the amount of ATP on a surface indicates how much living material or food residue is present.
parts.answer: All living cells (bacteria, yeast, and cells in food) contain ATP because it is the universal energy currency; more cells / residue means more ATP.
parts.working: B1 all cells contain ATP / universal energy currency; B1 more ATP = more cells / organic residue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in RLU achieved by cleaning the milk tank. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State, with a reason, what the factory should do about the conveyor belt.
parts.answer: Clean it again (and retest), because 820 RLU is above the 150 RLU limit.
parts.working: B1 reclean because above limit.

practice.stem: Stearic acid (C₁₈H₃₆O₂, Mr 284) is a fatty acid and glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆, Mr 180) is a carbohydrate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of hydrogen atoms per unit of relative molecular mass (H atoms ÷ Mr) for each molecule, and how many times greater this is for stearic acid. Give the final answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: stearic acid 0.127; glucose 0.067; 1.9 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to explain why respiring 1 g of lipid releases more energy than respiring 1 g of carbohydrate.
parts.answer: Most energy from respiration comes from oxidising hydrogen; more hydrogen atoms per gram means more reduced NAD / FAD formed; more electrons pass along the electron transport chain and more protons are pumped, so more ATP is made by chemiosmosis (and more water formed).
parts.working: B1 more hydrogen per gram; B1 more reduced NAD / reduced FAD; B1 more proton pumping / more ATP via oxidative phosphorylation.

practice.stem: An adult body contains about 250 g of ATP at any one time, yet hydrolyses about 70 kg of ATP per day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of times each ATP molecule is resynthesised from ADP and Pi per day.
parts.answer: 280 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: The relative molecular mass of ATP is 507. Hydrolysis of one mole releases 30.5 kJ. Calculate the energy released per day by hydrolysis of ATP, in kJ, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why cells do not store large amounts of ATP.
parts.answer: ATP is unstable / readily hydrolysed so cannot be stored for long; it is quickly regenerated from ADP and Pi when needed, so a small pool recycled rapidly is enough; energy is stored instead in glycogen or lipid.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: ATP unstable / hydrolyses easily; rapid turnover from ADP + Pi makes storage unnecessary; would affect water potential / takes up space; energy stored as glycogen / starch / lipid instead.

practice.stem: A kidney tubule cell pumps 1.5 × 10⁸ sodium ions per second out of the cell using sodium–potassium pumps. Each pump hydrolyses one ATP to move 3 sodium ions out (and 2 potassium ions in). Assume 32 ATP per glucose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of ATP molecules hydrolysed per second by the pumps.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of glucose molecules the cell must respire aerobically each second to supply this ATP. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the ATP is used to move sodium ions against their concentration gradient.
parts.answer: ATP binds to the carrier protein and is hydrolysed; the phosphate attaches to the protein (phosphorylation), changing its shape; the shape change moves the bound sodium ions to the other side of the membrane and releases them.
parts.working: B1 ATP hydrolysed at the carrier / ATPase site; B1 phosphate binds to carrier changing its shape (conformational change); B1 ions carried across / released on other side.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why kidney tubule cells contain many mitochondria.
parts.answer: To produce large amounts of ATP by aerobic respiration for active transport.
parts.working: B1 large ATP supply for active transport.

practice.stem: Complete aerobic oxidation of one molecule of glucose (Mr 180) yields 32 ATP. Complete oxidation of one molecule of the fatty acid palmitic acid (Mr 256) yields 106 ATP.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of ATP produced per gram of each substrate, to 3 significant figures, and how many times greater the yield per gram is for palmitic acid (to 3 significant figures).
parts.answer: glucose 0.178 mol g⁻¹; palmitic acid 0.414 mol g⁻¹; 2.33 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Despite this, mammals store some carbohydrate as glycogen in muscles and liver. Suggest two advantages of glycogen over lipid as an energy store.
parts.answer: Glycogen can be hydrolysed to glucose very quickly when energy is suddenly needed; glucose can be respired anaerobically, but fatty acids cannot (they need oxygen / Krebs cycle); glucose is the main fuel for the brain.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: rapid mobilisation; can supply anaerobic respiration / glycolysis; glucose needed by brain / red blood cells.

practice.stem:
Isolated frog muscle fibres were placed in three dishes and observed for 2 minutes:
dish 1: Ringer's salt solution only — no contraction
dish 2: Ringer's solution + 1 % glucose — no contraction
dish 3: Ringer's solution + 0.25 % ATP — fibres contracted within seconds

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the fibres in dish 3 contracted.
parts.answer: ATP was hydrolysed by ATPase in the muscle fibres, releasing energy (and phosphate) directly used for contraction (cross-bridge cycling).
parts.working: B1 ATP is the immediate energy source for contraction; B1 hydrolysed by ATPase releasing energy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why glucose did not cause contraction in dish 2.
parts.answer: Glucose is not used directly for contraction; it must first be respired (glycolysis, Krebs, oxidative phosphorylation) to make ATP, which takes time; isolated fibres may have little glucose uptake / the stimulus to contract was absent.
parts.working: B1 glucose must be respired to make ATP first; B1 multi-step / slow, or no stimulus / limited uptake.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why dish 1 was included.
parts.answer: As a control to show that the salt solution alone does not cause contraction, so the effect in dish 3 is due to ATP.
parts.working: B1 control: shows contraction is due to ATP not the solution.

practice.stem: When protein is burned completely in a calorimeter, it releases about 23.6 kJ g⁻¹. When it is respired in the human body, the useful energy is only about 17.0 kJ g⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the energy in protein that is not released in the body. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the energy released from protein in the body is less than in a calorimeter.
parts.answer: In the body amino acids are deaminated; the amino groups are converted to urea, which is excreted; urea still contains carbon and hydrogen that have not been oxidised, so its chemical energy is lost; in the calorimeter the protein is completely oxidised (including nitrogen).
parts.working: B1 deamination; B1 nitrogen excreted as urea; B1 urea contains unoxidised C / H / energy that is lost, whereas calorimeter oxidises completely.

practice.stem: A student plans to investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of carbon dioxide production by yeast in glucose solution, collecting the gas in a gas syringe.

parts.label: a
parts.text: List the apparatus the student needs, apart from yeast and glucose solution.
parts.answer: Conical flask / boiling tube with bung and delivery tube; gas syringe; thermostatically controlled water baths (or water bath and thermometer); stopwatch; measuring cylinder or syringe for volumes; balance.
parts.working: 2 marks for five suitable items; 1 mark for three or four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student should make sure that the yeast suspension is at the required temperature when timing starts.
parts.answer: Place the yeast suspension and glucose solution separately in the water bath for about 10 minutes before mixing (equilibration); check the temperature with a thermometer inside the tube before starting.
parts.working: B1 pre-incubate both solutions in water bath / equilibrate for stated time (e.g. 5–10 min); B1 check with thermometer in the mixture.

practice.stem: A student has 100 cm³ of 10 % glucose solution and distilled water. She needs 20 cm³ of each of these concentrations: 10 %, 8 %, 6 %, 4 % and 2 % glucose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the volumes of 10 % glucose solution and distilled water needed to make each concentration.
parts.answer: 10 %: 20 cm³ + 0 cm³; 8 %: 16 + 4; 6 %: 12 + 8; 4 %: 8 + 12; 2 %: 4 + 16 (volumes of glucose solution + water)
parts.working: M1 volume of stock = required concentration ÷ 10 × 20; A2 all five correct (A1 for three or four).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name a suitable piece of apparatus for measuring these volumes accurately.
parts.answer: Graduated pipette or syringe (or burette)
parts.working: B1 pipette / syringe / burette (not beaker).

practice.stem: A student compares carbon dioxide production by yeast in two sugar solutions by counting the bubbles that leave the end of a delivery tube placed under water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a better way of measuring the carbon dioxide produced.
parts.answer: Collect the gas in a gas syringe or in an inverted measuring cylinder filled with water (displacement), and read the volume at regular time intervals.
parts.working: B1 gas syringe / inverted measuring cylinder over water; B1 record volume at fixed intervals / over fixed time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why your method gives more accurate results than counting bubbles.
parts.answer: Bubbles can be different sizes, so the number of bubbles does not represent volume; bubbles may be missed when produced quickly; the volume is a quantitative measurement in cm³.
parts.working: B1 bubbles vary in size; B1 volume measured directly in cm³ / bubbles hard to count at high rate.

practice.stem: A student will use respirometers containing soda lime (or potassium hydroxide solution) and live blowfly larvae (maggots) to compare respiration rates at 15 °C, 20 °C and 25 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards in this investigation and state a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Soda lime / KOH is corrosive (alkali): wear eye protection and gloves, do not touch, wrap soda lime in gauze. Maggots may carry microorganisms: wash hands after handling / wear gloves. Glass capillary may break: handle carefully. Hot water bath: avoid scalding.
parts.working: For each of two hazards: B1 hazard identified; B1 matching precaution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way to make sure the investigation is ethical.
parts.answer: Keep the temperature range within what the larvae survive naturally (not above about 30 °C), keep them separated from the soda lime by gauze, use the fewest larvae possible and return them to suitable conditions afterwards.
parts.working: B1 any one sensible welfare point.

practice.stem: A student wants to find out whether yeast respires glucose, sucrose, maltose and lactose at different rates.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how you would make 50 cm³ of a 2 % sugar solution of each sugar, from solid sugar and distilled water.
parts.answer: Weigh 1.0 g of sugar, dissolve in some distilled water and make up to 50 cm³ in a volumetric flask (or measuring cylinder).
parts.working: M1 2 g per 100 cm³ → 1.0 g per 50 cm³; A1 dissolve and make up to total volume 50 cm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student could compare the rate of respiration of yeast with each sugar by measuring carbon dioxide production.
parts.answer: Mix the same volume (e.g. 20 cm³) of each sugar solution with the same mass of yeast (e.g. 1 g) in a flask connected to a gas syringe; keep at 30 °C in a water bath; allow 5 min to equilibrate; measure volume of gas collected every minute for 10 min (or total volume in a fixed time); rate = volume ÷ time; control with water and no sugar; repeat 3 times.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: same yeast mass / suspension volume; same volume and concentration of each sugar; collect CO₂ in gas syringe / inverted measuring cylinder over water; constant temperature water bath; equilibration time; measure volume over a fixed time / calculate rate; control with no sugar; repeats and mean.

practice.stem: DCPIP is a blue dye that becomes colourless when it is reduced by hydrogen released by dehydrogenase enzymes in respiring yeast. A student wants to investigate the effect of pH on the rate of respiration in yeast using DCPIP.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method the student could use. Your method should allow the student to collect valid and reliable results.
parts.answer: Use buffer solutions at pH 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 (at least five values); in each tube put the same volume (e.g. 5 cm³) of yeast suspension of the same concentration, the same volume of buffer and the same volume and concentration of glucose; equilibrate at 30 °C in a water bath; add the same volume of DCPIP (e.g. 1 cm³), mix, start timing; record time for blue colour to disappear (compare with a colour standard of yeast without DCPIP); control tube with boiled yeast at each pH; repeat three times at each pH and calculate means; rate = 1/time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: at least five pH values using buffers; same volume and concentration of yeast (and glucose); constant temperature with water bath (stated value); same volume of DCPIP added and timing started; end point judged against a colour standard / time to colourless; boiled yeast control or no-yeast control; three repeats and mean; rate = 1/t. Max 6.

practice.stem: A student wants to compare the rate of oxygen uptake of germinating wheat grains with that of dry (dormant) wheat grains using a respirometer with a syringe.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student should carry out this comparison so that the results are valid.
parts.answer: Use the same mass of grains in each respirometer (e.g. 5 g, weighed on a balance); place soda lime (CO₂ absorbent) in each, separated by gauze; keep both at the same temperature in a water bath and leave to equilibrate with tap open; close tap, start timing, measure distance moved / reset with syringe after a fixed time (e.g. 10 min); set up a control with glass beads or boiled grains of the same mass/volume; repeat three times and calculate a mean rate per gram per hour.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: same mass of grains; CO₂ absorbent; constant temperature / water bath; equilibration time before closing tap; measurement of volume over fixed time (syringe / capillary); control with beads or boiled grains; replicates and mean; rate per g per h. Max 5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the student should not use grains that have been soaked in water for very different times.
parts.answer: The stage of germination affects the respiration rate, so it would be an uncontrolled variable.
parts.working: B1 stage of germination / water content would differ and affect respiration rate.

practice.stem: A student has a carbon dioxide sensor connected to a data logger. She wants to investigate the effect of glucose concentration on the rate of respiration of yeast.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline how she could use the sensor to obtain a rate of respiration for each glucose concentration.
parts.answer: Place a fixed volume of yeast suspension and glucose solution in a sealed chamber containing the CO₂ sensor; record CO₂ concentration at intervals (e.g. every 10 s) for a fixed time (e.g. 10 minutes); plot CO₂ concentration against time; the rate is the gradient of the linear part of the graph (change in CO₂ ÷ time); flush the chamber with air and rinse between trials.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: sealed chamber with sensor; same volume of yeast and glucose solution; record at regular intervals for fixed time; rate from gradient / change ÷ time; reset / flush chamber between runs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a suitable range and interval of glucose concentrations.
parts.answer: e.g. 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 % (at least five concentrations including 0 %).
parts.working: B1 at least five concentrations, evenly spaced, sensible range.

practice.stem: A student thinks that ripening mangoes respire faster than unripe mangoes. Mangoes of three ripeness stages (green, turning, fully ripe) are available.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student could test this idea.
parts.answer: Place one whole mango of known mass in a sealed container of known volume with a CO₂ (or O₂) sensor / data logger; keep at constant temperature in the dark; record CO₂ concentration at start and after a fixed time (e.g. 30 minutes); calculate rate as change in CO₂ per kg per hour; use at least three mangoes of each stage (same variety, similar size); use an empty container as a control.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: sealed container and CO₂/O₂ sensor (or limewater/hydrogencarbonate indicator with colour standards); constant temperature; dark (to avoid photosynthesis in green skin); fixed time; rate per unit mass; replicates of each stage, same variety; control. Max 5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the mangoes should be kept in the dark during the measurements.
parts.answer: Green skin may photosynthesise in light, taking up CO₂ and giving out O₂, which would affect the measurements.
parts.working: B1 avoid photosynthesis altering gas concentrations.

practice.stem: A student plans to investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of oxygen uptake by woodlice.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest a suitable range of temperatures and explain your choice.
parts.answer: e.g. 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30 °C; at least five values within the range woodlice meet naturally, so they are not harmed (ethical) and enzymes are not denatured.
parts.working: B1 five or more temperatures in a sensible range (about 5–30 °C); B1 reason: ethical / natural range / avoid harm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student would make sure that differences in oxygen uptake were due to temperature only.
parts.answer: Use the same mass (or number and size) of woodlice for each trial; same volume of soda lime and same respirometer / capillary size; allow the same acclimatisation time at each temperature; same time of day / woodlice not recently fed; measure for the same length of time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three standardised variables with how they are kept constant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Methylene blue is a redox indicator that turns colourless when it is reduced by the hydrogen released by dehydrogenase enzymes in respiring yeast. Describe a method to investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of respiration of yeast using methylene blue.
parts.answer: Prepare yeast suspension (e.g. 10 g dried yeast in 100 cm³ of 5 % glucose solution) and leave to activate; place 10 cm³ yeast suspension in tubes in thermostatically controlled water baths at 5 temperatures (e.g. 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 °C) for 10 min to equilibrate; add 1 cm³ of 0.05 % methylene blue, mix by inverting once, start timer; record time for blue colour to disappear (compare with a colour standard of yeast suspension without indicator); do not shake (oxygen would reoxidise the dye); control: boiled yeast; rate = 1/time; 3 repeats at each temperature and mean; standardise yeast concentration, glucose concentration and volume, dye volume and concentration.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any seven of: at least 5 temperatures with suitable range; method of controlling temperature (water bath, thermometer check); equilibration of yeast and dye separately before mixing; same volume and concentration of yeast suspension; same concentration of glucose; same volume of methylene blue; measure time taken to decolourise; end point standardised (colour standard); avoid shaking / cover with liquid paraffin to keep oxygen out; control with boiled yeast; rate = 1/t; 3 repeats and mean; safety (e.g. methylene blue stains, hot water).

practice.stem: Baker's yeast and a yeast strain used in sugar-cane ethanol distilleries are thought to differ in their tolerance to ethanol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to compare the effect of ethanol concentration on the rate of respiration of the two yeast strains. Include a hypothesis and how you would analyse the results.
parts.answer: Hypothesis: the distillery strain respires faster than baker's yeast at high ethanol concentrations (or: rate falls less with increasing ethanol). Prepare ethanol solutions 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 % by dilution of stock; equal cell density of each strain (same mass of yeast per volume or matched turbidity with colorimeter); same volume and concentration of glucose; constant temperature 30 °C with water bath; equilibrate; measure CO₂ volume with gas syringe (or DCPIP time / CO₂ sensor) over fixed time; three or more replicates; control with no yeast / boiled yeast; calculate mean rate and SD; plot rate against ethanol concentration for both strains on one graph; use a t-test at each concentration (or compare concentrations giving 50 % reduction in rate); risk: ethanol is flammable — no naked flames.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 8: testable hypothesis; independent variable with at least five concentrations and how made; both strains with matched cell density; dependent variable measured (method + units); temperature controlled with stated value; glucose controlled; replicates (≥3); control; graph of mean rate vs concentration for each strain; statistical test (t-test) and why; safety (flammable ethanol).

practice.stem: A student wants to find the respiratory quotient (RQ) of germinating sunflower seeds at 25 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student could use respirometers to obtain the measurements needed, and how the RQ is then calculated.
parts.answer: Set up two identical respirometers with the same mass of seeds in a water bath at 25 °C; one contains KOH / soda lime to absorb CO₂, the other contains the same volume of water instead; equilibrate with taps open, then close and measure the distance moved by the liquid after the same time; the movement in the KOH tube gives oxygen uptake (x); the movement in the water tube gives the difference between O₂ taken in and CO₂ given out (y, towards seeds if O₂ > CO₂); CO₂ produced = x − y; RQ = (x − y) ÷ x; repeat and use means; use a thermobarometer for each.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: two respirometers same mass of seeds; one with KOH / soda lime, one with water; constant temperature / equilibration; KOH reading = O₂ uptake; water reading = O₂ − CO₂; RQ = CO₂ ÷ O₂ with formula; repeats / thermobarometer.

practice.stem: Caffeine is found in tea, which is drunk widely in Pakistan. A student wonders whether caffeine affects the rate of respiration of yeast.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a null hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the rate of respiration of yeast with caffeine and without caffeine (or: caffeine concentration has no effect on the rate).
parts.working: B1 null hypothesis correctly expressed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Plan an investigation to test this hypothesis. Include the statistical test you would use.
parts.answer: Prepare caffeine solutions (e.g. 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 g dm⁻³) by dilution; same volume of yeast suspension of same concentration and same glucose concentration in each tube; constant temperature (water bath 30 °C), equilibrate; measure rate using DCPIP decolourisation time or CO₂ volume in gas syringe over fixed time; at least 5 replicates per concentration; control with 0 caffeine (distilled water); compare 0 and each caffeine concentration with a t-test (or use Spearman's rank / correlation for concentration vs rate); 5 % significance level.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: range of caffeine concentrations; matched yeast and glucose; temperature controlled; rate measurement method; replicates; control; named appropriate statistical test with comparison / p = 0.05.

practice.stem: Mung bean seeds were soaked and left to germinate. A student wants to find out how the rate of respiration changes over the first 10 days of germination.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student could obtain reliable results for the rate of respiration on each day.
parts.answer: Germinate a large batch of seeds of the same variety at the same time under the same conditions (temperature, water, dark/light); each day take a random sample of seedlings; measure oxygen uptake in a respirometer with soda lime at a constant temperature for a fixed time; repeat with three samples each day; calculate rate per gram.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: same batch / variety, same start; same germination conditions; random sample each day; respirometer / sensor at constant temperature; fixed time; replicates; rate per unit mass.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate should be expressed per gram of dry mass rather than per gram of fresh mass, and state one disadvantage of using dry mass.
parts.answer: Fresh mass changes greatly as seedlings take up water, which does not respire, so fresh mass would not reflect the amount of tissue; but dry mass is found by drying (killing) the seedlings, so a separate sample must be used.
parts.working: B1 water content varies / water uptake increases fresh mass; B1 drying kills the seedlings so measurements need a different sample.

practice.stem:
The time taken for methylene blue to decolourise in tubes of yeast suspension at different temperatures:
20 °C: 480 s
30 °C: 300 s
40 °C: 190 s
50 °C: 120 s
60 °C: 260 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of respiration at each temperature as 1000/t, where t is time in seconds. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 1000/t for each; A1 all five correct to 1 d.p.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in rate between 20 °C and 50 °C, using unrounded rates. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

practice.stem: Ten seeds of maize had a total dry mass of 2.40 g before germination. After six days of germination in the dark, ten seedlings had a total dry mass of 2.04 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in dry mass. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the decrease in dry mass.
parts.answer: Stored starch (and lipid) is respired to release energy for growth; carbon is lost as carbon dioxide; seedlings in the dark cannot photosynthesise to replace it.
parts.working: B1 food stores respired; B1 carbon lost as CO₂ / no photosynthesis in dark.

practice.stem: Four replicate tubes of yeast in sucrose solution produced these volumes of CO₂ in 5 minutes: 4.2 cm³, 4.5 cm³, 6.9 cm³ and 4.3 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result.
parts.answer: 6.9 cm³
parts.working: B1 6.9 cm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean volume, excluding the anomalous result, to 2 decimal places, and the mean rate of CO₂ production in cm³ min⁻¹ to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: mean 4.33 cm³; rate 0.87 cm³ min⁻¹

practice.stem: A respirometer containing germinating peas showed an oxygen uptake of 0.45 cm³ in 15 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert this volume to mm³.
parts.answer: 450 mm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen uptake in mm³ per hour.
parts.answer: 1800 mm³ h⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: The peas had a mass of 6.0 g. Calculate the rate in mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹.
parts.answer: 300 mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹

practice.stem:
Time taken for DCPIP to become colourless in tubes of yeast with different glucose concentrations:
0.5 %: 85 s
1.0 %: 64 s
2.0 %: 52 s
4.0 %: 47 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of decolourisation (1/t) for each concentration in s⁻¹. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: 2 marks all four correct to 3 s.f.; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why 1/t can be used as a measure of the rate of respiration.
parts.answer: Rate is inversely proportional to the time taken to reach the same end point (same amount of DCPIP reduced), so a shorter time means a faster rate.
parts.working: B1 same amount of DCPIP reduced each time so rate ∝ 1/time.

practice.stem:
A respirometer containing 2.0 g of woodlice and soda lime was set up at 20 °C. The distance moved by the liquid in the capillary (radius 0.4 mm) from the start was recorded.
1 min: 8 mm
2 min: 17 mm
3 min: 25 mm
4 min: 33 mm
5 min: 42 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen absorbed between the readings at 1 minute and 5 minutes. Use V = πr²l and give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 17.1 mm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen uptake in mm³ per gram per hour. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 128 mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹

practice.stem:
Total volume of CO₂ in a gas syringe attached to a flask of yeast and glucose solution:
0 min: 0.0 cm³; 2 min: 3.5 cm³; 4 min: 7.8 cm³; 6 min: 12.0 cm³; 8 min: 15.2 cm³; 10 min: 17.4 cm³; 12 min: 18.6 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of CO₂ production in cm³ min⁻¹ for each 2-minute interval.
parts.working: M1 difference ÷ 2; A2 all six correct (A1 four or five).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease from the highest interval rate to the rate in the final interval. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason for the fall in rate.
parts.answer: Glucose is being used up (substrate concentration falls) or ethanol accumulates.
parts.working: B1 substrate depletion / ethanol build-up.

practice.stem: The temperature coefficient Q₁₀ = rate at (T + 10 °C) ÷ rate at T. The rate of oxygen uptake by germinating barley was 0.62 cm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹ at 20 °C and 1.18 cm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹ at 30 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Q₁₀ for this temperature range. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming Q₁₀ stays the same, predict the rate at 40 °C. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 2.25 cm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹
parts.working: B1 1.18 × 1.903 (unrounded Q₁₀) = 2.25.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the actual rate measured at 40 °C was lower than your prediction.
parts.answer: At high temperatures respiratory enzymes begin to denature (hydrogen bonds break, active sites change shape), so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form; Q₁₀ does not stay constant.
parts.working: B1 enzyme denaturation; B1 active site changes / fewer E–S complexes.

practice.stem: A graph shows the volume of oxygen absorbed by blowfly larvae against time. A student drew a tangent to the curve at 5 minutes. The tangent passes through the points (2 min, 1.0 cm³) and (8 min, 7.6 cm³).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen uptake at 5 minutes, with units.
parts.answer: 1.1 cm³ min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the student chose two points far apart on the tangent.
parts.answer: Reading points far apart reduces the percentage error in reading the coordinates, giving a more accurate gradient.
parts.working: B1 smaller percentage error in readings.

practice.stem: Yeast respiring anaerobically produced 480 cm³ of CO₂ at room temperature. One mole of gas occupies 24 000 cm³ at room temperature. The equation for ethanol fermentation is C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. Mr of glucose = 180.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of glucose that was fermented.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the mass of glucose that would be needed to produce the same volume of CO₂ by aerobic respiration, and explain why it is different.
parts.answer: 0.60 g; in aerobic respiration each glucose produces 6 CO₂ instead of 2.
parts.working: B1 0.60 g (0.020 ÷ 6 × 180); B1 6 CO₂ per glucose aerobically.

practice.stem:
Oxygen uptake (mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹) of two groups of germinating seeds, three replicates each:
seeds at 20 °C: 12.1, 12.9, 12.2
seeds at 30 °C: 16.5, 17.2, 16.7

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean for each group to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in mean oxygen uptake from 20 °C to 30 °C, to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the range of each group and comment on what the ranges suggest about the reliability of the data.
