parts.answer: 20 °C range 0.8; 30 °C range 0.7; replicates are close together and the ranges do not overlap, suggesting the results are repeatable and the difference is likely to be real.
parts.working: B1 both ranges; B1 small ranges / no overlap so reliable.

practice.stem: At rest, a 25 g mouse uses 2.0 cm³ of oxygen per minute, and a 70 kg human uses 250 cm³ of oxygen per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the oxygen uptake of each, in cm³ per kg per hour. Give the human value to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: mouse 4800 cm³ kg⁻¹ h⁻¹; human 214 cm³ kg⁻¹ h⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the mouse's rate per kg is. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 22.4 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a biological explanation for the difference.
parts.answer: The mouse has a much larger surface area to volume ratio, so it loses heat faster; it must respire faster per kg to generate heat and keep body temperature constant.
parts.working: B1 larger SA:V ratio / faster heat loss; B1 more respiration to replace heat / maintain body temperature.

practice.stem: In a respirometer experiment the liquid moved 12 mm in 300 s. The ruler reads to the nearest 1 mm, so the uncertainty is ±0.5 mm. The stopwatch uncertainty is ±1 s. The capillary radius is 0.50 ± 0.01 mm. Volume V = πr²l.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the distance, in the time and in r². Give each to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: distance 4.2 %; time 0.33 %; r² 4.0 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Estimate the total percentage uncertainty in the rate of oxygen uptake (V ÷ t) by adding the percentage uncertainties. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one change that would most reduce the total percentage uncertainty.
parts.answer: Measure for longer so that the liquid moves a greater distance (reducing the percentage uncertainty in distance), or use a capillary with a more precisely known radius.
parts.working: B1 longer time / larger distance (or more precise capillary bore).

practice.stem:
Five replicate measurements of the rate of CO₂ production by yeast at 35 °C (mm³ min⁻¹): 14.2, 15.8, 13.5, 16.1, 15.4.
Standard deviation s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and the standard deviation. Give the standard deviation to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: mean 15.0 mm³ min⁻¹; s = 1.11 mm³ min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: At 25 °C the mean rate was 9.6 mm³ min⁻¹ with s = 0.95. Explain what the standard deviations suggest about whether the difference between 25 °C and 35 °C is likely to be real.
parts.answer: The difference between means (5.4) is much larger than either standard deviation, and mean ± 2s ranges do not overlap, so the difference is probably real / significant (a t-test would confirm).
parts.working: B1 difference in means much greater than SDs / no overlap of mean ± s (or 2s); B1 likely significant, confirm with t-test.

practice.stem: When carbohydrate is respired, about 20.1 kJ of energy is released for every 1 dm³ of oxygen used. A resting student uses 0.30 dm³ of oxygen per minute. During a 45-minute brisk walk his oxygen uptake is 1.2 dm³ per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy released in 24 hours at rest, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the extra energy released during the 45-minute walk compared with resting for the same time, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 814 kJ

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the figure of 20.1 kJ per dm³ would be inaccurate if the student were respiring mainly lipid.
parts.answer: The energy released per dm³ of oxygen depends on the substrate; lipid needs more oxygen per unit of CO₂ (RQ 0.7), so the energy per dm³ O₂ is different (slightly lower).
parts.working: B1 different substrate gives a different energy per dm³ O₂ (RQ differs).

practice.stem: A student collected the CO₂ produced by yeast in an inverted measuring cylinder full of water held in a trough of water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the volume of gas collected may be less than the volume of CO₂ produced.
parts.answer: Some CO₂ dissolves in the water in the cylinder / trough (CO₂ is quite soluble), and some may dissolve in the yeast solution before leaving.
parts.working: B1 CO₂ dissolves in water; B1 so not all is collected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an improvement to the method.
parts.answer: Use a gas syringe instead (or saturate the water with CO₂ first / collect over oil).
parts.working: B1 gas syringe / pre-saturate water / layer of oil.

practice.stem: A student measured the time for methylene blue to decolourise in a single tube of yeast suspension at each of five temperatures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the student should repeat the experiment at each temperature.
parts.answer: To check that the results are repeatable / reliable, to identify anomalous results and to allow a mean to be calculated, which reduces the effect of random errors.
parts.working: B1 identify anomalies; B1 calculate a mean / reduce effect of random error / check repeatability.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the student would decide whether a result is anomalous.
parts.answer: It does not fit the pattern / is very different from the other replicates at that temperature (or does not lie close to the line of best fit).
parts.working: B1 differs greatly from other replicates / pattern.

practice.stem: In an experiment with DCPIP and yeast, the student judged by eye when the blue colour had disappeared.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this is a source of error.
parts.answer: Judging the end point is subjective; it is difficult to decide exactly when the blue colour has gone, especially as the yeast suspension is cloudy / cream coloured, so the times may be inaccurate.
parts.working: B1 subjective end point; B1 gradual colour change / cloudy yeast makes it hard to see.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two improvements to reduce this error.
parts.answer: Compare each tube with a colour standard (yeast + water without DCPIP) against a white background; use a colorimeter to measure absorbance at fixed times; same person judges every tube.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: A student investigated the effect of temperature on yeast respiration by placing tubes in beakers of water that had been heated to the required temperature with a Bunsen burner and then left on the bench.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this method could give unreliable results.
parts.answer: The water would cool towards room temperature during the experiment, so the temperature of the yeast would not stay constant; the actual temperature would differ from the stated one.
parts.working: B1 temperature falls / fluctuates; B1 so the independent variable is not controlled.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an improvement.
parts.answer: Use a thermostatically controlled water bath and check the temperature with a thermometer in the tube during the experiment.
parts.working: B1 thermostatic water bath (with thermometer check).

practice.stem: A student used respirometers to compare respiration rates of maggots at two temperatures. He used 10 maggots in each respirometer, picked at random from a container.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why using 10 maggots in each tube may make the comparison unfair.
parts.answer: Maggots vary in size / mass, so the total mass of respiring tissue in each tube may be different; rate depends on mass.
parts.working: B1 maggots differ in mass / size / age; B1 more tissue gives more oxygen uptake.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an improvement.
parts.answer: Use the same total mass of maggots (weighed) in each tube and express the rate per gram.
parts.working: B1 same mass / rate per gram.

practice.stem: A student measured the oxygen uptake of germinating seeds using a simple respirometer on the laboratory bench next to a sunny window. She sealed the tube with a rubber bung, started timing immediately and took one reading of the position of the liquid after 15 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three sources of error in this investigation and suggest an improvement for each.
parts.answer: e.g. room temperature changed during the experiment → place respirometer in a thermostatically controlled water bath; no thermobarometer, so pressure changes not allowed for → set up a control tube with glass beads of the same volume; leaks at joints → seal with petroleum jelly and test for leaks; difficult to read meniscus position → use a scale with mm divisions and read at eye level / mark with fine pen; seeds not given time to equilibrate → leave for 10 min with tap open before starting; only one reading → repeat three times.
parts.working: For each of three: B1 error relevant to this method; B1 matching improvement.

practice.stem: A student set up a respirometer with germinating seeds and soda lime. After 20 minutes the coloured liquid had hardly moved, although the seeds were known to be respiring.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two possible reasons for this result.
parts.answer: The apparatus was not airtight (air leaked in through a loose bung or joint); the soda lime was exhausted / no longer absorbing CO₂; the tap was left open.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student could test whether the apparatus is airtight.
parts.answer: With the tap closed, push the syringe plunger in a little: if the apparatus is airtight the liquid moves and stays in its new position; if it gradually returns, there is a leak. Seal joints with petroleum jelly.
parts.working: B1 move syringe / apply pressure and observe whether liquid stays displaced; B1 seal with petroleum jelly / check bungs.

practice.stem: A student pipetted yeast suspension from a stock bottle into six tubes, one after the other, over 15 minutes. The tubes filled last showed the fastest rates of respiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest an explanation for this result.
parts.answer: Yeast cells settle at the bottom of the stock bottle over time, so later samples taken from lower down (or from a more concentrated suspension) contain more yeast cells.
parts.working: B1 yeast settles / sediments; B1 later samples had more cells (uneven concentration).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how to improve the method.
parts.answer: Stir or swirl the stock suspension immediately before taking each sample; prepare all tubes quickly; randomise the order in which treatments are filled.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: A student took a respirometer containing seeds from a cool store room at 15 °C, placed it in a water bath at 30 °C, closed the tap immediately and started timing. The liquid first moved away from the seeds, then towards them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the liquid first moved away from the seeds.
parts.answer: The air inside the tube was warming up and expanding, increasing the volume / pressure and pushing the liquid away; this was greater than the volume of oxygen taken in.
parts.working: B1 gas warmed and expanded; B1 outweighed oxygen uptake.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the student should change the method.
parts.answer: Leave the respirometer in the water bath with the tap open for 10–15 minutes to equilibrate before closing the tap; use a thermobarometer to correct for any remaining changes.
parts.working: B1 equilibrate with tap open for stated time; B1 thermobarometer.

practice.stem:
Three students each measured the rate of oxygen uptake by germinating mung beans at 25 °C using the same method. Results (mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹):
student A: 34, 36, 35
student B: 22, 41, 30
student C: 35, 34, 52

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the reliability of the results of the three students.
parts.answer: A's results are close together so they are repeatable / reliable; B's results are widely spread (range 19) so not reliable; C has two close results and one anomalous result (52), which should be excluded or repeated.
parts.working: B1 A reliable / small range; B1 B unreliable / large range; B1 C has an anomaly (52).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why student B's results might vary so much.
parts.answer: Different masses / stages of germination of beans in each run; leaks in the apparatus; temperature not equilibrated; inaccurate reading of the meniscus; timing errors.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sensible reasons.

practice.stem: A student tested whether peas or maize grains produce more CO₂ by passing the air from containers of each through limewater and noting which limewater went cloudy first.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this method gives only limited information.
parts.answer: Limewater gives a qualitative result (cloudy or not) or only a time; the degree of cloudiness is difficult to judge and does not measure the volume of CO₂; different masses of seeds may have been used.
parts.working: B1 qualitative / subjective judgement of cloudiness; B1 no quantitative volume / rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a method that would give quantitative results.
parts.answer: Use a CO₂ sensor and data logger in sealed containers with equal masses of seeds, or use hydrogencarbonate indicator and a colorimeter calibrated with known CO₂ concentrations, and measure over a fixed time.
parts.working: B1 CO₂ sensor / colorimeter with indicator / respirometer; B1 equal masses and fixed time.

practice.stem:
In a respirometer investigation, the student made these errors:
1 the capillary tube was labelled as having a radius of 0.50 mm but it was actually 0.45 mm
2 the room temperature varied by up to 2 °C during the experiment
3 the student read the meniscus from different angles

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each error, state whether it is a systematic error or a random error, and explain your choice.
parts.answer: 1 systematic: every volume would be calculated too large by the same proportion. 2 random: changes in temperature affect readings unpredictably up or down. 3 random: parallax error varies from reading to reading in either direction.
parts.working: B1 each correct classification with reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain which of these errors would not affect a comparison of rates at two temperatures if the same capillary tube was used for both.
parts.answer: Error 1: the radius error multiplies every volume by the same factor, so the relative difference / ratio between temperatures is unchanged (only the absolute values are wrong).
parts.working: B1 error 1 (systematic radius error); B1 same proportional error in both, so comparison / ratio still valid.

practice.stem: A student investigated the effect of temperature on yeast respiration. He used one tube at each of 20 °C, 40 °C and 60 °C, measuring CO₂ volume after 10 minutes. Results: 20 °C: 3 cm³; 40 °C: 11 cm³; 60 °C: 2 cm³. He concluded that the optimum temperature for yeast respiration is 40 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the reliability of the method and the validity of the conclusion.
parts.answer: Only one tube at each temperature so no repeats / no way to identify anomalies or calculate means; only three temperatures with large 20 °C intervals, so the optimum could be anywhere between about 30 °C and 50 °C; a single 10-minute reading does not give the initial rate; no evidence that other variables (yeast and glucose concentration, equilibration) were controlled; conclusion that the optimum is exactly 40 °C is not justified — only that it is between 20 °C and 60 °C, most likely near 40 °C.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: no replicates; too few temperatures / intervals too large; optimum could be anywhere between 20/30 and 50/60 °C; single end-point reading not a rate; control variables not stated; conclusion only tentative.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the investigation should be improved to locate the optimum more precisely.
parts.answer: Repeat with smaller intervals around 40 °C (e.g. 30, 35, 40, 45, 50 °C) with at least three replicates each, and measure volume at several times to find initial rates.
parts.working: B1 smaller intervals around 40 °C; B1 replicates / initial rate from several readings.

practice.stem: A dissolved-oxygen probe was used to follow oxygen uptake by a yeast suspension. Before the experiment, the probe gave a reading of 9.6 mg dm⁻³ in air-saturated water at 25 °C, whose true value is 8.3 mg dm⁻³. At the end of the experiment, the probe gave a reading of 10.1 mg dm⁻³ in the same water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage error in the probe reading at the start, to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the problems shown by these readings and suggest how to deal with them.
parts.answer: The probe was not calibrated (systematic error — readings too high); the reading drifted during the experiment, so the error changed over time; calibrate the probe against air-saturated water and oxygen-free water (zero) before use, re-check calibration during the experiment and correct readings for drift.
parts.working: B1 probe not calibrated / systematic error; B1 drift during experiment; B1 calibrate before (two-point) and check / correct during or after.

practice.stem: A student measured oxygen uptake of germinating seeds over 48 hours in a sealed respirometer at 25 °C. The rate increased steadily throughout. When the seeds were examined at the end, there was white fungal growth on them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the fungal growth could have affected the results.
parts.answer: Fungi (microorganisms) also respire and take up oxygen, so the measured oxygen uptake includes their respiration and is greater than that of the seeds alone; the increase over time may be partly due to fungal growth.
parts.working: B1 fungi respire / use oxygen; B1 overestimate of seed respiration / rising rate partly due to fungi.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways the method could be improved to deal with this.
parts.answer: Surface-sterilise the seeds (e.g. with dilute sodium hypochlorite, then rinse) before use; use sterile apparatus; set up a control with boiled (dead) seeds that are not sterilised to measure microbial respiration; use a shorter experiment time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: A student used respirometers to investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of respiration of fly maggots.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable, the dependent variable and two standardised variables.
parts.answer: IV: temperature. DV: rate of oxygen uptake (distance moved by liquid per minute). Standardised (any two): mass of maggots; number / age / species of maggots; volume and mass of soda lime; diameter of capillary; time allowed to equilibrate; time of measurement.
parts.working: B1 IV temperature; B1 DV rate of oxygen uptake / distance per unit time; B1 any two standardised variables.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a control for this experiment and explain why it is needed.
parts.answer: A respirometer with an equal volume of glass beads (or dead maggots) instead of living maggots, to show that movement of the liquid is due to respiration and to correct for temperature and pressure changes.
parts.working: B1 tube with glass beads / no living organisms; B1 shows changes are due to respiration / allows correction.

practice.stem: A student investigated whether yeast respires glucose, fructose and galactose at different rates, by measuring the volume of CO₂ produced in 10 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: type of sugar (respiratory substrate). Dependent: volume of CO₂ produced in 10 minutes (rate of CO₂ production).
parts.working: B1 IV type of sugar; B1 DV volume of CO₂ in 10 min / rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three variables that should be standardised.
parts.answer: Any three: temperature; concentration of sugar; volume of sugar solution; mass / concentration of yeast; pH; time yeast was activated / age of yeast suspension; type of yeast.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

practice.stem: Two respirometers were set up in a water bath. Tube A contained 10 g of germinating seeds and soda lime. Tube B contained 10 cm³ of glass beads and soda lime.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the purpose of tube B.
parts.answer: It is a control (thermobarometer) that shows changes in volume due to temperature or atmospheric pressure only, not respiration, so tube A's readings can be corrected.
parts.working: B1 control / thermobarometer; B1 detects volume changes caused by temperature / pressure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why tube B contains glass beads of the same volume as the seeds rather than being empty.
parts.answer: So that the volume of air in both tubes is the same, so a given temperature or pressure change causes the same volume change.
parts.working: B1 same air volume in both tubes.

practice.stem: In an investigation of CO₂ production by yeast in glucose solution, a student set up an extra tube containing yeast that had been boiled and cooled, with glucose solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this tube was set up.
parts.answer: As a control to show that CO₂ production is due to respiration by living yeast (enzymes), and not to any other reaction or factor; boiling denatures the enzymes.
parts.working: B1 control; B1 boiled yeast enzymes denatured / shows CO₂ comes from living yeast respiration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one other suitable control tube.
parts.answer: Living yeast with distilled water instead of glucose (or glucose solution without yeast).
parts.working: B1 yeast without glucose / glucose without yeast.

practice.stem:
A student measured how the rate of oxygen uptake by woodlice changed with the temperature of the respirometer. The following were listed:
mass of woodlice; temperature; volume of oxygen taken up per minute; time of day; volume of soda lime

parts.label: a
parts.text: From the list, identify the independent variable, the dependent variable and three variables that should be controlled.
parts.answer: Independent: temperature. Dependent: volume of oxygen taken up per minute. Controlled: mass of woodlice, time of day, volume of soda lime.
parts.working: B1 IV; B1 DV; B1 all three controlled variables.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why time of day should be controlled.
parts.answer: Woodlice may be more active at certain times (e.g. at night), changing their respiration rate.
parts.working: B1 activity / metabolic rate varies with time of day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how each of these variables can be kept constant in an investigation of yeast respiration: temperature; pH; volume of glucose solution.
parts.answer: Temperature: thermostatically controlled water bath (check with thermometer). pH: add the same volume of a buffer solution of fixed pH. Volume: measure with a graduated pipette or syringe.
parts.working: B1 each correct method.

practice.stem: A student will investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of respiration in yeast using DCPIP. She must make sure every tube contains the same concentration of yeast cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways in which she could standardise the concentration of yeast.
parts.answer: Weigh the same mass of dried yeast and dissolve in the same volume of water; or use a colorimeter to adjust the suspension to the same absorbance (turbidity); or count cells with a haemocytometer and dilute to the same density.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two methods.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why yeast suspensions should be activated in glucose solution for the same length of time before each trial.
parts.answer: The respiration rate of yeast increases as it becomes active after rehydration (and cell number may increase with time); different activation times would add an uncontrolled variable affecting rate.
parts.working: B1 rate / activity of yeast changes with time after rehydration; B1 would affect dependent variable.

practice.stem: Volunteers had their RQ measured after eating a meal, to find out how the type of meal affects the respiratory substrate used.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest three variables, other than the meal, that should be controlled.
parts.answer: Any three: time since meal; activity / exercise level (measure at rest); time since last meal before the test (overnight fast); mass of food / energy content of meal; age, sex or fitness of volunteers; room temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the same volunteers should be tested with each type of meal.
parts.answer: Individuals differ in metabolic rate and RQ; using the same people removes the effect of these differences so changes can be attributed to the meal.
parts.working: B1 individuals vary in metabolism; B1 same people controls this / fair comparison.

practice.stem: A student compared the respiration rates of germinating seeds of chickpea, wheat and sunflower using a respirometer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the comparison may not be valid if the student used 20 seeds of each species.
parts.answer: The seeds differ greatly in size / mass, so the mass of respiring tissue would differ; rate should be compared per unit mass.
parts.working: B1 seeds differ in size / mass; B1 use the same mass / rate per gram.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two other variables that would be difficult to control between species and explain why each matters.
parts.answer: Stage of germination (species germinate at different rates); water content of seeds; type of stored food (lipid vs starch) changing oxygen uptake relative to CO₂.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two variables with reason.

practice.stem: A student made 2 % (20 g dm⁻³) solutions of glucose (Mr 180) and sucrose (Mr 342) to compare respiration by yeast with each sugar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of each solution in mol dm⁻³, to 3 significant figures, and how many times more molecules of glucose there are per dm³. Give the ratio to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: glucose 0.111 mol dm⁻³; sucrose 0.0585 mol dm⁻³; ratio 1.9

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why using equal molar concentrations might be a better way to control the substrate concentration in this investigation.
parts.answer: Each sucrose molecule is hydrolysed into one glucose and one fructose, so equal percentage solutions do not provide equal numbers of hexose units / molecules; equal molarity (or equal hexose content) makes the comparison of sugars fair.
parts.working: B1 equal % gives different numbers of molecules; B1 fairer comparison of substrate available / sucrose gives two hexoses.

practice.stem: A student used a respirometer to measure the rate of respiration of leaves from a mint plant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the respirometer must be kept in the dark.
parts.answer: In light the leaves photosynthesise, taking in CO₂ and releasing oxygen; this would counteract / mask oxygen uptake by respiration, so the measured volume change would not show respiration only.
parts.working: B1 photosynthesis in light; B1 releases O₂ / alters gas volume so respiration not measured accurately.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the student could check that no light was reaching the leaves.
parts.answer: Wrap the tube in aluminium foil / black paper and use a light meter / check no oxygen output in a tube without soda lime (or work in a darkened room).
parts.working: B1 any sensible check / method of exclusion.

practice.stem: A drug that may block the electron transport chain is only soluble in ethanol. Researchers will test its effect on oxygen uptake by isolated mitochondria by adding 0.1 cm³ of the drug dissolved in ethanol to 5 cm³ of mitochondrial suspension.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the control experiments that should be carried out and explain the purpose of each.
parts.answer: Add 0.1 cm³ of ethanol alone (solvent control) to show that any effect is due to the drug, not the ethanol; mitochondria with no additions (to measure normal oxygen uptake); suspension buffer without mitochondria plus drug (to show the drug does not react with oxygen itself / affect the electrode); a known inhibitor (e.g. cyanide) as a positive control to show the method detects inhibition.
parts.working: B1 solvent (ethanol) control; B1 explanation; B1 any other control (no mitochondria / no addition / positive control); B1 its purpose.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two variables that must be kept constant when adding the drug to the suspension.
parts.answer: Concentration / volume of mitochondria (protein content); temperature; concentration of respiratory substrate; concentration of ADP and phosphate; pH (buffer); oxygen concentration at the start.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: A student compared the rate of respiration of soil microorganisms in soil samples from a wheat field, a mango orchard and a roadside verge near Multan. She sealed 100 g of each soil in a jar with a CO₂ sensor for 1 hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest three variables that would be difficult to control in this study and explain how she could deal with each.
parts.answer: Soil moisture: measure and adjust to same water content (or record); soil temperature at collection: equilibrate all samples at the same temperature before measurement; organic matter / plant roots / invertebrates: sieve soil to remove roots and animals; time since collection / depth of sampling: collect at the same depth on the same day.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three variables with a sensible way of dealing with them (control, standardise or record).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why she should take several samples from different places in each site.
parts.answer: Soil is very variable within a site; several random samples give a representative mean and allow variability to be assessed (e.g. with standard deviation / statistical test).
parts.working: B1 variation within site; B1 representative mean / allows statistical comparison.

practice.stem: A student wants to investigate whether sodium chloride concentration affects the rate of respiration of yeast. He realises that adding salt also lowers the water potential of the solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest how he could design a control to find out whether any effect is caused by the low water potential rather than by sodium chloride itself.
parts.answer: Set up a second series using a solute that is not toxic and not respired by yeast (e.g. mannitol / sorbitol) at concentrations giving the same water potentials as each NaCl solution; if the rate falls equally with mannitol, the effect is due to water potential; if NaCl reduces the rate more, the ions themselves have an effect.
parts.working: B1 another solute not used as a substrate (mannitol / sorbitol / PEG); B1 matched water potential (osmotic concentration); B1 compare the two series to separate the effects.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the independent variable and two standardised variables in the main experiment.
parts.answer: IV: NaCl concentration. Standardised: any two of glucose concentration, temperature, yeast concentration, volume, pH.
parts.working: B1 IV; B1 two standardised variables.

practice.stem: A study tested whether a caffeine drink increases resting metabolic rate (measured by oxygen uptake) in adults. Volunteers drank either the caffeine drink or an identical-tasting drink without caffeine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the drink without caffeine was used and why it was made to taste the same.
parts.answer: It is a placebo control showing the effect of drinking (fluid, volume, sugar) without caffeine; identical taste means volunteers do not know which they received, so expectations / behaviour do not affect the results.
parts.working: B1 placebo / control for drink itself; B1 volunteers unaware so no psychological bias.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the study should be double-blind.
parts.answer: So the researchers measuring oxygen uptake also do not know which drink each volunteer had, preventing unconscious bias in measurement or recording.
parts.working: B1 researchers unaware, avoiding bias.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two variables relating to the volunteers that should be controlled.
parts.answer: Habitual caffeine intake (tea/coffee drinking); time since last meal (fasting); activity before the test (rest period); time of day; age / body mass; smoking.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem:
Volume of CO₂ produced by yeast in glucose solution in 10 minutes at different temperatures:
10 °C: 0.8 cm³; 20 °C: 2.1 cm³; 30 °C: 4.6 cm³; 40 °C: 6.3 cm³; 50 °C: 2.4 cm³; 60 °C: 0.2 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the results between 10 °C and 40 °C.
parts.answer: As temperature rises, the enzymes and substrate molecules of respiration have more kinetic energy; more frequent successful collisions, more enzyme–substrate complexes, so faster respiration and more CO₂.
parts.working: B1 more kinetic energy / more collisions; B1 more enzyme–substrate complexes so faster respiration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the results between 40 °C and 60 °C.
parts.answer: Respiratory enzymes are denatured: hydrogen bonds break, the active site changes shape so substrates no longer fit; fewer enzyme–substrate complexes; at 60 °C nearly all enzymes denatured / yeast killed.
parts.working: B1 denaturation / bonds broken; B1 active site shape changed so fewer E–S complexes.

practice.stem: Oxygen uptake of dry wheat grains was 0.02 mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹. Wheat grains soaked in water for 2 days took up 145 mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference in oxygen uptake.
parts.answer: Water activates the enzymes in the grains (and hydrolyses stored starch to sugars); respiration increases greatly to provide ATP for growth (cell division, protein synthesis) of the embryo; dry grains are dormant with very little metabolic activity.
parts.working: B1 water needed to activate enzymes / metabolism; B1 starch hydrolysed to glucose for respiration; B1 ATP needed for growth / dry grains dormant.

practice.stem: Yeast was placed in tubes containing 5 % solutions of different sugars. After 30 minutes, CO₂ had been produced with glucose, fructose and sucrose, but not with lactose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why no CO₂ was produced with lactose.
parts.answer: The yeast has no lactase enzyme (and no lactose carrier), so it cannot hydrolyse lactose into glucose and galactose; lactose cannot enter glycolysis.
parts.working: B1 yeast lacks lactase / cannot hydrolyse lactose; B1 so no respiratory substrate enters glycolysis / no uptake.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why CO₂ was produced with sucrose.
parts.answer: Yeast produces sucrase (invertase), which hydrolyses sucrose into glucose and fructose that can be respired.
parts.working: B1 sucrase / invertase hydrolyses sucrose to monosaccharides.

practice.stem: Tube 1 contained living yeast, glucose and DCPIP. Tube 2 contained boiled yeast, glucose and DCPIP. After 10 minutes, tube 1 was colourless and tube 2 was still blue.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the results.
parts.answer: In tube 1 dehydrogenase enzymes removed hydrogen from respiratory intermediates (e.g. in glycolysis); the hydrogen reduced the DCPIP, which became colourless; in tube 2 boiling had denatured the dehydrogenase enzymes, so no hydrogen was released and DCPIP stayed blue.
parts.working: B1 dehydrogenases remove hydrogen in respiration; B1 DCPIP reduced / accepts hydrogen → colourless; B1 enzymes in boiled yeast denatured.

practice.stem:
Blood lactate concentration of a footballer running on a treadmill at increasing speeds:
8 km h⁻¹: 1.2 mmol dm⁻³; 10 km h⁻¹: 1.4; 12 km h⁻¹: 1.9; 14 km h⁻¹: 3.8; 16 km h⁻¹: 7.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why lactate rises only slightly up to 12 km h⁻¹ but sharply above this speed.
parts.answer: At low speeds oxygen supply to muscles is enough for most ATP to come from aerobic respiration; above about 12 km h⁻¹ the demand for ATP exceeds what aerobic respiration can supply because oxygen delivery is limited; muscles respire anaerobically, pyruvate is reduced to lactate (to regenerate NAD) and lactate builds up in the blood.
parts.working: B1 low speed: aerobic respiration meets ATP demand; B1 high speed: oxygen supply insufficient / ATP demand exceeds aerobic supply; B1 anaerobic respiration / pyruvate → lactate.

practice.stem:
Rate of CO₂ production by yeast at different glucose concentrations (cm³ min⁻¹):
0 %: 0.0; 0.5 %: 0.8; 1 %: 1.5; 2 %: 2.4; 4 %: 2.9; 8 %: 3.0; 16 %: 3.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the increase in rate between 0 % and 2 % glucose.
parts.answer: Glucose is the limiting factor; more glucose molecules means more glucose taken into cells and more frequent collisions with glycolytic enzymes, so more enzyme–substrate complexes and faster respiration.
parts.working: B1 glucose limiting; B1 more E–S complexes / more substrate for glycolysis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate levels off above 4 % glucose.
parts.answer: Another factor is now limiting: all the active sites of the enzymes (or glucose carrier proteins in the membrane) are occupied / saturated; extra glucose cannot increase the rate; rate limited by enzyme / carrier number or temperature.
parts.working: B1 enzymes / carriers saturated; B1 another factor limiting (e.g. enzyme concentration, temperature).

practice.stem:
Time for methylene blue to decolourise in yeast suspensions buffered at different pH values:
pH 3: 410 s; pH 4: 190 s; pH 5: 120 s; pH 6: 135 s; pH 7: 260 s; pH 8: 600 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the pH at which the rate of respiration was fastest.
parts.answer: pH 5
parts.working: B1 pH 5 (shortest time).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate is lower at pH 8 than at pH 5.
parts.answer: At pH 8 the concentration of hydrogen ions is far from the optimum; ionic and hydrogen bonds in the enzymes (dehydrogenases) are disrupted; the shape of the active site changes so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form and less hydrogen is released to reduce methylene blue.
parts.working: B1 pH away from optimum; B1 ionic / hydrogen bonds affected, active site shape changed; B1 fewer E–S complexes so slower dehydrogenation / methylene blue reduction.

practice.stem:
Mitochondria isolated from beef heart were given different substrates and their oxygen uptake measured (nmol O₂ min⁻¹ mg⁻¹ protein):
no substrate: 2; glucose: 2; pyruvate: 85; succinate: 110

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why glucose did not increase oxygen uptake but pyruvate did.
parts.answer: Glycolysis enzymes are in the cytoplasm, not in mitochondria, so glucose cannot be converted to pyruvate; pyruvate is actively transported into the matrix where the link reaction and Krebs cycle produce reduced NAD and FAD; these pass electrons along the electron transport chain to oxygen.
parts.working: B1 glycolysis does not occur in mitochondria; B1 pyruvate enters matrix / link reaction / Krebs; B1 reduced NAD / FAD donate electrons to ETC, oxygen used.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why there was a small oxygen uptake with no substrate added.
parts.answer: Some respiratory substrates / intermediates remained inside the mitochondria from the cells.
parts.working: B1 endogenous substrate left in mitochondria.

practice.stem: Apples harvested in Kalam (Swat) are stored in cold stores at 2 °C with 2 % oxygen and 3 % carbon dioxide. They stay fresh for months. If the oxygen concentration falls below 1 %, the apples develop an alcoholic taste.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the storage conditions slow the deterioration of the apples.
parts.answer: Low temperature reduces kinetic energy so enzymes of respiration (and ripening) work slowly; low oxygen limits aerobic respiration (less oxygen as final electron acceptor); high CO₂ also slows respiration; less substrate (sugar) is used, so fruit stays firm and sweet for longer.
parts.working: B1 low temperature slows enzyme activity; B1 low oxygen reduces aerobic respiration; B1 less sugar / stored food used up.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the alcoholic taste when oxygen falls below 1 %.
parts.answer: Too little oxygen for the electron transport chain; the apple cells respire anaerobically, converting pyruvate to ethanol (to regenerate NAD), which accumulates in the fruit.
parts.working: B1 anaerobic respiration; B1 ethanol produced / accumulates.

practice.stem: A student squeezed a clothes peg as many times as possible with one hand. Number of squeezes in each 30-second interval: 0–30 s: 62; 30–60 s: 51; 60–90 s: 40; 90–120 s: 31.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the number of squeezes fell.
parts.answer: Muscles needed ATP faster than aerobic respiration could supply because oxygen delivery was limited; anaerobic respiration produced lactate, lowering pH, which inhibits enzymes (and contraction); fewer ATP available, muscle fatigue.
parts.working: B1 oxygen supply insufficient / anaerobic respiration; B1 lactate accumulates / pH falls; B1 less ATP / enzymes inhibited so fatigue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the student's other hand, used after a 5-minute rest, performed at the starting rate again.
parts.answer: The rested muscles had normal ATP and oxygen supplies and no lactate accumulation.
parts.working: B1 no lactate / oxygen debt / full ATP and creatine phosphate / glycogen stores.

practice.stem:
Yeast was added to a sealed flask containing 5 % glucose solution at 30 °C. The total volume of CO₂ released (cm³) was recorded every 10 hours.
0 h: 0
10 h: 4
20 h: 11
30 h: 19
40 h: 24
50 h: 26
60 h: 26

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the changes in the total volume of CO₂ produced over the 60 hours.
parts.answer: CO₂ production rose slowly at first (0–10 h), then rapidly between 10 and 30 h, then slowed and stopped at 26 cm³ after 50 h.
parts.working: B1 initial slow increase then rapid increase; B1 levels off / no further increase at 26 cm³ from 50 h.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain these results using your knowledge of respiration in yeast.
parts.answer: At first the yeast population is small / adjusting, so little CO₂; yeast then multiplies and respires glucose rapidly, aerobically while oxygen lasts then anaerobically, releasing CO₂ in the link reaction and Krebs cycle and by decarboxylation of pyruvate to ethanal; CO₂ production stops because glucose is used up and/or ethanol accumulates to a toxic concentration, killing yeast / inhibiting enzymes.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: lag – few yeast cells / enzymes being synthesised; population increases so more respiration; oxygen used up so anaerobic respiration (fermentation); CO₂ from decarboxylation (pyruvate → ethanal, or Krebs cycle while aerobic); glucose substrate runs out; ethanol accumulates and is toxic / denatures enzymes; pH falls as CO₂ dissolves.

practice.stem:
Yeast was placed in a sealed flask of glucose solution with an air space above it. Readings at intervals:
time / min: 0, 20, 40, 60, 80
O₂ uptake per 20 min / cm³: —, 4.0, 3.1, 0.9, 0.1
CO₂ output per 20 min / cm³: —, 4.0, 4.6, 6.2, 6.8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the RQ for each 20-minute interval to 2 significant figures where possible.
parts.working: M1 CO₂ ÷ O₂ for each; A1 1.0, 1.5, 6.9 and 68 (all four).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the changes in RQ.
parts.answer: At first all respiration is aerobic using glucose (carbohydrate RQ 1.0); as oxygen in the flask is used up, an increasing proportion of glucose is respired anaerobically to ethanol; this releases CO₂ (decarboxylation of pyruvate) without oxygen uptake, so RQ rises far above 1.
parts.working: B1 RQ 1 = aerobic respiration of carbohydrate; B1 oxygen depleted so more anaerobic respiration; B1 CO₂ produced without O₂ uptake, RQ rises.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the total CO₂ output per interval increased even though less oxygen was used.
parts.answer: Anaerobic respiration yields only 2 ATP per glucose, so the yeast must break down glucose much faster to meet its ATP needs; each glucose fermented releases 2 CO₂, so total CO₂ rises.
parts.working: B1 less ATP per glucose anaerobically so faster glycolysis; B1 more glucose fermented releasing CO₂.

practice.stem:
Oxygen uptake by isolated rat liver mitochondria at different ADP concentrations (all other substrates in excess):
ADP / µmol dm⁻³: 0, 20, 50, 100, 200, 400
O₂ uptake / nmol min⁻¹: 10, 28, 45, 58, 64, 65

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why oxygen uptake increases as ADP concentration increases from 0 to 100 µmol dm⁻³.
parts.answer: ADP is a substrate for ATP synthase; more ADP means more ATP synthesis, so more protons flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase; the proton gradient is reduced, so electron transport and proton pumping can proceed faster; more electrons reach oxygen per minute.
parts.working: B1 ADP substrate for ATP synthase; B1 more protons flow back / gradient used; B1 electron transport faster so more O₂ reduced.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why oxygen uptake levels off above 200 µmol dm⁻³ ADP.
parts.answer: ATP synthase molecules are working at their maximum rate (saturated with ADP) or the electron transport chain is working at its maximum rate; another factor such as number of carriers / ATP synthase is limiting.
parts.working: B1 ATP synthase / ETC saturated / at maximum rate; B1 another factor limiting.

practice.stem:
Blood lactate concentration at a running speed of 14 km h⁻¹:
untrained students (mean of 12): 6.1 mmol dm⁻³
students after 10 weeks of endurance training (same 12 students): 2.7 mmol dm⁻³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest explanations for the lower lactate concentration after training.
parts.answer: Training increases the number of mitochondria (and cristae) in muscle fibres, so more aerobic respiration; more capillaries in muscles and larger stroke volume increase oxygen delivery; more myoglobin stores oxygen; so less anaerobic respiration and less lactate formed; faster removal of lactate by the liver / heart.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: more mitochondria; more capillaries / better blood supply; increased cardiac output / stroke volume; more myoglobin; higher proportion of ATP from aerobic respiration; faster lactate removal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the same students were tested before and after training.
parts.answer: To remove the effect of differences between individuals (genetic, fitness), so any change is due to training.
parts.working: B1 controls for individual variation.

practice.stem:
Pea seeds were germinated in the light. Every two days, 20 seedlings were dried and weighed, and the oxygen uptake of another 20 was measured.
day: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12
dry mass of 20 seedlings / g: 4.0, 3.9, 3.6, 3.3, 3.2, 3.5, 4.1
oxygen uptake / mm³ h⁻¹: 2, 60, 210, 380, 420, 410, 400

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the changes in dry mass between day 0 and day 8.
parts.answer: Dry mass falls because stored starch is respired to provide ATP for growth; carbon is lost as CO₂; the seedlings cannot yet photosynthesise (no / few green leaves) to replace it.
parts.working: B1 stored food respired, carbon lost as CO₂; B1 little or no photosynthesis yet.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the changes in dry mass after day 8, even though oxygen uptake remained high.
parts.answer: Leaves have opened and photosynthesis begins; the rate of photosynthesis exceeds the rate of respiration, so there is a net gain in organic material / dry mass.
parts.working: B1 photosynthesis begins in green leaves; B1 photosynthesis > respiration so net gain.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why oxygen uptake rose so sharply between day 0 and day 6.
parts.answer: Water uptake activates enzymes and hydrolysis of stores provides substrate; rapid cell division and growth need large amounts of ATP, and the mass of respiring tissue increases.
parts.working: B1 enzymes activated / substrate made available; B1 ATP for growth / more cells respiring.

practice.stem:
Two investigations were carried out with yeast:
Investigation 1: volume of CO₂ produced in 10 minutes with five different sugars (glucose, fructose, sucrose, maltose, lactose).
Investigation 2: volume of CO₂ produced in 10 minutes at 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of graph or chart that should be used to present the results of each investigation. Explain your choices.
parts.answer: Investigation 1: bar chart, because the independent variable (type of sugar) is categorical / discontinuous, with bars separated. Investigation 2: line graph, because temperature is a continuous variable, with points joined by straight lines or a smooth curve.
parts.working: B1 bar chart; B1 sugar type is categorical / discontinuous; B1 line graph; B1 temperature is continuous.

practice.stem: A student is plotting a graph of oxygen uptake by germinating seeds (cm³) against time (min).

parts.label: a
parts.text: List four features of a well-drawn graph of these results.
parts.answer: Independent variable (time) on the x-axis and dependent variable (oxygen uptake) on the y-axis; both axes labelled with quantity and unit (e.g. time / min); linear scales chosen so the points fill more than half the grid; points plotted accurately as small crosses or circled dots; a smooth line of best fit or straight lines joining points, not extended beyond the data.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

practice.stem: Total volume of CO₂ produced by yeast: 4 min: 7.8 cm³; 6 min: 12.0 cm³. The points are joined by a straight line on a graph.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the straight line between these points to estimate the volume at 5 min.
parts.answer: 9.9 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the name for estimating a value between plotted points and explain why it is more reliable than estimating a value beyond the last point.
parts.answer: Interpolation; values between measured points are supported by data on both sides, whereas extrapolation assumes the trend continues beyond the data, which may not be true (e.g. glucose may run out).
parts.working: B1 interpolation; B1 extrapolation assumes trend continues / no data beyond range.

practice.stem: A student must plot volumes of CO₂ from 0 to 18.6 cm³ on the y-axis of a grid that has 10 large squares vertically.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest a suitable scale for the y-axis and explain your choice.
parts.answer: 2 cm³ per large square (0 to 20 cm³): it uses over half the grid (18.6 of 20) and is easy to read; awkward scales such as 1.86 per square or 3 per square should be avoided.
parts.working: B1 2 cm³ per large square (0–20); B1 data fill most of the grid and scale is easy to read / in simple multiples.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why the line of best fit should not be extended past the last data point.
parts.answer: There is no evidence of what happens beyond the measured range.
parts.working: B1 no data / trend may change.

practice.stem: A bar chart shows the mean rate of respiration of yeast with glucose and with maltose. Each bar has an error bar showing ± 2 standard errors. The error bars for glucose and maltose overlap.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the error bars show.
parts.answer: The variability / spread of the replicate results about the mean (an estimate of the range within which the true mean probably lies — about 95 % confidence).
parts.working: B1 spread of data / reliability of mean / 95 % confidence interval.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what can be concluded from the overlapping error bars.
parts.answer: The difference between the means is probably not significant; it could be due to chance / random variation, so we cannot conclude that yeast respires glucose and maltose at different rates.
parts.working: B1 difference not significant / could be due to chance; B1 no valid conclusion about a real difference.

practice.stem:
The volume of oxygen absorbed by 20 g of germinating pea seeds was measured.
0 min: 0.0 cm³
2 min: 1.8 cm³
4 min: 3.6 cm³
6 min: 5.5 cm³
8 min: 7.3 cm³
10 min: 9.0 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how you would plot these results on a graph.
parts.answer: Time (min) on the x-axis and volume of oxygen absorbed (cm³) on the y-axis; both axes labelled with units; scale using more than half the grid with even intervals; points plotted as small crosses; line of best fit drawn (points lie close to a straight line).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: correct axes orientation; labels with units; suitable linear scale using > half the grid; accurate plotting; ruled line of best fit (or point to point if justified).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen uptake between 2 and 8 minutes, in cm³ per minute, to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.92 cm³ min⁻¹

practice.stem: A line graph of oxygen uptake by germinating wheat against temperature was drawn. Two points on the straight part of the line are (10 °C, 4.2 mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹) and (30 °C, 15.6 mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gradient of this part of the line, with units.
parts.answer: 0.57 mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹ °C⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the gradient represents.
parts.answer: The increase in the rate of oxygen uptake for each 1 °C rise in temperature.
parts.working: B1 change in rate per °C.

practice.stem:
Mean rate of CO₂ production by yeast (cm³ min⁻¹) and standard deviation (SD), 5 replicates each:
20 °C: mean 0.42, SD 0.05
30 °C: mean 0.95, SD 0.07
40 °C: mean 1.38, SD 0.21
50 °C: mean 0.61, SD 0.18

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to show the variability of the data on a line graph of mean rate against temperature.
parts.answer: Plot each mean, then draw a vertical error bar through each point extending one SD above and below the mean (e.g. 40 °C from 1.17 to 1.59), with short horizontal caps.
parts.working: B1 error bars at each mean; B1 extending ± 1 SD (correct example values).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the SD values are larger at 40 °C and 50 °C than at 20 °C.
parts.answer: At higher temperatures enzymes in different samples are partly denatured to different extents / small differences in temperature have larger effects; more random variation in rate between replicates.
parts.working: B1 denaturation begins / rate very sensitive to small temperature differences; B1 more variable results between replicates.

practice.stem: A graph of oxygen uptake by maggots was plotted at 10, 15, 20 and 25 °C. A student used the line to predict the uptake at 45 °C and at 17 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain which of the two predictions is more reliable.
parts.answer: 17 °C is within the measured range (interpolation), so it is supported by data on either side; 45 °C is far outside the range (extrapolation) and enzymes may be denatured / maggots may die, so the trend is unlikely to continue.
parts.working: B1 17 °C more reliable – interpolation; B1 45 °C extrapolation beyond range / denaturation changes the trend.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an additional range of temperatures that would allow the student to find the temperature at which the rate is highest.
parts.answer: e.g. 30, 35, 40 °C (ethical limits permitting) — extend the range above 25 °C with small intervals.
parts.working: B1 extend range above 25 °C with suitable intervals.

practice.stem: A student recorded the following total volumes of oxygen absorbed by germinating peas: 0 min 0.0 cm³; 2 min 0.9; 4 min 1.9; 6 min 2.7; 8 min 3.8; 10 min 4.6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain whether the student should join the points dot to dot or draw a line of best fit.
parts.answer: A straight line of best fit, because the points follow a linear trend and the small irregularities are due to experimental error; the line shows the overall rate and averages out random errors.
parts.working: B1 line of best fit (straight); B1 data scattered about a linear trend / averages out random error.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Estimate the rate of oxygen uptake from the overall trend in cm³ min⁻¹, using the first and last values.
parts.answer: 0.46 cm³ min⁻¹

practice.stem: Rate of oxygen uptake of blowfly larvae (mm³ g⁻¹ min⁻¹): 10 °C: 0.9; 15 °C: 1.3; 20 °C: 1.9; 25 °C: 2.8; 30 °C: 3.9; 35 °C: 3.5; 40 °C: 1.2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the results shown, using figures from the data.
parts.answer: The rate increases as temperature increases from 10 °C (0.9) to a maximum at 30 °C (3.9); the increase gets steeper with temperature (0.4 per 5 °C at first, 1.1 between 25 and 30 °C); above 30 °C the rate falls, sharply to 1.2 at 40 °C.
parts.working: B1 increase to maximum at 30 °C with figures; B1 increase becomes steeper (accelerates); B1 decrease above 30 °C with figure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the shape of the curve you would draw through these points.
parts.answer: A smooth curve rising more and more steeply to a peak near 30 °C, then falling steeply.
parts.working: B1 smooth curve with peak near 30 °C and steep fall.

practice.stem: In a respirometer study, both the oxygen uptake and the CO₂ output of germinating castor-oil seeds (cm³ per day per 10 seeds) were measured over 10 days. Oxygen uptake ranged from 2 to 48, and CO₂ output from 1.4 to 47.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how both sets of data could be shown on one graph, and why this is useful.
parts.answer: Plot both against time on the same axes with one y-axis (same units, same scale) and a key distinguishing the two lines; it shows directly how the ratio CO₂ : O₂ (RQ) changes over time.
parts.working: B1 same axes / key (same units so one y-axis); B1 allows comparison / RQ changes visible.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a second graph that would show the change in respiratory substrate more clearly, and describe what it might show.
parts.answer: A graph of RQ (CO₂ ÷ O₂) against time: RQ near 0.7 early (lipid stores used) rising towards 1.0 as seedlings begin to use carbohydrate (e.g. after photosynthesis begins).
parts.working: B1 RQ against time; B1 shows change from about 0.7 (lipid) towards 1.0 (carbohydrate).

practice.stem: The body mass of five mammals ranges from a 0.02 kg mouse to a 600 kg horse (rat 0.25 kg, rabbit 3.0 kg, human 60 kg). A student wants to plot mass-specific oxygen uptake against body mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate log₁₀ of each body mass, to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: mouse −1.70; rat −0.60; rabbit 0.48; human 1.78; horse 2.78
parts.working: 2 marks all five correct; 1 mark three or four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why plotting log₁₀(body mass) on the x-axis is better than plotting body mass itself.
parts.answer: The masses range over more than four orders of magnitude; on a linear scale the four small animals would be crowded together near zero; a log scale spreads the points evenly so the trend can be seen.
parts.working: B1 very wide range (several orders of magnitude); B1 small values crowded on linear scale / log scale spreads them out.

practice.stem:
Total volume of CO₂ from yeast at two glucose concentrations:
time / min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
2 % glucose / cm³: 0, 1.6, 3.0, 4.1, 4.9, 5.4
8 % glucose / cm³: 0, 2.0, 3.9, 5.7, 7.4, 9.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the mean rate over 5 minutes is not a good measure for comparing the two concentrations, and state what should be used instead.
parts.answer: For 2 % glucose the rate decreases over time (curve flattens as glucose is used), so the mean rate over 5 minutes underestimates the true rate at the start; the initial rate (gradient of a tangent at t = 0, or over the first minute) should be compared.
parts.working: B1 rate not constant / curve flattens for 2 %; B1 use initial rate / tangent at time 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the first minute of data, calculate the ratio of the initial rates (8 % : 2 %).
parts.answer: 1.25 (8 % rate 2.0 cm³ min⁻¹, 2 % rate 1.6 cm³ min⁻¹)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete a frequency table using the classes 10.0–11.9, 12.0–13.9, 14.0–15.9 and 16.0–17.9.
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark for three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of chart that should be drawn from this table and describe how it differs from a bar chart.
parts.answer: A histogram: the variable on the x-axis is continuous, so the bars touch (no gaps) and the area / height represents frequency; a bar chart is used for categorical data with gaps between bars.
parts.working: B1 histogram; B1 bars touch because data are continuous (bar chart has gaps / categories).

practice.stem: A student plans to measure the rate of CO₂ production by yeast in glucose solutions of 0, 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a suitable hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: The rate of respiration of yeast increases as glucose concentration increases (until a maximum is reached).
parts.working: B1 testable hypothesis linking glucose concentration and rate, with direction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the shape of the graph of rate of CO₂ production against glucose concentration and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Rate increases steeply at low glucose concentrations, then levels off at high concentrations; at low concentration glucose is the limiting factor; at high concentration enzymes / glucose transport proteins are saturated (or yeast concentration limits), so rate cannot rise further; very high concentrations may decrease the rate by causing water loss by osmosis.
parts.working: B1 rises then levels off (plateau); B1 glucose limiting at low concentration / more collisions with enzymes; B1 enzymes / carrier proteins saturated or another factor limiting at high concentration (allow fall due to osmotic water loss).

practice.stem: A student will measure the rate of oxygen uptake of maggots at 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a testable hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: As temperature increases from 10 °C to 30 °C, the rate of oxygen uptake by maggots increases.
parts.working: B1 clear relationship between IV and DV that can be tested.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the biological basis for your hypothesis.
parts.answer: Maggots are ectotherms, so their body temperature follows the surroundings; higher temperature gives respiratory enzymes more kinetic energy, more enzyme–substrate collisions, faster respiration and more oxygen used.
parts.working: B1 body temperature follows environment / ectotherm; B1 enzyme activity increases with temperature (below optimum).

practice.stem: A student will compare the rate of CO₂ production by baker's yeast and brewer's yeast in the same glucose solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a null hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the rates of CO₂ production by baker's yeast and brewer's yeast.
parts.working: B1 'no (significant) difference' between the two strains.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name a statistical test the student could use to test the null hypothesis, and state what the student must collect to use it.
parts.answer: t-test; several replicate measurements (e.g. at least 5) of rate for each strain, so means and standard deviations can be calculated.
parts.working: B1 t-test; B1 replicate data for each strain / means and SD.

practice.stem: Two respirometers each contain 5 g of germinating wheat grains, which respire only carbohydrate. Respirometer A contains soda lime; respirometer B contains water instead.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the movement of the liquid in each respirometer. Explain your predictions.
parts.answer: A: liquid moves towards the grains because oxygen is taken in and the CO₂ given out is absorbed. B: liquid does not move (or hardly moves) because with carbohydrate the RQ is 1, so the volume of CO₂ released equals the volume of oxygen taken in.
parts.working: B1 A moves towards grains; B1 O₂ used, CO₂ absorbed; B1 B no movement; B1 RQ = 1 / equal volumes of O₂ and CO₂.

practice.stem: With 1 cm³ of yeast suspension, methylene blue took 240 s to decolourise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the time taken with 2 cm³ of the same yeast suspension (all other conditions the same). Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: About 120 s (about half the time), because there are twice as many yeast cells / dehydrogenase enzymes, so methylene blue is reduced twice as fast.
parts.working: B1 about half / ~120 s; B1 more enzymes / cells so faster reduction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the actual time might not be exactly half.
parts.answer: Other factors such as glucose concentration or oxygen concentration may become limiting, or the end point is judged inaccurately.
parts.working: B1 another limiting factor / measurement error.

practice.stem: Cyanide stops the electron transport chain. A suspension of yeast in glucose solution was given a small dose of cyanide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict what would happen to the oxygen uptake and the CO₂ production of the yeast. Explain your predictions.
parts.answer: Oxygen uptake stops (falls to almost zero) because electrons can no longer be passed to oxygen; CO₂ production continues (at a lower or similar rate) because yeast can respire anaerobically, converting pyruvate to ethanol and CO₂.
parts.working: B1 oxygen uptake stops; B1 electron transport chain blocked / oxygen not final acceptor; B1 CO₂ production continues; B1 anaerobic respiration / ethanol fermentation releases CO₂.

practice.stem: Germinating sunflower seeds store mainly lipid; germinating wheat grains store mainly starch.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a hypothesis about the RQs of these seeds during early germination.
parts.answer: Germinating sunflower seeds have a lower RQ (about 0.7) than germinating wheat grains (about 1.0).
parts.working: B1 sunflower RQ lower than wheat (with or without values).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain your hypothesis.
parts.answer: Sunflower seeds respire lipid, which contains relatively little oxygen, so more O₂ is needed per CO₂ released (RQ 0.7); wheat respires carbohydrate from starch (RQ 1.0).
parts.working: B1 lipid RQ 0.7 because less oxygen in molecule; B1 starch / carbohydrate RQ 1.0.

practice.stem: A respirometer containing soda lime and germinating sunflower seeds (RQ 0.70) showed 40 mm of liquid movement in 30 minutes. An identical respirometer contained water instead of soda lime.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the distance and direction the liquid would move in the respirometer with water in 30 minutes.
parts.answer: 12 mm towards the seeds
parts.working: M1 CO₂ produced = 0.70 × 40 = 28 mm equivalent; A1 net movement 40 − 28 = 12 mm towards the seeds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the direction of movement.
parts.answer: More oxygen is taken in than CO₂ released, so the gas volume in the tube falls.
parts.working: B1 O₂ uptake > CO₂ output so volume decreases.

practice.stem: A researcher plans to grow yeast in glucose solutions containing 0, 4, 8, 12 and 16 % ethanol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how the rate of CO₂ production will change as the ethanol concentration increases. Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: The rate will decrease as ethanol concentration increases, possibly falling to almost zero at 12–16 %; ethanol is toxic: it damages cell membranes (dissolves in the phospholipid bilayer) and denatures enzymes, so respiration slows.
parts.working: B1 rate decreases with increasing ethanol; B1 ethanol damages membranes; B1 denatures / inhibits enzymes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a small concentration of ethanol (4 %) may have little effect.
parts.answer: Yeast is tolerant of low ethanol concentrations because it produces ethanol naturally in fermentation.
parts.working: B1 yeast tolerates low ethanol / adapted to its own product.

practice.stem:
Hydrogencarbonate indicator is red at atmospheric CO₂ concentration, yellow at higher CO₂ concentrations and purple at lower CO₂ concentrations. Three sealed tubes each contain indicator and a gauze platform:
tube 1: germinating mung beans
tube 2: mung beans boiled and cooled
tube 3: glass beads

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the colour of the indicator in each tube after 2 hours. Explain each prediction.
parts.answer: Tube 1 yellow: the beans respire and release CO₂; tube 2 red: boiled beans are dead, enzymes denatured, no respiration; tube 3 red: glass beads do not respire.
parts.working: B1 tube 1 yellow with reason; B1 tube 2 red with reason; B1 tube 3 red with reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the tubes should be kept in the dark if green seedlings are used.
parts.answer: Green seedlings would photosynthesise in light, removing CO₂ (indicator may stay red or turn purple).
parts.working: B1 photosynthesis removes CO₂.

practice.stem: A biologist thinks that smaller mammals have higher respiration rates per gram of body mass than larger mammals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write this idea as a testable hypothesis and predict the shape of a graph of oxygen uptake per kg against body mass.
parts.answer: Hypothesis: as body mass increases, the rate of oxygen uptake per kg of body mass decreases. Graph: a curve falling steeply at low masses and levelling off at high masses (negative correlation).
parts.working: B1 testable hypothesis with direction; B1 decreasing curve / negative correlation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the biological reason for this prediction.
parts.answer: Smaller mammals have a larger surface area to volume ratio, so they lose heat faster; they respire faster per gram to produce heat and maintain a constant body temperature.
parts.working: B1 larger SA:V / greater heat loss; B1 more respiration to replace heat.

practice.stem: Muscle from the breast of pigeons (which fly long distances) and from the breast of domestic chickens (which fly only in short bursts) are to be compared.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Formulate a hypothesis relating the number of mitochondria in a muscle to the type of activity it performs, and make three predictions that would follow if the hypothesis is correct.
parts.answer: Hypothesis: muscles used for long periods of sustained activity contain more mitochondria per unit volume than muscles used for short bursts. Predictions: pigeon breast muscle has a greater volume of mitochondria per cell; pigeon muscle takes up more oxygen per gram at rest / when stimulated; chicken breast muscle has higher lactate dehydrogenase activity / produces more lactate; pigeon muscle has more myoglobin / capillaries (darker colour).
parts.working: B1 hypothesis linking mitochondria number to sustained activity; 1 mark each for up to three valid predictions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a correlation between mitochondria number and sustained activity would not prove the hypothesis.
parts.answer: Other differences between species (e.g. capillary density, myoglobin, enzyme concentrations) may also explain endurance; correlation does not show cause.
parts.working: B1 other variables / correlation is not causation.

practice.stem: A trained runner takes part in a 3-hour marathon, drinking only water. Her RQ was 0.95 at the start of the race.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how her RQ changes over the 3 hours. Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: RQ falls gradually from about 0.95 towards about 0.75–0.8; at first carbohydrate (muscle and liver glycogen, blood glucose) is the main substrate; as glycogen stores become depleted, an increasing proportion of energy comes from lipid (fatty acids from adipose tissue), which has an RQ of 0.7.
parts.working: B1 RQ falls (towards 0.7–0.8); B1 glycogen / carbohydrate used first and depleted; B1 more lipid respired, RQ 0.7.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the effect on her RQ of drinking a glucose drink at 2 hours, and explain.
parts.answer: RQ would rise towards 1.0 because the glucose is absorbed and respired, providing more carbohydrate as substrate.
parts.working: B1 RQ increases; B1 more carbohydrate respired.

practice.stem: Succinate dehydrogenase from mitochondria reduces the blue dye DCPIP as it oxidises succinate. Malonate is a competitive inhibitor of the enzyme. A student plans to measure the rate of DCPIP reduction at different succinate concentrations, with and without a fixed concentration of malonate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how the curves of rate against succinate concentration with and without malonate will compare. Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Both curves rise and level off; the curve with malonate is lower at low succinate concentrations; at high succinate concentrations the two curves approach the same maximum rate. Malonate competes with succinate for the active site; at high succinate concentrations succinate molecules outcompete malonate, so most active sites bind succinate.
parts.working: B1 rate lower with malonate at low succinate; B1 same maximum rate reached at high succinate; B1 malonate competes for active site (similar shape); B1 high succinate outcompetes inhibitor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State a null hypothesis that could be tested at one succinate concentration.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the rate of DCPIP reduction with and without malonate (at this succinate concentration).
parts.working: B1 correct null hypothesis.

practice.stem: The oxygen uptake of a lizard (an ectotherm) and a mouse (an endotherm) of similar mass will be measured at environmental temperatures of 10 °C and 30 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how the oxygen uptake of each animal will change from 10 °C to 30 °C. Explain your predictions.
parts.answer: Lizard: uptake increases at 30 °C because its body temperature rises with the environment, increasing enzyme activity / metabolic rate. Mouse: uptake decreases at 30 °C because it needs to generate less heat by respiration to maintain its body temperature (more heat needed at 10 °C).
parts.working: B1 lizard increases; B1 body temperature follows environment / enzymes faster; B1 mouse decreases (higher at 10 °C); B1 respiration produces heat to keep constant body temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict which animal will have the higher oxygen uptake at 10 °C.
parts.answer: The mouse (much higher).
parts.working: B1 mouse.

practice.stem:
Mean volume of CO₂ produced by yeast in 15 minutes (cm³), three replicates each:
glucose 8.4; fructose 8.1; sucrose 6.2; maltose 3.5; starch 0.2

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two conclusions that can be drawn from these results.
parts.answer: Yeast respires glucose and fructose fastest (at similar rates); disaccharides sucrose and maltose are respired more slowly than monosaccharides; starch is hardly respired at all.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid conclusions supported by the figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why starch produced almost no CO₂.
parts.answer: Yeast does not secrete amylase (cannot hydrolyse starch), and starch molecules are too large to enter the cells.
parts.working: B1 no amylase / starch not hydrolysed / too large to be absorbed.

practice.stem:
Rate of oxygen uptake (mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹) of seeds soaked for 2 days at 25 °C:
maize 95; chickpea 140; mustard 210

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student concluded that mustard seeds respire faster than maize seeds because mustard seeds are smaller. Explain whether the data support this conclusion.
parts.answer: The data show mustard has the highest rate per gram (210 vs 95), but no data on seed size were collected, so the reason cannot be concluded from these results; other differences (e.g. stored food type, germination stage) could explain it.
parts.working: B1 data show mustard faster per gram; B1 no data on size / cause not tested.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what further information would be needed to judge whether the differences are significant.
parts.answer: Replicate results with a measure of spread (standard deviation / error bars) or a statistical test.
parts.working: B1 replicates / SD / statistical test.

practice.stem: The RQ of germinating seeds of a plant was measured: day 1: 0.72; day 3: 0.71; day 5: 0.78; day 7: 0.90; day 9: 0.99.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what conclusion can be drawn about the main respiratory substrate during the 9 days.
parts.answer: On days 1–3 the main substrate is lipid (RQ about 0.7); from day 5 onwards there is a change to a mixture and then to carbohydrate by day 9 (RQ about 1.0).
parts.working: B1 lipid early (RQ ≈ 0.7); B1 changes to carbohydrate by day 9 (RQ ≈ 1.0).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a reason for the change.
parts.answer: Lipid stores are used up and/or the seedlings begin to photosynthesise, producing carbohydrate.
parts.working: B1 lipid stores depleted / photosynthesis provides carbohydrate.

practice.stem: Two cricketers ran the same 400 m shuttle test. Blood lactate (mmol dm⁻³) immediately after: player A 4.2; player B 9.6. Both had 1.1 at rest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a conclusion about the two players' respiration during the test.
parts.answer: Player B relied more on anaerobic respiration (produced more lactate) than player A.
parts.working: B1 B more anaerobic respiration / A more aerobic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason for the difference and explain why it cannot be confirmed from these data alone.
parts.answer: Player A may be fitter / have more mitochondria or better oxygen supply to muscles; but only one test was done on each player, and speed / effort may have differed, so the cause is not shown by the data.
parts.working: B1 reason (fitness, more mitochondria, capillaries); B1 single measurement / effort not controlled / other variables.

practice.stem:
Oxygen uptake (mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹) of seeds kept at 25 °C:
dry seeds: 0.1, 0.1, 0.2
seeds soaked for 24 h: 48, 52, 50

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a conclusion and use the data to support it.
parts.answer: Soaked (germinating) seeds respire much faster than dry seeds: mean about 50 compared with about 0.13 mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹ (several hundred times faster).
parts.working: B1 conclusion; B1 supporting figures / comparison of means.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the conclusion is valid only for this type of seed at 25 °C.
parts.answer: Only one species and one temperature were tested, so the results cannot be generalised to other species or conditions.
parts.working: B1 only one species / one temperature tested.

practice.stem:
Rate of oxygen uptake by germinating wheat grains (mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹) at different temperatures:
10 °C: 4.2
20 °C: 8.1
30 °C: 15.6
40 °C: 18.0
50 °C: 6.3

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of temperature on the rate of oxygen uptake.
parts.answer: Rate increases from 4.2 at 10 °C to a maximum of 18.0 at 40 °C, then falls sharply to 6.3 at 50 °C.
parts.working: B1 increase up to 40 °C, then decrease; B1 data quoted with units, e.g. maximum 18.0 mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹ at 40 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the results between 40 °C and 50 °C.
parts.answer: Respiratory enzymes (dehydrogenases, ATP synthase) are denatured: hydrogen bonds break, the active site changes shape so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form.
parts.working: B1 enzymes denatured / bonds in tertiary structure broken; B1 active site shape changed, substrate no longer fits.

parts.label: c
