parts.text: A student concluded that the optimum temperature for respiration in these seeds is 40 °C. Evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: The highest rate recorded was at 40 °C, but the true optimum could be anywhere between 30 and 50 °C because readings were taken only every 10 °C; more readings between 35 and 45 °C would be needed; no repeats shown.
parts.working: B1 highest rate at 40 °C so supports; B1 large intervals — optimum could be between 30 and 50 °C / need smaller intervals / repeats.

practice.stem: A student compared the rate of CO₂ production by yeast at 30 °C in 0.5 mol dm⁻³ glucose and 0.5 mol dm⁻³ maltose (5 replicates each). A t-test gave t = 3.42. The critical value at p = 0.05 with 8 degrees of freedom is 2.31.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what conclusion can be drawn from the t-test.
parts.answer: t (3.42) is greater than the critical value (2.31), so the null hypothesis is rejected; there is a significant difference between the rates with glucose and with maltose (the probability that the difference is due to chance is less than 5 %).
parts.working: B1 3.42 > 2.31 so reject null hypothesis; B1 significant difference / less than 5 % probability due to chance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the degrees of freedom were calculated.
parts.answer: Total number of replicates minus 2: (5 + 5) − 2 = 8.
parts.working: B1 n₁ + n₂ − 2 = 8.

practice.stem:
Data from five rat tissues:
tissue: mitochondria per cell; oxygen uptake / µl g⁻¹ h⁻¹
skin: 60; 210
liver: 1700; 1150
kidney: 1300; 1700
heart muscle: 3000; 2400
brain: 900; 1800

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between number of mitochondria and oxygen uptake, using data, and identify any tissue that does not fit the pattern.
parts.answer: Only a weak, broadly positive trend: skin (60 mitochondria, uptake 210) has the fewest mitochondria and the lowest uptake, and heart (3000, 2400) has the most mitochondria and a high uptake. But brain (900 mitochondria) has a higher uptake (1800) than liver (1700 mitochondria, 1150), and kidney (1300) has a higher uptake than liver despite fewer mitochondria. Brain and liver do not fit the pattern.
parts.working: B1 weak / broadly positive trend stated, with data quoted; B1 brain and/or liver (or kidney) identified as not fitting; B1 the data do not show a clear positive correlation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why these data do not prove that the number of mitochondria determines the rate of oxygen uptake.
parts.answer: Correlation does not show causation; other factors differ between tissues (size of mitochondria, cristae density, ATP demand, enzyme activity); only one sample from each tissue / no replicates.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem:
Two yeast strains were grown in glucose solution with different ethanol concentrations. Rate of CO₂ production as a percentage of the rate with 0 % ethanol:
ethanol / %: 0, 4, 8, 12, 16
strain P: 100, 92, 70, 31, 5
strain Q: 100, 75, 38, 9, 0

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a conclusion about the ethanol tolerance of the two strains. Support it with data.
parts.answer: Strain P is more tolerant of ethanol than strain Q: at 8 % P still respires at 70 % of its maximum rate while Q is at 38 %; at 12 % P 31 % vs Q 9 %.
parts.working: B1 P more tolerant; B1 comparative figures at the same concentration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest which strain is better for producing a fuel ethanol solution of about 12 %. Explain your choice.
parts.answer: Strain P, because it continues to respire / ferment at 12 % ethanol (31 % of maximum), whereas Q almost stops.
parts.working: B1 P with reason.

practice.stem:
Mean rate of oxygen uptake (mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹) ± standard deviation, 6 replicates each, for woodlice kept in dry and damp soil:
dry: 52 ± 9
damp: 58 ± 10

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student concluded that woodlice in damp soil respire faster than those in dry soil. Evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: The mean is higher in damp soil (58 vs 52); but the difference (6) is smaller than either standard deviation and the ranges mean ± SD overlap widely (43–61 and 48–68), so the difference is probably not significant / may be due to chance; a t-test is needed; conclusion not supported.
parts.working: B1 mean higher in damp; B1 SDs overlap / difference smaller than SD; B1 not likely to be significant / needs statistical test so conclusion not valid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the investigation could be changed to give a more certain conclusion.
parts.answer: Increase the number of replicates (larger sample) and use a t-test (also standardise mass / temperature).
parts.working: B1 more replicates / statistical test.

practice.stem:
Rate of oxygen uptake of aphids feeding on cotton plants in Faisalabad was measured before and 2 hours after spraying a new insecticide (mm³ g⁻¹ h⁻¹):
before: 3.1
after: 5.8
unsprayed control aphids, same times: 3.0 and 3.2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the rate of the sprayed aphids, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What conclusion can be drawn about the effect of the insecticide? Use the control data in your answer.
parts.answer: The insecticide increases the respiration rate of the aphids, since the control rate hardly changed (3.0 to 3.2), so the increase is not due to time of day or handling.
parts.working: B1 insecticide increases rate; B1 control unchanged so effect due to insecticide.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way the insecticide might cause this effect.
parts.answer: It may act as an uncoupler, allowing protons to leak across the inner mitochondrial membrane so more oxygen is used without making ATP (or it increases activity / stress).
parts.working: B1 sensible suggestion, e.g. uncoupling oxidative phosphorylation.

practice.stem: For eight mammal species, a student ranked body mass and resting oxygen uptake per kg. Spearman's rank correlation coefficient was rₛ = −0.89. The critical value at p = 0.05 for n = 8 is 0.738.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the conclusion that can be drawn.
parts.answer: The magnitude 0.89 is greater than 0.738, so there is a significant negative correlation: as body mass increases, oxygen uptake per kg decreases (less than 5 % probability the correlation is due to chance).
parts.working: B1 0.89 > 0.738 so significant; B1 negative correlation described.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this result does not show that body mass itself causes the lower oxygen uptake.
parts.answer: Correlation does not show causation; another factor linked to mass, such as surface area to volume ratio / heat loss, or activity level, may be the cause.
parts.working: B1 correlation ≠ causation; B1 named alternative factor (SA:V, activity, diet).

practice.stem:
Oxygen concentration in a chamber containing isolated mitochondria was recorded. Additions and rates of oxygen uptake (nmol min⁻¹):
0–2 min: mitochondria + pyruvate: 8
2–5 min: ADP added: 45
5–8 min: compound X added: 1
8–11 min: DNP (an uncoupler that makes the inner membrane permeable to protons) added: 1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the change in rate when ADP was added.
parts.answer: ADP allows ATP synthase to work; protons flow back through ATP synthase, reducing the gradient, so electron transport and proton pumping speed up and more oxygen is used.
parts.working: B1 ADP substrate for ATP synthase / protons flow through ATP synthase; B1 electron transport faster / more O₂ reduced.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce whether compound X acts on the electron transport chain or on ATP synthase. Explain how the data support your conclusion.
parts.answer: X acts on the electron transport chain. If X blocked only ATP synthase, adding DNP would let protons leak back, the gradient would be removed and electron transport (oxygen uptake) would restart; but oxygen uptake stayed at 1 after DNP, so electrons cannot reach oxygen — the chain itself is blocked.
parts.working: B1 ETC; B1 DNP would restore O₂ uptake if only ATP synthase blocked; B1 no restoration so electron flow to O₂ blocked.

practice.stem:
A company claims that a slimming supplement 'burns fat by speeding up metabolism'. In a trial, 10 mice given the supplement for 4 weeks were compared with 10 control mice:
oxygen uptake: +28 % compared with controls
ATP concentration in muscle: −15 %
body temperature: +0.9 °C
body mass change: −6 % (controls +1 %)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest a conclusion about how the supplement acts, using all four results.
parts.answer: The supplement probably uncouples oxidative phosphorylation: oxygen uptake (electron transport) increases but less ATP is made, so the energy from the proton gradient is released as heat (higher body temperature); more substrate including fat is respired to meet ATP needs, causing mass loss.
parts.working: B1 uncoupling / protons leak across inner membrane; B1 more O₂ used but less ATP, energy lost as heat; B1 more fat respired to compensate so mass falls.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether the trial supports the company's claim for use in humans.
parts.answer: Supports increased respiration and mass loss in mice; but small sample (10 per group), no statistical test given; mice not humans; 4 weeks only — long-term safety unknown; raised temperature and reduced ATP suggest possible danger (like DNP); mass loss not shown to be fat (could be water / muscle).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three valid evaluation points (max 1 for support).

practice.stem:
Soil respiration (CO₂ release, g m⁻² day⁻¹) was measured monthly in a field in Punjab, together with soil temperature and soil moisture:
Jan: 1.2 (12 °C, 22 %)
Apr: 3.6 (28 °C, 15 %)
Jun: 2.1 (38 °C, 5 %)
Aug: 6.4 (32 °C, 30 %)
Oct: 3.0 (25 °C, 18 %)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student concluded that soil respiration increases with temperature. Evaluate this conclusion using the data.
parts.answer: Partly supported: January (12 °C) has the lowest rate and April/August have higher rates; but June has the highest temperature (38 °C) and only a low rate (2.1), while August (32 °C) has the highest rate; moisture also varies — June was very dry (5 %) and August wettest (30 %); so moisture is a confounding variable and temperature alone does not explain the pattern; only one reading per month, no replicates.
parts.working: B1 some support with data; B1 June anomaly / not a consistent increase; B1 moisture confounding / no replicates or statistics.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a biological explanation for the low rate in June.
parts.answer: Very dry soil: microorganisms and roots lack water for enzyme activity / metabolism, so they become dormant or die; very high temperature may also denature enzymes.
parts.working: B1 lack of water limits microbial / root metabolism; B1 high temperature may denature enzymes / kill organisms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline how bacteria can be genetically modified to produce human insulin.
parts.answer: mRNA for insulin is extracted from pancreatic β-cells; reverse transcriptase makes cDNA (no introns); sticky ends added / DNA cut with a restriction enzyme; plasmids cut with the same restriction enzyme; insulin gene and plasmid joined by DNA ligase (recombinant plasmid); plasmids taken up by bacteria (transformation); bacteria with the plasmid identified using a marker gene; cultured in a fermenter; insulin extracted and purified
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: mRNA from β-cells; reverse transcriptase → cDNA; restriction enzyme / complementary sticky ends; plasmid as vector cut with same enzyme; DNA ligase; promoter added; transformation (e.g. heat shock with Ca²⁺); marker gene (e.g. GFP) to identify transformed cells; cloning/culture in fermenter; extraction and purification.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the role of each of the following in gene transfer: (i) restriction enzyme, (ii) DNA ligase, (iii) plasmid, (iv) sticky ends.
parts.answer: (i) cuts DNA at a specific base sequence (recognition site); (ii) joins sugar–phosphate backbones of DNA fragments by forming phosphodiester bonds; (iii) vector that carries the gene into the host cell (and replicates there); (iv) short single-stranded overhangs that pair with complementary sticky ends by hydrogen bonding, so fragments join
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why cDNA made from mRNA, rather than the gene cut from human chromosomes, is inserted into bacteria.
parts.answer: Human genes contain introns; bacteria cannot remove introns (no splicing), so the gene would not be expressed correctly; cDNA from mature mRNA has no introns
parts.working: 1 mark: genomic gene contains introns / cDNA does not. 1 mark: bacteria cannot splice out introns.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the gene for green fluorescent protein (GFP) can be used as a marker to identify bacteria that have taken up a recombinant plasmid.
parts.answer: GFP gene is placed in the plasmid alongside the desired gene; bacteria that take up the plasmid express GFP; under ultraviolet (blue) light these colonies fluoresce green, so they can be identified and selected
parts.working: 1 mark each: GFP gene inserted with/next to the gene of interest (same plasmid); transformed bacteria make GFP; glow green under UV light / can be picked out.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Antibiotic-resistance genes were once widely used as markers. Suggest two reasons why fluorescent markers are now often preferred.
parts.answer: Avoids spreading antibiotic resistance genes to other (pathogenic) bacteria; cells can be identified without killing non-transformed cells / no need for antibiotics; results seen quickly and easily
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sensible reasons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a plant cell can be genetically modified using the bacterium Agrobacterium tumefaciens and its Ti plasmid.
parts.answer: The desired gene is inserted into the T-DNA region of a disarmed Ti plasmid. Agrobacterium infects the plant at a wound and transfers the T-DNA into the plant cell. The T-DNA is inserted into a chromosome of the plant cell. Transformed cells are identified using a marker gene (e.g. antibiotic or herbicide resistance) and grown into whole plants.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: gene placed in the T-DNA of the Ti plasmid; bacterium infects wounded plant tissue; T-DNA transferred into the plant cell; T-DNA integrates into the plant chromosomal DNA; marker gene used to select transformed cells; transformed cells regenerated into whole plants. Accept disarmed = tumour-causing genes removed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the recombinant plasmid must be taken up by bacteria (transformation) before the inserted gene can be expressed in large amounts.
parts.answer: Plasmid DNA cannot pass through the bacterial membrane unaided, so it must be introduced by transformation (for example heat shock in cold calcium chloride). Once inside, the bacterium replicates the plasmid and expresses the inserted gene, so large amounts of the product are made.
parts.working: 1 mark: DNA cannot cross the membrane unaided, so transformation is needed. 1 mark: inside the bacterium the plasmid replicates and the gene is expressed, giving large amounts of product.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why some bacteria may take up a plasmid that has re-joined to itself, without the gene of interest.
parts.answer: The cut plasmid has complementary sticky ends, so its two ends can pair and be ligated back together without inserting the gene.
parts.working: 1 mark: the plasmid ends are complementary, so it can re-ligate to itself (the gene is not inserted).

practice.stem:
The restriction enzyme EcoRI recognises the sequence GAATTC and cuts between G and A on each strand, leaving sticky ends. One strand of a 43-nucleotide linear DNA molecule is:
5′ ATCGGAATTCTAGCCTAGGCATTACGGAATTCAGTTCAGCATG 3′

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of fragments produced when this DNA is cut with EcoRI.
parts.working: Two recognition sites (GAATTC at positions 5–10 and 27–32), so a linear molecule gives 3 fragments.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the length, in nucleotides, of each fragment of the strand shown.
parts.answer: 5, 22 and 16 nucleotides
parts.working: Cuts after the G of each site (after nucleotides 5 and 27): 5, 27 − 5 = 22 and 43 − 27 = 16. 1 mark for two correct; 2 marks all three.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the same restriction enzyme must be used to cut the plasmid and the DNA containing the gene.
parts.answer: It produces complementary sticky ends on both; the sticky ends can base pair (hydrogen bond) with each other so ligase can join gene and plasmid
parts.working: 1 mark: same/complementary sticky ends. 1 mark: base pairing allows fragments to join before ligase seals them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bt cotton, widely grown in Pakistan, contains a gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis that codes for a protein toxic to caterpillars such as bollworms. Explain two benefits of growing Bt cotton.
parts.answer: Plants are protected from insect pests so yield increases; less insecticide spraying needed, which reduces costs for farmers and harm to the farmer's health and to non-target insects/environment; toxin is specific to certain insects
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: reduced crop damage/higher yield; less pesticide spraying; lower cost; less exposure of farm workers to sprays; fewer non-target organisms killed (beneficial insects); toxin is specific.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss two concerns about growing Bt cotton.
parts.answer: Pests may evolve resistance to the Bt toxin (selection), especially if refuges are not used; the gene may spread to wild relatives by pollen; seed is costly and must often be bought each year; other (secondary) pests not affected may increase; effects on non-target insects
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three points, at least one explained (e.g. resistance: individuals with resistance alleles survive and reproduce, so allele frequency rises).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Golden rice has been genetically modified to produce β-carotene in its endosperm (the part of the grain that is eaten). The body converts β-carotene to vitamin A. Explain why the inserted genes are joined to a promoter that is active only in endosperm cells.
parts.answer: A promoter is needed for RNA polymerase to bind and transcribe the gene; an endosperm-specific promoter means the genes are expressed only in the grain (the eaten part), not wasting resources in leaves/roots
parts.working: 1 mark: promoter allows transcription (RNA polymerase binding). 1 mark: expression limited to endosperm/edible part.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why golden rice was developed and discuss one objection that has been raised against it.
parts.answer: Vitamin A deficiency causes blindness and weak immunity in children in countries where rice is the staple food; golden rice provides vitamin A cheaply in the normal diet. Objections: a varied diet/supplements could solve the problem; possible gene flow to other rice; concerns about control by companies or farmers' acceptance; unknown long-term effects
parts.working: 1 mark: vitamin A deficiency/blindness in rice-dependent populations. 1 mark: provides vitamin A in staple food. 1 mark: one objection explained.

practice.stem: A GM Atlantic salmon contains a growth hormone gene from another salmon species, joined to a promoter from a fish called the ocean pout. In one trial the GM salmon reached market mass in 18 months, compared with 36 months for non-GM salmon.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in the time to reach market mass.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the growth hormone gene was joined to a promoter from the ocean pout rather than its own promoter.
parts.answer: The normal promoter is only active in certain seasons/conditions; the ocean pout promoter is active all year, so growth hormone is produced continuously and the fish grow faster
parts.working: 1 mark: promoter controls when the gene is transcribed. 1 mark: pout promoter switched on all year → continuous growth hormone production.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The GM salmon are all sterile females and are farmed only in tanks on land. Explain why.
parts.answer: To prevent GM fish escaping and breeding with wild salmon; this avoids spreading the transgene into wild populations / GM fish outcompeting wild fish
parts.working: 1 mark: sterile so cannot reproduce if they escape. 1 mark: land tanks prevent escape; protects wild populations from gene flow/competition.

practice.stem: A plasmid carries an ampicillin-resistance gene and a tetracycline-resistance gene. A DNA fragment was inserted into the ampicillin-resistance gene, which inactivates it. Bacteria were transformed with the plasmid mixture and spread on a tetracycline plate, where 960 colonies grew. The same colonies were then replica-plated onto a plate containing both tetracycline and ampicillin; 288 colonies grew on this plate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the 288 colonies grew on the plate containing both tetracycline and ampicillin.
parts.answer: These bacteria took up a plasmid with an intact ampicillin-resistance gene, so there was no insert. The plasmid also carries the tetracycline-resistance gene, so they grow on both plates.
parts.working: 1 mark: no gene inserted, so the ampicillin-resistance gene is intact. 1 mark: the plasmid also carries the tetracycline-resistance gene, so the colonies grow on both plates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of colonies that contain a recombinant plasmid. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Recombinant colonies (insert in the ampicillin gene, so no ampicillin resistance) = 960 − 288 = 672. 672 ÷ 960 × 100 = 70.0 %. M1 for finding 672; A1 for 70.0 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one concern that has been raised about the effect of GM crops on non-target organisms, such as pollinating insects or soil microbes, and describe one piece of evidence that would be needed to judge the concern.
parts.answer: Concern: GM crops could harm beneficial non-target organisms (e.g. pollinators or soil organisms) through the toxin, or through effects on the food web. Evidence needed: field or laboratory studies comparing populations of the organism or its food web in GM and non-GM crop fields, with controls and replicates.
parts.working: 1 mark: a named concern about non-target organisms or the food web. 1 mark: an effect that could arise (e.g. toxin harms pollinators, reduced food for predators). 1 mark: a suitable evidence source such as comparative field studies with controls and replicates.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline how the CRISPR–Cas9 system can be used to inactivate (knock out) a specific gene in a plant.
parts.answer: A guide RNA is made with a base sequence complementary to part of the target gene; it is combined with the Cas9 enzyme (a nuclease); the guide RNA base pairs with the target DNA, so Cas9 cuts both strands at that point; the cell repairs the break, often with errors (insertions/deletions), causing a frameshift so the gene no longer codes for a functional protein
parts.working: 1 mark each: guide RNA complementary to target sequence; Cas9 nuclease guided to site; cuts both DNA strands (double-strand break); repair introduces mutation / frameshift, inactivating gene.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how CRISPR–Cas9 could instead be used to insert a corrected allele.
parts.answer: Supply a DNA template containing the desired allele with sequences matching either side of the cut; the cell uses this template to repair the break, so the new sequence is incorporated
parts.working: 1 mark: provide repair template with the correct sequence. 1 mark: template has ends matching the DNA around the cut, so it is used in repair.

practice.stem: A plasmid carries two antibiotic-resistance genes: one for ampicillin and one for tetracycline. A human gene is inserted into the middle of the tetracycline-resistance gene. After transformation, bacteria are spread on agar containing ampicillin and 200 colonies grow. The colonies are then copied, in the same positions, onto agar containing tetracycline; 46 colonies grow.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how growing the colonies on the two types of agar allows bacteria containing the recombinant plasmid to be identified.
parts.answer: Only bacteria with a plasmid (either type) grow on ampicillin, because all plasmids carry the ampicillin-resistance gene; inserting the gene into the tetracycline-resistance gene inactivates it; so bacteria with recombinant plasmids grow on ampicillin but not on tetracycline, while those with the original plasmid grow on both
parts.working: 1 mark each: ampicillin selects bacteria that took up any plasmid; insert disrupts tetracycline resistance gene; recombinant colonies are those that grow on ampicillin but fail to grow on tetracycline (replica plating).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of colonies on the ampicillin plate that contain the recombinant plasmid.
parts.working: M1: 200 − 46 = 154 colonies did not grow on tetracycline. A1: 154 ÷ 200 × 100 = 77 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Erythropoietin (EPO) is a human glycoprotein hormone. It is produced commercially using genetically modified mammalian cells grown in culture rather than bacteria. Suggest why.
parts.answer: EPO has carbohydrate chains added after translation (in the Golgi body / ER); bacteria have no Golgi or ER so cannot add these chains; without them the protein may be inactive or quickly removed; mammalian cells modify the protein like human cells
parts.working: 1 mark each: EPO needs glycosylation/post-translational modification; bacteria lack ER/Golgi (cannot glycosylate); mammalian cells can produce the correctly modified/functional protein.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Before GM bacteria were used, diabetics were treated with insulin extracted from pigs and cattle. Give three advantages of insulin made by GM bacteria.
parts.answer: Identical to human insulin so fewer immune/allergic reactions; can be produced in large quantities to meet demand; cheaper/faster; no ethical or religious objections to animal source; no risk of transmitting animal diseases; consistent quality
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A research team wants to show that a promoter from a plant gene is switched on in root hairs but not in leaves. They have the promoter DNA, a plasmid with a gene for green fluorescent protein (GFP) that has no promoter in front of it, and the bacterium Agrobacterium tumefaciens. Describe how they could use these materials to test the promoter, and explain the control they should include.
parts.answer: Insert the promoter DNA upstream of (in front of) the GFP gene in the plasmid. Transfer the construct into plant cells with Agrobacterium, then regenerate plants. Examine root hairs and leaves under UV or fluorescence microscopy. Green fluorescence in root hairs but not leaves shows the promoter is active only there. Use a control plant transformed with the GFP plasmid without the promoter, which should show no fluorescence.
parts.working: 1 mark: promoter placed in front of the GFP gene (promoter–GFP construct). 1 mark: construct transferred into plant cells using Agrobacterium (transformation). 1 mark: fluorescence seen only where the promoter is active. 1 mark: root hairs and leaves examined under UV/fluorescence microscope. 1 mark: control with promoterless GFP to show the GFP gene alone does not produce fluorescence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) caused by a faulty gene for the enzyme ADA has been treated by gene therapy. Describe how this is done.
parts.answer: Stem cells (or T-lymphocytes) are taken from the patient's bone marrow/blood; a normal allele of the ADA gene is inserted into a virus vector (e.g. a retrovirus/lentivirus); the virus infects the cells and inserts the gene into their DNA; the modified cells are returned to the patient, where they produce ADA
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: cells removed from patient (bone marrow stem cells/T-cells); normal allele/functional gene; viral vector (retrovirus/lentivirus); gene inserted into cells' DNA; cells cultured and returned; cells now produce ADA so immune system works.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why gene therapy in humans is carried out on body (somatic) cells but not on egg, sperm or embryo cells.
parts.answer: Germ-line changes would be passed to future generations; who could not consent, and long-term effects are unknown (ethical concerns; not permitted in most countries)
parts.working: 1 mark: germ-line changes inherited by offspring. 1 mark: ethical issue – no consent / unknown effects / 'designer babies'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by genetic screening.
parts.answer: Testing a person's (or embryo's) DNA to find out whether they carry a particular allele, e.g. one that causes a genetic disease
parts.working: Testing DNA for presence of specific alleles/mutations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: β-thalassaemia is a recessive genetic disorder that is common in Pakistan. Suggest two ways in which genetic screening could be used to reduce the number of children born with β-thalassaemia.
parts.answer: Screening couples before marriage/pregnancy to find carriers so they can make informed decisions; prenatal testing of a fetus; screening embryos from IVF (pre-implantation genetic diagnosis) so only unaffected embryos are implanted
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: carrier screening of couples/relatives; prenatal diagnosis; embryo (PGD) screening with IVF.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two ethical concerns about genetic screening.
parts.answer: Decisions to terminate pregnancies; stress/anxiety from results; confidentiality and discrimination (e.g. employers, insurance, marriage prospects); results may reveal information about relatives; could lead to selecting embryos for non-medical traits
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Viral vectors are modified so that they cannot cause disease. Describe two ways this is done.
parts.answer: Genes that the virus needs to replicate or that cause disease are removed from the viral genome, so the virus cannot make new infective particles. The therapeutic gene is inserted in place of the removed genes, so the vector delivers only the useful gene.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: disease-causing or replication genes deleted from the viral DNA/RNA; therapeutic gene inserted into the space left; vector cannot replicate or spread to form complete virus particles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Antisense oligonucleotides are short single-stranded pieces of nucleic acid used to treat some diseases. Describe how an antisense oligonucleotide can reduce the amount of a harmful protein made in a cell.
parts.answer: The oligonucleotide has a base sequence complementary to the target mRNA, so it base pairs with the mRNA. The double-stranded hybrid is then broken down by enzymes (e.g. RNase H), or it blocks ribosomes from translating the mRNA. Less of the harmful protein is therefore made.
parts.working: 1 mark: base sequence complementary to the target mRNA. 1 mark: forms a double-stranded hybrid with the mRNA. 1 mark: mRNA is degraded or translation is blocked, so less protein is made.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Gene therapy for a blood disorder is often carried out using stem cells removed from the patient's own bone marrow. Explain why the patient's own cells are preferred to cells from a donor.
parts.answer: The patient's own cells are not recognised as foreign, so the immune system does not attack them. Donor cells would need tissue matching, and the patient would need immunosuppressive drugs to prevent rejection.
parts.working: 1 mark: the patient's own cells are not recognised as foreign, so there is no immune rejection. 1 mark: donor cells need tissue matching and immunosuppressive drugs would be needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the use of viruses and liposomes as vectors for gene therapy.
parts.answer: Viruses enter cells efficiently and some insert genes into host DNA, so the effect is long-lasting; but they may trigger an immune response and may insert into/disrupt another gene. Liposomes (lipid spheres) fuse with cell surface membranes, cause little immune response and cannot cause infection; but they are less efficient at delivering genes and the gene is not integrated, so the effect is temporary
parts.working: Max 4: virus – efficient entry; may integrate (long-lasting); immune response; risk of insertional mutation. Liposome – fuses with membrane; little immune response/safe; less efficient; temporary expression.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Gene therapy for cystic fibrosis using liposomes in an inhaled spray must be repeated regularly. Suggest why.
parts.answer: The gene is delivered to epithelial cells lining the airways; these cells are short-lived and are replaced by new cells that do not carry the gene; the gene is not inserted into stem cells/host chromosomes
parts.working: 1 mark: airway epithelial cells are constantly replaced. 1 mark: new cells lack the gene / gene not integrated or passed on.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Screening shows that a husband and wife are both carriers of β-thalassaemia (heterozygous). Calculate the probability that their first child will have β-thalassaemia.
parts.working: Tt × Tt gives 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, so P(tt) = 0.25.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the probability that their first two children will both be unaffected. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1: P(unaffected) = 0.75 for each child (independent events). A1: 0.75 × 0.75 = 0.5625 → 0.56.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why marriages between close relatives (for example, first cousins) increase the chance of a child having a recessive disorder such as β-thalassaemia.
parts.answer: Relatives share many alleles inherited from common ancestors; so both partners are more likely to carry the same recessive allele, increasing the chance of a homozygous recessive child
parts.working: 1 mark: shared alleles from common ancestor. 1 mark: both more likely to be heterozygous for the same allele → more homozygous recessive offspring.

practice.stem: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an autosomal recessive disorder. Affected people cannot break down the amino acid phenylalanine, which builds up in the blood and damages the developing brain. Newborn babies are screened using a few drops of blood taken from the heel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why newborn babies are screened for phenylketonuria (PKU) rather than waiting for symptoms to appear.
parts.answer: PKU is inherited as a recessive allele. Phenylalanine builds up if it cannot be broken down, and this causes brain damage that cannot be reversed. Early detection allows a diet low in phenylalanine to start before the brain is damaged, so normal development is possible.
parts.working: 1 mark: brain damage from phenylalanine build-up is irreversible. 1 mark: early diagnosis means a low-phenylalanine diet can start immediately. 1 mark: treatment before symptoms appear prevents brain damage and allows normal development.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the genotype of a baby who has PKU, using the letters A (dominant) and a (recessive).
parts.answer: aa
parts.working: 1 mark: homozygous recessive, aa.

practice.stem: A screening programme tested 12 000 pregnant women for a genetic disorder. 60 women tested positive. Follow-up testing showed that 42 of these 60 women had the disorder. One further woman, who had the disorder, tested negative. All other women tested negative and did not have the disorder.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of women who tested positive but did not have the disorder.
parts.working: 60 − 42 = 18 false positives. 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the sensitivity of the test. Give your answer as a percentage to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Affected women = 42 + 1 = 43. Sensitivity = 42 ÷ 43 × 100 = 97.7 %. M1 for 43 affected (42 true positives plus 1 false negative); A1 for 97.7 %.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a positive screening result is confirmed with a second, more accurate test before a diagnosis is given.
parts.answer: A screening test can give false positives, which would cause unnecessary anxiety and procedures. A second test confirms whether the person really has the disorder.
parts.working: 1 mark: screening tests give false positives. 1 mark: confirmatory testing avoids unnecessary distress or treatment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between ex vivo and in vivo gene therapy, and give one advantage of ex vivo gene therapy.
parts.answer: Ex vivo: cells are removed from the patient, the gene is inserted in the laboratory, and the modified cells are returned to the patient. In vivo: the vector is delivered directly into the patient's body or tissue. An advantage of ex vivo therapy is that the modified cells can be checked and selected before they are returned, and the vector is not released directly into the patient.
parts.working: 1 mark: ex vivo – cells removed, modified outside the body and returned. 1 mark: in vivo – vector delivered directly into the body/tissue. 1 mark: any valid advantage (cells can be checked/selected before return; vector not released into the patient).

parts.label: a
parts.text: In early gene therapy trials for one form of SCID, a retrovirus vector was used. Some of the treated children later developed leukaemia. Suggest how the gene therapy could have caused leukaemia.
parts.answer: Retroviruses insert their DNA at random positions in host chromosomes; in some cells the vector inserted next to/within a gene controlling cell division (proto-oncogene); this activated the gene (or disrupted a tumour suppressor gene), so the cell divided uncontrollably
parts.working: 1 mark each: random insertion into host DNA; inserted near a proto-oncogene/tumour suppressor gene; abnormal activation/disruption → uncontrolled mitosis (cancer).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways in which the risks of this type of gene therapy could be reduced.
parts.answer: Use vectors that do not integrate (e.g. AAV or liposomes) or that integrate more safely (modified lentiviruses with self-inactivating promoters); use gene editing to correct the gene at its normal position; screen treated cells before returning them; monitor patients
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sensible suggestions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In one study, women with a harmful BRCA1 allele had a 72 % lifetime risk of breast cancer, compared with 12 % for women in the general population. Calculate how many times greater the risk was for women with the BRCA1 allele.
parts.answer: 6 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of offering screening for harmful BRCA1 alleles to women whose relatives have had breast cancer.
parts.answer: Advantages: women with the allele can have more frequent checks so cancer is found early; can choose preventive treatment (e.g. surgery); relatives can be tested. Disadvantages: a positive result does not mean cancer will develop (risk not certainty), causing anxiety; a negative result does not rule out cancer; possible discrimination (insurance/employment/marriage); results affect relatives who did not choose testing; costly
parts.working: Max 3 for one side; need both sides for 4 marks. 1 mark each for valid points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A test for a rare inherited condition has a sensitivity of 99 % (99 % of affected people test positive) and a specificity of 95 % (95 % of unaffected people test negative). The condition affects 1 in 500 people. Calculate the probability that a person who tests positive actually has the condition. Give your answer as a percentage to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Affected = 1/500 = 0.002. True positives = 0.99 × 0.002 = 0.00198. Unaffected = 0.998; false positives = 0.05 × 0.998 = 0.0499. Probability = 0.00198 ÷ (0.00198 + 0.0499) × 100 = 3.82 %. M1 for true positive fraction; M1 for false positive fraction; A1 for 3.82 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a positive result from this test should be followed by a second test.
parts.answer: Most positive results come from unaffected people (false positives), so only a small fraction of positive results are truly affected. A second test helps to confirm the diagnosis and avoid unnecessary treatment or distress.
parts.working: 1 mark: most positives are false positives because the condition is rare. 1 mark: a second test confirms the diagnosis.

practice.stem: A dominant disease is caused by a mutant allele that makes a protein with a harmful new function, which kills cells. Patients have one normal allele and one mutant allele. A scientist proposes treating patients by using a viral vector to add a normal copy of the gene to their cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why adding a normal copy of the gene might not cure this disease.
parts.answer: The patient still makes the mutant protein from the mutant allele, and that protein continues to kill cells. Adding a normal allele does not remove the harmful new function of the mutant protein. Treatment would need to silence or remove the mutant mRNA or edit the mutant allele, for example by RNA interference or CRISPR–Cas9 knockout.
parts.working: 1 mark: mutant protein is still produced. 1 mark: the harmful new function of the mutant protein continues. 1 mark: the mutant allele/mRNA must be silenced or edited (e.g. RNAi or CRISPR knockout).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether adults should be offered predictive genetic testing for a dominant disease with no cure, such as Huntington's disease.
parts.answer: Arguments for: adults can plan their lives, careers and family decisions; reduces uncertainty for people who would otherwise worry; allows reproductive choices such as prenatal testing; those who test negative are relieved; people have a right to know their own genetic information. Arguments against: no treatment exists, so a positive result causes distress and possible depression or suicidal thoughts; the test cannot say when symptoms will start; results affect relatives who may not want to know; risk of discrimination by employers or insurers; counselling and informed consent are essential. A reasoned conclusion should be given, such as offering the test only with counselling and a support plan.
parts.working: Up to 8 marks: 1–3 marks for relevant points on benefits (planning, relief, reproductive choice, right to know); 1–3 marks for points on harms (no cure, distress, discrimination, relatives, cannot predict onset); 1–2 marks for a reasoned judgement that refers to counselling, consent or a support system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the steps of one cycle of the polymerase chain reaction (PCR), giving the approximate temperature of each step.
parts.answer: Denaturation at about 95 °C: hydrogen bonds break and the DNA strands separate; annealing at about 55–65 °C: primers bind (base pair) to complementary sequences at each end of the target sequence; extension at about 72 °C: Taq polymerase adds free nucleotides to the primers to build new complementary strands
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: 95 °C (90–98 °C) denaturation; strands separate/H bonds broken; 50–65 °C annealing of primers to complementary sequences; 72 °C extension; Taq polymerase adds nucleotides from primer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Taq polymerase, from a bacterium living in hot springs, is used in PCR.
parts.answer: It is thermostable – it is not denatured at 95 °C; so it does not need to be replaced after every cycle, and its optimum temperature is about 72 °C
parts.working: 1 mark: not denatured at high (95 °C) temperature. 1 mark: does not need to be added each cycle / works at 72 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the PCR mixture must contain primers, and why the DNA polymerase used must be heat-stable.
parts.answer: Primers provide a short double-stranded starting point with a free 3′ end, so DNA polymerase can add nucleotides. Primers anneal to the sequences flanking the target region, defining the part that is copied. Heat-stable polymerase (e.g. Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus) is not denatured at the 95 °C denaturation step, so it can be used in every cycle without being added again.
parts.working: 1 mark: primers give the start point (free 3′ end) for DNA polymerase. 1 mark: primers bind to sequences either side of the target, so only that region is copied. 1 mark: Taq polymerase is not denatured at high temperature so works through repeated cycles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe one use of PCR in forensic science and one use of reverse transcriptase PCR (RT-PCR) in diagnosing a viral infection.
parts.answer: Forensic: PCR amplifies DNA from a very small sample, such as a single hair root or a trace of blood, so that a DNA profile can be produced. RT-PCR: viral RNA is converted into cDNA by reverse transcriptase, and the cDNA is amplified, so a very small amount of virus can be detected in a patient sample.
parts.working: 1 mark each: forensic – amplifies a tiny sample to give a DNA profile; RT-PCR – converts viral RNA to cDNA which is amplified and detected.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In Sanger (chain-termination) sequencing, dideoxynucleotides (ddNTPs) are added to the reaction. Explain why this stops the DNA chains at different positions.
parts.answer: A ddNTP lacks a 3′-OH group, so once it is incorporated into a growing strand no further nucleotide can be added. Because ddNTPs are incorporated at random positions, fragments of all different lengths are produced, each ending at a known base.
parts.working: 1 mark: ddNTP lacks a 3′-OH group, so chain elongation stops once it is added. 1 mark: random incorporation gives fragments of many lengths, each ending in a known base.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the gel must be immersed in a buffer solution during electrophoresis.
parts.answer: The buffer conducts electricity, completing the circuit between the electrodes so the current can flow through the gel. It also keeps the pH stable, so the DNA keeps its negative charge and migrates at a consistent rate.
parts.working: 1 mark: buffer conducts the current so the circuit is complete. 1 mark: buffer keeps pH constant so DNA stays charged and migrates consistently.

practice.stem: A forensic scientist has a sample containing 50 copies of a target DNA sequence from a hair root found at a crime scene in Islamabad.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of copies of the target DNA after 25 cycles, assuming the number doubles in every cycle. Give your answer in standard form to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Each cycle takes 3 minutes. Calculate the total time for 25 cycles.
parts.answer: 75 minutes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why two different primers are needed.
parts.answer: Each primer is complementary to the 3′ end of one of the two strands of the target sequence; DNA polymerase needs a primer to start adding nucleotides; using one for each strand means both strands are copied and only the region between them is amplified
parts.working: 1 mark: one primer per strand (strands have different sequences/are antiparallel). 1 mark: polymerase needs a primer to start / defines the region copied.

practice.stem:
A DNA profile was used in a family court case. Bands (fragment lengths in kilobases, kb) were:
child: 1.2, 2.5, 3.1, 4.0, 5.6
mother: 1.2, 3.1, 4.8, 6.0
man X: 2.5, 4.0, 5.6, 7.2
man Y: 2.5, 3.9, 6.0, 8.1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments.
parts.answer: DNA is negatively charged (phosphate groups), so in an electric field it moves towards the positive electrode (anode); the gel acts as a sieve/mesh; smaller fragments move more easily and travel further in a given time
parts.working: 1 mark each: negative charge on phosphates; moves to anode/positive terminal; smaller fragments move faster/further through gel pores.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which man could be the biological father. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Man X; the child's bands that are not from the mother (2.5, 4.0 and 5.6 kb) all match bands of man X, but man Y lacks the 4.0 and 5.6 kb bands
parts.working: 1 mark: man X. 1 mark: all non-maternal bands of the child are present in man X (man Y lacks two of them).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why DNA sequencing of a disease-causing gene can give more information than a DNA profile.
parts.answer: Sequencing shows the exact order of bases, so a specific mutation (e.g. a single base change) can be identified; a profile only shows fragment lengths
parts.working: Exact base sequence revealed / identifies specific mutations.

practice.stem: A PCR has an efficiency of 90 %. Each cycle therefore multiplies the number of copies by 1.9, not by 2. The reaction starts with 1000 copies of the target DNA.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of copies of DNA after 20 cycles. Give your answer in standard form to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Copies = 1000 × 1.9²⁰ = 3.759e+08. M1 for 1.9 raised to the power 20 (or 1000 × 1.9^20); A1 for 3.76 × 10⁸.

practice.stem: A Sanger sequencing gel was run with four lanes, one for each chain-terminating reaction (A, C, G and T). Bands were read from the bottom of the gel (shortest fragment) to the top (longest fragment). The lane containing each band, from bottom to top, was: T, A, G, G, C, A, T, T.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Read the sequence of the newly synthesised strand, written 5′ to 3′, from the bottom of the gel upwards.
parts.answer: 5′-TAGGCATT-3′
parts.working: 1 mark: reads from the bottom (shortest fragment) upwards, which gives the 5′ to 3′ direction. 1 mark: correct sequence TAGGCATT.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the sequence of the template strand, written 5′ to 3′.
parts.answer: 5′-AATGCCTA-3′
parts.working: The template is complementary and antiparallel to the new strand. Reverse complement of TAGGCATT is AATGCCTA. 1 mark: complementary bases correct; 1 mark: written antiparallel (5′ to 3′).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the minimum number of PCR cycles needed to produce at least 10⁹ copies from a single template molecule, assuming the number of copies doubles perfectly in every cycle.
parts.answer: 30 cycles
parts.working: 2ⁿ ≥ 10⁹. 2²⁹ = 536 870 912 (too few); 2³⁰ = 1 073 741 824 (enough). Minimum = 30 cycles. 1 mark for trying powers of 2; 1 mark for 30.

practice.stem: The coding sequence of the normal (wild-type) allele of a gene reads 5′-ATG GAG AAG-3′. A patient has the sequence 5′-ATG GTG AAG-3′ in the same region. The codons are read in the same frame.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of base change and the codon position it affects.
parts.answer: Substitution of A by T in the second base of codon 2.
parts.working: 1 mark: substitution (point mutation) of one base. 1 mark: second base of the second codon (GAG → GTG, A → T).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of this change on the amino acid, using the codons GAG (glutamic acid) and GTG (valine).
parts.answer: Glutamic acid is replaced by valine (a missense mutation).
parts.working: 1 mark: the amino acid changes from glutamic acid to valine, so the mutation is missense.

practice.stem:
A DNA ladder was run alongside a PCR product. Distances moved by the ladder bands from the well:
1000 bp: 12 mm | 500 bp: 24 mm | 250 bp: 36 mm | 125 bp: 48 mm
The PCR product moved 30 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the ladder to estimate the size of the unknown fragment. Give your answer to the nearest base pair.
parts.answer: 354 bp
parts.working: M1: each extra 12 mm halves the size (size = 1000 ÷ 2^((d − 12)/12)). M1: unknown at 30 mm is 18 mm beyond the 1000 bp band, so 1000 ÷ 2^1.5. A1: 1000 ÷ 2.828 = 353.6 → 354 bp. (Allow 350–360 bp read from a semi-log graph for 2 marks.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a ladder of fragments of known size is run in a separate lane of the same gel.
parts.answer: Distance moved depends on conditions (voltage, time, gel concentration), so the ladder must experience the same conditions; it gives a calibration to compare the unknown with
parts.working: 1 mark: same conditions/same gel and run time. 1 mark: allows size of unknown to be determined by comparison.

practice.stem: A PCR starts with 40 copies of the target DNA. After 28 cycles there are 1.2 × 10⁹ copies. Each cycle multiplies the number of copies by the same factor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the efficiency of the reaction as a percentage. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.working: 40 × f²⁸ = 1.2 × 10⁹, so f = (1.2 × 10⁹ ÷ 40)^(1/28) = 1.85 (3.0 × 10⁷ has a 28th root of 1.85). Efficiency = (f − 1) × 100 = 85 %. M1 for dividing 1.2 × 10⁹ by 40 and taking the 28th root; M1 for (f − 1) × 100; A1 for 85 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A negative control with no template DNA shows a band of the correct size after the reaction. Suggest one cause.
parts.answer: Contamination of the reagents or equipment with target DNA from an earlier PCR.
parts.working: 1 mark: contamination (e.g. carry-over of product or DNA into the reaction).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A forensic laboratory finds a DNA profile in a sample from a crime scene that matches a suspect. Explain how contamination of a PCR with DNA from an earlier sample could give a false positive result. Describe two precautions the laboratory should take.
parts.answer: PCR amplifies very small amounts of DNA, so any carry-over of DNA from an earlier sample, or from the analyst, is also amplified and detected. This can create a profile that appears to match the suspect. Precautions: use separate clean areas for setting up reactions; use disposable tips and sterile reagents; include negative controls with no template DNA; wear gloves and a lab coat; handle one sample at a time.
parts.working: 1 mark: PCR amplifies tiny amounts, so contaminant DNA is also copied. 1 mark: this gives a profile that matches the suspect falsely. 1 mark each for any two precautions (separate work areas; disposable tips; negative controls; clean reagents; gloves/lab coat).

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a Sanger reaction, the ratio of ddTTP to dTTP is 1 : 100. Explain how this ratio determines the range of fragment lengths produced, and why chain termination occurs at many different T positions along the strand.
parts.answer: Because ddTTP is present at a low concentration relative to dTTP, chain elongation usually continues past each T position. At any T position, there is a small chance that ddTTP is incorporated instead of dTTP, stopping that chain. Across millions of copies, termination occurs at many different T positions, so fragments of all lengths are made. The low ratio makes the fragments long enough to cover the whole sequence.
parts.working: 1 mark: ratio means most copies are extended past each T. 1 mark: at each T there is a random chance of incorporating ddTTP, which stops the chain. 1 mark: many copies with terminations at different positions give fragments of all lengths, covering the sequence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a microarray can be used to compare the genes being expressed in cancer cells and in normal cells from the same tissue.
parts.answer: mRNA is extracted from each type of cell; reverse transcriptase makes cDNA, labelled with a different fluorescent dye for each sample (e.g. red for cancer, green for normal); the cDNA is added to the microarray, where it hybridises (base pairs) with complementary DNA probes for thousands of genes; unbound cDNA is washed off; the array is scanned and the colour/intensity of each spot shows which genes are expressed in which sample
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: mRNA extracted; converted to cDNA; fluorescent labels (two colours); hybridisation to complementary probes on the chip; washing; scanning – colour/intensity shows expression level.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term genome, and give one way in which genome sequencing is used in medicine.
parts.answer: The genome is the complete set of genetic material (DNA) of an organism. Genome sequencing can be used to find the mutation responsible for an inherited disease, or to choose drugs that suit a patient's genotype (pharmacogenomics).
parts.working: 1 mark: complete set of DNA/genetic material of an organism. 1 mark: any valid medical use (e.g. identifying disease-causing mutations; pharmacogenomics; tracing a pathogen).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two genes from different species that share a common ancestor are described as homologous. Explain why comparing homologous sequences is useful in bioinformatics.
parts.answer: Similar sequences in homologous genes indicate common ancestry, so they can be used to build phylogenetic trees. The function of a gene of unknown function can be predicted from a well-studied homologous gene.
parts.working: 1 mark: similar sequences show common ancestry / relationship between species. 1 mark: function of an unknown gene can be predicted from a homologous gene of known function.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the term proteome.
parts.answer: The full set of proteins produced by a cell, tissue or organism at a given time.
parts.working: 1 mark: the complete set of proteins produced by a cell/organism (at a given time).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the proteome of a cell can differ from what its genome alone would predict.
parts.answer: Different genes are expressed in different cells and under different conditions, so different proteins are made. Alternative splicing of one gene can produce several different proteins, and proteins can be changed after translation (e.g. by addition of sugars or phosphate groups).
parts.working: 1 mark: not all genes are expressed in every cell, or expression changes with conditions. 1 mark: alternative splicing or post-translational modification produces more protein variants than genes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is attached to the surface of each spot on a DNA microarray, and how the labelled sample is detected.
parts.answer: Each spot contains many identical single-stranded DNA probes of a known sequence, one for each gene. Labelled cDNA from the sample hybridises (base pairs) with the complementary probes; the intensity of the fluorescent label in each spot shows how much of that gene is expressed.
parts.working: 1 mark: spots contain single-stranded DNA probes of known sequence. 1 mark: labelled (fluorescent) cDNA binds by complementary base pairing and spot brightness is measured.

practice.stem:
Researchers compared gene expression in leaves of drought-stressed and well-watered wheat plants using a microarray. cDNA from drought-stressed plants was labelled with a red dye and cDNA from watered plants with a green dye. Mean intensities (arbitrary units):
gene P: red 1200, green 300
gene Q: red 400, green 400
gene R: red 150, green 600

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of red to green intensity for each gene.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using your ratios, describe the expression of each gene in the drought-stressed plants compared with the watered plants.
parts.answer: P is expressed four times more in drought-stressed plants (switched on/up-regulated); Q is unchanged; R is expressed four times less (down-regulated)
parts.working: 1 mark: P up-regulated, R down-regulated. 1 mark: Q unchanged, with use of the factor of four.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the experiment should be repeated with samples from several plants.
parts.answer: Individual plants vary; repeats show whether the differences are consistent/reliable (and allow statistical testing)
parts.working: Natural variation between plants; check reliability.

practice.stem: A DNA microarray with 22 000 spots was used to compare gene expression in cancer cells and normal cells from the same tissue. 1430 spots showed higher expression in the cancer cells and 610 spots showed lower expression.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of spots that showed a change in expression. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the microarray result alone does not show which change causes the cancer.
parts.answer: Changes in expression may be a result of the cancer rather than its cause, or may be unrelated to the disease. Further experiments are needed to show which genes are causally involved.
parts.working: 1 mark: differences may be a consequence of the disease, not its cause. 1 mark: correlation does not prove causation, further experiments are needed.

practice.stem: The same 80-amino-acid region of the haemoglobin beta-chain was aligned for two mammal species. 71 of the 80 positions are identical in both sequences.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage identity of the two sequences. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: 71 ÷ 80 × 100 = 88.75 %. M1 for dividing identical positions by the total length; A1 for 88.8 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the percentage identity is a useful measure of how closely two species are related.
parts.answer: A higher percentage identity suggests the two sequences have been conserved since the species shared a common ancestor, so the species are more closely related.
parts.working: 1 mark: high identity means sequences are similar, so the species share a recent common ancestor. 1 mark: identity reflects the number of changes accumulated since divergence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a two-colour microarray experiment is repeated with the dyes swapped (the cancer cells labelled green and the normal cells labelled red).
parts.answer: Some dyes are incorporated or detected more efficiently than others, which could make a gene appear over-expressed simply because of the dye. Swapping the dyes shows whether the difference follows the sample or the dye. If the same gene shows the same change in both experiments, the difference in expression is real.
parts.working: 1 mark: dyes can have different labelling or detection efficiency (dye bias). 1 mark: swapping shows whether the result follows the dye or the sample. 1 mark: consistent results in both experiments confirm a real change in expression.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a gene expression profile from a microarray can be used to classify a cancer into subtypes, and how this can help a doctor choose treatment.
parts.answer: Tumours of the same subtype show similar patterns of expressed genes, so comparing a patient's profile with known profiles can place the tumour into a subtype. Each subtype may respond differently to particular drugs, so the doctor can choose the treatment most likely to work for that subtype.
parts.working: 1 mark: profiles of tumours show characteristic patterns of gene expression. 1 mark: a patient's profile is compared with known subtype profiles. 1 mark: subtype predicts response to a particular treatment, so treatment can be targeted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A short gene sequence of 60 bases from a newly discovered bacterium was compared with the matching sequence of a known species using a database search. The sequences differed at 9 positions. Calculate the percentage identity of the two sequences.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by bioinformatics and outline how databases of DNA and protein sequences can be used to identify an unknown pathogen.
parts.answer: Bioinformatics is the collection, storage and analysis of biological data (e.g. sequences) using computers; the sequence of the unknown organism is entered into a search program; it is compared/aligned with sequences in the database; the most similar sequences suggest the identity or closest relatives of the pathogen
parts.working: 1 mark: definition (computer storage/analysis of biological information). 1 mark: unknown sequence compared/aligned with database sequences. 1 mark: closest match identifies organism/relationship.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why comparing a longer sequence would give a more reliable result.
parts.answer: A short sequence may match several species by chance / gives fewer differences to compare; longer sequences give more data so the comparison is more accurate
parts.working: More bases compared, chance matches less important.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two BLAST alignments are reported for an unknown bacterial gene. Alignment X covers 40 bases with 99 % identity. Alignment Y covers 400 bases with 90 % identity. Explain which alignment gives stronger evidence of a real evolutionary relationship with the known gene.
parts.answer: Alignment Y gives stronger evidence. A short match of 40 bases could arise by chance, and a short region may not reflect the whole gene. A long alignment with 90 % identity is much less likely to occur by chance, so it indicates a genuine shared ancestry, even though its identity is lower.
parts.working: 1 mark: a short alignment can occur by chance (low statistical significance). 1 mark: a longer alignment covers more of the gene so is more informative. 1 mark: the high-identity long alignment is much less likely to occur by chance, giving stronger evidence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A study compares the expression of 20 000 genes in two groups of patients using t-tests, with a significance level of p < 0.05 for each gene. Calculate the number of genes that would be expected to show a significant difference by chance alone.
parts.answer: 1000 genes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of genes expected to show a significant difference by chance if the threshold were p < 0.01 instead of p < 0.05.
parts.answer: 200 genes

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the limitations of using microarray data alone to identify the gene responsible for an inherited disease.
parts.answer: Microarrays measure expression of genes already on the chip, so a mutated gene may not be detected if its level of expression does not change. Expression levels may change because of the disease rather than causing it. Thousands of genes are tested, so some results are false positives and need statistical correction. Probes can cross-hybridise with similar sequences, giving false signals. Mutations that change the protein but not the amount of mRNA are missed. Follow-up work such as sequencing, knockout or family studies is needed to confirm the gene.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks: 1–2 marks for a point about expression level not identifying mutations; 1–2 marks for point about cause versus consequence; 1–2 marks for multiple-testing or cross-hybridisation; 1 mark for a suggested follow-up (sequencing, family study, functional test).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two causes of background noise (false signal) in microarray results, and how each can be reduced.
parts.answer: Cross-hybridisation: a labelled sample binds weakly to probes with a similar but not identical sequence; reduce by designing specific probes and using stringent washing and hybridisation conditions. Non-specific binding of labelled DNA or dye to the glass surface; reduce by blocking the surface and washing thoroughly. Also accept unequal labelling or dust/scratches on the slide, reduced by careful handling and background subtraction in the scanner software.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two causes (cross-hybridisation; non-specific binding of dye/sample; uneven labelling; slide dust or scratches); 1 mark each for a matching reduction (specific probes and stringent conditions; blocking and washing; background subtraction).

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: A researcher weighed six seeds from a GM maize line, in grams: 0.42, 0.45, 0.39, 0.51, 0.44, 0.47.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean mass of the seeds. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the sample standard deviation of the masses. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: Use n − 1 = 5 in the denominator: sum of squared deviations ÷ 5, then square root gives 0.04 g. M1 for squared deviations summed correctly; A1 for 0.04 g.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: The leaf lengths of 36 randomly chosen seedlings of one variety were measured. The standard deviation of the lengths was 5.8 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard error of the mean. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: SE = SD ÷ √n = 5.8 ÷ √36 = 5.8 ÷ 6 = 0.967 mm, so 0.97 mm. 1 mark for dividing by √36; 1 mark for the answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the standard error is smaller than the standard deviation.
parts.answer: The standard error divides the standard deviation by the square root of the sample size, so it estimates how precisely the mean is known rather than how spread out the individual values are.
parts.working: 1 mark: SE = SD ÷ √n, so it is reduced by the square root of n, and it describes the precision of the mean rather than the spread of the data.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: The t-test comparing the two groups gave p = 0.03. State what this value means.
parts.answer: If there were no real difference between the groups, a difference at least as large as the one observed would occur by chance in about 3 % of repeated experiments. Because p is below 0.05, the difference is treated as statistically significant.
parts.working: 1 mark: the probability of a result at least this extreme if the null hypothesis is true is 0.03. 1 mark: 0.03 is less than 0.05, so the result is significant and the null hypothesis is rejected.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a suitable null hypothesis for a Spearman rank correlation test of the relationship between light intensity and the number of stomata per mm² on leaves of the same plant species.
parts.answer: There is no correlation between light intensity and the number of stomata per mm² on the leaves of this species.
parts.working: 1 mark: no correlation (rho = 0) between light intensity and stomatal density in the population.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A chi-squared test is used to compare the observed counts of four phenotypes with those expected from a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio. State the number of degrees of freedom and explain how it is found.
parts.answer: 3 degrees of freedom. The number of categories (4) minus 1 gives 3 when the expected values are fixed by the ratio.
parts.working: 1 mark: df = 3. 1 mark: df = number of categories − 1 (4 − 1 = 3).

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: Soil pH and the number of earthworms were recorded in eight quadrats of a field. pH values: 6.1, 5.4, 7.0, 6.6, 5.9, 7.4, 6.3, 5.1. Earthworm counts respectively: 12, 9, 15, 11, 14, 18, 10, 7. There are no tied values.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (rho). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the correlation and state whether it supports a positive or a negative relationship between soil pH and the number of earthworms.
parts.answer: Strong positive correlation (rho = 0.79): as soil pH increases, the number of earthworms tends to increase.
parts.working: 1 mark: positive correlation. 1 mark: strength stated (strong because rho close to +1) with the pattern in the data.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: A dihybrid cross between two pea plants was predicted to give offspring in a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio. Of 240 offspring, the observed counts were: 128 (type A), 46 (type B), 40 (type C), 26 (type D). The expected counts are based on the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the chi-squared value for these data. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: Expected: 135, 45, 45, 15. χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E = 9.01. M1 for expected values; M1 for correct squared differences; A1 for 9.01.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the conclusion at the 0.05 level, using a critical value of 7.81 for 3 degrees of freedom, and explain what it means for the genetic model.
parts.answer: 9.01 is greater than 7.81, so the null hypothesis is rejected: the observed ratio does not fit a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio, so the genes are not assorting independently in this cross.
parts.working: 1 mark: χ² greater than the critical value, so reject the null hypothesis. 1 mark: the phenotype ratio is not 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, so the genes are probably not independent (linked or affected by another factor).

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: The chlorophyll index was measured on seven wheat plants before and after a 14-day treatment with a foliar nutrient spray. Before: 31, 28, 35, 30, 33, 27, 29. After: 36, 30, 38, 33, 36, 30, 33. Each plant was measured before and after, so the difference (after − before) is used.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the t value for the paired t-test. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: Mean difference = 3.286; sample SD of differences = 0.951; SE = 0.951 ÷ √7 = 0.360; t = 3.286 ÷ 0.360 = 9.14. M1 for differences; M1 for SD and SE; A1 for 9.14.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The critical value of t for 6 degrees of freedom at p = 0.05 (two-tailed) is 2.45. State the conclusion.
parts.answer: 9.14 is greater than 2.45, so the increase in chlorophyll index is significant (the null hypothesis of no change is rejected).
parts.working: 1 mark: t greater than critical value, so reject the null hypothesis of no change.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: The length of the fruiting body of 12 mushrooms collected from one woodland was measured. The mean length was 34.6 mm and the standard deviation was 5.1 mm. Use t = 2.20 for 11 degrees of freedom at the 95 % level.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the 95 % confidence interval for the mean. Give both limits to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: SE = 5.1 ÷ √12 = 1.472; half-width = 2.20 × 1.472 = 3.24; limits 31.36 and 37.84, so 31.4 to 37.8. M1 for SE; M1 for multiplying by t; A1 for both limits.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the interval tells us about the population mean.
parts.answer: The interval is the range within which the true population mean is likely to lie. If the same sampling were repeated many times, about 95 % of such intervals would contain the true mean.
parts.working: 1 mark: the population mean is likely within this range. 1 mark: 95 % of intervals from repeated samples would contain the true mean (not a 95 % chance for this one interval).

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: A student scored 15 leaves of rice for yellowing on an ordinal scale from 1 (green) to 5 (completely yellow), and measured the time since the last nitrogen fertiliser in days. The student wants to test whether the score of yellowing is related to the time since fertiliser.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a Spearman rank correlation is used rather than a Pearson correlation for these data.
parts.answer: The scores are ordinal (ranked by colour), not measured on a continuous scale with equal intervals, and the relationship may not be linear. Spearman's test uses ranks, so it does not assume a normal distribution or equal intervals, and is suitable for ordinal data.
parts.working: 1 mark: data are ordinal / ranked rather than interval. 1 mark: Pearson assumes a linear relationship and normally distributed continuous data. 1 mark: Spearman uses ranks so it suits ordinal data and non-linear monotonic relationships.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
An agricultural researcher in Punjab compared seed-cotton yield per plant (g) for Bt cotton and non-Bt cotton grown in the same field.
Bt cotton: n = 10, mean = 92.4 g, standard deviation = 8.1 g
non-Bt cotton: n = 10, mean = 81.7 g, standard deviation = 9.3 g

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a null hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the mean yield per plant of Bt cotton and non-Bt cotton
parts.working: Must refer to no (significant) difference in mean yield between the two varieties.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of t, using t = (x̄₁ − x̄₂) ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of t at p = 0.05 for 18 degrees of freedom is 2.10. Explain what your result shows.
parts.answer: 2.74 is greater than 2.10, so the null hypothesis is rejected; there is a significant difference in mean yield (the difference is unlikely to be due to chance, p < 0.05)
parts.working: 1 mark: compares calculated t with critical value (greater). 1 mark: reject null hypothesis / difference is significant (not due to chance).

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: In a survey of a plant population, a table of observed and expected counts was prepared for four habitat types and three flower colours. Most cells had expected values of about 10 to 30, but one cell had an expected value of 3.2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The expected count in one cell of a chi-squared table is 3.2. Explain why this may make the test unreliable, and state one way the student could deal with it.
parts.answer: The chi-squared approximation is unreliable when expected counts are small (usually below 5). The calculated value may then be too large or inaccurate. The student could combine categories with small expected values, so that every expected count is 5 or more, or increase the sample size.
parts.working: 1 mark: small expected values make the chi-squared approximation unreliable. 1 mark: rule of thumb expected count of at least 5 (or similar). 1 mark: combine categories or increase the sample size.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: The standard deviation of the fungal colony diameter in a set of replicate plates was 4.2 mm. A student could use either 10 or 40 plates.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard error of the mean for each sample. Then explain by how much the SE changes when the sample size increases from 10 to 40 with the same standard deviation.
parts.answer: SE for n = 10: 4.2 ÷ √10 = 1.33; SE for n = 40: 4.2 ÷ √40 = 0.66. The SE halves (√(40 ÷ 10) = 2), because SE is inversely proportional to the square root of n.
parts.working: 1 mark: SE(10) = 1.33 (4.2 ÷ √10). 1 mark: SE(40) = 0.66 (4.2 ÷ √40). 1 mark: SE falls by a factor of √4 = 2, so it halves; SE ∝ 1 ÷ √n.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: The chi-squared test gave a value of 12.4 with 4 degrees of freedom. The critical value at p = 0.05 is 9.49. A student says that the two genes must be linked. Evaluate this claim.
