parts.answer: The result is significant (12.4 > 9.49), so the observed counts differ from the expected ones and the null hypothesis of independent assortment is rejected. However, a significant chi-squared test shows only that the expected pattern does not fit; it does not show linkage. The student should check the data for errors, consider other causes such as selection or sampling bias, and test for linkage with a further cross.
parts.working: 1 mark: χ² is greater than the critical value, so the null hypothesis is rejected. 1 mark: a significant result does not prove linkage; other causes are possible. 1 mark: a justified suggestion such as a follow-up cross or checking sampling.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: Two strains of tomato were grown in the same greenhouse and the fruit mass was recorded. Strain A had a 95 % confidence interval for the mean of 12.1 g to 15.3 g. Strain B had a 95 % confidence interval of 14.0 g to 18.6 g. The two intervals overlap between 14.0 g and 15.3 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why overlapping 95 % confidence intervals do not by themselves prove that there is no significant difference between the two groups, and name a suitable test to compare the groups.
parts.answer: Two intervals can overlap while the difference between the means is still statistically significant, because the test looks at the difference between the means relative to their standard errors, not at whether the intervals overlap. The appropriate test is an unpaired t-test (for normally distributed data).
parts.working: 1 mark: overlap of intervals is not the test criterion; the difference of means relative to the SEs is. 1 mark: the test statistic depends on the difference and the standard errors, so a significant difference can still arise. 1 mark: an appropriate test named (unpaired t-test).

practice.stem: A fluorescence micrograph of a plant cell nucleus shows the nucleus 15 mm wide on the printed image. The magnification of the image is ×1500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual width of the nucleus in micrometres (µm).
parts.answer: 10 µm
parts.working: Actual size = image size ÷ magnification = 15 mm ÷ 1500 = 0.01 mm = 10 µm. M1 for dividing by the magnification; A1 for 10 µm (accept unit conversion to µm).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the magnification that would make the same nucleus appear 30 mm wide.
parts.working: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size = 30 mm ÷ 0.01 mm = 3000. 1 mark.

practice.stem: The band intensity of a PCR product on a gel was measured by a scanner. Intensity was 240 arbitrary units after 20 cycles and 618 arbitrary units after 30 cycles, from the same starting sample.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in band intensity between the two samples.

practice.stem: A student measured the absorbance at 595 nm of four replicate samples of a protein assay: 4.2, 4.5, 9.8 and 4.3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean absorbance of the three replicates that are not anomalous. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: Mean of 4.2, 4.5 and 4.3 = 13.0 ÷ 3 = 4.33. M1 for summing the three values; A1 for 4.33.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the anomalous value should be excluded from the mean, and what should be recorded in the report.
parts.answer: The value 9.8 is far above the other three, so it is likely to be an error such as a contaminated cuvette, a bubble or a misread value. It should be excluded only with a stated reason, and the excluded value and reason should be recorded in the report.
parts.working: 1 mark: the value is far from the other replicates and is likely an error. 1 mark: the exclusion and reason are recorded, so the decision is transparent.

practice.stem: A stock solution of a DNA ladder has a concentration of 0.8 mg/ml. A student makes three serial dilutions, each by taking 1 volume of solution and adding 3 volumes of water (1 in 4).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of the diluted stock in µg/ml after three serial dilutions, each 1 in 4. Give your answer in µg/ml.
parts.answer: 12.5 µg/ml
parts.working: Dilution factor = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64. 0.8 mg/ml = 800 µg/ml; 800 ÷ 64 = 12.5 µg/ml. M1 for the dilution factor 64; A1 for 12.5 µg/ml.

practice.stem: An electron micrograph shows a bacterium of length 2.5 µm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert the length of the cell to nanometres (nm) and to millimetres (mm).
parts.answer: 2500 nm and 0.0025 mm
parts.working: 1 µm = 1000 nm, so 2.5 µm = 2500 nm. 1 mm = 1000 µm, so 2.5 µm = 0.0025 mm. 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A student transformed E. coli with 0.05 µg of plasmid carrying a GFP gene and an ampicillin-resistance gene. After heat shock, the bacteria were mixed with nutrient broth to a total volume of 1000 µl. 100 µl of this mixture was spread on an agar plate containing ampicillin, and 380 glowing colonies grew.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total number of transformed cells produced in the 1000 µl mixture.
parts.working: 100 µl gave 380 colonies, so 1000 µl contains 380 × 10 = 3800.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Transformation efficiency is the number of transformed cells per µg of plasmid DNA. Calculate the transformation efficiency. Give your answer in standard form.
parts.answer: 7.6 × 10⁴ transformants per µg

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why only 100 µl of the mixture, rather than all of it, was spread on the plate.
parts.answer: So that colonies are separate/countable (not overlapping)
parts.working: Too many colonies would merge and could not be counted.

practice.stem: Onion root tip cells were squashed and stained. In total 1380 cells were counted across the fields of view and 97 of them were in mitosis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mitotic index (percentage of cells in mitosis). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the cells were counted in several different fields of view rather than in one field.
parts.answer: Counting several fields gives a larger, more representative sample of cells and reduces the effect of uneven distribution across the slide.
parts.working: 1 mark: a larger, more representative sample reduces error and bias.

practice.stem: A DNA fragment moved 18.5 mm from the well during electrophoresis, which ran for 35 minutes at a constant voltage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of movement of the band in mm per minute. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 0.53 mm/min
parts.working: 18.5 ÷ 35 = 0.5286 mm/min = 0.53 mm/min. M1 for distance ÷ time; A1 for 0.53 mm/min.

practice.stem: A culture of a bacterium had 500 cells per ml at the start. After 150 minutes at 25 °C, the count was 3.2 × 10⁶ cells per ml. Assume the population doubled at a constant rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of doublings that occurred. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean doubling time in minutes. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: Time per doubling = 150 ÷ 12.64 = 11.86 min. M1 for dividing time by the number of doublings; A1 for 11.86 min.

practice.stem: Lichen cover on a limestone wall was estimated using 20 quadrats, each 0.5 m × 0.5 m. The total area of lichen found within all the quadrats was 1.45 m².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage cover of lichen across the sampled area. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

practice.stem: Three colonies of a fungus grew on the same agar plate. Their radii after 7 days were 2.1 mm, 2.4 mm and 2.0 mm. Area of a circle = πr².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean area of the colonies. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: Areas = πr²: 13.85, 18.10, 12.57 mm². Mean = 14.84 mm². M1 for calculating each area; A1 for the mean.

practice.stem: A student measured the absorbance of a DNA extract at 260 nm. The sample was diluted 1 in 40 before measurement, and the absorbance of the diluted sample was 0.420.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of the DNA in the original sample, in µg/ml. Use 1 absorbance unit at 260 nm = 50 µg/ml of double-stranded DNA.
parts.answer: 840 µg/ml
parts.working: Concentration in the diluted tube = 0.420 × 50 = 21.0 µg/ml; multiply by dilution factor 40: 21.0 × 40 = 840 µg/ml. M1 for the 50 µg/ml conversion; A1 for 840 µg/ml.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The A260/A280 ratio of the sample was 1.92. State what this suggests about the purity of the DNA.
parts.answer: The ratio is close to 1.8 for pure DNA, so the sample is fairly pure with little protein contamination.
parts.working: 1 mark: ratio near 1.8 indicates pure DNA with little protein contamination.

practice.stem: A stock solution of a buffer has a concentration of 100 mM. A student needs 25 ml of a 5 mM working solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of the 100 mM stock needed to make 25 ml of a 5 mM solution.
parts.working: Using C₁V₁ = C₂V₂: V₁ = 5 × 25 ÷ 100 = 1.25 ml. 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of water that must be added to make up the 25 ml.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the student would make the solution accurately, using a pipette.
parts.answer: Use a calibrated micropipette or graduated pipette to transfer 1.25 ml of the stock into a 25 ml volumetric flask, then add water up to the mark and mix.
parts.working: 1 mark: calibrated pipette used to measure 1.25 ml of stock. 1 mark: transferred into a volumetric flask, made up to 25 ml with water and mixed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of plasmid in the 0.5 µg sample. Assume an average molecular mass of 650 g/mol for each base pair, and that the plasmid is 4000 base pairs long.
parts.working: Molar mass = 4000 × 650 = 2.6 × 10⁶ g/mol; moles = 0.5 × 10⁻⁶ g ÷ 2.6 × 10⁶ g/mol = 1.92 × 10⁻¹³ mol. M1 for molar mass; A1 for the moles.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence calculate the number of plasmid molecules in the sample. Give your answer in standard form to 3 significant figures. (Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
parts.working: 1.92 × 10⁻¹³ × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.16 × 10¹¹. M1 for multiplying by the Avogadro constant; A1 for 1.16 × 10¹¹.

practice.stem: A suspension of yeast cells was counted two ways. A haemocytometer gave 4.8 × 10⁶ cells per ml. A spectrophotometer calibrated with a known standard gave 5.6 × 10⁶ cells per ml. Take the spectrophotometer result as the accepted value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage error of the haemocytometer count compared with the spectrophotometer result. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the haemocytometer count may be lower than the spectrophotometer result, and one way to reduce this error.
parts.answer: Dead cells or clumps of cells are counted by the spectrophotometer but may be missed or counted as one cell by the haemocytometer; use a stain to count only live cells and mix the sample thoroughly before counting.
parts.working: 1 mark: reason (e.g. clumping, uneven mixing, miscount of squares). 1 mark: method to reduce it (mix well, count more squares, use replicates, a stain).

practice.stem: E. coli cells were treated with a plasmid and given a heat shock at 42 °C for different times. The number of colonies that grew on ampicillin plates after each treatment (one plate per time) was: 0 s: 4; 15 s: 38; 30 s: 105; 45 s: 97; 60 s: 41.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the pattern shown by the results.
parts.answer: The number of colonies rises from 4 at 0 s to a peak of 105 at 30 s, then falls to 41 at 60 s. The numbers at 45 s (97) are close to the peak, so the response is greatest between 30 and 45 s.
parts.working: 1 mark: number of colonies increases with heat shock time up to a peak. 1 mark: decreases after the peak (30 s to 60 s), with the highest values between 30 and 45 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the conclusion the student can draw about the best heat shock time.
parts.answer: The best heat shock time is about 30 s, because this gives the most transformed colonies.
parts.working: 1 mark: 30 s (or 30–45 s) as the best time, supported by the number of colonies.

practice.stem: A student counted colonies on four replicate agar plates after plating the same bacterial culture: 38, 41, 37 and 112 colonies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and state what the student should do with it.
parts.answer: The fourth plate (112 colonies) is anomalous, as it is far from the other three (37 to 41). The student should check the plate for contamination or a counting or plating error. The result can be excluded only with a stated reason, and it should be repeated.
parts.working: 1 mark: 112 is the anomalous value because it is far from the other replicates. 1 mark: check the cause (e.g. contamination, plating error) and repeat or justify exclusion; do not silently discard it.

practice.stem: Newly hatched caterpillars of a moth pest were fed for 7 days on either a standard artificial diet (control) or a diet containing purified Bt toxin. Each group had 25 caterpillars. Survival after 7 days was 92 % for the control group and 18 % for the Bt diet group.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the conclusion the data support.
parts.answer: The Bt diet reduced caterpillar survival compared with the control diet.
parts.working: 1 mark: Bt diet reduces survival (lower survival with Bt than without).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a control group fed on the standard diet is needed.
parts.answer: The control group shows the survival expected without the Bt toxin, so any difference in survival can be attributed to the Bt diet. Without it, the low survival could be due to other factors such as the diet itself or the conditions in the container.
parts.working: 1 mark: provides a baseline to compare with the Bt treatment. 1 mark: allows the effect of Bt to be separated from other factors (diet, conditions).

practice.stem: Expression ratios (tumour tissue ÷ normal tissue) for four genes measured on a microarray: gene A 8.1, gene B 1.0, gene C 0.5, gene D 0.98. A ratio of 1.0 means no change in expression.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Gene D has a ratio of 0.98. Explain why this should not be reported as a real decrease in expression, and say what extra information is needed before a change is reported.
parts.answer: A ratio of 0.98 is a difference of only 2 %, which is within the random variation expected in microarray measurements, so it is not evidence of a real change. Replicate arrays and a statistical test across several samples are needed before a change is reported.
parts.working: 1 mark: a 2 % difference is within normal experimental (random) variation. 1 mark: replicate arrays and a statistical test are needed to judge significance.

practice.stem: Fold changes (expression in the test sample ÷ expression in the control) for five genes on a microarray: gene P 2.0, gene Q 0.5, gene R 16.0, gene S 1.1, gene T 0.06.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the gene with the largest up-regulation and the gene with the largest down-regulation.
parts.answer: Gene R has the largest up-regulation (16-fold). Gene T has the largest down-regulation (0.06, about 17 times lower than normal).
parts.working: 1 mark: gene R (16-fold increase). 1 mark: gene T (0.06, the smallest ratio, a 16.7-fold decrease).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a fold change of 0.5 (down-regulated) should be considered as important as a fold change of 2.0 (up-regulated).
parts.answer: On a log scale, a 2-fold increase (log₂ = +1) and a 2-fold decrease (log₂ = −1) are equal in size. Decreases below 1 are therefore as important as increases above 1 by the same factor.
parts.working: 1 mark: 0.5 is a 2-fold decrease and 2.0 is a 2-fold increase; they are equal changes on a log scale.

practice.stem:
Three lines of GM rice (A, B and C) carrying genes for β-carotene synthesis were grown together with non-GM rice. β-carotene content of the grain was measured in three samples from each line (µg per g of grain):
non-GM: 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 (mean 0.0)
line A: 1.4, 1.9, 1.5 (mean 1.6)
line B: 6.2, 7.5, 6.8 (mean 6.8)
line C: 21.0, 28.5, 36.0 (mean 28.5)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student concludes that line C is the best line to grow for vitamin A. Using the data, discuss the extent to which this conclusion is supported.
parts.answer: Support: line C has the highest mean β-carotene (28.5 µg/g), about four times line B; its range does not overlap with A or B. Against: line C has the largest variation (range 21.0–36.0), so results are less consistent; only three samples per line; plants grown in one place/season only; β-carotene content is not the same as vitamin A delivered (losses in storage/cooking, absorption); yield and other traits not measured; no statistical test done
parts.working: 1 mark: highest mean quoted. 1 mark: no overlap with other lines / clear difference. Max 2 limitations from: large spread in C; small sample (3); one site/season; β-carotene may be lost in storage/cooking; yield/taste not considered; no statistical test.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the non-GM rice was included.
parts.answer: As a control to show that β-carotene is produced because of the inserted genes (non-GM rice has none)
parts.working: Control/comparison showing the effect is due to the genetic modification.

practice.stem: Strain P and strain Q of rice were grown on six plots each. Yields (tonnes per hectare): strain P mean 8.2, standard deviation 1.1; strain Q mean 9.0, standard deviation 2.6. A student claims that strain Q gives a higher yield than strain P.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the data, discuss the extent to which the claim that strain Q gives a higher yield than strain P is supported.
parts.answer: The mean for Q (9.0 t/ha) is higher than for P (8.2 t/ha), so the claim has some support. However, the standard deviation of Q (2.6) is much larger than that of P (1.1), and the ranges overlap widely. With only six plots per strain, the difference may be due to chance. A statistical test (such as an unpaired t-test) is needed before the claim can be accepted, and Q is less consistent than P.
parts.working: 1 mark: means show Q higher. 1 mark: large SD and overlap mean the difference may not be significant; small sample. 1 mark: a suitable test is needed and Q is less consistent, so the claim is only partly supported.

practice.stem: A student collected data from 10 cotton farms in different districts. A Spearman rank correlation between mean hours of sunshine per day and yield per hectare gave rho = 0.82. The student concludes that sunshine causes the higher yield.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the student's conclusion that sunlight causes the higher yield.
parts.answer: A Spearman correlation shows a strong positive association, but it does not prove causation. Other factors that vary with sunlight (such as rainfall, soil type, temperature or the sites chosen) could be responsible. Only a controlled experiment that changes sunlight alone would show a causal link.
parts.working: 1 mark: correlation does not prove causation (confounding variables). 1 mark: a controlled experiment is needed to test the causal relationship.

practice.stem: A student measured the intensity of a PCR band after 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30 cycles. The intensity rose from 40 units at 10 cycles to 2900 units at 30 cycles, a roughly exponential increase within this range.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The student predicts that 40 PCR cycles would give a band intensity of about 4000 units. Evaluate this prediction.
parts.answer: The prediction is not reliable. PCR plateaus as the reagents are used up and the enzyme loses activity, so the band intensity stops increasing exponentially. Extrapolating the data beyond the range measured (up to 30 cycles) assumes the reaction keeps the same efficiency, which is unlikely.
parts.working: 1 mark: the reaction plateaus as reagents are used up (no longer exponential). 1 mark: extrapolating beyond the data assumes unchanged efficiency, which is unreliable.

practice.stem: Gibberellin was applied to rice seeds at four concentrations and the percentage germination was measured. Mean germination (± standard error) was: 0 µM: 22 % (± 3); 5 µM: 48 % (± 4); 10 µM: 71 % (± 3); 20 µM: 73 % (± 6).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the concentration that gives the best germination and explain whether a higher concentration is justified, referring to the standard errors.
parts.answer: About 10 µM. Germination at 20 µM (73 %) is not clearly higher than at 10 µM (71 %) because the means differ by only 2 % and the error bars (±6 and ±3) overlap, so the extra gibberellin does not give a significant improvement. The higher concentration would cost more without a clear benefit.
parts.working: 1 mark: 10 µM identified as best (or plateau from 10 µM). 1 mark: the difference between 10 and 20 µM is small. 1 mark: the standard errors overlap, so there is no significant improvement at 20 µM.

practice.stem: DNA was extracted from five samples and used in PCR to amplify a target gene, using a primer pair known to work. Lane 1 (sample A) showed a band of the correct size. Lanes 2 and 5 (samples B and E) showed no bands. Lanes 3 and 4 (samples C and D) showed a band of the correct size.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the conclusion about whether the sample contains the gene.
parts.answer: Samples B and E (lanes 2 and 5) do not appear to contain the target gene, since no band is seen in those lanes.
parts.working: 1 mark: no target gene in those samples (or PCR failed; check with a control).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what additional lane or check is needed before this conclusion can be accepted.
parts.answer: A positive control lane containing DNA known to have the gene, which shows that the PCR worked. Without it, a missing band could be due to a failed reaction (for example, a reagent or enzyme problem) rather than an absence of the gene.
parts.working: 1 mark: positive control (known DNA with the gene) to show the PCR works. 1 mark: a failed PCR can cause a missing band, so the absence cannot be concluded without it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The mRNA level of a gene is six times higher in the tumour cells, but the amount of protein is unchanged. Discuss what this result means for the hypothesis that increased expression of this gene causes the tumour to grow.
parts.answer: The higher mRNA does not lead to more protein, so the protein may not be the cause of growth. Translation may be blocked or the protein may be degraded faster, so the hypothesis is weakened. The result suggests that regulation after transcription is important, and protein levels should be measured directly before a causal role is accepted.
parts.working: 1 mark: more mRNA does not mean more protein (post-transcriptional control). 1 mark: the link between this gene and tumour growth is weakened. 1 mark: suggests further study of translation or protein levels before a conclusion is drawn.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Samples 1, 2 and 3 were digested with the same restriction enzyme and run on a gel. Sample 1 showed one band at 850 bp. Sample 2 showed two bands at 500 bp and 350 bp. Sample 3 showed three bands at 850 bp, 500 bp and 350 bp. Explain what these results show about the genotypes of the three samples.
parts.answer: The wild-type allele has a restriction site that cuts a 850 bp fragment into 500 bp and 350 bp. The mutant allele has lost the site and stays at 850 bp. Sample 1 has only uncut DNA, so it is homozygous mutant. Sample 2 has only the cut fragments, so it is homozygous wild-type. Sample 3 shows both, so it is heterozygous.
parts.working: 1 mark: the mutant allele lacks the site (uncut 850 bp fragment) and the wild-type allele is cut into 500 + 350 bp. 1 mark: sample 1 is homozygous mutant and sample 2 is homozygous wild-type. 1 mark: sample 3 is heterozygous, carrying one of each allele.

practice.stem: A researcher compared the diameter of the zone of inhibition around filter paper discs soaked in a new antibiotic and an existing antibiotic. Three replicate plates were used for each antibiotic. The mean diameter was 18 mm for the new antibiotic and 16 mm for the existing one.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a single experiment with three replicate plates per antibiotic is not enough to conclude that a new antibiotic is more effective than an existing one. Suggest two improvements to the design.
parts.answer: Three replicates give little information about variation and cannot show whether differences are reliable or statistically significant. Results might also depend on the batch of bacteria or the day. Improvements: use more replicates or repeat the experiment on different days; use a control with the existing antibiotic and a no-antibiotic control; use the same bacterial strain and standard conditions, then use a suitable statistical test.
parts.working: 1 mark: three replicates too few to measure variation or show significance. 1 mark: results may depend on batch or day, so repetition is needed. 1 mark each for two improvements (more replicates; repeat on different days; include controls; standardised conditions; statistical test).

practice.stem: A student grew E. coli on agar plates at 37 °C and counted the colonies after different incubation times. One plate was used for each time: 12 h: 18 colonies; 24 h: 65 colonies; 36 h: 120 colonies; 48 h: 122 colonies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the data, discuss the hypothesis that longer incubation always produces more colonies.
parts.answer: The hypothesis is only partly supported. The count rises from 18 at 12 h to 120 at 36 h, but from 36 h to 48 h it hardly changes (120 to 122), so longer incubation does not always give more colonies. Nutrients may run out, or the colonies may crowd and merge, so the count levels off. One plate per time is too few to judge the plateau reliably; replicate plates are needed.
parts.working: 1 mark: counts rise and then level off, so the hypothesis is not supported beyond about 36 h. 1 mark: a reason for the plateau (nutrients used up, space, colonies merging). 1 mark: a justified conclusion with a need for replicates.

practice.stem: E. coli cells that were not transformed were spread on an agar plate containing ampicillin. No colonies grew.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the bacteria that did not take up the plasmid failed to grow on the ampicillin plate.
parts.answer: Ampicillin inhibits the enzymes that cross-link peptidoglycan in the bacterial cell wall, so bacteria without the ampicillin-resistance gene cannot build a stable wall and are killed or cannot grow. Only bacteria that took up the plasmid carry the ampicillin-resistance gene (for a beta-lactamase enzyme that breaks down ampicillin) and can grow.
parts.working: 1 mark: ampicillin stops cell wall synthesis (peptidoglycan cross-linking) so the cells are killed. 1 mark: cells lacking the plasmid have no ampicillin-resistance gene, so cannot produce the enzyme that inactivates ampicillin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why longer DNA fragments travel more slowly through the agarose gel than shorter ones.
parts.answer: The gel is a mesh of agarose fibres that acts as a molecular sieve. Larger fragments are more hindered by the mesh and move through the pores more slowly, while smaller fragments pass through more easily.
parts.working: 1 mark: the gel acts as a sieve (mesh of agarose fibres). 1 mark: larger fragments are more hindered so move more slowly (smaller fragments move faster).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the bacteria are placed in cold calcium chloride solution before the heat shock.
parts.answer: Calcium ions neutralise the negative charges on the phosphate groups of the bacterial cell surface and membrane, which allows the DNA (also negatively charged) to be taken in and makes the membrane more permeable to the plasmid.
parts.working: 1 mark: calcium ions reduce the repulsion between the negatively charged DNA and the cell surface. 1 mark: they make the membrane/cell wall more permeable so DNA can enter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the transformed colonies glow green under ultraviolet light.
parts.answer: The GFP protein contains a fluorophore that absorbs ultraviolet (or blue) light. The energy is absorbed by electrons, which become excited, and then released as green light when the electrons return to their ground state.
parts.working: 1 mark: GFP absorbs UV (or blue) light. 1 mark: energy is re-emitted as lower-energy green light when electrons return to ground state.

practice.stem: A transgenic plant was made in which a gene for green fluorescent protein (GFP) was placed under a promoter from a root-specific gene. Under UV light, the roots of the plant glow green but the leaves do not.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the leaves of the transgenic plant show no fluorescence, while the roots do.
parts.answer: The promoter used is only switched on in root cells. Because the promoter is inactive in leaves, the GFP gene is not transcribed there, so no GFP is made and no fluorescence is seen.
parts.working: 1 mark: promoter is only active in roots, so GFP is not transcribed in the leaves. 1 mark: no GFP protein is made, so no fluorescence.

practice.stem: A transgenic tobacco plant carries a gene for a fluorescent protein under a strong promoter. Under UV light, the leaves show green patches, with some areas giving no fluorescence at all, even though all cells carry the transgene.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the transgene is expressed in some cells of the leaf but not in others, giving a mechanism for the silencing.
parts.answer: Expression varies between cells because in some cells the transgene is silenced. The promoter of the transgene may become methylated in some cells, which prevents transcription of the gene. Alternatively, RNA silencing degrades the mRNA of the transgene, so less protein is made in those cells.
parts.working: 1 mark: patchy (variegated) expression due to silencing in some cells. 1 mark: DNA methylation of the promoter blocks transcription, or the transgene is repressed in some cells. 1 mark: RNA silencing (e.g. small RNAs degrading the mRNA) reduces protein made.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the Bt toxin kills the caterpillars of the moth but does not harm people who eat the GM crop.
parts.answer: The toxin is a protoxin that is activated by proteases and the alkaline conditions in the insect midgut, forming a toxin that binds to specific receptors on the midgut cells of the caterpillar. This forms pores in the membrane, causing the cells to lyse and the caterpillar to die. Humans have a stomach with acid conditions and lack the specific receptors, so the toxin is digested and does not bind.
parts.working: 1 mark: toxin is activated by proteases and high pH in the insect gut. 1 mark: binds to specific receptors on the midgut cells of the insect. 1 mark: humans lack the receptors and the acidic stomach/digestion inactivates the toxin, so no harm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why two sequences of a highly conserved protein can have DNA sequences that differ at many bases, even though the amino acid sequences are identical.
parts.answer: The genetic code is degenerate: most amino acids are coded for by more than one codon. Most of the differing bases are in the third position of codons, and a change in the third base often still codes for the same amino acid (a silent mutation). Only changes that alter the codon to another amino acid change the protein.
parts.working: 1 mark: genetic code is degenerate, more than one codon per amino acid. 1 mark: differences mostly occur at the third base of the codon. 1 mark: synonymous (silent) substitutions do not change the amino acid sequence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a primer with a high proportion of guanine and cytosine bases needs a higher annealing temperature than a primer with a high proportion of adenine and thymine bases of the same length.
parts.answer: Guanine and cytosine pair with three hydrogen bonds, whereas adenine and thymine pair with two. More energy (higher temperature) is needed to break the stronger G–C pairs and form stable bonds with the target. A higher annealing temperature is therefore needed for a GC-rich primer to avoid non-specific binding.
parts.working: 1 mark: G–C has three hydrogen bonds, A–T has two. 1 mark: GC-rich primers are more stable, so need a higher temperature to anneal specifically (or to prevent non-specific binding).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why genetically modified bacteria that produce human insulin are grown in closed fermenters, and why the product must be purified before it is used as a medicine.
parts.answer: Closed fermenters keep the GM bacteria contained, so they do not escape into the environment or contaminate the product, and temperature, pH, oxygen and nutrients can be controlled for maximum growth and protein production. The product is purified to remove bacterial proteins and other contaminants (for example endotoxins), so the medicine is safe for patients.
parts.working: 1 mark: closed fermenter contains the GM bacteria and prevents contamination or escape. 1 mark: conditions (temperature, pH, oxygen, nutrients) are controlled for maximum production. 1 mark: purification removes bacterial proteins and toxins so the medicine is safe.

practice.stem:
A student ran PCR to amplify one gene from the DNA of a chickpea plant, using different annealing temperatures. Products were run on a gel. Results:
50 °C: strong band of correct size plus three other bands
55 °C: one strong band of correct size
60 °C: one strong band of correct size
65 °C: one faint band of correct size
70 °C: no bands

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why no product was formed at 70 °C.
parts.answer: At high temperature the hydrogen bonds between primer and template are unstable / break, so the primers cannot remain base-paired (anneal) to the template; without primers Taq polymerase cannot start making new strands
parts.working: 1 mark: primers cannot anneal / hydrogen bonds not stable at 70 °C. 1 mark: polymerase needs bound primer to begin extension.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why extra, unexpected bands appeared at 50 °C.
parts.answer: At low temperature primers can bind to sequences that are only partly complementary (mismatches tolerated, some hydrogen bonds still form); so other regions of DNA are also copied, giving products of different lengths
parts.working: 1 mark: primers bind to partly complementary/non-target sites. 1 mark: other DNA regions amplified, giving different-sized fragments.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest the best annealing temperature from these results and give a reason.
parts.answer: 55–60 °C, because a single strong band of the correct size was produced
parts.working: 55 or 60 °C (or between) with reason: single, strong correct band.

practice.stem: The normal coding sequence of a gene is 5′-ATG GCT AAG GAT GTA AAA TGA-3′, which codes for Met–Ala–Lys–Asp–Val–Lys then stop. A patient has a mutation in which the G at the start of the fourth codon (GAT) is deleted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Work out the sequence of the first five codons of the patient's mutant gene, and explain why the patient's protein is non-functional and much shorter than normal.
parts.answer: Mutant codons: ATG GCT AAG ATG TAA. The protein is Met–Ala–Lys–Met then stops: 4 amino acids, instead of 6 in the normal protein, and the protein is non-functional.
parts.working: 1 mark: deletion shifts the reading frame for all later codons (frameshift). 1 mark: correct mutant codons ATG GCT AAG ATG TAA, giving a stop codon TAA at codon 5. 1 mark: a truncated (4 amino acid) protein that is non-functional.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the antibiotic-resistance gene in the GM bacteria used to make insulin could spread to bacteria in the gut of a person who drinks water that contains the GM bacteria.
parts.answer: The plasmid carrying the resistance gene can be transferred to other bacteria by horizontal gene transfer, such as conjugation or transformation with DNA released from dead cells. Bacteria in the gut that receive the plasmid become resistant, and if the antibiotic is used, the resistant bacteria are selected and increase in number.
parts.working: 1 mark: horizontal gene transfer (e.g. conjugation or uptake of free plasmid DNA). 1 mark: recipient bacteria acquire the resistance gene. 1 mark: antibiotic use selects for the resistant bacteria so they spread.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the annealing step in PCR is carried out at a lower temperature (about 50–65 °C) than the extension step (72 °C).
parts.answer: At the lower annealing temperature the short primers form stable hydrogen bonds with their complementary sequences, so they bind specifically to the target. At 72 °C, the optimum temperature for Taq polymerase, the enzyme extends the primers fastest.
parts.working: 1 mark: at the lower annealing temperature primers form stable hydrogen bonds with complementary sequences (specific binding). 1 mark: 72 °C is the optimum temperature for Taq polymerase, so extension is fastest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A gene therapy vector delivers a therapeutic gene to liver cells. After several months, the expression of the gene falls. Explain two possible reasons why the expression of the gene decreases.
parts.answer: The vector DNA may not have integrated into the chromosome, so it is lost as the liver cells divide or are replaced, reducing the number of cells expressing the gene. The promoter of the transgene may become methylated and silenced, so transcription declines. An immune response to the vector or the protein can also destroy the modified cells.
parts.working: 2 marks each for any two reasons (1 for the reason, 1 for its effect on expression): vector DNA not integrated into the chromosome, so it is lost as cells divide or are replaced; promoter methylation or silencing; immune response destroys the modified cells.

practice.stem: A student loaded PCR products into the wells of an agarose gel. The student added each sample to the well with a pipette by holding the tip just above the well and releasing the liquid quickly. Several bands ran in the wrong place and some lanes showed faint bands.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one error in this procedure that could cause the DNA bands to appear at the wrong positions, and suggest an improvement.
parts.answer: The bands were loaded into the well by pipetting without a loading dye, so some sample may have floated out or diffused. Improvement: add loading dye containing glycerol to make the sample sink into the well, and load carefully with a fresh tip for each sample.
parts.working: 1 mark: an error (sample lost or spilled from the well, no loading dye, uneven loading). 1 mark: improvement such as adding loading dye/glycerol, slow careful loading, new tip per sample.

practice.stem: A student weighed 0.50 g samples of dried leaf powder on a balance. Before each weighing, the balance was not reset to zero, and the readings were always about 0.02 g higher than expected.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of error (systematic or random) that the balance causes, and explain how it can be detected.
parts.answer: A systematic error: every reading is too high by the same amount. It can be detected by weighing a known standard mass, which will give a reading different from its true value; zeroing the balance before weighing corrects it.
parts.working: 1 mark: systematic error (all readings offset in the same direction). 1 mark: detected by weighing a known mass or checking zero reading.

practice.stem: A student plated 0.1 ml of a bacterial culture on each of three agar plates. Plate 1 had about 600 colonies that were very close together, plate 2 had 84 colonies and plate 3 had 91 colonies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one reason why the colony counts from the replicate plates could be unreliable, and suggest how to improve the count.
parts.answer: Some plates had dense growth with colonies touching, so colonies were counted as one and the count is too low. Improvement: dilute the culture so that 30 to 300 colonies grow on each plate, and count each plate twice.
parts.working: 1 mark: colonies merged on overcrowded plates (or colonies missed at edges). 1 mark: dilute the culture so fewer colonies grow, and count each plate more than once.

practice.stem: A student measured the absorbance of a DNA sample at 260 nm. The spectrophotometer was switched on and the cuvette containing the DNA was placed into the instrument straight away. No blank was used.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the error that the blank was not measured against and state its effect on the reported concentration.
parts.answer: The spectrophotometer was not zeroed (blanked) with the buffer alone, so the absorbance of the buffer and cuvette was included. This is a systematic error that makes the reported concentration too high. Improvement: set the instrument to zero using a blank of the same buffer in the same cuvette before reading each sample.
parts.working: 1 mark: error (no blank, so absorbance of buffer/cuvette is included, giving a systematic error and results too high). 1 mark: improvement (zero with a matched blank before each measurement).

practice.stem: Restriction fragments of a plasmid were loaded onto an agarose gel and run for 10 minutes at 100 V. After staining, the fragments appeared as a single smeared band at the top of the gel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the main reason why the gel did not separate the fragments, and suggest an improvement.
parts.answer: The gel was run for only 10 minutes, too short a time for the fragments to separate, so the bands overlap. Improvement: run the gel for a longer time at a suitable voltage, until the dye front has moved about two-thirds of the way down the gel, and check with a DNA ladder.
parts.working: 1 mark: electrophoresis run too short, so fragments have not separated. 1 mark: run longer (until dye front is far enough) or use a suitable voltage; use a DNA ladder to check.

practice.stem: A class in Peshawar used gel electrophoresis to compare DNA fragments from three plant samples. Several groups reported that: bands were smeared, some lanes were empty, the smallest fragments were not visible, and different groups obtained different band positions for the same sample. The method: wells were made with a comb before the gel had fully set; samples were added with a dropper; the gel was run at a high voltage for 2 hours; no DNA ladder was used.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two sources of error in this procedure that could explain the poor results, and suggest an improvement for each.
parts.answer: Samples loaded unevenly / overflowing wells → use a micropipette with fresh tips and load the same volume carefully; gel run too long so small fragments ran off → run for a shorter time / check with loading dye; voltage too high causing smearing/overheating → use a lower voltage; DNA degraded/contaminated → use fresh samples/sterile equipment; wells damaged → let the gel set fully before removing comb; no ladder → include a DNA ladder
parts.working: 1 mark for each error linked to the observations (max 2) and 1 mark for each matching improvement (max 2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between repeatability and accuracy in this investigation.
parts.answer: Repeatability: getting the same band pattern when the procedure is repeated; accuracy: how close the estimated fragment sizes are to the true sizes
parts.working: 1 mark each correct definition applied to the context.

practice.stem: A student carried out a heat shock at 42 °C for 15, 30, 45 and 60 seconds. The tube was placed in a water bath and removed by hand after a stopwatch was started at the moment the tube entered the water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the reliability of the method used to time the heat shock, and suggest an improvement.
parts.answer: Timing by hand with a stopwatch is subject to human reaction time, so each tube may have been removed a fraction of a second early or late. This is a random error that affects the reliability of the results, especially for short times such as 15 s. Improvement: use a water bath with a timer that sounds automatically, time each sample with the same method, and repeat the investigation.
parts.working: 1 mark: reaction time causes random error in timing. 1 mark: importance for short times, so the results are less reliable. 1 mark: improvement such as an automatic timer or repeat of the experiment.

practice.stem: A student ran a PCR to detect a plant pathogen in leaf samples. The student did not include a control with no template DNA. The thermal cycler had not been checked for several months. Positive bands were found in four of the twenty samples.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two sources of error in this procedure that could cause a false result, and suggest an improvement for each.
parts.answer: A negative control was not included, so contamination of reagents with DNA from an earlier PCR could give a false band. The thermal cycler was not calibrated, so the annealing temperature was not the set value. Improvement: include a no-template control in every run, and calibrate the thermal cycler or check the block temperature with a thermometer.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two sources (no negative control; uncalibrated thermal cycler; pipette not calibrated; contaminated reagents). 1 mark each for an improvement (add no-template control; calibrate; use fresh reagents and separate work areas).

practice.stem: To estimate the percentage of leaves infected with a fungal disease in a wheat field, a student collected 12 leaves from the edge of the field nearest the road.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the student's sample of 12 leaves from the edge of the field may not be representative, and suggest a better sampling method.
parts.answer: Leaves from the edge of the field may have been affected by wind, pesticide drift or different light and water, so they may not represent the whole field (sampling bias). A better method is random sampling, such as a grid of quadrats or randomly chosen points across the whole field.
parts.working: 1 mark: edge leaves are biased by location (wind, light, pests, drift) so are not representative. 1 mark: random or systematic sampling across the whole area (e.g. quadrats).

practice.stem: A student measured the concentration of a DNA sample three times with a spectrophotometer and obtained 52.1, 52.2 and 52.1 ng/µl. The known concentration of the standard is 60 ng/µl.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The student reports a very small standard deviation for these three replicate measurements. State why this does not show that the method is accurate, and explain the difference between accuracy and precision.
parts.answer: A small standard deviation shows the readings are close to each other (precise), but not that they are close to the true value. A systematic error, such as an incorrectly calibrated instrument, can give consistent but inaccurate results. Accuracy is closeness to the true value, precision is closeness of repeated values to each other.
parts.working: 1 mark: small SD means precision (repeatable), not accuracy. 1 mark: systematic error can give consistent but wrong readings, so accuracy must be checked against a known value.

practice.stem: A sequencing gel for a short gene region had clear bands near the top of the gel, but the bands near the bottom were faint and smeared. A group of four adjacent bands could not be assigned to a base with confidence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the sequence could not be read accurately from the band pattern in the lower part of the gel, and suggest how the sequence could be checked.
parts.answer: Bands in a region with many repeated bases, or GC-rich sequence, may be compressed or form secondary structure, so they run as a smear and bases cannot be assigned. Bands close together in size may be unresolved if the gel is too short or the run too quick. Improvement: run a second sequencing reaction from the reverse primer and compare the two reads; use a longer gel or capillary sequencing.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two reasons (band compression or secondary structure in GC-rich regions; bands too close together; gel too short). 1 mark for a suitable check (reverse primer read, longer gel or capillary sequencing).

practice.stem: A student measured the turbidity (absorbance at 600 nm) of a bacterial culture every hour, using the same cuvette each time. The cuvette was placed in the spectrophotometer with a different side facing the light path each time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the error in the way the absorbance was read, and state how it changes the reported growth rate.
parts.answer: The cuvette was placed with a different side facing the light path each time. Each side has different marks, scratches or fingerprints, which scatter or absorb light differently, so the absorbance of the same culture changes from reading to reading. This random variation makes the readings unreliable, so the growth rate calculated from them is inaccurate, possibly too high or too low. Improvement: mark the cuvette and always place it in the same orientation, and wipe it before each reading.
parts.working: 1 mark: cuvette orientation (different sides, marks or dirt) changes light scattering, so absorbance readings vary. 1 mark: this makes the growth rate unreliable (random error); improvement: same orientation and a clean cuvette each time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between random and systematic error in the context of a microarray experiment, and give one example of each together with a way to reduce it.
parts.answer: Random error: variation in scanner readings or spot intensity from one spot to the next, which averages out with replicates and larger sample sizes. Systematic error: a dye that is consistently taken up better than the other, or a batch effect in the chips, which shifts all results the same way; reduce by dye-swap experiments and normalisation of the data across arrays.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition of random error (unpredictable, varies around true value). 1 mark: definition of systematic error (consistent bias in one direction). 1 mark: example with reduction for random error (replicates). 1 mark: example with reduction for systematic error (dye-swap, normalisation, calibration).

practice.stem: A researcher used a new primer pair to detect a gene in plant DNA. The PCR was run twice on the same day, using the same reagents, and gave a band of the correct size both times.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher reports that a new primer pair is reliable because it gave the same result on two occasions. Evaluate this claim.
parts.answer: Two repeats show some consistency, but reliability needs more evidence. Both repeats could share the same error (for example the same batch of reagents or the same operator), and two results are not enough to estimate variation. The primer should be tested on several independent occasions, with different batches of reagents and a range of known samples including a negative control, before reliability is claimed.
parts.working: 1 mark: two repeats are too few to show reliability. 1 mark: repeats may share the same systematic error (same batch, same operator). 1 mark: needs more independent repeats, different batches and known controls.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher found a gene in a bacterium by BLAST search. The search used a database that was two years old, and the researcher reported that the gene had no close match in any other species. Evaluate this conclusion and suggest how the error could be avoided.
parts.answer: The conclusion may be wrong because the database was out of date, so newer sequences from other species were not included, and a close match may have been missed. The result is therefore incomplete and not reliable. The researcher should search the current version of the database, use several databases, and report the database version and the search settings with the result.
parts.working: 1 mark: an old database lacks recent sequences, so a match can be missed. 1 mark: the conclusion is therefore unreliable/incomplete. 1 mark: use the current database (or several), and record the version and settings.

practice.stem: Bacteria were spread on agar plates containing four different concentrations of ampicillin: 0, 10, 50 and 100 µg/ml. After incubation, the number of colonies on each plate was counted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent variable: concentration of ampicillin in the agar (0, 10, 50 and 100 µg/ml). Dependent variable: number of bacterial colonies that grow on each plate.
parts.working: 1 mark: independent variable is ampicillin concentration. 1 mark: dependent variable is number of colonies.

practice.stem: A student is testing how annealing temperature affects the yield of a PCR product from a fixed amount of plant DNA.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name three variables that must be kept the same in every PCR run, and explain why one of them must be kept the same.
parts.answer: Any three of: the amount of template DNA, the concentration of primers, the concentration of Mg²⁺ ions, the volume of the reaction mix, the number of cycles, the temperatures and times of each step. Keeping the amount of template the same is needed so that differences in the product band are due to the factor being tested and not to the amount of starting DNA.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three controlled variables (template DNA amount, primer concentration, Mg²⁺ concentration, number of cycles, temperatures and times, reaction volume). 1 mark for an explanation of why the stated variable is controlled (e.g. so that differences are caused by the tested variable).

practice.stem: In a transformation experiment, one agar plate contains ampicillin and bacteria treated with the plasmid. A second plate contains ampicillin and bacteria treated with no plasmid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the purpose of the negative control in this investigation.
parts.answer: The negative control has no plasmid, so it shows whether any colonies grow without the plasmid, for example because the ampicillin plate is not working or because the bacteria are contaminated. Colonies on the negative control indicate a false positive or a problem with the method.
parts.working: 1 mark: shows whether colonies grow without plasmid (checks antibiotic selection works and no contamination). 1 mark: any growth on this plate indicates a fault in the method.

practice.stem: A student tested how a salt solution affects the germination of lettuce seeds. Five dishes with 20 seeds each were set up for each concentration of the solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the dependent variable would be measured, and give its unit.
parts.answer: Percentage germination = number of seeds germinated ÷ total number of seeds sown × 100, counted at the same time on each dish (for example after 7 days). The unit is percent (%).
parts.working: 1 mark: counting the germinated seeds and dividing by the total, then multiplying by 100. 1 mark: unit given as percent.

practice.stem: A student will test how the temperature of an amylase solution (10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 °C) affects the time taken to digest starch.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify whether the independent variable is continuous or categorical, and state how its levels should be chosen so that the results can show a trend.
parts.answer: Temperature is continuous, because it is a measurable quantity that can take any value within a range. Choose evenly spaced levels across a suitable range, including the temperature expected to give the fastest reaction, so that the shape of the trend can be seen.
parts.working: 1 mark: continuous (a measurable quantity), not categorical. 1 mark: evenly spaced levels over a suitable range, including the expected optimum.

practice.stem: A student plans to investigate how the duration of heat shock at 42 °C (0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 90 s) affects the uptake of a plasmid containing GFP and ampicillin-resistance genes by E. coli. Transformed bacteria are spread on ampicillin agar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable, and state how the dependent variable would be measured.
parts.answer: Independent: duration of heat shock (s); dependent: transformation efficiency / number of colonies (glowing colonies) on the plate, counted after incubation (e.g. 24 h at 37 °C)
parts.working: 1 mark: IV and DV correctly named. 1 mark: DV measured by counting (fluorescent) colonies after fixed incubation time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how three other variables should be controlled.
parts.answer: Temperature of heat shock kept at 42 °C using a thermostatically controlled water bath; same mass/volume of plasmid DNA added (using a micropipette); same volume and concentration of bacteria (same culture, same optical density); same time on ice before and after; same volume spread and incubation temperature/time
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three variables each with a method of control (variable alone = 0).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a suitable control and explain its purpose.
parts.answer: Bacteria treated in the same way but with no plasmid added; shows that colonies arise only from transformation (no growth on ampicillin/no glowing)
parts.working: No-plasmid (or no heat shock) control with purpose.

practice.stem: A student compared the transformation efficiency of the same plasmid after a 42 °C heat shock with a 37 °C control treatment (no heat shock). The 42 °C tubes were incubated in one incubator, and the 37 °C tubes were incubated in another incubator in a different room, after the treatment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one confounding variable in this investigation and explain how it could be controlled.
parts.answer: Different incubators may have different temperatures, which would affect the rate of heat shock damage and growth. The confounding variable is the incubator temperature; it can be controlled by using the same incubator (or incubators checked to the same temperature) for all plates.
parts.working: 1 mark: confounding variable identified (incubator temperature, or other unequal condition). 1 mark: controlled by using the same incubator or checking each to the same temperature.

practice.stem: A student compared the bands made by four PCR products on an agarose gel. The four samples had different concentrations of DNA.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the amount of DNA loaded into each well should be controlled, so that the bands can be compared fairly.
parts.answer: Measure the concentration of each sample first (for example with a spectrophotometer), then load the same mass of DNA (for example 200 ng) in the same volume of loading dye into each well using a fresh tip.
parts.working: 1 mark: measure concentration and calculate the volume needed for the same mass of DNA. 1 mark: load the same volume with fresh tips, using a loading dye.

practice.stem: A student wants to find out how calcium chloride concentration affects the number of transformed colonies. The student will prepare bacteria in calcium chloride at several concentrations, then add the same plasmid to each sample.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent variable, suggest one controlled variable that must be kept the same at every level, and give a suitable range of concentrations.
parts.answer: Independent variable: concentration of calcium chloride in the solution used to prepare the cells (e.g. 0, 20, 50, 100 mM). Controlled variable: the number of bacterial cells (or the volume and density of culture) added to each sample, the amount of plasmid, and the time and temperature of the heat shock.
parts.working: 1 mark: independent variable correctly identified as Ca²⁺ or CaCl₂ concentration. 1 mark: a suitable controlled variable named (amount of plasmid, cell density, heat shock time/temperature). 1 mark: a suitable range of at least four levels, including 0 mM.

practice.stem: A researcher compared gene expression in two cell samples by microarray. Each sample was labelled with a different fluorescent dye and hybridised to the same chip.

parts.label: a
parts.text: List two variables that must be kept constant in every microarray hybridisation and explain why.
parts.answer: The same amount of starting RNA (or cDNA) in each sample, and the same labelling time and hybridisation conditions (temperature and time). These must be kept constant so that differences in spot intensity are due to differences in gene expression, not to differences in the amount of material or the conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two variables (amount of RNA or cDNA; labelling time; hybridisation temperature/time; washing conditions), with 1 mark for explaining why they must be the same so the difference is due to expression.

practice.stem: A laboratory uses RT-PCR to detect a plant virus in leaf samples from different fields.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a positive control and a negative control for a PCR test that detects a plant virus in leaves. State the result expected from each.
parts.answer: Positive control: DNA or RNA from a known infected plant, or a plasmid carrying the target sequence. Expected: a band of the correct size. Negative control: DNA or RNA from a healthy plant, or a no-template reaction. Expected: no band.
parts.working: 1 mark: positive control with known target. 1 mark: expected band of the correct size. 1 mark: negative control (healthy plant or no template) with expected no band.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Design an investigation to find out how the length of ligation time affects the number of recombinant colonies. Identify the independent variable, the dependent variable and two controlled variables.
parts.answer: Independent variable: ligation time (for example 5, 15, 30 and 60 minutes). Dependent variable: number of recombinant colonies per plate (identified by a selectable marker, for example loss of one antibiotic resistance). Controlled variables: the ratio of insert to vector, the same amount of ligase, the same temperature, and the same volume of transformation mix. Any two are acceptable.
parts.working: 1 mark: independent variable is ligation time (with a range of values). 1 mark: dependent variable is number of recombinant colonies, measured by a suitable marker. 1 mark: two valid controlled variables (insert:vector ratio, ligase amount, temperature, volume).

practice.stem: A student changed both the voltage (50 V and 100 V) and the buffer (TAE and TBE) for the same DNA sample, and found that the bands moved further at 100 V with TBE than at 50 V with TAE.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a control variable can also be a confounding variable if it is not kept constant, using the example of a student who changes both the voltage and the buffer used in a gel electrophoresis experiment.
parts.answer: A confounding variable is one that changes along with the independent variable and so affects the result, making it impossible to say which change caused the effect. If both the voltage and the buffer change, the difference in band movement might be due to the buffer, the voltage, or both. Only one variable should be changed at a time; the other must be held constant so that it is a controlled variable.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition of confounding variable (varies with the independent variable). 1 mark: both voltage and buffer change, so the effect cannot be attributed to one. 1 mark: only one independent variable at a time; others held constant.

practice.stem: A student planned an investigation of heat shock time and transformation. In the write-up the student wrote: "The independent variable was the number of colonies, which was counted on each plate."

parts.label: a
parts.text: The student states that the independent variable is the number of colonies. Explain why this is incorrect, and correct the error.
parts.answer: The number of colonies is the dependent variable because it is measured and changes as a result of the independent variable, which is the amount of plasmid or the heat-shock time that the experimenter sets. Correct statement: the independent variable is the heat shock time and the dependent variable is the number of colonies.
parts.working: 1 mark: colonies depend on the variable being tested, so it is the dependent variable. 1 mark: correct independent variable (set by the experimenter) given.

practice.stem: A teacher planned a class experiment on a DNA-modifying enzyme and changed the temperature and the pH of the buffer in each tube at the same time, using 10 tubes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why changing both the temperature and the pH in the same experiment makes the results hard to interpret, and suggest a better plan.
parts.answer: If both change, any difference in enzyme activity or DNA yield could be due to the temperature, the pH or their combination, so the effect of each cannot be separated. A better plan is to change one variable at a time, for example vary the temperature at a fixed pH, then vary the pH at the best temperature, keeping all other variables constant and using replicates.
parts.working: 1 mark: two changes at once confound the results (cannot separate effects). 1 mark: change one at a time while holding the other constant. 1 mark: replicates and a controlled method, so results can be compared.

practice.stem: Ecologists want to know whether pollen from Bt maize, which drifts onto wild plants beside fields, harms the caterpillars of a butterfly that feeds on those plants. Caterpillars will be fed leaves dusted with Bt maize pollen, leaves dusted with non-Bt maize pollen, or leaves with no pollen, and survival after 7 days recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a hypothesis that the investigation could test.
parts.answer: Caterpillars fed on leaves dusted with Bt maize pollen have a lower survival rate than those fed on leaves with non-Bt pollen (or: Bt maize pollen reduces survival of these caterpillars)
parts.working: Testable statement linking pollen type to survival.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the null hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference in survival between caterpillars fed on leaves with Bt pollen and those fed on leaves with non-Bt pollen
parts.working: No significant difference in survival between the groups.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the results if Bt toxin in pollen harms these caterpillars, and explain why caterpillars fed on leaves with no pollen should also be included.
parts.answer: Prediction: survival lower (and growth slower) in the Bt pollen group than in the non-Bt pollen group. The no-pollen group shows whether pollen itself (not the toxin) affects survival / gives a baseline
parts.working: 1 mark: correct directional prediction. 1 mark: no-pollen control separates effect of pollen from effect of toxin.

practice.stem: A student plans to run restriction fragments of a plasmid of known sizes on an agarose gel and measure how far each band moves.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a hypothesis that the investigation could test about the relationship between DNA fragment size and distance moved in the gel.
parts.answer: Smaller DNA fragments move further through the agarose gel than larger fragments, so distance moved is inversely related to fragment size.
parts.working: 1 mark: hypothesis stated as a testable relationship (smaller fragments move further).

practice.stem: A farmer plants GM and non-GM varieties of maize on separate plots and records yield per plot at harvest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a suitable null hypothesis for a t-test comparing the mean yield of the GM and the non-GM plots.
parts.answer: There is no difference in the mean yield between the GM and the non-GM plots.
parts.working: 1 mark: no difference in the mean (population) yield between the two types of plot.

practice.stem: A linear DNA fragment of 3000 base pairs contains two recognition sites for the same restriction enzyme. The DNA is digested completely with the enzyme and run on a gel. The sites are 800 bp and 2000 bp from the same end of the molecule.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the number of bands seen on the gel after digestion with the enzyme, and state the reason for your prediction.
parts.answer: Three bands, of 800 bp, 1000 bp and 1200 bp: a linear DNA molecule cut at two sites is cut into three fragments, and here they all differ in length. Each cut site produces one extra fragment (2 cuts = 3 fragments).
parts.working: 1 mark: 3 bands. 1 mark: two cuts in a linear DNA molecule produce three fragments (800, 1200 and 1000 bp).

practice.stem: A researcher uses CRISPR–Cas9 to knock out a gene that is thought to control the production of a pigment in petals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a testable hypothesis about the effect of the CRISPR knockout on the trait, and predict the result if the hypothesis is correct.
parts.answer: Hypothesis: knocking out the target gene in the plant will remove the trait (for example a pigment) because the gene is needed to produce it. Prediction: plants with the knocked-out gene will lack the pigment, while control plants with the normal gene will show it.
parts.working: 1 mark: testable hypothesis linking gene and trait. 1 mark: prediction for knockout plants (trait absent). 1 mark: comparison with control plants that have the normal gene.

practice.stem: A student runs the same 500 bp DNA fragment on gels made with different concentrations of agarose, keeping the voltage and time the same.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how the distance moved by a 500 bp fragment changes as the agarose concentration increases from 0.8 % to 2.0 %. Give a reason.
parts.answer: The distance moved will decrease as agarose concentration increases, because a denser mesh with smaller pores hinders the fragment more. A higher-percentage gel is better for resolving small fragments such as 500 bp, whereas a lower-percentage gel suits larger fragments.
parts.working: 1 mark: prediction: distance moved decreases. 1 mark: reason: denser mesh with smaller pores gives more hindrance. 1 mark: a higher percentage gives better separation of small fragments, while a lower percentage suits large ones.

practice.stem: In a Sanger sequencing reaction, all four dNTPs are present, together with ddCTP only (no ddATP, ddGTP or ddTTP). The template strand, written 3′ to 5′, is 3′-TAGCCGTA-5′. The primer anneals to the 3′ end of the template.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the fragments that will be seen after electrophoresis, giving their lengths in nucleotides (counted from the 5′ end of the new strand, excluding the primer), and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: The new strand is 5′-ATCGGCAT-3′. Chains stop only where ddCTP is incorporated, so only fragments ending in C are seen: two bands, of 3 and 6 nucleotides. No bands are seen for the positions of A, G or T, because no chain can stop there.
parts.working: 1 mark: the new strand is the complement, 5′-ATCGGCAT-3′. 1 mark: C occurs at positions 3 and 6, giving two fragments of 3 and 6 nucleotides. 1 mark: chains stop only at C, so there are no bands for A, G or T.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a prediction about the brightness of GFP fluorescence if a strong promoter is used instead of a weak one, and explain the prediction.
parts.answer: A strong promoter will produce more GFP mRNA and therefore more GFP protein, so the cells will be brighter than with a weak promoter.
parts.working: 1 mark: brighter fluorescence with the strong promoter. 1 mark: more transcription and translation leads to more GFP protein.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The hypothesis is that the gene is expressed at higher levels in tumour cells than in normal cells. State the prediction the researcher should test, and the result that would reject the hypothesis.
parts.answer: Prediction: the mRNA level (or the fold change on the microarray) is higher in tumour cells than in normal cells. Rejection: the expression is the same or lower in the tumour cells, with no significant difference.
parts.working: 1 mark: prediction of higher expression in tumour cells. 1 mark: rejection result (no difference or lower expression in tumour cells).

practice.stem: A student transforms E. coli with a fixed volume of competent cells and a plasmid. The number of transformed colonies on each plate is counted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict whether the number of transformed colonies per plate will increase, decrease or stay the same if the amount of plasmid in each sample is doubled, and state one assumption that your prediction makes.
parts.answer: The number of transformed colonies is likely to increase, because more plasmid molecules are available to enter the cells. The prediction assumes that the cells are not saturated (not all of the competent cells are already taking up plasmid) and that the extra plasmid is not toxic to the cells.
parts.working: 1 mark: increase (more plasmid molecules available for uptake). 1 mark: stated assumption (cells not saturated, or the plasmid not toxic at this concentration).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Observations: the number of transformed colonies was 350 per µg of plasmid at 50 mM CaCl₂ and 40 per µg at 5 mM CaCl₂. Formulate a hypothesis that explains these results and predict the result at 150 mM.
parts.answer: Hypothesis: higher calcium ion concentration increases the uptake of plasmid DNA, because Ca²⁺ neutralises the charges on the cell surface and makes the membrane more permeable. Prediction: at 150 mM the number of colonies will be higher than at 50 mM, unless the concentration becomes toxic to the cells and reduces survival, in which case it will level off or fall.
parts.working: 1 mark: hypothesis that Ca²⁺ increases uptake (neutralises charges or permeabilises membrane). 1 mark: prediction of higher colonies at 150 mM. 1 mark: a reasoned limit (toxicity or saturation) that could cause a plateau or fall.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict and explain the shape of a graph of Spearman rank correlation values if the true relationship between two variables is a curve that rises then falls, and the test is applied to data from the whole range.
parts.answer: The rank correlation would be weak or close to zero, because Spearman's test measures a monotonic (consistently increasing or decreasing) relationship. A curve that rises then falls is not monotonic, so the ranks do not show a consistent trend across the whole range.
parts.working: 1 mark: rho is close to zero or weak. 1 mark: the relationship is not monotonic, so ranks do not follow a single trend.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict what would happen to the PCR product if the Taq polymerase was replaced by a polymerase that is destroyed at 95 °C, and explain the result for cycles 2 and 3.
parts.answer: Only the first cycle would produce product. The enzyme is denatured at 95 °C in the first denaturation step, so no new strands are made after cycle 1 unless more enzyme is added at each cycle. The amount of product would therefore not increase exponentially, and in cycles 2 and 3 no further product would be made.
parts.working: 1 mark: enzyme denatured at 95 °C, so it cannot work in later cycles. 1 mark: the product does not double each cycle. 1 mark: explanation that enzyme must be added at each cycle, or the reaction stops after cycle 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Formulate a hypothesis about how the proportion of resistant caterpillars changes if a refuge of non-Bt plants is provided, and predict how the frequency of the resistance allele will change over several generations.
parts.answer: Hypothesis: a refuge of non-Bt plants keeps susceptible caterpillars alive, so resistant caterpillars mate with susceptible ones and the resistance allele is diluted. Prediction: the frequency of the resistance allele will rise more slowly in populations with a refuge than in populations without one, and the population will remain susceptible to Bt for longer.
parts.working: 1 mark: testable hypothesis linking refuge and resistance. 1 mark: susceptible moths survive and mate with resistant moths, diluting the allele. 1 mark: prediction that allele frequency rises more slowly (resistance evolves more slowly).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Observations: a new gene is only found in strains of bacteria that grow on tetracycline. Formulate two hypotheses that could explain this, and predict one result for each that would support it.
parts.answer: Hypothesis 1: the gene confers tetracycline resistance. Prediction: strains without the gene are killed by tetracycline, and inserting the gene into a sensitive strain makes it resistant. Hypothesis 2: the gene is part of a plasmid that also carries the tetracycline resistance genes. Prediction: the gene is always found on the same plasmid, and curing the plasmid removes both the gene and the resistance.
parts.working: 1 mark each: a hypothesis that links the gene to resistance or plasmid location. 1 mark: a prediction for each that would support it (e.g. transfer or removal experiments).

subtopics.name: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

subtopics: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row correctly matches the disease with the type of causative organism?
A cholera – virus; malaria – protoctist
B tuberculosis – bacterium; HIV/AIDS – virus
C malaria – bacterium; measles – virus
D tuberculosis – protoctist; cholera – bacterium
parts.answer: B tuberculosis – bacterium; HIV/AIDS – virus
parts.working: TB is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis (or M. bovis) and HIV/AIDS by a virus. Malaria is caused by the protoctist Plasmodium and cholera by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae, so A, C and D each contain an error.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
After heavy monsoon floods, health officials want to reduce the spread of cholera in a camp for displaced families. Which measure would be most effective?
A spraying insecticide to kill mosquitoes
B giving every person the BCG vaccine
C supplying chlorinated water and building proper latrines
D isolating people who are coughing
parts.answer: C supplying chlorinated water and building proper latrines
parts.working: Cholera is spread by the faecal–oral route in water or food contaminated with Vibrio cholerae, so clean water and sanitation break transmission. A targets malaria; B and D target TB, which is airborne.

practice.stem: Floods in Sindh were followed by many cases of acute watery diarrhoea, some of which were confirmed as cholera.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the causative organism of cholera.
parts.answer: Vibrio cholerae
parts.working: B1 Vibrio cholerae (correct spelling of genus).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why cholera outbreaks often follow floods.
parts.answer: Floods mix sewage with drinking-water supplies, so water is contaminated with faeces containing Vibrio cholerae; people drink the water or eat food washed in it.
parts.working: B1 sewage / faeces contaminate drinking water (pipes and latrines overflow); B1 bacteria ingested in water or food (faecal–oral route).

parts.label: c
