parts.text: Suggest two ways in which the spread of cholera could be reduced in flood-affected villages.
parts.answer: Any two of: boiling or chlorinating drinking water; providing clean bottled/tanker water; building latrines away from water sources; handwashing with soap; cooking food thoroughly; oral vaccination; treating sewage.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid measures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of causative organism of HIV/AIDS and two ways in which HIV is transmitted.
parts.answer: Virus (retrovirus). Any two of: unprotected sexual intercourse; sharing needles; transfusion of unscreened blood; from mother to baby across the placenta, at birth or in breast milk.
parts.working: B1 virus; 1 mark each for any two transmission routes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why screening donated blood for HIV is important in a hospital blood bank.
parts.answer: Infected blood would transmit HIV directly into the recipient's bloodstream.
parts.working: B1 transfusion of infected blood passes the virus straight into the recipient.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why it is difficult to stop the spread of HIV by giving the antibiotics that are used to treat TB.
parts.answer: Antibiotics do not affect viruses: HIV has no cell wall or bacterial ribosomes / enzymes for the antibiotic to act on.
parts.working: B1 antibiotics target bacterial structures / metabolism; viruses lack these.

practice.stem: In one year a city with a population of 2 400 000 recorded 6 360 new cases of tuberculosis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of new TB cases per 100 000 people in this city in that year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why health departments give the number of cases per 100 000 people rather than the total number of cases.
parts.answer: It allows comparison between places or years with different population sizes.
parts.working: B1 allows fair comparison between populations of different sizes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why TB is difficult to eradicate in large cities.
parts.answer: Any two of: overcrowding; poor ventilation; people do not complete the long course of treatment; multidrug-resistant strains; HIV co-infection; poverty / malnutrition; people may carry the bacteria without symptoms (latent TB).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A health worker wants to reduce the number of dengue cases in a city.
Which action targets the vector most directly?
A Boiling drinking water before use
B Emptying and covering containers of stagnant water where Aedes aegypti lays its eggs
C Giving antibiotics to every patient with a fever
D Adding chlorine to the piped water supply
parts.answer: B Emptying and covering containers of stagnant water where Aedes aegypti lays its eggs
parts.working: Dengue is a virus carried by the Aedes aegypti mosquito, so removing its breeding sites reduces the vector population. A does not stop mosquitoes breeding; C is wrong because antibiotics act only on bacteria, not viruses; D treats drinking water and does not affect mosquitoes.

practice.stem: Dengue is a viral disease that spreads through cities during the monsoon season. The mosquitoes that carry it lay their eggs in stagnant water held in containers such as buckets, tyres and flower pots.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of organism that causes dengue, and name the vector that carries it.
parts.answer: Dengue is caused by a virus; the vector is the Aedes (Aedes aegypti) mosquito.
parts.working: B1 virus; B1 Aedes mosquito (accept Aedes aegypti).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how emptying containers of stagnant water reduces the number of dengue cases.
parts.answer: Removing breeding sites reduces the number of mosquito larvae and adults; fewer infected mosquitoes are available to transmit the virus to people.
parts.working: B1 fewer larvae/adult mosquitoes develop, so fewer vectors; B1 fewer infected mosquitoes available to pass the virus on.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which cells are infected and destroyed by HIV, leading to AIDS?
A red blood cells
B helper T-lymphocytes
C neutrophils
D plasma cells
parts.answer: B helper T-lymphocytes
parts.working: HIV infects helper T-lymphocytes (which carry the CD4 receptor), so their number falls and the immune system cannot respond to other pathogens. D is wrong: plasma cells are not the main target, although antibody production falls because helper T-cells are lost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how tuberculosis (TB) is transmitted between people.
parts.answer: By airborne droplets: an infected person coughs or sneezes droplets containing Mycobacterium tuberculosis which are inhaled by others, especially in close contact.
parts.working: B1 droplets / aerosol released when infected person coughs, sneezes or talks; B1 inhaled by uninfected person.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why TB spreads more easily in crowded, poorly ventilated housing.
parts.answer: People are close together for long periods, so droplets reach others; poor ventilation means droplets stay in the air longer, so more bacteria are inhaled.
parts.working: B1 close contact / many people sharing small rooms; B1 droplets not dispersed / remain in the air.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how people can be infected with Mycobacterium bovis, and one way of preventing this.
parts.answer: Drinking unpasteurised milk (or eating undercooked meat) from infected cattle; prevent by pasteurising or boiling milk / testing and slaughtering infected cattle.
parts.working: B1 unpasteurised / raw milk or meat from infected cattle; B1 pasteurise / boil milk or test cattle herds.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why people who are HIV positive are more likely to develop active TB.
parts.answer: HIV destroys helper T-cells, so the immune system cannot control the TB bacteria.
parts.working: B1 fewer helper T-cells / weakened immune system so cannot fight M. tuberculosis.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A patient with HIV has no symptoms for many years, and then develops AIDS.
Which statement best explains the long delay?
A The virus is destroyed by antibodies within weeks, so no virus remains in the body.
B HIV replicates at a low level for years and destroys helper T-lymphocytes slowly until the immune system can no longer defend the body.
C HIV stays inactive in red blood cells, which cannot be infected by any pathogen.
D HIV only infects the lungs, and symptoms appear only when the lungs are fully damaged.
parts.answer: B HIV replicates at a low level for years and destroys helper T-lymphocytes slowly until the immune system can no longer defend the body.
parts.working: HIV infects and gradually depletes helper T-lymphocytes, so the body is weakened over a long period; AIDS is diagnosed when defence fails. A is wrong because antibodies do not clear HIV completely; C is wrong because red blood cells are not infected by HIV; D is wrong because HIV infects immune cells throughout the body.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a vaccine against seasonal influenza must be updated every year.
parts.answer: The influenza virus changes its surface antigens over time (antigenic drift), so antibodies made against last year's strain no longer bind well to the new strain; a new vaccine must contain antigens of the predicted strain.
parts.working: B1 surface antigens of the virus change (mutation / antigenic drift); B1 antibodies (and memory cells) from the old vaccine no longer match or bind the new strain; B1 each year's vaccine uses antigens of the strains predicted to circulate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the vector of malaria and describe how it transmits the disease.
parts.answer: The female Anopheles mosquito; when she takes a blood meal from an infected person she takes in Plasmodium gametocytes (sexual stages); they develop in the mosquito and the infective stages move to her salivary glands; she injects them in saliva when she bites another person.
parts.working: B1 female Anopheles mosquito; B1 takes up Plasmodium in blood from an infected person; B1 parasites injected (with saliva / anticoagulant) into the blood of the next person bitten.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it has been difficult to develop a fully effective vaccine against malaria.
parts.answer: Plasmodium is a eukaryote with many stages in its life cycle, each with different antigens; it spends time inside liver cells and red blood cells, hidden from the immune system; antigens vary between strains.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: different antigens at each stage of life cycle; parasite lives inside host cells (liver, red blood cells) so not exposed to antibodies; antigenic variation / many strains; short time in the blood before entering cells.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why malaria cases in parts of Pakistan rise sharply in the months after the monsoon.
parts.answer: Standing water after the rains provides breeding sites for mosquitoes, and warm temperatures speed up mosquito and parasite development, so the vector population and transmission increase.
parts.working: B1 stagnant water / pools → more mosquito breeding sites (larvae); B1 warm and humid conditions → more mosquitoes / faster development of Plasmodium in the mosquito.

practice.stem: A town introduced a piped, chlorinated water supply. In the two years before the project there were 1840 reported cases of cholera; in the two years after it there were 412.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in the number of cases of cholera after the project. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Cases did not fall to zero. Suggest two reasons for this.
parts.answer: Any two of: some people still drank untreated water from wells/canals; poor hygiene or contaminated food spread infection; infected visitors / carriers without symptoms; pipes damaged so supply contaminated; some households not connected.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid reasons linked to cholera transmission.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A health worker said the fall in cases proves that the water project caused the decrease. Give one reason why this might not be correct.
parts.answer: Other factors could also have changed, e.g. a vaccination campaign, hygiene education, weather (fewer floods), or improved reporting.
parts.working: B1 another variable changed at the same time / correlation does not show causation (with example).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the stages of the life cycle of Plasmodium in a human host, including where it multiplies.
parts.answer: Sporozoites injected by the mosquito enter liver cells and multiply; merozoites are released from the liver into the blood; they invade red blood cells and multiply asexually; the infected red cells burst, releasing more merozoites, which infect other red cells; some develop into gametocytes that can be taken up by a mosquito.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks, 1 each for any four of: sporozoites enter liver cells and multiply; merozoites are released into the blood; merozoites invade red blood cells and multiply asexually; infected red cells burst, releasing merozoites; some merozoites develop into gametocytes that are taken up by a mosquito.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Heterozygous individuals with the sickle cell allele have partial protection against severe malaria. Explain how this protection arises.
parts.answer: Parasites develop poorly in the red blood cells of heterozygotes, so fewer parasites multiply and the disease is less severe.
parts.working: B1 Plasmodium reproduces less well in red cells that contain sickle haemoglobin (abnormal shape); B1 so fewer parasites survive and the infection is less severe / heterozygote advantage.

practice.stem: A wedding meal in Multan was followed by an outbreak of typhoid fever, caused by the bacterium Salmonella Typhi. Investigators recorded what each of the 150 guests ate. 60 guests ate the rice, and 36 of them became ill. 90 guests did not eat the rice, and 12 of them became ill.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the attack rate (percentage of people who became ill) among guests who ate the rice.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the relative risk of illness for guests who ate the rice compared with guests who did not. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 attack rate in those who did not eat rice = 12 ÷ 90 = 13.3 %; M1 relative risk = 60 ÷ 13.3 (or 0.60 ÷ 0.133); A1 = 4.5.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why this result does not prove that the rice was the source of the infection.
parts.answer: Any two of: guests who ate rice may also have eaten other contaminated foods; guests may not remember accurately what they ate (recall bias); the groups may differ in other ways; laboratory tests on the rice or on stool samples are needed to confirm the source; numbers are small so chance is possible.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three ways in which the development of antibiotic resistance can be reduced.
parts.answer: Any three of: only prescribe antibiotics for bacterial infections; complete the full course; do not sell antibiotics without prescription; use narrow-spectrum antibiotics where possible; limit antibiotics in farming / for animal growth; rotate antibiotics; improve hygiene and infection control in hospitals so fewer infections need treating.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a patient should finish the full course of an antibiotic even after feeling better.
parts.answer: Some bacteria, often the more resistant ones, may still be alive; stopping early lets them survive and multiply, so the infection returns and resistant bacteria increase.
parts.working: B1 not all bacteria killed / partly resistant ones survive; B1 they reproduce, increasing the proportion of resistant bacteria / infection returns.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A population of bacteria contains a few cells with a random mutation that makes them resistant to an antibiotic. The antibiotic is then used to treat an infection.
What happens next?
A The antibiotic causes all the bacteria to mutate, and the resistant mutation is passed on to all of them.
B The susceptible bacteria are killed, while the resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, so the resistant allele becomes more common.
C The bacteria recognise the antibiotic and choose to develop resistance to it.
D The antibiotic is absorbed by the bacteria, making the resistant cells shrink and then grow stronger.
parts.answer: B The susceptible bacteria are killed, while the resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, so the resistant allele becomes more common.
parts.working: This is natural selection: the mutation arose at random before exposure, and the antibiotic selects for it. A is Lamarckian (the antibiotic does not cause the mutation); C wrongly gives bacteria intention; D has no basis.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Tetracycline is an antibiotic that binds to the 70S ribosomes of bacteria and stops protein synthesis.
Explain why tetracycline does not stop protein synthesis in human cells.
parts.answer: Human cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S, which differ in structure from bacterial 70S ribosomes, so tetracycline does not bind to them and protein synthesis in the human cell cytoplasm is not stopped.
parts.working: B1 human cytoplasmic ribosomes (80S) differ in structure from bacterial 70S ribosomes; B1 tetracycline binds to the bacterial 70S ribosomes, not to the 80S ribosomes in the cytoplasm, so human protein synthesis is largely unaffected.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Penicillinase is an enzyme produced by some bacteria. Describe how penicillinase makes a bacterium resistant to penicillin.
parts.answer: Penicillinase hydrolyses (breaks) the β-lactam ring of penicillin, so the antibiotic is inactivated before it can reach and block the enzymes that make the cell wall.
parts.working: B1 enzyme hydrolyses / breaks the β-lactam ring of penicillin; B1 penicillin is inactivated so it cannot inhibit cell wall synthesis (peptidoglycan cross-linking).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why is penicillin not effective against measles?
A The measles virus has a cell wall made of chitin.
B Viruses have no peptidoglycan cell wall for penicillin to act on.
C The measles virus produces penicillinase that breaks down penicillin.
D Penicillin cannot enter the blood.
parts.answer: B Viruses have no peptidoglycan cell wall for penicillin to act on.
parts.working: Penicillin stops bacteria building peptidoglycan cell walls; viruses have no cell wall or metabolism of their own, so penicillin has no target. C is wrong because penicillinase is made by some bacteria, not viruses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how penicillin kills bacteria that are growing and dividing.
parts.answer: Penicillin inhibits the enzymes that form cross-links between peptidoglycan chains in the cell wall; new wall is weak; water enters by osmosis and the weakened wall cannot withstand the pressure, so the cell bursts (lysis).
parts.working: B1 inhibits enzymes (transpeptidases) that make cross-links in peptidoglycan; B1 cell wall weakened as it grows; B1 water enters by osmosis → cell bursts / osmotic lysis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why penicillin does not harm human cells.
parts.answer: Human cells do not have cell walls / peptidoglycan.
parts.working: B1 human (animal) cells lack a cell wall / peptidoglycan.

practice.stem:
Paper discs (6 mm diameter) soaked in four antibiotics, P, Q, R and S, were placed on an agar plate spread with a non-pathogenic strain of bacterium. After 24 hours at 25 °C the diameter of each clear zone (including the disc) was measured.
P: 24 mm
Q: 18 mm
R: 6 mm
S: 30 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the area of the clear zone around antibiotic P, not including the disc. Use π = 3.142 and give your answer to the nearest mm².
parts.answer: 424 mm²

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which antibiotic is most effective against this bacterium and which one the bacterium is resistant to. Give reasons.
parts.answer: S is most effective (largest clear zone, 30 mm); the bacterium is resistant to R (no clear zone beyond the 6 mm disc).
parts.working: B1 S, largest zone of inhibition; B1 R, zone diameter equals disc diameter so no bacteria killed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the size of the clear zone is not always a reliable guide to which antibiotic a doctor should use.
parts.answer: Antibiotics diffuse through agar at different rates (molecule size), and different starting concentrations were used; it also may behave differently in the body.
parts.working: B1 any one: different diffusion rates / molecular size / concentration in disc / effect in the body (toxicity, absorption) differs from agar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how plasmids carrying a resistance gene can spread antibiotic resistance between bacteria in a hospital.
parts.answer: Bacteria that carry the resistance gene on a plasmid pass a copy of the plasmid to other bacteria through direct contact (conjugation, using a pilus). The recipient bacteria, including bacteria of a different strain or species, then become resistant, so resistance spreads quickly and not only by vertical inheritance.
parts.working: B1 plasmid with resistance gene is copied and transferred between bacteria; B1 by conjugation (direct contact through a pilus); B1 recipients become resistant, which can include different species, so resistance spreads quickly.

practice.stem:
A hospital laboratory recorded the percentage of Staphylococcus aureus isolates from patients that were MRSA (methicillin-resistant):
2019: 22 %
2020: 27 %
2021: 31 %
2022: 36 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage-point increase in the proportion of MRSA isolates from 2019 to 2022.
parts.answer: 14 percentage points
parts.working: B1 36 % − 22 % = 14 percentage points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the relative (percentage) increase in the proportion from 2019 to 2022. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two factors, other than antibiotic use, that could explain the rise in MRSA in this hospital.
parts.answer: Any two of: poor hand hygiene by staff or visitors; longer hospital stays or more patients in intensive care; more patients with weakened immune systems or invasive devices (such as catheters); spread of MRSA between patients; a single resistant strain spreading through the wards.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A patient stops taking an antibiotic as soon as the symptoms disappear, so some bacteria are not killed. Explain how this can lead to the spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria.
parts.answer: Some surviving bacteria may be slightly less susceptible, or resistant, and reproduce; over several generations these resistant bacteria become more common in the patient and can be transmitted to other people.
parts.working: B1 bacteria that survive are the less susceptible or resistant ones; B1 they reproduce, so resistant strains become more common (natural selection); B1 resistant bacteria can be passed on to other people.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a population of bacteria becomes resistant to an antibiotic.
parts.answer: A random mutation produces an allele giving resistance (e.g. an enzyme that breaks down the antibiotic); the antibiotic kills susceptible bacteria; resistant bacteria survive and reproduce by binary fission; the resistance allele is passed on so its frequency increases; plasmids carrying the gene can be passed to other bacteria by conjugation.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: mutation (random) gives resistance gene / allele; antibiotic is a selection pressure; non-resistant bacteria killed; resistant bacteria survive and reproduce; allele passed to offspring (vertical) so frequency increases; resistance genes on plasmids transferred between bacteria (horizontal / conjugation).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Typhoid fever caused by Salmonella Typhi strains resistant to many antibiotics has spread in parts of Pakistan. Suggest why antibiotics sold without a prescription contribute to this.
parts.answer: People take antibiotics they do not need (e.g. for viral fevers) or take incomplete courses, so bacteria are exposed to antibiotics more often, giving more selection for resistant strains.
parts.working: B1 overuse / unnecessary use / wrong antibiotic / incomplete course; B1 increases selection pressure so resistant bacteria survive and multiply.

practice.stem:
A hospital laboratory in Lahore recorded the percentage of Escherichia coli isolates from patients that were resistant to one class of antibiotic.
2017: 12 %
2019: 31 %
2021: 54 %
2023: 68 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the trend shown by the data.
parts.answer: The percentage of resistant isolates increased every year, from 12 % in 2017 to 68 % in 2023; the largest rise was between 2019 and 2021 (23 percentage points).
parts.working: B1 increase throughout; B1 data quote with years, e.g. 12 % (2017) to 68 % (2023).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean increase in percentage of resistant isolates per year between 2017 and 2023.
parts.answer: 9.3 percentage points per year

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why hospital wards may contain a higher proportion of resistant bacteria than the general community.
parts.answer: Antibiotics are used heavily in hospitals, giving strong selection for resistant bacteria; many ill / immunocompromised patients close together allow resistant bacteria to spread between them (via hands, equipment).
parts.working: B1 high antibiotic use = strong selection pressure; B1 transmission between patients / staff / equipment, patients with weak immune systems.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bacterium divides every 30 minutes. A patient's infection starts with 500 bacteria. Calculate the number of bacteria after 4 hours if no antibiotic is given.
parts.answer: 128 000 bacteria
parts.working: M1 4 hours = 8 divisions, so 500 × 2⁸; A1 = 128 000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why penicillin is much less effective against a population of bacteria that has stopped dividing.
parts.answer: Penicillin inhibits the synthesis of peptidoglycan cell walls, which happens mainly in growing and dividing cells; bacteria that are not dividing make little new cell wall, so the antibiotic has little effect.
parts.working: B1 penicillin acts on cell wall synthesis, which occurs during growth and division; B1 dormant bacteria are not synthesising new peptidoglycan, so the drug has no target.

practice.stem: A patient is given 800 mg of an antibiotic intravenously. The antibiotic has a half-life of 3 hours in the blood (the time for the concentration to halve).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of antibiotic remaining in the blood 12 hours after a dose of 800 mg, if its half-life in the blood is 3 hours.
parts.answer: 50 mg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a doctor prescribes repeated doses, rather than one large dose, so that the drug concentration stays above the minimum inhibitory concentration for long enough.
parts.answer: Between doses the concentration falls below the level that stops the bacteria growing, so bacteria can recover; repeated doses keep the concentration above this level for the whole course, while avoiding a single very high dose that could cause toxic side effects.
parts.working: B1 concentration falls below the minimum inhibitory concentration between doses and bacteria can recover; B1 repeated doses maintain effective concentration without a single toxic peak.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss how the routine use of antibiotics in livestock may increase the number of antibiotic-resistant bacteria that infect people.
parts.answer: Low, repeated doses in animals select for resistant bacteria in the gut of the livestock; resistant bacteria and their resistance plasmids can reach humans through contaminated meat, food, water or direct contact with animals; resistant infections in people are harder and more expensive to treat, so antibiotics become less effective; resistance genes may be transferred to human pathogens.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks, 1 mark each for any four well-developed points: selection of resistant bacteria in animals; transfer of resistant bacteria or plasmids to humans through food, water or contact; resistant infections in humans need stronger or alternative drugs; plasmid-borne genes can spread to other bacterial species that infect people.

practice.stem:
A student grew Bacillus subtilis (a harmless soil bacterium) in nutrient broth at five temperatures for 24 hours. Bacterial density was estimated from absorbance at 600 nm, a higher reading meaning more bacteria.
15 °C: 0.12
25 °C: 0.38
30 °C: 0.61
37 °C: 0.84
45 °C: 0.19

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the trend in absorbance between 15 °C and 37 °C.
parts.answer: Absorbance (and so bacterial density) rises steadily as temperature increases from 15 °C to 37 °C, from 0.12 to 0.84.
parts.working: B1 absorbance increases with temperature; B1 quotes values (e.g. from 0.12 at 15 °C to 0.84 at 37 °C) or describes it as a steady rise.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the absorbance was much lower at 45 °C.
parts.answer: Enzymes in the bacteria are denatured at 45 °C, so growth and reproduction stop or slow sharply.
parts.working: B1 high temperature denatures enzymes / proteins needed for growth (the bacterium is not adapted to 45 °C).

practice.stem:
Paper discs soaked in an antibiotic at four concentrations were placed on agar spread with a sensitive bacterium. The mean clear-zone diameter (including the 6 mm disc) was:
1 µg cm⁻³: 9 mm
2 µg cm⁻³: 12 mm
4 µg cm⁻³: 15 mm
8 µg cm⁻³: 15 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between antibiotic concentration and the mean diameter of the clear zone, using the data.
parts.answer: The clear zone gets larger as concentration increases, but the increase levels off (no further increase) between 4 and 8 µg cm⁻³.
parts.working: B1 diameter increases as concentration increases; B1 the increase stops / levels off above 4 µg cm⁻³ (quote values).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a reason why the diameter did not increase between 4 and 8 µg cm⁻³.
parts.answer: All the sensitive bacteria near the disc were already killed or inhibited at 4 µg cm⁻³, so a higher concentration could not reveal more clear area; or the antibiotic has reached its maximum effect.
parts.working: B1 maximum effect reached: all susceptible bacteria already inhibited (or the antibiotic has diffused to its limit).

practice.stem:
A health department recorded vaccination coverage and the number of measles cases per 100 000 people in five districts:
District A: coverage 40 %, cases 120
District B: coverage 60 %, cases 84
District C: coverage 70 %, cases 60
District D: coverage 85 %, cases 22
District E: coverage 92 %, cases 9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between vaccination coverage and the number of cases, and state whether the data show a positive or negative correlation.
parts.answer: Negative correlation: as vaccination coverage increases, the number of cases decreases.
parts.working: B1 negative correlation; B1 stated as coverage rising, cases falling (quote data).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why these data alone cannot prove that the vaccine caused the fall in cases.
parts.answer: Other factors may differ between the districts, such as income, sanitation, population density or access to health care; the correlation shows association, not cause.
parts.working: B1 correlation does not show causation; B1 an uncontrolled variable (e.g. wealth, hygiene, population density) may explain the pattern.

practice.stem:
Clear-zone diameters (mm), measured from five wells on agar plates seeded with the same bacterium:
Honey A: 12, 14, 13, 15, 16
Honey B: 8, 9, 7, 10, 8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean zone diameter for honey A and for honey B.
parts.answer: Honey A: 14.0 mm; honey B: 8.4 mm

parts.label: b
parts.text: State a conclusion from these data and give one reason why the conclusion is limited.
parts.answer: Honey A inhibits the bacterium more than honey B does. Limitation: only five replicate zones per honey were measured, from one batch of agar, so the difference may not be generalisable (or variables such as honey concentration were not controlled).
parts.working: B1 honey A gives larger zones, so is more effective (more inhibition); B1 limitation such as small sample, single batch, or uncontrolled concentration.

practice.stem:
The percentage of households using insecticide-treated bed nets and the number of malaria cases per 1000 people in one year were recorded for five villages.
Village A: bed nets 15 %; cases 41 per 1000
Village B: bed nets 32 %; cases 30 per 1000
Village C: bed nets 48 %; cases 22 per 1000
Village D: bed nets 66 %; cases 15 per 1000
Village E: bed nets 81 %; cases 9 per 1000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between bed-net use and malaria cases.
parts.answer: Negative correlation: as the percentage of households using bed nets increases, the number of malaria cases per 1000 people decreases, from 41 at 15 % to 9 at 81 %.
parts.working: B1 negative correlation / inverse relationship; B1 data quoted with units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A newspaper reported that 'bed nets cause the fall in malaria'. Discuss whether the data support this claim.
parts.answer: Data show a strong negative correlation, and bed nets prevent mosquito bites, so it is plausible; but correlation does not prove causation: other factors may differ between villages (e.g. distance from water, insecticide spraying, wealth, access to treatment, altitude); only five villages; one year of data.
parts.working: B1 supports: strong negative correlation / biologically plausible because nets stop mosquito bites at night; B1 correlation ≠ causation; B1 named other variable not controlled or small sample / no statistics.

practice.stem:
A student pressed the fingertips onto agar plates before and after washing with soap and water. The colony counts were:
Before washing: 280 colonies
After washing: 35 colonies

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in colonies after hand washing. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether you would conclude that soap removes most bacteria, and give one reason why one plate per condition is not enough to be sure.
parts.answer: Yes, soap and water removed most bacteria in this test; one plate per condition does not show the variation between hands or plates, so the result could be due to chance and repeats are needed.
parts.working: B1 conclusion: hand washing with soap reduced bacteria greatly (supported by the large reduction); B1 one plate gives no measure of variability or repeatability.

practice.stem:
A survey of 200 children recorded whether they were vaccinated against a bacterial infection and whether they became infected.
Vaccinated (100 children): 12 infected, 88 not infected
Not vaccinated (100 children): 30 infected, 70 not infected

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected number of vaccinated people who became infected, if vaccination had no effect.
parts.working: M1 expected = row total × column total ÷ grand total = 100 × 42 ÷ 200; A1 = 21.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The chi-squared value for these data is 9.76. The critical value at the 5 % level with one degree of freedom is 3.84. Write a conclusion about whether vaccination is associated with infection.
parts.answer: The calculated value (9.76) is greater than the critical value (3.84), so there is a significant association between vaccination and infection; vaccinated people were infected less often than expected by chance.
parts.working: B1 9.76 > 3.84 so reject the null hypothesis; B1 significant association: vaccinated group had fewer infections than expected.

practice.stem: A study of 12 hospitals found that, between 2015 and 2024, the percentage of E. coli samples resistant to a common antibiotic rose from 12 % to 31 %. Over the same period, the amount of that antibiotic prescribed in the same hospitals also rose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An author concluded that increased antibiotic use caused the rise in resistant E. coli. Evaluate this conclusion, giving one reason why the data do not support it fully and one way of testing it.
parts.answer: The data show a correlation over time, but other factors (for example infection control, changes in patients, or spread of one resistant strain) could also cause the rise; a controlled study comparing wards with different antibiotic use, or tracking resistance genes in strains, would test the claim.
parts.working: B1 correlation is not causation; B1 another variable (e.g. infection control, patient mix, strain spread) may explain the rise; B1 a suitable test such as comparing wards with different prescribing or tracking the strains.

practice.stem: Four replicate plates were counted for one water sample: 88, 92, 240 and 90 colonies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and explain why it should not simply be included in the mean without comment.
parts.answer: The result 240 is anomalous because it is much larger than the others (88, 92 and 90); it may be due to contamination or a counting or technical error, so it should be checked and reported.
parts.working: B1 identify 240; B1 anomalous results may be errors (contamination, counting mistake); should be checked or reported and not included without comment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean with and without the anomalous result. Give both answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: With all four values: 127.5 colonies; without the anomalous value: 90.0 colonies.

practice.stem: A hospital introduced a hand-hygiene programme. Infection rates per 1000 bed-days were 18.0 before and 11.7 after the programme.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in the infection rate after the programme. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the infection rate (per 1000 bed-days) is a better measure than the total number of infections for comparing the two periods.
parts.answer: The number of infections depends on how many patients were in the ward and how long they stayed; the rate corrects for different numbers of patients and bed-days, so the periods can be compared fairly.
parts.working: B1 total counts depend on the number of patients/bed-days; B1 the rate standardises for patient exposure so the two periods are comparable.

practice.stem:
A school in Peshawar ran a handwashing campaign. The mean number of episodes of diarrhoea per child per year, with standard error (SE), was recorded.
before campaign: mean 3.8, SE 0.4
after campaign: mean 2.1, SE 0.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: The 95 % confidence intervals are mean ± 2 × SE. Calculate the 95 % confidence interval for each period.
parts.answer: Before: 3.0 to 4.6; after: 1.1 to 3.1 cases per child per year

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to discuss whether the campaign significantly reduced diarrhoea.
parts.answer: The intervals overlap (3.0–3.1), so the difference may not be significant; the mean did fall, but we cannot be confident the decrease is real rather than due to chance.
parts.working: B1 confidence intervals overlap; B1 so difference not shown to be significant (although mean is lower).

practice.stem:
A district recorded tuberculosis cases in two years:
2010: 540 cases; population 1 800 000
2020: 520 cases; population 2 400 000
A local newspaper reported that TB had hardly changed because the number of cases fell only slightly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the case rate per 100 000 people in 2010 and in 2020. Give each answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in cases and the percentage fall in the case rate, then explain why the rate fell by much more than the number of cases did.
parts.answer: Cases fell by 3.7 % (540 to 520) but the rate fell by 27.8 % (30.0 to 21.67 per 100 000, using unrounded figures). The population grew by 33 %, so the same number of cases is spread across more people and the rate falls more than the count.
parts.working: B1 correct percentage fall in cases (3.7 %) and in rate (27.8 %); B1 population grew by 33 %, so the rate per head falls more than the raw count.

practice.stem:
Survival (%) of a bacterium after 10 minutes in a disinfectant was measured in five replicates at each concentration. Results are given as mean ± SE:
0.5 % disinfectant: mean 62 %, SE 3
1 % disinfectant: mean 41 %, SE 4

parts.label: a
parts.text: The mean percentage survival with 95 % confidence intervals, estimated as mean ± 2 × SE, is given for two disinfectant concentrations. Calculate the 95 % confidence interval for each concentration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to decide whether the disinfectant at 1 % is likely to kill significantly more bacteria than at 0.5 %. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Yes: the intervals do not overlap (56 % to 68 % and 33 % to 49 %), so the difference in survival is likely to be real at the 95 % level; survival is lower at 1 %.
parts.working: B1 the intervals do not overlap; B1 the lower survival at 1 % is therefore likely to be a real effect; B1 justification referring to the non-overlapping 95 % intervals (the 95 % intervals are approximate here, as they use mean ± 2 SE).

practice.stem: Two sources of standing water were sampled for Aedes mosquito larvae on the same day. Site X had 58 larvae per litre, and site Y had 21 larvae per litre. Water temperature was 31 °C at site X and 27 °C at site Y. The student concluded that the water at site X supports more larvae.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the larvae count in site X being higher than in site Y does not, on its own, show that water X supports more larvae. Identify one uncontrolled variable and explain its effect.
parts.answer: The sites differed in temperature (about 4 °C warmer at site X), and warmer water speeds larval development and increases survival, so the difference may be caused by temperature rather than the water source; the number of larvae is also affected by predators, food and the amount of water, which were not controlled.
parts.working: B1 correlation between site and larvae count is not proof of a cause; B1 identify an uncontrolled variable (temperature, food, predators, water volume); B1 explain its effect on larval survival or development; B1 a fair test would keep this variable the same or measure it.

practice.stem: On an agar plate, a clear zone of 14 mm surrounds an antibiotic disc on a sensitive strain of Staphylococcus aureus, but only 7 mm on a second strain of the same species from a hospital patient. Both discs contained the same amount of antibiotic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, using biology, why a resistant strain of bacteria may give a smaller clear zone than a sensitive strain on the same antibiotic disc.
parts.answer: Resistant bacteria possess a mechanism (such as an enzyme that breaks down the antibiotic, a modified target, or a pump that removes the drug), so the antibiotic is less effective and bacteria grow closer to the disc; this gives a smaller clear zone.
parts.working: B1 resistance mechanism (enzyme, altered target or efflux pump) reduces the effect of the antibiotic; B1 resistant cells keep growing near the disc; B1 smaller clear zone as fewer cells are killed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one further test the student could do before concluding that the strain has a resistance gene.
parts.answer: Use a molecular test (for example PCR) to detect the resistance gene, or test against a known resistant control strain.
parts.working: B1 PCR or sequencing to detect a resistance gene, or a minimum inhibitory concentration test with comparison to a control.

practice.stem: A student wants to find out which concentration of ethanol in a hand sanitiser is most effective at killing bacteria.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how you would prepare 20 cm³ of each of 70 %, 60 %, 50 % and 40 % ethanol solutions from a 70 % stock solution and distilled water.
parts.answer: 70 %: 20 cm³ stock + 0 water; 60 %: 17.1 cm³ stock + 2.9 cm³ water; 50 %: 14.3 cm³ stock + 5.7 cm³ water; 40 %: 11.4 cm³ stock + 8.6 cm³ water.
parts.working: M1 volume of stock = (required % ÷ 70) × 20; A1 all four correct (to 1 decimal place).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student could use these solutions to compare their effect on the number of bacteria on the hands.
parts.answer: Volunteer presses fingertips on a nutrient agar plate (before); applies a fixed volume (e.g. 2 cm³) of one concentration for a fixed time (30 s), lets hands dry, presses fingertips on a second plate (after); incubate plates at 25 °C for 48 h; count colonies; calculate percentage reduction; repeat with several volunteers/days for each concentration; tape lid, do not open plates.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: before and after samples on agar; same volume of sanitiser and same rubbing time; same fingers / same pressure and time of contact; incubation ≤ 30 °C for a stated time; count colonies and calculate % reduction; repeats / several volunteers; safety (lids taped, plates autoclaved after).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how you would use serial dilution and plate counting to estimate the number of bacteria in a liquid culture, including how you would keep the work sterile.
parts.answer: Make a series of tenfold dilutions (for example 10⁻¹ to 10⁻⁴) using sterile distilled water and a sterile pipette, mixing each step; spread 0.1 cm³ of selected dilutions onto nutrient agar plates using a sterile spreader; incubate upside down at a safe temperature (e.g. 25–30 °C) for 24–48 hours; count colonies on a plate with 30–300 colonies; multiply by the dilution factor and divide by the volume plated; sterility: flame the loop/spreader, work near a Bunsen flame, use sterile equipment, seal plates with tape, and include a sterile (no bacteria) control plate.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks, 1 each: serial dilution in sterile water with mixing; known volume spread on agar using sterile technique; incubation with lid taped and inverted, safe temperature and time; count plate with 30–300 colonies; calculation (colonies × dilution factor ÷ volume); aseptic technique and control plate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how you would investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of growth of mould on bread. Include the independent, dependent and control variables and one safety precaution.
parts.answer: Cut identical slices of bread; inoculate each with the same amount of spores (or a standard spore suspension); place slices in sealed bags at different temperatures (e.g. 5 °C, 15 °C, 25 °C, 35 °C) in incubators or water baths; use the same humidity and light; measure the area of mould (for example by counting squares on graph paper) every day for 7 days; repeat with at least three slices per temperature; independent variable: temperature; dependent: mould area; controls: same bread, spore amount, humidity, time; safety: do not open the bags, wash hands, wear gloves, avoid inhaling spores.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks: identical bread slices with standard inoculation; range of temperatures in a controlled apparatus; measure mould area at regular intervals (e.g. daily); repeats (at least three); IV, DV and named control variables; safety (sealed bags, no opening, gloves).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how you would set up a disc diffusion (clear zone) test to compare three antibiotics, including a positive control and a negative control.
parts.answer: Spread a sensitive bacterium evenly over the surface of an agar plate; place three discs soaked in the three antibiotics at equal spacing; use a sterile disc soaked in distilled water as the negative control and a disc of a known antibiotic as the positive control; incubate lid-down at 25–30 °C for 24 hours; measure each clear zone with a ruler in mm, at several points, and calculate the mean.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks: spread bacteria evenly (lawn); discs at equal spacing, same amount of antibiotic; negative control (water disc) and positive control; incubation; measure diameters in several directions and calculate mean.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how you would investigate the effect of exposure time to ultraviolet (UV) light on the number of living bacteria in a suspension.
parts.answer: Spread a sample of a non-pathogenic bacterium suspension onto agar plates; expose the plates to a UV lamp at a fixed distance for times such as 0, 30, 60, 120 and 180 seconds, covering the other plates; keep a control plate that is not exposed; incubate and count colonies; repeat each time three times; independent variable: exposure time; dependent variable: number of colonies; control: same distance, same bacteria concentration, same incubation; safety: do not look at UV lamp, wear UV-blocking eye protection, switch off the lamp when handling plates.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks: plates spread with the same suspension; fixed distance and lamp intensity; range of times with a zero control; count colonies and calculate means from repeats; IV, DV and controls; UV safety (eye protection, no direct exposure).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how you would test whether the concentration of household bleach affects the growth of a bacterium. Explain how you would prepare the bleach concentrations from a stock solution.
parts.answer: Prepare bleach concentrations (for example 0 %, 0.1 %, 0.5 %, 1 %) by diluting a known stock with distilled water using a measuring cylinder or pipette so the total volume is fixed (e.g. 10 cm³); soak sterile filter paper discs in each solution and place them on a lawn of the bacterium on agar; use a disc soaked in water as the control; incubate and measure the clear zones; repeat each concentration; independent: bleach concentration; dependent: clear zone diameter; control: same disc size, same bacterium, same incubation.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks: calculate dilutions, with a fixed total volume; discs soaked equally; distilled water control; lawn on agar; measurement of zones with repeats; IV, DV and controlled variables.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how you would investigate the effect of water temperature on the development time of Aedes mosquito larvae. Include one ethical or safety consideration.
parts.answer: Collect early-stage larvae from a container and place a fixed number (e.g. 20) of similar-stage larvae in identical containers of water at 20 °C, 25 °C and 30 °C, with the same amount of food; keep at each temperature with a thermometer checking; record the day each larva reaches adulthood (or pupation); repeat in three containers per temperature; independent: temperature; dependent: development time; control: same larvae stage, water volume, food, and light; ethics: rear the larvae in sealed containers and release none; dispose of them by freezing or boiling and wash hands after handling.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks: standard number and stage of larvae; identical containers, measured water temperatures; regular recording of development; repeats; IV, DV and controlled variables; ethical/safety (no release of mosquitoes, sealed containers, disposal).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how you would investigate whether the concentration of sodium chloride (salt) affects the growth of a non-pathogenic yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, in sugar solution. Include how you would measure growth and one control.
parts.answer: Prepare sugar solutions with 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8 % sodium chloride, keeping the sugar concentration the same; add equal volumes of the same yeast suspension to each in identical tubes or flasks; measure growth as the volume of gas (or the displacement of a gas collection tube) or the turbidity of the culture every 10 minutes for 60 minutes; repeat each concentration at least three times; plot the results and calculate the rate of growth from the steepest part of each curve; control: same yeast, sugar concentration, volume, temperature (e.g. 30 °C), and a control with no salt.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks: range of salt concentrations with sugar kept constant; equal yeast inoculum and volumes; growth measured at regular intervals (gas or turbidity); repeats; rate from gradient; controlled variables with a no-salt control.

practice.stem: Neem (Azadirachta indica) leaves are traditionally used in Pakistan as an antiseptic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student could investigate the effect of the concentration of neem leaf extract on the growth of the bacterium Bacillus subtilis. Include how the results would be recorded and processed.
parts.answer: Make a stock extract (e.g. 20 g leaves blended in 100 cm³ distilled water, filtered and sterilised by filtration); dilute to five concentrations (e.g. 100, 80, 60, 40, 20 % plus 0 % control) using distilled water; spread the same volume (0.1 cm³) of the same culture on nutrient agar plates using aseptic technique; soak 6 mm sterile paper discs in each concentration for the same time and place them on the agar; incubate at 25 °C for 48 h; measure diameter of clear zone in two directions at right angles and calculate mean / area; three replicate plates per concentration; calculate mean; plot graph of zone diameter against concentration.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any seven of: preparation of extract and dilution method with volumes; at least 5 concentrations and suitable range; control discs soaked in distilled water; same volume / density of bacterial culture spread on each plate; same type and depth of agar; same disc size and soaking time; incubation temperature (≤ 30 °C) and time stated; measure clear zone diameter (mean of two perpendicular diameters) or area; at least 3 replicates and calculate mean; aseptic technique (flame loop, sterile equipment, lid taped not sealed); record in table and plot graph.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student wants to compare two hand sanitisers by the number of bacteria left on fingertips after use. Describe how the student would collect and count the bacteria, and how the results would be made reliable.
parts.answer: Each volunteer touches a sterile agar plate (contact plate) or swabs the fingertips before use; apply the sanitiser as directed, then sample again after 30 seconds, using the same finger and pressure; incubate plates and count colonies; use the same volunteers for both sanitisers (or a repeated-measures design) and randomise the order of use; take at least five volunteers and at least three samples each; calculate the percentage reduction; control: same volunteers, time and technique, and a control with no sanitiser; reliability: repeat, calculate means and standard deviations, and check for outliers.
parts.working: Up to 8 marks: contact plate or swab before use; apply sanitiser exactly; sample afterwards at the same time and place; incubate and count colonies; percentage reduction; repeat with several volunteers; randomise order / repeated measures; control for technique and time; calculate mean and SD.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how you would investigate the effect of pH on the growth rate of Escherichia coli (non-pathogenic strain) in broth, measuring growth with a colorimeter. Include how you would calibrate the colorimeter.
parts.answer: Prepare broth at pH 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 using dilute acid or alkali and check with a pH meter; inoculate equal volumes with the same starting culture; calibrate the colorimeter with a blank of sterile broth at the same pH set to zero absorbance and a series of known dilutions of a culture (or a standard) to give a calibration curve; take absorbance readings at fixed times (e.g. every hour for 6 hours) at a fixed wavelength; repeat each pH at least three times; plot absorbance against time and calculate growth rate from the steepest part of each curve; controls: same temperature, same starting density, sterile technique.
parts.working: Up to 8 marks: buffered or pH-adjusted broth checked with pH meter; equal inoculum; colorimeter blank and calibration curve; readings at fixed times and wavelength; repeats; growth rate from gradient; controlled variables and sterile technique.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how you would test whether the concentration of garlic extract affects the clear-zone diameter produced on a lawn of a non-pathogenic bacterium. Name the statistical test you would use to compare the diameters at two concentrations, and justify it. Assume the diameters are normally distributed.
parts.answer: Prepare garlic extract at concentrations such as 0 %, 25 %, 50 % and 100 % (serial dilution with water); soak discs of equal size in each extract and a water control; place on a lawn of bacteria with equal spacing; incubate at 25–30 °C; measure diameters in two directions and calculate the mean; repeat at least five times; an unpaired (independent samples) t-test, justified because two separate groups of plates are compared and the continuous diameter data are normally distributed (a Mann-Whitney test would only be needed if normality failed); controls: same disc size, bacteria, agar depth and incubation.
parts.working: Up to 8 marks: serial dilution of extract with water control; equal discs, equal soaking; lawn with equal spacing; measure clear zone and calculate mean; repeats (at least five); unpaired t-test, justified (two independent groups, continuous and normal data); controlled variables.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how you would investigate the effect of storage temperature on the time taken for milk to turn sour, using a pH indicator, and state how you would decide when the milk had soured.
parts.answer: Pour equal volumes of fresh milk into identical sealed containers; store at 4 °C, 15 °C, 25 °C and 35 °C; add the same amount of a pH indicator or measure pH with a pH meter at regular intervals; define sour as the time when pH falls below a set value (for example pH 4.6, the point at which milk curdles) or when the colour changes; repeat each temperature with replicate containers; IV: temperature; DV: time to souring; control: same milk batch, volume, container type, and time of measurement.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks: identical volumes and containers; range of temperatures; measure pH or indicator colour at regular intervals; define endpoint clearly; replicates; IV, DV and controls.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how you would count the number of viable bacteria in a soil sample after incubation at 25 °C and at 37 °C, and explain how you would make the comparison fair.
parts.answer: Weigh and suspend equal masses of soil in sterile water and shake; make a serial dilution; spread equal volumes (0.1 cm³) of two suitable dilutions onto identical nutrient agar plates in triplicate; incubate one set at 25 °C and one at 37 °C for the same time (e.g. 48 hours); count colonies on plates with 30–300 colonies; calculate colonies per gram of soil by multiplying by the dilution factor and dividing by the mass used; fair: same soil sample, same dilution, same agar batch, same time, same volume spread; use sterile technique and a control plate; treat all soil microorganisms as potentially harmful, keep plates taped and do not open them; wash hands and disinfect the bench.
parts.working: Up to 8 marks: equal masses of soil; serial dilution; equal volumes spread in triplicate; identical plates and time; incubation at each temperature; calculation per gram; fair comparison (same sample, equal conditions); sterile technique and safety.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how you would investigate the effect of boiling time on the number of viable bacteria in a water sample. Include how you would use the results to decide the minimum safe boiling time.
parts.answer: Collect one large well-mixed sample of water and divide it into equal volumes; boil each for 0, 1, 2, 5 and 10 minutes, then cool; use a sterile technique to spread a fixed volume of each sample onto agar plates; incubate at 30 °C for 48 hours and count colonies; repeat each time at least three times; plot mean colonies against time and identify the shortest time that gives no colonies; use a control of unboiled water; state a safety limit and that the result is only as good as the replicates.
parts.working: Up to 8 marks: one well-mixed sample divided into equal volumes; a range of boiling times including 0; spreading fixed volume with aseptic technique; incubation and count; replicates and means; plot and identify minimum time giving zero colonies; control and limitation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student measures clear-zone diameters with a plastic ruler marked in millimetres. Give one random error and one systematic error in these measurements, and suggest an improvement for each.
parts.answer: Random error: reading the edge of the clear zone differently each time (judging where the zone ends); systematic error: the ruler's zero mark is worn, so every measurement is too small (or the disc diameter is not subtracted); improvement: take readings from several points and average; calibrate the ruler against a known length.
parts.working: B1 random error (judgement of edge); B1 systematic error (zero error / parallax); B1 improvement for random error (repeats, mean, a clearly defined edge); B1 improvement for systematic error (check against a standard / zero the ruler).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student measures 5 cm³ of antibiotic solution with a 10 cm³ measuring cylinder, which has a scale of 0.5 cm³ divisions. Suggest an improvement that would reduce the uncertainty in the volume.
parts.answer: Use a smaller pipette (for example a 5 cm³ pipette or a 1 cm³ pipette with a graduated scale) so each division is smaller relative to the volume.
parts.working: B1 use a more precise, smaller measuring instrument (pipette/syringe); B1 smaller scale divisions give a smaller percentage uncertainty.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by reliability in an experiment, and state one way to make a measurement more reliable.
parts.answer: Reliability means that the results are consistent or repeatable: similar values are obtained when the experiment is repeated under the same conditions; repeating each measurement and calculating the mean makes results more reliable.
parts.working: B1 reliability = consistency / repeatability of results under the same conditions; B1 repeat the measurements and calculate a mean (or control variables more carefully).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student measures the turbidity of bacterial cultures with a colorimeter. Identify two sources of error that could affect the absorbance readings, and suggest how each could be reduced.
parts.answer: Fingerprints or scratches on the cuvette; air bubbles in the culture; the colorimeter not zeroed with a blank; cells settling out during the reading. Reduce by wiping cuvettes and handling them by the top; mixing and tapping out bubbles; zeroing with sterile broth before each set of readings; mixing well and reading immediately.
parts.working: B1 and B2 any two sources (cuvette marks, bubbles, not zeroed, settling); B1 and B2 suitable improvements for each.

practice.stem: A student placed paper discs soaked in different antibiotics on agar plates spread with bacteria. After incubation she measured the diameter of each clear zone with a ruler. The edges of some zones were blurred and some zones were oval rather than circular.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two sources of error in measuring the clear zones and suggest an improvement for each.
parts.answer: e.g. zones are not perfect circles → measure two diameters at right angles and take the mean; edge of the clear zone is blurred → use a hand lens / measure against a dark background with a fixed criterion; ruler measured only to the nearest mm → use digital calipers; discs not equally soaked → soak for a fixed time and drain on filter paper.
parts.working: For each of two: B1 error relevant to this experiment; B1 improvement that would reduce it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why each antibiotic should be tested on three separate plates.
parts.answer: To identify anomalous results and calculate a mean, making the results more reliable.
parts.working: B1 identify anomalies / calculate mean / check repeatability.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how contamination of agar plates by airborne bacteria or fungal spores could give misleading results, and describe one way the student could detect contamination.
parts.answer: Contaminating microorganisms grow on the plates and add extra colonies or clear zones of their own, so colony counts are too high and the effect of the treatment is not measured correctly; detection by including an uninoculated control plate that is incubated alongside the others and remains free of growth.
parts.working: B1 contaminant colonies add to the count / confuse clear zones, giving false results; B1 explanation of how the results are then misleading; B1 detect with an unseeded (sterile) control plate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student used an incubator that varied by ±3 °C during an experiment. Explain how this error affects the reliability and the accuracy of the results, and suggest an improvement.
parts.answer: The variation in temperature makes the growth rates inconsistent between repeats, so results are less reliable; if the average temperature is not the intended value, the results are not accurate; an improvement is to use a water bath or a calibrated incubator with a data logger and record the temperature throughout.
parts.working: B1 variation changes growth rate, so reliability (repeatability) is reduced; B1 average temperature may not match the target, reducing accuracy; B1 improvement: calibrated incubator, water bath or data logger.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how selective reporting, such as recording only the largest clear zone on each plate, could make the conclusions of an experiment unreliable.
parts.answer: Only the largest zones are recorded, so the mean is biased upwards and the apparent effect of the antiseptic is exaggerated; the results are then not representative of all the zones measured; all zones should be measured and reported, including any that are small or absent.
parts.working: B1 biased (overestimated) mean because only high values are included; B1 results not representative / not reproducible; B1 measure and report all zones.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student tested a disinfectant on three plates only and concluded that the disinfectant kills all bacteria. Suggest two limitations of the investigation and one improvement for each.
parts.answer: Limitation 1: three plates is a small sample, so the results may not be reliable; improvement: use more replicates (for example 5 or more) and calculate the mean and spread. Limitation 2: only one bacterial species was tested, so the conclusion cannot be applied to all bacteria; improvement: test several species, including ones that are resistant.
parts.working: B1 and B2 small number of replicates and improvement; B1 and B2 one species only and improvement; (1 mark each for limitation and improvement, max 4).

practice.stem: Researchers asked 40 families in a village whether they washed their hands with soap before eating and how many times family members had had diarrhoea in the past year. They concluded that handwashing halves the risk of diarrhoea.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest three limitations of this survey that could make the conclusion unreliable.
parts.answer: Any three of: data on handwashing were self-reported (people may overstate); small sample size; households not randomly chosen; other variables (water source, sanitation, income, family size) not controlled; diarrhoea recalled from memory over a long period; cause of diarrhoea not confirmed by laboratory tests.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one improvement to the study design.
parts.answer: e.g. larger random sample; observe handwashing directly; match households for water source; confirm cases by stool tests; record cases weekly.
parts.working: B1 any valid improvement linked to a limitation in (a).

practice.stem: A student diluted a bacterial culture for plate counting. The student's dilution step used the same pipette each time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student pipetted 1.0 cm³ of a bacterial culture into a dilution tube, but the pipette delivered only 0.9 cm³ every time. Calculate the percentage error in the volume. Explain why this is a systematic error and state its effect on the colony count of a sample. Give your answer as a percentage to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 10.0 % (percentage error) — systematic because the pipette consistently delivers too little; the count appears to be 10 % too low (the bacterial concentration is underestimated by about 10 %), unless the calculation is corrected for the actual volume.
parts.working: M1 (1.0 − 0.9) ÷ 1.0 × 100 = 10.0 %; B1 systematic: same error in every reading in the same direction; B1 counts underestimated by 10 %, so the calculated concentration is too low.

practice.stem: A student weighs a sample of dried soil for a bacterial count.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A balance reads to the nearest 0.01 g. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in a mass of 0.50 g, taking the uncertainty as ±0.01 g. Explain how the percentage uncertainty could be reduced when weighing a dried sample of soil.
parts.answer: ±2 %; weigh a larger mass of soil, so the same ±0.01 g uncertainty is a smaller percentage of the total mass (or use a balance that reads to more decimal places).
parts.working: M1 0.01 ÷ 0.50 × 100 = 2.0 %; B1 use a larger sample mass; B1 or use a more precise balance (smaller smallest division).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Colonies on a plate were counted by eye. Some colonies had grown together, and small colonies were difficult to see. Evaluate this method of counting and suggest a more reliable method.
parts.answer: The method is subjective and inaccurate because merged colonies are counted as one and faint colonies are missed; counts from different observers differ. A more reliable method is to count with a grid or magnifier, mark each colony as it is counted, use a plate with 30–300 colonies, or use image analysis software with a fixed threshold; count each plate more than once.
parts.working: B1 merged colonies undercounted; B1 faint colonies missed / subjective; B1 use of a grid, marker or magnifier, or a plate with 30–300 colonies; B1 software or repeat counts by more than one person.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two groups of students incubated identical plates. One group incubated for 24 hours and the other for 48 hours. The 48-hour plates had more colonies. Explain why the time of incubation is an uncontrolled variable and how it could be controlled.
parts.answer: Incubation time affects the number of colonies visible because bacteria keep dividing, so the group with longer incubation counts more colonies even if the starting numbers are the same; this makes the comparison unfair. Control it by using the same incubation time for all plates and recording it.
parts.working: B1 longer time means more cell divisions and visible colonies; B1 this makes the groups not comparable (uncontrolled variable); B1 standardise incubation time and temperature for all plates.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student measured the mean diameter of a clear zone as 14.0 mm with a standard deviation of 1.2 mm from three plates. Explain whether the student can be confident that a second set of plates would give a mean of 14.0 mm, using the words precision, accuracy and reliability in your answer.
parts.answer: The SD of 1.2 mm shows the three values are fairly close together (fairly precise), but the student cannot be confident about the true mean from three plates: a second set could give a different mean, so the result is not yet shown to be reliable, and accuracy cannot be judged without a known value; the student should repeat with more plates and calculate the standard error of the mean.
parts.working: B1 precision: SD of 1.2 mm indicates a fairly precise set of values; B1 accuracy: unknown from three plates; B1 reliability: needs repeat sets; B1 more replicates and standard error would give a more reliable estimate of the mean.

practice.stem: A student compares the antibacterial effect of four brands of mouthwash using paper discs on agar plates spread with a harmless bacterium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent and dependent variables.
parts.answer: Independent: type of mouthwash. Dependent: diameter (or area) of the clear zone around each disc.
parts.working: B1 IV type of mouthwash; B1 DV clear zone diameter / area.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two variables that should be standardised and how each could be controlled.
parts.answer: e.g. volume of bacterial culture – use a pipette to spread 0.1 cm³; temperature of incubation – incubator at 25 °C; size of discs – cut with the same hole punch; soaking time – 10 minutes timed with a stopwatch.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a variable with its method of control (max 2).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a suitable control and explain its purpose.
parts.answer: Disc soaked in sterile distilled water, to show that the paper disc itself does not inhibit growth.
parts.working: B1 disc in sterile water and showing any clear zone is due to the mouthwash.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student compares the growth of bacteria on agar plates kept at 25 °C for 24 hours with plates kept at 25 °C for 48 hours. State one control variable and explain why it must be controlled.
parts.answer: Control variable: the number and volume of bacteria spread on each plate (or the type of agar); it must be controlled so that any difference in colony count is due to the incubation time, not to different starting numbers.
parts.working: B1 named control variable (e.g. starting inoculum, agar type, temperature); B1 it must be kept constant so that only the independent variable affects the result.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A trial tests whether a new antiseptic reduces infection after surgery. One group receives the antiseptic and a second group receives a placebo. Explain why the placebo group is needed.
parts.answer: It acts as a control: it allows the effect of the antiseptic to be separated from other factors (such as the effect of being treated or of the surgery itself), so any difference in infection rates can be attributed to the antiseptic.
parts.working: B1 provides a baseline / control to compare against; B1 so that any difference in outcome is due to the antiseptic and not to other factors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student tests three disinfectants on a lawn of bacteria using discs. Explain why a disc soaked in distilled water is placed on the same plate.
parts.answer: It is a negative control; it shows the clear zone (or lack of one) produced by the disc and the solvent alone, so that any clear zone from the disinfectant can be interpreted as due to the disinfectant.
parts.working: B1 negative control with no active agent; B1 allows the effect of the disinfectant to be separated from the effect of the disc/water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student measures the turbidity of cultures of a bacterium as they grow. Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable if the student is testing the effect of pH on growth.
parts.answer: Independent variable: pH of the broth; dependent variable: turbidity (absorbance) of the culture, which indicates bacterial density.
parts.working: B1 IV = pH of the broth; B1 DV = absorbance / turbidity (bacterial population).

practice.stem: Health researchers compared the number of cases of measles in children who had received two doses of measles vaccine and in children who had not, in a district of Balochistan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this study.
parts.answer: Independent: whether children received the vaccine (vaccinated or not). Dependent: number / percentage of children who developed measles.
parts.working: B1 IV vaccination status; B1 DV incidence / percentage with measles.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two variables that the researchers should try to match between the two groups and explain why matching is necessary.
parts.answer: Any two of: age; nutrition / health status; living conditions (crowding); area / exposure to cases; access to health care; plus explanation: these also affect the chance of catching measles, so must be similar for a valid comparison.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid variables; B1 explanation that they could affect the dependent variable / make the comparison fair.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student investigates whether storing bread in a sealed bag reduces mould growth. Identify the independent variable, the dependent variable and two variables that must be controlled.
parts.answer: Independent variable: whether the bread is sealed or open (or humidity inside the bag); dependent variable: area of mould after a fixed number of days; control variables: starting mould spores (inoculum), type and size of bread slice, temperature and light.
parts.working: B1 IV: sealed or not (storage condition); B1 DV: mould area / number of days to mould; B1 and B2 any two controlled variables (inoculum, bread type, size, temperature, time).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A survey found that children who drank water from a well had more diarrhoea than those who drank piped water. Name one confounding variable that could explain this, and state how a researcher could control it.
parts.answer: Confounding variable: household sanitation (or family income); researchers could match children by household income or sanitation level, or measure the variable and include it in the analysis.
parts.working: B1 named confounding variable (income, sanitation, hand washing, age); B1 explain why it affects both water source and illness; B1 control by matching, stratifying or measuring and adjusting for it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In an experiment on the effect of a disinfectant on bacteria, a student used a different batch of agar for each concentration. Explain why this is a poor design, and state what the student should have done instead.
parts.answer: Different batches of agar may differ in nutrient content, thickness or pH, which would change bacterial growth and clear zone size, so differences could be due to the agar rather than the disinfectant; the student should use one batch of agar for all concentrations.
parts.working: B1 agar batches differ, so an uncontrolled variable is introduced; B1 this could change growth or zone size; B1 use the same batch (and pour plates together) for all treatments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student uses a sterile cotton-wool swab to spread a suspension of bacteria on agar, and each plate receives a different volume of suspension. Identify the variable that is not controlled and explain its effect on the results of an antibiotic disc test.
parts.answer: The volume (and so the density) of bacteria on the lawn is uncontrolled; a denser lawn grows more thickly, which can reduce the clear zone, so differences in clear zone size may reflect the lawn density rather than the antibiotic.
parts.working: B1 inoculum volume/density of the lawn is uncontrolled; B1 denser lawns give smaller zones (or uneven growth); B1 so differences cannot be attributed to the antibiotic alone; standardise inoculum.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student changed both the incubation temperature and the type of agar at the same time, and then concluded that temperature was the reason for the difference in growth. Explain the error in the design and describe how the investigation should be redesigned.
parts.answer: Two independent variables were changed at once, so the effect of temperature cannot be separated from the effect of the agar; redesign by changing only the temperature while keeping the agar the same (or changing only the agar at one temperature), so that each variable has its own controlled comparison.
parts.working: B1 two variables changed together (confounding), so the cause cannot be identified; B1 explain that only one variable should change; B1 redesign with a fixed agar and a range of temperatures; B1 keep all other variables constant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An antiseptic trial uses a double-blind design. Explain what is meant by double-blind, and describe how this design reduces bias in the recording of infection outcomes.
parts.answer: Neither the patients nor the staff who record and assess the infection outcome know who received the antiseptic and who received the placebo; this prevents expectation effects from influencing the reported symptoms or the assessment of the infection, so the outcome data are less biased.
parts.working: B1 neither patients nor researchers/assessors know the treatment allocation; B1 prevents patients' expectations affecting reported symptoms; B1 prevents the assessor's expectations affecting the classification of infection; B1 reduces bias in the results.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student measures the number of bacteria in river water at five sites. The sites differ in distance from a sewage outlet, depth and water flow. Identify the independent variable, and explain how the other two factors should be controlled or taken into account.
