parts.answer: Independent variable: distance from the sewage outlet; depth and water flow are uncontrolled variables that could affect bacterial counts, so they should be measured at each site and kept as similar as possible (for example, by sampling at the same depth and time), or the data should be analysed using them as covariates.
parts.working: B1 IV = distance from outlet; B1 depth and flow are uncontrolled and could change counts; B1 measure and record them; B1 keep them as constant as possible (same depth, same time, same flow) or account for them in the analysis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a water bath could be used to keep the incubation temperature constant in an investigation into the growth of a bacterium. Explain why the temperature of the water bath should be checked during the experiment.
parts.answer: Place the tubes or plates in a water bath set at the chosen temperature; use a thermostat and a thermometer in the bath, stir the water, and place tubes in a rack so that they are all surrounded by water; check the temperature regularly during the experiment because the bath can drift or the room temperature can change, which would change growth rates and invalidate the comparison.
parts.working: B1 water bath at fixed set temperature with thermostat; B1 thermometer and stirring so temperature is uniform; B1 plates or tubes fully immersed/surrounded; B1 check regularly because temperature can change and affect growth rates.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher tested whether a herbal extract reduces bacterial growth in a patient group. Explain why the researcher must keep the patient's diet, age and other medicines as similar as possible between groups, and describe one way to achieve this.
parts.answer: These factors could affect bacterial growth or immunity independently of the extract, so they could confound the results; the groups should be matched on age, diet and other medicines, or patients should be randomly allocated so that such factors are evenly spread between groups, and any remaining differences recorded.
parts.working: B1 these are confounding variables that could affect the outcome; B1 they could cause a difference independently of the extract; B1 matching groups on these factors; B1 random allocation spreads unknown factors evenly and/or record them for analysis.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the sample standard deviation of the five clear-zone diameters 4, 6, 5, 7 and 8 mm. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 mean = 6.0; M1 sum of squared deviations = 4 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 4 = 10; M1 √(10 ÷ (5 − 1)) = 1.58 mm.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard error of the mean for a sample of 16 bacterial counts with a standard deviation of 2.4 units. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why the standard error is smaller than the standard deviation.
parts.answer: The standard error is divided by √n, so it becomes smaller as the sample size increases; the SE describes how precisely the mean is estimated, not the spread of individual values.
parts.working: B1 SE = SD/√n, so it decreases with sample size; it measures uncertainty in the mean, not the spread of the data.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher compares the mean healing time of wounds treated with two antiseptics. The healing times for each group are normally distributed and the two groups are independent. Name the most suitable statistical test and state the null hypothesis.
parts.answer: An unpaired (independent samples) t-test; null hypothesis: there is no difference in the mean healing time between the two antiseptic groups.
parts.working: B1 unpaired / independent-samples t-test (normal data, two independent groups); B1 null hypothesis of no difference in mean healing time.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 95 % confidence interval for the mean number of infections is given as 3.2 to 5.8 per month. Explain what this interval tells you.
parts.answer: We are 95 % confident that the true (population) mean number of infections per month lies between 3.2 and 5.8; the interval reflects the uncertainty in estimating the mean from a sample.
parts.working: B1 95 % confident that the true population mean lies within the range; B1 the interval reflects uncertainty from sampling (narrower with larger samples).

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Clear zone diameters (mm) around eight discs soaked in garlic extract on plates of a harmless bacterium:
14.5, 16.0, 15.5, 13.0, 17.0, 15.0, 14.0, 16.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean diameter of the clear zone.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The standard deviation is 1.33 mm. Calculate the standard error, SE = s ÷ √n. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The 95 % confidence interval for a second extract was 11.2 to 12.3 mm. Calculate the 95 % confidence interval (mean ± 2 × SE) for this extract and state whether the difference between the two extracts is likely to be significant.
parts.answer: 14.2 to 16.1 mm; the intervals do not overlap, so the difference is likely to be significant.
parts.working: B1 15.19 ± 0.94 = 14.2–16.1 mm; B1 no overlap with 11.2–12.3 so difference likely significant.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: A student counted bacteria on the fingertips of 20 volunteers before and after washing with soap, and carried out a paired t-test on the differences.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A t-test comparing the number of bacteria on hands before and after washing gave t = 2.45 with 19 degrees of freedom. The critical value at the 5 % level (two-tailed) is 2.093. State and justify a conclusion.
parts.answer: t = 2.45 is greater than the critical value 2.093, so the difference is significant at the 5 % level; reject the null hypothesis: the mean number of bacteria changed after washing.
parts.working: B1 compare calculated t (2.45) with critical value (2.093); B1 significant, so reject H₀ and conclude that washing changed the number of bacteria.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the conclusion that would have been reached if t had been 1.80.
parts.answer: 1.80 is less than 2.093, so the difference is not significant; the null hypothesis would not be rejected.
parts.working: B1 not significant; do not reject H₀ (there is not enough evidence of a difference).

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: Eight sites along a river were ranked by distance from a sewage outlet and by the number of coliform bacteria per 100 cm³ of water. The Spearman's rank correlation coefficient was calculated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient was calculated for eight pairs of values, and rs = −0.95. The critical value from a table at the 5 % level (two-tailed) for n = 8 is 0.738. Interpret the result.
parts.answer: rs = −0.95 is a strong negative correlation between the two variables (as one increases, the other decreases); because −0.95 is more negative than the critical value (−0.738), the correlation is significant at the 5 % level.
parts.working: B1 negative correlation; B1 strong (close to −1); B1 significant because |rs| > 0.738, so reject H₀ of no correlation.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A chi-squared test on counts of two species in three habitats gave χ² = 6.8 with 2 degrees of freedom. The critical value at the 5 % level is 5.99. State the conclusion.
parts.answer: χ² = 6.8 is greater than 5.99, so the null hypothesis of no association is rejected: the species is not distributed independently of the habitat.
parts.working: B1 6.8 > 5.99 so reject H₀; B1 there is a significant association between species and habitat (not independent).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why a chi-squared test should not be used if the expected value in any cell is less than 5.
parts.answer: The chi-squared approximation is unreliable with very small expected values, so the test statistic may not follow the chi-squared distribution.
parts.working: B1 small expected values make the chi-squared approximation inaccurate.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two bars on a graph show means with error bars of ±SE. The mean and SE for the first group are 14.2 mm ± 0.8 mm and for the second group 12.9 mm ± 1.0 mm. Explain whether the bars overlap and what this suggests about the difference.
parts.answer: The ranges (13.4–15.0 mm and 11.9–13.9 mm) overlap, so the difference between the means may not be significant at the usual level; the data do not give clear evidence of a real difference, and a formal test is needed.
parts.working: B1 calculate ranges of ±1 SE: 13.4–15.0 and 11.9–13.9; B1 they overlap; B1 overlap suggests no clear difference, but a formal test (e.g. t-test) should be used to decide significance.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student tested 20 different antiseptics for a significant effect at the 5 % significance level. Calculate the number of antiseptics expected to give a significant result by chance alone if none of them has any real effect. Explain why this matters.
parts.answer: 20 × 0.05 = 1 antiseptic expected to show a significant result by chance (a Type I error); reporting only the significant results would be misleading, so repeats or a correction for multiple testing are needed.
parts.working: M1 20 × 0.05 = 1; B1 Type I error: a false positive; B1 the result must be checked with replication or a multiple-testing correction.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
The number of malaria cases in a rural health centre was recorded in each season of one year.
Winter (Dec–Feb): 48; spring (Mar–May): 112; summer and monsoon (Jun–Aug): 186; autumn (Sep–Nov): 74.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a null hypothesis for this test.
parts.answer: There is no difference between the numbers of malaria cases in the four seasons (cases are evenly spread through the year); any difference is due to chance.
parts.working: B1 no (significant) difference between observed number of cases in each season / cases distributed equally.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of χ² using χ² = Σ (O − E)²/E. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of χ² at p = 0.05 for 3 degrees of freedom is 7.82. Explain what the result shows.
parts.answer: χ² (103.0) is much greater than 7.82, so the null hypothesis is rejected; the difference between seasons is significant (p < 0.05) – malaria cases are not evenly spread through the year.
parts.working: B1 χ² > critical value (df = 4 − 1 = 3); B1 reject null hypothesis / significant difference between seasons, not due to chance.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher tests whether a vaccine is associated with infection. Vaccinated: 15 infected, 45 not infected. Unvaccinated: 28 infected, 32 not infected. Calculate the chi-squared value and state the expected count for vaccinated people who were infected. Give the chi-squared value to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Expected count for vaccinated and infected = 60 × 43 ÷ 120 = 21.5; χ² = 6.13 (df = 1), which is greater than the 5 % critical value 3.84, so there is a significant association between vaccination and infection: vaccinated people were infected less often than expected.
parts.working: M1 row total × column total ÷ grand total = 60 × 43 ÷ 120 = 21.5; M1 sum of (O − E)² ÷ E across all four cells = 6.13; B1 compare with the critical value 3.84 (df = 1) and reject H₀; B1 significant association, with fewer infections than expected in vaccinated people.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Eight pairs of values were recorded: the distance from a sewage outlet in metres and the number of coliform bacteria per 100 cm³: (10, 900), (20, 700), (30, 820), (40, 450), (50, 500), (60, 300), (70, 260), (80, 120). Calculate the Spearman's rank correlation coefficient. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: B1 rank both variables (1 = lowest); B1 d values, with d² totalling 164; M1 rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ n(n² − 1) = 1 − 984 ÷ 504; A1 = −0.95.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student measured the mass (g) of six samples of dried soil: 1.42, 1.38, 1.51, 1.45, 1.40 and 1.47. Calculate the mean, the sample standard deviation and the 95 % confidence interval (mean ± 2 × SE). Give each answer to 2 decimal places.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student's results give p = 0.04 for the difference between two antiseptics. Explain what this value means, and explain why the student should not conclude that there is a 96 % probability that the antiseptic works.
parts.answer: p = 0.04 means that, if there were no real difference, the probability of obtaining a difference at least as large as the one observed is 4 %; it is not the probability that the hypothesis is true; so 96 % is not a valid interpretation; the result is significant at the 5 % level only if the test assumptions are met.
parts.working: B1 p is the probability of results at least this extreme if H₀ is true; B1 it is not the probability that H₀ or the antiseptic works; B1 significance at the 5 % level depends on test assumptions and sample design.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a village of 1600 children, 1240 children received the full course of a vaccine. Calculate the percentage of children vaccinated. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bacterium population of 400 cells grew to 3200 cells in 3 hours. Calculate the number of generations, and the mean doubling time in minutes.
parts.answer: 3 generations; 60 minutes per doubling (mean doubling time).
parts.working: M1 2ⁿ = 8, so n = 3 generations; M1 180 min ÷ 3 = 60 min; A1 doubling time = 60 min.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bacterium is 2.5 µm long. Convert this length to mm, and to nm. (1 µm = 10⁻³ mm; 1 µm = 1000 nm.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage inhibition of growth caused by the disinfectant, using the colony counts: control plate 240 colonies, disinfectant plate 36 colonies. Use the formula (control − treated) ÷ control × 100.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A child weighs 18 kg. The total daily antibiotic dose is 15 mg per kg of body mass, split into three equal doses given every 8 hours. Calculate the mass of each dose and the total mass given in one day.
parts.answer: Each dose is 90 mg; total 270 mg per day.
parts.working: M1 15 × 18 = 270 mg total per day; M1 270 ÷ 3 = 90 mg per dose; A1 total 270 mg per day.

practice.stem: A district recorded 960 new cases of a disease in 2015, when its population was 1 200 000, and 735 cases in 2024, when its population was 1 500 000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the incidence of the disease per 100 000 people in each year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in incidence between 2015 and 2024.
parts.answer: −38.8 % (a decrease of 38.8 %)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the change in the total number of cases gives a misleading impression of the change in risk of infection.
parts.answer: The population grew, so the number of cases per person (the risk) fell more than the total number of cases suggests.
parts.working: B1 population size changed, so cases per 100 000 is the fair measure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a screening programme, 84 of 1200 people tested positive for a bacterial infection. Calculate the prevalence as a percentage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why prevalence is not the same as incidence.
parts.answer: Prevalence is the proportion of people who have the disease at a given time (new and existing cases), whereas incidence is the rate of new cases over a period of time.
parts.working: B1 prevalence counts all current cases, incidence counts only new cases in a time period.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A culture of bacteria increased from 2.0 × 10⁴ cells per cm³ at the start to 6.4 × 10⁵ cells per cm³ after 4 hours. Calculate the number of generations and the doubling time in minutes.
parts.answer: 5 generations; doubling time 48 minutes.
parts.working: M1 6.4 × 10⁵ ÷ 2.0 × 10⁴ = 32 = 2⁵, so 5 generations; M1 240 min ÷ 5 = 48 min; A1 doubling time = 48 min.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 50 cm³ sample of river water was filtered through a membrane and 37 colonies grew. Calculate the number of colony-forming units per cm³. Give your answer to 2 decimal places, and state how many colony-forming units would be expected in a 100 cm³ sample if the same concentration applied.
parts.answer: 0.74 cfu per cm³; 74 cfu in 100 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bacterial population doubles every 25 minutes. Starting from 1000 cells, calculate the number of minutes needed to reach 1 000 000 cells. Give your answer to the nearest minute.
parts.answer: 249 minutes (about 4 hours 9 minutes).

practice.stem: A water sample from a village well was diluted in a serial dilution so that the final tube was a 10⁻⁵ dilution of the original. 0.1 cm³ of this tube was spread on nutrient agar and incubated. 47 colonies grew.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of bacteria per cm³ in the original water sample. Give your answer in standard form.
parts.answer: 4.7 × 10⁷ bacteria per cm³
parts.working: M1 colonies per cm³ of diluted sample = 47 / 0.1 = 470; M1 × dilution factor 10⁵; A1 4.7 × 10⁷ per cm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one assumption made in this calculation.
parts.answer: Each colony grew from a single bacterium / all bacteria were able to grow on the agar.
parts.working: B1 one colony = one cell (cells not clumped) or all viable cells grow.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the plate from the 10⁻³ dilution, which had colonies that had merged into one another, was not used.
parts.answer: Overlapping colonies cannot be counted accurately.
parts.working: B1 colonies merge / too many to count individually.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Three plates were counted after 10⁻³ dilution of a sample: 84, 92 and 88 colonies. The volume spread on each plate was 0.1 cm³. Calculate the mean number of colonies per plate and the number of bacteria per cm³ in the original sample. Give your answer in standard form to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: Mean = 88 colonies; 88 ÷ 0.1 = 880 per cm³ in the 10⁻³ dilution; × 1000 = 8.8 × 10⁵ bacteria per cm³.
parts.working: M1 (84 + 92 + 88) ÷ 3 = 88; M1 88 ÷ 0.1 = 880 cells per cm³ in the diluted sample; M1 × 10³ dilution factor = 8.8 × 10⁵ per cm³; A1 standard form.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A stock disinfectant is 10 % (w/v). Calculate the volume of stock needed to make 200 cm³ of a 0.5 % (w/v) solution, and the volume of water to add. Show your working.
parts.answer: 10 cm³ of stock and 190 cm³ of water.
parts.working: M1 C₁V₁ = C₂V₂, so V₁ = 0.5 × 200 ÷ 10; M1 = 10 cm³ of stock; A1 add 190 cm³ of water to make 200 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student measures the concentration of a bacterial suspension by absorbance. The calibration data show that absorbance 0.40 corresponds to 2.0 × 10⁸ cells per cm³ and absorbance 0.80 corresponds to 4.0 × 10⁸ cells per cm³. Assuming a straight-line relationship through zero, calculate the concentration for an absorbance of 0.60. Give your answer in standard form.
parts.answer: 3.0 × 10⁸ cells per cm³
parts.working: M1 gradient = 2.0 × 10⁸ ÷ 0.40 = 5.0 × 10⁸ per unit absorbance; A1 0.60 × 5.0 × 10⁸ = 3.0 × 10⁸ cells per cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The mean diameter of clear zones with antibiotic A is 18.4 mm and with antibiotic B is 15.2 mm. Calculate the percentage difference between the two means, using the mean of antibiotic B as the reference value. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. Explain why this percentage does not, on its own, show that antibiotic A is clinically more useful.
parts.answer: 21.1 % larger (or (18.4 − 15.2) ÷ 15.2 × 100 = 21.1 %); clear-zone size in agar does not show how the antibiotic would act in the body, its toxicity, cost, or the resistance of the target bacterium.
parts.working: M1 (18.4 − 15.2) = 3.2; M1 3.2 ÷ 15.2 × 100 = 21.1 %; B1 zone size in vitro does not measure the antibiotic's effect in patients (absorption, toxicity, dose); B1 resistance patterns and cost also matter.

practice.stem: A student investigates whether honey from the Swat valley inhibits the growth of bacteria. Wells are cut in agar plates spread with bacteria and filled with honey diluted to different concentrations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a hypothesis that could be tested in this investigation.
parts.answer: The greater the concentration of honey, the larger the area of the clear zone around the well (the fewer bacteria grow).
parts.working: B1 testable statement linking honey concentration to bacterial growth / clear zone size, with direction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the results you would expect if manuka-type honey contains an antibacterial substance in addition to its high sugar concentration, compared with a sugar solution of the same concentration. Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Honey would give larger clear zones than sugar solution of the same concentration, because both cause water loss from bacteria by osmosis, but honey also contains an extra antibacterial substance.
parts.working: B1 larger zones with honey than with sugar solution; B1 osmotic effect is the same in both so the extra inhibition is due to the antibacterial substance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student wants to test whether a soap solution reduces the number of bacteria on a surface. State a suitable hypothesis that could be tested in this investigation.
parts.answer: As the concentration of soap solution increases, the number of bacteria remaining on the surface decreases.
parts.working: B1 a testable statement linking the independent variable (soap concentration) and the dependent variable (bacterial number) in a direction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bacterium is grown in broth at pH 2 and at pH 7, with all other conditions the same. Predict the difference in the growth of the bacterium and give a biological reason.
parts.answer: Growth will be much lower at pH 2 than at pH 7, because extreme acidity denatures the bacterium's enzymes and damages its cell membrane, so fewer cells can reproduce.
parts.working: B1 prediction: lower growth at pH 2 (near-optimal growth at pH 7); B1 reason: acid denatures enzymes/proteins and disrupts the membrane.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a null hypothesis for an investigation into whether lemon juice affects the growth of yeast cells.
parts.answer: There is no difference in the growth of yeast between lemon juice and the control (no lemon juice).
parts.working: B1 states no difference / no effect of lemon juice on yeast growth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one prediction, in an if–then form, that would support the alternative hypothesis.
parts.answer: If lemon juice inhibits yeast growth, then fewer colonies (or a smaller increase in turbidity) will appear in the lemon juice treatment than in the control.
parts.working: B1 if … then … form linking lemon juice to lower growth than control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a student should state the hypothesis before collecting data.
parts.answer: The hypothesis gives a clear aim and a prediction, so the student knows which variables to change, which to measure and what results would support or reject the idea; this stops the results being interpreted to fit the expected outcome.
parts.working: B1 gives a clear, testable prediction that guides the design; B1 prevents bias when interpreting results / defines what would count as support or rejection.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bacteriophage kills only one species of bacterium. Clear plaques form on a lawn of Escherichia coli but not on a lawn of Salmonella. Predict the result if the same phage is added to a lawn of a third species, and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: No clear plaques will form on the third species, because the phage can only attach to bacteria that carry the specific surface receptor proteins it recognises; a different species lacks these receptors, so the phage cannot enter or replicate in its cells.
parts.working: B1 prediction: no plaques (for a different species); B1 explanation: specificity of attachment to surface receptor proteins; B1 phage cannot enter/replicate in cells lacking the receptor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher predicts that increasing the dose of an antibiotic will reduce the number of resistant colonies on a plate. Explain why this prediction may be incorrect at very low doses.
parts.answer: At very low (sub-lethal) doses, the antibiotic may not kill the sensitive bacteria but selects for and allows resistant bacteria to survive and reproduce, so the number of resistant colonies can increase.
parts.working: B1 at low doses, sensitive bacteria are only partly inhibited; B1 resistant bacteria survive and multiply (selection); B1 so resistant colony numbers may rise at low doses, reversing the trend.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two hypotheses are proposed to explain why dengue cases rise after heavy rain: (1) the rain increases the number of mosquito breeding sites; (2) people spend more time indoors and so are bitten more. State which hypothesis is easier to test in a school investigation, and explain how a prediction would be tested.
parts.answer: Hypothesis 1 is easier to test: a student can count mosquito larvae in containers of rainwater before and after rain at several sites; a prediction is that larvae numbers increase after rain; hypothesis 2 is harder because it involves human behaviour and would require surveys.
parts.working: B1 hypothesis 1 identified as more testable; B1 a measurable prediction (more larvae in containers after rain); B1 method (count larvae at sites over time); B1 hypothesis 2 involves behaviour that is hard to measure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the effect of incubating larvae of Aedes mosquitoes at 38 °C instead of 25 °C, and explain your prediction in terms of enzyme action.
parts.answer: The larvae will develop more slowly or die, because at 38 °C enzymes in the larvae become denatured (their tertiary structure changes), so metabolic reactions cannot proceed normally and growth is impaired.
parts.working: B1 prediction: slower development or death at 38 °C; B1 enzymes denature at high temperature; B1 metabolic reactions/growth slow or stop.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bacterium has an enzyme that makes peptidoglycan cross-links in its cell wall. A new compound is found to bind to this enzyme and stop it working. Predict the effect of this compound on bacteria that are dividing, and on bacteria in a stationary phase, and explain each prediction.
parts.answer: Dividing bacteria will be affected strongly: they cannot build new cell walls for their daughter cells, so the cells may lyse or fail to divide; stationary-phase bacteria make little new peptidoglycan, so the compound will have much less effect on them.
parts.working: B1 dividing cells: cannot make new wall; B1 these cells lyse or stop dividing; B1 stationary cells synthesise little wall so are less affected; B1 explanation linked to growth-dependent cell wall synthesis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a city, the proportion of children vaccinated against measles is 70 % in one district and 95 % in another. Predict how the number of measles infections in a large outbreak would differ, and explain how herd immunity leads to your prediction.
parts.answer: More infections in the 70 % district, because a larger proportion of susceptible children allows the virus to spread between people; in the 95 % district, the high level of immunity (above the herd immunity threshold for measles, which is high, about 92–95 %) limits spread so that chains of transmission are interrupted.
parts.working: B1 prediction: more infections at 70 %; B1 explanation: more susceptible people allows continued spread; B1 herd immunity threshold for measles is high; B1 at 95 % most chains of infection are broken/fewer susceptible people to infect.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Thirty wells sampled in a village show that wells close to pit latrines are more often contaminated with E. coli than wells far from latrines. Suggest a hypothesis that accounts for this pattern and state a prediction that would test your hypothesis.
parts.answer: Hypothesis: faecal material from latrines seeps into groundwater and contaminates nearby wells; prediction: contamination will decrease with increasing distance from the latrine, and wells that are sealed or lined will show less contamination.
parts.working: B1 a testable hypothesis about transport of faecal bacteria through soil/groundwater; B1 a prediction relating distance to contamination; B1 a further prediction (e.g. lined or sealed wells contaminated less).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student suggests that tuberculosis cases are higher in crowded rooms because the bacteria spread by droplets. Write a prediction that could be tested with a comparison of two groups, and explain what result would make you reject the student's hypothesis.
parts.answer: Prediction: households with more people per room will have a higher proportion of TB infections among contacts than households with fewer people per room; rejection: if the infection rate is the same at all crowding levels (no difference, or a difference that does not follow the crowding trend), the hypothesis would be rejected.
parts.working: B1 prediction stated as a comparison of groups; B1 identifies a measurable outcome (infection rate); B1 rejection criterion (no or inconsistent difference); B1 explains that results must be compared with a control or adjusted for other factors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a prediction should be stated before data are collected, and why a single unexpected result does not automatically mean the hypothesis is false.
parts.answer: A prior prediction avoids bias in interpretation; a single unexpected result may be caused by error, anomalies, poor controls or sampling variation; repeats and statistical testing are needed before rejecting a hypothesis; a hypothesis may be modified rather than discarded.
parts.working: B1 avoids post hoc fitting of results; B1 unexpected result may be an error or chance; B1 repeats and statistical tests needed; B1 hypothesis may be refined rather than rejected.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher predicts that the number of new cases of a waterborne disease will fall by at least half after a new water-treatment plant is installed. Write a suitable null hypothesis for this prediction, and state the type of statistical comparison needed to test it.
parts.answer: Null hypothesis: the new water-treatment plant does not change the number of new cases (the case rate is the same before and after installation); test: compare case rates before and after installation (or between communities with and without the plant), using a chi-squared test on the counts or a comparison of rates with a measure of uncertainty, such as a confidence interval.
parts.working: B1 a null hypothesis of no change (or no change of the stated size); B1 identifies a comparison of before and after or between groups; B1 names an appropriate statistical test.

practice.stem:
Set 1: diameter of clear zones around five different antibiotics.
Set 2: number of new cases of dengue fever in a city each week for 12 weeks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of graph that should be drawn for each data set. Explain each choice.
parts.answer: Set 1: bar chart, because the independent variable (type of antibiotic) is categoric / discontinuous. Set 2: line graph, because both variables (time and number of cases) are continuous.
parts.working: B1 bar chart for categoric data; B1 line graph for continuous data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the line graph for Set 2 should be drawn.
parts.answer: Time on the x-axis, number of new cases on the y-axis; axes labelled with units; linear scale using more than half the grid; points plotted accurately as small crosses; points joined with ruled straight lines (point to point) as intermediate values are not known.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: independent variable (week) on x-axis; both axes fully labelled with units; even scale using most of the grid; points plotted precisely (× or ⊙); point-to-point ruled lines (no extrapolation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the most suitable type of graph for each data set: (1) the percentage of isolates that are resistant to five antibiotics at one time; (2) the number of TB cases recorded each year for ten years.
parts.answer: (1) bar chart (separate categories, percentages); (2) line graph (continuous time, trends over time).
parts.working: B1 bar chart for separate categories; B1 line graph for time series.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write suitable axis labels, including units, for a graph of bacterial growth (absorbance) over time. Suggest a suitable scale for the x-axis if the experiment runs for 12 hours.
parts.answer: x-axis: time (hours), 0 to 12 with divisions of 1 or 2 hours; y-axis: absorbance at 600 nm (no units, or arbitrary units), starting at zero.
parts.working: B1 x-axis labelled 'time (hours)' with an even scale covering 0–12; B1 y-axis labelled 'absorbance at 600 nm' (or bacterial density) starting from zero or a suitable value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student plots the diameter of clear zones against antibiotic concentration. Points are (1, 9), (2, 12), (4, 15), (8, 15), (16, 22). Identify the point that does not fit the general pattern of the others, and suggest why it might be an error.
parts.answer: The point (16, 22) does not fit the pattern (the trend from the other points levels off around 15 mm); it may be a measurement error, a different disc, or an incorrect concentration.
parts.working: B1 identifies (16, 22) as anomalous (or any clear-cut reason it differs from the trend, e.g. too high compared with the levelled trend); B1 suggests a measurement, recording or preparation error and that it should be repeated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Twenty clear-zone diameters were measured: 4 zones were 6–8 mm, 7 zones 9–11 mm, 6 zones 12–14 mm and 3 zones 15–17 mm. State the type of graph that should be drawn, and explain how the bars should be drawn.
parts.answer: A histogram; the bars should touch because the data are continuous; the x-axis shows the diameter classes with equal class widths (3 mm); the y-axis shows frequency (the number of zones).
parts.working: B1 histogram (continuous data); B1 bars touching with no gaps; B1 equal class widths with frequency on the y-axis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two points on the line of best fit for absorbance (y-axis) against time in hours (x-axis) for a bacterial culture treated with a disinfectant are (2.0 h, 0.84) and (6.0 h, 0.20). Calculate the gradient of the straight line through these two points, including its sign and units.
parts.answer: −0.16 absorbance units per hour
parts.working: M1 gradient = (0.20 − 0.84) ÷ (6.0 − 2.0); A1 = −0.16 absorbance units per hour (the absorbance falls with time).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what the error bars on a bar chart of mean values show, and state what it means if two sets of error bars overlap.
parts.answer: The error bars show the spread of the data (for example standard deviation) or the uncertainty of the mean (for example standard error or a 95 % confidence interval); overlapping error bars suggest the difference between the means may not be significant, so a statistical test is needed before concluding there is a difference.
parts.working: B1 error bars show variability or uncertainty of the mean (SD, SE or CI); B1 state which measure is used; B1 overlap suggests no clear difference, but this must be tested statistically.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student plotted a line graph of the number of cholera cases against month, with points joined by straight lines. Explain why it is useful to show the line of best fit or the trend rather than only joining each point, and identify one feature of the graph you would expect the student to label.
parts.answer: Joining each point shows the random variation between months; a trend line shows the overall pattern more clearly and can show the direction of change or seasonality; the graph should be labelled with the units, months on the x-axis and the number of cases on the y-axis, with a title.
parts.working: B1 trend line shows overall pattern / reduces effect of random variation; B1 explains the advantage (direction, seasonality); B1 labels: units, axis titles or title.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The bacterial counts in a culture are 1 × 10², 1 × 10⁴, 1 × 10⁶ and 1 × 10⁸ cells per cm³ at four times. Explain why a logarithmic scale on the y-axis is useful, and state the value of log₁₀ for the last count.
parts.answer: A log scale compresses very large ranges of values so that all points can be shown and the exponential growth appears as a straight line; log₁₀(1 × 10⁸) = 8.
parts.working: B1 log scale allows a very large range to be plotted on the same graph; B1 exponential growth looks linear on a log scale; B1 log₁₀(10⁸) = 8.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student has plotted the mean number of colonies against dilution on a graph with points joined by straight lines. Identify two improvements to the graph.
parts.answer: Add error bars (SD or SE) to show variation; add a title and label the axes with units; use a suitable scale and a line of best fit or smooth curve instead of joining the points directly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: error bars; labelled axes with units; title; suitable scale; line of best fit or smooth curve rather than joined points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student measured clear-zone diameters for 40 discs and used intervals of 1 mm to draw a histogram. The results ranged from 6 mm to 18 mm. Suggest a better choice of class width and explain why.
parts.answer: A class width of 2 or 3 mm would give a more manageable number of bars (about 4 to 6), so that the shape of the distribution can be seen; a width of 1 mm produces many bars with very few values in each, which makes the pattern hard to see.
parts.working: B1 a suitable class width of about 2–3 mm; B1 yields around 4–6 classes; B1 too narrow classes make the distribution unclear.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A graph of the growth of a bacterial population over 24 hours shows four phases. Describe each of the four phases (lag, log or exponential, stationary, death) and explain why growth changes in the stationary phase.
parts.answer: Lag: little growth as cells adapt to the medium and synthesise enzymes; log/exponential: rapid division, doubling at a constant rate while nutrients are plentiful; stationary: birth rate equals death rate as nutrients run out and waste accumulates; death: population declines as nutrients are exhausted and waste levels are toxic.
parts.working: B1 lag phase described; B1 log phase: rapid, constant-rate doubling; B1 stationary phase: no net growth; B1 death phase: numbers fall; B1 explanation of stationary phase: nutrient depletion and accumulation of waste; B1 linked to limiting factors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A table shows the incidence of a disease in five districts, but the incidence values are given as percentages that do not sum to 100 %. Explain why the student should not present these values as a pie chart, and suggest an alternative graph.
parts.answer: The values are not parts of a single total (they are rates in different populations), so a pie chart would be misleading; a bar chart of rates per 100 000 for each district would show the comparison correctly.
parts.working: B1 values are not parts of one whole; B1 pie chart would misrepresent the comparison; B1 bar chart of rates per 100 000 (or similar) is suitable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A scatter graph of the relationship between water temperature and the time taken for Aedes larvae to pupate shows a curve, not a straight line. Explain how the student should draw the curve, and why a straight line of best fit would give a misleading result.
parts.answer: The student should draw a smooth curve that passes through or near the points, following the trend; a straight line would not match the pattern, so it would misrepresent the relationship and any prediction made from it (for example at temperatures outside the range measured).
parts.working: B1 smooth curve drawn through the trend, not connecting every point; B1 straight line misrepresents relationship; B1 predictions from the line may be wrong, especially outside the measured range.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a student could decide on a suitable scale for the y-axis when plotting clear-zone diameters that range from 6 mm to 16 mm, and why the scale should start at 0 when possible.
parts.answer: Choose a scale that uses at least half of the graph paper for the data, for example from 0 to 20 mm in 2 mm steps; starting at 0 shows the true proportion of change and avoids exaggerating differences, though a non-zero start may be used when clearly labelled.
parts.working: B1 scale covering the full data range using most of the paper; B1 equal, easy-to-read divisions; B1 starting at zero avoids exaggerating differences.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student uses a Bunsen burner to sterilise an inoculating loop before transferring bacteria to an agar plate. Identify one hazard and state one control measure.
parts.answer: Hazard: open flame and hot loop (burns, ignition of nearby flammable material); control: keep the flame away from bags, papers and alcohol, tie back hair, and allow the loop to cool before touching the culture.
parts.working: B1 hazard named (flame / hot loop / flammable material); B1 control measure (tie hair, keep area clear, cool loop, use heat-resistant mat).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A school investigation uses a non-pathogenic strain of bacterium. Explain why a school should use a non-pathogenic strain rather than a pathogenic one.
parts.answer: A pathogenic strain could cause infection in students and staff if it escapes or is inhaled or touched; a non-pathogenic strain reduces the risk of disease while still allowing bacterial growth to be investigated.
parts.working: B1 pathogenic strains could infect people (risk of disease) if they escape; B1 non-pathogenic strains are safer and allow the same investigation without serious risk.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student uses glass Petri dishes that are cracked. Identify the hazard and the risk, and suggest a control measure.
parts.answer: Hazard: cracked glass (sharp edges); risk: cuts and contamination of the bench or the culture; control: use undamaged plastic Petri dishes, check dishes before use and dispose of broken glass in a sharps container.
parts.working: B1 hazard: cracked glass; B1 risk: cuts / spilled culture; B1 control: replace dishes, check before use, sharps disposal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student shines a UV lamp on bacterial plates to test whether UV kills bacteria. Identify one hazard and suggest two control measures.
parts.answer: Hazard: ultraviolet light (eye damage and skin burns); controls: wear UV-blocking eye protection, keep the lamp in a closed box or behind a UV shield, and switch the lamp off before handling the plates.
parts.working: B1 hazard: UV light causes eye/skin damage; B1 and B2 any two controls (UV goggles, shield or box, switch off before handling, limit exposure time).

practice.stem: A student cultures bacteria from a soil sample on nutrient agar plates and tests the effect of an antibacterial cream. Loops are sterilised in a Bunsen flame and the bench is wiped with 70 % ethanol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards in this investigation and describe how the risk from each could be reduced.
parts.answer: e.g. Bacteria could be pathogenic / contaminants may grow → use a non-pathogenic strain, aseptic technique, tape lid with two strips (not sealed all round), incubate at ≤ 30 °C, never open plates, autoclave after use. Flame / ethanol for sterilising loop is flammable → keep ethanol away from Bunsen, tie back hair. Hot agar → use heat-proof gloves.
parts.working: For each of two hazards: B1 hazard identified; B1 appropriate precaution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete a risk assessment table for three hazards in a microbiology practical: (1) ethanol used to clean the bench; (2) household bleach used as a disinfectant; (3) a scalpel used to cut agar. For each, give the hazard, the risk and one control measure.
parts.answer: Ethanol: flammable (fire); keep away from flames, small volumes, store in a cool place. Bleach: corrosive/irritant to eyes and skin and releases chlorine gas when mixed with acids or ammonia; wear goggles and gloves, never mix with other chemicals, use in a ventilated area. Scalpel: cuts; use a blade holder, cut away from the body, dispose in a sharps container.
parts.working: 2 marks for each hazard: 1 mark for identifying the hazard and risk, 1 mark for an appropriate control measure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Soil samples are collected from a school garden for a bacterial count. Explain two risks from handling soil, and describe the precautions the students should take.
parts.answer: Risks: soil may contain pathogenic bacteria, fungi or parasites, and sharp objects; precautions: wear gloves, wash hands thoroughly after handling, do not eat or drink during the practical, and do not culture any sample from the soil for pathogenic organisms.
parts.working: B1 and B2 any two risks (pathogens, sharp objects, contamination of food); B1 and B2 any two precautions (gloves, hand washing, no eating, do not open the plates).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student plans to transfer a culture of bacteria from a test tube to a Petri dish by mouth pipetting. Identify the hazard and suggest a safer method.
parts.answer: Hazard: the bacteria or chemicals could be swallowed or inhaled; safer method: use a sterile pipette with a pipette filler or a sterile loop.
parts.working: B1 hazard: ingestion or inhalation of the culture; B1 safer method: pipette filler / sterile loop.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student autoclaves used agar plates before disposing of them. Explain one hazard associated with the autoclave, and one precaution that reduces the risk.
parts.answer: Hazard: hot steam and high pressure can cause burns or scalding when the door is opened; precaution: allow the autoclave to cool and the pressure to fall to zero before opening, and wear heat-resistant gloves and eye protection.
parts.working: B1 hazard: scalding steam / hot surfaces / pressure; B1 precaution: wait until pressure is zero and cool; B1 heat-resistant gloves and goggles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a risk assessment should be reviewed and updated during an investigation, using an example in which the hazards change.
parts.answer: Risks can change as the experiment proceeds, for example when a new substance is added, a culture unexpectedly grows a different organism, or a piece of equipment is damaged; the assessment must be updated so that new controls are in place before work continues.
parts.working: B1 hazards change during the work (new chemicals, unexpected organisms, damaged equipment); B1 controls must be updated; B1 review before continuing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a risk assessment for an investigation into the effect of hand sanitisers on bacteria on the hands of students. Identify three hazards, state the level of risk (high, medium or low) for each after control measures, and explain your judgement.
parts.answer: Hazards: alcohol-based sanitiser (flammable and can irritate eyes or skin); contaminated agar plates (contain bacteria that could become a risk if mishandled); bacterial culture (if a pathogen is used). After controls (non-pathogenic bacteria, no open flames, plates taped and not opened, sanitiser used as directed, hands washed after): low risk for each; judgement is based on the severity of the harm and the likelihood of exposure.
parts.working: 2 marks each for three hazards: 1 mark for a relevant hazard, 1 for a control and risk level with justification (severity and likelihood).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student wants to collect pond water to culture microorganisms. Identify three risks and explain for each how the risk would be reduced.
parts.answer: Risks: pond water may contain pathogenic bacteria and parasites (for example Giardia or leptospira), so avoid direct contact and use gloves; slippery banks or deep water (falls and drowning), so collect from a safe edge with supervision; open culture plates may contaminate the environment, so keep lids on and sterilise after use; each risk reduced by supervision, PPE, safe location and disposal of cultures by autoclaving.
parts.working: 2 marks each for three risks: one for a relevant risk, one for an effective control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says, 'The bacteria are the hazard, and keeping the plates taped shut reduces the risk.' Explain whether the student is correct, using the terms hazard and risk.
parts.answer: The student is correct: the pathogenic bacteria are the hazard (the source of potential harm). Taping the plates shut does not remove the bacteria, but it reduces the risk, the likelihood that people are exposed to them and harmed.
parts.working: B1 hazard = the bacteria (a source of potential harm); B1 risk = the likelihood and severity of harm on exposure; B1 taping reduces the chance of exposure, it does not remove the hazard.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Students plan to keep live Aedes larvae for an investigation into their development. Describe two ways in which the risk of mosquitoes escaping can be reduced, and explain why this risk matters.
parts.answer: Escaped adult mosquitoes could establish a breeding population or spread disease; controls include rearing larvae in sealed containers with fine mesh lids, keeping them indoors, not releasing any adults, and destroying the cultures by freezing or boiling at the end.
parts.working: B1 why escape matters (establish population, disease vector); B1 and B2 two control methods (sealed/meshed containers, no release, end-of-study disposal by boiling/freezing).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student sets up a bacterial investigation at home on a kitchen table without a sterile working area. Identify two hazards and explain why the school practical rules should be followed instead.
parts.answer: Hazards: food preparation surfaces may contaminate the culture and spread bacteria to food; bacteria may be inhaled or touched and spread to family members; the school setting provides controlled surfaces, disinfection, waste disposal and supervision, so the investigation is safer and the results are more reliable.
parts.working: B1 and B2 two hazards (contamination of food surfaces, spread to family, exposure to a bacterium); B1 school practice provides supervision, sterile area and disposal; B1 more reliable results.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement describes the induced-fit hypothesis of enzyme action?
A The active site has a rigid shape that matches the substrate exactly before the substrate binds.
B The active site changes shape slightly as the substrate binds, so that it fits the substrate more closely.
C The substrate changes shape to fit an active site that cannot change shape.
D The enzyme can bind any substrate of a similar size because the whole enzyme moulds around it.
parts.answer: B The active site changes shape slightly as the substrate binds, so that it fits the substrate more closely.
parts.working: B: in induced fit the active site is not exactly complementary at first; binding of the substrate causes a small change in the shape of the active site, giving a closer fit and straining bonds in the substrate. A describes the lock-and-key hypothesis. D is wrong because enzymes remain specific.

practice.stem:
Catalase is found inside the cells of potato tubers, liver and yeast. It breaks down hydrogen peroxide, a toxic by-product of metabolism, into water and oxygen:
2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether catalase is an intracellular or an extracellular enzyme. Name one enzyme that is extracellular.
parts.answer: Intracellular; extracellular example: salivary amylase / trypsin / pancreatic lipase (any one).
parts.working: B1 intracellular. B1 any correct extracellular enzyme (one secreted out of the cell that made it).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how catalase increases the rate of this reaction.
parts.answer: Hydrogen peroxide binds to the active site forming an enzyme–substrate complex; this lowers the activation energy; products are released and the enzyme is unchanged and reused.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: substrate binds to the complementary active site; enzyme–substrate complex forms; activation energy is lowered; bonds in the substrate are strained / substrate held in a position that favours reaction; enzyme–product complex forms and products leave the active site; enzyme is not used up and can bind another substrate molecule.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a cell needs only a small amount of catalase to deal with the hydrogen peroxide it produces.
parts.answer: Each catalase molecule is not used up and has a very high turnover, so it can break down many substrate molecules per second.
parts.working: B1 enzyme reused / high turnover number.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement explains why an enzyme usually catalyses only one type of reaction?
A The enzyme is made of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.
B The active site has a specific shape, set by the enzyme's tertiary structure, that is complementary to one substrate.
C The enzyme lowers the activation energy of the reaction.
D The enzyme is not used up in the reaction and can be used again.
parts.answer: B The active site has a specific shape, set by the enzyme's tertiary structure, that is complementary to one substrate.
parts.working: B: specificity comes from the 3D shape (and charges) of the active site, which is complementary to only one substrate. C and D are true of enzymes but are not the reason for specificity; A is true of all proteins.

practice.stem: Tears and saliva contain lysozyme, an enzyme that hydrolyses glycosidic bonds in peptidoglycan, the main substance in bacterial cell walls. Lysozyme is made in cells of the tear glands and secreted onto the surface of the eye.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an enzyme.
parts.answer: A globular protein that acts as a biological catalyst: it speeds up a (metabolic) reaction without being used up or permanently changed.
parts.working: B1 (globular) protein. B1 biological catalyst / speeds up reaction and is not used up.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why lysozyme hydrolyses bonds in bacterial cell walls but has no effect on the cellulose cell walls of plant cells.
parts.answer: Lysozyme's active site is complementary only to its substrate in peptidoglycan; cellulose has a different shape, so it cannot bind to the active site and no enzyme–substrate complex forms.
parts.working: B1 active site complementary to (part of) peptidoglycan / enzyme is specific. B1 cellulose a different shape, does not fit / bind, no E–S complex.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how lysozyme forms an enzyme–substrate complex.
parts.answer: The substrate collides with and enters the active site; it is held there by temporary bonds (hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds) with R groups of amino acids in the active site.
parts.working: B1 substrate collides with / binds to active site. B1 held by temporary bonds (H bonds / ionic) with R groups of the active site.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest how lysozyme in tears helps to protect the eye.
parts.answer: It weakens bacterial cell walls so bacteria burst (lysis) and die, which helps prevent eye infections.
parts.working: B1 bacteria killed / burst because cell wall weakened → fewer infections.

practice.stem:
Statements P to T describe stages in the action of an enzyme.
P  The products are released from the active site.
Q  A substrate molecule collides with the active site.
R  An enzyme–product complex forms.
S  An enzyme–substrate complex forms.
T  Bonds in the substrate are put under strain, lowering the activation energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put statements P to T in the order in which they happen during an enzyme-catalysed reaction.
parts.answer: Q, S, T, R, P
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark if one pair is reversed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens to the enzyme after step P.
parts.answer: The enzyme is unchanged and its active site is free to bind another substrate molecule.
parts.working: B1 unchanged / reused / binds another substrate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction depends on how often enzyme and substrate molecules collide.
parts.answer: An enzyme–substrate complex can only form when a substrate molecule collides with an active site; more collisions per unit time give more enzyme–substrate complexes and so more product formed per unit time.
parts.working: B1 E–S complex forms only after collision with active site. B1 more (successful) collisions per unit time → more E–S complexes → faster rate.

practice.stem: One molecule of an enzyme in a yeast cell converts 4500 substrate molecules into product every second at 30 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many substrate molecules one enzyme molecule converts in 2.5 minutes.
parts.answer: 675 000 (6.75 × 10⁵) molecules

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why one enzyme molecule can convert so many substrate molecules.
parts.answer: The enzyme is not used up or changed by the reaction; once the products leave, the active site is free to bind another substrate molecule.
parts.working: B1 not used up / unchanged. B1 products released, active site free for next substrate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way in which enzymes differ from inorganic catalysts.
parts.answer: Enzymes are proteins (so they are specific / denatured by high temperature or extreme pH / work at body temperature).
parts.working: B1 any one: protein; highly specific; denatured by heat or pH; work at mild temperatures.

practice.stem: Sucrase is an enzyme produced by cells lining the small intestine. It hydrolyses sucrose into glucose and fructose. It does not hydrolyse lactose, even though lactose is also a disaccharide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why sucrase can hydrolyse sucrose but cannot hydrolyse lactose.
parts.answer: The active site of sucrase has a specific shape complementary to sucrose; this shape depends on the enzyme's tertiary structure (its sequence of amino acids and their R groups); lactose has a different shape, so it cannot fit/bind and no enzyme–substrate complex forms.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: active site has a specific/complementary shape to sucrose; shape is determined by the tertiary structure / bonds between R groups / primary structure; lactose is not complementary / does not fit the active site; so no enzyme–substrate complex can form with lactose.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of reaction catalysed by sucrase and the bond that is broken.
parts.answer: Hydrolysis; (1,2) glycosidic bond.
parts.working: B1 hydrolysis. B1 glycosidic bond.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Outline one difference between the lock-and-key hypothesis and the induced-fit hypothesis.
parts.answer: In lock-and-key the active site is a fixed shape exactly complementary to the substrate; in induced fit the active site changes shape slightly when the substrate binds, so that it fits more closely.
parts.working: B1 lock and key: rigid/fixed active site, exact fit. B1 induced fit: active site (and enzyme) changes shape on binding the substrate.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a reaction without a catalyst, the activation energy is 75 kJ mol⁻¹. With an enzyme, the activation energy is 29 kJ mol⁻¹. The products have 18 kJ mol⁻¹ less energy than the reactants.
Which statement is correct?
A The enzyme lowers the activation energy by 46 kJ mol⁻¹ and the energy released by the reaction stays at 18 kJ mol⁻¹.
B The enzyme lowers the activation energy by 46 kJ mol⁻¹ and increases the energy released to 64 kJ mol⁻¹.
C The enzyme lowers the activation energy to 46 kJ mol⁻¹ and the energy released stays at 18 kJ mol⁻¹.
D The enzyme lowers the activation energy by 29 kJ mol⁻¹ and the energy released stays at 18 kJ mol⁻¹.
parts.answer: A The enzyme lowers the activation energy by 46 kJ mol⁻¹ and the energy released by the reaction stays at 18 kJ mol⁻¹.
parts.working: A: 75 − 29 = 46 kJ mol⁻¹ lower; an enzyme does not change the energy of reactants or products, so the overall energy change is unchanged. B wrongly adds the reduction to the energy released; C confuses the new value with the reduction.

practice.stem:
Hexokinase catalyses the first reaction of glycolysis in many cells:
glucose + ATP → glucose 6-phosphate + ADP
When glucose enters the active site, the two lobes of the enzyme move towards each other and the active site closes around the glucose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the model of enzyme action that this observation supports.
parts.answer: Induced fit
parts.working: B1 induced fit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the change in shape of the active site helps hexokinase to catalyse the reaction.
parts.answer: The active site moulds more closely around the substrates, so more temporary bonds form between R groups and the substrates; this strains bonds and holds glucose and the phosphate group of ATP close together in the correct orientation, lowering the activation energy.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: closer fit / more bonds between R groups and substrate; strain / distortion of bonds; glucose and ATP held close together / correctly orientated; activation energy lowered.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest an advantage of the active site closing around glucose before the phosphate group is transferred from ATP.
parts.answer: Water is excluded from the active site, so ATP is not simply hydrolysed (wasting energy); the phosphate group is transferred to glucose instead.
parts.working: B1 water excluded / kept out. B1 so ATP not hydrolysed / energy not wasted; phosphate goes to glucose.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the lock-and-key hypothesis cannot fully account for the behaviour of hexokinase.
parts.answer: The lock-and-key hypothesis treats the active site as rigid, but in hexokinase the active site changes shape when the substrate binds.
parts.working: B1 lock-and-key = rigid / fixed active site; here shape changes.

practice.stem: In germinating barley grains used for malting, amylase hydrolyses starch to maltose. Maltase then hydrolyses maltose to glucose. Both starch and maltose contain α-1,4 glycosidic bonds between α-glucose units.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Amylase and maltase both break α-1,4 glycosidic bonds. Explain why they are still described as specific enzymes.
parts.answer: Each enzyme's active site is complementary to the shape of its own substrate: amylase binds a section of the long starch chain, while maltase's active site fits only the disaccharide maltose, so maltase cannot bind starch and amylase does not bind maltose effectively.
parts.working: B1 active site of each complementary to its own substrate's shape. B1 maltose (disaccharide) and starch (long polysaccharide chain) have different shapes, so each only binds one.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of reaction catalysed by both enzymes and the molecule that must be present for it.
parts.answer: Hydrolysis; water
parts.working: B1 hydrolysis. B1 water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student tested the barley extract with Benedict's solution to show that maltase was active. Explain why a positive Benedict's test does not show this.
parts.answer: Both maltose and glucose are reducing sugars, so Benedict's solution gives a positive result whether or not maltase has converted maltose into glucose.
parts.working: B1 maltose is a reducing sugar (as well as glucose). B1 so a positive result could be due to maltose alone / cannot tell which sugar is present.

practice.stem: Starch and cellulose are both polymers of glucose. Starch contains α-glucose units joined by α-1,4 and α-1,6 glycosidic bonds. Cellulose contains β-glucose units joined by β-1,4 glycosidic bonds. Humans secrete amylase but do not make cellulase. Buffaloes and cattle digest cellulose with cellulase made by microorganisms in their stomachs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why human amylase cannot hydrolyse cellulose.
parts.answer: Cellulose is made of β-glucose, in which alternate glucose units are inverted, so the chain and its β-1,4 bonds have a different shape from starch; cellulose is not complementary to the active site of amylase, so it cannot bind and no enzyme–substrate complex forms.
parts.working: B1 β-glucose / β-1,4 bonds / alternate units inverted. B1 different shape, not complementary to amylase active site. B1 no E–S complex / bond not hydrolysed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Textile mills in Faisalabad use cellulase to give cotton fabric a smoother finish. Suggest why cellulase does not damage woollen garments, which are made of the protein keratin.
parts.answer: Cellulase is specific: its active site is complementary only to β-1,4 glycosidic bonds in cellulose. Keratin is a protein with peptide bonds and a different shape, so it does not bind to the active site.
parts.working: B1 enzyme specific / active site complementary to cellulose only. B1 keratin a protein / peptide bonds / different shape, cannot bind.

practice.stem: A single base substitution in the gene for an enzyme replaces one amino acid with another. The changed amino acid is in a part of the enzyme that is far from the active site. The enzyme made from the mutated gene has only about 5 % of its normal activity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a change in an amino acid far from the active site can reduce the activity of the enzyme.
parts.answer: The primary structure changes, so a different R group is present; this changes the bonds (hydrogen, ionic, disulfide, hydrophobic interactions) that hold the tertiary structure; the protein folds differently so the shape of the active site changes and the substrate fits less well, so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: change in primary structure / different R group; different bonds form or bonds lost (hydrogen / ionic / disulfide / hydrophobic interactions); tertiary structure changes / folds differently; active site shape changes; substrate no longer complementary / fewer enzyme–substrate complexes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A second mutation replaces an amino acid inside the active site with a different amino acid of similar size and charge. The enzyme's activity does not change. Suggest why.
parts.answer: The new R group has similar properties, so it forms the same bonds/interactions; the shape and charge of the active site are unchanged, so the substrate still binds.
parts.working: B1 similar R group forms the same bonds / interactions. B1 active site shape (and charge) still complementary to substrate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, in terms of activation energy, why enzymes allow metabolic reactions to take place quickly at 37 °C.
parts.answer: Enzymes lower the activation energy, so at 37 °C a much larger proportion of substrate molecules have enough energy to react; without the enzyme a high temperature would be needed.
parts.working: B1 enzymes lower activation energy. B1 so reactions occur fast at body temperature without needing high temperatures (which would denature proteins / damage cells).

practice.stem: An enzyme from a bacterium that lives in hot springs at 80 °C is made of two identical polypeptide chains. Its active site is formed from R groups belonging to both chains. When the two chains are separated without any other change, neither chain shows any activity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the level of protein structure that involves more than one polypeptide chain.
parts.answer: Quaternary structure
parts.working: B1 quaternary.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the separated chains have no activity.
parts.answer: The active site is made from R groups of both chains, so a single chain has an incomplete active site that is not complementary to the substrate; the substrate cannot bind and no enzyme–substrate complexes form.
parts.working: B1 active site incomplete / needs R groups from both chains / shape not complementary. B1 substrate cannot bind / no E–S complex.

parts.label: c
parts.text: This enzyme has more disulfide bonds and ionic bonds than a similar enzyme from a bacterium that lives at 30 °C. Explain how this allows the enzyme to stay active at 80 °C.
parts.answer: More bonds (and covalent disulfide bonds are strong) hold the tertiary/quaternary structure together, so more energy is needed to break them; at 80 °C the bonds are not broken, the active site keeps its shape and remains complementary to the substrate, so the enzyme is not denatured.
parts.working: B1 more / stronger bonds holding tertiary (and quaternary) structure. B1 more (heat) energy needed to break them / vibrations do not break them at 80 °C. B1 active site shape kept / still complementary / not denatured.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why this enzyme has a low rate of activity at 30 °C.
parts.answer: At 30 °C enzyme and substrate molecules have less kinetic energy, so there are fewer collisions and fewer enzyme–substrate complexes per unit time; the rigid structure may also be unable to change shape enough for induced fit.
parts.working: B1 less kinetic energy → fewer collisions / E–S complexes. B1 fewer molecules reach activation energy OR structure too rigid / inflexible for induced fit.

practice.stem:
Trypsin and chymotrypsin are proteases that act in the small intestine. In this question assume that:
• trypsin hydrolyses the peptide bond on the carboxyl side of lysine (Lys) and arginine (Arg), whose R groups are long and positively charged;
• chymotrypsin hydrolyses the peptide bond on the carboxyl side of phenylalanine (Phe), tryptophan (Trp) and tyrosine (Tyr), whose R groups are large and hydrophobic.
A peptide has this sequence (amino end first):
Gly–Lys–Ala–Phe–Ser–Arg–Leu–Trp–Val–Lys–Met

parts.label: a(i)
parts.text: State the number of fragments produced when the peptide is completely hydrolysed by trypsin.
parts.answer: 4 fragments
parts.working: Cuts after Lys(2), Arg(6), Lys(10): Gly–Lys | Ala–Phe–Ser–Arg | Leu–Trp–Val–Lys | Met. B1 4.

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.text: State the number of fragments produced when the peptide is completely hydrolysed by chymotrypsin.
parts.answer: 3 fragments
parts.working: Cuts after Phe(4) and Trp(8): Gly–Lys–Ala–Phe | Ser–Arg–Leu–Trp | Val–Lys–Met. B1 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The peptide is treated with both enzymes together. List the fragments produced.
parts.answer: Six fragments: Gly–Lys, Ala–Phe, Ser–Arg, Leu–Trp, Val–Lys, Met
parts.working: Cuts after positions 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10. B2 all six correct; B1 for 6 stated with one error.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the active site of trypsin is adapted to its specificity.
parts.answer: The pocket in the active site is long/deep and contains a negatively charged R group (e.g. aspartate) that forms an ionic bond with the positively charged R group of lysine or arginine, so only those residues are held in position.
parts.working: B1 negatively charged R group in active site. B1 forms ionic bond / attracts positive R group of Lys/Arg; deep pocket fits long side chain.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the substrate-binding pocket of chymotrypsin is lined with non-polar R groups.
parts.answer: Non-polar R groups form hydrophobic interactions with the large hydrophobic R groups of Phe, Trp and Tyr, holding them in the active site.
parts.working: B1 hydrophobic interactions with hydrophobic R groups.

practice.stem: For a reaction X → Y in a cell, the activation energy without a catalyst is 92 kJ mol⁻¹. With the enzyme that catalyses it, the activation energy is 38 kJ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in activation energy produced by the enzyme. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how an enzyme lowers the activation energy of a reaction.
parts.answer: The substrate binds to the active site, forming an enzyme–substrate complex; R groups in the active site form temporary bonds with the substrate, distorting/straining bonds in it; the active site holds reacting molecules close together in the correct orientation and may provide charged groups that help the reaction.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: E–S complex formed; temporary bonds with R groups in active site; strain / distortion of substrate bonds; substrates held close / correct orientation; favourable charge environment.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The enzyme does not change the amount of energy released by the reaction. Explain why it still allows the reaction to happen quickly at 37 °C.
parts.answer: Because the activation energy is lower, a much larger proportion of substrate molecules at 37 °C have enough energy to react, so more successful reactions happen per unit time.
parts.working: B1 more molecules have energy ≥ (the lower) activation energy at 37 °C. B1 more successful collisions / reactions per unit time.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A student writes: 'The enzyme provides the energy needed for the reaction.' Explain why this is wrong.
parts.answer: The enzyme does not supply energy; it provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy.
parts.working: B1 alternative route / pathway with lower activation energy; no energy supplied.

practice.stem:
A bakery in Lahore uses a fungal amylase to help bread dough rise. A technician measured the rate of starch breakdown by the amylase at different temperatures.
Temperature / °C: 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70
Rate / arbitrary units: 0.8, 1.5, 2.6, 3.4, 1.2, 0.1

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the optimum temperature of the amylase from these data.
parts.working: B1 50 °C (highest rate of the temperatures tested).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the increase in rate between 20 °C and 50 °C.
parts.answer: Molecules gain kinetic energy so enzyme and substrate move faster and collide more often; more enzyme–substrate complexes form per unit time.
parts.working: B1 more kinetic energy / faster movement. B1 more frequent (successful) collisions / more enzyme–substrate complexes per unit time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the decrease in rate above 50 °C.
parts.answer: Vibrations break hydrogen bonds (and ionic bonds) holding the tertiary structure; the shape of the active site changes; starch no longer fits, so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form – the enzyme is denatured.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: hydrogen / ionic bonds broken; tertiary structure changes; active site changes shape; substrate no longer complementary / cannot bind; enzyme denatured (permanently).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in rate between 50 °C and 60 °C. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In an investigation the substrate is in excess. The concentration of the enzyme is doubled and all other conditions are kept the same.
What happens to the initial rate of reaction?
A It doubles, because twice as many active sites are available.
B It stays the same, because the substrate concentration limits the rate.
C It halves, because the enzyme molecules compete for substrate.
D It doubles, because the activation energy is halved.
parts.answer: A It doubles, because twice as many active sites are available.
parts.working: A: with substrate in excess, the number of active sites limits the rate, so doubling the enzyme doubles the number of enzyme–substrate complexes formed per unit time. B would only apply if substrate were limiting; enzymes do not change activation energy in proportion to their concentration (D).

practice.stem:
Invertase from yeast hydrolyses sucrose into glucose and fructose. The same volume of invertase solution was added to sucrose solutions of different concentrations at 30 °C.
Sucrose concentration / mmol dm⁻³: 0, 5, 10, 20, 40, 60, 80
Initial rate / µmol min⁻¹: 0, 3.1, 5.8, 9.6, 12.9, 13.8, 14.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of sucrose concentration on the rate of reaction.
parts.answer: Rate increases as sucrose concentration increases, steeply at first (almost in proportion up to about 10 mmol dm⁻³), then more slowly, and it levels off at about 14 µmol min⁻¹ above about 60 mmol dm⁻³.
parts.working: B1 rate increases (steeply / proportionally) at low concentrations. B1 levels off / plateau at about 14 µmol min⁻¹ from 60–80 mmol dm⁻³ (data quoted).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate increases between 0 and 20 mmol dm⁻³ sucrose.
parts.answer: More substrate molecules means more frequent collisions with free active sites, so more enzyme–substrate complexes form per unit time; substrate concentration is the limiting factor.
parts.working: B1 more collisions with active sites / more E–S complexes per unit time. B1 substrate concentration is limiting (active sites free).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate hardly changes between 60 and 80 mmol dm⁻³ sucrose.
parts.answer: Almost all active sites are occupied at any moment (the enzyme is saturated), so extra substrate cannot form more enzyme–substrate complexes; the enzyme concentration now limits the rate.
parts.working: B1 active sites all occupied / saturated. B1 enzyme concentration limiting / near Vmax.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one change that would increase the rate at 80 mmol dm⁻³ sucrose.
parts.answer: Increase the concentration of invertase (more active sites); also accept raising the temperature towards the optimum.
parts.working: B1 more enzyme / more active sites (or temperature closer to optimum).

practice.stem:
A student blended white radish (mooli) with water and filtered it to make a catalase extract, then diluted it to make 20 %, 40 %, 60 %, 80 % and 100 % extract. A small filter-paper disc was soaked in each extract and dropped into a tube of 3 % hydrogen peroxide at 25 °C. The disc sank and then rose to the surface. The time for the disc to rise was recorded.
Extract concentration / %: 20, 40, 60, 80, 100
Time to rise / s: 48, 25, 17, 13, 10

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate, as 1 ÷ time, for the 20 % and the 100 % extract. Give each answer in s⁻¹ to 3 significant figures.
