parts.working: M1 H1 using Vmax 20 and Km 5. A1 H1 values. A1 H2 values (Vmax 40, Km 15).

parts.label: b
parts.text: With the inhibitor, the measured rates were 3, 10, 22 and 30. State which hypothesis is supported and explain how the results at high substrate concentration distinguish between the two.
parts.answer: H2 (competitive). At high substrate concentration the rate approaches the uninhibited value (30 at 40 mmol dm⁻³, close to the H2 prediction of 29.1 and above the H1 prediction of 17.8), whereas a non-competitive inhibitor would keep the rate at or below 20 however much substrate is added; at low concentrations the two predictions are similar and cannot distinguish them.
parts.working: B1 H2. B1 reasoning based on high-[S] values / maximum rate.

practice.stem: The rate of a reaction catalysed by a yeast enzyme at 25 °C is 12 units. A student hypothesises that between 25 °C and 40 °C the rate doubles for every 10 °C rise (temperature coefficient Q₁₀ = 2). Rate at T₂ = rate at T₁ × Q₁₀^((T₂ − T₁) ÷ 10).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the predicted rates at 35 °C and at 40 °C. Give your answers to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 35 °C: 24 units; 40 °C: 34 units

parts.label: b
parts.text: The measured rates were 23 units at 35 °C and 26 units at 40 °C. Evaluate the hypothesis using these data.
parts.answer: Supported at 35 °C (23 is close to 24) but not at 40 °C (26 is well below 34); above about 35 °C the rate rises less than predicted, probably because some enzyme molecules are starting to denature, so Q₁₀ = 2 only holds at lower temperatures.
parts.working: B1 35 °C fits, 40 °C does not, with data. B1 explanation: denaturation begins.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a prediction for the rate at 60 °C, with a reason.
parts.answer: Much lower than at 40 °C (close to zero), because most of the enzyme molecules will be denatured.
parts.working: B1

practice.stem:
A student hypothesised: 'Adding calcium ions increases the activity of a bacterial amylase.' She measured activity (mean ± 2SE, n = 5) at four calcium chloride concentrations:
0 mmol dm⁻³: 20.0 ± 1.6
1 mmol dm⁻³: 24.5 ± 1.8
5 mmol dm⁻³: 25.8 ± 2.0
20 mmol dm⁻³: 21.0 ± 1.7

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the extent to which the data support the hypothesis.
parts.answer: Partly supported: activity at 1 and 5 mmol dm⁻³ is higher than with no calcium and the intervals do not overlap with 0 mmol dm⁻³ (18.4–21.6 vs 22.7–26.3 and 23.8–27.8), so this increase is significant; but 1 and 5 mmol dm⁻³ overlap, so more calcium beyond 1 mmol dm⁻³ gives no significant further increase; at 20 mmol dm⁻³ activity is not significantly different from 0 (19.3–22.7 overlaps 18.4–21.6), so high concentrations do not increase activity.
parts.working: B1 significant increase at 1 and 5 compared with 0, using intervals. B1 no significant difference between 1 and 5. B1 20 mmol dm⁻³ not different from 0 / hypothesis needs to be limited to low concentrations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a revised hypothesis that fits these data.
parts.answer: Low concentrations of calcium ions (about 1–5 mmol dm⁻³) increase amylase activity, but higher concentrations do not.
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: An enzyme has Vmax = 60 µmol min⁻¹ and Km = 4 mmol dm⁻³. Initial rate = Vmax × [S] ÷ (Km + [S]).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the initial rate at [S] = 2, 4, 12 and 36 mmol dm⁻³.
parts.answer: 20, 30, 45, 54 µmol min⁻¹
parts.working: M1 substitution. A1 all four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why increasing [S] from 12 to 36 mmol dm⁻³ has less effect on the rate than increasing it from 2 to 4 mmol dm⁻³.
parts.answer: Doubling from 2 to 4 raises the rate by 10 (50 %), but tripling from 12 to 36 raises it by only 9 (20 %); at high [S] most active sites are already occupied, so the rate approaches Vmax and enzyme concentration becomes limiting.
parts.working: B1 comparison using calculated values. B1 active sites near saturation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the effect on Vmax and on Km of doubling the enzyme concentration.
parts.answer: Vmax doubles (120 µmol min⁻¹) because there are twice as many active sites; Km stays the same (4 mmol dm⁻³) because the affinity of each enzyme molecule for the substrate does not change.
parts.working: B1 Vmax doubles. B1 Km unchanged with reason.

practice.stem: A student plans to compare the activity of catalase and trypsin at temperatures from 20 °C to 60 °C. She will use 3 % hydrogen peroxide, 1 % trypsin solution made from powder, a water bath and glass test-tubes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three hazards in this investigation and state a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Hydrogen peroxide is an irritant to eyes and skin – wear goggles and gloves; trypsin powder/solution can cause allergic reactions if inhaled or on skin – make solutions carefully, avoid raising dust, wear gloves; water bath at 60 °C can scald – handle tubes with a test-tube holder; glassware can break and cut – handle carefully, report breakages.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard with a matching precaution, max 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the overall level of risk in this investigation is low.
parts.answer: The solutions used are dilute and only small volumes are used.
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: In a risk assessment, students must distinguish between a hazard and a risk.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a hazard and a risk.
parts.answer: A hazard is something that has the potential to cause harm (e.g. a corrosive chemical, hot water); a risk is the likelihood (chance) that harm will actually happen, and how serious it would be, in the way the hazard is used.
parts.working: B1 hazard = potential to cause harm. B1 risk = likelihood/chance of harm (and severity).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student uses 1 % trypsin solution. Give one hazard of trypsin and explain how the risk can be reduced without removing the hazard.
parts.answer: Trypsin is a protein that can cause allergic reactions / is an irritant to skin and eyes (sensitiser); wear gloves and eye protection and avoid splashing or making aerosols, so contact is less likely.
parts.working: B1 hazard. B1 precaution reducing likelihood of exposure.

practice.stem: To prepare potato pieces for a catalase investigation, a student uses a cork borer to cut cylinders from a potato and a scalpel to cut them into discs of equal thickness.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the main hazard and describe two precautions.
parts.answer: Sharp blades (scalpel and cork borer) can cut the skin. Precautions: cut on a white tile (on a firm surface), cutting away from the body and fingers; push the cork borer down onto the tile rather than towards the hand; carry and store the scalpel with the blade covered/pointing down; never try to catch a falling blade.
parts.working: B1 hazard (cuts from sharp blades). 1 mark each for any two precautions.

practice.stem: A student tests samples for starch with iodine solution and for reducing sugars by heating samples with Benedict's solution in a water bath at about 90 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one hazard of each reagent and one hazard of the heating, and give a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Iodine solution: stains and is an irritant to eyes/skin — wear eye protection, wipe up spills. Benedict's solution: contains copper sulfate (harmful/irritant) — wear eye protection/gloves, wash hands. Water bath at 90 °C: scalds / spitting of boiling tubes — use a test-tube holder, point tubes away from people, use an electric water bath rather than a flame.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard with a matching precaution, max 3.

practice.stem: A class plans to investigate the effect of pH on salivary amylase, using each student's own saliva collected by spitting into a beaker.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the main hazard of using saliva and give two precautions.
parts.answer: Saliva may contain pathogens (risk of spreading infection). Precautions: each student uses only their own saliva; label beakers so they are not mixed up; wash hands; disinfect (e.g. with 1 % Virkon) and dispose of saliva and rinse glassware after use; do not share equipment.
parts.working: B1 hazard. 1 mark each for any two precautions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an alternative to saliva that would remove this hazard.
parts.answer: A commercial amylase solution (fungal or bacterial amylase).
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: A technician makes up a 1 % amylase solution from powdered enzyme. Enzyme powders are respiratory sensitisers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why enzyme powders are a greater hazard than the dilute enzyme solution.
parts.answer: Fine powder can form dust that is breathed in, which can cause asthma/allergy; the solution cannot be inhaled as dust (unless sprayed).
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two precautions the technician should take.
parts.answer: Weigh and dissolve the powder in a fume cupboard or with a dust mask; avoid raising dust (add powder gently to water, do not shake the container); wear gloves and eye protection; clean up spilled powder with a damp cloth.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: Fungi from soil samples are grown on starch agar plates to find which produce amylase. After incubation, the plates will be flooded with iodine solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why soil microorganisms present a hazard.
parts.answer: Soil may contain pathogenic microorganisms (and spores can be released), and culturing increases their numbers.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe three precautions that should be taken when growing and handling the cultures.
parts.answer: Use aseptic technique (flame loop, work near a Bunsen flame, sterilised equipment); tape the lid on with two or four short strips (do not seal completely); incubate at 25 °C, not 37 °C, to avoid growing human pathogens; do not open plates after incubation except to add iodine under supervision / in a safety cabinet; autoclave plates before disposal; wash hands.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

practice.stem: A student wants to measure the rate of oxygen release from 20 vol (6 %) hydrogen peroxide by blended liver, collecting the gas in a 50 cm³ gas syringe connected to a sealed flask.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards specific to this set-up and suggest a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Hydrogen peroxide at 6 % is an irritant/harmful to eyes and skin — use the lowest concentration that works (e.g. 3 %) and wear eye protection. A fast reaction in a sealed flask may build up pressure, forcing the plunger out of the syringe or the bung out of the flask — use a small volume of extract/peroxide so that the gas produced is less than 50 cm³, and check the syringe moves freely. Raw liver may carry pathogens — wear gloves, wash hands, disinfect surfaces.
parts.working: B1 each hazard (any two). B1 each matching precaution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why using a lower concentration of hydrogen peroxide reduces the risk but may affect the investigation.
parts.answer: Lower concentration is less irritant and gives less gas; but the rate will be lower, so readings may be smaller and need longer timing.
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: A student investigates inhibition of urease by copper(II) sulfate and lead(II) nitrate solutions at concentrations up to 0.1 mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the hazards of the inhibitor solutions and describe precautions for using them and for disposing of them.
parts.answer: Lead nitrate is toxic (and may harm an unborn child) and an oxidising agent; copper sulfate is harmful if swallowed and an irritant, and harmful to aquatic life. Use: wear gloves and eye protection, use the lowest concentrations needed, do not pipette by mouth, wash hands, clean spills at once. Disposal: collect waste in a labelled container for heavy-metal waste — do not pour down the sink.
parts.working: B1 lead toxic. B1 copper sulfate harmful/environmental. B1 handling precautions. B1 disposal via waste container, not the drain.

practice.stem: To show denaturation, a student heats amylase solution in a boiling tube in a beaker of boiling water on a hot plate for 10 minutes, and then cools the tube. An electric water bath at 40 °C is on the same bench, near the sink.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three hazards in this procedure and give a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Boiling water / hot glass can scald or burn — use tongs or a test-tube holder, let it cool, stand while working. Tube contents can 'bump' and spit when heated — point the tube away from people, do not fill more than one-third, use anti-bumping granules. Electrical equipment near water — keep the hot plate and water bath away from the sink, dry hands, check cables. Hot plate surface stays hot after use — label it / do not touch.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three hazards with matching precautions.

practice.stem: A student plans to use pectinase to extract juice from mangoes. She will peel and chop the fruit with a kitchen knife, blend it in a food blender, add pectinase solution and leave it at 40 °C. She plans to taste the juice at the end.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete a risk assessment by describing three hazards, the risk from each and a precaution.
parts.answer: Sharp knife and blender blades: cuts — use a chopping board, cut away from fingers, unplug blender before removing blades. Pectinase solution: irritant/allergen — gloves and eye protection. Electrical blender near liquids: shock — keep dry, do not overfill. Warm fruit pulp left for a long time: microbial growth.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard with risk and matching precaution, max 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the student must not taste the juice.
parts.answer: Food must never be eaten in a laboratory: the juice and equipment may be contaminated with laboratory chemicals or microorganisms, and the enzyme preparation is not food grade.
parts.working: B1

practice.stem:
A student wrote this risk assessment for an experiment on the effect of temperature (20–70 °C) on catalase from celery, using 3 % hydrogen peroxide:
1 'Hydrogen peroxide is dangerous — be careful.'
2 'Celery is a hazard — wear gloves.'
3 'Water baths are hot — risk of burns.'
4 'Overall risk: high, so the experiment should be done by the teacher.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate each statement and suggest a better version.
parts.answer: 1 Too vague: name the hazard (3 % hydrogen peroxide is an irritant to eyes/skin) and the precaution (wear eye protection; rinse with water if splashed). 2 Celery is not a significant hazard (unless allergic); gloves are not needed for celery — they would be sensible for hydrogen peroxide. 3 Identifies hazard but no precaution: use tongs/test-tube holders, keep water at 70 °C or below, do not touch the bath walls. 4 Overestimated: low concentrations and small volumes, with simple precautions, make the overall risk low; students can do it.
parts.working: B1 for each statement evaluated with an improved version.

practice.stem: Lipase activity can be followed using milk, sodium carbonate solution and phenolphthalein indicator. Phenolphthalein is supplied dissolved in ethanol. The tubes are warmed in a water bath at up to 50 °C. A student suggests speeding up warming by holding the tubes over a Bunsen flame.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why heating over a Bunsen flame is unsuitable here.
parts.answer: The phenolphthalein solution contains ethanol, which is highly flammable — the vapour could ignite near a flame; heating directly also gives uneven, uncontrolled temperature (and contents may spit).
parts.working: B1 ethanol flammable. B1 uncontrolled temperature / spitting.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two other hazards in this experiment and give a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Sodium carbonate solution: irritant to eyes — wear eye protection. Lipase solution: allergen/irritant — avoid skin contact, gloves. Phenolphthalein: harmful (possible carcinogen in large amounts) — use only a few drops, avoid contact, wash hands. Hot water bath — tongs.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two hazards with precautions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a safer way to warm the tubes.
parts.answer: Use a thermostatically controlled electric water bath (no naked flames), allowing time for tubes to reach the temperature.
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: Protease activity is measured by the biuret test: biuret reagent contains sodium hydroxide and copper(II) sulfate. The student also uses a centrifuge to remove undigested solid protein before testing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the hazards of biuret reagent and give precautions, including first aid if it splashes into the eye.
parts.answer: Sodium hydroxide is corrosive/irritant to eyes and skin (alkali can cause serious eye damage); copper sulfate is harmful/irritant. Precautions: wear eye protection (goggles), gloves, use small volumes, add reagent carefully. First aid: rinse the eye with plenty of clean running water for at least 10 minutes and get medical help.
parts.working: B1 NaOH corrosive / eye damage. B1 goggles + gloves / small volumes. B1 first aid: flood eye with water for ≥ 10 min, seek help.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two precautions when using the centrifuge.
parts.answer: Balance the tubes (equal masses opposite each other); close the lid before starting and do not open it until the rotor has stopped; use tubes that are not cracked and are capped.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: A student plans to compare catalase activity in leaves of trees growing beside a busy highway near Islamabad and in a park 1 km away. She will collect the leaves herself, then grind them with sand and test the extracts with 3 % hydrogen peroxide in the school laboratory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify hazards in the fieldwork part of the investigation and give suitable precautions.
parts.answer: Traffic: risk of being hit by vehicles — work away from the road edge, wear a high-visibility vest, go with a partner. Plants (thorns, sap, insects/stinging insects, allergies) — gloves, long sleeves. Air pollution / exhaust fumes — limit time spent near the road. Permission/lone working — tell someone where you are going, get permission from the landowner/park authority.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard with a matching precaution, max 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify one hazard in the laboratory part and give a precaution.
parts.answer: Sand and pestle grinding can splash extract/sand into eyes — eye protection; or hydrogen peroxide irritant — goggles; or dust/pollutants on leaves — wash leaves and hands.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a risk assessment should consider people other than the student.
parts.answer: Others nearby (classmates, the public, drivers) could be harmed by the activity, e.g. spills on the floor, broken glass, or a student stepping into traffic, so precautions must protect them too.
parts.working: B1

subtopics.name: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
Skill: recording results in a table

subtopics: Skill: recording results in a table

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An electron micrograph of a cell from the pancreas shows four structures, described below.
P: a stack of flattened, curved membrane-bound sacs with small vesicles budding from the edges
Q: an organelle with a double membrane; the inner membrane is folded into shelves
R: a network of flattened membrane-bound sacs with many small dark granules attached to the outer surface
S: a large structure bounded by two membranes with gaps (pores) in them
Name structures P, Q, R and S.
parts.answer: P Golgi body (Golgi apparatus); Q mitochondrion; R rough endoplasmic reticulum; S nucleus (nuclear envelope)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept Golgi complex for P. Do not accept 'ER' alone for R.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two functions of structure P.
parts.answer: Any two: modifies proteins (e.g. adds carbohydrate to make glycoproteins); packages proteins into (secretory) vesicles; makes lysosomes
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: modifies/processes proteins (or lipids); adds carbohydrate / forms glycoproteins; packages/sorts into vesicles for secretion (exocytosis); forms lysosomes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which structure is found in both plant and animal cells but is never found in prokaryotic cells?
A 70S ribosome
B Golgi body
C cell wall
D circular DNA
parts.answer: B Golgi body
parts.working: The Golgi body is a membrane-bound organelle, found only in eukaryotic cells. Prokaryotes have 70S ribosomes, circular DNA and a cell wall (peptidoglycan), so A, C and D are found in prokaryotes; a cell wall is also absent from animal cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A palisade mesophyll cell from a mango leaf is compared with a liver cell (hepatocyte). Name three structures found in the palisade mesophyll cell that are not found in the liver cell.
parts.answer: Cell wall; chloroplasts; large permanent vacuole (with tonoplast) — also accept plasmodesmata
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: cellulose cell wall; chloroplast; large (permanent) vacuole / tonoplast; plasmodesmata.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one structure found in the liver cell that is not found in the palisade mesophyll cell.
parts.answer: Centrioles (centrosome)
parts.working: Centriole(s). Also accept microvilli. Do not accept lysosome or mitochondrion (both types of cell have these).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Liver cells contain a large amount of smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER). State two functions of SER.
parts.answer: Synthesis of lipids (including steroids/phospholipids); detoxification of drugs/toxins (e.g. alcohol)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: lipid synthesis; steroid synthesis; detoxification; storage of calcium ions (in muscle).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the organelle in which most ATP is produced in a cell respiring aerobically.
parts.answer: Mitochondrion
parts.working: Mitochondrion / mitochondria.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the structure of a mitochondrion as seen in an electron micrograph.
parts.answer: Surrounded by an envelope of two membranes; the inner membrane is folded into cristae; the inside is a fluid matrix; the matrix contains 70S ribosomes and circular DNA
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: double membrane / envelope; inner membrane folded into cristae; matrix; 70S (small) ribosomes in matrix; circular DNA (loop) in matrix; intermembrane space.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The middle section of a human sperm cell is packed with mitochondria. Suggest why.
parts.answer: The tail (flagellum) needs a lot of ATP for movement; mitochondria release energy/produce ATP by aerobic respiration close to where it is used
parts.working: 1 mark: (aerobic) respiration produces large amounts of ATP. 1 mark: ATP needed for beating of the tail / swimming to the egg.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the function of the nucleolus?
A makes ribosomal RNA and assembles ribosome subunits
B makes proteins that are secreted from the cell
C controls the movement of molecules into and out of the nucleus
D stores the chromosomes during interphase
parts.answer: A makes ribosomal RNA and assembles ribosome subunits
parts.working: The nucleolus is where rRNA is transcribed and combined with proteins to form ribosome subunits. Secreted proteins are made on the rough ER (B); the nuclear envelope and its pores control movement in and out (C).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Chloroplasts contain two structures that are also found in prokaryotic cells. Name these two structures.
parts.answer: 70S ribosomes; circular DNA
parts.working: 1 mark each: 70S/small ribosomes; circular DNA (loop of DNA).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the stacks of membranes inside a chloroplast and state their function.
parts.answer: Grana (stacks of thylakoids); site of the light-dependent stage / contain chlorophyll that absorbs light
parts.working: Grana/thylakoids AND absorb light / light-dependent reactions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the fluid surrounding these stacks.
parts.answer: Stroma
parts.working: Stroma.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which structure in an animal cell is made of microtubules arranged as nine triplets in a cylinder?
A centriole
B ribosome
C microvillus
D Golgi body
parts.answer: A centriole
parts.working: Centrioles are short cylinders of nine triplets of microtubules; they lie in pairs in the centrosome. Ribosomes are made of rRNA and protein; microvilli are folds of the cell surface membrane, not built of microtubule triplets; the Golgi body is a stack of membrane-bound cisternae.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe one difference in appearance between rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) and smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) in an electron micrograph.
parts.answer: RER has ribosomes attached to the outer surface of its membranes; SER has no ribosomes (and is often more tubular).
parts.working: 1 mark: ribosomes on RER / none on SER. Accept RER = flattened sacs (cisternae), SER = tubules as an extra detail, but the ribosome point is needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two functions of SER.
parts.answer: Any two: synthesis of lipids (e.g. phospholipids); synthesis of steroids (e.g. steroid hormones); storage of calcium ions (in muscle); detoxification of drugs (in liver)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: lipid/phospholipid synthesis; steroid synthesis; Ca²⁺ storage; detoxification. Do not accept 'protein synthesis'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Proteins made on RER are transported to the Golgi body. State how they are carried between these two organelles.
parts.answer: In (transport) vesicles that bud off the RER and fuse with the Golgi body
parts.working: 1 mark: vesicles (pinched off from RER, fusing with Golgi).

practice.stem:
Researchers in a laboratory in Karachi supplied pancreatic cells with radioactive amino acids for a short time and then followed where the radioactivity was found. The time after supply at which radioactivity was highest in each place is shown.
rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER): 3 min
Golgi body: 20 min
secretory vesicles: 40 min
outside the cell: 90 min

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the order in which the radioactivity peaks in the structures listed above.
parts.answer: Amino acids are joined into protein on ribosomes of the RER first; the protein is moved in vesicles to the Golgi body where it is modified and packaged; secretory vesicles carry it to the cell surface membrane; it is then released from the cell
parts.working: 1 mark each: (1) protein synthesised by ribosomes on RER (first peak at 3 min); (2) transported in (transport) vesicles to Golgi body; (3) modified/packaged in Golgi, e.g. glycosylated, (peak 20 min); (4) secretory vesicles (40 min) move to and fuse with cell surface membrane, so protein appears outside (90 min).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the process by which the protein leaves the cell.
parts.answer: Exocytosis
parts.working: Exocytosis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Vesicles move through the cytoplasm towards the cell surface membrane. Explain the role of microtubules in this movement.
parts.answer: Microtubules form tracks along which vesicles are carried; motor proteins (using ATP) move the vesicles along the microtubules
parts.working: 1 mark: microtubules act as tracks/part of the cytoskeleton. 1 mark: vesicles moved along them by motor proteins / using ATP.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cells lining the bronchi of people living in a city with heavy winter smog have both cilia and microvilli. Describe two differences between cilia and microvilli in structure and function.
parts.answer: Cilia contain microtubules (9 + 2 arrangement) and are longer; microvilli are small finger-like folds of the cell surface membrane with no microtubules. Cilia beat to move mucus; microvilli increase the surface area for absorption
parts.working: Max 3: cilia contain microtubules, microvilli do not; cilia are larger/longer; cilia move/beat (to waft mucus), microvilli do not move; microvilli increase surface area (for absorption/exchange); both covered by cell surface membrane (no credit alone).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Particles in smog can stop the cilia in the bronchi from beating. Suggest and explain one effect this has on the person.
parts.answer: Mucus (with trapped dust and bacteria) is no longer moved up and out of the airways; it builds up in the bronchi, so the risk of infection increases / the person coughs to remove it
parts.working: 1 mark: mucus not moved towards the throat / accumulates in airways. 1 mark: trapped bacteria/particles remain, so more infections (e.g. bronchitis) / coughing / narrowed airways.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of a lysosome.
parts.answer: A small vesicle surrounded by a single membrane, containing hydrolytic (digestive) enzymes
parts.working: Membrane-bound sac/vesicle containing hydrolytic enzymes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A neutrophil engulfs a bacterium. Explain how lysosomes are involved in destroying the bacterium.
parts.answer: The bacterium is enclosed in a phagocytic vacuole; lysosomes fuse with the vacuole; hydrolytic enzymes are released into it and digest (hydrolyse) the bacterium
parts.working: 1 mark each: bacterium in phagocytic vacuole/phagosome; lysosome fuses with vacuole; enzymes (e.g. proteases, lysozyme) hydrolyse/digest the bacterium.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Lysosomal enzymes work best at about pH 5, but the cytoplasm is at about pH 7.2. Suggest how this protects the cell if a lysosome bursts.
parts.answer: At pH 7.2 the enzymes have much lower activity (are partly denatured / active site shape is changed), so they do little damage to the cell's own molecules
parts.working: 1 mark: enzymes are less active at cytoplasm pH. 1 mark: so cell components are not digested / cell protected from self-digestion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which organelles are surrounded by a double membrane?
1 nucleus
2 mitochondrion
3 Golgi body
4 chloroplast
A 1, 2 and 4
B 2 and 4 only
C 1, 2 and 3
D 2, 3 and 4
parts.answer: A 1, 2 and 4
parts.working: The nuclear envelope, mitochondrial envelope and chloroplast envelope each have two membranes. The Golgi body is made of single-membrane sacs, so any option containing 3 is wrong. B forgets that the nuclear envelope is a double membrane.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure and function of plasmodesmata.
parts.answer: Narrow channels through the cell walls of adjacent plant cells, lined with cell surface membrane and containing cytoplasm; allow movement of substances (water, ions, sugars) / communication between cells
parts.working: 1 mark structure: pores/channels through cell walls connecting cytoplasm of neighbouring cells. 1 mark function: transport of substances/communication between cells (symplast pathway).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the large permanent vacuole helps to support a non-woody plant such as a spinach seedling.
parts.answer: The vacuole (cell sap) has a low water potential so water enters by osmosis; the vacuole swells and pushes the cytoplasm against the cell wall, making the cell turgid
parts.working: 1 mark: water enters vacuole by osmosis (across tonoplast). 1 mark: cell becomes turgid, pressing on the cell wall, so tissues are firm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Root hair cells do not contain chloroplasts. Suggest why.
parts.answer: They are underground / receive no light, so cannot photosynthesise
parts.working: Roots are in the dark so photosynthesis is not possible.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A liver cell has a volume of 4800 µm³. Mitochondria make up 21 % of this volume and the mean volume of one mitochondrion is 0.56 µm³. Calculate the number of mitochondria in the cell.
parts.answer: 1800 mitochondria

parts.label: b
parts.text: A cardiac muscle cell has a volume of 15 000 µm³, of which 35 % is mitochondria. Calculate how many times greater the total mitochondrial volume is in the cardiac muscle cell than in the liver cell. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 5.21 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why cardiac muscle cells have such a large volume of mitochondria.
parts.answer: Cardiac muscle contracts continuously throughout life, so needs large amounts of ATP; ATP is made by aerobic respiration in mitochondria
parts.working: 1 mark: mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration / ATP production. 1 mark: continuous contraction needs much ATP / energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Fish living in the sea lose water to the sea water and gain salts. 'Chloride cells' in their gills pump chloride ions out of the blood into the sea water, against a concentration gradient. Electron micrographs show that these cells contain very many mitochondria. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Pumping ions against a concentration gradient is active transport, which needs ATP; mitochondria supply ATP by aerobic respiration
parts.working: 1 mark: active transport (against gradient). 1 mark: requires ATP from (aerobic) respiration in mitochondria.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The cell surface membrane of a chloride cell is highly folded. Suggest the advantage of this.
parts.answer: Increases the surface area of membrane; more carrier proteins/pumps can be present so more ions transported per unit time
parts.working: 1 mark: larger surface area. 1 mark: more transport (carrier) proteins / faster rate of ion transport.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict and explain the effect of a respiratory poison such as cyanide on the movement of chloride ions by these cells.
parts.answer: Movement of chloride ions out would (almost) stop, because no/little ATP is made, so the pumps cannot work
parts.working: 1 mark: active transport stops/decreases. 1 mark: aerobic respiration inhibited so ATP not produced.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plasma cells develop from B-lymphocytes and secrete large quantities of antibody. Explain why plasma cells have an extensive rough endoplasmic reticulum.
parts.answer: Antibodies are proteins; RER has ribosomes that synthesise proteins (and transports them / folds them) for secretion
parts.working: 1 mark: antibodies are proteins (glycoproteins). 1 mark: ribosomes on RER synthesise proteins; RER transports/folds them.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why plasma cells also have a large Golgi body.
parts.answer: The Golgi body modifies the antibody (adds carbohydrate to form glycoprotein) and packages it into secretory vesicles for exocytosis
parts.working: 1 mark: modification/glycosylation. 1 mark: packaging into (secretory) vesicles.

parts.label: c
parts.text: In one study, RER made up 5 % of the cytoplasm volume in a resting B-lymphocyte and 35 % in a plasma cell. Calculate how many times greater the proportion of RER is in the plasma cell.
parts.answer: 7 times

parts.label: a
parts.text: Leydig cells in the testis secrete the steroid hormone testosterone. Beta cells in the pancreas secrete the protein hormone insulin. Suggest and explain which organelle is likely to be more abundant in each cell type.
parts.answer: Leydig cells: much smooth ER, because steroids are lipids made by SER. Beta cells: much rough ER (and Golgi), because insulin is a protein made by ribosomes on RER
parts.working: 1 mark: Leydig – SER. 1 mark: Beta – RER (and Golgi). 1 mark: correct reason linking SER to lipid/steroid synthesis and RER to protein synthesis (both needed).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Both cell types contain many secretory vesicles. Testosterone, however, can pass straight through membranes. Suggest why testosterone does not need to be released by exocytosis.
parts.answer: Steroids are lipid-soluble/non-polar, so they can diffuse through the phospholipid bilayer of the cell surface membrane
parts.working: 1 mark: lipid-soluble/non-polar. 1 mark: diffuses through phospholipid bilayer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Colchicine is a drug that stops tubulin molecules joining together to form microtubules. Predict and explain the effect of colchicine on a dividing cell in a root tip.
parts.answer: Spindle cannot form (spindle fibres are microtubules), so chromosomes / chromatids cannot be separated and mitosis stops (at metaphase)
parts.working: 1 mark: no spindle formed. 1 mark: chromatids not pulled apart / mitosis cannot be completed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest the effect of colchicine on a pancreatic cell that is secreting enzymes.
parts.answer: Secretion reduced, because vesicles from the Golgi are moved along microtubules to the cell surface membrane; without microtubules they are not transported
parts.working: 1 mark: less exocytosis/secretion. 1 mark: vesicle transport depends on microtubules.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Centrioles are made of microtubules. State where centrioles are found in an animal cell.
parts.answer: In the centrosome, near the nucleus
parts.working: Near the nucleus / in the centrosome (a pair at right angles).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement is true of BOTH a ribosome and a centriole?
A It is not surrounded by a membrane.
B It contains RNA.
C It is made of microtubules.
D It is found in prokaryotic cells.
parts.answer: A It is not surrounded by a membrane.
parts.working: Neither ribosomes nor centrioles have a membrane. Only ribosomes contain RNA (rRNA); only centrioles are made of microtubules; prokaryotes have (70S) ribosomes but no centrioles. Distractor D is tempting because ribosomes occur in prokaryotes, but centrioles do not.

practice.stem: Cells in the root cap of a maize seedling secrete a slimy layer of polysaccharide that coats the root tip. In electron micrographs, these cells have very large Golgi bodies with many vesicles near the cell surface membrane.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the role of the Golgi body in the production of this slime.
parts.answer: Golgi body makes/modifies the polysaccharide (and adds it to proteins); packages it into vesicles; vesicles move to and fuse with the cell surface membrane, releasing slime by exocytosis
parts.working: 1 mark each: Golgi synthesises/modifies polysaccharide (or makes glycoproteins); packages into (secretory) vesicles; vesicles fuse with cell surface membrane / exocytosis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Electron micrographs show that root cap cells also contain many mitochondria. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration to make ATP; ATP is needed for synthesis of the slime and for movement of vesicles/exocytosis
parts.working: 1 mark: aerobic respiration releases energy as ATP. 1 mark: ATP used for polysaccharide synthesis / vesicle transport / exocytosis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Root cap cells are worn away and replaced as the root grows through soil. Suggest one advantage to the plant of the slime layer.
parts.answer: Lubricates the root tip so it pushes through soil more easily / reduces damage to cells by friction
parts.working: 1 mark: lubrication / less friction / protects growing tip.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An electron micrograph shows a mitochondrion with an image length of 24 mm. The magnification is ×12 000. Calculate the actual length of the mitochondrion in µm.
parts.answer: 2 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert your answer to nm.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A transmission electron microscope can show ribosomes but a light microscope cannot. What is the reason?
A Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than light, so resolution is higher.
B Electron microscopes have higher magnification, so small objects appear larger.
C Ribosomes are stained only by heavy metals.
D Light passes straight through ribosomes.
parts.answer: A Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than light, so resolution is higher.
parts.working: Resolution depends on wavelength: the shorter wavelength of electrons lets two points closer together than about 200 nm be distinguished. Magnifying more (B) without better resolution only gives a larger, blurred image.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between magnification and resolution.
parts.answer: Magnification is how many times larger the image is than the actual object; resolution is the ability to distinguish two points close together as separate (the smallest distance between two points that can be seen as separate)
parts.working: 1 mark each correct definition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A red blood cell has a diameter of 7.5 µm. In a textbook drawing its diameter is 30 mm. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is 0.25 mm expressed in nanometres?
A 2.5 × 10³ nm
B 2.5 × 10⁴ nm
C 2.5 × 10⁵ nm
D 2.5 × 10⁶ nm
parts.answer: C 2.5 × 10⁵ nm
parts.working: 1 mm = 1000 µm and 1 µm = 1000 nm, so 1 mm = 10⁶ nm. 0.25 × 10⁶ = 2.5 × 10⁵ nm. B results from multiplying by only 10⁵.

practice.stem: Use the formula: magnification = image size ÷ actual size.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the image length of a cell of actual length 12 µm viewed at a magnification of ×1500. Give your answer in mm.
parts.answer: 18 mm

parts.label: b
parts.text: An image of a chloroplast is 45 mm long at a magnification of ×15 000. Calculate the actual length in µm.
parts.answer: 3 µm

parts.label: c
parts.text: A virus particle with an actual diameter of 250 nm has an image diameter of 20 mm on a micrograph. Calculate the magnification.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a student would calibrate an eyepiece graticule using a stage micrometer.
parts.answer: Place stage micrometer on stage and focus; rotate eyepiece so graticule scale lies alongside/overlaps the micrometer scale; line up the zero marks / find a point where two lines coincide; count eyepiece units equal to a known number of micrometer divisions; calculate the length of one eyepiece unit (= micrometer length ÷ number of eyepiece units)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: micrometer on stage, focused; scales lined up/superimposed; count graticule divisions matching a known micrometer length; divide to find µm per eyepiece unit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The stage micrometer scale is 1 mm long and is divided into 100 equal divisions. State the length of one division in µm.
parts.answer: 10 µm

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a stage micrometer cannot simply be used to measure cells directly in the same view.
parts.answer: The cells and the micrometer cannot be on the stage/in focus at the same time (the micrometer is a separate slide)
parts.working: 1 mark: specimen slide and micrometer slide cannot be viewed together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages of an electron microscope compared with a light microscope.
parts.answer: Higher resolution (about 0.5 nm compared with about 200 nm); can produce higher useful magnification; shows ultrastructure such as ribosomes, membranes and cristae
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: higher resolution; higher (useful) magnification; organelles/ultrastructure visible.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two advantages of a light microscope compared with an electron microscope.
parts.answer: Any two: living cells can be viewed; natural colour / coloured stains can be seen; cheaper / portable; simpler and quicker specimen preparation; no vacuum needed
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid points.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why specimens for transmission electron microscopy must be very thin.
parts.answer: Electrons must pass through the specimen; thick specimens would absorb/scatter all the electrons so no image forms
parts.working: 1 mark: electrons have low penetrating power / must be transmitted through specimen.

practice.stem: A student in Faisalabad looks at a leaf epidermis with a light microscope fitted with an eyepiece graticule. Using the ×40 objective lens, 40 eyepiece graticule units line up exactly with 25 divisions of a stage micrometer. Each stage micrometer division is 0.01 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the length of one eyepiece graticule unit in µm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The lengths of five guard cells measured in eyepiece units were 11, 12, 10, 13 and 12. Calculate the mean actual length of the guard cells in µm.
parts.working: M1: mean = 58 ÷ 5 = 11.6 eyepiece units. A1: 11.6 × 6.25 = 72.5 µm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the eyepiece graticule must be calibrated again if the student changes to the ×10 objective lens.
parts.answer: The eyepiece graticule stays the same size in the eyepiece, but the specimen's image size changes with magnification, so each eyepiece unit represents a different actual length
parts.working: 1 mark: graticule scale does not change when objective changes. 1 mark: magnification of specimen changes so value of each unit changes.

practice.stem: A micrograph of a leaf cell has a scale bar labelled 5 µm. The scale bar is 18 mm long on the micrograph. A chloroplast in the same micrograph is 27 mm long.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the micrograph.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the actual length of the chloroplast in µm.
parts.answer: 7.5 µm
parts.working: M1: 27 mm = 27 000 µm. A1: 27 000 ÷ 3600 = 7.5 µm (allow ecf from a).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A nucleus has a diameter of 8 µm. A student draws it at a magnification of ×2500. What is the diameter of the drawing?
A 2.0 × 10¹ mm
B 2.0 × 10⁰ mm
C 3.2 × 10⁻³ mm
D 2.0 × 10² mm
parts.answer: A 2.0 × 10¹ mm
parts.working: 8 µm × 2500 = 20 000 µm = 20 mm = 2.0 × 10¹ mm. B comes from dividing by 10 000 instead of 1000 when converting µm to mm.

practice.stem: A student in Multan examines a stained blood smear with a light microscope. With the ×40 objective lens, one eyepiece graticule unit has been calibrated as 2.5 µm. The diameters of six red blood cells, in eyepiece units, are: 3.0, 2.8, 3.2, 3.0, 2.9, 3.1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean diameter of the red blood cells in µm.
parts.answer: 7.5 µm
parts.working: M1: mean = 18.0 ÷ 6 = 3.0 eyepiece units. A1: 3.0 × 2.5 = 7.5 µm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student draws one red blood cell with a diameter of 45 mm. Calculate the magnification of the drawing, using the mean diameter.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A white blood cell on the same slide is 5.0 eyepiece units across. Calculate its actual diameter in µm.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the student measured six red blood cells rather than one.
parts.answer: Red blood cells vary in size, so a mean of several cells gives a more representative (reliable) value
parts.working: 1 mark: variation between cells / one cell may be unusual; mean is more representative.

practice.stem: A student draws a group of guard cells seen with a light microscope. The drawing has a magnification of ×800.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the length, in mm, that the student should draw a 25 µm scale bar on this drawing.
parts.answer: 20 mm

parts.label: b
parts.text: A guard cell on the drawing is 36 mm long. Calculate its actual length in µm.
parts.answer: 45 µm

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student enlarges the drawing so that the magnification becomes ×3200. Explain why no further detail can be seen in the enlarged drawing.
parts.answer: Resolution is limited by the light microscope (about 200 nm); enlarging the drawing increases magnification but not resolution, so details closer together than the resolution limit still cannot be distinguished
parts.working: 1 mark: resolution / resolving power does not change. 1 mark: points closer than about 200 nm still appear as one / no new detail.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the meaning of the term resolution.
parts.answer: The ability to distinguish between two points that are close together as separate points (the smallest distance between two points that can be seen as separate)
parts.working: 1 mark: two close points distinguished as separate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A light microscope has a resolution of 200 nm. State which of these structures could be seen as separate objects with this microscope: nucleus (diameter 6 µm); chloroplast (length 5 µm); ribosome (diameter 25 nm); thickness of cell surface membrane (7.5 nm).
parts.answer: Nucleus and chloroplast only
parts.working: 1 mark for nucleus and chloroplast. 1 mark for correctly excluding both ribosome and membrane thickness (both smaller than 200 nm).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The resolution of a light microscope is about half the wavelength of the light used. Calculate the resolution when blue light of wavelength 450 nm is used and explain why blue light gives a better image of fine detail than red light of wavelength 700 nm.
parts.answer: 225 nm; shorter wavelength gives smaller resolution distance (red gives 350 nm), so finer detail can be distinguished
parts.working: B1: 225 nm. B1: shorter wavelength → better resolution (smaller distance between distinguishable points).

practice.stem: A transmission electron micrograph of the nucleus of a pancreatic cell has a magnification of ×80 000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: On the micrograph, one nuclear pore has an image diameter of 9.6 mm. Calculate the actual diameter of the pore in nm.
parts.answer: 120 nm

parts.label: b
parts.text: The whole nuclear envelope (both membranes and the space between them) is 2.4 mm wide on the same micrograph. Calculate its actual width in nm.
parts.answer: 30 nm

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using your answer to (a), explain why nuclear pores cannot be seen with a light microscope.
parts.answer: 120 nm is smaller than the resolution of a light microscope (about 200 nm), so the pore cannot be distinguished
parts.working: 1 mark: pore smaller than ~200 nm resolution limit (magnification is not the problem).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A ribosome has a diameter of 25 nm. Calculate the diameter of its image in mm if it is viewed at a magnification of ×1500.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The resolution of a light microscope is about 200 nm. Explain why ribosomes cannot be seen as separate structures with a light microscope, even though their image could be made larger by greater magnification.
parts.answer: Ribosomes (25 nm) are much smaller than the resolution limit, and are closer together than 200 nm; the wavelength of light is too long, so they cannot be distinguished as separate points – increasing magnification only enlarges a blurred image
parts.working: 1 mark: ribosomes smaller than/closer together than 200 nm limit (wavelength of light too long). 1 mark: magnifying beyond the resolution limit gives no more detail / image is blurred.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of using a light microscope rather than an electron microscope to study malaria parasites inside red blood cells.
parts.answer: Living cells can be observed (e.g. to watch movement); or colour can be seen with stains; or cheaper/portable for field clinics
parts.working: Any one: living specimens can be viewed; natural/stained colour seen; quicker/simpler preparation; cheaper/portable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: On an electron micrograph a bacterium that is 2 µm long has an image length of 50 mm. Calculate the magnification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A bacteriophage virus attached to the same bacterium has an image length of 2.5 mm. Calculate the actual length of the virus in nm.
parts.answer: 100 nm

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one feature that would be visible in a transmission electron micrograph of the bacterium but would not be seen in a scanning electron micrograph.
parts.answer: Internal structures, e.g. ribosomes / DNA (nucleoid) / cell wall in section
parts.working: SEM shows only the surface; TEM shows internal detail, e.g. ribosomes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
With a ×100 total magnification, the diameter of the field of view of a light microscope is 1.8 mm. The student then switches to ×400 total magnification. A cheek cell stretches across 0.3 of the diameter of the new field of view. What is the approximate width of the cheek cell?
A 13.5 µm
B 54 µm
C 135 µm
D 540 µm
parts.answer: C 135 µm
parts.working: Field diameter is inversely proportional to magnification: 1.8 mm × 100/400 = 0.45 mm. 0.3 × 0.45 mm = 0.135 mm = 135 µm. D (540 µm) uses the ×100 field diameter without scaling.

practice.stem: A scanning electron micrograph of a yeast cell from a bakery culture in Lahore has a magnification of ×6000. The image of the cell is circular with a diameter of 36 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual diameter of the yeast cell in µm.
parts.answer: 6 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Treating the cell as a sphere, calculate its volume in µm³. Use V = 4/3 πr³. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 113 µm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using surface area = 4πr², calculate the surface area : volume ratio of the cell.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A second yeast cell in the same micrograph has an image diameter of 72 mm. Without further measurement, state its surface area : volume ratio and explain your answer.
parts.answer: 0.5 : 1; the diameter (radius) is doubled and SA:V of a sphere = 3/r, so the ratio halves
parts.working: B1: 0.5. B1: SA increases ×4 but volume ×8 / ratio = 3/r, so doubling r halves ratio.

practice.stem: An electron micrograph labelled ×5000 is enlarged to 150 % of its original size on a photocopier. The label is not changed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the enlarged copy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A mitochondrion is 30 mm long on the enlarged copy. Calculate its actual length in µm.
parts.answer: 4 µm
parts.working: M1: uses ×7500 (not ×5000). A1: 30 000 µm ÷ 7500 = 4 µm. (Using ×5000 gives 6 µm — no credit.)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a scale bar printed on the original micrograph would still give correct measurements on the enlarged copy, but the printed magnification would not.
parts.answer: The scale bar is enlarged by the same factor as the image, so its length still represents the same actual length; the printed magnification number stays the same even though the image has become larger, so it is now wrong
parts.working: 1 mark: scale bar scales with image. 1 mark: written magnification value is not changed by enlarging.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The human eye can just distinguish two points 0.1 mm apart. Calculate the minimum magnification needed so that two points 200 nm apart appear 0.1 mm apart.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A light microscope can magnify up to ×1500. Explain why magnifying a specimen more than about ×1500 with a light microscope does not help to see more detail.
parts.answer: Resolution is limited to about 200 nm by the wavelength of light; any further magnification just makes the blurred image larger ('empty magnification') without separating more points
parts.working: 1 mark: resolution limited by wavelength of light. 1 mark: extra magnification enlarges blur / no extra detail.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A transmission electron microscope has a resolution of 0.5 nm. Calculate the useful magnification needed for two points 0.5 nm apart to appear 0.1 mm apart.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Vibrio cholerae is the bacterium that causes cholera. State four ways in which the structure of Vibrio cholerae differs from the structure of a cell lining the inside of the human cheek.
parts.answer: Vibrio: no nucleus (DNA free in cytoplasm); circular DNA (not linear chromosomes with histones); 70S ribosomes (not 80S); peptidoglycan cell wall (cheek cell has no wall); no membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria/ER/Golgi; may have plasmids and a flagellum; much smaller
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four comparative points: no nucleus/nuclear envelope; circular DNA not linear; DNA not associated with histones; 70S v 80S ribosomes; cell wall of peptidoglycan present; no membrane-bound organelles (named); plasmids present; smaller size (1–5 µm v about 50 µm).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which structure is present in all viruses?
A a protein capsid
B a phospholipid envelope
C ribosomes
D DNA
parts.answer: A a protein capsid
parts.working: Every virus has nucleic acid surrounded by a protein coat (capsid). Only some viruses, such as HIV and influenza, have an envelope (B); some viruses contain RNA instead of DNA (D), and no virus has ribosomes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which structure is found in many bacteria but not in an animal cell?
A plasmid
B 80S ribosome
C mitochondrion
D Golgi body
parts.answer: A plasmid
parts.working: Plasmids (small circles of DNA) occur in many bacteria but not in animal cells. 80S ribosomes, mitochondria and Golgi bodies are eukaryotic features; bacteria have 70S ribosomes and no membrane-bound organelles.

practice.stem: Salmonella bacteria from a contaminated food sample were examined with an electron microscope. Four structures were described.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name structures P, Q, R and S.
P: a rigid outer layer made of peptidoglycan
Q: one large loop of DNA lying in the cytoplasm
R: small extra loops of DNA, often carrying genes for antibiotic resistance
S: small particles in the cytoplasm, about 20 nm across, where polypeptides are made
parts.answer: P cell wall; Q circular DNA / bacterial chromosome; R plasmids; S 70S ribosomes
parts.working: 1 mark each. For Q accept 'nucleoid'. For S, '70S' not required for the mark but 'ribosome' is.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the typical diameter range of a prokaryotic cell.
parts.answer: About 1–5 µm (accept 0.5–5 µm)
parts.working: 1 mark; units required.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An E. coli cell is 2 µm long. A human liver cell is 25 µm across. Calculate how many times longer the liver cell is than the bacterium.
parts.answer: 12.5 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: In ideal conditions an E. coli cell divides by binary fission every 20 minutes. Calculate the number of cells produced from one cell after 2 hours, and state one assumption you have made.
parts.answer: 64 cells; assumption: every cell divides every 20 minutes / no cells die / nutrients are not limiting
parts.working: B1: 2 h = 6 generations; 2⁶ = 64. B1: any valid assumption (all cells divide at the same rate, none die, nutrients/space not limiting).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one structure found in E. coli but not in the liver cell.
parts.answer: Any one: cell wall (peptidoglycan); plasmid; 70S ribosomes in the cytoplasm; flagellum (some strains)
parts.working: 1 mark. Do not accept 'ribosomes' without '70S'.

practice.stem: Dengue fever is caused by an enveloped virus that is carried by Aedes mosquitoes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three ways in which the structure of a dengue virus particle differs from the structure of a bacterium such as E. coli.
parts.answer: Any three: virus has RNA (not DNA) as genetic material; virus has a protein capsid, not a peptidoglycan cell wall; virus has no cytoplasm or ribosomes; virus envelope comes from the host cell membrane (bacterium has its own cell surface membrane); virus is much smaller (about 50 nm, not 1–5 µm); no plasmids
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three valid comparative differences.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Doctors in Rawalpindi do not prescribe antibiotics to treat dengue fever. Explain why antibiotics would not cure dengue.
parts.answer: Antibiotics act on bacterial structures/processes (e.g. peptidoglycan cell wall or 70S ribosomes); viruses lack these / are not cells and use the host cell's ribosomes and enzymes
parts.working: 1 mark: antibiotics target bacterial features. 1 mark: viruses have no cell wall/ribosomes/metabolism of their own.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why viruses are not considered to be cells.
parts.answer: They have no cytoplasm, ribosomes or cell surface membrane of their own / no metabolism; they can only reproduce inside a host cell using the host's machinery
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: no cytoplasm; no ribosomes/organelles; no cell surface membrane (envelope comes from host); cannot carry out metabolism/respire; only replicate inside host cells.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the structure of an enveloped virus such as influenza.
parts.answer: Nucleic acid (RNA in influenza) core; surrounded by a protein capsid; outer envelope of phospholipid (from host cell membrane) with (glyco)protein spikes / attachment proteins
parts.working: 1 mark each: nucleic acid core (RNA or DNA); capsid made of protein (capsomeres); phospholipid envelope with surface glycoproteins.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cells of a Streptococcus bacterium have a diameter of 0.8 µm. Calculate how many of these cells could fit side by side in a line 1 mm long.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some antibiotics bind to 70S ribosomes. Explain why these antibiotics stop bacteria growing but have little effect on the cells of the person taking them.
parts.answer: Bacteria have 70S ribosomes, so their protein synthesis is stopped; human cells make proteins in the cytoplasm on 80S ribosomes, which have a different shape and are not affected
parts.working: 1 mark: bacterial protein synthesis inhibited at 70S ribosomes. 1 mark: human cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S / different shape so antibiotic does not bind.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the main polymer in the cell wall of a bacterium.
parts.answer: Peptidoglycan (murein)
parts.working: Peptidoglycan. Do not accept cellulose or chitin.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about prokaryotic cells is correct?
A The DNA is linear and enclosed by a nuclear envelope.
B The ribosomes are 70S and are free in the cytoplasm.
C The cell wall is made of cellulose.
D Aerobic respiration takes place in mitochondria.
parts.answer: B The ribosomes are 70S and are free in the cytoplasm.
parts.working: Prokaryotes have only 70S ribosomes, which are not attached to any membranes. Their DNA is circular and not enclosed (A), the wall is peptidoglycan (C) and they have no mitochondria (D).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row correctly compares a bacterial cell with a plant cell?
(ribosomes in bacterium | main component of bacterial cell wall | DNA in bacterium)
A 70S | peptidoglycan | circular, not in a nucleus
B 70S | cellulose | circular, not in a nucleus
C 80S | peptidoglycan | linear, in a nucleus
D 80S | cellulose | circular, in a nucleus
parts.answer: A 70S | peptidoglycan | circular, not in a nucleus
parts.working: Bacteria have 70S ribosomes, cell walls of peptidoglycan (murein) and circular DNA lying free in the cytoplasm. B is wrong because cellulose is the main component of plant, not bacterial, cell walls.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For a sphere, surface area = πd² and volume = πd³/6, so the surface area : volume ratio = 6/d. Calculate the surface area : volume ratio for a spherical bacterium of diameter 1 µm and for a spherical eukaryotic cell of diameter 20 µm.
parts.answer: Bacterium 6.0 µm⁻¹ (6 : 1); eukaryotic cell 0.3 µm⁻¹ (0.3 : 1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times larger the ratio is for the bacterium.
parts.answer: 20 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why bacteria do not need specialised transport systems.
parts.answer: Large SA:V means a large surface for exchange relative to the volume needing supplies; diffusion distances are very short, so diffusion across the cell surface is fast enough
parts.working: 1 mark: large SA relative to volume. 1 mark: short diffusion distance / diffusion alone is enough.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three differences between the DNA of a prokaryotic cell and the DNA in the nucleus of a eukaryotic cell.
parts.answer: Prokaryotic DNA is circular, eukaryotic is linear; prokaryotic is free in the cytoplasm, eukaryotic is in a nucleus (enclosed by an envelope); prokaryotic is not associated with histones ('naked'), eukaryotic is wound round histones to form chromatin/chromosomes; prokaryotes often have plasmids too
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three paired differences.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Bacteria have no mitochondria but many species respire aerobically. Suggest where the enzymes for the later stages of aerobic respiration are found in these bacteria.
parts.answer: On / in the cell surface membrane (and the cytoplasm)
parts.working: 1 mark: cell surface membrane (accept infoldings of membrane).

practice.stem: Poliovirus particles have a diameter of about 30 nm. HIV particles have a diameter of about 120 nm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the diameter of HIV is than the diameter of poliovirus.
parts.answer: 4 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Both viruses are roughly spherical. Calculate how many times greater the volume of HIV is.
parts.answer: 64 times
parts.working: M1: volume ∝ d³. A1: 4³ = 64.

parts.label: c
parts.text: HIV has an envelope but poliovirus does not. State the origin of the envelope of HIV.
parts.answer: The cell surface membrane of the host cell it left (taken as the virus buds out)
parts.working: 1 mark: host cell (surface) membrane.

practice.stem: During hot summers, the water of a lake in Punjab turns green because of a bloom of cyanobacteria (photosynthetic bacteria).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why cyanobacteria are classified as prokaryotes even though they photosynthesise.
parts.answer: They have no chloroplasts / photosynthetic membranes lie free in the cytoplasm; they have no nucleus or other double-membrane-bound organelles (circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, peptidoglycan wall)
parts.working: 1 mark: no chloroplasts (membrane-bound organelle). 1 mark: any other prokaryotic feature (no nucleus, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, peptidoglycan wall).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sample of lake water contained 3.6 × 10⁶ cyanobacteria per cm³. Calculate the number in 2.5 dm³ of lake water. Give your answer in standard form.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Giardia is a single-celled organism that lives in the human gut and causes diarrhoea, often after drinking contaminated water. Studies of Giardia show:
• it has two nuclei, each surrounded by a nuclear envelope
• its DNA is linear and associated with proteins
• it has 80S ribosomes and endoplasmic reticulum
• it has no mitochondria
• it has several flagella
A student says Giardia is a prokaryote because it is unicellular and has no mitochondria. Explain why the student is wrong.
parts.answer: Giardia is a eukaryote: it has a nucleus with a nuclear envelope, linear DNA with proteins, 80S ribosomes and ER; prokaryotes never have these. Being unicellular and lacking mitochondria does not make it a prokaryote (many eukaryotes are unicellular)
parts.working: 1 mark: has nuclei/nuclear envelope (prokaryotes have none). 1 mark: 80S ribosomes / ER / linear DNA with histones are eukaryotic features. 1 mark: eukaryotes can be unicellular / absence of mitochondria is not enough to classify it as prokaryotic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A Giardia cell is about 12 µm long. A typical gut bacterium is 1.5 µm long. Calculate how many times longer the Giardia cell is.
parts.answer: 8 times

parts.label: a
parts.text: A coronavirus particle has a diameter of 120 nm. In an electron micrograph its image diameter is 6 mm. Calculate the magnification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why viruses can be seen only with an electron microscope.
parts.answer: They are smaller than the resolution limit of a light microscope (about 200 nm); electron microscopes have much higher resolution
parts.working: Virus (120 nm) is below the 200 nm resolution of the light microscope.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Patients with a viral infection sometimes ask doctors for antibiotics. Explain why antibiotics are not effective against viruses.
parts.answer: Antibiotics act on bacterial structures/processes such as peptidoglycan cell walls or 70S ribosomes; viruses do not have these (they use the host cell's machinery)
parts.working: 1 mark: antibiotics target bacterial cell walls/70S ribosomes/bacterial enzymes. 1 mark: viruses have no cell wall/ribosomes/metabolism of their own.

practice.stem: A bacteriophage is a virus that infects bacteria. After one phage infects a bacterium, the cell bursts 25 minutes later, releasing 150 new phages.

parts.label: a
parts.text: One phage infects one bacterium. Assuming every new phage infects a fresh bacterium and all bacteria burst at the same time, calculate the number of phages present 50 minutes after the first infection.
parts.working: M1: two cycles in 50 min. A1: 150 × 150 = 22 500.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of phages after 75 minutes. Give your answer in standard form.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the phage cannot reproduce in a nutrient broth that contains no bacteria.
parts.answer: Viruses have no ribosomes/enzymes/metabolism of their own; they must use the host cell's ribosomes, ATP and nucleotides/amino acids to make new viral nucleic acid and proteins
parts.working: 1 mark: no cellular machinery (ribosomes/enzymes). 1 mark: needs host cell to replicate nucleic acid and make capsid protein.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four features of mitochondria and chloroplasts that support the idea that they were once free-living prokaryotes.
parts.answer: Contain their own circular DNA; have 70S ribosomes; are about the size of bacteria (1–5 µm); surrounded by two membranes (the inner one like a prokaryotic cell membrane); divide by a process like binary fission
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some antibiotics that target 70S ribosomes can cause side effects in human cells. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Mitochondria contain 70S ribosomes; the antibiotic may stop protein synthesis in mitochondria, reducing aerobic respiration/ATP production in human cells
parts.working: 1 mark: mitochondrial ribosomes are 70S. 1 mark: mitochondrial protein synthesis / ATP supply affected.

practice.stem: A student views a rod-shaped bacterium using an oil-immersion objective. One eyepiece unit = 0.25 µm. The bacterium is 10 eyepiece units long and 3.2 eyepiece units wide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual length and width of the bacterium in µm.
parts.answer: Length 2.5 µm; width 0.8 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Treating the bacterium as a cylinder (V = πr²h), calculate its volume in µm³. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 1.26 µm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: A yeast cell has a diameter of 5 µm. Treating it as a sphere (V = 4/3 πr³), calculate how many times greater its volume is than that of the bacterium. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 52.1 times

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hand sanitiser containing ethanol rapidly inactivates coronaviruses but is much less effective against norovirus. Using your knowledge of virus structure, suggest an explanation.
parts.answer: Coronavirus has a phospholipid envelope; ethanol (and soap) dissolves/disrupts lipid, destroying the envelope and its attachment proteins, so the virus cannot enter host cells; norovirus has no envelope, only a protein capsid, which is less affected
parts.working: 1 mark: coronavirus is enveloped (phospholipid). 1 mark: ethanol/soap disrupts lipid envelope → attachment glycoproteins lost/cannot infect. 1 mark: norovirus has only a capsid (no lipid).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Norovirus has RNA as its genetic material. State two ways in which the RNA of norovirus differs from the DNA of a bacterium.
parts.answer: Any two: RNA is single-stranded, bacterial DNA is double-stranded; RNA contains ribose, DNA deoxyribose; RNA contains uracil, DNA thymine; norovirus RNA is linear, bacterial DNA is circular
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two paired differences.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which components of the cell surface membrane are mainly involved in cell recognition?
A the fatty acid tails of phospholipids
B glycoproteins and glycolipids
C cholesterol molecules
D channel proteins
parts.answer: B glycoproteins and glycolipids
parts.working: The carbohydrate chains of glycoproteins and glycolipids (the glycocalyx) act as recognition sites / antigens. Cholesterol (C) only regulates fluidity and stability; channel proteins (D) let ions and polar molecules through.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substance crosses the phospholipid bilayer of a cell surface membrane most rapidly by simple diffusion?
A glucose
B carbon dioxide
C potassium ions
D amino acids
parts.answer: B carbon dioxide
parts.working: CO₂ is small and non-polar, so it passes between the hydrophobic fatty acid tails. Glucose and amino acids are polar and K⁺ is charged, so they need channel or carrier proteins.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State the function of each of these components of a cell surface membrane:
(i) channel protein
(ii) carrier protein
(iii) cholesterol
(iv) glycolipid
parts.answer: (i) forms a water-filled pore that lets specific ions/polar molecules through by facilitated diffusion; (ii) binds a specific molecule and changes shape to move it across (facilitated diffusion or active transport); (iii) regulates fluidity/stability of the membrane, reduces permeability to water and ions; (iv) cell recognition / acts as antigen / receptor, helps cells attach to each other.
parts.working: 1 mark each: (i) hydrophilic pore for ions/polar molecules; (ii) binds specific solute, changes shape; (iii) controls fluidity / mechanical stability / reduces leakage of polar substances; (iv) recognition / antigen / cell adhesion / receptor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Membranes are found inside eukaryotic cells as well as around them. State three roles of membranes inside cells, giving an example of an organelle for each.
parts.answer: Compartmentalisation – keeps enzymes/reactions separate, e.g. lysosome keeps hydrolytic enzymes away from cytoplasm; site of attachment of enzymes / electron carriers, e.g. inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae) or thylakoid membranes in chloroplasts; transport/packaging of proteins in vesicles, e.g. rough ER and Golgi body; control of entry/exit of substances, e.g. nuclear envelope with pores.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three roles each with a correct example: separating reactions (lysosome/nucleus); holding enzymes or electron carriers (cristae/thylakoids); forming vesicles for transport (ER/Golgi); controlling what enters an organelle (nuclear envelope).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the structure of the cell surface membrane is described as a 'fluid mosaic'.
parts.answer: Fluid: phospholipids (and many proteins) can move about / diffuse sideways within the bilayer. Mosaic: proteins are scattered among the phospholipids in a pattern, like tiles of a mosaic.
parts.working: 1 mark: fluid – molecules move laterally within their layer. 1 mark: mosaic – proteins (of different kinds) scattered/embedded through the phospholipid bilayer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Fish living in very cold water under polar ice have cell membranes with a different composition from fish in tropical rivers such as the Indus. State the role of cholesterol in a cell membrane.
parts.answer: Cholesterol regulates membrane fluidity: it stops phospholipids packing too closely at low temperature (keeps the membrane fluid) and restricts their movement at high temperature (keeps it stable); it also reduces permeability to ions/polar molecules.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: regulates/buffers fluidity; prevents tight packing / keeps membrane fluid at low temperature; reduces fluidity / adds stability at high temperature; reduces permeability to water-soluble ions/polar molecules; mechanical stability.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why sodium ions cannot cross the phospholipid bilayer by simple diffusion.
parts.answer: Sodium ions are charged (and surrounded by water molecules); the interior of the bilayer is made of hydrophobic fatty acid tails, which repel/do not let charged particles through, so they must use channel or carrier proteins.
parts.working: 1 mark: ions are charged / hydrated / water-soluble. 1 mark: core of bilayer is hydrophobic (fatty acid tails), so ions need channel/carrier proteins.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Proteins in the membrane of a human cell were labelled with a green fluorescent dye, and proteins of a mouse cell with a red dye. The two cells were fused. After 40 minutes at 37 °C the red and green labels were evenly mixed over the whole hybrid cell. At 5 °C the labels stayed in separate halves.
What do these results show?
A Membrane proteins are fixed in position by the cytoskeleton at all temperatures.
B Membrane proteins can move sideways in the bilayer, and this movement is faster at higher temperature.
C Membrane proteins are made faster at 37 °C than at 5 °C.
D Phospholipids flip between the two layers of the membrane at 37 °C.
parts.answer: B Membrane proteins can move sideways in the bilayer, and this movement is faster at higher temperature.
parts.working: Mixing shows lateral movement of proteins (the 'fluid' in fluid mosaic); it needs kinetic energy so it is slowed at 5 °C. C is wrong because the labels were on existing proteins; D is about phospholipids, which were not labelled.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Wheat plants that survive cold winters in the north of Pakistan increase the proportion of cholesterol-like sterols and unsaturated fatty acids in their membranes in autumn. What is the main effect of this change at low temperatures?
A The membrane becomes more rigid, so fewer ions leak out.
B The membrane stays fluid enough for membrane proteins to work.
C Glycoproteins are replaced by glycolipids.
D The phospholipids form a single layer instead of a bilayer.
parts.answer: B The membrane stays fluid enough for membrane proteins to work.
parts.working: Kinks in unsaturated fatty acid tails stop phospholipids packing tightly, and sterols disrupt close packing at low temperature, so the membrane does not become a rigid gel and carriers/channels/enzymes can still move and function. A is the opposite effect; C and D are not caused by this change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the stages of cell signalling in which a signalling molecule released by one cell causes a response in a target cell some distance away.
parts.answer: Signalling cell releases the signal molecule (e.g. by exocytosis); it travels (by diffusion or in the blood) to the target cell; binds to a specific receptor (protein/glycoprotein) on the cell surface membrane with a complementary shape; receptor changes shape and activates a G protein/enzyme inside; a second messenger (e.g. cyclic AMP) is produced; this starts a cascade of enzyme activation that amplifies the signal and produces the response.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: release by signalling cell; transport to target; binding to complementary receptor on cell surface membrane; change in receptor shape / G protein activated; second messenger formed (e.g. cAMP); amplification / enzyme cascade → specific response.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a signalling molecule that is a small, lipid-soluble steroid does not need a receptor on the cell surface membrane.
parts.answer: It is non-polar/lipid-soluble so it diffuses through the phospholipid bilayer; it binds to a receptor in the cytoplasm or nucleus instead.
parts.working: 1: dissolves in / diffuses through bilayer; 1: receptor inside the cell (cytoplasm/nucleus).

practice.stem:
Barley seedlings were grown at 5 °C or at 25 °C. The fatty acids of the root cell membrane phospholipids were analysed.
Growth temperature / °C: 5, 25
Percentage of fatty acids that are unsaturated / %: 78, 54

parts.label: a
