parts.answer: Label axes with quantities and units (concentration / mol dm⁻³; percentage change in mass / %); choose linear scales that use over half the grid and include negative values with a clear zero line; plot points accurately as small crosses; join points with ruled straight lines (or a smooth best-fit line) without extrapolating beyond the data.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: full axis labels with units; linear scale using most of grid, including negative values; points plotted exactly (small × or encircled dot); ruled lines point to point / best-fit line, not extended beyond data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Estimate, by linear interpolation between the readings at 0.4 and 0.6 mol dm⁻³, the sucrose concentration at which there would be no change in mass. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 0.45 mol dm⁻³

practice.stem: A student plotted absorbance of the liquid around beetroot discs (y-axis) against time / min (x-axis). Over the first 12 minutes the points lie close to a straight line. The line of best fit passes through the points (2, 0.10) and (10, 0.42).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gradient of the line and state its units.
parts.answer: 0.04 min⁻¹ (absorbance units per minute)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the gradient represents biologically.
parts.answer: The rate of release of pigment from the beetroot cells (rate of leakage through the membranes).
parts.working: 1: rate of pigment loss through membranes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the student should use points read from the line rather than two of her original readings.
parts.answer: The line is an average of all the readings, so it reduces the effect of random error in any single reading.
parts.working: 1: line averages all points / reduces effect of errors.

practice.stem:
The mean rate of water uptake by Visking tubing 'cells' at two temperatures was found, with error bars showing ± 1 standard deviation.
20 °C: mean 0.82 cm³ h⁻¹, SD 0.10
30 °C: mean 0.95 cm³ h⁻¹, SD 0.12

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the upper and lower ends of each error bar.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The error bars overlap. Explain what this suggests about the effect of temperature in this investigation.
parts.answer: The ranges overlap, so the difference in means may be due to variation/chance; we cannot conclude that temperature had a significant effect (a statistical test would be needed).
parts.working: 1: overlap means difference may not be significant/real; 1: cannot conclude effect / need test or more repeats.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain when a student should join the plotted points of a graph with straight lines between each point, rather than draw a line or curve of best fit. Give an example from an osmosis investigation.
parts.answer: Join points with ruled straight lines when the values between the readings are not known and it would be wrong to assume a trend (e.g. too few points or the relationship is unknown); draw a best-fit line/curve when there is an expected smooth trend and scatter from random error, e.g. % change in mass against sucrose concentration usually shows a clear trend so a best-fit line is drawn to find where it crosses zero.
parts.working: 1: point-to-point when intermediate values cannot be predicted/trend not established; 1: best-fit when a trend is expected and readings contain random error; 1: suitable osmosis example with reasoning (best-fit for % change v concentration to find intercept).

practice.stem:
A teacher checked a student's graph of 'time for agar cube to change colour' against 'surface area : volume ratio'. The teacher noted:
• time was plotted on the x-axis
• the y-axis label read 'SA:V' with no units
• the x-axis scale went 0, 50, 100, 200, 400
• the points were plotted as large dots about 3 mm across
• the points were joined with a freehand wavy line through every point

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify four mistakes the student made and state how each should be corrected.
parts.answer: Axes reversed – SA:V (independent variable) should be on the x-axis and time on the y-axis; label should include units – 'SA:V ratio / cm⁻¹' (or 'time / s' with unit); scale is not linear – use equal steps (e.g. 0, 50, 100, 150…); points too large – plot small crosses or dots in circles; freehand line through every point – draw a smooth curve of best fit (or ruled lines) with a sharp pencil.
parts.working: 1 mark each for four mistake + correction pairs.

practice.stem:
The diameters of 92 red blood cells in an isotonic solution were measured using an eyepiece graticule.
Diameter / µm: 6.0–6.4, 6.5–6.9, 7.0–7.4, 7.5–7.9, 8.0–8.4, 8.5–8.9
Number of cells: 3, 11, 24, 31, 18, 5

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of chart that should be drawn and describe two features of how it should be drawn.
parts.answer: A histogram: diameter (continuous) on the x-axis with bars of equal width for each class, bars touching (no gaps); frequency / number of cells on the y-axis starting at zero; axes labelled with units.
parts.working: 1: histogram; 1 each for any two features: touching bars/no gaps; equal class width; frequency on y-axis from 0; labelled axes with units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the modal class and check that the frequencies add up to the number of cells measured.
parts.working: 1: modal class 7.5–7.9 µm; 1: total 92.

practice.stem:
Beetroot discs were placed in water or in solutions of three household products for 20 minutes. The absorbance of the surrounding liquid was measured (higher absorbance = more pigment released).
Treatment: water | detergent P | detergent Q | ethanol solution R
Mean absorbance: 0.20 | 1.14 | 0.79 | 0.34
95 % confidence interval (±): 0.05 | 0.10 | 0.08 | 0.07

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of graph that should be used to display these results and give a reason.
parts.answer: A bar chart, because the independent variable (type of treatment) is categorical / discontinuous.
parts.working: 1 mark: bar chart (bars of equal width, not touching). 1 mark: independent variable is categorical / not continuous.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the 95 % confidence intervals should be shown on the graph.
parts.answer: As error bars drawn above and below the top of each bar, from (mean − 95 % CI value) to (mean + 95 % CI value).
parts.working: 1 mark: vertical error bars centred on each mean extending ± the CI value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student concluded that all three solutions damaged the membranes more than water did, and that detergent P damaged them most. Use the confidence intervals to evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: The intervals are water 0.15–0.25, P 1.04–1.24, Q 0.71–0.87 and R 0.27–0.41. None of P, Q or R overlaps with water (R's lower limit 0.27 is just above water's upper limit 0.25), so all three released significantly more pigment than water, though R only just. P's interval does not overlap with Q's or R's, so P is significantly the most damaging. The conclusion is supported, but only for these concentrations and this time.
parts.working: 1 mark: calculates/compares intervals – water 0.15–0.25 does not overlap with P, Q or R, so all significantly greater than water. 1 mark: P's interval (1.04–1.24) does not overlap Q (0.71–0.87), so P significantly the most damaging. 1 mark: R only just separated from water / limited to these conditions / small sample, so treat with caution.

practice.stem: A student wants to plot surface area : volume ratio against body length for organisms ranging from a bacterium (2 µm) to a blue whale (25 m).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a graph with ordinary (linear) scales would be unsuitable, and suggest a better way to plot the data.
parts.answer: The lengths range over about 7 orders of magnitude (2 × 10⁻⁶ m to 25 m), so on a linear scale almost all the small organisms would be squashed together near zero and could not be distinguished; plot log₁₀ of length (and of SA:V) or use logarithmic scales on both axes.
parts.working: 1: range spans many orders of magnitude (≈ 10⁷); 1: small values crowded at origin / unreadable; 1: use log scale (log–log).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of the largest to the smallest length.

practice.stem:
Mass gained by a potato cylinder in distilled water:
Time / min: 0, 5, 10, 20, 30
Mass gained / g: 0.00, 0.62, 1.05, 1.52, 1.70

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of mass gain during the first 5 minutes and during 20–30 minutes. Give units.
parts.answer: 0.124 g min⁻¹ and 0.018 g min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student should find the initial rate from a graph of these results, and explain whether it would be higher or lower than your first answer to (a).
parts.answer: Draw a smooth curve of best fit, then draw a tangent to the curve at t = 0 and calculate its gradient (Δy ÷ Δx using a large triangle); the curve is already flattening between 0 and 5 min, so the tangent at 0 is steeper – the initial rate is higher than 0.124 g min⁻¹.
parts.working: 1: tangent at time 0; 1: gradient from a large triangle; 1: higher because rate falls during first 5 minutes (curve).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate decreases with time.
parts.answer: As water enters, the water potential of the cells rises and pressure potential builds up, so the water potential gradient between solution and cells becomes smaller; net movement slows and stops when they are equal.
parts.working: 1: water potential gradient decreases; 1: cells become turgid / ψp increases / equilibrium.

practice.stem:
Two students drew lines of best fit for percentage change in mass (y) against sucrose concentration in mol dm⁻³ (x). The equations of their lines were:
Potato: y = −42x + 9.2
Carrot: y = −35x + 14.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the sucrose concentration at which there is no change in mass for each tissue. Give answers to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: potato 0.22 mol dm⁻³; carrot 0.40 mol dm⁻³

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which tissue has the lower water potential and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Carrot – a more concentrated sucrose solution (lower water potential) is needed to stop net water movement, so the carrot cells must have a lower water potential than the potato cells.
parts.working: 1: carrot; 1: no-change point at higher solute concentration = lower water potential.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the two lines have different gradients.
parts.answer: The tissues differ in how much water they gain or lose per unit difference in water potential – e.g. different cell wall elasticity, proportion of air spaces or starch/water content.
parts.working: 1: any sensible difference in tissue structure/composition affecting the size of mass change.

practice.stem: A cell is placed in a solution containing substance P. In experiment 1, P enters only by facilitated diffusion. In experiment 2, P enters only by active transport. The concentration of P inside the cell is measured every minute for 30 minutes; the starting concentration inside is zero and the outside concentration stays constant at 5 mmol dm⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the shape of the graph of internal concentration against time you would expect for each experiment, giving the final concentrations.
parts.answer: Facilitated diffusion: concentration rises quickly at first, then the curve levels off (plateau) at 5 mmol dm⁻³, equal to the outside concentration. Active transport: concentration rises steadily and continues above 5 mmol dm⁻³, levelling off only at a value much higher than outside (when carriers are limited or a steady state is reached).
parts.working: 1: FD curve rising and levelling; 1: FD plateau at 5 mmol dm⁻³ (equal to outside); 1: AT continues rising past 5; 1: AT final concentration higher than outside / accumulation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the curve for experiment 2 would change if a respiratory inhibitor were added at 15 minutes, and explain why.
parts.answer: The rise stops at 15 min (and the concentration may fall back towards 5 mmol dm⁻³ as P leaks out); no ATP is available for the carrier proteins/pumps.
parts.working: 1: curve flattens/falls after 15 min; 1: no ATP for active transport.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A potato cylinder had a mass of 2.45 g before and 2.71 g after being left in a dilute sucrose solution. Calculate the percentage change in mass. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what this result shows about the water potential of the potato tissue compared with the solution.
parts.answer: The tissue had a lower water potential than the solution, so it gained water by osmosis.
parts.working: 1 mark: tissue water potential lower than solution / water moved into tissue.

practice.stem:
Carrot discs were weighed, left in sodium chloride solutions for 1 hour, blotted and reweighed.
NaCl concentration / mol dm⁻³: 0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4
Initial mass / g: 5.12, 5.08, 4.96, 5.20, 5.04
Final mass / g: 5.66, 5.30, 4.91, 4.94, 4.62

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in mass for each concentration. Give your answers to 1 decimal place and include the sign.
parts.working: % change = (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100 (M1). All five correct with signs (A2); three or four correct (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Between which two concentrations does the carrot tissue have the same water potential as the solution?
parts.answer: between 0.1 and 0.2 mol dm⁻³
parts.working: Sign changes from + (0.1) to − (0.2).

practice.stem: Four agar cubes of the same size were timed until they became colourless in acid: 112 s, 118 s, 154 s, 115 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous time and calculate the mean of the remaining times to the nearest second.
parts.answer: anomaly 154 s; mean 115 s
parts.working: 154 s is far from the others (1); (112 + 118 + 115) ÷ 3 = 115 s (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason for the anomalous result.
parts.answer: That cube was cut larger than the others / not fully covered by acid / end point misjudged.
parts.working: 1: any sensible reason.

practice.stem: Agar cubes of three sizes were placed in acid. Time to become colourless: 1 cm cube 45 s; 2 cm cube 120 s; 3 cm cube 260 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of colour change for each cube as 1000 ÷ time, in s⁻¹. Give answers to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why 1000 ÷ time can be used as a measure of rate.
parts.answer: Rate is inversely proportional to time taken – a shorter time means a faster rate; ×1000 just gives convenient numbers.
parts.working: 1: rate ∝ 1/time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of 0.60 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution and the volume of distilled water needed to make 50 cm³ of 0.15 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution.
parts.answer: 12.5 cm³ of 0.60 mol dm⁻³ sucrose + 37.5 cm³ water

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the most suitable apparatus for measuring 12.5 cm³ accurately.
parts.answer: A graduated pipette or burette (or 20 cm³ syringe).
parts.working: 1: pipette/burette.

practice.stem: A cylinder of potato was cut with a cork borer of internal diameter 8 mm and trimmed to 30 mm long.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of the cylinder in cm³. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Volume = πr²l)
parts.answer: 1.51 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total surface area of the cylinder, including both ends, in mm². Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 855 mm²
parts.working: Ends 2πr² = 100.5; side πdl = 754.0 (M1); total 854.5 → 855 mm² (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate its SA:V ratio in mm⁻¹ to 2 decimal places.

practice.stem:
A drop of potassium manganate(VII) was placed in a well cut in agar. The distance the purple colour had spread from the edge of the well was measured.
Time / min: 0, 10, 20, 30, 40
Distance / mm: 0, 2.1, 3.0, 3.6, 4.2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of diffusion in mm min⁻¹ for the first 10 minutes and for the last 10 minutes. Give answers to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 0.21 mm min⁻¹ and 0.06 mm min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in rate from the first to the last 10 minutes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate decreases.
parts.answer: The concentration gradient becomes less steep as the dye spreads out (and the distance from the source increases), so net diffusion slows.
parts.working: 1: concentration gradient decreases; 1: greater diffusion distance.

practice.stem: Beetroot cylinders were left for 20 minutes in water or ethanol solutions. Absorbance of each solution: water 0.08; 10 % ethanol 0.15; 30 % ethanol 0.41; 50 % ethanol 0.86.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in absorbance in 50 % ethanol compared with water. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the absorbance is in 30 % ethanol than in 10 % ethanol, to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 2.7 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the effect of ethanol on the membranes.
parts.answer: Ethanol is a solvent that dissolves/disrupts the phospholipid bilayer (and denatures membrane proteins), making the membranes more permeable so betalain pigment leaks out of the vacuole and cell.
parts.working: 1: ethanol dissolves lipids / disrupts bilayer; 1: increased permeability → pigment leaks from vacuole/cell.

practice.stem: A calibration curve for beetroot pigment gave the straight line: absorbance = 0.42 × concentration + 0.02, where concentration is in arbitrary units (au).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sample has an absorbance of 0.65. Calculate the pigment concentration.
parts.answer: 1.5 au

parts.label: b
parts.text: Another sample read 1.38, above the highest standard used for the calibration (absorbance 0.86). Explain what the student should do before using the equation.
parts.answer: Dilute the sample by a known factor (e.g. 1 in 2) so that its absorbance falls within the calibration range, read it again, then multiply the result by the dilution factor – the relationship may not be linear outside the range.
parts.working: 1: dilute by known factor and re-measure; 1: multiply by dilution factor / extrapolation unreliable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A piece of potato of initial mass 2.40 g gained 0.18 g in 45 minutes in distilled water. Calculate the mean rate of water uptake in g per g of tissue per hour.
parts.answer: 0.10 g g⁻¹ h⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming 1 g of water has a volume of 1 cm³, calculate the volume of water taken up per hour by 1 kg of this tissue in cm³.
parts.answer: 100 cm³

practice.stem: A length of Visking (dialysis) tubing was filled with 1.0 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution, attached to a vertical capillary tube of internal radius 0.5 mm and placed in a beaker of distilled water. In 15 minutes the liquid in the capillary tube rose by 36 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of solution that entered the tubing in 15 minutes. Use π r² l and give your answer in mm³ to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 28.3 mm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 1.88 mm³ min⁻¹
parts.working: 28.27 ÷ 15 = 1.88 mm³ min⁻¹ (allow error carried forward).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the liquid in the capillary tube rises.
parts.answer: The sucrose solution in the tubing has a lower water potential than the distilled water outside; water moves in by osmosis through the partially permeable tubing (sucrose molecules are too large to leave), increasing the volume inside.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower water potential inside / water potential gradient. 1 mark: water enters by osmosis through partially permeable membrane; sucrose cannot pass out.

practice.stem:
Potato cylinders of diameter 6 mm and lengths 10, 20 and 40 mm were left in distilled water for 30 minutes.
Length / mm: 10, 20, 40
Mass gained / g: 0.052, 0.094, 0.180

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total surface area (sides plus both ends) of each cylinder in mm² to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: 10 mm: 245 mm², 20 mm: 434 mm², 40 mm: 811 mm²
parts.working: SA = 2πr² + 2πrl with r = 3 mm: 245, 434, 811 mm². 2 marks all three; 1 for two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass gained per mm² of surface in mg mm⁻². Give answers to 3 decimal places.
parts.working: e.g. 52 mg ÷ 245 mm² = 0.212. 2 marks all three correct; 1 for two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to suggest why mass gained is not exactly proportional to length.
parts.answer: Mass gained per unit surface area is similar for all three, so uptake depends mainly on surface area; surface area is not proportional to length because of the two ends.
parts.working: 1: uptake related to surface area, which includes ends so not ∝ length.

practice.stem: The rate of leakage of potassium ions from root tissue was measured as the conductivity of the surrounding water. At 30 °C the rate was 0.18 arbitrary units min⁻¹; at 40 °C it was 0.33; at 60 °C it was 2.40.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the temperature coefficient (Q₁₀) between 30 °C and 40 °C, using Q₁₀ = rate at (T + 10 °C) ÷ rate at T. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times faster leakage is at 60 °C than at 40 °C, to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why the effect of temperature above 40 °C cannot be explained only by increased kinetic energy of ions.
parts.answer: A Q₁₀ of about 2 is typical of increased kinetic energy/diffusion and enzyme-controlled processes; between 40 and 60 °C the increase (7.3 times over 20 °C, i.e. far more than 2 × 2 = 4) is much greater; this is because membrane proteins denature and the bilayer becomes more fluid/disrupted, so the membrane becomes much more permeable.
parts.working: 1: Q₁₀ ≈ 2 consistent with kinetic energy; 1: 7.3 > expected ~4 for 20 °C; 1: proteins denature / bilayer disrupted → holes, permeability rises steeply.

practice.stem: Pigment was extracted from beetroot discs heated at 70 °C. 2.0 cm³ of the extract was mixed with 8.0 cm³ of water. The diluted sample had an absorbance of 0.48. The calibration line is absorbance = 0.40 × concentration + 0.02 (concentration in µg cm⁻³).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the dilution factor.
parts.working: Total volume 10.0 cm³ ÷ 2.0 cm³ = 5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the pigment concentration in the original extract in µg cm⁻³. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 5.75 µg cm⁻³
parts.working: (0.48 − 0.02) ÷ 0.40 = 1.15 µg cm⁻³ in diluted sample (M1); × 5 = 5.75 µg cm⁻³ (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The extract volume was 25 cm³. Calculate the total mass of pigment released in µg.
parts.answer: 144 µg

practice.stem:
Three Visking tubing bags of equal size contained 0.25, 0.50 or 1.00 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution and were placed in distilled water. Mass gained / g at 0, 10, 20 and 30 minutes:
0.25 mol dm⁻³: 0.00, 0.31, 0.60, 0.92
0.50 mol dm⁻³: 0.00, 0.58, 1.19, 1.76
1.00 mol dm⁻³: 0.00, 1.10, 2.21, 3.30

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of water uptake for each bag over 30 minutes in cm³ min⁻¹ (1 g of water = 1 cm³). Give answers to 3 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of the rate for 1.00 mol dm⁻³ to the rate for 0.25 mol dm⁻³, to 1 decimal place, and comment on the relationship between concentration and rate.
parts.answer: 3.6; rate is roughly proportional to concentration (a 4-fold increase in concentration gives about 3.6 times the rate).
parts.working: 3.30 ÷ 0.92 = 3.6 (1); approximately proportional / rate increases with water potential gradient, slightly less than proportional (1).

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: Six agar cubes of side 1.5 cm took these times (s) to change colour in acid: 132, 128, 141, 135, 130, 138.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean time to 1 decimal place and the range.
parts.answer: mean 134.0 s; range 13 s

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the standard deviation is a better measure of the spread of these results than the range.
parts.answer: SD uses every value (deviation of each from the mean), while the range uses only the two extreme values, which may be anomalous.
parts.working: 1: SD uses all data / range affected by extremes.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Percentage gain in mass of five turnip cubes in distilled water: 4.2, 5.1, 3.8, 4.6, 4.8.
Standard deviation s = √[Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the standard deviation. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: Nine Visking tubing bags were used to measure the rate of osmosis. The mean rate was 1.84 cm³ h⁻¹ and the standard deviation was 0.36 cm³ h⁻¹. Standard error SE = s ÷ √n.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard error of the mean.
parts.answer: 0.12 cm³ h⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the 95 % confidence interval (mean ± 2 × SE).
parts.answer: 1.60 to 2.08 cm³ h⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the standard error tells you that the standard deviation does not.
parts.answer: How reliable / close to the true population mean the sample mean is likely to be (SD shows the spread of individual values).
parts.working: 1: SE measures reliability of the mean / how far the sample mean is likely to be from the true mean.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student used a t-test to compare the mean rate of pigment loss from beetroot at 25 °C and at 45 °C. State a suitable null hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the mean rate of pigment loss at 25 °C and at 45 °C.
parts.working: 1: no significant difference between the means.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Another student used Spearman's rank correlation to test whether there is a relationship between sucrose concentration and the percentage of onion cells plasmolysed. State a suitable null hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is no correlation between sucrose concentration and the percentage of cells plasmolysed.
parts.working: 1: no correlation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Spearman's rank correlation, not a t-test, is suitable for the second investigation.
parts.answer: It tests for a correlation/relationship between two variables measured on the same samples, whereas a t-test compares the means of two groups.
parts.working: 1: looking for correlation between two variables, not comparing two means.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Mean time for 10 pieces of dye-soaked agar to lose their colour in water, with 95 % confidence intervals:
At 15 °C: 12.4 min ± 1.1 min
At 35 °C: 15.0 min ± 0.9 min
(The longer time at 35 °C was unexpected; the student found that the 35 °C pieces had been cut larger.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the limits of each confidence interval and state whether the intervals overlap.
parts.answer: 15 °C: 11.3 to 13.5 min; 35 °C: 14.1 to 15.9 min; they do not overlap

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the lack of overlap suggests, and explain why the student still cannot conclude that temperature caused the difference.
parts.answer: The difference between the means is likely to be significant/not due to chance; but the size of the pieces (a confounding variable) was not controlled, so the difference may be caused by size not temperature.
parts.working: 1: difference is significant; 1: uncontrolled variable (size) – invalid conclusion about temperature.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Beetroot discs were left in 20 % or 30 % ethanol. Ten discs were used for each concentration.
20 %: mean absorbance 0.42, standard deviation 0.05
30 %: mean absorbance 0.47, standard deviation 0.06

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the 95 % confidence interval (mean ± 2SE, SE = s/√n) for each concentration. Give limits to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to explain whether there is a significant difference between the two concentrations.
parts.answer: The intervals overlap (0.43–0.45 is in both), so the difference between the means is not significant at the 95 % level; the true means could be the same.
parts.working: 1: intervals overlap; 1: so not significant / difference may be due to chance.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
The rate of water uptake by cubes of two varieties of mango, Sindhri and Chaunsa, was compared (8 cubes each).
Sindhri: mean 6.3 µl min⁻¹, s = 0.9
Chaunsa: mean 7.6 µl min⁻¹, s = 1.1
t = |x̄₁ − x̄₂| ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂). Critical value of t at p = 0.05 for 14 degrees of freedom = 2.14.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate t. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show how the number of degrees of freedom is obtained.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what your value of t shows.
parts.answer: 2.59 > 2.14, so reject the null hypothesis: the difference in mean rate between the two varieties is significant (probability of being due to chance < 5 %).
parts.working: 1: t greater than critical value; 1: significant difference / reject null hypothesis.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
SA:V ratio and time for an agar block to change colour:
SA:V / cm⁻¹: 6.0, 3.0, 2.0, 1.5, 1.2, 1.0
Time / s: 38, 95, 172, 160, 248, 305
rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n(n² − 1)). Critical value for n = 6 at p = 0.05 is 0.886.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Interpret your value.
parts.answer: |−0.94| > 0.886 so there is a significant negative correlation: blocks with a larger SA:V change colour in less time.
parts.working: 1: compared with critical value, significant; 1: negative correlation described.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State which statistical test (t-test, Spearman's rank correlation or chi-squared test) is most suitable for each investigation, with a reason.
(i) Do onion cells in a 0.4 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution plasmolyse in the ratio of 1 : 1 that a student predicted?
(ii) Is there a relationship between the length of time beetroot is boiled and the absorbance of the water?
(iii) Is the mean surface area of red blood cells different in people living at high altitude in Gilgit and at sea level in Karachi?
parts.answer: (i) chi-squared – compares observed counts in categories with expected counts; (ii) Spearman's rank – tests for correlation between two variables; (iii) t-test – compares two means of continuous data (normally distributed).
parts.working: 1 each, with reason.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: A student measured soil salinity and the solute potential of root cells of eight wheat plants and calculated rs = 0.43. The critical value for n = 8 at p = 0.05 is 0.738.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the student should conclude.
parts.answer: 0.43 < 0.738, so accept the null hypothesis – there is no significant correlation; any apparent relationship may be due to chance.
parts.working: 1: value below critical; 1: no significant correlation / accept null.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways the student could improve the investigation to test the relationship more effectively.
parts.answer: Use more plants/sites (larger n); use a wider range of salinities; control other variables such as plant age, variety and time of sampling; take repeat measurements for each plant.
parts.working: 1 each for any two.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
A student compared two potato varieties grown in Okara. Six cylinders of each were left in 0.3 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution and the percentage change in mass was found.
Variety P: mean −4.2 %, standard deviation 1.1, n = 6
Variety Q: mean −6.9 %, standard deviation 1.4, n = 6

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a null hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the mean percentage change in mass of the two varieties (any difference is due to chance).
parts.working: 1 mark: no (significant) difference between means of P and Q.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of t, using t = |x̄₁ − x̄₂| ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of t at p = 0.05 for 10 degrees of freedom is 2.23. Explain what your value of t shows.
parts.answer: 3.71 is greater than 2.23, so the null hypothesis is rejected: the difference between the varieties is significant (probability of it being due to chance is less than 5 %); variety Q loses more water, so its tissue has a higher water potential.
parts.working: 1 mark: t > critical value so reject null hypothesis. 1 mark: difference significant / not due to chance (p < 0.05).

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Electrolyte leakage (a measure of membrane damage) from leaves of wheat seedlings was measured at eight sites in Punjab with different soil salinity.
Salinity / dS m⁻¹: 2.1, 3.4, 5.0, 5.0, 7.8, 9.2, 11.5, 14.0
Leakage / %: 12, 18, 17, 25, 31, 29, 40, 46
Critical value of rs for n = 8 at p = 0.05 = 0.738.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, using the mean rank for tied values. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Interpret the result and suggest a biological explanation.
parts.answer: 0.93 > 0.738 so there is a significant positive correlation between salinity and leakage. High salt lowers the soil water potential and causes ion toxicity/osmotic stress; this damages membrane lipids and proteins (e.g. by oxidative damage), so membranes become leakier and ions escape.
parts.working: 1: significant positive correlation; 1: salt causes osmotic stress / ion toxicity; 1: membrane damage increases permeability. (Correlation does not prove cause – credit if stated.)

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Rate of osmosis (mm³ min⁻¹) into Visking tubing with two kinds of tubing, five replicates each:
Tubing P: 3.1, 2.6, 3.8, 3.3, 2.9
Tubing Q: 4.4, 3.9, 4.8, 4.1, 4.6
Critical t at p = 0.05 for 8 degrees of freedom = 2.31; at p = 0.001 = 5.04.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and standard deviation of each set. Give means to 2 decimal places and SDs to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate t to 2 decimal places and interpret it.
parts.answer: t = 4.71; significant at p = 0.05 but not at p = 0.001 (4.71 < 5.04) – reject the null hypothesis at the 5 % level
parts.working: 1.22 ÷ √(0.451²/5 + 0.365²/5) (M1) = 4.71 (A1); 4.71 > 2.31 so difference significant at p < 0.05 but not at p = 0.001 (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a reason for the difference between the tubing types.
parts.answer: Tubing Q has larger pores/more pores or is thinner, so water crosses it faster.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
A student predicted that at 0.42 mol dm⁻³ sucrose, half of the red onion cells would be plasmolysed. She counted 200 cells: 118 plasmolysed and 82 not plasmolysed.
χ² = Σ (O − E)² ÷ E. Critical value at p = 0.05 for 1 degree of freedom = 3.84.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate χ².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the result shows about the student's prediction and what it suggests about the water potential of the onion cells.
parts.answer: 6.48 > 3.84 so the difference from 1 : 1 is significant – reject the null hypothesis; more than half are plasmolysed, so 0.42 mol dm⁻³ is above the incipient plasmolysis concentration, meaning the cells' solute potential is higher (less negative) than that of 0.42 mol dm⁻³ sucrose.
parts.working: 1: significant / reject prediction; 1: more cells plasmolysed than expected; 1: cell water potential (solute potential) is higher than that of the solution / incipient point is at a lower concentration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of degrees of freedom and how it is found.
parts.answer: 1 – number of categories (2) minus 1.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: In a pilot study, 4 cylinders of yam were used per sucrose concentration. The standard deviation of percentage change in mass was 2.4 % and the standard error was 1.2 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show how the standard error of 1.2 % was obtained.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student wants to halve the standard error. Calculate how many cylinders she must use per concentration, assuming the standard deviation stays the same.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why halving the standard error makes it easier to detect a difference between two concentrations.
parts.answer: The 95 % confidence intervals (± 2SE) become narrower, so they are less likely to overlap when there is a real difference between the means; the mean is a more reliable estimate of the true mean.
parts.working: 1: narrower confidence intervals / error bars; 1: less overlap, so smaller real differences show as significant.

practice.subtopic: Skill: recording results in a table
practice.stem: A student cut four potato strips, each 50.0 mm long, and placed one in each of four sucrose solutions. After 1 hour she wrote in her notebook: '0.00 mol dm⁻³ strip now 53.5 mm; 0.25 mol dm⁻³ strip 51.0 mm; 0.50 strip 48.5 mm; 0.75 strip 47.0 mm.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student should set out a table to record these results, including the headings.
parts.answer: Columns (or rows) for: sucrose concentration / mol dm⁻³; initial length / mm; final length / mm; percentage change in length / %. Units only in the headings, not with each value; independent variable in the first column; all lengths to the same number of decimal places (1 d.p.).
parts.working: 1 mark: table with ruled columns and IV (concentration) in first column. 1 mark: headings include initial length, final length and % change. 1 mark: units in headings only (mol dm⁻³, mm, %) and consistent decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in length for each concentration.
parts.working: M1: (final − 50.0) ÷ 50.0 × 100. A1: all four correct with signs.

practice.subtopic: Skill: recording results in a table
practice.stem:
A student recorded her osmosis results like this:
Row 1: Solution | Mass at start | Mass at end | Change
Row 2: 0.0 | 2.31 g | 2.5 g | +0.19
Row 3: 0.2 | 2.28 g | 2.21g | −0.07 g
Row 4: 0.4 | 2.30 g | 2.14 | −.16

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify four errors in the way the results are recorded and state how each should be corrected.
parts.answer: Headings have no units: write 'sucrose concentration / mol dm⁻³', 'mass at start / g', 'mass at end / g', 'change in mass / g'; units are repeated in the body of the table (2.31 g, 2.21g): write numbers only; the decimal places are inconsistent (2.5 and 2.14 should be 2.50 and 2.14 to 0.01 g, the balance resolution); −.16 needs a leading zero (−0.16) and the signs/units of the change column should be stated in the heading.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four error + correction pairs.

practice.subtopic: Skill: recording results in a table

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student will place agar cubes of sides 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 cm in acid, time how long each takes to change colour (three repeats), and calculate the SA:V ratio and the mean time. Describe the table she should draw before starting, giving all the column headings.
parts.answer: Columns: 'length of side / cm' (independent variable first); 'SA:V ratio / cm⁻¹'; 'time to change colour / s' split into 'trial 1', 'trial 2', 'trial 3'; 'mean time / s'. One row per cube size, in increasing order; units only in headings.
parts.working: 1: IV in first column with unit; 1: SA:V column with unit cm⁻¹; 1: three raw-data columns under one heading with unit; 1: mean column / processed data to right, units only in headings.

practice.subtopic: Skill: recording results in a table
practice.stem: A student used a balance that reads to 0.01 g. She recorded masses of beetroot discs as: 2.4, 2.35, 2, 2.50, 2.4 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is wrong with the way these readings were recorded and rewrite them correctly.
parts.answer: Readings must be recorded to the same number of decimal places as the balance shows (2 d.p.): 2.40, 2.35, 2.00, 2.50, 2.40 g.
parts.working: 1: inconsistent / should all be to 0.01 g; 1: corrected list.

practice.subtopic: Skill: recording results in a table

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the correct way to write the heading for a column showing the volume of water taken up, measured in cm³, and explain why units are not written next to each value.
parts.answer: 'volume of water taken up / cm³' (or with units in brackets); the unit applies to every value in the column, so writing it once in the heading avoids repetition and makes the numbers clear.
parts.working: 1: quantity / unit format; 1: unit in heading applies to all values.

practice.subtopic: Skill: recording results in a table
practice.stem:
Counts of epidermal cells from three strips of red onion:
0.30 mol dm⁻³ sucrose: 47 cells counted, 3 plasmolysed
0.40 mol dm⁻³ sucrose: 52 cells counted, 19 plasmolysed
0.50 mol dm⁻³ sucrose: 49 cells counted, 38 plasmolysed

parts.label: a
parts.text: Draw up a suitable table (describe the columns) and calculate the percentage of cells plasmolysed for each concentration to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: Columns: sucrose concentration / mol dm⁻³; total number of cells; number of plasmolysed cells; percentage of cells plasmolysed / %. Percentages: 6 %, 37 %, 78 %
parts.working: 1: headings with units; 1: raw counts before % column; 1: 6, 37, 78 %.

practice.subtopic: Skill: recording results in a table
practice.stem:
Change in mass of potato cylinders (g) in three trials:
0.0 mol dm⁻³: 1.92, 1.88, 1.95
0.2 mol dm⁻³: 0.61, 0.70, 0.64
0.4 mol dm⁻³: −0.48, −0.55, −0.41

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a table to show these results with a column for the mean, and calculate the means to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Headings: sucrose concentration / mol dm⁻³ | change in mass / g – trial 1, trial 2, trial 3 | mean change in mass / g. Means: +1.92, +0.65, −0.48
parts.working: 1: headings with units and trials grouped; 1: mean column last; 1: means 1.92, 0.65, −0.48 with signs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the mean is given to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Same number of decimal places as the raw data (the balance resolution), as it cannot be more precise than the readings.

practice.subtopic: Skill: recording results in a table
practice.stem: A student timed agar cubes with a stopwatch and wrote the times as minutes:seconds: 1 cm cube 1:52; 2 cm cube 4:05; 3 cm cube 7:38.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert each time to seconds for the results table.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why recording time as '4.05 min' would be wrong.
parts.answer: 4.05 min means 4 min 3 s (0.05 × 60 = 3 s), not 4 min 5 s; decimal minutes are not the same as seconds.
parts.working: 1: confuses decimal minutes with seconds.

practice.subtopic: Skill: recording results in a table

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student measures absorbance of the water around beetroot discs at five temperatures, with three repeats at each, using a colorimeter that displays absorbance to 2 decimal places. Describe a table that would allow her to record all raw data and processed results, including how the values should be written.
parts.answer: First column 'temperature / °C' with values in ascending order; three columns under the heading 'absorbance / arbitrary units' for repeats 1–3; a final column 'mean absorbance / AU'; all absorbance values recorded to 2 d.p. (e.g. 0.20, not 0.2); table ruled with headings and units only in headings.
parts.working: 1: temperature column with unit; 1: repeats grouped under one heading; 1: mean column; 1: values to 2 d.p. consistently / no units in cells.

practice.subtopic: Skill: recording results in a table
practice.stem: Initial and final masses (to 0.01 g) of carrot discs: 4.62 → 4.79 g; 4.55 → 4.60 g; 4.70 → 4.58 g. A student wrote the percentage changes as 3.679653680 %, 1.1 % and −3 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage changes and give them to an appropriate and consistent number of decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the first value written by the student is not appropriate.
parts.answer: It has far more significant figures than the data justify – the masses are measured to 3 s.f., so the result should not be given to 10 s.f.
parts.working: 1: too many s.f. for precision of the raw data.

practice.subtopic: Skill: recording results in a table
practice.stem: Visking tubing containing starch and glucose was placed in water. Every 5 minutes for 20 minutes, 2 cm³ samples of the outside water were tested with Benedict's reagent (heated for 5 min) and with iodine solution. Colours observed with Benedict's: 0 min blue; 5 min green; 10 min yellow; 15 min orange; 20 min brick red. Iodine stayed orange-brown in every sample.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a table to record these qualitative results, including a column for an interpretation.
parts.answer: Columns: 'time / min'; 'colour with Benedict's reagent'; 'colour with iodine solution'; 'interpretation' (e.g. none / trace / low / moderate / high concentration of reducing sugar; starch absent). One row per sampling time.
parts.working: 1: time column with unit; 1: separate columns for each test with colours in words; 1: interpretation/semi-quantitative column.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the student could make the Benedict's results more quantitative.
parts.answer: Use a colorimeter on the supernatant after filtering / compare with colour standards made from known glucose concentrations / measure time for first colour change.
parts.working: 1: colour standards / colorimeter / timing.

practice.subtopic: Skill: recording results in a table

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student investigates the effect of both temperature (20, 40 and 60 °C) and ethanol concentration (0 % and 20 %) on pigment release from beetroot, with three repeats of each combination. Describe a single table that records all raw and mean results clearly.
parts.answer: Rows for temperature / °C (20, 40, 60); for each temperature, two sub-rows (or columns) for ethanol concentration / % (0 and 20); columns for absorbance repeats 1, 2, 3 under one heading 'absorbance / AU', then 'mean absorbance / AU'; or a grid with temperature down the side and ethanol across the top with mean values, plus separate raw data columns; units only in headings; consistent 2 d.p.
parts.working: 1: both independent variables identified with units; 1: every combination (6) has its own row/cell; 1: repeats grouped and mean column; 1: consistent d.p./units only in headings.

practice.subtopic: Skill: recording results in a table
practice.stem:
A student's notebook for potato strips in sucrose solutions reads:
'0.0 mol dm⁻³: start 52 mm, end 5.3 cm. 0.1 mol dm⁻³: start 50 mm, end 5.05 cm. 0.2 mol dm⁻³: start 5.0 cm, end 48 mm.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert all lengths to mm and calculate the percentage change in length for each strip to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: Conversions: 5.3 cm = 53 mm, 5.05 cm = 50.5 mm, 5.0 cm = 50 mm (1); % change calculated (1); +1.9, +1.0, −4.0 (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Comment on the precision of the recorded lengths and explain why this makes the data hard to record in one consistent table.
parts.answer: Lengths were recorded to different precisions (whole mm v 0.5 mm / 0.1 cm), so they cannot all be given to the same number of decimal places; a ruler with mm divisions should be read to the nearest 0.5 mm or 1 mm consistently and all in mm.
parts.working: 1: inconsistent precision/units; 1: all should be in mm to the same resolution.

practice.subtopic: Skill: recording results in a table
practice.stem: A student measured the height of liquid in a capillary tube attached to Visking tubing, using a ruler graduated in mm. Her readings every 2 minutes were: 0, 7, 15, 22.5, 30, 36.75 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the problems with the precision of these readings and state how they should be recorded.
parts.answer: A mm ruler can be read only to the nearest mm (or 0.5 mm at best), so 36.75 has false precision and 22.5 is inconsistent; record all to the same resolution, e.g. 0, 7, 15, 23 (or 22.5 with all to 0.5 mm: 0.0, 7.0, 15.0, 22.5, 30.0, 37.0) mm.
parts.working: 1: 36.75 more precise than instrument allows; 1: consistent resolution for all values.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of rise over the 10 minutes using the corrected final reading of 37 mm.
parts.answer: 3.7 mm min⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a table that includes these readings and a processed column showing the rise in each 2-minute interval.
parts.answer: Columns: 'time / min'; 'height of liquid / mm'; 'rise during previous 2 min / mm'; consistent decimal places; time in first column.
parts.working: 1: time and height with units; 1: processed column for interval rise.

practice.subtopic: Skill: recording results in a table
practice.stem:
Strips of pumpkin tissue, each 10.0 mm long at the start, were placed in sucrose solutions of 0.1, 0.3 and 0.5 mol dm⁻³. Their lengths (mm) were measured after 10, 20 and 30 minutes:
0.1: 9.8, 9.5, 9.1
0.3: 9.9, 10.2, 10.4
0.5: 10.0, 11.3, 12.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a single results table that records all of these readings, the starting length, and a processed column for the mean rate of change in length over 30 minutes.
parts.answer: Rows: sucrose concentration / mol dm⁻³ (0.1, 0.3, 0.5); columns: 'length of strip / mm' subdivided into 0, 10, 20, 30 min (starting length 10.0 included); final column 'mean rate of change in length / mm min⁻¹' with sign; all lengths to 1 d.p.
parts.working: 1: concentration column with unit; 1: time sub-columns under one 'length / mm' heading including 0 min; 1: processed rate column with unit and sign.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of change in length over 30 minutes for each concentration, to 3 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The results are unexpected. Suggest what mistake the student most probably made when labelling the tubes, and explain your answer.
parts.answer: The labels of 0.1 and 0.5 mol dm⁻³ were probably swapped: tissue should lose length (water) in the most concentrated solution (lowest water potential) and gain in the most dilute, but the opposite is shown.
parts.working: 1: labels of 0.1 and 0.5 swapped / reversed; 1: strongest solution should cause shrinkage (water loss by osmosis).

practice.stem: A leaf of the pondweed Elodea was mounted in 1.0 mol dm⁻³ sodium chloride solution and viewed with a microscope. After a few minutes the chloroplasts were clustered in the middle of each cell and there was a clear gap between the cytoplasm and the cell wall.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain these observations.
parts.answer: The solution has a lower water potential than the cell contents; water leaves the vacuole/cytoplasm by osmosis across the partially permeable cell surface membrane and tonoplast; the protoplast shrinks and pulls away from the cell wall (plasmolysis), carrying the chloroplasts with it.
parts.working: 1: lower water potential outside; 1: water lost by osmosis; 1: protoplast shrinks away from wall – plasmolysis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what fills the gap between the cell wall and the cell surface membrane.
parts.answer: The sodium chloride solution – the cell wall is fully permeable.
parts.working: 1: external solution (wall freely permeable).

practice.stem: Dried apricots from Hunza swell and become soft when soaked in water overnight.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the apricots swell.
parts.answer: The dried fruit cells contain a high concentration of sugars, giving them a very low (negative) water potential; water has a higher water potential, so water enters the cells by osmosis through partially permeable membranes (and is absorbed by cell walls); the cells gain volume and become turgid.
parts.working: 1: high sugar/solute concentration → low water potential; 1: water enters by osmosis; 1: cells swell/turgid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the apricots swell more slowly in a sugar syrup than in water.
parts.answer: The water potential gradient between the syrup and the fruit is smaller.
parts.working: 1: smaller water potential gradient.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Fish is traditionally preserved in coastal Balochistan by covering it with dry salt. Explain why bacteria cannot grow on salted fish.
parts.answer: The salt gives a very low water potential outside the bacterial cells; water leaves the bacteria by osmosis; the bacteria are dehydrated/plasmolysed, so their enzymes cannot work and they cannot grow or reproduce (they may die).
parts.working: 1: low water potential around bacteria; 1: water lost from bacteria by osmosis; 1: metabolism/enzymes stop, no growth/reproduction.

practice.stem: A drop of food dye was placed in the centre of each of two Petri dishes of agar, one at 10 °C and one at 30 °C. After 1 hour the coloured circle had a diameter of 14 mm at 10 °C and 21 mm at 30 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference in results.
parts.answer: At 30 °C the dye molecules have more kinetic energy and move faster, so the rate of diffusion is higher and the dye spreads further in the same time.
parts.working: 1: more kinetic energy at higher temperature; 1: faster diffusion → further spread.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why the dye spreads outwards from the drop.
parts.answer: Net movement of dye molecules from high concentration (the drop) to low concentration (the surrounding agar) – diffusion down a concentration gradient.
parts.working: 1: down concentration gradient.

practice.stem: Vegetable sellers in Lahore sprinkle water over spinach leaves on their stalls on hot afternoons. Wilted spinach becomes firm again after being sprinkled.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the spinach leaves wilt on a hot afternoon.
parts.answer: The leaves lose water by evaporation/transpiration faster than they can take it in (they have been cut from the roots), so cells lose water, vacuoles shrink and the cells become flaccid – the leaf loses support.
parts.working: 1: water lost by evaporation not replaced; 1: cells lose turgor/flaccid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how sprinkling water makes the leaves firm again.
parts.answer: Water enters the leaf cells by osmosis because their water potential is lower than that of the water; the cells swell and push against their cell walls, increasing pressure potential, so they become turgid and the leaf is supported.
parts.working: 1: water enters by osmosis (cells lower water potential); 1: cells become turgid / pressure potential increases.

practice.stem:
Samples of sheep red blood cells were placed in sodium chloride solutions of different concentrations. After 30 minutes the percentage of cells that had burst (haemolysed) was found and the cells were examined with a microscope.
NaCl / %: 0.30, 0.45, 0.60, 0.85, 1.20
Cells burst / %: 100, 50, 5, 0, 0
At 1.20 % the cells appeared shrunken with a crinkled outline.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the results for the 0.30 % and 0.45 % solutions.
parts.answer: These solutions have a higher water potential than the cytoplasm of the red blood cells; water enters the cells by osmosis; the cells swell and, with no cell wall, the membrane bursts (haemolysis); at 0.45 % the gradient is smaller, so only the cells with the weakest membranes burst (50 %).
parts.working: 1 mark: solution has higher water potential than cell. 1 mark: water enters by osmosis, cells swell and burst (no cell wall). 1 mark: smaller gradient at 0.45 % so fewer burst / cells vary in resistance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why cells in the 1.20 % solution appeared shrunken with a crinkled outline.
parts.answer: The 1.20 % solution has a lower water potential than the cells, so water leaves the cells by osmosis and they shrink (crenation).
parts.working: 1 mark: lower water potential outside. 1 mark: water lost by osmosis, cells shrink / crenated.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a 0.85 % sodium chloride solution is used when giving fluid to a dehydrated patient through a drip.
parts.answer: It has the same water potential as blood (is isotonic), so blood cells neither gain nor lose water.
parts.working: 1 mark: same water potential as plasma/cells, no net osmosis, no haemolysis or crenation.

practice.stem:
Beetroot discs were kept for 15 minutes in water at different temperatures, and the absorbance of the water was measured.
Temperature / °C: 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70
Absorbance: 0.05, 0.07, 0.10, 0.38, 0.85, 0.92

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the results.
parts.answer: Absorbance increases only slightly from 20 to 40 °C (0.05 to 0.10), then increases sharply between 40 and 60 °C (to 0.85), then levels off at 70 °C (0.92).
parts.working: 1: small increase to 40 °C; 1: steep rise 40–60 °C with data, levels off.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the results between 40 °C and 60 °C.
parts.answer: Membrane proteins (channel/carrier proteins) denature at high temperatures – hydrogen bonds break and their shape changes, leaving gaps in the membrane; the phospholipid bilayer becomes more fluid; both the tonoplast and cell surface membrane become very permeable so the red pigment leaks out of the vacuole into the water.
parts.working: 1: proteins denature (bonds break); 1: phospholipids more fluid / bilayer disrupted; 1: pigment leaks from vacuole through tonoplast and cell surface membrane.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why absorbance levels off above 60 °C.
parts.answer: Almost all the pigment has already leaked out / membranes fully disrupted.

practice.stem: Red blood cells were placed in two solutions with the same total concentration of solute particles as plasma: an isotonic sodium chloride solution and an isotonic urea solution. Cells in sodium chloride kept their shape; cells in urea swelled and burst within minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the cells in the urea solution burst.
parts.answer: Urea is a small molecule that can cross the cell surface membrane (through the bilayer / urea channels), so it diffuses into the cells down its concentration gradient; this lowers the water potential inside the cells; water then follows by osmosis; red blood cells have no wall, so they swell and burst (haemolysis).
parts.working: 1: urea crosses the membrane; 1: urea entering lowers water potential inside cells; 1: water enters by osmosis → cell bursts, no wall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the cells in sodium chloride did not burst.
parts.answer: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ cross the membrane only slowly (and Na⁺ is pumped out), so the water potential inside and outside stays equal – no net osmosis.
parts.working: 1: ions do not enter readily so water potentials stay equal.

practice.stem: In cystic fibrosis, the CFTR protein, a chloride ion channel in the cell surface membrane of cells lining the airways, does not work. In healthy cells, Cl⁻ ions move out of the cells through CFTR into the mucus, and water follows.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why people with cystic fibrosis have thick, sticky mucus in their airways.
parts.answer: Cl⁻ ions are not moved out of the cells into the mucus; so the water potential of the mucus is not lowered (stays higher than inside cells); less water moves out of the cells into the mucus by osmosis (water may even be absorbed from it), so the mucus is dehydrated and sticky.
parts.working: 1: no Cl⁻ secreted into mucus; 1: mucus water potential not lowered; 1: less water moves into mucus by osmosis → thick/sticky.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why thick mucus leads to frequent lung infections.
parts.answer: Cilia cannot move the thick mucus away, so bacteria trapped in it stay in the airways and multiply.

practice.stem: A gardener in Faisalabad added a large amount of granular fertiliser around young tomato plants and did not water it in. Two days later the plants were wilting, although the soil was moist.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the plants wilted.
parts.answer: Dissolving fertiliser makes the soil solution very concentrated, so its water potential becomes lower than that of the root hair cells; water cannot enter the roots by osmosis and may even leave the root cells; the plant cannot replace water lost in transpiration, so cells lose turgor and the plant wilts.
parts.working: 1: soil water potential lowered by solutes; 1: lower than root cells → water not taken up / lost by osmosis; 1: water lost by transpiration not replaced → loss of turgor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest what the gardener should have done.
parts.answer: Use less fertiliser / water it in well to dilute it (raising soil water potential).

practice.stem:
Beetroot cylinders were placed in different concentrations of washing-up liquid for 10 minutes.
Detergent concentration / %: 0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0
Absorbance: 0.06, 0.21, 0.45, 0.68, 0.70

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why absorbance increases as detergent concentration increases from 0 % to 2.0 %.
parts.answer: Detergent molecules have hydrophobic and hydrophilic parts; they dissolve/emulsify the lipids of the phospholipid bilayer (and disrupt membrane proteins), creating gaps; the tonoplast and cell surface membrane become more permeable, so more betalain pigment leaks out; higher concentrations disrupt more membrane.
parts.working: 1: detergent dissolves/disrupts phospholipids; 1: membranes (tonoplast and cell surface) more permeable; 1: more pigment escapes with more detergent.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why there is little difference between 2.0 % and 4.0 %.
parts.answer: Membranes are already almost completely disrupted at 2.0 %, so nearly all pigment has been released.

practice.stem: Oral rehydration solution (ORS), given to children with severe diarrhoea, contains both sodium chloride and glucose. Drinking a solution of sodium chloride alone, or of glucose alone, is much less effective at restoring water to the body.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use your knowledge of transport across membranes to explain why ORS is effective.
parts.answer: Epithelial cells of the small intestine have co-transporter proteins that carry Na⁺ and glucose into the cell together; the Na⁺ gradient is maintained by Na⁺/K⁺ pumps (ATP) on the blood side; so Na⁺ and glucose are both absorbed together even if Na⁺ alone is poorly absorbed; this lowers the water potential of the epithelial cells and blood; water follows by osmosis from the lumen into the cells and blood.
parts.working: 1: Na⁺–glucose co-transport; 1: Na⁺ gradient maintained by Na⁺/K⁺ pump using ATP; 1: absorption of solutes lowers water potential in cells/blood; 1: water absorbed by osmosis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the solution must not be too concentrated.
parts.answer: A very concentrated solution would give the intestinal contents a lower water potential than the cells, so water would move out of the body into the lumen by osmosis, making dehydration worse.
parts.working: 1: lumen water potential too low; 1: water drawn out of cells into gut.

practice.stem: Barley root tissue was placed in a solution containing potassium ions. When a respiratory inhibitor was added, the rate of K⁺ uptake fell by 85 %, but the rate of water uptake by the same tissue fell by only 10 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between the effects of the inhibitor on K⁺ uptake and on water uptake.
parts.answer: K⁺ is taken up mainly by active transport against its concentration gradient, which needs ATP from respiration; the inhibitor stops ATP production, so K⁺ uptake falls greatly; water enters by osmosis, which is passive and does not need ATP, so it continues; the small fall in water uptake occurs because less K⁺ is accumulated, so the water potential of the cells is not lowered as much (smaller water potential gradient).
parts.working: 1: K⁺ active transport needs ATP; 1: inhibitor reduces ATP; 1: water by osmosis – passive; 1: small fall explained by reduced solute uptake → smaller gradient.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why K⁺ uptake does not fall by 100 %.
parts.answer: Some K⁺ enters by facilitated diffusion through channels / down a gradient, or some ATP is still made by anaerobic respiration.

practice.stem:
The rate of glucose uptake by red blood cells (which take in glucose only by facilitated diffusion) was measured at different temperatures.
Temperature / °C: 10, 20, 30, 37, 45, 55
Rate / arbitrary units: 12, 22, 39, 50, 41, 9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the shape of the curve between 10 °C and 37 °C.
parts.answer: Increasing temperature gives glucose molecules and the carrier proteins more kinetic energy, so glucose collides with/binds to carriers more often and carriers change shape faster – rate rises.
parts.working: 1: more kinetic energy; 1: more frequent binding / faster carrier shape change.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the results above 37 °C.
parts.answer: The carrier proteins (GLUT proteins) begin to denature – their tertiary structure changes so the glucose binding site no longer fits glucose; fewer functional carriers so the rate falls, very low at 55 °C.
parts.working: 1: carrier proteins denature / binding site shape changes; 1: fewer functional carriers → lower rate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the fall in rate above 37 °C shows that glucose does not enter these cells by simple diffusion through the bilayer.
parts.answer: Simple diffusion would continue to increase with temperature (no proteins to denature), so a fall shows a protein is involved.
parts.working: 1: simple diffusion would keep increasing with temperature.

practice.stem:
Cylinders of sweet potato were kept in 1.0 mol dm⁻³ sodium chloride solution and weighed at intervals.
Time / h: 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 24
Change in mass / %: 0, −12, −18, −21, −21, −15

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the change in mass during the first 4 hours.
parts.answer: The solution has a lower water potential than the cells, so water leaves by osmosis; the loss slows as the cells' water potential falls towards that of the solution (smaller gradient) and stops at equilibrium.
parts.working: 1: water lost by osmosis down water potential gradient; 1: gradient decreases → rate slows → equilibrium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an explanation for the increase in mass between 8 h and 24 h.
parts.answer: After a long time in strong salt, the cells are damaged/die and their membranes lose partial permeability; Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions then diffuse into the cells (cell walls and cytoplasm), lowering their water potential; water re-enters by osmosis (or solution soaks into the dead tissue), so mass increases.
parts.working: 1: cells die / membranes damaged; 1: membranes no longer partially permeable – ions enter; 1: water potential inside falls → water re-enters / tissue absorbs solution.

practice.stem: A student measured the change in mass of potato cylinders after 30 minutes in sucrose solutions. Each cylinder was cut by hand with a kitchen knife, blotted with a paper towel and weighed to 0.1 g before and after the 30 minutes. She used one cylinder for each sucrose concentration. The starting masses were about 1.2 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two sources of error in this method and suggest an improvement for each.
parts.answer: Blotting removes a different amount of surface water each time: blot every cylinder the same way for the same time. The 0.1 g balance is too coarse for masses of about 1.2 g: use a balance reading to 0.001 g. Hand cutting gives cylinders of unequal size and surface area: use a cork borer and a ruler. Only one cylinder per concentration: use several cylinders per concentration and calculate a mean.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two sources of error and 1 mark for each matching improvement (max 4). Accept any two of: variable blotting; coarse balance; unequal cylinder size; no replicates.

practice.stem: A student prepared a sucrose solution for an osmosis experiment. To make 10 cm³ of solution she measured 2.0 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ sucrose in a 10 cm³ measuring cylinder and added distilled water up to the 10 cm³ mark. She read the bottom of the curved surface of the liquid by looking down from above the cylinder.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two errors in this method and explain how each affects the solution.
parts.answer: Using a 10 cm³ measuring cylinder to measure 2.0 cm³ is imprecise, because a small volume in a large cylinder gives a large percentage error: use a 2 cm³ graduated pipette. Reading the meniscus from above (parallax) gives the wrong volume of water added, so the total volume and concentration are not exact: read at eye level with the bottom of the meniscus.
parts.working: 1 mark for each error and 1 mark for each effect on the solution (max 4). Accept: imprecise measuring cylinder for a small volume (large percentage error); parallax from looking down (wrong volume of water added).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the sucrose concentration of the final 10 cm³ solution, assuming the volumes are exact.
parts.working: Concentration = 1.0 × 2.0 ÷ 10.0 = 0.20 mol dm⁻³ (1 mark).

practice.stem: A student measured how long it took the first visible colour to appear in water outside a dialysis tube. She started a stopwatch when she placed the tube in the water and stopped it when she first saw colour, judging by eye. Her repeat times at 10 °C were 245 s, 252 s and 311 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the source of error in starting and stopping the timer and explain its effect on the results.
parts.answer: Human reaction time when starting and stopping the stopwatch, and judging the first colour by eye. This adds random error, so repeat times vary; a consistent delay would shift all the times in the same direction.
parts.working: 1 mark: reaction time in starting or stopping the timer (or subjective colour judgement). 1 mark: this adds variation between repeats (or a systematic shift if consistent).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean time at 10 °C without the anomalous repeat, and give a reason for leaving it out.
parts.answer: (245 + 252) ÷ 2 = 248.5 s. The 311 s repeat is far from the other two (about 60 s longer) and no mistake was recorded for it; without a recorded error it should be repeated rather than removed.
parts.working: 1 mark for the mean 248.5 s. 1 mark for a justification (anomalous and far from the other repeats; no recorded error, so repeat the experiment).

practice.stem: A student investigated the effect of sodium chloride concentration on the mass of carrot cylinders. She used 0 %, 1 %, 2 % and 3 % sodium chloride solutions, with one cylinder in each, and measured the mass change after 2 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two ways to improve the reliability of this investigation.
parts.answer: Use at least three cylinders for each concentration and calculate a mean; cut cylinders to the same size with a cork borer and blot them the same way; keep the time and temperature the same for all tubes.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid suggestions (replicates and a mean; equal cylinder size; same blotting; same temperature and time).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way to improve the range of the investigation.
parts.answer: Use more concentrations spread over a wider range, including values close to the point where the mass change is zero, such as 0.25 %, 0.5 % and 0.75 %.
parts.working: 1 mark: more concentrations over a wider range, including values near the isotonic point.

practice.stem: A student measured how far a purple dye diffused into cubes of gelatin in 10 minutes. She cut each 2 cm cube by hand with a knife and placed each cube in a beaker of dye solution. She did not stir the solution in some of the beakers. She measured the distance the dye had diffused with a ruler, once only, by eye.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two errors and suggest an improvement for each.
parts.answer: Cubes cut by hand are not all the same size, so the surface area differs: use a template or ruler to cut identical cubes. Some solutions were not stirred, so the dye concentration around each cube is not the same: stir all beakers in the same way. The distance was measured once by eye, so reading errors are not averaged out: measure several points and take a mean. Timing may be inconsistent: use a stopwatch.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two errors and 1 mark for each matching improvement (max 4). Accept any two of: unequal cubes; unstirred solutions; single reading by eye; timing not controlled.

practice.stem: A student cut pieces of beetroot of about the same size with a kitchen knife and placed one piece straight into a test-tube of water at each of five temperatures, heating the water over a Bunsen burner in a beaker. After about 15 minutes she judged the depth of red colour in each tube by eye, on a scale from 0 (none) to 5 (very dark).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three sources of error in this method and suggest an improvement for each.
parts.answer: Pieces cut by knife differ in size/surface area – use a cork borer and ruler to cut equal cylinders; pigment from cells damaged by cutting not washed off – rinse pieces in water until the water stays clear; water bath temperature not controlled – use a thermostatically controlled water bath and check with thermometer; colour judged by eye is subjective – use a colorimeter to measure absorbance; only one tube per temperature – do three replicates and calculate means; timing not the same – use a stopwatch and fixed time.
parts.working: Award 1 mark for each error and 1 mark for its matching improvement, for three pairs (max 6): unequal size → cork borer/scalpel and ruler; unwashed cut cells → rinse until no pigment; uncontrolled temperature → thermostatic water bath; subjective colour → colorimeter; no replicates → at least 3 repeats + mean; time varied → stopwatch, same time.

practice.stem: A student filled a length of Visking tubing with 1 % glucose solution, tied both ends and placed it in a beaker of distilled water at 20 °C. Every 5 minutes she took 2 cm³ of the water outside the tubing, added Benedict's reagent and heated the mixture in a water bath. She judged the colour of each mixture by eye, from blue through green and yellow to brick red. She used one length of tubing for the whole experiment and did not rinse it before starting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the student's method could give unreliable results, and suggest two improvements.
parts.answer: Judging the colour by eye is subjective, so end points differ between readings and people: use a colorimeter or a colour standard. Only one tubing is used, so there are no repeats: use several tubings and calculate a mean. The tubing was not rinsed, so residual sugar could be present at the start: rinse and soak it first. Readings every 5 minutes may miss the early change: take readings more often.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two unreliability points (subjective colour judgement; no replicate tubings; unrinsed tubing; coarse time intervals) and 1 mark each for matching improvements (colorimeter or colour standard; several tubings and a mean; rinse and check the tubing; more frequent readings). Max 4.

practice.stem: A student tested whether yeast cells were alive. She mixed a yeast suspension with methylene blue stain, which passes into dead cells and turns them blue, while living cells stay colourless. She put a drop of the mixture into a haemocytometer and counted the cells in one large square under the microscope. She counted the cells by eye and recorded 23 blue and 61 colourless cells in that square. She did not shake the suspension before taking the drop.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three sources of error or weaknesses in this method and suggest an improvement for each.
parts.answer: Suspension not mixed, so the cells are unevenly spread: shake or stir it before sampling. Only one square counted: count several squares and calculate a mean. Counting by eye is subjective and easy to repeat or miss: use a second counter or count from a photograph. Cells touching the lines are counted inconsistently: state a rule, for example count cells on two of the four boundaries only. Stain time not fixed: time the staining.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of three errors and 1 mark for each matching improvement (max 6). Accept any three of: unmixed suspension; one square only; subjective counting; edge cells counted inconsistently; staining time not controlled.

practice.stem: A student measured the pigment released from red cabbage discs heated at different temperatures. For each temperature she placed discs in 10 cm³ of water for 10 minutes, poured the liquid into a cuvette and measured its absorbance in a colorimeter at 540 nm. She set the colorimeter to zero using a cuvette of distilled water. The outside of the cuvette had a fingerprint on it, and she used the same cuvette for every sample without rinsing it between samples.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three errors in these readings and suggest an improvement for each.
parts.answer: Fingerprint on the cuvette absorbs or scatters light, so absorbance is too high: wipe the outside with a lint-free tissue before each reading. Cuvette not rinsed between samples, so pigment carries over and later readings are too high: rinse it with the next sample or use a clean cuvette. No repeats: use three new sets of discs for each temperature and calculate a mean.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of three errors and 1 mark for each matching improvement (max 6). Accept any three of: fingerprint; carry-over between samples; no replicates; zeroing not repeated; discs not the same size.

practice.stem: A student measured the distance that liquid moved up a glass capillary tube attached to Visking tubing. She read the meniscus position with a ruler held beside the tube, not against it, and she read the scale from a position above the tube. The liquid moved from a start mark at 2.0 mm to a finish mark that she recorded as 9.9 mm. The true finish position was 9.4 mm, so the true distance moved was 7.4 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how each of the two reading methods could cause error.
parts.answer: Holding the ruler beside the tube, not against it, means the scale and the meniscus are not at the same level, so the reading is wrong (parallax). Reading from above also makes the meniscus appear at a different position, so the recorded position differs from the true position.
