parts.text: Suggest why the solution should be as dilute as the experiment allows.
parts.answer: A more dilute solution is less corrosive and less likely to cause severe burns, so the risk is reduced.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower concentration gives a lower risk.

practice.stem: Students grow a yeast culture at 30 °C in a flask on the bench for an experiment on membrane transport. At the end of the experiment the culture is poured down the sink.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two hazards and a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Yeast cultures can contaminate the bench and hands: wipe the bench with disinfectant and wash hands after handling. Pouring the culture down the sink can contaminate the drains: disinfect the culture first and then pour it away with plenty of water, following the school's disposal rules.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two hazards and 1 mark for each matching precaution (max 4).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the overall level of risk and give a reason.
parts.answer: Low risk: yeast is a non-pathogenic microorganism, and hygiene and disinfection control the risk.
parts.working: 1 mark: low, with a reason.

practice.stem: A student uses 0.5 mol dm⁻³ sulfuric acid to adjust the pH of a buffer solution for an osmosis experiment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the hazard and suggest a precaution.
parts.answer: Sulfuric acid is corrosive and burns the skin and eyes, and damages clothing: wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves, add the acid to water slowly and wash spills with plenty of water.
parts.working: 1 mark: corrosive (burns skin and eyes). 1 mark: a valid precaution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why 0.5 mol dm⁻³ acid is safer than 2.0 mol dm⁻³ acid.
parts.answer: A lower concentration is less corrosive, so a splash causes less severe injury.
parts.working: 1 mark: less corrosive at lower concentration.

practice.stem: A student heats a water bath with a Bunsen burner to 60 °C for an osmosis experiment. A bottle of ethanol, used to make a dye solution, is kept on the bench close to the burner.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards and give a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Ethanol is highly flammable, and its vapour can catch fire from the flame: keep ethanol away from the flame and keep the bottle closed. Hot water can scald: use a thermostatically controlled electric water bath, or handle the beakers with tongs and wear eye protection.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two hazards and 1 mark for each matching precaution (max 4). Accept: beaker tipping (stable tripod, heatproof mat); burns from hot apparatus (let it cool).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the overall level of risk and give a reason.
parts.answer: Medium risk: a flammable liquid is kept close to an open flame and hot water is used, so the risk is higher unless the precautions are followed.
parts.working: 1 mark: medium, with the reason that flammable liquid and flame are close.

practice.stem: A student plans to hold cells in a water bath at 60 °C for 30 minutes to denature the membrane proteins. The water bath is an electric model standing on the bench near a sink.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards and a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Hot water can scald the skin: use tongs and heatproof gloves, and let the bath cool before emptying it. Electricity and water near the sink: keep the cable and plug away from water, keep the bath on a dry surface and switch off before handling; avoid spills.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two hazards and 1 mark for each matching precaution (max 4).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the overall level of risk and give a reason.
parts.answer: Medium risk: hot water and electrical equipment near water are both hazards, but they can be controlled with simple precautions.
parts.working: 1 mark: medium, with a reason.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way to check the temperature safely and accurately.
parts.answer: Use a thermometer placed in the water bath, and read it through the glass or without touching the hot water.
parts.working: 1 mark: thermometer in the bath, read without contact with hot water.

practice.stem: A student prepares wet mounts of cells on glass slides, covers them with coverslips and views them under a microscope with an electric lamp.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards and a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Broken glass slides or coverslips can cut the fingers: handle by the edges and put broken glass in a glass bin. The electric lamp can give an electric shock and gets very hot: check the cable, switch off and let it cool before changing the bulb. Accept also: liquid spilt near the lamp (wipe spills at once and keep liquids away from the lamp).
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two hazards and 1 mark for each matching precaution (max 4).

practice.stem: A student heats 100 cm³ of water in a beaker on a tripod over a Bunsen burner to 80 °C, to test the effect of temperature on red blood cell membranes. She then transfers the hot water to test-tubes using a glass pipette.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards and suggest a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Hot water spilling or scalding: use a heatproof beaker, tongs and a stable tripod or heatproof mat. The glass pipette can break and cut: wrap it in a cloth, or use a plastic pipette. Accept also: a Bunsen flame near loose hair or flammable items (tie back hair, keep items away).
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two hazards and 1 mark for each matching precaution (max 4).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the risk is higher than in an experiment at 30 °C.
parts.answer: Water at 80 °C can cause severe burns, and it can boil and spit, so injuries are more serious if it spills. The precautions must be stricter.
parts.working: 1 mark: more severe burns or spitting at 80 °C. 1 mark: stricter precautions are needed.

practice.stem: A student grows a non-pathogenic bacterial culture on an agar plate at 25 °C for 2 days, and makes a second plate of sterile agar as a control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards and a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Bacteria can contaminate hands and benches: wash hands and disinfect the bench before and after work. The plate lid can be opened and let bacteria into the air: keep the lid taped shut and do not open the plates. Accept also: plates must be sterilised before disposal (for example in an autoclave).
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two hazards and 1 mark for each matching precaution (max 4).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the overall level of risk.
parts.answer: Low risk for a non-pathogenic strain used with aseptic technique.
parts.working: 1 mark: low, with the reason.

practice.stem: A student plans to collect cheek cells from her own mouth with a cotton bud, place them in a salt solution, add a stain and view them under a microscope.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one biological hazard and one chemical hazard, and state a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Biological: cells from the mouth may carry microorganisms, so use only her own cells, do not share the cotton bud, and disinfect the bench afterwards. Chemical: the stain (for example methylene blue) is harmful if swallowed and irritates the eyes, so wear goggles and gloves and wipe up spills.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard and 1 mark for each matching precaution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the overall level of risk and justify it. Say how the risk would change if the cells came from other people.
parts.answer: Low risk with the student's own cells, dilute solutions and simple precautions. The risk would be higher if cells from other people were used, because of possible infections.
parts.working: 1 mark: low risk, with a justification based on own cells and controls. 1 mark: higher risk if other people's cells are used.

practice.stem: A student views cells stained with a fluorescent dye under an ultraviolet (UV) lamp. She holds the lamp close to the cells and does not wear eye protection.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the hazard and explain why it is a risk.
parts.answer: Ultraviolet light can damage the eyes and skin. The damage may not be felt at the time and can appear later, and it is greater when the lamp is close and the exposure is long.
parts.working: 1 mark: UV damages eyes and skin. 1 mark: damage may be delayed, and risk rises with closeness and time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two precautions.
parts.answer: Wear UV-blocking goggles or safety glasses; keep the lamp at a distance and switch it off when not in use; limit the exposure time; use a shield or box around the lamp.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two valid precautions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the overall level of risk, before and after the precautions are used.
parts.answer: Medium risk without precautions, because the lamp is held close and no eye protection is worn; low risk once goggles, distance and short exposure are used.
parts.working: 1 mark: medium before precautions. 1 mark: low after precautions, with a reason.

practice.stem: A student proposes to dissolve a stain in ethanol, apply it to cells on a slide, and then dry the slide over a Bunsen burner before viewing it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the proposed method. Identify the main hazard, explain why it is a risk, and suggest a safer alternative.
parts.answer: The main hazard is ethanol, which is highly flammable: its vapour can ignite near the open flame and cause a fire. A safer alternative is a water-based stain, with the slide air-dried at room temperature or dried on a heat block with no open flame.
parts.working: 1 mark: ethanol is highly flammable. 1 mark: vapour can ignite near the flame. 1 mark: a water-based stain or air-drying. 1 mark: overall unacceptable as proposed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the level of risk as proposed, and whether the method should go ahead.
parts.answer: High risk as proposed. It should not go ahead with the flame; the safer method should be used and approved by the teacher before work starts.
parts.working: 1 mark: high risk. 1 mark: do not proceed as proposed; use the safer method with teacher approval.

practice.stem: A student plans an experiment with four parts: (1) cutting tissue with a scalpel; (2) using 1.0 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide; (3) heating water to 60 °C with a Bunsen burner; and (4) using an electric balance on the bench next to the water bath.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Rank the hazards from most to least serious, and justify your order.
parts.answer: Most serious: sodium hydroxide, which is corrosive and can cause permanent eye damage. Next: the open flame with hot water, which can cause fire and burns. Then the scalpel, which can be controlled, and the balance, which only becomes a hazard if water is spilt on it.
parts.working: 1 mark: sodium hydroxide ranked as most serious, with a reason. 1 mark: flame and hot water ranked next, with a reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For each hazard, state one control measure.
parts.answer: Sodium hydroxide: goggles and gloves, and wash splashes at once. Bunsen flame: tie back hair, keep flammable items away, or use an electric water bath. Scalpel: cut on a tile, away from the body, and keep the blade covered. Electric balance: keep it away from water and wipe spills at once.
parts.working: 1 mark for each sensible control measure (max 4).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the overall risk level before and after the controls, and give a reason.
parts.answer: Medium before the controls, because of the corrosive chemical and the flame; low after the controls, because each hazard is reduced to an acceptable level.
parts.working: 1 mark: medium before controls, low after. 1 mark: reason based on the controls reducing each hazard.

subtopics.name: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
Skill: recording results in a table

subtopics: Skill: recording results in a table
Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the process of transcription in a eukaryotic cell.
parts.answer: The DNA double helix unwinds and hydrogen bonds break at the gene; one strand acts as the template; free RNA nucleotides pair with complementary bases (U with A); RNA polymerase joins the nucleotides with phosphodiester bonds; this forms a primary transcript, which is spliced (introns removed) to form mRNA
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: occurs in nucleus; DNA unwinds/H bonds broken; only template strand used; free (activated) RNA nucleotides; complementary base pairing, uracil pairs with adenine; RNA polymerase; phosphodiester bonds; primary transcript; introns removed/exons joined to form mRNA.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The base sequence of a triplet on the template strand of DNA is GCA. What is the anticodon on the tRNA molecule that brings the matching amino acid?
A CGT
B CGU
C GCA
D GCU
parts.answer: C GCA
parts.working: Template GCA is transcribed into the mRNA codon CGU. The tRNA anticodon is complementary to the codon: GCA. B is the codon, not the anticodon; A contains thymine, which is not found in RNA.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the roles of mRNA, tRNA and ribosomes in translation.
parts.answer: mRNA carries the code (sequence of codons) from the nucleus to the ribosome; tRNA carries a specific amino acid and its anticodon pairs with the complementary codon; the ribosome holds the mRNA and tRNA in place and moves along the mRNA; peptide bonds form between adjacent amino acids on the ribosome
parts.working: 1 mark each: mRNA – sequence of codons / template; tRNA – brings specific amino acid; anticodon–codon complementary base pairing; ribosome – binding site for mRNA and two tRNAs / catalyses peptide bond formation / moves one codon at a time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by saying that the genetic code is degenerate.
parts.answer: Most amino acids are coded for by more than one triplet/codon
parts.working: More than one codon for (most) amino acids.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The coding sequence of the mature mRNA for a polypeptide has 1203 nucleotides, including one stop codon. Calculate the number of amino acids in the polypeptide.
parts.working: M1: 1203 ÷ 3 = 401 codons. A1: 401 − 1 stop codon = 400 amino acids.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The primary transcript of this gene is much longer than 1203 nucleotides. Explain why.
parts.answer: The primary transcript contains introns (non-coding sequences); these are removed by splicing, and the exons are joined to form the mature mRNA
parts.working: 1 mark: introns present in primary transcript. 1 mark: introns removed / exons joined (splicing).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where in a eukaryotic cell (i) transcription and (ii) translation take place.
parts.answer: (i) nucleus; (ii) ribosomes in the cytoplasm / on rough ER
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the enzyme that catalyses transcription.
parts.answer: RNA polymerase
parts.working: RNA polymerase. Not DNA polymerase.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the type of bond formed between amino acids during translation.
parts.answer: Peptide bond
parts.working: Peptide bond.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substance is NOT needed for translation?
A RNA polymerase
B ATP
C tRNA
D amino acids
parts.answer: A RNA polymerase
parts.working: RNA polymerase catalyses transcription (making mRNA from DNA), not translation. Translation needs mRNA, ribosomes, tRNA, amino acids and ATP (e.g. to attach amino acids to tRNA). B is wrong because energy from ATP is used during translation.

practice.stem: The primary transcript of a gene in a cow contains 8400 nucleotides. Its introns contain 5250 nucleotides in total.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the primary transcript that is made of introns.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assume that the whole mature mRNA codes for the polypeptide and ends in one stop codon. Calculate the number of amino acids in the polypeptide.
parts.working: M1: mature mRNA = 8400 − 5250 = 3150 nucleotides; 3150 ÷ 3 = 1050 codons. A1: 1050 − 1 = 1049 amino acids.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The same gene can produce two different polypeptides in muscle cells and in liver cells. Explain how this is possible.
parts.answer: Alternative splicing: different combinations of exons are kept in the mRNA in different cell types, so the mRNAs have different base sequences and code for different amino acid sequences
parts.working: 1 mark: different exons included/removed (alternative splicing). 1 mark: different mRNA sequence → different primary structure.

practice.stem:
Part of an mRNA molecule has this sequence of codons:
AUG GCU UUU GAU CCA UGG AAA UAA
Codons: AUG = Met (start); GCU = Ala; UUU = Phe; GAU = Asp; CCA = Pro; UGG = Trp; AAA = Lys; UAA = stop.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the sequence of amino acids coded for by this mRNA.
parts.answer: Met – Ala – Phe – Asp – Pro – Trp – Lys (then stop)
parts.working: 2 marks all correct in order; 1 mark if one error. Stop codon UAA adds no amino acid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the base sequence of the DNA template strand for the first two codons.
parts.answer: TAC CGA
parts.working: Complementary to AUG GCU, with T instead of U: TAC CGA.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A mutation changes the codon UGG to UGA, which is a stop codon. Explain the effect on the polypeptide.
parts.answer: Translation stops at this codon, so the polypeptide is shorter (only Met–Ala–Phe–Asp–Pro); it will have a different structure and probably not function
parts.working: 1 mark: translation ends early / shorter polypeptide (five amino acids). 1 mark: missing amino acids alter folding/tertiary structure, so protein likely non-functional.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Some events in making a secreted protein are listed.
1 tRNA anticodon pairs with an mRNA codon
2 RNA polymerase joins RNA nucleotides
3 mRNA leaves the nucleus through a nuclear pore
4 a peptide bond forms between two amino acids
5 introns are removed
What is the correct order?
A 2, 5, 3, 1, 4
B 2, 3, 5, 1, 4
C 5, 2, 3, 4, 1
D 2, 5, 3, 4, 1
parts.working: Transcription (2) and splicing (5) occur in the nucleus before the mRNA leaves (3); on the ribosome, tRNA must pair with the codon (1) before a peptide bond can form (4). B splices outside the nucleus, which is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A ribosome adds 15 amino acids per second to a growing polypeptide. Calculate how long it takes one ribosome to make a polypeptide of 450 amino acids.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a cell making large amounts of this protein, many ribosomes are attached to each mRNA molecule at the same time. Explain the advantage of this.
parts.answer: Many polypeptides are made from one mRNA at the same time, so a large amount of protein is made quickly without extra transcription
parts.working: 1 mark: several polypeptides translated simultaneously (polysome). 1 mark: faster/greater production of protein from one mRNA.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a tRNA molecule carries the correct amino acid to the ribosome.
parts.answer: Each tRNA has a specific anticodon; a specific amino acid is attached to the tRNA (by an enzyme, using ATP) according to that anticodon, at the amino acid binding site
parts.working: 1 mark: specific amino acid attached to tRNA at binding site (3′ end), using ATP/enzyme. 1 mark: anticodon is specific to that amino acid and pairs with the codon.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which event takes place during translation but NOT during transcription?
A Hydrogen bonds form between complementary bases.
B Peptide bonds form.
C A nucleic acid strand is used as a template.
D Energy from nucleoside triphosphates (such as ATP) is used.
parts.answer: B Peptide bonds form.
parts.working: Peptide bonds join amino acids only in translation. A happens in both (DNA–mRNA pairing in transcription; codon–anticodon pairing in translation); C happens in both (DNA template; mRNA read); D happens in both (activated nucleotides in transcription; ATP to load amino acids onto tRNA).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Rifampicin, an antibiotic used to treat tuberculosis, inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase. Explain why this stops the bacteria making proteins.
parts.answer: No transcription, so no new mRNA is made; without mRNA no translation can take place
parts.working: 1 mark: transcription prevented / no mRNA. 1 mark: no template for translation at ribosomes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Death cap mushrooms contain α-amanitin, which inhibits the RNA polymerase that makes mRNA in human cells. Symptoms of liver failure often appear only two to three days after eating the mushroom. Suggest why.
parts.answer: mRNA and proteins already present in the liver cells continue to work; as these are broken down over time they are not replaced; when key enzymes/proteins run out the cells die
parts.working: 1 mark: existing mRNA still translated for a time. 1 mark: existing proteins/enzymes still function. 1 mark: they are gradually broken down and not replaced, so cell function fails later.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why rifampicin does not stop transcription in the nuclei of human cells.
parts.answer: Human nuclear RNA polymerase has a different structure/shape so rifampicin does not bind to it
parts.working: Different shape of human RNA polymerase (no binding site for rifampicin).

practice.stem:
The coding (non-template) strand of a short gene section is:
5′ ATG GTC ACC TGA 3′
Codons: AUG = Met; GUC = Val; ACC = Thr; UGA = stop.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the base sequence of the mRNA transcribed from this gene section, showing the 5′ and 3′ ends.
parts.answer: 5′ AUG GUC ACC UGA 3′
parts.working: Same as coding strand with U in place of T, same direction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the base sequence of the template strand, showing the 5′ and 3′ ends.
parts.answer: 3′ TAC CAG TGG ACT 5′
parts.working: Complementary to the coding strand and antiparallel (accept 5′ TCA GGT GAC CAT 3′).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using the information given, state the number of amino acids coded for by this section, and name them in order.
parts.answer: 3 amino acids: Met – Val – Thr
parts.working: 1 mark: 3 (UGA is a stop codon and codes for no amino acid). 1 mark: Met, Val, Thr in order.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why only one strand of a gene is transcribed.
parts.answer: Only the template strand has the base sequence complementary to the required mRNA; transcribing the other strand would give a different (complementary) sequence of codons and the wrong amino acid sequence
parts.working: 1 mark: mRNA must be complementary to the template strand only. 1 mark: the other strand would give a different codon sequence/different polypeptide (or a non-functional one).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A gene has six exons. In different tissues, exon 1 and exon 6 are always kept, but each of exons 2, 3, 4 and 5 can either be kept or removed during splicing. Calculate the maximum number of different mature mRNAs that this gene could produce.
parts.working: M1: each of 4 exons has 2 possibilities (kept or removed). A1: 2⁴ = 16.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the existence of alternative splicing means that the human genome, with only about 20 000 protein-coding genes, can produce many more different proteins.
parts.answer: One gene can give several mRNAs with different exon combinations; each codes for a polypeptide with a different primary structure, so the number of proteins exceeds the number of genes
parts.working: 1 mark: one gene → several mRNAs. 1 mark: different amino acid sequences / different proteins.

practice.stem: A mature mRNA molecule in a human cell is 1650 nucleotides long. It has 120 untranslated nucleotides before the start codon and 210 untranslated nucleotides after the stop codon. The coding region begins with the start codon and ends with one stop codon.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of amino acids in the polypeptide.
parts.working: M1: coding region = 1650 − 120 − 210 = 1320 nucleotides = 440 codons. A1: 440 − 1 stop codon = 439 amino acids.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The mean mass of an amino acid residue in the polypeptide is 110 Da. Estimate the mass of the polypeptide in kDa. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 48.3 kDa

parts.label: c
parts.text: One ribosome adds 6 amino acids per second. Calculate the time for one ribosome to make the polypeptide. Give your answer to the nearest second.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the 120 nucleotides before the start codon are not translated, and suggest how the ribosome finds the correct place to begin translation.
parts.answer: Translation begins only at the start codon (AUG), so bases before it are not read as codons; the ribosome binds near the 5′ end of the mRNA and moves along it until it reaches the start codon, where the tRNA carrying methionine (anticodon UAC) pairs with it
parts.working: 1 mark: translation starts at start codon AUG. 1 mark: ribosome attaches/scans along mRNA to the start codon (tRNA-Met anticodon UAC pairs).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the three components of a DNA nucleotide.
parts.answer: Deoxyribose (a pentose sugar); a phosphate group; a nitrogenous (organic) base
parts.working: All three for 2 marks; any two for 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the bond that joins adjacent nucleotides in one strand of DNA.
parts.answer: Phosphodiester bond
parts.working: Phosphodiester. Do not accept 'hydrogen bond' or 'peptide bond'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the two purine bases found in DNA.
parts.answer: Adenine and guanine
parts.working: Both needed.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two differences between the structure of a DNA molecule and the structure of an mRNA molecule.
parts.answer: DNA has deoxyribose, mRNA has ribose; DNA has thymine, mRNA has uracil; DNA is double-stranded, mRNA is single-stranded; DNA is much longer
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two comparative differences.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A sample of double-stranded DNA from a goat contains 18 % adenine. What percentage of the bases are cytosine?
A 18 %
B 32 %
C 36 %
D 64 %
parts.working: A = T = 18 %, so A + T = 36 % and G + C = 64 %. Since G = C, cytosine = 64 ÷ 2 = 32 %. D gives G + C together, not cytosine alone.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which type of bond holds the two polynucleotide strands of a DNA molecule together?
A phosphodiester bonds
B hydrogen bonds
C glycosidic bonds
D peptide bonds
parts.answer: B hydrogen bonds
parts.working: Complementary bases (A–T and C–G) are joined by hydrogen bonds between the strands. Phosphodiester bonds (A) join nucleotides WITHIN one strand, forming the sugar–phosphate backbone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two pyrimidine bases found in DNA.
parts.answer: Cytosine and thymine
parts.working: 1 mark for both.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the pyrimidine base that is found in RNA but not in DNA.
parts.answer: Uracil
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one structural difference between a purine and a pyrimidine.
parts.answer: Purines have two (fused) rings; pyrimidines have one ring
parts.working: 1 mark: double ring vs single ring. Accept purines are larger.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why, in DNA, a purine always pairs with a pyrimidine.
parts.answer: A purine–pyrimidine pair has three rings in total, so every base pair is the same width; this keeps the distance between the two sugar–phosphate backbones constant (so the double helix has a uniform width)
parts.working: 1 mark: each pair same size (two rings + one ring). 1 mark: constant distance between backbones / uniform helix width. (Two purines would be too wide, two pyrimidines too narrow.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the reaction that joins two nucleotides together.
parts.answer: Condensation
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how two nucleotides are joined in a polynucleotide.
parts.answer: The phosphate group of one nucleotide bonds to the pentose sugar (3′ carbon) of the next nucleotide; forming a phosphodiester bond; water is released
parts.working: 1 mark: phosphate of one nucleotide joined to sugar of the next. 1 mark: phosphodiester bond (with release of water).

parts.label: c
parts.text: A molecule of ATP is similar to one of the nucleotides found in RNA. State two ways in which ATP differs from an RNA nucleotide containing adenine.
parts.answer: ATP has three phosphate groups, the RNA nucleotide has one; ATP is a free molecule / is not joined into a polynucleotide chain
parts.working: 1 mark: three phosphates vs one. 1 mark: ATP not part of a polynucleotide / free in cytoplasm. (Both contain adenine and ribose — do not accept differences in sugar or base.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of a molecule of ATP.
parts.answer: Adenine (base) joined to ribose (pentose sugar), with a chain of three phosphate groups attached to the ribose
parts.working: 1 mark each: adenine; ribose; three phosphate groups. (Accept 'a nucleotide with adenine, ribose and three phosphates' as 3 marks.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why ATP is well suited to be the immediate energy source in cells.
parts.answer: Hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate releases energy in one step / quickly; releases a small, usable amount of energy; it is small and soluble so moves easily in the cell; it is quickly regenerated from ADP + Pi
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: energy released by a single hydrolysis reaction; small manageable quantities of energy (less wasted as heat); water soluble/easily transported; rapidly resynthesised; can phosphorylate other molecules making them more reactive.

practice.stem: Strand 1 of a short DNA molecule from a rice gene has the base composition: adenine 22 %, thymine 30 %, guanine 28 %, cytosine 20 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the percentages of each base in strand 2 (the complementary strand).
parts.working: 2 marks all four correct; 1 mark for two or three correct. Base pairing A–T and G–C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Strand 1 is used as the template for transcription. Give the percentages of each base in the mRNA.
parts.working: 1 mark: uracil replaces thymine (U 22 %). 1 mark: other three correct.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of guanine in the whole double-stranded molecule.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which describes the structure of ATP?
A adenine, deoxyribose and three phosphate groups
B adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups
C adenosine, ribose and two phosphate groups
D adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups joined by hydrogen bonds
parts.answer: B adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups
parts.working: ATP is adenine + ribose (together adenosine) + three phosphate groups, joined by covalent bonds. A has the DNA sugar; C describes ADP; D is wrong because the phosphates are linked covalently, not by hydrogen bonds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The molar mass of ATP is 507 g/mol. A resting adult turns over (makes and hydrolyses) about 50 kg of ATP per day. Calculate the number of moles of ATP hydrolysed per day. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 98.6 mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hydrolysis of 1 mol of ATP to ADP and phosphate releases 30.5 kJ. Calculate the energy released per day from this ATP. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The body contains only about 50 g of ATP at any time. Explain how the cell can hydrolyse so much ATP each day.
parts.answer: ATP is constantly regenerated: ADP and phosphate are recombined by condensation using energy from respiration (catalysed by ATP synthase); each ATP molecule is recycled about 1000 times per day
parts.working: 1 mark: ADP + Pi → ATP / recycled. 1 mark: energy from respiration / ATP synthase. Accept calculation 50 000 ÷ 50 = 1000 recycles.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why ATP, rather than glucose, is used as the immediate energy source in cells.
parts.answer: ATP releases energy in small, manageable amounts in a single-step hydrolysis (glucose would release too much energy at once / needs many steps)
parts.working: 1 mark: small amount of energy released per molecule / one-step reaction / quickly.

practice.stem:
The table shows the percentage of each base in nucleic acid samples.
Sample | A | T | G | C | U
Wheat | 27.3 | 27.1 | 22.7 | 22.9 | 0
Bacterium X | 15.2 | 15.0 | 34.9 | 34.9 | 0
Virus Y | 24.0 | 31.0 | 18.0 | 27.0 | 0
Sample Z | 23.0 | 0 | 27.0 | 24.0 | 26.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio (A + G) ÷ (T + C) for wheat DNA. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the sample that is single-stranded DNA. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Virus Y; amounts of A and T are not equal and amounts of G and C are not equal, so the bases are not complementary-paired
parts.working: B1: Virus Y. B1: A ≠ T and G ≠ C (no base pairing rule).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what sample Z is. Give a reason.
parts.answer: RNA, because it contains uracil instead of thymine
parts.working: 1 mark: RNA with uracil reason.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Of the double-stranded DNA samples, suggest which would need the highest temperature to separate its two strands. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Bacterium X; it has the highest proportion of G–C pairs (69.8 %), which are joined by three hydrogen bonds rather than two
parts.working: B1: bacterium X. B1: more G–C pairs, each with three hydrogen bonds (A–T has two).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by saying that the two strands of DNA are antiparallel.
parts.answer: The strands run in opposite directions: one runs 5′ to 3′ and the other 3′ to 5′ (the deoxyribose sugars point in opposite directions)
parts.working: 1 mark: opposite directions. 1 mark: reference to 5′/3′ ends or orientation of the sugar–phosphate backbone.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why adenine pairs with thymine but not with cytosine.
parts.answer: A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine so the molecule has a constant width; adenine and thymine form two hydrogen bonds with each other, but adenine and cytosine cannot form matching hydrogen bonds
parts.working: 1 mark: purine–pyrimidine pairing (both A and C fit the width rule, so this alone is not enough). 1 mark: A and T form 2 hydrogen bonds / hydrogen-bonding positions match only for A–T (G–C forms 3).

parts.label: c
parts.text: A DNA fragment is 120 base pairs long, and 35 % of its bases are guanine or cytosine. Calculate the total number of hydrogen bonds holding the two strands together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of a tRNA molecule.
parts.answer: Single polynucleotide strand of RNA folded into a clover-leaf shape, held by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases; has an anticodon (three bases) at one end/loop; an amino acid attachment site at the 3′ end
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: single strand of RNA nucleotides; folded (clover-leaf) with some base pairing/hydrogen bonds; anticodon of three bases; amino acid binding site (3′ end, CCA).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A polynucleotide contains 250 nucleotides. State how many molecules of water are needed to hydrolyse it completely into separate nucleotides.
parts.working: One water molecule per phosphodiester bond; 250 − 1 = 249 bonds.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two differences between the structure of a tRNA molecule and an mRNA molecule.
parts.answer: tRNA is folded (clover-leaf) with hydrogen-bonded regions, mRNA is a straight/unfolded strand; tRNA has an anticodon and amino acid binding site, mRNA has codons; tRNA is much shorter (about 80 nucleotides); all tRNA molecules have the same length/shape
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid comparisons.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which molecules contain ribose?
1 ATP
2 mRNA
3 tRNA
4 DNA
A 1, 2 and 3 only
B 2 and 3 only
C 1, 2, 3 and 4
D 2, 3 and 4 only
parts.answer: A 1, 2 and 3 only
parts.working: ATP is adenine + ribose + three phosphates; all RNA (mRNA, tRNA) contains ribose. DNA contains deoxyribose, so 4 is excluded. B forgets that ATP contains ribose.

practice.stem: Human chromosome 1 is one double-stranded DNA molecule containing about 249 million base pairs. Adjacent base pairs are 0.34 nm apart along the length of the double helix.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the length of this DNA molecule in cm. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The double helix makes one complete turn every 10 base pairs. Calculate the number of complete turns in the molecule.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The nucleus containing this chromosome has a diameter of about 6 µm. Suggest how such a long molecule fits inside the nucleus.
parts.answer: DNA is wound around histone proteins / coiled and supercoiled (forming chromatin); this packs the molecule into a much shorter, compact structure
parts.working: 1 mark: histones / DNA–protein (chromatin). 1 mark: coiling/folding at several levels.

practice.stem: A linear double-stranded DNA fragment cut from a plasmid contains 5800 nucleotides in total. 1218 of these nucleotides contain guanine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of each base (A, T, G and C) in the molecule.
parts.working: M1: C = G = 1218 (complementary). A1: (5800 − 2436) ÷ 2 = 1682 each for A and T.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The mean mass of one nucleotide in this DNA is 330 Da. Calculate the mass of the fragment in kDa. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the number of phosphodiester bonds in the molecule.
parts.working: M1: each strand has 2900 nucleotides, so 2899 phosphodiester bonds. A1: 2 × 2899 = 5798.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a molecule of DNA is replicated by semi-conservative replication.
parts.answer: DNA helicase breaks hydrogen bonds between bases and the strands separate; both strands act as templates; free DNA nucleotides pair with complementary bases (A–T, C–G); DNA polymerase joins nucleotides by phosphodiester bonds (in the 5′ to 3′ direction); each new molecule contains one original strand and one new strand
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: helicase; breaks hydrogen bonds/unwinds; both strands are templates; free (activated) nucleotides; complementary base pairing; DNA polymerase; phosphodiester bonds formed; DNA ligase joins fragments (lagging strand); each daughter molecule has one old and one new strand.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Bacteria grown for many generations with only heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N) were moved to a medium containing only light nitrogen (¹⁴N). DNA was extracted after two generations in ¹⁴N. Which result supports semi-conservative replication?
A all DNA hybrid (¹⁵N/¹⁴N)
B 50 % hybrid DNA and 50 % light DNA
C 25 % hybrid DNA and 75 % light DNA
D 50 % heavy DNA and 50 % light DNA
parts.answer: B 50 % hybrid DNA and 50 % light DNA
parts.working: After one generation every molecule is hybrid. In the second generation each hybrid molecule gives one hybrid and one light molecule, so half are hybrid and half light. A is the result after one generation; D is what conservative replication would give.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
During which stage of the cell cycle is DNA replicated?
A prophase
B S phase of interphase
C G2 phase of interphase
D anaphase
parts.answer: B S phase of interphase
parts.working: DNA replication takes place in the S (synthesis) phase of interphase, so each chromosome has two identical chromatids by the start of mitosis. In G2 (C) the cell checks the replicated DNA and prepares for division; replication is already complete.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why DNA replication is described as semi-conservative.
parts.answer: Each new DNA molecule contains one original (parental) strand and one newly made strand
parts.working: 1 mark: one old strand kept. 1 mark: one new strand made in each daughter molecule.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how complementary base pairing makes sure that the new DNA molecules are identical to the original.
parts.answer: Each exposed base on the template can pair with only one type of free nucleotide (A with T, C with G); so the sequence of the new strand is determined by the template and both molecules have the same base sequence as the original
parts.working: 1 mark: A–T, C–G only. 1 mark: base sequence copied exactly / new strand complementary to template, matching the other old strand.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why it is important that DNA is copied exactly before a cell divides by mitosis.
parts.answer: So that both daughter cells receive identical genetic information (all the genes needed)
parts.working: 1 mark: genetically identical daughter cells / no mutations passed on.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the passage by giving the word for each gap (1)–(6).
'The enzyme DNA helicase breaks the (1) bonds between the bases, so the double helix unwinds and the two strands separate. Each strand acts as a (2). Free (3) in the nucleus pair with the exposed bases by (4) base pairing. The enzyme DNA (5) joins adjacent nucleotides, forming (6) bonds in the new strand.'
parts.answer: (1) hydrogen; (2) template; (3) (activated) nucleotides; (4) complementary; (5) polymerase; (6) phosphodiester
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct gap.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the role of each of these enzymes in DNA replication: (i) DNA helicase, (ii) DNA polymerase, (iii) DNA ligase.
parts.answer: (i) unwinds DNA and breaks hydrogen bonds between bases; (ii) joins new nucleotides to form a new strand (forms phosphodiester bonds); (iii) joins short fragments (Okazaki fragments) of the lagging strand
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why one new strand (the leading strand) is made continuously while the other (the lagging strand) is made in short sections.
parts.answer: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides in one direction (to the 3′ end, building 5′ to 3′); the two template strands are antiparallel; so on one template the polymerase follows the replication fork, but on the other it must work away from the fork in short fragments that are later joined
parts.working: 1 mark: polymerase works only 5′ → 3′ / adds to 3′ end. 1 mark: strands are antiparallel. 1 mark: on lagging strand synthesis is away from the fork, so fragments are made and joined by ligase.

practice.stem: A student repeats a classic experiment using E. coli grown first in ¹⁵N medium, then transferred to ¹⁴N medium. DNA is separated by density after each generation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of DNA molecules that would be hybrid (one ¹⁵N strand and one ¹⁴N strand) after three generations in ¹⁴N.
parts.working: M1: after 3 generations there are 2³ = 8 molecules from each original; only 2 contain an original ¹⁵N strand. A1: 2 ÷ 8 × 100 = 25 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the results after one generation ruled out the conservative model of replication.
parts.answer: After one generation all DNA was of intermediate (hybrid) density; conservative replication would have given one band of heavy DNA and one band of light DNA
parts.working: 1 mark: all intermediate/single hybrid band. 1 mark: conservative model predicts heavy + light bands (no hybrid).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Part of a template strand of DNA has the sequence 3′-TACGGA-5′. Which new strand is made against this template?
A 5′-ATGCCT-3′
B 3′-ATGCCT-5′
C 5′-AUGCCU-3′
D 5′-TACGGA-3′
parts.answer: A 5′-ATGCCT-3′
parts.working: Bases pair A–T and C–G, and the new strand is antiparallel to the template, so it runs 5′→3′ opposite the 3′→5′ template: 5′-ATGCCT-3′. B has the correct bases but the wrong orientation; C contains uracil, which is in RNA, not DNA.

practice.stem: In a section of a human chromosome, the lagging strand is 60 000 nucleotides long. It is made in fragments with a mean length of 150 nucleotides.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the lagging strand is made as short fragments.
parts.answer: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to the 3′ end of a growing strand (so works only in the 5′→3′ direction); on the lagging strand this direction is away from the replication fork, so the enzyme must keep restarting as more DNA is unwound
parts.working: 1 mark: DNA polymerase adds only to 3′ end / synthesises 5′→3′. 1 mark: strands antiparallel, so lagging strand made away from fork in short pieces.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of fragments made on the lagging strand of this section.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assuming the section begins and ends with complete fragments, calculate the number of joins that DNA ligase must make within the section, and name the bond it forms.
parts.answer: 399 joins; phosphodiester bond
parts.working: B1: 400 − 1 = 399. B1: phosphodiester.

practice.stem: A temperature-sensitive mutant of E. coli makes a DNA polymerase that works normally at 30 °C but is inactive at 42 °C. All its other enzymes work at both temperatures. At 30 °C the population doubles every 40 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A culture at 30 °C starts with 2.0 × 10⁶ cells. Calculate the number of cells after 2 hours. Give your answer in standard form.
parts.answer: 1.6 × 10⁷ cells

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the mutant DNA polymerase is inactive at 42 °C although the normal enzyme still works at this temperature.
parts.answer: The mutation changed an amino acid, so some bonds holding the tertiary structure are weaker; at 42 °C these bonds break, the active site changes shape and nucleotides can no longer bind (enzyme denatured)
parts.working: 1 mark: changed primary structure / weaker bonds (hydrogen/ionic) in the mutant protein. 1 mark: broken at 42 °C → active site shape changed / denatured.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The culture is moved to 42 °C. Explain why the cells soon stop dividing.
parts.answer: New DNA strands cannot be made because DNA polymerase cannot join nucleotides (no phosphodiester bonds); so DNA is not replicated and each daughter cell could not receive a complete copy, so division stops
parts.working: 1 mark: no joining of nucleotides / no new strand synthesis. 1 mark: DNA not replicated → no complete copy for each daughter cell, so cell cannot divide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The circular chromosome of a bacterium contains 4.6 million base pairs. Replication starts at a single origin and proceeds in both directions around the circle. Each replication fork adds 1000 nucleotides per second to each new strand. Calculate the time to replicate the whole chromosome, in minutes, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 38.3 min

parts.label: b
parts.text: A human chromosome contains about 50 times as much DNA, but replication forks in human cells move more slowly. Suggest how human cells can still replicate each chromosome within a few hours.
parts.answer: Replication starts at many origins along each chromosome at the same time, so many forks work simultaneously
parts.working: 1 mark: many origins of replication. 1 mark: replication happens simultaneously in many places/replication bubbles join.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A mutant bacterium makes a non-functional DNA ligase. What is the most likely result when it replicates its DNA?
A The lagging strand stays as many separate short fragments.
B Hydrogen bonds between the template strands are not broken.
C Free nucleotides cannot pair with the template strands.
D The leading strand is made as many short fragments.
parts.answer: A The lagging strand stays as many separate short fragments.
parts.working: DNA ligase joins the Okazaki fragments of the lagging strand with phosphodiester bonds. Breaking hydrogen bonds (B) is done by helicase; the leading strand is made continuously (D), so it does not need ligase in this way.

practice.stem: A eukaryotic chromosome contains 150 million base pairs. Replication proceeds in both directions from each origin of replication (two forks per origin). Each fork copies 50 base pairs per second.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time, in days, needed to replicate this chromosome if it had only ONE origin of replication. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 17.4 days
parts.working: M1: each fork copies 75 × 10⁶ bp; 75 × 10⁶ ÷ 50 = 1.5 × 10⁶ s. A1: ÷ 86 400 = 17.4 days.

parts.label: b
parts.text: S phase in these cells lasts 8 hours. Calculate the minimum number of origins of replication needed to copy the chromosome in this time, assuming all origins start together.
parts.working: M1: one origin copies 2 × 50 × 28 800 = 2.88 × 10⁶ bp in 8 h. A1: 150 × 10⁶ ÷ 2.88 × 10⁶ = 52.1 → 53 (must round up).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why bacteria can replicate their DNA using a single origin, while eukaryotic cells need many.
parts.answer: Bacterial DNA is much shorter (a few million bp), so two forks can copy it in a short time; eukaryotic chromosomes are much longer and replication forks move more slowly
parts.working: 1 mark: eukaryotic DNA far longer (and/or slower forks).

practice.stem: Without correction, DNA polymerase inserts about 1 wrong nucleotide in every 10⁵. Proofreading by DNA polymerase removes 99 % of these errors (reducing them 100-fold). A separate mismatch repair system reduces the remaining errors by a further 1000-fold. A diploid human cell contains 6.4 × 10⁹ nucleotide pairs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of errors made per replication of the genome before proofreading.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of errors remaining after proofreading and after mismatch repair.
parts.answer: 640 after proofreading; 0.64 after mismatch repair

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why an error that remains after replication is described as a gene mutation if it lies within a gene, and explain why it is passed on to all the cells descended from the cell in which it occurred.
parts.answer: It is a change in the base sequence of DNA (of a gene); when this DNA is replicated, the changed sequence acts as a template and is copied exactly, so it is passed on to all cells descended from it
parts.working: 1 mark: change in base sequence = mutation. 1 mark: replicated / copied semi-conservatively into later cells.

practice.stem: Onion root tips were placed for 20 minutes in a solution containing radioactive thymidine (a nucleoside of thymine). The tips were then washed, squashed and the cells examined. 48 of 150 cells in the zone of cell division had radioactive nuclei.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why thymidine, rather than uridine, was used to label replicating DNA.
parts.answer: Thymine is found only in DNA (not RNA), so radioactivity shows DNA synthesis only; uridine (uracil) would be built into RNA made in transcription, which happens in all phases
parts.working: 1 mark: thymine only in DNA. 1 mark: uracil/uridine would label RNA / transcription, not replication.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of cells that were labelled.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what this percentage shows about the cell cycle of these cells.
parts.answer: About a third (32 %) of the cells were in S phase during the 20 minutes, so S phase takes roughly a third of the cell cycle (assuming cells are dividing non-synchronously)
parts.working: 1 mark: proportion of cells in S phase ≈ proportion of cycle time in S phase.

parts.label: d
parts.text: No radioactivity was found in the chromosomes of cells that were in metaphase at the end of the 20 minutes. Explain this result.
parts.answer: Cells in metaphase had already finished replicating their DNA (in S phase) before the thymidine was added; there was not enough time (20 min) for labelled cells to pass through G2 into mitosis
parts.working: 1 mark: replication completed before label added / no replication during mitosis. 1 mark: 20 min too short for labelled cells to reach metaphase (G2 too long).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term gene mutation.
parts.answer: A change in the base (nucleotide) sequence of DNA of a gene
parts.working: Change in base sequence of DNA (in a gene).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name three types of gene mutation.
parts.answer: Substitution, insertion (addition), deletion
parts.working: All three for 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the deletion of a single base near the start of a gene usually has a greater effect than the substitution of a single base.
parts.answer: Deletion causes a frameshift: every codon after the deletion is changed, so many amino acids change (and a stop codon may appear early); a substitution changes only one codon, which may code for the same amino acid (degenerate code) or only one different amino acid
parts.working: 1 mark: deletion causes frameshift. 1 mark: all following triplets/amino acids altered (or premature stop). 1 mark: substitution affects only one codon / may be silent because the code is degenerate.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Sickle cell anaemia is caused by a mutation in the gene for the β-globin polypeptide of haemoglobin. Which row describes this mutation?
A substitution; glutamic acid replaced by valine
B deletion; valine replaced by glutamic acid
C substitution; valine replaced by glutamic acid
D insertion; glutamic acid replaced by valine
parts.answer: A substitution; glutamic acid replaced by valine
parts.working: A single base substitution (GAG → GTG on the coding strand, GAG → GUG in the mRNA) changes one codon, so glutamic acid is replaced by valine. C has the amino acids the wrong way round; an insertion would cause a frameshift.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change in a gene is most likely to have NO effect on the polypeptide it codes for?
A insertion of one base near the start of the gene
B deletion of one base near the middle of the gene
C substitution of the third base of a codon in the coding sequence
D substitution that changes a codon for an amino acid into a stop codon
parts.answer: C substitution of the third base of a codon in the coding sequence
parts.working: Because the genetic code is degenerate, many codons differing only in the third base code for the same amino acid, so a third-base substitution is often silent. A and B cause frame shifts; D gives a shortened polypeptide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two mutagens.
parts.answer: Any two: ultraviolet light; X-rays / gamma rays (ionising radiation); chemical mutagens such as benzene, mustard gas or carcinogens in tobacco smoke
parts.working: 1 mark each; 'radiation' alone not enough — must name type.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a gene mutation can result in an enzyme that does not work.
parts.answer: Change in base sequence of DNA changes the mRNA codon(s) / sequence of triplets; so the amino acid sequence (primary structure) changes; so the protein folds differently (different tertiary structure), changing the shape of the active site so the substrate no longer fits
parts.working: 1 mark each: changed triplet/codon; changed primary structure; changed tertiary structure/active site shape → no enzyme–substrate complexes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a gene and an allele.
parts.answer: A gene is a length of DNA that codes for a polypeptide (and has a fixed locus); an allele is one of the different versions (base sequences) of the same gene
parts.working: 1 mark: gene definition. 1 mark: allele = alternative form of a gene.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a new allele arises.
parts.answer: By a gene mutation: a change in the base sequence of the gene (substitution, insertion or deletion)
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The allele for a darker coat colour in a population of desert mice arose by a single base substitution. State why a substitution may change only one amino acid in the polypeptide.
parts.answer: It changes only one triplet/codon (no frame shift), so the rest of the triplets are read normally
parts.working: 1 mark: only one codon affected / reading frame unchanged.

practice.stem:
Part of an mRNA for an enzyme reads: AUG CUU GAA GGA …
Codons: AUG = Met; CUU = Leu; GAA = Glu; GAG = Glu; AAA = Lys; GGA = Gly; UAA = stop.
Three different mutations each change the third codon (GAA):
Mutation 1: GAA → GAG
Mutation 2: GAA → AAA
Mutation 3: GAA → UAA

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each mutation, state the change, if any, in the amino acid sequence.
parts.answer: Mutation 1: no change (GAG still codes for Glu); Mutation 2: Glu replaced by Lys; Mutation 3: translation stops – polypeptide ends after Leu (Met–Leu only)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain which mutation is most likely to produce a non-functional protein.
parts.answer: Mutation 3: a stop codon is formed, so the polypeptide is very short / most amino acids are missing, so it cannot fold into the correct tertiary structure
parts.working: 1 mark: mutation 3 (nonsense/stop codon). 1 mark: truncated polypeptide, wrong tertiary structure/shape.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why mutation 2 may have little effect on the function of the protein in some cases.
parts.answer: If the amino acid is not in the active site/an important region, or Lys has similar properties, the tertiary structure may hardly change
parts.working: Change outside active site / does not change folding much.

practice.stem:
The mRNA for a short peptide is:
AUG GCU AAA GGC UUU GAU UGG UAA
Codons: AUG = Met; GCU = Ala; AAA = Lys; GGC = Gly; UUU = Phe; GAU = Asp; UGG = Trp; UAA = stop; UUG = Leu; AUU = Ile; GGU = Gly.
A mutation in the gene deletes the first G of the fourth codon (GGC).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the amino acid sequence coded for by the mutated mRNA, as far as the codons given allow.
parts.answer: Met – Ala – Lys – Ala – Leu – Ile – Gly (then incomplete codon AA…)
parts.working: Mutated sequence: AUG GCU AAA GCU UUG AUU GGU AA… 2 marks all correct; 1 mark first three correct and frame shifted.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the name for this kind of effect and explain why the stop codon is lost.
parts.answer: Frameshift; the reading frame moves one base, so the triplets are read differently and UAA is no longer read as a codon in frame
parts.working: 1 mark: frameshift. 1 mark: codons regrouped so original stop codon no longer in reading frame.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the deletion of three adjacent bases is often less harmful than the deletion of one base.
parts.answer: Removes one codon/one amino acid only; reading frame is kept for the rest of the gene
parts.working: One amino acid lost, no frameshift.

practice.stem: The coding sequence of a gene for an enzyme is 1500 nucleotides long, including the stop codon.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of amino acids in the normal polypeptide.
parts.working: 1500 ÷ 3 = 500 codons; minus 1 stop codon = 499.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In one family, a substitution changes codon 132 into a stop codon. Calculate the number of amino acids in the mutant polypeptide and express it as a percentage of the normal length. Give the percentage to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 131 amino acids; 26.3 %

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why this mutation is likely to have a more serious effect than a substitution in codon 132 that replaces one amino acid with another of similar properties.
parts.answer: The stop codon ends translation early, so most of the polypeptide (including e.g. regions needed for the active site / correct folding) is missing and the protein is non-functional; a similar amino acid would probably not change the tertiary structure much
parts.working: 1 mark: truncated polypeptide lacks most of its sequence / cannot fold correctly. 1 mark: conservative substitution has little effect on shape/function.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mutation X inserts one extra base after the 30th base of the coding sequence of a gene. Mutation Y inserts three extra bases at the same place. Explain why mutation X is likely to have a much greater effect on the polypeptide than mutation Y.
parts.answer: X causes a frame shift: every codon after the insertion is read in a different frame, so all following amino acids change (and a premature stop codon is likely); Y adds one extra codon (one extra amino acid) without changing the reading frame, so the rest of the sequence is normal
parts.working: 1 mark: frame shift in X. 1 mark: all downstream codons/amino acids altered (or early stop). 1 mark: Y adds one amino acid / reading frame kept.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why a single base insertion very near the END of the coding sequence may have little effect.
parts.answer: Only the last few codons/amino acids are changed, so most of the polypeptide is normal
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: In the gene for the β-globin polypeptide of haemoglobin, the sixth triplet of the template strand is CTC. In people with sickle cell anaemia this triplet is CAC.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the mRNA codon transcribed from the normal triplet and from the mutated triplet.
parts.answer: Normal GAG; mutated GUG
parts.working: 1 mark each (complementary to template; U replaces T).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of mutation.
parts.answer: Substitution (base substitution)
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The normal codon codes for glutamic acid and the mutated codon codes for valine. Glutamic acid has a charged R group; valine has a non-polar (hydrophobic) R group. Explain how this change leads to sickle-shaped red blood cells when oxygen concentration is low.
parts.answer: Valine on the surface of the β-globin chain is hydrophobic; at low oxygen, haemoglobin molecules stick together via these hydrophobic regions; forming long fibres/chains that distort the red blood cell into a sickle shape
parts.working: 1 mark each: hydrophobic amino acid at surface; haemoglobin molecules bind/aggregate (less soluble); fibres distort cell shape.

practice.stem: Huntington's disease is caused by an allele in which a run of repeated CAG triplets near the start of a gene is longer than normal. People with 40 or more repeats develop the disease.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The codon CAG codes for glutamine. In one person's allele, the repeated region is 135 nucleotides long. Calculate the number of CAG repeats in this allele.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A normal allele has 20 repeats. Calculate how many extra glutamine residues the polypeptide from the person's allele contains.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the type of gene mutation that has increased the number of repeats.
parts.answer: Insertion (of bases / of whole triplets)
parts.working: 1 mark: insertion (accept duplication/expansion of triplets).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why this change adds amino acids but does not alter the amino acids coded for after the repeat region.
parts.answer: The extra bases are added in multiples of three (whole codons), so the reading frame is not shifted; so codons after the repeat are read normally
parts.working: 1 mark: multiples of three / whole codons. 1 mark: no frame shift → downstream sequence unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The most common mutation causing cystic fibrosis deletes three nucleotides from the CFTR gene, so phenylalanine at position 508 is missing. Explain why the rest of the amino acid sequence is unchanged.
parts.answer: Three bases = one whole codon is removed, so the reading frame is not shifted; all codons after the deletion are read as normal
parts.working: 1 mark: three nucleotides correspond to one codon/triplet. 1 mark: no frameshift so downstream codons unchanged.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The normal CFTR protein contains 1480 amino acids. Calculate the number of nucleotides in the coding sequence of the normal mRNA, including the stop codon.

parts.label: c
parts.text: CFTR is a channel protein in the cell surface membrane. Suggest why the loss of one amino acid can stop the protein from working.
parts.answer: Changes the primary structure, so the polypeptide folds into a different tertiary structure; misfolded protein does not form a working channel / is broken down and does not reach the cell surface membrane
parts.working: 1 mark: altered folding/tertiary (3D) shape. 1 mark: channel not formed or protein not inserted in the membrane / destroyed by the cell.

practice.stem:
The start of an mRNA reads:
AUG CCA GUU ACG GAU AAA UGG UAA
Codons: AUG = Met; CCA = Pro; GUU = Val; ACG = Thr; GAU = Asp; AAA = Lys; UGG = Trp; UAA = stop; CAG = Gln; UUA = Leu; CGG = Arg; AUA = Ile; AAU = Asn; GGU = Gly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the amino acid sequence of the normal polypeptide.
parts.answer: Met–Pro–Val–Thr–Asp–Lys–Trp
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Mutation 1 deletes the fifth base (C). Give the first seven amino acids coded for by the mutant mRNA.
parts.answer: Met–Gln–Leu–Arg–Ile–Asn–Gly
parts.working: M1: reading frame shifted: AUG CAG UUA CGG AUA AAU GGU. A1: correct amino acids.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A second mutation in the same gene inserts a G immediately after the 12th base of the mutant mRNA (straight after the CGG codon). Give the amino acid sequence now coded for.
parts.answer: Met–Gln–Leu–Arg–Asp–Lys–Trp (then stop)
parts.working: M1: new mRNA AUG CAG UUA CGG GAU AAA UGG UAA. A1: sequence.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Compare the polypeptide in (c) with the normal polypeptide and explain why its function may be restored.
parts.answer: Only amino acids 2–4 differ (Gln–Leu–Arg instead of Pro–Val–Thr); the insertion restores the reading frame, so the rest of the polypeptide is normal and if the changed amino acids are not in a critical region (e.g. active site) the protein may still fold and function
parts.working: 1 mark: only three amino acids changed / same length. 1 mark: reading frame restored so remaining sequence normal (function may be kept if changes not critical).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A mutation occurs in the DNA of a skin cell on a farmer's arm after years of exposure to sunlight. Explain why this mutation cannot be passed on to the farmer's children.
parts.answer: Skin cells are body (somatic) cells that do not produce gametes; only mutations in cells that give rise to gametes (in the testes/ovaries) are inherited
parts.working: 1 mark: somatic cell. 1 mark: only germ-line/gamete mutations inherited.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Two different substitutions each change one amino acid in an enzyme. One has no detectable effect on enzyme activity; the other stops the enzyme working completely. Suggest explanations for this difference.
parts.answer: First: amino acid replaced by one with similar R group / change is on the surface away from the active site, so tertiary structure and active site unchanged; second: change in or near the active site or at a position that forms important bonds (e.g. ionic/disulfide/hydrogen bonds), altering folding/tertiary structure so the active site changes shape and substrate no longer binds
parts.working: 1 mark: similar R group / position not important. 1 mark: second in active site or affects bonds holding tertiary structure. 1 mark: active site shape altered → substrate cannot bind.

practice.stem:
Yeast cells were exposed to different doses of ultraviolet (UV) light and then spread on agar to grow. Mutant colonies (unable to make a particular amino acid) were counted.
UV dose / J m⁻² | surviving cells / 10⁶ | mutant colonies
0 | 50 | 20
10 | 32 | 410
20 | 18 | 650
40 | 5 | 380

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mutation frequency (mutant colonies per 10⁶ surviving cells) for 20 J m⁻². Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 36.1 per 10⁶ survivors

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the effect of UV dose on the mutation frequency and on the number of surviving cells.
parts.answer: As UV dose increases, mutation frequency increases (from 0.4 to 76 per 10⁶ survivors, a 190-fold rise); the number of survivors decreases (from 50 to 5 × 10⁶)
parts.working: 1 mark: frequency increases with data. 1 mark: survival decreases with data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the number of mutant colonies is lower at 40 J m⁻² than at 20 J m⁻², although the mutation frequency is higher.
parts.answer: Many more cells are killed at 40 J m⁻² (only 5 × 10⁶ survive), so even though a higher proportion of survivors are mutants, the total number of mutant cells is smaller
parts.working: 1 mark: far fewer survivors. 1 mark: frequency is a proportion of survivors, so total can fall.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why UV light kills cells as well as causing mutations.
parts.answer: UV damages DNA in many places, so essential genes may be damaged / DNA cannot be replicated or transcribed
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of an antibody molecule.
parts.answer: Four polypeptide chains: two heavy and two light; held together by disulfide bonds; variable regions at the tips form two antigen-binding sites; constant region (same in all antibodies of that class); hinge region gives flexibility
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: four polypeptides; two heavy and two light chains; disulfide bonds; variable region(s); antigen-binding sites (two); constant region; hinge region; Y-shape.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how antibodies cause bacteria to clump together (agglutination) and why this helps to protect the body.
parts.answer: Each antibody has two antigen-binding sites so it can bind to antigens on two different bacteria, linking many together; clumps cannot spread easily and are easier for phagocytes to engulf
parts.working: 1 mark: two binding sites link several bacteria. 1 mark: clumped bacteria easily engulfed by phagocytes / cannot spread/enter cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which cells secrete antibodies?
A plasma cells
B T-helper cells
C memory T-cells
D macrophages
parts.answer: A plasma cells
parts.working: Plasma cells are differentiated B-lymphocytes that make and secrete antibodies. T-helper cells (B) release cytokines that stimulate B-lymphocytes, but do not make antibodies themselves.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the comparison of B-lymphocytes and T-lymphocytes by stating, for each type: (i) where it matures, (ii) one way in which it helps to destroy pathogens.
parts.answer: B-lymphocytes: mature in bone marrow; become plasma cells that secrete antibodies (humoral response). T-lymphocytes: mature in the thymus; T-helper cells release cytokines / T-killer (cytotoxic) cells destroy infected cells
parts.working: 1 mark each: B – bone marrow; B – antibodies via plasma cells; T – thymus; T – cytokines from T-helper cells or killing infected cells by T-killer cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term antigen.
parts.answer: A molecule (usually a protein or glycoprotein, often on the surface of a cell or virus) that is recognised as foreign by the immune system and stimulates a specific immune response.
parts.working: 1 mark: foreign (non-self) molecule that triggers an immune response, e.g. stimulates a lymphocyte to make a specific antibody.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by clonal selection when a B-lymphocyte meets its specific antigen.
parts.answer: Only the B-lymphocyte whose surface antibody (receptor) is complementary in shape to the antigen binds it; this cell is selected and divides by mitosis to form a clone of identical cells, some of which differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antibody and some into memory cells.
parts.working: 1 mark: only the lymphocyte with a complementary receptor binds the antigen and is selected; 1 mark: that cell divides by mitosis to make many identical cells (a clone); 1 mark: clone differentiates into plasma cells (antibody secretion) and memory cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement explains why a second infection with the same pathogen produces a faster and larger antibody response than the first?
A Memory cells are already present in larger numbers and divide and differentiate quickly into plasma cells.
B Plasma cells from the first infection keep making antibody at a constant rate, so no new cells are needed.
C The pathogen has become less antigenic after the first infection.
D Antibodies from the first infection are converted into T-killer cells.
parts.answer: A Memory cells are already present in larger numbers and divide and differentiate quickly into plasma cells.
parts.working: A is correct: memory cells from the first infection give a rapid secondary response. B is wrong because plasma cells are short-lived and do not persist at a constant rate for long; C is wrong because antigenicity does not decrease; D is wrong because antibodies are not converted into cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how B-lymphocytes respond during the primary immune response to a bacterium that the body has never met before.
parts.answer: Only a B-lymphocyte with receptors (antibody) complementary to the antigen binds to it (clonal selection); stimulated by cytokines from T-helper cells; divides by mitosis to form a clone (clonal expansion); some cells differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antibodies; others become memory cells
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: specific B-cell receptor binds antigen; clonal selection; activation by T-helper cells/cytokines; mitosis/clonal expansion; plasma cells; secrete antibodies specific to antigen; memory cells formed; response is slow (several days).

practice.stem:
A volunteer received an injection of a harmless antigen on day 0 and the same antigen again on day 28. Antibody concentration in the blood (arbitrary units, a.u.):
day 0: 0 | day 7: 10 | day 14: 40 | day 21: 15 | day 28: 12 | day 35: 350 | day 42: 400

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the antibody response to the first exposure with the response to the second exposure. Use the data in your answer.
parts.answer: Second response is faster (high levels within 7 days of the second exposure v about 14 days); much larger (peak 400 v 40 a.u.); lasts longer / antibody stays high
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three, at least one with data: faster; greater; longer-lasting; quoted values (e.g. 400 v 40, peak at day 42 v day 14).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the peak antibody concentration was after the second exposure.
parts.answer: 10 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the difference between the two responses.
parts.answer: Memory cells were made during the first response; on second exposure memory B-cells recognise the antigen quickly; they divide rapidly to produce many plasma cells, so more antibody is made sooner
parts.working: 1 mark each: memory cells formed in primary response; memory cells remain in blood/long-lived; rapid clonal expansion/differentiation into plasma cells on second exposure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the roles of T-helper cells and T-killer (cytotoxic) cells in the immune response.
parts.answer: T-helper cells: bind to antigen presented by macrophages; release cytokines; stimulate B-cells to divide/become plasma cells and stimulate macrophages/T-killer cells. T-killer cells: recognise antigens on the surface of infected cells; attach and release substances (e.g. perforin/toxins) that kill the infected cell
parts.working: Max 2 for T-helper: recognise antigen-presenting cells; secrete cytokines; activate B-cells/T-killer cells/phagocytes. Max 2 for T-killer: bind infected/cancer cells with matching antigen; secrete toxins/perforin making holes; destroy infected cells.

parts.label: b
parts.text: HIV infects and destroys T-helper cells. Explain why people with untreated HIV infection become ill with other infections such as tuberculosis.
parts.answer: Fewer T-helper cells so B-cells are not stimulated to make antibodies and T-killer cells are not activated; the immune system cannot respond effectively to other pathogens (opportunistic infections)
parts.working: 1 mark: less activation of B-cells/T-killer cells/phagocytes. 1 mark: weakened immune response so other pathogens not destroyed.

practice.stem:
A patient was infected for the first time with a bacterium. The concentration of antibody specific to this bacterium in the blood was measured:
day 0 – 0 arbitrary units; day 7 – 15 arbitrary units; day 14 – 120 arbitrary units.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in antibody concentration between day 7 and day 14.
parts.answer: 700 % (increase of 105 units on a base of 15: 105 ÷ 15 × 100)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why there is no specific antibody at day 0, and why the concentration is still low at day 7.
parts.answer: Before infection no B-lymphocyte has been selected for this bacterium, so there is no specific antibody. Clonal selection, mitosis and differentiation into plasma cells take several days, so only a low concentration has built up by day 7.
parts.working: 1 mark: no clone of B-cells with the matching receptor exists until the antigen is met; 1 mark: selection, clonal expansion and differentiation into plasma cells take time (lag phase), so levels are low at day 7.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature of a plasma cell is most directly linked to its job of producing large amounts of antibody?
A many lysosomes that digest engulfed pathogens
B an extensive rough endoplasmic reticulum with many ribosomes
C many cilia that move mucus away from the cell
D a flagellum that allows the cell to swim towards a pathogen
parts.answer: B an extensive rough endoplasmic reticulum with many ribosomes
parts.working: B is correct: plasma cells synthesise and secrete large amounts of protein (antibody), so they have extensive rough endoplasmic reticulum and many ribosomes. A describes phagocytes; C and D describe structures not found in plasma cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by an autoimmune disease.
parts.answer: The immune system fails to distinguish self from non-self; it makes antibodies/T-cells against the body's own antigens and attacks its own cells
parts.working: 1 mark: immune system attacks body's own cells/tissues. 1 mark: self antigens treated as non-self / lymphocytes not removed during maturation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In myasthenia gravis, antibodies bind to acetylcholine receptors on the muscle cell membranes at neuromuscular junctions. Suggest how this causes muscle weakness.
parts.answer: Antibodies block receptor binding sites so acetylcholine cannot bind; receptors may also be destroyed/removed; fewer sodium ion channels open so less depolarisation of the muscle membrane; fewer action potentials so muscle contracts weakly
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: antibodies block/compete with acetylcholine; receptors destroyed/fewer receptors; less depolarisation (fewer Na⁺ channels open); threshold not reached / fewer impulses in muscle fibre; weaker contraction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why an antibody that binds to an antigen on the surface of the measles virus cannot bind to an antigen on the mumps virus.
parts.answer: The antigen-binding site (variable region) has a specific shape determined by its amino acid sequence; it is complementary only to the shape of the measles antigen; the mumps antigen has a different shape so it cannot fit/bind
parts.working: 1 mark each: variable region/antigen-binding site; specific amino acid sequence gives specific tertiary structure/shape; complementary to one antigen only (mumps antigen different shape). Do not credit 'active site' or 'receptor'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some antibodies neutralise bacterial toxins. Suggest how binding of an antibody to a toxin molecule prevents it harming cells.
