parts.answer: The antibody covers the part of the toxin that binds to cell receptors / changes its shape, so it cannot attach to or enter body cells; antibody–toxin complexes are removed by phagocytes
parts.working: 1 mark: blocks toxin's binding site/prevents entry into cells. 1 mark: complex engulfed by phagocytes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
During their development, some lymphocytes are found to have receptors that bind to the body's own (self) antigens. What happens to these lymphocytes?
A They are destroyed or made inactive.
B They develop into memory cells.
C They divide to form a clone of plasma cells.
D They become T-helper cells.
parts.answer: A They are destroyed or made inactive.
parts.working: Lymphocytes that react with self antigens are removed (by programmed cell death) so that the immune system does not attack the body. If they became memory or plasma cells (B, C), an autoimmune response would result.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bacterium has many different antigens and epitopes on its surface. Explain why this bacterium stimulates several different clones of B-lymphocytes, and why the mixture of antibodies it produces is more effective than a single antibody type.
parts.answer: Each epitope has its own shape, so only the B-lymphocytes whose receptors are complementary to a given epitope bind and are selected; several clones therefore divide and produce different antibodies. Several different antibodies bound to the same bacterium can cause agglutination, opsonisation and neutralisation more effectively than one type, so the bacterium is removed more effectively.
parts.working: 1 mark: different epitopes have different shapes; 1 mark: each is recognised by a different complementary receptor, so several clones are selected; 1 mark: the mixture of antibodies binds many sites on the bacterium; 1 mark: effective destruction (agglutination, opsonisation, phagocytosis or neutralisation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why T-killer (cytotoxic) cells destroy body cells infected with a virus but do not destroy free virus particles circulating in the blood.
parts.answer: T-killer cells have receptors that bind to an antigen displayed on the infected cell surface together with an MHC class I protein. Free virus particles do not carry an MHC protein displaying the antigen in this way, so the T-killer cell cannot bind them; free viruses are instead bound and neutralised by antibodies and removed by phagocytes.
parts.working: 1 mark: T-killer receptor binds viral antigen displayed with MHC class I on the infected cell; 1 mark: free virus does not present antigen with MHC so is not recognised by T-killer cells; 1 mark: free virus is dealt with by antibodies (neutralisation/opsonisation) and phagocytes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Classify each example as natural active, natural passive, artificial active or artificial passive immunity:
(i) a baby receives antibodies in its mother's breast milk
(ii) a child is given oral polio vaccine drops
(iii) a man recovers from measles and does not catch it again
(iv) a farmer in Sindh bitten by a snake is given an injection of antivenom
parts.answer: (i) natural passive; (ii) artificial active; (iii) natural active; (iv) artificial passive
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which would give long-term immunity to measles?
A an injection of an attenuated (weakened) measles virus vaccine
B an injection of antibodies against measles
C antibodies crossing the placenta from an immune mother
D a course of antibiotics
parts.answer: A an injection of an attenuated (weakened) measles virus vaccine
parts.working: A vaccine stimulates an active immune response, producing memory cells that last for years. Injected or placental antibodies (B, C) give passive immunity, which lasts only weeks because no memory cells are made; antibiotics do not affect viruses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how vaccination provides protection against a disease.
parts.answer: The vaccine contains antigens (dead/weakened pathogen, toxoid or parts of the pathogen); it stimulates a primary immune response; B- and T-lymphocytes specific to the antigen form clones and memory cells; on infection memory cells give a fast secondary response, destroying the pathogen before symptoms appear
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: vaccine contains antigens; specific lymphocytes activated/clonal selection; antibodies produced; memory cells formed; secondary response faster and greater on infection; pathogen destroyed before causing disease.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term herd immunity.
parts.answer: A high proportion of a population is immune (through vaccination or previous infection), so the pathogen cannot spread easily and unvaccinated or susceptible people are protected because chains of transmission are broken.
parts.working: 1 mark: a large proportion of the population is immune; 1 mark: the pathogen cannot spread easily, so unvaccinated individuals are protected.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about the primary response to a vaccine is correct?
A It is faster than the primary response to a natural infection.
B Antibodies appear in the blood only after the pathogen has caused symptoms.
C Memory cells are produced and persist after the antibody concentration has fallen.
D Plasma cells are converted into memory cells that then secrete antibody.
parts.answer: C Memory cells are produced and persist after the antibody concentration has fallen.
parts.working: C is correct: the primary response produces memory cells that persist long after antibody levels fall, giving long-term immunity. A is wrong because the vaccine primary response is the same as for a natural infection, with no symptoms; B is wrong because antibodies are made after vaccination before symptoms; D is wrong because plasma and memory cells are different cell types.

practice.stem: A district health office ran a measles vaccination campaign. Before the campaign there were 840 cases per year. Two years later, with 95 % of children vaccinated, there were 63 cases per year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in measles cases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some children in the district were too young or too ill to be vaccinated, but their risk of catching measles still fell. Explain why.
parts.answer: Herd immunity: so many people are immune that the virus has few susceptible hosts; chains of transmission are broken; so unvaccinated individuals are less likely to meet an infected person
parts.working: 1 mark each: herd immunity (named or described); fewer infected people/carriers to pass on the virus; transmission chain broken so contact with infected people unlikely.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why a few vaccinated children still caught measles.
parts.answer: Some people do not respond fully to the vaccine (e.g. poor immune response, malnutrition); vaccine may have been stored incorrectly (cold chain broken); only one dose received; vaccinated too young while maternal antibodies were present
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sensible reasons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Smallpox was eradicated worldwide by 1980. Explain the features of smallpox and its vaccine that made eradication possible.
parts.answer: The virus had stable antigens (did not mutate much), so one vaccine worked everywhere; the vaccine was live, effective and gave long-lasting immunity; infected people were easy to identify (clear symptoms) so cases could be isolated and contacts vaccinated (ring vaccination); no animal reservoir / only infected humans; vaccine was heat-stable/freeze-dried and easy to give
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: little antigenic variation; effective live vaccine; long-lasting immunity; easy to identify cases; ring vaccination/isolation; no animal reservoir; heat-stable vaccine.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why it has been much more difficult to develop a highly effective vaccine against malaria.
parts.answer: Plasmodium is a eukaryote with many antigens and several stages in its life cycle; it hides inside liver cells and red blood cells, and shows antigenic variation, so antibodies cannot reach it easily
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: different antigens at different life-cycle stages; intracellular (liver/red blood cells) so hidden from antibodies; antigenic variation; many strains.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A newborn baby has antibodies against tetanus that came from its mother across the placenta. Why does this protection last for only a few weeks?
A The baby makes no memory cells and the antibodies are gradually broken down.
B The baby's memory cells die soon after birth.
C The antibodies are destroyed by the baby's plasma cells.
D The antibodies are digested in the baby's stomach.
parts.answer: A The baby makes no memory cells and the antibodies are gradually broken down.
parts.working: This is natural passive immunity: the antibodies were made by the mother, so the baby has no memory cells for tetanus and the antibodies are broken down. B is wrong because no memory cells were formed in the first place.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some vaccines are given as a first course followed later by a booster dose. Explain why a booster dose is needed.
parts.answer: Antibody concentration and the number of memory cells fall with time. The booster stimulates the existing memory cells to divide and differentiate quickly into plasma cells, producing a faster, larger antibody response (secondary response) that restores protection.
parts.working: 1 mark: antibody levels and memory cell numbers decline over time; 1 mark: the booster re-stimulates memory cells, giving a faster and larger (secondary) response.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Tetanus vaccine contains a toxoid: tetanus toxin that has been chemically inactivated so that it no longer causes harm. Explain how the toxoid gives immunity to tetanus even though the vaccine contains no live Clostridium tetani bacteria.
parts.answer: The toxoid keeps the shape of the toxin's antigens, so it is recognised as foreign. The B-lymphocyte with a complementary receptor is selected and divides, and its plasma cells make antibody that neutralises the toxin. Memory cells are also formed, giving a faster response if active toxin is released later.
parts.working: 1 mark: toxoid retains the antigenic shape of the toxin, so it is recognised as foreign; 1 mark: complementary B-lymphocytes are selected and differentiate into plasma cells that make antibody against the toxin; 1 mark: memory cells are formed, giving a rapid secondary response if the toxin is encountered later.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is a disadvantage of a vaccine that contains live but attenuated (weakened) pathogens, compared with one containing only dead pathogens or their antigens?
A It cannot stimulate memory cells.
B The weakened pathogen may revert to a virulent form, which can cause disease in people with weak immune systems.
C It contains no antigens and so cannot stimulate lymphocytes.
D It must be given as a preformed antibody injection.
parts.answer: B The weakened pathogen may revert to a virulent form, which can cause disease in people with weak immune systems.
parts.working: B is correct: live attenuated vaccines carry a small risk of reversion to virulence, so they can be unsafe for immunocompromised people. A is wrong because live vaccines stimulate memory cells well; C is wrong because attenuated pathogens carry antigens; D is wrong because vaccines stimulate the body to make its own antibodies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A new influenza vaccine is produced every year. Explain why.
parts.answer: The influenza virus mutates frequently, changing its surface antigens (antigenic variation/drift); memory cells and antibodies from earlier vaccines are not complementary to the new antigens; so a new vaccine matching the current strains is needed
parts.working: 1 mark each: mutation/antigenic variation; new antigen shapes not recognised by existing memory cells/antibodies; vaccine updated to match strains expected that season.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some vaccines contain mRNA coding for a viral surface protein, enclosed in lipid droplets. Explain how such a vaccine leads to immunity.
parts.answer: Lipid droplets fuse with/enter body cells; the mRNA is translated by the cell's ribosomes to make the viral protein (antigen); this protein is displayed on the cell surface/released, triggering a primary immune response with production of antibodies and memory cells
parts.working: 1 mark each: mRNA enters cells; translated to produce viral antigen; antigen presented/displayed and activates lymphocytes, forming memory cells (and antibodies).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A boy in Multan is bitten by a dog that may have rabies. Doctors inject both rabies antibodies and rabies vaccine. Explain the reason for giving both.
parts.answer: The antibodies give immediate (artificial passive) protection by binding to/neutralising the virus straight away; but they are broken down within weeks and no memory cells form; the vaccine stimulates artificial active immunity, but antibodies take a week or more to appear; the vaccine gives long-term protection through memory cells
parts.working: 1 mark each: antibodies act immediately (passive); antibodies short-lived/no memory cells; vaccine stimulates own immune response (active) but slower; vaccine gives memory cells/long-term protection.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The rabies virus travels slowly along nerves from the bite to the brain, which can take weeks. Suggest why this makes vaccination after the bite effective.
parts.answer: There is time for the primary immune response to produce antibodies and T-cells before the virus reaches the brain; so the virus is destroyed before it causes disease
parts.working: 1 mark: long incubation period gives time for primary response/antibody production. 1 mark: virus neutralised before reaching the central nervous system.

practice.stem: Two groups of volunteers were given a hepatitis B vaccine. Group X received two doses, 28 days apart. Group Y received one dose only. Antibody concentration was measured 60 days after the first dose: group X – 800 arbitrary units; group Y – 150 arbitrary units.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of the antibody concentration in group X to that in group Y. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why group X had a much higher antibody concentration than group Y at day 60.
parts.answer: Group X received a second dose, which gives a secondary response. The memory cells made after the first dose were stimulated to divide rapidly and differentiate into many plasma cells, producing a larger antibody concentration. Group Y had only a primary response, which produces fewer memory cells and less antibody by day 60.
parts.working: 1 mark: group X had a second (booster) dose giving a secondary response; 1 mark: memory cells from the first dose divide quickly and differentiate into plasma cells; 1 mark: group Y had only a primary response, so fewer plasma cells and less antibody.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A subunit vaccine contains only a purified surface protein from a virus, and no whole virus particles. Explain why this vaccine cannot cause the disease, and why it may produce a weaker and shorter-lasting response than a live attenuated vaccine.
parts.answer: It contains no live or replicating virus, so it cannot infect cells or cause the disease. Only one protein is present, so fewer antigens stimulate fewer lymphocytes, and because the pathogen does not replicate there is no build-up of stimulus; the response is therefore weaker and produces fewer memory cells, so protection may be shorter-lasting.
parts.working: 1 mark: no live or replicating virus, so it cannot cause disease; 1 mark: fewer antigens so fewer lymphocytes are stimulated; 1 mark: no replication of the pathogen, so a weaker response and fewer memory cells (less long-lasting protection, boosters may be needed).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how monoclonal antibodies are produced using the hybridoma method.
parts.answer: Inject a mouse with the antigen; mouse makes B-lymphocytes/plasma cells specific to the antigen; remove B-cells from the spleen; fuse them with myeloma (cancer) cells to form hybridoma cells; select hybridomas making the required antibody; clone these cells and culture them; collect and purify antibody
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: antigen injected into mouse; B-lymphocytes/plasma cells taken from spleen; fused with myeloma cells; using polyethylene glycol/electric shock; hybridoma cells; screened for correct antibody; cloned/cultured (divide indefinitely); antibody harvested.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why are B-lymphocytes fused with myeloma cells when producing monoclonal antibodies?
A Myeloma cells can divide indefinitely.
B Myeloma cells make large quantities of antibody of their own.
C Myeloma cells provide the specificity of the antibody.
D Myeloma cells prevent the mouse rejecting the antibody.
parts.answer: A Myeloma cells can divide indefinitely.
parts.working: B-lymphocytes do not divide in culture; fusing them with cancerous myeloma cells gives hybridomas that both divide continuously and secrete the specific antibody. The specificity comes from the B-lymphocyte, not the myeloma cell (C).

practice.stem: A home pregnancy test strip detects the hormone hCG in urine. Near the bottom of the strip are mobile monoclonal antibodies against hCG, each attached to a coloured bead. Further up are a test line of immobilised antibodies against hCG and, above it, a control line of immobilised antibodies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a positive result appears at the test line.
parts.answer: hCG in the urine binds to the mobile antibodies, which carry coloured beads/dye; the hCG–antibody complex moves up the strip with the urine; at the test line, immobilised antibodies that are also specific to hCG bind the complex; coloured beads build up so a coloured line appears
parts.working: 1 mark each: hCG binds to mobile (labelled) antibody; complex moves up strip; immobilised antibody at test line binds hCG (at a different site); colour accumulates at test line.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a coloured line should always appear at the control line, whether or not the woman is pregnant.
parts.answer: Immobilised antibodies at the control line bind to the mobile antibody itself (not to hCG); so mobile antibodies with coloured beads always collect there, showing the urine has moved up the strip and the test has worked
parts.working: 1 mark: control antibodies bind the mobile antibodies (with or without hCG). 1 mark: shows test is working / liquid has flowed past test line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the term monoclonal antibody, and why such antibodies are highly specific.
parts.answer: Monoclonal antibodies are identical antibody molecules produced by a single clone of cells. All the molecules have identical antigen-binding sites, so each one binds to the same single epitope of one antigen.
parts.working: 1 mark: all identical antibodies from one clone of cells; 1 mark: identical binding sites so each binds one specific epitope only.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement explains why a monoclonal antibody gives fewer false-positive results than a polyclonal antibody in a diagnostic test?
A It binds to several different epitopes, so it detects more antigen molecules.
B All of its molecules are identical and bind one epitope, so it is less likely to react with unrelated molecules.
C It is collected from the serum of an immunised animal, so it contains only one antibody type.
D It is made from many B-lymphocyte clones, so it has more binding sites.
parts.answer: B All of its molecules are identical and bind one epitope, so it is less likely to react with unrelated molecules.
parts.working: B is correct: identical molecules with one binding site give fewer cross-reactions. A is wrong because binding several epitopes increases cross-reactions. C is wrong because serum contains many antibody types (polyclonal). D is wrong because having many clones gives variety, not specificity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Trastuzumab is a monoclonal antibody used to treat some breast cancers. It binds to a receptor protein (HER2) found in very large numbers on the surface of these cancer cells. Explain why trastuzumab binds to the cancer cells but rarely to other cells.
parts.answer: Its antigen-binding sites are complementary to HER2 only; normal cells have few HER2 receptors, so little binding occurs
parts.working: 1 mark: specific/complementary binding site to HER2. 1 mark: HER2 present in large numbers only on these cancer cells.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Monoclonal antibodies for treatment are usually 'humanised'. Explain why antibodies made entirely by mouse cells are not suitable for repeated treatment.
parts.answer: Mouse antibodies have mouse-specific (constant region) amino acid sequences that act as foreign antigens; the patient's immune system makes antibodies against them, destroying them / causing an allergic reaction, so later doses work less well
parts.working: 1 mark: mouse antibodies are non-self/antigenic. 1 mark: patient produces an immune response (antibodies) that removes them or causes side-effects.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why patients need repeated doses of trastuzumab over several months.
parts.answer: Antibodies are proteins that are broken down in the body over time; cancer cells continue to be present and divide, so the antibody concentration must be kept high
parts.working: 1 mark: antibodies broken down/removed (no memory cells, passive). 1 mark: need to keep binding to cancer cells as they continue to divide.

practice.stem:
A rapid test for dengue fever uses a monoclonal antibody against a dengue virus protein (NS1). In a hospital in Lahore it was tested on 400 patients. A laboratory method showed that 150 patients were infected and 250 were not.
Of the 150 infected patients, 138 tested positive.
Of the 250 uninfected patients, 10 tested positive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate (i) the percentage of infected patients correctly identified by the test (its sensitivity), (ii) the percentage of uninfected patients correctly identified as negative (its specificity).
parts.working: (i) 138 ÷ 150 × 100 = 92 % (2 marks; M1 correct division). (ii) uninfected testing negative = 250 − 10 = 240; 240 ÷ 250 × 100 = 96 % (1 mark).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why some uninfected patients tested positive.
parts.answer: The monoclonal antibody may bind to a similar antigen from another related virus (cross-reaction), e.g. a protein of shape similar to NS1; or contamination/misreading of a faint line
parts.working: 1 mark: antibody binds a different antigen of similar shape (cross-reactivity). 1 mark: e.g. related virus such as Zika / or a technical error.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about a sample of one type of monoclonal antibody is correct?
A All the molecules have identical antigen-binding sites.
B The molecules are made by many different clones of B-lymphocytes.
C The molecules bind to several different antigens.
D The molecules have different constant regions.
parts.answer: A All the molecules have identical antigen-binding sites.
parts.working: Monoclonal antibodies come from a single clone of hybridoma cells, so every molecule is identical and binds the same antigen. B describes polyclonal antibodies produced in a normal immune response.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare monoclonal antibodies with polyclonal antibodies (made by immunising an animal and collecting its serum). Give three differences, and state which type gives more consistent results in a diagnostic test.
parts.answer: Monoclonal antibodies come from one clone and have identical binding sites that bind one epitope; polyclonal antibodies are a mixture from many B-lymphocyte clones that bind several epitopes. Monoclonal antibodies give more consistent results between batches and fewer cross-reactions, so they are more consistent in a diagnostic test.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: monoclonal from a single clone, polyclonal from many clones; monoclonal bind one epitope, polyclonal bind several; monoclonal are identical and consistent between batches; polyclonal vary between animals and batches; polyclonal are more likely to cross-react; monoclonal give more consistent results (state monoclonal).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the monoclonal type is produced in cell culture rather than by immunising animals every time.
parts.answer: A hybridoma cell line can be grown in culture indefinitely, giving a continuous and reproducible supply of the same antibody. Immunising animals would produce a mixture of antibodies and would be less reliable.
parts.working: 1 mark: hybridoma cells divide indefinitely, giving a continuous supply; 1 mark: the same identical antibody every time, without variation between animals.

practice.stem: A dipstick test for a bacterium uses monoclonal antibodies. It was tested on 500 people with the following results: 90 people had the infection and tested positive; 10 people had the infection and tested negative; 380 people did not have the infection and tested negative; 20 people did not have the infection but tested positive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of positive results that were true positives (the positive predictive value). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: 1 mark: positive results = 90 + 20 = 110; 1 mark: 90 ÷ 110 × 100 = 81.8 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two problems that a high number of false positives could cause for an individual patient and for the health service.
parts.answer: Patients without infection may be given unnecessary treatment (for example antibiotics), with side effects and a risk of antibiotic resistance; false positives also cause anxiety and waste money and time on further tests and treatment.
parts.working: Any two, 1 mark each: unnecessary treatment or side effects; increased antibiotic use and resistance; anxiety for the patient; wasted resources or extra tests on uninfected people.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A monoclonal antibody that binds specifically to the CD20 protein on the surface of B-lymphocytes is given to a patient with a B-cell cancer. What is the most likely result?
A B-lymphocytes make more antibody against the cancer.
B B-lymphocytes are destroyed or marked for destruction, so fewer B-lymphocytes survive.
C T-helper cells are destroyed, so the patient cannot make antibody.
D Red blood cells are destroyed because they also carry CD20.
parts.answer: B B-lymphocytes are destroyed or marked for destruction, so fewer B-lymphocytes survive.
parts.working: B is correct: the antibody binds to CD20 on B-cells, which are then removed by the immune system (for example by complement or killer cells). A is wrong because the antibody does not stimulate antibody production; C is wrong because T-helper cells do not carry CD20; D is wrong because red blood cells do not carry CD20.

practice.stem: A sandwich ELISA test detects a virus antigen in blood serum. A monoclonal antibody against the antigen is fixed to the bottom of a plastic well. The serum is added, then the well is washed. A second monoclonal antibody, which binds to a different part of the antigen and is linked to an enzyme, is added; the well is washed again. Finally a colourless substrate is added that the enzyme converts to a coloured product.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the wells must be washed after the sample is added, and again after the second antibody is added.
parts.answer: Washing removes any unbound antigen/proteins, and then any unbound enzyme-linked antibody; otherwise unbound enzyme would cause a colour change even when no antigen is present (false positive)
parts.working: 1 mark: removes unbound molecules (sample proteins/second antibody). 1 mark: prevents colour change not caused by antigen / false positive.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the intensity of colour indicates the amount of antigen in the sample.
parts.answer: The second antibody can only stay in the well if it is bound to antigen held by the first antibody; more antigen means more enzyme bound, so more substrate is converted to coloured product
parts.working: 1 mark: second (enzyme-linked) antibody binds only where antigen is captured. 1 mark: more enzyme → more coloured product.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the two antibodies used must bind to different parts (epitopes) of the antigen.
parts.answer: If both bound the same site, the first (fixed) antibody would block it so the second antibody could not bind
parts.working: Second antibody must bind while the antigen is held by the first.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest a suitable control well for this test.
parts.answer: A well with a sample known to contain no antigen (e.g. buffer or serum from an uninfected person), treated in the same way
parts.working: Negative control with no antigen (or a positive control with known antigen).

practice.stem: After a single dose, the concentration of a humanised therapeutic antibody in a patient's blood was 160 µg cm⁻³. Its concentration halves every 21 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration remaining 63 days after the dose.
parts.answer: 20 µg cm⁻³
parts.working: M1: 63 ÷ 21 = 3 half-lives. A1: 160 × (½)³ = 20 µg cm⁻³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The same antibody made entirely by mouse cells had a much shorter half-life in patients after the first few doses. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Patient's immune system recognised the mouse antibody as foreign/non-self; antibodies against it were produced and the complexes were removed by phagocytes, so it disappeared faster
parts.working: 1 mark: mouse protein is antigenic / triggers immune response. 1 mark: anti-mouse antibodies bind and remove it (phagocytosis) more quickly.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Outline how scientists 'humanise' a mouse monoclonal antibody.
parts.answer: Genetic engineering: keep the mouse variable regions (antigen-binding sites) but replace the constant regions (and most other parts) with human antibody sequences
parts.working: 1 mark: variable/antigen-binding region from mouse retained. 1 mark: rest/constant region changed to human sequence (by altering the genes).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A monoclonal antibody that binds to a protein found only on the surface of a tumour cell is linked to a toxic drug. Describe how this antibody–drug conjugate could kill the cancer cells, and explain why it causes fewer side effects than the drug given on its own.
parts.answer: The antibody binds specifically to the tumour antigen on cancer cells, so the drug is delivered to the tumour. After binding, the complex is taken into the cell (endocytosis) and the toxic drug is released, killing the cancer cell. Because the antibody binds only to cells with the antigen, most healthy cells are not exposed to the drug, so side effects are reduced.
parts.working: 1 mark each: antibody binds specifically to the tumour antigen; drug is delivered to the tumour; complex is taken into the cell and the drug is released; drug kills the tumour cell; healthy cells lack the antigen so are not targeted and damage is reduced.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A monoclonal antibody is linked to a radioactive isotope and injected into a patient so that a tumour can be located by imaging. Explain why the label becomes concentrated in the tumour rather than in healthy tissue.
parts.answer: The antibody is specific to an antigen found on the tumour cells, so it binds there and the label accumulates in the tumour. Healthy cells lack the antigen, so little label binds to them and unbound antibody is cleared from the body.
parts.working: 1 mark: the antibody binds the tumour-specific antigen; 1 mark: little binds to healthy tissue (no antigen) and unbound antibody is cleared, so the label is concentrated in the tumour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the isotope used for imaging should emit gamma rays rather than alpha particles.
parts.answer: Gamma rays are penetrating, so they pass out of the body and can be detected by a detector outside the patient. Alpha particles are absorbed within a few cells of their source, so they would not reach a detector outside the body.
parts.working: 1 mark: gamma rays penetrate tissue and can be detected outside the body; 1 mark: alpha particles have a very short range and are absorbed by the tissue near the source.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a neutrophil destroys a bacterium by phagocytosis.
parts.answer: Neutrophil is attracted to the bacterium (by chemicals/chemotaxis); receptors on its membrane bind to the bacterium (or to antibodies on it); it engulfs the bacterium by endocytosis, forming a phagocytic vacuole; lysosomes fuse with the vacuole and hydrolytic enzymes digest the bacterium
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: chemotaxis/moves towards bacterium; attachment/recognition; engulfing by cell surface membrane/pseudopodia (endocytosis); phagocytic vacuole (phagosome); lysosomes fuse; hydrolytic enzymes digest/hydrolyse bacterium.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row correctly compares neutrophils and macrophages?
A neutrophils are short-lived and arrive first; macrophages are long-lived and act as antigen-presenting cells
B neutrophils are long-lived and present antigens; macrophages are short-lived and arrive first
C neutrophils secrete antibodies; macrophages engulf bacteria
D neutrophils have a round nucleus; macrophages have a lobed nucleus
parts.answer: A neutrophils are short-lived and arrive first; macrophages are long-lived and act as antigen-presenting cells
parts.working: Neutrophils are the first, short-lived phagocytes to reach an infection; macrophages live longer and present antigens to lymphocytes. Neither secretes antibodies (C), and it is the neutrophil that has a lobed nucleus (D).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the non-specific defences that prevent pathogens from entering the body or stop them once they reach the body surface.
parts.answer: Intact skin forms a physical barrier. Mucus traps microorganisms and cilia sweep the mucus away from the lungs. Stomach acid kills many pathogens, and lysozyme in tears and saliva hydrolyses the cell walls of some bacteria.
parts.working: Any three, 1 mark each: skin is a physical barrier; mucus traps pathogens; cilia move mucus away (up the airways); stomach acid (low pH) kills pathogens; lysozyme hydrolyses bacterial cell walls.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term antigen presentation, and name one type of phagocyte that carries it out.
parts.answer: After engulfing and digesting a pathogen, the phagocyte displays fragments of its antigens on its cell surface bound to MHC class II proteins. A macrophage (or dendritic cell) does this.
parts.working: 1 mark: antigen fragments displayed on the cell surface bound to MHC protein after digestion of the pathogen; 1 mark: macrophage (or dendritic cell).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement correctly describes the role of lysosomes in phagocytosis?
A They engulf the pathogen by pinching off the cell membrane.
B They fuse with the phagocytic vacuole and release hydrolytic enzymes that digest the pathogen.
C They produce antibodies that bind to the pathogen.
D They display the pathogen’s antigens on the cell surface.
parts.answer: B They fuse with the phagocytic vacuole and release hydrolytic enzymes that digest the pathogen.
parts.working: B is correct: lysosomes fuse with the phagocytic vacuole (phagosome) and release hydrolytic (digestive) enzymes. A describes the engulfment process rather than the lysosome role; C is wrong because phagocytes do not make antibody; D describes antigen presentation, not the function of lysosomes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two signs of inflammation at an infected cut.
parts.answer: Any two of: redness, swelling, heat, pain.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: redness (vasodilation); swelling (fluid leaks into tissue); heat (increased blood flow); pain (chemicals stimulate nerve endings).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where phagocytes are produced.
parts.answer: Bone marrow
parts.working: Bone marrow.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A blood smear is viewed with a light microscope. State one visible feature that identifies a cell as a neutrophil.
parts.answer: Lobed (multi-lobed) nucleus / granular cytoplasm
parts.working: Lobed nucleus (accept 3–5 lobes) or granules in cytoplasm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how macrophages help to activate the specific immune response.
parts.answer: Macrophages engulf and partly digest pathogens; they display the pathogen's antigens on their cell surface membrane (antigen presentation); T-helper cells with complementary receptors bind and are activated, then stimulate B-cells/T-killer cells
parts.working: 1 mark each: phagocytosis/digestion of pathogen; antigens displayed on the surface (antigen-presenting cell); activation of specific T-helper lymphocytes (which then activate B-cells).

practice.stem:
A patient with a bacterial skin infection had blood tests. Neutrophil counts (× 10⁹ per dm³):
0 h: 4.0 | 6 h: 9.5 | 24 h: 11.2 | 48 h: 10.1 | 96 h: 5.3

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in neutrophil count between 0 h and 6 h. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the number of neutrophils in the blood increases rapidly after infection.
parts.answer: Chemicals (cytokines) released from infected tissue/immune cells stimulate the bone marrow to release (and make) more neutrophils; more phagocytes are needed to engulf the bacteria
parts.working: 1 mark: chemical signals (cytokines/histamine) released at infection. 1 mark: bone marrow releases/produces more neutrophils.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the neutrophil count falls again after 48 h.
parts.answer: Bacteria have been destroyed so fewer signals; neutrophils are short-lived and die
parts.working: Infection controlled / neutrophils short-lived.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how inflammation helps phagocytes destroy bacteria at the site of an infection.
parts.answer: Damaged cells release histamine and cytokines, which cause vasodilation and increased blood flow to the area, bringing more phagocytes. The capillary walls become more permeable, so phagocytes (neutrophils) can leave the blood and move towards the bacteria by chemotaxis. The phagocytes then engulf and digest the bacteria.
parts.working: 1 mark: chemicals released from damaged cells cause vasodilation/increased blood flow; 1 mark: more phagocytes are brought to the site; 1 mark: capillaries become more permeable so phagocytes leave the blood and move towards the bacteria (chemotaxis); 1 mark: phagocytes engulf and digest the bacteria.

practice.stem: In a laboratory test, 240 neutrophils were mixed with a suspension of bacteria. After 10 minutes, 186 of the neutrophils had engulfed at least one bacterium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of neutrophils that had engulfed at least one bacterium. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why not every neutrophil had engulfed a bacterium after 10 minutes.
parts.answer: Some neutrophils had not yet come into contact with a bacterium, because bacteria are distributed unevenly in the suspension; some neutrophils may already have been busy engulfing bacteria, and the 10-minute time may have been too short for all cells to finish.
parts.working: Any two, 1 mark each: not all neutrophils contacted a bacterium (random distribution); some were still moving towards or attaching to bacteria; phagocytosis takes time, so 10 minutes was too short; some bacteria may resist engulfment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is engulfed by macrophages in the lungs but is not killed. It prevents lysosomes from fusing with the phagocytic vacuole. Explain how this allows the bacterium to survive.
parts.answer: Hydrolytic enzymes from lysosomes are not released into the vacuole; so the bacterium is not digested; it can remain/divide inside the macrophage
parts.working: 1 mark each: no lysosomal enzymes in vacuole; bacterium not hydrolysed/digested; survives and multiplies inside macrophage (protected).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why antibodies are not effective at destroying Mycobacterium tuberculosis once it is inside macrophages.
parts.answer: Antibodies are large proteins that stay outside cells/in blood and tissue fluid; they cannot cross the cell surface membrane to reach bacteria inside the vacuole
parts.working: 1 mark: antibodies cannot enter cells. 1 mark: bacteria hidden from antibodies inside the macrophage (needs T-cell response instead).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a macrophage activates a T-helper cell, and explain how this leads to the activation of a specific B-lymphocyte.
parts.answer: The macrophage engulfs the pathogen, digests it and displays the antigen fragments on its surface bound to MHC class II. A T-helper cell whose receptor is complementary to the antigen–MHC complex binds to it and is activated, dividing by mitosis. The activated T-helper cell releases cytokines (interleukins), which stimulate a B-lymphocyte with a complementary antibody receptor to divide and differentiate into plasma cells and memory cells.
parts.working: 1 mark each: macrophage engulfs and digests pathogen; antigen displayed on MHC class II; T-helper cell with complementary receptor binds and is activated/clones; T-helper releases cytokines; cytokines stimulate the matching B-lymphocyte to divide and differentiate into plasma and memory cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Patients receiving chemotherapy often have very low neutrophil counts (neutropenia). Explain why these patients are at risk from bacteria that are normally destroyed by phagocytosis.
parts.answer: There are fewer neutrophils to engulf bacteria, so less phagocytosis takes place and the bacteria are not removed. Bacteria can therefore multiply and spread. Inflammation is also less effective because fewer phagocytes are recruited to the site of infection.
parts.working: 1 mark: fewer neutrophils, so less phagocytosis; 1 mark: bacteria are not destroyed and can multiply; 1 mark: fewer phagocytes are recruited to the infection site (reduced inflammation); 1 mark: infection spreads more easily.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some bacteria have a polysaccharide capsule around the cell wall. Explain why bacteria with capsules are harder for phagocytes to engulf.
parts.answer: The capsule masks the surface molecules that the phagocyte recognises. It also prevents antibodies and complement proteins from binding to the bacterium, so opsonisation is reduced and the phagocyte does not attach to the bacterium effectively. Fewer bacteria are engulfed and digested.
parts.working: 1 mark: capsule masks the surface molecules that phagocytes recognise; 1 mark: antibodies or complement cannot bind to the surface (less opsonisation); 1 mark: attachment and engulfment are reduced, so fewer bacteria are digested.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the role of opsonins in phagocytosis.
parts.answer: Opsonins such as antibodies and complement proteins bind to antigens on the surface of the pathogen. Their other end binds to receptors on the phagocyte membrane, so the phagocyte attaches to the pathogen more readily and engulfs it more efficiently.
parts.working: 1 mark: opsonins bind to antigens on the pathogen surface; 1 mark: other part of the opsonin binds to receptors on the phagocyte; 1 mark: this increases attachment; 1 mark: more efficient engulfment and digestion of the pathogen.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
During which stage of mitosis do the centromeres divide and the sister chromatids move to opposite poles of the cell?
A prophase
B metaphase
C anaphase
D telophase
parts.answer: C anaphase
parts.working: In anaphase the centromeres split and spindle microtubules shorten, pulling the chromatids (now chromosomes) to opposite poles. B is wrong: at metaphase the chromosomes are lined up on the equator but the chromatids are still joined.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about mitosis is correct?
A Homologous chromosomes pair up during prophase.
B The daughter cells are genetically identical to the parent cell.
C The chromosome number is halved in each daughter cell.
D Crossing over between chromatids produces new combinations of alleles.
parts.answer: B The daughter cells are genetically identical to the parent cell.
parts.working: Mitosis produces two genetically identical nuclei with the same chromosome number as the parent. A, C and D all describe meiosis.

practice.stem: A farmer in Punjab cuts his hand on a sickle. Over the next ten days the skin heals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three roles of mitosis in multicellular organisms.
parts.answer: Any three of: growth; repair of damaged tissue; replacement of worn-out cells; asexual reproduction; clonal expansion of lymphocytes in an immune response.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: growth (increase in cell number); repair / wound healing; replacement of cells such as skin or gut lining or red blood cell precursors; asexual reproduction (e.g. potato tubers, Hydra budding); clonal expansion of B and T lymphocytes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is important that the daughter cells produced by mitosis are genetically identical to the parent cell when skin is repaired after a cut.
parts.answer: The new cells must have the same genes so they can produce the same proteins and function as skin cells; genetic stability keeps the tissue working and avoids harmful mutations.
parts.working: B1 same genetic information / same alleles as the parent cells; B1 so new cells can carry out the same function / make the same proteins as the cells they replace.

practice.stem: A student looks at a stained onion root tip squash under high power and describes three cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Identify the stage shown by each cell. Give one reason for each.
Cell P: chromosomes are short and thick and lie in a line across the middle of the cell; no nuclear envelope is visible.
Cell Q: two groups of V-shaped chromosomes are near opposite ends of the cell, with arms trailing behind.
Cell R: a nucleus with a clear nuclear envelope and a dark nucleolus; no individual chromosomes visible.
parts.answer: P metaphase (chromosomes on the equator); Q anaphase (chromatids being pulled to the poles, centromeres leading); R interphase (intact nucleus, chromatin not condensed).
parts.working: 1 mark per correct stage with reason: P metaphase – on equator/metaphase plate; Q anaphase – chromatids moving to opposite poles, V shape as centromere leads; R interphase – nuclear envelope and nucleolus visible / chromosomes not condensed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why most cells in the field of view look like cell R.
parts.answer: Interphase is the longest stage of the cell cycle.
parts.working: B1 cells spend most of the cell cycle in interphase.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A plant cell has a diploid number of 6 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are present in each daughter nucleus immediately after telophase of mitosis?
A 3
B 6
C 12
D 24
parts.answer: B 6
parts.working: Mitosis gives daughter nuclei with the same chromosome number as the parent cell, so each has 6. Sister chromatids separate in anaphase and each becomes a chromosome. A (3) is the haploid number; C (12) counts chromatids before anaphase.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Tomato cells have a diploid number of 24 chromosomes. How many chromatids are present in one tomato cell at metaphase of mitosis?
A 12
B 24
C 48
D 96
parts.working: DNA was replicated in S phase, so each of the 24 chromosomes consists of two sister chromatids: 24 × 2 = 48. B is the number of chromosomes, not chromatids.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A cell in G1 of interphase contains 16 arbitrary units of DNA. How much DNA is in the cell at the end of G2, and in each daughter cell immediately after cytokinesis?
A end of G2 16; each daughter cell 8
B end of G2 32; each daughter cell 16
C end of G2 32; each daughter cell 32
D end of G2 16; each daughter cell 16
parts.answer: B end of G2 32; each daughter cell 16
parts.working: DNA is replicated in S phase so G2 has 2 × 16 = 32 units; mitosis shares this equally, so each daughter has 16 units, the same as the parent in G1. A halves the DNA as if this were meiosis.

practice.stem:
A student made a squash of a stained garlic root tip and counted the cells in each stage of the cell cycle.
Interphase 412; prophase 46; metaphase 18; anaphase 9; telophase 15.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mitotic index of this root tip. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 cells in mitosis = 46 + 18 + 9 + 15 = 88; total = 500. A1 mitotic index = 88/500 = 0.176.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The cell cycle in this root tip lasts 24 hours. Assuming the number of cells seen in a stage is proportional to the time spent in that stage, calculate how long the cells spend in metaphase. Give your answer in minutes to the nearest minute.
parts.answer: 52 minutes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a root tip, rather than a region 2 cm behind the tip, was used to find the mitotic index.
parts.answer: The root tip contains a meristem where cells are actively dividing, so many cells are in mitosis.
parts.working: B1 meristem / zone of cell division at the tip; cells further back are elongating or differentiating and no longer divide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the behaviour of the chromosomes during prophase and metaphase of mitosis.
parts.answer: Prophase: chromosomes condense / shorten and thicken and become visible as two sister chromatids joined at a centromere; nuclear envelope breaks down. Metaphase: chromosomes attach to spindle microtubules at their centromeres/kinetochores and line up on the equator.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: chromosomes condense / coil / become visible (prophase); each seen as two chromatids joined at the centromere; nuclear envelope / nucleolus disappears so chromosomes lie in the cytoplasm; spindle fibres attach at centromere / kinetochore; chromosomes lined up on the equator / metaphase plate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what happens during telophase.
parts.answer: Chromosomes arrive at the poles and uncoil / decondense; a nuclear envelope reforms around each group, giving two nuclei; spindle breaks down.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: chromatids reach poles; chromosomes uncoil / become less visible; nuclear envelope and nucleolus reform; spindle disappears.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how cytokinesis differs in an animal cell and a plant cell.
parts.answer: Animal: cell membrane pinches in to form a cleavage furrow that divides the cytoplasm. Plant: vesicles from Golgi form a cell plate across the equator, which becomes the new cell wall.
parts.working: B1 animal: cleavage furrow / membrane constricts inwards; B1 plant: cell plate / new cell wall built from the centre outwards (from vesicles).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a plant cell cannot divide its cytoplasm in the same way as an animal cell.
parts.answer: The rigid cellulose cell wall prevents the cell surface membrane from pinching inwards.
parts.working: B1 rigid / cellulose cell wall cannot be constricted.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student observed a cell in a stained root tip squash with two nuclei and a thin line between them across the middle of the cell. State the stage the cell was in.
parts.answer: Late telophase / cytokinesis.
parts.working: B1 telophase / cytokinesis (cell plate forming).

practice.stem: During a typhoid infection in Karachi, a patient's immune response involves rapid division of lymphocytes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A single activated B-lymphocyte divides by mitosis every 8 hours. Calculate the number of identical cells produced from this one cell after 48 hours, assuming every cell divides each cycle.
parts.answer: 64 cells
parts.working: M1 number of cycles = 48/8 = 6; A1 2^6 = 64.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is important that these lymphocytes are produced by mitosis rather than meiosis.
parts.answer: Mitosis gives genetically identical cells, so all of the clone have the same genes for the same specific antibody / receptor that binds the antigen.
parts.working: B1 genetically identical / clones; B1 all make the same antibody / have the same receptor complementary to the pathogen's antigen (meiosis would give variation and half the chromosome number).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A cell has 8 chromosomes at the end of G1 of interphase. Which row correctly gives the number of chromosomes and the number of chromatids in this cell at prophase, after S phase is complete?
A 8 chromosomes, 8 chromatids
B 8 chromosomes, 16 chromatids
C 16 chromosomes, 16 chromatids
D 16 chromosomes, 32 chromatids
parts.answer: B 8 chromosomes, 16 chromatids
parts.working: S phase replicates each chromosome, so each now has two sister chromatids joined at a centromere, but the chromosome number stays at 8. 8 × 2 = 16 chromatids. C wrongly counts each chromatid as a separate chromosome.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Colchicine prevents tubulin molecules joining together to form microtubules. Explain why cells treated with colchicine do not complete mitosis.
parts.answer: No spindle forms, so chromosomes cannot attach to spindle fibres, cannot line up at the equator, and chromatids cannot be pulled apart to the poles in anaphase.
parts.working: B1 spindle (fibres) made of microtubules cannot form; B1 chromosomes not attached at centromeres / cannot line up at equator; B1 sister chromatids not separated / pulled to opposite poles (so mitosis halts at metaphase).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Onion root tips were placed in colchicine for 4 hours and then squashed. Suggest and explain how the mitotic index and the percentage of dividing cells in metaphase would differ from untreated root tips.
parts.answer: Mitotic index higher and a higher proportion of dividing cells in metaphase, because cells keep entering mitosis but become stuck at metaphase and cannot leave it.
parts.working: B1 higher proportion of dividing cells in metaphase (and mitotic index increases); B1 cells continue to enter mitosis but cannot progress beyond metaphase so accumulate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Some cancer drugs act in a similar way to colchicine. Suggest why patients receiving these drugs often lose hair.
parts.answer: Hair follicle cells divide rapidly, so their mitosis is also blocked.
parts.working: B1 hair follicle cells divide frequently by mitosis and are affected as well as cancer cells.

practice.stem:
Mammalian cells growing in culture were synchronised so that they all began the cell cycle at the same time. The mean mass of DNA per cell (arbitrary units) was measured.
time 0 h: 10
time 4 h: 10
time 8 h: 10
time 10 h: 13
time 12 h: 17
time 14 h: 20
time 16 h: 20
time 18 h: 20
time 18.5 h: 10
time 22 h: 10

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the time interval during which S phase occurs. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: 8 to 14 hours; DNA mass doubles from 10 to 20 a.u. as DNA is replicated.
parts.working: B1 8–14 h; B1 DNA content rises / doubles, showing DNA replication.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the change in DNA mass between 18 and 18.5 hours.
parts.answer: The DNA mass halves because the cell divides (telophase / cytokinesis): each daughter cell receives one copy of each chromosome, i.e. half the replicated DNA.
parts.working: B1 DNA halves from 20 to 10; B1 sister chromatids separated into two nuclei / cytokinesis produces two cells, each with the original DNA content.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using the data, calculate the length of G1 for these cells, assuming the next cycle begins at 18.5 hours and is the same as the first. State one other assumption you have made.
parts.answer: 8 hours; assumes all cells are synchronised / DNA starts to rise immediately at the end of G1.
parts.working: B1 G1 = time from start of cycle to start of DNA replication = 8 − 0 = 8 h; B1 assumption: cells synchronised / readings frequent enough to show exact start of S phase.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paclitaxel binds to microtubules and stops them from shortening. Explain why this prevents a cell from completing anaphase.
parts.answer: Chromatids are separated by shortening of spindle microtubules attached at their centromeres; if microtubules cannot shorten, chromatids are not pulled to opposite poles.
parts.working: B1 spindle fibres attached to centromeres / kinetochores must shorten (depolymerise); B1 so chromatids cannot be pulled apart to the poles.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a trial, the mitotic index in a breast tumour fell from 0.21 to 0.06 after treatment, while in the lining of the small intestine it fell from 0.15 to 0.11. Calculate the percentage decrease in mitotic index in the tumour. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the drug also reduced the mitotic index in the small intestine and explain one consequence for the patient.
parts.answer: Intestinal lining cells divide rapidly (stem cells constantly replace epithelium), so they are also affected; the gut lining is not replaced, causing poor absorption / diarrhoea / sores.
parts.working: B1 intestinal epithelium divides frequently / rapidly; B1 consequence: lining not renewed → damage, diarrhoea, poor absorption of nutrients, infection risk.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement correctly describes telomeres?
A They are regions of a chromosome where the spindle fibres attach.
B They are repeated, non-coding base sequences at the ends of chromosomes.
C They are genes that code for proteins controlling the cell cycle.
D They are protein molecules around which DNA is wound.
parts.answer: B They are repeated, non-coding base sequences at the ends of chromosomes.
parts.working: Telomeres are many repeats of a short non-coding sequence at chromosome ends. A describes the centromere/kinetochore; D describes histones.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of a chromosome as it appears at the start of mitosis.
parts.answer: Two identical sister chromatids joined at a centromere; each chromatid is one long DNA molecule wound around histone proteins (chromatin), tightly coiled / condensed; telomeres at the ends.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: two (sister) chromatids; joined at centromere; each chromatid contains one DNA molecule (double helix); DNA associated with / wound round histones; condensed / supercoiled; telomeres at ends.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the role of histone proteins in the nucleus.
parts.answer: They package / coil the DNA so the long molecules fit into the nucleus (and help control access to genes).
parts.working: B1 DNA wound around histones for packaging / condensing (accept: regulating gene expression).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which enzyme adds repeats of the telomere sequence to the ends of chromosomes in germ cells and in many cancer cells?
A DNA polymerase
B DNA ligase
C DNA helicase
D telomerase
parts.answer: D telomerase
parts.working: Telomerase carries its own RNA template and extends the 3′ end of the chromosome. DNA polymerase needs an existing template to copy; ligase joins DNA fragments; helicase unwinds the double helix.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the region of a chromosome to which spindle microtubules attach during mitosis.
parts.answer: The centromere
parts.working: 1 mark: centromere.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe where this region lies on the chromosome compared with a telomere.
parts.answer: The centromere is a fixed point between the two arms (between the sister chromatids), not at the end; telomeres are at the tips of the chromatids.
parts.working: 1 mark: centromere is internal / at a fixed point between the arms, whereas telomeres are at the ends.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the proteins around which the DNA of a eukaryotic chromosome is wound.
parts.answer: Histones
parts.working: 1 mark: histone proteins (forming nucleosomes).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one function of this packaging.
parts.answer: It compacts the long DNA molecule so that it fits inside the nucleus (also protects DNA or helps control gene expression).
parts.working: 1 mark for any one of: compaction into the nucleus; protection of DNA; regulation of gene expression.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the ends of a DNA molecule become shorter each time the DNA is replicated, and why this does not normally cause the loss of genes.
parts.answer: DNA polymerase cannot replicate the very end of the lagging strand, so a short length of DNA is lost each replication; the lost DNA comes from the telomere, which is non-coding, so genes are protected.
parts.working: B1 the extreme end of the (lagging) strand is not copied; B1 so the chromosome loses a short length each division; B1 the lost section is telomere / non-coding repeats, so no genes are lost (telomeres act as a buffer).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Stem cells in bone marrow continue to divide throughout life. Suggest how their telomeres are kept long.
parts.answer: They have active telomerase, an enzyme that adds repeats back onto the telomeres.
parts.working: B1 telomerase adds (telomere) repeats / extends telomeres.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement explains why telomeres are shorter in most human somatic cells than in germ cells?
A Germ cells do not have telomeres, so their DNA does not shorten.
B Somatic cells make more telomerase than germ cells do.
C Germ cells make telomerase, which restores telomere length, while most somatic cells make little or none.
D Telomeres in somatic cells contain genes, so they are lost by mutation.
parts.answer: C Germ cells make telomerase, which restores telomere length, while most somatic cells make little or none.
parts.working: Telomerase is active in germ cells and restores the repeats lost during replication, but most somatic cells have little telomerase, so telomeres shorten with each division. A is wrong because germ cells do have telomeres; B reverses the true pattern; D is wrong because telomeres are non-coding.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how telomeres help to protect the genes near the ends of chromosomes during DNA replication.
parts.answer: Telomeres are non-coding repeats, so the lost end sequence does not remove genes; the telomere cap stops the chromosome end being recognised as broken DNA; this prevents end-to-end fusion and degradation of coding DNA.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: telomeres are non-coding so their loss removes no genes; the repeats are lost instead of coding DNA; the protein cap stops the end being recognised as DNA damage; prevents chromosomes fusing with each other; prevents degradation of the coding DNA near the end.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A germ-line cell line has telomeres of 11 500 base pairs at the start. Each division removes 72 base pairs from the telomere, but telomerase adds 120 base pairs per division. Calculate the telomere length after 20 divisions. Show your working.
parts.answer: 12 460 base pairs
parts.working: M1 net change per division = +120 − 72 = +48 base pairs; A1 11 500 + 20 × 48 = 12 460 base pairs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why most adult somatic cells cannot keep their telomeres at a constant length.
parts.answer: Most somatic cells have little or no telomerase, so the lost telomere repeats are not replaced and the telomeres shorten with each division.
parts.working: 1 mark for any one: telomerase is largely switched off in somatic cells; lost repeats are not replaced; so telomeres shorten each division.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A human cell has a diploid number of 46 chromosomes in G1 of interphase. Calculate the number of chromatids in this cell at metaphase of mitosis, after S phase is complete.
parts.answer: 92 chromatids
parts.working: 1 mark: each of the 46 chromosomes has been replicated in S phase to give two sister chromatids, so 46 × 2 = 92 chromatids.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the structure of one chromosome at metaphase, naming the two parts that are joined at the centromere.
parts.answer: Two sister chromatids, each containing one copy of the DNA (identical copies made by replication in S phase), joined at a centromere.
parts.working: 1 mark: two sister chromatids. 1 mark: they are identical copies of DNA made during S phase, joined at the centromere.

practice.stem:
The mean telomere length in white blood cells was measured in healthy volunteers in Lahore.
age 20 years: 9.8 kb
age 35 years: 9.2 kb
age 50 years: 8.5 kb
age 65 years: 7.9 kb
age 80 years: 7.4 kb
(1 kb = 1000 base pairs)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of telomere shortening between ages 20 and 80, in base pairs per year. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: 40 bp per year
parts.working: M1 (9.8 − 7.4) kb / (80 − 20) years = 0.04 kb per year; A1 × 1000 = 40 bp per year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why telomere shortening may limit the number of times a body cell can divide.
parts.answer: When telomeres become very short, further replication would remove coding DNA / genes, so the cell stops dividing (or dies) to avoid losing genes.
parts.working: B1 telomeres eventually too short to protect chromosome ends; B1 genes would be lost / chromosomes unstable, so cell stops dividing (senescence) or undergoes apoptosis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Cancer cells can divide an unlimited number of times. Suggest one feature of telomeres in cancer cells that explains this.
parts.answer: Telomerase is active, so telomeres are maintained at a constant length.
parts.working: B1 telomerase active / telomere length maintained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The telomere on one chromosome end is 10000 base pairs long and consists of repeats of the sequence TTAGGG. Calculate how many repeats are lost before the telomere reaches a critical length of 4000 base pairs.
parts.answer: 1000 repeats

parts.label: b
parts.text: The telomere loses 60 base pairs at each division. Calculate the number of divisions possible before the critical length is reached.
parts.answer: 100 divisions

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a short repeated sequence is better at protecting chromosome ends than a gene would be.
parts.answer: The repeats do not code for anything, so losing some of them has no effect on protein synthesis; the many repeats provide a long buffer that can be shortened many times.
parts.working: B1 non-coding, so loss does not change any polypeptide; B1 many repeats so a long length can be lost over many divisions before genes are reached.

practice.stem: Telomere lengths were measured in a stem cell line grown in culture (hypothetical data). Mean telomere length: division 0: 9.80 kb; division 10: 9.31 kb; division 20: 8.85 kb; division 30: 8.42 kb; division 40: 7.98 kb. (1 kb = 1000 base pairs.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean loss of telomere length per cell division between division 0 and division 40, in base pairs. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 45.5 bp per division

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the loss per division is not exactly constant.
parts.answer: Any two of: telomerase is active in some cells, so loss varies; each figure is a mean over many cells and chromosomes, so random variation occurs; differences in DNA damage or repair between cells; differences in how often cells divide.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of the points listed.

practice.stem: A drug that blocks the activity of telomerase is tested on a human cancer cell line. Telomeres in these cancer cells are initially long.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the drug's effect on the rate of cell division is delayed, rather than immediate, in a cancer cell line whose telomeres are initially long.
parts.answer: Telomerase normally adds repeats to replace those lost each division; blocking it means the telomeres shorten by the usual amount every division. Because the telomeres start long, many divisions are needed before they reach a critical length. Only then do the cells stop dividing or die, so the drug slows growth only after many generations.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: telomerase normally replaces lost repeats; blocking it stops replacement so telomeres shorten each division; telomeres start long, so many divisions are needed; critically short telomeres trigger senescence or apoptosis; the effect on growth is therefore delayed.

practice.stem: Mean telomere lengths in three tissues of one adult (hypothetical data): intestinal epithelium 5.2 kb; liver 6.4 kb; skeletal muscle 7.0 kb. Cells of the intestinal epithelium are replaced every few days from stem cells; skeletal muscle fibres rarely divide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the pattern shown by the data.
parts.answer: Telomeres are shortest in the tissue where cells divide most often (intestine) and longest in the tissue with the least cell division (muscle).
parts.working: 1 mark: inverse relation between telomere length and rate of cell division.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the pattern using your knowledge of telomeres.
parts.answer: Stem cells in the intestine divide frequently, so telomeres lose length at each division; telomerase activity is low in these cells, so the repeats are not replaced; once critically short, cells stop dividing. Muscle fibres divide rarely, so telomeres lose little length.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: frequent division means repeated loss per division; little telomerase means lost repeats are not replaced; critically short telomeres stop division; muscle fibres divide rarely so little telomere loss.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement describes a stem cell?
A a cell that can no longer divide and has a specialised function
B a cell that can divide by mitosis to give cells that can differentiate into specialised cells
C a cell that divides only by meiosis to produce gametes
D a cell that has lost its nucleus to make room for haemoglobin
parts.answer: B a cell that can divide by mitosis to give cells that can differentiate into specialised cells
parts.working: Stem cells self-renew by mitosis and their daughter cells can differentiate. A describes a fully differentiated cell; D a red blood cell.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where stem cells that produce blood cells are found in an adult.
parts.answer: Bone marrow (red marrow).
parts.working: B1 bone marrow.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Children with thalassaemia major in Pakistan may be treated with a bone marrow transplant from a matched sibling. Explain how the donor stem cells can cure the condition.
parts.answer: Donor stem cells settle in the bone marrow, divide by mitosis to self-renew, and differentiate into red blood cells containing normal haemoglobin, so regular blood transfusions are no longer needed.
parts.working: B1 donor stem cells divide by mitosis / self-renew; B1 differentiate into (red) blood cells; B1 these have normal genes / make normal haemoglobin (for life, so transfusions no longer needed).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term totipotent. Name one natural example of a totipotent cell in a mammal.
parts.answer: Totipotent: able to differentiate into any type of cell, including those needed to form a whole organism (in mammals this includes placental cells). Example: the zygote (fertilised egg) or the cells of an early embryo up to the 8-cell stage.
parts.working: 1 mark: any cell type possible including extra-embryonic/whole organism. 1 mark: a valid example (zygote, or early embryo cells up to about 8 cells).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the region of a plant where stem cells are found, and state what these stem cells can produce.
parts.answer: Meristem (e.g. the apical meristem at the root or shoot tip); they produce cells that differentiate into the tissues of the plant, such as xylem, phloem and epidermis.
parts.working: 1 mark: meristem. 1 mark: they differentiate into all the tissues of the plant (e.g. xylem, phloem, epidermis).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the stem cells in the basal layer of the epidermis must keep dividing throughout life.
parts.answer: They replace cells lost from the skin surface through wear and abrasion; they continuously produce new keratinocytes to maintain the epidermis.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: replacement of cells lost from the surface; continuous production of new cells; maintenance of the tissue.

practice.stem: Lung cancer is one of the most common cancers in men in Pakistan, and most cases are linked to smoking cigarettes, bidis or shisha.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a mutation in a gene that controls cell division can lead to the formation of a tumour.
parts.answer: The mutated gene produces a faulty protein (or no protein), so mitosis is no longer controlled; the cell divides repeatedly and uncontrollably; its daughter cells inherit the mutation, forming a mass of cells (tumour).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: mutation changes the protein that regulates the cell cycle; cell divides by mitosis without control / continuously; daughter cells have the same mutation (clone); mass of abnormal cells = tumour; cells do not respond to signals to stop dividing / undergo apoptosis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Tobacco smoke contains carcinogens. State what is meant by a carcinogen.
parts.answer: A substance or agent that causes cancer (by increasing the rate of mutation of DNA).
parts.working: B1 agent / substance that causes cancer / mutations leading to cancer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by cell differentiation.
parts.answer: The process by which an unspecialised cell becomes specialised for a particular function, by switching on (expressing) some genes and not others.
parts.working: B1 cell becomes specialised (changes structure for a function); B1 only certain genes expressed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why stem cells taken from an early embryo can produce more types of cell than stem cells taken from adult bone marrow.
parts.answer: Embryonic stem cells have not yet started to differentiate, so they can express any genes and form any cell type; adult marrow stem cells are already partly committed and can form only blood cell types.
parts.working: B1 embryonic cells can form (almost) all cell types / are totipotent or pluripotent; B1 adult stem cells only form a limited range (multipotent), e.g. blood cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how asymmetric cell division allows one daughter cell to remain a stem cell while the other differentiates.
parts.answer: One daughter receives factors or positions that keep it as a stem cell, while the other receives different components and starts to differentiate; so one stem cell is retained and the other becomes a specialised cell.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: unequal distribution of cell components or signalling molecules; one daughter stays in a stem-cell niche/keeps stem-cell signals; the other begins to differentiate; the stem-cell population is maintained.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The gene TP53 codes for the p53 protein. Mutated forms of this gene are found in many cancers, and cells lacking functional p53 may keep dividing after their DNA is damaged. What type of gene is TP53?
A oncogene
B tumour suppressor gene
C telomerase gene
D homeobox gene
parts.answer: B tumour suppressor gene
parts.working: Tumour suppressor genes normally stop division when something goes wrong; losing their function removes this control. An oncogene is an overactive gene that promotes division; telomerase is an enzyme; homeobox genes control development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how cells from a malignant tumour can spread to other parts of the body to form secondary tumours.
parts.answer: Tumour cells lose adhesion to their neighbours; they invade the surrounding tissue through the basement membrane; they enter blood or lymph vessels; they lodge in another tissue and divide to form a secondary tumour.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: loss of cell adhesion; invasion through the basement membrane; entry into blood or lymph vessels; transport and lodging in another tissue; division to form a secondary tumour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A study in Lahore followed 900 adults for 10 years. 60 of 400 smokers and 12 of 500 non-smokers developed lung cancer. Calculate the percentage of smokers, and the percentage of non-smokers, who developed lung cancer. Give each answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Smokers 15.0%; non-smokers 2.4%
parts.working: M1 60 ÷ 400 × 100 = 15.0%, and 12 ÷ 500 × 100 = 2.4%; A1 both values correct to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why these data alone cannot show that smoking causes lung cancer.
parts.answer: Other factors, such as diet, air pollution or occupation, may differ between the two groups, so they could explain some of the difference; this was an observational study, not a controlled experiment.
parts.working: 1 mark for any one: confounding factors (other variables differ between the groups); observational study rather than a controlled experiment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two differences between the behaviour of the cells in a malignant tumour and the cells of normal tissue.
parts.answer: Malignant cells divide uncontrollably/more often and do not stop dividing on contact or by apoptosis; they can spread (metastasise) into other tissues; they do not differentiate normally.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: divide more often / without control; do not undergo apoptosis; not specialised / undifferentiated; invade other tissues / spread through blood or lymph; telomerase active / unlimited divisions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why exposure to radiation, such as UV light in a sunny region, increases the risk of skin cancer.
parts.answer: UV damages DNA in skin cells, causing mutations; if the mutation affects genes controlling the cell cycle, cells divide uncontrollably.
parts.working: B1 UV is a mutagen / damages DNA (base sequence changed); B1 in genes controlling cell division, causing uncontrolled mitosis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why cancer is not an infectious disease.
parts.answer: It is not caused by a pathogen and cannot be passed from person to person.
parts.working: B1 not caused by a pathogen / not transmissible.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a series of mutations can lead to a malignant tumour.
parts.answer: Mutations in proto-oncogenes produce overactive oncogenes that drive division; mutations in tumour suppressor genes (e.g. p53) remove brakes on division; each mutation can give a growth advantage so the cells form a clone; further mutations accumulate over time, e.g. loss of contact inhibition or avoidance of apoptosis; the cells then invade tissue and may metastasise.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five: oncogene activation by mutation of a proto-oncogene; loss of tumour suppressor function; selective growth advantage forming a clone; accumulation of further mutations over time; loss of contact inhibition or apoptosis control; invasion or metastasis.

parts.label: a
