parts.text: Bone marrow transplants are used to treat some blood cancers. Explain why transplanted cells can restore blood cell production in the patient.
parts.answer: Bone marrow contains haematopoietic stem cells, which divide by mitosis and differentiate into red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. Transplanted stem cells lodge in the patient's bone marrow and renew blood cell production.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: bone marrow contains haematopoietic stem cells; they divide by mitosis; they differentiate into the different blood cell types; transplanted cells move to and establish in the marrow; they renew production.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A population of cancer cells in culture doubles every 36 hours. The culture starts with 2.0 × 10⁵ cells. Calculate the smallest whole number of doublings needed for the population to reach at least 1.0 × 10⁹ cells.
parts.answer: 13 doublings
parts.working: M1 after 12 doublings: 2.0 × 10⁵ × 2¹² = 8.2 × 10⁸ (too few); A1 after 13 doublings: 2.0 × 10⁵ × 2¹³ = 1.6 × 10⁹, so 13.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time, in days, taken to reach this number of cells.
parts.answer: 19.5 days

practice.stem: A student makes a drawing of an onion cell. In the drawing the cell is 45 mm across. The actual diameter of the cell, found with a graticule and stage micrometer, is 15 µm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the drawing. Show your working.
parts.working: M1 image size 45 mm = 45 000 µm; A1 magnification = image size ÷ actual size = 45 000 ÷ 15 = 3000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert the actual diameter of 15 µm into nanometres.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert 0.0064 mm into micrometres (µm).
parts.answer: 6.4 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert 0.0064 mm into nanometres (nm).

parts.label: a
parts.text: At ×100 magnification the field of view has a diameter of 1.8 mm. Calculate the magnification needed to give a field of view of diameter 0.36 mm, using the same eyepiece.
parts.working: M1 field of view is inversely proportional to magnification, so magnification = 1.8 × 100 ÷ 0.36; A1 ×500.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why a specimen is harder to find when the magnification is increased.
parts.answer: At higher magnification the field of view shows a smaller area of the specimen, so the feature being looked for is less likely to be in view.
parts.working: 1 mark: a smaller area of the specimen is seen, so the object is harder to locate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A photomicrograph of a root hair cell includes a scale bar labelled 50 µm. The scale bar measures 4.0 cm on the printed page, and the cell measures 6.4 cm. Calculate the actual length of the cell in µm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why an eyepiece graticule must be calibrated separately for each objective lens.
parts.answer: Each objective gives a different magnification, so one graticule division represents a different actual length; the calibration (µm per unit) changes with the objective.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: the magnification changes with the objective; the length represented by one graticule unit changes; so a new calibration (using a stage micrometer) is needed.

practice.stem: A student calibrated an eyepiece graticule using a stage micrometer in which each division is 0.01 mm. Using the ×40 objective, 40 eyepiece units lined up exactly with 25 stage micrometer divisions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the length of one eyepiece graticule unit, in µm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A cell in metaphase measured 4 eyepiece units from one end to the other. Calculate its actual length in µm.
parts.answer: 25 µm

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the eyepiece graticule must be calibrated again if the student changes to a higher-power objective lens.
parts.answer: The graticule scale stays the same size but the specimen is magnified more, so each eyepiece unit represents a smaller actual length.
parts.working: B1 each eyepiece unit corresponds to a different (smaller) distance on the specimen at a different magnification.

parts.label: a
parts.text: At ×100 magnification, 25 eyepiece graticule units coincide with 6 stage micrometer divisions. Each stage division is 0.01 mm. Calculate the length of one eyepiece unit, in µm.
parts.answer: 2.4 µm
parts.working: M1 6 × 0.01 mm = 0.06 mm = 60 µm; A1 60 ÷ 25 = 2.4 µm per eyepiece unit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A root cell measures 17 eyepiece units at the same magnification. Calculate its length in µm.
parts.working: M1 use the calibration from (a); A1 17 × 2.4 = 40.8 µm.

practice.stem: A student measured the diameter of five nuclei in one onion root tip, using an eyepiece graticule calibrated at this magnification. The diameters in eyepiece units were: 12, 15, 11, 14, 13.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean diameter of the five nuclei in eyepiece units.
parts.answer: 13.0 units

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the calibration 1 eyepiece unit = 1.8 µm, calculate the mean diameter of the nuclei in µm. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

practice.stem: A mitotic cell is drawn from a microscope image. The drawing is 62 mm across. The actual diameter of the cell is 25 µm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the drawing. Give your answer as ×n.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way to make the measurement of the image more accurate.
parts.answer: Measure the cell several times and calculate a mean, or use a ruler marked to 0.5 mm.
parts.working: 1 mark for any one: repeat the measurement and average; use a finer ruler; measure a larger structure to reduce relative error.

practice.stem: A student uses a light microscope to estimate the density of cells in a squashed tissue sample. The field of view is a circle of diameter 0.50 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The circular field of view has a diameter of 0.50 mm. Calculate its area in mm². Give your answer to 3 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark: area = πr² = π × 0.25² = 0.196 mm².

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student counts 14 cells in this field of view. Calculate the number of cells per mm². Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 71.3 cells per mm²
parts.working: M1 14 ÷ 0.19635 mm²; A1 = 71.3 cells per mm².

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the approximate resolution of a light microscope.
parts.answer: About 0.2 µm (200 nm)
parts.working: 1 mark: about 200 nm (0.2 µm).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student says that a 0.1 µm structure will be seen clearly with a light microscope if the magnification is made high enough. Evaluate this claim.
parts.answer: The claim is not valid: 0.1 µm is below the resolution limit, so two points this close blur together; increasing magnification only enlarges the blur, and an electron microscope would be needed.
parts.working: 1 mark: resolution limit is about 0.2 µm, so 0.1 µm cannot be resolved; 1 mark: higher magnification does not improve resolution, so an electron microscope is needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A chromosome measures 6.6 cm long in an electron micrograph printed at a magnification of ×15 000. Calculate the actual length of the chromosome in µm.
parts.answer: 4.4 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the actual length in nanometres.

parts.label: a
parts.text: With the ×40 objective, one eyepiece unit is 12.5 µm. Calculate the length of one eyepiece unit with the ×400 objective, keeping the same eyepiece.
parts.working: M1 magnification is ten times greater, so each unit represents one tenth of the length; A1 12.5 ÷ 10 = 1.25 µm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A cell spans 36 eyepiece units at ×400. Calculate its length in µm.
parts.answer: 45 µm

parts.label: a
parts.text: The length of a root cell is 35 eyepiece units. The reading is uncertain by ±1 unit. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in this length. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way the uncertainty in the length could be reduced.
parts.answer: Measure a longer structure, or measure several cells and calculate a mean.
parts.working: 1 mark: a larger measured value reduces the percentage uncertainty; repeat readings and average.

practice.stem: A photomicrograph of a nucleus includes a scale bar labelled 5 µm. On the printed page the scale bar measures 25 mm and the nucleus measures 33 mm across.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual diameter of the nucleus in µm. Show your working.
parts.answer: 6.6 µm
parts.working: M1 the scale bar 25 mm = 5 µm, so 1 mm = 0.2 µm; A1 33 mm × 0.2 = 6.6 µm (33 ÷ 25 × 5 = 6.6).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the photomicrograph.

practice.stem:
Sections of a mung bean root were cut at different distances behind the tip, and the mitotic index of each section was found.
1 mm: 0.18
2 mm: 0.12
3 mm: 0.05
4 mm: 0.01
5 mm: 0.00

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship shown by the data.
parts.answer: As distance from the tip increases, mitotic index decreases; it falls from 0.18 at 1 mm to 0 at 5 mm, falling most steeply between 2 and 3 mm.
parts.working: B1 negative trend / mitotic index decreases with distance; B1 data quote with units, e.g. 0.18 at 1 mm to 0.00 at 5 mm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student concluded that no cell division takes place more than 4 mm from the root tip. Evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: Partly supported: mitotic index is 0 at 5 mm, but 0.01 at 4 mm and only one root/one sample was used and only a limited number of cells counted, so some dividing cells may be missed beyond 4 mm.
parts.working: B1 supported because MI is 0.00 at 5 mm / 0.01 at 4 mm; B1 limitation: only one root / small sample / no readings between 4 and 5 mm / no repeats, so cannot be sure.

practice.stem: Onion root tips were treated with a colchicine solution. The mitotic index (percentage of cells in mitosis) was measured at intervals: 0 h 4.1%; 2 h 6.3%; 4 h 9.8%; 6 h 12.6%; 8 h 12.9%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the pattern shown by the data.
parts.answer: The mitotic index rises from 4.1% at 0 h to about 12.9% at 8 h; the increase is rapid up to about 6 h and then levels off.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: an increase over time from 4.1% to about 13%; the rate of increase slows and levels off (plateau) after about 6 h.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a conclusion that the data support.
parts.answer: The longer the root tips are exposed to colchicine (up to about 6–8 h), the greater the proportion of cells in mitosis; the increase then levels off.
parts.working: 1 mark: a conclusion that matches the data (more cells in mitosis with longer exposure, levelling off after about 6–8 h). A claim that colchicine causes metaphase arrest needs further evidence and is not supported by these data alone.

practice.stem: A student counted 500 cells in a garlic root tip squash and classified each cell by stage: interphase 441; prophase 32; metaphase 9; anaphase 9; telophase 9.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of cells in interphase. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why these data support the statement that interphase is the longest stage of the cell cycle.
parts.answer: Most cells (88.2%) were in interphase; since a random sample shows cells in proportion to the time spent in each stage, interphase must take up most of the cell cycle.
parts.working: 1 mark: most cells are in interphase. 1 mark: the proportion of cells in a stage reflects the time spent in it, so interphase takes the most time.

practice.stem: Root tips of broad bean seedlings were exposed to different doses of gamma radiation and the mitotic index was measured. Dose (Gy) and mitotic index (%): 0 Gy 5.2; 1 Gy 3.9; 2 Gy 2.4; 4 Gy 1.1; 6 Gy 0.6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between radiation dose and mitotic index.
parts.answer: As the dose increases, the mitotic index decreases; the fall is steepest at low doses (0–2 Gy), and the index falls to about 0.6% at 6 Gy.
parts.working: 1 mark: an inverse (negative) relationship; 1 mark: quote figures, e.g. falls from 5.2% to 0.6% over 0–6 Gy, with a steep fall at low doses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the mitotic index falls as the dose increases.
parts.answer: Radiation damages DNA; checkpoints stop cells from entering or completing mitosis, so fewer cells are in mitosis.
parts.working: 1 mark: DNA damage causes cell-cycle arrest at checkpoints, so fewer cells enter mitosis.

practice.stem: A student took three root tips from one onion bulb. She made one slide from each root and calculated the mitotic index: 5.8%, 6.1% and 5.5%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a conclusion that the data support.
parts.answer: The mitotic index of this onion sample is about 5.8%.
parts.working: 1 mark: mean of 5.8, 6.1 and 5.5 = 5.8%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one limitation of these data for drawing a general conclusion about onions.
parts.answer: Only one bulb and one slide per root were used, so the results may not represent onions in general.
parts.working: 1 mark for any one: only one bulb (small sample of plants); only one slide per root; only three cells sampled per root.

practice.stem: The percentage of cells in mitosis was counted in four tissues of an adult mouse: bone marrow 6.5%; intestinal crypts 4.0%; liver 0.3%; adult brain 0.1%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which tissue has the highest proportion of cells in mitosis.
parts.answer: Bone marrow
parts.working: 1 mark: bone marrow (6.5%).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between the bone marrow and the brain in terms of cell turnover.
parts.answer: Bone marrow continually produces new blood cells, so many cells divide; adult brain cells rarely divide, so almost no cells are in mitosis.
parts.working: 1 mark: bone marrow has continuous cell replacement / high rate of division; 1 mark: brain cells are largely non-dividing so very few are in mitosis.

practice.stem: The mitotic index of onion root tips was measured for seedlings of different ages (days after germination): day 1 3.2%; day 2 5.8%; day 3 7.4%; day 4 6.1%; day 5 4.9%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the pattern shown by the data.
parts.answer: The mitotic index rises to a peak on day 3 (7.4%), then falls to 4.9% by day 5.
parts.working: 1 mark: rises to a maximum at day 3; 1 mark: falls after day 3 (or quote the values).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the pattern using your knowledge of root growth.
parts.answer: Rapid cell division in the root meristem increases during the first days of growth, peaking as the root grows fastest; later, cells in the root differentiate and elongate and fewer cells divide.
parts.working: 1 mark: meristem cells divide fastest when root growth is greatest; 1 mark: after the peak, cells differentiate and elongate rather than dividing.

practice.stem: A fluorescent stain that binds DNA was used to measure the DNA content of 1000 cultured cells. Cells with the G1 DNA content (2C) numbered 620; cells in S phase (between 2C and 4C) numbered 210; cells with 4C DNA content numbered 170.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of cells in the G2/M population. Give your answer as a whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why cells with twice the DNA content of the G1 population are found in the G2/M population.
parts.answer: These cells have replicated their DNA during S phase, so they have 4C DNA; they are in G2 or undergoing mitosis, and have not yet divided into two daughter cells.
parts.working: 1 mark: DNA is replicated in S phase, giving twice the DNA. 1 mark: they are in G2 or M and have not yet completed cell division.

practice.stem: A student tested a drug on onion root tips. She made one slide at each of two concentrations: 0 mM (control) with a mitotic index of 4.8%, and 0.1 mM with a mitotic index of 6.2%. She concluded that the drug increases the mitotic index.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one reason why one slide per concentration does not allow a firm conclusion.
parts.answer: One slide gives no information about variation between slides, so random error cannot be judged.
parts.working: 1 mark: no measure of variability/repeatability; a single count may be unrepresentative.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the experiment should be improved.
parts.answer: Use at least three slides (or roots) per concentration and calculate a mean and standard deviation.
parts.working: 1 mark: repeat each concentration on several slides or roots and report mean with spread.

practice.stem: Three slides were made at each time point. Mitotic index (%): 0 h: 4.0, 4.3, 3.9; 2 h: 6.8, 6.2, 9.9; 4 h: 9.1, 9.5, 8.8.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous value and justify your choice.
parts.answer: 9.9% at 2 h is anomalous: the other two values at 2 h (6.8% and 6.2%) are much lower and the value does not fit the trend that follows.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies 9.9% at 2 h. 1 mark: compares with the other replicates at that time, which are about 6–7%, and/or the trend.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the anomalous value should be treated.
parts.answer: Recount the slide and check the technique; if no error is found, report the value and state whether the mean changes with and without it.
parts.working: 1 mark: check the slide/recount and report transparently rather than discarding without a reason.

practice.stem: A population of cells was synchronised so that all cells began the cycle together. The mitotic index peaked at 9 h and again at 27 h after synchronisation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the duration of the cell cycle from these data, in hours.
parts.working: 1 mark: 27 − 9 = 18 h between successive peaks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the mitotic index rises and falls in a population of synchronised cells.
parts.answer: All the cells began the cycle together, so they reach mitosis at about the same time, giving a peak; as the cells move into interphase the proportion in mitosis falls, and a second peak occurs one cycle later.
parts.working: 1 mark: the cells pass through mitosis together, causing a peak; 1 mark: the index falls as cells pass into interphase, and a new peak appears after one full cycle.

practice.stem: Mitotic index (mean ± SD, n = 5 slides for each group): control 4.8 ± 0.6%; treated with a drug 6.3 ± 0.9%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why the means and standard deviations alone do not show whether the difference is significant.
parts.answer: Significance depends on the sample size and the spread; the overlap between values must be tested with a statistical test.
parts.working: 1 mark: a statistical test (e.g. t-test) is needed to judge significance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name a suitable test for comparing these two independent means.
parts.answer: Student's t-test (independent samples).
parts.working: 1 mark: t-test for two independent samples with normally distributed data.

practice.stem: Two cell lines were started with 1000 cells each in culture. Normal cells have a doubling time of 36 hours and cancer cells have a doubling time of 18 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of cells in each culture after 72 hours. Give each answer to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: Normal cells: 4000 cells; cancer cells: 16 000 cells.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times more cancer cells there are than normal cells after 72 hours.
parts.answer: 4 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one assumption made in predicting these numbers.
parts.answer: No cell death and no contact inhibition or nutrient limitation, so the population grows exponentially at the given doubling time.
parts.working: 1 mark for any one assumption: no cell death; constant doubling time; unlimited nutrients or space.

practice.stem: Root tips were treated with colchicine. The mitotic index rose from 4.2% at 0 h to 11.8% at 6 h. The total number of cells counted in each sample stayed about the same over the same period.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student claims that colchicine increases the rate of mitosis. Evaluate this claim using the data.
parts.answer: The claim is not supported: colchicine stops cells at metaphase, so cells accumulate in mitosis and the mitotic index rises, but this does not show that cells divide faster. The total number of cells did not increase, so no more cells completed division. A rate would need cell number over time or a measure of cell-cycle duration.
parts.working: 1 mark: the index rises because cells are arrested in metaphase (not faster division). 1 mark: total cell number did not increase, so no extra divisions. 1 mark: the data show a proportion, not a rate. 1 mark: a valid test would count cells completing division over time or measure cycle duration.

practice.stem: The mitotic index of onion root tips was measured on three slides in each group. Control (no extract): 5.1%, 4.6%, 5.4%. Treated with 0.5% plant extract: 6.2%, 5.0%, 6.8%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain whether these data support the conclusion that the extract increases the mitotic index.
parts.answer: The mean is higher in the extract group (6.0% against 5.0%), but the ranges overlap (5.0% lies within the control range), so the difference is not clearly significant with only three replicates.
parts.working: 1 mark: means differ (6.0 vs 5.0%). 1 mark: values overlap, so a t-test is needed and the evidence is weak.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one improvement to the experiment that would give a more reliable conclusion.
parts.answer: Use more replicate slides or roots per treatment, and test for significance; include a range of concentrations.
parts.working: 1 mark: more replicates; 1 mark: statistical test (t-test) or a dose range.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a random error and a systematic error. Give one example of each when measuring the length of a root with a millimetre ruler.
parts.answer: A random error varies unpredictably between readings, so it can be reduced by repeating and averaging; a systematic error shifts all readings in the same direction, so repeating does not remove it. Example of random: uncertainty in lining up the root end each time. Example of systematic: a ruler whose zero mark is worn/ not at the end of the scale.
parts.working: 1 mark: random error varies unpredictably. 1 mark: systematic error shifts all readings the same way. 1 mark: a valid example of each (e.g. reading errors vs a zero error on the ruler).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student counted cells from one slide only. Explain why this reduces the reliability of the mitotic index, and suggest one improvement.
parts.answer: One slide may not be representative of the root tip, so the result may vary a lot if another slide were used; counting several slides from different roots and calculating a mean improves reliability.
parts.working: 1 mark: one slide is not representative / gives high variability. 1 mark: count several slides or roots and calculate a mean.

practice.stem: A student made a squash of an onion root tip and placed a coverslip over it. Air bubbles were trapped under the coverslip in several places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the effect of air bubbles trapped under the coverslip on the counts.
parts.answer: Bubbles hide or distort cells, so some dividing cells are missed or misidentified and the count is inaccurate.
parts.working: 1 mark: cells are obscured or miscounted.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the student could avoid trapping air bubbles.
parts.answer: Lower the coverslip gently at an angle, or add a drop of stain/water so the coverslip spreads evenly.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower the coverslip at an angle, or apply gentle pressure to spread the liquid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student counted cells that overlapped each other in the squash. Explain why this is an error and suggest how it could be avoided.
parts.answer: Overlapping cells may be counted twice or missed, so the counts are inaccurate; counting in a fixed pattern across a single layer of cells, or using a thinner squash, avoids this.
parts.working: 1 mark: overlapping cells are counted twice or missed (inaccurate count). 1 mark: thin squash / systematic counting of non-overlapping cells in a single layer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student started a stopwatch by hand each time the root tips were placed into the hydrochloric acid, so the start time varied by about ±2 s. State whether this error is random or systematic.
parts.answer: Random error.
parts.working: 1 mark: it varies unpredictably between timings.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how this error could be reduced.
parts.answer: Use a timer with a fixed start signal, or time all samples together and repeat.
parts.working: 1 mark: a standard timing procedure, or repeating the timed step and comparing results.

practice.stem: A student wanted to find the mitotic index of onion root tips. She cut 1 cm from the end of one root, heated it in hydrochloric acid, stained it, placed it on a slide under a coverslip and pressed gently. She counted the dividing and non-dividing cells in one field of view at ×100 magnification.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two sources of error in this procedure and suggest an improvement for each.
parts.answer: e.g. (1) cells overlapping because the squash was too thick → press harder / thinner squash so cells form a single layer; (2) only one field of view counted → count several fields of view / at least 200 cells from several root tips; (3) difficult to decide the stage of some cells (e.g. early prophase vs interphase) → use agreed criteria / higher magnification; (4) different root tips from different bulbs / different ages → use roots of the same length taken at the same time.
parts.working: For each of two errors: B1 error stated in terms of this method; B1 matching improvement. Credit: overlapping cells / thick squash; small sample of cells / one field of view; subjective identification of stages; cells counted twice when moving the slide; roots of different lengths.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The student counted cells only near one edge of the slide. Identify the type of error this causes and suggest an improvement.
parts.answer: This gives a biased (unrepresentative) sample, a systematic error; the student should count cells from several randomly chosen fields of view across the whole squash.
parts.working: 1 mark: sampling bias/systematic error because the sample is not representative. 1 mark: count randomly chosen fields across the whole slide.

practice.stem: A student prepared a squash from a root tip by hydrolysing it in hydrochloric acid for 20 minutes instead of the recommended 5 minutes, then staining it and squashing it under a coverslip. The mitotic index of this root was low.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two sources of error in the preparation of the root tips, other than counting.
parts.answer: Leaving the root in hydrochloric acid for too long damages the cells and makes chromosomes hard to see; the squash may be made too thick, so cells overlap and are hard to count.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: over-hydrolysis in HCl damages cells; cells not spread; squash too thick; root tip cut too long so cells are mixed with other tissue; stain too strong or too weak.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two students counted the same slide and recorded different numbers of cells in prophase. Identify the type of error this shows and suggest a way to reduce it. Give one reason why it occurs.
parts.answer: This is observer (subjective) error: the two observers apply different judgements about which cells are in prophase. It may be random between counts or systematic if one observer is consistently different. It can be reduced by agreeing clear criteria for each stage, training the observers, and counting blind or by one observer.
parts.working: 1 mark: observer (subjective) error or variation between observers. 1 mark: reason, e.g. differing criteria for identifying prophase. 1 mark: agreed criteria, training, or blind counting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how parallax error can occur when reading the eyepiece graticule against the stage micrometer.
parts.answer: The eye is not directly above the scale, so the apparent position of the marks shifts and the reading is wrong.
parts.working: 1 mark: the scale is viewed from an angle, so the apparent position shifts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how parallax error can be reduced.
parts.answer: Keep the eye directly above the scale and align the marks so they are seen in the same line.
parts.working: 1 mark: view along the line of sight directly over the scale.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The student did not control the temperature of the root tips between the replicate samples. Explain the effect this has on the reliability of the results, and suggest an improvement.
parts.answer: Cell division rate depends on temperature, so the mitotic index varies between replicates for reasons not related to the treatment; this lowers reliability (and may be systematic if one group is warmer). Improvement: keep all samples at the same temperature (e.g. in a water bath or incubator) and record the temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark: temperature affects mitotic rate. 1 mark: different temperatures add variation/bias between replicates. 1 mark: control and record temperature (water bath or incubator).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two samples of onion root tips were counted: one with 100 cells, one with 1000 cells. Both gave a mitotic index of 5%. Explain why the count of 1000 cells gives a more reliable estimate of the mitotic index.
parts.answer: Counting more cells reduces the effect of chance variation: a few extra or missing dividing cells change the percentage much less in a larger sample; with 100 cells, one cell changes the index by 1 percentage point, but with 1000 cells it changes it by only 0.1 points, so the estimate is more precise.
parts.working: 1 mark: larger sample reduces the effect of random variation. 1 mark: with 100 cells one cell changes the value by a large proportion (1%) versus 0.1% with 1000. 1 mark: the larger sample gives a more precise and reliable estimate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term validity, as applied to an experiment.
parts.answer: The extent to which the experiment measures what it claims to measure, with no relevant confounding variables.
parts.working: 1 mark: measures what it is intended to measure; free from confounding variables.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student concludes that her results are valid because they match a textbook value of 5%. Evaluate this reasoning.
parts.answer: Agreement with a textbook value does not prove validity: the value may have been measured under different conditions, and the student's method could still be biased or affected by confounding variables; agreement could be coincidence.
parts.working: 1 mark: agreement with a reference value does not establish validity; 1 mark: the method may still have systematic errors or confounding variables.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way to test the validity of the method.
parts.answer: Compare the results with those from a different, independent method, or test a sample of known mitotic index.
parts.working: 1 mark: an independent method or known standard.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student finds that all her eyepiece graticule measurements are 10% too large. Explain what type of error this is and why repeating the measurements does not remove it.
parts.answer: It is a systematic error caused by a wrong calibration, so every measurement is shifted in the same direction; repeating the measurement gives the same systematic error each time.
parts.working: 1 mark: systematic error from incorrect calibration. 1 mark: each repeat repeats the same wrong calibration so the error is not averaged out.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student could detect and correct the calibration error.
parts.answer: Recalibrate the graticule against the stage micrometer at the same magnification, and check that the result matches a second calibration.
parts.working: 1 mark: recalibrate with a stage micrometer and check agreement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two experiments on the same root tip material gave mitotic indices of 5.2% on Monday and 7.9% on Thursday. Identify four variables that could have changed between the two days and explain how each could affect the result.
parts.answer: Any four, each with an effect: the temperature of the room or water bath (affects rate of division); the age or batch of the onion bulbs (different growth rates); the time of day or light exposure (affects cell cycle timing); the concentration or age of the HCl or stain (affects staining or hydrolysis); the observer (different judgement of stages).
parts.working: 1 mark for each of four valid variables, with its effect on mitotic index (e.g. temperature, age or batch of bulbs, time of day/light, concentration/age of reagents, observer, timing of hydrolysis).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to prepare a squash slide of an onion root tip for counting mitotic cells.
parts.answer: Cut the root tip (about 1–2 mm), hydrolyse it in warm 1 M hydrochloric acid for about 5 minutes, rinse it, stain it (e.g. acetic orcein or toluidine blue), place it on a slide, cover it with a coverslip and press gently to spread the cells in a single layer.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: cutting the tip and hydrolysing it in HCl; staining; squashing under a coverslip into a single layer with gentle pressure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to calibrate an eyepiece graticule against a stage micrometer for one objective lens.
parts.answer: Place the stage micrometer on the stage and align the scales so that the two scales coincide; count how many stage divisions (each 0.01 mm) match a known number of eyepiece units; calculate the length of one eyepiece unit as (stage divisions × 0.01 mm × 1000) ÷ number of units, in µm; repeat and calculate a mean.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: aligning the two scales at the same objective; counting the coinciding divisions over a large number of units; calculating the length of one unit and repeating.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to calculate the mitotic index of a root tip from a squash slide.
parts.answer: Count the total number of cells and the number of cells in mitosis (prophase to telophase) in several randomly chosen fields of view; count at least 500 cells in total; calculate the mitotic index as (number of cells in mitosis ÷ total number of cells) × 100; repeat for several root tips and calculate the mean.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: counting cells in mitosis and total cells in several fields; calculating the mitotic index correctly; repeating for several roots and averaging.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to choose fields of view on a slide so that they are random.
parts.answer: Divide the slide into a grid, or use random numbers or a random number generator to choose coordinates; move the stage to each chosen position, avoiding the edges and the overlapping areas of the squash; record each field before counting, and count each cell only once.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: a method for choosing random positions (grid or random numbers); avoiding edges or overlapping cells; recording each field and counting each cell once.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to prepare 100 cm³ each of 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 mol/dm³ sodium chloride solutions, starting from a 1.0 mol/dm³ stock solution and distilled water.
parts.answer: Use a measuring cylinder or pipette: 20 cm³ of stock diluted to 100 cm³ with distilled water gives 0.2 mol/dm³; 40 cm³ of stock to 100 cm³ gives 0.4; 60 cm³ gives 0.6; 80 cm³ gives 0.8. Mix each thoroughly and label it.
parts.working: 1 mark for the volumes of stock (20, 40, 60, 80 cm³); 1 mark for making up to 100 cm³ with distilled water; 1 mark for mixing, using a measuring cylinder and labelling.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to investigate the effect of gamma radiation exposure time on the mitotic index of onion root tips. Your method should be detailed enough for another person to follow.
parts.answer: Independent variable: exposure time (e.g. 0, 10, 20 and 30 min) to a source at a fixed distance; dependent variable: mitotic index. Control: roots kept at 0 min; keep the dose rate, distance, temperature and root length constant. Grow at least three roots per time, fix/hydrolyse, stain and squash identically; count at least 500 cells per root from random fields, calculate the mitotic index, repeat and calculate means. Radiation safety must be followed and the source used under supervision.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five: independent and dependent variables named; a range of exposure times with a 0-min control; controlled variables (distance, dose rate, temperature, root size); replicate roots; standard hydrolysis, staining and squashing; counting method with random fields and sufficient cells; mean and repeat; radiation safety.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to investigate the effect of ethanol concentration on the mitotic index of onion root tips.
parts.answer: Prepare a range of ethanol concentrations (e.g. 0%, 2%, 5%, 10%) by dilution with water; place the root tips in each for the same time at the same temperature; use water as a control; wash, hydrolyse, stain and squash identically; count cells in random fields from at least three roots per concentration; calculate mitotic indices and repeat.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five: concentration series with a control; independent and dependent variables; same time and temperature for all treatments; identical slide preparation; counting method with random fields, enough cells and replicate roots.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to investigate the effect of sodium chloride (salt) solution concentration on the mitotic index of onion root tips grown in the solution.
parts.answer: Grow onion bulbs or roots in a series of salt concentrations (e.g. 0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2 mol/dm³) with water as control; keep light, temperature and time constant; use at least three roots per concentration; prepare slides identically; count at least 500 cells per root from random fields; calculate mean mitotic index and repeat.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five: independent variable and series of concentrations; control with water; controlled variables (time, light, temperature); replicate roots; slide preparation and counting method with random fields.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to investigate how the age of seedlings affects the mitotic index of their root tips, using onion or broad bean seedlings from day 1 to day 5 after germination.
parts.answer: Germinate seeds at the same time under the same conditions (temperature, light, water); sample roots from several seedlings on each day (day 1 to day 5); cut root tips the same length; prepare slides identically; count cells from random fields; calculate mitotic indices and means for each day; repeat the whole experiment.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five: seeds germinated together under the same conditions; independent variable is age in days; several seedlings sampled each day; standard preparation and length of root tip; counting method with random fields and enough cells; repetition.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to investigate the effect of ultraviolet (UV) exposure time on the mitotic index of Allium root tips.
parts.answer: Expose root tips to UV at a fixed distance and intensity for different times (e.g. 0, 5, 10, 15 min) with a dark control; keep temperature constant; grow at least three roots per time; hydrolyse, stain and squash identically; count at least 500 cells per root from random fields; calculate and average the mitotic indices; wear eye protection.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five: a range of exposure times with a control; fixed distance and intensity; replicate roots; identical slide preparation; counting method with random fields and sufficient cells; safety measures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method the student could use to investigate the effect of temperature on the mitotic index of garlic root tips. Your method should be detailed enough for another person to follow.
parts.answer: Grow garlic cloves with roots in water at 5 different temperatures (e.g. 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 °C) in incubators/water baths for the same time; cut 5 mm tips at the same time of day; hydrolyse in 1 mol dm⁻³ HCl at 60 °C for a fixed time; stain (e.g. acetic orcein / toluidine blue); squash; count cells in mitosis and total cells (at least 200 per tip, several fields); MI = dividing ÷ total; at least 3 roots per temperature; calculate mean MI.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: IV with at least 5 temperatures and stated range; method of keeping temperature constant (incubator / thermostatic water bath); time roots grown at each temperature standardised; same variety / size of clove; tips cut to same length at same time of day; hydrolysis with HCl, fixed concentration, temperature and time; stain named; squash to a single layer; count number in mitosis and total (≥ 200 cells, random fields); calculate mitotic index; replicates ≥ 3 roots per temperature and mean.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to investigate the effect of colchicine concentration on the proportion of cells in metaphase in onion root tips. Include how you would control variables, how you would take replicates and how you would analyse the results.
parts.answer: Prepare colchicine solutions at several concentrations (e.g. 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1 mg/cm³) and a water control; place root tips in each for the same time at the same temperature; identical hydrolysis, staining and squashing; count at least 500 cells from random fields of at least three roots per concentration; calculate the percentage of mitotic cells in metaphase; calculate means and standard deviations; plot a graph and compare treatments with a statistical test.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: concentration series with a control; controlled variables (time, temperature, root length); replicate roots; standard slide preparation; counting of cells in metaphase with random fields and enough cells; mean, SD and statistical test or graph to compare treatments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to compare the mitotic index of root tips from two garlic varieties grown under the same conditions. Explain how you would select samples to avoid bias.
parts.answer: Grow both varieties in the same conditions (soil, light, temperature, water, time) in identical containers, with randomly assigned positions; take root tips from several randomly chosen bulbs or plants of each variety; cut tips of the same length; prepare and count slides identically, blind to variety if possible; use random fields and at least 500 cells per root; calculate means and SD for each variety and use a t-test to compare them.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: same growing conditions; random allocation/positions; several bulbs per variety; standard tip length and slide preparation; blind or randomised counting with random fields; means, SD and a t-test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to investigate whether the length of storage of onion bulbs before planting affects the mitotic index of their root tips.
parts.answer: Store bulbs for different times (e.g. 1, 2, 4, 8 weeks) under the same conditions of temperature and humidity; plant bulbs at the same time after storage and grow them under identical conditions; sample root tips of the same length from several bulbs per storage time; prepare and count slides identically with random fields; calculate the mean mitotic index for each storage time and repeat; use a control of bulbs planted immediately.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: range of storage times with control; controlled storage conditions; same growth conditions after storage; several bulbs per treatment; identical sampling and slide preparation; random-field counting and means with repeats.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to investigate the effect of gibberellin concentration on the mitotic index of bean root tips. Include a control, the range of concentrations, and how you would count the cells.
parts.answer: Prepare a dilution series of gibberellin solution (e.g. 0, 10, 50, 100 mg/dm³) and grow seedlings in each for the same time at constant temperature and light; a water control; take root tips of the same length from at least three seedlings per concentration; hydrolyse, stain and squash identically; count at least 500 cells per root from randomly chosen fields; calculate the mitotic index for each root and the mean for each concentration; repeat the experiment.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: concentration series with water control; controlled variables (time, temperature, light); replicate seedlings; identical root tip length and slide preparation; random-field counting with enough cells; calculation of means and repetition.

practice.stem: A student investigated the effect of the concentration of caffeine solution on the mitotic index of onion root tips.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation.
parts.answer: Independent: concentration of caffeine. Dependent: mitotic index (number of cells in mitosis ÷ total cells counted).
parts.working: B1 IV caffeine concentration; B1 DV mitotic index.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three variables that should be standardised, and explain why one of them must be kept constant.
parts.answer: e.g. temperature; time in solution; length of root tip cut; type/age of onion; hydrolysis time and acid concentration; stain and time in stain. Explanation e.g. temperature affects enzyme activity and the rate of mitosis, so would change mitotic index.
parts.working: B1 × 2 for any three valid standardised variables (two correct = 1 mark, three = 2 marks); B1 valid explanation for one.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a suitable control for this investigation.
parts.answer: Roots grown in distilled water with no caffeine, treated in the same way.
parts.working: B1 0 % caffeine / distilled water, all other conditions the same.

practice.stem: A student placed onion root tips in a colchicine solution and measured the mitotic index of the root tips after 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation.
parts.answer: Independent variable: time spent in the colchicine solution (hours). Dependent variable: mitotic index (percentage of cells in mitosis).
parts.working: 1 mark: independent variable is time in colchicine (named with units). 1 mark: dependent variable is mitotic index (percentage of cells in mitosis).

practice.stem: The same investigation as above: onion root tips placed in colchicine solution for different times, with the mitotic index measured at each time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two variables that should be kept constant in this investigation, and explain why one of them must be kept constant.
parts.answer: Any two of: temperature; concentration of the colchicine solution; length of the root tips; staining and squashing time; light. Keeping the temperature constant matters because the rate of cell division changes with temperature, so a temperature change would alter the mitotic index.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two named constant variables; 1 mark for explaining why one (e.g. temperature) affects the rate of division.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a control in an experiment.
parts.answer: A treatment or condition in which the independent variable is not changed, used for comparison with the other treatments.
parts.working: 1 mark: a standard for comparison with no change in the independent variable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a control using distilled water is needed in an experiment on the effect of a drug on the mitotic index.
parts.answer: It shows the mitotic index without the drug, so any change in the other treatments can be attributed to the drug rather than to the procedure.
parts.working: 1 mark: provides a baseline to show the effect is due to the drug, not to handling or the solvent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why all root tips should be cut to the same length before they are treated.
parts.answer: The root tip contains a zone of dividing cells that varies in size and position; cutting to the same length keeps the amount of meristem tissue constant, so that differences in mitotic index are due to the treatment.
parts.working: 1 mark: standardises the amount of meristem tissue/dividing cells; 1 mark: so differences are due to the treatment, not to the material.

practice.stem: Bean seedlings were grown under lamps at different light intensities and the mitotic index of their root tips was measured after 10 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable in this investigation and name one variable that must be controlled.
parts.answer: Independent variable: light intensity. Controlled variable: temperature (or time in the light, or the species/age of the seedlings).
parts.working: 1 mark: light intensity named as the independent variable. 1 mark: a valid controlled variable (temperature, time, species/age of seedlings) with a reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent and dependent variables, and describe how you would control two other variables in an investigation of the effect of gamma radiation dose on the mitotic index.
parts.answer: Independent variable: dose of radiation (Gy); dependent variable: mitotic index (%); controlled variable e.g. distance from the source, which is kept the same by a fixed jig; controlled variable e.g. time of fixation/ root length, which is kept the same by cutting roots to the same length and fixing them at the same time after irradiation.
parts.working: 1 mark: independent variable (dose). 1 mark: dependent variable (mitotic index). 1 mark: a named controlled variable with method (e.g. fixed distance from source). 1 mark: a second controlled variable with method (e.g. same root length or same time after exposure).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the investigation should include a positive control (colchicine) and a negative control (water).
parts.answer: The negative control (water) shows the normal mitotic index, so the effect of the test solution can be compared with it; the positive control (colchicine) is a substance known to affect the mitotic index, so it shows that the method can detect a change in the mitotic index.
parts.working: 1 mark: negative control gives the baseline for comparison. 1 mark: positive control confirms the method can detect an effect. 1 mark: both help to show the results are reliable or valid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student changed the temperature between the replicate samples. Explain why this is a problem, and describe how the temperature should be controlled.
parts.answer: Temperature affects the rate of mitosis, so differences in mitotic index may be due to temperature rather than the treatment; this makes the results unreliable. The temperature should be kept constant using a water bath or incubator, with the temperature checked by a thermometer during the experiment.
parts.working: 1 mark: temperature changes the rate of cell division. 1 mark: so the results cannot be attributed to the treatment. 1 mark: control by a water bath or incubator with thermometer checks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable, the dependent variable and two variables that must be kept constant in an investigation of the effect of ethanol concentration on the mitotic index of root tips.
parts.answer: Independent: ethanol concentration (%); dependent: mitotic index (%); constant: time in ethanol solution, temperature of the solution, length of the root tips, and the hydrolysis and staining times.
parts.working: 1 mark: independent variable. 1 mark: dependent variable. 1 mark and 1 mark: two valid constant variables (time, temperature, root length, staining time).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the same stain must be applied for the same time to all slides in this investigation.
parts.answer: Staining time affects how strongly the chromosomes stain, which can change how easily cells in mitosis are identified; if the time differs, the proportion of cells counted as dividing may differ for reasons unrelated to the treatment.
parts.working: 1 mark: staining affects visibility of chromosomes. 1 mark: different staining times cause different counts. 1 mark: this would be a confounding variable that makes comparison unreliable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two cultivars of garlic are compared, but they were grown in different greenhouses. Identify the confounding variable and explain how the investigation should be designed to avoid it.
parts.answer: The confounding variable is the greenhouse (its temperature, light and humidity), because any difference in mitotic index could be due to the greenhouse rather than the cultivar; to avoid this, grow both cultivars in the same greenhouse, arranged randomly, so that conditions affect both equally.
parts.working: 1 mark: names the greenhouse (environment) as a confounding variable. 1 mark: explains that it changes both the independent variable and the outcome. 1 mark: grow both in the same environment. 1 mark: random arrangement of plants across the space.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student kept the root tips at room temperature, which varied between 18 °C and 26 °C during the day. Explain how this could affect the results, and describe how the student could improve the design.
parts.answer: Mitotic rate increases with temperature, so the mitotic index could vary with the time of day rather than the treatment; this is an uncontrolled variable. The student should use a water bath or incubator at a fixed temperature, record the temperature for each sample, and run all treatments at the same time.
parts.working: 1 mark: temperature affects mitotic rate. 1 mark: variation means it is an uncontrolled (confounding) variable. 1 mark: water bath or incubator at fixed temperature. 1 mark: record temperature and run all treatments at the same time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some onion bulbs in a study cannot be sourced from the same field. Explain how the design of the investigation can reduce the effect of this uncontrollable variable.
parts.answer: Use many bulbs from different sources and allocate them randomly to the treatment groups, so the variation between bulbs is spread across all treatments; use a larger number of replicates so that the effect of any one bulb is small; treat the bulb as a source of variation in the analysis.
parts.working: 1 mark: many bulbs/replicates. 1 mark: random allocation to treatments. 1 mark: spreads variation so it does not favour one treatment. 1 mark: larger sample reduces the effect of one bulb.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why random allocation of root tips to treatments reduces bias in an experiment on the effect of a drug.
parts.answer: Random allocation means that differences between root tips (size, age, position on the bulb) are spread across the treatments by chance, so no treatment group is systematically better or worse; this prevents the researcher's choices from influencing which tips receive which treatment, and makes the groups comparable.
parts.working: 1 mark: spreads uncontrolled differences between tips across groups. 1 mark: prevents researcher bias in allocation. 1 mark: makes groups comparable at the start. 1 mark: so differences are more likely due to the drug.

practice.stem: A student wants to investigate the effect of colchicine on the mitotic index of onion root tips.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a suitable alternative hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: Increasing the concentration of colchicine increases the proportion of cells in mitosis (mitotic index) in onion root tips.
parts.working: 1 mark: a testable, directional statement linking colchicine concentration to the mitotic index.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the corresponding null hypothesis.
parts.answer: Colchicine concentration has no effect on the mitotic index of onion root tips.
parts.working: 1 mark: no difference / no effect, stated for the same variables.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how the mitotic index of root tips kept at 4 °C for 24 hours compares with root tips kept at 20 °C for 24 hours. Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: The mitotic index would be lower at 4 °C, because enzyme-controlled stages of the cell cycle proceed more slowly at low temperature, so fewer cells pass through mitosis in the same period.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower mitotic index at 4 °C. 1 mark: explanation that low temperature slows enzyme-controlled cell-cycle processes so fewer cells reach mitosis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a testable hypothesis for this observation: older bean roots have fewer dividing cells than younger roots.
parts.answer: Root tips from older bean seedlings have a lower mitotic index than root tips from younger seedlings.
parts.working: 1 mark: states a measurable relationship (mitotic index compared between ages). 1 mark: directional statement (lower in older roots).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the statement 'Colchicine is good for root growth' cannot be tested as written.
parts.answer: The statement does not name a measurable variable or specify what 'good' means, so there is no way to collect data to support or refute it.
parts.working: 1 mark: 'good' is not defined or measurable. 1 mark: no independent or dependent variable is named.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how the mitotic index of onion root tips exposed to 2 Gy of gamma radiation compares with unirradiated roots. Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: The mitotic index would be lower after 2 Gy, because radiation damages DNA, cell-cycle checkpoints stop cells before mitosis, and fewer cells enter division.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower mitotic index after irradiation. 1 mark: DNA damage triggers checkpoints that arrest cells, reducing entry into mitosis.

practice.stem: A researcher compares the mitotic index of bean root tips grown in a plant growth regulator solution with those grown in water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a null hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the mean mitotic index of root tips grown in the plant growth regulator and those grown in water.
parts.working: B1 no significant difference in mean mitotic index between the two treatments (must name both groups and the measured variable).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The plant growth regulator is thought to stimulate cell division. Make a prediction about the results and explain it.
parts.answer: Mean mitotic index will be higher in the treated roots, because more cells will enter mitosis at any one time if division is stimulated.
parts.working: B1 prediction: higher mitotic index with regulator; B1 explanation: more cells dividing / shorter cell cycle so greater proportion in mitosis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A drug blocks DNA replication. Predict the effect of the drug on the mitotic index of root tips after 4 hours and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: The mitotic index falls. Cells cannot complete S phase, so they cannot progress to G2 and mitosis; they are held at checkpoints, and the proportion of cells in mitosis decreases as cells already in mitosis complete it.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower mitotic index. 1 mark: cells cannot complete S phase. 1 mark: fewer cells enter G2 and mitosis (checkpoint arrest).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict how the mitotic index of onion root tips changes as the temperature of the growth medium falls from 30 °C to 10 °C. Explain your prediction in terms of molecular movement and enzymes.
parts.answer: The mitotic index falls as temperature falls. Molecules have less kinetic energy, so there are fewer successful collisions; enzyme-controlled steps of the cell cycle proceed more slowly, so cells take longer to pass through each stage.
parts.working: 1 mark: mitotic index decreases. 1 mark: lower kinetic energy and fewer successful collisions. 1 mark: enzymes controlling the cell cycle slow down, lengthening each stage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Variety A of bean grows faster than variety B under the same conditions. Predict which variety has the higher mitotic index in its root tips, and explain your prediction. State one reason why the prediction may be wrong.
parts.answer: Variety A has the higher mitotic index, because faster growth needs more cell division in its root tips; one reason it could be wrong is that the mitotic index is a snapshot of one moment, and cells in B may be dividing at a different time or be more numerous in another part of the root.
parts.working: 1 mark: variety A is predicted to have a higher mitotic index. 1 mark: faster growth requires more cell division. 1 mark: a valid reason the prediction may be wrong (snapshot timing, root zone sampled, differences in cell-cycle length).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a testable hypothesis about the effect of salt stress on the mitotic index of onion root tips. Then state the null hypothesis you would test.
parts.answer: Hypothesis: root tips grown in a higher salt concentration have a lower mitotic index than those grown in water. Null hypothesis: salt concentration has no effect on the mitotic index of root tips.
parts.working: 1 mark: a directional, measurable hypothesis. 1 mark: identifies salt concentration and mitotic index as variables. 1 mark: a correctly stated null hypothesis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a hypothesis linking the growth rate of seedling roots to their mitotic index, and describe how you would test it.
parts.answer: Hypothesis: seedlings with a faster root growth rate have a higher mitotic index. Test: measure root length each day for several seedlings to calculate growth rate, measure the mitotic index of the root tips for each seedling, and calculate a correlation coefficient.
parts.working: 1 mark: testable hypothesis with a predicted direction. 1 mark: measure growth rate (root length over time) and mitotic index for each seedling. 1 mark: test using correlation with a sufficient number of seedlings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assume that in an unsynchronised population, the proportion of cells in mitosis is approximately the time spent in mitosis divided by the cell cycle time. Mitosis takes 1 hour. Calculate the expected mitotic index (%) for a tissue with a cycle time of 20 hours and for one with a cycle time of 40 hours. Then state whether the first tissue should have the higher mitotic index.
parts.answer: Tissue 1 (20 h cycle): 1 ÷ 20 × 100 = 5.0%; tissue 2 (40 h cycle): 1 ÷ 40 × 100 = 2.5%. The 20-hour tissue has the higher mitotic index.
parts.working: 1 mark: 5.0% for the 20-hour cycle. 1 mark: 2.5% for the 40-hour cycle. 1 mark: the faster-dividing tissue has the higher mitotic index. 1 mark: states the assumption that the time in mitosis is the same for both tissues (and the population is unsynchronised).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The predicted mitotic index for a root tip population is 5%, but the observed value is 1.5%. Evaluate possible reasons for the difference, and state one change to the prediction that would make it closer to the observed value.
parts.answer: The population may be unrepresentative, e.g. counting from the wrong region of the root; the cell cycle may be longer than the assumed value, so less time is spent in mitosis; most cells may be in G1 or G2 or in a non-dividing state; time in mitosis may be shorter than 1 hour. A better prediction would use the actual mitosis time and cycle time of the material.
parts.working: 1 mark for each: a valid reason for the difference (sampling region, longer cycle time, non-dividing cells, shorter mitosis time); 1 mark for a reasonable change to the prediction (use measured mitosis and cycle times).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a null hypothesis is tested statistically rather than the alternative hypothesis, and what a p-value below 0.05 indicates.
parts.answer: The null hypothesis is the statement of no difference or no effect, which is assumed true until the data show otherwise; statistical tests give the probability of obtaining results at least as extreme if the null hypothesis is true. A p-value below 0.05 means such results would occur by chance less than 5% of the time, so the null hypothesis is rejected.
parts.working: 1 mark: the null hypothesis is the default that can be tested/rejected. 1 mark: tests give the probability of the result if H0 is true. 1 mark: p < 0.05 means the result would arise by chance less than 5% of the time. 1 mark: so H0 is rejected in favour of the alternative.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a null hypothesis for a comparison of the mitotic index of two independent groups of root tips, name the statistical test you would use, and state the degrees of freedom when there are 6 slides in each group.
parts.answer: Null hypothesis: there is no difference in mean mitotic index between the two groups. Test: Student's t-test for two independent samples. Degrees of freedom: (6 + 6) − 2 = 10.
parts.working: 1 mark: null hypothesis of no difference in means. 1 mark: independent (Student's) t-test. 1 mark: degrees of freedom = n1 + n2 − 2. 1 mark: degrees of freedom = 10.

practice.stem: The mitotic index (%) of six slides prepared from onion root tips was: 4.8, 5.1, 4.6, 5.5, 4.9, 5.2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean mitotic index of these six slides. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the range of the values.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: The mitotic index (%) of six slides prepared from onion root tips was: 4.8, 5.1, 4.6, 5.5, 4.9, 5.2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the sample standard deviation of these six values (divide by n − 1). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 squared deviations from the mean 5.0167 sum to 0.5083 (sum of squares ÷ (n − 1) = 0.5083 ÷ 5 = 0.1017); A1 square root = 0.32.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the standard deviation tells you about these data.
parts.answer: How spread out the values are around the mean (a typical distance of each value from the mean).
parts.working: 1 mark: a measure of the spread or variability of the values about the mean.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: Six slides gave a standard deviation of 0.31% for the mitotic index.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard error of the mean. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the standard error is smaller than the standard deviation.
parts.answer: The standard error estimates how precisely the mean is known and divides the spread by √n, so it becomes smaller as the sample size increases.
parts.working: 1 mark: SE divides the SD by √n, so it measures the precision of the mean, which improves with larger n.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: The mitotic index of control root tips was 5.2% with a 95% confidence interval of 4.9% to 5.5%. The mitotic index of treated root tips was 6.2% with a 95% confidence interval of 5.6% to 6.8%. Each mean is based on six slides.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the 95% confidence intervals, state whether the two means are likely to differ significantly.
parts.answer: The intervals do not overlap, which suggests the difference is likely to be significant at the 5% level (a t-test should confirm this).
parts.working: 1 mark: non-overlapping intervals suggest a significant difference; overlap would suggest caution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why this comparison may still be unreliable.
parts.answer: The sample sizes are small, so the intervals are wide and the assumption of normal distribution may not be met.
parts.working: 1 mark for any one: small samples; assumptions of the test not checked; the test not actually performed.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what a p-value of 0.03 means for the result of the test.
parts.answer: If the null hypothesis were true, a difference at least this large would occur by chance in about 3 of 100 repeats.
parts.working: 1 mark: probability of obtaining a result this extreme (or more) if H0 is true.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the conclusion at the 5% significance level.
parts.answer: The result is significant: the null hypothesis is rejected.
parts.working: 1 mark: 0.03 < 0.05, so reject the null hypothesis.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: The mitotic index (%) of ten onion root tips grown in one condition: 7.1, 6.4, 8.0, 7.6, 6.9, 7.3, 6.7, 7.8, 7.0, 7.2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean of the ten values. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the sample standard deviation. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark: sum of squared deviations = 2.20; ÷ 9 = 0.244; √ = 0.494.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the 95% confidence interval for the mean. Use t = 2.262 for 9 degrees of freedom. Give each limit to 2 decimal places.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: The mitotic index (%) of five onion root tips in group A: 5.2, 6.1, 5.8, 6.5, 5.9. In group B: 4.1, 4.8, 4.4, 5.0, 4.6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the t value for these two independent groups. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the degrees of freedom, the critical t value at the 5% level (two-tailed), and the conclusion.
parts.answer: df = 8; critical t = 2.306; 5.01 > 2.306, so the difference is significant and the null hypothesis is rejected.
parts.working: 1 mark: df = 5 + 5 − 2 = 8 and critical t = 2.306. 1 mark: t exceeds the critical value, so the means differ significantly at the 5% level.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: A student measured the mitotic index (%) of onion root tips exposed to eight concentrations of a growth regulator (concentration levels 0 to 7 in increasing order). The mitotic index was: 4.1, 4.5, 4.4, 5.2, 5.0, 5.9, 6.2, 6.0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (rs). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 ranks for mitotic index: 1, 3, 2, 5, 4, 6, 8, 7; differences d (rank of concentration − rank of MI): 0, −1, 1, −1, 1, 0, −1, 1; Σd² = 6; M1 rs = 1 − (6 × 6) ÷ (8 × 63) = 0.929 → A1 0.93.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the correlation between concentration and mitotic index, and state what it does not show.
parts.answer: There is a strong positive correlation: the mitotic index tends to rise as the concentration rises. It does not show that the concentration causes the rise, since other factors could be involved.
parts.working: 1 mark: strong positive correlation. 1 mark: correlation does not prove causation.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: Two treatments were compared, each with 1000 root-tip cells counted. Control: 48 cells in mitosis, 952 not in mitosis. Treated: 92 cells in mitosis, 908 not in mitosis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected number of mitotic cells in the control group if there is no association between treatment and mitosis.
parts.working: 1 mark: total mitotic cells = 140; 140 ÷ 2 = 70 (each group has 1000 cells).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the chi-squared value for this table. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 each expected value is 70 (mitotic) or 930 (non-mitotic); M1 sum of (O − E)² ÷ E = 6.91 + 0.52 + 6.91 + 0.52; A1 14.9.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the degrees of freedom and the conclusion at the 5% significance level, given the critical value 3.84 for 1 degree of freedom.
parts.answer: df = 1; 14.9 > 3.84, so reject the null hypothesis: mitosis is associated with the treatment.
parts.working: 1 mark: df = 1 and reject H0 because 14.9 > 3.84.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: In a count of 100 dividing cells, the observed numbers in three categories were: prophase 50; metaphase 30; anaphase and telophase 20. The null hypothesis is that the three categories are equally represented.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the chi-squared value for these observed counts. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 expected count if phases are equally represented: 100 ÷ 3 = 33.3 per phase; M1 sum of (O − E)² ÷ E = (16.7² + 3.3² + 13.3²) ÷ 33.3; A1 = 14.0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the degrees of freedom.
parts.working: 1 mark: number of categories − 1 = 3 − 1 = 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the conclusion at the 5% level, given the critical value 5.99 for 2 degrees of freedom.
parts.answer: 14.0 > 5.99, so the null hypothesis is rejected: the three phases are not equally represented.
parts.working: 1 mark: reject H0 because the calculated value exceeds the critical value.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: The standard deviation for root tips grown at 25 °C is 0.80 and for those at 15 °C is 0.68. Calculate the mean mitotic index (as a percentage) for each group.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the formula t = |x̄₁ − x̄₂| ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂) to calculate the value of t. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 √(0.80²/10 + 0.68²/10) = 0.3320; A1 2.83/that = 8.52 (using unrounded SDs gives 8.52; accept 8.4–8.6).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of t at p = 0.05 for 18 degrees of freedom is 2.10. State what the student can conclude.
parts.answer: t (about 8.5) is greater than 2.10, so the null hypothesis is rejected: the difference in mean mitotic index between 25 °C and 15 °C is significant (probability of it being due to chance is less than 5 %).
parts.working: B1 calculated t > critical value 2.10 (df = 10 + 10 − 2 = 18); B1 reject null hypothesis / difference is significant, not due to chance (p < 0.05).

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: Two independent samples of six root tips each gave these values of length (mm): group A 12.1, 11.4, 13.0, 12.6, 11.8, 12.3; group B 10.2, 10.9, 9.8, 10.5, 11.0, 10.1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the degrees of freedom for this t-test.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the t value. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the conclusion at the 5% level, given the critical value 2.228 for 10 degrees of freedom.
parts.answer: The difference is significant, because 5.91 exceeds 2.228; the null hypothesis is rejected.
parts.working: 1 mark: reject H0 because t > critical value.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: Seven bean seedlings were measured. Root length (mm): 12, 25, 31, 18, 40, 22, 35. Mitotic index (%) of their root tips: 5.2, 4.1, 3.8, 3.6, 2.9, 4.6, 3.1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient for these seven seedlings. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 ranks of root length 1, 4, 5, 2, 7, 3, 6 and of mitotic index 7, 5, 4, 3, 1, 6, 2; Σd² = 100; M1 rs = 1 − (6 × 100) ÷ (7 × 48) = −0.79.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why Spearman's rank correlation is more suitable than Pearson's correlation for these data.
parts.answer: The data are not assumed to be normally distributed, and the method uses ranks, so it tests a monotonic relationship.
parts.working: 1 mark: non-parametric; ranks do not require normal data or linearity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the correlation and state what it means for the relationship between root length and mitotic index.
parts.answer: A strong negative correlation: seedlings with longer roots tend to have lower mitotic indices.
parts.working: 1 mark: strong negative correlation with the stated direction.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: In a count of 200 root-tip cells, 100 were treated with a growth regulator and 100 were controls. Treated: 30 cells in mitosis, 70 not. Control: 18 cells in mitosis, 82 not.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected number of cells in mitosis in the treated group if there is no association between treatment and mitosis.
parts.working: 1 mark: total cells in mitosis = 48; 48 ÷ 2 = 24.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the chi-squared value. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 sum of (O − E)² ÷ E across four cells with expected values 24 and 76; M1 (36/24) + (36/76) + (36/24) + (36/76); A1 = 3.95.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the conclusion at the 5% level, using the critical value 3.84 for 1 degree of freedom.
parts.answer: 3.95 > 3.84, so the null hypothesis is rejected; the treatment is associated with mitosis, although the result is close to the critical value.
parts.working: 1 mark: reject H0; state that the result is only just significant.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem: Group X: mean 6.0%, 95% CI 5.1% to 6.9%. Group Y: mean 6.8%, 95% CI 5.9% to 7.7%. Each group has 8 slides.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why overlapping 95% confidence intervals do not prove that there is no significant difference between the two means.
parts.answer: Two intervals can overlap while the difference between the means is still statistically significant, because the test for a difference uses the spread of the difference, not the separate intervals; overlapping intervals are a weaker check than a formal test.
parts.working: 1 mark: the overlap check is a conservative guide; the difference in means is tested separately. 1 mark: a t-test on the raw data (which accounts for both groups together) may still give significance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the test that should be used to check this difference.
parts.answer: An independent samples t-test on the raw data.
parts.working: 1 mark: t-test for two independent samples.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the reason why the t-test is more informative than the overlap check.
parts.answer: It gives a p-value for the actual difference in means, based on the sample sizes and variances of both groups.
parts.working: 1 mark: it uses the sample size and spread of both groups to test the difference directly.

subtopics.name: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

subtopics: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which tissue is present in the wall of the trachea but absent from the wall of a bronchiole?
A smooth muscle
B cartilage
C ciliated epithelium
D elastic fibres
parts.answer: B cartilage
