parts.working: Bronchioles have no cartilage; their walls are mainly smooth muscle and elastic fibres, and larger bronchioles are still lined by ciliated epithelium. Smooth muscle (A) and elastic fibres (D) occur in both.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the function of the elastic fibres in the walls of the airways and alveoli?
A to contract and narrow the airways
B to stretch during inspiration and recoil during expiration, helping to push air out
C to trap dust and bacteria
D to keep the trachea open when air pressure inside it falls
parts.answer: B to stretch during inspiration and recoil during expiration, helping to push air out
parts.working: Elastic fibres stretch as the lungs fill and recoil to help expel air. Contraction (A) is done by smooth muscle; keeping the trachea open (D) is the role of cartilage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the cartilage differs in the trachea, the bronchi and the bronchioles.
parts.answer: Trachea: C-shaped rings of cartilage. Bronchi: irregular plates/blocks of cartilage. Bronchioles: no cartilage.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the function of the cartilage in the trachea.
parts.answer: It supports the trachea and keeps it open, preventing it collapsing when air pressure inside falls during inspiration.
parts.working: 1 mark: support / keeps airway open. 1 mark: prevents collapse when pressure falls (inspiration).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how goblet cells and ciliated cells work together to protect the lungs from infection.
parts.answer: Goblet cells secrete mucus, which traps dust, bacteria and viruses; cilia on ciliated cells beat in a coordinated (wave-like) way; they move the mucus up towards the throat (larynx) where it is swallowed, so pathogens are removed before reaching the alveoli.
parts.working: 1 mark: goblet cells secrete mucus that traps particles/pathogens. 1 mark: cilia beat (in waves/synchrony). 1 mark: mucus moved up to throat and swallowed / away from alveoli.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why there are no goblet cells or cilia in the alveoli.
parts.answer: A layer of mucus or cilia would increase the diffusion distance (and ciliated cells are thicker than squamous cells), slowing gas exchange; mucus could also fill the small air spaces.
parts.working: 1 mark: would increase diffusion distance / thicker barrier. 1 mark: would reduce rate of gas exchange / block air spaces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the cartilage in the trachea is C-shaped rather than a complete ring.
parts.answer: The gap at the back allows flexibility / lets the oesophagus, which lies behind the trachea, expand when food is swallowed.
parts.working: 1 mark: gap at back next to oesophagus. 1 mark: allows oesophagus to expand / food bolus to pass, or allows trachea to flex.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of the smooth muscle in the walls of the bronchi and bronchioles.
parts.answer: Contracts to narrow (constrict) the airways, controlling the diameter of the lumen and the flow of air.
parts.working: 1 mark: contraction changes diameter / constricts airways.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the structure in the airways where gas exchange takes place.
parts.answer: The alveoli.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the cilia in the trachea move mucus.
parts.answer: The cilia beat (move back and forth) in a coordinated, wave-like rhythm; this sweeps the mucus upwards towards the larynx/throat.
parts.working: 1 mark: cilia beat in coordinated waves. 1 mark: move mucus upward / towards throat.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Whooping cough is caused by bacteria that release a toxin which damages ciliated cells. Suggest why people with whooping cough cough violently and often.
parts.answer: Cilia no longer move mucus, so mucus builds up in the airways; coughing is the only way to remove it.
parts.working: 1 mark: mucus accumulates because cilia damaged. 1 mark: coughing needed to clear the mucus/airways.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which type of tissue forms most of the lining of the alveoli?
A ciliated epithelium
B squamous epithelium
C columnar epithelium with goblet cells
D smooth muscle
parts.answer: B squamous epithelium
parts.working: Alveoli are lined by very thin, flattened squamous epithelial cells, giving a short diffusion distance. Ciliated epithelium (A) lines the trachea, bronchi and larger bronchioles but not the alveoli.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A child inhales a small bead that completely blocks the right main bronchus. Suggest and explain the effect on gas exchange in the alveoli of the right lung.
parts.answer: Alveoli of the right lung are no longer ventilated; oxygen in them is used up / carbon dioxide builds up, so the concentration gradients disappear and little or no gas exchange occurs there (the left lung still works)
parts.working: 1 mark: no fresh air reaches right-lung alveoli / no ventilation. 1 mark: gradients for O₂ and CO₂ fall → gas exchange stops/greatly reduced.

parts.label: b
parts.text: During exercise, the smooth muscle in the walls of the bronchioles relaxes. Describe and explain the effect on air flow to the alveoli.
parts.answer: Bronchioles widen (lumen diameter increases); less resistance so more air reaches the alveoli per minute
parts.working: 1 mark: airways dilate/widen. 1 mark: lower resistance → increased air flow/ventilation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the tissue that allows the alveoli to return to their original size during expiration.
parts.answer: Elastic fibres
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the human lungs, each airway divides into two smaller airways. The trachea is generation 0, the two main bronchi are generation 1, and so on. Calculate the number of airways in generation 16.
parts.working: M1: number = 2ⁿ. A1: 2¹⁶ = 65 536.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Each generation-16 airway has a diameter of 0.50 mm; the trachea has a diameter of 18 mm. Calculate how many times greater the total cross-sectional area of all generation-16 airways is than the cross-sectional area of the trachea. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 50.6 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how this affects the speed at which air moves in the smallest airways.
parts.answer: Air moves much more slowly (the same volume flows through a much larger total cross-section), so near the alveoli gases move mainly by diffusion
parts.working: 1 mark: much slower air flow in small airways.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A photomicrograph shows an airway about 0.8 mm in diameter. Its wall has no cartilage, a thick layer of smooth muscle, elastic fibres and a lining of ciliated cells with very few goblet cells.
What is the airway?
A trachea
B bronchus
C bronchiole
D alveolar duct
parts.answer: C bronchiole
parts.working: No cartilage, much smooth muscle and a small diameter identify a bronchiole. A bronchus (B) would contain plates of cartilage; the trachea (A) has C-shaped cartilage rings and many goblet cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which structures produce the mucus that lines the trachea?
A goblet cells and mucous glands
B ciliated cells and goblet cells
C cartilage and mucous glands
D squamous epithelial cells and goblet cells
parts.answer: A goblet cells and mucous glands
parts.working: Mucus is secreted by goblet cells in the epithelium and by mucous glands below it. Ciliated cells (B) move mucus but do not secrete it; squamous cells (D) line alveoli, not the trachea.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
During an asthma attack the airways narrow and breathing becomes difficult. Which tissue contracts to cause this narrowing?
A cartilage
B elastic fibres
C smooth muscle
D squamous epithelium
parts.answer: C smooth muscle
parts.working: Smooth muscle in the walls of bronchi and especially bronchioles contracts, reducing the diameter of the lumen. Elastic fibres (B) recoil but do not actively contract.

practice.stem:
The wall of the trachea was examined from the lumen outwards. Four structures were described:
P: a layer of tall cells with tiny hair-like projections on their free surface
Q: single cup-shaped cells scattered among the cells of P, filled with pale-staining vesicles
R: clusters of secretory cells in the connective tissue beneath P, with ducts opening onto the surface
S: a thick C-shaped band of bluish, glassy tissue with cells in small spaces (lacunae)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the tissues P, Q, R and S.
parts.answer: P ciliated (pseudostratified columnar) epithelium; Q goblet cell; R mucous gland (in submucosa); S cartilage (hyaline).
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept 'ciliated epithelium' for P.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of tissue S and one other tissue named in your answer to (a).
parts.answer: S: keeps trachea open / prevents collapse. P: cilia move mucus up to the throat (or Q/R: secrete mucus to trap particles).
parts.working: 1 mark for S; 1 mark for a correct function of P, Q or R.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In cystic fibrosis the mucus in the airways is much thicker and stickier than normal. Suggest why people with cystic fibrosis suffer from frequent lung infections.
parts.answer: Cilia cannot move the thick mucus (mucociliary escalator fails); mucus and trapped bacteria stay in the airways; bacteria multiply in the warm, moist mucus, causing infection.
parts.working: 1 mark: cilia unable to move/clear thick mucus. 1 mark: bacteria/pathogens trapped and not removed. 1 mark: bacteria multiply in the mucus / reach lower airways.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why people with cystic fibrosis may also become breathless.
parts.answer: Mucus blocks or narrows bronchioles, so less air reaches the alveoli; less oxygen diffuses into the blood (smaller surface area for gas exchange).
parts.working: 1 mark: mucus blocks/narrows airways. 1 mark: less ventilation of alveoli / less gas exchange.

practice.stem: A student viewed a transverse section of trachea with a light microscope. With the objective used, one eyepiece graticule division equals 4.0 µm. The ciliated epithelium measured 12 divisions thick and the cartilage measured 85 divisions thick.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual thickness of the ciliated epithelium and of the cartilage.
parts.answer: Epithelium 48 µm; cartilage 340 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times thicker the cartilage is than the epithelium. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 7.1 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: On a photomicrograph of a bronchiole, a scale bar 20 mm long represents 100 µm. The diameter of the bronchiole on the photomicrograph is 96 mm. Calculate the actual diameter of the bronchiole in µm.
parts.answer: 480 µm

parts.label: a
parts.text: An electron micrograph of the surface of a ciliated cell has a magnification of ×6000. A cilium on the micrograph is 45 mm long. Calculate the actual length of the cilium in µm.
parts.answer: 7.5 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert your answer to nanometres.
parts.working: 7.5 × 1000 = 7500 nm (error carried forward).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Ciliated cells contain many mitochondria close to the bases of the cilia. Explain why.
parts.answer: Mitochondria produce ATP by aerobic respiration; ATP provides the energy for the cilia to beat (continuously).
parts.working: 1 mark: mitochondria make ATP / site of aerobic respiration. 1 mark: cilia beating needs energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a rare inherited condition, enzymes released by white blood cells in the lungs break down elastic fibres faster than normal. Suggest and explain how this would affect breathing out.
parts.answer: Fewer elastic fibres, so the walls of the alveoli and airways recoil less; less air is pushed out during expiration; air remains trapped in the alveoli (so the concentration gradient for gas exchange is reduced); breathing out needs more effort.
parts.working: 1 mark: less elastic recoil. 1 mark: less air expelled / air trapped / harder to exhale. 1 mark: stale air reduces concentration gradient / gas exchange or extra muscular effort needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Alveolar walls damaged in this way may break down so that several alveoli merge into one larger air space. Explain why this reduces the rate of gas exchange.
parts.answer: Merging alveoli reduces the total surface area available for diffusion, so less oxygen can diffuse into the blood per unit time.
parts.working: 1 mark: smaller (total) surface area. 1 mark: less diffusion of O₂/CO₂ per unit time.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Copy and complete the table by writing present or absent in each box.
Feature | trachea | bronchiole | alveolus
cartilage | ? | ? | ?
ciliated epithelium | ? | ? | ?
smooth muscle | ? | ? | ?
elastic fibres | ? | ? | ?
parts.answer:
cartilage: present, absent, absent
ciliated epithelium: present, present, absent
smooth muscle: present, present, absent
elastic fibres: present, present, present
parts.working: 1 mark per correct row. Accept 'present in larger bronchioles' for ciliated epithelium in bronchiole.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of epithelium that lines the alveoli and explain how it is adapted for its function.
parts.answer: Squamous epithelium; the cells are very thin/flattened, giving a short diffusion distance for oxygen and carbon dioxide.
parts.working: 1 mark: squamous. 1 mark: thin/flattened cells → short diffusion distance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mucus contains glycoproteins. Name two organelles that you would expect to be abundant in a goblet cell and explain the role of each in producing mucus.
parts.answer: Rough endoplasmic reticulum: ribosomes on it synthesise the protein part of the glycoproteins. Golgi body: adds carbohydrate to the proteins (glycosylation) and packages mucus into secretory vesicles. (Also accept mitochondria: ATP for synthesis and exocytosis.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each organelle (max 2) and 1 mark for each matching role (max 2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the process by which mucus is released from the goblet cell.
parts.answer: Exocytosis.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row correctly matches a tissue of the gas exchange system with its function?
A goblet cells — move mucus towards the throat
B cartilage — contracts to narrow the airways
C mucous glands — secrete mucus that traps dust and bacteria
D elastic fibres — prevent the trachea collapsing during inspiration
parts.answer: C mucous glands — secrete mucus that traps dust and bacteria
parts.working: Mucous glands (below the epithelium of the trachea and bronchi) secrete mucus that traps particles and pathogens. Goblet cells secrete mucus but cilia move it (A); smooth muscle, not cartilage, contracts (B); cartilage, not elastic fibres, keeps the trachea open (D).

practice.stem: A student viewed a stained section of mammal lung through a light microscope with a grid of 100 points in the eyepiece. In one field of view, 68 points fell on air spaces, 26 on alveolar walls and 6 on blood vessels.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of points that fell on tissue (alveolar walls and blood vessels together).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of air space to tissue. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student repeated the count in four more randomly chosen fields of view. The percentages of air space were 68, 71, 64, 70 and 67. Calculate the mean and state why using several fields gives a better estimate.
parts.answer: Mean 68 %; one field may not be representative of the whole section (reduces effect of variation)
parts.working: B1: (68 + 71 + 64 + 70 + 67) ÷ 5 = 68 %. B1: more representative / reduces effect of an unusual field.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why it is difficult to decide which tissue a point falls on when it lies on the edge of an alveolar wall, and how the student could deal with this.
parts.answer: Alveolar walls are very thin so boundaries are unclear; set a rule before counting (e.g. count edge points as half, or count only points clearly inside)
parts.working: 1 mark: thin walls / boundary unclear. 1 mark: consistent rule decided in advance.

practice.stem:
Descriptions of four airways from a human lung:
W: diameter 8 mm; irregular plates of cartilage; ciliated epithelium with goblet cells; mucous glands
X: diameter 0.4 mm; no cartilage; smooth muscle; no goblet cells; epithelium cells cuboidal with few or no cilia
Y: diameter 18 mm; C-shaped rings of cartilage; ciliated epithelium with goblet cells; mucous glands
Z: diameter 0.9 mm; no cartilage; thick smooth muscle layer; ciliated epithelium with a few goblet cells

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify each airway W, X, Y and Z as trachea, bronchus, larger bronchiole or terminal (smallest) bronchiole.
parts.answer: W bronchus; X terminal bronchiole; Y trachea; Z larger bronchiole
parts.working: 1 mark each. W: irregular cartilage plates + cilia/goblet cells = bronchus. Y: C-shaped cartilage = trachea. Z: no cartilage, cilia present, few goblet cells = larger bronchiole. X: no cartilage, no goblet cells, few/no cilia = terminal bronchiole.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the terminal bronchiole has no goblet cells.
parts.answer: Mucus would block such a narrow airway / could not be cleared without cilia; most particles have already been trapped higher up
parts.working: 1 mark for either reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statements about the wall of a bronchus are correct?
1 It contains irregular plates of cartilage.
2 It is lined by ciliated epithelium with goblet cells.
3 It contains smooth muscle.
A 1, 2 and 3
B 1 and 2 only
C 2 and 3 only
D 1 only
parts.answer: A 1, 2 and 3
parts.working: A bronchus has irregular blocks of cartilage (not complete C-rings), ciliated epithelium with goblet cells, and smooth muscle. B is a common error: smooth muscle is present in bronchi as well as bronchioles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe four differences between the wall of the trachea and the wall of a bronchiole.
parts.answer: Trachea has C-shaped cartilage rings, bronchiole has no cartilage; trachea has many goblet cells, bronchiole few or none; trachea has mucous glands, bronchiole none; trachea has relatively little smooth muscle, bronchiole has a relatively thick layer of smooth muscle; trachea lined by tall (pseudostratified) ciliated epithelium, bronchiole by shorter (cuboidal) ciliated epithelium (none in the smallest); trachea wall much thicker / lumen wider.
parts.working: 1 mark for each comparative difference, max 4: cartilage; goblet cells; mucous glands; proportion of smooth muscle; height/type of epithelium; wall thickness/diameter.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why bronchioles can change their diameter but the trachea cannot do so to the same extent.
parts.answer: Bronchioles have no cartilage and a high proportion of smooth muscle, so when the muscle contracts or relaxes the lumen narrows or widens; the trachea is held open by rigid cartilage rings.
parts.working: 1 mark: bronchioles have smooth muscle and no cartilage. 1 mark: trachea's cartilage is rigid / prevents narrowing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three rules a student should follow when making a plan diagram of a transverse section of a bronchus.
parts.answer: Draw only the outlines of tissue layers (no individual cells); use clear, continuous thin lines with no shading; draw tissues in the correct proportions/relative thickness; use a large drawing (over half the space); label lines ruled, not crossing, touching the tissue.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: no cells drawn; sharp continuous lines, no shading; correct proportions of layers; large size; ruled label lines to the correct tissues.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In the bronchus section the total wall thickness was 60 eyepiece divisions, of which 38 divisions were cartilage. Calculate the percentage of the wall thickness made up of cartilage. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A second section was of a bronchiole. Suggest two features that the student would see in the bronchiole that would allow her to distinguish it from the bronchus.
parts.answer: No cartilage; smaller diameter / thinner wall; relatively thicker smooth muscle layer; few or no goblet cells / no mucous glands; epithelium shorter (cuboidal).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem:
A woman in Karachi with asthma measured her peak flow (the fastest rate at which she could breathe out) before and 15 minutes after using an inhaler.
Before: 220 dm³ min⁻¹
After: 380 dm³ min⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in peak flow after using the inhaler. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The inhaler contains a drug that causes smooth muscle to relax. Explain how this increases peak flow.
parts.answer: Relaxed smooth muscle in the walls of bronchioles (and bronchi) allows the airways to widen; the larger lumen means less resistance, so air can flow out faster.
parts.working: 1 mark: bronchioles widen / dilate when smooth muscle relaxes. 1 mark: larger lumen / less resistance, faster airflow.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Her reading before using the inhaler was 55 % of the expected peak flow for a healthy woman of her age and height. Calculate her expected peak flow.
parts.answer: 400 dm³ min⁻¹

practice.stem:
The table shows the percentage of inhaled particles of different diameters that are trapped in the trachea and bronchi.
Particle diameter / µm: 0.5, 2.5, 5, 10
Trapped in trachea and bronchi / %: 5, 40, 70, 90

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain the pattern shown by the data.
parts.answer: The larger the particle, the greater the percentage trapped in the trachea and bronchi (90 % at 10 µm, 5 % at 0.5 µm); large particles hit and stick to the mucus in the upper airways and are removed by cilia; small particles stay suspended in the air and are carried deep into the bronchioles and alveoli.
parts.working: 1 mark: larger particles more trapped (data quote). 1 mark: trapped by mucus (from goblet cells) and removed by cilia. 1 mark: small particles follow air flow into bronchioles/alveoli.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Smog in Lahore contains many particles smaller than 2.5 µm. Suggest why these particles are more harmful to the lungs than larger particles.
parts.answer: They reach the alveoli, where there is no mucus or cilia to remove them; they can damage the thin alveolar walls / cause inflammation, reducing gas exchange (they must be removed by phagocytes/macrophages).
parts.working: 1 mark: reach alveoli. 1 mark: no mucus/cilia there so not removed / cause inflammation or damage to exchange surface.

practice.stem:
Samples of bronchus lining were taken during routine medical procedures from adults living in a large industrial city and from adults in rural villages. The number of goblet cells per mm of epithelium was counted.
City group: mean 41 goblet cells per mm
Village group: mean 25 goblet cells per mm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which the mean number of goblet cells in the city group is greater than in the village group.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an explanation for the difference between the two groups.
parts.answer: City air has more particles/pollutants; the epithelium responds by producing more goblet cells, so more mucus is secreted to trap the extra particles.
parts.working: 1 mark: more pollution/particles in city air. 1 mark: more goblet cells → more mucus to trap particles.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one disadvantage to the city group of having more goblet cells.
parts.answer: Excess mucus may be too much for the cilia to remove, so it collects, narrows airways and allows bacteria to multiply (more infections, coughing).
parts.working: 1 mark: excess mucus blocks airways / harbours bacteria / causes cough.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cilia in a healthy trachea move mucus at 5 mm per minute. Calculate the time taken for mucus to travel the full 12 cm length of the trachea.
parts.answer: 24 minutes
parts.working: 120 mm ÷ 5 mm min⁻¹ = 24 min.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In winter, breathing very cold, dry air reduces the speed to 2 mm per minute. Calculate the percentage increase in the time for mucus to clear the trachea.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why dry air slows mucus clearance.
parts.answer: Water evaporates from the airway lining so the watery layer around the cilia becomes thinner / mucus becomes thicker and stickier; cilia cannot beat freely / mucus is harder to move
parts.working: 1 mark: drying of lining / mucus more viscous. 1 mark: cilia beating impaired / less effective.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain how slower clearance could increase the risk of lung infections.
parts.answer: Bacteria and viruses trapped in mucus stay in the airways longer; more time to multiply / infect epithelial cells or reach the alveoli
parts.working: 1 mark: pathogens remain longer. 1 mark: more chance to multiply/invade.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Air-flow resistance in an airway is inversely proportional to the fourth power of its radius (resistance ∝ 1/r⁴). In a person with long-term asthma, thickening of the smooth muscle layer reduces the lumen radius of a bronchiole from 0.50 mm to 0.40 mm. Calculate how many times greater the resistance becomes. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 2.44 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use this calculation to explain why bronchioles, rather than the trachea, are the main site of airway narrowing in an asthma attack.
parts.answer: Bronchioles have no cartilage but have a relatively thick layer of smooth muscle, so contraction can greatly reduce their radius; the trachea is held open by cartilage; because resistance depends on r⁴, even a small decrease in bronchiole radius causes a large rise in resistance
parts.working: 1 mark: bronchioles lack cartilage. 1 mark: smooth muscle contraction narrows lumen (trachea supported by cartilage). 1 mark: r⁴ relationship → small change in radius has large effect.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three features of alveoli and explain how each increases the rate of gas exchange.
parts.answer: Very many alveoli give a large surface area; walls one cell thick of squamous epithelium give a short diffusion distance; close network of capillaries carries O₂ away/brings CO₂, keeping a steep concentration gradient; ventilation renews air, maintaining the gradient; moist lining lets gases dissolve.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three feature + explanation pairs: large surface area; thin wall/short distance; good blood supply maintains gradient; ventilation maintains gradient; moist surface.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the process by which oxygen moves from the alveolar air into the blood.
parts.answer: Diffusion.
parts.working: 1 mark (not active transport).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the route taken by a molecule of carbon dioxide as it leaves the blood and passes out of the body.
parts.answer: From plasma (or red blood cell) through the capillary endothelium, through the alveolar epithelium into the alveolar air; then out through the bronchiole, bronchus and trachea during expiration.
parts.working: 1 mark: through capillary wall/endothelium. 1 mark: through alveolar wall/epithelium into alveolus. 1 mark: bronchiole → bronchus → trachea (in correct order) during expiration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Alveolar walls contain macrophages. Suggest the role of these cells.
parts.answer: They engulf (by phagocytosis) bacteria and dust particles that reach the alveoli.
parts.working: 1 mark: phagocytosis of pathogens/particles.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
How does oxygen move from the air in an alveolus into the blood?
A by active transport through the alveolar wall
B by diffusion down a concentration gradient through the alveolar wall and capillary wall
C by osmosis through the capillary wall
D by facilitated diffusion through channel proteins in the squamous cells
parts.answer: B by diffusion down a concentration gradient through the alveolar wall and capillary wall
parts.working: Oxygen is small and non-polar, so it diffuses passively through the phospholipid bilayers of the squamous epithelium and capillary endothelium, from high concentration in the alveolus to low concentration in the blood. A is wrong because no ATP is used.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the passage by giving the word for each gap (1)–(5).
'Oxygen in the alveolar air first dissolves in the thin layer of (1) lining the alveolus. It then diffuses through the flattened (2) epithelium of the alveolus and the (3) of the capillary into the plasma, and then into the red blood cells, where it combines with (4). Carbon dioxide diffuses in the (5) direction.'
parts.answer: (1) water / moisture; (2) squamous; (3) endothelium / wall; (4) haemoglobin; (5) opposite
parts.working: 1 mark for each gap.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In one part of the lung, the alveolar epithelium is 0.15 µm thick, the shared basement membrane 0.10 µm and the capillary endothelium 0.15 µm. Calculate the total diffusion distance from alveolar air to blood plasma, in nm.
parts.answer: 400 nm

parts.label: b
parts.text: A red blood cell has a diameter of 7.5 µm. Calculate how many times greater this is than the diffusion distance in (a). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 18.8 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a short diffusion distance is important for gas exchange.
parts.answer: Rate of diffusion is faster over a shorter distance, so more oxygen/carbon dioxide is exchanged per second
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between ventilation and gas exchange.
parts.answer: Ventilation is the movement of air into and out of the lungs (breathing); gas exchange is the diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide between alveolar air and the blood
parts.working: 1 mark: ventilation = air moved in/out of lungs. 1 mark: gas exchange = diffusion of O₂/CO₂ across alveolar wall between air and blood.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Gas exchange takes place in the alveoli but not in the trachea. Suggest two reasons why.
parts.answer: Any two: trachea wall is thick (many cell layers, cartilage), so diffusion distance is long; no capillary network pressed against its lining; small surface area compared with millions of alveoli; mucus layer adds to the distance
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the inner surface of each alveolus is covered with a thin film of water.
parts.answer: Oxygen must dissolve in water before it can diffuse across the cell membranes; the film keeps the cells moist so gases can pass through
parts.working: 1 mark: gases dissolve. 1 mark: then diffuse through (moist) alveolar wall / cells would dry out and die.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one disadvantage of having a moist surface in the lungs.
parts.answer: Water is lost by evaporation in exhaled air (or: moist surface could allow growth of pathogens)
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three differences between inhaled and exhaled air.
parts.answer: Exhaled air has less oxygen; more carbon dioxide; more water vapour (and is warmer)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: less O₂; more CO₂; more water vapour; warmer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why exhaled air contains more carbon dioxide than inhaled air.
parts.answer: Cells produce CO₂ in (aerobic) respiration; it is carried in the blood to the lungs and diffuses from the blood into the alveoli (down its concentration gradient)
parts.working: 1 mark: produced in respiration. 1 mark: diffuses from blood to alveolar air.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student at rest breathes in 0.50 dm³ of air in each breath and takes 14 breaths per minute. Calculate the volume of air breathed in per minute.
parts.answer: 7.0 dm³ per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Inhaled air contains 21 % oxygen and exhaled air contains 16 % oxygen. Calculate the volume of oxygen absorbed per minute, in cm³.
parts.answer: 350 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how breathing in fresh air helps to maintain the rate of oxygen diffusion into the blood.
parts.answer: It replaces alveolar air with air of higher oxygen concentration; so a steep concentration gradient between alveolar air and blood is maintained
parts.working: 1 mark: brings in high-O₂ air / removes air with lower O₂. 1 mark: maintains steep concentration gradient.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how breathing (ventilation) and blood flow both help to maintain a steep concentration gradient of oxygen between alveolar air and blood.
parts.answer: Ventilation regularly replaces alveolar air with fresh air, keeping the oxygen concentration in the alveoli high (and removing CO₂). Blood flow continuously carries oxygenated blood away from the alveoli and brings deoxygenated blood (low O₂) to them, keeping the oxygen concentration in the capillaries low. Oxygen binding to haemoglobin also keeps the plasma oxygen concentration low.
parts.working: 1 mark: ventilation brings fresh air / keeps alveolar O₂ high. 1 mark: removes CO₂-rich air. 1 mark: blood flow removes oxygenated blood / brings deoxygenated blood. 1 mark: keeps blood O₂ low (helped by uptake by haemoglobin).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the capillaries around the alveoli are so narrow that red blood cells pass through them in single file, pressed against the capillary wall.
parts.answer: This reduces the diffusion distance between the alveolar air and the haemoglobin; red blood cells move more slowly, giving more time for gas exchange.
parts.working: 1 mark: short diffusion distance. 1 mark: slows red cells / more time for diffusion / larger area of contact.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In pulmonary fibrosis, scar tissue forms in the walls of the alveoli. In one patient the distance between alveolar air and blood increased from 0.5 µm to 3.0 µm. Assuming the rate of diffusion is inversely proportional to the diffusion distance, calculate how many times slower diffusion became.
parts.answer: 6 times slower

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why patients with pulmonary fibrosis become breathless, especially during exercise.
parts.answer: Oxygen diffuses into the blood more slowly, so the blood is less fully oxygenated; less oxygen reaches respiring muscle cells; during exercise the demand for oxygen rises, so breathing rate increases to try to compensate. Scar tissue may also make the lungs stiffer, so less air is breathed in.
parts.working: 1 mark: slower diffusion of O₂ into blood / less O₂ absorbed. 1 mark: less O₂ to cells for aerobic respiration. 1 mark: exercise raises O₂ demand → faster/deeper breathing (or stiff lungs reduce ventilation).

practice.stem: Climbers on their way to K2 spend time at a base camp at about 5000 m above sea level. The partial pressure of oxygen in the air is 21.2 kPa at sea level and 11.2 kPa at 5000 m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in the partial pressure of oxygen between sea level and the base camp. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why climbers at the base camp become breathless even when resting.
parts.answer: Lower partial pressure of oxygen in the air means a lower partial pressure in the alveoli; the gradient between alveolar air and blood is smaller, so oxygen diffuses into the blood more slowly; less oxygen is carried to the tissues, so breathing rate increases to compensate.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower pO₂ in alveoli. 1 mark: smaller diffusion gradient / slower diffusion into blood. 1 mark: less O₂ delivered / haemoglobin less saturated, so breathing faster/deeper.

practice.stem:
Typical percentages of gases:
Inhaled air: oxygen 21 %, carbon dioxide 0.04 %
Alveolar air: oxygen 14 %, carbon dioxide 5.3 %
Exhaled air: oxygen 16 %
Exhaled air is a mixture of alveolar air and air from the airways (trachea, bronchi, bronchioles) that still has the composition of inhaled air.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the oxygen percentages to calculate the percentage of exhaled air that comes from the alveoli. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: M1: fraction f from alveoli: 21 − f(21 − 14) = 16, so f = 5 ÷ 7. A1: 71.4 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to (a) to predict the percentage of carbon dioxide in exhaled air. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why air in the airways has the same composition as inhaled air.
parts.answer: The airways have no alveoli / thick walls without close capillaries, so no gas exchange takes place there; the last air breathed in stays in them and is breathed out first
parts.working: 1 mark: no gas exchange in airways. 1 mark: air there is unchanged inhaled air (dead space).

practice.stem:
Partial pressure of oxygen / kPa:
Alveolar air: rest 13.3, exercise 13.3
Blood arriving at the alveoli: rest 5.3, exercise 2.7

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the partial pressure difference for oxygen between alveolar air and blood arriving at the alveoli, at rest and during exercise.
parts.answer: Rest 8.0 kPa; exercise 10.6 kPa

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in this difference during exercise.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the partial pressure of oxygen in blood arriving at the lungs is lower during exercise.
parts.answer: Muscle cells respire faster during exercise and use more oxygen; so more oxygen is released from haemoglobin / removed from the blood in the muscles
parts.working: 1 mark: increased respiration rate in muscles. 1 mark: more O₂ unloaded/used, so less returns.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the alveolar partial pressure stays at about 13.3 kPa even though more oxygen is being absorbed.
parts.answer: Ventilation rate (breathing rate and depth) increases, so oxygen in the alveoli is replaced faster
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In pneumonia, some alveoli fill with fluid and white blood cells. Explain why this reduces oxygen uptake into the blood.
parts.answer: Fluid increases the diffusion distance; air cannot reach the fluid-filled alveoli, so the surface area available for gas exchange is reduced; concentration gradient of oxygen is reduced (no fresh air ventilates these alveoli)
parts.working: 1 mark each: longer diffusion distance; smaller surface area; smaller concentration gradient / less ventilation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a patient with pneumonia breathes faster than normal.
parts.answer: Less oxygen absorbed and less CO₂ removed, so blood CO₂ concentration rises (and O₂ falls); this is detected and breathing rate increases to increase ventilation of the remaining alveoli
parts.working: 1 mark: low blood O₂ / high blood CO₂. 1 mark: faster breathing increases ventilation/gradient in working alveoli.

practice.stem:
Five students in a school in Peshawar counted their breaths per minute while sitting, then again immediately after 3 minutes of step-ups.
Student | before | after
1 | 14 | 28
2 | 15 | 30
3 | 13 | 27
4 | 16 | 33
5 | 12 | 32

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean breathing rate before and after exercise.
parts.answer: Before 14 breaths per minute; after 30 breaths per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in mean breathing rate. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two variables that should be kept the same for all students.
parts.answer: Any two: type and duration/intensity of exercise (e.g. same number of step-ups per minute for 3 min); time after exercise at which breaths were counted; length of counting period; position (sitting/standing); time allowed to rest before the first count
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain how the increase in breathing rate helps gas exchange in the alveoli during exercise.
parts.answer: More fresh air enters the alveoli per minute, keeping alveolar O₂ high and CO₂ low; this maintains steep concentration gradients for O₂ into and CO₂ out of the blood
parts.working: 1 mark: increased ventilation. 1 mark: steep gradients maintained for both gases.

practice.stem:
The partial pressure of oxygen was estimated in blood at different points along a capillary next to an alveolus (alveolar oxygen partial pressure = 13.3 kPa).
Distance along capillary / % of length: 0, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100
Partial pressure of oxygen / kPa: 5.3, 9.8, 12.2, 13.1, 13.3, 13.3

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the partial pressure of oxygen in the blood changes along the capillary.
parts.answer: Rises rapidly over the first part of the capillary (from 5.3 to 12.2 kPa in the first 20 %); then levels off / reaches 13.3 kPa by 50 % of the length and stays constant
parts.working: 1 mark: rapid increase at start with data. 1 mark: plateau at 13.3 kPa (equal to alveolar air) from halfway.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the shape of the curve.
parts.answer: At first the concentration gradient between alveolar air (13.3 kPa) and blood is steep, so diffusion is fast; as blood gains oxygen the gradient becomes smaller, so diffusion slows, until partial pressures are equal (equilibrium) and there is no net diffusion
parts.working: 1 mark: steep gradient → fast diffusion at start. 1 mark: gradient decreases → equilibrium / no net movement.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why it is an advantage that equilibrium is normally reached well before the end of the capillary.
parts.answer: Blood can still be fully oxygenated when it flows faster (e.g. during exercise) and spends less time in the capillary
parts.working: 1 mark: safety margin when transit time is shorter.

practice.stem: Patients with severe lung infections in a hospital in Islamabad are given air enriched with oxygen through a face mask.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Air at the hospital's location has a total pressure of 101 kPa. Calculate the partial pressure of oxygen in a gas mixture containing 40 % oxygen.
parts.answer: 40.4 kPa

parts.label: b
parts.text: Room air contains 21 % oxygen. Explain how breathing the 40 % mixture helps a patient whose alveolar walls are thickened by infection.
parts.answer: Higher partial pressure/concentration of oxygen in the alveoli; steeper concentration gradient between alveolar air and blood; increases rate of diffusion, compensating for the longer diffusion distance
parts.working: 1 mark each: higher alveolar O₂; steeper gradient; faster diffusion despite thicker barrier.

practice.stem: Normal blood contains 150 g of haemoglobin per dm³. Each gram of haemoglobin can carry up to 1.34 cm³ of oxygen. A woman with anaemia has only 60 % of the normal haemoglobin concentration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum volume of oxygen carried by haemoglobin in 1 dm³ of normal blood and of the woman's blood. Give the second answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: Normal 201 cm³; anaemic 121 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: The partial pressure of oxygen in the woman's alveoli is normal. Suggest why her blood still takes up less oxygen in the lungs.
parts.answer: Less haemoglobin to bind oxygen, so the haemoglobin present becomes saturated and dissolved oxygen in the plasma rises; the concentration gradient from alveolar air disappears sooner, so less oxygen in total diffuses in
parts.working: 1 mark: less haemoglobin to bind/remove O₂ from plasma. 1 mark: gradient lost sooner → less total uptake.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why she becomes breathless during exercise.
parts.answer: Less oxygen reaches respiring muscles, so breathing rate rises to try to increase oxygen supply
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation using agar cubes containing phenolphthalein indicator and dilute sodium hydroxide (pink) to model the effect of diffusion distance on the time for an acid to diffuse to the centre of the cube. Describe the method, including the independent and dependent variables and how other variables would be standardised.
parts.answer: Cut agar cubes of different side lengths (e.g. 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5 cm) with a ruler and scalpel; place each cube in the same volume and concentration of hydrochloric acid at the same temperature; start a stopwatch; measure time for the pink colour to disappear completely; repeat three times for each size and calculate the mean; diffusion distance = half the side length
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: IV = cube size / distance to centre (half side length), at least five sizes stated; DV = time for complete colour loss (decolourisation); same volume of acid (cubes fully covered); same acid concentration; same temperature (water bath); same agar/indicator/NaOH concentration in all cubes; cubes cut accurately / measured; stir or turn cubes; repeats and mean; safety: goggles/gloves for acid and alkali.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the results of this model relate to the structure of the alveoli.
parts.answer: Larger cubes (longer distance) take much longer to decolourise, showing diffusion is slow over long distances; alveolar walls are very thin, giving a short diffusion distance so exchange is rapid
parts.working: 1 mark: time increases with distance. 1 mark: link to thin alveolar/capillary walls.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
How many cell surface membranes does an oxygen molecule cross as it diffuses from the air in an alveolus to a haemoglobin molecule inside a red blood cell?
A 2
B 3
C 4
D 5
parts.answer: D 5
parts.working: In and out of the alveolar epithelial cell (2), in and out of the capillary endothelial cell (2), into the red blood cell (1) = 5. C (4) forgets the red blood cell membrane.

practice.stem: A pair of adult human lungs contains about 480 million alveoli. Assume that each alveolus has a diameter of 0.2 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the surface area of one alveolus, treating it as a sphere (surface area = πd²). Give your answer in mm² to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total surface area of the alveoli in m², to 2 significant figures. (1 m² = 10⁶ mm²)
parts.answer: 60 m²

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one assumption in this calculation that may make the answer inaccurate, and explain why.
parts.answer: Alveoli are not complete, separate spheres: part of each opens into an alveolar duct and neighbouring alveoli share walls, so not all of the calculated surface is in contact with air (or alveoli vary in size, so 0.2 mm is only an average).
parts.working: 1 mark: alveoli not complete/separate spheres (open to ducts, share walls) or diameters vary / not all alveoli the same size / not all surface covered by capillaries – with a reason.

practice.stem:
The table shows partial pressures of gases (kPa).
Gas: inspired air | alveolar air | deoxygenated blood arriving at lungs
Oxygen: 21.0 | 13.3 | 5.3
Carbon dioxide: 0.04 | 5.3 | 6.1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the partial pressure of oxygen in alveolar air is lower than in inspired air.
parts.answer: Inspired air mixes with the air that remains in the lungs (residual air / air in airways) which has less oxygen; oxygen is continuously diffusing from alveolar air into the blood.
parts.working: 1 mark: mixing with stale/residual air. 1 mark: O₂ constantly removed by diffusion into blood.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the difference in partial pressure (the diffusion gradient) between alveolar air and deoxygenated blood for oxygen and for carbon dioxide.
parts.answer: Oxygen: 8.0 kPa; carbon dioxide: 0.8 kPa

parts.label: c
parts.text: Carbon dioxide still diffuses out of the blood as quickly as oxygen diffuses in, even though its gradient is much smaller. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide is much more soluble in water (in the moist alveolar lining and plasma) than oxygen, so it diffuses through the barrier faster for a given gradient.
parts.working: 1 mark: CO₂ much more soluble.

practice.stem: In emphysema, the walls between neighbouring alveoli break down and the alveoli merge into larger air spaces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the diameter of the single large air space formed when 10 spherical alveoli of diameter 0.20 mm merge into one sphere with the same total volume. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: M1: volume ∝ d³, so new d³ = 10 × 0.20³. A1: d = 0.20 × ∛10 = 0.431 mm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using surface area = πd², calculate the percentage decrease in surface area for gas exchange. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using your answer to (b), explain why a person with emphysema has low blood oxygen during exercise even though their breathing rate increases.
parts.answer: Surface area for gas exchange is much smaller, so less oxygen diffuses into the blood per second; during exercise oxygen demand rises (and blood passes the alveoli faster), so faster breathing cannot make up for the lost surface area
parts.working: 1 mark: reduced surface area → less diffusion per second. 1 mark: higher O₂ demand in exercise not met / ventilation cannot compensate.

practice.stem:
Of each breath, 150 cm³ stays in the trachea, bronchi and bronchioles (where no gas exchange happens) and does not reach the alveoli.
Breathing pattern 1: 500 cm³ per breath, 12 breaths per minute.
Breathing pattern 2: 250 cm³ per breath, 24 breaths per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that both patterns move the same volume of air into the lungs per minute.
parts.answer: Both 6000 cm³ per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of fresh air reaching the alveoli per minute for each pattern.
parts.answer: Pattern 1: 4200 cm³ min⁻¹; pattern 2: 2400 cm³ min⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in alveolar ventilation for pattern 2 compared with pattern 1. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why rapid, shallow breathing is less effective for gas exchange.
parts.answer: A larger fraction of each breath only fills the airways, so less fresh air reaches the alveoli; alveolar oxygen falls and carbon dioxide rises, so concentration gradients with the blood are less steep and diffusion is slower
parts.working: 1 mark: less fresh air to alveoli. 1 mark: smaller gradients → slower diffusion of O₂ in / CO₂ out.

practice.stem:
Rate of diffusion ∝ (surface area × difference in partial pressure) ÷ thickness of the exchange surface.
Athlete: surface area 70 m²; partial pressure difference 8 kPa; thickness 0.5 µm
Patient with lung disease: surface area 45 m²; partial pressure difference 6 kPa; thickness 0.8 µm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times faster oxygen would diffuse into the blood of the athlete than into the blood of the patient. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 3.32 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest which ONE of the three changes in the patient has the greatest effect on the rate, and justify your answer with a calculation.
parts.answer: The increase in thickness: it reduces the rate by a factor of 0.8 ÷ 0.5 = 1.60, compared with 70 ÷ 45 = 1.56 for the smaller surface area and 8 ÷ 6 = 1.33 for the smaller partial pressure difference
parts.working: B1: increase in thickness (factor 1.60). B1: compared with surface area (1.56) and gradient (1.33).

practice.stem: An alveolar capillary is 0.75 mm long. At rest, blood flows through it at a mean speed of 1.0 mm per second.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time a red blood cell spends in this capillary at rest.

parts.label: b
parts.text: During hard exercise the blood flows three times faster. Calculate the new time in the capillary.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Oxygen loading of a red blood cell is complete about 0.25 s after it enters the capillary in a healthy person. Explain why a person with thickened alveolar walls may have normal blood oxygen at rest but low blood oxygen during exercise.
parts.answer: Thicker walls slow diffusion, so loading takes longer than 0.25 s; at rest there is still enough time (0.75 s) to load fully; during exercise the time falls to 0.25 s, which is not enough, so blood leaves partly oxygenated
parts.working: 1 mark: diffusion slower / takes longer. 1 mark: at rest transit time long enough. 1 mark: exercise transit time too short → incomplete loading.

practice.stem: At rest, 5.0 dm³ of blood flows through the lungs per minute. Blood leaving the lungs contains 200 cm³ of oxygen per dm³, and blood arriving at the lungs contains 150 cm³ of oxygen per dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen taken up by the blood in the lungs per minute at rest.
parts.answer: 250 cm³ per minute
parts.working: M1: 200 − 150 = 50 cm³ per dm³. A1: 50 × 5.0 = 250 cm³ min⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: During intense exercise, blood flow through the lungs rises to 20 dm³ per minute and the oxygen content of blood arriving at the lungs falls to 50 cm³ per dm³. Assuming blood leaving the lungs still contains 200 cm³ per dm³, calculate the factor by which oxygen uptake increases.
parts.answer: 12 times (3000 cm³ per minute)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how features of the alveoli and their blood supply make this large increase in oxygen uptake possible.
parts.answer: Very large total surface area of alveoli (and capillaries) — extra capillaries open; short diffusion distance (squamous epithelium and endothelium one cell thick); steeper concentration gradient because returning blood has less oxygen and ventilation increases
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: large surface area; short diffusion distance; steeper gradient (lower venous O₂); increased ventilation; increased blood flow carries O₂ away.

practice.stem: Some cells in the alveolar walls secrete surfactant, a mixture of phospholipids and proteins that spreads over the water film lining the alveoli and lowers its surface tension. Babies born very early may not yet make enough surfactant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the alveoli of a premature baby lacking surfactant tend to collapse after each breath.
parts.answer: Without surfactant the surface tension of the water film is high; the water molecules pull the alveolar walls inwards (cohesion), so the alveoli collapse when air leaves at expiration
parts.working: 1 mark: high surface tension (cohesion between water molecules). 1 mark: pulls walls together / alveoli collapse.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the baby's blood oxygen concentration is low.
parts.answer: Collapsed alveoli are not ventilated, so the surface area available for gas exchange is reduced; less oxygen diffuses into the blood
parts.working: 1 mark: reduced surface area / fewer alveoli open. 1 mark: less diffusion of O₂.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the baby has to use much more energy to breathe.
parts.answer: Each breath must re-inflate collapsed alveoli against high surface tension, which needs greater muscle effort
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Data for three mammal species:
Species P: body mass 0.025 kg; total alveolar surface area 0.10 m²
Species Q: body mass 2.0 kg; total alveolar surface area 4.4 m²
Species R: body mass 65 kg; total alveolar surface area 72 m²

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the alveolar surface area per kg of body mass for each species. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: P 4.00 m² kg⁻¹; Q 2.20 m² kg⁻¹; R 1.11 m² kg⁻¹
parts.working: M1: area ÷ mass for at least one. A1: all three correct (0.10/0.025 = 4.00; 4.4/2.0 = 2.20; 72/65 = 1.11).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the relationship between body mass and alveolar surface area per kg.
parts.answer: As body mass increases, alveolar surface area per kg decreases
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest an explanation for this relationship.
parts.answer: Smaller mammals have a larger surface area : volume ratio, so lose heat faster to the surroundings; they have a higher metabolic rate / respiration rate per kg to maintain body temperature; so need to absorb more oxygen per kg of body mass
parts.working: 1 mark each: larger SA:V / more heat loss; higher metabolic/respiration rate per kg; greater O₂ demand per kg → more alveolar area needed.

practice.stem:
One student in Islamabad skipped for different lengths of time and measured her pulse rate immediately afterwards, resting for 15 minutes between trials.
0 min: 72 beats per minute
1 min: 98 beats per minute
2 min: 118 beats per minute
3 min: 131 beats per minute
4 min: 134 beats per minute

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between the duration of skipping and the pulse rate.
parts.answer: Pulse rate increases as duration increases, from 72 beats per minute at rest to 134 after 4 minutes; the increase gets smaller each minute and the rate levels off between 3 and 4 minutes.
parts.working: B1 positive relationship / increases; B1 levels off (increase of only 3 between 3 and 4 min) with data quote.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in pulse rate after 2 minutes compared with resting.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why these results cannot be used to draw a conclusion about all students.
parts.answer: Only one student was tested (no repeats, no range of ages, fitness or sex).
parts.working: B1 single individual / small sample.

practice.stem:
A student counted the stomata in ten fields of view on each surface of bean (Phaseolus) leaves.
upper surface: mean 36 stomata per mm², standard deviation 9
lower surface: mean 248 stomata per mm², standard deviation 22

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the stomatal density on the two surfaces.
parts.answer: The lower surface has many more stomata (mean 248 per mm²) than the upper surface (mean 36 per mm²), about seven times as many; the lower surface also shows more variation (SD 22 compared with 9).
parts.working: B1 lower surface has more stomata, with figures; B1 comparison of spread (SD) or ratio ≈ 7 times.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an advantage to the plant of having most stomata on the lower surface.
parts.answer: Less water loss by transpiration, because the lower surface is shaded and cooler / not in direct sunlight.
parts.working: B1 reduces water loss (cooler, shaded, less air movement).

practice.stem:
A student in Peshawar mixed 2 cm³ of yeast suspension with 2 cm³ of glucose solution and 1 cm³ of dilute methylene blue in a test tube at 35 °C. Methylene blue becomes colourless when it is reduced by hydrogen released in respiration. The time for the blue colour to disappear was recorded.
glucose 0 %: no colour change after 600 s
glucose 1 %: 312 s
glucose 2 %: 205 s
glucose 3 %: 158 s
glucose 4 %: 151 s
glucose 5 %: 149 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of glucose concentration on the time taken for the methylene blue to decolourise.
parts.answer: As glucose concentration increases from 1 % to 3 % the time falls steeply (312 s to 158 s); above 3 % the time falls only slightly / levels off (151 s, 149 s); no decolourisation without glucose.
parts.working: B1 time decreases as concentration increases; B1 levels off above 3 % with data quoted (or no change in 600 s at 0 %).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The rate of decolourisation can be found as 1000 ÷ time. Calculate the rate for 2 % glucose. Give your answer to 3 significant figures and state the unit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student concluded: 'The rate of respiration of yeast is directly proportional to the glucose concentration.' Use the data to explain whether this conclusion is supported.
parts.answer: Not supported: doubling glucose from 2 % to 4 % does not double the rate (205 s → 151 s, rate 4.88 → 6.62 s⁻¹); rate levels off at high concentration.
parts.working: B1 not supported; B1 calculated or quoted comparison showing rate not doubling / plateau.

practice.stem:
Strips of red onion epidermis were placed in sodium chloride solutions for 20 minutes. For each strip, 100 cells were observed with a light microscope and the number of plasmolysed cells was counted.
0.00 mol dm⁻³: 0 %
0.10 mol dm⁻³: 4 %
0.20 mol dm⁻³: 18 %
0.30 mol dm⁻³: 42 %
0.40 mol dm⁻³: 76 %
0.50 mol dm⁻³: 95 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between sodium chloride concentration and the percentage of plasmolysed cells.
parts.answer: Percentage plasmolysed increases as concentration increases; few cells plasmolysed up to 0.10 mol dm⁻³, steepest increase between 0.20 and 0.40 mol dm⁻³, almost all (95 %) at 0.50 mol dm⁻³.
parts.working: B1 positive trend; B1 detail with data (e.g. steepest rise 0.30–0.40, 95 % at 0.50).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming a straight line between the two readings either side of 50 %, estimate the sodium chloride concentration at which 50 % of the cells are plasmolysed. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 0.32 mol dm⁻³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what can be concluded about the epidermal cells at the concentration found in (b).
parts.answer: This is incipient plasmolysis: the water potential of the solution is about equal to the (mean) water potential of the cell contents / cell sap; cells vary, so half have lower and half higher water potential.
parts.working: B1 water potential of solution ≈ water potential of cells; B1 idea of an average / cells differ in water potential.

practice.stem:
A student placed single Daphnia (water fleas) in caffeine solutions for 5 minutes and counted heartbeats using a microscope. Each value is the mean for 5 Daphnia.
0 mg dm⁻³: 212 beats per minute
10 mg dm⁻³: 228 beats per minute
20 mg dm⁻³: 241 beats per minute
40 mg dm⁻³: 262 beats per minute
80 mg dm⁻³: 270 beats per minute

parts.label: a
parts.text: The hypothesis was: 'The heart rate of Daphnia increases as caffeine concentration increases.' State whether the results support the hypothesis and give a reason using the data.
parts.answer: Supported (partly): heart rate rises from 212 to 270 beats per minute between 0 and 80 mg dm⁻³; but the increase is much smaller between 40 and 80 mg dm⁻³ (262 to 270).
parts.working: B1 supports with data; B1 note that increase slows / levels off at higher concentrations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in heart rate between 0 and 80 mg dm⁻³ caffeine. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the result cannot be used to predict the effect of caffeine on human heart rate.
parts.answer: Daphnia is a different organism (invertebrate, ectotherm, different heart/regulation and metabolism of caffeine); concentrations reaching the human heart are unknown.
parts.working: B1 any one valid reason.

practice.stem:
100 wheat grains were placed on filter paper soaked in sodium chloride solutions of different concentration. The percentage that germinated after 7 days was recorded.
0 mmol dm⁻³: 96 %
50 mmol dm⁻³: 90 %
100 mmol dm⁻³: 71 %
150 mmol dm⁻³: 38 %
200 mmol dm⁻³: 9 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a conclusion that can be drawn from the data.
parts.answer: Increasing salt concentration decreases the percentage germination of wheat seeds (most sharply above 50 mmol dm⁻³).
parts.working: B1 higher salt concentration → lower germination.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your knowledge of water potential to explain the results.
parts.answer: Salt lowers the water potential of the solution; the water potential gradient between the solution and the seed is reduced (or reversed), so less water enters the seed by osmosis; water is needed to activate enzymes / mobilise food stores (e.g. amylase hydrolysing starch) so fewer seeds germinate.
parts.working: B1 solution has lower (more negative) water potential; B1 less water absorbed by osmosis / imbibition; B1 water needed for enzyme activity / hydrolysis of stores / cell expansion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Farmers in parts of Punjab have soils that are becoming more saline. Suggest one further investigation that would help them choose which wheat variety to plant.
parts.answer: Compare germination (or growth) of several varieties at the same salt concentrations found in their soil.
parts.working: B1 compare different varieties at a range of salt concentrations / test using their own soil samples.

practice.stem:
A microbiologist in Lahore spread a lawn of bacteria on agar plates and placed four discs, each soaked in a different antibiotic, P, Q, R and S, on each plate. After 24 hours the diameter of the clear zone around each disc was measured on 6 plates.
P: mean 18.2 mm, standard deviation 1.1 mm
Q: mean 24.6 mm, standard deviation 3.8 mm
R: mean 22.9 mm, standard deviation 1.2 mm
S: mean 9.5 mm, standard deviation 0.6 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text: The paper discs had a diameter of 6 mm. Calculate the mean area of the clear zone for antibiotic R, not including the area of the disc. Use π = 3.14 or the π key. Give your answer to the nearest mm².
parts.answer: 384 mm²

parts.label: b
parts.text: The microbiologist concluded that antibiotic Q was the most effective. Use the data to evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: Q has the largest mean diameter, so supports; but Q has a very large standard deviation (3.8 mm) so results are variable; mean ± SD for Q (20.8–28.4 mm) overlaps R (21.7–24.1 mm), so the difference between Q and R may not be significant; a t-test would be needed.
parts.working: B1 Q largest mean; B1 Q large SD / less reliable; B1 overlap of ranges with R so difference may not be significant / need statistical test.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons, other than how effective each antibiotic is at killing bacteria, why the clear zones might differ in size.
parts.answer: Antibiotics diffuse through agar at different rates (molecule size/solubility); different concentration or amount of antibiotic on each disc; different time for diffusion before bacterial growth.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem:
A leafy shoot of a guava plant was set up in a potometer. A fan was placed at different distances from the shoot to give different air speeds, and the rate of water uptake was measured.
0 m s⁻¹: 4.2 mm³ min⁻¹
1 m s⁻¹: 7.9 mm³ min⁻¹
2 m s⁻¹: 10.8 mm³ min⁻¹
3 m s⁻¹: 12.0 mm³ min⁻¹
4 m s⁻¹: 12.3 mm³ min⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of air speed on the rate of water uptake.
parts.answer: Rate increases as air speed increases from 0 to 3 m s⁻¹ (4.2 to 12.0 mm³ min⁻¹); the increase is smaller at higher speeds and rate almost levels off between 3 and 4 m s⁻¹ (12.0 to 12.3).
parts.working: B1 increase; B1 levels off with data quoted.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your knowledge of transpiration to explain the results.
parts.answer: Moving air removes the layer of humid air / water vapour near the stomata; this keeps the water potential gradient between air spaces in the leaf and the outside air steep; so more water vapour diffuses out of the stomata; at high air speed another factor limits, e.g. stomatal aperture / rate of evaporation from mesophyll cell walls / stomata may partly close.
parts.working: B1 humid layer removed; B1 steeper water potential / water vapour gradient, faster diffusion through stomata; B1 levelling explained by another limiting factor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the potometer measures the rate of water uptake rather than the rate of transpiration.
parts.answer: Some of the water taken up is used by the shoot (photosynthesis, kept in cells for turgor), so uptake is not exactly equal to water lost.

practice.stem:
Lipase was added to full-cream milk containing sodium carbonate solution and phenolphthalein indicator, which is pink in alkaline conditions. As fatty acids are released the pH falls and the pink colour disappears. The time taken for the colour to disappear was recorded at five temperatures.
15 °C: 540 s
25 °C: 290 s
35 °C: 170 s
45 °C: 205 s
55 °C: 610 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate (1000 ÷ time, in s⁻¹) at each temperature. Give each value to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 1000 ÷ time; A1 all five correct to 2 d.p.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student concluded that the optimum temperature of lipase is 35 °C. Explain why this conclusion is not fully justified and describe how the experiment could be changed to find the optimum more precisely.
parts.answer: Readings are 10 °C apart, so the optimum could be anywhere between 25 °C and 45 °C (rate at 45 °C is quite high, so likely between 35 and 45 °C); repeat with smaller intervals, e.g. every 2 °C from 30 °C to 44 °C; repeat each temperature at least three times and calculate means.
parts.working: B1 interval too large / optimum between 25 and 45 °C; B1 extra temperatures at smaller intervals around 35–45 °C; B1 replicates and means.

practice.stem: A student measured the light intensity and the height of 12 plants of one species growing along a path from under trees into open ground. Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, rs, was calculated as 0.81.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the value of rs shows about the relationship between the two variables.
parts.answer: A strong positive correlation: plants receiving more light grew taller.
parts.working: B1 strong positive correlation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The critical value of rs at p = 0.05 for 12 pairs of readings is 0.587. State what the student can conclude.
parts.answer: 0.81 > 0.587 so the null hypothesis (no correlation) is rejected; the positive correlation is significant – the probability it is due to chance is less than 5 %.
parts.working: B1 compares rs with critical value correctly; B1 reject null / significant correlation (not due to chance).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student then concluded that light intensity causes plants to grow taller. Explain why this conclusion is not fully justified by the data.
parts.answer: Correlation does not show cause; other factors that vary with light in the field (e.g. soil moisture, temperature, nutrient levels, trampling) were not controlled and may affect height.
parts.working: B1 correlation ≠ causation; B1 named uncontrolled variable that could vary with position.

practice.stem:
Potato cylinders were left in sucrose solutions for 24 hours. The mean percentage change in mass was:
0 mol dm⁻³: +12.4 %
0.2 mol dm⁻³: +5.8 %
0.4 mol dm⁻³: −1.6 %
0.6 mol dm⁻³: −7.9 %
0.8 mol dm⁻³: −12.1 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Estimate the sucrose concentration at which there would be no change in mass, assuming a straight line between the two readings either side of zero. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 0.36 mol dm⁻³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what this concentration tells you about the potato tissue.
parts.answer: At this concentration the water potential of the sucrose solution equals the water potential of the potato cells, so there is no net movement of water by osmosis.
parts.working: B1 water potential of tissue = water potential of solution; B1 no net osmosis / no net water movement.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the results are given as percentage change in mass rather than change in mass.
parts.answer: The cylinders had different starting masses, so percentage change allows a fair comparison.
parts.working: B1 different initial masses.

practice.stem:
Students measured their reaction time using a ruler-drop test after drinking either an energy drink or water.
energy drink: mean 0.250 s, standard error 0.007 s
water: mean 0.270 s, standard error 0.0085 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the 95 % confidence interval (mean ± 2 × SE) for each group.
parts.answer: Energy drink: 0.236 to 0.264 s; water: 0.253 to 0.287 s

parts.label: b
parts.text: The company that makes the drink claims that it 'significantly improves reaction time'. Use the data to evaluate this claim.
parts.answer: Mean reaction time is shorter after the drink (0.250 s compared with 0.270 s), but the confidence intervals overlap (0.253–0.264 s), so the difference is not shown to be significant; also the sample size, whether the trial was blind, and other variables (sleep, time of day, practice effect) are not stated.
parts.working: B1 mean is lower with drink; B1 confidence intervals overlap so difference not significant; B1 further limitation (sample size / no placebo or blinding / practice effect / variables not controlled).

practice.stem:
The chlorophyll content of mango leaves was measured in an orchard near Multan. Two leaves from the sunny outer canopy and two leaves from the shaded inner canopy were taken from each of 8 trees (n = 16 in each group).
sun leaves: mean 1.42 mg chlorophyll per g fresh mass, standard deviation 0.24
shade leaves: mean 1.86 mg chlorophyll per g fresh mass, standard deviation 0.32

parts.label: a
parts.text: The 95 % confidence interval is mean ± 2 × standard error, where standard error = SD ÷ √n. Calculate the 95 % confidence interval for each group. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: sun leaves: 1.30 to 1.54 mg g⁻¹; shade leaves: 1.70 to 2.02 mg g⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the confidence intervals show about the difference in chlorophyll content between sun and shade leaves.
parts.answer: The intervals do not overlap, so the difference is (very likely) significant / not due to chance; shade leaves have a higher chlorophyll content per gram.
parts.working: B1 no overlap → significant; B1 shade higher.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a higher chlorophyll content is an advantage to leaves in the shade.
parts.answer: Light intensity is low in the shade, so light is the limiting factor; more chlorophyll (more photosystems) absorbs a greater proportion of the available light, so more light-dependent reaction / ATP and reduced NADP for photosynthesis.
parts.working: B1 low light intensity limiting; B1 absorbs more of available light → more photosynthesis.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the leaves in both groups were taken from the same 8 trees.
parts.answer: To control genetic differences / age / health of trees between groups, so only light (position) differs.

practice.stem: Students measured the nitrate concentration and the number of algal cells per cm³ of water in 10 farm ponds near Sheikhupura. They calculated Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, rs = 0.89.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a null hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: There is no correlation between nitrate concentration and the density of algal cells in the ponds.
parts.working: B1 must refer to correlation and both variables (not 'no difference').

parts.label: b
parts.text: The critical value of rs for 10 pairs at p = 0.05 is 0.648. State what can be concluded from rs = 0.89.
parts.answer: 0.89 is greater than 0.648, so reject the null hypothesis; there is a significant positive correlation between nitrate concentration and algal density (probability of this being due to chance is less than 5 %).
parts.working: B1 compare with critical value, reject null hypothesis; B1 significant positive correlation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The students also calculated rs = −0.55 between nitrate concentration and the number of invertebrate species found in each pond. Using the same critical value, state and explain what this result shows.
parts.answer: There is a negative correlation, but 0.55 (ignoring the sign) is less than 0.648, so it is not significant at p = 0.05; accept the null hypothesis – the apparent trend could be due to chance (more ponds would need to be sampled).
parts.working: B1 compares magnitude 0.55 with 0.648 (sign ignored), not significant / accept null hypothesis; B1 trend may be due to chance / no significant correlation shown.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A farmers' group said: 'The data prove that nitrate fertiliser running off fields causes the growth of algae.' Discuss whether this statement is justified.
parts.answer: Not justified: correlation does not show cause; other variables may vary with nitrate, e.g. phosphate, temperature, light / pond depth; the source of the nitrate was not identified (could be animal waste or sewage); only 10 ponds sampled once, so "prove" is too strong; but a causal link is plausible because algae need nitrogen to make amino acids and nucleotides; an experiment adding nitrate to identical tanks would test cause.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: correlation ≠ causation; named other variable; source of nitrate not shown; small sample / single sampling; biological reason it is plausible; suggested controlled experiment.

practice.stem:
The rate of photosynthesis of the pondweed Cabomba was measured by counting bubbles per minute at different light intensities (arbitrary units) in two sodium hydrogencarbonate concentrations, at 25 °C.
light intensity: 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10
low hydrogencarbonate (0.01 mol dm⁻³): 6, 11, 19, 23, 24, 24
high hydrogencarbonate (0.05 mol dm⁻³): 6, 12, 23, 34, 41, 42

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Identify the factor limiting the rate of photosynthesis at the low hydrogencarbonate concentration
(i) at light intensities 1 and 2
(ii) at light intensities 8 and 10.
Give a reason for each answer.
parts.answer: (i) light intensity – rate is the same at both hydrogencarbonate concentrations / rate rises as light rises; (ii) carbon dioxide (hydrogencarbonate) concentration – rate no longer rises with light but is higher with more hydrogencarbonate.
parts.working: B1 each with reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the rate at light intensity 10 when the hydrogencarbonate concentration is increased. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The rate at the high hydrogencarbonate concentration levels off at about 42 bubbles per minute. Suggest two factors that could be limiting the rate at this point.
parts.answer: Temperature; amount / activity of rubisco (enzymes of the Calvin cycle); amount of chlorophyll / number of chloroplasts; carbon dioxide still limiting.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using a 1.0 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution and distilled water, describe how to make 10 cm³ of each of 1.0, 0.8, 0.6, 0.4 and 0.2 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solutions. Present the volumes in a table.
parts.answer: 1.0 mol dm⁻³: 10.0 cm³ sucrose + 0.0 cm³ water; 0.8 mol dm⁻³: 8.0 cm³ sucrose + 2.0 cm³ water; 0.6 mol dm⁻³: 6.0 cm³ sucrose + 4.0 cm³ water; 0.4 mol dm⁻³: 4.0 cm³ sucrose + 6.0 cm³ water; 0.2 mol dm⁻³: 2.0 cm³ sucrose + 8.0 cm³ water
parts.working: B1 correct volumes of stock (concentration ÷ 1.0 × 10 cm³); B1 correct water volumes making 10 cm³ each, table with headings and units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a simple dilution was used here rather than a serial dilution.
parts.answer: The concentrations form an even (linear) series; a serial dilution gives concentrations that fall by the same factor each time (e.g. halving).
parts.working: B1 equal intervals needed / serial dilution gives proportional (e.g. 1.0, 0.5, 0.25) concentrations.

practice.stem: A student in Rawalpindi is preparing solutions for an investigation into the hydrolysis of starch by amylase.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using a 2.0 % starch solution and distilled water, describe how to make 20 cm³ of each of these starch concentrations: 0.25 %, 0.50 %, 1.00 %, 1.50 % and 2.00 %. Show the volumes in a table.
parts.working: B1 table with headings and units (concentration / %, volume of 2.0 % starch / cm³, volume of water / cm³); B1 starch volumes correct; B1 water volumes correct (each pair totals 20 cm³).

parts.label: b
