practice.subtopic: Skill: recording results in a table
practice.stem:
Catalase from mung bean extract was added to hydrogen peroxide and the total volume of oxygen in a gas syringe was read every 30 s.
0 s: 0.0 cm³; 30 s: 4.2 cm³; 60 s: 8.0 cm³; 90 s: 11.3 cm³; 120 s: 13.9 cm³; 150 s: 15.8 cm³; 180 s: 17.0 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a table showing time, total volume and volume produced in each 30 s interval.
parts.working: B1 headings with units; B1 total volumes recorded to 1 d.p.; B1 interval volumes correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of oxygen production over the first 2 minutes in cm³ min⁻¹.
parts.answer: 6.95 cm³ min⁻¹ (allow 7.0)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the table to explain why the rate decreases.
parts.answer: Volume per interval falls (4.2 → 1.2 cm³); substrate (hydrogen peroxide) is used up, so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form per unit time.
parts.working: B1 data; B1 substrate concentration falls.

practice.subtopic: Skill: recording results in a table
practice.stem: A student investigates the effect of both temperature (20, 30 and 40 °C) and pH (5, 7 and 9) on the activity of an amylase.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a single results table that would show the mean rate for every combination of temperature and pH.
parts.answer: A grid: rows for temperature / °C (20, 30, 40) and columns for pH (5, 7, 9) under a heading 'mean rate of reaction / s⁻¹'; each cell is the mean for that combination.
parts.working: B1 two-way layout with both IVs and units; B1 heading for values in cells with unit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many tubes are needed if each combination is tested three times.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why recording raw data from such an experiment in a separate table is still necessary.
parts.answer: Means hide variation/anomalies; raw data allow reliability to be judged and anomalies identified.

practice.subtopic: Skill: recording results in a table
practice.stem: A student timed how long it took for a colour change in tubes with different concentrations of enzyme. She stopped timing at 600 s. Tube 1 (lowest concentration) showed no change in 600 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the student should record the result for tube 1, which had not changed after 600 s.
parts.answer: Write '> 600' (or 'no colour change after 600 s') rather than 0 or 600, so it is clear that the end point was not reached; explain in a note under the table.
parts.working: B1 '> 600' / no change recorded; B1 not 0 or 600 (would be misleading).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a rate cannot be calculated for tube 1 and state how this result should be shown on a graph of rate against concentration.
parts.answer: The time is unknown, so 1 ÷ time cannot be found (rate is less than 1/600 s⁻¹); it can be plotted as approximately zero / shown with an arrow below 1.7 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹, or omitted with a note.
parts.working: B1 time unknown; B1 suitable way of showing it.

practice.subtopic: Skill: recording results in a table
practice.stem:
The time taken for a piece of pondweed to release 10 bubbles was measured with a lamp at different distances.
10 cm: 48 s; 15 cm: 67 s; 20 cm: 95 s; 25 cm: 143 s; 30 cm: 260 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a table with columns for distance, time and rate. Calculate the rates (1000 ÷ time) to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: B1 headings with units; B1 raw times as whole seconds; M1 1000 ÷ time; A1 all rates to 3 s.f., including 6.99 and 3.85.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rates are given to 3 significant figures rather than a fixed number of decimal places.
parts.answer: The raw times are given to 2–3 significant figures; using 3 s.f. keeps the same precision for large and small values (2 decimal places would give 20.83, which is 4 s.f., but 3.85, which is 3 s.f.).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether a line graph, a bar chart or a histogram should be used for each set of data. Give a reason for each.
(i) mean mass of seeds from five varieties of sunflower
(ii) volume of oxygen released by catalase every minute for 10 minutes
(iii) the number of students in each class of hand span: 16–17.9 cm, 18–19.9 cm, 20–21.9 cm, 22–23.9 cm
parts.answer: (i) bar chart – independent variable is categoric (variety); (ii) line graph – both variables continuous; (iii) histogram – frequencies of a continuous variable grouped into classes, bars touching.
parts.working: B1 each with reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one rule for drawing the bars in a bar chart that differs from a histogram.
parts.answer: Bars in a bar chart are separate (gaps between bars, same width); in a histogram bars touch.

practice.stem:
Volume of oxygen released by yeast catalase and hydrogen peroxide:
0 min: 0.0 cm³; 1 min: 2.4 cm³; 2 min: 4.9 cm³; 3 min: 7.3 cm³; 4 min: 9.8 cm³; 5 min: 11.0 cm³; 6 min: 11.6 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the time interval during which the rate of oxygen release is constant. Give a reason.
parts.answer: 0 to 4 minutes – the volume increases by about the same amount (about 2.4–2.5 cm³) each minute, giving a straight line.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the gradient of the line between 1 and 4 minutes, with units. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 2.47 cm³ min⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the graph changes after 4 minutes and suggest why.
parts.answer: The gradient decreases / the curve levels off (11.0 then 11.6 cm³); substrate is being used up / hydrogen peroxide concentration falling.
parts.working: B1 levels off with data; B1 reason.

practice.stem: A student must plot data on graph paper that has 8 large squares across and 12 large squares up (each large square is 2 cm). The temperatures used were 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 °C and the volumes of gas collected ranged from 2.1 cm³ to 17.4 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which variable should be plotted on each axis.
parts.answer: temperature on the x-axis; volume of gas on the y-axis

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a suitable scale for each axis and explain why your scales are suitable.
parts.answer: x-axis: 1 large square (2 cm) = 10 °C, 0 to 60 °C uses 6 of 8 squares; y-axis: 1 large square = 2 cm³, 0 to 18 cm³ uses 9 of 12 squares; both scales are easy to read (multiples of 1, 2, 5, 10) and use more than half the grid in each direction.
parts.working: B1 x scale; B1 y scale; B1 reason – plotted points occupy at least half the grid and scale is easy to read (not 3s or 7s).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The axis labels should include units. Write the full label for each axis.
parts.answer: temperature / °C; volume of gas collected / cm³
parts.working: B1 both.

practice.stem: A student drew a graph of the height of a germinating maize seedling against time. The graph had: an x-axis labelled 'time' with no units; a y-axis scale of 0, 5, 10, 20, 40 mm at equal spacing; large blobs for points; a thick line drawn freehand from the origin (where no reading had been taken) through every point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify four faults in this graph and state how each should be corrected.
parts.answer: Line drawn through the origin without a reading at 0 – start the line at the first plotted point; points plotted as large dots – use small crosses (×) or dots in circles; x-axis label has no unit – 'time / min'; y-axis scale uneven (0, 5, 10, 20, 40) – use an even scale; line drawn freehand / thick – use a thin ruled line or smooth curve; points joined dot-to-dot with a curve – use a line of best fit or ruled lines.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four faults with corrections.

practice.stem:
Percentage change in mass of onion tissue in salt solutions:
0 mol dm⁻³: +8.2 %
0.1 mol dm⁻³: +4.9 %
0.2 mol dm⁻³: +2.1 %
0.3 mol dm⁻³: −1.0 %
0.4 mol dm⁻³: −3.8 %
0.5 mol dm⁻³: −6.9 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how you would draw a graph of these results.
parts.answer: Concentration (mol dm⁻³) on the x-axis, percentage change in mass on the y-axis, with the x-axis crossing at 0 % and the y-axis extending to negative values; axes labelled with units; scales even and using more than half the grid; points plotted as small crosses; ruled line of best fit (or smooth curve) through the points.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: correct axes with labels and units; negative values shown / x-axis at y = 0; suitable linear scales; accurate plotting; line of best fit (not extended beyond data).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how you would use your graph to find the concentration of salt solution at which there is no change in mass, and explain why the line of best fit should be used rather than the two plotted points nearest to zero.
parts.answer: Find where the line of best fit crosses the line of 0 % change in mass (the x-axis) and read the concentration vertically down from that point; the line of best fit uses all six readings, so it reduces the effect of an error in any single reading.
parts.working: B1 read the x-value where the line crosses 0 % change (draw a vertical guide line to the x-axis); B1 line of best fit is based on all the data / averages out random errors in individual points (answer about 0.27 mol dm⁻³).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete a frequency table using the classes 30–34, 35–39, 40–44, 45–49, 50–54 and 55–59 mm.
parts.working: M1 tally method / at least four classes correct; A1 all correct (total 20).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how to draw a histogram of these data.
parts.answer: x-axis: leaf length / mm with class boundaries on a continuous scale; y-axis: frequency (number of leaves); bars of equal width touching each other, height = frequency.
parts.working: B1 axes with labels; B1 touching bars of equal width.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the shape of the histogram suggests about the distribution of leaf length.
parts.answer: Roughly normal distribution – most leaves near the middle class (40–44 mm), fewer at either extreme (continuous variation).

practice.stem: A student plotted the amount of product formed by a phosphatase against time. The curve started at the origin and levelled off after about 6 minutes. A tangent drawn to the curve at time zero passed through the origin and through the point (50 s, 2.4 µmol).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the initial rate of reaction in µmol min⁻¹ from the tangent.
parts.answer: 2.88 µmol min⁻¹
parts.working: M1 gradient 2.4 ÷ 50 = 0.048 µmol s⁻¹; A1 × 60 = 2.88 µmol min⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the initial rate is used to compare enzyme activity rather than the mean rate over 10 minutes.
parts.answer: At the start the substrate concentration is known / highest and not yet limiting; later the rate falls as substrate is used up (or product inhibits), so the mean rate depends on how long the reaction ran.
parts.working: B1 substrate concentration known/not depleted; B1 rate falls later.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the student should draw the tangent at time zero.
parts.answer: Use a ruler to draw a straight line that touches the curve at the origin and follows its initial slope, extended across a large part of the grid to read the gradient.

practice.stem:
Glucose standards were reacted with a reagent that forms a coloured product, and absorbance was measured.
0.0 %: 0.02; 0.2 %: 0.18; 0.4 %: 0.35; 0.6 %: 0.51; 0.8 %: 0.66; 1.0 %: 0.80
A diluted sample of sugarcane juice gave an absorbance of 0.43.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the calibration data, assuming a straight line between the two nearest standards, to find the glucose concentration of the diluted juice.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The juice had been diluted 10 times before testing. Calculate the glucose concentration of the undiluted juice.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the juice was diluted before testing.
parts.answer: So that its absorbance fell within the range of the calibration standards (0–1.0 %), where the curve can be used; reading outside the range would need extrapolation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each set of data state whether the points should be joined by a line of best fit (straight or curved) or by ruled straight lines from point to point, and explain why.
(i) rate of an enzyme reaction at 10 °C intervals from 10 °C to 70 °C
(ii) the number of a fish species counted in a lake at the end of each month for one year
parts.answer: (i) smooth curve of best fit – temperature and rate are related by a continuous trend and readings contain random error; (ii) ruled lines point to point – the values between months are not known and do not follow a smooth predictable trend.
parts.working: B1 each with reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a line of best fit should not be forced through the origin unless a reading at zero has been taken or is certain.
parts.answer: The origin is an extra data point that was not measured; it may not be true (e.g. reaction may occur at 0 °C or a value may not be zero), so forcing it changes the line and any gradient read from it.
parts.working: B1 not a measured point; B1 effect on line/gradient.

practice.stem:
At a fish hatchery near Muzaffargarh, tilapia fry were fed one of three diets, P, Q and R, for 4 weeks. The mean length of the fry was found (n = 16 fish for each diet).
P: mean 24.6 mm, SD 2.4 mm
Q: mean 27.9 mm, SD 3.2 mm
R: mean 26.0 mm, SD 2.0 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text: The means are to be shown on a bar chart with error bars of ± 2 × SE, where SE = SD ÷ √n. Calculate 2 × SE for each diet and give the upper and lower limits of each error bar. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 SE = SD ÷ 4 (0.6, 0.8, 0.5 mm); A1 2SE values 1.2, 1.6, 1.0 mm; A1 all limits.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which pairs of diets give significantly different mean lengths. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Only P and Q – their error bars (95 % confidence intervals) do not overlap (25.8 < 26.3); R overlaps with both P (25.0 < 25.8) and Q (26.3 < 27.0), so those differences may be due to chance.
parts.working: B1 P and Q only; B1 reasoning based on overlap / non-overlap of error bars.

practice.stem: A student in Faisalabad grew tomato plants with three different fertilisers, A, B and C, and calculated the mean yield per plant and the standard error for each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of chart that should be drawn and describe how the error bars should be added.
parts.answer: A bar chart (fertiliser type is categoric); bars of equal width, not touching; each bar height = mean yield; error bars drawn as a vertical line from mean − 2SE to mean + 2SE (95 % CI) with short horizontal caps.
parts.working: B1 bar chart because categoric independent variable; B1 bars separated, labelled axes with units; B1 error bars extend 2 × SE (or 1 SD as stated) above and below the mean.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The error bars for fertilisers A and B overlap but those for B and C do not. State what this suggests.
parts.answer: The difference between A and B may not be significant (could be due to chance); the difference between B and C is likely to be significant.
parts.working: B1 A and B not significantly different; B1 B and C probably significantly different.

practice.stem:
The number of bacterial cells per cm³ in a culture was measured every hour.
0 h: 2.0 × 10³; 1 h: 2.2 × 10³; 2 h: 8.1 × 10³; 3 h: 3.2 × 10⁴; 4 h: 1.3 × 10⁵; 5 h: 5.1 × 10⁵; 6 h: 9.8 × 10⁵

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate log₁₀ of the number of cells at each time. Give each value to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 log₁₀ used; A1 all correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why log₁₀ (number of cells) is plotted against time rather than the number of cells.
parts.answer: The numbers range over almost three orders of magnitude (2000 to almost a million), so small values could not be read on a linear scale; exponential growth gives a straight line on a log scale, making the log phase easy to identify.
parts.working: B1 wide range; B1 exponential → straight line.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Between 2 h and 4 h the graph is a straight line. Calculate the mean generation (doubling) time in this period, in minutes.
parts.answer: 30 min
parts.working: M1 1.3 × 10⁵ ÷ 8.1 × 10³ = 16 = 2⁴, so 4 generations in 120 min (or log difference 1.20 ÷ log 2 = 4.0); A1 30 min.

practice.stem:
The absorbance of a chlorophyll extract (chlorophyll a and b only) and the relative rate of photosynthesis of the whole leaf were measured at different wavelengths.
wavelength / nm: 400, 450, 500, 550, 600, 650, 700
absorbance: 0.62, 0.85, 0.30, 0.18, 0.25, 0.55, 0.08
relative rate of photosynthesis: 70, 92, 48, 25, 35, 80, 8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how both sets of data could be plotted on one graph.
parts.answer: Wavelength / nm on the x-axis; absorbance on a left-hand y-axis and relative rate of photosynthesis on a right-hand y-axis, each with its own scale; points for each set joined by a different style of line (e.g. solid and dashed) with a key.
parts.working: B1 shared x-axis with two y-axes; B1 different lines and key.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of relative rate of photosynthesis to absorbance at 450 nm and at 500 nm. Give your answers to the nearest whole number.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to (b) to suggest why the rate of photosynthesis at 500 nm is higher than expected from the absorbance of the chlorophyll extract.
parts.answer: The ratio is much higher at 500 nm, so light at 500 nm is absorbed by other (accessory) pigments, such as carotenoids, not present in the chlorophyll extract; they pass energy to chlorophyll a in the photosystems.
parts.working: B1 accessory pigments / carotenoids absorb 500 nm; B1 energy transferred to reaction centre / used in photosynthesis.

practice.stem:
The initial rate of an invertase reaction was measured at different sucrose concentrations.
0.5 mmol dm⁻³: 1.9 µmol min⁻¹
1 mmol dm⁻³: 3.3
2 mmol dm⁻³: 5.0
4 mmol dm⁻³: 6.6
8 mmol dm⁻³: 7.8
16 mmol dm⁻³: 8.4
32 mmol dm⁻³: 8.6

parts.label: a
parts.text: The student estimated Vmax as 8.8 µmol min⁻¹ from where the curve levels off. Explain why Vmax was estimated rather than read from the highest result.
parts.answer: The rate is still rising slightly at 32 mmol dm⁻³; Vmax is only reached at infinite / very high substrate concentration, so the curve approaches but never quite reaches it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Estimate Km, assuming a straight line between the two readings either side of ½Vmax. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 1.6 mmol dm⁻³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a smooth curve drawn through the points would give a more accurate value of Km than the straight-line method in (b).
parts.answer: The true relationship is curved between 1 and 2 mmol dm⁻³, so a straight line between the points gives a slightly wrong value; a curve of best fit also averages out random errors.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A competitive inhibitor was added. State how Vmax and Km would change.
parts.answer: Vmax unchanged (can still be reached at high substrate concentration); Km increases (higher substrate concentration needed to reach ½Vmax).
parts.working: B1 each.

practice.stem:
The percentage cover of a dune grass was recorded along a transect from the strandline at Sandspit beach, Karachi.
0 m: 0 %; 2 m: 12 %; 4 m: 36 %; 6 m: 58 %; 8 m: 40 %; 10 m: 14 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using a scale of 1 mm width = 2 % cover, calculate the half-width (the distance above and below the centre line) of the kite at each distance.
parts.working: M1 total width = % ÷ 2, half-width = % ÷ 4; A1 all correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the kite diagram is drawn and explain why it is useful.
parts.answer: Distance along the transect on the x-axis; for each species a horizontal centre line, with points marked the half-width above and below it and joined to form a symmetrical shape; several species can be drawn one above another on the same distance scale, so changes in distribution along the transect can be compared easily.
parts.working: B1 construction; B1 compares distribution of several species along the transect.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a kite diagram is not suitable for testing whether the cover of this species is correlated with distance.
parts.answer: It only shows the pattern visually; a statistical test (e.g. Spearman's rank) is needed to test for a significant correlation; and the relationship here rises then falls so is not a simple correlation.

practice.stem: A piece of carrot tissue had a mass of 2.45 g. After 4 hours in distilled water its mass was 2.71 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in mass. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of mass change in g per hour over the 4 hours.
parts.answer: 0.065 g per hour

practice.stem: Pieces of potato were added to hydrogen peroxide. At 30 °C it took 40 s to collect 5.0 cm³ of oxygen in an upturned measuring cylinder.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of gas production in cm³ min⁻¹ at 30 °C.
parts.answer: 7.5 cm³ min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: At 20 °C the same volume took 64 s. Calculate how many times faster the reaction was at 30 °C than at 20 °C. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 1.6 times

practice.stem: A student needs sodium chloride solutions of different concentrations for an investigation into osmosis in red blood cells of a goat (from a butcher's shop).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volumes of 0.60 mol dm⁻³ sodium chloride solution and distilled water needed to make 50 cm³ of 0.15 mol dm⁻³ solution.
parts.answer: 12.5 cm³ of 0.60 mol dm⁻³ + 37.5 cm³ water
parts.working: M1 C₁V₁ = C₂V₂: V₁ = 0.15 × 50 ÷ 0.60; A1 12.5 and 37.5 cm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of 0.60 mol dm⁻³ solution needed to make 20 cm³ of 0.24 mol dm⁻³ solution.
parts.answer: 8.0 cm³ (+ 12.0 cm³ water)

practice.stem:
Three cubes of turnip were left in 0.3 mol dm⁻³ sucrose for 1 hour.
cube 1: 1.52 g → 1.47 g
cube 2: 1.48 g → 1.44 g
cube 3: 1.55 g → 1.49 g

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in mass for each cube. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100; A1 all three with negative signs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean percentage change in mass. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the negative sign shows about the movement of water.
parts.answer: The cubes lost mass: water left the cells by osmosis, so the solution has a lower water potential than the tissue.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Convert each value to the unit shown.
(i) 0.35 dm³ to cm³
(ii) 2500 mg to g
(iii) 0.045 mm to µm
(iv) 0.25 mol dm⁻³ to mmol dm⁻³
parts.answer: (i) 350 cm³; (ii) 2.5 g; (iii) 45 µm; (iv) 250 mmol dm⁻³
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A rate of 18 cm³ per hour is to be compared with rates given in cm³ min⁻¹. Convert it.
parts.answer: 0.3 cm³ min⁻¹

practice.stem: A student painted clear nail varnish on the lower surface of a neem leaf, peeled it off and viewed it with a microscope. The diameter of the field of view was 0.40 mm. The numbers of stomata in five fields of view were 14, 17, 15, 13 and 16.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the area of the field of view in mm². Use the π key. Give your answer to 4 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean stomatal density in stomata per mm², to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: 119 stomata per mm²

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the student counted stomata in five fields of view chosen at random.
parts.answer: Stomata are not evenly spread over the leaf (fewer over veins); random fields give a representative mean / avoid bias.

practice.stem: A respirometer contained 2.5 g of germinating sesame seeds and soda lime to absorb carbon dioxide. The coloured liquid in the capillary tube, of internal radius 0.5 mm, moved 34 mm in 5 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen absorbed in 5 minutes, using volume = πr²l. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 26.7 mm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen uptake per gram of seeds per minute. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 2.14 mm³ g⁻¹ min⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate is expressed per gram of seeds.
parts.answer: So that results from samples with different masses of seeds / other experiments can be compared fairly.

practice.stem:
Two respirometers contained the same mass of germinating seeds at 25 °C. In 10 minutes:
with potassium hydroxide (absorbs CO₂): gas volume decreased by 4.8 cm³
with water instead of potassium hydroxide: gas volume decreased by 0.6 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide released in 10 minutes.
parts.answer: 4.2 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the respiratory quotient (RQ = CO₂ released ÷ O₂ absorbed). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what respiratory substrates are being used. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: A mixture of carbohydrate (RQ 1.0) and lipid (RQ about 0.7) / or protein (RQ about 0.9); the value 0.88 lies between them.
parts.working: B1 substrate(s); B1 reference to standard RQ values.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of glucose (Mr = 180) needed to make 250 cm³ of a 0.20 mol dm⁻³ solution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Express the concentration of this solution as a percentage (g per 100 cm³).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the solution should be made up so that its concentration is accurate.
parts.answer: Weigh the glucose on a balance, dissolve in less than 250 cm³ of distilled water in a beaker, transfer to a 250 cm³ volumetric flask with washings and make up to the mark, then mix.
parts.working: B1 dissolve in a smaller volume first; B1 make up to 250 cm³ in volumetric flask / measuring cylinder.

practice.stem: Students at an agricultural college in Tando Jam caught 48 ground beetles in pitfall traps, marked them with a dot of non-toxic paint and released them. Two days later they caught 52 beetles, of which 12 were marked.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the Lincoln index to estimate the population of ground beetles in the field.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two assumptions made in this estimate.
parts.answer: Marks are not lost and do not affect survival/behaviour (e.g. predation); marked beetles mix randomly with the population; no births, deaths, immigration or emigration between samples; all beetles equally likely to be caught.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: Numbers of five species of invertebrate found in leaf litter samples from a garden in Multan: 34, 21, 12, 8, 5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Simpson's index of diversity, D = 1 − Σ(n/N)². Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A second plot near a busy road had D = 0.42. Compare the diversity of the two plots.
parts.answer: The first plot (0.71) is more diverse than the plot near the road (0.42), because D closer to 1 means higher diversity.
parts.working: B1 first plot more diverse; higher D = greater diversity.

practice.stem: A potato cylinder is 4.0 cm long and 1.0 cm in diameter. It is cut across its length into 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 equal pieces. Cutting does not change the total volume.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total surface area of the potato when it is in 1 piece and when it is cut into 16 pieces. Use surface area of a cylinder = 2πrl + 2πr². Give your answers to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 1 piece: 14.14 cm²; 16 pieces: 37.70 cm²
parts.working: M1 curved area 2π × 0.5 × 4 = 12.57 cm² is unchanged by cutting; M1 each piece adds two ends of π × 0.5²; A1 14.14 and 37.70 cm².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the surface area : volume ratio for 1 piece and for 16 pieces. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 volume = π × 0.5² × 4 = 3.14 cm³; A1 4.5 and 12.0.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict how cutting the cylinder into more pieces would affect the initial rate of mass loss in a concentrated salt solution. Explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Initial rate of mass loss increases; larger surface area for the same volume, so more water leaves by osmosis per unit time.
parts.working: B1 prediction; B1 explanation.

practice.stem: A sample of raw milk from a dairy in Okara was serially diluted by factors of 10. 0.1 cm³ of each dilution was spread on agar and incubated. The 10⁻⁵ dilution plate had about 520 colonies and the 10⁻⁶ dilution plate had 47 colonies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of bacteria per cm³ in the original milk sample. Give your answer in standard form.
parts.answer: 4.7 × 10⁸ cells per cm³
parts.working: M1 47 colonies from 0.1 cm³ → 470 per cm³ of diluted sample; M1 × 10⁶ dilution factor; A1 4.7 × 10⁸.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the plate from the 10⁻⁵ dilution was not used.
parts.answer: About 520 colonies – too many to count accurately; colonies merge / overlap so one colony may come from more than one cell.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one assumption made in this calculation.
parts.answer: Each colony grows from a single bacterium; all live bacteria grow on the agar in the conditions used.

practice.stem: Phosphatase releases a yellow product from a colourless substrate. A calibration line showed that absorbance = 0.85 × concentration of product (in mg cm⁻³). The absorbance of the reaction mixture was 0.00 at the start, 0.34 at 2 minutes and 0.68 at 6 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of product at 2 minutes and at 6 minutes.
parts.answer: 2 min: 0.40 mg cm⁻³; 6 min: 0.80 mg cm⁻³
parts.working: B1 each: absorbance ÷ 0.85.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of product formation from 0 to 2 minutes and from 2 to 6 minutes, in mg cm⁻³ min⁻¹.
parts.answer: 0–2 min: 0.20; 2–6 min: 0.10 mg cm⁻³ min⁻¹
parts.working: M1 change in concentration ÷ time; A1 0.20 and 0.10.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the rate between 2 and 6 minutes is lower.
parts.answer: Substrate concentration falls as it is used, so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form per unit time (or product inhibition).

practice.stem: A 0.50 g piece of cashew nut was burned under a boiling tube containing 20 cm³ of water. The temperature of the water rose by 45 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy released per gram of cashew nut in kJ g⁻¹. Energy = mass of water × 4.2 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ × temperature rise, and 1 cm³ of water has a mass of 1 g. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 7.56 kJ g⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: The energy content of cashew nuts given on the packet is 23 kJ g⁻¹. Calculate the student's value as a percentage of this. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the student's value is lower, and one improvement.
parts.answer: Heat lost to the air / surroundings and to the tube; incomplete burning (black residue); heat used to warm the boiling tube/thermometer; improvement: use a calorimeter with insulation / a lid / burn in oxygen / bring the tube closer and shield from draughts.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two reasons; 1 mark for improvement.

practice.stem: Students cut samples of potato, apple and onion with scalpels, crushed them with water, and tested the extracts with iodine solution and with Benedict's solution in a boiling water bath.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three hazards in this practical and state a precaution for each.
parts.answer: e.g. scalpel – sharp, cut on a tile away from the body; hot water bath / boiling water – scalds, use tongs and a test-tube holder; Benedict's solution (copper sulfate) – irritant, wear goggles and wash skin; iodine solution – stains / irritant, wear gloves and goggles; glassware breaking – handle with care, sweep up with brush.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three hazards with matching precautions.

practice.stem: Students culture bacteria from samples of garden soil on nutrient agar plates.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards in this investigation and state a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Soil may contain pathogenic bacteria / fungal spores – wear gloves, wash hands, use aseptic technique (flame loop, work near a Bunsen); cultures may grow pathogens – tape lid with two strips (not sealed all round), never open plates after incubation, incubate at 25–30 °C not 37 °C; Bunsen flame / ethanol for sterilising – keep ethanol away from the flame, tie hair back; disposal – autoclave plates before disposal.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard and 1 for a matching precaution, two pairs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why plates should be incubated at 25 °C rather than 37 °C.
parts.answer: 37 °C is human body temperature, which favours growth of human pathogens.

practice.stem: A class dissects a sheep heart bought from a butcher in Lahore, using scalpels, scissors and a dissecting board.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three hazards in this practical and suggest how the risk from each can be reduced.
parts.answer: Sharp scalpel / scissors – cut away from the body on a board, carry blades pointing down; microorganisms on raw meat – wear gloves, disinfect surfaces, wash hands; disposal of tissue – place in a sealed bag; slippery fluids on the floor – clean spills immediately.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three hazard + precaution pairs.

practice.stem: Students add pieces of liver to 20 volume hydrogen peroxide and collect the oxygen produced in a gas syringe.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the hazard of 20 volume hydrogen peroxide and a suitable precaution.
parts.answer: Irritant / harmful to eyes and skin (oxidising) – wear eye protection and gloves; wash off any spills with plenty of water.
parts.working: B1 hazard; B1 precaution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest the overall level of risk (low, medium or high) for this practical and give a reason.
parts.answer: Low – small volumes of dilute solutions are used and simple precautions such as goggles reduce the risk.
parts.working: B1 level with reason.

practice.stem: A student plans to measure the heart rate of classmates before and after running on the spot for 5 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two risks to the volunteers and describe how each should be reduced.
parts.answer: Volunteers with medical conditions (asthma, heart problems) could be harmed – use a health questionnaire / exclude them; overexertion, dizziness or falling – stop immediately if unwell, supervise, use a stable step and non-slip floor.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two risks with precautions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one ethical requirement before the investigation starts.
parts.answer: Informed consent (volunteers told what will happen and can withdraw at any time).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a hazard and a risk.
parts.answer: A hazard is something that could cause harm (e.g. a corrosive chemical); risk is the chance / likelihood of harm happening and how serious it would be.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student describes the risk of using dilute iodine solution as 'high'. Suggest why most teachers would describe it as low, and state one precaution.
parts.answer: Iodine solution is dilute and used in small amounts; it is only a mild irritant / stains skin and clothes; precaution: wear gloves / eye protection and wash skin if splashed.
parts.working: B1 reason; B1 precaution.

practice.stem: Students carry out a quadrat survey on a steep hillside along a walking trail in the Margalla Hills in June.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three hazards of this fieldwork and suggest how the risk from each can be reduced.
parts.answer: Steep or slippery slopes – stay on paths, wear boots with grip; sun / heat stroke – hats, sunscreen, carry water; stings or bites from insects and snakes – long trousers, look before putting hands in vegetation; getting lost / separated – work in groups with a teacher, carry a phone, tell someone the route; uncertain weather – check the forecast.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three hazard + precaution pairs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a risk assessment should be written before the trip rather than on the day.
parts.answer: So precautions (equipment, clothing, first aid, supervision) can be planned and prepared in advance.

practice.stem: The biuret test uses sodium hydroxide solution and dilute copper sulfate solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the hazard associated with each solution and explain whether this makes the risk of the biuret test medium rather than low.
parts.answer: Sodium hydroxide is corrosive at 0.5 mol dm⁻³ and above (irritant when more dilute) and can cause serious eye damage; dilute copper sulfate solution is of low hazard / harmful if swallowed or irritant; with small volumes and eye protection the risk is low, but if sodium hydroxide of 0.5 mol dm⁻³ or more is used, or eye protection is not worn, the risk becomes medium.
parts.working: B1 sodium hydroxide corrosive / damages eyes (irritant only when very dilute); B1 copper sulfate low hazard / harmful / irritant; B1 risk depends on concentration and precautions, with a conclusion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what a student should do if sodium hydroxide splashes into the eye.
parts.answer: Wash the eye immediately with plenty of running water (eye wash) for at least 10 minutes and tell the teacher / seek medical help.

practice.stem: A student heats a test tube containing glucose solution and Benedict's solution by holding it directly in a Bunsen burner flame.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards in this method and suggest a safer method for each.
parts.answer: Heating directly over a Bunsen flame can make the mixture boil and spit out (scalding) – use a beaker of boiling water / water bath instead; tube held by hand / pointing at people – use a test-tube holder or rack, point the tube away from people; hot water bath – handle with tongs, place on heat-proof mat.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard and 1 for a matching safer method, two pairs.

practice.stem: Students scrape cells from the inside of their own cheeks with a cotton bud, smear them onto a slide and stain them with methylene blue.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards and the precautions needed.
parts.answer: Body cells / fluids can carry pathogens – use only your own cheek cells; methylene blue stains and is harmful if swallowed – wear gloves, do not eat or drink in the lab; glass slides and cover slips can break – handle carefully.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two with precautions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how used cotton buds and slides should be disposed of.
parts.answer: Placed in disinfectant (e.g. 1 % sodium chlorate(I)) / a bag for autoclaving before disposal.

practice.stem: Students separate photosynthetic pigments from spinach leaves by grinding them with propanone and running a thin-layer chromatogram in a solvent containing ethanol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the main hazard and state two precautions.
parts.answer: Propanone / ethanol is highly flammable; no naked flames in the room (warm with a water bath heated electrically, if needed); use small volumes, keep containers closed; work in a well-ventilated area / fume cupboard because vapour is harmful.
parts.working: B1 flammable solvent; 1 mark each for two precautions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the solvent should not be left in an open beaker.
parts.answer: Vapour escapes – can be inhaled / increases fire risk; also the solution becomes more concentrated.

practice.stem: A student plans an investigation of the effect of temperature (20–60 °C) on the hydrolysis of milk protein by trypsin. The pH is followed with phenolphthalein (dissolved in ethanol) and sodium carbonate solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a risk assessment for this practical in a table with columns for hazard, risk and precaution. Include at least three different hazards.
parts.answer: trypsin powder / solution – can cause allergic reaction / sensitiser if inhaled or on skin – make solution in a fume cupboard or have it made by technician, wear gloves and goggles; sodium carbonate solution – irritant – goggles; phenolphthalein in ethanol – flammable / irritant – no flames nearby; hot water bath (up to 60 °C) – scalding – handle with care, use tongs, place on stable surface; broken glass – sweep up with brush, do not use bare hands.
parts.working: 1 mark for a correct table layout; 1 mark each for up to three hazards with risk and matching precaution; 1 mark for identifying the enzyme as a sensitiser / allergen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the overall level of risk and justify your answer.
parts.answer: Low (to medium) – dilute solutions in small volumes and temperatures below 60 °C, with goggles and gloves; enzyme sensitisation is reduced by using solutions not powder.
parts.working: B1 level with justification.

practice.stem: A student uses a respirometer containing soda lime to measure the oxygen uptake of woodlice at temperatures from 10 °C to 40 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards to the student in this investigation and suggest precautions.
parts.answer: Soda lime is corrosive / irritant – handle with a spatula and gloves, keep it in a gauze-covered compartment; glass capillary tubes may break – handle gently; coloured liquid / ethanol may be flammable or toxic.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two hazard + precaution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss the ethical issues of using live woodlice and describe how harm to them can be minimised.
parts.answer: Animals should not suffer unnecessarily; soda lime must not touch them (use a gauze platform); keep the experiment short and at temperatures they would meet in nature (not above about 30 °C); ensure enough oxygen and a damp environment; use the smallest number needed; return them to their habitat afterwards; consider using germinating seeds instead.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three points.

practice.stem: A student wrote this risk assessment for an investigation into the effect of antibiotic concentration on the growth of bacteria: 'Hazards: chemicals and equipment. Precautions: be careful, wear a lab coat. Risk: none.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate this risk assessment, identifying three weaknesses.
parts.answer: It lists no specific hazards (e.g. the ethanol used to sterilise is flammable, hot water bath) – too general; 'be careful' and 'wear a lab coat' are not specific precautions matched to hazards; does not mention bacteria / need for aseptic technique and disposal by autoclaving; gives no risk level; nothing about what to do in an emergency (spills, burns).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three weaknesses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Rewrite one entry so that it is a good risk assessment entry.
parts.answer: Hazard: ethanol used to flame-sterilise spreaders is highly flammable; risk: fire if the beaker of ethanol is near the Bunsen flame (medium); precaution: keep ethanol beaker covered and well away from the flame, dip only the end of the spreader and let it burn off away from the beaker.
parts.working: B1 specific hazard with harm; B1 matching specific precaution.

practice.stem: A student plans to investigate the effect of the time of exposure to ultraviolet (UV) light on the survival of yeast cells spread on agar plates.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the main hazard of the UV lamp and describe how the risk can be reduced.
parts.answer: UV radiation damages the eyes (and skin) – may cause burns / is a mutagen; use the lamp inside a closed box / cabinet, switch on only when covered, wear UV-protective goggles and gloves, limit exposure time.
parts.working: B1 hazard; B1 precaution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two other hazards in this investigation and precautions for each.
parts.answer: Yeast cultures could be contaminated with other microorganisms – aseptic technique, dispose of cultures by autoclaving; mutated yeast cells – do not release into environment; hot agar / Bunsen burner – heat-resistant gloves; glass Petri dishes breaking.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two with precautions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the overall risk of this investigation is higher than that of a typical enzyme practical.
parts.answer: It involves a mutagenic radiation source and culturing microorganisms, so harm could be serious unless strict precautions are followed.

practice.stem: With a ×10 objective, 40 eyepiece graticule divisions lined up exactly with 25 divisions of a stage micrometer. Each stage micrometer division is 10 µm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the length of one eyepiece graticule division.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A xylem vessel measured 18 eyepiece divisions across. Calculate its actual width.

practice.stem: A chloroplast has an actual length of 5 µm. In an electron micrograph its image is 30 mm long.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the electron micrograph.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the formula linking image size, actual size and magnification.
parts.answer: magnification = image size ÷ actual size

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Convert:
(i) 0.25 mm to µm
(ii) 4500 nm to µm
(iii) 7.2 µm to nm
(iv) 1.8 mm to µm
parts.working: B1 each.

practice.stem: A student's drawing of a stoma from a maize leaf has a magnification of × 800. The length of the stoma on the drawing is 46 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual length of the stoma (pair of guard cells) in µm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the student should write the magnification of the drawing, not the magnification of the microscope, under the drawing.
parts.answer: The drawing may be larger or smaller than the image seen in the microscope, so its magnification is different.

practice.stem: With the ×10 objective, one eyepiece graticule division was 10 µm. With the ×40 objective it was 2.5 µm. A xylem vessel in a sunflower stem was 12 divisions wide with the ×40 objective.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual width of the vessel.
parts.answer: 30 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the eyepiece graticule must be calibrated again when the objective lens is changed.
parts.answer: The eyepiece graticule stays the same size in the eyepiece, but the specimen is magnified more/less; so each division represents a different actual length at each objective.
parts.working: B1 graticule not magnified by objective; B1 value of a division changes.

practice.stem: A photomicrograph of a leaf epidermis has a scale bar labelled 100 µm that is 25 mm long. One epidermal cell measures 38 mm long on the photomicrograph.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual length of the cell, in µm.
parts.answer: 152 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the photomicrograph.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why measuring several cells and finding the mean gives a better estimate of cell length.
parts.answer: Cells vary in size and may be cut at different angles; a mean reduces the effect of this variation.
parts.working: B1 variation between cells / sectioning angle.

practice.stem: With a ×10 objective the diameter of the field of view is 1.6 mm. A student counted 20 onion epidermal cells end to end across the diameter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean length of one cell in µm.
parts.answer: 80 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the diameter of the field of view when the ×40 objective is used instead of the ×10.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one source of error in this method.
parts.answer: Cells are not all the same length; partial cells at the edges must be estimated; cells may not lie exactly along the diameter.

practice.stem: A photomicrograph of cells in a root tip has a scale bar labelled 20 µm. The scale bar is 16 mm long.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the photomicrograph.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The nucleus of one cell measures 9.3 mm on the photomicrograph. Calculate its actual diameter. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

practice.stem: One eyepiece graticule division = 2.5 µm. The lengths of ten guard cells from a lily leaf, in eyepiece divisions, were: 16, 18, 17, 15, 19, 18, 17, 16, 18, 16.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean length of the guard cells in µm.
parts.working: M1 mean 17 divisions; A1 × 2.5 = 42.5 µm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the range of guard cell lengths in µm.
parts.answer: 37.5 µm to 47.5 µm

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why it is better to measure ten guard cells than one.
parts.answer: Guard cells vary in length; a mean of several is more representative / reduces the effect of an unusual cell.

practice.stem: With a ×40 objective, 100 eyepiece graticule divisions matched 0.25 mm on a stage micrometer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the length of one eyepiece division in µm.
parts.answer: 2.5 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: A root hair measured 5 divisions wide and 240 divisions long. Calculate its width and its length in µm.
parts.answer: width 12.5 µm; length 600 µm
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the root hair's large length compared with its width is an advantage to the plant.
parts.answer: Large surface area for absorption of water (osmosis) and mineral ions.

practice.stem: A student draws a hibiscus pollen grain with an actual diameter of 40 µm. The drawing is 60 mm across.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the student's drawing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student wants to show the pollen grain at × 2000 instead. Calculate the diameter the drawing should have, in mm.
parts.answer: 80 mm

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two features of a good biological drawing.
parts.answer: Clear, continuous thin pencil lines; no shading; correct proportions; drawn large (fills the space); labels with ruled label lines that do not cross.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: A student viewed a filament of the alga Spirogyra with a ×40 objective. One eyepiece graticule division = 2.5 µm. Student X measured one cell as 32 divisions long. Student Y lined the graticule up along a row of 5 cells end to end and found the row was 156 divisions long. Each reading has an uncertainty of ± 0.5 division.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cell length in µm found by each student.
parts.answer: X: 80.0 µm; Y: mean 78.0 µm per cell

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in each student's reading. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 0.5 ÷ number of divisions × 100; A1 1.6 % and 0.3 %.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain which student's method gives the better estimate of the mean length of a Spirogyra cell.
parts.answer: Student Y – the reading covers more divisions so the percentage uncertainty is smaller, and measuring 5 cells averages out variation between cells.
parts.working: B1 Y with reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Calculate the actual size of each structure. Give each answer in the most suitable unit.
(i) a structure 1.0 mm in diameter on a micrograph at × 40 000
(ii) a structure 18 mm long on a micrograph at × 12 000
parts.working: B1 each with suitable unit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest the identity of each structure, giving a reason.
parts.answer: (i) ribosome – about 20–30 nm in diameter; (ii) mitochondrion – about 1–2 µm long (0.5–1 µm wide); prokaryotic cell also accepted with reason.
parts.working: B1 each with size reasoning.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why structure (i) cannot be seen with a light microscope, however high the magnification.
parts.answer: Its size (25 nm) is less than the resolution of the light microscope (about 200 nm), limited by the wavelength of light.

practice.stem: A transverse section of a young stem was viewed with a ×4 objective, where one eyepiece division = 25 µm. The stem was 64 divisions across and the central pith was 30 divisions across.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual diameter of the stem and of the pith in mm.
parts.answer: stem: 1.6 mm; pith: 0.75 mm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming the stem and pith are circular in section, calculate the percentage of the cross-sectional area occupied by pith. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why measurements of the pith diameter should be taken in two directions at right angles and averaged.
parts.answer: The section is not perfectly circular / may be cut at an angle, so one diameter may not be typical.

practice.stem: A student calibrated an eyepiece graticule: one division = 10 µm with the ×10 objective, 2.5 µm with the ×40 objective and 1.0 µm with the ×100 oil-immersion objective.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many eyepiece divisions a red blood cell 7.5 µm in diameter would cover with each objective.
parts.working: M1 7.5 ÷ division length; A1 all three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which objective should be used to measure the diameter of red blood cells and calculate the percentage uncertainty if each reading is ± 0.5 division. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: ×100 (oil immersion); 6.7 %

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student wants to measure the thickness of the cell surface membrane (about 7 nm) of a red blood cell. Explain why no objective on this microscope can be used.
parts.answer: 7 nm is far below the resolution of the light microscope (about 200 nm), so the membrane's two edges cannot be distinguished; an electron microscope is needed.
